assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteremia) complicated by acute bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and toxic encephalopathy. Blood culture at 24 hours grew Salmonella Typhi, sensitive to ceftriaxone but resistant to ciprofloxacin. Management: Empiric IV normal saline, IV ceftriaxone (2 g every 12 h), IV vancomycin (1 g/day), IV acyclovir (750 mg every 8 h), and IV dexamethasone (3 mg/kg loading, then 1 mg/kg every 6 h, transitioned to oral prednisolone 60 mg/day after 2 days). Coverage was empirically broadened to IV meropenem (2 g every 8 h) and oral azithromycin (500 mg/day) due to risk of Pakistani XDR strain, but de-escalated to IV ceftriaxone monotherapy once sensitivities confirmed ceftriaxone susceptibility, completing a 14-day antibiotic course. Prednisolone was tapered over 3 weeks. Fever subsided and hearing improved 5 days post-treatment; hearing loss almost completely resolved by 1 month of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 88-year-old woman visited our emergency department due to hemoptysis. She had hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and dementia due to cerebral infarction. She also had interstitial pneumonia and had been followed up at our hospital but had voluntarily interrupted treatment.
At the time of this admission, her vital signs were normal, and fine crackles were heard from bilateral lower lungs. White blood cells count was increased (19,140 /microL) and serum level of C-reactive protein was slightly increased (3.71 mg/dL). Her hemoglobin level was 8.0 g/dl, hematocrit was 23.1 %, Mean Corpuscular Volume was 80.5 fL, platelet count was 290,000 /microL. Antinuclear antibody, perinuclear-antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) and C-ANCA were all negative. The result of Interferon-Gamma Release Assay was indeterminate. Chest radiography (Figure 1(Fig. 1)) showed bilateral reticular shadows but no finding of cavity lesions. Contrast-enhanced chest CT showed a honeycomb lung in the right lower lung field and infiltrative shadow and ground glass shadow in the left lower lung field (Figure 2A(Fig. 2)). A contrast-enhancing aneurysm was seen within the infiltrative shadow in the left lower lung, but no obvious cavitary lesion was seen (Figure 2B-D(Fig. 2)).
We thought the patient's hemoptysis was caused by an aneurysm in the lower left lung field. We performed angiography (Figure 3(Fig. 3)) and successfully performed endovascular coil embolization of an aneurysm in the pulmonary artery. After these treatments, sputum screening tested positive for acid-fast bacillus. She was diagnosed with pulmonary TB based on the result of polymerase chain reaction positive for mycobacterium TB. She was treated with isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RFP), and ethambutol (EB) without pyrazinamide (PZA) due to problems with liver function. No recurrence of hemoptysis was observed after successfully treating pulmonary TB.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 88-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An 88-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with acute hemoptysis. She had a known history of interstitial pneumonia previously managed at the hospital, but had voluntarily discontinued her treatment.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, vascular dementia secondary to cerebral infarction, and interstitial pneumonia (treatment voluntarily discontinued). Prior TB history, travel, and animal/TB contacts not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports hemoptysis; denies fever, chest pain, dyspnea, chills, hematemesis, or melena. Home medications and drug allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs within normal limits. Chest auscultation: fine crackles audible over bilateral lower lung fields. Cardiovascular, abdominal, and extremity examinations unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 19,140/microL; CRP: 3.71 mg/dL; Hemoglobin: 8.0 g/dL; Hematocrit: 23.1%; MCV: 80.5 fL; Platelets: 290,000/microL; ANA, p-ANCA, and c-ANCA: all negative; Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (IGRA): indeterminate. Chest radiography: bilateral reticular opacities without evident cavitary lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced chest CT: honeycomb changes in right lower lung field, infiltrative shadow and ground-glass opacities in left lower lung field, and a contrast-enhancing aneurysm within the infiltrative shadow in left lower lung without obvious cavitary lesions. Angiography: confirmed a left pulmonary artery branch aneurysm.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Pulmonary tuberculosis presenting with a pulmonary artery pseudoaneurysm (Rasmussen's-type aneurysm) and hemoptysis, superimposed on chronic interstitial pneumonia.
Confirmation: Sputum screening was positive for acid-fast bacilli (AFB), and sputum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Differentials ruled out: ANCA-associated vasculitis and systemic autoimmune diseases (p-ANCA, c-ANCA, ANA negative), non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection.
Treatment & Outcome: Urgent endovascular coil embolization of the left pulmonary artery aneurysm was successfully performed via angiography, arresting hemoptysis. Following confirmation of tuberculosis, antituberculous therapy was started with isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (RFP), and ethambutol (EB); pyrazinamide (PZA) was omitted due to baseline hepatic dysfunction. Complete resolution of pulmonary tuberculosis was achieved with no recurrence of hemoptysis.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old, otherwise healthy, male was admitted to the emergency room with a four-day history of malaise, myalgia, and high-grade fever. Laboratory tests showed increased liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase [AST] 2216 U/L and alanine aminotransferase [ALT] 1611 U/L), but normal bilirubin. Dengue Fever (DF) rapid test (NS1) and serology (ELISA IgM and IgG) were performed with negative results. Two days later the patient developed jaundice (total bilirubin 6.36 mg/dL and direct bilirubin 5.60 mg/dL) with a decrease in platelet count (52000 /mm3), normal international normalized ratio (INR) (0.85), and moderate proteinuria. At that time, abdominal ultrasonography showed hepatomegaly. Serology for viral hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus, and Cytomegalovirus were negative. Dengue serology was repeated, and found positive, suggesting DF-related hepatitis. Despite an uncertain patient report of prior YF vaccination, YF polymerase chain reaction (YF-PCR) was performed considering the epidemiological risk and YF outbreak context. The patient was discharged after one week with improvement of laboratorial parameters (AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 153 U/L, platelets 294000 /mm3, and total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL). The YF-PCR result was not available prior to discharge.
After 40 days, he was readmitted to the hospital with persistent fatigue, jaundice, and pruritus. Liver enzymes and bilirubin had increased (total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1037 U/L, ALT 2289 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase [GGT] 669 U/L, and INR 1.05). Extensive workup including serologies, ceruloplasmin, and ferritin was performed, but not indicative of a specific etiology. A hypothesis of autoimmune liver disorder was discarded by negative autoantibodies (i.e., anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, and anti-mitochondria antibodies) and normal serum gamma-globulin. Liver biopsy demonstrated lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration (Figure 1). The remaining parenchymal cells showed frequent hepatocyte ballooning, macro- and microvacuolar steatosis, and rare apoptotic bodies. The patient was discharged again after a small decrease in total bilirubin without a definitive diagnosis. A follow-up hepatology appointment was scheduled for five days later. 
Upon hepatologist consultation, it was found that the YF-PCR ordered during the first hepatitis episode was positive, thus corroborating the suspicion of relapsing hepatitis due to YF. A pathological review was performed, including YF virus immunohistochemistry stain, but it was negative. The patient was started on ursodeoxycholic acid (10 mg/kg) and within three days improved his pruritus and bilirubin levels. In the two-week follow-up period, liver enzymes were normal, and the medication was suspended.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with malaise, myalgia, and high-grade fever for 4 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency room with a 4-day history of high-grade fever, generalized myalgia, and malaise. Two days after admission, he developed jaundice, moderate proteinuria, and worsening thrombocytopenia. His transaminases gradually improved, and he was discharged after 1 week. Forty days later, he was readmitted due to persistent fatigue, worsening scleral icterus, and intense pruritus, with severe rebound in transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Uncertain documentation of prior arboviral immunization. Epidemiological exposure: lived/worked in an area experiencing an active viral epidemic.
subjective.review_of_systems: High-grade fever, malaise, diffuse myalgia, fatigue, jaundice, and intense generalized pruritus.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: clinical jaundice; abdominal palpation revealed hepatomegaly. Readmission at day 40: deep jaundice, excoriations secondary to pruritus, persistent fatigue; no stigmata of chronic liver disease.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: AST 2216 U/L, ALT 1611 U/L, normal total bilirubin. Day 2: total bilirubin 6.36 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.60 mg/dL, platelet count 52,000/mm3, international normalized ratio (INR) 0.85, moderate proteinuria. Discharge (day 7): AST 259 U/L, ALT 638 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 153 U/L, platelets 294,000/mm3, total bilirubin 2.25 mg/dL. Readmission (day 40): total bilirubin 19.2 mg/dL, AST 1037 U/L, ALT 2289 U/L, GGT 669 U/L, INR 1.05. Abdominal ultrasound: hepatomegaly. Serologies: Dengue rapid test (NS1) and ELISA IgM/IgG negative on day 1; repeat dengue serology later positive (cross-reactive flavivirus antibody). Viral hepatitis panel (hepatitis A, B, C), Epstein-Barr virus, and Cytomegalovirus serologies: negative. Autoimmune markers (anti-nuclear, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial antibodies): negative; normal serum gamma-globulin; ceruloplasmin and ferritin not indicative of a specific etiology.
objective.advanced_workup: Percutaneous liver biopsy (second admission): lobular hepatitis with mild neutrophilic infiltration, diffuse hepatocyte ballooning, macro- and microvacuolar steatosis, and rare apoptotic bodies. Immunohistochemical staining for specific viral antigen on liver tissue was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of relapsing hepatitis due to Yellow Fever: Serum RT-PCR obtained during the initial acute hepatitis episode was positive for Yellow Fever virus RNA. Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C, EBV, CMV) and autoimmune liver diseases were ruled out by negative serologies and autoantibodies. Pathological review confirmed lobular hepatitis with steatosis and apoptotic bodies, though immunohistochemistry was negative on late biopsy. Treatment: The patient was initiated on oral ursodeoxycholic acid 10 mg/kg daily; pruritus and bilirubin improved within 3 days. Transaminases completely normalized at 2-week follow-up, and ursodeoxycholic acid was successfully discontinued.

raw_case_text:
To the Editor: A 37-year-old woman, a logistics director for a nongovernment organization, returned to France in March 2004 from an 18-day trip to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone. Fever, chills, and myalgia developed in the woman 3 days before she returned to France, and she treated herself with aspirin and paracetamol (acetaminophen). Malaria prophylaxis was taken neither during nor after the trip.
The day after returning to France, the woman's condition progressively worsened; diarrhea and extreme weakness that led to the inability to walk developed. Ten days after her return, she was admitted to the local hospital and treated with intravenous quinine and oral doxycycline (2 g per day) after thick and thin blood films showed 3% parasitemia with Plasmodium falciparum. Three days later, she was still febrile and had conjunctival jaundice, vomiting, insomnia, and moderate hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, blood in urine and feces). Three days after initial hospitalization, the patient was transferred to the Infectious Diseases Unit in Marseille; fever (39.5 C) continued, and hepatosplenomegaly developed. Biologic analyses showed disseminated intravascular coagulation with platelet count of 22,000/mL, an elevated prothrombin time (54% higher than the control value), a longer activated clotting time (51 seconds versus a control value of 34 seconds), a fibrinogen level of 0.9 g/dL, exaggerated plasma fibrin formation and degradation, and hepatic cytolysis with both aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels of 80 U/L.
Although acute malaria had been diagnosed, viral serologic tests were performed because the patient had returned from a tropical country with a fever. Persons in these circumstances are systematically administered a series of tests to determine the cause of their fever. Serologic tests for dengue performed on the acute-phase serum (collected 13 days after onset of symptoms) and convalescent-phase serum (collected 23 days after onset of symptoms) showed the presence of immunoglobulin (Ig) M (titers 1:800 and 1:3,200, respectively) and IgG (titers 1:400 and 1:3,200, respectively), which suggested that the patient had dengue fever and malaria concurrently. These results were obtained by using the Dengue Duo IgM-capture and IgG-indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (Biotrin, PanBio Pty. Ltd., Brisbane, Australia). The same acute-phase serum was tested for flavivirus RNA by seminested reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) by using flavivirus consensus primers PF1S and PF2R as previously described in conjunction with the sense primer PF3S (GCIATHTGGTAYATGTGGYT). Attempts to isolate viruses by using C6/36 and Vero cells were unsuccessful, which might be expected given the delay between the onset of symptoms and specimen collection.
Sequence analysis of the 163-bp (primers excluded) PCR product (GenBank accession no. AY862501) showed 89%-99.4% range of homology with 34 dengue 3 virus strains by using the BLAST nucleotide program. Similarities obtained with sequences of dengue virus 1, 2, and 4 were <=87%. Phylogenetic analysis performed with the patient sequence together with homologous sequences from dengue viruses and other flaviviruses showed that it corresponded to dengue 3 virus species. RT-PCR amplification on the convalescent-phase serum was negative. Based on World Health Organization criteria, the patient was diagnosed with dengue fever. The patient's interview showed a previous dengue fever episode in Haiti in 1995 and a previous malaria episode in Burundi in 2002, but biologic confirmation was not available, and serum was not collected before this episode. Therefore, we could not determine definitively whether this patient experienced primary or secondary dengue. In light of virologic tests results, the diagnosis of secondary dengue infection was more likely.
A PubMed search using the keywords dengue, mixed infections, dual infections, simultaneous infections, and concurrent infections retrieved 14 references published since 1958. In most cases, concurrent infection was with 2 dengue virus strains from 2 different serotypes in a single patient. Only 6 published studies reported concurrent infection with dengue virus and a bacterium (Salmonella typhi, Shigella sonnei, Leptospira spp.) or with a virus such as Chikungunya virus.
To our knowledge, this is the first report of mixed dengue-parasite infection, dengue virus with P. falciparum. The authors previously questioned the accuracy of a serologic test to diagnosis dengue fever in patients experiencing malaria because reactivity was nonspecific on certain rapid serologic assays; however, serologic tests used in this study have demonstrated good specificity, and molecular tests are not prone to such specificity problems. Classifying this case as dengue hemorrhagic fever is questionable since some of the hemorrhagic signs may have been caused by acute malaria. In cases of concurrent infections involving a dengue virus, questions related to the influence of mixed infection on severity and prognosis are, therefore, impossible to address because of lack of information. Further investigations are required because this situation likely occurs frequently in nature, despite scant available data.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old female presented with high fever, chills, myalgias, diarrhea, extreme weakness, and bleeding manifestations following travel to West Africa.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three days prior to returning from an 18-day trip to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone, the patient developed fever, chills, and myalgias, self-medicating with aspirin and paracetamol. Upon returning, her condition deteriorated with watery diarrhea, profound asthenia, and inability to ambulate. Ten days post-return, she was hospitalized locally and initiated on IV quinine and oral doxycycline for Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia (3%). Three days later, persistent high fever (39.5 C), conjunctival icterus, persistent vomiting, epistaxis, hematuria, and hematochezia prompted transfer to a specialized infectious disease unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previous documented episode of severe tropical febrile illness in Haiti in 1995, and malaria in Burundi in 2002. Non-adherent to malaria chemoprophylaxis during recent 18-day travel to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, chills, severe myalgia, diarrhea, vomiting, severe weakness, insomnia, epistaxis, hematuria, and bloody stools. Self-medicated with aspirin and paracetamol.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature 39.5 C. Scleral and conjunctival icterus was evident. Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatosplenomegaly. Active mucocutaneous and visceral bleeding was noted, including epistaxis, hematuria, and rectal bleeding.
objective.routine_investigations:
Peripheral blood smear: Demonstrated 3% Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia.
Coagulation and hematology: Platelet count 22,000/mL, prothrombin time elevated (54% above control), activated clotting time prolonged at 51 seconds (control: 34 seconds), plasma fibrinogen 0.9 g/dL, with marked plasma fibrin formation and degradation complexes (disseminated intravascular coagulation).
Liver function tests: AST 80 U/L and ALT 80 U/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Concurrent acute infection with Dengue virus serotype 3 (DENV-3) and Plasmodium falciparum malaria, presenting with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), severe thrombocytopenia, hemorrhagic diathesis, and hepatosplenomegaly. Confirmed by positive Dengue RT-PCR with nucleotide sequence analysis demonstrating 89%-99.4% homology to Dengue 3 virus strains (GenBank AY862501), alongside rising Dengue IgM (1:800 to 1:3,200) and IgG (1:400 to 1:3,200) titers. Viral culture in C6/36 and Vero cells was negative.
Treatment and outcome: Treated with intravenous quinine and oral doxycycline (2 g daily) alongside intensive supportive care for DIC and coagulopathy, resulting in clearance of parasitemia, resolution of coagulopathy, and clinical recovery.

raw_case_text: The patient is a 72-year-old woman. She presented to the outpatient department of internal medicine with a chief complaint of fever and dyspnea that persisted for 3 days. Her daughter and husband had been diagnosed with COVID-19. She had bronchial asthma, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.6%). She had no smoking history. The SARS-Cov-2 antigen test and SARS-Cov-2 PCR test were positive, and a diagnosis of COVID-19 was made. On admission, the patient was conscious and clear (Glasgow Coma Scale: E4V5M6). She had no headache on admission or during the clinical course. She had a temperature of 38.0C38.0 C (axillary), respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, and hypoxemia with SpO2 of 88% (in room air). Respiratory investigation revealed diffuse bilateral coarse crackles, but no wheeze. Physical examination was otherwise normal. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 21,240/microL (74% neutrophils, 10.9% lymphocytes) (reference range (RR), 1000-4800/microL). Additionally, serology showed revealed elevated lactate dehydrogenase level of 292 IU/L (RR 124-222 IU/L), C-reactive protein levels of 7.61 mg/dL (RR < 0.3 mg/dL), and elevated creatinine level of 1.61 mg/mL (RR < 1.0 mg/dL). Urinalysis was normal. Chest CT showed bilateral pneumonia. Dexamethasone 6 mg/day and Remdesivir 100 mg/day (initially 200 mg/day) were started on the first day of treatment for COVID-19 moderate disease with oxygen demand. Oxygen demand was initially 4 L/min on the oximizer, but increased during the night on the first day, and oxygen administration by High Flow Nasal Cannula (FiO2 0.65, Flow 50 L/min) was started. On the fourth day of the illness, oxygen demand increased, requiring FiO2 of 0.8, and the patient was admitted to the ICU and endotracheal intubation was performed. On the same day, a single dose of Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg/day was administered, and Remdesivir was discontinued. The patient remained in a lull state until the ninth day of treatment when fever developed. The patient's level of consciousness was difficult to assess because she was under sedation. Physical examination and abdominal ultrasonography revealed no heat source. Microscopic pyuria was observed, but since there were no change of other vital sign, blood and urine cultures were obtained and the patient was monitored for a febrile form. On the 10th day, blood culture was positive for 6/6 Gram-positive cocci (streptococci). Considering the possibility of catheter infection, the catheters (central venous catheter, arterial line, and venous line) were replaced and Vancomycin 1.5 g/day was started. On the 11th day, the Gram-positive cocci was identified as streptococcus pneumoniae. Since streptococcus pneumoniae was the causative organism of bacteremia, catheter infection was unlikely, and we considered the possibility of meningitis. Although the patient did not have rigidity of the neck, a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) puncture was performed, and the CSF was grossly thick (Fig. 1). The CSF examination showed an increased cell count (Number of cells 2998/microL, (Mono 6.8%, Poly 93.,2%), Protein 468.5 mg/dL, Glucose 24 mg/dL.), and a diagnosis of bacterial meningitis was made. Gram staining of CSF and CSF culture were negative, possibly due to post-antimicrobial administration. The patient was started on a meningitis dose of ceftriaxone 4 g/day and vancomycin 2 g/day. An additional blood culture taken on the 12th day was positive for Gram-negative rods in 2/2 sets and considering the possibility of Extended Spectrum beta Lactamase (ESBL-s)-producing organisms, antimicrobial escalation from Ceftriaxone to Meropenem 6 g/day was performed. The Gram-negative rods were Klebsiella spp. The Gram-negative rod was found to be Klebsiella pneumoniae, which was de-escalated to 3rd cephem after confirming susceptibility. The main pathogenesis was meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, but the possibility that Klebsiella pneumoniae was the pathogen of meningitis could not be ruled out, and antimicrobial agents were administered for a total of 21 days. On the 13th day, we confirmed that the patient's level of consciousness had improved, and we performed a spontaneous awakening trial and a spontaneous breathing trial before performing extubation. After extubation, the patient's respiratory status and level of consciousness stabilized, and fortunately, no sequelae of meningitis were observed. On the 34th day, the patient was transferred to a rehabilitation hospital. After leaving the rehabilitation hospital, she returned to society.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old female presenting with a 3-day history of persistent fever and dyspnea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the outpatient internal medicine clinic with a 3-day history of persistent fever and dyspnea following close household exposure to her husband and daughter, both diagnosed with viral respiratory infections. She was admitted for moderate pneumonia with hypoxemia. During her first hospital night, her oxygen requirements surged, prompting high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC). By illness day 4, hypoxemia progressed (FiO2 0.8), requiring ICU admission, endotracheal intubation, and mechanical ventilation. She remained stable until treatment day 9, when she developed a new high fever. On day 10, blood cultures turned positive. On day 11, diagnostic lumbar puncture revealed purulent meningitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bronchial asthma, essential hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.6%). Non-smoker. Epidemiological history: Close household contact with family members diagnosed with confirmed viral respiratory infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Persistent fever and dyspnea. Denies headache on admission or throughout hospitalization. Denies nausea, vomiting, or neck pain.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: T 38.0 °C (axillary), RR 24 breaths/min, SpO2 88% on room air. Glasgow Coma Scale: E4V5M6 (fully conscious). Pulmonary: Diffuse bilateral coarse crackles without wheezing. ICU course (day 4): Severe respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation. Day 9: New fever while under sedation; no nuchal rigidity on examination. Day 13: Neurological status normalized following sedation hold.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC 21,240/μL (74% neutrophils, 10.9% lymphocytes; reference 1,000–4,800/μL), LDH 292 IU/L (reference 124–222 IU/L), CRP 7.61 mg/dL (reference < 0.3 mg/dL), serum creatinine 1.61 mg/dL (reference < 1.0 mg/dL). Urinalysis normal on admission; microscopic pyuria noted on day 9. Day 9 abdominal ultrasound: No intra-abdominal focus of infection. Lumbar puncture / CSF (day 11): Grossly turbid/thick purulent fluid, WBC 2,998/μL (polymorphonuclear 93.2%, mononuclear 6.8%), protein 468.5 mg/dL, glucose 24 mg/dL; CSF Gram stain and culture were negative (post-antimicrobial administration).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (admission): Bilateral pneumonia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia (confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 antigen and RT-PCR tests on admission) complicated by severe acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, secondary Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia and purulent bacterial meningitis, and subsequent Klebsiella pneumoniae catheter-related bloodstream superinfection.

Confirmation: Day 10 blood cultures grew Gram-positive cocci in 6/6 bottles, identified as Streptococcus pneumoniae. Day 12 repeat blood cultures grew Klebsiella pneumoniae in 2/2 sets. CSF pleocytosis and biochemical profile confirmed bacterial meningitis.

Management and outcome: Initial treatment with IV dexamethasone 6 mg/day, remdesivir (200 mg loading, then 100 mg/day; discontinued on day 4), single-dose tocilizumab 8 mg/kg on day 4, and mechanical ventilation. For secondary bacteremia/meningitis, central and arterial catheters were replaced, and therapy escalated to vancomycin (1.5 g/day, then 2 g/day) and ceftriaxone (4 g/day), followed by escalation to meropenem (6 g/day) for Klebsiella bacteremia and de-escalation to a third-generation cephalosporin based on susceptibility, completing a 21-day antimicrobial course. Successfully extubated on day 13 following spontaneous breathing trial without neurological sequelae. Transferred to a rehabilitation facility on hospital day 34 and ultimately achieved full functional recovery and return to community life.

raw_case_text: Case 3: A 21 year old patient that reported fever in the second trimester of pregnancy. Her IgM serology for ZIKV was positive and non-reactive for dengue, chikungunya, rubella, toxoplasmosis, HIV, syphilis and cytomegalovirus. The PRNT90% was positive for neutralizing antibodies. Her IgG serology was positive for cytomegalovirus and rubella. At 41 weeks of gestation, her baby girl was born by cesarean delivery that presented a cephalic circumference of 36 cm.

subjective.chief_complaint: 21-year-old pregnant female presenting with fever in the second trimester of gestation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced an episode of fever during the second trimester of pregnancy. The pregnancy continued without documented maternal complications to 41 weeks of gestation, when she delivered an infant girl via cesarean section.
subjective.past_medical_history: Second trimester of pregnancy; no prior medical illnesses reported.

objective.physical_examination: Maternal: Documented fever during second trimester. Neonatal: Female infant delivered at 41 weeks gestation via cesarean delivery with cephalic circumference of 36 cm.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Maternal second-trimester Zika virus infection confirmed by positive ZIKV IgM serology and positive PRNT90% for neutralizing antibodies. Serological differential testing was non-reactive for dengue, chikungunya, rubella, toxoplasmosis, HIV, syphilis, and cytomegalovirus IgM (positive IgG for CMV and rubella indicated prior immunity). Delivery at 41 weeks gestation yielded a normocephalic infant girl (head circumference 36 cm).

raw_case_text: Patient 2. A 21-year-old student presented with fever, drenching sweats, headache, generalized fatigue, and joints pain for three weeks. The general examination was normal except for fever and (R) ankle swelling. The joint was hot and tender with restricted range of movement. US and MRI of the (R) ankle showed large effusion with tibialis posterior tenosynovitis (Figures 2 and 3). His WBC was 7.7 x 109, ESR 45 mm/hr., and CRP 53 mg/L. Synovial fluid was cloudy straw colored. The cell count was 3.3 x 109 with 53% polymorphs. Brucella serology done by immunocapture assay was significantly raised 1 : 10240. Blood culture isolated Brucella species but synovial fluid culture was negative. He, his father, and his brother developed brucellosis concurrently. They all consumed the same raw milk. He received two weeks of streptomycin and a total of three-month rifampicin and doxycycline with full recovery. Follow-up CRP was 2 and ESR 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old male student presented with a 3-week history of fever, drenching sweats, headache, generalized fatigue, and joint pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute fever, drenching sweats, headache, generalized fatigue, diffuse joint pain, and right ankle swelling over a 3-week duration. His father and brother concurrently developed identical febrile symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: university student. Epidemiological exposure: shared consumption of unpasteurized raw milk with his father and brother. Prior medical history and medications not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, drenching sweats, headache, generalized fatigue, arthralgias, right ankle swelling. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile; right ankle: swollen, hot, and tender to palpation with restricted range of movement. General examination otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 7.7 x 10^9/L; ESR: 45 mm/hr; CRP: 53 mg/L. Right ankle ultrasound: large joint effusion with tibialis posterior tenosynovitis. Synovial fluid analysis: cloudy straw-colored fluid, cell count 3.3 x 10^9/L with 53% polymorphonuclear leukocytes; synovial fluid culture negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Right ankle MRI: confirmed large ankle effusion with prominent tibialis posterior tenosynovitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute brucellosis with peripheral osteoarticular involvement (right ankle septic arthritis and tibialis posterior tenosynovitis) and bacteremia, as part of a familial foodborne outbreak.
Confirmation: Brucella immunocapture assay significantly elevated at a titer of 1:10240; blood culture isolated Brucella species. (Synovial fluid culture negative).
Differentials ruled out: Non-brucellar bacterial septic arthritis ruled out by negative synovial fluid culture and isolation of Brucella from blood.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with parenteral streptomycin for 2 weeks combined with a 3-month course of oral rifampicin and doxycycline, resulting in full clinical recovery and normalization of inflammatory markers (follow-up CRP 2 mg/L, ESR 1 mm/hr).

raw_case_text:
A 68-year-old female, a resident of Karnal (Haryana, North India), a known case of diabetes mellitus (for 5 years on diet control), and chronic liver disease (for 3 years) presented with complaints of cough, generalized weakness, and significant weight loss since one month. The cough was insidious in onset, dry in nature, and not associated with any aggravating or relieving factor. She was diagnosed with chronic liver disease 3 years ago and an evaluation was done earlier for the same and was found to be cryptogenic in origin. There were no similar complaints among her family members. On examination, she was thin built and pale. The patient was afebrile and haemodynamically stable. There were no palpable lymph nodes. Systemic examination was unremarkable.
Initial blood investigations revealed anaemia (haemoglobin 10.2 g/dl), total leucocyte count 12x109 cells/l, platelet count 150x109 cells/l, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 59 mm/hour and differential count was neutrophil 41%, lymphoctes 27% and eosinophils 32%. Mean corpuscular volume and mean corpuscular haemoglobin concentration were 84 fL and 32 g/dl, respectively. Peripheral blood smear showed normocytic normochromic anaemia with eosinophilia (figure 1). Absolute eosinophil count was 4x109 cells/l. Hepatic functions were normal except for hypoalbuminemia (2.78 g/dl). Renal function tests were normal. ELISA for HIV-1 and HIV-2, anti-hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B surface antigen were negative. Reaction to the tubercular skin test was less than 10 mm. Chest radiograph showed increased bronchovascular markings with right hilar prominence (figure 2). Stool samples tested two times but did not reveal any ova or parasite. Ultrasound abdomen showed coarse liver echotexture. During the course of hospital stay, the patient continued to have a dry cough and generalized weakness. The patient was given deworming measures (albendazole and diethylcarbamazine). Repeat blood counts revealed persistent eosinophilia. Test for echinococcus serology was negative. Anti-filarial antibodies were negative. Tests for anti-nuclear and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative. Echocardiography was normal with no evidence of vegetation. A contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen was done, which revealed enlarged non-necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes with features suggestive of chronic liver disease. Microscopic examination of needle-aspirated bone marrow and biopsy examination revealed increased eosinophilic precursors with no abnormal cells. Endoscopic bronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration of mediastinal lymph nodes was consistent with tubercular inflammation with acid-fast stain positive for bacilli. Acid-fast bacilli culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis over a period of 3 weeks in the BACTEC medium. The patient was started on anti-tubercular treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide) and her eosinophil counts gradually returned to normal levels with in 1 week.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old female presented with dry cough, generalized weakness, and significant weight loss for one month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 68-year-old female presented with an insidious, non-productive cough, progressive generalized weakness, and significant weight loss over a 1-month period. The cough was non-paroxysmal without aggravating or relieving factors. She had a history of diet-controlled diabetes mellitus and cryptogenic chronic liver disease.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus for 5 years on diet control; chronic liver disease of cryptogenic origin for 3 years. Resident of Haryana, North India. No family history of similar complaints.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for persistent dry cough, generalized weakness, and weight loss. Negative for fever, hemoptysis, or dyspnea. Home medications (diet-controlled) and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Thin built, pale, afebrile, hemodynamically stable. No palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, MCV 84 fL, MCHC 32 g/dL, total leukocyte count 12 x 109 cells/L (neutrophils 41%, lymphocytes 27%, eosinophils 32%), absolute eosinophil count 4 x 109 cells/L, platelets 150 x 109 cells/L, ESR 59 mm/hr. Peripheral smear: normocytic normochromic anemia with marked hypereosinophilia. Serum albumin 2.78 g/dL; liver and renal function tests normal. HIV-1/2 ELISA, anti-HCV, and HBsAg negative. Tuberculin skin test induration <10 mm. Stool examinations (x2) negative for ova/parasites. Serology for Echinococcus, anti-filarial antibodies, ANA, and ANCA negative. Echocardiography normal without vegetations. Abdominal ultrasound: coarse liver echotexture. Chest X-ray: increased bronchovascular markings with right hilar prominence. Empirical deworming with albendazole and diethylcarbamazine yielded no change in eosinophilia.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced CT thorax and abdomen: enlarged non-necrotic mediastinal lymph nodes and changes of chronic liver disease. Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy: increased eosinophilic precursors without dysplastic or neoplastic cells. Endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) of mediastinal lymph nodes performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Mediastinal tuberculous lymphadenitis presenting with marked peripheral hypereosinophilia and leukemoid reaction, confirmed by EBUS-guided fine-needle aspiration of mediastinal lymph nodes demonstrating granulomatous inflammation with acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on stain and mycobacterial culture growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis in BACTEC medium at 3 weeks. Parasitic infections, allergic conditions, hypereosinophilic syndrome, and hematological malignancies were ruled out. Management & Outcome: Prescribed 4-drug antitubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide). Peripheral eosinophil counts completely normalized within 1 week of therapy, accompanied by resolution of cough and constitutional symptoms.

raw_case_text: We report a 39-year-old caucasian man who has lived in Angola for 4 years. He presented to a hospital in California, during a trip, with a flu-like syndrome, jaundice and altered state of consciousness. On hospital admission, he had hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, acidemia and acute renal failure. After the diagnosis of Plasmodium falciparum malaria, the patient initiated therapy with quinine and doxycycline, although developing severe encephalopathy (coma). After therapy with artesunate, he had hematologic and neurological improvement, and was transferred to Portugal. On initial eye examination at our hospital, he had 20/20 visual acuity in the right eye and a central scotoma in the left eye. Right eye indirect ophthalmoscopy revealed round deep layer retinal hemorrhage, with one disc diameter of radius, in the superior temporal arcade (Figure 1 (Fig. 1)). Left eye indirect ophthalmoscopy showed a foveal hemorrhage, several superficial hemorrhages in the interpapillomacular bundle (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)) and a deep white-centered peripheral hemorrhagic lesion (Figure 3 (Fig. 3)). Fluorescein angiography was not performed given the deterioration of the renal function warranting hemodialysis. At one-month follow-up, the patient had 20/20 visual acuity in both eyes and on examination almost all lesions shown on retinography had regressed (Figure 4 (Fig. 4) and Figure 5 (Fig. 5)).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old male presenting with a flu-like illness, jaundice, acute visual scotoma, and rapid progression to altered consciousness while traveling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had lived in Angola for 4 years, developed a progressive flu-like syndrome, jaundice, and deteriorating sensorium while traveling in California. Upon hospital admission, he was found to have acute hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, metabolic acidemia, and acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis. Despite initial oral therapy, his encephalopathy progressed to deep coma, prompting conversion to intravenous artesunate. Following neurological recovery, he noted acute central vision loss in the left eye and was repatriated to Portugal for specialized ophthalmologic and nephrologic management.
subjective.past_medical_history: Lived in Angola for 4 years prior to presentation. No prior ocular or nephrologic history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, jaundice, altered sensorium, and left eye central visual scotoma. Negative for prior visual impairment. Medications: quinine, doxycycline, and artesunate received during hospitalization. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Initially comatose with deep encephalopathy and jaundice; later fully conscious and oriented. Visual acuity: Right eye 20/20, left eye with central scotoma (subsequently improving to 20/20 at 1 month). Dilated fundoscopic examination: Right eye revealed round deep intraretinal hemorrhage (one disc diameter in radius) along the superior temporal vascular arcade; left eye revealed prominent foveal hemorrhage, multiple superficial flame-shaped hemorrhages within the papillomacular bundle, and a deep white-centered peripheral hemorrhagic lesion (Roth spot). Systemic examination: Hemodialysis catheter in situ; lungs clear, abdomen soft.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory investigations demonstrated acute hemolytic anemia, marked thrombocytopenia, systemic acidemia, and severe acute renal failure with azotemia necessitating hemodialysis.
objective.advanced_workup: Color retinal photography / indirect ophthalmoscopy: Documented multifocal malarial retinopathy including foveal hemorrhage, papillomacular hemorrhages, and white-centered intraretinal hemorrhages (fluorescein angiography contraindicated and deferred due to renal dysfunction).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe cerebral Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by malarial coma, acute hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, severe metabolic acidemia, acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis, and acute malarial retinopathy with foveal hemorrhage and left central scotoma.
Diagnostic confirmation: Detection and laboratory confirmation of Plasmodium falciparum malaria on admission blood films.
Plan & Outcome: Initial treatment with oral quinine and doxycycline was escalated to parenteral artesunate upon development of deep coma, resulting in successful parasite clearance and neurological revival. Acute renal failure was managed with temporary hemodialysis. Left central scotoma and retinal hemorrhages were managed conservatively; by 1-month follow-up, visual acuity normalized to 20/20 bilaterally with near-total regression of all fundoscopic hemorrhages and complete renal recovery.

raw_case_text: As of now, he was 8 years old and his insulin dosage was 1.1 IU/kg/d. Even under fluconazole therapy, he developed oral mucocutaneous Candida fungi twice every month, but he did not develop recurrent viral or bacterial infections. He was given antituberculosis drugs (isoniazide, rifampicin) for tuberculosis infection. The liver function was normal at the last follow-up, and the HbA1c was 6.5%. Ruxolitinib was recommended to the patient's parents, but they refused because of concerns about side effects.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old boy with diabetes mellitus and recurrent oral candidiasis presented for follow-up of tuberculosis infection.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An 8-year-old boy with insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus presented for clinical follow-up. Despite continuous fluconazole prophylaxis, he experienced recurrent episodes of oral mucocutaneous candidiasis twice monthly, without recurrent bacterial or viral infections. He was diagnosed with tuberculosis infection and commenced on antituberculosis therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (insulin requirement 1.1 IU/kg/day); chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis on prophylactic fluconazole. Antituberculosis therapy with isoniazid and rifampicin. Prior hospitalizations, travel, or TB contacts not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports recurrent oral mucocutaneous candidiasis; denies fever, chronic cough, or gastrointestinal complaints. Home medications: subcutaneous insulin (1.1 IU/kg/day), fluconazole, isoniazid, rifampicin. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Oral examination: recurrent oral candidiasis mucosal lesions noted during flares. General physical exam otherwise stable.
objective.routine_investigations: HbA1c: 6.5%; Liver function tests: normal at last follow-up.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Tuberculosis infection in an 8-year-old child with autoimmune polyendocrinopathy / immune dysregulation syndrome manifested by insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.
Confirmation: Clinical and microbiological diagnosis of tuberculosis infection managed with targeted anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy; recurrent mucocutaneous Candida infection documented despite fluconazole.
Differentials ruled out: Severe combined immunodeficiency (denied recurrent severe viral or bacterial infections).
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with antituberculosis drugs (isoniazid and rifampicin), subcutaneous insulin therapy (1.1 IU/kg/day maintaining HbA1c at 6.5%), and oral fluconazole. Liver function tests remained strictly normal throughout therapy. Ruxolitinib therapy was offered for the underlying immune condition, but declined by the parents due to concern for potential adverse effects.

raw_case_text:
This was a second case of a 43-year-old male laborer, diagnosed as HIV positive 2 years back who was on ART and anti-tubercular treatment for the past 9 months. He presented with a 7 month history of asymptomatic skin lesions all over his body. Physical examination revealed multiple bilateral asymmetrical diffuse, papulonodular, non-itchy skin lesions of size 2-25 mm on the face, trunk and extremities. Lesions first appeared on the arm and progressively spread to involve the face, legs and trunk [Figure 3]. There were no signs of ulceration and scarring. There was no lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. There was no history of travel to endemic areas of leishmaniasis. The patient was initially suspected to be suffering from histoplasmosis, but skin biopsy taken from the nodules ruled it out. Laboratory investigations revealed anemia (Hb-9.1 g/dL). Liver function tests, renal function tests and lipid profile were normal. Ultrasonography of the abdomen was normal. His CD4 count was 50 cells/muL and HIV viral load was 1750 copies/mL. Punch biopsy of skin lesions revealed sheets of histiocytic cells in the sub epithelial tissue, stuffed with numerous amastigotes of Leishmania. Mild lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate was also noted [Figure 4].
The patient was treated with ketoconazole 200 mg twice daily and 450 mg rifampicin daily for 1 month along with ART (nevirapine, stavudine and lamivudine). The patient initially responded to treatment but later on expired due to chest infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old HIV-positive male presented with a 7-month history of widespread, non-itchy skin nodules on his face, trunk, and extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 7-month history of progressive, asymptomatic papulonodular eruptions that began on his arm and sequentially spread across his face, trunk, and lower limbs. He was concurrently receiving antiretroviral and antitubercular therapies.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 2 years prior on ART (nevirapine, stavudine, and lamivudine). Tuberculosis infection on antitubercular therapy for the past 9 months. Occupation: laborer. Denied travel to known leishmaniasis endemic areas.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports skin nodules are completely non-pruritic and asymptomatic; denies fever, night sweats, or constitutional symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic examination revealed multiple bilateral, asymmetrical, diffuse, papulonodular, non-pruritic skin lesions measuring 2 mm to 25 mm in diameter distributed across the face, trunk, and extremities, with no ulceration or scarring. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 9.1 g/dL. Liver function tests, renal function tests, and lipid profile: within normal limits. CD4 cell count: 50 cells/muL; HIV viral load: 1,750 copies/mL. Abdominal ultrasound: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy: subepithelial sheets of histiocytes with mild lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, heavily packed with intracellular microorganisms; fungal elements absent.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Histopathological examination of cutaneous punch biopsy revealed dermal histiocytic sheets stuffed with numerous Leishmania amastigotes, confirming cutaneous leishmaniasis in a patient with advanced HIV disease. Cutaneous histoplasmosis was formally ruled out on tissue morphology. Management and Outcome: Treated with oral ketoconazole 200 mg twice daily and oral rifampicin 450 mg once daily for 1 month along with continuing ART (nevirapine, stavudine, and lamivudine). The patient demonstrated initial cutaneous improvement but subsequently succumbed to an intercurrent pulmonary chest infection.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old previously healthy male presented with high grade fever associated with constitutional symptoms of five days' duration. He was complaining of right hypochondrium pain and tea-coloured urine for two days associated with yellowish discolouration of the eyes. He had severe loss of appetite to food and water, but his bowel habits had been normal throughout the illness. On admission, he was afebrile with normal vital signs but was deeply icteric. His abdominal examination revealed a tender, mild hepatomegaly while his cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous system examination was normal.
His full blood count revealed a white cell count of 3 x 103 muL with a platelet count of 116 x 103 muL. His aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were 5162 U/L and 3964 U/L, respectively. Initial total bilirubin was found to be 61.7 mumol/L with an increased direct fraction. His prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (PT/INR) and serum protein were normal throughout the illness. His dengue IgM antibody done by chromatographic immunoassay was positive on the 6th day of the illness. Hepatitis A IgM antibody done by the ELISA technique was positive on day 6 of the illness, while hepatitis A IgG antibody was negative. Other investigations done during the hospital stay are summarized in Table 1.
During the course of the illness, the patient was closely monitored for features of development of liver failure while continuing with the precritical monitoring of the dengue fever. The patient's hospital stay was uneventful, and he did not develop features of acute liver failure or features of plasma leakage as in DHF. He was discharged on day 10 of the illness. On follow-up, his AST, ALT, and bilirubin have become normal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, constitutional symptoms, right hypochondrial pain, tea-colored urine, and deep jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 34-year-old previously healthy male presented with high-grade fever and constitutional symptoms of 5 days' duration. Two days prior to presentation, he developed right hypochondrial abdominal pain, dark tea-colored urine, yellowish scleral discoloration, and severe anorexia to both solids and liquids. Bowel habits remained normal throughout.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no chronic medical conditions or known liver diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, malaise, right upper quadrant pain, dark urine, jaundice, and severe anorexia. Negative for nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or bleeding manifestations. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile, vital signs normal. Deeply icteric. Abdomen: Tender mild hepatomegaly. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological examinations were completely normal.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count: 3 x 10^3/muL, platelet count: 116 x 10^3/muL. Liver biochemistry: AST 5,162 U/L, ALT 3,964 U/L, total bilirubin 61.7 mumol/L (with elevated direct bilirubin fraction). Coagulation and synthetic function: PT/INR and serum total protein/albumin remained normal throughout illness.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute co-infection of Dengue fever and acute Hepatitis A virus (HAV) presenting with marked acute transaminitis and cholestatic jaundice without acute liver failure or plasma leakage. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus IgM antibody by chromatographic immunoassay on illness day 6; positive Hepatitis A IgM antibody by ELISA on day 6 (Hepatitis A IgG antibody negative).
Plan & Outcome: Monitored closely for acute liver failure and plasma leakage while undergoing supportive dengue care and fluid management. Hospital course remained uneventful without coagulopathy or bleeding; discharged on day 10. Complete normalization of AST, ALT, and bilirubin documented on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Clinical data: A 21-year-old female patient who experienced fever, myalgia and headache for 8 days and symptoms progressed to metrorrhagia, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. Before hospitalization, she was examined in another health service with a hypothesized dengue diagnosis due to severe leukopenia and thrombocytopenia (platelet 10.000/mm3). The patient was admitted in the intensive care unit (ICU) at the Hospital Universitario Clementino Fraga Filho with respiratory failure, followed by the evolution of multiple organ failure and refractory shock. Biochemical parameters evaluated in the serum: aspartate aminotransferase 149 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase 66 IU/L; glucose 158 mg/dL; creatinine 1.10 mg/dL; urea 9.0 mg/dL.
 Necropsy data: Ecchymosis, conjunctival hemorrhage, bilateral pleural effusion, pulmonary hemorrhage, renal congestion and splenomegaly.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old female presenting with an 8-day history of fever, myalgia, and headache, progressing to metrorrhagia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced fever, myalgia, and headache for 8 days, which progressed to nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and metrorrhagia. She was initially evaluated at another clinic and found to have profound bicytopenia, before being admitted to the university intensive care unit due to acute respiratory failure, rapid clinical deterioration, and refractory shock.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, myalgia, headache, metrorrhagia, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely ill in respiratory failure; clinical progression to refractory shock and multiorgan failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Severe leukopenia and profound thrombocytopenia with platelet count 10,000/mm3. Serum biochemistry: AST 149 IU/L, ALT 66 IU/L, glucose 158 mg/dL, creatinine 1.10 mg/dL, urea 9.0 mg/dL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Fatal severe dengue / dengue hemorrhagic fever presenting with profound thrombocytopenia, metrorrhagia, acute respiratory failure, and refractory shock. Necropsy confirmation: Widespread ecchymoses, conjunctival hemorrhage, bilateral pleural effusions, pulmonary hemorrhage, marked renal congestion, and splenomegaly.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to the intensive care unit and managed with critical care resuscitation and mechanical respiratory support. Despite intensive measures, she suffered multiorgan failure and refractory shock, resulting in death.

raw_case_text:
Six-year-old female child, first product of nonconsanguineous marriage resident of New Delhi, presented with fever for four days, yellowish discoloration of eyes, and urine for two days, progressive swelling of whole body starting from feet for one day. Fever was moderate to high grade, intermittent in type associated with chills and rigor subsided with medication and profuse sweating. She was having high coloured urine for two days. Progressive swelling of whole body for last one day starting from feet then involved the whole body. Stools were normal in colour. There was no history of black coloured stools, vomiting, bleeding from any site, and any change in conscious level, jaundice in the past, any history of blood transfusion, and intravenous medication in the past or any history of drug intake. There was no history suggestive of respiratory tract infections, skin infection, decreased micturition, and reddish coloured urine. There was no significant past, antenatal, perinatal, or family history. The child was fully immunized and was receiving adequate calories and proteins for her age.
On examination, the child was conscious, cooperative, and orientated. At admission her pulse was 78 per minute, respiratory rate 26 per minute, and blood pressure 98/68 mm of mercury. There were severe pallor, and icterus. Lymph nodes were not palpable. On abdominal examination liver was palpable 4 cms below costal margin with span of 10 cm the spleen was palpable 1 cms below costal margin. Her respiratory, cardiovascular (CVS), and central nervous system (CNS) examination was unremarkable.
On investigation haemoglobin was 4.9 g/dL, total leucocyte count 10.6 x 103 per muL with polymorphs 54%, lymphocytes 42%, monocyte 4%, platelet count 11x103 per muL and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/1st hour by Westergren method. Blood sugar was 84 mg/dL. Total serum bilirubin was 27.5 mg/dL, indirect fraction of 18 mg/dL. SGOT was 495 and SGPT 210. Serum total protein was 2.8 gram (gm) and albumin 1 gm per 100 mL of blood. Blood urea nitrogen was 189 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, sodium 136 meq/L, potassium 4.1 meq/L. Prothrombin time was 17.3/12 with INR of 1.44. Viral markers (HBsAg, IgM hepatitis C, A and E) were negative. Chest X-ray was normal and ultrasonography abdomen showed hepatosplenomegaly. On peripheral smear trophozoites and schizonts of P. vivax and trophozoites and gametocytes of P. falciparum were seen. Rapid malarial antigen test was positive. Arterial blood gas analysis showed pH 7.45, partial pressure (PP) of oxygen 104, PP of carbon dioxide 45, and standard bicarbonate 28 meq/L. Urine routine and microscopy were normal. She was given injection of Artesunate 2.4 gm per kilogram body weight, along with cefotaxime and vitamin K. She received fresh frozen plasma, packed red cell, platelets along with inotropes. Within five hours of admission she developed profuse upper gastrointestinal bleeding, along with deterioration of consciousness. She went into shock, then cardiorespiratory arrest from which she could not be revived.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old female presenting with fever for four days, jaundice for two days, and generalized body swelling for one day.

One day prior, she developed rapidly progressive generalized edema (anasarca) beginning in the lower extremities and involving the entire body. Stools remained normal in color. There was no history of melena, hematemesis, epistaxis, altered consciousness, oliguria, or red urine. Within five hours of hospital admission, she developed catastrophic upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, progressive shock, and cardiac arrest.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious, cooperative, and oriented on admission. Pulse rate 78 beats/min, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, blood pressure 98/68 mmHg. Severe pallor, deep icterus, and generalized anasarca present. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. Abdominal examination: tender hepatomegaly palpable 4 cm below the costal margin (liver span 10 cm); splenomegaly palpable 1 cm below the costal margin. Respiratory, cardiovascular, and central nervous system examinations were normal on admission. Terminal examination at 5 hours: massive hematemesis, altered consciousness, unrecordable blood pressure (shock), and cardiorespiratory arrest.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 4.9 g/dL, total leukocyte count 10.6 x 10^3/muL (polymorphs 54%, lymphocytes 42%, monocytes 4%), platelets 11 x 10^3/muL (severe thrombocytopenia), ESR 8 mm/1st hr (Westergren). Blood glucose 84 mg/dL. Total serum bilirubin 27.5 mg/dL (indirect fraction 18 mg/dL). AST/SGOT 495 U/L, ALT/SGPT 210 U/L. Total serum protein 2.8 g/dL, serum albumin 1.0 g/dL. Blood urea nitrogen 189 mg/dL, creatinine 0.6 mg/dL, sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.1 mEq/L. Coagulation: prothrombin time 17.3/12 sec, INR 1.44. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.45, PaO2 104 mmHg, PaCO2 45 mmHg, standard bicarbonate 28 mEq/L. Urinalysis: normal routine and microscopy. Viral hepatitis serologies (HBsAg, IgM anti-HCV, IgM anti-HAV, IgM anti-HEV): all negative. Chest X-ray: normal. Bedside abdominal ultrasound: hepatosplenomegaly. Peripheral blood smear performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe mixed Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by profound hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin 4.9 g/dL), severe thrombocytopenia (11,000/muL), extreme hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 27.5 mg/dL), severe hypoalbuminemia with anasarca, prerenal azotemia (BUN 189 mg/dL), coagulopathy (INR 1.44), massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and fatal shock.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrating trophozoites and schizonts of Plasmodium vivax along with trophozoites and gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum; positive rapid malarial antigen test; negative acute viral hepatitis serologies (HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV).
Treatment & Outcome: Managed urgently with intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg), IV cefotaxime, intravenous vitamin K, transfusions of fresh frozen plasma, packed red blood cells, and platelets, along with inotropic support. Despite intensive resuscitation, the patient developed profuse upper gastrointestinal bleeding within five hours of admission, rapidly deteriorated into refractory shock, and suffered cardiorespiratory arrest with unsuccessful resuscitation.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 30-year-old female healthcare worker with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, pancreatitis, reflux and recurrent pneumonia. Her home medications included mirtazapine, quetiapine, dicycloverine, pantoprazole, and pancreatic enzyme replacement. She presented in March 2020 with fever, fatigue, sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy, nasal congestion, chest tightness and dry cough. She was diagnosed with COVID-19 by PCR and was treated with a course of azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine. After full recovery, nasal PCR swab was negative twice prior to returning to work. Her SARS-CoV-2 IgG nucleocapsid protein (N-protein) antibodies were negative 8 weeks after her initial infection. Six months later in October 2020, she once again developed upper respiratory symptoms which included headaches, fever, and sinus congestion. She again tested positive for COVID-19 by PCR. The symptoms felt milder with the second infection with less chest tightness. On immune work-up after recovery, she was found to have a decreased level of mannose binding lectin (<50ng/mL), normal immunoglobulin levels, and protective Streptococcus pneumoniae IgG antibodies for 18 of the 23 serotypes with appropriate vaccine response. Her SARS-CoV-2 IgG N- protein returned as positive 8 weeks after her second infection. With both infections, hospitalization was never required, and her symptoms remained mild overall.
Antibodies against COVID-19 are typically found in most patients within 2 weeks of infection. However, it is not known to what degree this provides immunity to COVID-19.   Some studies revealed severe cases of COVID-19 tend to have a greater IgG response than milder cases, and in some mild cases, the immune system does not produce adequate IgG antibodies.   Given the novelty of the virus and unclear long-term immune response to the virus, it is difficult to know for sure exactly how long these IgG antibodies last. One study on health care workers in Germany found that 22% percent of COVID-19 positive workers did not develop IgG after an 8-12-week period.   Findings from a study in 2005 of SARS-CoV infection demonstrated that MBL-deficient individuals are more susceptible to SARS, however the paper did not comment on recurrent coronavirus infection rates.  
MBL has been shown to cause microvascular injury in COVID-19 viral infections. In a study of critically ill COVID-19 patients, extensive deposits of the terminal complement complex C5b-9 as well as C4d and MASP2 were found in the lungs on histology.   These findings are consistent with sustained systemic activation of the complement pathway.   Studies with influenza H1N1 revealed that MBL knockout mice developed mild disease as evidenced by lower cytokine and chemokine production.   This suggests that MBL could increase inflammatory responses and worsen tissue damage.   Perhaps in the case of our patient, her mannose-binding lectin deficiency prevented her from developing a severe case of COVID-19. Her failure to seroconvert after her first infection may be indirectly related to her MBL deficiency by means of her milder case.   This however remains hypothetical.
Reported cases of COVID-19 reinfection have been rare. A study from Hong Kong revealed that a patient tested positive on two separate occasions months apart. Genomic analysis was performed, and two different strains of the virus were found. In this study, the individuals were asymptomatic during the recurrence despite the different strains.   This is in contrast to the individual in this case who did not seroconvert after the first exposure to the virus has had two negative SARS-CoV-2 PCR test in the interim. She was symptomatic with both infections. In a recent study from Denmark, it was found that individuals ages 65 and over were more susceptible to reinfection, in contrast to this case.  
This case presents details of a patient with mannose binding lectin deficiency who developed reinfection with COVID-19 after seroconversion failure with initial infection. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report regarding recurrent COVID-19 infection in a patient mannose binding lectin deficiency and delayed seroconversion. Additional studies would be required to determine if those with MBL deficiency are at greater risk of reinfection than the general population or failure to seroconvert.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Recurrent SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 reinfection) occurring in a patient with mannose-binding lectin (MBL) deficiency (< 50 ng/mL). The initial March 2020 infection was confirmed by positive RT-PCR, with absence of SARS-CoV-2 IgG nucleocapsid protein (N-protein) antibodies at 8 weeks post-infection and two negative intervening swabs. The second episode in October 2020 was confirmed by repeat positive RT-PCR, followed by successful seroconversion with positive SARS-CoV-2 IgG N-protein antibodies 8 weeks post-reinfection.
Plan & Outcome: Initial infection was treated on an outpatient basis with a course of azithromycin and hydroxychloroquine with complete resolution. The second episode was managed symptomatically without requiring hospitalization. The patient recovered completely from both episodes.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, chills and one episode of vomiting. On admission, he had a single seizure episode, followed by an altered sensorium and deteriorating neurological status. He also had an erythematous macular rash over his body. The patient tested positive for dengue non-structural (NS1) antigen and immunoglobulin M (IgM) dengue antibody, while the test for dengue immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody was negative. The haematological investigations at the time of presentation revealed a reduced haemoglobin (7 gm/dL) and thrombocytopaenia with a platelet count of 60 000/microl, which reduced to 40 000/microl over the subsequent two days. The platelet count steadily improved thereafter and was 80 000/microl on the sixth day.
CT imaging of the brain (Figures 1a-c) revealed ill-defined symmetrical bilateral hypodensities in the thalami, cerebellar white matter and bilateral frontal subcortical and deep white matter. Tiny hyperdense haemorrhagic foci were observed within some of these hypodense areas (Figure 1c). Repeat CT Brain imaging (Figures 1d-f), performed a day later due to the patient's clinical deterioration, revealed an increase in the haemorrhagic foci with intraventricular extension, obstructive hydrocephalus and generalized cerebral oedema.
MRI of the brain (Figures 2a-i) performed on the second day of admission revealed multiple, bilaterally symmetrical, hyperintense areas on fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T2-weighted images involving the thalami, cerebellum, bilateral frontal and parietal subcortical and deep white matter, with patchy restricted diffusion at diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) (Figure 2g). Multiple internal foci of blooming were seen on gradient recalled echoplanar (GRE) images, representing haemorrhages (Figures 2h and 2i).
A diagnosis of dengue-associated haemorrhagic encephalitis was made based on the clinical presentation, imaging and laboratory findings.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever, chills, and vomiting for five days, complicated by an acute seizure and deteriorating sensorium.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 25-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever, chills, and one episode of emesis. On admission, he experienced a single seizure followed by acute sensorium alteration and rapidly progressive neurological deterioration. He also displayed a generalized erythematous macular rash. Hematology revealed progressive thrombocytopenia followed by gradual recovery over six days.
subjective.review_of_systems: Emesis, chills; no focal motor symptoms preceding seizure.

Repeat Brain CT (day 2): Increase in hemorrhagic foci with intraventricular hemorrhage extension, obstructive hydrocephalus, and generalized cerebral edema. Brain MRI (day 2): Multiple bilaterally symmetrical hyperintense areas on T2/FLAIR involving the thalami, cerebellum, and bilateral frontal and parietal subcortical/deep white matter, patchy diffusion restriction on DWI/ADC, and multiple foci of blooming on GRE images confirming parenchymal hemorrhages.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus hemorrhagic encephalitis complicated by intraventricular hemorrhage, obstructive hydrocephalus, cerebral edema, severe thrombocytopenia, and anemia. Confirmed by positive Dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen and positive Dengue IgM antibody, with negative Dengue IgG antibody.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted for emergent neurocritical care and supportive management with intracranial pressure monitoring, anti-edema measures, blood component support, and neurological observation, achieving platelet stabilization and neurological monitoring.

raw_case_text: A male aged 43 years, residing in Bengaluru sought emergency services in July 2010. He presented with high-grade fever since four days and headache, myalgia, abdominal pain with distension since two days. He was a known diabetic (blood sugars were under control throughout the course, was on oral hypoglycemic agents) and was a social drinker (occasional alcohol consumption). Patient did not have any history of trauma. On examination he was febrile, anicteric, without any rash or lymphadenopathy. The complete blood count (CBC) showed total leukocyte count-6100 cells/mm3, differential count-neutrophils-50%, lymphocytes-45%, platelet count-96,000 cells/mm3 and packed cell volume-30%. The dengue serology was positive for both IgM and IgG antibodies (immunochromatography) serological test and peripheral smear for malaria was negative. The titers (ELISA) of dengue immunoglobulins was IgM : IgG = 4:1 and 14 days later IgM : Ig G = 5:2. With rising titers new dengue illness was diagnosed. The blood culture was sterile and ultrasound abdomen reported gross ascites, bilateral minimal pleural efflusion and borderline hepatosplenomegaly. We supposed the ascites is transudative and a part of the viral illness and as self-limiting. But the abdominal distension and pain continued to bother the patient so peritoneal tap was planned. Simultaneously, patient developed progressive pallor with drop in hemoglobin (from 9.6 gm/dl to 6.9 gm/dl) and hematocrit (from 30 to 23%), for which patient underwent blood transfusion (twice-packed red blood cells). During the initial two attempts of peritoneal tap, 500 ml of hemorrhagic ascitic fluid was drained. Even after drainage the abdominal pain and distention persisted with drop in hemoglobin, so laparoscopy was planned. Laparoscopic exploration showed 1.5 liters of peritoneal fluid with blood clots in the peritoneal cavity and mild diffuse congestion of the peritoneum. Liver, spleen, bladder and blood vessels were normal. His coagulation profile was within normal limits throughout the course (Prothrombin time (PT)-15.9 sec, Activated Patial thromboplastin time(APTT)-29 sec, International Normalized Ratio(INR)-1.48). Patient underwent blood transfusion (two packed red blood cells) again. The histopathological examination of the peritoneum showed mild hyperemia. Peritoneal drain was there for two days, abdominal discomfort and distention reduced over a week and hemoglobin improved and repeat ultrasound showed that the peritoneum was free of collection. Patient was discharged on oral hypoglycemic agents. The patient was asked to follow up with repeat hemoglobin, fasting and post-prandial blood sugar. During follow-up he is doing fine.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever for 4 days and progressive abdominal pain with distension, headache, and myalgia for 2 days.

He denied any trauma. During hospital observation, abdominal pain and distension worsened and he developed progressive pallor with a marked drop in hemoglobin and hematocrit.

subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, myalgia, abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. Negative for prior bleeding diathesis or trauma. Home medications: oral hypoglycemic agents. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, anicteric, without rash or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Abdomen: Distended with generalized abdominal tenderness. Progressive pallor noted on serial examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Total leukocyte count: 6,100 cells/mm3 (differential: neutrophils 50%, lymphocytes 45%), platelet count: 96,000 cells/mm3, packed cell volume: 30%. Hemoglobin dropped from 9.6 g/dL to 6.9 g/dL with hematocrit falling from 30% to 23%. Peripheral smear for malaria: Negative. Blood cultures: Sterile. Coagulation profile: PT 15.9 sec, aPTT 29 sec, INR 1.48 (within normal limits). Abdominal ultrasound: Gross ascites, bilateral minimal pleural effusion, borderline hepatosplenomegaly; repeat ultrasound post-drainage showed resolution of peritoneal collection.
