The ARVs were delivered monthly from June 2012 to February 2015 by courier pharmacy and no parcels were returned. She attended all monitoring visits and initially had an excellent response to the third-line regimen.
However, by 2013 the patient was not coping well and had developed urinary and faecal incontinence without a physiological cause. She had nearly been raped, had failed grade 9 and had become socially isolated. By December 2013, her viral load reflected the impact of the psychological problems on her adherence. Her mother passed away in 2015 and with that the patient lost her medical aid benefits and was referred back to the state sector. A fourth DRT (Table 1) showed that resistance to the non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and protease inhibitors had worsened and also now included resistance to the integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs).
Currently, neither the patient nor the family seem to have grasped the seriousness of her condition. Despite multiple adherence counselling sessions and even contracting with the family that her pill-taking will be supervised, there is still inadequate supervision. She has poor coping skills, has not entirely accepted her illness and is ambivalent about taking her ART. She is now on a holding regimen consisting of FTC, TDF, AZT and abacavir (ABC). A tropism assay predicted that CCR5-antagonists are likely to be effective.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old female presenting for management of perinatally acquired retroviral disease and multidrug-resistant virologic treatment failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented following referral for complex antiretroviral management due to persistent medication non-adherence driven by taste aversion. Over a two-year period, serial genotypic resistance assays demonstrated progression from single-class resistance to extensive three-class drug resistance. Although she initially showed virologic response to third-line salvage therapy initiated in 2012, severe psychosocial trauma (including an attempted sexual assault, academic failure, and the death of her mother in 2015) led to social isolation, non-physiological urinary and fecal incontinence, and severe treatment default culminating in four-class antiretroviral resistance.
subjective.past_medical_history: Perinatally acquired human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection; maternal HIV infection on ART (deceased in 2015); history of poor adherence to first- and second-line antiretroviral regimens due to medication unpalatability; no underlying structural genitourinary or gastrointestinal pathology.
subjective.review_of_systems: Psychogenic urinary and fecal incontinence, social withdrawal, emotional distress; denies chronic fever, opportunistic infections, respiratory distress, or localized pain.

objective.physical_examination: Adolescent female in stable general physical condition; absence of physiological causes for urinary or fecal incontinence; normal cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurological examinations.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial genotypic drug resistance testing (DRT): DRT 1-3 demonstrated progressive development of high-level resistance to nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), and ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors (PIs). Fourth DRT demonstrated extensive cross-class resistance including emerging resistance to integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs). Viral tropism assay: Predicted functional coreceptor tropism with likelihood of response to CCR5-antagonists (maraviroc).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Perinatally acquired human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection complicated by multiclass drug resistance (pan-resistant to NRTIs, NNRTIs, PIs, and INSTIs) secondary to severe psychosocial trauma, grief, and treatment non-adherence, presenting with functional/psychogenic encopresis and enuresis.
Plan & Outcome: Placed on an interim nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor holding regimen comprising tenofovir (TDF), emtricitabine (FTC), zidovudine (AZT), and abacavir (ABC) to maintain replicative fitness impairment while salvage regimens are formulated. Initiated intensive multidisciplinary adolescent adherence counseling, psychological support, social services involvement, and directly observed therapy agreements with family caregivers, with future consideration of CCR5 coreceptor antagonist-based regimens.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old female who was referred to a rheumatologic outpatient clinic, complaining of fever for 8 months, initially daily but changing to an irregular pattern along the course, predominantly in the afternoon, and associated with arthralgia in small and large joints, malaise, pallor, increased abdominal volume, and involuntary weight loss (20 kilograms during the period). The patient lived in the metropolitan area of Sao Paulo. Laboratory tests showed pancytopenia associated with increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein, polyclonal gammopathy, and a weakly positive rheumatoid factor. The abdominal tomography showed great splenomegaly (reaching > 26 cm in greater diameter) and hepatomegaly. A bone marrow aspirate was performed and did not show any hematological diseases or etiological agents. The initial clinical diagnosis was Still's disease, and she was treated with a 2-month course of prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (tapered to 0.6 mg/kg/day) and methotrexate (MTX) 15 mg/week.
The patient progressed with significant worsening of symptoms and required hospitalization due to poor general condition, presenting cachexia, persistent fever, abdominal distension, and pancytopenia. She was admitted to HCFMUSP, in a ward reserved for cases without clinical suspicion of COVID-19 ('non-COVID-19 area'). Upon admission, we retrieved a detailed clinical history, showing that she toured to many places, from the north and coastal areas of Sao Paulo State to the south region of Minas Gerais State, all considered endemic areas for leishmaniasis in Southeastern Brazil (Figure 1), from September 2018 to September 2019. A new laboratory work-up showed no helminthic diseases in stool samples, and serologies for systemic mycoses were non-reactive. The initial blood sample taken for Polymerase Chain Reaction of KDNA for Leishmania was negative on the third day of hospitalization (DH). On the eighth DH, the patient progressed with dyspnea associated with ground-glass opacity and consolidations on the chest tomography. In this context, SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and influenza B infections were ruled out by molecular tests, and piperacillin-tazobactam was started. Blood cultures were negative, and the patient presented an improvement in respiratory status after the antibiotic treatment. On the thirteenth DH, serologies to detect anti-Leishmania antibodies were collected (rapid immunochromatographic test for qualitative detection of anti-recombinant antigen K39 and indirect immunofluorescence), showing positive results. At this time, the patient was taking 10 mg/day of prednisone, without MTX for 45 days. Treatment with liposomal amphotericin 300 mg/day was started, but on the second day of treatment, the patient developed hypoglycemia, torpor, dyspnea, and shock, evolving within a few hours to cardiac arrest, unresponsive to cardiopulmonary resuscitation maneuvers. An autopsy was requested to clarify the cause of the acute respiratory failure, with pulmonary thromboembolism, nosocomial infection or COVID-19 as the main clinical hypotheses.
The MIA-US was performed after written consent from the next-of-kin, using a portable SonoSite M-Turbo R (Fujifilm, Bothell, WA, USA) ultrasound, with C60x (5-2 MHz Convex) multifrequency broadband transducers and DICOM standard images, to guide the tissue sampling from the liver, spleen, lungs, heart and kidneys, with Tru-Cut semi-automatic coaxial needles (14G; 20 cm in length). Additional sampling of skeletal muscle (quadriceps femoris) and skin (left thigh) was performed with a 5-mm punch needle; the brain was sampled through transsphenoidal puncture, and the bone marrow through sternal puncture. This autopsy protocol was approved by the HCFMUSP Ethical Committee (protocol No 3951.904) and was previously described in detail  .
The US showed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly and lungs with irregular and thickened pleura, B lines, and subpleural hyperechogenicity, indicative of pneumonia (Figure 2A). Microscopic analysis showed: hypocellular bone marrow aspirate with hemophagocytosis and several macrophages containing amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. (Figure 2B); spleen with necrotic red pulp and hyperplastic sinusoidal cells containing amastigotes (Figure 2C); liver with hyperplastic Kupffer cells containing amastigotes, hepatic steatosis, and gram-negative bacilli in vessels. The immunohistochemistry labeled amastigotes forms, using as the primary antibody a polyclonal anti-Leishmania in the bone marrow, liver and spleen samples (Figure 2D). The lungs exhibited pulmonary edema and foci of suppurative pneumonia (Figure 2E), with numerous gram-negative bacilli in the alveoli and vessels (Figure 2F). Other findings included: acute tubular necrosis, hyperplasia of mesangial cells, and reactive microglia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old female presented with an 8-month history of daily-to-irregular fevers, widespread arthralgia, abdominal distension, and a 20-kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed daily fevers peaking in the afternoon 8 months prior, which evolved into an irregular pattern, accompanied by arthralgia in small and large joints, malaise, progressive pallor, abdominal distension, and an involuntary 20-kg weight loss. She was initially diagnosed with adult-onset Still's disease at an outside rheumatology clinic and treated with prednisone (1 mg/kg/day tapered to 0.6 mg/kg/day) and methotrexate (15 mg/week) for 2 months. She experienced clinical deterioration with worsening cachexia, persistent fever, and abdominal distension, prompting acute hospital admission. On hospital day 8, she developed acute dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Presumed adult-onset Still's disease treated with prednisone and methotrexate (discontinued 45 days prior to admission). Epidemiological history: resident of metropolitan Sao Paulo with extensive travel to coastal/northern Sao Paulo State and southern Minas Gerais State between September 2018 and September 2019.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, malaise, diffuse arthralgias, pallor, abdominal distension, severe weight loss, and progressive dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Cachectic female in poor general condition. Abdominal examination revealed marked abdominal distension with massive splenomegaly and hepatomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests revealed pancytopenia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), polyclonal gammopathy, and weakly positive rheumatoid factor. Stool examinations: negative for helminths. Blood cultures: negative. Serologies for systemic mycoses: non-reactive. Molecular testing for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, and influenza B: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT: marked hepatomegaly and massive splenomegaly measuring >26 cm in greatest diameter. Chest CT: bilateral ground-glass opacities and pulmonary consolidations. Initial bone marrow aspirate: no hematologic malignancy or etiology identified. Initial blood kDNA PCR: negative on hospital day 3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Anti-Leishmania serology by rapid immunochromatographic rK39 test and indirect immunofluorescence returned positive on hospital day 13, establishing visceral leishmaniasis. Postmortem minimally invasive ultrasound-guided tissue sampling confirmed abundant intracellular Leishmania amastigotes in bone marrow aspirates with hemophagocytosis, splenic red pulp, and hepatic Kupffer cells, verified by polyclonal anti-Leishmania immunohistochemistry. Lung autopsy demonstrated suppurative pneumonia with intra-alveolar gram-negative bacilli. Still's disease ruled out; COVID-19, influenza, and systemic mycoses excluded. Management and Outcome: Received IV piperacillin-tazobactam for hospital-acquired pneumonia. Liposomal amphotericin B (300 mg/day) was initiated on hospital day 13; on treatment day 2, she developed acute hypoglycemia, torpor, dyspnea, and refractory septic shock leading to cardiac arrest and death.

raw_case_text:
A 32-year-old woman presented to the Ear, Nose and Throat clinic with a tender lump on her right side of the upper neck that had appeared for 2 weeks. She had a mild fever initially but did not have a loss of appetite, weight loss or night sweats. She also did not experience any cough, chest pain, nasal obstruction or otologic symptoms. There was no recent contact history of tuberculosis. She was treated for cervical lymphadenitis with amoxicillin by a general practitioner before coming to us. However, her neck lump persisted. On examination, there was a firm 1.5 x 1 cm right upper neck lump which was mildly tender. We performed nasal endoscopy, which showed a nasopharyngeal mass almost obliterating the fossa of Rosenmuller on both sides (Figure 1).
The surface of the mass looked irregular with yellowish secretions on it. The rest of the ear, nose and throat examinations were unremarkable. Our working diagnosis was NPC with neck metastasis. We ordered an ultrasound scan of the neck and fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the neck lump. A biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mass was taken. The ultrasound scan reported multiple hypoechoic enlarged cervical nodes bilaterally with distortion of the fatty hilum. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the nasopharynx and neck was ordered to further evaluate the neck lump and nasopharyngeal mass.
The FNAC was reported as showing 2 foci of atypical cells arranged in a sheet, composed of enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei. The nuclear membranes were found to be irregular with moderate cytoplasm in the background of abundant polymorphous lymphoid cells and red blood cells. The Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain of the FNAC was negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Metastatic carcinoma of the neck node was suspected. The CT scan showed a heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass measuring 2 x 1.4 x 3.9 cm in the nasopharynx, obliterating the bilateral fossa of Rosenmuller and extending inferiorly to the upper part of the oropharynx (Figure 2). Multiple enlarged, homogenously enhancing cervical nodes were seen on both sides. The visualized apical lungs showed minimal consolidation and centrilobular nodules with tree-in-bud appearances.
The radiologist's impression from the CT scan finding was that of nasopharyngeal cancer with multiple cervical lymphadenopathy. Lesions in the lung apices were suspected of being active lung infections. Histopathological examination of the nasopharyngeal mass biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells. No malignant cells were seen. Stains for AFB and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain for fungal hyphae were negative.
A repeat biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mass was sent due to strong suspicion of nasopharyngeal cancer with neck metastasis. The repeat biopsy showed caseating granuloma with dense chronic inflammatory cells forming lymphoid follicles and the ZN stain demonstrated a few AFB (Figure 3(a)-(c)). Malignant cells were again not detected and GMS staining was negative for fungal hyphae.
The repeat biopsy was again negative for malignant cells and fungal hyphae. We ordered sputum smears for microscopy and a chest x-ray to exclude pulmonary tuberculosis. The chest x-ray was normal, but her sputum smears for AFB tested positive. Her white blood cell (WBC) count was 6.99 x 109/L, neutrophil count 70.4%, lymphocyte count 19%, Hb level was 12.2 g/dL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate was (ESR) 60 mm/h and anti HIV and HBsAg tests were negative. A diagnosis of nasopharyngeal tuberculosis secondary to pulmonary tuberculosis was made. We referred her to a pulmonologist colleague who put her on first-line anti-tubercular drugs. The patient was admitted to the tuberculosis ward for 2 weeks to be observed for any drug reactions and acute side-effects as per the protocol. The patient responded well to standard treatment of a 2 months intensive phase (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), and a 4 months continuation phase (isoniazid and rifampicin). Her neck node was not palpable after 2 months of treatment and the nasopharyngeal mass disappeared in 3 months. She remained asymptomatic at 6 months follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old woman presented with a tender right upper neck lump of two weeks' duration and mild fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 32-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of a tender right upper neck mass and mild fever. She received empiric oral amoxicillin from a general practitioner for suspected cervical lymphadenitis without improvement. She denied cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, nasal obstruction, otologic symptoms, anorexia, weight loss, or night sweats.
subjective.past_medical_history: Empiric amoxicillin therapy for cervical lymphadenitis. Denies personal or contact history of tuberculosis, prior chronic medical conditions, or travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports tender right neck lump, mild fever; denies nasal obstruction, epistaxis, ear discharge, hearing loss, cough, chest pain, anorexia, weight loss, or night sweats. Home medications: amoxicillin. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Firm, mildly tender 1.5 x 1 cm right upper cervical lymph node. Nasal endoscopy: irregular nasopharyngeal mass with yellowish secretions almost obliterating the bilateral fossa of Rosenmuller. Ear, nose, and throat exam otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 6.99 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 70.4%, lymphocytes 19%); Hemoglobin: 12.2 g/dL; ESR: 60 mm/h; Anti-HIV: negative; HBsAg: negative; Chest X-ray: normal lung fields.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial FNAC of cervical lymph node: two foci of atypical cells in sheets with enlarged hyperchromatic irregular nuclei against lymphoid/RBC background; Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain negative for AFB. Contrast CT of neck and nasopharynx: heterogeneously enhancing soft tissue mass (2 x 1.4 x 3.9 cm) in nasopharynx obliterating bilateral fossa of Rosenmuller and extending to upper oropharynx; multiple bilateral homogenously enhancing cervical lymph nodes; apical lung fields showed minimal consolidation and centrilobular tree-in-bud nodules. Initial biopsy of nasopharyngeal mass: necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells; malignant cells absent; AFB and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) fungal stains negative. Repeat nasopharyngeal biopsy: caseating granulomas with dense chronic lymphoid infiltration; malignant cells absent; GMS stain negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Primary nasopharyngeal tuberculosis with cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis secondary to subclinical pulmonary tuberculosis, mimicking nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
Confirmation: Repeat nasopharyngeal biopsy demonstrated caseating granulomas with Ziehl-Neelsen stain demonstrating acid-fast bacilli; sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli were positive; neck CT showed characteristic centrilobular tree-in-bud nodules in lung apices.
Differentials ruled out: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma with nodal metastasis (ruled out by absence of malignant cells on two consecutive deep biopsies and resolution on ATT), fungal granulomatous disease (GMS stains negative on both biopsies), pyogenic bacterial lymphadenitis (unresponsive to amoxicillin).
Treatment & Outcome: Standard first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy: 2 months intensive phase with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 4 months continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampicin. Inpatient monitoring for 2 weeks in TB ward confirmed excellent drug tolerance. Cervical lymphadenopathy resolved completely by 2 months, and nasopharyngeal mass disappeared completely by 3 months. The patient remained completely asymptomatic at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: An antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naive woman was asymptomatic for tuberculosis (TB) at presentation and started on first-line ART (see Table 1 for more information). She rapidly deteriorated and presented again after 10 days with night sweats, a cough, and abdominal pain. She met the criteria for AlereLAM testing on this date, which revealed a strongly positive (4+) result. The patient was placed onto TB treatment and sputum was sent for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and mycobacterial culture, along with urine for mycobacterial culture.

subjective.chief_complaint: An adult female presenting with acute clinical deterioration, cough, night sweats, and abdominal pain ten days after commencing antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, initially asymptomatic for active opportunistic infections, commenced first-line antiretroviral therapy. Within 10 days of ART initiation, she experienced rapid clinical deterioration characterized by the onset of persistent cough, drenching night sweats, and severe abdominal pain, prompting urgent medical re-evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Newly diagnosed chronic retroviral illness, previously antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naive prior to commencing first-line regimen 10 days earlier.
subjective.review_of_systems: Cough, drenching night sweats, and abdominal pain; denies hemoptysis or focal neurologic deficits.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely unwell female meeting clinical criteria for severe illness and lateral flow screening; detailed vital signs not documented in raw text.
objective.routine_investigations: Sputum and urine samples collected and submitted for mycobacterial culture and specialized diagnostic antigen screening.
objective.advanced_workup: Sputum submitted for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra molecular testing.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis unmasked as tuberculosis-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (TB-IRIS) following initiation of first-line antiretroviral therapy for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Diagnostic confirmation: Strongly positive (4+) urine lipoarabinomannan (AlereLAM) lateral flow test, supported by diagnostic workup with sputum Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and concurrent sputum and urine mycobacterial cultures. Plan & Outcome: Promptly commenced on standard weight-based antitubercular therapy while continuing clinical monitoring and antiretroviral management.

raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old healthy male volunteer was enrolled in a double blind, randomized, controlled trial that assessed the safety, tolerability, and protective efficacy against CHMI by PfSPZ-infected mosquitoes of intradermal administration of aseptic purified cryopreserved PfSPZ (PfSPZ Challenge) in volunteers taking weekly 300 mg chloroquine prophylaxis, the PfSPZ-CVac approach. His medical history was unremarkable, and he did not smoke or use illicit drugs. His mother had a history of hypertension and his paternal grandfather had a history of heart valve defects and a possible myocardial infarction at the age of 70. At inclusion, physical examination was within normal limits with a blood pressure of 139/76 mmHg, heart rate of 55 beats per minute and a body mass index of 20.2 kg/m2. Electrocardiography (ECG) showed a commonly seen normal variant of incomplete right bundle branch block (see Additional file 1). Standard laboratory tests at inclusion were normal (see Table 1).
From October to December 2012, he received three intradermal injections at four-week intervals of 7.5 x104 PfSPZ of PfSPZ Challenge (PfNF54) diluted in phosphate buffered saline with 1% human serum albumin. From day 3 until day 8 after the first immunization he reported a sore throat and symptoms of a common cold (i.e., stuffy nose and coughing) with mild chills for a few hours. No complaints were reported after the second and third immunizations. No clinically significant laboratory abnormalities were found during the immunization period.
Fifty-nine days after the third and last immunization and 32 days after his last dose of chloroquine, he underwent CHMI by the bites of five P. falciparum-infected mosquitoes (PfNF54). On day 9 post-CHMI he complained of a sore throat. On day 11 post-CHMI his thick blood smear became positive (6 P. falciparum/muL blood; 0.00012% infected erythrocytes) and standard treatment with Malarone  (1,000 mg atovaquone plus 400 mg proguanil once daily for three days) was initiated. Retrospective assessment of parasitaemia by quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) revealed 13,293 parasites/mL (0.00026% infected erythrocytes) on day of thick smear positivity. On that day he complained of minor chills and headache for a few hours with a highest recorded sublingual temperature of 37.5 C. Platelet and lymphocyte counts decreased to 97 x109/L (normal range = 141 - 400 x109/L) and 0.60 x109/L (normal range = 1.0 - 3.5 x109/L), respectively, as often seen in malaria positive individuals. The level of troponin T by a highly sensitive assay was normal (i.e., 8 ng/L; upper limit of normal = 14 ng/L). Troponin T is a specific marker for myocardial tissue damage.
On the second day of Malarone treatment (day 12 post-CHMI) the troponin T level was elevated at 45 ng/L and increased to 63 ng/L in the evening. No abnormalities were seen on ECG. Apart from mild headache and fatigue on the following day (day 13 post-CHMI) the volunteer was asymptomatic, but the troponin T was 197 ng/L in the morning and 299 ng/L in the afternoon. The blood pressure was 114/60 mmHg and the ECG revealed mild repolarization disturbances with diffuse ST-T-segment elevation, suggestive of pericarditis (see Additional file 2). The echocardiogram showed mild hypokinesia of the inferior wall and a slightly diminished global left ventricle (LV)-function (calculated LV ejection fraction of 53%; normal range for a young man is > 55%). Malarone treatment was completed and qPCR for P. falciparum was negative on day 13 post-CHMI. Although the subject did not have any cardiac or chest symptoms, he was hospitalized at the cardiology department according to safety protocol for telemetric ECG-monitoring and follow-up of troponin T levels.
That night at ~01:00 AM he experienced retrosternal pain and a heavy feeling in his left arm. After approximately 10 minutes sublingual nitroglycerin spray was administered; the chest pain did not disappear immediately, but only 10 minutes after administration of nitroglycerin. The pain was not related to breathing and there were no concomitant complaints or signs of dyspnoea, pyrosis or ructus. The subject never had another episode of chest pain. Cardiac MRI several hours later on day 14 post-CHMI showed: i) slightly increased T2-weighted signal intensity in the basal- and mid-inferolateral and partly in the mid-anterolateral myocardial segments, matching minor oedema (see Figure 1A); ii) focal areas of subepicardial and midwall delayed enhancement in the basal- and mid-inferior and basal- and mid-inferolateral segments after administration of gadolinium contrast (see Figure 1B and C); iii) hypokinesia basal- and mid-inferior and mild hypokinesia basal- and mid-inferolateral. These findings were interpreted as indicative of myocarditis. Treatment was started on day 14 post-CHMI with a beta-blocker, metoprolol (25 mg twice daily), to reduce the chance of cardiac arrhythmia and according to the treatment guidelines for patients with reduced LV-function.
Troponin T levels continued to rise with a peak of 1,115 ng/L on day 16 after CHMI. The following days troponin T decreased and eventually returned to normal 16 days after initial increase, corresponding to 28 days post-CHMI. Creatine kinase (CK) showed a similar pattern of rising and falling, but returned to normal on day 16 post-CHMI. A biochemical marker of cardiac wall stress, N-terminal pro-hormone brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), was slightly elevated on days 15 and 17 post-CHMI, but was normal on day 20 post-CHMI (see Table 1). A limited rise and fall of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) were found. The nonspecific marker for increased coagulation and inflammation, D-dimer, remained within the normal range and was only minimally elevated on the first day after thick smear positivity. Similarly, the inflammatory acute-phase protein, C-reactive protein (CRP) was only slightly elevated on days 13, 14, and 15 after CHMI (see Table 1). Four days after admission (day 17 post-CHMI) ECG and echocardiogram had normalized (see Additional file 3 and calculated LV ejection fraction was 62%; normal range is > 55%) and the volunteer was discharged.
Apart from the single short episode of chest pain and a longer period of fatigue with occasional mild headache during and shortly after hospitalization, no other complaints were reported. The fatigue diminished after halving the dose of metoprolol to 25 mg once daily on day 23 post-CHMI. The remaining mild fatigue completely disappeared three weeks later on day 44 post-CHMI. After discharge the volunteer did not complain about occasional mild headache anymore.
The volunteer received pre-travel vaccines for diphtheria, tetanus, polio, typhus, hepatitis A and hepatitis B 14 days after the third injection of PfSPZ Challenge (46 days before CHMI). He had booster vaccinations for hepatitis A and B 40 days after the third injection (20 days before CHMI).
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analyses of throat smear, faeces and whole blood were carried out for viruses and bacteria known to cause myocarditis (see Table 2). Throat smear PCR was positive for rhinovirus; all other PCR results were negative (Table 2). Virological, bacteriological and parasitological serology was performed on samples obtained three weeks before inclusion and on day 17 post-CHMI (see Table 3) with repeat testing 18 days later (day 35 post-CHMI and 23 days after first elevation of troponin T). All serologic results were negative. Furthermore, urine toxicology screening for amphetamine-derivatives, cocaine, cannabinoids, diazepam, methadone, tramadol hydrochloride, and opiates was negative on day 17 after CHMI.
At almost five months after the first MRI, repeat cardiac MRI demonstrated good function of the left ventricle (calculated LV ejection fraction of 67%) with persistence of mild hypokinesia in the mid-inferior and mid-inferolateral segments of the left ventricle. The oedema had disappeared completely (see Figure 1A) and concomitantly the delayed enhancement had decreased, mostly in the basal-inferolateral segment (see Figure 1B and C). However, patchy midwall and subepicardial delayed enhancement was still present in four myocardial segments (i.e., the basal-inferolateral, mid-inferolateral, basal-inferior, and mid-inferior segments). Follow-up ECG did not show any abnormalities except for a minimally widened QRS complex compared to the pre-trial ECG and the persistence of incomplete right bundle branch block (see Additional file 4). In addition, ECG during a cardiac stress test did not show ST-T-segment changes, rhythm abnormalities, or other changes with respect to the pre-trial ECG. The cardiac stress test used a cycling protocol starting at 50 watt and with increasing steps of 20 watt per minute. He reached a maximally achieved power of 270 watt (i.e., 122% of expected for his age group and gender). He had an adequate increase in blood pressure and heart rate. His heart rate pressure product was 35,854 mmHg/min (normal is > 25,000 mmHg/min). Metoprolol 25 mg once daily was stopped and the volunteer has remained without complaints in good condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old male presenting with low-grade fever, chills, sore throat, and headache following controlled mosquito challenge, subsequently developing acute chest pain and troponin elevation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient participated in a clinical trial and developed a sore throat on day 9 after controlled mosquito challenge. On day 11, he experienced minor chills, headache, and sublingual temperature of 37.5 C, for which oral atovaquone-proguanil was initiated. On day 12, asymptomatic high-sensitivity troponin elevation was detected. On day 13, ECG revealed diffuse ST-T elevations and echocardiography showed mild inferior hypokinesia. On the night of day 13-14, he experienced retrosternal chest pain and left arm heaviness responsive to sublingual nitroglycerin, prompting cardiology admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Healthy volunteer. Received pre-trial vaccinations (diphtheria, tetanus, polio, typhoid, hepatitis A, hepatitis B) and completed trial-mandated chloroquine prophylaxis 32 days prior to challenge. No prior cardiovascular disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for sore throat, mild chills, headache, fatigue, retrosternal chest pain, and left arm heaviness. Negative for dyspnea, pyrosis, or orthopnea. Medications: oral atovaquone-proguanil. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 37.5 C, blood pressure: 114/60 mmHg. Cardiovascular: Normal heart sounds, no rubs or gallops. Lungs clear to auscultation. Neurological and general examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: 97 x 10^9/L (normal: 141-400 x 10^9/L), lymphocyte count: 0.60 x 10^9/L (normal: 1.0-3.5 x 10^9/L). High-sensitivity troponin T: Baseline 8 ng/L (normal: <14 ng/L), rose to 45 ng/L and 63 ng/L on day 12, 197-299 ng/L on day 13, peaking at 1,115 ng/L on day 16, normalizing by day 28. Creatine kinase (CK): Transient elevation, normalized by day 16. NT-proBNP: Mildly elevated on days 15 and 17, normal by day 20. Limited transient elevations of AST, LDH, and CRP (days 13-15). D-dimer: Minimally elevated on day 12, otherwise normal. Urine toxicology screen: Negative. Comprehensive infectious serology panel (viral, bacterial, parasitic): All negative. Throat swab PCR: Positive for rhinovirus. ECG: Diffuse ST-T segment elevation on day 13; normalized by day 17. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Day 13 showed mild inferior wall hypokinesia and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 53%; normalized on day 17 to LVEF 62%.
objective.advanced_workup: Cardiac MRI (day 14): Increased T2-weighted signal intensity (edema) in basal-, mid-inferolateral, and mid-anterolateral myocardium; focal subepicardial and midwall delayed gadolinium enhancement in basal- and mid-inferior and inferolateral segments; basal/mid-inferior hypokinesia consistent with acute myocarditis. Follow-up cardiac MRI at 5 months: Complete resolution of myocardial edema, normalized global LV function (LVEF 67%), and diminished residual focal delayed enhancement. Exercise stress test at 5 months: Normal exercise tolerance (270 W, 122% of predicted), no ischemia or arrhythmias.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria acquired during controlled human malaria infection (CHMI), complicated by acute perimyocarditis with transient left ventricular dysfunction.
Diagnostic confirmation: Thick blood smear positive for Plasmodium falciparum (6 parasites/muL blood; 0.00012% infected erythrocytes) on day 11 post-CHMI; quantitative PCR confirmed 13,293 P. falciparum parasites/mL (0.00026% parasitemia), with rapid clearance and negative qPCR by day 13. Other cardiotropic viral/bacterial pathogens excluded by negative blood PCR and paired serologies (incidental upper respiratory rhinovirus detected on throat swab).
Plan & Outcome: Completed a 3-day course of oral Malarone (atovaquone 1,000 mg plus proguanil 400 mg once daily), achieving rapid parasite clearance. Acute myocarditis was managed with telemetry, sublingual nitroglycerin for acute chest pain, and oral metoprolol (25 mg twice daily, subsequently tapered to 25 mg once daily and discontinued). Cardiac enzymes, ECG, and echocardiography normalized, with full recovery and excellent exercise capacity confirmed on long-term follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old man with Type 2 diabetes presented with fever, arthralgia, and myalgia for three days after working in paddy fields. On admission, he was febrile, icteric, dyspneic, and hypotensive (blood pressure 93/60 mmHg), with bibasal lung crepitations. He had not urinated for over 6 hours.
Initial tests indicated neutrophilic leukocytosis, severe thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes and serum creatinine (Table 2). Arterial blood gas analysis showed hypoxemia and metabolic acidosis with a lactate level of 7.1 mmol/L. Chest radiograph suggested severe pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome. Leptospira MAT was positive at a titer of 1 : 640.
After fluid resuscitation noradrenaline was initiated, the patient was transferred to the ICU. He was electively intubated due to severe hypoxemia. Intravenous ceftriaxone was commenced. Renal replacement therapy by continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration was commenced, and multiple platelet concentrates were given to correct thrombocytopenia. Once stabilized, intermittent hemodialysis was initiated.
On Day 13, the patient developed blood-stained nasogastric aspirate and significant anemia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed gastric erosions. Anemia was corrected with multiple blood transfusions. The patient was gradually improving by this time with no fever and minimum ventilator support until Day 15, when abdominal tenderness and sluggish bowel sounds were detected. There was intolerance of nasogastric feeds and melena. The abdomen was distended, and an anteroposterior radiograph (Figure 3) showed dilated multiple small bowel loops, a collapsed large bowel but no free gas in the peritoneal cavity. An ultrasound scan confirmed small bowel obstruction. The patient was hemodynamically unstable for contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography scan or for any surgical intervention. He succumbed on Day 21 of illness.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old male with diabetes presenting with a 3-day history of fever, arthralgia, and myalgia following work in paddy fields.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 3 days prior to admission following labor in agricultural paddy fields, characterized by acute fever, arthralgias, and generalized myalgias. He was anuric for over 6 hours prior to hospital arrival. In the hospital, he rapidly deteriorated into severe hypoxemia, lactic acidosis, and hypotensive shock requiring endotracheal intubation, vasoactive agents, and continuous renal replacement therapy. On day 13, he developed blood-stained nasogastric aspirate and anemia. On day 15, he developed acute abdominal distension, sluggish bowel sounds, feed intolerance, and melena.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus. Epidemiological exposure: occupational exposure working in agricultural paddy fields.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, arthralgias, generalized myalgias, anuria, blood-stained nasogastric aspirate, and melena. Home medications: not documented. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: febrile, deeply icteric, tachypneic/dyspneic, and hypotensive (blood pressure 93/60 mmHg). Respiratory: bibasal lung crepitations auscultated. Renal: anuria (>6 hours without urine). On day 15: distended abdomen with diffuse tenderness and sluggish/hypoactive bowel sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas: severe hypoxemia and metabolic acidosis with serum lactate of 7.1 mmol/L. Complete blood count: neutrophilic leukocytosis, severe thrombocytopenia, and subsequent severe anemia on day 13. Biochemistry: marked elevation in serum creatinine (acute renal failure) and elevated liver transaminases. Chest radiograph: severe pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome. Abdominal radiograph (anteroposterior): dilated multiple small bowel loops with collapsed large bowel, without pneumoperitoneum. Bedside abdominal ultrasound: confirmed mechanical small bowel obstruction.
objective.advanced_workup: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: multiple gastric mucosal erosions. Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT and emergency laparotomy were deferred due to extreme hemodynamic instability.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) confirmed by Leptospira microscopic agglutination test (MAT) positive at a titer of 1:640. Complex presentation included severe pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome, severe lactic acidosis (7.1 mmol/L), septic shock, anuric acute kidney injury requiring continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) and intermittent hemodialysis, severe thrombocytopenia, gastric stress erosions, and acute mesenteric ischemia resulting in small bowel obstruction.
Plan & Treatment: Intravenous fluid resuscitation, noradrenaline infusion; IV ceftriaxone; elective endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation; continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) transitioned to intermittent hemodialysis; multiple platelet concentrate transfusions; packed red blood cell transfusions for acute anemia.
Outcome: Patient was hemodynamically unstable for surgical exploration or advanced CT angiography; condition deteriorated inexorably, and he succumbed on Day 21 of illness due to multiorgan failure.

raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old previously healthy Sri Lankan Sinhala man was admitted with an acute febrile illness lasting for three days. He had high fever associated with severe myalgia, arthralgia and headache. He also had vomiting associated with a severe loss of appetite for two days. There was no photophobia. He did not complain of cough, chest pain or shortness of breath. There was no dysuria, increased frequency of urination, loin pain, diarrhea or abdominal pain. He did not have any bleeding manifestations. He had no history of skin rash or joint swelling. He had not noticed any significant reduction of urine output and his urine color was normal.
On examination, our patient was febrile and appeared ill. He was not icteric and not pale. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. There was a mild conjunctival injection but no conjunctival hemorrhages. There were no peripheral stigmata to suggest bacterial endocarditis. Neck stiffness and Kernig's sign were absent. There were no features of joint inflammation but his muscles were mildly tender. No skin rashes or eschars were observed.
A cardiovascular examination found our patient to be tachycardic with a regular pulse rate of 104 beats per minute. His jugular venous pressure was not elevated. His blood pressure was 110/68 mmHg with no postural decline. His heart was in dual rhythm and there were no murmurs. His apex beat was not deviated.
He was not dyspnoic and had a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute. His breath sounds were symmetrically vesicular and there was no evidence of consolidation. No rhonchi or crepitations were observed.
His abdomen was soft to superficial palpation. There were no abnormal masses on deep palpation and his liver and spleen were not palpable, nor were there any ballotable masses. There was no free fluid.
A nervous system examination revealed an alert and conscious middle-aged man who was mildly distressed due to headache and myalgia. A cranial nerve examination and neurological examination did not reveal any abnormality and he had a normal gait.
Basic laboratory investigations were sent and our patient was initially managed as having an unspecified viral fever pending results of the investigations. A full blood count revealed his hemoglobin level to be 13.4 g/dL, his white blood cell count (WBC) 4400/muL (neutrophils, 76%; lymphocytes, 24%) and a platelet count of 48,000/muL. His serum creatinine was 83 mumol/L, serum sodium was 141 mmol/L and potassium was 3.7 mmol/L. His liver enzyme results were as follows: aspartate transaminase, 153 U/L, alanine transaminase, 207 U/L; and alkaline phosphatase, 387 U/L. His total protein level was 70 g/dL with albumin of 43 g/dL. His international normalized ratio was 0.97 and activated partial thromboplastin time 32 seconds.
The initial investigations were compatible with dengue fever. Blood was taken to screen for the dengue antibody and blood cultures were sent. His fluid intake was maintained according to the national guidelines on dengue fever, as there was a widespread dengue epidemic with hundreds of patients getting admitted daily. His fever was treated symptomatically with paracetamol.
His fever settled on the fourth day of fever and our patient was symptomatically better. However, he developed mild slurring of speech six days after the onset of fever. On the seventh day, he had marked slurring of speech and he found it difficult to walk due to severe unsteadiness. An examination revealed a bilaterally impaired finger-to-nose test and heel-to-shin test. He had dysdiadochokinesia and an ataxic gait. There was no nystagmus. An examination of the fundus of his eye did not reveal any abnormality. An examination of his cranial nerves continued to be normal. There were no peripheral sensory or motor deficits. His deep tendon reflexes and plantar reflexes remained normal.
Due to the sudden onset of bilateral cerebellar signs, an urgent non contrast computed tomography scan was performed. There were bilateral hypodense areas in his cerebellum but his ventricles and cerebral hemispheres appeared normal. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of his head was performed, which revealed bilateral diffuse hyperintense areas in his cerebellar hemispheres spreading across the vermis (Figures 1 and 2). The appearance in the MRI scan was compatible with acute postinfective cerebellitis. Serological studies were performed for the possible viral etiologies that can cause cerebellitis. Hepatitis B and C serology, herpes simplex virus serology and Japanese encephalitis immunoglobulin M were negative. An enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for human immunodeficiency virus was negative. Dengue virus immunoglobulin M (IgM) and immunoglobulin G (IgG) were both detected in our patient's serum on day six after the onset of the symptoms. EBV IgM antibody was detected in his blood by ELISA on the eighth day of illness. Serological studies for Salmonella typhi and paratyphi were negative. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a WBC of 10 cells/muL (lymphocytes, nine cells and neutrophils, one cell), red blood cells 1 cell/muL, proteins 0.88 g/dL and sugar 3.1 mmol/L with a random blood sugar of 5.4 mol/L, all of which were compatible with viral central nervous system infection. Cerebrospinal fluid cultures were negative and viral studies were negative for Herpes simplex virus, EBV antibody and Japanese encephalitis virus. Dengue IgG was detected in his CSF while IgM was negative. Dengue virus non-structural protein 1 antigen was not detected in his CSF.
Dependent on the clinical findings and serology, a diagnosis of post-infectious cerebellitis was made. Our patient was managed with maximum supportive care and physiotherapy combined with gait training. Speech therapy was also commenced. At discharge two weeks after the onset of symptoms, our patient was able to walk without support and his speech was markedly improved. His platelet count, WBC and differential counts were within normal limits at the time of discharge.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presented with high fever, severe myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and vomiting for 3 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-day history of acute high fever accompanied by severe myalgia, arthralgia, headache, vomiting, and profound anorexia. His fever resolved on illness day 4. However, on illness day 6, he developed acute slurring of speech, which progressed by day 7 to marked dysarthria and severe gait ataxia resulting in inability to walk independently.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy Sri Lankan man. No prior chronic illnesses, neurological diseases, or psychiatric history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, anorexia, vomiting, dysarthria, and gait unsteadiness. Denied diplopia, sensory loss, weakness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination:
Admission: Heart rate 104 bpm, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg without postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min. Chest clear; abdomen soft and non-tender without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Initial neurological exam was normal.
Illness day 7: Alert and conscious. Speech was severely slurred (scanning/cerebellar dysarthria). Bilateral dysmetria on finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing, bilateral dysdiadochokinesia, and marked cerebellar ataxic gait. Cranial nerves were intact without nystagmus; fundoscopy was normal; motor power, sensory modalities, deep tendon reflexes, and plantar reflexes were entirely normal.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, white blood cell count 4,400/muL (76% neutrophils, 24% lymphocytes), platelet count 48,000/muL (normalized by discharge).
Biochemistry & liver panel: Serum creatinine 83 mumol/L, sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, AST 153 U/L, ALT 207 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 387 U/L, total protein 70 g/dL, albumin 43 g/dL.
Coagulation & cultures: INR 0.97, aPTT 32 seconds; blood cultures showed no bacterial growth.
objective.advanced_workup:
Non-contrast head CT: Bilateral hypodense areas within the cerebellar hemispheres with normal ventricles and cerebral hemispheres.
Brain MRI: Bilateral diffuse hyperintense lesions in the cerebellar hemispheres spreading across the vermis, diagnostic of acute post-infectious cerebellitis.
Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis: White blood cells 10 cells/muL (9 lymphocytes, 1 neutrophil), red blood cells 1 cell/muL, protein 0.88 g/dL, glucose 3.1 mmol/L (paired blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L). Bacterial CSF cultures were sterile; viral PCR and serology for herpes simplex virus, Japanese encephalitis virus, and Epstein-Barr virus in CSF were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute post-infectious cerebellitis complicating Dengue virus infection, confirmed by detection of serum Dengue virus IgM and IgG antibodies on day 6 of illness and Dengue IgG in CSF. Differential etiologies including hepatitis B, hepatitis C, herpes simplex virus, Japanese encephalitis, HIV, Epstein-Barr virus, and Salmonella typhi/paratyphi were excluded.
Treatment and outcome: Treated supportively with intravenous hydration, symptomatic paracetamol, gait retraining, physiotherapy, and speech therapy. Symptoms progressively resolved; at discharge two weeks post-onset, he was ambulating independently with markedly improved speech and normalized hematologic indices.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old man with HIV and a history of cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma presented with left eyelid droop and left-sided facial numbness five days after restarting antiretroviral therapy following a long hiatus. He was diagnosed with HIV 21 years prior and had a nadir CD4 cell count of 107. His CD4 cell count when he restarted his antiretroviral regimen was 159 cells/mm3, viral load 511,000 c/mL. He had been intermittently compliant with antiretroviral therapy in the past and since resumption of therapy. In 2005, he had a recurrence of Kaposi's sarcoma and received five cycles of paclitaxel with clinical remission by 2006. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable at the time and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was read as having no significant abnormalities. His symptoms initially were stable, but in the subsequent two months, they worsened, with hypoesthesia and paresthesia over all three branches of the trigeminal nerve on the left, severe headaches, ataxia, dysarthria, and dysphagia. He also began to experience fatigue, weight loss, and night sweats. A repeat MRI revealed enhancing leptomeningeal masses with associated mass effect involving the trigeminal nerve, middle cerebellar peduncle, pons, and upper spinal cord. Review of his prior MRI showed a suggestion of enhancement of the left trigeminal nerve intradurally. 
A lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein (205 g/dL), slightly depressed glucose (45 g/dL), with 106 leukocytes (32% lymphocytes, 26% monocytes, and 42% unclassified cells), and no erythrocytes. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) cytology was notable for atypical appearing cells, which were suspicious for, but not sufficient for a primary diagnosis of malignancy (see Figure 2(a)). CSF flow cytometry demonstrated no clonal B- or T-cell populations, and IGH gene rearrangement was not detected by PCR. CSF PCR for EBV was negative.
A bone marrow biopsy was unremarkable and core needle biopsy of a modestly enlarged retroperitoneal lymph node showed no evidence of lymphoproliferative disease. There was no evidence of pleural, peritoneal, or pericardial effusions on computed tomography and ultrasound studies. A positron emission tomography with computed tomography (PET/CT) was then performed and demonstrated increased uptake at the known cerebellopontine lesion, as well as in the posterior inferior wall and papillary muscle of the left ventricle of the heart (Figure 1). An endomyocardial biopsy of the left ventricle was performed via left heart catheterization. Pathology revealed large atypical discohesive cells infiltrating the myocardium. Immunostains of the atypical lymphoid cells were strongly KSHV+ (Figure 2), MUM1/IRF4+, CD79a rare+, CD20-. In situ hybridization for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) using a probe for EBER showed no staining. Comparison with the CSF specimens showed that these atypical cells were morphologically similar to the suspicious cells in the CSF (Figure 2(a)).
A preliminary diagnosis of large B-cell lymphoma was made based on morphologic appearance, and the patient was initiated on treatment with R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) along with intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine, and hydrocortisone for the leptomeningeal disease. He was observed on telemetry for one week without cardiac ectopy and was discharged home. One day following discharge, he had syncope and was found to be in ventricular tachycardia with preserved blood pressure, for which he was treated with lidocaine and amiodarone with successful conversion to sinus rhythm. CD20 staining on his pathology returned negative and so treatment with cycle 2 was changed to EPOCH (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin) without rituximab. High-dose systemic methotrexate was included to treat the CNS disease. Six weeks into treatment, restaging PET CT imaging showed no persistent FDG-avid disease of the heart, and MRI showing significant resolution of his intracranial tumor. Spinal fluid examination demonstrated no persistent circulating disease in the CSF. Clinically, his headaches, dysarthria, and dysphagia improved, but he still had numbness of his left face along the V1 and V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve along with an upper motor facial nerve palsy on the left. Some residual gait ataxia was notable on examination.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presenting with left eyelid ptosis and left facial numbness five days after restarting combination antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient resumed combination antiretroviral therapy after a prolonged hiatus; five days later, he noted left eyelid droop and ipsilateral facial numbness. Over the subsequent two months, symptoms progressed with severe headaches, ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and hypoesthesia/paresthesia across all three divisions of the left trigeminal nerve, prompting extensive neuro-oncologic investigation.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic retroviral infection diagnosed 21 years prior with intermittent compliance (nadir CD4 107 cells/mcL; resumption CD4 159 cells/mm3, viral load 511,000 copies/mL). History of cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma in 2005, treated with five cycles of paclitaxel with complete clinical remission by 2006.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left-sided facial numbness, ptosis, headaches, dysarthria, dysphagia, gait ataxia, fatigue, night sweats, and weight loss; negative for focal limb weakness or bowel/bladder incontinence. Home medications: combination antiretroviral therapy. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Neurologic examination: left eyelid ptosis, sensory deficit (hypoesthesia and paresthesia) across V1, V2, and V3 branches of the left trigeminal nerve, left upper motor facial nerve paresis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and gait ataxia. Remainder of physical examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Lumbar puncture CSF analysis: leukocytes 106/mcL (32% lymphocytes, 26% monocytes, 42% unclassified atypical cells), protein elevated at 205 g/dL (as documented in text), glucose depressed at 45 g/dL, erythrocytes: 0. CSF PCR for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): negative. CSF flow cytometry: no clonal B- or T-cell population; IGH gene rearrangement by PCR: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: enhancing leptomeningeal masses with mass effect involving the left trigeminal nerve, middle cerebellar peduncle, pons, and upper spinal cord (retrospective review showed subtle enhancement of left trigeminal nerve intradurally). Bone marrow biopsy: unremarkable. Retroperitoneal lymph node core biopsy: no lymphoproliferative disease. Chest/abdominal/pelvic CT and ultrasound: no pleural, peritoneal, or pericardial effusions. 18F-FDG PET/CT: increased uptake at the left cerebellopontine angle lesion and hypermetabolic foci in the posterior inferior wall and papillary muscle of the left cardiac ventricle. Left ventricular endomyocardial biopsy: large atypical discohesive lymphoid cells infiltrating the myocardium, strongly positive for KSHV/HHV-8, MUM1/IRF4, and rare CD79a, negative for CD20 and EBER in situ hybridization.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Extracavitary solid-variant Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus (KSHV/HHV-8)-associated large B-cell lymphoma / primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) with myocardial infiltration and leptomeningeal involvement in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Confirmed by endomyocardial biopsy showing atypical discohesive large lymphoid cells strongly positive for KSHV and MUM1/IRF4 (CD20-negative, EBER-negative), morphologically matching atypical cells in CSF cytology. EBV-driven lymphoma ruled out by negative EBER and negative CSF EBV PCR. Management & Outcome: Initially treated empirically with R-CHOP plus intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine, and hydrocortisone; after CD20 returned negative, switched to EPOCH without rituximab, augmented with high-dose intravenous methotrexate for CNS penetration. Post-discharge ventricular tachycardia was successfully converted with lidocaine and amiodarone. At 6 weeks, restaging PET/CT demonstrated complete cardiac metabolic response, brain MRI showed marked intracranial tumor regression, and CSF cytology cleared, with substantial clinical improvement in headaches, dysarthria, and dysphagia.

raw_case_text: Patient B: The patient, a 27-year-old man, was just diagnosed with HIV/AIDS (3 months ago) after being tested for HIV serostatus following notification that his wife had tested positive for the virus at a nearby clinic. He has no complaints about anything else. All of the physical evidences were unremarkable. Except for the CD4 count, which was determined to be 77cells/mm3, all baseline examinations, including tuberculosis investigations using a sputum gene expert, were non-revealing, and he subsequently tested for TB LAM, which yielded a positive result. He was subsequently started on anti-TB as recommended, and after a month, he was started on HAART withTenofovir+Lamivudine+Dolutegravir (TLD). He is using his medications without any problems so far, and the viral load will be sent on his six month of HAART initiation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male presenting for evaluation following partner notification of retroviral seropositivity.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented as an asymptomatic contact following spousal notification of seropositivity three months earlier. He reported no active constitutional, respiratory, gastrointestinal, or neurological symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposure: Heterosexual contact with a partner with confirmed retroviral infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Completely asymptomatic; denies fevers, night sweats, cough, weight loss, or gastrointestinal disturbances.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination was completely unremarkable; vital signs, nutritional status, and systemic evaluations were within normal limits.
objective.routine_investigations: Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF: Negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Urine submitted for lipoarabinomannan (TB LAM) lateral flow testing.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Subclinical disseminated tuberculosis in a patient with profound human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) immunodeficiency (CD4+ T-cell count 77 cells/mm3). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive urine TB LAM test despite negative sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF in an asymptomatic HIV-seropositive individual. Plan & Outcome: Initiated on first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy according to guidelines. One month into anti-TB treatment, commenced combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART) with tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir (TLD). Patient tolerated the regimen uneventfully without adverse events, with viral load monitoring scheduled at 6 months post-ART initiation.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 60 year old European homosexual man who had HIV infection diagnosed in 1985. Zidovudine monotherapy was commenced in 1988 and three-drug combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) in 1996. His ART between 2001 and 2013 consisted of lopinavir/ritonavir, lamivudine and nevirapine. He had a prompt sustained response to ART and from 1997-2013 consistently had an undetectable HIV viral load. Despite this, his CD4 count, which had a nadir of 39 in 1996, never rose above 140 despite consistent adherence to his ART (Fig 1A).
In April 1996 he developed drenching sweats and hepato-splenomegaly, and in March 1997 the diagnosis of VL was confirmed by the visualization of amastigotes in bone marrow samples. Infection with Leishmania infantum had probably been acquired during a visit to Spain in 1992. Initial treatment with sodium stibogluconate 20 mg/kg for 44 days over 8 weeks achieved a clinical improvement and clearance of parasites from his bone marrow.
Visceral leishmaniasis relapsed in July 1997 and persisted for the next 15 years, despite combination treatment with: paromomycin 15 mg/kg and stibogluconate; stibogluconate, liposomal amphotericin 3mg/kg and gamma interferon 2 megaunits subcutaneously; and since 2000 with 7 days liposomal amphotericin 3 mg/kg daily every 6 weeks, increasing to every 3 weeks in May 2012. Miltefosine 50 mg twice daily, for 28 days every 3 months, was added in March 2005.
 Leishmania amastigotes were visualized in bone marrow samples collected in September 2004, March, May, and December 2005, November 2006, October 2007, and February 2011; and also in skin lesions biopsied in November 2003, September 2007, and May 2009; lymph nodes biopsied in May 2009 and September 2011; and a sigmoid biopsy in March 2000. An isolate of Leishmania infantum cultured from a bone marrow aspirate in October 2007 was tested at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine in January 2008 and reported to be resistant to stibogluconate (IC50 > 60 mg/L) but susceptible to amphotericin B (IC50 = 0.3 muM), miltefosine (IC50 = 8 muM) and paromomycin (IC50 = 4 muM).
Treatment of VL was complicated by significant adverse drug effects including: marked visual impairment presumed secondary to antimonial toxicity; hearing loss presumed secondary to various agents including paromomycin; and multiple episodes of bacteremia arising from the indwelling cannula used for his IV infusions of liposomal amphotericin B. The patient suffered increasing discomfort from his splenomegaly and had an increasing requirement for red cell transfusions. In view of his worsening symptoms and pancytopenia, and the consistent increase in the density of amastigotes in his bone marrow samples despite maximal conventional treatment, alternative therapeutic approaches were discussed at length with the patient and with experts elsewhere.
With written informed consent from the patient, and agreement from the Hospital Medicines Committee, he received six doses of intravenous liposomal daunorubicin: 34mg on 24 October 2012, 50mg on 7 November, 50 mg on 21 November, 40mg on 7 January 2013, 50mg on 21 January, and 50mg on 4 February. Daunorubicin was chosen instead of doxorubicin because of personal and institutional experience in the use of this agent for the treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma in patients with HIV infection. The treatment regimen was based on that recommended for the treatment of Kaposi's sarcoma in patients with HIV infection and mild renal impairment. The patient was carefully monitored for evidence of cardiotoxicity, and other potential adverse effects of daunorubicin therapy. Each treatment resulted in a temporary worsening of his pancytopenia but there were no significant infectious, bleeding or other adverse effects (Fig 1B). There was no decrease in his splenomegaly either on clinical examination or on abdominal imaging (Fig 2). The density of amastigotes in the bone marrow trephine collected 7 days after the last dose of daunorubicin was greater than that in the most recent previous trephine which had been collected in February 2011 (Fig 3). Urine samples collected on May 8 2013, 3 months after the last dose of daunorubicin, showed 3+ agglutination using the KAtex Leishmania urinary antigen detection test. In September 2013, 7 months after the completion of the trial of daunorubicin, the patient was in an unchanged clinical condition compared to the immediate pre-treatment period, with persistent abdominal pain due to severe hepato-splenomegaly, pancytopenia and disabling lethargy. The patient decided to cease all treatment of his HIV infection, VL, and other medical conditions. He died of complications of VL within one month of stopping treatment.
The patient provided written informed consent for all procedures (skin biopsy, bone marrow biopsy, and sigmoidoscopy and biopsy) and written informed consent for the trial of liposomal daunorubicin. The Hospital Medicines Committee approved the trial of liposomal daunorubicin.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male with HIV infection presented with drenching sweats, massive splenomegaly, and pancytopenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 60-year-old HIV-infected male presented in April 1996 with drenching night sweats and hepatosplenomegaly. Parasitic visceral infection was diagnosed in March 1997. Despite initial antimonial response, the illness relapsed in July 1997 and persisted for 15 years as refractory disease despite multidrug antileishmanial regimens. He developed progressive splenomegaly causing severe abdominal pain, worsening pancytopenia requiring frequent red cell transfusions, and adverse drug toxicities. In October 2012 to February 2013, he consented to an experimental trial of intravenous liposomal daunorubicin. In September 2013, facing persistent severe hepato-splenomegaly, transfusion-dependent pancytopenia, and disabling lethargy, he elected to withdraw all therapy and entered palliative care.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 1985; treated with zidovudine monotherapy (1988), combination ART (1996), and lopinavir/ritonavir, lamivudine, nevirapine (2001-2013). Travel history: travel to Spain in 1992. Chronic medical complications: mild renal impairment, marked visual impairment attributed to antimonial toxicity, hearing loss secondary to paromomycin, and recurrent central line-associated bacteremias.
subjective.review_of_systems: Drenching sweats, severe abdominal discomfort and fullness from splenomegaly, profound fatigue and disabling lethargy, visual impairment, hearing loss. Denied fever during late stages.

objective.physical_examination: Severe, massive hepatosplenomegaly causing abdominal distension and palpable splenic enlargement filling the left abdomen. Indwelling central venous catheter in situ. Conjunctival pallor.
objective.routine_investigations: Progressive pancytopenia requiring repeated packed red blood cell transfusions. HIV-1 RNA viral load consistently undetectable (< 50 copies/mL) from 1997 to 2013. CD4+ T-cell count had a nadir of 39 cells/muL in 1996 and remained persistently < 140 cells/muL despite adherence to ART. Mild renal impairment. Urine KAtex urinary antigen test: 3+ agglutination (May 2013).
objective.advanced_workup: Serial bone marrow trephine biopsies (1997, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2011, and post-daunorubicin 2013) demonstrated heavy and increasing infiltration of macrophages with intracellular microorganisms. Histopathology of skin biopsies (2003, 2007, 2009), lymph node biopsies (2009, 2011), and sigmoid colon biopsy (2000) revealed disseminated intracellular organisms. Abdominal imaging (CT) confirmed persistent massive splenomegaly without regression. Serial electrocardiograms and cardiac monitoring revealed no daunorubicin cardiotoxicity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Refractory, multidrug-resistant visceral leishmaniasis with multiorgan dissemination (skin, lymph nodes, and sigmoid colon) in a patient with HIV-1 infection and severe immunological non-response.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct visualization of Leishmania amastigotes in serial bone marrow aspirates/trephines, skin lesions, lymph nodes, and sigmoid mucosa. Culture from bone marrow (October 2007) yielded Leishmania infantum; in vitro susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to sodium stibogluconate (IC50 > 60 mg/L), but susceptibility to amphotericin B (IC50 = 0.3 muM), miltefosine (IC50 = 8 muM), and paromomycin (IC50 = 4 muM). Positive urine KAtex antigen detection test (3+ agglutination).
Differentials Ruled Out: Kaposi's sarcoma (biopsies negative for spindle cell proliferation / HHV8), lymphoma, mycobacteriosis, and opportunistic fungal infections.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Multiple combination antileishmanial regimens over 15 years: sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg), paromomycin (15 mg/kg), liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg daily, transitioned to maintenance every 6 then 3 weeks), subcutaneous interferon-gamma (2 MU), and oral miltefosine (50 mg BID). In October 2012-February 2013, administered 6 cycles of liposomal daunorubicin (34-50 mg IV per dose) with transient bone marrow suppression but no reduction in parasite density or spleen size. In September 2013, the patient ceased all medical therapy and died of visceral leishmaniasis complications within one month.

raw_case_text:
We report a case of a 48-year-old Caucasian male patient with a past medical history of type II diabetes mellitus, obesity, dyslipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and hypertension. He was initially referred to our multidisciplinary clinic for chronic lower back pain. The clinical evaluation revealed a 3-year history of chest pain caused by multiple recurrent pericarditis of unknown origin.
The patient underwent multiple para-clinical evaluations for his pericarditis, with no determined etiology. The initial transthoracic ultrasound showed a reduced ejection fraction at 33% with moderate hypokinesis of the left ventricle and left ventricular asynchrony. Subsequently, ventriculography was performed, which showed severe hypokinesis of the left ventricle, with an associated ejection fraction of 26% and no signs of mitral insufficiency. A normal coronary angiogram excluded coronary heart disease as the culprit of heart failure. Rheumatological evaluations and a search for auto-immune diseases were performed, which did not reveal any underlying disorders. With regard to lombalgia investigations, neuraxial and sacroiliac joint MRI showed evidence of facet arthritis at the levels of L3-L4, L4-L5, and L5-S1, but no signs of canal stenosis, bone lesions, or indications of ankylosing spondylitis were observed.
Our multidisciplinary pain clinic evaluated the patient for his persistent low back pain. Initially, there was no indication for spinal surgical intervention. Instead, medical treatment with interventional spine procedures was offered. Over a period of 4 years and 7 months, hydromorphone was titrated up to a maximal equivalent dose of morphine of 428 mg. Gabapentin was initiated, which was then discontinued due to the absence of a therapeutic response. Pregabalin was also tried, but the patient reported dizziness and drowsiness. Regarding co-analgesia, he was prescribed maximal doses of acetaminophen and duloxetine at 90 mg/day. With regard to his chest pain, the medical treatment for pericarditis was optimized, which improved his left ventricle ejection fraction from 26% to 40%. However, no significant reduction of his severe chest pain ensued, rated as 10/10 on the visual analog scale (VAS) despite maximal medical therapy including scheduled narcotic intake. At this point, a stellate ganglion block (SGB) was performed by an interventional pain physician, granting temporary pain relief as measured by a VAS score of 5/10, without changes in the medical management.
After a comprehensive evaluation of the patient, he was determined as an ideal candidate for SCS to address his chronic lower back pain. Due to his history of refractory pericarditis and chronic chest pain, the pain physician and neurosurgeon jointly decided to offer him the option of placing the stimulator at the cervicothoracic junction instead of the lower thoracic level. The decision aimed to target and potentially alleviate his chest pain and lower back pain. The risks of the operation and the likelihood of trial failure were thoroughly discussed. In the event of failure of the initial procedure, the possibility of a second surgical intervention to reposition the epidural paddle to the low thoracic spine was also addressed. These discussions took place separately at the pain clinic and the neurosurgeon's office. The patient was subsequently evaluated during a multidisciplinary round, and after considering all information, he provided consent for the procedure.
A 14-day trial period of SCS was conducted using an eight-contact Lamitrode  paddle with bipolar stimulation, provided by Abbott and inserted through an interlaminar approach (Figure 1). The configuration was optimized after multiple trials of changing the contact levels performed mainly on days 0 and 1. The programming utilized the burst mode, with 500 ms of pulse width, 50 Hz of frequency, and 0.8-1 mA of stimulation with cycling (Abbott ). During the trial, the patient reported a 60% reduction in chest pain and an 80% reduction in back pain. There was also an improvement in his sleeping pattern, with uninterrupted 5 h of sleep per night compared with his previous pattern of 1-2 h, and a reduction of equivalent dose of morphine by 164 mg, from 428 to 264 mg of daily morphine equivalent dose. Sham stimulation was conducted between days 5 and 7 of the trial period. Following the patient's evaluation, a reprogramming session was conducted, maintaining the same stimulation frequency and pulse width but setting the intensity to 0. On day 8, a clinical reassessment was performed to determine success, which is determined by the recurrence of pain or the indication of ineffectiveness compared with the initial 5-day period. This strategy has been used since the inception of our neuromodulation program and has been documented in the literature.
Following a successful trial period and sham stimulation test, the spinal cord stimulator was internalized using a Proclaim internal pulse generator provided by Abbott  while maintaining the burst programming parameters. The initial follow-up was virtually conducted after 2 months, where the patient tested positive for COVID-19 and was hospitalized.
At 6 months post-SCS implantation, a transthoracic cardiac ultrasound performed on the patient showed an increase in ejection fraction to 45% despite having no changes in his previous medical treatment, and he became narcotic-free.
During the 8- and 12-month follow-ups, the patient reported consistent pain control without needing any narcotic intake. In addition, the pain relief allowed him to initiate an exercise program for weight loss.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old male presenting with chronic lower back pain and a 3-year history of refractory chest pain secondary to recurrent pericarditis of undetermined etiology.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 48-year-old male presented with chronic severe lower back pain and a 3-year history of severe refractory chest pain (rated 10/10 on the visual analog scale) secondary to recurrent idiopathic pericarditis. Despite medical management with high-dose opioids (hydromorphone titrated to a daily morphine equivalent dose of 428 mg), duloxetine (90 mg/day), acetaminophen, gabapentin, and pregabalin, as well as a temporary response to a stellate ganglion block, pain persisted. He subsequently underwent evaluation and implantation of a cervicothoracic spinal cord stimulator (SCS).
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, obesity, dyslipidemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypertension, and recurrent idiopathic pericarditis with secondary cardiomyopathy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe chest pain, chronic low back pain, sleep disturbance (averaging 1–2 hours of uninterrupted sleep per night), and medication-related dizziness and drowsiness with pregabalin. Other systems not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Baseline physical examination not detailed; visual analog scale (VAS) score for chest pain: 10/10 prior to intervention, improving to 5/10 following stellate ganglion block, and achieving 60% chest pain reduction and 80% back pain reduction following SCS trial.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial transthoracic echocardiogram: left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 33% with moderate LV hypokinesis and LV asynchrony; repeat echocardiogram following optimized pericarditis medical therapy showed LVEF improvement to 40%; 6-month follow-up echocardiogram showed LVEF 45%. Autoimmune and rheumatological screening panels: negative for underlying connective tissue disorders.
objective.advanced_workup: Left ventriculography: severe left ventricular hypokinesis with an ejection fraction of 26% and absence of mitral regurgitation. Coronary angiography: normal coronary arteries without obstructive coronary artery disease. Neuraxial and sacroiliac joint MRI: facet arthritis at L3-L4, L4-L5, and L5-S1 without spinal canal stenosis, osseous lesions, or evidence of ankylosing spondylitis.
