raw_case_text: A 4-year-old female child from Vizianagaram district, Andhra Pradesh, having fever for 5 days was tested positive for PF on smear examination. She was started on IV artesunate as monotherapy. She developed ascites, icterus, severe anemia, and hemoglobinuria requiring multiple blood transfusion. She was referred after 7 days of IV artesunate as she had persistent fever. At admission, her blood smear showed multiple PF. She was started on quinine and clindamycin, along with primaquine. Serial smears were obtained and parasitological clearance was documented after 4 days of therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-old female presenting with fever for five days, dark urine, jaundice, and abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child had a 5-day history of fever when she was diagnosed with malaria at an outside hospital and initiated on intravenous artesunate monotherapy. Over the course of seven days of therapy, she developed persistent fever, progressive jaundice, abdominal distension, severe anemia, and dark hemoglobinuria requiring multiple blood transfusions, prompting tertiary referral.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Vizianagaram district, Andhra Pradesh, India. Received 7 days of IV artesunate monotherapy and multiple blood transfusions prior to transfer.

objective.physical_examination: Persistent fever, mucosal pallor, jaundice, and clinically evident ascites on abdominal examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Severe anemia requiring multiple blood transfusions; presence of hemoglobinuria.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Artesunate-resistant Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by blackwater fever (severe intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria), ascites, and severe anemia. Initial and referral peripheral blood smears confirmed persistent P. falciparum parasitemia despite 7 days of IV artesunate.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on rescue therapy with parenteral quinine and clindamycin along with primaquine, alongside blood transfusions and supportive care. Serial blood smears documented complete parasitological clearance after 4 days of therapy.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 38-year-old HIV + male, well controlled (CD4 count of 213 cells/mm3 with an undetectable viral load) on dolutegravir and emtricitabine-tenofovir, without any prior ocular problems. He presented with a nonulcerative papulonodular hypopigmented rash with lesions scattered along the bilateral upper and lower extremities, trunk, and abdomen [Figure 1]. H and E staining of the cutaneous biopsy showed Leishmaniasis chassis and infantum. Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly were also noted. The patient immigrated to the US from Nicaragua at the age of 20 and he has remained in the US since his arrival. The patient was treated with intravenous amphotericin B liposome (7 of 9 doses) and then lost to follow-up. He presented a year later with the same papulonodular rash consistent with cutaneous leishmaniasis. He was retreated with amphotericin (14-dose course) and miltefosine for a 28-day course. Two days after stopping miltefosine, he developed progressive left eye redness, pain, and photophobia.
On day 7 of his symptoms, visual acuity declined to count fingers in the affected left eye. Biomicroscopy showed unilateral 3+ conjunctival and ciliary injections, corneal peripheral haze with focal areas of whitening without epithelial loss or ulceration, and 1+ anterior chamber cell [Figure 2]. No vitreoretinal involvement was noted; however, there was a shallow temporal choroidal effusion of the left eye. Anterior chamber paracentesis was performed for polymerase chain reaction (PCR) analysis for leishmaniasis. No corneal scrapings were performed since the epithelium was intact. Additional infectious workup included HZV aqueous PCR, serum RPR/FTA, QuantiFERON Gold, and serum VZV. All tests were found to be noncontributory. HIV monitoring laboratories revealed a rise in the HIV viral load to 10,500 copies/mL and a decline in CD4 count to 213 cells/mm3. No changes in medications or compliance were noted at that time.
Cautious initiation of topical steroid (prednisolone acetate 1%) every 2 h and cycloplegic (cyclopentolate 1%) three times per day was done under close monitoring and with the plan to change to topical amphotericin if any worsening occurred. The patient responded rapidly to the application of topical steroids with complete clearing of corneal infiltration and resolution of anterior uveitis [Figure 3]. The visual acuity returned to 20/20 by the Snellen chart. Ocular quiescence has remained off steroids for 2 years even though concurrent cutaneous and visceral disease did recur.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old HIV-positive male presented with progressive redness, pain, and photophobia in the left eye of 7 days duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, with a history of treated cutaneous and visceral lesions, presented with acute progressive left eye redness, pain, and photophobia that developed 2 days after completing a 28-day course of miltefosine and a 14-dose course of amphotericin B for recurrent papulonodular skin lesions. Over 7 days, visual acuity in the left eye deteriorated markedly to counting fingers.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection on dolutegravir and emtricitabine-tenofovir. Prior cutaneous and visceral disease treated initially with 7 doses of liposomal amphotericin B, and retreated 1 year later with a 14-dose course of amphotericin and 28 days of miltefosine. Denied prior ocular disease. Epidemiological history: immigrated to the United States from Nicaragua at age 20 and resided in the US continuously thereafter.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports left eye redness, ocular pain, and photophobia; denies other acute systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: nonulcerative papulonodular hypopigmented rash distributed across bilateral upper and lower extremities, trunk, and abdomen. Abdomen: splenomegaly noted. Ophthalmic examination (left eye): visual acuity reduced to counting fingers; biomicroscopy showed 3+ conjunctival and ciliary injection, peripheral corneal haze with focal areas of whitening without epithelial loss or ulceration, and 1+ anterior chamber cells; shallow temporal choroidal effusion on fundus exam; no vitreoretinal involvement.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed thrombocytopenia. HIV viral load: 10,500 copies/mL; CD4 count: 213 cells/mm^3. Infectious serologies and tests: serum RPR/FTA non-reactive; QuantiFERON-TB Gold negative; serum VZV antibodies noncontributory.
objective.advanced_workup: Cutaneous biopsy: hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed dermal histiocytic infiltration with intracellular organisms. Anterior chamber paracentesis: performed for diagnostic PCR analysis; herpes zoster virus (HZV) aqueous PCR was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Cutaneous biopsy H&E staining demonstrated Leishmania infantum amastigotes, confirming cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis with secondary ocular anterior uveitis/interstitial keratitis. Anterior chamber paracentesis performed for Leishmania PCR. Alternative etiologies (herpes zoster, syphilis, tuberculosis) ruled out by negative HZV aqueous PCR, serum RPR/FTA, and QuantiFERON Gold. Management and Outcome: Initiated on topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 2 hours and cyclopentolate 1% three times daily under close monitoring (with backup plan for topical amphotericin B). Rapid resolution of corneal infiltration and anterior uveitis was achieved, with visual acuity restoring to 20/20 on Snellen chart. Ocular quiescence was maintained off topical steroids for 2 years, despite subsequent recurrence of systemic cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis.

raw_case_text:
A 16-year-old female was admitted to Kyungpook National University Children's Hospital with complaints of diarrhea, hematochezia, and weight loss for a year. She had been diagnosed with latent TB 1 month before her visit, and a latent TB treatment regimen with isoniazid (INH) for 9 months had been started. She had completed Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccination. Family history revealed that her father had a history of pulmonary TB, which was treated 3 years ago.
On admission, vital signs were within normal range. On physical examination, a perianal fistula with the discharge was observed in the perianal area. Initial laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 5,130/muL, a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dl, a platelet count of 462,000/muL, an albumin level of 3.5 g/dl, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 99 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein (CRP) of 3.51 mg/dl. The fecal immunochemical test was positive and fecal calprotectin was 589.9 mg/kg. No pathogens were detected in stool culture and stool polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Chest x-ray showed no abnormal findings in the lungs. However, the interferon-gamma release assay was positive. Ileocolonoscopy showed multifocal ulcers throughout the terminal ileum and colon (Figures 1A,B). Histology revealed cryptitis, crypt abscesses, and noncaseating granulomas; however, the acid-fast bacillus smear, culture, and PCR for TB were negative. Magnetic resonance enterography showed multifocal wall thickening in the colon, ileum, and jejunum and two intersphincteric perianal fistulas (Figures 1C,D). Upper GI endoscopy was unremarkable. The patient was diagnosed with CD with a phenotype of A1b, L3+L4b, B1p, G0 according to the Paris classification. Her pediatric CD activity index (PCDAI) score was 50 and the Simple Endoscopic Score for CD (SES-CD) was 26.
Treatment was begun with exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN), mesalazine, and azathioprine, which were effective. Two weeks after the diagnosis, she underwent seton placement. However, 1 month after finishing her 8-week treatment with EEN, her disease relapsed. Azathioprine was changed to methotrexate (MTX). However, symptoms did not improve, and infliximab (IFX) was started 1 month later, considering that she had taken sufficient latent TB treatment with INH for 5 months. The patient chose to take IFX as her biologic agent between IFX and adalimumab, which are the only biologic agents currently approved for the treatment of moderate-to-severe CD. Chest x-ray before starting IFX showed no abnormal findings in the lungs. After starting IFX, INH therapy for latent TB treatment was extended for a total of 12 months.
Ileocolonoscopy at 1-year follow-up after IFX treatment revealed endoscopic healing. PCR for TB was negative again from specimens of the ileum and cecum. However, ESR and CRP gradually increased 1 month after the ileocolonoscopy, and she developed diarrhea. IFX trough level was 2.4 mug/mL, and IFX antibody was negative. Considering the suboptimal trough level and negative anti-drug antibody status of the patient, secondary loss of response due to nonimmunogenic pharmacokinetic failure was suspected. Therefore, the IFX interval was shortened from every 8 weeks to every 4 weeks.
However, 1 month later, she newly developed symptoms of fever, cough, and sputum. Chest x-ray and chest computed tomography (CT) showed multiple small nodules in both lungs indicating miliary TB (Figure 2A). Bronchoscopy was conducted, and TB was confirmed by a positive TB PCR test of the tracheal biopsy specimen and bronchial washing fluid. IFX treatment was discontinued and the standard TB treatment regimen with INH, ethambutol, rifampin, and pyrazinamide for 2 months followed by INH, ethambutol, and rifampin for 4 months was started. MTX and mesalazine were maintained to treat CD. Miliary TB was completely cured after 6 months of TB treatment (Figure 2B).
Three months later, an abdominal CT was performed to evaluate her CD after failed ileocolonoscopy due to poor bowel preparation. No active CD involvement was observed in the bowel, whereas a newly developed left psoas muscle abscess and spinal bony destruction were incidentally identified (Figure 3). Surprisingly, the patient did not have any back pain. Spinal MRI was conducted to confirm the diagnosis of TB spondylitis (Figure 4A). Ultrasound-guided aspiration for the paraspinal abscess was conducted, and TB PCR was positive. Abscess culture grew M. tuberculosis later. Bacterial and fungus culture grew no isolates. Follow-up chest CT revealed no aggravation of miliary TB. Thus, she was diagnosed with TB spondylitis.
She discontinued all medications for CD treatment and maintained TB treatment for a total of 12 months because extrapulmonary TB had developed within 3 months after the end of her miliary TB treatment. TB treatment regimen included INH, ethambutol, rifampin, and pyrazinamide for a total of 12 months. Spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at 1-year follow-up after TB treatment revealed that her spinal lesions were cured (Figure 4B).
MTX and mesalazine were restarted thereafter. However, symptoms of diarrhea and abdominal pain developed 2 months later. Her PCDAI score was 35 and the exacerbation of CD was confirmed by ileocolonoscopy. Again, acid-fast bacillus smear, culture, and PCR for TB were all negative. Due to the fear of another severe active TB with IFX treatment, vedolizumab (VDZ) was initiated instead. The patient is currently on VDZ for over a year and is maintaining clinical and biochemical remission. No serious adverse events, including TB reactivation, have occurred. Spinal MRI conducted 1 year after VDZ initiation showed no reactivation of her TB spondylitis (Figure 4C).
This case report was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Kyungpook National University Chilgok Hospital (No. 2020-09-018). All procedures performed in studies involving human participants were in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and national research committees and the Helsinki Declaration (as revised in 2013). Written informed consent was obtained from the patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old female presented with chronic diarrhea, hematochezia, and weight loss of one year's duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 16-year-old female presented with a 1-year history of diarrhea, hematochezia, and progressive weight loss. One month prior, she was diagnosed with latent tuberculosis and started on isoniazid (INH). Following comprehensive workup, Crohn's disease was diagnosed and treated with exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN), mesalazine, azathioprine, and seton placement for perianal fistula. One month after stopping EEN, she relapsed. Azathioprine was transitioned to methotrexate without response. Infliximab (IFX) was started after 5 months of INH therapy (with INH extended to 12 months). After 1 year of IFX, endoscopic mucosal healing was observed. One month later, inflammatory markers rose and diarrhea recurred; IFX was intensified to every 4 weeks. One month after dose escalation, she developed fever, cough, and sputum. Three months after completing 6 months of antituberculous therapy, surveillance imaging revealed a paraspinal abscess without back pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Latent tuberculosis treated with isoniazid for 12 months; completed BCG vaccination. Family history: father had pulmonary tuberculosis successfully treated 3 years prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports diarrhea, hematochezia, weight loss, fever, cough, sputum, and perianal discharge; denies back pain. Home medications: mesalazine, azathioprine/methotrexate, infliximab, isoniazid. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs within normal limits on admission. Perianal inspection: perianal fistula with active discharge. Neurological: no spinal tenderness or motor deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 5,130/muL; Hemoglobin: 11.6 g/dL; Platelets: 462,000/muL; Albumin: 3.5 g/dL; ESR: 99 mm/h; CRP: 3.51 mg/dL; Fecal immunochemical test: positive; Fecal calprotectin: 589.9 mg/kg; Stool culture and stool PCR: negative for enteric pathogens; Chest X-ray (initial and pre-biologic): normal; IGRA: positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial ileocolonoscopy: multifocal ulcerations throughout terminal ileum and colon (SES-CD 26, PCDAI 50); mucosal biopsy histology: cryptitis, crypt abscesses, and noncaseating granulomas, with negative AFB smear, culture, and TB PCR. MR enterography: multifocal wall thickening in colon, ileum, jejunum and two intersphincteric perianal fistulas. Upper GI endoscopy: normal. Chest CT (at miliary relapse): multiple small nodules in both lungs indicating miliary pattern. Abdominal CT: left psoas muscle abscess and spinal bony destruction without active bowel inflammation. Spinal MRI: destructive lesions in lumbar spine; follow-up MRI at 1 year showed healed spinal lesions. Ultrasound-guided paraspinal abscess aspiration: bacterial and fungal cultures sterile.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Crohn's disease complicated by infliximab-induced reactivation miliary pulmonary tuberculosis and subsequent extrapulmonary tuberculosis (tuberculous spondylitis with left psoas abscess).
Confirmation: Miliary pulmonary TB confirmed by positive TB PCR of tracheal biopsy and bronchial washing fluid; paraspinal abscess confirmed by positive TB PCR and culture growing Mycobacterium tuberculosis; bacterial and fungal cultures were negative.
Differentials ruled out: Intestinal tuberculosis (colonic biopsy AFB smear, culture, and TB PCR all negative); pyogenic psoas abscess (routine bacterial/fungal cultures negative).
Treatment & Outcome: Infliximab discontinued; standard 4-drug anti-TB therapy (INH, ethambutol, rifampin, pyrazinamide) given for 2 months followed by INH, ethambutol, rifampin for 4 months, curing miliary TB. When psoas abscess and spondylitis appeared 3 months later, 4-drug ATT was restarted for 12 months, achieving complete spinal cure on follow-up MRI. Vedolizumab was subsequently initiated for Crohn's flare with sustained clinical/biochemical remission and no TB reactivation for >1 year.

raw_case_text: Patient B: The patient, a 27-year-old man, was just diagnosed with HIV/AIDS (3 months ago) after being tested for HIV serostatus following notification that his wife had tested positive for the virus at a nearby clinic. He has no complaints about anything else. All of the physical evidences were unremarkable. Except for the CD4 count, which was determined to be 77cells/mm3, all baseline examinations, including tuberculosis investigations using a sputum gene expert, were non-revealing, and he subsequently tested for TB LAM, which yielded a positive result. He was subsequently started on anti-TB as recommended, and after a month, he was started on HAART withTenofovir+Lamivudine+Dolutegravir (TLD). He is using his medications without any problems so far, and the viral load will be sent on his six month of HAART initiation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old asymptomatic male presented for routine evaluation following a diagnosis of HIV infection three months prior.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 27-year-old male was diagnosed with HIV/AIDS 3 months prior after undergoing contact tracing when his wife tested positive for HIV. He reported no complaints or physical symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 3 months prior (contact of HIV-positive spouse). Denies prior opportunistic infections, chronic medical illnesses, or known TB contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Completely asymptomatic; denies cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Home medications: none. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination was completely unremarkable; vitals normal; no lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, or rash.
objective.routine_investigations: CD4 count: 77 cells/mm^3; routine baseline laboratory investigations unremarkable; sputum GeneXpert: negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Subclinical disseminated tuberculosis in advanced HIV infection (CD4 77 cells/mm^3).
Confirmation: Urine lipoarabinomannan (TB LAM) test was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Differentials ruled out: Active pulmonary tuberculosis (sputum GeneXpert negative), cryptococcal disease.
Treatment & Outcome: Standard anti-tuberculosis therapy commenced. One month following ATT initiation, HAART was started with tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD). Patient tolerated therapy without adverse events, with viral load assessment planned at 6 months.

raw_case_text: A 39-year-old woman - a known case of HIV infection from 1 year ago - who was admitted to our hospital (Shahid Faghihi Hospital, Shiraz, Iran) with a 6-month history of skin lesions that initially was present on her face, later extending onto the chest, abdomen, and extremities. Our physical examination revealed varying size skin papules and nodules (Figure-1). Laboratory data showed the only leukopenia (WBC: 1700 cells / mm3) and a CD4 cell count of 280 cells / mm3. Skin lesion biopsy was performed, and histopathological studies showed a busy dermis with infiltration of many inflammatory cells, including histiocytes-macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells (Figure-2). High power field images revealed aggregates of macrophages filled with numerous leishman bodies (Figure-2). These findings confirmed the diagnosis of CL. Regarding patient's immune deficiency and the extent of skin lesions, the diagnosis of diffuse CL was made. She received liposomal amphotericin B with a total dose of 40 mg/kg as a case of diffuse CL. Her skin lesions showed significant improvement in follow-up visits after completion of treatment (particularly after six months).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old female presented with a 6-month history of progressive skin lesions spreading from the face to the trunk and extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed skin lesions initially appearing on her face 6 months prior to admission, which subsequently extended progressively onto the chest, abdomen, and all four extremities.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection diagnosed 1 year prior.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed variable-sized skin papules and nodules distributed over the face, chest, abdomen, and extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell (WBC) count: 1,700 cells/mm^3 (leukopenia); CD4+ T-cell count: 280 cells/mm^3.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin lesion biopsy with histopathological examination showed a busy dermis infiltrated with numerous inflammatory cells, including histiocytes-macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) complicating HIV infection: high-power field histopathology of the skin biopsy revealed aggregates of macrophages densely filled with numerous Leishman bodies (amastigotes). Given the patient's underlying immunosuppression and widespread lesion dissemination, a diagnosis of diffuse CL was established. She was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B at a cumulative total dose of 40 mg/kg. Follow-up evaluations following treatment completion demonstrated significant clinical regression and healing of skin lesions, particularly evident at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old female presented with complaints of generalized abdominal distension, weight loss, swelling of legs, and muscle weakness extant for several weeks. Her past medical history was significant for a well-controlled HIV infection of 6 years on highly active anti-retroviral therapy, hypertension, ESRD secondary to HIV-associated nephropathy, and secondary hyperparathyroidism. She was a non-smoker and had no history of alcohol or drug abuse. Her initial renal biopsy revealed collapsing focal glomerular sclerosis, microcystic dilation of renal tubules, lymphocytic interstitial infiltrates, and interstitial fibrosis. She received chronic cycler-assisted peritoneal dialysis (PD) for 5 years and was well controlled clinically regarding uremic and volume status with no abnormalities regarding color, viscosity, or volume of exchanges. Subsequently, she was transitioned to intermittent hemodialysis (HD) due to personal preferences. A few weeks after the transition to intermittent HD, ascites of unclear etiology developed, ultimately requiring repeated large-volume paracentesis with ~ 5 - 7 L ascitic fluid removals every other week. 
There were no associated symptoms of coughing, palpitations, or shortness of breath. She was chronically anuric. Vital signs showed blood pressure of 160/80 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats/min (regular), respiratory rate 16/min and temperature 36.9  C. Oxygen saturation was 98% on ambient room air. Her physical examination was remarkable for moderate ascites and edema of the lower extremities. Otherwise neurological, respiratory, and cardiovascular examinations were normal without organomegaly and without clinical stigmata or symptoms of chronic liver disease or heart failure. 
Laboratory investigations showed normocytic, normochromic anemia with a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL and uncorrected serum calcium of 8.6 mg/dL. Other labs were as follows: CD4 T-cell count: 600/mm3, HIV viral load: 986 copies/mL (reference: < 40 copies/mL), serum creatinine: 10.3 mg/dL, aspartate aminotransferase: 13 U/L (normal range: 5 - 34 U/L), alanine aminotransferase: 17 U/L (5 - 45 U/L), bilirubin: 0.4 mg/dL, prothrombin time INR: 1.01, serum albumin: 2.3 mg/dL, serum amylase: 105 IU/L (27 - 130 U/L), serum lipase: 40 IU/L (8 - 78 U/L). Her tumor antigens (Ag) were within reference range for cancer antigen (CA) 15-3 and CA19-9. CA 125 levels were repeatedly elevated (197 - 416 U/mL (normal: < 34.9 U/mL)), but no further follow-up was obtained. Analysis of the ascites fluid showed an albumin level of 1.5 g/dL and protein of 3.5 g/dL. The serum-to-ascites albumin gradient was < 1.1 excluding portal hypertension as a cause of ascites. The culture of peritoneal fluid was negative for acid-fast bacilli. There were no fungi seen by calcofluor white stain. Histoplasma Ag and Aspergillus Ag were negative. The pancreas was reported normal on computed tomography. Her beta-2 microglobulin was elevated to 47.30 mg/L (normal: 0.80 - 2.3). Serum protein electrophoresis showed hypoalbuminemia and decreased total protein, with minimal monoclonal M-component only (IgG-kappa 0.30 g/dL in the gamma zone). Immunofixation electrophoresis showed polyclonal immunoglobulins (Ig) with polyclonal light chains. kappa and lambda light chains were increased to 66.86 mg/dL (normal: 0.33 - 1.94) and 18.55 mg/dL (normal: 0.57 - 2.63), respectively, yielding a ratio of 3.6 (normal: 0.26 - 1.65) (Table 1). Ascitic fluid analysis showed a marked increase in plasma cells with an abnormal kappa : lambda ratio, i.e., > 5 : 1. 
Liver biopsy was essentially normal, hence an omental biopsy was performed which on immunohistochemistry showed similar findings as the ascitic fluid with predominant kappa and faint lambda staining (Figure 1). Multiple myeloma work-ups with skeletal surveys revealed no focal osseous lesions, apart from the osseous changes of hyperparathyroidism. Accordingly, the diagnosis of omental EMP with malignant ascites was established. Omental resection and radiation were offered to the patient, but she refused further intervention. Two years of follow-up, she remained stable without any further complication, apart from requiring regular paracenteses.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old female presenting with progressive abdominal distension, bilateral leg swelling, muscle weakness, and weight loss for several weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a multi-week history of worsening painless abdominal distension, bilateral lower extremity edema, proximal muscle weakness, and unintentional weight loss. Several weeks after transitioning from long-term peritoneal dialysis to intermittent hemodialysis, she developed rapid, recurrent, high-volume ascites requiring therapeutic paracentesis of 5 to 7 liters every two weeks.
subjective.past_medical_history: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection diagnosed 6 years prior, maintained on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART); end-stage renal disease (ESRD) secondary to biopsy-proven HIV-associated nephropathy (HIVAN, characterized by collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis), managed with cycler peritoneal dialysis for 5 years before elective transfer to intermittent hemodialysis; hypertension; secondary hyperparathyroidism; chronic anuria. No history of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit substance use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal distension, peripheral edema, generalized weakness, weight loss; denies dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, cough, chest pain, palpitations, or abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals: Blood pressure 160/80 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.9 °C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Abdomen: Prominent abdominal distension with shifting dullness consistent with moderate ascites, soft and non-tender; no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider angiomas, palmar erythema). Extremities: Bilateral pitting pedal edema. Cardiovascular and Respiratory: Normal heart sounds without gallop or murmur; clear breath sounds bilaterally.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 10.0 g/dL (normocytic, normochromic anemia). Comprehensive metabolic panel: Serum creatinine 10.3 mg/dL, serum albumin 2.3 g/dL, uncorrected serum calcium 8.6 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.4 mg/dL, AST 13 U/L, ALT 17 U/L, serum amylase 105 IU/L, serum lipase 40 IU/L, prothrombin time INR 1.01. Paracentesis / Ascitic fluid: Total protein 3.5 g/dL, albumin 1.5 g/dL, serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) < 1.1 (exudative ascites); calcofluor white fungal stain negative; Histoplasma and Aspergillus antigens negative; acid-fast bacilli (AFB) culture negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Tumor and hematologic biomarkers: CA-125 elevated (197-416 U/mL; reference < 34.9 U/mL), CA 15-3 and CA 19-9 normal; serum beta-2 microglobulin 47.30 mg/L. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation: Hypoalbuminemia, minimal monoclonal IgG-kappa M-spike (0.30 g/dL in gamma zone); serum free kappa light chains 66.86 mg/dL, lambda 18.55 mg/dL (ratio 3.6). Ascitic fluid cytology: Markedly elevated monoclonal plasma cell infiltrate with kappa:lambda ratio > 5:1. Abdominal CT: Moderate-to-severe ascites with normal pancreas and liver parenchyma. Core needle liver biopsy: Histologically normal liver tissue. Omental biopsy: Sheets of atypical plasma cells with monotypic kappa light chain restriction on immunohistochemistry. Skeletal radiographic survey: Absence of osteolytic lesions (findings limited to hyperparathyroid osteopathy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Primary omental extramedullary plasmacytoma (EMP) presenting with recurrent malignant ascites, in a patient with well-controlled HIV infection (CD4 count 600/mm3, HIV viral load 986 copies/mL) and ESRD on maintenance hemodialysis; peritoneal tuberculosis, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, ovarian malignancy, cirrhosis, and systemic multiple myeloma were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Offered definitive surgical omental resection and adjuvant radiotherapy, which the patient declined. Managed conservatively with continued HAART, maintenance hemodialysis, and serial therapeutic paracenteses (5-7 L evacuated every other week). Remained clinically stable without disease progression over two years of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 60-year-old woman presented with fatigue and weight loss, along with pain in the proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands, wrists, elbows, shoulders, knees, and metatarsophalangeal joints. She was diagnosed with RA at a local clinic six months ago. Her symptoms were not relieved with six months of continuous treatment of DMARDs, and the patient had fever. When the patient referred to our hospital, she experienced severe pain in the small- and medium-sized joints throughout the body and significant swelling in the interphalangeal joints of all painful joints. She described her joints as having a burning sensation, accompanied by significant morning stiffness. She was positive for antinuclear antibody and negative for RF. Additionally, she had a high titer of anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 48 mm/h, and a CRP level of 13.3 mg/L (Table 2). Using the 28-Joint Disease Activity Scale (DAS28), her diagnosis of RA was confirmed with a disease activity score of 6.04, suggesting a high degree of disease activity.
Next, we initially administered methotrexate (MTX), tofacitinib, and etoricoxib because of the ineffectiveness of multiple DMARDs, for which the patient experienced insignificant joint pain relief. The patient experienced vomiting after MTX administration. For several reasons, the patient refused low-dose steroids to relieve pain. As this patient was resistant to first-line DMARDs, we initiated adalimumab (40 mg subcutaneously every other week) (Hisun Biopharmaceutical Co., Ltd.) therapy after screening the patient for hepatitis virus infection, LTBI, and other infectious conditions according to the British Society for Rheumatology DMARDs safety guidelines. Compared to DMARDs, the patient responded better to adalimumab therapy. Unfortunately, the patient had a concealed history of a sexual partner with HIV/AIDS. However, her DAS28 score decreased to 4.9 after two weeks of ADA treatment, and symptoms such as joints pain and weakness were significantly relieved. Nonetheless, after RA was in control, HIV was detected in her blood, with a quantitative HIV-1 RNA test revealing values of 1.31E+5 IU/mL, accompanied by a decreased CD4+ lymphocyte count. Considering that she had difficult-to-treat RA combined with HIV/AIDS, her swollen and painful joints were uncontrolled. In addition, the patient was ineffective against DMARDs. Steroids may have accelerated the replication of HIV-RNA and induce other infections. After discussion with the patient, adalimumab therapy was continued, and HAART was initiated. HIV-1 RNA viral replication was controlled, and the CD4+ lymphocyte count continued to increase (Figure 1). After one year of ADA therapy, LTBI and other infections did not occur. She had no fever, and her fatigue had significantly improved. Her case was considered as RA remission, with a DAS28 score of 1.40.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old female presenting with severe polyarticular joint pain, morning stiffness, fever, fatigue, and weight loss for six months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-month history of severe polyarthritis involving the proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands, wrists, elbows, shoulders, knees, and metatarsophalangeal joints, accompanied by morning stiffness, burning arthralgias, intermittent fevers, fatigue, and weight loss. She had been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis at a local clinic six months earlier but failed multiple conventional synthetic and targeted synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, tofacitinib, and etoricoxib), suffering drug intolerance with emesis from methotrexate. She declined systemic corticosteroid therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed 6 months prior, refractory to DMARD therapy; screened negative for latent tuberculosis (LTBI) and viral hepatitis prior to biologic therapy. Epidemiological risk: Unprotected heterosexual contact with a partner known to have a chronic retroviral illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Polyarticular joint pain and swelling, morning stiffness, fever, fatigue, weight loss, and nausea/vomiting associated with methotrexate; denies photosensitivity, malar rash, or mucosal ulcerations.

objective.physical_examination: Musculoskeletal: Severe tenderness and pronounced symmetric synovitis/swelling involving the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of both hands, wrists, elbows, shoulders, knees, and metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints; baseline 28-Joint Disease Activity Score (DAS28) was 6.04, indicating severe active rheumatoid disease.
objective.routine_investigations: Inflammatory markers: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 48 mm/h; C-reactive protein (CRP) 13.3 mg/L. Autoimmune serologies: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) positive; anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies strongly positive in high titer; rheumatoid factor (RF) negative. Infectious screening: Negative for hepatitis B and C viruses and negative screening for latent tuberculosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Active seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (DAS28 score 6.04) complicated by newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection (quantitative HIV-1 RNA 1.31 x 10^5 IU/mL, accompanied by severe CD4+ T-lymphocyte depletion). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive HIV serology and quantitative HIV-1 RNA testing of 1.31 x 10^5 IU/mL; high-titer anti-CCP confirming RA. Plan & Outcome: Initiated on subcutaneous adalimumab 40 mg every other week, resulting in rapid decrease of DAS28 to 4.9 at 2 weeks. Upon identification of HIV infection, combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART) was safely co-administered with adalimumab without systemic corticosteroids. At 1-year follow-up, viral replication was completely suppressed, CD4+ count reconstituted, no opportunistic infections occurred, and rheumatoid arthritis attained complete clinical remission with a DAS28 score of 1.40.

raw_case_text: The second patient was a 17-year-old girl without family history of TB. She presented with numerous bilateral cervical lymphadenopathies and nasal obstruction. Nasal endoscopy found a polypoid uprising of the superior and posterior nasopharyngeal walls. CT scan showed a nasopharyngeal mass with central hypodensity suggesting tissue necrosis (Figure 3), with multiple cervical lymphadenopathies. A biopsy was performed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old female presented with nasal obstruction and bilateral neck swelling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with nasal obstruction and numerous bilateral cervical swellings.
subjective.past_medical_history: No family history of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Patient reported nasal obstruction. Systemic symptoms, home medications, and allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Presence of numerous bilateral cervical lymphadenopathies.
objective.advanced_workup: Nasal endoscopy: revealed polypoid swelling and mucosal uprising of the superior and posterior nasopharyngeal walls. CT scan: demonstrated a nasopharyngeal mass with central hypodensity suggestive of tissue necrosis, accompanied by multiple cervical lymphadenopathies. Nasopharyngeal biopsy was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Primary nasopharyngeal tuberculosis presenting with central necrosis mimicking nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Diagnostic biopsy was performed; across this patient series, histopathology confirmed granulomatous nasopharyngitis with epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans multinucleated giant cells, and caseous necrosis. Managed with antitubercular regimen comprising rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day), isoniazid (5 mg/kg/day), and pyrazinamide (20 mg/kg/day) for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months, achieving favorable clinical and radiological resolution.

raw_case_text: Laboratory tests such as complete blood count revealed a white blood cells (WBCs) count of 26,900/muL, 90.9% of them were neutrophils. They also showed elevated inflammatory markers; C-reactive protein (CRP) was 71.3, and later erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) test was 60 mm/h. His other tests which included liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, and urine examination were all within normal limits. MRI study of the entire spine with gadolinium contrast provided evidence of T2 hyperintense signal changes at the level of (10-11-12) thoracic vertebrae, often related to an inflammatory process with no compressive lesion (Figure 1), so electromyography (EMG) was not performed. The patient was managed with short courses of intravenous (IV) antibiotic methylprednisolone solumedrol for 5 days, but he did not get better. During that time we continued with testing the CSF which was turbid with WBCs count of 30/muL, 95% of them are neutrophils with 2760 RBCs, glucose of 63 mg/dL, elevated levels of protein about 67 mg/dL, and immunoglobulin G (IGg) value in the CSF of 5.22 mg/dL with normal CSF IgG Index. There are no malignant cells detected in the examined CSF sample. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest excluded the tuberculosis (TB) infection and when (GeneXpert) PCR in the CSF was performed, it was negative. Immunology tests of anti-aquaporin-4 (APQ-4)-IgG autoantibodies and anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) autoantibodies were negative. Electrophoresis showed positive oligoclonal bands correlated with systemic inflammation. The patient mentioned a history of unpasteurized dairy products so a real-time PCR for brucella bacteria was performed and it was positive, while it is not usual for brucella bacteria to cause transverse myelitis. We were not able to identify the brucella type because that is not available in our country. The patient opted to transfer his care to another hospital, where the medical team considered the potential benefit of plasmapheresis. However, the intervention proved ineffective due to the advanced disease stage. At that time the patient was commenced on a 6-week course of doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and rifampicin 600 mg once daily, alongside an intensive physical therapy program aimed at optimizing good outcomes.

subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposure: History of consuming unpasteurized dairy products. No other prior medical history, chronic conditions, or prior medications documented.

objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: white blood cells (WBC) 26,900/muL (90.9% neutrophils); C-reactive protein (CRP): 71.3; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 60 mm/h. Liver function tests, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, and urinalysis: all within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: Spinal MRI with gadolinium contrast demonstrated T2 hyperintense signal changes at the level of T10-T12 thoracic vertebrae suggestive of an inflammatory process without compressive lesion; EMG was not performed. Chest CT excluded pulmonary tuberculosis. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: turbid CSF, WBC count 30/muL (95% neutrophils), RBC 2,760/muL, glucose 63 mg/dL, protein 67 mg/dL, CSF IgG 5.22 mg/dL with normal CSF IgG index; cytology negative for malignant cells; CSF GeneXpert PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. Autoantibody testing: anti-aquaporin-4 (AQP-4)-IgG and anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) autoantibodies negative; protein electrophoresis showed positive oligoclonal bands.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Real-time PCR for Brucella bacteria was positive (specific species typing unavailable locally), establishing Brucella-induced transverse myelitis. Differential diagnoses ruled out: Compressive myelopathy excluded by spine MRI; tuberculosis excluded by chest CT and negative CSF GeneXpert PCR; neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) and MOGAD excluded by negative anti-AQP-4 and anti-MOG antibodies; malignancy ruled out by CSF cytology. Management and Outcome: Initially treated with short courses of IV antibiotics and methylprednisolone (Solu-Medrol) for 5 days without improvement. Plasmapheresis was considered and attempted at a transfer facility but was ineffective due to advanced disease stage. The patient was then treated with a 6-week course of oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily, combined with intensive physical therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old Italian patient with a 20-year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriasis arthropathica presented to our hospital with numerous ulcerations or nodules within his psoriatic lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been treated with subcutaneous methotrexate (25 mg per week) for the past 9 years and adalimumab (40 mg every other week) for the past 7 years. Topical treatment included halometasone 0.05% plus triclosan 1% cream and calcipotriol plus betamethasone dipropionate foam in the weeks before hospitalization.
The obese patient (BMI 39 kg/m2) showed multiple psoriatic lesions characterized by erythemato-squamous plaques disseminated over the integument (PASI 16.6). Moreover, the patient showed erosive and partly ulcerating plaques and nodules, some of them covered by distinct brown crusts, at the right forearm, right knee, left flank and the abdomen (Figures 1A,B). Physical examination showed no pathological findings. There was no lymphadenopathy.
The histopathology of an externally performed lesion biopsy reported dermal T-cell infiltrates without evidence repeated of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies and histologies from morphologically different lesions on the right forearm and right flank revealed an interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, thickening of the epidermis, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular, periadnexal, superficially accentuated lymphocytic infiltrates with a preponderance of T cells (Figures 2A,B). Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence did not detect any IgG, IgM, IgA, or C3 depositions. Syphilis serology, carried out due to numerous plasma cells in the tissue, yielded negative results. Moreover, an HIV infection, borreliosis and tuberculosis were ruled out by negative antibody or PCR tests. A serum sample was negative for antibodies against (extractable) nuclear antigens. Complement factors were within normal ranges. In hematoxylin-eosin (Figure 1C), Giemsa (Figure 1D) and Feulgen stains, intracellular Leishmania amastigotes with kinetoplasts were seen, which were identified by culture, miniexon PCR and restriction fragment length polymorphism-analysis as L. infantum. The patient also had a positive anti-Leishmania serology (maximum titer detected by indirect immunofluorescence using viable L. major promastigotes was 1:1,600). Since the patient originated from and repeatedly visited southern Italy, it is likely that he acquired the infection during his temporary stays.
The therapy with adalimumab was stopped, while treatment with methotrexate was continued (Figure 2). Interestingly, the ulcerations already started to heal under intensive topical treatment with salicylic acid, dithranol, and clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment. Visceral involvement was excluded based on clinical parameters and sonography of liver and spleen. Therefore, we pursued a watch-and-wait strategy without specific therapy for leishmaniasis. The ulcerative skin lesions, which were clinically compatible with cutaneous leishmaniasis, completely regressed. After switching the systemic treatment to secukinumab (anti-IL-17A) or apremilast, the psoriatic lesions remained unaltered, but finally improved with ixekizumab (anti-IL-17A). During regular medical follow-up for almost 5 years the clinical condition of the patient remained stable (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male with psoriasis on immunosuppressive therapy presented with a 6-month history of ulcerating nodules developing within psoriatic plaques.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had longstanding psoriasis on combined immunosuppressive therapy, developed progressive erosive and ulcerating nodular lesions covered with brown crusts arising within preexisting psoriatic plaques on his right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen over the preceding 6 months.
subjective.past_medical_history: 20-year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis treated with subcutaneous methotrexate (25 mg weekly for 9 years) and adalimumab (40 mg every other week for 7 years); recent topical therapy with halometasone-triclosan and calcipotriol-betamethasone foam; originating from and frequent temporary traveler to southern Italy (endemic area).

objective.physical_examination: Obese male (BMI: 39 kg/m^2). Skin: multiple disseminated erythemato-squamous plaques over the integument (PASI 16.6); erosive and ulcerating plaques and nodules with thick brown crusts on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. Lymph nodes: no palpable lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver and spleen dimensions without hepatosplenomegaly. Serum complement factors were within normal ranges. Serology for syphilis was negative; tests for HIV, Borrelia, and tuberculosis (antibody and PCR) were negative. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA/ENA) were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: External lesion biopsy reported dermal T-cell infiltrates without clear malignancy. Repeat biopsies of lesions on the right forearm and right flank demonstrated interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, epidermal thickening, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and perivascular/periadnexal T-cell lymphocytic infiltrates. Tissue clonality analysis demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR-gamma gene rearrangements, ruling out cutaneous lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgG, IgM, IgA, and C3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania infantum in an immunosuppressed patient on adalimumab: tissue histopathology with hematoxylin-eosin, Giemsa, and Feulgen stains revealed intracellular Leishmania amastigotes with kinetoplasts; culture, miniexon PCR, and restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis definitively identified Leishmania infantum; anti-Leishmania indirect immunofluorescence serology was positive (maximum titer 1:1,600 using viable L. major promastigotes). Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, syphilis, deep mycoses, and visceral leishmaniasis were excluded. Adalimumab was discontinued while methotrexate was maintained; ulcerative lesions completely regressed under intensive topical keratolytic and anti-inflammatory therapy (salicylic acid, dithranol, clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment) using a watch-and-wait approach without systemic antileishmanial drugs. Psoriasis was subsequently stabilized with ixekizumab (anti-IL-17A), remaining disease-free and stable over 5 years of follow-up.

raw_case_text: In July 2013, 53-year-old male, Caucasian, unemployed, from Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil, attended to the Stomatology Clinic at University Hospital, presenting with pain, nasal obstruction, and complaints of odynophagia and dysphagia. Physical examination showed painful, hyperemic and friable lesion in the right nasal cavity, associated with infiltrative lesion on the hard and soft palate, and uvula ( Figure 1c). We observed ulcerated lesion on the left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent secretion, a small ulcer on the lower eyelid, on the lobe of the right ear and a lesion in the malar region. The patient was admitted for diagnosis and treatment of disseminated skin lesions. A biopsy of the palate lesions revealed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process. The patient was HIV negative and positive for Montenegro reaction. Treatment with amphotericin B was initiated at a dose of 150 mg/d up to a maximum dose of 2,410 mg. Lesions regressed after drug treatment and oral treatment was initiated during hospitalization. We removed dental foci without any intercurrence. One month later, the patient was discharged. However, in August 2013, in outpatient medical consultation, the lesions were observed in nasal mucosa and palate. He was followed up in the outpatient clinic and treatment with glucantime 20 mg/kg/day was prescribed for one month. The follow-up period was eight months, and the result was negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old male presented with facial ulcers, nasal pain, nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the stomatology clinic in July 2013 with nasal pain, persistent nasal obstruction, odynophagia, and dysphagia. He had noted progressive ulcerated lesions appearing on his eyelids, face, and earlobe, alongside destructive lesions inside the nasal cavity and oropharynx. He was admitted for diagnostic workup and inpatient therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Dental infectious foci. Negative for HIV. Resident of Mundo Novo, State of Bahia, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Nasal pain, nasal blockage, odynophagia, dysphagia. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: HEENT and Dermatologic: painful, hyperemic, and friable lesion in the right nasal cavity; extensive infiltrative lesions involving the hard palate, soft palate, and uvula. Multiple ulcerated skin lesions: ulcer on left eyebrow and right eye with seropurulent discharge, small ulcer on the right lower eyelid, ulcer on the right earlobe, and an ulcerated lesion in the right malar region.
objective.routine_investigations: Serology: HIV serology negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Palate lesion biopsy: histopathological examination revealed a non-specific erosive chronic inflammatory process.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated American tegumentary leishmaniasis with extensive mucocutaneous involvement (nasal, palatal, uvular, and facial skin).
Diagnostic confirmation: Positive Montenegro intradermal reaction (MIT); palate biopsy demonstrated non-specific chronic inflammatory process consistent with mucosal leishmaniasis.
Differentials ruled out: Paracoccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, squamous cell carcinoma, syphilis, tuberculosis, and HIV co-infection.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated initially with intravenous amphotericin B (150 mg/day up to a cumulative dose of 2,410 mg) with lesion regression, alongside dental focus removal. Upon outpatient follow-up in August 2013, persistent mucosal lesions prompted treatment with meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime, 20 mg/kg/day for 1 month). Followed for 8 months with complete clinical resolution and no active lesions.

raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old Asian male with no significant medical history presented to us with complaints of pain in the right gluteal region radiating down to right thigh since 6 days and fever since 2 days. There was no history of recent trauma to lower extremity or back. He denied any history of rash, joint pains, weight loss, or high-risk behavior. History of travel was absent. Family history was noncontributory. There was no history of tuberculosis contact or intravenous drug abuse. There was no history of raw milk consumption or undercooked meat exposure. There was no history of contact with pet animals. On presentation, he was tachycardic and febrile with respiratory rate 24/min and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg. Regional lymphadenopathy was absent. Local tenderness over the right gluteal region was present with no overlying skin changes of inflammation seen. Straight leg raising test was negative. Lower limb reflexes were normal.
Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis with neutrophilic predominance and eosinopenia (Hb 12.7 g%, total leukocyte count 14,580/cmm, neutrophils 81.7%, and eosinophils 0.1%). Blood chemistry showed normal renal function and electrolyte levels. Malaria antigen test was negative. He was empirically started on intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g 24 h after sending blood culture. Liver function test showed borderline elevated enzymes (serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase 62 IU/L, serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase 69 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 415 IU/L) with normal bilirubin levels. HbA1C level was 5.5%. C-reactive protein (CRP) was positive (32.37 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was raised 34 mm/h.
Chest, pelvis radiographs, and abdominal ultrasonography were unremarkable. Pelvis magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed peripherally enhancing fluid collection within the right piriformis muscle measuring 3.2 cm x 3.0 cm size, representing an abscess with subtle bony involvement of the right sacroiliac joint [Figure 1a and b]. Surgical incision and drainage of abscess were deferred taking the small size and deep seatedness of abscess into consideration. Brucella antibodies tested was negative. HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen serology were negative. However, blood culture sent earlier yielded Gram-negative bacilli, later identified to be Salmonella serotype typhi. Ceftriaxone was continued as per antibiotic sensitivity pattern for 2 weeks more following which fever intensity reduced to a significant extent. Meanwhile, Widal test done 1 week after symptom onset yielded significant titers of Salmonella agglutinogens (1:240 Salmonella typhi O, >1:1920 S. typhi H).
Repeat pelvis MRI after 2 weeks showed no interval change in size of abscess but marrow edema involving iliac and sacral portions of the right sacroiliac joint was more pronounced, with postcontrast enhancement [Figure 1c and d]. Intravenous ceftriaxone dose was stepped up to 2 g 12 h and was continued for 4 weeks more on outpatient basis taking into consideration the deep seatedness of abscess and the bony involvement. After 4 weeks, ESR normalized to 07 mm/h and CRP was negative (0.00 mg/L). Pelvis MRI after 4 weeks showed the signs of resolution with a significant reduction in abscess size and reduced marrow edema of the involved sacroiliac joint [Figure 2a-c]. A gradual improvement was seen clinically, laboratory-wise, and radiologically over 6 weeks course of intravenous ceftriaxone and complete recovery was noted without any complication.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old Asian male presented with pain in the right gluteal region radiating down to the right thigh for 6 days and fever for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced pain in the right gluteal region radiating down to the right thigh starting 6 days prior to presentation, followed by onset of fever 2 days prior. He reported no history of recent trauma to the lower extremity or back.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history. No history of tuberculosis contact or intravenous drug abuse. Denied raw milk consumption or undercooked meat exposure. No contact with pet animals. History of travel was absent. Family history was noncontributory.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denied rash, joint pains, weight loss, or high-risk behavior.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile and tachycardic; blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min. Regional lymphadenopathy was absent. Local tenderness was present over the right gluteal region without overlying inflammatory skin changes. Straight leg raising test was negative. Lower limb reflexes were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 12.7 g%; total leukocyte count: 14,580/cmm; neutrophils: 81.7%; eosinophils: 0.1%. Normal renal function and electrolyte levels. HbA1c: 5.5%. LFTs: SGOT 62 IU/L, SGPT 69 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 415 IU/L, normal bilirubin levels. C-reactive protein (CRP): positive at 32.37 mg/L; ESR: raised at 34 mm/h. Malaria antigen test: negative. Chest and pelvis radiographs: unremarkable. Abdominal ultrasonography: unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup: Pelvis MRI revealed a peripherally enhancing fluid collection within the right piriformis muscle measuring 3.2 cm x 3.0 cm, representing an abscess with subtle bony involvement of the right sacroiliac joint. Repeat pelvis MRI at 2 weeks demonstrated no interval change in abscess size, with more pronounced marrow edema involving iliac and sacral portions of the right sacroiliac joint and postcontrast enhancement. Follow-up pelvis MRI at 4 weeks showed significant reduction in abscess size and reduced marrow edema of the sacroiliac joint. Brucella antibodies, HIV serology, and hepatitis B surface antigen serology were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Piriformis abscess with secondary sacroiliac joint osteomyelitis due to Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi. Confirmed by blood culture yielding Gram-negative bacilli identified as Salmonella serotype Typhi, along with Widal test titers of 1:240 Salmonella typhi O and >1:1920 S. typhi H. Empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g every 24 h was initiated; surgical incision and drainage was deferred due to abscess depth and size. Ceftriaxone was continued according to susceptibility for 2 weeks, then stepped up to 2 g every 12 h for 4 additional weeks (total 6-week course). ESR normalized to 7 mm/h and CRP normalized to 0.00 mg/L, with complete clinical and radiological resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 5-week-old female presented to hospital with 3 days of diarrhea, poor feeding, decreased activity, and two episodes of unilateral leg shaking that self-resolved in less than 1 min. of 2 weeks prior, she had 1 day of fever. She had no respiratory symptoms, vomiting, rash, or decreased level of consciousness.
The infant's mother migrated from Nigeria 9 years prior. This pregnancy was conceived during travel to Nigeria. The mother returned to Canada at 5-months gestation. Testing for HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis was negative at 7-months gestation.
The infant was delivered by caesarean section at 37 + 5 weeks gestation for breech presentation. The mother had fever at delivery and on post-operative day one, then defervesced without antibiotics. The baby's birth weight was 3.1 kg. Neonatal examination was normal. She fed and gained weight appropriately until the current illness.
In the Emergency Department (ED), the infant was afebrile, with vital signs in normal range. Examination revealed lethargy and a soft flow murmur. Hemoglobin was 64 g/L, hematocrit 20%, white blood cells 8.5 x 109/L, platelets 331 x 109/L, and glucose 5.2 mmol/L.
The Hematology technician contacted the ED to report having seen malaria parasites (at 0.1% parasitemia) on the blood smear performed for complete blood count with manual differential. Rapid diagnostic test for malaria (BinaxNOW; Abbott, Chicago, IL, USA) was done and was negative.
Further history revealed that the mother was treated for malaria at 6-weeks' gestation in Nigeria (see case timeline in Supplemental Figure 1). She did not know the causative species or medication. Fever recurred at 6-months gestation in Canada. The mother contacted her physician in Nigeria, who advised to take a course of antimalarial therapy she had brought back from Nigeria. Fever resolved.
The infant was transferred to the pediatric hospital and the Infectious Diseases service was consulted. The infant was alert but pale, and noted to have tachycardia, retractions, and desaturations with feeding. Hepatosplenomegaly was palpated. Hemoglobin was 55 g/L, hematocrit 17.3%, and lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Liver panel, creatinine, and C-reactive protein were normal.
Red blood cells were transfused due to symptomatic anemia. Congenital malaria was presumed given absence of endemic malaria transmission in Canada, and managed as a severe case given progressive anemia and possible seizures. IV artesunate was initiated (3.0 mg/kg/dose at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h). Ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir were started pending full septic workup. Repeat peripheral blood smear confirmed 0.1% parasitemia, and Plasmodium ovale was identified by microscopy and polymerase chain reaction at the provincial reference laboratory.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-week-old female infant presenting with diarrhea, poor feeding, decreased activity, and brief unilateral leg shaking episodes for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 5-week-old female infant presented with a three-day history of loose stools, poor feeding, decreased activity, and two self-limiting episodes of unilateral leg shaking each lasting under one minute. Two weeks prior, she had experienced a single day of fever. She was brought to the emergency department where anemia and lethargy were noted, prompting transfer to a tertiary pediatric intensive care unit for progressive respiratory distress and pallor during feeds.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born at 37+5 weeks gestation via Cesarean section for breech presentation (birth weight 3.1 kg, normal neonatal exam) to a mother who immigrated from Nigeria 9 years prior and traveled to Nigeria during pregnancy (conception in Nigeria, return to Canada at 5 months gestation). Mother was treated for malaria at 6 weeks gestation in Nigeria, experienced recurrent fever at 6 months gestation treated with self-administered Nigerian antimalarials, and had peripartum fever. Mother tested negative for HIV, HBV, and syphilis at 7 months gestation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for poor feeding, lethargy, diarrhea, and brief unilateral focal shaking. Negative for vomiting, cough, rhinorrhea, rash, or decreased level of consciousness. Medications: none. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: In emergency department: afebrile, vital signs normal; lethargic with a soft systolic flow murmur. Upon transfer to pediatric ICU: alert but marked pallor, tachycardia, subcostal retractions and oxygen desaturations during feeding. Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Emergency department labs: hemoglobin 64 g/L, hematocrit 20%, white blood cells 8.5 x 10^9/L, platelets 331 x 10^9/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L. Pediatric hospital labs: hemoglobin 55 g/L, hematocrit 17.3%, lactate 2.1 mmol/L; normal hepatic transaminases, normal creatinine, and normal C-reactive protein. Rapid diagnostic test (BinaxNOW) was negative. Peripheral blood smear performed for complete blood count with manual differential.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe congenital Plasmodium ovale malaria complicated by severe progressive hemolytic anemia (hemoglobin nadir 55 g/L), feeding desaturations, hepatosplenomegaly, and suspected focal seizures.
Diagnostic confirmation: Routine CBC blood smear manual differential identifying intraerythrocytic parasites at 0.1% parasitemia (false-negative BinaxNOW rapid diagnostic test); repeat smear confirmed 0.1% parasitemia, and Plasmodium ovale was definitively identified by reference laboratory light microscopy and species-specific PCR. Full septic workup was negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with emergency packed red blood cell transfusion for symptomatic severe anemia, intravenous artesunate (3.0 mg/kg/dose at 0, 12, 24, and 48 hours), and empiric IV ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir pending microbiological culture and viral results.

raw_case_text:
We diagnosed the first case of disseminated-CL in Ecuador and named it as "generalized CL". The patient was a 40-year-old female, as of the time of examination (August 1979). The patient came from a small village, Balao Chico, Guayas province, a mountainous area located at 200 m a.s.l. (Fig. 1 (2)). At the early phase of the disease, the lesion appeared on the lumbar region, and then papular lesions were seen, which became pustulous vesicles at the right lumber region and disseminated all over the body, demonstrating 308 generalized lesions counted. The patient revealed a marked right lumbar pain, and some of the lesions in the body surface suspecting herpes zoster were observed. The patient was admitted for 16 days in a private hospital and then was taken to a national hospital "Hospital Luis Vernaza" in Guayaquil city, Ecuador. She was admitted to the hospital under the suspected diagnosis of smallpox, being registered No. 03739 in August 1979, without a precise diagnosis. As there was no improvement of her lesions on the 15th day of admission, she was taken to receive differential diagnosis at the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene, Guayaquil city, Ecuador. The presumptive clinical diagnoses were paracoccidioidomycosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, or staphylococcal infections. Firstly, the case was considered as paracoccidioidomycosis suggesting a generalized cutaneous form of the disease. But either Paracoccidioides braziliensis or Staphylococcus aureus were not observed in the examination of ulcer materials. Laboratory examinations revealed positive for betahemolytic streptococcus and sensitive for erythromycin, cephalexin, amikacin, and ampicillin and stool examination positive for Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale.
Most of the ulcer was crusty. When lifting the crusts, they were excavated with a purulent fluid because of sever secondary infections. The ulcers had different sizes ranging from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter. Some lesions had thick, prominent, and adhered crusts that bleed easily when they were separated. Others were small crusty ulcers that left an excavation, and some of them were erythematous and papulous, and confluent plaques were found on the lumbar-dorsal region. Several smear samples from diverse regions of the body surface were taken at random. The samples were positive for the Leishmania amastigote, though the number was scanty in smear specimens. The parasite isolated was identified as L. (V.) panamensis (designated as MHOM/EC/95/NA-03) by ELISA species-specific monoclonal antibodies (serodeme) analysis. No Montenegro skin test and rK39 kit test were performed in the case. The patient responded well to Glucantime  treatment (6.5 mg/kg/day for 12 days). In this case, both metronidazole per os and its ointment were also used as a supplementary treatment; probably, these accelerated the patient's healing within a short regimen, in spite of a relatively low dose of the drug.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female presented with severe right lumbar pain and extensive disseminated pustulovesicular and crusted skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old female presented in August 1979 with acute-onset right lumbar pain followed by an initial lumbar skin lesion. The eruption progressed rapidly into papules and pustular vesicles on the right flank, subsequently disseminating over the entire body, totaling 308 lesions. She was hospitalized for 16 days in a private clinic and transferred to Hospital Luis Vernaza under suspicion of smallpox (reg. No. 03739). Lacking improvement by day 15 of admission, she was referred to the National Institute of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene in Guayaquil for differential diagnosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Balao Chico, Guayas province, Ecuador (mountainous area at 200 m a.s.l.). Prior medical conditions and prior antibiotic therapy not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe right lumbar pain, widespread ulcerative skin eruptions. Denied systemic fever, chills, cough, or gastrointestinal bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Total of 308 disseminated cutaneous lesions counted over the entire body surface. Erythematous, papular, and confluent plaques on the lumbodorsal region. Lesions ranged from 0.5 to 20 mm in diameter; most were crusted, and removal of crusts revealed excavated ulcers with purulent exudate due to secondary bacterial infection; some crusts were thick, prominent, and bled easily on separation.
objective.routine_investigations: Ulcer exudate culture grew beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (sensitive to erythromycin, cephalexin, amikacin, and ampicillin); negative for Staphylococcus aureus and Paracoccidioides braziliensis. Stool microscopy revealed Trichuris trichiura, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Ancylostoma duodenale.
objective.advanced_workup: Multiple random skin lesion smears stained with Giemsa: light microscopy revealed intracellular microorganisms within phagocytes, present in scanty numbers.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (generalized CL) caused by Leishmania (Viannia) panamensis, complicated by secondary beta-hemolytic streptococcal pyoderma and intestinal helminthiasis.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct smear specimens revealed Leishmania amastigotes. Parasite isolate (MHOM/EC/95/NA-03) identified as Leishmania (Viannia) panamensis by ELISA species-specific monoclonal antibodies (serodeme analysis). Montenegro skin test and rK39 test were not performed.
Differentials Ruled Out: Smallpox (initial hospital misdiagnosis), herpes zoster, paracoccidioidomycosis, and primary staphylococcal ecthyma.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Secondary streptococcal infection treated with sensitive antibiotics. Antileishmanial therapy administered with intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) at 6.5 mg/kg/day for 12 days, supplemented with oral and topical metronidazole. The patient responded rapidly and achieved complete healing of all 308 lesions.

raw_case_text: A 61-year-old woman presented with intermittent low back pain that persisted for past one month. The pain worsened within one week and became unbearable. Three months previously, the patient was admitted to a local hospital for productive cough. Lung CT showed suspicious TB lesions, and T-SPOT was positive. After excluding other diseases, the local hospital started diagnostic anti-tuberculosis treatment consisting of HRZE. The patient took the medication irregularly because of gastrointestinal reaction. A physical examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory results were white blood cells, 7.22x109/L; hemoglobin, 122 g/L; platelets, 216 x109/L; CRP, 32.97 mg/dl; and procalcitonin, 0.213ng/mL. The sputum GeneXpert test result was positive and sensitive to rifampicin. Multiple infections and diffuse miliary nodules in both lungs suggested tuberculosis. Thoracic and abdominal aortic CTA examination showed a 51x28 mm2 pseudoaneurysm arising from the lower abdominal aorta, surrounded by a patchy shadow and lymphadenopathy (Figure 5). Combined with the patient's medical history, tuberculous aortic pseudoaneurysm was considered. Emergency digital subtraction angiography was performed after admission, and two coated stents were implanted in the abdominal aorta and iliac artery. Angiography showed that the stents were well- positioned, blood flow was smooth, and a pseudoaneurysm did not develop. The patient was discharged from the hospital 2 days post-operation and received anti-tuberculosis drug treatment, including isoniazid 0.6 g once daily, rifapentine 0.45 g twice a week, ethambutol 0.75 g once daily, pyrazinamide 0.5 g three times daily, and moxifloxacin 0.4 g once daily. Abdominal aortic CTA performed two weeks later revealed that the aneurysm did not recur (Figure 6). Our follow-up plan was consistent with that of the patient in case 1. The patient tolerated the anti-tuberculosis drugs well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 61-year-old woman presented with intermittent low back pain of one month's duration, which worsened severely over the prior week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 61-year-old woman presented with low back pain for 1 month, which became unbearable over the preceding week. Three months prior, she was admitted to a local hospital for productive cough; chest CT showed suspicious pulmonary lesions and T-SPOT was positive. She had been prescribed HRZE but took medications irregularly due to gastrointestinal adverse effects.
subjective.past_medical_history: Productive cough and suspected pulmonary tuberculosis 3 months prior (positive T-SPOT); irregular HRZE adherence due to GI intolerance. No other chronic illnesses, travel, or animal exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports severe low back pain, prior productive cough, gastrointestinal adverse reactions to anti-TB drugs; denies numbness, weakness, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Home medications: irregular HRZE. Allergies: GI intolerance to HRZE.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed no abnormalities; vitals normal.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 7.22 x 10^9/L; Hemoglobin: 122 g/L; Platelets: 216 x 10^9/L; CRP: 32.97 mg/dL; Procalcitonin: 0.213 ng/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic and abdominal aortic CTA: a 51 x 28 mm pseudoaneurysm arising from the lower abdominal aorta, surrounded by patchy shadow and lymphadenopathy, alongside diffuse miliary nodules in both lungs. Emergency digital subtraction angiography: confirmed abdominal aortic pseudoaneurysm. Abdominal aortic CTA at 2 weeks post-procedure: confirmed stent graft integrity without pseudoaneurysm recurrence.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Tuberculous pseudoaneurysm of the lower abdominal aorta (51 x 28 mm) associated with miliary pulmonary tuberculosis in the context of irregular anti-tuberculosis therapy.
Confirmation: Sputum GeneXpert was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and sensitive to rifampicin; CTA demonstrated 51 x 28 mm pseudoaneurysm surrounded by inflammatory lymphadenopathy; prior T-SPOT was positive.
Differentials ruled out: Atherosclerotic abdominal aneurysm, pyogenic bacterial mycotic aneurysm.
Treatment & Outcome: Emergency digital subtraction angiography with implantation of two coated stents across the abdominal aorta and iliac artery, successfully sealing the pseudoaneurysm with smooth blood flow. Discharged on postoperative day 2 on oral anti-TB therapy: isoniazid 0.6 g daily, rifapentine 0.45 g twice weekly, ethambutol 0.75 g daily, pyrazinamide 0.5 g TID, and moxifloxacin 0.4 g daily. Follow-up CTA at 2 weeks confirmed successful exclusion without recurrence.

raw_case_text:
Control 3: 72-year-old male with diabetes mellitus, chronic ischemic cardiopathy and dyslipaemia, attending the emergency department for cough and fever during the last 15 days without improvement and accompanied by diarrhea. He also had partial respiratory failure. His blood pressure score was 154/81, and he had a heart rate of 80 beats per minute, SpO2 87%, and elevated D-Dimer levels. Chest X-Ray: A bilateral alveolar reticulum interstitial pattern of peripheral predominance and right base was observed, indicating an atypical infectious process. Confirmation of COVID-19 was made by RT-PCR using a throat swab, as well as testing positive for pneumococcus. He was treated with hydroxychloroquine, prednisone, lopinavir-ritonavir, vancomycin, and tacrolimus. The patient remains in the intensive care unit.
The effects of lithium treatment between dependent variables were evaluated with regression analyses using GraphPad Prism 7.0 software. Multiple linear regression is one of the most important statistical methods used to model the linear relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables to fit an exponential decay curve. We calculated a nonlinear regression with one phase exponential decay.
