assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute pericarditis secondary to Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Blood smear examination confirmed the presence of Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites. Coronary angiography ruled out STEMI/coronary occlusion.
Plan & Outcome: Treated for malaria with oral artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for 3 days. Pericarditis was treated with oral ibuprofen 600 mg every 8 hours for one week, followed by 600 mg twice daily for a second week. Symptoms resolved within one week, repeat blood smear showed complete clearance of malarial parasites, and follow-up ECG at 15 days showed complete normalization.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old previously healthy female presented with generalised body swelling, disproportionate ascites, loss of appetite, and loss of weight for four months' duration. She denied any fever, night sweats, yellowish discolouration of the eyes, hematemesis, melena, chronic cough, and haemoptysis. She reported no history of orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and her urine output remained normal.
Her past medical history was not significant for any liver, renal, or cardiac disease. She denied any past or contact history of TB. She reported no use of alcohol or herbal medications and no intravenous drug abuse. She was in a monogamous relationship and she denied any family history of liver or renal disease.
She was afebrile on admission and her vitals included a pulse rate within normal limits. On exam, she was emaciated with a body mass index of 18, and she had significant ascites with mild ankle oedema. She was anicteric and did not have any lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or the peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease. Respiratory system and cardiovascular examinations were within normal limits. On eye exam, there was no evidence of choroid tubercles.
The initial laboratory findings are summarised in Table 1.
The anaemia workup, including serum iron studies, vitamin B12, and folate testing, was normal. A blood picture revealed normochromic normocytic anaemia and thrombocytosis, suggestive of anaemia of chronic disease. Thyroid function tests were normal. She did not have any proteinuria, and her international normalised ratio (INR) was normal. Repeated blood cultures, urine culture, and sputum culture were sterile, and a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) fourth-generation test was negative. CA 125 was mildly elevated to 175 U/ml (<46 U/ml).
The initial chest x-ray (CXR) was normal, and her transthoracic two-dimensional echocardiography showed normal systolic and diastolic functions and no evidence of constrictive pericarditis. A transvaginal ultrasound (US) did not reveal any ovarian pathology. Meanwhile, an abdomen US revealed a mildly hyperechoic liver with moderate ascites. Contrast Enhanced Computed Tomography (CECT) of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a normal-sized liver with evidence of heterogenicity of the liver parenchyma with minimal nodularity of the liver surface and moderate ascites with no portal vein thrombosis or lymphadenopathy. The spleen, gallbladder, biliary tract, and intestines were normal, as were the ovaries. The findings were in favour of possible decompensated chronic liver disease (CLD). However, the CLD workup did not reveal any potential aetiology (Table 2). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGIE) was normal and did not show any evidence of portal gastropathy or varices.
The initial diagnosis of possible cryptogenic CLD was made, and the patient was started on spironolactone and furosemide. Even though the diagnostic paracentesis was planned on admission, it was delayed due to the patient's refusal, but we were to do initiate after a few days. The analysis of the ascitic fluid revealed an exudative picture. There was no evidence of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and the ascitic fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells.
With elevated inflammatory markers and an exudative type of ascites, we decided to proceed with further investigations to rule out possible peritoneal TB. The ascitic fluid acid-fast bacilli (AFB) test was negative. The ascitic fluid bacterial, TB culture, and TB Gene Xpert were negative. The tuberculin sensitivity test (Mantoux) was positive at 17 mm without ulceration. Her repeated sputum for AFB, TB culture, and GeneXpert were negative.
Because the clinical picture did not fit the imaging findings, we decided to proceed with diagnostic laparoscopy and peritoneal biopsy. The laparoscopy was in favour of miliary TB (Figure 1) and the peritoneal biopsy revealed granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis favouring TB. She was started on anti-TB treatment (ATT), and on initial follow-up, she showed improvement in her clinical, biochemical, and radiological parameters. Her fever settled with ATT, and her ESR was 15 mm/1st hour and CRP was 12 mg/l at 3 weeks after the initiation of ATT.

She denied fever, night sweats, jaundice, hematemesis, melena, chronic cough, hemoptysis, orthopnea, or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and noted normal urine output.

Abdomen: marked distention with significant ascites; mild bilateral ankle edema. Anicteric; no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease, no palpable lymphadenopathy, and no hepatosplenomegaly. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. Fundoscopy: no evidence of choroid tubercles.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and blood smear: normochromic normocytic anemia and thrombocytosis consistent with anemia of chronic disease. Serum iron studies, vitamin B12, and folate levels: normal. Thyroid function tests: normal. Urinalysis: no proteinuria; international normalized ratio (INR): normal. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures: sterile. HIV fourth-generation antibody/antigen test: negative. Serum CA 125: mildly elevated at 175 U/mL (reference <46 U/mL). Initial chest X-ray: normal. Diagnostic laparoscopy and peritoneal biopsy: laparoscopy revealed diffuse peritoneal tubercles; peritoneal biopsy demonstrated granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Peritoneal tuberculosis (miliary peritoneal tuberculosis) presenting with severe exudative ascites mimicking decompensated chronic liver disease. Confirmed by diagnostic laparoscopy demonstrating peritoneal tubercles and peritoneal biopsy revealing granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis, supported by a positive tuberculin skin test (Mantoux 17 mm); ascitic fluid AFB smear, GeneXpert, and mycobacterial cultures were negative, and repeated sputum AFB, GeneXpert, and cultures were negative. Malignancy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and chronic liver disease etiologies were ruled out.
Treatment & Outcome: Started on standard antitubercular therapy (ATT). Experienced rapid clinical and biochemical improvement; fever settled, with ESR decreasing to 15 mm/1st hour and CRP decreasing to 12 mg/L at 3-week follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 8-year-old girl, from a rural area in Choco (Colombian Pacific Coast), presented with 20 days of fever, hiporexia, asthenia, and arthralgias, associated with emesis and diarrhea. She was found to have anemia and was prescribed ferrous bisglycinate without improvement. The fever was persistent and was associated with chills, abdominal pain, and dark urine; she was admitted to a rural hospital and diagnosed with pancytopenia; 2 units of packed red blood cells were transfused; and she was transferred to our hospital with a clinical suspicion of lymphoproliferative disorder. Her vital signs showed tachycardia (131 bpm), tachypnea (45 per min), and limit-low oxygen saturation (91%). Physical examination revealed jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly of 6 cm and of 2 cm below the costal margin, respectively; fine right basal crackles and a soft systolic heart murmur were heard at the left sternal border and the third intercostal space. Her past medical history was relevant for posttraumatic osteomyelitis of the right humerus and septic arthritis of the right elbow; her parents were not consanguineous, and she did not have pseudoalbinism.
Test results revealed thrombocytopenia and lymphopenia (Hg 11.5 g/dL, WBCs 4600/microL, neutrophils 3404/microL, lymphocytes 1058/microL, and platelets 59000/microL), elevated C-reactive protein (21.57 mg/dL), and altered liver function tests (ALT 349 U/L, AST 135 U/L, total bilirubin 6.67 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL, LDH 1376 IU/L, and albumin 2.1 g/dL). Infectious workup was negative for HIV, dengue, malaria, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, CMV, EBV, and Mycoplasma. Additional laboratory tests showed hypertriglyceridemia (787 mg/dL) and hyperferritinemia (>2000 ng/mL) with normal fibrinogen (311 mg/dL). Echocardiogram showed minimal pericardial effusion and preserved ventricular function without anatomic defects or signs of endocarditis. Abdominal ultrasound showed a small right pleural effusion, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and retroperitoneal and hepatic hilar lymphadenopathies. Abdominal computed tomography showed the same findings, with hypodensity areas corresponding to splenic infarcts. She was diagnosed with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and started on piperacillin-tazobactam and intravenous immunoglobulin (1 g/kg/d for 2 days); while waiting for blood cultures and bone marrow analysis, CSF was within normal limits. On her third hospital night, she presented hematemesis and rectorrhagia with hypovolemic shock that required fluid resuscitation, intravenous infusion of omeprazole, tranexamic acid, phytomenadione, packed red blood cell, and platelets transfusion. She was stabilized; upper and lower endoscopies did not show signs of active bleeding, but just some residual melena. On the fourth day of hospitalization, both blood and bone marrow cultures were positive for Salmonella typhi; and the antibiotic regimen was changed to ciprofloxacin; bone marrow specimen showed hematopoietic precursors with no signs of malignancy; and no hemophagocytosis was appreciated. Repeated blood cultures were negative; during the hospital stay, she was started on enalapril to maintain a tight control on blood pressure. She completed 14 days of antibiotic treatment with resolution of the fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and the abdominal pain. Laboratory investigations before discharge showed resolution of the cytopenias, down trending of liver function tests and triglycerides levels, and ferritin was still elevated.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever due to Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi, complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), gastrointestinal hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock, and splenic infarcts. Confirmed on hospital day 4 by positive blood and bone marrow cultures for Salmonella typhi (repeat blood cultures were negative). Initially treated empirically with intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and IVIG (1 g/kg/day for 2 days). Hypovolemic shock managed with fluid resuscitation, IV omeprazole, tranexamic acid, phytomenadione, PRBCs, and platelet transfusions. Following culture confirmation, antibiotics were switched to ciprofloxacin to complete 14 days of therapy, and enalapril was initiated for blood pressure control. Achieved resolution of fever, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and abdominal pain. Pre-discharge testing showed resolution of cytopenias, downtrending transaminases and triglycerides; ferritin remained elevated.

raw_case_text: A 42-year-old man with no particular history was hospitalized for drowsiness, 38.9 C fever and a heart rate of 140 beats/minute. He weighed 55 kg. The thick peripheral blood smear was positive with 17,400 Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites per mm3. The hemoglobin concentration was 10.3 g/dl, and blood glucose was 9.4 mmol/L. Quinine treatment at a dose of 25 mg/kg per 24 hours was instituted in the emergency department. Obnubilation-type consciousness disorders and conjunctival jaundice appeared after 12 hours of hospitalization. Even though the patient was afebrile, the diagnosis of BWF was evoked due to the port wine color of his urine. The emergency bioassay showed a creatinemia of 720 mumol, urea of 28 mmol, and hemoglobin of 5.5 g/dl. Quinine was immediately stopped, in favor of intramuscularly injected artemether prescribed at a dose of 3.2 mg/kg daily on day 1 and 1.6 mg/kg daily from day 2 to day 5. Unfortunately, the patient only received the first dose because he died less than 24 hours after admission of shock in coma and with anuria.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with fever, drowsiness, and rapid heart rate.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute onset of high fever, somnolence, and palpitations. Twelve hours after admission and initiation of parenteral antimalarial therapy, he developed acute clinical deterioration characterized by deep stupor/obnubilation, severe jaundice, and dark port wine-colored urine.

objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, blood glucose 9.4 mmol/L. Repeat emergency labs (12 hours later): Hemoglobin dropped acutely to 5.5 g/dL; serum creatinine 720 micromol/L; blood urea 28 mmol/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute blackwater fever (quinine-induced massive intravascular hemolysis, acute hemoglobinuric renal failure with anuria, and refractory shock). Admission thick peripheral blood smear demonstrated 17,400 P. falciparum trophozoites/mm3.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated in the emergency unit on intravenous quinine at 25 mg/kg/24h. Upon appearance of port wine urine and catastrophic drop in hemoglobin from 10.3 to 5.5 g/dL, quinine was immediately ceased and intramuscular artemether (3.2 mg/kg) administered. However, the patient developed uncal/neurologic herniation or refractory circulatory collapse with anuria, dying within 24 hours of hospital presentation.

raw_case_text:
This twenty-seven years old male presented with complaints of fever with rigor and chills and sore throat for ten days. It was associated with myalgia and recurrent vomiting followed by diffuse maculopapular rash all over the body with sparing of mucous membranes and periorbital tissues. On examination, he had conjunctival congestion with toxic facies. He had a past history of gout for which he received allolpurinol for twenty days and phenytoin for sudden loss of consciousness in another institution. There was no past history of tuberculosis, diabetes or hypertension.
Bilateral hard indurated cervical lymphadenopathy and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy was also observed along with bilateral parotid and submandibular gland enlargement. Hepatosplenomegaly was detected on ultrasonography. Hemogram on several occasions from admission revealed normal hemoglobin and red blood cell morphology. There was transient neutrophilic leukocytosis, whereas platelet counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were normal throughout. During his treatment with ceftriaxone, he suddenly developed shock, cyanosis and acute renal failure for which he was given inotropic support, amoxicillin, ceftazidine and steroids. He gradually responded and recovered in due course of time. A clinical diagnosis of shock syndrome due to Dengue fever or Epstein Barr virus (EBV) or streptococcus or phenytoin induced hypersensitivity syndrome was made. The Dengue virus IgM antibody Elisa was positive and serum D-dimer levels were positive (>200 ng/ml). Anti EBV IgG antibody test was positive but EBV IgM antibody test was negative. The serology tests for anti- cytomegalovirus antibody, anti leptospira antibody, Widal test, brucella (abortus and melitensis), and HIV were negative. The blood, throat swab and urine cultures were sterile. Paul-Bunnel and Weil-Felix tests were negative. Cervical lymph node biopsy was undertaken for histopathology.
Gross examination revealed four lymph nodes, the largest one measuring 1.5 cm and the rest below 1 cm. On microscopy, two of the lymph nodes (including the largest one) showed near total infarction of the parenchyma with preservation of cellular outlines of the lymphocytes (Fig 1). A thin rim of viable subcapsular normal mature lymphocytes along with neutrophils and plasma cells were identified. The medullary vessels showed vascular congestion however the blood vessels in the perinodal adipose tissue showed multiple fibrin thrombi with congestion in some of the vessels (Fig 2).
Multiple deeper sections revealed perinodal granulation tissue with viable subcapsular lymphoid tissue but no atypical cells, histiocytes or granulomas were seen. Stains for fungi and acid-fast bacilli were negative. The adjacent two uninvolved lymph nodes showed features of reactive change. Immunohistochemistry with B- cell (CD20) and T- cell (CD3) markers was performed. The viable lymphoid tissue showed an admixture of both B and T-cells. The infarcted tissue showed variable positivity and these markers highlighted few reactive follicles (Fig 3). The uninvolved lymph nodes also showed a normal positivity pattern.
The patient was asymptomatic thereafter and had complete regression of the lymph nodes. He was lost to follow up after two months of discharge from the hospital.
Lymph node infarction is a rare phenomenon reported in literature in association with various neoplastic and non-neoplastic conditions. The non-neoplastic conditions associated with infarction are namely polyarteritis nodosa, viral infections (Parvovirus B19, Infectious mononucleosis), cholesterol atheromatous embolism, thrombosis, gold injections, intestinal volvulus, postmediastinoscopy, mononeuritis multiplex, fine needle aspiration cytology and finally may be idiopathic. Hemorrhagic infarction of hilar lymph nodes has also been reported recently in association with heart lung transplantation. 
The neoplastic lesions most commonly associated with infarction are malignant lymphoma and metastatic melanoma. The differential diagnosis pertaining to the present case would be the above mentioned two conditions along with necrotizing lymphadenitis (Kikuchi's lymphadenitis), mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, and necrotizing granulomatous inflammation.
Serial deeper sections failed to reveal any evidence of either lymphoma or melanoma, any granulomatous inflammation, and vasculitis or monocytoid histiocytes, thus ruling out the above mentioned conditions. Drug induced hypersensitivity reactions in a lymph node especially due to phenytoin are known in the form of inter follicular expansion by a mixed infiltrate of immunoblasts, plasma cells and eosinophils with varying degrees of vascular proliferation. Focal necrosis has also been observed. Other drugs have been reported to show reactive change. These changes were not seen in the present case in the non-infarcted lymph nodes. In the present case it appears that infarction of the lymph node occurred before the DIC became clinically evident.
A completely infarcted lymph node should alert the pathologist to the high possibility of malignant lymphoma, as it is the most common cause of spontaneous lymph node infarction. Further investigation can be carried out by taking multiple deeper sections of the infarcted lymph node to visualize the viable subcapsular tissue for any clue of malignancy. Immunohistochemistry has been done on the infarcted lymph node sections to establish the underlying pathology. Although it is widely believed that necrotic tissue is not suitable for immunohistochemical study, this view may be inaccurate. 
The detection of spontaneous lymph node infarction should alert the pathologist and the clinician alike for an associated or underlying impending pathology. In a multicentre study of 51 cases of lymph-node infarction seen in the 30-year period, Maurer et al identified 14 cases of malignant lymphoma synchronously with the infarct. Of the remaining 37 patients, six showed manifestations of malignant lymphoma in the follow-up period within 2 years of the lymph-node infarction.
On analyzing other cases in the literature these authors also confirmed that a minority (26 of 81) have developed malignant lymphoma, which appeared within 2 years of infarction. Therefore, a thorough examination of both the infarcted lymph nodes and others resected at the same time is mandatory in order to exclude concomitant or underlying malignant lymphoma. The risk of development of malignant lymphoma after infarction was found to be negligible after two years.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male presented with fever with rigors, sore throat, myalgia, and recurrent vomiting for 10 days, followed by a diffuse rash.

Following admission and initiation of ceftriaxone, he abruptly developed cyanosis, hypotensive shock, and acute renal failure requiring inotropic and ventilatory resuscitation.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of gout treated with allopurinol for 20 days, and receipt of phenytoin for an episode of sudden loss of consciousness at an outside hospital. No past history of tuberculosis, diabetes mellitus, or hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, chills, rigors, sore throat, generalized myalgias, recurrent vomiting, and generalized rash. Denied joint swelling or chronic cough.

objective.physical_examination: Patient appeared toxic with marked bilateral conjunctival congestion. Examination revealed bilateral hard, indurated cervical lymphadenopathy, bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, and bilateral parotid and submandibular salivary gland enlargement. Developed cyanosis and profound hypotensive shock during hospitalization.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood counts: Normal hemoglobin and red blood cell morphology, transient neutrophilic leukocytosis, and normal platelet counts and erythrocyte sedimentation rate throughout hospitalization.
Renal & coagulation tests: Acute renal failure with elevated blood urea/creatinine; positive serum D-dimer (>200 ng/mL).
Microbiology & infectious serologies: Sterile blood, throat swab, and urine cultures. Serologies negative for acute EBV (IgM negative, IgG positive), cytomegalovirus, Leptospira, Widal test, Brucella abortus/melitensis, HIV, Paul-Bunnell test, and Weil-Felix reaction.
Abdominal ultrasound: Hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Excisional cervical lymph node biopsy and histopathology: Four lymph nodes examined (largest 1.5 cm); two demonstrated near-total parenchymal coagulative necrosis/infarction with preservation of cellular outlines, a thin rim of viable subcapsular mature lymphocytes, neutrophils, and plasma cells, and multiple fibrin thrombi within congested perinodal blood vessels. Acid-fast and fungal stains were negative. Immunohistochemistry (CD20 and CD3) confirmed preserved mixed B- and T-cell architecture without monoclonal expansion, ruling out malignant lymphoma, Kikuchi's necrotizing lymphadenitis, and phenytoin hypersensitivity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue virus infection presenting with spontaneous hemorrhagic lymph node infarction, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and shock syndrome, confirmed by positive Dengue virus IgM ELISA and elevated D-dimer. Malignant lymphoma, Kikuchi lymphadenitis, drug-induced hypersensitivity, Epstein-Barr virus, CMV, leptospirosis, and bacterial sepsis were ruled out.
Treatment and outcome: Managed aggressively in the intensive care unit with inotropic support, systemic corticosteroids, intravenous fluids, and broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftazidime and amoxicillin). The patient stabilized, renal function recovered, lymphadenopathy completely regressed, and he was asymptomatic at 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: Patient 5: 68-year-old male, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia, attending the emergency department for increased dyspnoea in the last 48 h, together with cough and dark expectoration. His blood pressure was 112/81, heart rate 82 beats per minute, SpO2 95%, and elevated D-Dimer levels. Chest X-ray: He had a small nodular infiltrate in the upper left lobe suggesting an infectious process. The radiological pattern was indicative of emphysema (two-basal, varicose bronchiectasis in left hemithorax). Confirmation of COVID-19 was made by RT-PCR using a throat swab. He was treated with hydroxychloroquine (for 5 days), risperidone, lopinavir-ritonavir and lithium carbonate (first dose on day 12, 200 mg/12 h and second dose on day 15, with 600 mg/12 h). The patient was discharged 9 days later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old male presented to the emergency department with increased dyspnoea for 48 hours, cough, and dark expectoration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 68-year-old male presented to the emergency department with increased dyspnoea in the last 48 hours, together with cough and dark expectoration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure 112/81 mmHg, heart rate 82 beats per minute, SpO2 95%.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated D-Dimer levels. Chest X-ray: Small nodular infiltrate in the upper left lobe suggesting an infectious process; radiological pattern was indicative of emphysema (two-basal, varicose bronchiectasis in left hemithorax).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation of COVID-19 was made by RT-PCR using a throat swab. He was treated with hydroxychloroquine (for 5 days), risperidone, lopinavir-ritonavir, and lithium carbonate (first dose on day 12, 200 mg/12 h and second dose on day 15, with 600 mg/12 h). The patient was discharged 9 days later.

raw_case_text: In February 2016, a male in his 40s was admitted to the neurology department of a hospital in Paramaribo, Suriname, because of muscle weakness in the legs, which started 7 days prior to admission. At presentation in the hospital, the patient was unable to walk without help. Two weeks before muscle weakness started he visited the hospital because of urinary retention. Acute myelitis and a cauda syndrome were excluded with an MRI-scan, which showed no abnormalities. The week before muscle weakness started he had an influenza-like syndrome and had a short episode of diplopia. At first physical examination after admission, muscle weakness was observed in predominantly the legs (MRC score 4). Areflexia in both legs and arms was noted. The patient complained of paresthesias and pain in the legs but did not have a sensory level or other signs of myelum involvement. A lumbar puncture was performed 2 days after admission, and a high protein level was found in the CSF (4.4 g/L) while the cell count was slightly increased (32.7 x 106/L). A urine sample, taken at day two after admission, was tested positive for ZIKV RNA with a Ct-value of 35.7. Four days after admission his muscle power improved (MCR score arms 5, legs; proximal 5, distal 4), while the areflexia in arms and legs persisted. Because of the little availability of IVIg in Suriname and because PE is not possible in Suriname, the patient did not received immunotherapy. A motor NCS, performed 15 days after the start of muscle weakness, showed severe decreased NCV and a prolonged DML in all tested nerves. The CMAP was decreased in predominantly the legs (see Table S2 in Supplementary Material). These results were consistent with the demyelinating subtype of GBS. At discharge, 7 days after admission, he was still unable to walk without help due to muscle weakness in the legs. Four months after hospital discharge he was able to walk a few steps without assistance, but he still could not live independently or return to work.

subjective.chief_complaint: Male in his 40s presenting with progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness for 7 days, resulting in inability to ambulate unassisted.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three weeks prior to admission, the patient presented with acute urinary retention. Two weeks later (one week before admission), he experienced an influenza-like illness and a transient episode of diplopia. Seven days prior to admission, he developed progressive muscle weakness in both legs, culminating in inability to walk without assistance upon hospital presentation. He reported paresthesias and pain in both legs. Four days post-admission, motor strength showed slight improvement, but areflexia persisted.
subjective.past_medical_history: Episode of acute urinary retention 3 weeks prior to admission; resident of Paramaribo, Suriname.
subjective.review_of_systems: Transient diplopia, paresthesias and pain in bilateral lower extremities; denies sensory level or bowel dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: At admission: Predominant lower extremity muscle weakness (MRC score 4/5); generalized areflexia in bilateral upper and lower extremities; no sensory level or signs of spinal cord involvement. Four days post-admission: Muscle strength improved (MRC score arms 5/5; legs proximal 5/5, distal 4/5), with persistent areflexia in all four extremities. At discharge (day 7): Unable to walk without assistance.
objective.advanced_workup: MRI scan of the spine (performed 2 weeks prior to weakness onset): No abnormalities, excluding acute myelitis and cauda equina syndrome. Lumbar puncture (day 2 post-admission): Cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated elevated protein (4.4 g/L) and slightly increased cell count (32.7 x 10^6/L). Motor nerve conduction study (NCS) (day 15 post-onset): Severely decreased nerve conduction velocity (NCV) and prolonged distal motor latency (DML) across all tested nerves, with decreased compound muscle action potential (CMAP) predominantly in the lower extremities, consistent with the demyelinating subtype of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy subtype) associated with acute Zika virus infection, confirmed by detection of ZIKV RNA in urine collected on day 2 post-admission (Ct value 35.7). The patient did not receive intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) or plasma exchange due to local unavailability. Managed supportively; at discharge (day 7) he remained unable to ambulate unassisted. At 4-month follow-up, he could walk a few steps without assistance but was unable to live independently or return to work.

raw_case_text:
Further history revealed that among the family of four members, his 53-year-old paternal grandmother was a known case of HIV infection and receiving antiretroviral therapy since January 2013. Her existing documented medical records showed an absolute CD4+ count of 123 cells/mm3(13.9%) and plasma viral load of 11,612 copies/ml at the initiation of cART, which consisted of tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. Her plasma viral load was undetectable reflecting her excellent adherence in September 2015. The paternal grandmother was the primary caregiver of the child at home as both the parents were working. She helped him in feeding, giving a bath, and other routine activities. The child was treated with cART consisting of zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine from October 2015 and followed periodically.
The investigation of this child was further done at the National AIDS Research Institute, Pune, India, through interviews with the available involved adults and through a review of the available documented medical records. Written informed consent for HIV testing and other-related tests was obtained from adult family members, while in case of a child, assent was obtained from his parents. HIV testing was performed as recommended by the WHO. Blood specimens from the child and HIV-infected parental grandmother were used for the amplification and sequencing of HIV-1 partial pol regions.
The pol gene sequence analysis showed 97.18% (94.37% nucleotide identity) amino acid identity between HIV strain from the child and his paternal grandmother. Phylodynamic analysis showed clustering of both the sequences at one node with posterior probability of 1.0, implying that the paternal grandmother was probably the source of HIV-1 infection [Figure 1].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3.5-year-old male presenting for molecular epidemiological evaluation of non-vertical retroviral transmission and initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Following the diagnosis of advanced retroviral infection in a young child with seronegative parents, extended epidemiological screening identified the primary household caregiver (paternal grandmother) as a known retroviral patient on long-term therapy. The child was referred to a national research institute for molecular sequencing and phylogenetic transmission tracking, and commenced on pediatric combination therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pediatric retroviral infection presenting with recurrent respiratory infections and severe immunosuppression. Epidemiological exposure: Primary daytime childcare provided by the 53-year-old paternal grandmother (known HIV-1 infection on tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz since January 2013; baseline CD4 123 cells/microL, viral load 11,612 copies/mL; undetectable viral load by September 2015) who assisted with bathing, feeding, and daily activities.

objective.advanced_workup: Molecular phylogenetic and sequencing analysis (partial pol gene): HIV-1 pol gene sequence comparison between the child and his paternal grandmother demonstrated 97.18% amino acid identity and 94.37% nucleotide identity; Bayesian phylodynamic analysis demonstrated monophyletic clustering at a single node with a posterior probability of 1.0.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Pediatric HIV-1 infection confirmed to be transmitted non-vertically from the primary caregiver (paternal grandmother) via phylogenetic and partial pol gene sequencing (posterior probability 1.0).
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on pediatric combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) consisting of zidovudine, lamivudine, and nevirapine in October 2015 with periodic clinical, immunological, and virological monitoring.

raw_case_text: An 18-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus presented with focal convulsions in September 2012. She was detected to have multiple tuberculomas. Biopsy of one of the lesion grew MTB. She was on second-line ATT since September 2012 as drug-sensitivity testing (DST) of the tuberculous lesion showed resistance to isoniazid (INH), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), ethambutol (E), moxifloxacin (Mfx), ofloxacin (Ofx) and ethionamide (Eth). Her cererbrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was normal. She was put on capreomycin, PAS, cycloserine (Cys), clofazimine and linezolid (Lnz) along with carbamazepine and levetiracetam and prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for 30 days and then tapered off in next 1 month). In February 2013, she had moderate sensorineural hearing loss, and capreomycin was omitted. Her serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain till August 2013 showed decrease in size and number of the granulomas in the frontal periventricular parenchyma bilaterally, but the left frontoparietal granuloma remained the same. In February 2014, Lnz and Cys were stopped and clarithromycin was added due to tingling and numbness in the right leg. In February 2015, computed tomography (CT) brain still showed presence of left frontal granuloma. In May 2015, her ATT was stopped, as she had completed 2 years 6 months of therapy and was asymptomatic except for persistence of left frontal granuloma. In April 2016 (Figure 1), granulomas remained the same in the frontal parenchyma, while the rest of the lesions had calcified, but the patient remained asymptomatic.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old female with type 1 diabetes mellitus presented with focal convulsions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in September 2012 with new-onset focal convulsions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus.

objective.advanced_workup: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination: normal. Serial brain MRI (through August 2013): multiple bilateral frontal periventricular and left frontoparietal parenchymal granulomas, demonstrating regression in size and number of frontal periventricular lesions while the left frontoparietal lesion remained stable. Brain CT (February 2015): persistent left frontal granuloma. Follow-up imaging (April 2016): stable frontal parenchymal granulomas with calcification of the remaining lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Extensively drug-resistant central nervous system tuberculomas (Mycobacterium tuberculosis). Biopsy of an intracranial lesion grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis; drug-sensitivity testing (DST) confirmed resistance to isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, moxifloxacin, ofloxacin, and ethionamide.
Treatment and course: Initiated on second-line antitubercular therapy consisting of capreomycin, para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), cycloserine, clofazimine, and linezolid, alongside carbamazepine, levetiracetam, and oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day for 30 days, then tapered over 1 month). In February 2013, capreomycin was discontinued due to moderate sensorineural hearing loss. In February 2014, linezolid and cycloserine were discontinued and clarithromycin was substituted due to peripheral neuropathy (right leg tingling and numbness). Antitubercular therapy was successfully completed and discontinued in May 2015 after 2.5 years; at follow-up in April 2016, the patient remained clinically asymptomatic with calcification of intracranial lesions.

raw_case_text: A-3 months-old-boy presented with severe malnutrition, known cholestatic jaundice diagnosed as congenital cytomegalovirus infection and contact of his father who was diagnosed with MDR-TB but was not compliant with his treatment. His tuberculin skin test was positive, chest radiograph revealed right perihilar infiltrate and X-pert MTB/RIF on gastric aspirate was positive for M. tuberculosis complex with resistance to rifampicin. Other baseline investigations revealed a small atrial septal defect on echocardiography, mild to moderate hearing loss on audiology, normal vision and retinas on ophthalmological evaluation, raised bilirubin and liver enzymes (alanine and aspartate transaminases) and positive cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM with a negative CMV PCR. He was HIV-unexposed and his HIV ELISA was negative, but CD4% was low (19%). Culture of the gastric aspirate eventually was positive, confirming M. tuberculosis resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin on line-probe assay as well as resistant to second-line injectable agents with second-line LPA, but susceptible to the fluoroquinolones. He was therefore confirmed as pre-XDR-TB. The mother's sputum was X-pert MTB/RIF negative. The chest x-ray showed active tuberculosis with infiltrates at the right upper-middle lung field with an increased of bronchovascular marking (Fig. 1). We treated him with five kind of less hepatotoxic anti tuberculosis drugs by individualized treatment based on the updated WHO 2018 guidelines. He commenced the treatment with moxifloxacin (10 mg/kg/day divided in tow dose), linezolid (10 mg/kg/day once daily), cycloserin (10 mg/kg/day once daily), ethambutol (20 mg/kg/day once daily) and para-aminosalysilic acid (200 mg/kg/day divided in two dose). After seven days receiving the pre- XDR-TB treatment, the liver enzymes improved, no adverse reaction such as vomiting, dhiarrea was reported. He also recieved gancyclovir for the CMV infection. He was followed every one month, he shows weight increment to 5.8 kg from 3.6 kg in 3 months and increased gradually every month. His nutritional status improved to normal from severe malnutrition after 20 months of treatment. No adverse reaction such as vomiting nor dhiarrea was reported. The growth and milestones development were appropriate. Laboratory evaluation showed improvement of liver function. Hematologic and neurologic (peripheral and toxic optic neuropathy) adverse effects were monitored during linezolid treatment. No anemia nor thrombocytopenia was found. For the optic toxic neuropathy evaluation, normal vision was concluded through examination of response to light, pupil response, ability to follow a target and ophthalmoscopy examination of the retina was also done to exclude CMV retinitis symptom and the result was normal. The M.tuberculosis culture evaluation result was negative on the first and third month of treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-month-old male infant presented with severe malnutrition, cholestatic jaundice, and known household contact with his father who had drug-resistant tuberculosis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 3-month-old infant was brought for clinical evaluation due to failure to thrive, severe malnutrition, and persistent jaundice. He had a prior diagnosis of congenital cytomegalovirus infection. Epidemiological investigation revealed close household contact with his father, who had diagnosed multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and was non-compliant with therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection with cholestatic jaundice. Close household contact of father with non-compliant MDR-TB. Mother's sputum tested negative on GeneXpert. No prior antibiotic therapy reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports severe failure to thrive, malnutrition, jaundice; denies vomiting, diarrhea, cough, or respiratory distress. Home medications: none prior to admission. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Severe malnutrition (body weight 3.6 kg). Cutaneous and scleral icterus present. Ophthalmology: normal vision and retinas without evidence of retinitis. Audiology: mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss. Cardiac: normal heart sounds with soft systolic murmur. Normal developmental milestones for age.
objective.routine_investigations: Tuberculin skin test (TST): positive. Total bilirubin, AST, and ALT: elevated. CMV IgM: positive; CMV PCR: negative. HIV ELISA: negative (HIV-unexposed); CD4%: 19% (low). Echocardiography: small atrial septal defect. Chest radiograph: active pulmonary infiltrates in right upper-middle lung field, right perihilar infiltrate, and increased bronchovascular markings.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Early infantile pre-extensively drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (pre-XDR-TB) and congenital cytomegalovirus infection with cholestatic jaundice.
Confirmation: Gastric aspirate Xpert MTB/RIF was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex with rifampicin resistance. Gastric aspirate culture confirmed M. tuberculosis resistant to isoniazid and rifampicin on line-probe assay (LPA) and resistant to second-line injectable agents on second-line LPA, but susceptible to fluoroquinolones (pre-XDR-TB). Tuberculin skin test was positive. Sputum Xpert MTB/RIF of mother was negative.
Differentials ruled out: HIV infection (HIV ELISA negative, HIV-unexposed), CMV retinitis (normal retinal exam).
Treatment & Outcome: Commenced on an individualized 5-drug less-hepatotoxic regimen per WHO 2018 guidelines: moxifloxacin (10 mg/kg/day divided BID), linezolid (10 mg/kg/day once daily), cycloserine (10 mg/kg/day once daily), ethambutol (20 mg/kg/day once daily), and para-aminosalicylic acid (200 mg/kg/day divided BID), alongside ganciclovir for CMV. Liver enzymes normalized within 7 days. Monthly monitoring demonstrated weight gain from 3.6 kg to 5.8 kg at 3 months, and full nutritional recovery after 20 months of therapy without optic, hematologic, or gastrointestinal toxicity. Gastric aspirate M. tuberculosis cultures converted to negative at months 1 and 3.

raw_case_text:
Forty-nine days after receiving his second dose of SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccine BNT162b2 a 42-year old, otherwise healthy male tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 in a rapid antigen test, which was confirmed in a laryngopharyngeal swab by RT-PCR for two viral targets (E and S genes as previously described), two days later (see Figure 1). All four members of the household equally tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 (the two children 9 days before the individual whose case is presented here, and the wife 10 days after that) and all individuals had asymptomatic infections, except for the wife who reported one mild symptom (loss of sense of taste). At the time of her first positive test she had been vaccinated once with ChAdOx1-S (AstraZeneca) 3 weeks prior. Subsequent sequential testing of the male subject for SARS-CoV-2 RNA demonstrated an increase in viral load with a peak at day 6 after the first positive SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test. The first negative test was confirmed on day 10. Virus Propagation showed high titers after 5 day culture on Caco-2 cells (E gene RT-PCR Ct = 9.44, S gene Ct = 14.53) and capable productively infecting and lysing 100% of VeroE6 cells in 3 days (E gene Ct = 14.28, S gene Ct = 13.23). NextGen Sequencing using the Qiagen protocol on a miSeq (Illumina) platform identified the virus from the laropharyngeal swab as SARS-CoV-2 B.1.525, identical to the reference sequence EPI_ISL_1571188, except for three silent base substitutions in the spike gene (A23746G, T24070C, and G25767T). This variant had been detected at varying but low frequencies in the German population in recent months, but remained a minor variant under investigation.
We next investigated the ability of SARS-CoV-2 recognition by the vaccine-induced immune responses. Using the Roche whole antibody ELISA (spike subdomain S1-specific) we first detected anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies 16 days after the first vaccination. Maximum levels were reached 9 days after the second vaccination (Figure 1). To determine the patient's ability to recognize and neutralize the SARS-CoV-2 variant B.1.525 as well as other variants we performed plaque reduction neutralization assays as previously described. We longitudinally tested plasma from the patient in the neutralization assays against four major SARS-CoV-2 variants B.3, B.1.117 (alpha variant), B.1.351 (beta), and B.1.525 (eta). Surprisingly, the plasma was equally capable of neutralizing B.1.525 virus as the other variants with slightly lower NT activity against B.1.351 (see Figure 2). Overall we observed a general trend for an increase in neutralization between day 5 and 13 after SARS-CoV-2 breakthrough infection (Figure 3). This boost detected in neutralization capacities of the individual's plasma from day 5 to day 13 was similar irrespective of the virus tested, i.e., at least a doubling of the NT90 values was observed against all four virus variants. Surprisingly, in these neutralizing samples no nucleocapsid (N)-specific antibodies could be detected up to 20 days after infection (Figure 1, Roche Elecsys  Anti-SARS-CoV-2 immunoassay and Supplementary Figure 1), while spike (S)-specific antibodies stayed at the highest detectable levels or above (Euroimmun SARS-CoV-2 ELISA).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting asymptomatic following a positive rapid antigen screening test.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 42-year-old male who remained completely asymptomatic throughout his clinical course. Forty-nine days after receiving his second dose of mRNA vaccine, he underwent screening due to known household exposures and tested positive on rapid antigen testing, which was confirmed on follow-up molecular testing two days later. Longitudinal viral monitoring demonstrated peak viral load on day 6 and complete viral clearance by day 10.
subjective.past_medical_history: Otherwise healthy with no chronic medical conditions. Vaccination history: Received two doses of mRNA vaccine (BNT162b2), with the second dose administered 49 days prior to positive testing. Epidemiological exposure: Household contact with three infected family members (two children testing positive 9 days prior).
subjective.review_of_systems: Review of systems was negative for fever, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, anosmia, ageusia, or gastrointestinal symptoms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 vaccine breakthrough infection caused by the B.1.525 (Eta) variant, confirmed by RT-PCR for viral E and S genes from a laryngopharyngeal swab.
Virological, Sequencing & Serological Confirmation: High viral titers were isolated after 5-day culture on Caco-2 cells (E gene Ct 9.44, S gene Ct 14.53) with complete cytolysis of VeroE6 cells in 3 days (E gene Ct 14.28, S gene Ct 13.23). Next-generation sequencing (Illumina MiSeq) identified SARS-CoV-2 lineage B.1.525 (Eta variant) with three silent spike substitutions (A23746G, T24070C, and G25767T). Roche whole antibody ELISA demonstrated anti-S1 spike antibodies persisting at peak levels; plaque reduction neutralization assays demonstrated neutralizing titers against B.3, B.1.117 (Alpha), B.1.351 (Beta), and B.1.525 (Eta) with at least doubling of NT90 titers between days 5 and 13 post-infection; anti-nucleocapsid (N) antibodies remained undetectable up to 20 days post-infection (Roche Elecsys).
Plan & Outcome: Outpatient home isolation and serial clinical, virological, and serological surveillance. No pharmacological therapy was required. The patient remained entirely asymptomatic with documented viral clearance by day 10.

raw_case_text:
Patient 2 was a 3-year-old girl who presented with 3 days of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and retroorbital headache. There had been one episode of gum bleeding on the first day of illness. She had been apparently a well child without any significant illnesses in the past. WBC count done on day 2, on request of the general practitioner, was 8.15 x 103 with 85% neutrophils and platelet count was 120,000 mm3. She had right hypochondrial tenderness with just palpable liver on day 5. ALT and AST were 16 mEq/L and 69.7 mEq/L, respectively, on day 3 and they increased to 29.7 mEq/L and 122.2 mEq/L on day 5. Initial C-reactive protein was 6 mg/dL and remained normal. She was monitored for vital signs including urine output and packed cell volume (PCV). Baseline PCV was 32 and the highest noted was 35. The lowest platelet count documented was 67,000/mm3 and the lowest WBC count was 2.27 x 103. She did not show signs of fluid leakage. However, there was a second episode of gum bleeding on day 5 with normal clotting profile (INR: 1.1 and APTT: 35). She was positive for IgM and negative for IgG antibodies for dengue virus.
On the 5th day of illness, she developed tremors in her upper limbs. She had cogwheel rigidity, mask like face, and staccato speech. Power was grade four in all four limbs with normal reflexes. CT scan of brain revealed diffuse hypodense areas in bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus with predominant involvement of right side (Figure 2). During the first 48 hours after the onset of neurological symptoms, she showed rapid deterioration and became aphasic with severe paucity of movements. Cerebrospinal fluid examination showed 2 lymphocytes without any polymorphs and normal proteins. She recovered dramatically and showed complete recovery within 3 weeks after onset of illness.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3-year-old girl presenting with a 3-day history of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, retro-orbital headache, and gum bleeding.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 3-year-old girl presented with 3 days of continuous high fever, intermittent abdominal pain, vomiting, and retro-orbital headache, accompanied by an episode of gum bleeding on day 1. On illness day 5, she experienced a second episode of gum bleeding and acutely developed upper limb tremors, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like facies, and staccato speech, rapidly deteriorating over the subsequent 48 hours into aphasia and severe paucity of movement. No clinical signs of plasma leakage were observed.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously well child with no significant illnesses in the past.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, gum bleeding, tremors, rigidity, and loss of speech. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Day 5: Right hypochondrial tenderness with a palpable liver edge. Neurological examination: Upper extremity tremors, cogwheel rigidity, mask-like face, staccato speech progressing to aphasia and severe paucity of movements; motor power grade 4/5 across all four limbs with preserved normal deep tendon reflexes. Vital signs stable without fluid leakage.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 2: WBC 8.15 x 10^3/muL (85% neutrophils), platelets 120,000/mm3. Day 3: ALT 16 mEq/L, AST 69.7 mEq/L. Day 5: Lowest platelets 67,000/mm3, lowest WBC 2.27 x 10^3/muL, ALT 29.7 mEq/L, AST 122.2 mEq/L, CRP 6 mg/dL (normal), coagulation profile: INR 1.1, aPTT 35 sec. Packed cell volume (PCV): Baseline 32%, peak 35%.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT scan: Diffuse hypodense areas in bilateral basal ganglia and thalamus with predominant involvement of the right side. Lumbar puncture / CSF examination: 2 lymphocytes, 0 polymorphonuclear cells, normal protein concentration.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue encephalitis / parkinsonian neurodengue presenting with extrapyramidal features (cogwheel rigidity, tremors, mask-like facies, mutism) and bilateral basal ganglia/thalamic CT hypodensities. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus IgM antibodies and negative IgG antibodies, confirming primary acute dengue infection; CSF pleocytosis absent with normal protein.
Plan & Outcome: Supportive management with close clinical monitoring of vital signs and fluid balance. Neurological signs resolved dramatically, leading to complete clinical and neurological recovery within 3 weeks of illness onset.

raw_case_text: A 37-year-old foreign domestic worker with no history of major infection and 3 previous vaginal births presented with a one-week history of suprapubic pain associated with fever. The patient also experienced loss of appetite and loss of weight. On examination, she was tachycardic with high-grade fever of 38.9 C. Abdomen examination revealed tenderness over her suprapubic area; however, pelvic examination showed no abnormality. Her total white cell count was 5.9 x 109/L, with predominantly lymphocytes (16.5 x 109/L) and monocytes (2.6 x 109/L). Her C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were elevated at 29.9 mg/dl and 100 mm/Hr. Chest radiograph showed bilateral perihilar opacities which could represent enlarged hilar nodes. There was no evidence of fibrosis, pleural effusion, or infective changes (Figure 1). Ultrasound scan showed presence of right complex mass measured 12 x 6 x 6 cm with minimal free fluid at the pouch of Douglas. Cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) was elevated at 97 u/ml. Working diagnosis of tuboovarian abscess was made, and she was treated with a broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic. Despite 48 hours of parenteral antibiotic, she did not improve clinically. After discussion, she opted for exploratory laparotomy. There were moderate amount of ascitic fluid with the presence of slough and cheesy materials covering the entire abdominal and pelvic cavities. However, there was no tubercle noted over the peritoneal surface. There was a right ovarian cyst measuring 12 x 6 cm and features suggestive of a mature cystic teratoma. Right salpingo-oophorectomy was performed (Figure 2). Peritoneal fluid cytology showed no malignant cells, and there was no acid-fast bacilli (AFB) seen on AFB staining. Mycobacterium culture did not yield any positive AFB even after 6 weeks. In view of high index of suspicion for TB, peritoneal fluid was also sent for polymerase chain reaction (semiauto TB PCR machine, Rotor-Gene Q , Qiagen) testing, which was positive for NTM but negative for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Bronchoalveolar lavage was done as the patient was unable to produce sputum, which was negative for TB as well. Infective screening such as HIV, venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL), and hepatitis was nonreactive. Histopathological examination confirmed a right mature cystic teratoma. She remained well postoperatively and completed intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole for 10 days. She was initially planned for anti-TB (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and streptomycin) following positive PCR testing for NTB. However, upon discharge, she was sent back to home town immediately by her employer. Hence, we have no further information about her progress.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old female presented with a 1-week history of suprapubic pain, high-grade fever, loss of appetite, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old female domestic worker presented with a 1-week history of worsening suprapubic abdominal pain accompanied by high-grade fever, anorexia, and weight loss. She had no relief after 48 hours of broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics for presumed tubo-ovarian abscess, prompting surgical exploration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Foreign domestic worker; para 3 (3 previous spontaneous vaginal deliveries). No history of major infections or tuberculosis contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for suprapubic pain, high-grade fever, anorexia, and weight loss. Negative for abnormal vaginal discharge or bleeding. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Tachycardic, febrile with temperature of 38.9 °C. Abdomen: marked tenderness over suprapubic region. Pelvic examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count 5.9 x 109/L (predominantly lymphocytes 16.5 x 109/L, monocytes 2.6 x 109/L), CRP 29.9 mg/dL, ESR 100 mm/h. Cancer antigen 125 (CA-125) elevated at 97 U/mL. Serologic screening for HIV, syphilis (VDRL), and viral hepatitis non-reactive. Chest radiograph: bilateral perihilar opacities suggestive of hilar adenopathy, without pulmonary infiltrates, cavities, or pleural effusion. Pelvic ultrasound: 12 x 6 x 6 cm right complex adnexal mass with minimal free fluid in pouch of Douglas.
objective.advanced_workup: Exploratory laparotomy with right salpingo-oophorectomy: cheesy exudate coating abdominal and pelvic cavities without discrete peritoneal tubercles; 12 x 6 cm right ovarian mass. Histopathology confirmed benign mature cystic teratoma. Peritoneal fluid cytology negative for malignant cells; acid-fast staining showed no acid-fast bacilli; 6-week mycobacterial cultures were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Mature cystic teratoma of the right ovary with coexisting pelvic/peritoneal mycobacterial infection, confirmed by ovarian histopathology demonstrating benign mature cystic teratoma and peritoneal fluid PCR (Rotor-Gene Q) testing positive for non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) while negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Acid-fast stains and 6-week mycobacterial cultures were negative. Initial presentation mimicked tubo-ovarian abscess and peritoneal tuberculosis. Management & Outcome: Treated surgically with right salpingo-oophorectomy and completed a 10-day course of intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, streptomycin) was planned based on positive mycobacterial PCR, but the patient was repatriated to her home country upon discharge.

raw_case_text: On hospital day 1, despite continued management, he showed no significant improvement with an elevated uric acid of 13.8 mg/dL. His renal function remained severely compromised with persistent severe metabolic acidosis; creatine kinase (CK) remained elevated at 2185 U/L with continued electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypermagnesemia). Chest X-ray showed persistent patchy peripheral infiltrates in the right lung with lesser patchy peripheral infiltrates just above the left lung base (Figure 2). Given his intractable acidosis, a hemodialysis catheter was placed for emergent dialysis. Lopinavir and ritonavir were held due to nephrotoxicity. Viral HIV load was low at 47 HIV-1 RNA copies/mL. Patient was closely monitored in supplementary ICU area until discharged on hospital day 7.

subjective.chief_complaint: A male inpatient presenting with acute renal failure, persistent intractable metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and severe electrolyte abnormalities on hospital day one.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient demonstrated lack of clinical improvement on hospital day 1 of admission, developing severe acute kidney injury, intractable metabolic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and rhabdomyolysis accompanied by persistent bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral condition managed with lopinavir/ritonavir (held on hospital day 1); active respiratory illness and severe metabolic decompensation.

objective.physical_examination: Inpatient ICU monitoring: Intractable metabolic derangement and respiratory compromise.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum biochemistry: Uric acid 13.8 mg/dL, creatine kinase (CK) 2185 U/L, persistent severe metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and hypermagnesemia. Chest X-ray: Persistent patchy peripheral infiltrates in the right lung with lesser patchy peripheral infiltrates just above the left lung base.
objective.advanced_workup: Vascular access: Hemodialysis catheter placed for emergent renal replacement therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute kidney injury with intractable metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis (CK 2185 U/L, hyperuricemia 13.8 mg/dL, multiple electrolyte disturbances), and bilateral pneumonia in a patient with virologically controlled human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; plasma HIV-1 RNA viral load 47 copies/mL).
Management & Outcome: Lopinavir and ritonavir were discontinued due to nephrotoxicity. A hemodialysis catheter was placed and emergent hemodialysis was initiated for refractory acidosis and uremia. The patient was managed in a supplementary intensive care unit with supportive therapy and clinical stabilization, successfully discharged on hospital day 7.

raw_case_text: Patient 4: 54-year-old male, healthy carrier of the hepatitis B virus, attending the emergency department for bilateral pneumonia, fever and with respiratory failure. He was treated with lithium carbonate (400mg/12h). The patient was discharged after 18 days.

raw_case_text: A 42-year-old man presented with a six-month history of nonbloody diarrhea associated with the clinical triad of fever, splenomegaly, and pancytopenia. Anti-Leishmania antibodies serological tests (indirect immunofluorescence title 1 : 640 and rapid test with the recombinant k39) were positive. The diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis was firmed by the detection of amastigotes in a bone marrow aspirate smears. Because of upper gastrointestinal symptoms (mild dysphagia and vomiting), an esophagogastroduodenoscopy was performed, revealing in duodenum the presence of erosions coated with fibrin, plates of enanthema, and thickened pleats with small whitish spots distributed diffusely. In a tissue fragment obtained by biopsy, the duodenal mucosa showed villous enlarged and filled with numerous histiocytes packed with intracytoplasmic round structures with morphology suggestive of amastigotes of Leishmania spp. The patient received liposomal amphotericin B, 4 mg/kg of body weight during 5 days with complete improvement of visceromegaly, fever and recovery of white blood cell and platelets counts. After treatment and hospital discharge, diarrhea and anemia persisted, and his condition continued to deteriorate. Four months later the patient was admitted once again to hospital with worsening diarrhea, dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and electrolyte imbalance. Blood tests revealed a normochromic normocytic anemia, profound hipoalbuminemia (1.9 g/dL), and a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (120 mm/1 hour). Laboratory examinations also revealed low serum folic acid and iron levels. Both vitamins were replaced and nutritional support was beginning. This time, an extensive search for parasites in stool microscopy was done and eggs of S. mansoni were identified on stool microscopy. The patient was treated with praziquantel 60 mg/kg of body weight. After four weeks, diarrhea remained unchanged, and his condition continued to deteriorate with anorexia and weight loss. Abdominal computer tomography showed mild splenomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, and a normal liver size. There was mild dilatation of intestinal loops of the colon. A bone marrow aspiration was also performed showing only reactive changes and no Leishmania amastigotes. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) assessment on whole blood and bone marrow samples showed positive results using the ribosomal RNA small subunit gene (SSU rRNA) from Leishmania spp. as DNA target. Patient's lymphocyte counts were TCD4+: 539/mm3, TCD8+: 503/mm3 e TCD3+: 1,094/mm3. A colonoscopy was normal. Despite the absence of symptoms of upper gastrointestinal system, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, and it showed the presence of diffuse pallor in stomach and duodenum with swollen appearance without ulceration. Duodenal mucosa histopathology showed the persistence of amastigotes, as four months before (Figure 1). The immunohistochemical study confirmed the presence of numerous immunolabeled amastigotes forms of Leishmania (Figure 2). Tests to detect anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies, a protozoan also endemic in Brazil and with tropism for the gastrointestinal tract, and the anti-HIV testing were negative. The patient was treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate, 0.8 mg/kg of body weight for 30 days, and diarrhea resolved completely within two weeks. Two months after the end of treatment the patient had reached its normal weight and normalized erythrocyte levels. The plasmatic levels of IFN-gamma and IL-10 were measured before and after treatment by sandwich-enzyme-linked immuonosorbent assay, as previously described. The results were expressed as picograms per milliliter (pg/mL) based on a standard curve. IFN-gamma was undetectable before and after treatment, while IL-10 levels decreased from 36 pg/mL at initial evaluation to 16.3 pg/mL (55% reduction) after amphotericin treatment and clinical improvement.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presented with persistent worsening nonbloody diarrhea, dehydration, and weight loss 4 months following treatment for visceral leishmaniasis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient originally presented 10 months prior with a 6-month history of nonbloody diarrhea, fever, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, dysphagia, and vomiting. He received a 5-day course of liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg/day) with resolution of fever and cytopenias, but diarrhea and anemia persisted. Four months later, he was readmitted with severe chronic diarrhea, profound dehydration, metabolic acidosis, and progressive cachexia. A course of praziquantel for coinfection produced no improvement in diarrhea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated visceral leishmaniasis 4 months prior with liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg for 5 days). Schistosoma mansoni intestinal coinfection treated with praziquantel (60 mg/kg). Country of residence: Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports intractable nonbloody watery diarrhea, dehydration, anorexia, significant weight loss, mild dysphagia, and postprandial vomiting; denies current fevers.

objective.physical_examination: Patient appeared dehydrated and malnourished with metabolic distress. Abdominal examination revealed mild splenomegaly without hepatomegaly or peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed normocytic normochromic anemia. Serum albumin: 1.9 g/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 120 mm/1 hour; low serum folic acid and ferritin/iron levels. T-lymphocyte subsets: CD4+ count 539/mm^3, CD8+ count 503/mm^3, CD3+ count 1,094/mm^3. Stool microscopy: positive for Schistosoma mansoni ova. Anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies: negative. HIV serology: negative. Cytokines: plasma IFN-gamma was undetectable; IL-10 level was 36 pg/mL (decreasing to 16.3 pg/mL post-treatment).
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT scan: mild splenomegaly with normal liver size and no lymphadenopathy; mild dilatation of colonic loops. Initial bone marrow aspirate: reactive changes without intracellular organisms on light microscopy. Colonoscopy: normal colonic mucosa. Upper endoscopy (EGD): diffuse mucosal pallor and swollen appearance of the gastric and duodenal mucosa without ulceration. Duodenal mucosal biopsy: enlarged intestinal villi packed with histiocytic infiltrates containing intracellular protozoa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) targeting the Leishmania small subunit ribosomal RNA (SSU rRNA) gene was positive in whole blood and bone marrow aspirate. Repeat duodenal mucosal biopsy and immunohistochemistry demonstrated abundant immunolabeled Leishmania amastigotes within lamina propria histiocytes, confirming persistent gastrointestinal mucosal leishmaniasis. Anti-Leishmania rK39 rapid test and indirect immunofluorescence (titer 1:640) were positive. Chagas disease, HIV, and intestinal schistosomiasis (eradicated with praziquantel) excluded as causes of persistent diarrhea. Management and Outcome: Nutritional rehabilitation and electrolyte/acidosis correction were initiated with folic acid and iron supplementation. Re-treated with amphotericin B deoxycholate at 0.8 mg/kg/day for 30 days. Diarrhea resolved completely within 2 weeks of therapy initiation. At 2-month post-treatment follow-up, the patient regained baseline body weight and normalized hemoglobin and erythrocyte levels.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old female presented to the ED in March 2014 with complaints of a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and anorexia. On evaluation she had dry oral mucosa, and laboratory results demonstrated leukocytosis and elevated serum creatinine, amylase (130 units per liter [u/L]), and lipase (118 u/L). Ultrasound examination revealed evidence of cholelithiasis. The initial diagnostic impression was acute kidney injury with dehydration, IV piperacillin-tazobactam and IV fluids were initiated, and the patient was hospitalized.
On day 3 of hospitalization, the patient developed shortness of breath and had bibasilar crackles. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral confluent alveolar opacities. Echocardiogram demonstrated mild tricuspid and mitral valve regurgitation. Laboratory results demonstrated leukocytosis, a 15% drop in hematocrit, thrombocytopenia, and mildly elevated LFTs. Because of the onset of pulmonary edema, developing acute respiratory distress syndrome and concerns of respiratory tract infection, the patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and placed on oxygen supplementation. Furosemide was given, and antimicrobial therapy was changed to include azithromycin, imipenem, trimethoprine-sulfamethoxazole, linezolid, and oseltamivir. Laboratory results demonstrated worsening leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia and prominently elevated LFTs and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (9,976 u/L).
The following day she was feeling better, but with mild shortness of breath and continued bibasilar crackles. She continued to improve daily thereafter, was transferred to the regular ward on the seventh hospitalization day, and was discharged home on the 12th day of hospitalization.
All blood and sputum cultures were negative. A serum specimen drawn on the sixth day of symptoms (third day of hospitalization) was negative for Leptospira IgM antibody test performed at a commercial reference laboratory and also negative for mycoplasma IgM antibody and HIV. DNA specific to L. interrogans was detected by PCR in a serum specimen collected on day 2 of illness, which was negative by MAT. Serum collected upon patient discharge had a reciprocal MAT titer of 3,200 against serogroup Australis (serovar Bratislava).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old female presenting with a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and anorexia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in March 2014 with a 3-day history of fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and anorexia. She was admitted for dehydration and acute kidney injury. On hospital day 3, she developed acute shortness of breath and bibasilar crackles, with a 15% drop in hematocrit, thrombocytopenia, and bilateral alveolar opacities, prompting ICU transfer for acute respiratory distress syndrome and pulmonary edema. Her condition improved daily thereafter, allowing transfer to the medical ward on day 7 and discharge on day 12.

objective.physical_examination: Initial evaluation: Dry oral mucosa. Hospital day 3: Shortness of breath, bibasilar crackles, requiring supplemental oxygen. Hospital day 4: Mild shortness of breath with continued bibasilar crackles.
objective.routine_investigations:
Initial laboratory results: Leukocytosis, elevated serum creatinine, elevated amylase (130 u/L), and elevated lipase (118 u/L). Abdominal ultrasound: Cholelithiasis.
Hospital day 3: Leukocytosis, 15% drop in hematocrit, thrombocytopenia, and mildly elevated LFTs. Chest X-ray: Bilateral confluent alveolar opacities.
Follow-up labs: Worsening leukocytosis, worsening thrombocytopenia, prominently elevated LFTs, and markedly elevated LDH (9,976 u/L).
Negative routine infectious workup: Sputum and blood cultures were negative; serum Mycoplasma IgM and HIV screening were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Echocardiogram: Mild tricuspid and mitral valve regurgitation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Leptospira interrogans infection (leptospirosis) complicated by acute kidney injury, pancreatitis, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and pulmonary edema. Confirmed by positive PCR detection of L. interrogans DNA in serum collected on illness day 2 (initial MAT negative), followed by convalescent MAT reciprocal titer of 3,200 against serogroup Australis (serovar Bratislava) at discharge. Commercial serum Leptospira IgM on symptom day 6 was negative. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, Mycoplasma IgM, and HIV were negative.
Plan & Outcome: Initial therapy with IV fluids and IV piperacillin-tazobactam. Following ARDS/pulmonary edema onset in the ICU, managed with oxygen supplementation, IV furosemide, and expanded antimicrobial coverage with azithromycin, imipenem, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, linezolid, and oseltamivir. The patient achieved full clinical resolution and was discharged home on hospital day 12.

raw_case_text: A 15-month-old female infant from Georgia arrived in France in September 2010. She had fever, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and 213,000 Leishmania/ml. Leishmania amastigotes were observed in the bone marrow. There was no underlying immunosuppression. Treatment with 20 mg/kg of L-AmB resulted in complete resolution of symptoms and parasite clearance from the blood (PCR). Four months later, clinical symptoms recurred with 50 Leishmania/ml. The patient was treated with L-AmB then miltefosine for 28 days, resulting in complete clinical and parasitological response (Fig 1B). Five months later a second overt relapse occurred with typical symptoms and 20 Leishmania/ml. The patient was treated thereafter with meglumine antimoniate with a one-week break for QT interval prolongation. Upon EKG normalization, the course was reinstated with no further QT modifications. All VL clinical signs and laboratory abnormalities resolved. The patient remained relapse-free and PCR-negative 42 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-month-old female infant presented with fever, sweats, and abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 15-month-old female infant from Georgia arrived in France in September 2010 with fever, sweats, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. She achieved initial cure following liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB). Four months later, she experienced a clinical relapse, treated with L-AmB followed by 28 days of miltefosine with full response. Five months thereafter, she suffered a second overt clinical relapse with typical symptoms. Meglumine antimoniate was administered, briefly paused due to electrocardiographic changes, and completed successfully without further relapse.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born in Georgia; immigrated to France in September 2010. No underlying immunosuppression or congenital disease. Prior antibiotic therapy not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, diaphoresis, irritability, abdominal distension. Denied vomiting, diarrhea, or rash.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, irritable infant. Abdominal examination revealed marked hepatosplenomegaly. No peripheral lymphadenopathy or petechial lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Pancytopenia noted on complete blood count. Electrocardiogram (ECG) during antimonial therapy revealed QT interval prolongation, which completely normalized after a 1-week treatment interruption.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspirate revealed intracellular microorganisms within bone marrow mononuclear phagocytes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Recurrent visceral leishmaniasis in an immunocompetent infant.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Bone marrow aspirate demonstrated intracellular Leishmania amastigotes. Quantitative peripheral blood PCR revealed 213,000 Leishmania/mL at presentation, 50 Leishmania/mL at first relapse, and 20 Leishmania/mL at second relapse.
Differentials Ruled Out: Primary immunodeficiency, hematologic malignancy, and viral/bacterial sepsis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Initial treatment with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB; 20 mg/kg total) cleared parasitemia. First relapse treated with L-AmB followed by oral miltefosine for 28 days. Second relapse treated with meglumine antimoniate; therapy was held for 1 week upon detection of QT prolongation on EKG and safely resumed upon normalization. All clinical signs and lab abnormalities resolved completely; patient remained relapse-free and PCR-negative through 42 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 38-year-old Liberian female with a 12-week gestation presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of low-grade subjective fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, gradually worsening abdominal pain, and intermittent spotting. Vital signs were stable on presentation, physical exam noticeable for gravida abdomen, otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed beta hCG 118471, which was otherwise unremarkable. Pelvic ultrasound confirmed a 12-week viable intrauterine pregnancy. The patient was admitted to the hospital for close monitoring. Hospital course was complicated by massive pleural effusion, low-grade fever, progressive worsening abdominal pain, and spontaneous abortion.
