As listed in Table 1, laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia, anemia, and neutropenia. Her pT and pTT levels were prolonged, and fibrinogen was consumed, suggesting ongoing disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC).
Her chest X-ray showed an enlarged heart, slightly congested lungs with bilateral mild pleural effusion, and bibasilar reticulation/atelectatic changes. Blood cultures were taken. Four liters of normal saline as IV hydration were given, and FFPs 1U q 8 hours and 1 pool of platelets were transfused. Tazocin 4.5 g IVD q 6 hours was started, in addition to metronidazole 500 mg IVD q 8 hours. However, no improvement was seen, so vasopressors were given (Levophed 8 mg) with a target blood pressure > 110 mmHg. After her vitals stabilized, the patient underwent an urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiography (IOC), without a prior MRCP, due to her condition. No photos were taken during the surgery. Extubating the patient failed as she developed ARDS, complicated by alveolar hemorrhage, so she was reintubated and transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) immediately after the operation. In ICU, she was sedated with Dormicum and fentanyl, received nutritional feeding via a nasogastric tube at a rate of 60 cc/hr, and was given FFPs every 12 hours along with multiple blood transfusions. Blood cultures that were taken on admission on 23.11.2022 turned negative after the regular incubation period of 5 days.
During her ICU stay, our patient developed septic shock, so another set of blood cultures were taken and followed by initiating empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. Meropenem 1 gram every 8 hours and Tavanic 750 mg every 24 hours were started, in addition to colistin that was given for 2 days for persistent fever. However, no clinical or laboratory improvement was observed. One week later, blood cultures detected Brucella species, and Brucella tube agglutination titer was found to be higher than 1/5120. Laboratory workup done will be summarized in Table 2. Doxycycline 100 mg every 12 hours and rifampicin 600 mg once daily per IV were started immediately.
After initiation of anti-Brucella treatment, rapid clinical and laboratory improvement was perceived as platelets and WBC count were elevated. Repeated investigations such as chest X-rays and blood studies were found unremarkable. TTE was also done and showed normal heart function, with no signs of hypokinesia and no vegetations present. The patient was transferred to the regular floor a few days later and was discharged on oral doxycycline and rifampicin.

However, over the subsequent days she developed worsening lethargy, inability to tolerate oral intake, somnolence, and jaundice, prompting emergency hospital admission. Shortly after arrival, she deteriorated into hypotensive septic shock, underwent urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, and developed postoperative ARDS with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU admission.

Coagulation profile: prolonged PT and PTT, consumed fibrinogen (consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulopathy [DIC]). Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, slight lung congestion with bilateral mild pleural effusion, and bibasilar reticulation/atelectatic changes. assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe brucellosis (Brucella bacteremia) presenting with acalculous/reactive cholecystitis, septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) complicated by alveolar hemorrhage.
Confirmation: Repeat blood cultures drawn during ICU septic shock positive for Brucella species after extended incubation; Brucella tube agglutination titer >1/5120.
Differentials ruled out: Acute pyogenic cholecystitis / bacterial cholangitis and conventional gram-negative septic shock (non-responsive to piperacillin/tazobactam, metronidazole, meropenem, levofloxacin, and colistin; negative initial 5-day blood cultures); infective endocarditis (normal TTE without vegetations).
Treatment & Outcome: Managed in ICU with mechanical ventilation, sedation (midazolam, fentanyl), nasogastric tube feeding (60 cc/hr), fluid resuscitation, norepinephrine infusion (target SBP >110 mmHg), fresh frozen plasma, and platelet transfusions. Initial empiric antibiotics (Tazocin 4.5 g IV q6h plus metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h, escalated to meropenem 1 g IV q8h, levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h, and colistin for 2 days) produced no improvement. Following detection of Brucella, treatment was switched to intravenous doxycycline (100 mg q12h) and intravenous rifampicin (600 mg once daily). Marked clinical and laboratory recovery ensued with rising platelet and WBC counts and clearing of lung fields. Extubated, transferred to the ward, and discharged on oral doxycycline and rifampicin.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old male patient returned to a rural region of Colombia on 17 December 2020, from Africa, where he lived for 10 months in the city of Gul, Uganda. He went to the emergency room on 26 December 2020 due to 10-day history of fever, holocranial headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and retroocular pain associated with sudden onset epistaxis and choluria. Physical examination revealed blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, heart rate 89 beats/minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths/minute, temperature 39 C, oxygen saturation 97% room air, cold and sweaty skin without jaundice or skin lesions, with adequate ventilatory dynamics, with hepatosplenomegaly 5 cm below the costal margin, and without any neurological compromise.
Laboratory analysis showed anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dl reference value 12-14 mg/dl), thrombocytopenia (platelets 97 000/mm3 reference value 150 000-400 000/mm3) and abnormal serum transaminase. Various laboratory investigations were conducted to exclude any other likely cause of the fever and presence of an infection, including those for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody, both came out normal. Serologic tests for dengue performed on the acute-phase serum (collected 10 days after onset of symptoms) showed the presence of immunoglobulin (Ig) M (titers 1:800) and IgG (titers 1:400; Table 1). Diagnosis of dengue virus infection with warning signs (Group B) was made and admitted to hospitalization for management with intravenous hydration, antipyretic, and total abdominal ultrasound. Ultrasound scan shows pleural effusion in addition to moderate free fluid in the peritoneal cavity surrounding urinary bladder and gallbladder wall thickening, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and pleural effusion. A 72 hours after admission, the patient persisted with fever and presented a decrease in hematocrit (34.4%) with an increase in hemoglobin 12 g/dL and platelets to 137 000/mm3 (Table 1).
Although dengue virus infection had been diagnosed, parasitic tests were performed because the patient had returned from an endemic country with persistent prolonged febrile syndrome, a thick and thin blood smear stained with Giemsa was performed and revealed the characteristic intraerythrocytic ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum (trophozoites: a total of 215 000 parasites/mul, parasitemia index of 2.3% and gametocytes), which confirmed the diagnosis of malaria as uncomplicated. Antimalarial management was started with artemether-lumefantrine 20/120 mg twice a day for 3 days. To rule out false positives, the asexual parasites load was performed on the peripheral blood smear and MAC-ELISA (considering more than 5 days illness) was positive for dengue virus type 2 (DENV-2). The MAC-ELISA is based on capturing human IgM antibodies on a microtiter plate using anti-human-IgM antibody followed by the addition of dengue virus antigens. The antigens used for this assay are derived from the envelope proteins of the 4 dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1-4). Considering IgG detection by ELISA in a single serum sample is not useful for diagnostic testing because it remains detectable for life after a dengue virus infection, the patient was asked if he had had dengue infection before, which he denied, and IgG was negative. Therefore, a diagnosis of concurrent malaria and dengue infection was established.
The patient completed antimalarial treatment with clinical and paraclinical improvement, afebrile, without new episodes of epistaxis or obvious bleeding, without skin lesions or jaundice, normalization of platelets and transaminases with normal total abdominal ultrasound. PCR (molecular test) was performed to confirm the presence of dengue virus in the blood, being positive. After 7 days at hospital, he was fully discharged.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting with fever, severe holocranial headache, myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, epistaxis, and choluria for ten days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 34-year-old male returned to Colombia on December 17, 2020, after residing in Gulu, Uganda, for 10 months. On December 26, 2020, he presented to the emergency department with a 10-day history of high fever, holocranial headache, diffuse myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, sudden-onset epistaxis, and dark tea-colored urine (choluria). Initial serologic testing confirmed acute viral infection, and he was admitted with warning signs for fluid hydration. However, after 72 hours of persistent fevers, further parasitic investigations were initiated.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical conditions. Travel history: Resided for 10 months in Gulu, Uganda, returning to Colombia 9 days prior to emergency presentation. Denied any prior history of dengue infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Epistaxis, choluria, holocranial headache, retroocular pain, diffuse myalgias, arthralgias.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Febrile (39.0 °C), heart rate 89 beats/min, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on room air. Cold, diaphoretic skin without petechiae, purpura, or jaundice. Ventilatory dynamics intact. Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. Neurological examination intact.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL, platelet count 97,000/mm^3, elevated liver transaminases. Negative HBsAg and anti-HCV antibodies. Serology at day 10: Dengue IgM positive (titer 1:800), IgG negative (titer 1:400 initially, confirming primary dengue). Abdominal ultrasound: Bilateral pleural effusions, moderate peritoneal free fluid surrounding urinary bladder, gallbladder wall thickening, and hepatosplenomegaly. At 72h post-admission: Hemoglobin 12 g/dL, hematocrit 34.4%, platelets 137,000/mm^3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Concurrent coinfection of uncomplicated imported Plasmodium falciparum malaria and Dengue virus type 2 (DENV-2) infection with warning signs (plasma leakage, polyserositis, and bleeding). Malaria confirmed by Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood smears showing intraerythrocytic ring forms, trophozoites (215,000 parasites/μL, parasitemia index of 2.3%), and gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum. Dengue infection confirmed by positive IgM MAC-ELISA (titer 1:800) and positive blood RT-PCR for DENV-2. Viral hepatitis B and C were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with intravenous fluid hydration, antipyretics, and oral artemether-lumefantrine (20/120 mg twice daily for 3 days). Following antiparasitic therapy, the patient achieved complete defervescence, cessation of epistaxis, resolution of polyserositis on repeat ultrasound, and normalization of platelets and transaminases. Discharged in full health on hospital day 7.

raw_case_text:
A 22-year-old male was evaluated at the ED on March 24, 2014, because of a 3-day history of fever, malaise, myalgia, nausea, rhinorrhea, sore throat, and headache. Physical examination revealed fever, underweight (body mass index = 18.1), and tachycardia. He was given acetaminophen and discharged from the ED with a diagnosis of viral syndrome.
Serum collected on day 2 of illness was negative by PCR and MAT. Convalescent serum collected 18 days after illness onset was positive by MAT with a reciprocal titer of 800 against serogroups Bataviae (serovar Bataviae) and Canicola (serovar Canicola) and was also positive for detection of anti-dengue virus IgM antibodies.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old male presenting with a 3-day history of fever, malaise, myalgia, nausea, rhinorrhea, sore throat, and headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department on March 24, 2014, with a 3-day history of fever, malaise, myalgias, nausea, rhinorrhea, sore throat, and headache. Following clinical examination, he received symptomatic therapy and was discharged home with a diagnosis of viral syndrome.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis with dengue virus co-infection. Convalescent serum obtained 18 days post-onset demonstrated positive MAT with a reciprocal titer of 800 against serogroups Bataviae (serovar Bataviae) and Canicola (serovar Canicola), alongside positive anti-dengue virus IgM antibodies. Acute-phase serum drawn on illness day 2 was negative by both PCR and MAT.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral acetaminophen in the emergency department for presumptive viral syndrome and discharged home with uneventful recovery.

raw_case_text: Patient A; This is a 40-year-old male patient who came with a non-productive cough for one month and a three-month history of unquantified but significant weight loss. He also had a history of losing his appetite. On initial presentation, he appeared to be chronically ill, and all of his vital signs were within normal limits. The man weighed 52 kilograms and stood 1.74 meters tall, with a BMI of 17.2 kilograms per square meter, indicating that he was underweight. The lymphoglandular system revealed 3 by 4 cm enlarged masses that were mobile, had no overlying skin color change, and were tender in the cervical areas bilaterally, as well as 2 by 3 cm enlarged masses that were soft in consistency, mobile, had no overlying skin color change, and were non-tender on the submental areas. Other findings in the abdomen were a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant, about 5 cm below the right costal border, indicating hepatomegaly, and a soft mass along the line of spleen expansion, suggesting splenomegaly. He was then probed for a possible TB diagnosis, despite the fact that all of the standard TB diagnostic tests were negative. However, as shown below, the abdominal ultrasonography and FNAC (fine needle aspiration cytology) both supported the tuberculosis diagnosis. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed calcified and hypoechoic micronodules in the liver and spleen, as well as numerous enlarged centrally necrotic intra-abdominal lymphadenopathies, indicating disseminated tuberculosis (likely resolving). A FNAC biopsy revealed bilateral cervical and submental lymphadenopathies, with a tuberculous abscess as the most likely diagnosis. He was then tested for retrovirus infection and was found to be positive. The CD4 cell count was 14 cells per millimeter squared. He was offered urine LAM for tuberculosis diagnosis, and the result was positive for TB LAM. He began antiTB treatment, and on the tenth day of treatment, he was started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) with Tenofovir+Lamivudine+Dolutegravir (TLD) as per the recommendation. He is now on his 7th month and is apparently healthy, and taking his medication regularly. His weight also increased to 63 kilograms, with a BMI of 20.8, which is normal. The viral load was done 2 weeks back, and it was 800 copies, which is below the threshold for viral transmission (greater than 1000 copies).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented with a non-productive cough of one month's duration, accompanied by anorexia and significant weight loss over three months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of dry cough, anorexia, and progressive significant weight loss over 3 months. Initial standard outpatient evaluations had been inconclusive.
subjective.past_medical_history: Denies prior chronic illnesses, hospitalizations, or known TB contacts. HIV diagnosed during present hospitalization. Home medications and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports non-productive cough, anorexia, weight loss; denies fever, night sweats, or hemoptysis. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Chronically ill appearance; vital signs within normal limits. Weight 52 kg, height 1.74 m, BMI 17.2 kg/m^2. Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (3 x 4 cm mobile, tender masses) and submental lymphadenopathy (2 x 3 cm soft, mobile, non-tender masses). Abdominal exam: hepatomegaly palpable 5 cm below right costal margin, palpable splenomegaly.

objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal ultrasound: calcified and hypoechoic micronodules in liver and spleen, along with numerous enlarged centrally necrotic intra-abdominal lymph nodes. FNAC of cervical and submental lymph nodes: cytomorphology consistent with necrotic tuberculous abscess.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis (cervical/submental lymphadenitis, splenic and hepatic micronodules, necrotic intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy) in newly diagnosed advanced HIV infection (CD4 14 cells/mm^3).
Confirmation: Urine lipoarabinomannan (LAM) test was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis; FNAC of cervical and submental lymph nodes confirmed tuberculous abscess; abdominal ultrasound revealed disseminated hepato-splenic micronodules and necrotic retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.
Differentials ruled out: Lymphoma, Kaposi sarcoma, disseminated histoplasmosis/cryptococcosis.
Treatment & Outcome: Anti-tuberculosis therapy initiated; on day 10 of ATT, highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) was started with tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD). At 7-month follow-up, patient was clinically well, weight increased to 63 kg (BMI 20.8 kg/m^2), and HIV viral load was suppressed to 800 copies/mL.

raw_case_text:
A 54 years old male Ugandan presented to Kenyatta National Hospital, a major referral tertiary hospital, in Kenya. He had initially reported with headache and joint pain to a local health facility in Uganda and was diagnosed to have severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria infection, and thereafter treatment with intravenous quinine commenced.
Treatment at the facility had been responsive; however two days after the onset, the patient started experiencing episodes of headache, pain, numbness, coldness, and swelling of the extremities. This was followed by darkening of the digits of his toes and hands, which gradually progressed proximally.
On presentation at out institution, he was conscious, alert, oriented, but lethargic and unable to walk. He was a non-smoker and non-alcoholic, and had no history of diabetes, hypertension or any angiopathies. He however had a history of numerous episodes of malaria bouts and a family history of hypertension with his father having succumbed to a stroke.
On physical examination, apart from fever, abdominal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems were normal. Jaundice, pallor and cyanosis were absent. A right low paramedian scar was noted secondary to appendicectomy conducted in the year 1995. On local examination, the overlying skin cold, dry, wrinkled, and was darkened with a clear line of proximal demarcation (Figure 1). Pain was present in the regions proximal to the discolouration, and absent in the distal regions.
Investigations tested negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, and VDRL on ELISA. Urea, Electrolyte and creatinine tests were normal. Clotting profile showed a prolonged Prothrombin time of 19sec, Prothrombin time index of 74%, and an INR of 1.36. A haemogram showed macrocytic normochromic anaemia (Hb 9.03 g/dL, MCV 89.9fL, MCH 29.5pg, MCHC 27.2g/dL), Hct 33.2%, RBC 3.69x1012/L. WBC 4.39x109, Neutrophils 2.11x109 (48.2%), Lymphocytes 1.73x109 (39.5%), Monocytes 0.314x109 (7.16%), Eosinophils 0.193x109 (4.4%), Basophils 0.035x109 (0.796%).
An echocardiogram was normal except for type 1 left ventricular dysfunction and mild tricuspid regurgitation. The Dorsalis pedis pulses showed absence of blood flow, and a diagnosis of Symmetrical peripheral gangrene was made. Management was initiated with clopidogrel, Acetylsalicylic Acid, and Atorvastatin, and quad-amputation recommended. Time was allowed for marginalization of the gangrene, which was noted two months later. Meanwhile fresh frozen plasma was regularly administered to counter suspected thrombophilia.
Following satisfactory marginalization of the gangrene, the patient underwent surgical excision of the necrotic tissue. This involved transmetatarsal amputation of both feet and ray amputation of the hands. The wounds healed well thereafter facilitated by vacuum dressing at -7.5mmHg over one month. He was then referred to plastic surgeons for prosthesis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old male presenting with numbness, coldness, severe pain, and progressive symmetric blackening of the fingers and toes.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 54-year-old male initially presented to a health facility in Uganda with headache and arthralgias and was treated for a severe febrile illness. Two days following treatment initiation, he developed headache, intense limb pain, numbness, coldness, and swelling of his distal extremities, rapidly followed by symmetrical darkening of the digits of his feet and hands that progressed proximally. He was transferred to a tertiary referral hospital in Nairobi, Kenya, unable to walk due to dry gangrene.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ugandan male; history of numerous prior bouts of malaria. Non-smoker, non-drinker. No history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or angiopathies. Family history of hypertension and fatal stroke in father. Surgical history: appendectomy in 1995. Completed IV quinine prior to transfer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache, arthralgia, severe limb pain proximal to discoloration, distal numbness, coldness, and swelling. Negative for chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Medications: completed course of IV quinine. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious, alert, oriented, but lethargic and unable to walk. Febrile. Jaundice, pallor, and cyanosis were absent. Abdominal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems were normal. Abdomen showed a right lower paramedian appendectomy scar. Extremity examination: skin of bilateral distal hands and feet was cold, dry, wrinkled, and blackened with a clear line of proximal demarcation. Severe tenderness present proximal to demarcation; distal areas were insensate. Bilateral dorsalis pedis pulses were absent.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemogram: macrocytic normochromic anemia with hemoglobin 9.03 g/dL, MCV 89.9 fL, MCH 29.5 pg, MCHC 27.2 g/dL, hematocrit 33.2%, red blood cells 3.69 x 10^12/L; leukocytes 4.39 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 48.2%, lymphocytes 39.5%, monocytes 7.16%, eosinophils 4.4%, basophils 0.8%). Coagulation profile: prothrombin time 19 sec, prothrombin time index 74%, INR 1.36. Urea, electrolytes, and creatinine: normal. Serology: negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, and VDRL on ELISA.
objective.advanced_workup: Transthoracic echocardiogram: type 1 left ventricular diastolic dysfunction and mild tricuspid regurgitation, without intracardiac vegetations or thrombi. Peripheral vascular Doppler: confirmed complete absence of blood flow in bilateral dorsalis pedis arteries.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Symmetrical peripheral gangrene (purpura fulminans / post-infectious microvascular thrombosis of all four extremities) complicating severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
Diagnostic confirmation: Documented severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria initially treated with intravenous quinine; negative serologic screening for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis; echocardiography excluding central embolic sources; Doppler demonstrating peripheral arterial flow arrest.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed medically with clopidogrel, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), atorvastatin, and regular administration of fresh frozen plasma to counteract suspected hypercoagulability/thrombophilia. Following 2 months of conservative observation to allow complete ischemic demarcation, he underwent surgical amputation comprising bilateral transmetatarsal amputations of the feet and ray amputations of both hands. Wounds were managed with negative-pressure vacuum dressings at -7.5 mmHg for 1 month, achieving primary healing, and he was referred for plastic surgical prosthesis.

raw_case_text: A 36-year-old woman was admitted to Imam Khomeini Hospital, Tehran because of acute onset of fever and decreased level of consciousness. Her problem began 3 days prior to admission with hallucination, delusions and fever. She was single and unemployed, living in a small town, without previous history of brucellosis in herself and her family. She was not receiving any medication and had no history of illicit drug use. The only positive point in her past was regular consumption of unpasteurized dairy products. On admission, she had disorientation to time and place. She was agitated and had visual hallucination and grandiose delusion. Despite her high temperature (39 C) other vital signs were normal including blood pressure, pulse rate, and respiratory rate. Head and neck examination revealed nuchal rigidity. General physical examination was normal except for some abnormal neurologic findings including decreased deep tendon reflexes and forces of lower extremities at about 3/5. A lumbar puncture was done after brain computerized tomography scan did not reveal any abnormality. The results of initial tests and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis are listed in table 1. Presence of fever, decreased level of consciousness, and bizarre behavior raised the possibility of herpes simplex virus (HSV) meningoencephalitis, hence intravenous acyclovir started pending further evaluations. Brain MRI with contrast (gadolinium) showed meningeal enhancement in left frontal and right temporal lobes (fig. 1), suggesting meningoencephalitis. During the next few days no significant change was observed in the patient's condition. On the 6th day of hospitalization she developed nausea and vomiting and laboratory tests showed significant elevation of liver enzymes (aspartate aminotransferase, AST = 1,093, and alanine aminotransferase, ALT = 203). Since our patient showed raised levels of liver function tests, we further checked for HBsAg, HCV Ab, HAV Ab (IgM), HIV Ab, EBV Ab (VCA IgM), CMV Ab (IgM), anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, and liver kidney microsomal antibody; all were negative. Because of lack of clinical response to acyclovir therapy, negative CSF HSV PCR results, and possibility of drug-induced hepatotoxicity, acyclovir was discontinued after a 10-day course of therapy. At this time serology tests for brucellosis became positive including: Wright agglutination test = 1/40, Coombs Wright = 1/80, Brucella ELISA IgG = 146.6 U/ml (normal <8 U/ml). With probable diagnosis of neurobrucellosis, triple therapy including one intravenous drug with good penetration to CSF (ceftriaxone, doxycycline and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) was started. Rifampin was avoided at this time due to abnormal liver enzymes. Within a week, the patient's symptoms including fever and psychosis improved and she became completely alert without any neurological problems and regained ability to talk and eat. Five days after discontinuation of acyclovir, serum aminotransferase levels decreased (AST = 288 IU/l and ALT = 191 IU/l) and subsequently 9 days after discontinuation of acyclovir, liver enzymes reached near-normal levels (AST = 54 IU/l and ALT = 63 IU/l). Liver biopsy also showed unremarkable portal tracts and lobules. The patient was discharged with triple oral therapy (doxycycline, rifampin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). After 3 months, she became completely well. She received 6 months' treatment totally with clinical follow-ups showing no problem at 3 months and at the end of 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old female presented with an acute 3-day history of high fever, decreased level of consciousness, hallucinations, and delusions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute onset of high fever and altered mental status beginning 3 days prior to admission. She experienced agitation, visual hallucinations, grandiose delusions, and disorientation. On hospital day 6, she developed nausea and vomiting associated with marked acute liver enzyme elevation during empiric intravenous acyclovir therapy for suspected HSV meningoencephalitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous history of chronic febrile illness or zoonotic disease in herself or family. No history of illicit drug use; not receiving any medications prior to admission. Epidemiological history: regular consumption of unpasteurized dairy products; lived in a small town.
subjective.review_of_systems: Visual hallucinations, grandiose delusions, agitation, nausea, and vomiting. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39 °C; blood pressure, pulse rate, and respiratory rate were normal. Neurological exam: disoriented to time and place, agitated; nuchal rigidity present. Motor examination showed lower extremity muscle strength decreased to approximately 3/5, with decreased deep tendon reflexes in lower extremities. General physical examination was otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs and CSF analysis (Table 1). On hospital day 6: AST 1,093 IU/L, ALT 203 IU/L. Hepatitis and viral serologies all negative: HBsAg, anti-HCV, HAV IgM, HIV Ab, EBV VCA IgM, CMV IgM. Autoimmune liver serologies all negative: anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, liver-kidney microsomal antibody. Follow-up LFTs 5 days post-acyclovir: AST 288 IU/L, ALT 191 IU/L; 9 days post-acyclovir: AST 54 IU/L, ALT 63 IU/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT without contrast: normal. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: CSF HSV PCR negative. Brain MRI with gadolinium contrast: meningeal enhancement in left frontal and right temporal lobes, compatible with meningoencephalitis. Percutaneous liver biopsy: unremarkable portal tracts and lobules (consistent with drug-induced liver injury secondary to acyclovir).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis (meningoencephalitis with acute psychotic features) and acyclovir-induced hepatotoxicity. Confirmed by positive Brucella serology: Wright agglutination test 1/40, Coombs Wright 1/80, and Brucella ELISA IgG 146.6 U/mL (normal <8 U/mL). Herpes simplex virus meningoencephalitis, viral hepatitis (A, B, C, EBV, CMV), HIV, and autoimmune hepatitis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Empiric acyclovir was discontinued. Treated with IV ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (rifampin initially withheld due to acute hepatotoxicity). Fever and psychosis resolved within one week; patient became fully alert with normalized neurologic exam and recovered eating/speaking. Liver enzymes normalized following acyclovir cessation. Discharged on oral triple therapy (doxycycline, rifampin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) to complete a total 6-month regimen with complete recovery and no recurrence on 3- and 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 44-year-old male presented with sudden onset, diminution of vision in both eyes for 10 days. He gave history of fever, myalgia, and weakness one week prior to onset of ocular problem. He was previously healthy, not known to have diabetes mellitus or hypertension. There was no relevant family or social history of medical significance. During clinical evaluation and laboratory investigation for fever; typhoid, malaria, tuberculosis, syphilis, collagen vascular disease and bleeding disorders were absent. He was diagnosed to have dengue fever as NS1 antigen and IgM antibody were positive. After conservative management, his platelet count had improved from 49x103/microL to 176x103/microL (normal range, 150-450x103/microL) over a week period. At presentation, his best-corrected visual acuity was 1/60 in the right eye (OD) and 6/18 in the left eye (OS). Anterior segment findings were normal. Fundus examination revealed vitritis, perivascular exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, macular edema, peripapillary retinal whitening, and cotton wool spots in both eyes, with additional retinal whitening affecting the right macula (Figure 1). Fundus fluorescein angiography revealed disc and perivascular leakage limited to posterior pole along with patches of blocked fluorescence. In addition, there was capillary nonperfusion due to occlusion of multiple small arterioles supplying the macula of the right eye confirming macular ischemia (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography of both eyes demonstrated macular edema with subretinal fluid. A diagnosis of bilateral retinal vasculitis with right eye macular infarction was made. Echocardiography and carotid Doppler studies revealed normal cardiac and carotid artery status. The patient was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone which was futile even after three days of treatment. Then he was counseled for treatment with immunoglobulin, which the patient refused and left for a second opinion without returning back to us.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old male presenting with sudden-onset diminution of vision in both eyes for ten days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 44-year-old male developed fever, myalgia, and weakness lasting approximately one week, managed conservatively with resolution of systemic symptoms. One week after the onset of systemic symptoms, he experienced sudden-onset bilateral visual impairment progressing over 10 days, prompting ophthalmologic evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; no history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, bleeding disorders, or collagen vascular diseases. Family and social history non-contributory.
subjective.review_of_systems: Weakness and myalgia preceding visual symptoms; no focal neurologic or cardiopulmonary complaints at ocular presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmologic examination: Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) 1/60 in the right eye (OD) and 6/18 in the left eye (OS). Anterior segment examination normal bilaterally. Dilated fundus examination: Bilateral vitritis, perivascular exudates, intraretinal hemorrhages, macular edema, peripapillary retinal whitening, and cotton wool spots in both eyes, with additional retinal whitening affecting the right macula.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: Nadir of 49 x 10^3/microL during febrile phase, improving to 176 x 10^3/microL (reference range: 150-450 x 10^3/microL) within one week. Diagnostic testing negative for typhoid, malaria, tuberculosis, syphilis, collagen vascular diseases, and coagulopathies. Transthoracic echocardiography and carotid Doppler ultrasound: Normal cardiac valves, function, and carotid arterial status.
objective.advanced_workup: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA): Disc and perivascular leakage limited to the posterior pole with patches of blocked fluorescence bilaterally; capillary nonperfusion secondary to occlusion of multiple small arterioles supplying the right macula, confirming macular ischemia/infarction. Optical coherence tomography (OCT): Bilateral macular edema with subretinal fluid accumulation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection complicated by bilateral retinal vasculitis, bilateral macular edema, and right-sided macular branch retinal arteriolar occlusion/infarction. Dengue confirmation established by positive Dengue NS1 antigen and Dengue IgM antibody during the acute febrile illness. Typhoid, malaria, tuberculosis, syphilis, collagen vascular diseases, and cardiac/carotid embolic sources were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy for 3 days without functional visual improvement. Immunoglobulin therapy was recommended; however, the patient declined further intervention and discharged against medical advice to seek a second opinion.

raw_case_text: A 28-year-old woman was hospitalized for acute-onset high fever, myalgia, arthralgia and ocular pain. Detailed history- taking, hematological and serological investigations established the diagnosis of classic dengue fever (a positive IgM antibody titer); and ruled out mimicking infections like leptospirosis, typhoid, malaria, syphilis, as well as collagen vascular diseases. Seven days later, during the convalescent phase, the patient noticed blurring of the inferior visual field in the right eye. She presented to us two weeks after the ocular symptoms had started. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. On slit-lamp examination, anterior segment was unremarkable in both eyes; no anterior vitreous cells or flare was observed. Fundus examination of the right eye showed a patchy area of partially faded retinal whitening in the superotemporal quadrant of the macula, just encroaching into the fovea, with attenuation and sclerosis of the macular division of the superotemporal branch retinal artery [Fig. 1]. The left fundus revealed a single cotton-wool spot towards the edge of the inferotemporal arcade. Midphase fluorescein angiogram of the right eye showed narrowing of the affected arterial segment, blocked background fluorescence in the area of whitening and delayed arteriovenous transit in the affected vessels. Staining and leakage of the occluded artery was observed in the late phase [Fig. 2]. Kinetic central field charting with Bjerrum's screen showed an inferonasal field defect corresponding to the area of arterial occlusion. The patient was referred for a detailed cardiac and carotid evaluation - including carotid doppler study and echocardiography - which was unremarkable. She was followed up for three months. Her visual acuity remained 20/20 in both eyes, but the inferior field defect persisted in the right eye.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old female presented with blurring of the inferior visual field in the right eye following an acute febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was hospitalized initially for acute-onset high fever, severe myalgia, arthralgia, and retro-ocular pain. Seven days later, during her convalescent period, she developed sudden painless blurring of the inferior visual field of her right eye, presenting for ophthalmic evaluation two weeks after ocular symptom onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent acute febrile illness managed as an inpatient. No prior history of hypertension, thromboembolism, or collagen vascular disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported inferior visual field blurring in the right eye; preceding illness featured high fever, generalized arthralgias, myalgias, and retro-orbital pain. Denied eye pain at ophthalmic presentation, amaurosis fugax, or motor weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of anterior segments was unremarkable bilaterally without vitreous cells or flare. Right funduscopy revealed a patchy area of partially faded retinal whitening in the superotemporal macular quadrant encroaching on the fovea, with marked attenuation and sclerosis of the macular branch of the superotemporal retinal artery. Left funduscopy revealed an isolated cotton-wool spot near the inferotemporal vascular arcade.
objective.routine_investigations:
Hematologic profile demonstrated transient acute cytopenias and thrombocytopenia during initial febrile hospitalization.
Systemic vascular screening: Transthoracic echocardiogram and bilateral carotid Doppler ultrasound were entirely normal.
objective.advanced_workup:
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FA) of right eye: Mid-phase showed focal arteriolar narrowing, delayed arteriovenous transit, and blocked background choroidal fluorescence in the ischemic zone; late-phase demonstrated hyperfluorescent staining and vascular leakage of the occluded retinal arterial segment.
Visual field examination (Bjerrum screen kinetic perimetry): Demonstrated a dense inferonasal visual field defect corresponding geometrically to the occluded superotemporal macular retinal arteriole.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) secondary to Dengue virus infection, confirmed by a positive Dengue IgM antibody titer. Leptospirosis, typhoid fever, malaria, syphilis, systemic lupus erythematosus/collagen vascular diseases, and cardiac/carotid embolic sources were systematically ruled out.
Treatment and outcome: Managed conservatively with observation. Over three months of follow-up, visual acuity remained preserved at 20/20 bilaterally, but the dense right inferonasal visual field defect persisted permanently.

raw_case_text:
A 20 year old Saudi male was diagnosed to have severe acquired AA at King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre (KFSH&RC) in Riyadh on 9/4/2006. He presented with 2 week history of low grade pyrexia, mucosal bleeding and anemic symptoms and his physical examination revelaed: pallor, few ecchymotic areas over the limbs, no external lymphadenopathy, a clear chest, no palpable abdominal organomegaly, and normal cardiovascular and neurological systems. Complete blood count (CBC) showed: WBC: 1.5 x 109/L with neutrophils of 0.02, Hb: 72 g/L and PLT: 5 x 109/L. Blood film revealed severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia but no blast cells and bone marrow biopsy showed a hypocellular marrow with no blasts and a normal cytogenetic analysis. Renal, hepatic and coagulation profiles were normal. Screens for fanconi anemia, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, hepatitis, brucellosis, syphilis, viruses and autoimmune disorders were all negative. The patient was given supportive measures and after identifying an HLA identical and a healthy sibling donor, prepartions for allogeneic HSCT were made. The transplant conditioning was composed of fludarabine and cyclophophamide. The patient received acyclovir, fluconazole and trimethoprim-sulphamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ) as infection prophylaxis and cyclosporine-A and methotrexate as graft versus host disease (GVHD) prophylaxis. On 15/5/2006, the patient was given his allograft without any complication. The patient developed: grade I mucositis treated with IV morphine infusion and few febrile neutropenic episodes treated empirically with vancomycin, cefepime, amphotericin-B and metronidazole. However, no acute GVHD, cytomegalovirus infection, venoocclusive disease of the liver or hemorrhagic cystitis were encountered. The patient engrafted his leucocytes on day +24 and his platelets on day +16 HSCT. After the recovery of his blood counts, the patient was discharged on zantac, cyclosporine-A and prophylactic antimicrobials.
On 4/9/2006, he presented with 2 week history of high grade pyrexia, rigors and sweating. He denied intake of raw milk. Physical examination did not reveal any abnormality. CBC showed: WBC: 2.37 x 109/L with neutrophils of 1.59, Hb: 152 g/L and PLT: 97 x 109/L. Serum creatinine was 130 mumol/l [normal range: 0-122 mumole/L], bilirubin 30 mumol/L [normal range: 0-22 mumole/L], ALT: 194 U/L [normal range: 0-50 U/L], AST: 176 U/L [normal range: 0-40 U/L]. Blood cultures grew Brucella melitensis sensitive to: TMP/SMZ, streptomycin, tetracyclin, ciprofloxacin and imipenem. Brucella serology was strongly positive with 2-mercaptoethanol titer of 1:1280 and agglutination antibody titer of 1:20480. Initially, the patient was given streptomycin 1 gram intramuscularly twice daily and ciprofloxacin 400 mg orally twice daily for two weeks. Few days later, the clinical manifestation of brucellosis disappeared then the blood counts started to recover so streptomycin was replaced by doxycyline 100 mg orally twice daily and the patient was continued on ciprofloxacin for 4 more weeks. Subsequently, the blood cultures for Brucella became negative, the Brucella titers decreased significantly, the blood indices as well as the renal and the hepatic profiles normalized. When the patient was last seen on 29/4/2008, he was asymptomatic and his physical examination did not reveal any abnormality. CBC showed: WBC: 6.13 x 109/L with neutrophilis of 2.82, Hb: 142 g/L and PLT: 186 x 109/L. The renal and the hepatic profiles were normal. No new medication was prescribed and the patient was given a new follow up appointment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant presented with a 2-week history of high-grade pyrexia, rigors, and sweating.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had severe acquired aplastic anemia diagnosed in April 2006 and underwent successful HLA-identical sibling allogeneic HSCT on 15/5/2006 following fludarabine and cyclophosphamide conditioning, with leukocyte engraftment on day +24 and platelet engraftment on day +16. On 4/9/2006, he presented with a 2-week history of high-grade pyrexia, rigors, and profuse sweating. He denied consuming raw milk.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe acquired aplastic anemia diagnosed on 9/4/2006 (bone marrow biopsy showed hypocellular marrow without blasts and normal cytogenetics; baseline screens for Fanconi anemia, PNH, hepatitis, syphilis, brucellosis, and autoantibodies negative). Underwent allogeneic HSCT on 15/5/2006. Conditioning: fludarabine and cyclophosphamide. Prophylaxis: acyclovir, fluconazole, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMZ), cyclosporine-A, and methotrexate. Post-transplant course complicated by grade I mucositis (treated with IV morphine) and febrile neutropenia (treated empirically with vancomycin, cefepime, amphotericin B, and metronidazole). Discharged on ranitidine (Zantac), cyclosporine-A, and prophylactic antimicrobials. Epidemiological exposure: denied ingestion of raw milk.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high-grade pyrexia, rigors, and sweating. Denies consumption of raw milk. Current medications: ranitidine, cyclosporine-A, and prophylactic antimicrobials.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination on 4/9/2006 was completely unremarkable (clear chest, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, normal cardiovascular and neurological systems). Baseline examination on 9/4/2006 showed pallor and few limb ecchymoses.
objective.routine_investigations: At presentation on 4/9/2006: WBC 2.37 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 1.59 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin: 152 g/L, platelet count: 97 x 10^9/L. Serum creatinine: 130 mumol/L (normal range 0-122 mumol/L), total bilirubin: 30 mumol/L (normal range 0-22 mumol/L), ALT: 194 U/L (normal range 0-50 U/L), AST: 176 U/L (normal range 0-40 U/L). Initial pre-transplant CBC (9/4/2006): WBC 1.5 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 0.02), Hb 72 g/L, platelets 5 x 10^9/L; blood film showed severe neutropenia and thrombocytopenia without blast cells. Follow-up CBC on 29/4/2008: WBC 6.13 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 2.82), Hb 142 g/L, platelets 186 x 10^9/L; renal and hepatic profiles normalized.
objective.advanced_workup: Pre-transplant bone marrow biopsy demonstrated a hypocellular marrow without blasts and normal cytogenetic analysis. Susceptibility testing of the isolated pathogen showed susceptibility to TMP/SMZ, streptomycin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, and imipenem.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Blood cultures grew Brucella melitensis sensitive to TMP/SMZ, streptomycin, tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, and imipenem. Brucella serology was strongly positive with a 2-mercaptoethanol titer of 1:1,280 and an agglutination antibody titer of 1:20,480. Differential diagnosis: Viral infections (hepatitis viruses, CMV), syphilis, Fanconi anemia, PNH, and autoimmune disorders ruled out by pre-transplant workup; acute GVHD and veno-occlusive disease excluded. Management and Outcome: Initially treated with intramuscular streptomycin 1 g twice daily and oral ciprofloxacin 400 mg twice daily for 2 weeks. Following clinical resolution and hematological recovery, streptomycin was discontinued and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was started, with oral ciprofloxacin continued for an additional 4 weeks (total 6 weeks). Blood cultures became negative, Brucella antibody titers dropped significantly, and blood counts, renal function, and liver enzymes normalized. At follow-up on 29/4/2008, the patient remained fully asymptomatic with normal examination, normal blood counts, and normal hepatic and renal function.

raw_case_text:
In the fall of 2021, a 34-year-old woman presented to our retina clinic two days ago with a chief complaint of sudden onset, painless vision loss in her left eye 2 days ago after waking up in the morning. She complained about blurred vision with a scotoma at the inferior eye field. Five days before the onset of the ocular symptoms, the patient was diagnosed with a novel coronavirus infection (COVID-19) based on clinical features such as fever, myalgia, dry cough, dyspnea, and a positive PCR test of nasopharyngeal sample for COVID-19.
She had not been hospitalized because of her stable vital signs and had been under outpatient supportive care at her home. The patient had not done her COVID-19 vaccination, and the history of any previous ocular or systemic diseases was negative. The history of drug history was negative. She did not have a history of significant headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss, vomiting, double vision, or any other rheumatologic disease symptoms.
On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 1/10 in the left eye (OS) and 10/10 in the right eye (OD). Extraocular motility was in the normal range and painless. Relative afferent papillary defect (RAPD) was grade II positive in the left eye, and red/green color vision according to the Ishihara chart was impaired. On the examination by slit lamp, anterior segment was normal. IOP was 17 mmHg in both eyes. In fundoscopy, the right eye was completely normal, but a pale optic disc swelling, peripapillary hemorrhages, and adjacent macular cotton-wool exudate with edema were observed in the left eye as shown in Figure 1. The confrontational visual field demonstrated an inferior hemifield defect in her left eye. There was an inferior left visual field defect in the perimetry test, with no visual field abnormalities in the contralateral eye (Figure 2). All the blood tests such as the venereal diseases research laboratory (VDRL), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibody, hematological, rheumatological, and immunological tests were normal but high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP).
Based on the clinical features (unilateral painless visual decrease), laboratory tests (elevated levels of ESR and CRP), and ocular examination (pale optic disc swelling in fundoscopy), a diagnosis of AAION was considered. The patient was admitted to the hospital, and treatment with a high dose of intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day) for three days was started. In laboratory tests, an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) (3+) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (32 mm/h) with a decreased level of vitamin D3 (14 ng/ml) were detected. The results of the complete blood test, coagulopathy tests (PT, PTT, INR, protein C, protein S, and antithrombin), and rheumatologic tests (RF, ANA, and ANCA) were within the normal range. Brain and orbital MRI of the patient was normal; rheumatologic consultation also was done that suggested following up with the patient. After 3 days, the patient was discharged with oral prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day).
After one week at the follow-up visit, the patient's visual acuity of the left eye was 2/10, and disc edema was resolved. Finally, after four months of follow-up, the patient's left eye visual acuity improved to 3/10, fundoscopic examination revealed the resolution of left optic disc edema and optic nerve head paleness with restricted visual field, while the right eye was fortunately normal and not affected by the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old female presenting with sudden-onset, painless vision loss, blurred vision, and an inferior visual field scotoma in the left eye for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 34-year-old female presented with sudden-onset, painless visual loss in her left eye upon awakening two days prior, noting blurred vision and an inferior visual field scotoma. Five days prior to the ocular symptoms, she had developed an acute viral respiratory illness characterized by fever, myalgias, dry cough, and dyspnea, managed with supportive home care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable medical and ocular history. Denied history of systemic or rheumatologic diseases, prior ocular disorders, or medications. Had not received routine pandemic vaccinations.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, myalgias, dry cough, dyspnea, and left eye vision loss. Negative for headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, weight loss, vomiting, diplopia, or joint pain. Home medications: none. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic examination: Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA): 10/10 in the right eye (OD) and 1/10 in the left eye (OS). Extraocular motility: full and painless bilaterally. Intraocular pressure: 17 mmHg bilaterally. Pupils: grade II relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in the left eye. Color vision: impaired red/green perception on Ishihara testing in the left eye. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: anterior segments normal bilaterally. Fundoscopy: right eye unremarkable; left eye demonstrated pale optic disc swelling, peripapillary flame-shaped hemorrhages, and adjacent macular cotton-wool exudates with retinal edema. Visual field testing: confrontational and perimetric examination revealed an inferior hemifield defect in the left eye.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation: C-reactive protein (CRP): markedly elevated (3+); erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 32 mm/h; 25-hydroxyvitamin D3: decreased at 14 ng/mL. Complete blood count: within normal limits. Coagulation profile: PT, PTT, INR, protein C, protein S, and antithrombin levels were normal. Autoimmune and infectious serologies: negative for VDRL, HIV antibody, rheumatoid factor (RF), antinuclear antibodies (ANA), and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA).
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and orbital MRI: unremarkable without evidence of intracranial pathology, demyelination, or orbital mass lesions. Formal automated visual field perimetry: confirmed an inferior hemifield defect in the left eye with normal field in the contralateral eye.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (AAION) secondary to acute COVID-19 infection, confirmed by a positive nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Giant cell arteritis and systemic autoimmune vasculitides were clinically and serologically excluded. Management & Outcome: Inpatient admission and treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days), followed by oral prednisolone taper (1 mg/kg/day). At 1-week follow-up, left eye visual acuity improved to 2/10 with resolution of optic disc edema; at 4-month follow-up, left visual acuity reached 3/10 with optic disc pallor and persistent inferior visual field defect.

raw_case_text:
A 52-year-old farmer, L. M. B., woman, resident in a rural area, attended the Oral Medicine Service, referred by a head and neck surgeon, for evaluation of a granulomatous lesion on the palate and complaining of hoarseness, which she believed to be a sequela of a flu occurred three months earlier. According to the doctor's report, the patient presented extensive oral lesion, having undergone a laryngoscopy and biopsy, with a histopathological result of pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and an active chronic inflammatory process, suggesting a fungus investigation, the reason why the doctor referred her to our service.
During the health questionnaire, the patient did not reveal any systemic alteration as well as use of medications chronically. The patient reported having worked in the sugarcane fields for many years and had history of crusting and nasal bleeding, started about 4 years earlier. Physical examination showed nasal constipation, issuing nasal voice, and was mouth breather. The patient also reported to had been smoking for 6 months and the use of upper and lower total prosthesis.
Extrabuccal clinical examination revealed a lowering of the right side of the nasal wing and nasal septum perforation (Figures 1 and 2).
Intrabuccal examination revealed granulomatous lesion involving the entire palate and uvula, extending to the pharynx bilaterally with erythematous appearance and presence of scratchable white plaques distributed in some regions (Figures 3 and 4). The patient reported continuous use of the prosthesis.
Diagnostic hypotheses of mucosal leishmaniasis and paracoccidioidomycosis associated with candidosis were formulated. Mouth rinse using nystatin oral solution, hand hygiene instructions, and night removal of the prosthesis were prescribed. In posterior return, the hemogram and chest X-ray previously requested by the doctor were evaluated. The hemogram showed microcytosis and moderate hypochromia with basophilic dotting and discreet polychromatophilia. Chest X-ray analysis showed dense and congestive yarns. Radiographic examination of the bones of the nose, which demonstrated integrity of the nasal septum, was also requested.
Serology and mycological exams were requested. Direct mycological was negative. On clinical examination, no changes were noticed in the appearance of lesions after use of antifungal mouthwashes.
In view of the negative result of the direct mycological examination, sputum examination and the Montenegro intradermal test (MIT) for leishmaniasis were requested. In the same visit, incisional biopsy of the buccal lesion was also performed.
After 7 days, the patient returned with the result of the histopathological examination (Figure 5), which revealed signs compatible with leishmaniasis, but without demonstration of the etiological agent.
The MIT test was positive with an exacerbated reaction (bubble formation) (Figure 6).
Once the definitive diagnosis of mucosal leishmaniasis was formulated, the patient was referred to the Araraquara Health Service (SESA) for treatment. At the same time, Rx of nasal bone was requested, which demonstrated integrity of the nasal bone septum.
Patient treatment consisted of daily administration of 3 ampoules of 5 ml of glucantime 425 mg, diluted in 250 ml of saline solution, administered intravenously for about 2 hours in a hospital for 30 days.
In a follow-up visit to our service, after completing the treatment, the patient reported stomach pain in the first 2 days of treatment; arthralgia and swelling of the joints of hands and legs during the course of treatment were also reported. Intraoral clinical examination was conducted where complete regression of the lesion was observed, leaving only cicatricial aspect (Figures 7 and 8).
The patient reported nasal decongestion and improved breathing. She was then referred to an otolaryngologist for evaluation of the nasal and laryngeal region, since the patient showed improvement in hoarseness. At the moment, the patient is followed up by this service, showing no other manifestation of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old female presented with an extensive granulomatous lesion on her palate and hoarseness of three months duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 52-year-old female farmer who attended the oral medicine service referred by a head and neck surgeon for evaluation of a palatal granulomatous lesion and hoarseness, which she attributed to an upper respiratory infection 3 months prior. She reported a 4-year history of recurrent nasal crusting and epistaxis. A prior laryngoscopy and biopsy had demonstrated pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and active chronic inflammation, prompting referral for suspected fungal infection. Initial topical nystatin oral rinses produced no improvement. Further diagnostic workup, including mycological testing, Montenegro intradermal testing, and repeat mucosal biopsy, was conducted.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of working in sugarcane fields for many years; tobacco smoking for 6 months; use of complete upper and lower dental prostheses. Denies chronic systemic diseases or chronic medication use. Resident of a rural area in Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Nasal obstruction/congestion, epistaxis, hoarseness, mouth breathing. Home medications: nystatin oral suspension. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: General/Extrabuccal: mouth breather with nasal voice; lowering/flattening of the right nasal wing and perforation of the nasal septum. Intrabuccal: extensive granulomatous lesion involving the entire hard and soft palate and uvula, extending bilaterally to the pharynx, with an erythematous base and scrapable white plaques.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: microcytosis, moderate hypochromia, basophilic stippling, and discreet polychromatophilia. Chest radiograph: dense and congestive vascular markings. Radiography of nasal bones: preserved nasal bone structure / intact nasal bone septum. Mycological testing: direct mycological exam of oral scrapings was negative. Sputum examination: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Incisional biopsy of palatal mucosal lesion: histopathological examination revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and chronic active granulomatous inflammation compatible with leishmaniasis (without direct identification of the etiological agent). Prior outside laryngoscopy and biopsy: showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and active chronic inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Mucosal leishmaniasis (espundia) involving the palate, uvula, pharynx, and nasal septum.
Diagnostic confirmation: Positive Montenegro intradermal test (MIT) with an intense hyperergic reaction (bullous/bubble formation); palatal histopathology showing pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and granulomatous inflammation compatible with leishmaniasis.
Differentials ruled out: Paracoccidioidomycosis (direct mycological examination and sputum examination negative), oral candidiasis (no response to nystatin rinses), tuberculosis, squamous cell carcinoma, syphilis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated at the Araraquara Health Service (SESA) with intravenous meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime, 3 ampoules of 5 mL [425 mg each] diluted in 250 mL normal saline infused over 2 hours daily for 30 days). Experienced transient epigastric pain on days 1-2 and arthralgias with peripheral joint swelling of hands and legs during therapy. At completion of treatment, intraoral examination showed complete regression and scarring of the lesion, relief of nasal congestion, improved breathing, and marked improvement in hoarseness.

raw_case_text: In early January 2016, a 46-year-old Brazilian non-Caucasian female previously healthy arrived at the emergency department of the University Hospital of Sergipe with a history of 3 days with high fever (>39 C), joint pain, arthralgia, and a red cutaneous rash. She was treated with hydration and discharged from the hospital with a paracetamol prescription. She returned to the emergency department 4 days later with right upper extremity painful edema, with no prior peripherally inserted central catheter or intravenous infusions in the arm that had brachial thrombosis (Figure 1). An upper limb venous duplex scan revealed right brachial vein thrombosis. She was treated with unfractionated heparin followed by vitamin K antagonists (VKAs). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test confirmed Zika infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: 46-year-old female presenting with high fever (>39 °C), arthralgia, and red cutaneous rash for 3 days, returning 4 days later with painful edema of the right upper extremity.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of high fever (>39 °C), diffuse joint pain, and an erythematous cutaneous rash. She received intravenous hydration and was discharged on paracetamol. Four days later, she returned with acute painful swelling of the right upper extremity, with no prior peripherally inserted central catheter, vascular access, or intravenous infusions in that arm.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; non-Caucasian female residing in Sergipe, Brazil; no conventional predisposing risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
subjective.review_of_systems: High fever, diffuse joint pain, cutaneous rash, acute arm pain and swelling; denies chest pain or shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: High fever (temperature >39 °C), red cutaneous rash. Subsequent presentation: Painful edema of the right upper extremity without superficial skin breakdown.
objective.routine_investigations: Upper limb venous duplex ultrasound: Right brachial vein thrombosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute Zika virus infection confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), complicated by acute right brachial deep vein thrombosis. Patient was treated with therapeutic anticoagulation using intravenous unfractionated heparin bridged to oral vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), resulting in clinical resolution.

raw_case_text: A 15-day-old male infant was referred to our hospital with a history of recurrent apnea, suspected sepsis, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and thrombocytopenia. The infant was ventilated at the referring hospital for recurrent apnea and was treated with intravenous antibiotics and other supportive measures. General examination at admission revealed marked hyperpigmentation of the face (Figure 1) and genital region (Figure 2). Systemic examination was unremarkable. The possibility of neonatal chikungunya was considered due to classical hyperpigmentation, clinical presentation, and thrombocytopenia. The patient's mother reported having suffered a fever during the week preceding his delivery. The diagnosis in the neonate was confirmed by positive IgM antibodies to chikungunya. The child was treated symptomatically, recovered gradually, and was extubated on the third day of admission. Platelet count also normalized and the infant was discharged on the tenth day of admission. Transmission of chikungunya from mother to fetus is most likely when the mother is viremic at delivery. Though neurological, ocular, renal, and hematological manifestations have been described, the striking pigmentation of the nose, described as the "chik sign," is the most recognizable feature in the diagnosis of neonatal chikungunya  . Differential diagnoses include congenital lupus, drug rash (due to imipenem, for instance), and bacterial infections (Listeria monocytogenes, Staphylococcus epidermidis), fungi (Candida), and viruses (human herpesvirus 6, enteroviruses). Knowledge of the "chik sign" as a cutaneous feature of chikungunya could be useful in resource-poor settings to detect unrecognized outbreaks of this arboviral fever, especially when the facilities for serological confirmation are not available.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-day-old male infant was referred with recurrent apnea, suspected sepsis, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and thrombocytopenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 15-day-old male neonate was transferred from an outside hospital following intubation and mechanical ventilation for recurrent apnea in the setting of suspected sepsis, neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, and thrombocytopenia. He had received empiric intravenous antibiotics and supportive care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born to a mother who suffered from a febrile illness during the week preceding delivery; prior hospitalization and mechanical ventilation at referring facility.

objective.physical_examination: General examination: Marked hyperpigmentation involving the face (particularly the nose) and the genital region. Systemic examination: Unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Thrombocytopenia and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia documented (exact numerical values not reported in case text).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Positive IgM antibodies to Chikungunya virus, confirming vertically transmitted neonatal Chikungunya infection with characteristic facial ('chik sign') and genital hyperpigmentation. Management and course: Managed with supportive intensive care and mechanical ventilation; extubated on the third hospital day. Thrombocytopenia resolved, and the infant was discharged in stable condition on day 10.

raw_case_text: A man in his 40s with a history of HIV on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) and hypertension with a body mass index (BMI) of 34.9 presented to the Emergency Department (ED) after being seen at an urgent care clinic with hypotension and dyspnea. He visited his Primary Care Provider 2 weeks prior for fever, chills, and cough productive of grayish sputum; however, his symptoms persisted despite completing a course of azithromycin. During the interview, he denied recent travel or COVID-19 exposure. He endorsed fatigue, leg cramping, and poor appetite. CD4+ count and viral load were unknown to the patient. His vitals were unstable in ED with tachypnea (58 breaths/min) and hypotension (70/50 mmHg), heart rate of 91 beats/min, temperature of 37.1 C, and an oxygen saturation of 92% while on a non-rebreather mask at a flow rate of 15 L. On examination, he was in respiratory distress with decreased breath sounds in bilateral lung fields. The patients' baseline creatinine was unknown at the time of presentation. The remainder of the examination was noncontributory; patient had good skin turgor and appropriate capillary refill. Vital signs for the duration of the visit are provided in Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A male in his 40s presenting with severe dyspnea, hypotension, fever, chills, and productive cough refractory to outpatient azithromycin.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A man in his 40s presented with a 2-week history of fever, chills, and cough productive of grayish sputum that persisted despite outpatient azithromycin therapy. He subsequently developed worsening dyspnea, fatigue, poor appetite, and leg cramping, presenting to an urgent care clinic where hypotension and respiratory distress were identified, prompting immediate transfer to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral infection on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART; baseline CD4 count and viral load unknown to patient); hypertension; obesity (BMI 34.9 kg/m2); recent course of oral azithromycin. Denied recent travel or known COVID-19 contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue, leg cramping, anorexia, dyspnea, productive cough with grayish sputum, fever, and chills; denies other systemic complaints.

objective.physical_examination: General appearance: Severe respiratory distress. Vitals on admission: Blood pressure 70/50 mmHg (hypotension), respiratory rate 58 breaths/min (severe tachypnea), heart rate 91 beats/min, temperature 37.1 °C, oxygen saturation 92% on a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min. Respiratory: Decreased breath sounds throughout bilateral lung fields. Cardiovascular: Appropriate capillary refill, regular rate. Skin: Good skin turgor; remainder of examination noncontributory.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe refractory community-acquired / atypical pneumonia complicated by septic shock, severe type 1 respiratory failure, and acute respiratory distress in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection on HAART, class I/II obesity (BMI 34.9 kg/m2), and hypertension.
Plan & Emergency Management: Patient presented in shock with profound tachypnea and hypoxemia requiring maximal non-rebreather oxygen supplementation (15 L/min). Management prioritized hemodynamic stabilization, aggressive fluid resuscitation, escalation of broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage, and immediate intensive care unit admission.

raw_case_text: A 37-year-old male from Georgia came to France in October 2012. He had HIV infection since 2006 inconstantly treated with HAART. Other medical conditions were adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis due to chronic HCV, and treatment-controlled tuberculosis. VL was diagnosed in 2010 and treated in Georgia with meglumine antimoniate and L-AmB (doses and schedules unknown). In November 2012, he presented hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathies, infiltrated cutaneous lesions, anemia, number of CD4 lymphocytes = 133/mm3, viral load < 50 copies/mL, and parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/ml. He received a course of L-AmB followed by maintenance therapy for 5 months (Fig 1B). In May 2013, he had weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, number of CD4 lymphocytes = 177/mm3, viral load < 40 copies/mL and parasitemia of 12 Leishmania/ml. L-AmB treatment was intensified, but renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia occurred. In June, the splenomegaly and parasitemia remained unchanged. A course of meglumine antimoniate was administered. Despite pre-existing liver disorders, the treatment was well tolerated except for mild neutropenia. One month later, a marked clinical improvement was observed and parasitemia decreased to 0.2 Leishmania/ml. In July, maintenance treatment with miltefosine (150 mg/day for 3 months) was started. Parasitemia was negative, the number of CD4 lymphocytes increased from 169 to 540/mm3, and viral load was undetectable. Parasitemia remained negative through 18 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male presented with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and infiltrated skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old male from Georgia presented in November 2012 with hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathies, infiltrated skin lesions, and anemia. He was treated with an induction course of L-AmB followed by 5 months of maintenance therapy. In May 2013, he suffered a relapse with progressive weight loss, persistent hepatosplenomegaly, and anemia. Intensification of L-AmB induced acute renal insufficiency and thrombocytopenia without splenic reduction. In June 2013, he was transitioned to meglumine antimoniate, followed by oral miltefosine maintenance, which achieved complete clinical remission and parasitemia clearance.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 2006 (intermittently treated with HAART); adrenal insufficiency; liver cirrhosis secondary to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection; treatment-controlled pulmonary tuberculosis. Prior visceral leishmaniasis diagnosed in Georgia in 2010, treated with meglumine antimoniate and L-AmB.
subjective.review_of_systems: Weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, infiltrated skin lesions. Denied fever during late relapse.

objective.physical_examination: Cachectic male with palpable hepatosplenomegaly, generalized peripheral lymphadenopathies, and diffuse infiltrated cutaneous lesions. Spleen size remained enlarged despite initial therapy.
objective.routine_investigations: Anemia on presentation. Following intensified L-AmB, developed acute renal insufficiency and acute thrombocytopenia. Transient mild neutropenia occurred during antimonial therapy. CD4+ T-cell count: 133/mm^3 in November 2012; 177/mm^3 in May 2013; increased from 169 to 540/mm^3 in July 2013. HIV viral load < 50 copies/mL initially and < 40 copies/mL in May 2013.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Relapsing visceral leishmaniasis with cutaneous involvement (PKDL/disseminated) in an HIV-coinfected patient with HCV cirrhosis and adrenal insufficiency.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Quantitative blood PCR demonstrated parasitemia of 6 Leishmania/mL in November 2012, rising to 12 Leishmania/mL during the May 2013 relapse, declining to 0.2 Leishmania/mL following antimonial therapy, and becoming undetectable on miltefosine.
Differentials Ruled Out: Progression of HCV cirrhosis, recurrence of tuberculosis, and lymphoproliferative malignancy.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Received L-AmB induction and 5 months maintenance. Relapse in May 2013 failed intensified L-AmB due to nephrotoxicity and thrombocytopenia. In June 2013, treated with a course of meglumine antimoniate, which was well tolerated despite cirrhosis (mild neutropenia only) and reduced parasitemia to 0.2 Leishmania/mL. Switched in July 2013 to maintenance oral miltefosine (150 mg/day for 3 months), resulting in complete clinical recovery, CD4+ count reconstitution to 540/mm^3, and sustained undetectable parasitemia through 18 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old male presented to the medical emergency department with complaints of weakness and significant weight loss over 1 year. He had episodes of low-grade fever in the past year, for which the patient was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years back. At present, he was again put on antitubercular therapy (ATT) for the past 1 month; however, no improvement was noted and hence the patient was referred to our hospital. There was no significant family history. On general physical examination, the patient was found to be thin built, pale, and afebrile with abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were enlarged and measured 1.5 cm in diameter. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted, however no fluid thrill could be discerned. Ultrasound abdomen revealed enlarged multiple conglomerate of mesenteric lymph nodes with the largest node measuring 22 mm x 18 mm. Clinical chemistry revealed A:G reversal with total protein of 9.5 g%, albumin of 2.0 g%, globulin of 7.5 g%, and A:G ratio of 1:3.75. Other parameters of liver function test and kidney function test were found to be within normal limits. Complete hemogram revealed pancytopenia with hemoglobin: 6 g%, total leukocyte count: 1800/muL, differential leukocyte count: polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%, eosinophils 1%, monocytes 1%, platelets: 48,000/muL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear revealed the presence of rouleaux; however, no hemoparasite was noted.
Fine needle aspiration cytology was performed on the left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes, which yielded thick aspirate. Smears prepared showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete and aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells. Numerous intracellular as well as extracellular amastigote forms of Leishmania species were seen [Figure 1]. In view of strong clinical suspicion, Ziehl-Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was also done which came out to be negative. Both polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and AFB culture yielded negative result. Later on, rK39 antigen was also found to be positive.
