raw_case_text: A 46-year-old male patient presented to the dermatology outpatient department with 1-year history of sensory loss and paresthesia over bilateral lower legs. He was admitted and evaluated for Hansen's disease. On examination, there was no cutaneous lesion suggestive of leprosy. Peripheral nerve trunks were not thickened. Sensory loss to touch, pain, and temperature was present over the distal part of legs and feet bilaterally. Ankle jerk was diminished bilaterally. No trophic ulcer was present. Higher mental function and cranial nerve examination were within normal limits. There was no sign of meningeal irritation. Motor examination did not reveal weakness in any major muscle groups. Slit skin smear taken from earlobes did not demonstrate any acid-fast bacilli. A skin biopsy was taken from hypoesthetic skin of the right leg and sent for histopathology. Initial investigations including complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, fasting plasma glucose, and urine examination did not reveal any abnormality. In such a clinical scenario, the possibility of Hansen's disease was remote, and therefore, a neurologist's opinion was sought. The patient was then advised to go for HIV serology and to our surprise found to be reactive for HIV-1 with CD4 count of 160 cells/mm3. On retrospective questioning, the patient gave a history of on-and-off fever, fatigue, weight loss, and recurrent pyodermas. He also had multiple high-risk sexual exposures several years back. He was diagnosed as a case of HIV neuropathy-distal symmetric polyneuropathy (DSP) type and started on antiretroviral therapy (ART).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presenting with sensory loss and paresthesias in bilateral lower extremities for one year.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-year history of progressive, symmetrical numbness, paresthesias, and sensory loss in a glove-and-stocking distribution over both lower legs and feet. He was initially admitted to the dermatology unit for evaluation of suspected Hansen's disease. Subsequent retrospective clinical review elicited a multi-month history of intermittent fevers, generalized fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and recurrent cutaneous bacterial infections.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent pyodermas over preceding years; remote history of multiple high-risk unprotected sexual exposures. No history of diabetes mellitus, neurotoxic substance exposure, or heavy alcohol use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Bilateral lower extremity numbness, tingling, fatigue, weight loss, and intermittent fevers; denies focal motor weakness, gait ataxia, bowel or bladder incontinence, visual changes, or cranial neuropathies.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: Absence of hypopigmented or erythematous skin macules/plaques, trophic ulcers, or cutaneous lepromatous lesions. Neurologic: Intact cranial nerves and normal higher mental functions; bilateral symmetrical reduction to light touch, pinprick, and temperature sensation over the distal lower third of both legs and feet; bilateral ankle jerk reflexes diminished; motor power 5/5 across all major muscle groups; absence of peripheral nerve trunk thickening (ulnar, radial cutaneous, or common peroneal nerves); no signs of meningeal irritation.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, fasting plasma glucose, serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, liver function tests, and urinalysis were all within normal reference limits. Slit skin smear examination from bilateral earlobes: Negative for acid-fast bacilli.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic skin punch biopsy from hypoesthetic skin of the right lower leg: Histopathological evaluation revealed no evidence of neural granulomatous inflammation or Hansen's disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection (CDC Stage 3; confirmed by reactive HIV-1 serology, CD4 count 160 cells/microL) presenting with HIV-associated distal sensory polyneuropathy (DSP); Hansen's disease, diabetic neuropathy, and central nervous system pathologies were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) alongside symptomatic neuropathic pain management and close clinical follow-up for immunologic recovery.

raw_case_text: A 50-year-old Italian man was admitted to the hospital because of severe febrile illness associated with profound malaise, headache, sweating, and worsening jaundice of five-day duration. Two weeks before the onset of sickness he had returned from a business trip in Cameroon. The patient had not taken any chemoprophylaxis against malaria. He was obese (weight 98 Kg; height 176 cm), and an excessive use of alcohol was reported. He had not previously suffered from hypertension or any other known cardiovascular disease. Upon admission, he complained additionally of nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. He was fully conscious, normotensive with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm/Hg, but clinical examination revealed tachycardia and severe jaundice; his peripheral oxygen saturation was 95%. A neurological inspection did not show significant alterations. Full blood count revealed thrombocytopenia (17 x 109/L), haemoglobin at 14.6 g/dL, and white cell count at 10 x 109/L. Liver function tests documented hyperbilirubinaemia, moderate increase in serum transaminases, and moderate renal impairment; blood glucose levels were also raised. Coagulation screen did not show evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation. Cardiac enzymes were normal (Table 1). A blood film revealed a heavy P. falciparum parasitaemia of 20%. A chest X-ray was normal, and the unique alteration observed in the electrocardiogram (ECG) was a low amplitude in QRS complexes. Serological testing for Cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, seasonal influenza viruses A and B, adenoviruses, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, respiratory syncytial virus, the Widal-Wright reaction and the slide macro-agglutination test for leptospirosis were negative. The patient was treated with 10 mg/kg b.w. (namely, 1000 mg) of I.V. quinidine gluconate t.i.d., plus ceftriaxone 2 g q24h I.V. and oral doxycycline 100 mg b.i.d., while waiting for the results of blood cultures. Within 12 hours of admission, a slow but progressive worsening of multiorgan failure was observed despite a marked reduction of parasitaemia. Given the severity of clinical setting, I.M. artemisin (300 mg loading dose, followed by 100 mg/daily) was initiated. At 40 hours after admission, the patient worsened suddenly. He became restless, confused, bradiarythmical, hypotensive (80/60 mmHg), and died in spite of prompt mechanical ventilation and cardiac resuscitation. The post-mortem evaluation revealed acute heart failure (bilateral pulmonary oedema) but no signs of myocardial ischaemia. The liver and the spleen were not enlarged. However, an histology of severe acute myocarditis with myocardiolysis was detected: diffuse lymphocytic infiltrates were surrounding the myocardial capillaries, inside which some intravascular parasitized RBCs were visible (Figure 1). No sequestered parasites could be revealed in brain vessels.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presenting with a 5-day history of severe fever, profound malaise, headache, sweating, and worsening jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 50-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of severe febrile illness, profound malaise, severe headache, drenching diaphoresis, progressive scleral jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Symptoms began two weeks following his return from a business trip to Cameroon. He had taken no chemoprophylaxis. At 40 hours following hospital admission, he suffered acute cardiovascular collapse with restlessness, confusion, bradyarrhythmia, and severe hypotension.
subjective.past_medical_history: Travel history: returned 2 weeks prior from a business trip to Cameroon without malaria chemoprophylaxis. Obesity (weight 98 kg, height 176 cm); history of excessive alcohol consumption. No history of hypertension or known cardiovascular disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, profuse sweating, severe headache, profound malaise, progressive jaundice, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Denied chest pain or cough on presentation. Medications: none. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious and oriented. Normotensive on admission with blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, but tachycardic and severely jaundiced; peripheral oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Neurological exam: no focal abnormalities. Abdominal exam: soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. Terminal exam at 40 hours: restless, confused, severe bradyarrhythmia, and profound hypotension (80/60 mmHg).
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: platelets 17 x 10^9/L (severe thrombocytopenia), hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 10 x 10^9/L. Liver function tests: severe hyperbilirubinemia and moderate transaminitis. Renal profile: moderate renal impairment. Serum glucose elevated. Coagulation screen: no evidence of overt DIC. Cardiac biomarkers: normal initially. Chest X-ray: normal on admission. Electrocardiogram (ECG): low QRS voltage. Extensive negative serologies: CMV, EBV, influenza A/B, adenovirus, Chlamydia psittaci, Coxiella burnetii, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, RSV, Widal-Wright, and leptospirosis macro-agglutination. Peripheral blood smear performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Post-mortem autopsy and histological examination: acute heart failure with bilateral pulmonary edema without coronary or myocardial ischemic necrosis; normal liver and spleen size; cardiac histopathology revealed severe acute myocarditis with myocardiolysis, diffuse lymphocytic infiltrates surrounding myocardial capillaries containing intravascular intraerythrocytic inclusions. Brain vessels showed no sequestered cellular aggregates.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Hyperparasitemic Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute lethal malarial myocarditis, severe thrombocytopenia, hyperbilirubinemia, acute renal impairment, and fatal cardiogenic shock.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood film revealing heavy Plasmodium falciparum hyperparasitemia of 20%; post-mortem cardiac histology confirming severe acute lymphocytic myocarditis with myocardiolysis and capillaries packed with parasitized red blood cells.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous quinidine gluconate 10 mg/kg (1000 mg) every 8 hours, IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily, and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; intramuscular artemisinin (300 mg load, then 100 mg daily) was added due to clinical severity. Despite rapid reduction in parasitemia, the patient developed sudden refractory cardiogenic shock, bradyarrhythmia, and bilateral pulmonary edema at 40 hours post-admission, and died despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation and mechanical ventilation.

raw_case_text: A 14-year-old female was admitted to the hospital on June 5, 2016, at 2:20 am. The patient's symptoms started 12 h after clinical manifestation in her sister (Case 1). She had a 39  C fever and headache progression for 24 h. She presented with psychomotor agitation, followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizures. She was taken to Axochiapan Morelos Hospital for assessment. On admission, she exhibited neurological deterioration requiring orotracheal intubation and was sent to Children's Hospital of Morelos, where cranial computerized axial tomography (CAT) revealed severe cerebral edema and uncal herniation (Fig. 2). Her laboratory blood tests are presented in Table 1. She was transferred to the intensive care unit where hemodynamic and antiedema care was provided. On beginning intensive care, clinical data indicated brain death, which was confirmed by three isoelectric EEGs. The patient died in the hospital five days after admission. Serology positive for dengue NS1 by ELISA was reported, and PCR was performed to detect enterovirus in the CSF, with negative results.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old female presenting with high fever, progressive headache for 24 hours, psychomotor agitation, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 14-year-old female (sister of Case 1) developed high fever of 39 C and progressive headache for 24 hours, starting 12 hours after the onset of illness in her sister. She developed acute psychomotor agitation rapidly followed by generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Evaluated at a regional hospital, she exhibited rapid neurological deterioration necessitating emergent orotracheal intubation and transfer to a pediatric intensive care unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological history: Sibling (sister) developed fatal fulminant encephalitis 12 hours prior; younger sister also had acute febrile illness 2 days prior. No prior chronic medical illnesses. Family history negative for toxic exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, severe headache, psychomotor agitation, and seizures. Systemic review limited by intubation and coma. Medications: none. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Intubated, comatose. Neurological deterioration with loss of brainstem reflexes. Clinical findings consistent with brain death upon ICU admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory blood tests performed on admission (Table 1).
objective.advanced_workup: Cranial CT: Severe cerebral edema with uncal herniation. Electroencephalography (EEG): Three consecutive isoelectric EEGs confirming brain death. Lumbar puncture / CSF: PCR for enterovirus was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe neurodengue / fatal dengue encephalitis with uncal herniation and brain death. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus NS1 antigen by ELISA; negative CSF enterovirus PCR.
Plan & Outcome: Received intensive hemodynamic support and anti-cerebral edema therapy in the ICU. Clinical brain death was confirmed by three isoelectric EEGs, and the patient died 5 days after hospital admission.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old HIV-negative aboriginal male was initially admitted with community-acquired pneumonia, which progressively worsened. A subsequent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed acid-fast bacilli on ziehl-neelsen staining. A subsequent CT chest demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and cavitating lesions consistent with active pulmonary tuberculosis infection. His treatment was initiated with the standard 4-drug regimen: pyrazinamide, rifampin, ethambutol, and isoniazid (INH). Sputum mycobacterial TB culture demonstrated susceptibility to the 4-drug regimen. 
During his admission to hospital, he developed diffuse abdominal pain with peritonitis on examination. He also developed tachycardia and hypotension, and an abdominal X-ray revealed free air under the diaphragm. Arrangements were made for emergent exploratory laparotomy in the operating room. Intraoperatively a single contiguous inflammatory mass was found in the left upper quadrant, which revealed a gangrenous necrotic splenic colon. A left hemicolectomy was preformed. This revealed a region of necrotic-appearing pancreatic tissue which was likely associated with the necrosis of the adjacent splenic colon. Further exploration of this inflammatory mass demonstrated particulate matter and peritoneal fluid and a large perforation in the posterior wall of the stomach, which was the initial insult. Peritoneal fluid mixed with enteric contents from the gastric perforation was sent for culture and was positive for mycobacterium tuberculosis. An intraoperative gastroscopy was preformed which identified an ulcer approximately 5-10 cm from the gastroesophageal junction. The patient hemodynamic status worsened in the operating room despite ongoing resuscitation and significant quantities of norepinephrine intravenously were needed. It was decided to stabilize the patient with a damage control laparotomy and take the patient to the intensive care unit rather than perform a definitive repair of the gastric perforation because of the severe hemodynamic instability. Drains surrounding the ulcer were placed and the skin closed. Plans were made to return to the operating room in 24 hours for definitive treatment if the patient's hemodynamic status improved. 
The patient's condition stabilized in the intensive care unit, and he was brought to the operation room the following day. Multiple biopsies of the large 3 cm gastric ulcer were taken. The patient was deemed to be unable to tolerate a total gastrectomy at this time, and unfortunately wedge resection of the stomach was not possible due to the position and size of the ulcer. Thus, the ulcer was repaired with primary closure, and creation of a feeding jejunostomy was completed. The patient was returned to the intensive care unit. Biopsies from the gastric ulcer revealed no malignancy but did demonstrate fungal elements (Candida albicans) indicative of secondary infection. Also, focal reactive changes in the surface epithelium suggested a reactive process. No granulomata or giant cells were identified. Biopsies were also negative for Helicobacter pylori. The patient did not receive nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications and was on Pantoprazole to prevent stress-related ulceration. The peritoneal fluid cultures collected during operation for the gastric perforation demonstrated mycobacterium tuberculosis and fungal elements. Gastric tissue sent intraoperatively for culture was positive for mycobacterium TB, which led to the presumptive diagnosis of gastric perforation, associated with TB. Pathologic examination of the resected left colon revealed an area of necrosis, but no perforation. Microscopic examination demonstrated numerous caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, demonstrating mycobacterial colitis. 
The patient remained in the intensive care unit, and a small-bowel follow-through with contrast revealed no extravasation of contrast. The TB-associated gastric perforation was adequately repaired. Postoperatively the patient was continued on INH 300 mg intramuscularly and rifampin 600 mg intravenously daily according to sensitivities from peritoneal fluid cultures. Imipenum, levofloxacin, and fluconazole were also continued according to culture results. 
The patient's pulmonary tuberculosis persisted over the subsequent weeks despite appropriate antituberculosis treatment. Deteriorating lung function was likely a combination of previous smoking damage, edema secondary to recent aggressive fluid resuscitation, and persistent pneumothorax. Eventually multiorgan failure ensued, and life support was discontinued following discussion with the family.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male with worsening pneumonia presenting with acute severe abdominal pain, peritonitis, and hemodynamic collapse.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, an HIV-negative aboriginal male, was initially hospitalized with community-acquired pneumonia that progressively worsened despite antibiotics. Bronchoscopy with BAL was performed and chest CT showed cavitary lesions, leading to initiation of standard 4-drug antitubercular therapy. During his hospital stay, he developed acute diffuse abdominal pain, peritonitis, tachycardia, and hypotension, with radiographic evidence of pneumoperitoneum requiring emergent surgical exploration.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of cigarette smoking with chronic lung damage. HIV-negative. Denied use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs); was maintained on pantoprazole for stress ulcer prophylaxis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Acute diffuse abdominal pain, progressive respiratory failure. Denies NSAID ingestion.

objective.physical_examination: Patient was in severe distress, tachycardic, hypotensive, requiring significant intravenous norepinephrine infusions for hemodynamic support. Abdominal examination revealed diffuse abdominal tenderness with involuntary guarding and frank peritonitis.
objective.routine_investigations: Abdominal plain radiograph revealed free air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum).
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT demonstrated bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and cavitating lesions. Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed. Emergent exploratory laparotomy: single contiguous inflammatory mass in the left upper quadrant with gangrenous necrotic splenic flexure of the colon; left hemicolectomy performed; adjacent necrotic pancreatic tissue identified; intra-abdominal particulate matter and large perforation in the posterior wall of the stomach 5 to 10 cm distal to gastroesophageal junction. Damage-control closure with drainage; return to OR at 24 hours for primary closure of 3 cm gastric ulcer and feeding jejunostomy. Gastric ulcer biopsies revealed Candida albicans fungal elements and reactive surface epithelial changes without malignancy, H. pylori, or granulomas. Small-bowel follow-through with contrast showed no extravasation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis manifesting as severe cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis and tuberculous colitis with gangrene of the splenic colon, complicated by secondary posterior gastric wall perforation and Candida albicans superinfection.
Diagnostic confirmation: Bronchoalveolar lavage Ziehl-Neelsen stain positive for acid-fast bacilli; sputum culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis fully susceptible to first-line agents. Peritoneal fluid cultures and intraoperative gastric tissue cultures grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis (with fungal elements). Colon histopathology demonstrated numerous caseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells confirming tuberculous colitis.
Management and outcome: Initial treatment with standard oral pyrazinamide, rifampin, ethambutol, and isoniazid; following emergent laparotomies, transitioned to intramuscular isoniazid 300 mg daily and intravenous rifampin 600 mg daily alongside imipenem, levofloxacin, and fluconazole. Despite successful surgical repair, respiratory failure worsened due to pre-existing tobacco-related damage, fluid resuscitation-associated pulmonary edema, and persistent pneumothorax, progressing to multiorgan failure; life support was withdrawn following family discussion.

raw_case_text: A man who was on second-line ART and had a history of TB four times prior presented with weight loss, fatigue and diffuse, hypopigmented skin lesions suggestive of a superficial fungal infection (see Table 1 for more information). The patient was classified as meeting the WHO 'seriously ill' criteria and an AlereLAM revealed a strongly positive (4+) result; he was therefore started on TB treatment. A sputum and urine sample were collected, and both of these later cultured Mycobacterium kansasii. Once the two samples had isolated M. kansasii, a dual infection of M. tb and M. kansasii was diagnosed and azithromycin was added to the patient's regimen. Unfortunately, the patient disengaged from treatment after one year and died as an inpatient two years after initial presentation. Blood culture on that admission was positive for Mycobacterium kansasii. No Xpert MTB/RIF or cultures identified M. tb.

subjective.chief_complaint: An adult male presenting with progressive weight loss, severe fatigue, and diffuse skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with progressive constitutional symptoms including unintentional weight loss and debilitating fatigue, accompanied by widespread cutaneous eruptions. He met the World Health Organization 'seriously ill' clinical criteria at the time of evaluation. After one year of therapy, he disengaged from clinical care and required hospital admission two years after his initial evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Receiving second-line combination antiretroviral therapy; history of four prior episodes of treated tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Profound fatigue, weight loss, and widespread cutaneous rash; denies acute focal chest pain or focal neurologic complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Patient met WHO 'seriously ill' criteria. Dermatologic: Diffuse, hypopigmented maculopapular skin lesions suggestive of a superficial fungal infection; vital signs not documented in raw text.
objective.routine_investigations: Sputum and urine samples collected for diagnostic screening and mycobacterial cultures.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated Mycobacterium kansasii infection (with initial clinical diagnosis of concurrent Mycobacterium tuberculosis) in an advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-infected patient on second-line antiretroviral therapy. Diagnostic confirmation: Both sputum and urine cultures isolated Mycobacterium kansasii; follow-up blood culture during terminal hospitalization was positive for Mycobacterium kansasii; urine lipoarabinomannan (AlereLAM) test was strongly positive (4+); molecular assays (Xpert MTB/RIF) and cultures were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Plan & Outcome: Initially initiated on standard anti-tuberculosis therapy based on positive AlereLAM (4+); upon speciation of M. kansasii, oral azithromycin was added to the regimen. The patient disengaged from care at one year and subsequently died during inpatient hospitalization two years post-presentation secondary to disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease.

raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old male was referred to our emergency department with 8-10 days of worsening shortness of breath, fever, and dry cough. The patient had no prior medical history, took no medications at home, and had never had an endoscopy. Physical examination was significant for respiratory distress with bilateral crackles and oxygen saturation of 70% on room air requiring the initiation of high flow nasal cannula for oxygen support. Chest x-ray on presentation demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities and a left-sided consolidation consisted with viral pneumonia secondary to COVID-19. SARS-CoV-2 reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) viral testing was positive. His initial electrolytes, kidney functions, and complete blood count were within the normal range, serum albumin on presentation was 2.3 mg/dL. He was placed on hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone empirically. The patient was admitted to an intensive care unit. Of note, he reported significant hunger and asked several times for additional food.
On the second hospital day, the patient became increasingly hypoxic despite maximal non-invasive ventilatory support. He was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation. He was placed on pantroprazole for GI prophylaxis.
Throughout hospital days 2 and 3, the patient showed signs of acute kidney injury with metabolic acidosis. Vasopressors were administered as well as Bicarbonate drip. The patient gradually improved, requiring fewer vasopressors and ventilator support. Tube feeds were started on the fourth hospital day, and the patient appeared to tolerate feeding without issue.
On the evening of the fifth hospital day, the patient began to require higher levels of oxygenation to maintain saturation. His abdomen was noted to be acutely markedly distended. White blood cell count was elevated to 15,900 (94.4% Neutrophils). An abdominal x-ray remonstrated no evidence of air or stool in the rectum, a paucity of intestinal gas, and no evidence of obstruction (Figure 1). Chest x-ray demonstrated a small amount of pneumoperitoneum which was not present in the previous day chest x-ray. As the patient had worsening hypoxia with maximal ventilator support, CT scan was deferred. A bedside ultrasound was performed which demonstrated significant amounts of hypoechoic fluid. Bedside abdominal paracentesis was performed under ultrasound guidance, and a catheter was placed in the right lower quadrant. One liter of cloudy, milky-appearing fluid was aspirated immediately, and the catheter was left in place connected to a drainage bag. The fluid was sent for gram stain and culture. Analysis of this fluid revealed no neutrophils, 4000 red blood cells (pHF), lactate dehydrogenase of 3791 (U/L), and an amylase of 871 (U/L).
Due to the appearance of the fluid, which was similar to the tube feeds the patient had started the day before, and the fact that the fluid did not contain white blood cells or bacteria, it was suspected that the patient may have proximal gastrointestinal perforation. For confirmation, methylene blue was administered via the nasogastric tube (NGT) and was noted to appear in the drainage bag rapidly. The patient was made NPO (nothing by mouth), and broad spectrum antibiotic therapy was initiated in order to cover for any enteric anaerobic bacteria and fungi. Given the patients critical condition, we elected to offer the patient's family surgical exploration for diagnosis and treatment of gastrointestinal perforation. However, the patient's family elected to proceed with non-operative management. Following the drainage and the conservative treatment, over the next day, the patient's vasopressor and oxygen requirements improved dramatically.
On hospital days 6 and 7, the amount of fluid noted in the drainage bag decreased. Bile was noted in the NGT. Repeated bedside ultrasound did not demonstrate re-accumulation of fluid. The patient remained stable. Unfortunately, over the next several days, the patient's respiratory status began to decline and he demonstrated a clinical picture typical to severe COVID-19 infection with extreme respiratory failure. He further required renal replacement therapy, and expired on hospital day 9. Due to hospital policy during the pandemic surge, we could not perform autopsy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old male presenting with 8 to 10 days of worsening shortness of breath, fever, and dry cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 74-year-old male presented with an 8- to 10-day history of progressively worsening shortness of breath, high fever, and dry cough. On arrival, he exhibited severe hypoxemic respiratory failure with an oxygen saturation of 70% on ambient air, requiring high-flow nasal cannula. On hospital day 2, his respiratory failure escalated despite noninvasive ventilation, necessitating endotracheal intubation. On hospital day 5, while on mechanical ventilation and enteral feeding, he developed acute massive abdominal distension and worsening hypoxia.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior chronic medical conditions. Denied previous gastrointestinal endoscopy or prior hospitalizations.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive dyspnea, fever, dry cough, severe hunger upon admission, and subsequent acute abdominal distension. Home medications: none. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: severe respiratory distress; oxygen saturation: 70% on room air; chest auscultation revealed bilateral crackles throughout. Abdominal examination on hospital day 5: acute, tense, marked abdominal distension with tympany.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: serum albumin: 2.3 mg/dL; complete blood count, serum electrolytes, and baseline renal panel were within normal limits. Hospital day 5 labs: WBC count: 15,900/muL (94.4% neutrophils); acute kidney injury with metabolic acidosis. Peritoneal fluid analysis: cloudy, milky-appearing fluid containing 0 neutrophils, 4,000 RBC/hpf, LDH: 3,791 U/L, and amylase: 871 U/L. Enteral methylene blue dye test: rapid appearance of blue dye in the abdominal drainage catheter, confirming transmural proximal gastrointestinal tract perforation. Chest and abdominal radiographs: initial CXR revealed diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities and left-sided consolidation; day 5 CXR revealed interval pneumoperitoneum; abdominal X-ray demonstrated paucity of intestinal gas without mechanical obstruction. Bedside abdominal ultrasound: large volume hypoechoic free intraperitoneal fluid without fluid reaccumulation after drainage.
objective.advanced_workup: Bedside ultrasound-guided diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with right lower quadrant catheter placement, draining 1,000 mL of enteric/milky fluid. Abdominal computed tomography was deferred due to extreme ventilatory instability.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), complicated by spontaneous proximal gastrointestinal tract perforation, secondary peritonitis, acute kidney injury, and refractory septic/hypoxemic shock, confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Management & Outcome: Intubated and mechanically ventilated. Empiric antimicrobial therapy consisted of hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, and ceftriaxone, followed by broad-spectrum anaerobic and antifungal coverage. Following family decision for non-operative management of hollow viscus perforation, percutaneous abdominal catheter drainage, bowel rest (NPO), intravenous pantoprazole, and vasopressor/bicarbonate support produced transient hemodynamic stabilization. However, refractory ARDS and multi-organ failure ensued, requiring continuous renal replacement therapy, and the patient expired on hospital day 9.

raw_case_text:
A 6-month-old boy with hydrocephalus was referred to our hospital in 2008. The hydrocephalus during the first admission was confirmed by computed tomography (CT) scan. Examination of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) did not reveal any abnormality.
A VP shunt was inserted in June 2008 and the infant was discharged in acceptable condition, with good control of hydrocephalus confirmed by another CT scan on discharge day. Approximately 16 months after insertion of the VP shunt, the child was readmitted with a one-week history of fever (up to 38.5 C), and acute abdominal pain. The diagnosis was brucellosis based on serum agglutination test 1/640 and 1/1280 three days later. A titre of 1/320 measured in 2 mercaptoethanol (2ME) test. The patient was treated with trimethoprimsulfamethoxazole, rifampin, and gentamicin. His blood culture was negative.
The Ascitic fluid examination showed a glucose level of 89 mg/dL, a protein level of 5800 mg/dL, white blood cell (WBC) count was 480 (10% polymorphonuclear cells and 90% mononuclear), and the red blood cell (RBC) count was 4800.
After 4 months, he was again admitted to our hospital with drowsiness, vomiting and fever. Clinical diagnosis was suggestive for a VP shunt infection. Laboratory results were as follows: Hemoglobin, 9.1 g/dL; WBC count, 6.1x103 cells/mm3. 
A sample of ventricular CSF analyzed was slightly xanthochromic and contained a total of 4000 cells (70% polymorphonuclear cells and 30% lymphocytes), 80 mg/ dL glucose, and 192 mg/dL protein. No organisms were observed on the direct gram-stained smear. 
Blood culture was sterile and CSF serological test was positive (Brucella agglutinin titer was 1/80).
The patient responded well to a course of rifampin, gentamicin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily. Three days later the shunt was extracted. He was well on three follow-up visits at the outpatient clinic and the latest follow-up visit was 12 months after the diagnosis has been made. Figure 1 and 2 show Brain CT scan before and after extracting the VP shunt, respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-month-old boy with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt presented with drowsiness, vomiting, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was diagnosed with hydrocephalus at 6 months of age and received a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt in June 2008. Approximately 16 months later (at 22 months of age), he was readmitted with a 1-week history of fever (up to 38.5 °C) and acute abdominal pain, receiving trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampin, and gentamicin. Four months later (at 26 months of age), he presented with drowsiness, vomiting, and fever suggestive of VP shunt infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Infantile hydrocephalus treated with ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement in June 2008. Episode of febrile peritonitis/ascites 4 months prior. Animal contact or dairy exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Drowsiness, vomiting, fever; previous acute abdominal pain. Home medications: prior antibiotics (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, rifampin, gentamicin). Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature up to 38.5 °C; drowsiness/lethargy. Abdomen: acute abdominal pain noted during prior admission. Other physical exam details not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Ascitic fluid analysis (prior admission): glucose 89 mg/dL, protein 5,800 mg/dL, WBC count 480/mm^3 (10% polymorphonuclear, 90% mononuclear), RBC count 4,800/mm^3. Readmission blood labs: Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, WBC count 6.1 x 10^3 cells/mm^3. Blood cultures: sterile during both admissions.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT scan: hydrocephalus on initial presentation, with adequate control on post-shunt imaging; pre- and post-extraction CT scans confirmed ventricular configuration. Ventricular CSF analysis: slightly xanthochromic, total cell count 4,000 cells/mm^3 (70% polymorphonuclear cells, 30% lymphocytes), glucose 80 mg/dL, protein 192 mg/dL; Gram-stained smear: no organisms observed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt infection and neurobrucellosis / brucellar peritonitis.
Confirmation: Initial admission serum agglutination test was 1/640, rising to 1/1280 three days later, with 2-mercaptoethanol (2ME) titer of 1/320. Readmission ventricular CSF serology was positive with a Brucella agglutinin titer of 1/80. Blood cultures were sterile.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous/oral rifampin, gentamicin, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole daily, with complete surgical extraction of the infected VP shunt 3 days into therapy. Patient responded well and remained clinically healthy across outpatient follow-ups up to 12 months post-diagnosis.

raw_case_text: A 46-year-old female without a significant past medical history presented to the emergency room because of fever, myalgias, and body aches for past two days. She denied cough, dysuria, diarrhea, convulsions, and sick contact. However, she recently returned from Nigeria 7 days before presentation. Her initial vital signs were within the normal limit, but she spiked a fever of 101.7 F later on the same day of presentation. Physical examination was normal. She was alert and oriented to time, place, and person. She was ambulatory and was anicteric. Initial white blood cell count (6,000/mul) and hemoglobin (13 g/dl) levels were within normal limits; however, platelet count was low (83,000/muL). A comprehensive metabolic panel was normal with a random blood glucose of 136 mg/dl, creatinine of 1.1 mg/dl, and bicarbonate level of 25 mmoL/L, and a hepatic panel showed mild elevation in total bilirubin (1.2 mg/dL), aspartate transaminase (43 U/L), and alanine transaminase (59 U/L). Urinalysis was negative for blood, and red blood cell was 0-3/HPF. A chest X-ray was negative for an acute pulmonary mass, infiltrate, edema, effusion, or pneumothorax. She had a peripheral blood smear (Figure 1). Microbiology revealed a parasitemia level of 1.6% of Plasmodium falciparum at 1437 hours on Day 0. Despite being on the full dose of oral atovaquone and proguanil, the parasitemia level continued to rise from 1.6% to 7.6% at 0839 hours on Day 1 and then to 12.24% at 1154 hours on Day 2 with persistent intermittent fever spikes. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) was contacted, and the patient was supplied with three doses of intravenous artesunate at 2.4 mg/kg per dose. After the second dose, the parasitemia level was at 0.1% at 0458 hours on Day 3, and after the third dose it was negative. A repeat test also was negative. The patient continued to be on atovaquone and proguanil for 3 more days. The patient's symptoms resolved, and she stopped spiking fever and platelets count improved to 229,000/muL. She was discharged with scheduled repeat lab work weekly for 4 weeks as an outpatient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old female presenting with fever, myalgias, and body aches for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 46-year-old female presented to the emergency room with a 2-day history of fever, myalgias, and body aches. She reported no cough, dysuria, diarrhea, convulsions, or sick contacts. Initial vital signs were within normal limits, but she developed a fever spike later on the day of presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history. Epidemiological history: Recently returned from Nigeria 7 days prior to presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies cough, dysuria, diarrhea, convulsions, and sick contacts.

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs within normal limits; spiked a fever of 101.7 °F later on the day of presentation. Alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Ambulatory, anicteric. Physical examination was otherwise normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial WBC 6,000/μL, hemoglobin 13 g/dL, platelet count 83,000/μL. Comprehensive metabolic panel: random blood glucose 136 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, bicarbonate 25 mmol/L. Hepatic panel: total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, AST 43 U/L, ALT 59 U/L. Urinalysis: negative for blood, RBC 0-3/HPF. Chest X-ray: negative for acute pulmonary mass, infiltrate, edema, effusion, or pneumothorax.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria with progressive parasitemia during oral therapy. Peripheral blood smear microbiology revealed Plasmodium falciparum with an initial parasitemia of 1.6% at 1437 hours on Day 0. Despite oral atovaquone and proguanil, parasitemia increased to 7.6% at 0839 hours on Day 1 and 12.24% at 1154 hours on Day 2 with persistent intermittent fever spikes.
Plan & Outcome: Intravenous artesunate was obtained from the CDC and administered for three doses at 2.4 mg/kg per dose. Parasitemia fell to 0.1% at 0458 hours on Day 3 following the second dose, and cleared completely after the third dose; repeat test was negative. Oral atovaquone-proguanil was continued for an additional 3 days. Symptoms resolved, fevers ceased, and platelet count normalized to 229,000/μL. Discharged with weekly outpatient follow-up labs for 4 weeks.

raw_case_text: A 7-month-old male infant presented with fever for 10 days associated with hepatosplenomegaly, bicytopenia, pallor, anasarca, and increased ferritin. Immunochromatographic rapid test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania spp., and amastigotes were detected in a myelogram, which also presented hemophagocytosis. Complete treatment with lipossomal amphotericin was started and cefepime was used due to fever-associated neutropenia. In addition, he underwent transfusion of platelets, red blood cells, and albumin. After a diagnosis of HLHS, corticotherapy was started. The patient recovered after 3 days of treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-month-old male infant presented with a 10-day history of fever, pallor, and generalized swelling.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 7-month-old male infant developed persistent fever over 10 days, accompanied by progressive abdominal distension, severe cutaneous pallor, and generalized anasarca.

objective.physical_examination: Marked cutaneous pallor, generalized anasarca, and hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory testing showed bicytopenia, neutropenia, and markedly elevated serum ferritin.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspirate (myelogram) demonstrated active hemophagocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH/HLHS): rapid immunochromatographic test with rK39 antigen was positive for Leishmania spp., and bone marrow myelogram detected Leishmania amastigotes alongside active hemophagocytic histiocytes. The patient received complete treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B, intravenous cefepime for fever-associated neutropenia, transfusions of platelets, packed red blood cells, and albumin, and corticosteroid therapy for HLH. Rapid clinical recovery occurred within 3 days of initiating targeted therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old male laboratory worker was referred to a physician with recurrent fever, headache, arthralgia, weakness, and constipation, which had begun 1 month before. The patient worked in a laboratory that produced antigens for diagnostic use. Three weeks before symptoms began, he had been handling a dense culture of live B. canis M- and was using no personal protection; the procedures were not performed in a biological safety cabinet. Moreover, the patient had attempted resuspension by repeated pipetting with his mouth. The clinical examination disclosed cervical adenomegaly, and laboratory tests indicated a mild increase of hepatic enzymes (Aspartate aminotransferase 46 mu/L and alanine aminotransferase 65 mu/L) and neutropenia. The patient reported not having close contact with dogs or other animals. Taking into account the unprotected exposure to B. canis M-, brucellosis was suspected, and blood samples were drawn for culture and serologic studies. Two weeks later blood cultures indicated a Brucella species that was later typed as B. canis. Conventional tests for antibodies to smooth brucellae (agglutination, complement fixation) yielded negative results. In contrast, slide agglutination for B. canis was strongly positive with undiluted serum and was also positive at 1:10 dilution. Serologic tests for hepatotropic viruses and Toxoplasma gondii were negative.
After diagnosis, a course with oral doxycycline, 100 mg twice a day for 42 days, plus parenteral gentamicin, 180 mg once a day for 10 days, was started. The patient clinically recovered, but on the last day gentamicin was administered, symptoms of the left VIII cranial nerve occurred, which resolved with flunarizine and vitamin B12 administration.
Blood cultures performed 2 weeks after antimicrobial therapy ended were negative for B. canis. During follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic, his cervical adenitis resolved, and serum levels of hepatic enzymes returned to normal. On his last visit, 4 years after infection, the patient was asymptomatic. While he continues to handle B. canis M-, cultures are now performed under strict biological safety measures (biological safety cabinet, personal protection including goggles, gloves and mask, and autoclaving of contaminated material).
To assess the humoral immune response of the patient to Brucella antigens, the slide agglutination test with B. canis M- and 3 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) were used. ELISA used a hot-saline extract of B. canis M- (HS, mainly composed of rough lipopolysaccharide [LPS] and outer membrane proteins), a preparation of cytoplasmic proteins of B. abortus depleted of LPS (CP [cytoplasmic proteins]) or recombinant Brucella lumazine synthase (RBLS), which were obtained as described previously. As shown in the Figure, antibodies to the three antigens were detected at the time of diagnosis, but antibodies to proteinaceous antigens (CP and RBLS) were negative earlier than those against HS. The slide agglutination test that used B. canis M- and undiluted serum was strongly positive at diagnosis and 48 days later (beginning and end of therapy, respectively), weakly positive at 103 and 150 days, and negative at 190 days and 4 years after diagnosis. Positive samples were assayed in serial dilutions starting at 1:10; only the initial sample was positive at 1:10 dilution (negative at 1:20).
The cellular immune response against CP from Brucella in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCS) was also evaluated. In vitro proliferation and cytokine gene expression were investigated as previously described. For blastogenesis assays, PBMCS were cultured with CP (10 mug/mL), RBLS (5 mug/mL), or phytohemagglutinin (10 mug/mL). Results were expressed as stimulation index (counts per minute of stimulated cultures divided by counts per minute of unstimulated cultures). Stimulation indices (SI) >2 were considered positive. For reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), RNA was extracted from PBMCS cultured in the presence of CP, RBLS, or phytohemagglutinin for 24 hours. Results were expressed as fold increase over the messenger ribonucleic acid levels of cells cultured in the absence of antigen; increases >2 were considered specific.
CP and RBLS induced T-cell proliferation (SI >2) in PBMCS obtained from the patient before antimicrobial therapy (Table). PBMCS from a healthy person, which were run in parallel, showed no response to CP and RBLS (SI <2) (not shown). In addition, CP and RBLS induced a significant (p<0.001, nonparametric Mann-Withney u test) upregulation of interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma), interleukin (IL)-2, and IL-10 transcripts only in PBMCS from the patient. No IL-4 induction was observed with PBMCS from the patient or the healthy control (not shown). The cellular immune response declined with antimicrobial treatment (Table), but CP-specific IFN-gamma remained increased 55 days after therapy ended. In the last sample (obtained 250 days after therapy ended), all the parameters of the cellular immune response were normal (not shown).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male laboratory worker presented with a 1-month history of recurrent fever, headache, arthralgia, weakness, and constipation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed recurrent fever, headache, arthralgia, generalized weakness, and constipation beginning 1 month prior to medical evaluation. Three weeks before symptom onset, he was involved in handling dense live bacterial cultures in a diagnostic laboratory without personal protective equipment and performed mouth pipetting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: diagnostic laboratory worker producing diagnostic antigens. Epidemiological exposure: handled a dense culture of live bacterial antigens 3 weeks prior to symptom onset outside a biological safety cabinet without personal protective equipment, and performed mouth pipetting. Denied close contact with dogs or other animals. Prior medical history not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache, arthralgia, weakness, constipation, recurrent fever. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed cervical adenomegaly. Vital signs not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 46 mu/L; Alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 65 mu/L (mild elevation of transaminases). Complete blood count: neutropenia. Serologic tests for hepatotropic viruses and Toxoplasma gondii: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Cellular immune response testing: In vitro blastogenesis of PBMCs showed T-cell proliferation (stimulation index >2) upon stimulation with bacterial cytoplasmic proteins (CP) and recombinant lumazine synthase (RBLS). RT-PCR demonstrated significant upregulation of IFN-gamma, IL-2, and IL-10 mRNA transcripts (normalized at 250 days post-therapy).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Laboratory-acquired brucellosis due to Brucella canis.
Confirmation: Blood cultures grew Brucella species after 2 weeks, definitively typed as Brucella canis. Serology: conventional tests for antibodies to smooth brucellae (agglutination, complement fixation) were negative; slide agglutination with B. canis M- antigen was strongly positive with undiluted serum and positive at 1:10 dilution. ELISAs detected antibodies to hot-saline extract of B. canis M-, Brucella cytoplasmic proteins, and recombinant Brucella lumazine synthase.
Differentials ruled out: Viral hepatitis and toxoplasmosis ruled out by negative serologies.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 42 days) plus parenteral gentamicin (180 mg once daily for 10 days). On the final day of gentamicin, developed left cranial nerve VIII vestibulocochlear symptoms, which resolved following flunarizine and vitamin B12 therapy. Blood cultures 2 weeks post-treatment were negative; transaminases and cervical adenopathy resolved; remained asymptomatic at 4-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 64-year-old male patient, resident of Vadodara city, Gujarat state located in the western India, who is a known case of diabetes mellitus II, hypothyroidism, and ocular myasthenia gravis since 3 years presented to our tertiary care hospital named Sheth VS General hospital located in Ahmedabad city (Gujarat state) with 8 days history of acute fever, malaise, generalized rash, and multiple joint pains. He complained of an acute onset of sensorimotor quadriparesis and urinary retention since 7 days which was followed 1 day later by H/O altered sensorium. He had no history of headache, vomiting, seizure, dimness of vision, double vision, dysphagia, change in voice, and neck/back pain. The patient had already received methyl prednisolone injection pulse therapy 1 g each for 5 days before presenting to our institute to which he responded partially in form of improved level of consciousness. The patient had no recent history of travelling outside the state of Gujarat or India.
The patient was conscious oriented following verbal command and had no neck rigidity. Cranial nerves: left eye ptosis+; no facial/neck flexor weakness; and mixed dysarthria+.
Nutrition-no undue wasting or hypertrophy; tone: spastic both upper limbs (UL) with flaccid both lower limbs; power (according to the MRC scale): 4/5 in both UL and 1/5 in both LL; with B/L hand grip weakness and B/L dorsiflexor weakness;
Deep tendon reflexes (DTRs) were +3 in both UL with B/L pectoralis reflex and jaw jerk+; DTRs were absent in both lower limbs (LL), and planters were absent.
Impaired joint, position, and vibration sensations up to metatarsophalangeal joints in both the lower limbs and up to metacarpophalangeal joints in both the upper limbs were noted with normal cerebellar examination.
Including complete blood count, random blood sugar, renal and liver function tests, and serum electrolytes were within normal limits except for slightly raised WBC to 14500/microL, CRP 16, and CPK total 84. Serum CHIKV IgM detection by ELISA came positive. Serum chikungunya real-time PCR, which is a qualitative test of chikungunya RNA by a standard procedure, was positive. RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit (Qiagen). One-step RT-PCR was performed using the access quick RT-PCR kit (Promega), in accordance with the manufacturer's protocol, employing primer pairs targeting the E1 gene designed from the nucleotide sequence of the reference S27 strain (GenBank accession number AF490259; CK 13, TTA CAT CAC GTG CGA TA C; CK-14, CTT TC TCT CAG GG TGC GAC TTT). The amplification was performed in a 50 microL total reaction volume with the Promega Access Quick One-Step RT-PCR kit, 50 pmol of each forward and reverse primer, and 2 microL of extracted viral RNA, in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.
Electroencephalogram (EEG) showed generalized bilaterally symmetrical diffuse theta-delta slowing suggestive of diffuse encephalopathy. His electrophysiology study showed distal symmetrical sensory motor axonal polyneuropathy more in the lower limbs than the upper limbs. CSF routine micro: protein, 96 mg/dL, glucose, 60 mg/dL, and total cells, 140 with lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative Gram and ZN stain. CSF viral panel done by PCR was negative for neurotropic viruses. This included pan-flavivirus RNA, pan-enterovirus RNA, pan-paramyxovirus RNA detection and pan-herpes DNA detection. Patient's sample was positive for ANA (antinuclear antibody) by immunofluorescence with a dilution of 1 : 100 and 1 : 200, a homogeneous pattern, and +1 intensity. On further workup, ANA profile by immunoDOT was negative. Anti-aquaporin-4 Ab became negative. Serum and CSF investigations are depicted in Tables 1 and 2.
Multiple tiny altered signal intensity foci with restricted diffusion seen in subcortical and periventricular white matter of bilateral (B/L) cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, and b/L corona radiata with normal MR angiogram are shown in Figure 1. Axial T2W sagittal section showing D7 intramedullary hyperintensity is shown in Figure 2. Patchy areas of T2W hyperintensity in the cervicodorsal cord predominantly from the C7 to D9 level without significant postcontrast enhancement are shown in Figure 3. These findings were consistent with features of encephalomyelitis.
Our patient was managed with IV immunoglobulin (IgG) in a total dose of 140 grams as well as supportive treatment for his comorbidities. He was discharged in a stable hemodynamic condition with power 5/5 in both the UL and 3/5 in both the LL. The patient was advised supportive treatment and neurorehabilitation in form of active physiotherapy.
The patient responded well; his power improved; he was able to walk with one stick support with a normal bladder function with a current modified Rankin scale (mRS) of 4. No radiological investigations were done in follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male presented with fever, generalized rash, polyarthralgia, acute sensorimotor quadriparesis, urinary retention, and altered sensorium for 8 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 64-year-old male developed acute fever, malaise, generalized rash, and multiple joint pains 8 days prior to presentation. Seven days prior, he developed acute sensorimotor quadriparesis and urinary retention, followed 1 day later by altered sensorium. He received pulse IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day for 5 days at an outside hospital with partial cognitive recovery before transfer.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, and ocular myasthenia gravis diagnosed 3 years previously. Resides in Vadodara, Gujarat; no travel outside Gujarat or India.
subjective.review_of_systems: Urinary retention, malaise; denies headache, vomiting, seizures, visual dimness, diplopia, dysphagia, dysphonia, or neck/back pain. Medications: Not detailed outside pulse steroids. Allergies: Not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious, oriented, following commands; no neck rigidity. Cranial nerves: Left eye ptosis, mixed dysarthria, no facial or neck flexor weakness. Motor exam: No wasting/hypertrophy; spastic tone in bilateral upper limbs, flaccid tone in bilateral lower limbs; power (MRC scale): 4/5 upper limbs, 1/5 lower limbs, with bilateral hand grip and dorsiflexor weakness. Reflexes: DTRs +3 in upper limbs, bilateral pectoralis reflex and jaw jerk present; absent DTRs in lower limbs; plantars absent. Sensory exam: Impaired joint, position, and vibration sense up to MTP joints bilaterally and MCP joints bilaterally; normal cerebellar testing.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 14,500/microL; CRP: 16 mg/L; CPK total: 84 U/L. Complete blood count, random blood sugar, renal function, liver function, and serum electrolytes were otherwise normal. ANA by immunofluorescence positive at 1:100 and 1:200 (homogeneous pattern, +1 intensity), but ANA profile by immunoDOT was negative. Anti-aquaporin-4 antibody: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and Spine MRI: Multiple tiny restricted diffusion foci in subcortical and periventricular white matter of bilateral cerebral hemispheres, corpus callosum, and bilateral corona radiata; normal MR angiogram; axial T2W hyperintensity at D7 and patchy intramedullary T2W hyperintensity in cervicodorsal cord from C7 to D9 without significant post-contrast enhancement, consistent with encephalomyelitis. Lumbar puncture / CSF: Protein 96 mg/dL, glucose 60 mg/dL, total cell count 140/microL with lymphocytic pleocytosis; Gram and ZN stains negative; CSF PCR panel negative for pan-flavivirus, pan-enterovirus, pan-paramyxovirus, and pan-herpesviruses. Electroencephalogram (EEG): Generalized bilateral diffuse theta-delta slowing consistent with diffuse encephalopathy. Electrophysiology / EMG-NCS: Distal symmetrical sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy (lower > upper limbs).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Serum CHIKV IgM detection by ELISA was positive, and serum qualitative real-time RT-PCR for Chikungunya viral RNA (E1 gene) was positive, confirming Chikungunya-associated acute encephalomyelitis and polyradiculoneuropathy. Management and course: Treated with IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) total dose 140 g along with supportive treatment for comorbidities and active neurorehabilitation. Discharged with motor improvement (power 5/5 upper limbs, 3/5 lower limbs). At follow-up, patient was able to ambulate with single cane support, normal bladder function, and mRS of 4.

raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old man, in complete remission of a chronic lymphoid leukemia (CLL) after 6 cycles of rituximab and bendamustin (last therapy administrated in December 2019), presented to our emergency unit on April 1st 2020 with asthenia, loss of weight, dry cough and diarrhea since a month. He was otherwise healthy with well-controlled arterial hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected (7x106 copies/ml) from a nasopharyngeal swab (defined as day 1). Laboratory analyses showed a moderate neutropenia, but severe T (114 cell/mm3) and B (1 cell/mm3) lymphopenia with reduced total immunoglobulin (Ig) G and IgM levels (Supplementary Figure 1A), while inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein and ferritin) were elevated (Figure 1A). Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed bilateral multifocal subpleural and peribronchial ground-glass opacities typical of COVID-19 pneumonia (Figure 1B and Supplementary Figure 2). The clinical condition gradually deteriorated with sub-febrile episodes, persisting dry cough and diarrhea, and progressive weight loss and cognitive dysfunction (Figures 1C, D and Supplementary Information). Inflammatory parameters and blood cell counts remained abnormal (Figures 1A, E), while persisting SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed (Supplementary Figure 1B). Complementary investigations excluded other diagnoses (Supplementary Information). No specific antiviral agents were introduced given the mild symptoms of COVID-19 (e.g. absence of hypoxemia).
In summary, the patient developed a long-lasting SARS-CoV-2 infection likely related to his severe immunosuppressive status. Consequently, we hypothesized that convalescent plasma could be beneficial in this particular case, by providing virus-specific neutralizing antibodies as well as a potential anti-inflammatory effect. Plasma units (3x200 ml/donor) were obtained from three selected donors, who had fully recovered from mild COVID-19 disease (Supplementary Information). Each donor presented relatively high IgG antibody titers against the S1 (spike)-protein using Euroimmun ELISA (Supplementary Figure 3A). The first cycle of ABO-compatible plasma transfusion (two units on two consecutive days) was given on days 72 and 73 after diagnosis of SARS-CoV-2 infection, followed by three additional cycles, administered 10 to 15 days apart (Supplementary Figure 3A).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old male presenting with asthenia, weight loss, dry cough, and diarrhea for one month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency unit on April 1, 2020, with a 1-month history of asthenia, unintentional weight loss, dry cough, and diarrhea. Following admission, his clinical course was characterized by gradual deterioration with sub-febrile episodes, persistent dry cough and diarrhea, progressive weight loss, and cognitive dysfunction. He did not exhibit hypoxemia on initial evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic lymphoid leukemia (CLL) in complete remission following 6 cycles of rituximab and bendamustine (last administered in December 2019); well-controlled arterial hypertension; type 2 diabetes mellitus.

objective.physical_examination: Initial examination revealed absence of hypoxemia; subsequently exhibited sub-febrile episodes during hospitalization.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation revealed moderate neutropenia, severe T lymphopenia (114 cells/mm3) and B lymphopenia (1 cell/mm3), reduced total IgG and IgM levels, and elevated inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein and ferritin). Persistent abnormalities in inflammatory parameters and blood cell counts were observed throughout the clinical course.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Bilateral multifocal subpleural and peribronchial ground-glass opacities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia) detected via nasopharyngeal swab RT-PCR (7x10^6 copies/mL on day 1), with persistent infection confirmed on repeat testing. Other potential diagnoses were excluded by complementary investigations.
Plan & Outcome: Given the mild initial presentation without hypoxemia, no specific antiviral agents were introduced. Due to long-lasting infection secondary to profound immunosuppression, the patient was treated with convalescent plasma transfusions (ABO-compatible plasma units 3x200 mL/donor from three donors who recovered from mild COVID-19 with high IgG anti-S1 spike antibody titers). The first cycle (two units on consecutive days) was administered on days 72 and 73 post-diagnosis, followed by three additional cycles administered 10 to 15 days apart.

raw_case_text: We report a case of a 56-year-old man presenting acute fever, cutaneous rash, conjunctival hyperemia, intense joint pain, and self-reported use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) in the initial days of symptoms. The patient reported that for the last 30 days before Hospital admission, he started presenting fever, headaches, paresthesia, and pain in the right arm with visible red spots on the skin. These skin lesions worsened and spread through the lower limbs and trunk within a period of 10 days. The patient evolved to hypotension with some Hospital admissions and discharges. On the 15th day after skin disease onset, he developed thrombocytopenia, liver dysfunction with International Normalized Ratio (INR) of 1.45 and Prothrombin Time of 56%, edema in his hands and feet and hemorrhagic bullous lesions on the skin of the upper and lower limbs (Figures 1a-c), being admitted to the Intensive Care Unit. Immediately, therapy was started with meropenem and vancomycin, then maintained for 6 days, during which the patient presented some febrile peaks. Subsequently, intravenous administration of Intravenous Immunoglobulin (Human), 5% (Flebogamma  5% DIF, Instituto Grifols S.A., Barcelona, Spain) at 400 mg/Kg/day restarted for 5 days. Antibiotic therapy started again for 5 days. The patient showed a progressive increase in platelet levels from 43,000 to 201,000 and total leukocyte count, together with an important reductions of the edema, necrosis, and erythema. Ten days after globulin administration, a substantial improvement of the bullous lesions was observed (Figures 1g-l). The patient evolved with aphasia, thus being considered to be suffering a transient acute ischemic stroke. Laboratory analysis followed the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) recommendations, in which a single anti-CHIKV IgM-positive test (collected during acute or convalescence phase) is sufficient for confirmation of any suspected case of CHIKV. The blood test returned positive serology for Dengue (IgM-/IgG+) and Chikungunya (IgM+) at the 16th day after symptom onset, but results were negative for other infectious diseases and blood culture. Notably, laboratory tests excluded other confounding diseases such as: malaria, leptospirosis, rheumatic fever, septic arthritis, Zika, and Mayaro. Moreover, there is no report showing any Mayaro case detected in the state of Paraiba. This would definitively exclude the possibility of a cross-reactive IgM serology against another alphavirus as discussed elsewhere. No comorbidities were reported, except for alcoholism. Throughout hospitalization, imaging exams were normal and no vasoactive drugs were administered. Furthermore, no lesions were observed in oral, genital, or conjunctival mucosa. Nikolsky's sign was positive. A diagnosis of Stevens Johnson syndrome-Toxic epidermal necrolysis-like features was discarded. The patient was discharged and has not presented any other clinical sign of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male presented with fever, worsening rash with hemorrhagic bullae, conjunctival hyperemia, and severe joint pain for 30 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 56-year-old male developed fever, headaches, paresthesia, and pain in the right arm with red cutaneous macules 30 days prior to admission. The rash progressed over 10 days to involve the lower limbs and trunk. He experienced hypotension with repeated outpatient visits. On day 15 following rash onset, he developed hand and foot edema, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and hemorrhagic bullous skin lesions on upper and lower limbs, leading to ICU admission. During ICU stay, he experienced transient aphasia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Alcoholism. No other medical comorbidities. Recent self-administration of NSAIDs during early symptomatic days.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache, paresthesias in right arm, transient aphasia. Home medications: Self-medicated NSAIDs. Allergies: None reported.

objective.physical_examination: Hypotension; conjunctival hyperemia; edema in hands and feet; extensive hemorrhagic bullous lesions on upper and lower extremities with necrosis and erythema; Nikolsky's sign positive; no mucosal lesions on oral, genital, or conjunctival mucosa; intense joint tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelets: Nadir of 43,000/microL increasing to 201,000/microL with therapy; Prothrombin Time: 56%; INR: 1.45 (liver dysfunction/coagulopathy). Blood cultures: negative. Workup excluding malaria, leptospirosis, rheumatic fever, and septic arthritis was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Hospitalization imaging studies: Normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Serology at day 16 post-symptom onset was positive for anti-Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) IgM (meeting PAHO criteria for confirmed Chikungunya); Dengue serology was IgM negative / IgG positive (past infection); serology was negative for Zika and Mayaro viruses. SJS/TEN discarded in favor of severe atypical Chikungunya with hemorrhagic bullous dermatosis and transient ischemic attack. Management and course: Admitted to ICU; initial empiric meropenem and vancomycin for 6 days, followed by IVIG (Flebogamma 5% DIF) at 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days, and an additional 5 days of antibiotics. Platelet counts normalized (43,000 to 201,000/microL) with marked regression of bullae, necrosis, and edema 10 days post-IVIG. The patient achieved complete clinical recovery and was discharged.

raw_case_text:
A 49-year-old male shepherd presented at our hospital with complaints of severe chest and back pain persisting for 6 months. He also reported a recent onset of lower limb mobility limitation over the past 2 weeks, which notably worsened at night. His fevers spiked to 39 C. His professional background involved prolonged exposure to sheep, which was particularly relevant given our initial diagnostic considerations. Upon examination, he displayed significant tenderness and percussion pain at the T9 and T10 spinous processes. His neurological assessment revealed a muscle strength of grade 2 in both lower limbs, highlighting substantial functional impairment. Initial laboratory tests indicated an elevated white blood cell count of 11.5 x 109/L with 67% neutrophils, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 10 mm/h, and a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 9.8 mg/L, indicating the presence of inflammation. A positive result on the Rose Bengal plate agglutination test strongly suggested an infection with Brucella. Comprehensive imaging was undertaken to further evaluate the extent of the infection. Thoracic CT scans revealed considerable bone destruction and narrowing of the intervertebral spaces at T9 and T10, with local endplate destruction evident (Figures 1A-C). MRI scans demonstrated degenerative changes in the intervertebral disks and abnormal high signal changes on T2-weighted images (T2WI), indicative of an abscess compressing the spinal cord (Figures 1D-F).
Given the severity of the infection and its impact on the spinal column, we initiated an aggressive antimicrobial regimen. The patient was treated with doxycycline 200 mg daily and rifampicin 600 mg daily, supplemented with quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, for at least 2 weeks before any surgical intervention. The surgical approach involved transforaminal-assisted posterior debridement, internal fixation, and bone graft fusion under general anesthesia. The operation was carefully documented, showing the precise placement of guide wires and the thorough debridement process using various sizes of nucleus pulposus forceps for lesion clearance (Figures 2A-I). Postoperative care included continuing the antimicrobial regimen, with added nutritional support and blood transfusions as needed. The histopathological examination with HE and Gram staining showed the extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells and confirmed Brucella infection (Figures 3A,C). Real-time PCR further confirmed the presence of Brucella melitensis DNA (Figure 3E). The patient's recovery was notable; he was provided with a waist brace and began ambulating 1 week post-surgery. At the 12-week follow-up, he reported significant relief from back pain, and his muscle strength in the lower limbs improved to grade 3. Follow-up imaging showed stable surgical repairs and proper alignment (Figure 3G).

subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 49-year-old male shepherd presented with severe chest and back pain persisting for 6 months, along with a recent onset of lower limb mobility limitation over the past 2 weeks that notably worsened at night. His fevers spiked to 39 C.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar thoracic spondylodiscitis (T9-T10) complicated by epidural abscess and compressive myelopathy/paraparesis caused by Brucella melitensis.
Confirmation: Rose Bengal plate agglutination test positive; real-time PCR of debrided tissue positive for Brucella melitensis DNA; histopathology (HE and Gram stain) demonstrating extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells and bacterial presence.
Differentials ruled out: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) and pyogenic spondylodiscitis (clinically and radiologically considered; ruled out by Brucella-specific serology, histopathology, and PCR).
Treatment & Outcome: Initiated on aggressive antimicrobial therapy with oral doxycycline 200 mg daily and oral rifampicin 600 mg daily, supplemented with quinolones and third-generation cephalosporins for at least 2 weeks preoperatively. Underwent transforaminal-assisted posterior debridement, bone graft fusion, and internal fixation under general anesthesia. Postoperatively, antimicrobial therapy was continued alongside nutritional support and blood transfusions. Fitted with a waist brace and began ambulating 1 week post-surgery. At 12-week follow-up, reported significant relief from back pain, lower limb muscle strength improved to grade 3/5, and follow-up imaging showed stable surgical repairs and proper alignment.

raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old HIV-infected black African female presented with an 8-day history of painful swallowing, sore eyes, malaise and a worsening rash. She had been on antiretroviral (ARV) regimen of nevirapine (NVP) 400 mg daily, tenofovir 300 mg daily and lamivudine 300 mg daily for more than 4 years uneventfully. She was on no other medications and had not taken any other medication in the preceding 8 weeks. She had acquired HIV via heterosexual contact - the exact date of HIV infection was unknown. At the time of initiation of ARV therapy, her nadir CD4 cell count was 139 cells/mm 3 and her HIV RNA viral load at the time was unknown. Her last CD4 counts, done 31, 21 and 11 months before developing her current symptoms were 373, 356 and 387 cells/mm 3 respectively. The last HIV RNA viral load test, done 11 months prior to the onset of her symptoms showed an undetectable viral load.
She gave a history of forgetting to take her ARV medication for a day. The following day, 10 days before development of her symptoms she took 2 days equivalent of her ARVs in one day, in her own words "to make up for the missed dose".
On examination, she was normotensive and had a temperature of 38.8 C. She had conjunctivitis and hemorrhagic cheilitis but no involvement of the genital mucosa. She had epidermal necrosis involving predominantly her trunk and face and to a lesser extent palms, soles and extremities, totaling 10% of her body surface area, 3% of which was stripping. Initial laboratory studies showed normal blood count, except for an elevated eosinophil count of 0.70 x 10 9/L. The liver and renal function tests were normal. Her ARVs were stopped and her epidermal necrosis did not extend and eosinophil counts normalized. Over the next few days her skin condition improved and she was discharged 10 days later fully re-epithelialized with the exception of the lips, which were still eroded in areas. On review, 2 weeks after discharge, her skin had normalized except for residual hyperpigmentation. She was started on a single daily tablet of Odimune  , a fixed drug combination of tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg and efavirenz 600 mg. On follow-up, 4 weeks later she was tolerating the new ARV regimen.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old female presenting with painful swallowing, sore eyes, malaise, and a worsening rash for eight days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with an 8-day history of painful swallowing, sore eyes, malaise, and a progressive rash. Ten days prior to symptom onset, she missed her daily medications for one day and subsequently took a double dose (two days' equivalent in a single day) to compensate. Her symptoms progressed to blistering and skin peeling involving the face, trunk, and extremities, prompting hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection acquired via heterosexual contact; nadir CD4 cell count 139 cells/mm3; maintained on an antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimen of nevirapine 400 mg daily, tenofovir 300 mg daily, and lamivudine 300 mg daily for over 4 years uneventfully; serial CD4 counts 31, 21, and 11 months prior were 373, 356, and 387 cells/mm3, respectively, with undetectable viral load 11 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Painful swallowing, sore eyes, malaise; denies genital mucosal symptoms. Home medications: Nevirapine 400 mg daily, tenofovir 300 mg daily, lamivudine 300 mg daily; no other medications in preceding 8 weeks.

Dermatologic: Epidermal necrosis involving predominantly the trunk and face, and to a lesser extent palms, soles, and extremities, totaling 10% of body surface area (BSA) with 3% stripping.
