assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) secondary to nevirapine toxicity / double-dosing in an HIV-infected patient on established antiretroviral therapy.
Plan & Outcome: Antiretroviral therapy was immediately discontinued. Epidermal necrosis arrested without further extension, and eosinophilia normalized. The patient was discharged after 10 days fully re-epithelialized except for residual lip erosions. At 2 weeks follow-up, skin had normalized with residual hyperpigmentation. Antiretroviral therapy was safely resumed with a single daily tablet of Odimune (fixed-dose combination of tenofovir 300 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, and efavirenz 600 mg), which was well-tolerated at 4-week follow-up.

raw_case_text: In the meantime, he was tried with various antiretroviral drugs in combinations, i.e. lamivudine 150-300 mg, zidovudine 300 mg, nevirapine 600 mg, stavudine 20 mg, and tenofovir 300 mg. In 2014-2015, he was prescribed with EFV 600 mg in combination with nevirapine up to 600 mg and lamivudine up to 300 mg at different times. Around this time, the patient presented with decreased sleep, sadness, weeping spells, decreased interaction, decreased appetite, odd behavior, and irrelevant and inappropriate talk at times and had socio-occupational dysfunction. A diagnosis of "bipolar affective disorder, current episode severe depression with psychotic symptoms" was made, and the treatment was started with antidepressant tablet escitalopram 10 mg, which was increased to 20 mg, and antipsychotic olanzapine 5 mg tablet was added to it. This time, he did not improve with the treatment even after 3 months. Hence, olanzapine was discontinued, and tablet quetiapine 50 mg was started which was gradually increased to 300 mg. Electrocardiogram was done periodically while quetiapine was increased and it was found to be normal; no QTc (corrected QT interval of ECG) prolongation was there. As there was no improvement in depression, the antidepressant was changed to another selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, i.e., fluoxetine capsule at a dosage of 20 mg. Still, the patient did not improve at the end of 3 months, and the score on the Beck Depression Inventory was 55 which corresponded to severe depression. The status about lack of any improvement in depression was communicated to the physician who was aware that antiretroviral drugs may cause depression. Hence, he discontinued EFV and started nevirapine. After discontinuing EFV, the patient started to improve in a month and recovered completely in 3 months with good socio-occupational functioning. Quetiapine in the meantime was reduced and stopped (as he complained of increased sedation and found the drug to be costly), and he was continued on fluoxetine 20 mg and aripiprazole 2.5 mg. The score on the Beck Depression Inventory at the end of 3 months was 6 which corresponded to minimal depression.

subjective.chief_complaint: A male patient presenting with severe depression, decreased sleep, weeping spells, anorexia, social withdrawal, odd behavior, and inappropriate speech refractory to psychiatric therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with progressive psychiatric decompensation characterized by decreased sleep, persistent sadness, weeping spells, social withdrawal, anorexia, odd behavior, and inappropriate speech with marked socio-occupational impairment. The depressive episode began following modification of his antiretroviral therapy regimen in 2014-2015 to include efavirenz 600 mg daily. The depression proved refractory to successive antidepressant and antipsychotic trials, including escitalopram (titrated to 20 mg), olanzapine (5 mg), quetiapine (titrated to 300 mg), and fluoxetine (20 mg), with persistence of severe depression (Beck Depression Inventory score of 55) over more than six months.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of bipolar affective disorder; treated with sequential antiretroviral regimens including lamivudine 150-300 mg, zidovudine 300 mg, nevirapine 600 mg, stavudine 20 mg, and tenofovir 300 mg, followed by efavirenz 600 mg daily in combination with nevirapine and lamivudine.
subjective.review_of_systems: Decreased sleep, decreased appetite, sadness, weeping spells, social withdrawal, odd behavior, inappropriate speech; excessive sedation reported while taking quetiapine.

objective.physical_examination: Mental status examination: Profound depressive affect, weeping spells, psychomotor slowing, social withdrawal, odd behavior, and occasional irrelevant and inappropriate speech.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial electrocardiograms (ECGs): Normal tracing with normal corrected QT interval (no QTc prolongation) during quetiapine titration. Beck Depression Inventory (BDI): Admission/refractory score of 55 (severe depression); declined to 6 (minimal depression) after treatment modification.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Efavirenz-induced severe depression with psychotic symptoms in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and underlying bipolar affective disorder.
Plan & Outcome: Due to lack of response to escitalopram, olanzapine, quetiapine, and fluoxetine, efavirenz was identified as the offending neuropsychiatric agent and discontinued, replacing it with nevirapine. Following efavirenz cessation, the patient showed clinical improvement within one month and achieved full remission at three months with restored socio-occupational functioning. Psychotropic therapy was rationalized to fluoxetine 20 mg and aripiprazole 2.5 mg daily (quetiapine was tapered and discontinued due to sedation and cost). Beck Depression Inventory score decreased from 55 to 6.

raw_case_text: The child underwent tonsillectomy, for a clinical diagnosis of chronic tonsillitis. Histopathological examination of bilateral tonsils revealed caseating and noncaseating epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells (Figures 1, 2, and 3). Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid fast bacillus was positive (Figure 4). Features were consistent with a diagnosis of tuberculosis of tonsils.

subjective.history_of_present_illness: A pediatric patient underwent elective tonsillectomy for a clinical diagnosis of chronic tonsillitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Clinical diagnosis of chronic tonsillitis.

objective.advanced_workup: Histopathological examination of bilateral resected tonsils revealed caseating and noncaseating epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans giant cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Tuberculosis of the tonsils (primary tonsillar tuberculosis).
Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathological examination of bilateral tonsils demonstrated caseating and noncaseating epithelioid cell granulomas with Langhans multinucleated giant cells, and Ziehl-Neelsen staining was positive for acid-fast bacilli.
Management: Fragment of published case record; post-tonsillectomy antituberculosis chemotherapy detailed in subsequent clinical report.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old previously healthy man presented with fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, and dyspnea for three days after working in paddy fields. On admission, he was conscious, with low blood pressure (94/63 mmHg) and tachycardia (pulse rate 145 beats/min). There were bibasal lung crepitations, and urine output was only 10 mL over 4 hours. Admission blood tests indicated leucopenia and severe thrombocytopenia (Table 1).
After crystalloid fluid resuscitation noradrenaline was initiated to maintain blood pressure, intravenous ceftriaxone was commenced, and the patient was transferred to the medical intensive care unit (ICU). Due to severity of leptospirosis, intravenous methylprednisolone was administered for 3 days, and multiple platelet transfusions were given to correct thrombocytopenia. As oliguria persisted, intermittent hemodialysis was initiated. Dopamine was added due to persistent hypotension.
Chest radiograph indicated severe pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome (Figure 1). Echocardiogram showed hypokinetic anterior wall motion and moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation. The patient was electively intubated and ventilated due to respiratory acidosis and hypoxia. Despite treatment, thrombocytopenia and abnormal liver function tests persisted (Table 1). Therapeutic plasma exchange was performed, and meropenem was commenced.
By Day 8, the patient was stable and afebrile, allowing for gradual withdrawal of inotropes. Leptospira microscopic agglutination test (MAT) became positive with a high titer. Blood picture showed low-grade hemolysis with a few red cell fragments.
On Day 21, the patient experienced fresh rectal bleeding. Upper gastroesophageal endoscopy revealed multiple gastric erosions, and colonoscopy revealed features of ischemic colitis. Blood and fresh frozen plasma were transfused, and intravenous proton pump inhibitor infusion was commenced. Exploratory laparotomy revealed extensive bowel necrosis from terminal ileum to the hepatic flexure with perforation and abscess formation of posterior wall of the ascending colon. Histopathology of affected areas confirmed these changes (Figure 2). There was no evidence of vasculitis in the rest of the peritoneal viscera. Standard right hemicolectomy and elective tracheostomy were performed.
On postoperative Day 1, the patient became unstable with hypotension and severe acidosis. Intact exteriorized bowel ends which had looked healthy at surgery showed features of ischemic necrosis. Since the patient's condition was unstable, further surgical exploration was abandoned. He succumbed on Day 27 of illness due to multiorgan failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male presenting with fever, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, myalgias, and dyspnea for 3 days following agricultural work in paddy fields.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 3 days prior to admission following work in paddy fields, presenting with fever, watery diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, generalized myalgias, and shortness of breath. On arrival, he was severely oliguric (10 mL urine over 4 hours) with shock and respiratory distress. He deteriorated into severe acute respiratory failure and refractory shock requiring intubation, inotropes, hemodialysis, and plasma exchange. On illness day 21, he developed acute fresh rectal bleeding, severe anemia, and peritonitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Epidemiological exposure: agricultural work in paddy fields prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, generalized myalgias, dyspnea, and rectal bleeding. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: conscious, hypotensive (blood pressure 94/63 mmHg) and tachycardic (pulse rate 145 beats/min). Respiratory: bibasal lung crepitations. Renal: profound oliguria (10 mL over 4 hours). On day 21: abdominal tenderness, peritoneal signs, and ischemic exteriorized bowel stoma.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed leukopenia and severe thrombocytopenia; blood smear demonstrated low-grade microangiopathic hemolysis with red cell fragments. Liver function tests: persistently abnormal transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia. Renal function: severe oliguric acute kidney injury. Chest radiography: severe pulmonary hemorrhagic syndrome. Transthoracic echocardiogram: hypokinetic anterior wall motion with moderate mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.
objective.advanced_workup: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: multiple gastric mucosal erosions. Colonoscopy: findings of ischemic colitis. Exploratory laparotomy: extensive transmural bowel necrosis extending from the terminal ileum to the hepatic flexure, with perforation and localized abscess formation along the posterior wall of the ascending colon. Histopathology confirmed transmural necrosis without evidence of systemic vasculitis in other peritoneal viscera.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) confirmed by Leptospira microscopic agglutination test (MAT) positive with a high diagnostic titer. Disease manifestations included severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome, septic and cardiogenic shock with acute myocardial dysfunction (anterior wall hypokinesis, MR/TR), anuric acute kidney injury requiring hemodialysis, microangiopathic hemolytic thrombocytopenia, and extensive ischemic bowel necrosis with ascending colon perforation and abscess formation.
Plan & Treatment: Crystalloid resuscitation, noradrenaline and dopamine inotropic support; antimicrobial therapy with IV ceftriaxone, escalated to meropenem; IV methylprednisolone for 3 days; intermittent hemodialysis; multiple platelet concentrates, fresh frozen plasma, and packed red blood cell transfusions; therapeutic plasma exchange; invasive mechanical ventilation; IV proton pump inhibitor infusion; emergency exploratory laparotomy with right hemicolectomy, abdominal drainage, and elective tracheostomy.
Outcome: On postoperative day 1, patient developed recurrent ischemic necrosis of exteriorized bowel ends with refractory acidosis and shock; surgical exploration was abandoned due to extreme instability, and he succumbed on Day 27 of illness due to multiorgan failure.

raw_case_text:
A 65-year-old male with hypertension and atrial fibrillation was admitted to the University of Rochester Medical Center with fever, chest pain, and dyspnea. A CT Chest angiogram revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and no embolic disease. He was admitted to the general medicine service and was treated for community-acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone and doxycycline. His fevers persisted for the first three days. On hospital day 6 his antimicrobial therapy was broadened to vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam, and azithromycin due to worsening hypoxia and was continued for 10 days. He was found to be HIV positive with a RNA level greater than 500,000 copies/ml and a CD4 count of 15. On hospital day 9 he required intubation for worsening hypoxia. He underwent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with pneumocystis jiroveci identified on PCR testing and microscopy and CMV was identified on viral cell culture. Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and glucocorticoid therapy was empirically started and he completed 21 days of therapy.
On hospital day 23 he was extubated. Due to increasing lethargy he was reintubated on hospital day 27 for airway protection. After intubation he developed intermittent fevers for 25 days with altered mental status. Vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were restarted. An initial work up for encephalopathy was performed with normal ammonia (18 mumol/L), normal CT head with and without contrast, and negative evaluation for infection including blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool cultures. An electroencephalogram was performed and showed moderate encephalopathy without epileptiform abnormalities. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) with elvitegravir, cobicistat, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 33 after HIV genotype testing returned. There was concern for drug fever from dexmedetomidine and piperacillin-tazobactam and both drugs were discontinued on hospital day 32 and 37. After no improvement in fevers a MRI of the head with and without contrast was performed on hospital day 37 and showed acute infarcts in the bilateral thalami, right parietal lobe, and right basal ganglia. Neurology felt it was embolic phenomena from atrial fibrillation. He also developed persistent, nonbloody loose stools with negative bacterial and parasite stool studies so serum CMV PCR was checked on hospital day 43 showing 2,623,108 IU/mL. With new nuchal rigidity on exam and right lower extremity weakness a lumbar puncture was performed on hospital day 44 after another head CT was normal. Spinal fluid analysis was consistent with encephalitis and CSF PCR for CMV DNA was positive (Table 1). After serum CMV PCR positivity returned ganciclovir was started on hospital day 47. MRI imaging of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine showed extensive linear leptomeningeal enhancement along the lower spinal cord, conus medullaris, and roots of the cauda equine with thickening of the roots concerning for radiculomyelitis (Figure 1). At this point his mental status remained poor with quadriparesis and flaccid paraplegia. He underwent tracheostomy on hospital day 50.
Serum CMV DNA PCR and HIV RNA PCR were checked weekly to monitor treatment efficacy, and both decreased significantly on treatment (Table 2). No further lumbar punctures were performed. He received 30 days of IV ganciclovir 469mg twice daily before decreasing to IV ganciclovir 469mg daily after two consecutive weeks of undetectable serum CMV DNA PCR, hospital day 76. He received IV ganciclovir daily for 85 days total, before switching to oral valganciclovir 900mg daily. The serum HIV RNA PCR continued to decline and was 49 copies/mL on hospital day 128 (96 days after initiation of HAART therapy). He remained on mechanical ventilation and was able to move his upper extremities with assistance and could answer simple questions. He never regained function in his lower extremities. After minimal improvement he opted to stop mechanical ventilation and passed away on hospital day 147.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presenting with fever, chest pain, and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute-onset fever, pleuritic chest pain, and dyspnea. Initial empirical treatment for community-acquired pneumonia failed to improve fevers, and he developed progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation on hospital day 9. Following antimicrobial treatment for opportunistic pulmonary coinfections, he was successfully extubated on day 23. However, four days later he developed acute encephalopathy, recurrent fevers, diarrhea, and progressive lower extremity weakness requiring re-intubation and intensive care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Essential hypertension; non-valvular atrial fibrillation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, dyspnea, chest pain, followed by lethargy, confusion, non-bloody diarrhea, and bilateral lower extremity flaccid weakness; denies antecedent seizures, cranial nerve trauma, or focal visual loss.

objective.physical_examination: Initial examination: Febrile, tachypneic, and hypoxemic. ICU re-intubation (hospital day 27-44): Lethargic, encephalopathic; developed positive nuchal rigidity; motor examination revealed flaccid paraplegia with absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, progressing to quadriparesis with preserved partial upper limb movement.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood chemistry: Serum ammonia 18 micromol/L; serial routine blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool bacterial/parasitic cultures were negative. Electroencephalography (EEG): Diffuse background slowing consistent with moderate toxic-metabolic/infectious encephalopathy without epileptiform discharges.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): Performed for progressive hypoxemic infiltrates. Chest CT angiogram: Bilateral ground-glass opacities with mediastinal lymphadenopathy and absence of pulmonary embolism. Brain CT and MRI (hospital day 37): Acute embolic ischemic infarctions involving bilateral thalami, right parietal lobe, and right basal ganglia. Lumbar puncture / Cerebrospinal fluid analysis (day 44): Cerebrospinal fluid analysis consistent with encephalitis. Contrast-enhanced spine MRI: Extensive linear leptomeningeal enhancement along the lower thoracic spinal cord, conus medullaris, and cauda equina nerve roots with root thickening, diagnostic of myeloradiculitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infection / acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS; CD4 count 15 cells/microL, HIV-1 RNA > 500,000 copies/mL) presenting with severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (identified on BAL microscopy and PCR) and disseminated cytomegalovirus (CMV) disease (CMV isolated on BAL viral cell culture; serum CMV PCR 2,623,108 IU/mL; CSF CMV DNA PCR positive) manifesting as CMV enteritis, meningoencephalitis, and myeloradiculitis, alongside cardioembolic cerebral infarctions secondary to atrial fibrillation.
Plan & Outcome: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia treated with a 21-day course of intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and tapering systemic glucocorticoids. Combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART) was initiated on day 33 with elvitegravir, cobicistat, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide following resistance genotyping. Disseminated CMV treated with high-dose intravenous ganciclovir (469 mg BID for 30 days, then 469 mg daily for total 85 days, transitioned to oral valganciclovir 900 mg daily), resulting in complete clearance of CMV viremia and reduction of HIV viral load to 49 copies/mL by day 128. Despite virological clearance, he remained quadriplegic and ventilator-dependent via tracheostomy; following discussion of goals of care, mechanical ventilation was withdrawn, and he expired on hospital day 147.

raw_case_text:
A female patient is 56 years old and was born in Sao Tome and Principe. She has a medical history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, diagnosed seven years ago when she moved to Portugal. At the time of diagnosis, the patient's CD4 T lymphocyte count was 34 cells/muL with no opportunistic infections. The patient was started on antiretroviral therapy (ART) with lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (FTC/TDF) plus dolutegravir (DTG). The patient stopped attending follow-up appointments, and a few months later she was admitted to the hospital's emergency department, complaining of pain from an ulcer in her right foot that had begun three months prior (Figure 1). After a brief inquiry, she informed the medical team that she had been in Sao Tome and Principe for the previous nine months and that she stopped ART during that period. In Sao Tome and Principe, the patient lived at her family's home and was in contact with seawater and river water every day for cleaning and housekeeping purposes. A blood test revealed a haemoglobin level of 11.0 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 8.2 x 103 cells/muL, and a C-reactive protein level of 3.0 mg/dL. The patient's HIV-1 viral load was 79,300 copies/mL, and her CD4 T lymphocyte count was 240 cells/muL. The medical team collected pus from the ulcer for microbiologic analysis, and S. algae was isolated. The patient was treated with ciprofloxacin for 6 weeks, and ART was reinstated. The patient was evaluated by a plastic surgeon, and a skin graft was performed four weeks later. Figure 2 depicts the ulcer two weeks after the initiation of antibiotic treatment, and Figure 3 depicts the ulcer after the conclusion of the six-week antibiotic treatment and skin grafting. The patient currently maintains regular follow-up appointments at the infectious disease clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old female presenting with a painful, chronic cutaneous ulcer on her right foot for three months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-month history of a painful, non-healing ulcer on her right foot that developed while residing in Sao Tome and Principe. She had discontinued all chronic medications for nine months prior to admission, prompting emergency department presentation for wound care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic retroviral infection diagnosed seven years prior in Portugal; previously maintained on combination antiretroviral therapy (emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and dolutegravir) but defaulted from therapy and follow-up nine months prior. Epidemiological exposure: Born in Sao Tome and Principe; daily contact with marine and river freshwater environments for cleaning and housekeeping purposes during the preceding nine months.
subjective.review_of_systems: Painful foot ulceration; denies fevers, chills, nausea, vomiting, or respiratory symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic/Extremities: Chronic cutaneous ulcer on the right foot with purulent exudate and peripheral tissue inflammation; no systemic fevers; vital signs hemodynamically stable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 11.0 g/dL. White blood cell count: 8.2 x 10^3 cells/microL. C-reactive protein (CRP): 3.0 mg/dL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe cutaneous Shewanella algae soft tissue ulceration in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) virological rebound secondary to treatment default (CD4+ T-cell count 240 cells/microL, HIV-1 RNA 79,300 copies/mL; nadir CD4 34 cells/microL). Diagnostic confirmation: Isolation and microbiological identification of Shewanella algae from ulcer purulent exudate cultures, correlated with daily seawater and river water exposure. Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral ciprofloxacin for 6 weeks, alongside wound debridement and reinstatement of antiretroviral therapy (FTC/TDF plus dolutegravir). Underwent successful split-thickness autologous skin grafting by plastic surgery at four weeks, achieving complete re-epithelialization and sustained healing at outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old post-partum mother in area with known ZIKV infestation in Bangkok, Thailand had an uncomplicated natural birth of her child in February 2017 with no growth defect. Since birth, the child was exclusively breast-fed and the mother remained well until December 8, 2017 when she developed fever. Her husband was diagnosed with ZIKV a week before her becoming ill. Initially, she suffered a low-grade fever and fatigue, followed by morbilliform itchy red rash, bilateral orbital pain, and submandibular lymphadenopathy on the following day. Bilateral conjunctivitis and polyarthralgia were evident before presenting to Chulalongkorn University Hospital on December 12. All symptoms were resolved by December 20 (12 days). The baby was fed breast milk until December 12 when the mother tested positive for ZIKV, after which the mother decided to stop breastfeeding (Figure 1).
The mother's expressed breast milk was routinely stored at -20 C. Thence, a total of 22 consecutive milk specimens were collected from December 1 until her illness was resolved. The mother's serum and urine and her baby's urine were also collected at short intervals from December 12, 2017 until January 5, 2018. Both urine and serum samples were examined for ZIKV RNA using real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) (RealStar Zika Virus RT-PCR Kit; Altona, Germany), and serum for IgG and IgM by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) method (EUROIMMUN, Germany) at the WHO Collaboration Centre for Research and Training on Viral Zoonoses, Chulalongkorn University. Her baby's urine was also sent for RT-PCR (Figure 2).
ZIKV RNA was detected in the breast milk as early as 3 days before her symptoms started (December 5) and remained detectable in the breast milk for 11 days (December 15) (cycle threshold [Ct], with level of detection between 29.27 and 38.08). ZIKV RNA was still detected in the mother's urine until December 26 but not in blood. Urine collected on January 5, 2018 was negative for ZIKV RNA.

subjective.chief_complaint: 38-year-old postpartum female presenting with 4 days of fever, fatigue, pruritic morbilliform rash, bilateral orbital pain, conjunctivitis, and polyarthralgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, an exclusively breastfeeding mother 10 months postpartum, developed low-grade fever and fatigue on December 8, 2017. The following day, an itchy red morbilliform rash, bilateral retro-orbital pain, and submandibular lymphadenopathy developed, followed by bilateral conjunctivitis and polyarthralgia. She presented to the hospital on December 12. All symptoms resolved within 12 days (by December 20). Breastfeeding was discontinued on December 12 upon maternal diagnostic confirmation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uncomplicated vaginal delivery 10 months prior (February 2017); resident of Bangkok, Thailand; epidemiological exposure: husband diagnosed with an acute viral infection 1 week prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Bilateral retro-orbital pain, polyarthralgia, fatigue, pruritus; denies gastrointestinal or respiratory complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Low-grade fever, erythematous itchy morbilliform rash, bilateral conjunctival injection, and submandibular lymphadenopathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute Zika virus infection in a postpartum lactating mother with prolonged viral shedding in breast milk and urine. Confirmed by detection of Zika virus RNA via RT-PCR (RealStar Zika Virus RT-PCR Kit) in serial expressed breast milk samples from December 5 (3 days pre-symptom onset) to December 15 (Ct values 29.27 to 38.08), and in maternal urine through December 26 (negative on January 5, 2018; serum RT-PCR negative). Serum Zika virus IgG and IgM were detected by ELISA. Breastfeeding was suspended and infant urine monitored by RT-PCR; maternal symptoms resolved completely without complication.

raw_case_text: In 2017, an eight year-old Caucasian male from Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, presented with a hyperemic and pruritic lesion on the upper lip which had persisted for six months. Patient was treated with acyclovir cream, 5%, 5 times/day and cefadroxil (50 mg/kg/day) for seven days, with no response. He presented worsening of the lesion and Montenegro intradermal examination was performed ( Figure 2a). The patient was positive for American Tegumentary Leishmaniasis. Treatment with glucantime (10 mg/day) for 20 days was initiated. After three days of treatment, the patient developed vomiting episodes, intermittent fever, diarrhea, hypoglycemia, dark urine, and began developing a reaction of cardiotoxicity and hepatoxicity. Treatment with liposomal amphotericin B was initiated (3 mg/kg/day for 5 days, followed by 3 mg/kg). One month later, patient was discharged with remission of the lesion ( Figure 2b). Two months later, the patient was admitted at University Hospital with a new, erythematous and ulcerated lesion on the upper lip lesion, lymphadenopathy, and facial edema. Therapy with amoxicillin 250 mg (1g/day) and amphotericin B (100 mg/day) for 10 days was started. Patient is currently in psychological follow-up due to trauma caused by facial disfiguration and difficulty in returning to social life. Patient maintained outpatient follow-up and did not present with recurrence of the lesion.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of a persistent pruritic, hyperemic lesion on his upper lip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-month history of an erythematous, itchy lesion on his upper lip that failed to improve after treatment with topical acyclovir cream (5 times daily) and oral cefadroxil (50 mg/kg/day for 7 days). Because of clinical worsening, he underwent Montenegro testing and was diagnosed with American tegumentary leishmaniasis. He was started on meglumine antimoniate (10 mg/day for 20 days), but after 3 days developed acute vomiting, fever, diarrhea, hypoglycemia, dark urine, cardiotoxicity, and hepatotoxicity. He was switched to liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day for 5 days, followed by 3 mg/kg) and achieved remission at 1 month. Two months post-discharge, he relapsed with a new erythematous ulcerated upper lip lesion, facial edema, and lymphadenopathy, prompting readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior chronic medical illnesses. Resident of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pruritus of lip lesion; acute vomiting, diarrhea, dark urine, and fever during antimonial toxicity. Home medications: prior courses of acyclovir, cefadroxil, Glucantime, and liposomal amphotericin B. Allergies: Severe toxic reaction to meglumine antimoniate (cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity).

objective.physical_examination: Initial presentation: hyperemic, pruritic plaque on the upper lip. Relapse presentation: new erythematous, ulcerated lesion on the upper lip, diffuse facial edema, and regional cervical/submandibular lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Biochemical and toxicological monitoring: hypoglycemia, elevated liver enzymes (hepatotoxicity), and electrocardiographic abnormalities (cardiotoxicity) documented on day 3 of meglumine antimoniate therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: American tegumentary leishmaniasis of the upper lip with meglumine antimoniate-induced systemic toxicity and subsequent cutaneous relapse.
Diagnostic confirmation: Positive Montenegro intradermal reaction (skin test).
Differentials ruled out: Herpes simplex virus infection (unresponsive to acyclovir) and bacterial impetigo/cellulitis (unresponsive to cefadroxil).
Treatment and clinical course: Antimonial therapy was permanently discontinued due to life-threatening multiorgan toxicity. Relapse successfully treated with intravenous amphotericin B (100 mg/day for 10 days) alongside amoxicillin (250 mg PO, total 1 g/day), resulting in complete lesion healing without recurrence during follow-up. Enrolled in psychological support for facial disfigurement trauma.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old male farmer, presented with a history of multiple, recurrent discharging scrotal ulcers over a period of three (3) years. He had had multiple wound debridements and dressings done, but the ulcers had recurred a few months after complete healing. The discharging wounds occurred after the formation and subsequent rupture of pustules.
He was otherwise healthy with no constitutional symptoms, significant comorbidities, and no previous history or contact history of TB. He had received the BCG vaccination during infancy. He was an averagely built male with normal general and systemic examination. Genitourinary examination revealed bilateral craggy, hard epididymes, an enlarged and tender right testis, and multiple, superficial, noninfected scrotal ulcers (Fig. 1A and B).
Ultrasonography showed bilateral normal-sized testes. The right epididymis was enlarged and thickened with a 1.4 x 1 cm sized hypoechoic lesion in relation to the head of the right epididymis and a 2 cm x 1.8 cm sized hypoechoic lesion in relation to the lower pole of the right testis. Internal vascularity was noted. The right testis was not identified separately from the lesion. Furthermore, there was a 1.3 x 0.8 cm sized hypoechoic lesion in the left testis and a 0.7 x 0.6 cm sized hypoechoic lesion in relation to the left epididymis.
His complete blood count and chest radiograph were normal. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 90 mm/h, and the Mantoux was strongly positive with a diameter of 20 mm after 72 h. The urine full report (UFR) showed a field full of pus cells, and routine bacterial cultures were negative.
He underwent surgical exploration where the right epididymis was noted to be enlarged, irregular, and thickened with mild enlargement of the right testis with an irregular surface lesion, favoring chronic epididymo-orchitis (Fig. 2A and B). A right epididymal and testicular biopsy was performed, and histology revealed evidence of granulomatous inflammation with central caseous necrosis favoring mycobacterial TB infection. There was no evidence of intratubular germ cell neoplasia or malignancy. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain was negative for acid-fast bacilli. Pus from the scrotal discharge, the biopsy specimen, and the urine sent for TB culture returned negative.
He was started on category 1 antituberculosis therapy, that is, quadruple antimicrobial therapy for 2 months followed by dual therapy with rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months, for which there was a good response with healing of the scrotal ulcers. He was compliant, and no significant adverse effects of treatment were noted. However, three (3) months into therapy, he presented with worsening lower urinary tract symptoms, strangury, and acute urinary retention. He required suprapubic catheterization, and subsequent retrograde urethrography revealed a bulbar urethral stricture for which he is under urological care.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male presented with a 3-year history of multiple recurrent discharging scrotal ulcers.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 46-year-old male farmer presented with recurrent pustules on the scrotum that ruptured to form discharging ulcers over a period of 3 years. He had undergone multiple wound debridements and dressings, but ulcers consistently recurred a few months after complete epithelialization. He was otherwise healthy without constitutional symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: BCG vaccination during infancy. Multiple prior scrotal wound debridements and dressings. Denied significant comorbidities, previous history of tuberculosis, or known tuberculosis contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent discharging scrotal pustules and ulcers. Negative for fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, or cough. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Averagely built male; general and systemic examinations normal. Genitourinary examination: bilateral craggy, indurated epididymides; enlarged, tender right testis; multiple superficial, non-infected scrotal ulcers.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and plain chest radiograph normal. ESR 90 mm/h. Mantoux test strongly positive with 20 mm induration at 72 hours. Urinalysis: field full of pus cells (sterile pyuria); routine bacterial urine cultures negative. Scrotal ultrasound: right epididymis enlarged and thickened with 1.4 x 1 cm hypoechoic lesion in head; right testis not clearly demarcated from 2 x 1.8 cm hypoechoic lower pole lesion with internal vascularity; left testis contained 1.3 x 0.8 cm lesion and left epididymis contained 0.7 x 0.6 cm lesion.
objective.advanced_workup: Surgical exploration: enlarged, irregular, thickened right epididymis with mildly enlarged right testis displaying irregular surface lesions. Right epididymal and testicular biopsy: granulomatous inflammation with central caseous necrosis without intratubular germ cell neoplasia or malignancy; Ziehl-Neelsen stain was negative for acid-fast bacilli. Mycobacterial cultures of scrotal pus, biopsy tissue, and urine were negative. Retrograde urethrography performed subsequently revealed a bulbar urethral stricture.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Genitourinary tuberculosis presenting as chronic bilateral tuberculous epididymo-orchitis with recurrent scrotal ulceration and sterile pyuria, confirmed by testicular and epididymal histopathology showing necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with central caseous necrosis and a strongly positive Mantoux test (20 mm induration). AFB stains and mycobacterial cultures of pus, tissue, and urine were negative. Neoplasm was ruled out by biopsy. Management & Outcome: Treated with Category 1 antituberculosis therapy: 2 months of quadruple therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) followed by 4 months of dual therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid). Achieved complete healing of scrotal ulcers. At 3 months into therapy, developed lower urinary tract symptoms, strangury, and acute urinary retention due to bulbar urethral stricture, managed with suprapubic catheterization and urological follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old woman was referred to the emergency department with complaints of icterus, nocturnal fever, arthralgia, and abdominal pain. The patient had been well until two weeks earlier, when symptoms developed. She was a farmer in a village and owned a lot of sheep. There were no allergies and no history of recent use of drugs but she was consuming a large amount of nonpasteurized traditional cheese.
On physical examination, the patient was nonedematous. Her temperature was 38.5 C, with a blood pressure of 70/45 mm Hg, a pulse rate of 70 beats per minute, and respirations of 18 per minute. The oxygen saturation was 96 percent while she was breathing room air.
The liver edge was palpable 5 cm below the costovertebral margin. Her right upper quadrant of abdomen was diffusely tender to palpation. Additionally, there was marginal splenomegaly. The heart sounds and the results of the remainder of the examination were normal.
Laboratory studies performed at admission revealed a WBC count of 5400 cells/mm3, a hemoglobin level of 10.6 g/dL, a platelet count of 216.000 platelets/mm3, an aspartate aminotransferase level of 224 U/L, an alanine aminostransferase of 159 U/L, an alkaline phosphatase level of 2340 U/L, a gamma glutamyl transferase level of 597 U/L, a direct bilirubin level of 3.1 mg/dL, an albumin level of 3.3 g/dL, a globulin level of 4.3 g/dL and a uric acid level of 1.4 g/dL. Serum pituitary, thyroid, and adrenal function tests were in normal ranges.
Her other laboratory parameters included erythrocyte sedimentation rate 47 mm/hr, C-Reactive Protein level 26 U/L, serum sodium level 124 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 95 mmol/L, and plasma osmolality 262 mmol/kg/H2O. Urine biochemistry showed osmolality 274 mmol/kg/H2O and urinary sodium 64 mmol/L. Serologic tests for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis viruses were negative. Electrocardiographic examination showed minimal ST-T elevations.
Ultrasonography and Computed Tomography scan (CT scan) of the abdomen showed a small pericardial effusion with mild splenomegaly and hepatomegaly (Figures 1 and 2). However, there was no evidence of biliary dilatation or cholecystitis. CT scan of thorax and brain revealed no abnormality. Echocardiography detected mild pericardial effusion without cardiac dysfunction.
At the next day, serum agglutination test for Brucella was positive and its titer was 1/1240. The diagnosis of SIADH in association with cholestatic hepatitis and pericardial effusion due to Brucellosis was made. After intramuscular streptomycin (1000 mg/day for 20 days) with oral Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks), the patient's symptoms, cholestasis, pericardial effusion, and hyponatremia resolved dramatically.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old female presented with a 2-week history of jaundice, nocturnal fever, arthralgia, and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been well until 2 weeks prior to presentation, when she developed icterus, nocturnal fevers, generalized arthralgias, and abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Village farmer owning numerous sheep. Dietary exposure: regular consumption of large amounts of nonpasteurized traditional cheese. Denied allergies or recent use of medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports jaundice, nocturnal fever, arthralgia, and abdominal pain. Denies known drug allergies or recent medication use.

objective.physical_examination: Nonedematous. Temperature: 38.5 °C, blood pressure: 70/45 mmHg, pulse rate: 70 bpm, respiratory rate: 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation: 96% on room air. Abdomen: right upper quadrant diffusely tender to palpation; liver edge palpable 5 cm below the costovertebral margin; marginal splenomegaly. Heart sounds and remainder of physical examination were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count: 5,400 cells/mm^3, hemoglobin: 10.6 g/dL, platelet count: 216,000/mm^3. AST: 224 U/L, ALT: 159 U/L, alkaline phosphatase: 2,340 U/L, GGT: 597 U/L, direct bilirubin: 3.1 mg/dL, albumin: 3.3 g/dL, globulin: 4.3 g/dL, uric acid: 1.4 g/dL. ESR: 47 mm/hr, CRP: 26 U/L. Serum sodium: 124 mmol/L, potassium: 4.4 mmol/L, chloride: 95 mmol/L, plasma osmolality: 262 mmol/kg/H2O. Urine osmolality: 274 mmol/kg/H2O, urinary sodium: 64 mmol/L. Pituitary, thyroid, and adrenal function tests: within normal ranges. ECG showed minimal ST-T elevations. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated mild hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and a small pericardial effusion without biliary dilatation or cholecystitis. Echocardiography detected mild pericardial effusion without cardiac dysfunction.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen confirmed mild hepatosplenomegaly and small pericardial effusion with no evidence of biliary dilatation or cholecystitis. CT scans of the thorax and brain revealed no abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Serum agglutination test for Brucella was positive with a titer of 1:1,240, establishing the diagnosis of Brucellosis presenting with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), cholestatic hepatitis, and pericardial effusion. Differential diagnoses ruled out: Acute cholecystitis and biliary tree obstruction excluded by ultrasound and CT; viral hepatitis, EBV, and CMV ruled out by negative serologies; endocrine etiologies of hyponatremia excluded by normal thyroid, adrenal, and pituitary profiles. Management and Outcome: Treated with intramuscular streptomycin 1,000 mg/day for 20 days combined with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks. Following antimicrobial therapy, the patient's symptoms, cholestatic liver enzyme abnormalities, pericardial effusion, and hyponatremia resolved dramatically.

raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old man became aware that he was feeling fatigue the end of July 2020; he gradually also experienced lower leg pain and headache. He had diarrhea and vomiting; therefore, he visited a local hospital. He was referred to our hospital from the local hospital on the next day. We urgently hospitalized him, suspecting an infectious disease. His medical history only included a gastric ulcer. He was engaged in forestry and smoked for about 10 pack-years. He had no history of domestic or international travel and no recent history of sexual intercourse.
On examination, he was conscious and alert. His vital signs included a heart rate of 114 beats/min, blood pressure of 109/79 mmHg, and body temperature of 39.4 C. His blood oxygen saturation was 96%; however, bloody sputum was present. Chest auscultation revealed no rales. He complained of headache and severe pain in the lower legs. The clinical examination was otherwise unremarkable.
The laboratory data on admission have been shown in Table 1. In the peripheral blood, the white blood cell count was increased, predominantly, the neutrophils; his C-reactive protein level was also. Thrombocytopenia was present. His transaminase level was elevated; however, there was no hyperbilirubinemia. There was an increase in the urea nitrogen and serum creatinine levels. Granular casts and epithelial casts appeared in the urine, suggesting renal injury.
The imaging finding on admission have been shown in Figure. Chest radiographs did not reveal infiltration shadows (Fig. 1). Computed tomography showed central lobular shadows and pale ground-grass shadows in both the lungs (Fig. 2), suggesting alveolar hemorrhage along with bloody sputum symptoms.
The patient's clinical course has been described in Fig. 3. After admission, we administered 400 mg of moxifloxacin. On day 2 of admission, we received information that there were mice in the patient's living environment. Ceftriaxone at 2 g/d and minocycline at 200 mg/d were started, because we considered leptospirosis and rickettsia infection in the differential diagnosis. Immunoglobulin was also administered for 3 d for severe infection. Oxygen therapy was started with a high flow nasal cannula because of respiratory failure. On day 3 of admission, hyperemia of the bulbar conjunctiva and direct bilirubin-dominant bilirubin elevation appeared. Hemodialysis was started because of exacerbation of acute kidney injury by day 4 of admission. Leptospirosis was highly likely owing to the presence of symptoms, such as thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, liver injury, and hyperbilirubinemia. Thus, we requested the National Institute of Infectious Disease to perform tests using blood and urine samples. On day 10 of admission, the National Institute of Infectious Disease provided the results; the PCR of the urine samples showed positive leptospiral DNA; thus, a diagnosis of leptospirosis was established. Antimicrobial administration and hemodialysis were completed on day 15 of admission to reduce the inflammation and treat acute kidney injury. Thrombocytopenia also started subsiding. Oxygen therapy was completed on day 16 of admission to treat respiratory failure. He was transferred to a local hospital on day 23 of admission for rehabilitation. Thereafter, the results of a microscopic agglutination test (MAT) performed on blood samples on day 22 of admission were received (Table 2). The paired sera on day 4 and day 22 were significantly increased in the titers of the two types of antibodies (Leptospira interrogans serovar Autumnalis and Leptospira interrogans serovar Rachmati).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old male forestry worker presenting with acute fatigue, headache, lower leg pain, diarrhea, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fatigue at the end of July 2020, followed by progressive bilateral lower leg pain, headache, diarrhea, and vomiting. He visited a local hospital and was transferred the following day for urgent admission. Over the subsequent days, he developed hemoptysis, severe respiratory failure requiring high-flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy, direct hyperbilirubinemia, bulbar conjunctival hyperemia, and severe oliguric acute kidney injury requiring hemodialysis from hospital day 4. With targeted antimicrobial therapy and supportive care, his organ dysfunction improved, permitting cessation of hemodialysis on day 15 and weaning from oxygen on day 16.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical history of gastric ulcer. Occupation: Forestry worker. Social history: 10 pack-year cigarette smoking. Denied domestic or international travel, recent sexual contacts, or sick contacts. Epidemiological exposure: Mice present in his living environment.
subjective.review_of_systems: Complaints of headache, severe lower extremity muscle pain, diarrhea, vomiting, and bloody sputum.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Temperature 39.4 C, heart rate 114 beats/min, blood pressure 109/79 mmHg, SpO2 96% on room air. Conscious and alert. Chest auscultation revealed no rales. Severe calf/lower leg muscle tenderness. Presence of bloody sputum. Clinical examination otherwise unremarkable on day 1. Hospital day 3: Development of bulbar conjunctival hyperemia and visible jaundice.
objective.routine_investigations:
Admission laboratory findings: Peripheral blood leukocytosis with neutrophil predominance, elevated CRP, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases without initial hyperbilirubinemia, elevated blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine. Urinalysis: Granular casts and epithelial casts.
Hospital day 3: Direct bilirubin-predominant hyperbilirubinemia and worsening renal function.
Chest radiograph (admission): No infiltrative shadows.
Arterial blood gas / oxygenation: Hypoxemic respiratory failure managed with high-flow nasal cannula.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT (admission): Centrilobular nodules and faint ground-glass opacities bilaterally, consistent with alveolar hemorrhage.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed icteric leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, acute kidney injury, hepatic injury with direct hyperbilirubinemia, conjunctival suffusion, and thrombocytopenia. Confirmed on hospital day 10 by positive PCR detection of leptospiral DNA in urine by the National Institute of Infectious Diseases, and further validated by paired MAT sera (day 4 and day 22) showing significant titer rises against Leptospira interrogans serovar Autumnalis and Leptospira interrogans serovar Rachmati. Rickettsial infection was ruled out. Environmental exposure to mice was identified as the transmission source.
Plan & Outcome: Initial treatment with oral moxifloxacin (400 mg). Upon day 2, regimen changed to intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g/day) and minocycline (200 mg/day) along with intravenous immunoglobulin for 3 days. Managed with high-flow nasal cannula oxygenation and intermittent hemodialysis from day 4 to day 15. Antibiotics and hemodialysis were completed on day 15, oxygen therapy discontinued on day 16, and the patient was transferred for inpatient rehabilitation on day 23 in stable, recovering condition.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old female was referred to our clinic with double vision and restricted right eye abduction. In the ophthalmic examination, both pupils were round and reactive to light and accommodation. Extraocular movements were intact with the exception that the right eye was unable to abduct (Figure 1 (Fig. 1), Figure 2 (Fig. 2)). No nystagmus was detected and visual acuity was normal. Visual field examination revealed the enlargement of the blind spot and constriction of the peripheral fields. On fundus examination, bilateral papilledema with blurring of the disc margins was present.
Questioning her history revealed that the first symptoms were weakness and numbness in her lower limbs which had resolved spontaneously. Afterwards, she had developed an intractable headache associated with right gaze difficulty and diplopia and was referred from the emergency room to the neurology department. Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging revealed no pathology. After our finding of papilledema, despite the history of transient weakness in the lower limbs, the cause was firstly considered as idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) and lumbar puncture was planned. But because she developed fever and neck rigidity at that time, she was referred to the department of infectious diseases to rule out meningitis.
The patient underwent a lumbar puncture, opening pressure was 255 mm H2O and the examination of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed 85 leukocytes/mul. Her Rose Bengal test was positive and the CSF culture yielded Brucella melitensis and diagnosis of neurobrucellosis was established. The patient was treated with a combination of doxycycline, rifampin, cotrimoxazole, and dexamethasone for 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old female presented with persistent headache, diplopia, restricted right eye abduction, and acute fever with neck stiffness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially experienced transient weakness and numbness in her lower extremities that resolved spontaneously. She subsequently developed an intractable headache accompanied by difficulty looking to the right and binocular horizontal diplopia. Following an unremarkable brain MRI, idiopathic intracranial hypertension was initially suspected, but the acute emergence of fever and neck rigidity prompted referral for urgent evaluation of infectious meningitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior episode of transient weakness and numbness in the lower extremities that resolved spontaneously. Epidemiological exposure and prior medical comorbidities not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Diplopia, right gaze restriction, intractable headache, prior lower extremity numbness/weakness, fever, neck rigidity. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile with nuchal rigidity. Neuro-ophthalmic examination: visual acuity normal, pupils round and reactive to light and accommodation; extraocular movements intact except complete failure of right eye abduction (right cranial nerve VI / abducens nerve palsy); no nystagmus. Visual field testing: enlargement of the blind spot and peripheral field constriction. Fundoscopy: bilateral papilledema with blurring of the optic disc margins.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI): unremarkable, no structural pathology. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure elevated at 255 mm H2O; cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 85 leukocytes/microL.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis presenting with pseudotumor cerebri-like syndrome, intracranial hypertension, bilateral papilledema, and isolated right sixth cranial nerve (abducens) palsy. Confirmed by CSF culture isolating Brucella melitensis and positive serum Rose Bengal test. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) and non-brucellar infectious meningitis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with combination antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory therapy comprising oral doxycycline, rifampin, cotrimoxazole, and dexamethasone for a total duration of 6 months, resulting in resolution of intracranial hypertension and cranial neuropathy.

raw_case_text:
A summary reinfection case timeline is presented in Figure 1. A 49-year-old male resident of Tangerang, Banten, Indonesia, worked as a driver and utility worker at Tangerang District Hospital. He lived alone in a private room and commuted every day to the hospital on public transportation. He had not received COVID-19 vaccination, and his only known chronic condition was hypertension, for which he received no routine treatment. On January 10, 2021, the patient developed clinical symptoms consistent with COVID-19, including fever, cough, runny nose, anosmia, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia. On January 13, 2021, the patient was admitted to the emergency department. Physical examination revealed the patient was fully conscious, with high blood pressure (175/110 mmHg), fever (38 C), respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min, heart rate of 98 beats/min, and oxygen saturation of 97%. Nasopharyngeal (NP) and oropharyngeal (OP) swabs were collected for RT-PCR testing, and the following day he was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 infection (Ct values: Nucleocapsid (N) gene = 23.5 and ORF1ab gene = 30.2) but remained in the emergency department due to overloaded hospital COVID-19 wards. An initial chest X-ray showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and his laboratory tests showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) (66.3 mg/L), elevated D-dimer (241 ng/mL), leukocytosis (10.9 x 103/muL) with neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) of 9.6, and mild thrombocytopenia (134 x 103/muL). The patient was admitted to the COVID-19 ward on January 15 and received favipiravir, methylprednisolone, antihypertensives, and vitamin C. A repeated RT-PCR test showed that he was still positive (Ct values: N-gene = 23.0 and ORF1ab gene = 28.4). A summary of serial blood tests performed during hospitalization is shown in Table 1.
On January 17, the patient's oxygen saturation fell to 88% with marked shortness of breath, leading to his admission to the ICU and treatment with oxygen therapy at 10L/minute using a non-rebreathing mask. While in the ICU, his antiviral treatment was changed to a 5-day course of remdesivir and meropenem, per the attending physician's clinical judgment. No bacterial culture and antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) were performed. He also received heparin, which was then switched to fondaparinux sodium due to increased risk of bleeding, and a furosemide injection due to high blood pressure (up to 163/97 mmHg). After 3 days in the ICU, his condition improved, and his oxygen therapy was weaned to a nasal cannula. On January 22, the patient was moved to the regular COVID-19 ward, received oral levofloxacin for 5 days, and continued with oral cefixime, per clinical judgment due to an elevated leukocyte count (15.2 x 103/muL). A secondary bacterial infection was never confirmed. A follow-up RT-PCR test on January 25 detected low levels of viral RNA (Ct values: N-gene = 35.6 and ORF1ab gene = 35.8). The patient met discharge criteria [i.e., 10 days after onset of symptoms and at least three additional days without symptoms ] on January 29 and left the hospital. A summary of the patient's treatments is shown in Table 2.
On January 25, 2021, serum was collected and antibodies to the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein receptor binding domain (S-RBD) were detected by chemiluminescence immunoassay (CLIA) CL-900i  SARS-CoV-2 S-RBD IgG (Mindray, Shenzhen, China), with an IgG index of 350.8 U/mL. Further testing using a surrogate virus neutralization test (sVNT) (GenScript, Piscataway, United States) resulted in a percent inhibition value of 83%. Following the patient's discharge on January 29, follow-up RT-PCR tests on NP and OP specimens were performed on February 4 and 15, both of which were negative. Genomic sequencing of the SARS-CoV-2 Spike (S) gene from specimens collected on January 13, 2021, revealed S-D614G and S-N439K mutations. The full sequence of the S-gene (3,822-bp) was mapped and aligned to the reference genome obtained from the GISAID database. The sequence showed a 100% similarity with accession ID: EPI_ISL_1284133, belonging to Pango Lineage B.1.466.2 or GH clade on GISAID. Subsequent serological testing was performed at several timepoints after the initial COVID-19 episode (Figure 2A), with a peak S-RBD IgG index of 998.4 U/mL and a peak sVNT value of 88% on February 17. By May 24, the S-RBD IgG index declined to 230.5 U/mL and sVNT to a value of 76%.
The second episode of SARS-CoV-2 infection occurred around July 7, 2021, during the surge of the Delta variant in Indonesia. The patient developed mild symptoms consistent with COVID-19, including anosmia and runny nose. Two days later, he underwent RT-PCR testing at Tangerang District Hospital and was positive for SARS-CoV-2 (Ct values: N-gene = 20.1 and ORF1ab gene = 19.2). No routine blood test and chest imaging were performed. S-gene sequencing revealed mutations in the S gene (T19R, G142D, E156G, Del157/158, A222V, L452R, T478K, D614G, P681R, and D950N) that were consistent with the Delta variant, belonging to Pango Lineage B.1.617.2 or clade 21A on Nextstrain. Genomic analysis showed that the first episode viral genome belonged to a different clade/lineage from the second viral genome (Figure 2B). The patient underwent self-isolation at home and received treatment with vitamins, oseltamivir, paracetamol, and candesartan. His symptoms resolved 4 days later, with no follow-up on RT-PCR test. Serology testing from a blood specimen collected on July 9, 2021, revealed low antibody levels (S-RBD IgG = 142.7U/mL and sVNT = 71%). Subsequent testing on August 31, 2021, demonstrated boosting of humoral immunity (S-RBD IgG > 1,000 U/mL and sVNT = 91%). Details of the laboratory assays are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old male presenting with a 3-day history of fever, cough, rhinorrhea, anosmia, headache, myalgia, and arthralgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: On January 10, 2021, the patient developed fever, cough, runny nose, anosmia, headache, myalgias, and arthralgias, presenting to the emergency department on January 13, 2021. Due to hospital bed shortages, he remained in the ED until ward admission on January 15. On January 17, his oxygen saturation dropped to 88% with severe dyspnea, requiring ICU transfer for oxygen therapy at 10 L/min via non-rebreathing mask. Following ICU stabilization, he was weaned to nasal cannula on January 20, transferred to the regular ward on January 22, and discharged on January 29. Approximately six months later (around July 7, 2021), he developed a second episode consisting of anosmia and rhinorrhea lasting 4 days, managed in home isolation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Essential hypertension without routine therapy. Unvaccinated against pandemic respiratory virus. Occupational exposure: Driver and utility worker at a district hospital; commutes by public transportation.

objective.physical_examination: ED presentation (Jan 13, 2021): Fully conscious. BP 175/110 mmHg, HR 98 beats/min, T 38.0 °C, RR 22 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on room air. ICU transfer (Jan 17, 2021): Severe respiratory distress, SpO2 88% on room air; BP elevated up to 163/97 mmHg. Second episode (July 2021): Mild symptoms, hemodynamically stable.
