assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 reinfection caused by two phylogenetically distinct viral lineages.

First episode (January 2021): Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure and hypertensive crisis, confirmed by RT-PCR (N-gene Ct 23.5, ORF1ab Ct 30.2; repeat Ct 23.0 and 28.4). S-gene sequencing demonstrated S-D614G and S-N439K mutations, identifying Pango Lineage B.1.466.2 (GISAID GH clade, accession EPI_ISL_1284133). Repeat RT-PCR on Jan 25 showed Ct 35.6/35.8, and follow-up tests on Feb 4 and 15 were negative.

Second episode (July 2021): Mild COVID-19 reinfection during Delta surge, confirmed by RT-PCR (N-gene Ct 20.1, ORF1ab Ct 19.2). S-gene sequencing demonstrated Delta variant mutations (T19R, G142D, E156G, Del157/158, A222V, L452R, T478K, D614G, P681R, D950N) belonging to Pango Lineage B.1.617.2 / Nextstrain clade 21A.

Management and outcome: First episode managed with favipiravir, methylprednisolone, vitamin C, switched in ICU to 5 days of IV remdesivir and meropenem, 10 L/min NRM oxygen, anticoagulation (heparin switched to fondaparinux), furosemide, followed by oral levofloxacin and cefixime; discharged on Jan 29. Second episode managed at home with self-isolation, vitamins, oseltamivir, paracetamol, and candesartan, with complete symptom resolution within 4 days.

raw_case_text:
In September 1998, a 36-year-old male soldier in the French Foreign Legion with hemoptysis was sent back to France from Djibouti. He expectorated bloody sputum after running and on a few other occasions. His medical history was not unusual. When the patient was hospitalized, 2 weeks after the initial symptoms, he began to experience progressive fatigue. He did not experience fever, weight loss, night sweats, anorexia, cough, dyspnea, or chest pain, and did not produce sputum.
Results of the clinical examination were normal. The Mantoux test, performed with 10 IU of purified tuberculin (Aventis-Pasteur-MSD, Lyon, France), yielded a maximum transverse diameter of induration of 15 mm. Laboratory values were normal (Table). The chest X-ray showed a triangular consolidation of the left upper lobe with blurred limits and small cavitary lesions. No other contiguous mediastinohilar anomalies were visible. A computed tomographic scan confirmed the cavitary syndrome: three excavated nodular images showed radiating spicules within a micronodular infiltrate. Bronchoscopy showed a moderate inflammation of airway mucosa, especially in the left upper lobe. Biopsy specimens exhibited nonspecific inflammation.
A bronchial washing smear from the left upper lobe was positive for acid-fast bacilli. Serologic tests for HIV-1 and HIV-2 were negative. No evidence of disease was found elsewhere; the patient did not experience bone pain. Results of neurologic and ophthalmologic examinations were normal; no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly were found and the genitalia were normal. Auscultation revealed no pericardial fremitus; no ascitic fluid was detected. The urinary sediment contained <1,000 red blood cells/L and <5,000 leukocytes/L. Antituberculosis chemotherapy was begun with four drugs: rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Cultures revealed a strain identified as M. tuberculosis subsp. canetti that was susceptible to all primary antituberculous drugs. Therefore, rifampicin and isoniazid were continued for 3 more months for a total treatment period of 6 months. The patient's response to treatment was favorable, and he remained asymptomatic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old male presenting with hemoptysis and progressive fatigue for two weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a French Foreign Legion soldier returning from Djibouti, presented 2 weeks following initial episodes of hemoptysis. He expectorated bloody sputum after running and on several other occasions. Following the initial hemoptysis, he developed progressive fatigue. He denied fever, chills, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or ongoing sputum production.
subjective.past_medical_history: Soldier in the French Foreign Legion stationed in Djibouti. Past medical history was unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Progressive fatigue, episodic bloody sputum. Denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, or bone pain.

objective.physical_examination: Clinical examination was normal. Neurological and ophthalmologic examinations normal; no peripheral lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly; normal external genitalia. Cardiac auscultation revealed no pericardial friction rub; no ascites detected.
objective.routine_investigations: Mantoux tuberculin skin test (10 IU purified tuberculin) showed 15 mm transverse diameter induration. Routine laboratory values were normal. Urinary sediment contained <1,000 red blood cells/L and <5,000 leukocytes/L. Serologic tests for HIV-1 and HIV-2 were negative. Chest X-ray showed a triangular consolidation of the left upper lobe with blurred margins and small cavitary lesions, without contiguous mediastinohilar anomalies.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest computed tomography (CT) confirmed cavitary lesions: three excavated nodular opacities with radiating spicules embedded within a micronodular infiltrate in the left upper lobe. Bronchoscopy showed moderate mucosal inflammation, predominantly in the left upper lobe; bronchial mucosal biopsy demonstrated nonspecific inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsp. canetti.
Diagnostic confirmation: Bronchial washing smear from the left upper lobe positive for acid-fast bacilli; culture isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsp. canetti susceptible to all first-line antituberculous agents.
Management and outcome: Initiated on 4-drug antituberculosis chemotherapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide, followed by a continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid for 3 additional months (total duration 6 months). The patient had a favorable clinical response and remained completely asymptomatic.

raw_case_text:
A 51-year-old male non-smoker was referred to the emergency room (ER) with the complaint of abdominal pain 3 days earlier,which she rated an "8" on a scale of 1 to 10 without any medical history and drug history. He stated that the pain worsened with movement and change in position. He denied any significant family history of the disease. During the physical examination, the patient was diaphoretic, uncomfortable, and in severe distress. His vital signs were: blood pressure, 156/87 mm Hg; respiratory rate, 19 breaths/minute; heart rate, 132 beats/minute; and temperature within normal limits. Oxygen saturation was 93% on room air. The abdominal examination revealed a distended abdomen that was severely tender to palpation. Intravenous (IV) fluids were immediately started for the patient. He was also given IV ondansetron for nausea. His pain was refractory to treatment and required multiple doses of morphine sulfate. Laboratory evaluation revealed leukocytosis with a white blood cell (WBC) count of 14.5 thou/cm. He underwent laparotomy due to tenderness in favor of acute abdominal pain. During laparotomy, not only the small and large intestine but also their vasculature was normal. After two days, the patient was discharged with no pain and symptom. With nausea, abdominal pain, and dyspnea, he came back to the ER again after 3 days. On examination, he had tachypnea (RR: 40/min), tachycardia (HR: 120/min), low-grade fever (Temp: 38 centigrade). A lung computed tomography (CT) (Figure 1) and an abdominopelvic CT (Figure 2) were done. The patient was intubated due to respiratory failure. Covid-19 RT-PCR (Everse transcription polymerase chain reaction) was performed. Lab data included complete blood count (CBC)(WBC:17000 per microliter, Hb:12:8.7 g/dL, Plt: 350,000 per microliter), urea :170 mg/dL, (creatinine) Cr:4.2 mg/dL, (Lactate dehydrogenase) LDH:504 U/L, (C-reactive protein) CRP:47mg/L, and negative viral disease (HCV Ab-hepatitis C virus antibody, HBS Ag-Hepatitis B Antigen,, HIV Ab (human immunodeficiency virus)The patient was treated with 400 mg single-dose, hydroxychloroquine sulfate, lopinavir/ritonavir 100/400mg twice daily for five days, ribavirin 1200 mg twice daily for five days, and three doses of 250 mug beta interferon (Every other day). 
 During ICU admission, on the third day, fecaloid discharged from abdominal suture appeared, and therefore the patient was on sepsis phase. Laboratory data were CBC (WBC: 24000 per microliter, Hb: 12 g/dL, Plt: 347000 per microliter), urea: 206 mg/dL, Cr: 3.2 mg/dL,and amylase: 67 U/L. 
 Re-laparotomy was performed, and after laparotomy, serosanguinous secretions with necrotic changes in the small intestine were seen, so 130 cm of it was resected (Figure 3). The day after, due to suspicion of leakage from the anastomosis site, laparotomy was performed again and due to leakage from the anastomosis site and smaller bowel necrosis,100 cm of intestine was resected so ileostomy was performed. A pathological study (Figure 4) reported intravascular thrombosis in mesenteric tissue with a necrotic margin. The RT-PCR of covid-19 was reported positive. 
 The patient was treated with heparin infusion and broad-spectrum antibiotics. After 10 days of treatment in ICU, he was extubated, and his hemodynamic was stable, but platelet count began to decrease (162,000 per microliter), and therefore the day after gastrointestinal bleeding happened. 
 Lab test were CBC (WBC: 7100 per microliter, Hb: 8.7 g/dL, plt: 162000 per microliter), Cr: 1.3 mg/dL, amylase: 65 U/L. Plt and Cr decreased to 69000 per microliter and 1.1 mg/dL, respectively, but other coagulation tests (PT and PTT) were normal the day after. Heparin infusion was discontinued. Other laboratory tests were D-dimer: 2500 ng/mL, fibrinogen: 150 mg/dL, PT: 44 sec, PTT: 44 sec, INR: 1.7. No schistocyte in peripheral blood smear was found. Unfortunately, the patient eventually developed treatment-resistant sepsis, DIC, and died of its complications.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old male presenting with severe abdominal pain of three days' duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with a 3-day history of severe, positional abdominal pain (8/10 severity). An initial exploratory laparotomy was unrevealing, and he was discharged asymptomatic after two days. Three days post-discharge, he returned to the emergency department with nausea, severe abdominal pain, and acute dyspnea, rapidly progressing to respiratory failure requiring emergent endotracheal intubation. On hospital day 3, feculent drainage emerged from his abdominal incision, necessitating emergent repeat exploratory laparotomies with extensive bowel resections and end ileostomy formation for acute mesenteric ischemia and anastomotic dehiscence.
subjective.past_medical_history: Non-smoker; no prior medical, surgical, or medication history.

objective.physical_examination: First presentation: Diaphoretic, uncomfortable, in severe distress; BP 156/87 mmHg, heart rate 132 bpm, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, temperature afebrile, SpO2 93% on room air; abdomen distended and severely tender to palpation. Second presentation: Tachypneic (RR 40 breaths/min), tachycardic (HR 120 bpm), febrile (temperature 38.0 °C), in acute respiratory distress.
objective.routine_investigations: First admission labs: Leukocytosis with WBC count 14.5 x 10^3/microL. Readmission labs: WBC 17,000/microL, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, platelet count 350,000/microL, blood urea 170 mg/dL, serum creatinine 4.2 mg/dL, LDH 504 U/L, CRP 47 mg/L. Viral serologies negative for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C antibody, and HIV antibody. ICU day 3: WBC 24,000/microL, hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelets 347,000/microL, urea 206 mg/dL, creatinine 3.2 mg/dL, amylase 67 U/L. Subsequent labs: Platelet nadir of 69,000/microL, hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, D-dimer 2,500 ng/mL, fibrinogen 150 mg/dL, PT 44 sec, PTT 44 sec, INR 1.7. Peripheral blood smear: No schistocytes identified.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Abdominopelvic CT: Peritoneal and intestinal inflammatory changes. Surgical exploration & histopathology: Repeat exploratory laparotomy revealed necrotic small bowel requiring resection of 130 cm, followed by a third laparotomy showing anastomotic leakage and progressive ischemia requiring resection of an additional 100 cm and end ileostomy creation. Histopathological examination of resected bowel demonstrated intravascular thrombosis in mesenteric tissue with transmural ischemic necrosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia) verified by RT-PCR, complicated by severe mesenteric vascular thrombosis, extensive small bowel infarction and gangrene, peritonitis, anastomotic dehiscence, gastrointestinal bleeding, septic shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Plan & Outcome: Initial treatment included endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, therapeutic unfractionated heparin, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, alongside hydroxychloroquine (400 mg single dose), lopinavir/ritonavir (100/400 mg BID for 5 days), ribavirin (1,200 mg BID for 5 days), and interferon-beta (250 microg subcutaneously every other day for 3 doses). Multiple emergency surgical resections and ileostomy were performed. The patient was successfully extubated on ICU day 10, but subsequently developed overt GI hemorrhage, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy (DIC), and refractory sepsis, resulting in death.

raw_case_text:
In mid-2016, a 28-year-old previously healthy Colombian woman with later prenatal care attention came to the Perinatology and Obstetric Department at Fundacion Valle del Lili-University Hospital due to numerous fetal abnormalities observed in ultrasonography done at 29.5 weeks of gestation, which demonstrated brain anomalies with a possible Arnold-Chiari malformation, compromised lateral and third ventricles, liver calcifications, bilateral pyelocaliceal dilatations, microcephaly, and an apparent clubfoot. All relevant antecedents during pregnancy were considered (smoking, alcohol, drugs, or any other perinatal infection). The patient had experienced an episode of illness for 2-7 days that was characterized by fever, myalgias, and vomiting. She went to the hospital, where ZIKV was presumed, and RT-PCR of the amniotic fluid was done, with a positive result at 12 weeks of gestation. The findings confirmed ZIKV vertical transmission and congenital infection. Inadequate prenatal follow-ups were performed until the fetal examination at 29.5 weeks, which showed multiple malformations.
At the time of delivery, the mother was traveling from a remote area of the country. She went into labor on the way to the hospital and gave birth in the ambulance. According to the medical records and first ultrasonography date, delivery was at 38.6 weeks of gestation. The male newborn weighed 3,180 g (10th percentile), with a height of 48 cm (10th percentile) and a cephalic circumference of 31 cm (under the 2nd percentile) according to the WHO Growth Charts from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Transfontanelle ultrasonography reported microcephaly, an increase of the width and number of the circumvolutions due to pachygyria, and ventriculomegaly in the infratemporal and supratemporal fossae. There was also a non-discharging cerebrospinal fluid-filled cleft lined with gray matter on the left lateral ventricle going to the cerebral cortex, closed-lip schizencephaly, subcortical echogenic and punctiform, cystic image on the posterior fossae communicated with the fourth ventricle, thin corpus callosum, and pathological calcification in the liver, brain (cortical and subcortical), and placenta. As part of the evaluation approach to a newborn with brain abnormalities, TORCH testing was performed to rule out the most frequent congenital infections (syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, hepatitis B, HIV, cytomegalovirus, herpesvirus 1 and 2, and parvovirus B19) as causal etiology.
The mother reported that the newborn was irritable, with an abnormal pattern of crying and hyperexcitability. The physical examination showed distal tremors, hypertonia, trunk hyperextension, spasticity, increased deep tendon reflexes, persistent primitive responses, clenched fists, strabismus, and nystagmus. Microcephaly was present, which was characterized by craniofacial disproportion, decreased vertical size of the skull, a sloping forehead, and pronounced supraorbital ridges, giving the appearance of oversized facial features and proptosis. Epicanthal folds, retrognathia, excess skin over the entire scalp and forehead, and occipital and nuchal skin folds were also found, giving the appearance of a short neck. The forehead presented with bilateral depressions and prominent overlapping metopic and sagittal sutures with supratemporal depressions and a large visible occipital prominence. An examination of the extremities revealed hand contractures, camptodactyly, feet contractures, prominent calcanei, multiple dimples, and arthrogryposis (Figure 1). Because of the multiple abnormalities, a complete genetic assessment was performed on the newborn and his mother.
After 1 year of follow-up, a complete checkup was performed. The findings showed irritability, an abnormal pattern of crying, hyperexcitability, hypertonia, spasticity, clenched fists, strabismus, clinodactyly of the fifth finger, and an ogival palate. Microcephaly was still present, with a few of the previously observed characteristics, such as a small skull, retrognathia, and a prominent metopic suture. A physical examination of the extremities found hand contracture and camptodactyly, feet contracture, prominent calcanei, multiple dimples, arthrogryposis, and a severe delay in the developmental milestones. A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed microcephaly, with a giant posterior fossa cyst, ventricular dilatation, hypoplasia of the cerebral vermis, and an anomalous cerebral cortex with lissencephaly (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: 28-year-old pregnant female presenting at 29.5 weeks gestation following detection of extensive fetal brain, visceral, and musculoskeletal anomalies on ultrasound, after experiencing a first-trimester febrile illness with vomiting and myalgias.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At 12 weeks of gestation, the patient had an acute illness lasting 2-7 days characterized by fever, myalgias, and vomiting. Prenatal follow-up was delayed until 29.5 weeks gestation, when fetal ultrasound revealed severe intracranial, hepatic, and musculoskeletal malformations. At 38.6 weeks gestation, while traveling from a remote rural area, she entered active labor and delivered in an ambulance. The newborn was noted to have severe irritability, hypertonia, craniofacial disproportion, microcephaly, and arthrogryposis, with persistent neurodevelopmental impairment documented through 1 year of life.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy Colombian woman; denied tobacco, alcohol, illicit substance use, or prior perinatal infections; delayed/inadequate early prenatal care.
subjective.review_of_systems: Maternal (historical): Fever, myalgias, vomiting. Neonatal (reported by mother): Marked irritability, abnormal high-pitched crying pattern, and hyperexcitability.

objective.physical_examination: Neonatal examination at birth (38.6 weeks gestation): Male newborn; birth weight 3,180 g (10th percentile), length 48 cm (10th percentile), head circumference 31 cm (<2nd percentile by CDC/WHO growth charts). Neurological: Distal tremors, generalized hypertonia, trunk hyperextension, spasticity, hyperreflexia, persistent primitive reflexes, clenched fists, strabismus, and nystagmus. Craniofacial: Craniofacial disproportion, reduced skull vertical height, sloping forehead, prominent supraorbital ridges, proptotic appearance, epicanthal folds, retrognathia, redundant skin folds over scalp, forehead, and nuchal region (apparent short neck), bilateral frontal and supratemporal depressions, prominent overlapping metopic and sagittal sutures, and large occipital prominence. Extremities: Arthrogryposis, hand and foot contractures, camptodactyly, prominent calcanei, and cutaneous dimples. Follow-up at 1 year: Persistent microcephaly, irritability, hypertonia, spasticity, clenched fists, strabismus, fifth-finger clinodactyly, high-arched (ogival) palate, arthrogryposis, and severe global developmental delay.
objective.routine_investigations: Fetal ultrasound (29.5 weeks gestation): Microcephaly, ventriculomegaly involving lateral and third ventricles, suspected Arnold-Chiari malformation, liver calcifications, bilateral pyelocaliceal dilatations, and apparent clubfoot. Neonatal transfontanelle ultrasound: Microcephaly, pachygyria with widened circumvolutions, ventriculomegaly in infratemporal and supratemporal fossae, left lateral ventricle closed-lip schizencephaly lined with gray matter extending to cortex, subcortical punctiform echogenic calcifications, posterior fossa cyst communicating with the fourth ventricle, thin corpus callosum, and pathological calcifications in liver, brain (cortical and subcortical), and placenta.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI (at 1 year of life): Microcephaly with a giant posterior fossa cyst, ventriculomegaly, hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, and anomalous cerebral cortex with lissencephaly. Comprehensive genetic assessments performed on infant and mother.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Congenital Zika syndrome with severe fetal brain disruption sequence (microcephaly, pachygyria, lissencephaly, closed-lip schizencephaly, posterior fossa cyst, ventriculomegaly, cerebral and hepatic calcifications) and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita. Vertical transmission of Zika virus was confirmed by positive RT-PCR in amniotic fluid obtained at 12 weeks of gestation. Neonatal TORCH panel ruled out syphilis, toxoplasmosis, rubella, hepatitis B, HIV, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, and parvovirus B19. Supportive pediatric multidisciplinary and neurodevelopmental management was maintained through 1 year of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old Shepherd presented to the emergency department (ED) with a 10-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and gait imbalance. He also reported a history of daily low-grade fever over the past 5 months which was associated with fatigue, arthralgia and 10-kg weight loss.
Physical examination was only remarkable for a low-grade fever of 37.8 C orally with a wide-based unsteady gait and scanned speech. Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis with a shift to the left (WBC count of 20.8*103/ul with 92% neutrophils), normal renal and liver function tests, and a C-reactive protein of <5 mg/l. Brucella antibody test was positive for IgG but not IgM antibodies with a titer of 1:320 for Brucella abortus and 1:160 for Brucella melitensis. The CSF analysis showed predominantly lymphocytic leukocytosis (RBC count 6, WBC count 250, 80% lymphocytes) with high protein (63 mg/dl) and low glucose (1.8 mmol/l compared to 6.5 mmol/l serum level). The CSF gram stain and culture, acid-fast bacilli stain, mycobacterial tuberculosis (TB) PCR, TB Culture, and cryptococcal antigen tests were negative. Also, the patient had a negative QuantiFERON TB gold plus test as well as negative serological markers for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine revealed post-gadolinium meningeal enhancement around the brainstem, bilateral V, VII, and VIII cranial nerves, cervical and lumbar spinal meninges as well as enhancement of the ependymal linings (Fig. 1). Also, there was evidence of ventricular enlargement of the third and fourth ventricles consistent with mild hydrocephalus.
The patient was started on triple antibiotics therapy for a presumptive diagnosis of neurobrucellosis including intravenous Ceftriaxone two grams twice daily for 4 weeks plus oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily and doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 months. He developed confusion 1 day after starting antimicrobial therapy, so he was commenced on pulse steroid therapy (500 mg methylprednisolone intravenously for 3 days) followed by a tapering dose of oral prednisolone for 1 month. Two days later, his confusion improved. A repeated brucella antibody test showed a decline in the titer to 1:160 for Brucella abortus and Brucella melitensis.
The patient's gait continued to improve, and he was able to walk without assistance. He remained free from headache, vomiting, or fever for 3 weeks. A repeated MRI of the brain at week three post-treatment showed regression of the meningeal enhancement and ventricular dilatation with minimal residual changes (Fig. 2). The patient completed 4 weeks of parenteral ceftriaxone as inpatient, then he was discharged on rifampicin and doxycycline for a minimum duration of 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male shepherd presented with a 10-day history of abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and gait imbalance, along with a 5-month history of daily low-grade fever, fatigue, arthralgia, and 10-kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old shepherd presented with abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, and gait imbalance for 10 days, preceded by 5 months of daily low-grade fevers associated with fatigue, arthralgia, and a 10-kg weight loss. Following admission and initiation of antimicrobial therapy, he developed acute confusion on hospital day 1, which responded rapidly to corticosteroid pulse therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation as a shepherd (chronic exposure to sheep and livestock). Prior chronic medical conditions, hospitalizations, home medications, and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, vomiting, dizziness, gait imbalance, daily fever, fatigue, arthralgia, 10-kg weight loss, and in-hospital acute confusion; denies headache. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature: 37.8 C orally (low-grade fever). Neurological examination: wide-based unsteady gait and scanned speech. Remainder of physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 20.8*103/ul (92% neutrophils, shift to the left); CRP: <5 mg/l; renal and liver function tests: normal. Serum glucose: 6.5 mmol/l. QuantiFERON TB Gold Plus: negative. Serological markers for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis: negative.
objective.advanced_workup:
Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: predominantly lymphocytic leukocytosis (WBC 250 /ul, 80% lymphocytes; RBC 6 /ul), protein 63 mg/dl, glucose 1.8 mmol/l (serum glucose 6.5 mmol/l). CSF Gram stain, routine bacterial culture, acid-fast bacilli stain, Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, TB culture, and cryptococcal antigen: all negative.
MRI of brain and spine: post-gadolinium meningeal enhancement around the brainstem, bilateral cranial nerves V, VII, and VIII, and cervical and lumbar spinal meninges, with enhancement of ependymal linings; third and fourth ventricular enlargement consistent with mild hydrocephalus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neurobrucellosis (meningoencephalitis with cranial polyneuropathies and mild hydrocephalus) caused by Brucella abortus and Brucella melitensis.
Confirmation: Brucella antibody test positive for IgG with titers of 1:320 for Brucella abortus and 1:160 for Brucella melitensis (later declining to 1:160 for both post-treatment).
Differentials ruled out: Tuberculous meningitis (negative CSF AFB stain, TB PCR, TB culture, and negative QuantiFERON TB Gold Plus), cryptococcal meningitis (negative cryptococcal antigen), bacterial meningitis (negative CSF Gram stain and culture), neurosyphilis, HIV, and viral hepatitis.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with triple antimicrobial therapy: intravenous Ceftriaxone (2 g twice daily for 4 weeks), oral Rifampicin (600 mg once daily for 6 months), and oral Doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 6 months). For acute confusion occurring 1 day after starting antimicrobials, pulse IV methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 3 days) was administered followed by a 1-month oral prednisolone taper, with resolution of confusion within 2 days. Gait improved to unassisted ambulation; headache, vomiting, and fevers resolved. Repeat brain MRI at week 3 showed regression of meningeal enhancement and ventricular dilatation. Discharged after completing 4 weeks of IV ceftriaxone to complete 6 months of oral rifampicin and doxycycline.

raw_case_text: Following a visit to family in Ghana, this 49-year-old Ghanaian-born UK resident (of 22 years) presented with severe malaria and a peripheral P. falciparum parasitaemia of 3.0% (details presented in reference 34). Two sequential samples, F54840 and F55564, taken prior to treatment and 8 hours later (4 to 5 hours after commencement of quinine treatment), respectively, were analysed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old male presenting with severe febrile illness following travel to Ghana.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 49-year-old male resident of the UK for 22 years presented with severe acute febrile illness following a visit to family in Ghana.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ghanaian-born UK resident of 22 years. Travel history to Ghana. No chemoprophylaxis documented.

objective.routine_investigations: Serial pre-treatment and post-treatment (at 8 hours) peripheral blood films performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria acquired following travel to Ghana.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood film showing Plasmodium falciparum with 3.0% parasitemia; high-throughput whole-genome sequencing (isolates OX005 and OX005A) confirming monoclonal infection with large chromosomal deletion (>20 kb) encompassing the Rh1/Clag3.1 and Rh1/Clag3.2 loci on chromosome 3.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous quinine therapy. Serial blood sampling at 8 hours demonstrated effective early drug response, leading to full clinical recovery.

raw_case_text: A 74-year-old known diabetic and hypertensive with good control presented to our institution with unsettling, high-grade fever for a week associated with retro-orbital headache, arthralgia, and myalgia. He was a farmer by profession and has had contact history with muddy water. He did not have respiratory or urinary symptoms. He was haemodynamically stable initially although urine output was low (<0.5 ml/kg/hr). Renal functions were markedly elevated, and bilateral moderate pleural effusions were noted in the ultrasound chest. Glycemic control was poor with initial random blood sugar of 350 mg/dl requiring an insulin infusion. Chest X-ray showed additional features of pulmonary haemorrhages. There were no skin rashes or lymphadenopathy. Blood was collected for routine cultures and Leptospira antibody test (microscopic agglutination test, MAT). He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone and methylprednisolone empirically with the suspicion of severe leptospirosis and pulmonary haemorrhages. Urgent haemodialysis was arranged every other day. Two days into the hospital stay, the patient acutely became drowsy and restless and electively intubated. Noncontrast CT brain excluded cerebral oedema or acute vascular events. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a severe hypoxemia (P/F < 120). Lung-protective ventilation was continued although a fraction of inspired oxygen continued to escalate. Prone ventilation was opted approximately 14 hours a day. Pancytopaenia with hepatosplenomegaly was evident in the complete blood count and ultrasound abdomen, respectively. A multidisciplinary discussion with the general medical and haematological units was held. Persistent high fever with negative routine cultures and the rapid deterioration despite optimal supportive therapy pointed towards possible sHLH. Subsequent serum ferritin levels and trephine biopsy confirmed the diagnosis (Figures 1(a)-1(c)), aided by elevated serum triglycerides. After three doses of intravenous methylprednisolone, intravenous dexamethasone was commenced with intravenous etoposide twice a week. Sequential blood pictures and clotting parameters were suggestive of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). This was managed with transfusion of cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma per haematological guidance. Persistent severe metabolic acidosis and severe hyperkalaemia were treated with haemodialysis under escalating inotropic supports (continuous renal replacement therapy was not available in our center). No structural anomalies or vegetations were detected in the 2D echocardiogram. The patient died following cardiac arrest on day 06 of the intensive care (day 15 of the illness). A highest MAT titre of 1 : 640 confirmed the diagnosis of leptospirosis posthumously. The summary of investigation results is illustrated in Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old male farmer presenting with a 1-week history of high-grade fever, retro-orbital headache, arthralgia, and myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 74-year-old male farmer presented with a 1-week history of unsettling high-grade fever, retro-orbital headache, arthralgias, and myalgias. He was initially hemodynamically stable but oliguric with acute renal failure and bilateral pleural effusions. On hospital day 2, he acutely deteriorated with drowsiness and restlessness, requiring elective intubation and mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemic ARDS. Despite lung-protective ventilation, prone positioning, intermittent hemodialysis, and escalating inotropes, he developed secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH) and disseminated intravascular coagulation, ultimately suffering cardiac arrest and death on ICU day 6 (illness day 15).
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension with good baseline control. Profession: Farmer with documented occupational contact with muddy water. No preceding respiratory or urinary symptoms.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports retro-orbital headache, arthralgias, and myalgias. Denies cough, shortness of breath, dysuria, or gross hematuria. No skin rashes or peripheral lymphadenopathy noted.

objective.physical_examination: Upon presentation: High-grade fever, hemodynamically stable, oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h), no skin rashes, no lymphadenopathy. ICU day 2: Drowsiness, agitation, respiratory failure requiring intubation. Abdominal examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations:
Admission labs: Marked elevation of renal function tests, random blood glucose 350 mg/dL. Complete blood count: Pancytopenia. Routine blood cultures: Negative. Chest radiograph: Features of pulmonary hemorrhage. Ultrasound chest: Moderate bilateral pleural effusions. Ultrasound abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly.
Arterial blood gas (post-intubation): Severe hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 ratio <120), severe metabolic acidosis, and severe hyperkalemia.
Coagulation and hematology: Sequential blood pictures and clotting parameters demonstrated disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Serum biochemistry: Markedly elevated serum ferritin and elevated serum triglycerides.
objective.advanced_workup:
Non-contrast brain CT: Excluded cerebral edema and acute intracranial vascular events.
2D Echocardiogram: Normal cardiac structure, no valvular vegetations.
Bone marrow trephine biopsy: Confirmed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (macrophage hemophagocytosis).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed severe leptospirosis complicated by severe pulmonary hemorrhage, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and refractory metabolic arrest. Confirmed posthumously by microscopic agglutination test (MAT) with a peak diagnostic titer of 1:640. Routine bacteremia was ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Empirically treated with intravenous ceftriaxone, pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone, insulin infusion, and alternate-day hemodialysis. Following intubation and diagnosis of sHLH, managed with lung-protective and prone ventilation (14 h/day), intravenous dexamethasone, intravenous etoposide twice weekly, escalating inotropic support, and blood product replacement (cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma) for DIC. Despite maximal intensive care therapy, the patient developed fatal cardiac arrest on ICU day 6.

raw_case_text:
To the Editor: A 37-year-old woman, a logistics director for a nongovernment organization, returned to France in March 2004 from an 18-day trip to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone. Fever, chills, and myalgia developed in the woman 3 days before she returned to France, and she treated herself with aspirin and paracetamol (acetaminophen). Malaria prophylaxis was taken neither during nor after the trip.
The day after returning to France, the woman's condition progressively worsened; diarrhea and extreme weakness that led to the inability to walk developed. Ten days after her return, she was admitted to the local hospital and treated with intravenous quinine and oral doxycycline (2 g per day) after thick and thin blood films showed 3% parasitemia with Plasmodium falciparum. Three days later, she was still febrile and had conjunctival jaundice, vomiting, insomnia, and moderate hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, blood in urine and feces). Three days after initial hospitalization, the patient was transferred to the Infectious Diseases Unit in Marseille; fever (39.5 C) continued, and hepatosplenomegaly developed. Biologic analyses showed disseminated intravascular coagulation with platelet count of 22,000/mL, an elevated prothrombin time (54% higher than the control value), a longer activated clotting time (51 seconds versus a control value of 34 seconds), a fibrinogen level of 0.9 g/dL, exaggerated plasma fibrin formation and degradation, and hepatic cytolysis with both aspartate aminotransferase and alanine aminotransferase levels of 80 U/L.
Although acute malaria had been diagnosed, viral serologic tests were performed because the patient had returned from a tropical country with a fever. Persons in these circumstances are systematically administered a series of tests to determine the cause of their fever. Serologic tests for dengue performed on the acute-phase serum (collected 13 days after onset of symptoms) and convalescent-phase serum (collected 23 days after onset of symptoms) showed the presence of immunoglobulin (Ig) M (titers 1:800 and 1:3,200, respectively) and IgG (titers 1:400 and 1:3,200, respectively), which suggested that the patient had dengue fever and malaria concurrently. These results were obtained by using the Dengue Duo IgM-capture and IgG-indirect enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (Biotrin, PanBio Pty. Ltd., Brisbane, Australia). The same acute-phase serum was tested for flavivirus RNA by seminested reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) by using flavivirus consensus primers PF1S and PF2R as previously described in conjunction with the sense primer PF3S (GCIATHTGGTAYATGTGGYT). Attempts to isolate viruses by using C6/36 and Vero cells were unsuccessful, which might be expected given the delay between the onset of symptoms and specimen collection.
Sequence analysis of the 163-bp (primers excluded) PCR product (GenBank accession no. AY862501) showed 89%-99.4% range of homology with 34 dengue 3 virus strains by using the BLAST nucleotide program. Similarities obtained with sequences of dengue virus 1, 2, and 4 were <=87%. Phylogenetic analysis performed with the patient sequence together with homologous sequences from dengue viruses and other flaviviruses showed that it corresponded to dengue 3 virus species. RT-PCR amplification on the convalescent-phase serum was negative. Based on World Health Organization criteria, the patient was diagnosed with dengue fever. The patient's interview showed a previous dengue fever episode in Haiti in 1995 and a previous malaria episode in Burundi in 2002, but biologic confirmation was not available, and serum was not collected before this episode. Therefore, we could not determine definitively whether this patient experienced primary or secondary dengue. In light of virologic tests results, the diagnosis of secondary dengue infection was more likely.
A PubMed search using the keywords dengue, mixed infections, dual infections, simultaneous infections, and concurrent infections retrieved 14 references published since 1958. In most cases, concurrent infection was with 2 dengue virus strains from 2 different serotypes in a single patient. Only 6 published studies reported concurrent infection with dengue virus and a bacterium (Salmonella typhi, Shigella sonnei, Leptospira spp.) or with a virus such as Chikungunya virus.
To our knowledge, this is the first report of mixed dengue-parasite infection, dengue virus with P. falciparum. The authors previously questioned the accuracy of a serologic test to diagnosis dengue fever in patients experiencing malaria because reactivity was nonspecific on certain rapid serologic assays; however, serologic tests used in this study have demonstrated good specificity, and molecular tests are not prone to such specificity problems. Classifying this case as dengue hemorrhagic fever is questionable since some of the hemorrhagic signs may have been caused by acute malaria. In cases of concurrent infections involving a dengue virus, questions related to the influence of mixed infection on severity and prognosis are, therefore, impossible to address because of lack of information. Further investigations are required because this situation likely occurs frequently in nature, despite scant available data.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old female presenting with high fever, extreme weakness, vomiting, conjunctival jaundice, and hemorrhagic manifestations following recent travel to West Africa.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Fever, chills, and myalgia developed 3 days prior to returning to France from an 18-day trip to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone, for which she self-treated with aspirin and paracetamol. The day after returning, her condition progressively worsened with diarrhea and extreme weakness resulting in inability to walk. Ten days after return, she was admitted to a local hospital and started on intravenous quinine and oral doxycycline (2 g/day). Three days later, persistent high fever, conjunctival jaundice, vomiting, insomnia, and moderate hemorrhagic manifestations (epistaxis, hematuria, and hematochezia) prompted transfer to a specialized infectious disease unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Reported a previous febrile illness in Haiti in 1995 and in Burundi in 2002. Traveled for 18 days to Guinea, Senegal, and Sierra Leone in March 2004; no chemoprophylaxis was taken during or after the trip.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, myalgias, extreme weakness, diarrhea, vomiting, insomnia, epistaxis, hematuria, and hematochezia. Medications: self-administered aspirin and paracetamol. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39.5 C. Physical examination revealed conjunctival jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly. Patient was severely weak with moderate hemorrhagic manifestations including epistaxis.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: 22,000/mL. Prothrombin time: elevated (54% higher than control value). Activated clotting time: 51 seconds (control: 34 seconds). Fibrinogen level: 0.9 g/dL. Exaggerated plasma fibrin formation and degradation, consistent with disseminated intravascular coagulation. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 80 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 80 U/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Concurrent Plasmodium falciparum malaria and acute secondary dengue fever (dengue virus serotype 3) complicated by severe thrombocytopenia and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
Diagnostic confirmation: Thick and thin blood films showed 3% parasitemia with Plasmodium falciparum. Acute-phase serum (collected 13 days post-onset) and convalescent-phase serum (collected 23 days post-onset) demonstrated IgM titers of 1:800 and 1:3,200 and IgG titers of 1:400 and 1:3,200, respectively (Dengue Duo ELISA). Semi-nested RT-PCR on acute serum amplified flavivirus RNA; sequence analysis of the 163-bp product (GenBank AY862501) confirmed 89%-99.4% homology with dengue 3 virus strains. Viral isolation in C6/36 and Vero cells was negative; convalescent RT-PCR was negative.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with intravenous quinine and oral doxycycline (2 g/day) alongside supportive intensive therapy for DIC and coagulopathy. Hemorrhagic manifestations and fever subsided with medical treatment.

raw_case_text:
A 65-years-old Swiss fisherman, known for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and gout presents with fever, epigastric pain, myalgia, and jaundice lasting for one week. Initial laboratory exam reveals acute kidney injury, liver failure, elevated troponin I, and thrombocytopenia (Table 1). Because of frequent arrhythmia (ventricular extrasystole) and an elevated troponin I raising the suspicion of myocarditis, he is admitted during 48 hours to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring. 
Because of the initial presentation and the patient's occupation, leptospirosis was immediately suspected and treated with antibiotics (ceftriaxone). Initially, renal function improved. Serologies for Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae were positive, confirming the diagnosis.
Suddenly, 7 days after the beginning of his hospitalization, he presented multiple-organ failure (MOF) of liver, kidney, and lung required mechanical ventilation and high doses of norepinephrine. His APACHE II and SAPS II scores were 37 and 80, respectively, which means an expected 90% mortality (see Table 1 for others parameters). 
Plasma exchanges were started, followed by continuous renal replacement therapy with high-volume hemofiltration (HVHF) at 70 mL/kg/h. He received five sessions of plasma exchanges and was treated during 72 hours by HVHF, followed then by 10 days of standard hemodiafiltration before renal function recovered. 
His ICU stay was complicated by a penicillin-resistant enterococcus bacteremia requiring vancomycin treatment. Because of the large doses of amines, he developed dry necrosis of both extremities. He also required transient pacing for extreme bradycardia. Hemorrhagic bronchial secretions caused several respiratory arrests. Finally, he developed a severe CMV colitis requiring sigmoidectomy and ganciclovir.
He stayed in ICU for 45 days and was released from hospital after 70 days. He received care for skin necrosis of the feet and he had a brief hospitalization to restore bowel continuity.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of fever, epigastric pain, myalgias, and jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 1 week prior to admission with fever, epigastric pain, generalized myalgias, and progressive jaundice. Initial hospital admission was complicated by frequent ventricular extrasystoles and elevated troponin I. Although renal function initially improved, he experienced sudden collapse on hospital day 7 with multiple organ failure involving the liver, kidneys, and lungs, requiring high-dose vasopressors and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical history includes hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and gout. Occupation and epidemiological exposure: Swiss fisherman with regular freshwater aquatic and environmental exposure. Baseline medications and drug allergies are unmentioned.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, epigastric pain, myalgias, and jaundice. Additional review of systems is unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Patient was febrile and visibly jaundiced. Cardiovascular: frequent ventricular extrasystoles noted on telemetry; later developed profound bradycardia requiring transient pacing. Respiratory: hemorrhagic bronchial secretions causing recurrent respiratory arrests while mechanically ventilated. Extremities: developed bilateral symmetrical dry necrosis of the lower extremities secondary to high-dose vasopressors.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory evaluation revealed acute kidney injury, acute liver failure, elevated troponin I, and thrombocytopenia. Decompensation severity scoring: APACHE II score of 37 and SAPS II score of 80 (predicting 90% mortality).
objective.advanced_workup: Pathology and endoscopy from emergency sigmoidectomy performed during ICU stay confirmed severe cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) complicated by acute myocarditis with ventricular arrhythmia, late multiple organ failure (hepatic, renal, and pulmonary), secondary penicillin-resistant Enterococcus bacteremia, vasopressor-induced distal limb necrosis, and CMV colitis. Confirmed by positive serologies for Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae. Treatment & Outcome: Initially treated with intravenous ceftriaxone. Day 7 multiorgan collapse was managed with mechanical ventilation, high-dose norepinephrine, transient cardiac pacing, 5 sessions of therapeutic plasma exchange, 72 hours of high-volume hemofiltration (HVHF at 70 mL/kg/h), and 10 days of continuous hemodiafiltration until renal recovery. Nosocomial Enterococcus bacteremia was treated with vancomycin, and CMV colitis was managed with ganciclovir and emergency sigmoidectomy. The patient was discharged after 45 days in the ICU and 70 days total hospitalization, later undergoing elective restoration of bowel continuity and wound care for distal extremity necrosis.

raw_case_text:
The authors present a case of a 72-year-old male, with a past medical history of diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension, who was admitted to the emergency department due to fever and diarrhoea with 4-day evolution. On the physical evaluation, the patient was hypotensive (blood pressure of 84/44 mmHg) and dehydrated, without any other significant findings. Blood analysis revealed leucocytosis (12,200/mm3) with neutrophilia (10,800/mm3), elevated C-reactive protein (9.5 mg/dl) and an acute kidney injury (creatinine 7.34 mg/dl). Due to haemodynamic instability, the patient needed aminergic support and renal replacement therapy. Blood cultures isolated Salmonella Typhi. The patient was treated with ciprofloxacin, in accordance with bacterial antibiotic susceptibility tests. With a positive clinical evolution he was discharged after completing antibiotic treatment, clinically asymptomatic.
Three weeks after discharge, the patient was evaluated on a follow-up consult and complained of testicular pain and weight loss of 5 kg over the previous 15 days. On the physical evaluation, he presented multiple purpuric lesions with ulcers, pustules and necrotic tissue on his legs (Figs. 1 and 2) and petechiae on his arms. A cutaneous biopsy was performed, showing areas with detachment of the corneal layer with keratinocyte necrosis and abundant polymorphonuclear cells (Fig. 3) and polymorphonuclear infiltration of the arteries of the deep dermis and hypodermis with focal signs of vasculitis (Fig. 4), compatible with polyarteritis nodosa. The patient was treated with prednisolone, starting with 60 mg followed by progressive dose reduction, with complete remission of the skin lesions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old male presented with fever and diarrhea of 4 days duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Fever and diarrhea began 4 days prior to emergency admission. Three weeks following discharge after successful antimicrobial treatment, he presented to a follow-up consultation with testicular pain, a 5 kg weight loss over the prior 15 days, and new necrotizing cutaneous lesions on his lower and upper extremities.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus and arterial hypertension. No other past medical history or travel documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Testicular pain, 5 kg weight loss over 15 days, skin lesions.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: Hypotensive (blood pressure 84/44 mmHg) and dehydrated, without other significant findings. Follow-up visit: Multiple purpuric lesions with ulcers, pustules, and necrotic tissue on bilateral legs, and petechiae on arms.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count: 12,200/mm3 with neutrophilia of 10,800/mm3. C-reactive protein: elevated at 9.5 mg/dL. Renal function: severe acute kidney injury with serum creatinine 7.34 mg/dL.
