assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteremia) complicated by septic shock and acute renal failure, followed by post-infectious secondary polyarteritis nodosa (PAN). Blood cultures isolated Salmonella Typhi, susceptible to ciprofloxacin. Initial management: hemodynamic stabilization with aminergic (vasopressor) support, renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis), and intravenous ciprofloxacin according to susceptibility tests, resulting in resolution of infection and normal discharge. For secondary polyarteritis nodosa: oral prednisolone initiated at 60 mg daily with progressive tapering, achieving complete remission of cutaneous vasculitic lesions.

raw_case_text:
A 71-year-old female presented to our emergency room (ER) with two syncopal episodes. About three days prior to the presentation, she started having a fever, dry cough, body aches, and tested positive for COVID-19 at home. She was started on a 5-day treatment course of Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir/ritonavir). Subsequently, the patient developed episodes of nausea with vomiting. After the third dose of Paxlovid, she had sudden onset of dizziness with nausea and felt like she was about to pass out. She was able to slowly bring herself to the ground and then lost consciousness. This was an unwitnessed episode, and her family members noticed her on the ground about 10 minutes later. The patient was able to stand up, walked to the bed, and then lost consciousness again for 3-5 minutes. No seizure-like activity was noted. She presented to ER after the second syncopal episode.
She has no significant past medical history apart from the remote history of vasovagal syncopal episodes. Her last syncopal episode from vasovagal episodes was more than 30 years ago. She does not drink alcohol, smoke cigarettes, or use any recreational drugs. She is not on any other prescription medications.
An initial evaluation in the ER was reassuring. Her blood pressure (BP) was 143/87 mmHg, temperature 98.4 F, heart rate 62 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 16 per minute. Labs showed normal electrolytes, and renal and liver function. D-dimer was negative. Orthostatic vitals were unremarkable. High-sensitivity serial troponins were negative. EKG showed normal sinus rhythm with heart rate of 64, normal QRS wave, good R wave progression with no Q waves or significant ST-T abnormalities. She remained asymptomatic and appeared stable for discharge from the ER. While preparing for discharge, she suddenly developed lightheadedness, nausea with vomiting, and heart rate suddenly dropped to 28. BP was unrecordable. She was not on a cardiac monitor as patient was about to leave the hospital. She was given a dose of 1 mg IV atropine push with which her heart rate improved to 80s instantly and her BP improved to 141/79 mmHg. She was admitted to the hospital.
While monitoring, around the 30-hour mark since the last dose of Paxlovid, she developed an episode of sudden lethargy and passed out. She was noted to have several pauses with a maximum 10-second pause on telemetry (Figures 1-2) and was hypotensive. She was given 1 mg IV atropine push, with which her heart rate immediately restored to the 80s. Mild hypokalemia (3.4 mmol/L; reference range 3.5-5.1 mmol/L) was noted and corrected. Her heart rate remained stable in normal sinus rhythm without any further episodes or significant alarms on telemetry. 2D echocardiogram did not show any abnormal findings such as pericardial effusion or valvular abnormalities. The ejection fraction was 74%. The atrial size was normal and no evidence of pulmonary hypertension was noted. Thyroid studies were within normal range. She was monitored for a total of 72 hours in the hospital and no significant cardiac events were noted after the 30-hour mark of Paxlovid.
The cardiac electrophysiology team was consulted. Since these events happened after the initiation of Paxlovid and improved after discontinuation of medication, it was felt that this is a medication-related side effect. Hence, a pacemaker was deferred and she was sent home on a 14-day event monitor for further monitoring. A follow-up phone call was made to her 12 days after her discharge and she reported no further episodes of lethargy or syncope and was feeling much better.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 71-year-old female presenting with two syncopal episodes following three days of fever, dry cough, body aches, nausea, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three days prior to presentation, the patient developed fever, dry cough, and body aches, testing positive on a home viral antigen test. She was prescribed oral nirmatrelvir/ritonavir. After the third dose, she developed nausea, vomiting, acute dizziness, and lightheadedness, experiencing an unwitnessed syncopal episode lasting approximately 10 minutes. Upon standing and walking toward bed, she experienced a second witnessed syncope lasting 3–5 minutes without seizure activity, prompting emergency department evaluation. While being prepared for discharge from the ED, she suddenly became dizzy, nauseated, and collapsed with extreme bradycardia (HR 28 beats/min) and unrecordable blood pressure. Approximately 30 hours after her last dose of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir, she had another syncopal collapse on telemetry with sinus pauses up to 10 seconds.
subjective.past_medical_history: Remote history of vasovagal syncope over 30 years prior. No other chronic cardiovascular, neurological, or systemic illnesses. Denies alcohol, tobacco, or recreational drug use. No regular prescription medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, dry cough, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, and syncope. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or focal neurological deficits.

objective.physical_examination: Initial ER vitals: BP 143/87 mmHg, HR 62 beats/min, T 98.4 °F, RR 16 breaths/min. Orthostatic vital signs unremarkable. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations normal. Acute syncopal event 1 (ER): Heart rate abruptly dropped to 28 beats/min, blood pressure unrecordable; restored to HR 80s and BP 141/79 mmHg after atropine. Acute syncopal event 2 (inpatient telemetry at 30 hr): Profound hypotension, lethargy, loss of consciousness, and telemetry showing sinus pauses up to 10 seconds; restored to HR 80s after atropine.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, electrolytes, hepatic and renal panels normal. High-sensitivity troponins negative. D-dimer negative. Mild hypokalemia: potassium 3.4 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.1 mmol/L), which was corrected. Thyroid function studies normal. Serial ECGs showed normal sinus rhythm, normal QRS, normal R wave progression, and no ST-T abnormalities. Inpatient telemetry: Recorded several sinus pauses, the longest measuring 10 seconds, terminating after IV atropine.
objective.advanced_workup: Transthoracic 2D echocardiogram: Normal left ventricular systolic function with ejection fraction 74%, normal atrial dimensions, no valvular abnormalities, no pericardial effusion, and no evidence of pulmonary hypertension.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe symptomatic sinus arrest with prolonged sinus pauses (up to 10 seconds) and recurrent syncope secondary to adverse drug effect of nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid), initiated for acute mild COVID-19 infection (confirmed by home antigen test).

Management and outcome: Successfully resuscitated from profound bradycardic episodes with two separate doses of IV atropine 1 mg. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir was discontinued. Electrolyte abnormalities corrected. Cardiac electrophysiology consultation determined the sinus node dysfunction was drug-induced rather than intrinsic conduction system disease, deferring permanent pacemaker implantation. Monitored for 72 hours with complete cessation of bradycardic events after 30 hours post-drug discontinuation. Discharged on a 14-day cardiac event monitor; follow-up at 12 days confirmed no further syncopal or presyncopal events.

raw_case_text: A 40-year-old male experienced blurred vision and black shadows in both eyes 2 months after HAART initiation (3TC and Dolutegravir [DTG]). CD4 counts were 160/mul. VA was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye. Ophthalmic examination showed retinal necrosis and hemorrhages with vitritis (++) in zones 2 and 3. OCT was normal in the macular. He underwent PPV and silicone oil tamponades in the left eye and ganciclovir and steroid intravitreal injections for both eyes. Afterward, immediate PPV and silicone oil tamponades were conducted in the opposite eye for secondary retinal detachment 1 month later. Vitreous DNA sequencing showed a CMV sequence of 446,072 copies. Silicone oil removal was conducted 4 months later for both eyes. Intravitreal injections were conducted eight times separately for both eyes. VA of the patient was 20/20 in both eyes at the last follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presenting with bilateral blurred vision and floating shadows two months after initiating antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of bilateral blurred vision and dark shadows (floaters) starting two months after initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy. He underwent surgical and medical vitreoretinal management, followed one month later by acute retinal detachment in the contralateral right eye requiring urgent operative intervention.
subjective.past_medical_history: Receiving combination antiretroviral therapy consisting of lamivudine (3TC) and dolutegravir (DTG) initiated two months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Bilateral blurred vision and vitreous floaters; denies ocular pain, redness, or systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic Examination: Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left eye; fundoscopy revealed bilateral necrotizing retinitis and intraretinal hemorrhages with moderate vitritis (++) involving zones 2 and 3.
objective.advanced_workup: Optical coherence tomography (OCT): Normal macular architecture bilaterally. Vitreous fluid sampled for molecular diagnostic DNA sequencing.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Bilateral cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis complicated by secondary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment and immune recovery vitritis in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection on HAART (CD4+ T-cell count 160/microL). Diagnostic confirmation: High-titer vitreous CMV DNA (446,072 copies) on DNA sequencing, consistent with characteristic clinical necrotizing retinitis and vitritis. Plan & Outcome: Underwent urgent pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and silicone oil tamponade in the left eye, along with bilateral intravitreal ganciclovir and corticosteroid injections. Secondary retinal detachment in the right eye required emergency PPV with silicone oil tamponade one month later. Both eyes received a total of 8 intravitreal injections each. Bilateral silicone oil removal was performed at 4 months. Final visual acuity achieved 20/20 in both eyes at last follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old man from Chhapra, Bihar, visited the outpatient department of Rajendra Memorial Research Institute of Medical Sciences (RMRIMS), Indian Council of Medical Research, Patna, on December 10, 2018, with non-itching nodular eruptions on his face, hands, and abdomen. The patient had a history of VL 8 months back. On physical examination, the patient was afebrile and non-anemic, with no hepatosplenomegaly, and skin lesions with intact sensitivity. On investigation, his rK39 strip test was positive. Hence, PKDL was suspected,and the patient was advised to undergo skin smear microscopy and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis. His skin smear report was positive for Leishman-donovan bodies, and the parasite load for qPCR was 6723 parasites/microg of DNA. Hence, the patient was diagnosed with PKDL. 
The patient was prescribed 100 mg of oral miltefosine capsules daily for 28 days. After 15 days of miltefosine consumption, he developed blurred vision, redness, photophobia, and foreign body sensation in both eyes (Figure 1). He stopped taking miltefosine on his own, but his symptoms did not improve. Six days later, he visited RMRIMS, Patna. The patient was referred to a higher ophthalmological center for consultation by a trained ophthalmologist. His ophthalmic investigation revealed best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in the right and left eyeof 6/9 and 6/18, respectively. There was ciliary congestion in both eyes with no mucopurulent discharge. Anterior chamber examination revealed cells and flares in the anterior chamber along with fine keratic precipitates over the endothelium in both eyes. There was dense senile arcus in both eyes and mild posterior subcapsular cataract in the left eye. Posterior segment examination revealed no macular edema on +90D examination in either eye. Optical coherence tomography was not performed as the +90D examination showed no macular edema. Indirect ophthalmoscopy examinations were normal in both eyes. Routine laboratory examinations, including total blood cell count, differential white blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, chest radiography, Mantoux test, venereal disease research laboratory test, and antinuclear antibody test were performed to exclude other common causes of uveitis. The results were insignificant to establish any systemic association for uveitis. Therefore, a presumptive diagnosis of acute anterior non-granulomatous uveitis was made, and the routine treatment for typical anterior uveitis was started. He was treated with topical antibiotics and steroid eye drops. After 3 weeks of treatment, his ophthalmological examination revealed resolution of the uveitis. BCVA was recorded as 6/6 and 6/12 in the right and left eye, respectively. No cells or flare was present in the anterior segment examination. Posterior segment examination was normal on +90D and indirect ophthalmoscopy examination. The patient was administered 30 mg/kg of liposomal amphotericin B (6 doses of 5 mg/kg twice weekly for 3 weeks) in 5% dextrose intravenously. Six months post-treatment, all the skin lesions disappeared and the qPCR report showed negligible parasites.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male with post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis presented with blurred vision, bilateral eye redness, photophobia, and foreign body sensation after starting miltefosine.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to RMRIMS with non-itching nodular skin eruptions on his face, hands, and abdomen 8 months after completing treatment for visceral leishmaniasis. He was diagnosed with post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) and prescribed oral miltefosine capsules (100 mg daily for 28 days). After 15 days of miltefosine therapy, he developed acute blurred vision, bilateral ocular redness, photophobia, and foreign body sensation in both eyes. He self-discontinued miltefosine, but symptoms persisted, prompting referral to an ophthalmology center 6 days later.
subjective.past_medical_history: Visceral leishmaniasis treated 8 months prior. Origin: Chhapra, Bihar, India (endemic region).
subjective.review_of_systems: Bilateral ocular pain, redness, photophobia, foreign body sensation, blurred vision. Denies pruritus of skin lesions. Home medications: miltefosine 100 mg daily (discontinued). Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: General: afebrile, non-anemic, no hepatosplenomegaly. Dermatologic: non-itching nodular eruptions on the face, hands, and abdomen with intact tactile sensation. Ophthalmologic: best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) 6/9 in right eye and 6/18 in left eye; bilateral ciliary injection/congestion without mucopurulent discharge; anterior chamber revealed cells and flares with fine endothelial keratic precipitates in both eyes; bilateral dense senile arcus and mild posterior subcapsular cataract in left eye; posterior segment normal on +90D and indirect ophthalmoscopy (no macular edema).
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology and serology: total blood cell count, differential white blood cell count, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) normal/unremarkable. Chest radiography: normal. Infectious and autoimmune serologies: Mantoux tuberculin test, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) test, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) test were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin smear microscopy and quantitative PCR (qPCR): performed on facial/abdominal nodular lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) complicated by miltefosine-induced acute anterior non-granulomatous uveitis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Positive rK39 strip test; slit-skin smear microscopy demonstrated Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies; quantitative PCR (qPCR) demonstrated a parasite load of 6,723 parasites/microg of DNA.
Differentials ruled out: Lepromatous leprosy (intact sensation, no thickened nerves), ocular syphilis (negative VDRL), tuberculosis (negative Mantoux, normal chest X-ray), and autoimmune anterior uveitis (negative ANA).
Treatment and clinical course: Miltefosine was permanently withheld. Acute anterior uveitis was treated with topical antibiotics and corticosteroid eye drops, leading to complete resolution of uveitis within 3 weeks (BCVA improved to 6/6 OD and 6/12 OS; resolution of anterior chamber cells and flare). PKDL was subsequently treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (30 mg/kg cumulative dose given as 6 infusions of 5 mg/kg twice weekly for 3 weeks in 5% dextrose). At 6 months post-treatment, all cutaneous lesions completely resolved and repeat qPCR demonstrated negligible parasite load.

raw_case_text:
Patient 1 was a 10-year-old girl admitted with 2 days of fever, retroorbital headache, vomiting, and myalgia. Her white blood cell (WBC) count on the 3rd day was 2.2 x 103 with 65% neutrophils and platelet count of 117,000. Alanine transaminase (ALT) was 17.8 and aspartate transaminase (AST) was 55.2. Treatment was commenced as dengue fever in febrile phase. By the 4th day, she became sleepy and lethargic and the level of consciousness gradually deteriorated. She was moved to high dependency care for further management. On neurological examination, she had increased tone in all four limbs with cogwheel rigidity. The lowest Glasgow coma scale documented was 10/15. Her vital parameters and serial packed cell volume readings remained stable without signs of fluid leakage.
Lowest WBC count (1.9 x 103) was reported on day 5 of the illness and lowest platelet count was 50,000/mm3 on day 6. Liver enzymes deteriorated (ALT: 357, AST: 478) and serum albumin was 38 g/dL and INR was 1.17 on day 6. Tender liver was palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Renal functions (sodium: 142 mEq/L, potassium: 4.2 mEq/L, blood urea: 7.6 mmol/L, and serum creatinine: 52 mumol/L) remained normal. Serum calcium remained between 2.08 and 2.69 mmol/L. Primary dengue infection was suggested by the presence of IgM antibodies and absence of IgG antibodies to dengue virus. Dengue NS-1 antigen and the viral load were not performed due to lack of laboratory support. A CT scan revealed hypodense areas in bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia regions (Figure 1). Cerebrospinal fluid examination did not reveal any cells and had normal protein levels (42 mg/dL). Over the next 2 weeks following the acute illness, she showed complete recovery with no residual neurological disability.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old girl presenting with a 2-day history of fever, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and myalgia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 10-year-old girl presented with 2 days of fever, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, and myalgia. On illness day 4, she became progressively sleepy and lethargic, with deteriorating sensorium requiring transfer to high-dependency care. Vital parameters and serial hematocrit/packed cell volume remained stable without evidence of plasma leakage.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, retro-orbital headache, vomiting, myalgia, sleepiness, and lethargy. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination on day 4: Increased muscle tone in all four limbs with cogwheel rigidity; lowest Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score documented was 10/15. Abdominal examination: Tender hepatomegaly palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. Vital signs stable throughout.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 3: WBC 2.2 x 10^3/muL (65% neutrophils), platelets 117,000/muL, ALT 17.8 U/L, AST 55.2 U/L. Day 5: Lowest WBC 1.9 x 10^3/muL. Day 6: Lowest platelets 50,000/mm3, ALT 357 U/L, AST 478 U/L, serum albumin 38 g/L, INR 1.17, serum sodium 142 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, blood urea 7.6 mmol/L, serum creatinine 52 mumol/L, serum calcium 2.08-2.69 mmol/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT scan: Hypodense areas in bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia regions. Lumbar puncture / CSF examination: Acellular (no cells), normal protein level (42 mg/dL).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue encephalitis / neurodengue with bilateral basal ganglia and thalamic involvement and extrapyramidal signs (cogwheel rigidity). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus IgM antibodies and negative IgG antibodies, confirming primary dengue infection (NS1 antigen and RT-PCR unavailable due to laboratory constraints); CSF cellularity normal; characteristic CT hypodensities in basal ganglia and thalami.
Plan & Outcome: Managed in high-dependency care with close neuro-monitoring and supportive care. Over the subsequent 2 weeks, sensorium cleared and she achieved complete clinical recovery without residual neurological disability.

raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man, a resident of Uttar Pradesh, driver by occupation, a smoker for 25 years, and occasional alcohol consumer, having a previous history of dengue fever six years back, known patient of diabetes mellitus, presented with a history of acute onset intermittent, high-grade fever associated with chills during the last seven days followed by mild to moderate epigastric pain and two episodes of gum bleeding. He also noticed yellowish discoloration of eyes for three to four days, and throat pain for two days. On examination, the patient was hemodynamically stable with a random blood sugar of 180 mg/dL and had multiple ecchymoses over the arm and abdomen, icterus, and multiple creamy white patches over the tongue, posterior oro-pharyngeal wall and palate (Figures 2A, 2B). Tenderness was noted on the right hypochondriac region; on respiratory system examination, the patient had inspiratory crackles over bilateral infra-axillary and infra-scapular areas. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable.
Baseline blood investigation showed hematocrit of 39.7%, thrombocytopenia of 19,000/mm3, and total leukocyte count of 6,700/mm3; liver function test showed total bilirubin of 3.56 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 2.00 mg/dL, SGPT of 450 Units/liter and SGOT of 633 Units/liter, with alkaline phosphatase of 559 Units/liter. The renal function test was within normal limits. A tropical fever workup came positive for dengue NS1 (ELISA method), and viral markers (anti-HCV, anti-HIV I/II, and HBsAg) were non-reactive. Serum HBA1C level was 10%. Fundoscopy showed no evidence of hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy, and urine routine microscopy showed no evidence of proteinuria. Abdominal ultrasonography showed grade II fatty liver with coarse liver echotexture without any sign of portal hypertension or dilatation of biliary radicle. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed evidence of oro-pharyngeal candidiasis but not esophageal involvement or any varices there.
The patient improved with conservative management and transfusion of random donor platelets. Oral thrush improved with nystatin suspension, 4 mL four times a day. Over the next two weeks, the patient reported a complete resolution of throat pain. Blood glucose was optimized using subcutaneous regular insulin (10U three times a day) in the outpatient setting.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presented with high-grade fever with chills for 7 days, epigastric pain, gum bleeding, jaundice for 3-4 days, and sore throat for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 7-day history of acute intermittent high-grade fever with chills, followed by mild to moderate epigastric pain and two episodes of gingival bleeding. Over the preceding 3-4 days, he noted scleral icterus, and developed progressive odynophagia over the past 2 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Documented acute febrile illness 6 years prior. Driver by occupation residing in Uttar Pradesh, India. 25-pack-year smoking history and occasional alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, chills, epigastric discomfort, gingival bleeding, jaundice, and sore throat. Denied melena, hematemesis, or altered sensorium.

objective.physical_examination: Patient was hemodynamically stable. Scleral icterus was noted. Cutaneous examination showed multiple ecchymoses over the arms and abdomen. Oropharyngeal examination revealed multiple creamy white plaques over the tongue, posterior oropharyngeal wall, and soft palate. Abdominal examination demonstrated right hypochondrial tenderness without peritoneal signs. Respiratory examination revealed inspiratory crackles over bilateral infra-axillary and infra-scapular areas.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Hematocrit 39.7%, platelet count 19,000/mm3, total leukocyte count 6,700/mm3.
Liver function tests: Total bilirubin 3.56 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.00 mg/dL, SGOT 633 U/L, SGPT 450 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 559 U/L.
Renal function tests: Within normal limits.
Metabolic profile: Random blood glucose 180 mg/dL, HbA1c 10%.
Urinalysis: Normal without proteinuria.
Abdominal ultrasonography: Grade II hepatic steatosis with coarse echotexture; no evidence of portal hypertension or intrahepatic/extrahepatic biliary dilatation.
objective.advanced_workup:
Fundoscopy: No diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: Oropharyngeal candidiasis confirmed; no esophageal candidiasis or gastroesophageal varices.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue fever with hemorrhagic manifestations (gum bleeding, ecchymoses), severe thrombocytopenia, hepatic dysfunction, secondary oropharyngeal candidiasis, and uncontrolled type 2 diabetes mellitus. Confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen test (ELISA). Viral serologies for HIV I/II, HCV, and HBV (HBsAg) were non-reactive.
Treatment and outcome: Treated with supportive care and transfusion of random donor platelets. Oral candidiasis was successfully treated with oral nystatin suspension (4 mL four times daily), leading to complete resolution of odynophagia within 2 weeks. Diabetes was managed with regular subcutaneous insulin (10 units three times daily).

raw_case_text:
A 31-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital for the treatment of newly diagnosed drug-resistant (pre-extensively drug resistant) pulmonary tuberculosis (chest X-ray at time of diagnosis - Fig. 1). She was treated with second-line antituberculosis drugs: moxifloxacin, kanamycin, cycloserine, prothionamide, para-aminosalicylic acid. After 3 weeks of therapy she developed high fever (> 39 C), lymphadenopathy in the cervical and axillary regions and pruritic maculopapular eruption all over the body (Fig. 2). Hematologic abnormalities such as leukocytosis with eosinophilia (1.81 x 109/l) and monocytosis (1.85 x 109/l) were detected in peripheral blood of the patient. Hepatitis was asymptomatic and detected by the evaluation of liver function: serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 1379 IU/l and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 1221 IU/l; levels of liver enzymes were increased by approximately 30-40-fold above the normal limits. The positive diagnosis of Epstein-Barr infection was based on the onset of increase in the anti-Epstein-Barr immunoglobulin (Ig) G titer (> 200 U/ml), implicating Epstein-Barr virus re-activation. Based on the clinic and laboratory findings diagnosis of DiHS/DRESS was suspected, and all the drugs were discontinued. Symptoms and laboratory abnormalities gradually resolved over 4 weeks without additional treatment.
A patch test was performed and analyzed according to the recommendations. The results of the patch test are presented in Table 1 and Figure 3. Treatment was adjusted to ethambutol, kanamycin, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, and linezolid, and no new symptoms were observed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old woman presented with high fever (>39 °C), generalized pruritic maculopapular rash, and lymphadenopathy three weeks after starting second-line antituberculosis medications.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 31-year-old woman was admitted to the hospital and commenced on second-line antituberculosis medications. After 3 weeks of therapy, she acutely developed high-grade fever (>39 °C), bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, and a generalized pruritic maculopapular eruption. All second-line drugs were discontinued upon suspicion of a severe adverse drug reaction, with gradual symptom resolution over 4 weeks without additional systemic therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR) pulmonary tuberculosis. Prior hospitalizations, non-TB medical conditions, travel, or epidemiological exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high fever, generalized pruritic eruption, cervical and axillary swelling; denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or acute dyspnea outside baseline. Home medications: moxifloxacin, kanamycin, cycloserine, prothionamide, para-aminosalicylic acid. Allergies not documented prior to reaction.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature >39 °C. Dermatologic: generalized pruritic maculopapular eruption covering the entire body. Lymphatic: palpable lymphadenopathy in cervical and axillary regions. Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no overt jaundice on physical inspection.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC: leukocytosis with eosinophilia (1.81 x 10^9/L) and monocytosis (1.85 x 10^9/L); liver function tests: serum AST 1,379 IU/L, serum ALT 1,221 IU/L (transaminases elevated 30-40-fold above upper normal limit); Chest X-ray: baseline pulmonary infiltrates at time of diagnosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Anti-Epstein-Barr virus IgG titer: markedly increased (>200 U/mL), indicating EBV reactivation. Drug patch testing performed according to international guidelines.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Drug-induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome / Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DiHS/DRESS) with severe acute hepatitis and Epstein-Barr virus reactivation, secondary to second-line antituberculosis agents, in a patient with pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR) pulmonary tuberculosis.
Confirmation: Clinical triad of high fever (>39 °C), generalized rash, peripheral lymphadenopathy, marked peripheral eosinophilia (1.81 x 10^9/L) and monocytosis (1.85 x 10^9/L), 30-40-fold transaminitis (AST 1,379 IU/L, ALT 1,221 IU/L), rising anti-EBV IgG titers (>200 U/mL) demonstrating viral reactivation, and positive drug patch testing.
Differentials ruled out: Acute viral hepatitis (A, B, C) and primary EBV mononucleosis.
Treatment & Outcome: Immediate cessation of all second-line antituberculosis medications. Clinical symptoms and laboratory abnormalities completely resolved over 4 weeks without corticosteroids. Antituberculosis treatment was successfully adjusted to ethambutol, kanamycin, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, and linezolid, with no recurrence of adverse reactions.

raw_case_text:
A 29 year old previously asymptomatic male was admitted in a peripheral hospital with fever and jaundice of 1 week duration. He had anemia (hemoglobin [Hb] 8.8 g/dl), thromocytopenia (platelet count 55,000/mul), renal impairment (serum creatinine [s. creatinine] 1.5 mg/dl) and direct hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 3.9 mg/dl, direct 1.9 mg/dl). Peripheral smear showed the presence of schizonts of Plasmodium vivax. Antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was negative. He was treated with Artesunate and Clindamycin for 7 days and was discharged when asymptomatic, although improvement in thrombocytopenia or renal impairment was not observed. Two week later (1 week after being afebrile and getting discharged) he presented to us with vomiting and pain in the abdomen for 3 days and decreased urine output. He did not have fever, loose motions, rash, bleeding or alteration in sensorium. There was no history of treatment with quinine. He was hypertensive, pale, did not have edema and had unremarkable systemic examination except for the presence of haemic murmur. Severe anemia (hemoglobin 4.8 g/dl), thrombocytopenia (platelet count 61,000/mul) and azotemia (s. creatinine 8.3 mg/dl) were noted. Presence of schistocytes on peripheral smear, elevated reticulocyte count (13%), elevated serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 1242 U/L) and indirect hyperbilirubinaemia indicated ongoing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Urinalysis showed microhematuria and proteinuria of 3.75 g/day. Coagulation profile was normal. Serum C3 level was low (50 mg/dl), C4 level being normal. Antinuclear antibodies and enzyme-linked immuno sorbent assay for human immunodeficiency virus were negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-hepatitis C antibodies were negative. He underwent five sessions of 1.5 volume plasma exchanges with replacement with fresh frozen plasma. Hypertension was controlled. Intermittent hemodialysis was done. Anemia was corrected with packed red cells transfusion. After five sessions of plasma exchanges, platelet count increased to 150,000/mul Hb stabilized at 6 g/dl and then increased. S. LDH decreased to 206.3 U/L and s. creatinine stabilized at 5.5 mg/dl, patient being dialysis-independent. This hematological remission persisted at 4th week (Hb 9.1 g/dl, platelet count 163,000/mul) with C3 level being normal. Kidney biopsy was performed at this time. Enlarged glomeruli had capillary wall thickening, with double contours seen on silver Methanamine stain, endothelial swelling and increased mesangial cellularity. Arterioles with onion peel appearance were seen [Figures 1 and 2]. No immune deposit was seen on immunoflorescence study.
At the end of 4 months, he requires two antihypertensive drugs, has Hb 13.5 g/dl, platelet count 229,000/mul, s. creatinine 1.4 mg/dl and poteinuria 1.2 g/day.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presenting with abdominal pain, vomiting, severe oliguria, and extreme pallor 2 weeks after initial treatment for a febrile icteric illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two weeks prior to presentation, the patient was treated at a peripheral hospital for 1 week of fever and jaundice, receiving a 7-day course of artesunate and clindamycin. Although his fever resolved and he was discharged, laboratory abnormalities had not fully normalized. One week post-discharge, he developed persistent vomiting, abdominal pain, and progressive oliguria over 3 days without recurrent fevers, diarrhea, or gross bleeding, prompting referral to a nephrology service.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated with artesunate and clindamycin for 7 days 2 weeks prior for a febrile illness with jaundice, thrombocytopenia, and mild renal impairment. No prior hypertension or renal disease. Denied prior exposure to quinine.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, oliguria, and profound fatigue. Negative for fever, diarrhea, hematuria, hemoptysis, rash, or altered sensorium. Medications: artesunate and clindamycin completed 1 week prior. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure: elevated (hypertensive), afebrile. Marked pallor without peripheral edema or icterus. Cardiovascular: Hemic flow murmur; normal heart sounds. Abdominal, respiratory, and neurological examinations were otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial peripheral hospital labs: Hemoglobin: 8.8 g/dL, platelet count: 55,000/muL, serum creatinine: 1.5 mg/dL, total bilirubin: 3.9 mg/dL (direct bilirubin: 1.9 mg/dL). Readmission labs: Hemoglobin: 4.8 g/dL, platelet count: 61,000/muL, serum creatinine: 8.3 mg/dL. Peripheral blood smear: Presence of schistocytes, reticulocyte count: 13%. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 1,242 U/L (declined to 206.3 U/L post-plasmapheresis). Urinalysis: Microscopic hematuria, proteinuria: 3.75 g/24 hours. Coagulation profile: Normal. Complement levels: Serum C3 low at 50 mg/dL, C4 normal (C3 normalized at 4 weeks). Autoimmune and viral serologies: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA), HIV ELISA, HBsAg, and anti-HCV antibodies all negative. Hematologic recovery at 4 weeks: Hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, platelet count 163,000/muL; at 4 months: Hemoglobin 13.5 g/dL, platelet count 229,000/muL, serum creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, proteinuria 1.2 g/day.
objective.advanced_workup: Percutaneous renal biopsy: Enlarged glomeruli with capillary wall thickening, double contours on silver methenamine stain, endothelial swelling, and increased mesangial cellularity; arterioles demonstrated prominent 'onion-peel' intimal hyperplasia; immunofluorescence negative for immune complex deposits, confirming thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium vivax infection triggering secondary atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA/HUS) with severe acute kidney injury.
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial peripheral smear demonstrated schizonts of Plasmodium vivax; rapid antigen test for Plasmodium falciparum was negative. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and renal TMA were confirmed by peripheral schistocytes, elevated LDH, reticulocytosis, severe azotemia, low C3, and classic histologic features on renal biopsy.
Plan & Outcome: Completed initial antiparasitic therapy with artesunate and clindamycin. TMA and acute renal failure managed with five sessions of 1.5-volume therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) with fresh frozen plasma replacement, packed red blood cell transfusions, temporary intermittent hemodialysis, and antihypertensive therapy. Hematologic remission and dialysis independence were achieved, with creatinine stabilizing to 1.4 mg/dL at 4 months on two antihypertensive agents.

raw_case_text:
A 44-year-old female without past medical history who is healthcare personnel and had close contact with COVID-19 pneumonia patients recognized fever without any other symptoms (day 0). An RT-PCR test was positive on day 2, and she was admitted to our hospital on day 3. On admission, she was symptom-free without any abnormality on physical examination. Her laboratory test results were as follow: WBC 3,600/muL, lymphocyte 1,224/mL, sodium level 136 mmol/L, Ferritin 20 ng/mL, and CRP 0.06 mg/dL. She developed a fever and dry cough on day 5 but had no severe respiratory symptoms such as difficulty in breathing, chest pain, or productive sputum. However, infiltrative shadows were observed in the right upper and left lower area on chest X-ray on day 6, and CT scan showed consolidations in the same areas on day 7. After obtaining consent, we started LPV/r on day 8, but she suffered from gastrointestinal adverse events and discontinued LPV/r on day 11. She had no concurrent medication. Improvement of pneumonia was observed on day 15, and she was discharged after two consecutive negative RT-PCR results. Interestingly, following the improvement of pneumonia without any symptoms or abnormality in blood examinations, RT-PCR remained positive during her follow-up RT-PCR testing.
Patients 1 and 2 developed a fever over 38 C and required oxygen inhalation, but neither were observed throughout the clinical course in Patient 3 (Figures 1-3). Pneumonia developed 8, 12, and 7 days after the onset of illness in Patients 1, 2, and 3, respectively (Figure 4; P1A, P2A, and P3A). After LPV/r was initiated, body temperature decreased, with improvement of cough, lymphopenia, hyponatremia, hyper-ferritinemia, and infiltrative shadows in Patients 1 and 2 (P1B, P2B). This effect was rapid in Patient 1 and gradual in Patient 2. No abnormal laboratory test results except for increased CRP were observed in Patient 3. The duration of treatment with LPV/r was 10, 12, and 3 days for patients 1, 2, and 3, respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old female healthcare worker presenting with a 3-day history of transient fever following occupational exposure to patients with viral pneumonia.

Following positive diagnostic testing on day 2, she was admitted on day 3 asymptomatic. On illness day 5, she developed recurrent fever and a new dry cough, without dyspnea, chest pain, or sputum production.

Chest X-ray (day 6): infiltrative opacities in the right upper and left lower lung zones.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Mild COVID-19 pneumonia, confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on illness day 2. Management & Plan: Antiviral therapy with lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) was initiated on day 8; however, due to gastrointestinal adverse effects, LPV/r was discontinued after 3 days (on day 11). Radiographic and symptomatic pneumonia resolution was confirmed by day 15. The patient achieved full clinical recovery and was discharged following two consecutive negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR tests.

raw_case_text:
An 18-months-old male child presented with history of high-grade fever for 1 month, cough for 15 days and progressive breathlessness of 7 days duration without relief of symptoms by medications prescribed by a local medical practitioner. History of loose stools, vomiting, significant weight loss, and contact with tuberculosis were absent. He belonged to a low socioeconomic class. He was a predominantly breast fed baby, and his mother had been suffering from fever 2 months back, which responded to 10 days of antibiotic therapy.
On examination, it was seen that he was acutely ill, irritable, pale, and febrile (temperature 39  C). His weight was 9.6 kg. (> -2 SD as per WHO growth charts); the heart rate was 130/min; respiratory rate was 60/min with intercostal recession along with diminished air entry on the left side. Liver and spleen were not palpable. Diagnosis of left-sided pleural effusion was made and the same was confirmed on chest x-ray [Figure 1a]. Ultrasonography (USG) and CT further confirmed left-sided pleural effusion. Pleural tap was done and 150 mL of viscid purulent fluid was aspirated.
Cell count of pleural fluid revealed a total of 6800 cells/mm3 (84% polymorphs and 16% lymphocytes) and proteins of 4.6 gm/dL. Intercostal drain (ICD) was placed and intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin was started empirically. Gram stain of pleural fluid revealed Gram negative bacilli. After 48 hrs of incubation, culture growth obtained was subjected to biochemical testes. These tests were suggestive of S. typhi. The organism was further confirmed using serotyping method and the confirmed S. typhi was reported along with antibiogram. Antibiogram showed sensitivity to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, amikacin, ofloxacin, and ciprofloxacin. Ceftriaxone alone was continued. Blood and stool cultures were sterile and Widal test was positive (O titer of 1:120 and H titer of 1:240). Hemoglobin was 8.8 gm% and total leucocyte counts was 20,500 (Polymorphs 78%, Lymphocytes 20%, Eosinophils 2%,). Peripheral smear examination showed normocytic normochromic anemia with reticulocyte count of 2%. Liver function tests, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, iron profile, sickling test, and ultrasound abdomen were normal.
Intercostal drainage tube was removed after 5 days when no drainage was seen from the tube. However, even after 10 days of antibiotic therapy fever was persisting and x-ray chest was still hazy; therefore, a CT thorax was done that revealed loculated pus in the left pleural cavity [Figure 1b]. Based on pleural fluid culture sensitivity report, ofloxacin was added to the treatment. After 6 days of further treatment, the patient became afebrile and chest X-ray improved markedly with a total of fourteen days of ofloxacin therapy [Figure 2]. Repeat USG revealed minimal pleural effusion less than 30 cc. ELISA for HIV of both child and mother were negative and immunoglobulin profile (IgG, IgA, and IgM) of the child were normal. Echocardiography done to rule out pericardial involvement was normal. The patient was doing well during a year's follow up. To find out the source of infection in this child we investigated his mother, and performed cultures of her blood, urine, stool, and breast milk. Mother's stool culture was positive for S. typhi, and other cultures were sterile. A course of amoxicillin was prescribed for treatment of her carrier status and repeat stool culture after a month of follow up was sterile.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-month-old male infant presented with high-grade fever for 1 month, cough for 15 days, and progressive breathlessness for 7 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 1 month prior to admission with high-grade fever, followed by cough for 15 days and progressive breathlessness for 7 days, refractory to medications prescribed by an outpatient practitioner. Predominantly breastfed; mother had experienced a febrile illness 2 months prior that resolved with 10 days of antibiotics. No history of loose stools, vomiting, significant weight loss, or known contact with tuberculosis.

subjective.review_of_systems: Cough and progressive breathlessness. Denies diarrhea, vomiting, and significant weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Acutely ill, irritable, pale, and febrile with body temperature 39 °C. Weight 9.6 kg (> -2 SD for age on WHO growth charts). Heart rate 130 bpm, respiratory rate 60 bpm with intercostal retractions and diminished air entry over the left hemithorax. Abdominal exam showed non-palpable liver and spleen.
objective.routine_investigations: Body temperature 39 °C, HR 130 bpm, RR 60 bpm. Hemoglobin 8.8 gm%, total leukocyte count 20,500/cu.mm (neutrophils 78%, lymphocytes 20%, eosinophils 2%), reticulocyte count 2% (normocytic normochromic anemia). Liver function tests, renal function tests, serum electrolytes, iron profile, and sickling test were normal. Baseline chest X-ray revealed left-sided pleural effusion, with persistent haziness at day 10. Abdominal ultrasound was normal. Transthoracic echocardiogram was normal, ruling out pericardial involvement. Maternal and infant HIV ELISA were negative; infant immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM) were normal. Blood and stool cultures were sterile.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic ultrasonography and CT confirmed left-sided pleural effusion; repeat CT thorax on hospital day 10 showed loculated pus in the left pleural cavity. Thoracentesis yielded 150 mL of viscid purulent fluid. Pleural fluid analysis: total cell count 6800 cells/mm3 (84% polymorphs, 16% lymphocytes), protein 4.6 gm/dL. Gram stain of pleural fluid demonstrated Gram-negative bacilli. Antibiogram of the isolate showed susceptibility to ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, amikacin, ofloxacin, and ciprofloxacin.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi empyema thoracis / purulent pleurisy, confirmed by biochemical testing and serotyping of pleural fluid culture growth after 48 hours of incubation; supported by positive Widal test (O titer 1:120, H titer 1:240). Blood and stool cultures were sterile. Maternal investigation identified maternal chronic carrier state as the epidemiological source, with mother's stool culture positive for S. typhi (maternal blood, urine, and breast milk sterile). Tuberculosis, HIV, primary humoral immunodeficiency, and pericarditis were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Left intercostal drainage tube was inserted (draining 150 mL purulent fluid, removed after 5 days) and empirical IV ceftriaxone plus vancomycin was initiated, transitioning to ceftriaxone monotherapy. Due to persistent fever and CT evidence of loculated empyema on day 10, oral ofloxacin was added based on pleural culture antibiogram. Fever resolved after 6 days of dual therapy, with complete radiographic resolution achieved following a 14-day total course of ofloxacin (repeat ultrasound showed minimal residual effusion <30 cc). The mother was treated with oral amoxicillin, resulting in documented negative follow-up stool culture at 1 month. The patient remained healthy at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Congenital brucellosis was diagnosed in patients 1 and 2, who were 3-month-old twins (Technical Appendix Table). They were prematurely delivered by cesarean section on July 6, 2012, at the Provincial Maternity and Child Care Center (Guangzhou, China). The boy (patient 1, Apgar score 9-10/1-10 min) had a birthweight of 2.3 kg, and the girl (patient 2, Apgar score 9-10/1-10 min) had a birthweight of 1.8 kg. They received standard care for preterm neonates at the hospital. They were discharged once their weight reached 2.5 kg; this happened for patient 1 at 3 weeks of age and for patient 2 at 4 weeks of age (July 29 and August 3, 2012, respectively).
On October 2, 2012, the boy was examined at the hospital for irregular fever up to 39 C. On October 9, he was readmitted to the hospital with a fever of 38 C and weight of 5.0 kg. Chest radiograph showed signs of increased bronchovascular shadows. Mezlocillin sodium and sulbactam sodium (4:1) and ribavirin were administered, but the patient did not improve. On the same day, the girl had a cough and low-level fever (37-37.5 C) but was not hospitalized. On October 16, B. melitensis was isolated from a blood culture from patient 1, in whom brucellosis with alveobronchiolitis, abnormal hepatic function, and moderate anemia were initially diagnosed when he was 3 months and 10 days of age.
On October 17, the twins were transferred to an infectious disease hospital, where they had extensive physical and laboratory examinations (Table 1). During 57 days of hospitalization, the boy received general and specific therapies for brucellosis. Brucellosis and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency were diagnosed in the girl, and she received appropriate treatment. At the time of discharge (December 12), the twins were well and without fever. They left the hospital for home care, which was supervised by a local general practitioner who provided rifampin and sulfamethoxazole for up to 6 weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: Three-month-old premature twins presented with irregular fever up to 39 °C, low-grade fever (37-37.5 °C), and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The twins were delivered prematurely by cesarean section on July 6, 2012, and discharged after reaching 2.5 kg weight. On October 2, 2012, the male twin developed irregular fever up to 39 °C and was readmitted on October 9 with fever of 38 °C and respiratory distress unresponsive to mezlocillin/sulbactam and ribavirin. Concurrently, the female twin developed cough and low-grade fever (37-37.5 °C). On October 17, both infants were transferred to an infectious disease hospital for specialized evaluation and care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Premature delivery via cesarean section at 34 weeks and 2 days' gestation. Birth weights: 2.3 kg (twin 1, boy) and 1.8 kg (twin 2, girl); Apgar scores 9-10 at 1 and 10 minutes. Preterm neonatal care received until discharge at 3 weeks (boy) and 4 weeks (girl) of age upon reaching 2.5 kg. No known direct animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Cough and low-grade fever in twin 2; irritability, fever, and respiratory symptoms in twin 1. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Twin 1 (boy): temperature 38-39 °C, body weight 5.0 kg; signs of respiratory distress. Twin 2 (girl): temperature 37-37.5 °C, cough. Other detailed physical findings not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Twin 1: Chest radiograph showed increased bronchovascular shadows consistent with alveobronchiolitis; laboratory tests showed abnormal hepatic function and moderate anemia. Twin 2: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency identified.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Congenital brucellosis due to Brucella melitensis in twin infants, complicated by alveobronchiolitis, hepatic dysfunction, and moderate anemia in the male twin, and coexisting glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency in the female twin.
Confirmation: Blood culture in twin 1 isolated Brucella melitensis on October 16.
Treatment & Outcome: Initial empiric therapy with mezlocillin/sulbactam (4:1) and ribavirin failed. Following diagnosis, both twins received targeted anti-brucellosis therapy during a 57-day hospitalization, followed by outpatient oral rifampin and sulfamethoxazole for up to 6 weeks. At discharge, both infants were afebrile, clinically well, and had fully recovered.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old male known HIV-positive patient on antiretroviral therapy (TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg + EFV 600 mg) for the last 3 years was referred from Gidda Ayana District Hospital on May 26, 2021 to Wollega University referral hospital. Upon arrival to the emergency department, he complained of shortness of breath of five days' duration, which began suddenly, and became more and more persistent, associated with productive cough, high-grade fever, malaise, and severe headache. In addition, he had a loss of appetite, weight loss, chest pain, night sweats, and fatigue. Moreover, he had a history of bloody sputum one month prior to the current complaint. He has tolerated well but had poor adherence to his ART medication and had no previous history of alcohol consumption and other illicit drugs. He has reported receiving cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for three years, but often missed some doses. His current CD4 count was 266 cells/mm3, and HIV-1 RNA level was 9000 copies/mL.
Upon physical examination at presentation, the patient looked acutely sick, and blood pressure was measured at 110/60 mmHg, a body temperature of 39.3 C, and pulse rate of 112 beats per minute, classed as tachycardia. His respiratory rate was 38/minute, and his oxygen saturation was 87% on room air. His breathing was shallow, rapid, and used respiratory accessory muscles. There was dullness over the left lower lobe. Breathing sounds were vesicular on the right side but markedly reduced at the base. There was coarse crepitation over the left upper and lower lobes. He was conscious and oriented. Immediately the patient was admitted as a medical emergency and put on intranasal oxygen.
Necessary laboratory investigations were performed. Accordingly, random blood sugar was 110 mg/dL, complete blood count with differential revealed only leukocytosis (15.2 x 103/L) with lymphocyte predominance, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 86 mm/hour; blood film (BF) showed no hemoparasite, serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, and liver function test showed no abnormal value. Chest X-ray showed perihilar patchy opacities (Figure 1).
Gene Expert test was done from sputum and was positive for TB (no rifampin resistance), and nasopharyngeal sample for SARS CoV-2 PCR was positive. On his 2nd day of admission, he was transferred to a COVID-19 dedicated treatment center located in the same hospital with the diagnosis of severe COVID-19, pulmonary TB, and WHO stage-3 RVI.
During his stay, oxygen supplementation for an SpO2 target >=92-96% was provided with 6-10 L O2 via a nasal cannula. Conservative IV fluid management with empiric antimicrobials for possible bacterial infection was started with cefepime 2 g IV TID for 3 days then changed to an oral antibiotic. In addition, dexamethasone 6 mg once per day IV was given with close monitoring of vital signs, work of breathing, and mental status. Anti-TB drugs were initiated with RHZE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) at the intensive phase on the 3rd day of admission. Highly active antiretroviral therapy was continued with the same regimen he was taking before presentation to the hospital.
On his 6th day of admission, the patient became afebrile and started to maintain his oxygen saturation >94% with room air. The patient's general condition also improved. Follow-up RT-PCR test for COVID-19 was done, and the results were negative. On June 6, 2021 the patient was discharged from hospital after 10 days of hospital stay, and a follow-up appointment at the ART and TB clinic within two weeks was given.

He also reported an episode of hemoptysis one month prior. On presentation, he was in severe respiratory distress with profound hypoxemia requiring immediate supplemental oxygen.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV-1 infection on antiretroviral therapy (TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg + EFV 600 mg) for 3 years with reported poor adherence (CD4 count 266 cells/mm3, HIV-1 RNA 9,000 copies/mL); no history of alcohol or illicit drug use. Epidemiological history: Residence in an endemic region for tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) 300 mg, emtricitabine (FTC) 200 mg, efavirenz (EFV) 600 mg daily, and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis (with missed doses). Allergies: None reported.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Temperature 39.3 °C, pulse rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 110/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 87% on room air. General appearance: Acutely sick, shallow rapid breathing with accessory muscle use; conscious and oriented. Chest examination: Dullness to percussion over the left lower lobe, vesicular breath sounds on the right with markedly reduced basal breath sounds, and coarse crepitations over the left upper and lower lobes.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Random blood glucose 110 mg/dL, white blood cell count 15.2 x 10^3/microL with lymphocyte predominance, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 86 mm/hour, peripheral blood film negative for hemoparasites, serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and normal liver function tests. Chest radiograph: Perihilar patchy opacities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe SARS-CoV-2 infection (severe COVID-19 pneumonia) confirmed by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR, co-existing with active pulmonary tuberculosis (confirmed by sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF without rifampin resistance) and poorly adherent HIV-1 infection (WHO Stage 3).
Plan & Outcome: Managed with oxygen therapy (6-10 L/min via nasal cannula targeting SpO2 92-96%), IV dexamethasone (6 mg once daily), empiric IV cefepime (2 g TID for 3 days) stepped down to oral antibiotic, continuation of antiretroviral therapy (TDF/FTC/EFV), and initiation of intensive anti-tuberculosis therapy (RHZE: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) on hospital day 3. The patient became afebrile on day 6 with SpO2 > 94% on room air, achieved viral clearance with negative repeat SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR, and was discharged on hospital day 10 with scheduled ART and TB clinic follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 39-year-old Nigerian woman with history of sickle cell disease presented to our hospital with a chief complaint of increased swelling on her left flank for the past 2 years. She initially noticed the swelling "many years ago" as a 1 cm soft, painless mass. Over the years, the swelling progressively increased to the current size of approximately 10 cm on presentation. She reported no warmth, redness, or drainage of pus or fluid. Six months prior to presentation, the patient began experiencing a dull pain in the midline of her lower back, radiating laterally to the left lower quadrant. It fluctuated in severity but was aggravated with flexion of the back. She reported no recent fevers, fatigue, changes in weight, chills, sweats, hemoptysis, or dyspnea. She did not have any urinary or gastrointestinal symptoms nor did she experience weakness or sensory loss in her lower limbs. The patient immigrated to the United States from Nigeria one year ago. She has no known history of or exposure to TB but did receive the BCG vaccine as a child.
On examination, she was a well appearing young female. Vital signs included BP 118/60 mmHg, HR 66/min, temperature 98.8 F, O2 saturation 97% on room air, and BMI 20.3. She was noted to have icteric sclera and multiple enlarged, nontender, soft, mobile cervical lymph nodes (LNs), the largest being a 2 cm right anterior cervical LN. Inspection of her back revealed a 10 cm x 16 cm well-demarcated fluctuant area without erythema or other skin changes. The area was not tender to palpation, nor were there any areas of focal tenderness at the spine. Range of motion of her back and hips was fully intact. The remainder of the examination including cardiopulmonary, abdominal, and neurologic examination was unremarkable.
Review of her lab tests revealed hemoglobin of 94 g/L, MCV 92.5 fl, RDW 21.7%, reticulocyte count 0.08 of RBCs, leukocyte count 7.4 x 103/muL, and platelet count 317 x 103/muL. Other lab tests included blood urea nitrogen 2.86 mmol/L, serum creatinine 45 mumol/L, AST 65 U/L, ALT 29 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 19 U/L, total bilirubin of 148.8 mumol/L with indirect bilirubin 131.7 mumol/L, LDH 525 U/L, and ESR 28 mm/hr. Rapid HIV testing was negative. Blood cultures drawn at initial evaluation remained sterile after 48 hours.
A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed diskitis/osteomyelitis at the L4-L5 level with adjacent paraspinal and left retroperitoneal abscesses extending to the left lower back/flank subcutaneous tissue and into the epidural space. A follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine with and without contrast confirmed these findings of diskitis and osteomyelitis at L4-L5 with an expansile abscess within substance of the disk extending into ventral epidural space with involvement of left L5-S1 and right L4-L5 neural foramina (Figures 1 and 2).
Ultrasound guided drainage of the abscess was attempted but only a small amount of thick tan fluid could be collected as the contents were extremely viscous. Fluid analysis showed glucose <10 mg/dL, protein 5 g/dL, and LDH 4872 U/L. Cell count was unable to be performed due to the fluid's viscosity but differential showed 82% neutrophils. Gram stain and acid-fast staining were negative for any organisms.
Given her history and presentation, a tuberculous cold abscess was high on our differential and the patient was empirically started on the standard anti-TB regimen of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. Though she had no neurological symptoms, given the extension of the abscess, both orthopedic and neurosurgery specialists were consulted for surgical drainage of abscess. The patient and neurosurgeons were initially reluctant to perform the procedure and she was therefore discharged on anti-TB medications and pyridoxine.
Upon follow-up at a local TB clinic, she complained of right upper quadrant pain and was found to have elevated transaminases. All of her medications were stopped and a week later she was restarted on rifampin and ethambutol. Four weeks from presentation, cultures from drained abscess revealed Mycobacterium tuberculosis. At this time, the patient was reevaluated by neurosurgery and underwent paraspinal abscess drainage through paravertebral muscles. Following the procedure, she was briefly treated with moxifloxacin as per instructions from the regional TB clinic. At her last clinic visit, six months into her treatment course, she was on isoniazid, rifampin, and pyridoxine without any complaints.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 39-year-old female presented with progressive enlargement of a left flank swelling for 2 years and lower back pain radiating to the left lower quadrant for 6 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 39-year-old female noticed a soft, painless 1 cm mass on her left flank many years ago that progressively increased in size, becoming noticeably larger over the past 2 years to a diameter of 10 cm. Six months prior to presentation, she developed dull lower back pain radiating laterally to the left lower quadrant, fluctuating in intensity and aggravated by spinal flexion. She denied fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis, dyspnea, gastrointestinal/urinary symptoms, or neurologic deficits.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle cell disease. Immigrated to the United States from Nigeria 1 year prior. Childhood BCG vaccination. No known personal history of or exposure to tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dull lower back pain radiating to left lower quadrant, aggravated by spinal flexion. Negative for fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue, weight changes, hemoptysis, dyspnea, bowel/bladder dysfunction, lower extremity weakness, or numbness. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Well-appearing female. BP 118/60 mmHg, HR 66/min, T 98.8 °F, SpO2 97% on room air, BMI 20.3 kg/m2. Scleral icterus. Multiple enlarged, nontender, soft, mobile cervical lymph nodes (largest 2 cm right anterior cervical). Back: 10 cm x 16 cm well-demarcated, fluctuant mass on left flank without erythema, warmth, drainage, or tenderness; no focal spinal tenderness. Full range of motion of back and hips. Neurological, cardiopulmonary, and abdominal exams unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 94 g/L, MCV 92.5 fL, RDW 21.7%, reticulocyte count 0.08 of RBCs, leukocyte count 7.4 x 103/muL, platelet count 317 x 103/muL. BUN 2.86 mmol/L, serum creatinine 45 mumol/L, AST 65 U/L, ALT 29 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 19 U/L, total bilirubin 148.8 mumol/L (indirect bilirubin 131.7 mumol/L), LDH 525 U/L, ESR 28 mm/hr. Rapid HIV test negative. Blood cultures sterile at 48 hours.
objective.advanced_workup: CT abdomen/pelvis: L4-L5 diskitis and osteomyelitis with paraspinal and left retroperitoneal abscesses extending into left flank subcutaneous tissue and epidural space. MRI lumbar spine: expansile abscess within L4-L5 intervertebral disc extending into ventral epidural space and involving left L5-S1 and right L4-L5 neural foramina. Ultrasound-guided aspiration of abscess yielded viscous tan fluid (glucose <10 mg/dL, protein 5 g/dL, LDH 4872 U/L, 82% neutrophils); Gram stain and acid-fast stain were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott's disease) of L4-L5 with retroperitoneal, epidural, and subcutaneous cold abscess of the left flank, confirmed by fluid cultures from the drained abscess yielding Mycobacterium tuberculosis at 4 weeks. Management & Outcome: Started empirically on 4-drug therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) plus pyridoxine. Course was complicated by drug-induced transaminitis, necessitating temporary drug cessation and sequential reintroduction with rifampin, ethambutol, and brief moxifloxacin. Following microbiological confirmation, she underwent surgical drainage of the paraspinal abscess via a paravertebral approach. Maintained on isoniazid, rifampin, and pyridoxine at 6-month follow-up with complete symptom resolution and normalization of liver enzymes.

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old male with no significant past medical history presented to Shanxi Bethune Hospital with a 10-day history of dizziness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and joint pain, accompanied by a fever for the past 5 days, with a body temperature peaking at 40 C.
Body temperature was 38.6 C, a respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min, a pulse rate of 88 beats/min, and jaundice of the skin and conjunctival. Tenderness was noted in the right upper abdomen without rebound tenderness or muscle tension. The liver and spleen were not palpable, Murphy's sign was positive, and there was percussion pain over the liver. Bowel sounds were heard at a rate of 3 times/min.
Aspartate transaminase 778.7 IU/L (15-40 IU/L), alanine transaminase 371.6 IU/L (9-50 IU/L), total bilirubin 96.7 mumol/L (<=26 mumol/L), direct bilirubin 61.2 mumol/L (<=4 mumol/L; Figure 1(a) and (b)), gamma-glutamyl transferase 191.7 IU/L (10-60 IU/L), and ALP 351.8 IU/L (45-125 IU/L). Blood work revealed white blood cell (WBC) count 2.7 x 109/L (3.50-9.50 x 109/L), red blood cell count 4.3 x 1012/L (4.50-5.80 x 1012/L), and PLT count 45 x 109/L (125-350 x 109/L; Figure 1(c-e)). Trends in the laboratory test indicators during the patient's hospitalization can be observed in Figure 1.
The patient received symptomatic treatment, including fasting, fluid infusion, acid suppression, anti-inflammatory medication, liver protection measures, and albumin infusion. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed edema of the gallbladder wall and disappearance of intrahepatic bile ducts (Figure 2). Based on the patient's clinical presentation of abdominal pain and jaundice, along with elevated transaminases and ALP levels, a preliminary diagnosis of probable VBDS was made. However, the patient's blood routine examination showed a decrease in WBC count, red blood cell count, and PLT count, which is unusual for VBDS. Therefore, we began considering the possibility of other underlying diseases in the patient.
The patient underwent an extensive diagnostic workup, including blood culture (to exclude severe infection), the antinuclear antibody spectrum (to exclude autoimmune disease), all of which showed normal results. Fine-needle aspiration of cervical lymph nodes, along with immunohistochemical analysis, suggests reactive lymphoid hyperplasia (Table 1). Additional investigations for infectious etiologies such as EBV, hepatitis A, B, C, and E, HIV, and syphilis all returned negative results (Table 2).
Further examination revealed abnormal levels of fibrinogen 1.26 g/L (2.38-4.98 g/L), triglycerides 2.87 mmol/L (<=1.7 mmol/L), soluble IL-2 receptor alpha chain (sCD25) 938.93 U/ml (92-402 U/ml), NK cell activity 1.33% (47.6%-76.8%), and ferritin>15000 ng/ml (23.9-336.2 ng/ml). On July 18, a bone marrow biopsy revealed the presence of haemophilus cells (Figure 3), meeting criteria (1), (3), (4), (5), (6), and (8)of the updated HPS-2004 criteria. Confirming the diagnosis of HPS as the underlying cause of the probable VBDS. The patient was subsequently treated with the Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)-2004 protocol, consisting of Dexamethasone (17 mg/day) and Etoposide (250 mg/day),   The treatment effect was satisfactory, with improvements in fever, nausea, vomiting, and joint pain. By July 24, the patient's condition gradually stabilized. After taking the medication for 2 months, the patient reported no abnormalities and discontinued treatment. To determine the etiology of HPS, Further testing for infectious indicators such as kala-azar and brucellosis was conducted. The brucellosis antibody panel test, tube agglutination test, and tiger red plate agglutination test were performed on July 22, 2022, at Jin Yu Clinical Laboratory in Taiyuan city. The results showed positive Brucella immunoglobulin G (IgG ) antibodies, positive Brucella agglutination test (1:200 ++), and positive Brucella tiger red plate agglutination test (+) (Table 3). Combined with the patient's clinical symptoms, this confirms the diagnosis of Brucella infection. Symptomatic treatment medications include rifampicin capsules, doxycycline hydrochloride capsules, compound sulfamethoxazole tablets, bicyclol tablets, and prednisone acetate tablets. The patient achieved recovery after 8 weeks. Through further inquiry into the medical history, it was discovered that the patient had a history of contact with sheep. Therefore, the truth finally surfaced that the patient was eventually diagnosed with Brucella infection-induced HPS, which subsequently led to the development of probable VBDS.
He followed up as an outpatient, which normalized after completing anti-brucellosis and HLH-2004 therapy.
This case was attributed to Brucella infection, which resulted in HPS, subsequently leading to probable VBDS due to sustained damage to the biliary system. In the early stages of the disease, the clinical symptoms such as high fever, chills, abnormal liver function, and jaundice are similar to clinical symptoms of VBDS. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed severe edema of the gallbladder wall and disappearance of the intrahepatic bile ducts, which are typical features of VBDS (Figure 2). Although liver biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing VBDS, the underlying cause of the patient's condition has not been identified at present. Considering the patient's compromised liver and coagulation function, performing a liver biopsy to confirm VBDS could easily lead to massive bleeding and endanger the patient's life. Therefore, we can only highly consider it as VBDS and diagnose it as probable VBDS. Historically, our understanding of this disease has been limited, and invasive procedures have often resulted in uncontrolled bleeding and ultimately patient mortality. For example, Gao   reported a case of a patient admitted with the initial diagnosis of acute cholecystitis characterized by "gallbladder edema with significant wall thickening and intrahepatic bile duct disappearance," without fully considering HPS or VBDS. An emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed, but the patient's condition did not improve after surgery and even worsened. The postoperative pathological diagnosis confirmed gallbladder non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, and the patient eventually died. The MRCP imaging data presented in Gao's report the gallbladder edema observed in this case showed remarkable similarities, both demonstrating abnormal gallbladder edema and bile duct disappearance. Therefore, when we encountering patients with similar imaging presentations, it is crucial to remain vigilant regarding the possibility of HPS. Any invasive procedure at this stage could potentially result in patient death. Thus, it is essential to actively investigate the underlying cause and develop an appropriate treatment plan. In this case, as the disease progressed, the patient experienced a gradual decline in red blood cells, WBCs, and PLTs, along with increased ferritin levels, decreased NK cell activity, and elevated triglycerides. These findings met the criteria (1), (3), (4), (5), (6), and (8) of the updated HPS-2004 criteria. The bone marrow biopsy indicated the presence of haemophilus cells. At this point, confirming the diagnosis of HPS. Further investigations were conducted to determine the cause of HPS, including kala-azar, Brucella, ultimately leading to a diagnosis of brucellosis. In this case, the clinical manifestations of brucellosis, HPS, acute cholangitis, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, and VBDS overlap, posing challenges in terms of diagnosis and differential diagnosis for clinicians. If we make a single diagnosis to any these diseases, it may delay the condition, affect the prognosis, or even lead to death.
Therefore, early identification of the disease and the formulation of an appropriate treatment plan are crucial for ensuring a favorable prognosis. In this case, the absence of specific initial symptoms related to Brucella infection posed challenges for clinicians in establishing a connection between VBDS and brucellosis. Consequently, achieving an accurate diagnosis after admission assumes paramount importance.
We collected a series of case reports associated with Brucella infections and summarized them in (Table 4). These reports highlight that Human brucellosis remains the most prevalent zoonotic disease worldwide, affecting numerous countries and a wide range of age groups, including newborns, young adults, and elderly patients. The primary mode of transmission is through the consumption of unpasteurized milk from infected animals.   Transmission through placenta, breast milk, and sexual contact is extremely rare.   In our case report, upon further inquiry into the patient's medical history, a history of contact with sheep was identified. This literature review encompasses 10 case reports, where 10% of brucellosis cases presented with HPS as the initial symptom and 20% presented with liver failure as the initial symptom. Other initial symptoms included undulating fever, liver abscess, and cirrhosis, with varying manifestations. Consequently, the early and accurate diagnosis of brucellosis assumes significant importance. In clinical practice, when a patient presents with admission symptoms such as jaundice, dizziness, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting, along with abdominal pain and cholecystitis upon physical examination, and an MRI reveals notable gallbladder edema and bile duct disappearance, it is crucial to consider various factors, including the possibility of HPS. Simultaneously, it is imperative to differentiate HPS from surgical conditions like gallstones and acute cholangitis, and refrain from premature surgical intervention until a confirmed diagnosis is established.
