At 1-week postoperative follow-up: Trace swelling of right upper eyelid, mild inflammation-induced ptosis, and scabbing; normal visual acuity.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic incisional biopsy: Recurrent mucinous carcinoma. Surgical wide local excision specimen (15 mm x 10 mm pentagonal wedge with staged peripheral and deep margins totaling 7.5 mm): Dermal-based tumor cells arranged in clusters within pools of extracellular mucin, immunoreactive for Cytokeratin 7 and GCDFP-15, and negative for Cytokeratin 5/6 and p63; confirmed negative resection margins medially, temporally, superiorly, and deep.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Recurrent primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC) of the right upper eyelid and lateral canthus in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, hypertension, and bilateral senile nuclear cataract.
Surgical Treatment & Outcome: Managed with modified wide local excision utilizing pentagonal full-thickness lid resection and staged margin procurement (2.5 mm and 5.0 mm incremental margins achieving > 7.5 mm clear margins), lateral canthotomy, tarsal reapproximation with 6-0 Vicryl, and skin closure with 6-0 plain gut. Histopathology confirmed complete tumor eradication with clear surgical margins. At 6-month follow-up, the patient had complete cosmetic and functional preservation without evidence of local recurrence.

raw_case_text: The patient was a 75-year-old man patient with a medical history of atrial fibrillation taking warfarin. Fever and impaired consciousness were noted in mid-March 2020, and the patient was transferred to our hospital as an emergency. COVID-19 pneumonia was suspected due to a history of close contact with spouse who had COVID-19, increased fever and respiratory rate, decreased permeability of the right whole lung field on chest X-ray, and accumulation of pleural effusion. He was urgently admitted via the emergency department. A positive polymerase chain reaction test result for COVID-19 was confirmed, and a definitive diagnosis of COVID-19 pneumonia was made. After admission, an oral combination of lopinavir/ritonavir (800 mg/200 mg/ day, twice daily) was administered, and ciclesonide (800 microg/day, twice daily) was inhaled for 7 days. On the 7th day of hospitalization, aspiration pneumonia was observed. On the 14th day of hospitalization, white plaque began to appear in the oral cavity. At the first visit to our department on the 14th day, white plaque was found on both buccal mucosa and the back of the tongue, but there was no oral pain or dysgeusia. Candida albicans was identified by oral bacterial tests (oral swab culture), and a diagnosis of oral candidiasis was made. No fungi such as C. albicans were identified in blood cultures and sputum cultures. An intraoral examination revealed multiple pseudomembranous structures with white plaque on both buccal mucosa and tongue (Figure 1). The white plaque was easily wiped with gauze and exhibited an erythematous mucosa, suggesting oral candidiasis. Oral administration of syrup containing amphotericin B (400 mg /day) was initiated 4 times per day, and negative result for C. albicans was confirmed on the 35th hospital day. The mucosal surface of the oral cavity was also normalized (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old male presenting with fever and impaired consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever and altered mental status in mid-March 2020. Upon emergency transfer, he was noted to have high fever, tachypnea, and radiological abnormalities concerning for viral pneumonia. During hospitalization, he developed aspiration pneumonia on day 7, followed by the appearance of asymptomatic white oral mucosal plaques on hospital day 14.
subjective.past_medical_history: Atrial fibrillation. Epidemiological exposure: Close contact with his spouse who was diagnosed with viral respiratory illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: Warfarin. Allergies: None reported.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Pyrexia, tachypnea, and impaired level of consciousness. Oral cavity examination (hospital day 14): Multiple pseudomembranous white plaques on bilateral buccal mucosa and the dorsal tongue, which were non-tender and easily wiped away with gauze revealing an underlying erythematous mucosal base.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission chest X-ray: Decreased radiopermeability across the entire right lung field with accumulation of pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia) confirmed by RT-PCR, complicated by aspiration pneumonia and secondary pseudomembranous oral candidiasis (oral swab culture positive for Candida albicans). Sputum and blood cultures were negative for fungi.
Plan & Outcome: For COVID-19 pneumonia: Treated with oral lopinavir/ritonavir (800 mg/200 mg daily in divided doses) and inhaled ciclesonide (800 microg daily in divided doses) for 7 days. For oral candidiasis: Initiated on oral amphotericin B syrup (400 mg/day divided 4 times daily). Achieved complete clinical resolution of oral plaques with negative follow-up oral swab fungal cultures on hospital day 35.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old Italian man, who had been living in Nigeria because of his job since two years, was urgently repatriated following diagnosis of acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Fourteen days after anti-malarial treatment started, with quick resolution of fever, he suddenly complained of acute left flank pain.
At emergency department (ED) admission, his vital parameters appeared stable. Physical examination revealed tender left hemiabdomen without frank peritonism. Laboratory tests disclosed severe anemia (hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL), moderate leukocytosis, markedly elevated C-Reactive Protein (232 mg/L), plasma D-Dimer (2188 ug/L), lactic dehydrogenase (654 IU/L) and creatine kinase (1255 IU/L); platelet count and coagulation assays were within normal limits. Rapid blood assay tested positive for P. falciparum antigen, with negative blood cultures for bacteria and parasites.
Prompt investigation with multi-detector CT [Figure 1] allowed confident diagnosis of diffuse, moderately hyperdense peritoneal effusion consistent with hemoperitoneum and splenomegaly with hyperdense, stratified subcapsular and perisplenic clotted hematoma. Bilateral pleural effusion and lung base atelectasis were also present.
Urgent laparotomic surgery confirmed abundant hemorrhagic peritoneal effusion without detectable active bleeding. Splenomegaly with multiple blood clots was resected. Pathology specimen reported 850-g enlarged spleen measuring 17x14x8 cm after fixation, with large capsular interruption and underlying hematoma. Histologically, diffuse parenchymal hemorrhage and markedly hypertrophic red pulp were observed, without follicular structure abnormalities nor signs of malignancy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with sudden-onset acute left flank pain 14 days after starting treatment for a severe febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 42-year-old male who had resided in Nigeria for two years was urgently repatriated following diagnosis and treatment of an acute febrile tropical illness, with rapid defervescence. Fourteen days after starting antimalarial therapy, while convalescing, he experienced sudden-onset, severe left flank pain, prompting immediate emergency department evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Italian expatriate living in Nigeria for two years. Recently treated for acute tropical infection with antimalarials. No history of abdominal trauma, coagulopathy, hematologic disorder, or splenic disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for sudden acute left flank and left abdominal pain. Negative for recurrent fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, hematuria, or syncope. Medications: completed antimalarial regimen. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs stable on presentation. Abdomen: localized tenderness over left hemiabdomen, but without frank peritonitis, guarding, or rigidity. No palpable masses.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: severe anemia with hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; moderate leukocytosis; platelet count normal. Biochemistry: markedly elevated C-reactive protein (232 mg/L), plasma D-dimer (2,188 ug/L), lactate dehydrogenase (654 IU/L), and creatine kinase (1,255 IU/L). Coagulation assays: within normal limits. Blood cultures: sterile for bacteria and fungi. Peripheral blood smears performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Multidetector computed tomography (CT) of abdomen: diffuse, moderately hyperdense peritoneal fluid consistent with hemoperitoneum, marked splenomegaly with hyperdense stratified subcapsular and perisplenic hematoma, bilateral pleural effusions, and basal atelectasis. Urgent exploratory laparotomy: evacuation of abundant hemorrhagic peritoneal fluid and total splenectomy. Pathology: 850-g ruptured spleen measuring 17x14x8 cm with large capsular laceration, underlying hematoma, diffuse parenchymal hemorrhage, and marked red pulp hyperplasia without malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Spontaneous (non-traumatic) splenic rupture with acute hemoperitoneum complicating convalescent Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
Diagnostic confirmation: Rapid blood assay positive for Plasmodium falciparum antigen; multidetector CT identifying hemoperitoneum and subcapsular splenic hematoma; emergency laparotomy and surgical pathology confirming an 850 g ruptured spleen with red pulp hyperplasia and subcapsular hematoma. Bacterial blood cultures were negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with emergency exploratory laparotomy, evacuation of hemoperitoneum, and total splenectomy. The patient made an uneventful postoperative recovery with stabilization of hemoglobin and was discharged in good condition.

raw_case_text:
An 18-year old male from Myanmar was brought to the emergency department because of difficulty in swallowing and alteration of consciousness. He had been in good health and had arrived Bangkok 6 days earlier. Three days prior to admission, he developed fever and difficulty in swallowing. He also had pruritus of his right leg and buttock which resulted in extensive excoriation. He had became intermittently confused and refused to eat or drink. There were episodes of agitation and he was reported to have complained of shortness of breath incited by fanning.
One day prior to entry, he was unable to swallow his saliva. His mental status alternated between normal periods and confusion. He gave a history of dog bite 10 years previously but no post exposure vaccination was administered and he denied any recent animal bites or contact with bats.
On admission, he was conscious and well co-operative. He complained of a severely sore throat. He insisted on sitting and continuously spitting out saliva. His body temperature was 39.1 C, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 120 and respiration 30 per minute. There was crepitus on the left side of his neck without signs of inflammation. There were no focal neurological signs. His palatopharyngeal muscle functions were intact but the gag reflex was hyperactive. Aero- and hydrophobic spasms could not be induced. Indirect laryngoscopic examination showed no abnormality. Laboratory studies revealed a leucocytosis of 28,400 with 89.6% of neutrophils. His serum amylase level was slightly elevated (443 U/L, normal range 28-100 U/L). The computerized tomography (CT) scan of the brain was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed an acellular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and normal protein and sugar levels. Lateral neck radiographs showed air in retropharyngeal space (Figure 1) and a chest x-ray performed at the same time showed evidence of pneumomediastinum (Figure 2). A liquid barium esophagogram failed to show any point of leakage. Surgical consultation was obtained for exploration. Between admission and operation, his mental state was clear and he showed no signs of aggression and the differential diagnosis of possible rabies was disregarded.
Operative findings were unremarkable. There was no evidence of perforation in upper esophagus and oropharynx. Retropharyngeal area was normal without any accumulation of fluid or purulent discharge.
He required assisted ventilation postoperatively but was able to move limbs voluntarily. He remained rational and cooperative. His hypernatremia (Na 157 mOsm/L) was rapidly corrected to140 mOsm/L within the following 11 hours. On the second postoperative day, he developed brief generalized tonic- clonic seizures. Intravenous phenytoin was initiated. Serial seizures developed on day 6. Repeated lumbar puncture and CT scan were unremarkable. He was conscious but failed to communicate. Paralysis of all limbs with absence of deep tendon reflexes was noted on the same day. He became comatose on day 9. Paralytic rabies was then suspected and rabies virus RNA was demonstrable in saliva but not in the urine by nucleic acid sequence based amplification technique (3). The patient died after 12 days of hospitalization (15 days after first clinical onset). Autopsy findings showed wide spread Negri bodies through out the whole neural axis.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old male presenting with difficulty swallowing, fever, and intermittent alteration of consciousness for 3 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was in good health until 3 days prior to admission when he developed fever and difficulty swallowing, accompanied by severe pruritus of his right leg and buttock that resulted in extensive excoriation. He subsequently became intermittently confused, agitated, refused food and drink, and complained of shortness of breath incited by fanning. One day prior to admission, he became unable to swallow his saliva, with mental status alternating between normal periods and confusion.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of a dog bite 10 years previously without administration of post-exposure prophylaxis; denied recent animal bites or bat exposures. Travel history: arrived in Bangkok from Myanmar 6 days prior to presentation. Previously in good health.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe sore throat, refusal to eat or drink, aerophobia-induced dyspnea, pruritus of right leg and buttock. Denies other systemic complaints.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: conscious, rational, and well cooperative, sitting upright and continuously spitting out saliva, complaining of severely sore throat; temperature 39.1 C, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, heart rate 120 beats/min, respiratory rate 30 breaths/min. Palpable crepitus on the left side of the neck without erythema or local inflammatory signs. Neurological examination: no focal neurological signs; palatopharyngeal muscle function intact, gag reflex hyperactive; aerophobic and hydrophobic spasms could not be induced. Indirect laryngoscopic examination was unremarkable. Postoperative course: on day 2 developed brief generalized tonic-clonic seizures; by day 6 developed serial seizures, remained conscious but unable to communicate, with flaccid paralysis of all limbs and absence of deep tendon reflexes; deteriorated to coma on day 9.
objective.routine_investigations: Leukocytosis of 28,400/uL with 89.6% neutrophils. Serum amylase slightly elevated at 443 U/L (reference range 28-100 U/L). Serum sodium: initial hypernatremia of 157 mOsm/L, corrected to 140 mOsm/L within 11 hours. Lateral neck radiographs: air in the retropharyngeal space. Chest radiograph: evidence of pneumomediastinum. Liquid barium esophagogram: failed to demonstrate any point of esophageal leakage.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast head CT on admission: unremarkable. Repeat head CT on day 6: unremarkable. Lumbar puncture on admission: acellular cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with normal protein and glucose levels. Repeat lumbar puncture on day 6: unremarkable. Surgical exploration of neck and thorax: unremarkable operative findings, no evidence of perforation in upper esophagus or oropharynx, and normal retropharyngeal space without purulent discharge or fluid accumulation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of paralytic rabies: Rabies virus RNA was demonstrable in saliva by nucleic acid sequence-based amplification (NASBA) technique; urine NASBA was negative for rabies RNA. Post-mortem autopsy confirmed widespread Negri bodies throughout the entire neural axis. Surgical exploration was initially performed due to suspected upper digestive tract perforation and pneumomediastinum. Postoperatively, assisted mechanical ventilation was provided. Hypernatremia was corrected with intravenous fluids. Intravenous phenytoin was initiated for generalized tonic-clonic seizures. The patient progressed to coma and died after 12 days of hospitalization (15 days after initial clinical onset).

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 59-year-old male from Dammam, Saudi Arabia with a history of HIV for 15 years, who was non-compliant to HIV treatment for five years. The patient last visited the HIV clinic in December 2020 and blood tests showed a viral load of 9340 copies per mL. Furthermore, this person had a history of HBV (immune to hepatitis B due to natural immunity), chronic non-treated HCV, diabetes mellitus type II for three years, hypertension (HTN), smoking and active drug abuse for heroin and alcohol, chronic kidney disease stage III, and a previously treated cervical spine abscess with internal fixation surgery. The patient was prescribed tenofovir and emtricitabine; no antiretroviral resistance screening test was performed, and we could not obtain lymphocyte subset results. Prior to emergency department (ER) admittance, the patient had three months history of progressive neck pain, and sudden weakness in the upper and lower limbs the day before presenting to the ER; however, they experienced no numbness, loss of sphincter control, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. The results of the patient's physical examination, blood pressure and other vital signs were normal, and neuromuscular examination results were unremarkable. However, laboratory blood test results revealed a high white blood cell (WBC) count, decreased hemoglobin level (Hgb), and high platelet count (Plt). The patient's serum creatinine level was 2.54 mg/dL and blood urea nitrogen was 45 mg/dL. Notably, there were elevated levels of inflammatory markers, such as procalcitonin and C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A brain computed tomography (CT) revealed chronic small vessel disease, with a number of lytic lesions on the patient's first cervical vertebra.
Seven days post admission, the patient experienced fever (38.8 C), in addition to persistent and uncontrolled high blood pressure; however, a physical examination showed no evidence of limited movement or mobility. Prior to receiving blood culture results for sepsis testing, vancomycin and meropenem antibiotics were empirically prescribed. The patient received a complete work-up, and was tested for complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, and blood and urine cultures.
The septic workup results showed a high WBC count and high levels of inflammatory markers, including CRP and procalcitonin (Table 1). 
We incubated one set of blood culture vials in a BacT/Alert Virtuo system (BioMerieux, France) for 5 days, according to the internal policies and procedures of the microbiology laboratory at King Fahd Hospital of the University. After 72 hours of incubation, one of the two blood culture vials flagged positive, and direct Gram staining showed Gram-positive bacilli. Subsequently, the blood culture vials were sub-cultured on sheep blood, MacConkey, chocolate, and anaerobic Brucella agars.
After 48 hours incubation at 37 C, there was no growth present on sheep blood, MacConkey's, and chocolate agars. However, there was bacterial growth on anaerobic Brucella agar (Figure 1). We used Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight-mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS) (VITEK MS; bioMerieux) and the Knowledge Base database (version 3.0) with a confidence value of 99.9% to identify Clostridium paraputrificum. Antibiotics-susceptibility tests for anaerobic organisms were not available in our routine diagnostic laboratory; therefore, we depended on 2022 Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) cumulative data, which showed that Clostridium was sensitive to imipenem, meropenem, and metronidazole antibiotics. Urine analysis results were normal, and the urine culture showed no growth. 
Forty-eight hours following treatment with vancomycin and meropenem antibiotics, the patient clinically improved, the fever subsided, and blood cultures showed no growth. All subsequent cultures were negative, but inflammatory markers remained high. On day 12 of admission, the patient experienced sudden cardiac arrest due to reflex arrhythmia caused by atlantoaxial subluxation and passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old male presenting with a 3-month history of progressive neck pain and acute weakness in the upper and lower extremities.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced progressive neck pain over a 3-month period, followed by acute onset of weakness in the upper and lower extremities the day prior to emergency department presentation. He denied associated numbness, loss of sphincter control, fever, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. On post-admission day 7, he developed new high-grade fever (38.8 °C) with persistent, uncontrolled hypertension, prompting an evaluation for systemic infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of chronic retroviral illness diagnosed 15 years prior (non-compliant with therapy for 5 years; prior viral load 9,340 copies/mL; no lymphocyte subsets available); chronic untreated hepatitis C; hepatitis B (immune due to natural immunity); type 2 diabetes mellitus for 3 years; hypertension; chronic kidney disease stage III; and prior cervical spine abscess status post internal fixation surgery. Social history notable for cigarette smoking and active substance abuse with heroin and alcohol. Resides in Dammam, Saudi Arabia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for sensory loss/numbness, sphincter dysfunction, fever, diaphoresis, or weight loss on initial presentation. Home medications: prescribed tenofovir and emtricitabine. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Initial examination: blood pressure and other vital signs were normal; neuromuscular examination was unremarkable without focal deficits; cervical range of motion showed no evidence of limited mobility. Day 7 examination: body temperature 38.8 °C, persistent and uncontrolled high blood pressure; physical examination demonstrated no limitation of cervical movement or mobility.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood tests: leukocytosis with elevated white blood cell count, decreased hemoglobin, elevated platelet count; serum creatinine: 2.54 mg/dL; blood urea nitrogen: 45 mg/dL; elevated inflammatory markers including procalcitonin, C-reactive protein (CRP), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Day 7 sepsis workup: persistent leukocytosis with elevated CRP and procalcitonin; urinalysis: normal; urine culture: no growth.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain computed tomography (CT): chronic small vessel disease with multiple lytic lesions on the first cervical vertebra (C1).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Clostridium paraputrificum bacteremia and sepsis in a patient with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, chronic hepatitis C, and cervical spine osteolytic lesions. Blood culture vials incubated in BacT/Alert Virtuo system flagged positive after 72 hours, demonstrating Gram-positive bacilli on direct Gram staining; subcultures yielded bacterial growth exclusively on anaerobic Brucella agar at 48 hours, definitively identified as Clostridium paraputrificum by MALDI-TOF MS (VITEK MS; Knowledge Base version 3.0, 99.9% confidence). Susceptibility testing for anaerobes was unavailable; 2022 CLSI cumulative data indicated sensitivity to imipenem, meropenem, and metronidazole. Management & Outcome: Initiated on empiric intravenous vancomycin and meropenem. Fever subsided, clinical condition improved within 48 hours, and subsequent blood cultures confirmed clearance of bacteremia, although inflammatory markers remained elevated. On hospital day 12, the patient developed fatal reflex arrhythmia and sudden cardiac arrest secondary to atlantoaxial subluxation.

raw_case_text:
A 15-year-old female patient without any previous medical history presented at Amiri Hospital, Kuwait, on March 6, 2021, with a one-day history of facial asymmetry and weakness in the right upper and lower limbs, accompanied by impaired sensation. She reported feeling unwell with fatigue and loss of appetite a few days prior to admission. She had a low-grade fever on the day of admission with no other infective/coryzal symptoms. She had not received vaccination against Covid-19 infection. Her temperature was 37.8 Celsius, her pulse rate was 90 per minute, her blood pressure was 100/60 mm Hg, and her oxygen saturation was 98 percent on room air.
Neurological examination revealed normal cognition, mild dysarthria, right-sided upper motor neuron facial weakness, and monocular diplopia affecting the left eye. There was no ptosis or nystagmus, a full range of motion in the external ocular muscles, and normal swallowing. In the right upper and lower limbs, the muscle power was 0/5 according to the Medical Research Council (MRC) Scale for Muscle Strength, accompanied by hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and ankle clonus. Superficial sensations were impaired on the right side of the body, although deep sensation was preserved. She had no bladder or bowel incontinence.
She tested positive for nasopharyngeal COVID-19 real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test carried out on admission to the hospital.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the patient's brain revealed acute infarcts in the pons and left cerebellum (Figure 1). There were no definite features of demyelinating disease. A computed tomography (CT) angiogram of the cerebrovascular system and carotid doppler findings showed occluded left vertebral and basilar arteries (Figure 2). The MRI findings of the brain and neck (T1 with fat suppression) suggested a thrombotic etiology rather than dissection. A conventional angiogram was not performed, as the patient's family did not want to take the risks involved with the procedure. The findings of the transthoracic echocardiogram bubble study were unremarkable.
Laboratory investigations were normal except for mildly elevated D-dimer level, at 299 ng/ml (normal range: 0-250 ng/ml). Her coagulation profile was normal. Serum ferritin and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels were not elevated. The patient's thrombophilia and vasculitis screens were all negative. Tests for mycoplasma, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, and cytomegalovirus antibodies were also negative.
On admission, a preliminary diagnosis of a demyelinating disease was considered, and she was empirically treated with intravenous Methylprednisolone. When investigations revealed cerebrovascular thrombosis, Methyl Prednisolone was discontinued. She was then started on dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin and Plavix). Five weeks later the patient was transferred to the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Hospital, Kuwait, for rehabilitation. By this time, she exhibited partial motor recovery. Superficial sensations were still impaired on the right side. The cerebellar signs could not be assessed at this time due to the patient's muscle weakness. The functional assessment revealed that she could take a few steps with the assistance of one person. She needed assistance for the activities of daily living, and her functional independence measure (FIM) score was 82/126. The patient underwent a comprehensive rehabilitation program, which included physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and robotic hand therapy sessions, as an inpatient as well as an outpatient at the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Hospital and showed significant improvement.
The muscle power in her right upper and lower limbs had improved to grade 4/5 according to the MRC Scale, except for the finger extensors, intrinsic muscles of the hand, and ankle dorsiflexion, which were all graded 3/5. The patient had difficulty with her fine motor skills, especially handwriting, due to intention tremors in the fingers. She was trained to write with her left hand because she found doing so easier and faster than writing with her right hand. She exhibited mild incoordination. After eight months of rehabilitation, she could walk independently with a mild circumduction gait pattern. She was independent in all the activities of daily living and was able to return to school. At the time of discharge, her FIM score had improved to 123/126 (Figure 3).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-year-old female presenting with a 1-day history of acute facial asymmetry, right hemiplegia, and right-sided hemi-hypoesthesia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A previously healthy 15-year-old female developed generalized malaise, fatigue, and anorexia several days prior to presentation. On the day of admission, she developed low-grade fever accompanied by acute right-sided facial drooping, right upper and lower extremity weakness, sensory loss, and diplopia. She had no preceding catarrhal or respiratory symptoms. In the hospital, she was initially suspected of having an acute demyelinating syndrome and was treated with corticosteroids, but comprehensive neuroimaging demonstrated acute basilar and vertebral arterial thromboembolism with posterior circulation stroke.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical or surgical illnesses. Unvaccinated against pandemic respiratory virus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue, anorexia, low-grade fever, facial asymmetry, right arm and leg weakness, numbness on right side, diplopia affecting left eye. Denies headache, cough, shortness of breath, sore throat, or bowel/bladder incontinence.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: T 37.8 °C, HR 90 beats/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air. Neurological: Alert, oriented, mild dysarthria, right upper motor neuron facial nerve palsy, monocular diplopia of the left eye; no ptosis or nystagmus, full extraocular movements, intact swallowing. Motor: Right flaccid hemiplegia (MRC grade 0/5 in right upper and lower extremities) with hypertonia, hyperreflexia, and ankle clonus. Sensory: Impaired superficial sensation on the right side of the body; intact deep sensation. Discharge/rehabilitation exam: Motor power improved to MRC 4/5 in right upper and lower limbs (3/5 in hand intrinsics, finger extensors, and ankle dorsiflexors); mild intention tremor and incoordination; ambulating independently with mild circumduction gait.
objective.routine_investigations: D-dimer mildly elevated at 299 ng/mL (normal range 0–250 ng/mL). CBC, coagulation profile, serum ferritin, and LDH were normal. Comprehensive thrombophilia and vasculitis screens were negative. Infectious serologies negative for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, HSV, VZV, and CMV. Transthoracic echocardiogram bubble study: Unremarkable without intracardiac shunt.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: Acute ischemic infarctions in the pons and left cerebellum without demyelinating features; T1 with fat suppression suggested a thrombotic rather than dissecting etiology. CT angiogram of cerebrovascular system and carotid Doppler: Occlusion of the left vertebral and basilar arteries.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute basilar artery and left vertebral artery thrombosis causing pontine and cerebellar ischemic infarction, triggered by acute COVID-19 infection (confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal RT-PCR test on admission).

Management and outcome: Initial empiric intravenous methylprednisolone was discontinued upon confirmation of cerebral arterial thrombosis. Started on dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and clopidogrel). Transferred at 5 weeks to a specialized rehabilitation hospital (initial FIM score 82/126) for intensive physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and robotic hand therapy. After 8 months of comprehensive rehabilitation, motor power improved to 4/5 throughout (3/5 in distal hand/ankle muscles), FIM score improved to 123/126, and she achieved independent ambulation and full functional independence for activities of daily living and return to school.

raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old previously healthy girl with no prior remarkable medical history presented to our institution with fever following a one-week trip to Costa Rica. During this time, she stayed in a hotel in the rain forest where she took hikes with family members. She swam in the ocean as well as in chlorinated pools, saw many animals (including rodents), and was splashed with fresh water. Five days following her return from Costa Rica, she developed fever of one-week duration (up to 39.5 C), abdominal pain, nausea, and sore throat. None of the accompanying family members (parents and sibling) developed any signs of illness, nor was there any remarkable family history. The family resided in a metropolitan area in Los Angeles County, and there had been no recent floods or rodent exposures in the neighborhood preceding or following the trip. The patient was seen in her primary care physician's office one week into her illness. At that time, she had a negative throat beta streptococcus direct antigen screen. She developed bilateral eye pain and redness and was seen again by her primary care pediatrician two days later who performed further laboratory evaluations. Results included an alanine aminotransferase of 102 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase of 73 U/L, albumin 3.1 g/dL, total bilirubin 0.5 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.9 seconds, partial thromboplastin time 38.1 seconds, and alkaline phosphatase 314 U/L.
She was subsequently referred to our infectious disease clinic for further investigation. The first visit to our clinic was approximately 2 1/2 weeks following the return from Costa Rica. At that time, she was afebrile and showed complete symptomatic improvement. Further workup demonstrated a positive Leptospira indirect hemagglutination test (Focus technologies, Cypress, CA) with a titer of 1 : 200. After the results of the positive Leptospira test became available, she was reevaluated at our clinic (approximately 6 weeks following her return from Costa Rica). At that time, she was back to her normal state of health. A urine culture for Leptospira was obtained and incubated onto Ellinghausen McCullough Johnson Harris medium with 200 micrograms per mL of 5-Fluorouracil. Urine cultures 6 weeks following her trip were positive for spirochetes. A renal ultrasound was normal, while serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen values remained within normal range during this period. A convalescent serology was also obtained. Both acute and convalescent sera were sent to the CDC for confirmation and microscopic agglutination testing (MAT).
Acute and convalescent sera were positive with IgM Dip-S-Ticks (PanBio INDX, Inc., Baltimore, Maryland). The MAT test was negative for the acute serum. The convalescent serum had a positive MAT titer of 1 : 400 to serogroup Mini and serovar Georgia and strain LT117. The WHO/FAO Collaborating Centre for Reference and Research on Leptospirosis, Royal Tropical Institute (KIT, Amsterdam, The Netherlands) has identified the Leptospira spirochete as belonging to serovar Shermani using rabbit polyclonal sera. The patient was seen again 2 months following her trip to Costa Rica. She was doing well, and urine cultures for Leptospira were performed at the time with negative results.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old girl presented with a 1-week history of high fever up to 39.5 °C, abdominal pain, nausea, and sore throat following a trip to Costa Rica.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five days after returning from a 1-week family vacation in Costa Rica, the patient developed high fever up to 39.5 °C, abdominal pain, nausea, and sore throat. One week into the illness, a rapid streptococcal screen was negative. Two days later, she developed bilateral eye pain and conjunctival redness, leading to pediatric laboratory evaluation demonstrating elevated transaminases. She was referred to the infectious disease clinic 2.5 weeks post-travel, by which time she was afebrile and clinically improving.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no prior remarkable medical or family history. Travel and epidemiological exposures: 1-week stay in a Costa Rican rainforest hotel with hiking, swimming in the ocean and chlorinated pools, sighting wild animals including rodents, and being splashed with fresh water. No recent floods or rodent exposures at her home residence in Los Angeles County.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, sore throat, nausea, abdominal pain, and bilateral eye pain and redness. Denies current fever at clinic evaluation.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile, well-appearing child in no acute distress. Ocular examination revealed bilateral conjunctival redness without purulent discharge. General and systemic physical examinations were otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: ALT: 102 U/L; AST: 73 U/L; alkaline phosphatase: 314 U/L; albumin: 3.1 g/dL; total bilirubin: 0.5 mg/dL; PT: 12.9 seconds; PTT: 38.1 seconds. BUN and serum creatinine remained within normal limits. Throat group A streptococcal direct antigen screen was negative. Renal ultrasound was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Anicteric leptospirosis presenting with acute febrile illness, conjunctival suffusion, and mild hepatitis, complicated by prolonged urinary shedding of spirochetes. Confirmed by: (1) positive Leptospira indirect hemagglutination test (titer 1:200); (2) positive acute and convalescent IgM Dip-S-Ticks; (3) positive microscopic agglutination test (MAT) on convalescent serum at the CDC with a titer of 1:400 to serogroup Mini, serovar Georgia, strain LT117; and (4) positive urine culture on EMJH medium with 5-fluorouracil growing Leptospira spirochetes at 6 weeks post-exposure, identified as serovar Shermani by the WHO/FAO Reference Centre. Streptococcal pharyngitis was ruled out. Treatment & Outcome: Managed expectantly with complete spontaneous clinical resolution; repeat urine culture at 2 months was negative for Leptospira, confirming cessation of shedding.

raw_case_text:
Participant 1: Mrs. O. F, a 36-year-old married female police officer, admitted on account of a two-month history of recurrent fever and progressive weight loss. She had a weeping left facial vesicular rash and a day s history of right sided weakness. Not a known hypertensive or diabetic patient, not a known case of haemoglobinopathy. She neither consumed illicit drugs nor smoked cigarettes, but took two bottles of Guinness stout weekly. No seizure disorders. Examination revealed a young woman with a left sided herpetic rash pustular, distributed over the ophthalmic region of the trigeminal nerve. At entry, she was not febrile (36.5 C). Temperature during admission ranged between 36.8 - 37. 8 C. She was anicteric but pale (PCV 26%), conscious with right hemiparesis, with power of 3 in the upper and lower limbs. Her blood pressure was 120/80mm/Hg, No cardiac murmurs. Apart from hepatomegaly of 3cm on abdominal examination, other examinations were not remarkable. Serology was positive for HIV-1 with a CD4 count of 180 cells/cm3. Her renal function was normal. Entry random blood glucose was 128 mg/dl (7.1mmol/l), normal repeat and normal plasma lipids. Her cranial CT, was reported as normal. A routine chest X-ray was not remarkable. Herpes was suspected. She had Acyclovir, and antibiotics for the super-added bacterial infection on the facial rash.
Outcome: had sustained clinical improvement, was enrolled for HIV treatment/care and being followed up at the out patients  services.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old female presenting with a 2-month history of recurrent fever and weight loss, accompanied by a facial vesicular rash and acute right-sided hemiparesis for one day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of intermittent fevers and progressive unintentional weight loss. Over the days prior to admission, she developed a painful, weeping pustular rash over the left side of her face, followed by the acute onset of right-sided body weakness 24 hours prior to presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hemoglobinopathy, or seizure disorders. Social history: Police officer; consumes two bottles of stout beer weekly; denies cigarette smoking or illicit drug use.
subjective.review_of_systems: Recurrent fever, weight loss, weeping facial eruption, and right-sided hemiparesis; denies headache, neck stiffness, visual loss, or chest pain.

objective.physical_examination: General: Pale, anicteric, conscious. Vitals: Temperature 36.5 °C at presentation (ranging between 36.8 °C and 37.8 °C during admission), blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, no cardiac murmurs. Abdomen: Hepatomegaly palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Dermatologic: Pustular, weeping vesicular eruption distributed over the ophthalmic division (V1) of the left trigeminal nerve. Neurologic: Conscious with right hemiparesis, muscle power grade 3/5 in the right upper and lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Packed cell volume (PCV): 26% (anemia). Random blood glucose: 128 mg/dL (7.1 mmol/L), with normal repeat values. Plasma lipids: Normal lipid profile. Renal function: Normal serum urea and creatinine. Chest radiograph: Normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Cranial computed tomography (CT): Normal brain parenchyma without evidence of acute hemorrhagic or established ischemic infarction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Acute ischemic cerebrovascular accident (vasculopathy-induced stroke) and ophthalmic herpes zoster with secondary bacterial superinfection in a patient with newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection (CD4+ T-cell count 180 cells/mm3). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive HIV-1 serology; clinical diagnosis of herpes zoster ophthalmicus based on dermatomal vesicular-pustular distribution over the V1 branch. Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous acyclovir, broad-spectrum antibiotics for secondary bacterial skin infection, and supportive stroke care. She achieved sustained clinical recovery and functional improvement, and was initiated on combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) with longitudinal outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Our patient is a 28-year-old male from Gaza who was transferred to our hospital's medical intensive care unit (ICU) because of complicated leptospirosis. His past surgical and medical history was insignificant. Ten days before admission, the patient had a rat bite in his left big toe, so he sought medical advice, where he was given a tetanus vaccine and discharged with a recommendation to follow up at the infectious clinic. Later on, the patient started complaining of nonspecific symptoms of headache, general weakness, and myalgia, for which he took analgesics. However, his symptoms worsened, and he started to notice a yellowish discoloration all over his body, associated with fever. So, he was admitted to the medical ward in Gaza, where Investigations were performed and confirmed the diagnosis of leptospirosis. Those revealed alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury. The patient's condition rapidly deteriorated, requiring intubation and urgent transfer to our hospital for Advanced ICU management.
Upon arrival, the Patient was admitted to the ICU immediately. On examination, He was deeply sedated on mechanical ventilation SIMV, PEEP:10, FIO2: 100%, PS:20, RR:18). He was pale, deeply jaundiced, and ecchymosis was found on his hands and legs. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral basal crepitation. His vital signs showed a heart rate of 88 beats/min, blood pressure of 150/90 mmHg, and body temperature of 38.6 C. His blood oxygen saturation was 99% on the parameters as mentioned above. Upon admission, extensive laboratory investigations were obtained, including a full septic workup (Table 1). Arterial blood gases revealed a PH of 7.40, CO2:45.3 mmHG, and HCO3:28 mEq/L. The white blood cell count was elevated, primarily the neutrophils. He was anemic, and thrombocytopenia was present. The transaminases level was average. There was a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine levels were significantly increased, suggesting acute renal injury. Urine analysis showed no proteinuria. CT scan showed diffuse bilateral areas of patchy alveolar infiltration ground glass opacities, representing alveolar hemorrhage (Figure 1). The patient was started on broad-spectrum antibiotics, including vancomycin, meropenem, and doxycycline, as well as esomeprazole 40 mg orally and a Pulse dose of Methylprednisolone 1 g once daily for three days, then tapering gradually to 80 g. By the sixth day of admission, the patient developed Ventilator-associated pneumonia. Sputum culture showed pseudomonas aeruginosa sensitive for colistin.
Day by day, the Patient's condition dramatically resolved. His labs showed stable blood hemostasis The creatinine, liver enzymes, bilirubin, and CRP gradually subsided. Also, his respiratory conditions improved. The patient was successfully extubated on day 10 from admission. His condition was stable, and he was transferred to the medical ward to continue antibiotics therapy. On day 18 of admission, he suddenly developed abdominal pain and severe hematemesis of a large amount of blood (about 3 liters). He became unconscious with a GCC scale of 4/15; the blood pressure was unrecordable. An Urgent resuscitative strategy for hemorrhagic shock was started, including the following: two bores IV cannula, two central lines (femoral and internal jugular), massive blood product transfusion with a total of 30 units (10 units of PRBC, 10 FFP, 10 PLTS), several liters of IV Fluid (Normal saline and ringer lactate), and calcium gluconate administration. Then Intubation was done, and adrenaline and noradrenaline were started. An urgent upper endoscopy revealed an intact oesophagus and a stomach full of blood. Laboratory results showed a Hb of 4.22 mg/dl, HCT of 15.7%, MCH of 27 PG/ML, MCV of 88 microm3, RBC of 1.4 x 106/microl, wbc of 11 x 103/L, Platelets of 50 x 103/micro, SGPT of 94 U/L, SGOT of 37 U/L, BUN of 28 mg/dl, Cre of 0.9 mg/dl, Fibrinogen of 220 mg/dl, CRP of 12.4 mg/dl, D-dimer of 910 mg/dl, PT of 13.6, INR of 1.15, APTT of 20.6, T. bilirubin of 2 mg/dl, and D. Bilirubin of 1.3 mg/dl.
The patient underwent urgent exploratory laparotomy. Open stomach anterior wall and gastric lumen packing were done. The upper half of the mucosa of the stomach oozed fresh blood, and a Splenic artery aneurysm eroded into the gastroesophageal junction. So left gastric artery was ligated, Splenectomy and proximal partial gastrectomy with distal esophagectomy were performed. Intraoperatively, the Patient receives 8 PRPC, 10 FFP, 10 PLT,2500-unit prothrombin complex concentration, and 8,000 CC IV fluid. Afterward, the Patient was readmitted to the ICU, fully sedated and intubated. The next day, a second look procedure was done involving esophagogastric anastomosis and anterior continues repair of the wall. A jejunostomy feeding tube along with abdominal drains was applied. Figure 2 Showed the Patient's clinical course during the first 23 days of hospitalization.
5-6 days later, the Patient complained of shortness of breath and chest pain. A physical exam revealed tachypnea, desaturation, crackles on the right side, and decreased breath sounds on the left side. A portable chest x-ray showed pleural effusion and left-sided pneumothorax. CT scan findings were: Collapsed left lung due to complete obstruction of the left main bronchus. Mild to moderate left-sided pneumothorax, mild bilateral pleural effusion. A focal consolidation area is seen at the right lower lobe with surrounding ground glass opacities. Two Chest tubes were inserted at the left side, and the Patient's condition improved (Figure 3). The Patient underwent a bronchoscopy, which showed a left main bronchus occlusion. Multiple bronchoscopies were performed by which large amounts of secretions were removed.
The Patient developed an unresolved fever. Full septic work was done, and Antibiotics were upgraded. Chest and abdomen Ct scan with contrast revealed a right upper lobe cavitary lesion surrounded by ground glass opacities. Multiple intraabdominal fluid collections were noted (Figure 4). Ultrasound Guidance drainage was done. Fluid culture revealed stenotrophomonas bacteria sensitive for colistin, levofloxacin, and resprim. The patient was given Colistin and resprim.
Day by day, the Patient showed gradual resolution of his status and was successfully extubated. Extensive supportive strategies were followed for recovery from critical illness, including exercise rehabilitation and physiotherapy. He was transferred to the medical world and discharged home. On follow up the patient was in a good general condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presenting with headache, general weakness, myalgia, jaundice, and fever progressing to respiratory failure and multiorgan dysfunction following a rat bite 10 days prior.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days prior to admission, the patient sustained a rat bite on his left big toe, for which he received a tetanus vaccine. Subsequently, he developed headache, generalized weakness, and myalgias managed with analgesics. His symptoms progressively worsened with high fever and generalized yellowish skin discoloration. He was initially hospitalized in a local medical ward where alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury were identified. His condition deteriorated rapidly, requiring endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and urgent transfer to the intensive care unit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical and surgical history was insignificant. Epidemiological exposure includes a rat bite to the left big toe 10 days before admission. Prior therapy included tetanus vaccination and analgesics.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports headache, generalized weakness, and diffuse myalgias. Home medications: analgesics. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon ICU admission: deeply sedated on mechanical ventilation (SIMV mode, PEEP 10 cmH2O, FiO2 100%, PS 20 cmH2O, RR 18 breaths/min). Heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, body temperature 38.6 °C, blood oxygen saturation 99%. General: pale, deeply jaundiced, with ecchymoses on hands and legs. Respiratory: bilateral basal crepitations on chest auscultation. On day 18: Glasgow Coma Scale 4/15 with unrecordable blood pressure during acute hemorrhage. On day 23: tachypneic and desaturating, with right-sided crackles and decreased left-sided breath sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gases on admission: pH 7.40, PaCO2 45.3 mmHg, HCO3 28 mEq/L. Complete blood count showed elevated white blood cell count (predominantly neutrophils), anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Biochemistry: normal transaminases, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and significantly elevated blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine. Urinalysis: no proteinuria. Day 18 hemorrhage labs: Hb 4.22 mg/dL, HCT 15.7%, MCH 27 pg/mL, MCV 88 mcm^3, RBC 1.4 x 10^6/mcL, WBC 11 x 10^3/L, platelets 50 x 10^3/mcL, SGPT 94 U/L, SGOT 37 U/L, BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, fibrinogen 220 mg/dL, CRP 12.4 mg/dL, D-dimer 910 mg/dL, PT 13.6 s, INR 1.15, APTT 20.6 s, total bilirubin 2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 1.3 mg/dL. Portable chest X-ray: pleural effusion and left-sided pneumothorax.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest CT: diffuse bilateral areas of patchy alveolar infiltration and ground-glass opacities consistent with alveolar hemorrhage. Urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: intact esophagus and stomach full of blood. Diagnostic bronchoscopy: left main bronchus occlusion by copious secretions. Contrast chest and abdominal CT: collapsed left lung due to complete obstruction of the left main bronchus, mild-to-moderate left pneumothorax, mild bilateral pleural effusion, focal consolidation in right lower lobe with surrounding ground-glass opacities, right upper lobe cavitary lesion surrounded by ground-glass opacities, and multiple intra-abdominal fluid collections. Exploratory laparotomy: upper gastric mucosal bleeding and a splenic artery aneurysm eroding into the gastroesophageal junction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Complicated leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, cholestatic jaundice, and acute kidney injury following a rat bite, confirmed by investigations in Gaza. Hospitalization was complicated by ventilator-associated pneumonia secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa (sensitive to colistin), massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage from a ruptured splenic artery aneurysm eroding into the gastroesophageal junction, complete left main bronchus obstruction with lung collapse, left pneumothorax, and secondary intra-abdominal fluid collection infection with Stenotrophomonas (sensitive to colistin, levofloxacin, and resprim/co-trimoxazole).
Plan & Management: Initial broad-spectrum coverage with vancomycin, meropenem, and doxycycline, alongside esomeprazole 40 mg PO and pulse methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 days tapered to 80 mg. Emergent massive resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock (30 blood product units: 10 PRBC, 10 FFP, 10 platelets; IV fluids, calcium gluconate, adrenaline, noradrenaline) and exploratory laparotomy with splenic artery aneurysm ligation, splenectomy, proximal partial gastrectomy, distal esophagectomy, and subsequent second-look esophagogastric reconstruction with jejunostomy feeding tube. Left chest tube thoracostomy and therapeutic bronchoscopies. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous abdominal drainage with targeted colistin and resprim antimicrobial therapy. Physical therapy and rehabilitation. Successful extubation, resolution of organ failure, and discharge home in good general condition.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old male patient was referred to the emergency department with seizure. He had a history of fever and generalized weakness about 2 weeks before. According to having the history of consuming continuously dairy products made from unpasteurized milk, the serologic Brucella tests including wright, 2ME, and coombs wright were checked. Serum SAT test was positive at titer of 1/1,280, and with the diagnosis of brucellosis, the doxycycline and streptomycin were prescribed for him since about 2 weeks before admission. Two weeks later, the patient referred to our hospital with seizure. Convulsion was generalized, tonic, and colonic lasting about 5 min. He had no history of recent drug usage (except for treatment of brucellosis), alcohol consumption, and smoking. No history of head trauma was declared. Vital signs and general examination were not remarkable. He was afebrile. Complete blood cell count was in normal limits. HBS-Ag, HCV-Ab, HIV test, and serum toxic panel were all negative.
Brain computed tomography scan was performed, which was with no abnormality. The lumbar puncture (LP) was performed. Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) revealed no abnormality; it was colorless and clear; glucose = 67, protein = 15 mg/dL, red blood cell = 0, and white blood cell = 0. The CSF was also sent for Brucella and herpes simplex (HSV 1 and 2) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) studies. Status epilepticus was defined, and patient required intubation and mechanical ventilation. Antiepileptic drugs were started. According to brucellosis, with the clinical suspicious for neurobrucellosis, the treatment including ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 h intravenous (IV), doxycycline 100 mg every 12 h, and rifampin 600 mg daily in addition to IV acyclovir were started. In ICU, the clinical seizure classification was focal and lateralizing signs were right facial and arm clonic and right versive. The electroencephalography monitoring was performed, and the midazolam infusion was started. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance venography (MRV) were both normal. CSF PCR studies for Brucella and HSV, 1 and 2, were reported negative and CSF adenosine deaminase reported 10. Serologic test for brucellosis on CSF were negative. With the probable diagnosis of neurobrucellosis, the treatment with ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and rifampin were continued. Also, 14-day course of IV acyclovir was completed. After 1 month, the patient was stable and treatment with oral doxycycline, rifampin, and co-trimuxazole accompanied with antiepileptic drugs were continued. Two weeks after discharge the patient readmitted to hospital with status epilepticus and was intubated again. The LP was performed, which revealed normal CSF analysis. HSV, 1 and 2, PCR in addition to Brucella PCR were negative in CSF again. The patient underwent renewed brain MRI and MRV and both were normal. Extensive workup did not reveal any cause of the symptoms; however, NMDAR antibodies were positive in both serum and CSF; hence, the diagnosis of NMDAR encephalitis was established. He was started on IV methylprednisolone, which yielded limited improvement. According to intractable epilepsy, the patient's treatment consisting of plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin was started.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 5-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure following a 2-week history of fever and generalized weakness. Two weeks prior to admission, he had been evaluated for systemic febrile illness and commenced on antimicrobial therapy. In the emergency department, he progressed into refractory status epilepticus requiring endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and continuous intravenous midazolam infusion. Following initial stabilization and discharge, he was readmitted two weeks later with recurrent status epilepticus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior diagnosis of systemic febrile illness treated with doxycycline and streptomycin for 2 weeks prior to presentation. Denied alcohol use, tobacco smoking, or head trauma. Epidemiological exposure: continuous consumption of dairy products made from unpasteurized milk.
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized tonic-clonic convulsion, prior fever and generalized weakness. Denied toxic ingestions. Home medications: doxycycline and streptomycin. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile; vital signs and general physical examination were unremarkable. ICU neurological exam: focal motor seizures with lateralizing features (right facial and right upper limb clonic jerks, right versive head turning); comatose requiring mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: within normal limits. Infectious and toxicologic screening: HBsAg, HCV Ab, HIV test, and urine/serum toxicological panel were all negative. Continuous electroencephalography (EEG): documented status epilepticus.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT without contrast: normal. Initial and repeat lumbar puncture: colorless, clear CSF with glucose 67 mg/dL, protein 15 mg/dL, RBC 0/cumm, WBC 0/cumm, and adenosine deaminase (ADA) 10 U/L. Initial and repeat CSF PCR for HSV types 1 and 2 and targeted zoonotic bacterial PCR in CSF were negative. CSF agglutination serology was negative. Initial and repeat brain MRI and magnetic resonance venography (MRV): normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Anti-NMDA receptor (NMDAR) autoimmune encephalitis triggered in the setting of concurrent/preceding systemic brucellosis. Systemic brucellosis confirmed by positive serum standard agglutination test (SAT) at 1 : 1,280 titer, positive 2-mercaptoethanol (2-ME), and positive Coombs Wright. Direct central nervous system neurobrucellosis was ruled out by negative CSF Brucella PCR, negative CSF serology, normal CSF biochemistry, absent CSF pleocytosis, and normal brain MRI/MRV; HSV 1/2 encephalitis was excluded by negative CSF PCR. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis was confirmed by positive anti-NMDA receptor antibodies in both serum and CSF.
Plan & Outcome: Received empirical neurobrucellosis coverage with IV ceftriaxone (2 g every 12h), oral doxycycline (100 mg every 12h), oral rifampin (600 mg daily), cotrimoxazole, and a 14-day course of IV acyclovir alongside antiepileptic therapy (midazolam infusion). Following readmission for recurrent status epilepticus and autoimmune confirmation, he was treated with IV methylprednisolone, therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis), and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male patient, resident of West Bengal, was suffering from cough and chest pain for the last 6 months. He underwent initial management in a local hospital. He was a non-smoker and non-alcoholic. He had no history of fever, hematemesis, malena, diarrhea, headache, or body ache. He had not suffered from diseases like tuberculosis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). He was not taking any drugs at that time.
Initial clinical evaluation in the local hospital revealed that the patient had moderate pallor, cachexia but no lymphadenopathy. Auscultation of chest showed bilateral normal breath sounds, Chest radiograph showed a small left-sided pleural effusion. Routine hematological investigations detected pancytopenia with hemoglobin level of 7.7 g/dl. Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate was 100 mm/h. Mantoux test for tuberculosis was negative. Sputum culture for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was negative. Ziehl-Neelsen stain of the sputum smears was also negative for AFB.
The patient was prescribed antitussives and analgesics, but no significant improvement occurred. He was then referred to our hospital for further management.
After examining the patient, we obtained another chest radiograph that confirmed the presence of a small left-sided pleural effusion [Figure 1]. Known causes of pleural effusion like heart failure, pneumonia, tuberculosis, or carcinoma of lung were absent in this patient. He did not have any symptoms of arthritis, which is commonly found in autoimmune diseases. Therefore, the cause of pleural effusion remained unexplained.
On thorough examination, a mild splenomegaly was detected. To detect the cause of splenomegaly, serum bilirubin, liver enzymes, and prothrombin time were estimated which were within normal limits. HBsAg, anti-HCV and anti-HIV antibodies were negative by ELISA technique. Widal test for enteric fever and test for malaria antigens were negative.
Total serum protein estimation was done, which was found to be within normal limits. However, the albumin/globulin ratio was reversed, being 0.2. Napier's aldehyde test was then performed which is based on the principle of hypergammaglobulinemia, that occurs in VL. About 1 ml of patient's serum was mixed well with a drop of 40% formalin, shaken and kept at room temperature. Opacification and solidification of serum was seen after 10 min signifying a positive result. Subsequently, bone-marrow aspiration was undertaken, which showed both intracellular and extracellular amastigote forms of L. donovani. Slight excess of plasma cells was also noted [Figure 2].
The patient was treated with IV Sodium Stibogluconate with prompt clinical and laboratory improvement. Chest radiograph was done after 1 month, which showed resolution of preceding pleural effusion [Figure 3]. He was on follow-up for another 6 months, which was uneventful.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male presented with a 6-month history of chronic cough and left-sided chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a dry cough and dull left-sided chest pain 6 months prior to admission, receiving antitussives and analgesics without symptomatic relief. He experienced progressive pallor and weight loss but denied fevers, chills, hemoptysis, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
subjective.past_medical_history: Non-smoker and non-drinker. Denied history of tuberculosis, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or gastroesophageal reflux disease. Epidemiological history: resident of West Bengal, India.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports chronic cough and left chest pain; denies fever, night sweats, hematemesis, melena, diarrhea, headache, or arthralgias.

objective.physical_examination: Patient appeared cachectic with moderate pallor; no peripheral lymphadenopathy or peripheral edema. Chest auscultation: normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. Abdominal examination: mild splenomegaly palpable below the left costal margin; liver not enlarged.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia with hemoglobin 7.7 g/dL; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 100 mm/h. Total serum protein: normal, with marked reversal of albumin/globulin (A/G) ratio to 0.2. Serum bilirubin, liver enzymes, and prothrombin time: all within normal limits. Napier's aldehyde test: strongly positive (solidification and opacification within 10 minutes). Infectious workup: Mantoux test negative; sputum smears (Ziehl-Neelsen) and cultures for acid-fast bacilli negative; Widal test negative; malaria rapid antigen test negative; serologies for HIV, HBsAg, and anti-HCV negative. Chest radiograph: small left-sided pleural effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration: hypercellular marrow with a slight excess of plasma cells and numerous intracellular and extracellular protozoal amastigotes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated numerous intracellular and extracellular amastigote forms of Leishmania donovani with reactive plasmacytosis, confirming visceral leishmaniasis presenting atypically with reactive pleural effusion. Tuberculosis, bronchogenic carcinoma, parapneumonic effusion, heart failure, enteric fever, and malaria were ruled out. Management and Outcome: Treated with intravenous sodium stibogluconate, leading to rapid clinical recovery, resolution of pancytopenia, and complete radiological clearing of the left pleural effusion on chest X-ray at 1 month. Follow-up at 6 months was uneventful.

raw_case_text: 64-year-old man farmar was admitted to our department with low back pain radiating to the lower extremities. He had a history of febrile illness and loss of appetite 2 years before admission. Four months after the start of the febrile illness, the patient started to complain of backache and spinal movements were restricted and painful. He had no other neurologic symptoms. Radiography of the spine revealed parrot's peak appearance (Pedro Pons' sign) at the anterior superior end of the L3 vertebra which is characterized by osteosclerosis and osteophyte (A, arrows). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after the administration of gadolinium revealed L2-L3 epiduritis, an erosive change of the anterior portion of L4 and L5, abnormal signal change with enhancement in T12, L2, L3, L5 and S1 body with probable spondylodiscitis in L2/L3 and L5/S1 levels (B). Pathological analysis of a specimen obtained with CT-guided aspiration revealed non caseating granulomas, which were culture positive for Micrococcus melitensis. Rose Bengal test for brucellosis was positive and Brucella standard tube agglutination confirmed this finding with 1/321 titer. Antibiotic treatment (doxycyline 200 mg/d and rifampicin 600 mg/d) was initiated and the patient's complaints were diminished gradually. He was discharged from hospital and recommended to complete his treatment to 90 days and a follow-up MRI showed sclerosis and reactive osteophyte formation indicating the healing phase of inflammatory tissue at the same levels. Pedro Pons' sign, known as anterior superior end erosion, which occurs together with rounding of the vertebral end and level deformity, is a characteristic radiologic finding of brucellar spondylitis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male farmer presented with low back pain radiating to the lower extremities and restricted spinal mobility.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced a febrile illness associated with anorexia 2 years prior to admission. Four months after the febrile illness began, he developed persistent low back pain with restricted and painful spinal movements, which gradually radiated to both lower extremities. He had no other neurological symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: farmer. Past history of febrile illness and anorexia 2 years prior. Other medical comorbidities, prior antibiotic exposure, and animal contact details not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Low back pain radiating to lower extremities, painful restricted spinal mobility, anorexia. Denied other neurological symptoms. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Spinal mobility was severely restricted and painful. Neurological examination was otherwise normal without focal motor or sensory deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Spine radiography: 'parrot's peak' appearance (Pedro Pons' sign) at the anterior superior end of L3 vertebra characterized by osteosclerosis and osteophyte formation.
objective.advanced_workup: Spine MRI (gadolinium-enhanced): L2-L3 epiduritis, erosive changes of anterior L4 and L5, abnormal signal enhancement in T12, L2, L3, L5, and S1 vertebral bodies with probable spondylodiscitis at L2-L3 and L5-S1 levels. CT-guided vertebral aspiration: histopathology of aspirate revealed non-caseating granulomas. Follow-up MRI: demonstrated sclerosis and reactive osteophyte formation indicating healing of inflammatory tissue at affected levels.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar spondylodiscitis with multi-level vertebral involvement (T12, L2, L3, L4, L5, S1) and L2-L3 epiduritis.
Confirmation: Culture of CT-guided vertebral aspirate positive for Micrococcus melitensis (Brucella melitensis); Rose Bengal screening test positive; standard tube agglutination test confirmed Brucella titer of 1/321.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with oral doxycycline (200 mg/day) and oral rifampicin (600 mg/day). Symptoms diminished gradually, and he was discharged to complete a 90-day antimicrobial course; follow-up MRI confirmed resolution and healing with reactive sclerosis.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old Caucasian man was admitted our hospital with malaise, fatigue, and low-grade fever (up to 38 C), and a two-month history of rigors. He also reported anorexia and weight loss, night sweats, and generalized arthralgia. His medical history was non-contributory. He worked as a food handler.
On physical examination, the only abnormalities were a systolic murmur (grade II/VI) of the heart and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations revealed low haemoglobin 11.6 g/dL (normal range 13.0-18.0 g/dL), and raised aspartate aminotransferase (57 U/L; upper normal limit (UNL) 40 U/L), alaninoaminotransferase (57 U/L; UNL: 40 U/L) and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (55 U/L; UNL 37 U/L). Electrocardiography (ECG) was normal with sinus rhythm, but chest radiography revealed slight cardiomegaly. Stool, urine and pharynx cultures, and investigations for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), cytomegalovirus, enteric cytopathic human orphan (ECHO) virus, coxsackie viruses, herpes simplex virus (HSV), varicella-zoster virus (VSV), adenovirus, Coxiella burnetti, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Leptospira spp. and Mycoplasma pneumoniae were negative. However, serum agglutination tests were positive (titre >1:2560), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (SERION ELISA Classic IgG/IgM; Institute Virion/Serion GmbH, Wurzburg, Germany) tests for anti-Brucella IgG and IgM antibodies were strongly positive (118 U/ml and 35.5 U/ml; UNL 30 U/ml and 20 U/ml, respectively). In addition, Brucella spp. were isolated from consecutive blood cultures (six out of eight cultures positive). Two-dimensional trans-thoracic and trans-oesophageal echocardiography was performed to investigate for the possible presence of Brucella-related endocarditis because of our patient's systolic heart murmur, six positive blood cultures and presence of cardiomegaly on chest radiographs. The investigation showed normal valves without any sign of vegetation; however, there was marked pericardial effusion without signs of cardiac tamponade, even though our patient had not reported any chest pain.
Additional extensive laboratory blood tests were performed because of the asymptomatic pericardial effusion, including tumor markers, C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies, serum immunoglobulins, and C3 and C4 component, but did not reveal the cause. There were no clinical or radiologic signs (computed tomography and MRI scans) suggestive for the presence of spondylitis, splenic disease or epididymoorchitis.
Accordingly, a diagnosis of Brucella-related asymptomatic pericardial effusion in the absence of concomitant endocarditis was made and specific treatment with antibiotics only was started immediately. Our patient was given oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus oral rifampicin 900 mg once daily for three months, with intramuscular streptomycin 1 g once daily for the first three weeks. Our patient attended for treatment and follow-up to our outpatient clinic every two weeks. His symptoms regressed rapidly 10 days after initiation of treatment, and no recurrence or adverse drug reactions were observed during follow-up (to one year from the beginning of therapy). Echocardiographic studies three, six and 12 months after the start of treatment showed no pericardial effusion. When last seen, 12 months after starting therapy, our patient was well with no sign of relapse.

subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of rigors, malaise, fatigue, and low-grade fever up to 38 °C. He also experienced anorexia, weight loss, night sweats, and generalized arthralgias. He denied chest pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical history was non-contributory. Occupation: food handler. No prior hospitalizations or specific previous antibiotic therapy noted.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports malaise, fatigue, low-grade fever, rigors, anorexia, weight loss, night sweats, and generalized arthralgia. Denies chest pain.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed a grade II/VI systolic cardiac murmur and hepatosplenomegaly. Remainder of physical examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 11.6 g/dL (normal range 13.0-18.0 g/dL), aspartate aminotransferase (AST): 57 U/L (upper normal limit [UNL] 40 U/L), alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 57 U/L (UNL 40 U/L), gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT): 55 U/L (UNL 37 U/L). Electrocardiography (ECG) showed normal sinus rhythm. Chest radiography revealed slight cardiomegaly. Stool, urine, and pharyngeal cultures were negative. Extensive autoimmune and inflammatory panel (CRP, fibrinogen, rheumatoid factor, ANA, anti-dsDNA, immunoglobulins, C3, C4) and tumor markers revealed no abnormalities. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography showed normal cardiac valves without vegetations, but demonstrated marked pericardial effusion without signs of cardiac tamponade; follow-up echocardiograms at 3, 6, and 12 months showed complete resolution of the effusion.
