assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Serum agglutination tests were positive with a titer > 1:2,560; ELISA for anti-Brucella IgG and IgM was strongly positive (118 U/mL and 35.5 U/mL, respectively; UNL 30 U/mL and 20 U/mL); Brucella spp. was isolated from six out of eight consecutive blood cultures, confirming Brucella-related asymptomatic pericardial effusion without endocarditis. Differential diagnoses ruled out: Negative serologies and cultures for EBV, CMV, ECHO virus, Coxsackieviruses, HSV, VZV, adenovirus, Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Leptospira spp., and Mycoplasma pneumoniae; autoimmune screen and tumor markers were negative. Management and Outcome: Managed exclusively with medical antimicrobial therapy: oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus oral rifampicin 900 mg once daily for 3 months, combined with intramuscular streptomycin 1 g once daily for the first 3 weeks. Symptoms regressed rapidly within 10 days of treatment initiation. Serial echocardiograms at 3, 6, and 12 months documented sustained resolution of pericardial effusion, with no recurrence or relapse observed at 12-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 60-year-old man from Jiangxi province in China, was admitted to the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University with a 3-day history of fever and convulsions. The patient initially presented with sudden onset of fever and chills, with a maximum temperature of 40 C. Symptomatic treatment with over-the-counter cold medication did not result in improvement. On the second day of illness, the patient developed recurrent generalized seizures accompanied by vomiting of gastric contents, followed by progressive disturbance of consciousness. He had no past medical history, took no regular medications, and had no known drug allergies. He had no history of psychiatric illness and no family history of psychiatric disorders. He was a farmer living in a rural area and had no formal employment.
On admission, his vital signs were as follows: Respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, regular heart rate of 76 beats per minute, the patient was febrile with a temperature reading of 37.2 C and a blood pressure of 131/76 mmHg. His chest was clear anteriorly. Neurological examination revealed increased muscle tone and mild neck stiffness, but both Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs were negative.
Laboratory investigations on admission showed a markedly elevated procalcitonin level of 27.68 [0-0.05] ng/mL, heparin-binding protein of 75 [0-15] ng/mL and C- reactive protein level of 69.45 [0-8] mg/L. The white blood cell count was 6.46 x 109/L and the platelet count was decreased at 87 x 109/L. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a white blood cell count of 1 [0-10] /microL, protein levels of 1038 [150-450] mg/L, and glucose levels of 3.18 [2.8-4.4] mmol/L. Liver and kidney function tests revealed elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 128.7 [9-50] U/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 115.2 [15-40] U/L, with a serum creatinine level of 101.8 [57-97] micromol/L. The COVID-19 reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction test was negative.
Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities and patchy consolidations in both lungs (Fig. 1). Brain magnetic resonance (MRI) showed multiple, mildly asymmetric lesions with slightly prolonged T1 and T2 signals involving the bilateral parietal lobes, centrum semiovale, bilateral thalami, brainstem, and bilateral cerebellum. The lesions appeared slightly hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and hyperintense on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), with no significant enhancement on post-contrast images (Fig. 2). The imaging findings were considered most consistent with inflammatory lesions.
Cerebrospinal fluid Metagenomic Next-generation Sequencing (mNGS) confirmed leptospiral infection. Empirical antibiotics were adjusted from intravenous vancomycin (1000 mg q12h) and intravenous meropenem (1000 mg q8h) to definitive penicillin sodium (40 WU q8h). The patient achieved marked clinical improvement within two weeks, with follow-up MRI showing a significant reduction of the CNS lesions and chest CT revealing marked resolution of pulmonary infiltrates (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Approximately three years after the initial leptospiral infection, the patient developed progressive behavioral and psychiatric abnormalities. According to his family, he became increasingly irritable, emotionally unstable, and preoccupied with trivial matters. He exhibited persistent persecutory delusions, believing that his neighbors were encroaching on his land, and reacted with anger when family members attempted to reason with him. Episodes of auditory and visual hallucinations were reported, including hearing indistinct voices and seeing shadow-like figures. His personality gradually changed:he became socially withdrawn, rigid in thinking, and occasionally impulsive, including loudly singing patriotic songs to "protest" perceived injustices. A follow-up brain MRI performed in October 2025 revealed chronic lacunar infarctions in the pons, right thalamus, and bilateral basal ganglia, Fazekas grade 2 white matter degeneration, and a stable arachnoid cyst in the cisterna magna, but no evidence of active inflammation or recurrence. Neurology consultation suggested that his symptoms likely reflected a combination of post-meningitic neuropsychiatric sequelae and emotional dysregulation rather than a primary psychiatric disorder.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male presenting with a 3-day history of fever, chills, vomiting, and recurrent convulsions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 3 days prior to admission with abrupt fever and chills peaking at 40 °C, which failed to improve with over-the-counter cold medications. On the second day of illness, he developed recurrent generalized seizures accompanied by vomiting of gastric contents, followed by progressive deterioration of consciousness leading to emergency hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history, no regular medications, no known drug allergies. No personal or family history of psychiatric illness. Occupation: farmer living in a rural area of Jiangxi province, China.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports acute fever, shaking chills, nausea, vomiting of gastric contents, recurrent generalized seizures, and altered level of consciousness. Home medications: over-the-counter cold medication. Allergies: no known drug allergies.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: body temperature 37.2 °C (febrile peak 40 °C prior to admission), regular heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 131/76 mmHg. Chest: clear to auscultation anteriorly. Neurological: altered consciousness, increased generalized muscle tone, mild neck stiffness; negative Brudzinski and Kernig signs.

Complete blood count: white blood cell count 6.46 x 10^9/L, platelet count decreased at 87 x 10^9/L. Liver and renal panel: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 128.7 U/L (ref 9-50), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 115.2 U/L (ref 15-40), serum creatinine 101.8 mcmol/L (ref 57-97). COVID-19 RT-PCR: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: cerebrospinal fluid WBC count 1/mcL (ref 0-10), protein elevated at 1038 mg/L (ref 150-450), glucose 3.18 mmol/L (ref 2.8-4.4). Chest CT: diffuse ground-glass opacities and patchy consolidations in bilateral lungs; follow-up CT demonstrated marked radiographic resolution of pulmonary infiltrates. Brain MRI: multiple, mildly asymmetric lesions with slightly prolonged T1 and T2 signals involving bilateral parietal lobes, centrum semiovale, bilateral thalami, brainstem, and bilateral cerebellum; slightly hyperintense on DWI and FLAIR without significant contrast enhancement, consistent with inflammatory lesions; 2-week follow-up MRI showed marked lesion regression; 3-year follow-up MRI showed chronic lacunar infarctions (pons, right thalamus, basal ganglia), Fazekas grade 2 white matter degeneration, and stable cisterna magna arachnoid cyst without active inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospiral meningoencephalitis with diffuse inflammatory CNS lesions, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, acute hepatitis, and thrombocytopenia, definitively confirmed by cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) positive for Leptospira. Ruled out COVID-19 infection. Long-term course was complicated 3 years later by post-meningitic neuropsychiatric sequelae (persecutory delusions, auditory and visual hallucinations, irritability, emotional dysregulation, and personality change) rather than a primary psychiatric illness.
Plan & Treatment: Initial empiric antimicrobial coverage with intravenous vancomycin (1000 mg q12h) and intravenous meropenem (1000 mg q8h), de-escalated to targeted intravenous penicillin sodium (40 WU q8h) following mNGS pathogen confirmation. Supportive anticonvulsant and neurologic care; outpatient neuropsychiatric evaluation and supportive management for late sequelae.
Outcome: Acute clinical and radiographic resolution within two weeks, with marked clearance of pulmonary infiltrates and brain lesions; late development of post-encephalitic behavioral and psychiatric symptoms at three years.

raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old male was referred to Infectious Disease Clinic of Hamadan Sina Hospital in summer 2008 with acute onset of fever, headache, malaise, sweating and low back pain. On examination, the patient was conscious and his temperature was 39 C. There were no obvious systemic findings such as organomegaly on physical examination. Laboratory test findings were: white blood cell (WBC) count of 13350 (Neutrophil: 85%), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 48m/h, CRP+, RF-, ANA-, Wright's agglutination titer of 1/1280. Results of serologic testing for syphilis, hepatitis, tuberculosis and AIDS were negative. Outcomes of a lumbar puncture were normal. Blood levels, for sugar, sodium and potassium were normal. Blood cultures were negative and electrocardiogram and chest-X-ray (CXR) were normal. The patient was diagnosed with brucellosis, and treated with rifampin 600 mg/day and doxycycline 100 mg/twice daily.
After a week, the patient was referred for an Ophthalmology consult with complaints of ocular pain and redness and visual complaints. On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity in both eyes was 20/25. There was diffuse conjunctival injection bilaterally which was more prominent in the right eye. The conjunctional injection was a mixture of ciliary injection, episcleritis and conjunctivitis but more severe in the ciliary area. Neither eye had signs of intraocular inflammation. Pupillary light reflexes were sluggish bilaterally but no afferent pupillary defect was present. The patient was orthophoric without any muscle involvement and there was no diplopia. On funduscopy, there was bilateral optic disc swelling along with retinal hyperemia (optic disc hyperemia and vascular tortuosity) and diffuse intraretinal hemorrhage [Figure 1]. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 26 mmHg in the right eye and 24 mmHg in the left eye. The patient was hospitalized with a probable diagnosis of ocular brucellosis and was treated with co-trimoxazole adult two tablets, three times a day (tid), rifampin 600 mg/day doxycycline 100 mg/BID and prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 2 months. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging studies of the brain and optic nerve were requested. Both studies were unremarkable. A brief visual field limitation was reported on perimetry. Fever and headache diminished within 48 hours of the treatment however, ophthalmic complaints lingered. One week after treatment, visual acuity improved to 20/20. Conjunctival hyperemia had decreased but previous funduscopic findings remained unchanged. IOP was 19 mmHg OD and 16 mmHg OS using timolol. Four weeks after treatment, there were no visual complaints. Optic disc swelling and hyperemia had decreased and IOP bilaterally was within normal limits. Thirteen months after treatment, the funduscopic examination was normal [Figure 2].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presented with acute onset of fever (39 °C), headache, malaise, sweating, and low back pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in summer 2008 with acute onset of fever, headache, malaise, diaphoresis, and low back pain. He was evaluated at an infectious disease clinic and prescribed antimicrobial therapy. One week later, while on treatment, he developed new bilateral ocular pain, redness, and visual disturbances, prompting urgent ophthalmologic consultation and hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Denied prior chronic medical conditions. Prior antibiotic use and animal or unpasteurized dairy exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Low back pain, malaise, diaphoresis, headache, bilateral ocular pain, redness, and visual disturbances; denied diplopia. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious and alert; body temperature: 39 °C. Systemic exam: no organomegaly or other abnormal findings. Ophthalmic examination: visual acuity 20/25 in both eyes; diffuse conjunctival injection bilaterally (more prominent OD) consisting of ciliary injection, episcleritis, and conjunctivitis; pupillary light reflexes sluggish bilaterally without afferent pupillary defect; orthophoric without extraocular muscle palsy or diplopia; intraocular pressure (IOP) 26 mmHg OD and 24 mmHg OS. Funduscopy: bilateral optic disc swelling, optic disc hyperemia, vascular tortuosity, and diffuse intraretinal hemorrhage.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 13,350/mm^3 (neutrophils 85%); ESR: 48 mm/h; CRP: positive; Rheumatoid factor (RF): negative; ANA: negative; Blood sugar, sodium, and potassium: normal. Blood cultures: negative. CXR: normal. ECG: normal. Serologic tests for syphilis, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: normal CSF analysis. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain and optic nerves: unremarkable. Visual field perimetry: brief visual field limitation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neuro-ocular brucellosis presenting with bilateral optic disc swelling (papillitis), diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages, episcleritis, conjunctivitis, and secondary ocular hypertension.
Confirmation: Wright's serum agglutination test positive at a titer of 1/1280.
Differentials ruled out: Syphilis, viral hepatitis, tuberculosis, HIV/AIDS, intracranial space-occupying lesions or cerebral venous thrombosis (normal brain/optic nerve CT and MRI), and bacterial meningitis (normal CSF).
Treatment & Outcome: Initially treated with oral rifampin (600 mg/day) and doxycycline (100 mg BID). Upon developing ocular complications, admitted and intensified to triple therapy with adult co-trimoxazole (2 tablets TID), rifampin (600 mg/day), doxycycline (100 mg BID), and systemic prednisolone (1 mg/kg/day) for 2 months, along with topical timolol. Fever and headache resolved within 48 hours; visual acuity improved to 20/20 at 1 week with IOP decreasing to 19 mmHg OD and 16 mmHg OS; visual complaints and disc edema resolved by 4 weeks; normal funduscopy confirmed at 13-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
In June 2021, a 7-year-old male without comorbidities from the south of Bahia (northeastern Brazil), residing in a peri-urban area, reported fever, chills, fatigue, headache, myalgia, dyspnea, pallor, apathy, and reduced food intake. Other family members reported similar symptoms. The patient was transferred to a reference hospital for infectious diseases in Salvador/Bahia. The patient presented with pallor, tachycardia, and tachypnea without signs of respiratory distress. A physical examination revealed painless hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Laboratory tests identified hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, hematocrit 17.4%, leukocytes 5,820/mm3 and platelets 50,000/microL. The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) IgM rapid test result was positive, although the nasal swab SARS-CoV-2 reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) result was negative. 
Although a non-malaria-endemic region, a recent malaria outbreak was confirmed in a rural settlement neighboring the region where the patient and his family resided. A rapid test for malaria was positive for P. vivax, confirmed by microscopy and quantitative PCR (qPCR) after genomic DNA extraction from slides (). A thin blood-smear examination identified 378.3 parasites/microL of blood, parasitemia of half a cross. The patient was initially treated with three doses of intravenous artesunate 2.4 mg/kg/dose every 12 h, then two doses of 2.4 mg/kg/dose daily, followed by oral chloroquine with primaquine, resulting in full recovery.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old male presenting with fever, chills, fatigue, headache, myalgia, dyspnea, pallor, and apathy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 7-year-old boy from south Bahia, Brazil, presented with fever, chills, fatigue, headache, myalgia, dyspnea, marked pallor, apathy, and reduced oral intake of acute onset. Other family members experienced similar febrile illness. Due to progressive symptoms, he was transferred to a reference hospital for infectious diseases in Salvador, Bahia.
subjective.past_medical_history: No known comorbidities. Epidemiological exposure: resided in a peri-urban area of south Bahia (extra-Amazonian, non-endemic region) adjacent to a rural settlement experiencing a confirmed malaria outbreak.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, fatigue, headache, myalgia, dyspnea, pallor, apathy, and anorexia. Denied nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary complaints. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Significant pallor, tachycardia, and tachypnea without signs of respiratory distress. Abdomen: painless hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests: hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, hematocrit 17.4%, leukocytes 5,820/mm3, and platelets 50,000/microL. Rapid point-of-care test for SARS-CoV-2 IgM was positive, but nasopharyngeal swab SARS-CoV-2 RT-qPCR was negative. Peripheral blood smear performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium vivax malaria complicated by severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (50,000/microL), and hepatosplenomegaly, occurring within an extra-Amazonian outbreak in northeastern Brazil.
Diagnostic confirmation: Rapid diagnostic test positive for Plasmodium vivax; confirmed by thin blood smear microscopy demonstrating 378.3 parasites/microL (parasitemia of half a cross) and slide-extracted genomic DNA quantitative PCR (qPCR).
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous artesunate at 2.4 mg/kg/dose every 12 hours for three doses, followed by two daily doses of 2.4 mg/kg/dose, and completed with oral chloroquine and primaquine, achieving complete parasitological and clinical cure.

raw_case_text:
A 27-day-old boy presented to the emergency room with a 7-hour history of fever. After giving superficial skin cooling at home, the baby remained febrile. The peak temperature was 38.5 C. The baby had a poor appetite and symptoms of sneezing and a stuffy nose without vomiting and coughing. He was a term baby without extraordinary perinatal history. His parents had a history of sore throat and cough for several days during the Omicron epidemic, but they didn't test for SARS-CoV-2. After admission to our NICU, he was febrile at 38.3 C with a respiratory rate of 52 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 95%-99% while breathing ambient air. His examination was remarkable for congested nares, clear rhinorrhea, and mild subcostal retractions. There were coarse breath sounds in all lung fields. No murmur of the heart could be heard. The liver was palpated at 1 cm-2 cm under the costal margin (consistent with age), and the spleen was not palpated. Laboratory data revealed that the total WBC count and the proportions of the major leukocyte subsets in peripheral blood were normal. Blood gas, C reactive protein (CRP), and transaminase levels were in the normal range. RNA test for SARS-CoV-2 from a throat swab was positive. Then, the baby was given physical cooling and nasal secretion removal to keep the airway clear (see Table 1).
The baby presented febrile once daily in the following four days, and the peak temperature decreased from 38.4 to 38 C. Meanwhile, he developed a cough and sputum, along with a dropping of SpO2 to 80% when feeding. His lung demonstrated scattered crackles (see Figure 1). Because of continuous fever and pneumonia, more investigations were performed. The total WBC count and the proportions of the major leukocyte subsets were still in the normal range. CRP was 4.3 mg/L (0-10 mg/L). Anemia was noticed: RBC was 2.73 x 1,012/L, hemoglobin was 91.0 g/L, and hematocrit was 27.4%. Alanine transaminase (ALT) was 88 U/L(<=41 U/L), aspartate transaminase (AST) was 180 IU/L(<=40 U/L), and glutamyltranspeptidase (gamma-GT) was 109 U/L(6-42 U/L). Further, pathogens tests identified that parainfluenza virus RNA was positive, but there was no evidence of infection for other pathogens such as RSV, EBV, TORCH, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus (CA16/CVB), influenza A/B/H1N1/H3N2, adenovirus, mycoplasma, chlamydia, HIV, Human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, and hepatitis B/C virus. Ultrasonography for the heart and abdomen was normal. Therefore, the baby was given the nebulization treatment of budesonide and ipratropium bromide solution and given Glutathione for hepatoprotection. In addition, he inhaled oxygen intermittently to avoid hypoxia when feeding.
On the 7th day after admission, the patient was no longer febrile but was still coughing and had nasal congestion. On the 10th day, respiratory symptoms improved greatly, and we re-tested the liver function after 5 days of hepatoprotective treatment. The transaminase level elevated markedly. ALT was up to 645 U/L(<=41 U/L), AST increased to 480 IU/L(<=40 U/L), and gamma-GT was 491 U/L(6-42 U/L). However, bilirubin, blood ammonia, blood glucose, lipids, lactate, coagulation function, and albumin levels were within the normal range. The patient's perinatal medical history and family history were tracked carefully, and the possibility of inherited metabolic liver disease was ruled out. Furthermore, the patient's history of drug exposure before/after admission was also reviewed, and there was no evidence of drug-induced liver injury. So, virus infection may contribute to liver injury and the elevation of transaminase levels. When the immune system clears the virus, the injury should be alleviated. Thus, we only administered glycyrrhizin and bicyclol to promote recovery.
On the 14th day, the baby looked well with the normal physical examination. Laboratory tests demonstrated that ALT decreased to 125 U/L(<=41 U/L), AST was 44 IU/L(<=40 U/L), and gamma-GT was 283 U/L(6-42 U/L). He continued to take glycyrrhizin and bicyclol after being discharged home. The liver transaminase level returned to normal on 8 and 15 days after discharge (see Table 2 and Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-day-old male infant presenting with a 7-hour history of fever with a peak temperature of 38.5 °C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 27-day-old male infant presented with a 7-hour history of fever up to 38.5 °C that persisted despite superficial skin cooling at home. He exhibited poor appetite, sneezing, and nasal congestion, without vomiting or cough. Over the subsequent four days of hospitalization, he experienced daily fever spikes (38.0–38.4 °C), developed a cough with sputum production, and exhibited transient oxygen desaturations to 80% during feeds.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born at full term with an uneventful perinatal history. Epidemiological exposure: parents had a several-day history of sore throat and cough during a respiratory viral epidemic.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, poor appetite, sneezing, stuffy nose, rhinorrhea, and subsequent productive cough with feeding-related desaturations. Negative for vomiting. Home medications: none documented. Drug allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.3 °C, respiratory rate: 52 breaths/min, SpO2: 95%–99% on ambient air (dropping to 80% during feeds). Head and neck: congested nares with clear rhinorrhea. Respiratory: mild subcostal retractions, coarse breath sounds throughout all lung fields, with scattered crackles noted on follow-up. Cardiovascular: regular rate, no murmurs. Abdomen: liver palpable 1–2 cm below the costal margin; spleen not palpable. Day 14: examination normalized.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: total WBC count and leukocyte subsets normal; blood gas, CRP, and transaminases within normal ranges. Follow-up labs: WBC and leukocyte subsets remained normal; CRP: 4.3 mg/L (reference: 0–10 mg/L); RBC: 2.73 x 10^12/L; hemoglobin: 91.0 g/L; hematocrit: 27.4%. Initial hepatic panel: ALT: 88 U/L (reference: <=41 U/L), AST: 180 IU/L (reference: <=40 U/L), gamma-GT: 109 U/L (reference: 6–42 U/L). Peak hepatic panel (day 10): ALT: 645 U/L, AST: 480 IU/L, gamma-GT: 491 U/L; total bilirubin, blood ammonia, blood glucose, lipid panel, serum lactate, coagulation profile, and serum albumin were within normal limits. Day 14 labs: ALT: 125 U/L, AST: 44 IU/L, gamma-GT: 283 U/L. Echocardiogram and abdominal ultrasound: normal. Respiratory multiplex PCR: parainfluenza virus RNA positive; negative for RSV, influenza A/B/H1N1/H3N2, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and Chlamydia. Serologies/virology: negative for EBV, TORCH panel, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus (CA16/CVB), HIV, and hepatitis B/C viruses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Neonatal COVID-19 pneumonia with acute viral-induced liver injury and secondary parainfluenza virus co-infection, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RNA reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) from a throat swab. Inherited metabolic liver diseases and drug-induced liver injury were ruled out. Management & Plan: Physical cooling, airway clearance, intermittent oxygen supplementation during feeding, and nebulized budesonide and ipratropium bromide. Hepatoprotective therapy initiated with intravenous glutathione, followed by oral glycyrrhizin and bicyclol. Transaminases showed substantial improvement by day 14 (ALT 125 U/L, AST 44 IU/L) and completely normalized at 8 and 15 days post-discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old Omani female not known to have any significant medical history was referred to our hospital with a history of upper abdominal discomfort more localized to the epigastric region and associated with jaundice and dark urine. There was no history of fever or night sweat nor history of travel. On physical examination, the patient was jaundice; otherwise, the systemic examination was unremarkable.
Complete blood count was within normal limits with a normal white blood count (6.3 10*g/L). Liver function test revealed a picture of obstructive jaundice with a total bilirubin of 52 umil/L, Alkaline phosphatase 302 [iU] /L, and Alanine transaminase 457 [iU]/L. QuantiFERON-Tb gold test was positive.
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis showed a lobulated and heterogeneous liver hilar mass with a central necrosis, measuring 2.4 x 3.9 cm. The mass was obstructing the proximal common hepatic duct resulting in dilatation of the intrahepatic biliary tree (Figure 1). The mass was associated with multiple enlarged peripancreatic, porta hepatis and hepatoduodenal lymph nodes, measuring up to 1.2 cm. None of the lymph nodes were showing central necrosis. Features were suggestive of a cholangiocarcinoma of the common hepatic duct. Further work-up with a liver MRI redemonstrated the porta hepatis mass. The mass was T2 hyperintense and T1 hypointense and showed moderate enhancement on postcontrast sequence with severe diffuse restriction (Figures 2 and 3). On MRCP, the mass was causing severe narrowing of the proximal 1.8 cm of the common hepatic duct, reaching the confluence and causing moderate dilation of the intrahepatic biliary tree. In addition, the MRI revealed multiple foci of restriction scattered throughout the liver and some of them showed subtle enhancement on postcontrast sequence suggestive of liver microabscess (Figure 3).Constellation of MRI findings was suggestive of localized TB of the porta hepatis; however, neoplastic lesion such as rhabdomyosarcoma and lymphoma could not be excluded and further evaluation with a tissue biopsy was advised. Chest radiograph was normal. Tumor markers were within normal limits including Cancer Ag 19-9 (CA 19-9): 8U/mL (range, 0-37U/mL), Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA): 1.2 ug/L (range, 0-3ug/L), Alpha fetoprotein: 1.1 ug/L (range 0-15), and Chromogranin A: 47ug/L (range 26-92ug/L)
The patient underwent laparoscopic biopsy and was found to have enlarged porta hepatis lymph nodes. Biopsy was taken from the porta hepatis mass and histopathological examination showed a granulomatous inflammatory process. Although, no definite proof was obtained by culture or polymerase chain reaction (PCR), probable TB diagnosis was made based on the histological and imaging findings, and the patient was treated for 6 months with Rifampicin 150 mg and Isoniazid 75 mg. The patient showed significant response to treatment with dramatic improvement of liver function test. A follow-up liver function test 3 months after starting anti-TB medication showed normalization of Alkaline phosphatase 91 [iU] /L along with improvement of total bilirubin of 24 umil/L and Alanine transaminase 211 [iU]/L. After completion of anti-TB medication, liver function test was back to normal with a total bilirubin of 17 umil/L, Alkaline phosphatase 58 [iU] /L, and Alanine transaminase 16 [iU]/L. A follow-up CT abdomen was performed 10 months later and showed complete resolution of porta hepatis mass and intrahepatic biliary dilatation along with significant regression of previously noted enlarged upper abdomen lymph nodes.

Tumor markers: CA 19-9 8 U/mL (reference 0-37 U/mL), CEA 1.2 ug/L (reference 0-3 ug/L), alpha-fetoprotein 1.1 ug/L (reference 0-15 ug/L), chromogranin A 47 ug/L (reference 26-92 ug/L).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Probable tuberculosis of the porta hepatis presenting as an obstructive hilar mass mimicking cholangiocarcinoma, confirmed by positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold test and histopathology demonstrating granulomatous inflammation; tissue culture and PCR yielded no definite microbiological amplification. Cholangiocarcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, and lymphoma were ruled out.
Treatment and outcome: Treated for 6 months with rifampicin 150 mg/day and isoniazid 75 mg/day. Liver function tests significantly improved at 3 months (alkaline phosphatase 91 IU/L, total bilirubin 24 umol/L, ALT 211 IU/L) and fully normalized upon treatment completion (total bilirubin 17 umol/L, ALP 58 IU/L, ALT 16 IU/L). Follow-up abdominal CT at 10 months showed complete resolution of the porta hepatis mass and intrahepatic biliary dilatation, with marked regression of upper abdominal lymphadenopathy.

raw_case_text: A 34-year-old man presented with weight loss, progressively worsening gait, confusion, back pain and urinary incontinence. Initial examination of both lower extremities showed Muscle Power Assessment (MRC) 3 out of 5 in both extremities, spastic paraparesis with brisk knee reflexes, absent ankle jerk and diffuse sensory deficits. Skin examination was notable for seborrheic dermatitis and oral thrush. Initial laboratory workup showed lymphopenia with absolute lymphocyte count of 0.90 K/microL (normal 1-4.8 K/microL). MRI brain showed increased T2 signal intensity throughout the periventricular and juxtacortical white matter extending along the corticospinal tracts in the brain stem (Figure 1). MRI of the cervical spine was normal, while imaging of the thoracic spine showed mild diffuse cord atrophy most apparent from T3 to T10 (Figures 2 and 3). MRI lumbar spine showed a small right paracentral disc extrusion at the level of L5-S1 (Figure 4). Lumbar puncture was negative for syphilis, toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcus, Cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr Virus. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) counts were notable for elevated protein to 163 mg/dL and total white blood cell (WBC) count of 36 cells/microL with 95% lymphocytes. A fourth-generation HIV Ag/Ab assay was found to be positive. Initial HIV viral load was 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count was 89 cells/microL. He was started on emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and Raltegravir. Later, his Raltegravir was switched to dolutegravir.

Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: Protein elevated at 163 mg/dL, total WBC count 36 cells/microL with 95% lymphocytes; CSF studies negative for syphilis, toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcus, Cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus.

Definitive diagnosis: Newly diagnosed advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection complicated by HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy, HIV encephalopathy, and oral candidiasis.
Confirmatory Testing: Fourth-generation HIV Ag/Ab assay positive; baseline plasma HIV RNA viral load 300,000 copies/mL; baseline CD4+ T-cell count 89 cells/microL. CSF infectious workup ruled out neurosyphilis, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, CMV, and EBV.
Treatment & Course: Combination antiretroviral therapy was initiated with emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate plus raltegravir, subsequently transitioned to emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and dolutegravir.

raw_case_text: A 15-year-old boy, presented with a right leg swelling, which increased in size over 2 months. There was no history of fever or weight loss. Radiograph of right lower limb showed a lytic sclerotic mass in proximal meta-diaphysis of right fibula, which on biopsy was suggestive of Ewing's sarcoma. Whole body 18F-fluoro-deoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (FDG PET/CT) was performed as a part of staging work-up. Maximum intensity projection (MIP) image [Figure 1a] showed intense focus of tracer uptake in the right leg (arrow) and liver (arrow-head). Axial fused PET/CT images revealed intense tracer uptake in destructive lytic-sclerotic soft tissue mass in upper end of right fibula, with a maximum standardized uptake value (max SUV in milliCurie/kilogram of body weight) of 7.8. An intense solitary focus of FDG uptake was seen in hypodense lesion in caudate lobe of liver [Figure 1c - arrow], which was presumed to be metastatic on the basis of imaging findings. It measured 16 mm in transverse dimensions with a max SUV of 8.2. Rest of the study was unremarkable, except for reactive mediastinal nodes. Subsequently, patient underwent induction chemotherapy for 6 weeks. Follow-up FDG PET/CT study after treatment completion showed complete regression of tracer concentration at primary site in tibia on MIP image [Figure 1b - arrow], as well as reduction in size of the soft tissue mass with post treatment healing changes in the fibula seen on axial CT images. Contrary to this, the focal hepatic lesion in caudate lobe of liver showed significant increase in size and metabolic activity [Figure 1b - arrow head]; measuring 31 mm, with max SUV of 14.6 on axial fused PET/CT images [Figure 1d - arrow]. This prompted a histological correlation and fine-needle aspiration (FNA) was done from the liver lesion. Microscopic examination showed collection of epitheloid cells on Papanicolaou Stain [Figure 2a - arrows and Figure 2b] with pale oval shaped cells showing slipper shaped nuclei [Figure 2b - inset]. These findings were confirmatory for tuberculous etiology. Patient was immediately started on antituberculosis treatment, and follow-up is awaited.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-year-old boy presented with a right leg swelling that had enlarged over 2 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 15-year-old boy presented with progressive swelling of the right leg over 2 months. Lower limb radiography and biopsy of the proximal meta-diaphysis of the right fibula established a primary diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma. Staging whole-body FDG PET/CT revealed a hypermetabolic caudate liver lesion presumed to be metastasis. He completed 6 weeks of induction chemotherapy, after which repeat PET/CT showed response in the fibular lesion but paradoxical progression of the hepatic lesion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Proximal right fibular Ewing sarcoma diagnosed on biopsy; status post 6 weeks of induction chemotherapy. No prior tuberculosis history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denied fever, weight loss, or other systemic complaints. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right leg swelling corresponding to fibular mass. Remainder of physical examination normal.

objective.advanced_workup: Staging whole-body 18F-FDG PET/CT: intense tracer uptake in right fibula destructive mass (max SUV 7.8) and solitary hypodense lesion in caudate lobe of liver measuring 16 mm (max SUV 8.2); reactive mediastinal nodes. Post-chemotherapy PET/CT: complete metabolic regression of primary fibular mass with bone healing changes, but interval enlargement of caudate lobe liver lesion to 31 mm with increased metabolic activity (max SUV 14.6). Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of liver lesion: collection of epithelioid cells on Papanicolaou stain with pale oval-shaped cells and slipper-shaped nuclei.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Hepatic tuberculosis mimicking metastatic disease in a patient with Ewing sarcoma, confirmed by liver fine-needle aspiration cytology demonstrating epithelioid cell collections with characteristic slipper-shaped nuclei on Papanicolaou stain diagnostic of tuberculous etiology. Primary Ewing sarcoma demonstrated complete metabolic response to 6 weeks of induction chemotherapy while the hepatic lesion progressed due to untreated tuberculosis. Management & Outcome: Initiated immediately on antituberculosis treatment; ongoing clinical monitoring maintained.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old female presented with the left dull mid-back pain for 3 months' duration. The pain was moderate and radiated to the left breast/precordium. The physical examination just revealed focal tenderness over the inferior angle of the left scapula/7th costovertebral junction, without swelling or erythema.
The patient had a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 and C-reactive protein of 6. Serological testing for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C was all negative.
The anteroposterior X-rays of the thoracic spine showed that the T7 vertebral body was scalloped on the left side, and there erosion of the T7 left pedicle and adjoining rib [Figure 1]. The MR showed; a left-sided T7 enhancing periarticular erosive lesion, marrow edema in the posteromedial portion of the left 7th rib, the left posterolateral portion of the T7 vertebral body, and lateral left T7 pedicle. There was also thickening/ enhancement of the synovium of the left 7th costotransverse joint with enhancing soft tissue elevating the overlying pleura, and abutting the descending aorta [Figure 2]. A CT-guided biopsy was diagnostic for TB; it demonstrated caseous necrosis with epithelioid and Langerhans giant cells [Figure 3]. In addition, GeneXpert detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis that showed sensitivity to both isoniazid and rifampicin.
ATT for the first 4 months included rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (HRZE) (intensive phase). For the next 8 months, the patient received rifampicin and isoniazid (HR) (continuation phase). At follow-up (12 months), the patient showed clinical and radiological signs of healing [Figure 4].

subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 25-year-old female presented with a 3-month history of moderate, dull left mid-back pain radiating anteriorly to the left breast/precordium.
subjective.past_medical_history: Denies prior medical conditions, hospitalizations, prior antituberculous treatment, travel, or TB exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports left mid-back pain radiating to breast/precordium; denies fever, cough, night sweats, weight loss, or focal neurological deficits. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.routine_investigations: ESR: 40 mm/h; CRP: 6 mg/L; HIV, HBV, HCV serologies: negative; AP thoracic spine X-ray: scalloping of left T7 vertebral body with erosion of T7 left pedicle and adjoining rib.
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic spine MRI: left-sided T7 enhancing periarticular erosive lesion; marrow edema in posteromedial portion of left 7th rib, left posterolateral portion of T7 vertebral body, and lateral left T7 pedicle; synovial thickening/enhancement of left 7th costotransverse joint with soft tissue elevating overlying pleura and abutting descending aorta. CT-guided core biopsy: caseous necrosis with epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans giant cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Extrapulmonary musculoskeletal tuberculosis involving the left T7 vertebra, pedicle, 7th rib, and costotransverse joint (tuberculous costovertebral arthritis and spondylitis).
Confirmation: CT-guided biopsy showed caseous necrosis with epithelioid and Langhans giant cells; GeneXpert of biopsy specimen detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with demonstrated sensitivity to isoniazid and rifampicin.
Differentials ruled out: Primary bone neoplasm, metastatic malignancy, pyogenic spondylodiscitis, HIV and viral hepatitis (seronegative).
Treatment & Outcome: 12-month anti-tuberculosis therapy: 4 months of intensive HRZE (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), followed by 8 months of continuation HR (rifampicin, isoniazid). Complete clinical resolution of pain and radiological bone healing confirmed at 12-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 54-year-old Hispanic male who was diagnosed with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), and AIDS-related cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma (KS; affecting his nose, back, and left leg) 1 year earlier was seen by his primary care physician (PCP) with cough and exertional dyspnea. He was empirically treated with amoxicillin, but failed to show clinical improvement. During a follow-up visit to his PCP, he was noted to be hypoxemic on room air and was sent to our hospital emergency department for further evaluation.
At the time of his initial HIV diagnosis 9 months earlier, he was found to have a CD4 count of <20 (500-1,600) with 2% (25-65%) CD4 cells. Following the diagnosis, he was started on appropriate prophylactic therapy for opportunistic infections as well as highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Unfortunately, he consistently demonstrated a lack of adherence to his medications. One month after the initial HIV diagnosis, he was noted to have systemic KS involving the pulmonary tree and bone marrow following presentation with hemoptysis and pancytopenia. Both processes were biopsy-proven. His HAART regimen was adjusted, and his symptoms and cell counts subsequently improved. He also underwent multiple cycles of chemotherapy with doxorubicin for the visceral involvement of KS.
In the emergency department, he was found to be hemodynamically stable with a low-grade fever and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. A computed tomography (CT) scan of his chest revealed a large pericardial effusion, but did not show any focal pulmonary infiltrates or evidence of pulmonary embolism. In light of these findings, he was admitted to the intensive care unit for closer monitoring. Concerns regarding poor adherence to his medications were again raised.
On the second day of his hospitalization, a transthoracic echocardiogram was done and revealed a large anterior and moderate posterior pericardial effusion with evidence of early pericardial tamponade. A CT scan of the chest also showed the pericardial effusion (Fig. 1). He underwent a pericardiocentesis, and 900 cc of bloody fluid was aspirated. A pericardial tube was placed, and this drained an additional 300 cc of bloody fluid. Laboratory examinations including serologic tests for acute EBV and CMV viral infections were negative. Pericardial fluid bacterial, fungal, and acid fast cultures were negative. Pericardial fluid cytology was also negative. However, the pericardial fluid cell count was compatible with hemopericardium. At that time, he had a viral load of 1,395 copies/ml, with a CD4 count of 113 (500-1,600). Multiple follow-up echocardiograms performed during the hospitalization showed stable small residual pericardial effusion, prompting removal of the pericardial tube on the fifth day of hospitalization. Given his stable disease and absence of recurrence of the effusion, treatment with anti-inflammatory agents was deferred. He was discharged on the sixth day with instructions for close follow-up visits with transthoracic echocardiogram and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan.
The follow-up PET/CT (Figs. 2-4) scan done after 2 months of discharge showed FDG avid areas in the right paratracheal (SUV of 9.8) and subcarinal (SUV 5.6) tissues representing pericardial involvement of KS. The scan also showed FDG avid areas in the left upper abdominal quadrant. It, however, failed to show any pulmonary tree or bone marrow involvement. A repeat PET/CT (Figs. 5, 6) done after 3 months to monitor the progression of the disease showed diminished metabolic activity in the previously seen right paratracheal and subcarinal regions with SUV up to 3.9 compared to 9.8 on the previous scan. There was also no subdiaphragmatic involvement.
In light of the improved appearance of the lesions, resolution of the pericardial effusion, and improved medication adherence, the patient was continued on the same HAART regimen with close monitoring, and the lesions were attributed to KS.

On follow-up, room air hypoxemia was documented, prompting urgent referral to the emergency department. Following admission, he was found to have a large pericardial effusion with early tamponade.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable, low-grade fever, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Dermatologic: Cutaneous Kaposi sarcoma lesions involving the nose, back, and left leg. Cardiovascular: Early pericardial tamponade physiology.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests: Serologic tests for acute EBV and CMV viral infections were negative. Pericardial fluid analysis: Aspirated bloody fluid compatible with hemopericardium; fluid bacterial, fungal, and acid-fast cultures were negative; cytology was negative for malignant cells.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Large pericardial effusion without focal pulmonary infiltrates or pulmonary embolism. Transthoracic echocardiogram (day 2): Large anterior and moderate posterior pericardial effusion with evidence of early pericardial tamponade; serial follow-up echocardiograms showed stable small residual effusion. Pericardiocentesis: Therapeutic aspiration of 900 cc of bloody fluid with an additional 300 cc drained via an indwelling pericardial tube. assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS; CD4 count 113 cells/microL, HIV viral load 1,395 copies/mL) complicated by visceral pericardial Kaposi sarcoma presenting as hemopericardium and early pericardial tamponade in the setting of medication non-adherence.
Plan & Outcome: Emergency pericardiocentesis with indwelling pericardial tube drainage (evacuating 1,200 cc bloody fluid total); pericardial tube removed on hospital day 5 following demonstration of stable residual effusion on repeat echocardiograms. Specific anti-inflammatory therapy was deferred. Discharged on hospital day 6 with counseling on medication adherence and continuation of HAART. Follow-up PET/CT scans confirmed substantial interval regression of pericardial Kaposi sarcoma lesions without recurrence of pericardial effusion.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 32-year-old man started to develop flu-like symptoms 1 day after returning from a Caribbean cruise trip, which stopped in Jamaica, Mexico, and the Cayman Islands. The trip included freshwater swimming at National Park, with no apparent animal contact. His symptoms persisted, and he presented to the hospital after 10 days of fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, myalgia, nonproductive cough, and worsening dyspnea. Physical examination revealed normal vital signs, jaundice, and bilateral conjunctival suffusions. Laboratory workup showed neutrophil-predominant (62%) leukocytosis (24.6 x 103/microL), thrombocytopenia (78 x 103/microL), creatinine level of 5.29 mg/dL, aspartate transaminase of 736 U/L, alanine transaminase of 495 U/L, and markedly elevated levels of direct bilirubin (17.8 mg/dL) and creatine kinase (2426 U/L). The initial chest x-ray (CXR) was unremarkable.
He was initially admitted to the regular floor, but 1 day after admission, he developed worsening multiorgan dysfunction and episodic hypotension requiring intensive care unit admission. After 36 h of arrival, the patient developed massive hemoptysis and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, leading to acute respiratory distress syndrome. He received hemodynamic support with norepinephrine and vasopressin, mechanical ventilation, and renal replacement therapy.
There was a high clinical suspicion for severe leptospirosis, based on his history of exposures, and the clinical presentation of liver failure, pulmonary hemorrhage, and neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis in a relevant time frame. He was therefore started on ceftriaxone and doxycycline. Leptospirosis indirect hemagglutination assay eventually yielded positive results, and the patient completed a 14-day course of doxycycline and 7 days of ceftriaxone.
Repeat CXR revealed extensive bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, Pao2/Fio2 ratio (P/F) remained below 30 mm Hg, and plateau pressures remained above 40 cm H2O despite optimized ventilator support, deep sedation, and paralysis. At that point, the decision was made to start veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) to facilitate gas exchange. Patient was cannulated in a femoral-femoral approach, and VV-ECMO was introduced without complications. Oxygen saturation prior to VV-ECMO initiation ranged from 74% to 80%, improving to 98% to 100% within minutes after ECMO initiation. Consequently, P/F ratio continued to improve dramatically, allowing for a lung-protective ventilation strategy.
Hemoptysis persisted during VV-ECMO despite an adjusted heparin protocol with a target activated clotting time (ACT) range of 160 to 180 seconds (standard ECMO regimen dictates an ACT range: 180-220 seconds), requiring the use of a significant amount of blood products. To stop and prevent further alveolar hemorrhage, and based on previous studies on ECMO patients, initiation of continuous aminocaproic acid infusion at 20 mL/h was tried after about 13 days on ECMO for a duration of 6 days, which presumably resulted in improved lung aeration and significantly decreased transfusion requirements. Due to persistent thrombocytopenia, he required multiple platelet transfusions to maintain a count of about 60 to 120 x 103/microL. The last unit of platelets was given about 15 days after presentation, around the same time of ECMO discontinuation, which coincides with his clinical improvement.
Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was discontinued after 18 days of therapy. The patient was extubated and discharged home to continue with outpatient rehabilitation after a 40-day hospitalization. He achieved a complete recovery and had evidence of normal pulmonary function tests at 6-month follow-up.

Within 24 hours of admission, he developed episodic hypotension and worsening multiorgan failure, progressing at 36 hours to massive hemoptysis and acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU transfer.
