assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Shewanella algae bacteremia and complicated chronic foot ulceration in a patient with newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection (CD4+ T-lymphocyte count 167 cells/microL, HIV-1 viral load 7,180 copies/mL). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive HIV antibody screening and confirmatory assay; Shewanella algae isolated concurrently from multiple blood cultures and wound pus swab. Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous cefotaxime and gentamicin for 10 days, resulting in bacteremic clearance and defervescence. Combination antiretroviral therapy was initiated with emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (FTC/TDF) plus dolutegravir (DTG). At 1-month follow-up, the patient remained afebrile, inflammatory markers normalized, and the foot ulcer was progressively healing.

raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old female returning traveler presented to an emergency room in South Carolina for evaluation of syncope. Thirteen days prior she had returned from a 10-day trip to Lagos, Nigeria, where she visited family. While in Lagos, she felt well. Six days after returning to the U.S., she developed nausea and diarrhea. Three days later, she developed fevers and sweats that occurred multiple times daily. Twelve days after returning to the U.S., she experienced two episodes of syncope and then sought medical care. She had no headache, neck stiffness, sore throat, or respiratory symptoms. She reported that while in Lagos, she stayed in a home in an urban environment. She used mosquito repellent with N, N-diethyl-meta-toluamide (DEET), and slept indoors with closed windows but no mosquito net. She did not recall any mosquito bites. While in Lagos, she ate food prepared in the home after purchase from a local grocery store, and she drank only bottled water. She did not recall having been in contact with anyone who was sick while she was in Lagos. She reported having taken a prescription medication for malaria prevention, but we were unable to verify this. She had received oral typhoid, yellow fever, hepatitis A, TDaP, influenza, and meningococcal vaccines within the preceding year. The recent trip was her third to Nigeria; she had been well during and after her previous two trips. She was born and raised in South Carolina and had no other international travel. She had no significant past medical history and was not taking any medications at the time of presentation. She worked as a manager at a retail clothing store.
On examination at presentation, the temperature was 100.8 , pulse 117/minute and regular, blood pressure 127/78, respirations 18/minute and unlabored, and O2 saturation was 99% breathing ambient air. She appeared comfortable, well-nourished, and not chronically ill. There was no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Lungs were clear. Heart sounds were normal aside from tachycardia, and there was no murmur. The abdomen was not tender, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. She was alert, and neurologic exam was unremarkable. Laboratory test results are shown in Table 1.
There was no hemoglobin detected in the urine. Blood cultures were drawn. Thick and thin blood smears were prepared and Giemsa-stained. Microscopic examination showed a microcytic normochromic anemia, numerous erythrocytes with trophozoite rings, and rare banana gametocytes characteristic of P. falciparum malaria. Parasitemia was 3.5%. Rapid malaria diagnostic testing using the BinaxNOW  Malaria test (Alere Inc., Waltham Massachusetts) was positive for P. falciparum. An ARCHITECT HIV Ag/Ab Combo (Abbott, Wiesbaden, Germany) test was negative. Nucleic acid amplification-based testing of a stool specimen was negative for adenovirus, Campylobacter, Cyclospora cayetanensis, Clostridium difficile, enteroaggregative Escherichia coli, enteropathogenic E. coli, enterotoxigenic E. coli, Shiga-like toxin producing E. coli, Shigella, enteroinvasive E. coli, Entamoeba histolytica, Giardia lamblia, human astrovirus, norovirus GI/GII, Plesiomonas shigelloides, rotavirus A, Salmonella, sapovirus, Vibrio, Vibrio cholera, and Yersinia enterocolitica (FilmArray  Gastrointestinal Panel, BioFire Diagnostics LLC, Salt Lake City, UT). At 48 hours of incubation, blood cultures obtained at presentation grew gram-negative rods identified as a Salmonella species by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. A triple sugar iron agar slant showed a nontyphoidal Salmonella phenotype. The isolate was identified as Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar stanleyville (1,4,12,27:z4,z23:[1,2]) by the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control Public Health Laboratory using serotyping with specific O and H antisera according to the Kaufman-White scheme. She was treated for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria with oral doxycycline and quinidine for 7 days. Fevers resolved by day 3 at the hospital and repeat blood smear remained negative for malaria 16 days later. For nontyphoidal Salmonella bacteremia, she was treated with ceftriaxone for 2 weeks; diarrhea and all other signs/symptoms resolved within 10 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old female presenting with two syncopal episodes, fevers, sweats, nausea, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient returned 13 days prior from a 10-day trip to Lagos, Nigeria. Six days after return, she developed nausea and diarrhea. Three days later, she began experiencing daily paroxysmal fevers and diaphoresis. Twelve days after return, she had two syncopal episodes prompting emergency medical presentation. She denied headache, neck stiffness, sore throat, or respiratory symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history; retail clothing store manager. International travel: 10-day visit to Lagos, Nigeria, returning 13 days prior; reported taking unverified malaria prophylaxis; vaccinated with typhoid, yellow fever, hepatitis A, TDaP, influenza, and meningococcal vaccines within the preceding year.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for nausea, watery diarrhea, fevers, chills, diaphoresis, and syncope; negative for headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, sore throat, cough, dyspnea, or chest pain.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 100.8 °F, heart rate 117 beats/min (tachycardia), blood pressure 127/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, SpO2 99% on room air. General: Well-nourished, comfortable, no distress. HEENT: Anicteric sclerae, no cervical lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular: Regular tachycardia, no murmurs. Respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended, no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurologic: Alert, oriented, non-focal.
objective.routine_investigations: Urinalysis: Negative for hemoglobin. Complete blood count: Microcytic normochromic anemia. HIV Ag/Ab Combo: Negative. Stool multiplex PCR (FilmArray GI Panel): Negative for common enteric viral, bacterial, and parasitic pathogens.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria (parasitemia 3.5%) co-infected with Salmonella enterica subspecies enterica serovar stanleyville bacteremia. Giemsa-stained blood smears revealed P. falciparum ring trophozoites and rare banana-shaped gametocytes; BinaxNOW Malaria rapid test was positive for P. falciparum. Blood cultures flagged positive at 48 hours for gram-negative bacilli confirmed as Salmonella enterica serovar stanleyville by MALDI-TOF and Kauffmann-White serotyping.
Plan & Outcome: Treated for falciparum malaria with oral quinidine and doxycycline for 7 days, with fever resolution by hospital day 3 and negative repeat blood smear 16 days later. Salmonella bacteremia was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone for 14 days, resulting in complete resolution of diarrhea and systemic symptoms within 10 days.

raw_case_text:
A 78-year-old male patient was referred to the Imam Reza Hospital, North Khorasan University of Medical Sciences, Bojnurd, Iran, for evaluation of disseminated skin lesions over the arm and hemithorax. As shown in Figure 1 , he presented with one-month history of multiple skin lesions, which started with a small furuncle on the left forelimb which progressed to other parts of the arm and hemithorax. He was originally resident in Esfarayen city in the Northeastern region of Iran, which is one of the new endemic regions of cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL). The patient declared that prior to the dissemination of the lesion, he had edema and lymphedema over the arm and hemithorax. Physical examination was remarkable for mild peripheral edema and lymphedema, but in radiological and laboratory tests, there were no abnormalities. At the time of physical examination, mild peripheral edema and lymphedema, but no systemic symptoms such as fever, hepatosplenomegaly were observed; however, he had a 10-year history of opium smoking abuse, as well as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD ) which had previously been treated with Salbutamol (100 microg/4 times (puffs) per day) and Fluticasone/Salmeterol Spray (250/50 microg twice a day). The patient was hospitalized with an initial suspicion of diffuse bacterial infection due to lymphedema, opium smoking and history of respiratory disease. Physical examination showed that he had multiple, disseminated and wet-looking skin lesions which were papular, crusted and severely ulcerated all over the left arm and hemithorax ( Figure 1 ). Furthermore, the patient's lesions spread to his palm and all over the left finger nails which are very rare manifestations. It should be noted that three days before referring to the hospital, the patient bandaged up the lesions with plastic covers; therefore, all covered parts turned into creamy, wet-looking and severely inflammatory lesions which looked like second-degree burn wounds.
A hypothesis of leishmaniasis was made, and further evaluation by direct examination of the skin of the wrist and forearm using lesion scraping by a vaccinostyle, under sterile conditions was performed (Giemsa staining) revealing abundant intracellular Leishmania amastigotes inside and outside host cells (3+ parasitemia grade: 1-10 parasites/microscopic field) ( Figure 2A ). In addition, for histopathological examination, punch biopsy of lesions of the wrist and forearm were performed (Hematoxylin and Eosin staining: H&E). Histopathological smears of wrist and forearm skin lesions revealed mild hyperkeratotic epidermis based on dermis infiltrated by numerous mixed inflammatory cells including abundant macrophages at dermis filled with amastigote forms of Leishmania ( Figure 2B ). Direct microscopy skin smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative. According to positive Giemsa-stained slide and skin biopsy, diagnosis of diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) was made Bone marrow aspiration showed no detectable Leishmania parasites among myelogenous elements. All routine laboratory tests of the patient were normal. Viral markers (HIVAb, HBSAg, HCVAb), and anti-Brucella Ab (Wright, Coombs Wright and 2-mercaptoethanol) were negative. In addition, serous fluid from the patient's skin lesion were cultured in Schneider's Drosophila medium (Sigma, Darmstadt, Germany), supplemented with 5% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (HI-FBS) (Sigma, Germany). Isolated parasites were subcultured and monitored regularly to check promastigotes growth. In this experiment, 2 x 10 parasites/mL at the logarithmic (2 days) growth phases were counted and used for DNA extraction.
Total genomic DNA of Leishmania parasites was extracted from cultured parasites and also from paraffin-embedded blocks of the patient's skin biopsy using the GF-1 DNA extraction kit (GF-1, Vivantis, Canada), and Leishmania ITS1 was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). For identification of Leishmania species by PCR-RFLP, the PCR product was digested using HaeIII ( BsuRI ) enzyme   ; L. major parasites were identified as the causative agents of DCL.
The patient's first PCR product was subjected to sequence analysis using the forward and reverse primers according to the manufacturer's instructions (Bioneer, South Korea). GenBank was searched for similar sequences and a significant similarity was found with other Leishmania species. The patient's ITS1 sequence was similar to the Iranian strain of L. major (AB04/HU64) (99%).
The patient was initially treated with a bilayer wet dressing that was coated with silver sulfadiazine and petroleum salve/ointment along with vancomycin (1 g/kg/per 12 h) and ceftriaxone (1 g/kg/per 12 h) as broad spectrum antibiotics. At the same time, he received antileishmanial therapy including: meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) 20 mg/kg/day for 10 days. Since he showed no significant improvement with Glucantime and developed pancytopenia as a complication of therapy, his treatment was discontinued at day 10. Consequently, he was placed on amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/per day for 10 days) and showed progressive and marked improvement of cutaneous lesions ( Figure 3 ).
During hospitalization and successful treatment, he developed a severe lung infection and disseminated bronchiectasis probably due to his history of opium abuse and COPD; therefore, he was admitted to ICU and unfortunately died because of a systemic bacterial superinfection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of disseminated skin lesions over his left arm and hemithorax.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 78-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of multiple skin lesions originating as a furuncle on the left forearm and disseminating to the arm and hemithorax. Prior to dissemination, he noticed edema and lymphedema over the arm and hemithorax. Three days before admission, he bandaged the lesions with plastic wrapping, resulting in macerated, wet, inflammatory lesions resembling second-degree burns. He was hospitalized with initial suspicion of diffuse bacterial soft tissue infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Esfarayen, North Khorasan, Iran (endemic for cutaneous leishmaniasis). 10-year history of opium smoking abuse. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) managed with inhaled salbutamol (100 mcg 4 puffs/day) and fluticasone/salmeterol (250/50 mcg BID). Pre-existing left upper extremity lymphedema.
subjective.review_of_systems: Disseminated ulcerated skin lesions, localized lymphedema. Denied fever, chills, night sweats, or visceral symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Multiple, disseminated, wet-looking, creamy inflammatory lesions that were papular, crusted, and severely ulcerated across the left arm, hemithorax, left palm, and all left fingernails, resembling second-degree burns. Mild peripheral edema and localized lymphedema over the left arm and hemithorax. Afebrile; no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine hematological, biochemical, and radiological examinations were normal. Viral serologies negative for HIV, HBsAg, and HCV. Anti-Brucella antibodies (Wright, Coombs Wright, 2-mercaptoethanol) negative. Direct microscopy of skin smears for acid-fast bacilli was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Direct skin scraping of wrist and forearm lesions (Giemsa staining) revealed abundant intracellular and extracellular microorganisms (3+ parasitemia: 1-10 parasites/field). Punch biopsy of wrist and forearm lesions (H&E) showed mild epidermal hyperkeratosis and dermal infiltration by mixed inflammatory cells with abundant macrophages filled with intracellular organisms. Bone marrow aspiration revealed no detectable parasites. Skin lesion fluid cultured in Schneider's Drosophila medium with 5% HI-FBS yielded 2 x 10^7 flagellated organisms/mL at log phase.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) with unusual palmar and ungual involvement caused by Leishmania major, complicated by secondary bacterial infection.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Giemsa-stained scrapings and H&E punch biopsies revealed abundant Leishmania amastigotes (3+ grade); culture in Schneider's medium confirmed promastigotes; ITS1 PCR-RFLP with HaeIII and DNA sequencing demonstrated 99% identity with Leishmania major (Iranian strain AB04/HU64). Bone marrow aspirate was negative for Leishmania.
Differentials Ruled Out: Severe diffuse bacterial burn/cellulitis, cutaneous tuberculosis/leprosy (negative AFB), brucellosis, viral hepatitis/HIV, and visceral leishmaniasis (negative bone marrow).
Treatment & Clinical Course: Initial treatment included broad-spectrum antibiotics (IV vancomycin 1 g/12h and ceftriaxone 1 g/12h) and silver sulfadiazine dressings. Meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime; 20 mg/kg/day) was started but discontinued at day 10 due to poor response and drug-induced pancytopenia. Switched to intravenous amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day for 10 days), achieving progressive and marked resolution of skin lesions. However, during hospitalization, the patient developed severe pulmonary infection and disseminated bronchiectasis related to COPD and opium abuse, and died in the ICU from systemic bacterial superinfection.

raw_case_text:
A 58-year-old Hispanic woman with a history of chronic rhinitis, diabetes on insulin treatment, squamous cell carcinoma (remission), and sleep apnea using a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) device. The patient reported having a high fever, severe muscle and headache pain, sore throat, dry throat with a burning sensation, nasal congestion with postnatal drip, and cough for the last two days. The antigen on the day of the visit was positive for SARS-CoV-2. The patient was administered two doses of the COVID-19 vaccine two months prior. The patient also reported malaise, fever, and fatigue. In addition to CPM oral spray treatment was started with Vitamin C 1000 mg twice a day, zinc 100 mg once a day, Vitamin D3 5000IU once a day, and ibuprofen or acetaminophen as needed, plus daily phone call follow-ups. The patient reported significant improvement in the burning sensation immediately after the spray was applied. On the second day, she felt better as the hoarseness decreased; by day 3 of treatment, the sore throat, hoarseness, and burning had improved by more than 50% (Figure 2). The fever lasted four days, with muscle pain and tiredness persisting slightly until day 5.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old female presenting with a 2-day history of high fever, severe myalgias, headache, sore throat with a burning sensation, nasal congestion with postnasal drip, and cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-day history of high fever, severe myalgias, intense headache, severe sore throat, dry throat with an acute burning sensation, nasal congestion with postnasal drip, and cough. She also reported marked malaise and fatigue. Symptoms began acutely two days prior to presentation. She was treated in the outpatient setting with a topical cetylpyridinium chloride (CPM) oral spray along with supportive supplements and analgesics, with immediate relief of pharyngeal burning and progressive resolution of systemic symptoms over several days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic rhinitis, type 2 diabetes mellitus requiring insulin therapy, history of squamous cell carcinoma (in complete remission), and obstructive sleep apnea treated with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Vaccinated with two doses of pandemic respiratory vaccine 2 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high fever, headache, severe muscle aches, sore throat, throat burning, hoarseness, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, postnasal drip, cough, malaise, and fatigue.

objective.physical_examination: Outpatient clinical evaluation: Febrile, pharyngeal mucosal erythema and irritation. Vital signs otherwise stable. No acute respiratory distress on examination.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Mild COVID-19 upper respiratory tract infection (confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test on the day of presentation) in a vaccinated patient with comorbidities including diabetes mellitus and sleep apnea.

Management and outcome: Outpatient management consisting of topical cetylpyridinium chloride (CPM) oral spray, vitamin C 1,000 mg BID, zinc 100 mg daily, vitamin D3 5,000 IU daily, and as-needed ibuprofen/acetaminophen, accompanied by daily phone monitoring. Burning pharyngeal symptoms improved immediately after initial spray application, hoarseness improved on day 2, and sore throat/burning improved by > 50% by day 3. Fever resolved by day 4; residual myalgias and fatigue resolved by day 5.

raw_case_text:
A 43-year-old man presented to our clinic due to headache persisting for the previous 15 days, and with fever, vomiting, and altered consciousness for two days. At physical examination, the patient was somnolent, and signs of meningeal irritation were positive. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed microprotein: 138 mg/dL, chloride: 120 mmol/L, and glucose: 32 mg/dL (simultaneous blood sugar: 128 mg/dL). The headache persisted on the seventh day of anti-microbial therapy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a millimeter-scale cerebellar lesion (Figure 1). PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Quantiferon tests of CSF were positive. The patient was commenced on isoniazid, 300 mg/day, rifampicin 600 mg/day, ethambutol 2 g/day and pyrazinamide 2 g/day. CSF culture testing over the first month of treatment was reported as M. tuberculosis, susceptible to anti-tuberculous drugs. In the second month of treatment, the patient was reexamined, complaining of severe headache. MRI of the brain revealed an increased number of lesions and basilar occlusion (Figure 2). Moxifloxacin and anti-edematous therapy were added to four-drug anti-tuberculous therapy. The symptoms resolved in the third month of five-drug anti-tuberculous therapy, and treatment was maintained with two-drug anti-tuberculous therapy. Improvement was recorded by MRI in the fifth month of treatment (Figure 3).
Central nervous system tuberculosis is a rare form of tuberculosis in immunocompetent individuals. It can lead to excessive tuberculosis protein release in association with basilar obliteration, particularly in tuberculous meningitis, in patients receiving anti-tuberculous therapy. This protein can lead to tuberculoma expansion, or to identification of previously unseen tuberculomas  .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old male presented with a 15-day history of headache, and a 2-day history of fever, vomiting, and altered consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with persistent headache for 15 days, followed by acute worsening over 2 days with high fever, vomiting, and progressive somnolence.
subjective.review_of_systems: Complained of headache, fever, vomiting, and somnolence. Home medications and allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Somnolent with positive signs of meningeal irritation (nuchal rigidity).
objective.routine_investigations: Simultaneous blood glucose: 128 mg/dL.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: microprotein 138 mg/dL, chloride 120 mmol/L, glucose 32 mg/dL (CSF-to-blood glucose ratio 0.25). Brain MRI (initial): demonstrated a millimeter-scale focal cerebellar lesion. Brain MRI (month 2): demonstrated interval expansion with an increased number of intracranial lesions and basilar artery occlusion. Brain MRI (month 5): documented significant radiological resolution.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Tuberculous meningitis complicated by cerebellar tuberculoma and a paradoxical neuro-inflammatory reaction with basilar artery occlusion. Confirmed by positive CSF PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, positive CSF QuantiFERON test, and CSF cultures yielding Mycobacterium tuberculosis fully susceptible to first-line agents.
Treatment & Course: Initiated on four-drug antitubercular therapy: isoniazid 300 mg/day, rifampicin 600 mg/day, ethambutol 2 g/day, and pyrazinamide 2 g/day. Due to clinical deterioration in the second month with severe headache and basilar vasculopathy on MRI, moxifloxacin and anti-edematous corticosteroid therapy were added to make a five-drug regimen. Symptoms resolved by the third month, and the patient transitioned to two-drug maintenance therapy (isoniazid and rifampicin) with marked radiologic healing confirmed on month 5 MRI.

raw_case_text: A 75-year-old male from Algeria had HIV infection since 2001 treated with nevirapine and lamivudine/zidovudine. He had cerebral toxoplasmosis, chronic hepatitis B, gastrointestinal CMV infection, and anal squamous cell carcinoma. In 2013, the patient started treatment with darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir and emtricitabine. VL had been diagnosed in 2001, and treated with L-AmB 5 mg/Kg/d for 15 days with partial improvement. Maintenance therapy of 3 mg/kg weekly was planned but irregularly administered. Recurrence was reported in March 2011, the infecting specie was identified as L. infantum. The number of CD4 lymphocytes was 33/mm3, and viral load 75000 copies/mL. The patient received 40 mg/kg of L-AmB, followed by 3 mg/kg at 15-day interval. Clinical improvement was obtained but qualitative PCR remained positive. In 2012, L-AmB infusions were administered at 3-week intervals. In 2013, a last course of 50 mg/kg of L-AmB was administered, Despite this complete course of L-AmB, clinical symptoms worsened (weight loss, fatigue), clinical splenomegaly was present (greater diameter 20 cm on the CT scan), and parasitemia remained positive and stable (from 126 Leishmania/ml before treatment to 118 Leishmania/ml after completion of the course 3 weeks later). Meglumine antimoniate was thus administered, initially at low doses (4-10 mg/kg SbV every other day for 7 weeks) because of advanced age. Treatment was well tolerated except for moderate neutropenia. Fatigue resolved and weight increased from 50 to 61 Kg. The spleen was no longer palpable after 2 months of treatment. Number of CD4 lymphocytes increased from 75 to 134/mm3. Parasitemia cleared and remained negative through 13 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old male with HIV infection presented with worsening fatigue, weight loss, and marked splenomegaly.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 75-year-old male with HIV infection diagnosed in 2001 and visceral leishmaniasis diagnosed in 2001 presented with recurrent disease. He experienced a relapse in March 2011 treated with L-AmB (40 mg/kg, then biweekly maintenance), but qualitative PCR remained positive. In 2012, L-AmB was given every 3 weeks. In 2013, despite a full 50 mg/kg course of L-AmB, he deteriorated with progressive weight loss (weight 50 kg), profound fatigue, persistent massive splenomegaly, and unchanged parasitemia. He was treated with low-dose meglumine antimoniate, which produced rapid recovery.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 2001 (initially treated with nevirapine and lamivudine/zidovudine; switched in 2013 to darunavir, ritonavir, raltegravir, and emtricitabine). Past medical history included cerebral toxoplasmosis, chronic hepatitis B, gastrointestinal cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, and anal squamous cell carcinoma. Visceral leishmaniasis diagnosed in 2001.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe fatigue, unintentional weight loss, abdominal heaviness and fullness. Denied fever, vomiting, or diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Elderly, wasted male; body weight 50 kg (increased to 61 kg post-treatment). Abdominal examination revealed marked palpable splenomegaly (spleen became non-palpable after 2 months of antimonial therapy).
objective.routine_investigations: In March 2011: CD4+ count 33/mm^3, HIV viral load 75,000 copies/mL. During antimonial therapy: moderate neutropenia without other toxicities. Post-treatment: CD4+ count increased from 75 to 134/mm^3.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrated massive splenomegaly with a maximum diameter of 20 cm.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Liposomal amphotericin B-refractory recurrent visceral leishmaniasis in an elderly patient with advanced HIV-1 coinfection and multiple opportunistic infections.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Parasite identified as Leishmania infantum in March 2011. Quantitative peripheral blood PCR demonstrated persistent parasitemia (126 Leishmania/mL prior to 2013 L-AmB course, remaining at 118 Leishmania/mL after completion).
Differentials Ruled Out: Progression of opportunistic infections (toxoplasmosis, CMV, hepatitis B), hematologic malignancy, and anal carcinoma metastasis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Demonstrated clinical and parasitological failure to high-dose liposomal amphotericin B regimens (including 40 mg/kg and 50 mg/kg cumulative courses). Successfully treated with low-dose meglumine antimoniate (4-10 mg/kg SbV every other day for 7 weeks) adjusted for advanced age. Treatment was well tolerated aside from moderate neutropenia, resulting in complete resolution of fatigue, weight gain of 11 kg, disappearance of splenomegaly, CD4+ increase to 134/mm^3, and sustained clearance of blood parasitemia through 13 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 69-year-old male farmer with no prior medical history was admitted to a local hospital after experiencing fever for 5 days and dyspnea with hemoptysis for 1 day. He had a history of exposure to poultry manure while working on his farm 5 days prior. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed pulmonary infection and interstitial changes (Figure 1A). The primary diagnosis was severe pneumonia and acute respiratory failure, and the patient was placed on mechanical ventilation via endotracheal intubation. However, his oxygen saturation continued to deteriorate, and bloody sputum was aspirated from his airway. Twenty hours after intubation, he was transferred to our emergency intensive care unit (EICU).
Upon arrival at the EICU, the patient was in a sedated and analgesic state, with a body temperature of 36.8 C, respiratory rate of 17 breaths/min, pulse rate of 138 beats/min, and blood pressure of 137/90 mmHg (with norepinephrine infusion at 0.5 mug/kg/min). Oxygen saturation was 88%. He remained on mechanical ventilation in volume-controlled mode with a tidal volume of 350 mL, an FiO2 of 100%, and a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 15 cmH2O (1 mmH2O = 0.098 kPa). A large amount of fresh red bloody sputum was aspirated from the airway, and extensive moist rales were heard in both lungs. Laboratory results showed: P/F, 85 mmHg; Platelet count (PLT), 43 x 109/L; C-reactive protein (CRP), 213.74 mg/L; Procalcitonin (PCT), >100 ng/mL; Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), 36.8 s; Myoglobin (MYO), >2000 ng/mL; Creatinine (CR), 240 mg/dL; Alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 111 U/L; Total bilirubin (TBIL), 70 mumol/L. The primary diagnosis included severe pneumonia, DAH, severe ARDS, septic shock, and hepatic and renal dysfunction.
Despite optimized mechanical ventilation, his P/F remained below 80 mmHg for over 3 h. VV-ECMO and CRRT support were initiated, along with intermittent prone ventilation. Mechanical ventilation was switched to pressure control mode (inspiratory pressure 12 cmH2O, tidal volume 150-350 mL, PEEP 15 cmH2O, plateau pressure <=30 mmHg). Empirical antibiotic therapy included piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g every 8 h) combined with omadacycline (100 mg daily, initial dose 200 mg IV). The patient also received methylprednisolone (200 mg IV) for anti-inflammatory treatment, recombinant human thrombopoietin (15,000 U SC daily) to increase platelet count, platelet transfusion (10 U), fresh plasma, packed red blood cells, and norepinephrine (0.1-0.8 mug/kg/min) for blood pressure support. Bronchoscopic alveolar lavage was performed, and both blood and lavage fluid were sent for mNGS testing. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) anticoagulation was initiated at the 5th hour of VV-ECMO operation. On day 3, mNGS confirmed Leptospira interrogans infection, with a coverage rate of 1% and a relative abundance of 16.45% (Figure 1D). On day 5, VV-ECMO was discontinued, and omadacycline was stopped. Follow-up chest CT showed improvement in pulmonary hemorrhage compared to before (Figure 1B). The endotracheal tube was removed on day 6, the patient was transferred out of the EICU on day 9, and was discharged after recovery on day 20. A follow-up chest CT before discharge showed that pulmonary hemorrhage had significantly improved (Figure 1C). The treatment process is summarized in Figure 1E, and the trends in blood test results are detailed in Table 1. Changes in ventilator parameters, ECMO parameters, and medication dosages during ECMO are detailed in Table 2.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 69-year-old male presenting with a 5-day history of fever, and a 1-day history of dyspnea and hemoptysis following exposure to poultry manure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five days prior to admission, the patient was exposed to poultry manure while working on his farm, subsequently developing persistent fever. One day prior to admission, he developed acute dyspnea and hemoptysis. Admitted to a local hospital where chest CT showed diffuse infiltrates; he was intubated for acute respiratory failure. Due to progressive hypoxemia and copious bloody endotracheal secretions, he was transferred to the emergency intensive care unit 20 hours post-intubation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history. Occupation: farmer. Epidemiological exposure: direct exposure to poultry manure on his farm 5 days prior to illness onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon EICU arrival: sedated and analgesized on volume-controlled mechanical ventilation (tidal volume 350 mL, FiO2 100%, PEEP 15 cmH2O). Body temperature 36.8 °C, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min, pulse rate 138 beats/min, blood pressure 137/90 mmHg (supported by norepinephrine at 0.5 mcg/kg/min). Oxygen saturation 88%. Copious fresh red bloody sputum aspirated from endotracheal tube. Extensive moist rales auscultated bilaterally throughout both lungs.
objective.routine_investigations: PaO2/FiO2 ratio 85 mmHg (declined to <80 mmHg for >3 hours). Platelet count 43 x 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 213.74 mg/L. Procalcitonin >100 ng/mL. Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 36.8 s. Serum myoglobin >2000 ng/mL. Serum creatinine 240 mg/dL [or mcmol/L as reported]. ALT 111 U/L. Total bilirubin 70 mcmol/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest CT: diffuse pulmonary infection with bilateral interstitial changes consistent with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). Follow-up chest CT on day 5 and discharge day 20: progressive and marked absorption of pulmonary hemorrhage. Bedside bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage performed; alveolar lavage fluid and blood collected for genomic analysis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe pulmonary hemorrhagic leptospirosis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH), severe ARDS (P/F ratio <80 mmHg), septic shock, profound thrombocytopenia, rhabdomyolysis, and acute hepatic and renal impairment. Confirmed on hospital day 3 by blood and BALF mNGS detecting Leptospira interrogans (coverage rate 1%, relative abundance 16.45%).
Plan & Treatment: Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO) and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) support with intermittent prone positioning; lung-protective pressure-controlled ventilation; unfractionated heparin (UFH) initiated at hour 5 of ECMO. Empirical and targeted antimicrobials: piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g IV q8h) combined with omadacycline (initial dose 200 mg IV, then 100 mg IV daily; discontinued day 5). Anti-inflammatory therapy with methylprednisolone (200 mg IV daily); recombinant human thrombopoietin (15,000 U SC daily); transfusions of platelets (10 U), fresh plasma, and packed red blood cells; norepinephrine infusion (0.1-0.8 mcg/kg/min).
Outcome: VV-ECMO successfully discontinued on day 5, endotracheal tube removed on day 6, transferred out of EICU on day 9, and discharged home fully recovered on day 20.

raw_case_text:
A five-year-old male non-Caucasian patient presented with fever, myalgia, headache, and conjunctivitis for 5 days. His past medical history was unremarkable, with normal psychomotor development, no family history neurological diseases and no consanguinity. The patient was born and lived in Ceara, northeast Brazil, and family reported no recent travels.
After 1 week he developed tonic-clonic seizures. Neurological examination was normal at this point. Complete blood count, liver functions and acute reactants were normal. Serologies for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV, EBV, VZV, HIV, and toxoplasmosis were negative. Brain MRI was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 15 cells, protein 16.6 mg/dL and glucose 68 mg/dL. He was started on acyclovir and ceftriaxone.
Two weeks after seizure onset, he presented with dystonia (Video 1) and oromandibular dyskinesia. On physical examination the patient was awake, his speech output was decreased, pupils were normal. Cranial nerves examination was unremarkable. Muscle strength was symmetric and deep tendon reflexes were normoactive and symmetric. One week later he developed focal motor seizures followed by decreased level of consciousness, dysautonomia, and central apnea. EEG showed extreme delta brush and valproate and phenytoin were started. He also received methylprednisolone followed by intravenous immunoglobulin with seizure resolution and improvement of level of consciousness, dysautonomia and orofacial dyskinesias within 2 weeks.
Anti-NMDAR antibodies were detected in serum (titer 1:25600) and CSF (titer 1:1024) after 3 weeks of symptom onset using tissue and cell-based assays as previously reported. CHIK serology was positive for both IgM and IgG, suggesting a recent infection. Dengue and Zika serologies were negative. CSF PCR for herpes viruses and arboviruses (CHIK, Dengue and Zika) were negative. Whole body CT and testis ultrasound were normal. Because of partial improvement (persistence of orofacial dyskinesias and impaired speech), the patient received rituximab and cyclophosphamide with good response. After 8 months he is seizure-free and has returned to school with only mild restlessness and inattention. Figure 1 describes the timeline of clinical features, investigation and treatment of the case report.

raw_case_text:
An 8-month old baby boy presented with high-grade fever associated with chills and rigours for 15 days, abdominal distension for 5 days and diarrhoea for 5 days. He also had an erythematous rash over his face and back. On examination, his length was 73 cm (85th percentile) and weight was 7.3 kg (3rd percentile). He was afebrile, heart rate was 140/min, respiratory rate was 38/min and blood pressure was 102/74 mm Hg. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatomegaly. No neck stiffness or signs of meningeal irritation were seen. Investigations revealed a haemoglobin of 7.2 gm/dL; total white cell count, 8300/mm3 (neutrophils, 30%; lymphocytes, 69%; eosinophils, 0%; monocytes, 1%; basophils, 0%); and platelets, 81,000/mm3. Peripheral smear for malarial parasites was negative. Tests for dengue fever were negative. Widal test revealed the antibody titers to 'O' and 'H' antigens to be 1:160 each respectively. Liver function tests showed an elevation of the hepatic enzymes - alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 94 IU/L; aspartate aminotransferase (AST), 249 IU/L; and INR, 1.3. international normalized ratio (INR) Serum creatinine was 0.4 mg/dL. Urine examination and echocardiography were both normal. Ultrasound examination of the abdomen revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly with increased echogenicity of liver. Blood culture showed S. typhi sensitive to ampicillin-sulbactam and cotrimoxazole but resistant to fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins. The blood culture results were obtained on day 6 of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed lymphocytic pleocytosis (14 leucocytes/mm3 with 100% lymphocytes), 38 mg/dL of proteins and 74 mg/dL of glucose. CSF Gram stain, Zeil Neilson stain and culture were negative.
The child was initially treated with IV ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day) for 5 days but had no response. Antibiotics were changed to IV aztreonam and oral azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day) which were given for 5 days but still the fever persisted. Hence, antibiotics were switched to IV meropenem (40 mg/kg/dose 8 hourly), and oral azithromycin was continued. The fever subsided in 13 days. IV meropenem was given for 14 days and oral azithromycin was given for 7 days.

raw_case_text:
In April 2015, a 42-year-old married male visited the outpatient clinic suffering from high-grade fever and a large painful ulcer around the anus for the past 3 weeks.
Medical history revealed that he was seropositive and diagnosed with HIV in 1997. His history also confirmed high-risk behavior involving anal sexual intercourse with another man. Treatment was deferred repeatedly for antiretroviral treatment (ART) in 1997 and 2005 as his absolute CD4 counts were >400 cells/mm3. For the past 3 months, (2015), he was experiencing low-grade fever with rising temperature in the evening often associated with chills. He suffered from loss of appetite and had lost 15 kg weight in the past 4 months. He has no history of headache, vomiting, cough, breathlessness, and diarrhea.
Clinical Examination revealed oral candidiasis, a large ulcer measuring 8" X 2" around the anus that was painful and bled on touch as shown in Figure 1. There was no lymphadenopathy. Systemic examination was normal. As the ulcer was painful and bled on touch, a skin biopsy and Tzanck Smear test were recommended.
Four days later, on his 2nd visit, as per NACO, his HIV-1 status was confirmed by HIV-enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. His CD4 count (Absolute count and Percentage) was 10 cells/mm3, CD4-<4%, and plasma viral load was 43,803 copies/ml. Genotypic drug resistance (DR) testing for HIV-1 was done to rule out (r/o) transmitted DR (TDR) or primary DR.
Hemogram, blood sugar level, renal and liver function tests, urine tests were otherwise normal except thrombocytosis. For investigating fever, the following tests were done which were all negative: Malaria antigen test for Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum, Dengue NS1, IgM, IgG, HBsAg, hepatitis C virus, venereal diseases research laboratory/Treponema pallidum Hemagglutination, and Herpes IgM, IgG. Blood culture for aerobic and anaerobic organisms showed no growth. All the tests related to fever were insignificant. Koch's infection was also ruled out. He tested IgG positive for toxoplasmosis. He received chemoprophylaxis for opportunistic infections, (Co-trimoxazole, INH, and Azithromycin) and ART regimen of Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) + Emtricitabine (FTC) + Efavirenz (EFA) (TDF + FTC + EFV) fixed-dose combination while awaiting the results of DR, and skin biopsy.
There was no improvement in his symptoms despite treatment for over 3 weeks. Thereafter, he was admitted to the hospital with high-grade fever and large painful perianal ulcer. He received intravenous antibiotics along with ongoing medications.
His perianal biopsy report was suggestive of superficial aphthous ulcer. Tzanck smear test was done suspecting herpetic infection but was negative. 18F-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose positron emission tomography computed tomography (18FDG-PET) scan was done which did not show any abnormal uptake suggestive of malignancy. Thus, tuberculosis and malignancy were ruled out by the TB specialist and oncologist. The dermatologist treated the ulcer as a giant herpetic ulcer with valaciclovir 1 g thrice a day for 2 days, thereafter 500 mg thrice a day while continuing the chemoprophylaxis. While on valaciclovir, the ulcer size reduced in size and developed scarring and pigmentary changes.
While this treatment was ongoing, the ART DR report showed he was resistant to Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) and Non-NRTIs (NNRTIs) while being susceptible to protease inhibitors and integrase strand transfer inhibitors. Before switching the patients' regimen, CD4 and viral load tests were repeated which showed that his CD4 absolute count was 10 cells/mm3 and CD4- below 4% and plasma viral load was 52,935 copies/ml. The regimen selected post DR test report and counseling was Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) + Lamivudine (3TC) + Raltegravir (RAL). The patient was afebrile and asymptomatic. The skin lesion healed and he was discharged within 15 days while maintaining the ART regimen.
Five days later, while on the new ART regimen, the patient complained of giddiness and loss of balance. The patient was managed conservatively with oral betahistine (Vertin) by an Otorhinolaryngologist. Subsequently, within few days, the symptoms worsened with him developing headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision. Neurological evaluation revealed tendency to fall on either side during tandem walking, bilateral finger nose ataxia, and Romberg's sign was present. Magnetic Resonance Imaging brain suggested acute demyelination with a differential diagnosis of lymphoma.
FDG-PET scan was repeated after a gap of 40 days from the previous scan. It showed a single space-occupying lesion in the vermis of cerebellar area with no other abnormality as shown in Figure 2. Stereotactic biopsy suggested lymphoma- Non-Hodgkin's diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Immunohistochemistry showed positive expression for CD20 and negative expression for CD-10. Cultures of CSF and tissue did not reveal any aerobic or anaerobic infection. Fungal culture, TB-MGIT, and identification of MAC and Gene Xpert for MTB were negative. EBV was present.
The patient was eventually diagnosed with PCNSL through a process of elimination. The patient was started on chemotherapy but did not improve. Despite being on ART for 3 months and taking chemotherapy/radiotherapy, his CD4 counts did not rise although, his viral load was undetectable. The patient ultimately died in the 4th month of his treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with a 3-week history of high-grade fever and a large, exquisitely painful perianal ulcer.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-week history of high-grade fevers and a painful, bleeding perianal ulcer, preceded by three months of low-grade evening fevers with chills, anorexia, and a 15 kg weight loss over four months. Following initial antiviral therapy and ulcer healing, he developed acute-onset dizziness and dysequilibrium five days after discharge, which rapidly worsened to severe headaches, vomiting, visual blurring, and cerebellar ataxia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with retroviral infection in 1997; antiretroviral therapy was initially deferred in 1997 and 2005 due to preserved immune parameters; history of high-risk sexual behavior including condomless receptive and insertive anal intercourse with male partners. Denies prior history of headache, chronic cough, or diarrhea.
subjective.review_of_systems: High-grade fever, chills, anorexia, 15 kg weight loss, painful perianal ulcer, oral thrush, secondary dizziness, vomiting, headache, and visual blurring; denies cough, dyspnea, or diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: General: Febrile with evening spikes; oral examination revealed oral candidiasis (thrush). Abdomen/Perianal: Large perianal ulcer measuring 8 inches by 2 inches, exquisitely tender and bleeding upon contact; absence of peripheral lymphadenopathy. Neurologic (upon readmission): Bilateral finger-to-nose dysmetria, ataxia with tendency to fall on either side during tandem walking, positive Romberg sign, and visual impairment.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Reactive thrombocytosis; hemoglobin, white blood cell count, and differential were otherwise unremarkable. Biochemistry & Urinalysis: Normal blood glucose, renal panel, liver function tests, and urinalysis. Infectious & Fever Workup: Negative for malaria antigen (P. vivax and P. falciparum), dengue NS1 antigen and IgM/IgG, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis C antibody, VDRL/TPHA, and herpes simplex IgM/IgG; Toxoplasma gondii IgG positive; aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures were sterile.
objective.advanced_workup: Histopathology & Smears: Tzanck smear from perianal ulcer was negative; perianal biopsy demonstrated superficial aphthous ulceration without malignancy. Initial 18F-FDG PET/CT: No hypermetabolic lesions suggestive of malignancy. Brain MRI: Space-occupying lesion in the cerebellar vermis with surrounding edema suggestive of acute demyelination versus lymphoma. Repeat 18F-FDG PET/CT (day 40): Solitary hypermetabolic mass confined to the cerebellar vermis. Stereotactic cerebellar brain biopsy: Histopathology demonstrated atypical dense perivascular lymphocytic infiltration; tissue and CSF bacterial, fungal, TB-MGIT, GeneXpert MTB, and MAC testing were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL; diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, EBV-positive) and giant herpetic perianal ulcer in a patient with profound human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) immunodeficiency and multidrug resistance (baseline CD4 count 10 cells/mm3 [<4%], HIV RNA viral load 43,803 copies/mL). Diagnostic confirmation: Confirmation of HIV-1 by ELISA; genotypic drug resistance testing revealed high-level resistance to NRTIs and NNRTIs with susceptibility to protease inhibitors and INSTIs; stereotactic cerebellar biopsy confirmed CD20+ CD10- DLBCL with positive EBV. Plan & Outcome: Giant perianal ulcer healed following oral valacyclovir (1 g TID for 2 days, then 500 mg TID). ART was optimized to lopinavir/ritonavir, lamivudine, and raltegravir, achieving undetectable HIV viral load; however, CD4 count remained 10 cells/mm3. Initiated on systemic chemotherapy and cranial radiotherapy for PCNSL, but experienced refractory neurological decline and died in the fourth month of treatment.

raw_case_text:
A 14-year-old Japanese girl developed high-grade fever and headache during the COVID-19 pandemic. A SARS-CoV-2 rapid antigen test performed at a local clinic was positive. The following day, she developed difficulty in eating, and was admitted to our hospital. Her medical history included five episodes of MERS, at the ages of 3, 6, 7, 8 and 9 years (Table 1). Three of these five episodes were associated with influenza A. Her clinical course prior to the fourth episode has been reported elsewhere, and a heterozygous p.Gln403Arg variant of MYRF had been identified. There had been a few infectious events that were not associated with encephalopathy apart from the episodes of MERS. Neurological symptoms, including unconsciousness, convulsions, and numbness in the limbs, had developed 2-4 days after the onset of fever. She had completely recovered from a previous episodes within a week.
On admission, she had pyrexia of 37.8 C. All other vital signs were within the normal range. Physical examination was unremarkable, apart from slight erythema of the pharynx. Her level of consciousness was normal and there was no neck stiffness. Laboratory data were unremarkable except for mild hyponatremia (134 mEq/L). SARS-CoV-2 infection was diagnosed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test of a nasal swab. PCR of cerebrospinal fluid was not performed. Her headache gradually improved with supportive treatment; however she complained of numbness in her arms. On the fourth day after the onset, she developed generalized spasticity, speech disturbance, and had a fixed gaze eyes wide open. Smooth pursuit was preserved. She appeared to understood the spoken word, but was unable to speak herself. These manifestations were similar to those of her previous episodes of MERS (Table 1). Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed restriction of water diffusion in the entire corpus callosum (CC) and deep white matter (Figure 1). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed a cell count of 9/muL, a normal protein level (0.25 g/L), and a glucose level of 0.6 g/L. Myelin basic protein (MBP) in the CSF was below the limit of quantitation. A diagnosis of MERS was established on the basis of these findings. She was treated with a single course of intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1 g/day for 3 days), which resulted in an immediate improvement in her symptoms. A follow-up MRI on the 10th day after onset demonstrated resolution of the previously noted abnormalities. She was discharged on the 11th day after onset with no neurological sequelae. Although no formal examination of intellectual and behavioral function has not been performed, we confirmed that her school performance was average and had not been worsened until the last follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old female presenting with high-grade fever, headache, and difficulty eating for 1 day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high-grade fever and headache, followed the next day by difficulty eating, prompting hospital admission. While headache initially improved with supportive care, she developed numbness in both arms. On illness day 4, she developed generalized spasticity, speech disturbance (mutism despite intact auditory comprehension), and a fixed wide-eyed gaze with preserved smooth pursuit, closely resembling her previous episodes of encephalopathy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Five prior episodes of mild encephalopathy with reversible splenial lesion (MERS) at ages 3, 6, 7, 8, and 9 years (three triggered by influenza A; all recovered fully within 1 week). Confirmed heterozygous pathogenic p.Gln403Arg variant in the MYRF gene.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high fever, headache, poor oral intake, bilateral upper extremity numbness, mutism, and generalized stiffness. Denies neck stiffness or visual impairment.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: T 37.8 °C; other vital signs normal. General: Alert and oriented on admission. HEENT: Mild pharyngeal erythema. Neurological (day 4): Generalized spasticity, speech arrest/mutism with preserved comprehension of spoken language, fixed wide-eyed gaze, preserved smooth pursuit, no nuchal rigidity.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum sodium 134 mEq/L (mild hyponatremia). Other routine hematology and chemistry unremarkable. Lumbar puncture / CSF: Cell count 9/μL, protein 0.25 g/L (normal), glucose 0.6 g/L, myelin basic protein (MBP) below the limit of quantitation.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI (day 4): Restricted water diffusion in the entire corpus callosum and deep white matter, diagnostic of mild encephalopathy with reversible splenial lesion (MERS) type II. Follow-up brain MRI (day 10): Complete resolution of previously noted diffusion abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Mild encephalopathy with reversible splenial lesion (MERS type II) triggered by COVID-19 infection (confirmed by positive rapid antigen test at local clinic and positive nasal swab RT-PCR on admission; CSF PCR not performed), occurring in a patient with a hereditary predisposition due to heterozygous MYRF p.Gln403Arg mutation.

Management and outcome: Treated with a single course of intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone pulse therapy (1 g/day for 3 days), resulting in prompt and complete clinical resolution. Discharged on illness day 11 without neurological deficits; school performance and cognitive function remained normal at follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old Caucasian man was admitted to our hospital with a six-day history of high-grade fever (up to 39 C) and chest pain. He also reported fatigue, anorexia, generalized arthralgia, headache and night sweats. He had been treated with paracetamol by his general practitioner for an upper respiratory infection, but the symptoms remained and worsened. He was living in a rural area of central Greece and was working as a stock farmer. His medical history was unremarkable.
On physical examination, only tachypnoea and hepatosplenomegaly were seen. ECG demonstrated repolarization disturbances with T-wave inversion in the II, III, aVF and V2 to V6 leads.
Laboratory investigations found a raised white blood cell count of 11.15  109/l (normal range 4-11  109/L), creatine phosphokinase 305 IU/L (30-190 IU/L) and lactate dehydrogenase 247 IU/L (12-230 IU/L). Results of the remaining haematological and biochemical tests, including liver function tests, were within normal ranges. A qualitative determination of troponin was positive, which was confirmed by a quantitative method.
A diagnosis of myocarditis due to an infectious agent was suspected because of the history of chest pain in association with the positive troponin test and the ECG abnormalities. Two-dimensional trans-thoracic and trans-oesophageal echocardiography revealed a mild regional motion abnormality of the left ventricular wall but without pericardial effusion or valves vegetations. Blood, urine, and pharynx cultures were negative, as were serology tests for Influenza A and B, parvovirus, EBV, CMV, ECHO virus, coxsackie virus, HSV, VSV, adenovirus, Coxiella burnetti, Chlamydia pneumonia, Leptospira, Mycoplasma pneumonia. However, serum agglutination tests were positive at a titre >1:1280 and ELISA results for anti-Brucella IgG and IgM antibodies were strongly positive (92 U/ml and 48 U/ml, antibodies, respectively), and Brucella spp was isolated in two out of four sets of blood cultures. As for patient 1, there were no clinical and radiologic signs suggestive for the presence of other systemic features of the disease.
Accordingly, a diagnosis of Brucella-related myocarditis was made and our patient was treated only with the specific triple antibiotic regimen as for patient 1 (oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus oral rifampicin 900 mg once daily for three months, with intramuscular streptomycin 1 g once daily for the first three weeks). His symptoms regressed rapidly after initiation of treatment. His echocardiographic and ECG studies three and 12 months after the start of treatment were completely normal, and he showed no signs of relapse during 12 months of follow-up at our outpatient clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old Caucasian male presented with a 6-day history of high-grade fever and chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high-grade fever peaking up to 39 °C and chest pain 6 days prior to admission. He also experienced fatigue, anorexia, generalized arthralgia, headache, and night sweats. He was treated with paracetamol by his general practitioner for a suspected upper respiratory infection, but symptoms worsened.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical history was unremarkable. Occupation: stock farmer living in a rural area of central Greece. Prior therapy: paracetamol for suspected upper respiratory infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports high-grade fever, chest pain, fatigue, anorexia, generalized arthralgia, headache, and night sweats.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed tachypnea and hepatosplenomegaly. Remainder of physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell (WBC) count: 11.15 x 10^9/L (normal range 4-11 x 10^9/L), creatine phosphokinase (CPK): 305 IU/L (30-190 IU/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 247 IU/L (12-230 IU/L). Cardiac troponin was positive qualitatively and confirmed quantitatively. Other hematologic and biochemical tests, including liver function tests, were normal. ECG showed repolarization disturbances with T-wave inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V2-V6. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography revealed mild regional left ventricular wall motion abnormality without pericardial effusion or valvular vegetations; follow-up echocardiography and ECG at 3 and 12 months were completely normal. Routine blood, urine, and pharyngeal cultures were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Serum agglutination tests were positive with a titer > 1:1,280; ELISA was strongly positive for anti-Brucella IgG (92 U/mL) and IgM (48 U/mL); Brucella spp. was isolated in two out of four sets of blood cultures, confirming acute Brucella-related myocarditis. Differential diagnoses ruled out: Negative serologies for Influenza A and B, parvovirus, EBV, CMV, ECHO virus, Coxsackievirus, HSV, VZV, adenovirus, Coxiella burnetii, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Leptospira, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Management and Outcome: Treated with triple antibiotic regimen of oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily plus oral rifampicin 900 mg once daily for 3 months, combined with intramuscular streptomycin 1 g once daily for the initial 3 weeks. Symptoms regressed rapidly, and complete normalization of cardiac enzymes, ECG, and echocardiography was achieved, with no relapse at 12-month follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 54-year-old male, known diabetic patient presented to our urology OPD, with a chief complaint of dysuria, weak urine stream, suprapubic pain radiating to perineal area, urethral pus discharge, and fever for approximately 2-week duration. The symptoms did not improve post a course of antibiotics for 1 week. The patient reported ingestion of raw milk before the presentation of symptoms. On examination, vital signs were showing high-grade fever, otherwise unremarkable. Digital rectal examination showed enlarged tender prostate. Laboratory tests showed mild leukocytosis with elevated lymphocytes and monocytes. Urine analysis showed pus cells and red blood cells. Transrectal ultrasonography and computed tomography (CT) scan confirmed the diagnosis of prostatic abscess. Transurethral drainage of the abscess, performed for the patient and foly's and suprapubic catheter inserted to relive obstruction. Pus culture and titration were positive for Brucella Bactria. Postoperatively, the patient received intravenous (IV) fluids and antibiotics including sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and gentamicin. One week after surgery, the patient developed low-grade fever and urine culture showed Staphylococcus species and the patient received ciprofloxacin. Two weeks later, the patient improved and discharged home on Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim. A follow-up CT scan, performed, and no further collection of abscess detected with complete resolution.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old diabetic male presented with a 2-week history of dysuria, weak urine stream, suprapubic pain radiating to the perineum, urethral pus discharge, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-week history of dysuria, poor urinary stream, suprapubic pain radiating to the perineal region, purulent urethral discharge, and high-grade fever. Symptoms failed to improve following a 1-week course of outpatient antibiotics. In the postoperative period following transurethral abscess drainage, he developed low-grade fever at 1 week associated with secondary bacteriuria.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known history of diabetes mellitus. Prior 1-week course of outpatient antibiotics. Epidemiological exposure: reported ingestion of raw milk prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Dysuria, weak urinary stream, suprapubic and perineal pain, urethral pus discharge, fever. Home medications: prior 1-week antibiotic course. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: High-grade fever; other vital signs unremarkable. Digital rectal examination (DRE): enlarged, tender prostate.
objective.routine_investigations: Mild leukocytosis with elevated lymphocytes and monocytes. Urinalysis: pus cells (pyuria) and red blood cells (hematuria). Transrectal ultrasonography: confirmed prostatic abscess. Postoperative urine culture grew Staphylococcus species.
objective.advanced_workup: Pelvic/abdominal CT scan: confirmed prostatic abscess; follow-up CT scan demonstrated complete resolution with no recurrent fluid collection. Surgical procedure: transurethral drainage of prostatic abscess with Foley catheter and suprapubic catheter placement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Prostatic abscess secondary to Brucella infection, complicated by secondary hospital-acquired Staphylococcus urinary tract infection. Confirmed by pus culture and serological titration positive for Brucella bacteria. Urine culture grew Staphylococcus species postoperatively.
Plan & Outcome: Underwent transurethral drainage of prostatic abscess with Foley and suprapubic catheter decompression. Treated postoperatively with IV fluids, IV gentamicin, and oral sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (cotrimoxazole); ciprofloxacin was added for secondary staphylococcal bacteriuria. Discharged home after 2 weeks on oral sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim. Follow-up CT confirmed complete resolution without recurrence.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old man was hospitalized due to complaints of lower back and neck pains approximately 3 months ago. He had a history of atrial fibrillation and chronic obstructive liver disease, and was engaged in animal husbandry. The Rose Bengal test yielded a positive result, and the Wright test score was 1/160. Blood culture showed absence of bacterial growth, and vegetation was not detected on echocardiography (ECHO). Rifampicin and doxycycline were administered as the patient's clinical manifestations were compatible with those of brucellosis, and the Wright test at the external center yielded a positive result. The patient was discharged on volition. 
Three months later, the patient presented with worsening rhythm disturbance over the previous 4-5 days, shortness of breath, right leg pain, and elevated body temperature. Wright agglutination was 1/5120, and Ig M and Ig G were detected on enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Hence, ECHO was performed. Vegetation was detected in the mitral valve (Figures 1 and 2). The patient had a toxic appearance. He was administered with rifampicin, doxycycline, and cefotaxime for two weeks. Brucella growth was determined by blood culture. The patient was then transferred to the Department of Cardiovascular Surgery. The mitral valve was resected, and bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement was performed. The treatment was continued postoperatively, and the patient did not develop any complications. The patient survived and remained healthy. 
Brucellosis can affect several organs and tissues. It frequently involves the aortic valve, followed by the mitral valve. 
The prevalence of brucella endocarditis is 1% and is the most frequent cause of death. The prognosis is poor in young patients. Hence, short-term and long-term follow-ups must be performed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male presented with worsening heart rhythm disturbance for 4-5 days, shortness of breath, right leg pain, and fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Three months prior to presentation, the patient was hospitalized with lower back and neck pain and received rifampicin and doxycycline before self-discharging against medical advice. He re-presented 3 months later with acute worsening of cardiac rhythm disturbance over 4-5 days, progressive shortness of breath, right leg pain, and fever. Echocardiography identified a new mitral valve vegetation, necessitating surgical intervention.
subjective.past_medical_history: Atrial fibrillation, chronic obstructive liver disease; prior presentation 3 months earlier with lower back/neck pain and incomplete antimicrobial therapy. Epidemiological exposure/Occupation: Engaged in animal husbandry.
subjective.review_of_systems: Shortness of breath and right leg pain. Home medications: Incomplete prior course of rifampicin and doxycycline. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Patient had a toxic general appearance. Elevated body temperature (fever) present. Cardiac exam notable for worsening rhythm disturbance.
objective.routine_investigations: Transthoracic echocardiography (3 months prior): No vegetative lesions detected. Repeat echocardiography (current admission): Mitral valve vegetation detected.
objective.advanced_workup: Surgical pathology / intraoperative evaluation: Resected diseased mitral valve with bioprosthetic valve replacement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucella infective endocarditis involving the mitral valve, confirmed by positive blood cultures growing Brucella species, with Wright agglutination titer rising markedly to 1:5120 (from 1:160 three months prior) and positive Brucella IgM and IgG by ELISA (initial episode was also Rose Bengal positive).
Plan & Clinical Course: Initiated on two weeks of preoperative rifampicin, doxycycline, and cefotaxime. The patient was transferred to Cardiovascular Surgery and underwent mitral valve resection and bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement. Antimicrobial therapy was continued postoperatively. The patient recovered completely without complications.

raw_case_text: A seven-and-a-half-year-old boy had focal convulsions in February 2012. He was diagnosed to have tuberculomas on CT brain, and CSF examination was normal and was started on four drug ATT (HRZE) in February 2012 along with prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for a month and then tapered off in next 1 month) but had no response and had increase in size of granulomas even after 1 year of ATT. In February 2013, histopathological examination done on an excised lesion removed by right parietal craniotomy which showed large granulomatous lesions with central caseous necrosis. Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was not seen, and TB culture was also negative. He was started on second-line drugs consisting of Mfx, Eth, PAS, Cys, Lnz, amikacin (Am) and clofazimine along with prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for a month and then tapered off in the next 3 months). In August 2013, Am was discontinued. By August 2014, MRI brain showed calcified granulomas (left occipital 36 x 19 mm and right parietal 24 x 19 mm). ATT was stopped in August 2014. On last follow-up in October 2016, he continues to remain asymptomatic, and granulomas have regressed further but still are persistent.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7.5-year-old male presented with focal convulsions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with focal convulsions in February 2012.

objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT (initial): demonstrated multiple intracranial granulomatous lesions/tuberculomas. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination: normal. Histopathological examination of excised brain lesion (via right parietal craniotomy): large granulomatous lesions with central caseous necrosis. Follow-up brain MRI (August 2014): calcified granulomas in the left occipital (36 x 19 mm) and right parietal (24 x 19 mm) lobes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Central nervous system tuberculomas / tuberculosis with initial treatment failure on first-line therapy. Histopathology confirmed large granulomatous lesions with central caseous necrosis; acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain was negative and mycobacterial culture was negative.
Treatment and clinical course: Initially treated with four-drug first-line ATT (HRZE: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) plus prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for 1 month, then tapered over 1 month), but showed disease progression and lesion enlargement over 1 year. In February 2013, switched to second-line regimen: moxifloxacin, ethionamide, para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS), cycloserine, linezolid, amikacin, and clofazimine, alongside prednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for 1 month, tapered over 3 months). Amikacin was discontinued in August 2013. Therapy was completed and stopped in August 2014. At follow-up in October 2016, the patient remained asymptomatic with further regression of residual lesions.

raw_case_text: The male patient was born on June 6, 1960, in Acaua municipality, Piaui State, was a married and was diagnosed with kala-azar in January 2014 and had a negative serology to HIV. Since then, he evolved with recurrent pancytopenia, persistent splenomegaly and a history of five previous hospitalizations at the IDTNP for the kala-azar treatment. After unsuccessful attempts with all the existing drug treatments against kala-azar, such as pentavalent antimony (glucantime, 20 mg of Sb + 5 kg/d for 30 d at first hospitalization) and liposomal amphotericin B (for 14 d at a dose of 3 mg/kg/d, in three hospitalizations), and in the face of an evolution with hypersplenism, clinical and laboratory repercussions, the patient was admitted in July 2015 to undergo a splenectomy, and at that time, on the physical examination, he presented with a palpable spleen at 12 cm from the left costal margin. In the preoperative period, an ultrasound of the abdomen was performed showing an enlarged spleen extending to the left iliac fossa. CBC with Hb 8.7 g/dL; Ht 27.9%; leukocytes 1,090/microL and 155,000/microL platelets. He underwent splenectomy on August 04, 2015, progressing uneventfully in the intra and postoperative periods. The surgical specimen measured 19.5 x 14.5 x 6 cm and weighed 1,066g (Figures 1 and 2). The histopathological study confirmed the presence of Leihmania parasites within the splenic parenchyma. He also had 7 d of liposomal amphotericin B during hospitalization. In the outpatient follow-up, cholelithiasis was identified, which became symptomatic and the patient underwent, a video cholecystectomy surgery on November 03, 2017, performed by the same team of the splenectomy, also evolving without complications. Nowadays, he has been followed-up at the outpatient clinic, for more than 4 years after the surgery, remaining asymptomatic, without further hospitalizations due to kala-azar or medications, and with a normal hematological profile.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male with recurrent visceral leishmaniasis and refractory hypersplenism presented for scheduled therapeutic splenectomy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 55-year-old male diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis in January 2014 who experienced recurrent pancytopenia, persistent splenomegaly, and five hospitalizations at IDTNP for antileishmanial therapy. Despite multiple courses of pentavalent antimony and liposomal amphotericin B, he developed progressive hypersplenism and refractory cytopenias, prompting admission in July 2015 for therapeutic splenectomy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent visceral leishmaniasis diagnosed in 2014 with five prior hospitalizations; treated with pentavalent antimony (Glucantime 20 mg Sb5+/kg/day for 30 days) and liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day for 14 days across three hospitalizations). Negative HIV serology. Origin: Acaua municipality, Piaui State, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal fullness, fatigue, chronic left upper quadrant heaviness. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly with a palpable spleen extending 12 cm below the left costal margin.
objective.routine_investigations: Preoperative complete blood count: Hemoglobin: 8.7 g/dL; Hematocrit: 27.9%; Leukocyte count: 1,090/microL; Platelet count: 155,000/microL. Abdominal ultrasound: massive splenomegaly extending into the left iliac fossa. HIV serology: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Splenectomy surgical specimen: spleen measured 19.5 x 14.5 x 6 cm and weighed 1,066 g. Histopathological examination of splenic parenchyma: performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Drug-resistant, relapsing visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with severe secondary hypersplenism.
Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathological examination of the surgical specimen confirmed the presence of Leishmania parasites within the splenic parenchyma.
Differentials ruled out: HIV co-infection (negative serology) and primary hematologic malignancies.
Treatment and clinical course: Underwent successful open splenectomy on August 4, 2015, with an uneventful postoperative recovery, alongside a 7-day inpatient course of liposomal amphotericin B. Hematological counts completely normalized. In November 2017, he underwent elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis without complications. At greater than four years of outpatient follow-up, he remains entirely asymptomatic with normal hematological indices and no further leishmaniasis relapse.

raw_case_text: Control 1: 57-year-old male with obesity, attending the emergency department for fever that was present for 10 days, as well as a cough and respiratory failure. His blood pressure was 121/78, heart rate 110 beats per minute, SpO2 94-95%, and he had elevated D-Dimer levels. Chest X-ray: A bilateral alveolar reticulum interstitial pattern of peripheral predominance and right base was observed which was suggestive of an atypical infection. Confirmation of COVID-19 was made by RT-PCR using a throat swab. The patient was treated with hydroxychloroquine and lopinavir-ritonavir, and they remain in the hospital.
