Abdominal examination demonstrated firm, non-tender hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin, spleen extending 6 cm along its long axis). Vital signs were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Chronic active hepatitis B infection parameters on oral entecavir; routine laboratory evaluations were completed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of para-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) with visceral involvement and concurrent chronic active hepatitis B: slit skin smear from cutaneous lesions and splenic aspirate both demonstrated intracellular Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies; liver biopsy confirmed the presence of LD bodies in hepatic tissue without fibrosis. Entecavir antiviral therapy was maintained. He was initially treated with intramuscular sodium stibogluconate (SSG; 20 mg/kg deep IM for 5 cycles of 20 days injection followed by 10 days rest); however, skin lesions and splenomegaly remained unchanged and repeat slit skin smear and splenic aspirate confirmed persistent LD bodies, establishing SSG resistance. The patient was switched to intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg 2 days per week for 3 consecutive weeks). At 21 days post-initiation, skin lesions faded and spleen size regressed; at 1-month follow-up, repeat slit skin smear and splenic aspirate showed complete clearance of LD bodies.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old man was hospitalized with sudden-onset weakness in both lower extremities. The patient had been treated with isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 450 mg, and ethambutol 800 mg daily for pulmonary tuberculosis during the past two months. He had no history of exposure to antituberculosis antibiotics before beginning therapy. His compliance to antibiotics was excellent after the treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis and he denied the interruption on these regimens. He reported no constitutional symptoms, history of hyperthyroidism or paralysis.
A physical examination indicated that the muscle strength of the lower extremities was 2/5 of normal. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph revealed reticular opacities on the bilateral upper lung fields, consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis. His laboratory data included hemoglobin 13.0 mg/dL, leukocyte count 9900/muL, and platelet count 290,000/muL. His biochemical data for serum and urine on admission are shown in Table 1. Profound hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypouricemia were present. Serum pH, bicarbonate level and anion gap indicated hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap. The urinary anion gap was positive (10.2 mEq/L), suggesting the presence of renal tubular acidosis. Urinalysis showed normoglycemic glucosuria, beta2-microglobulinuria, pH 5.5, 2.5 g/day proteinuria and microscopic hematuria. The fractional excretion of potassium was 29.3% (normal range, 4%-16%); the calculated ratio of the maximal tubular transport of phosphate reabsorption to the glomerular filtration rate (TmP/GFR) was 0.24 mg/dL (normal range, 2.3-4.3 mg/dL); and the fractional excretion of uric acid was 77.4% (normal range, 6%-20%). Generalized hyperaminoaciduria was detected with liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. These findings suggest generalized proximal tubular dysfunction with wasting of bicarbonate, glucose, protein, potassium, phosphate, and uric acid.
Additional blood tests were performed to determine other possible causes of the patient's hypokalemia. His plasma renin activity and serum level of aldosterone were 21.6 ng/mL/h and 30.5 ng/dL, respectively. His thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine levels were within the normal ranges. Serum and urinary protein immunoelectrophoresis showed no evidence of monoclonal gammopathy, and immunological surveys of autoantibodies were negative. The patient's reticulocyte count, serum lactate dehydrogenase, and liver enzymes levels were within the normal ranges.
An ultrasonographic examination showed a normal-sized kidney, with slightly increased echogenicity in the bilateral renal parenchyma. A renal biopsy showed extensive mononuclear cell infiltrates, including epithelioid histiocytes and eosinophils, mild interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy (Figure 1A and B). Ziehl-Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli and PCR detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the renal biopsy specimen were negative. Focal granular deposits of immunoglobulin A (IgA) and complement 3 (C3) were demonstrated in the tubules (Figure 1C and D). The same immunofluorescent positivity was also shown in glomerular mesangium, and electron microscopy showed electron-dense deposits in the subendothelial and mesangial spaces (Figure 1E and F). These findings were consistent with IgA nephropathy accompanied by focal immune deposits along the tubules. Half the epithelial foot processes were effaced, and there were no pathological findings in the mitochondria.
Potassium chloride supplementation was given to treat the patient's hypokalemic paralysis. His muscle strength increased one day after potassium chloride supplementation. We substituted rifampin with levofloxacin, but his other antituberculosis antibiotics remained the same. Supplementation with potassium chloride and sodium bicarbonate was continued, and the patient was discharged on hospital day 14. The biochemical markers associated with Fanconi syndrome were significantly resolved, and he experienced no paralytic symptoms after discharge. His proteinuria and microscopic hematuria was also improved, and we discontinued supplementation with potassium chloride and sodium bicarbonate at the three-month follow-up. The patient's renal function and proximal tubular function remained stable at the last follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male receiving antituberculosis therapy presenting with acute lower extremity weakness and paralysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with sudden-onset bilateral lower extremity weakness leading to inability to walk. He had been receiving daily therapy with isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 450 mg, and ethambutol 800 mg for active pulmonary tuberculosis for the preceding two months, with strict medication adherence and no treatment interruptions. He denied constitutional symptoms, prior episodes of weakness, paralysis, or thyroid disease.
subjective.past_medical_history: Active pulmonary tuberculosis treated for 2 months with isoniazid 300 mg, rifampin 450 mg, and ethambutol 800 mg daily. No prior antituberculosis drug exposure before starting current therapy. Denies hyperthyroidism or familial periodic paralysis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Acute profound lower extremity muscle weakness. Denies fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, palpitations, or sensory disturbances.

objective.physical_examination: Neuromuscular examination revealed symmetrical flaccid weakness of the lower extremities with muscle strength graded at 2/5. Remainder of physical and neurological examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL (reported as 13.0 mg/dL), leukocyte count 9,900/muL, platelet count 290,000/muL. Serum biochemistry: profound hypokalemia (potassium 1.6 mEq/L), hypophosphatemia (phosphate 1.1 mg/dL), hypouricemia (uric acid 1.2 mg/dL). Arterial blood gas showed normal anion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Urinary anion gap was positive (+10.2 mEq/L) consistent with renal tubular acidosis. Urinalysis: normoglycemic glucosuria, beta2-microglobulinuria, pH 5.5, proteinuria 2.5 g/day, and microscopic hematuria. Fractional excretion of potassium was 29.3% (normal 4%-16%); TmP/GFR was 0.24 mg/dL (normal 2.3-4.3 mg/dL); fractional excretion of uric acid was 77.4% (normal 6%-20%). Reticulocyte count, serum LDH, and liver enzymes were within normal limits. Plasma renin activity 21.6 ng/mL/h, serum aldosterone 30.5 ng/dL. TSH and free T4 within normal limits. Serum and urine protein immunoelectrophoresis showed no monoclonal gammopathy; autoimmune serologies negative. Chest radiograph showed bilateral upper lung field reticular opacities consistent with pulmonary tuberculosis. Renal ultrasonography showed normal-sized kidneys with slightly increased bilateral parenchymal echogenicity.
objective.advanced_workup: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) revealed generalized hyperaminoaciduria, establishing generalized proximal tubular dysfunction. Renal biopsy demonstrated extensive interstitial mononuclear cell infiltration with epithelioid histiocytes and eosinophils, mild interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy; immunofluorescence revealed focal granular deposits of IgA and C3 in renal tubules and glomerular mesangium; electron microscopy showed subendothelial and mesangial electron-dense deposits with 50% epithelial foot process effacement (consistent with IgA nephropathy and acute tubulointerstitial nephritis); Ziehl-Neelsen stain and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on renal biopsy tissue were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Drug-induced Fanconi syndrome with severe hypokalemic paralysis and acute tubulointerstitial nephritis secondary to rifampin toxicity, superimposed on underlying IgA nephropathy, in a patient being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Clinical and biochemical proximal tubular wasting syndrome (renal hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypouricemia, normoglycemic glycosuria, aminoaciduria, beta2-microglobulinuria) and renal biopsy confirming acute tubulointerstitial nephritis with negative renal TB PCR and AFB stain, resolving completely upon withdrawal of rifampin.
Management and outcome: Emergency intravenous and oral potassium chloride supplementation restored lower extremity muscle strength within 24 hours. Rifampin was permanently discontinued and replaced with levofloxacin, while isoniazid and ethambutol were maintained. Potassium chloride and sodium bicarbonate supplementation was continued, leading to normalization of proximal tubular function; patient was discharged on day 14. Microscopic hematuria and proteinuria resolved, electrolyte supplements were stopped at 3-month follow-up, and renal and proximal tubular function remained stable.

raw_case_text: A 65-year-old male patient, with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, presented to us with painless, progressive diminished vision in both eyes over 4 months (asymmetrical involvement; right eye defect more than left eye). On examination, right eye had only perception of light and left eye had vision of counting fingers up to 2 feet. Fundus showed features of optic atrophy. His neurological examination was unremarkable. There were no signs of meningeal irritation. He was negative for  HIV, HBsAg and HCV done by ELISA as a routine presurgical investigation. His chest X-ray was unremarkable. Mantoux was negative. Sputum AFB (done in the postoperative period after the tissue cultures showed growth of tuberculosis) was negative. Sputum for acid fast bacilli was negative. He had an FBS = 176 mg/dl, PPBS = 231mg/dl, and Hb1Ac = 8.2%. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of brain with orbit showed a lesion, which was heterogeneously hypointense on T1W and hyperintense on T2W, located in the orbit, encircling the optic nerve and was extending through the optic foramen into the cranial cavity. On gadolinium contrast T1W imaging, the lesion was brilliantly enhancing and was extending onto the planum sphenoidale [Figure 1]. Mild enhancement was also noted in the right orbit. The paranasal sinuses were normal. A working diagnosis of orbital meningioma was made. A left supraorbital craniotomy and deroofing of the orbit was followed by subtotal excision of the lesion. The tumor was grayish, mildly vascular, firm, nonsuckable and was encircling the left optic nerve and was extending into the optic canal. The frozen section examination was suggestive of granulomatous pathology and hence the specimen was subjected to microbiological examination as per our departmental protocol for suspected infections (aerobic, tubercular and fungal staining, and cultures). Histopathological examination showed multi-septate hyphae suggestive of fungus. On day 5, growth of Aspergillus flavus was noted on fungal culture. The patient was started on antifungal drugs immediately (Inj. Voriconazole 400 mg on day 1 followed by 200 mg daily for 14 days, followed by oral Voriconazole 200 mg, twice daily for 4 weeks, to be reviewed with repeat imaging). On day 28, all three cultures tubes for tuberculosis [BACTEC 460 Tb system (Becton Dickinson, USA) using the 12 B vials] were positive. He was started on antitubercular drugs as per his body weight (Isoniazid 300 mg once a day, Rifampicin 600 mg once a day, Pyrazinamide 750 mg twice daily, Ethambutol 800 mg once a day, and Benadone 20 mg once a day). He was discharged on 14th postoperative day with no change in his visual status. He, however, had a cerebrovascular accident and succumbed to it on 38th postoperative day.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presented with painless, progressive loss of vision in both eyes over 4 months, affecting the right eye more than the left.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 65-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus experienced insidious, painless, progressive diminution of vision in both eyes over 4 months, with greater impairment in the right eye compared to the left.
subjective.past_medical_history: Poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. No other prior medical history, hospitalizations, or exposures documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for progressive bilateral visual loss. Negative for meningeal symptoms or systemic complaints. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right eye: vision limited to light perception only. Left eye: vision limited to counting fingers up to 2 feet. Fundus: bilateral optic atrophy. Neurological examination unremarkable; no signs of meningeal irritation.
objective.routine_investigations: Fasting blood sugar 176 mg/dL, postprandial blood sugar 231 mg/dL, HbA1c 8.2%. Chest X-ray unremarkable. Mantoux test negative. Sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear negative. Presurgical ELISA for HIV, HBsAg, and HCV negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and orbital MRI: heterogeneously T1-hypointense, T2-hyperintense mass in orbit encircling the optic nerve and extending through the optic foramen into the cranial cavity, intensely enhancing with gadolinium onto planum sphenoidale; mild enhancement in right orbit; normal paranasal sinuses. Left supraorbital craniotomy and deroofing of orbit performed with subtotal excision of grayish, firm, nonsuckable tumor. Frozen section revealed granulomatous pathology; histopathology showed multi-septate hyphae.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Co-infection of orbital-cranial tuberculoma and orbital Aspergillus flavus mimicking an orbital meningioma, confirmed by positive mycobacterial culture in all three tubes (BACTEC 460 TB system using 12B vials) on postoperative day 28, alongside culture isolation of Aspergillus flavus on day 5 and histopathologic demonstration of multi-septate fungal hyphae. Sputum AFB and Mantoux tests were negative. Management & Outcome: Treated initially with voriconazole (IV 400 mg loading, then 200 mg daily for 14 days, followed by oral voriconazole 200 mg twice daily). Upon mycobacterial culture positivity, weight-based antitubercular therapy was added: isoniazid 300 mg daily, rifampicin 600 mg daily, pyrazinamide 750 mg twice daily, ethambutol 800 mg daily, and pyridoxine (Benadone) 20 mg daily. Discharged on postoperative day 14 without visual recovery; subsequently suffered a cerebrovascular accident and died on postoperative day 38.

raw_case_text:
In September 2016, a 60-year-old male Austrian patient presented at the Department of Internal Medicine, Medical University of Graz, Graz, Austria, with a three-week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. Concomitant diseases were adequately treated diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypothyroidism. Travel history revealed a two-week trip to the south of Crete in September 2015 and a two-week trip the south of Spain in May 2016.
Laboratory parameters showed elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) ranging between 94.2 and 188.9 mg/L (normal range 0-5 mg/L), slight hypochromic, normocytic anemia without signs of hemolysis (hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombopenia (127,000/muL; normal range 140,000-440,000/muL) and a discreetly elevated gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) but were otherwise inconspicuous. The soluble interleukin 2-receptor (IL-2R) was elevated (5156.1 pg/mL, reference range 458.0-1997.0). Chest X-ray, urine analysis, abdominal sonography, transthoracic as well as transoesophageal echocardiography showed no focus of infection but revealed splenomegaly (7.2 x 16.4 cm). Serial blood cultures were negative, as were tests for influenza (negative PCR), other viral infections (negative IgM antibody test for Puumala, Dobrava, and Hantaan virus, negative PCR for cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus), leptospirosis (negative antibody test), malaria (negative blood smear), tuberculosis (negative interferon-gamma release assay), and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (negative antibody).
Empiric antibiotic therapy with initially ampicillin/sulbactam and later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin did not lead to improvement. Interestingly, in the course of the following 3 weeks, discrete bicytopenia turned into severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), initially normal, increased to 1107 U/L (reference range 120-240). Liver enzymes including GGT, alkaline phosphatase (AP), aspartate transaminase (AST) also increased. Fever persisted with levels up to 40 C.
Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (see Fig. 1A and B) showed tracer enhancement in the central and peripheral bone marrow. Bone marrow biopsy revealed microorganisms within macrophages (Fig. 2). PCR from peripheral blood and bone marrow confirmed infection with Leishmania donovani. Therapy with liposomal amphotericin B was initiated, causing rapid cessation of fever and a significant drop in CRP levels within days. Blood count ameliorated rapidly, and transfusions were no longer required. After release from hospital, regular follow-up visits at the outpatient clinic ensued. Until today, VL has not recurred.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male presented with a 3-week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and 6 kg unintentional weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In September 2016, a 60-year-old male presented with a 3-week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. Empirical antibiotic therapy with ampicillin/sulbactam, followed by piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin, produced no improvement. Over the next 3 weeks, mild bicytopenia evolved into severe transfusion-dependent pancytopenia with persistent fevers up to 40 °C and rising transaminases.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (well-controlled) and hypothyroidism. Travel history: two-week trip to southern Crete in September 2015 and two-week trip to southern Spain in May 2016. Prior empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: High fever up to 40 °C, fatigue, unintentional weight loss (6 kg). Denied localized pain, respiratory symptoms, or bowel changes.

objective.physical_examination: Initial physical examination was inconspicuous. During hospitalization, high spiking fevers reached 40 °C. Palpation revealed splenomegaly. No peripheral lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP: 94.2 to 188.9 mg/L; reference 0-5 mg/L). Mild hypochromic normocytic anemia (Hb 12.5 g/dL) and mild thrombocytopenia (127,000/muL), which progressed over 3 weeks into severe pancytopenia requiring blood transfusions. Elevated GGT, alkaline phosphatase (AP), and AST. LDH increased to 1,107 U/L (reference 120-240). Soluble IL-2 receptor (sIL-2R) elevated at 5,156.1 pg/mL (reference 458-1,997). Serial blood cultures sterile. Urine analysis normal. Negative PCR for influenza, CMV, and EBV; negative IgM serology for Puumala, Dobrava, and Hantaan hantaviruses; negative Leptospira antibodies; negative malaria blood smears; negative IGRA for tuberculosis; negative HIV antibody test.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest X-ray normal. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography: no infective endocarditis focus. Abdominal sonography demonstrated splenomegaly (7.2 x 16.4 cm). Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) showed intense metabolic tracer uptake in central and peripheral bone marrow. Bone marrow biopsy revealed microorganisms within macrophages.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Travel-acquired visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) caused by Leishmania donovani with hemophagocytic activation.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Bone marrow biopsy revealed amastigotes within macrophages; PCR from peripheral blood and bone marrow confirmed Leishmania donovani infection.
Differentials Ruled Out: Infective endocarditis, occult bacteremia, influenza, hantavirus infection, CMV/EBV mononucleosis, leptospirosis, malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, and lymphoproliferative malignancy.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics (ampicillin/sulbactam, piperacillin/tazobactam, vancomycin) were ineffective. Targeted therapy with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B led to rapid defervescence, sharp decline in CRP within days, rapid hematologic reconstitution without further transfusions, and sustained remission without relapse during outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
This was a case report of a 50-year-old male agriculturist, diagnosed as HIV positive 11/2 years back on antiretroviral therapy (ART), who presented with a 6 month history of asymptomatic skin lesions over his limbs. Physical examination revealed multiple, diffuse, non-ulcerating, papulonodular and non-itchy skin lesions of size 2-18 mm [Figure 1]. History revealed that the lesions first appeared on the feet and then over the hands. There was no history of travel to endemic areas of leishmaniasis. There was no hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. The laboratory investigations revealed anemia hemoglobin (Hb - 8.3 g/dL). The liver function tests, renal function tests, lipid profile and blood sugar were within the normal limits. The platelet count was 2 lacs/muL and the total leucocyte count was 5,100/muL.
Chest X-ray and ultrasound of abdomen were normal. His CD4 count was 126 cells/muL and HIV viral load was <47 copies/mL. The patient was initially suspected to be having histoplasmosis, which was ruled out by skin biopsy.
Punch biopsy of skin lesions showed sheets of histiocytic cells in the sub epithelial tissue, stuffed with numerous amastigotes of Leishmania. Mild lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate was also noted [Figure 2].
The patient was treated with ketoconazole 200 mg twice a day and 450 mg rifampicin daily for 1 month along with ART (nevirapine, stavudine and lamivudine). The patient improved on treatment but later was lost to follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old HIV-positive male presented with a 6-month history of painless, non-itchy skin lesions on his limbs.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-month history of gradual eruption of non-ulcerating, asymptomatic papulonodular lesions that first developed on his feet and progressively involved his hands.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed 1.5 years prior on antiretroviral therapy (nevirapine, stavudine, and lamivudine). Occupation: agriculturist. No history of travel to known leishmaniasis endemic areas.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports skin lesions are asymptomatic and non-pruritic; denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, or gastrointestinal disturbances.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic examination demonstrated multiple diffuse, non-ulcerating, non-pruritic papulonodular skin lesions ranging from 2 mm to 18 mm in size across the upper and lower extremities. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy was present.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed anemia with hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL; total leukocyte count: 5,100/muL; platelet count: 200,000/muL. Liver function tests, renal function tests, lipid profile, and blood glucose: all within normal limits. CD4 cell count: 126 cells/muL; HIV viral load: <47 copies/mL. Chest radiograph and abdominal ultrasound: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy: sheets of histiocytic cells in the subepithelial dermis with mild lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltrate, containing dense intracellular protozoan structures; fungal stains negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Punch biopsy of cutaneous nodules revealed dermal histiocytic sheets stuffed with numerous Leishmania amastigotes, confirming cutaneous leishmaniasis in an HIV-coinfected host. Histoplasmosis and other fungal/mycobacterial infections were excluded on biopsy. Management and Outcome: Treated with oral ketoconazole 200 mg twice daily and oral rifampicin 450 mg once daily for 1 month alongside continuing antiretroviral therapy (nevirapine, stavudine, lamivudine). The patient showed clinical improvement with regression of lesions but was subsequently lost to outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
Patient information: a 9-month-old female presented with a history of poor weight gain from birth, cough, and fever of 2 weeks, fast breathing of 1 week, and refusal to suck for one day. Weight loss was progressive despite adequate feeding. Cough was distressful, non-paroxysmal with no history of contact with an adult having a chronic cough. The fever was high-grade and continuous. Fast breathing was of insidious onset and had been progressive. She was unable to suckle from the breast for 24 hours prior to presentation despite her mothers  concerted effort to breastfeed her. A review of systems revealed she had orthopnea, easy fatigability, excessive sweating, no cyanosis, no body swelling, and no seizures. She was referred to another hospital where she was admitted and had a blood transfusion without remarkable improvement. Prior to this, she had no previous hospital admission. Pregnancy, birth, and neonatal period were normal. Although her mother did not remember the birth weight. She was exclusively breastfed and commenced satisfactory complementary feeds. She was also adequately immunized and her development was within normal limits. She is the third of 3 children. Both parents were in their early thirties and from a low socio-economic class.
Clinical findings: at presentation, she had dysmorphic features with upward slanting of the palpebral fissures, low-set ears, and flattened nasal bridge. She was also severely pale, in severe respiratory distress with subcoastal and intercoastal recessions, flaring alae nasi and she was saturating at 85% in room air. Her weight was 6kg (44% of expected and > -3 Z-score), height was 72cm (0.8 Z-score). She was tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 60 cycles per minute and had widespread crepitation. She also had an active precordium, apex beat was displaced to the fifth left intercostal space lateral to the mid-clavicular line, she had tachycardia with a heart rate of 160bpm and a grade 3/6 continuous systolic murmur, maximal at the left lower sternal border and radiating to the armpit. Abdominal examination showed a reducible umbilical hernia and tender hepatomegaly with liver 4cm below the right subcoastal margin. An initial working diagnosis was severe bronchopneumonia in heart failure in a child with acyanotic congenital heart disease and chromosomal abnormality probably Downs syndrome, failure to thrive with severe malnutrition.
Diagnostic assessment: full blood count showed absolute leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 22.7 x 109/L, and anemia with a packed cell volume of 28%, electrolytes urea, and creatinine showed hypokalemia of 2.4mmol/L, hypocalcemia with non-ionic calcium of 1.09mmol/L. The retroviral screening was seronegative. Chest X-ray (Figure 1), done showed: significant perihilar mottled and fluffy opacities involving all lung zones bilaterally, cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 61%, splaying of the carina suggestive of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Electrocardiograph showed: sinus tachycardia, with a heart rate of 168bpm, right (rt) atrial enlargement, rt ventricle hypertrophy, and rt axis deviation. Echocardiography showed: 0.4cm PDA with continuous left to rt shunt at 74mmHg. The malaria parasite was positive.
Therapeutic interventions: she was, commenced on parenteral antibiotics, diuretics, intranasal oxygen, nutritional rehabilitation, vitamin D supplementation, antimalarial medications, and hematinic. She was stabilized, discharged, and referred for PDA ligation which she had after 6 months. The operation was successful as there was good PDA ligation with no residual flow on the echocardiogram (Figure 2 A,B).
Follow-up and outcome of interventions: a month post-surgery she started coughing and though she had started gaining weight which was now 94% of expected, she had localized rhonchi in the left upper lung zone posteriorly, she was managed for early pneumonia with a possible localized lung obstruction as a post-PDA ligation complication. A chest X-ray was ordered which was not done although she was placed on antibiotics, and chest physiotherapy. She was managed for uncomplicated pneumonia two more times on an outpatient basis. The cough however progressively worsened over 3 months and she also developed a fever and started losing the previously gained weight. On subsequent examination, she was tachypneic, and had coarse crepitations, bilaterally. She also had tachycardia with a gallop rhythm and tender hepatomegaly. She was admitted for severe bronchopneumonia in heart failure to rule out PTB. Chest X-ray (Figure 3) showed bilateral perihilar mottled opacity. GeneXpert test showed mycobacteria tuberculosis was not detected. A diagnosis of PTB was made and she was commenced on anti-tuberculosis drugs with a good response. She has had no recurrence of pneumonia and started gaining weight adequately six months into the treatment.
Patient perspective: the mother was very satisfied and happy that her child has finally recovered.
Informed consent: a written informed consent was given by the mother to have her child s case published.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-month-old female presenting with poor weight gain since birth, cough and fever for two weeks, fast breathing for one week, and inability to suckle for one day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with progressive weight loss since birth despite adequate feeding. Two weeks prior to admission, she developed a persistent, distressing, non-paroxysmal cough and high-grade continuous fever, with no known contact with chronic cough. One week prior, she developed insidious and progressive tachypnea, culminating in refusal to suckle for 24 hours. She was initially hospitalized elsewhere and received a blood transfusion without significant improvement. She was diagnosed with a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and underwent successful surgical ligation at 6 months of age. One month post-surgery, she developed cough and localized rhonchi, and was treated for recurrent pneumonia three times on an outpatient basis. Over the subsequent 3 months, cough worsened with recurrent fever, failure to gain weight, and worsening respiratory distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Normal pregnancy, delivery, and neonatal period; exclusively breastfed followed by satisfactory complementary feeds; up-to-date immunizations. Prior hospitalization with blood transfusion at another facility. Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with continuous left-to-right shunt (0.4 cm, 74 mmHg) successfully ligated at 6 months of age with no residual shunt.
subjective.review_of_systems: Orthopnea, easy fatigability, excessive sweating. Denies cyanosis, generalized body swelling, or seizures.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature not specified; SpO2 85% on room air; HR 160 bpm; RR 60 cycles/min. Weight 6 kg (44% of expected, > -3 Z-score), height 72 cm (0.8 Z-score). Dysmorphic features (upward-slanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, flattened nasal bridge). Severely pale, in severe respiratory distress with subcostal/intercostal recessions and flaring alae nasi. Respiratory exam: widespread crepitations. Cardiovascular: active precordium, apex beat displaced to 5th left intercostal space lateral to midclavicular line, tachycardia, grade 3/6 continuous systolic murmur maximal at left lower sternal border radiating to axilla. Abdomen: reducible umbilical hernia, tender hepatomegaly (liver palpable 4 cm below right subcostal margin). Subsequent re-admission exam: tachypneic with bilateral coarse crepitations, tachycardia with gallop rhythm, tender hepatomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Full blood count: WBC 22.7 x 10^9/L, packed cell volume (PCV) 28%. Serum electrolytes, urea, and creatinine: potassium 2.4 mmol/L, non-ionic calcium 1.09 mmol/L. Retroviral screening seronegative. Malaria parasite smear positive. Initial chest X-ray: significant bilateral perihilar mottled and fluffy opacities across all lung zones, cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 61%), and splaying of the carina suggestive of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. Follow-up chest X-ray: persistent bilateral perihilar mottled opacities.
objective.advanced_workup: Electrocardiogram: sinus tachycardia (HR 168 bpm), right atrial enlargement, right ventricular hypertrophy, and right axis deviation. Echocardiogram: 0.4 cm PDA with continuous left-to-right shunt at 74 mmHg; post-ligation echocardiogram confirmed complete ductal closure without residual flow. Sputum/gastric GeneXpert: negative for mycobacterial DNA.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) in an infant with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome), severe malnutrition/failure to thrive, and post-PDA ligation; initial presentation complicated by severe bronchopneumonia, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, hypokalemia (2.4 mmol/L), hypocalcemia (1.09 mmol/L), and malaria parasitemia.
Diagnostic confirmation: Clinical and radiological diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis based on recurrent non-resolving pneumonia unresponsive to standard broad-spectrum antibiotics, progressive weight loss, persistent fever, and characteristic bilateral perihilar mottled opacities, despite negative GeneXpert.
Management and outcome: Commenced on anti-tuberculosis therapy along with supportive care (parenteral antibiotics, diuretics, oxygen therapy, nutritional rehabilitation, vitamin D supplementation, antimalarials, and hematinics). Follow-up demonstrated favorable clinical response with resolution of pneumonia, cessation of cough and fever, and adequate weight gain reaching 94% of expected at 6 months of treatment.

raw_case_text:
After obtaining the approval of the local ethics committee (Section Giovanni Paolo II- IRCCS Casa Sollievo della Sofferenza) and written informed consent, we report the case of a 66-year-old man with a history of hypertension and ocular MG. This disorder was diagnosed 2 years before the pandemic onset by electromyography (EMG) and frontal muscle jitter study at the neurology unit of our hospital (Figure 1). AChR antibodies were detected, and and the thymoma ascertainment results were negative. He undertook pharmacology therapy consisting of pyridostigmine at a dosage of 30 mg three times daily, which was efficacious in treating myasthenic symptoms. The strength quantification performed by the Medical Research Council (MRC) was normal before the pandemic. At the beginning of December 2020, he developed fever, cough, myalgia, and dyspnea with progressive severe respiratory failure, which required ICU admission. He underwent chest computer tomography (CT) and nasopharyngeal swab that were positive for COVID-19 and was treated with remdesivir and corticosteroids. The patient underwent mechanical ventilation and tracheotomy. Laboratory tests did not detect an increase in the serum CK level. He also developed infections caused by multi-drug resistant germs, including Klebsiella pneumonia, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and underwent multiple antibiotic therapies. The Simplified Acute Physiology Score was 35. During the ICU stay, 15 days after admission, he complained of muscle weakness that evolved into the manifestation of tetraparesis without ocular involvement. Despite this development, pyridostigmine was increased to 60 mg three times daily; the strength remained unchanged. The length of stay (LOS) in ICU was 35 days. After improvement of the clinical conditions, the patient was transferred to our neuro-rehabilitation (NR) unit. At admission, the patient breathed spontaneously but needed 3 L/m oxygen by mask. Capillary oximetry was 97%; he had a central venous catheter, a tracheal tube, and a nasal-gastric tube for nutrition. The neurological picture showed severe tetraparesis that involved predominantly the lower limbs, and he had absent tendinous reflexes. No deficit in ocular or facial muscles was detected, and superficial and deep sensibilities were normal. Given the neurological feature, on day 2 of admission, the patient underwent electroneurography (ENG), electromyography (EMG), and frontal muscle jitter study that confirmed MG and showed overlapping ICUAW. In this respect, the electrophysiological exam revealed signs characteristic of CIP (Table 1). However, a lumbar puncture was performed, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was collected and processed for standard analysis to exclude Guillain-Barre syndrome and polyneuropathies of different etiology. Pressure, cell count, and protein levels (<45 mg/dl) of the CSF were normal without albumin-cytologic disassociation. CSF/serum glucose ratio was normal. The CSF culture results for possible organisms, such as human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi, Borrelia, enteroviruses, Herpes viruses, and CMV, were negative. Similarly, the laboratory test for autoimmune disorders, including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, a panel of antiganglioside antibodies, including anti-GM1, -GM2, -GM3, -GD1a, -GD1b, -GT1b, and -GQ1b, and a panel for paraneoplastic syndrome, were negative.
Strength and functional evaluation were quantified through the MRC scale sum-score, the Disability Rating scale (DRS), the Barthel scale (BS), and the functional independence measure (FIM) at admission, discharge, and 6 months of follow-up. During NR stay, the patient underwent a personalized and tailored rehabilitation treatment for 3 h daily, 6 days a week. Furthermore, he performed 2 h of daily electrical muscular stimulation on the lower limbs by placing surface electrodes on the quadriceps and anterior tibial muscles bilaterally. The muscular strength improved progressively, and the MRC sum score was 50 at discharge. The anticholinesterase therapy with pyridostigmine at the dosage of 30 mg three times daily, the same that the patient was taking before he had COVID-19, was resumed. His motor abilities recovered and, at discharge, he was able to walk without support but remained with left foot drop, which required the application of an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO). Furthermore, he complained of mild fatigue with reduced endurance, which improved over time. At follow-up, the MRC scale sum score and all functional scale scores resulted to be normal (Table 2). The LOS in neuro-rehabilitation was 42 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old male with pre-existing ocular myasthenia gravis presenting with fever, cough, myalgia, and progressive dyspnea leading to severe acute respiratory failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In early December 2020, the patient developed fever, cough, myalgias, and dyspnea, rapidly progressing to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure that required intensive care unit admission and mechanical ventilation. During his ICU stay, he underwent tracheotomy and developed multidrug-resistant nosocomial infections. On ICU day 15, he developed new generalized muscular weakness that progressed to flaccid tetraparesis without ocular involvement, unresponsive to dose escalation of pyridostigmine. After a 35-day ICU stay, he was transferred to a neuro-rehabilitation unit for management of persistent tetraparesis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension and ocular myasthenia gravis diagnosed 2 years prior via EMG and frontal muscle jitter study, with positive anti-AChR antibodies and negative thymoma workup; maintained well on pyridostigmine 30 mg TID with normal baseline MRC strength scores.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports fever, cough, myalgias, dyspnea, and profound generalized limb weakness. Denies diplopia, ptosis, facial weakness, or sensory loss during the tetraparesis episode. Home medications: pyridostigmine 30 mg TID.

objective.physical_examination: Neuro-rehabilitation admission: Breathing spontaneously with 3 L/min oxygen mask, SpO2 97%. Tracheotomy tube, central venous catheter, and nasogastric tube in place. Neurological: Severe flaccid tetraparesis predominantly affecting lower extremities, absent deep tendon reflexes, intact cranial nerves without ocular or facial weakness, and normal superficial and vibration sensation. Discharge: Able to ambulate without assistance with left foot drop requiring an ankle-foot orthosis.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum CK level was normal. Lumbar puncture / CSF: Normal opening pressure, cell count, and protein (< 45 mg/dL) without albuminocytologic dissociation; normal CSF/serum glucose ratio. CSF microbiological investigations were negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, fungi, Borrelia, enteroviruses, herpesviruses, and CMV. Autoimmune and paraneoplastic serologies negative (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, antiganglioside antibodies anti-GM1, -GM2, -GM3, -GD1a, -GD1b, -GT1b, -GQ1b, and paraneoplastic panel).
objective.advanced_workup: Electroneurography (ENG), electromyography (EMG), and frontal muscle jitter study: Confirmed underlying myasthenia gravis and demonstrated concurrent critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) / intensive care unit-acquired weakness (ICUAW). Chest CT: Bilateral infiltrates consistent with severe viral pneumonia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia (confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal swab RT-PCR) complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation, tracheotomy, multiple nosocomial infections (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa), and intensive care unit-acquired weakness / critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) superimposed on ocular myasthenia gravis.

Management and outcome: Received remdesivir, systemic corticosteroids, mechanical ventilation, tracheotomy, and multiple targeted antibiotic courses in the ICU. In neuro-rehabilitation, treated with daily tailored physiotherapy (3 hr/day, 6 days/week), 2 hours of daily neuromuscular electrical stimulation to lower limbs, and resumed pyridostigmine 30 mg TID. Neurological strength and functional status progressively improved (MRC sum-score improved to 50 at discharge, and normalized at 6-month follow-up along with DRS, Barthel, and FIM scores); discharged after 42 days in neuro-rehabilitation with full functional independence.

raw_case_text: A man with recently diagnosed HIV and cryptococcal meningitis had been started on ART one month prior to this (see Table 1 for more information). He presented with WHO 'seriously ill' criteria and an AlereLAM was performed, revealing a strongly positive (4+) result. He was started on TB treatment on the same day. A month later, he deteriorated clinically and required hospital admission. A blood culture during this admission cultured Mycobacterium avium. With this result, azithromycin was added to his TB treatment and pyrazinamide was stopped. The patient died as an inpatient 17 months after initial presentation. No Xpert MTB/RIF or cultures identified M. tb, although he was diagnosed with TB meningitis based on CT brain features during the protracted illness course.

subjective.chief_complaint: An adult male presented with acute clinical deterioration meeting WHO 'seriously ill' criteria one month after starting antiretroviral therapy for HIV and cryptococcal meningitis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A male patient with recently diagnosed HIV and treated cryptococcal meningitis was commenced on antiretroviral therapy 1 month prior. He presented with severe clinical deterioration fulfilling WHO 'seriously ill' criteria. One month later, his condition worsened, necessitating hospitalization and prolonged inpatient care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recently diagnosed HIV infection; cryptococcal meningitis; commenced on antiretroviral therapy 1 month prior. Other medical conditions, travel, or TB exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports severe generalized deterioration and constitutional decline; denies localized symptoms on presentation. Home medications: ART. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Classified as meeting WHO 'seriously ill' criteria; detailed physical exam findings not documented.
objective.advanced_workup: CT scan of the brain demonstrated features characteristic of tuberculous meningitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated mycobacteriosis with Mycobacterium avium bacteremia and concurrent tuberculous meningitis in advanced HIV infection.
Confirmation: Urine AlereLAM was strongly positive (4+); blood culture during subsequent hospitalization grew Mycobacterium avium; brain CT features confirmed tuberculous meningitis; Xpert MTB/RIF and cultures did not isolate M. tuberculosis.
Differentials ruled out: Relapsed cryptococcal meningitis and other CNS opportunistic infections.
Treatment & Outcome: Empiric anti-tuberculosis therapy started on day of presentation based on positive AlereLAM; following isolation of M. avium from blood, azithromycin was added and pyrazinamide stopped. Patient had a protracted hospital course and died as an inpatient 17 months after initial presentation.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old female, with no previous PAH comorbidities, initially presented with fever, shortness of breath, dry cough, chest pain, nausea, and generalized body aches for seven days. On presentation in the hospital, the blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, pulse was 105 bpm, respiratory rate of 22/min, and oxygen saturation was 77%. On examination, there were bilateral coarse crackles in both lower lung fields. Based on the history and examination findings, a COVID-19 was suspected. The patient was admitted to the COVID-19 isolation unit and was started on oxygen by a simple face mask (5 L). The patient was started on intravenous (IV) azithromycin (500 mg/day) and ceftriaxone (75 mg/kg/day IV) along with enoxaparin sodium (40 mg for each 12 hours subcutaneously), dexamethasone (6 mg/day IV), vitamin C and Zinc. The baseline lab testing and a chest X-ray (CXR) were ordered. Moreover, a nasopharyngeal swab was collected for SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR.
Her initial lab reports showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, WBCs 17000/mm3 with polymorphonuclear neutrophils 90% and lymphocyte 7%, LDH 900U/L, serum ferritin 1100 ng/mL, CRP 12 mg/L, PT 14 sec, INR 1.1, aPTT 32 sec, ALT 57 U/L, AST 78 U/L, serum bilirubin total 2 mg/dl, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, and blood urea 40 mg/dL. Her CXR demonstrated bilateral infiltrates. RT-PCR result confirmed as SARS-CoV-2-positive. Arterial blood gas analysis was consistent with hypoxemia and respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.6, PaO2 42 mmHg, and PaCO2 22 mmHg). Over the course of treatment, the patient developed mild respiratory distress syndrome (PaO2/FiO2 250) and necessitated continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). The patient remained in the COVID-19 isolation unit for 18 days. On discharge, patient had improved clinically with oxygen saturation was 92% without oxygen and SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR was negative.
Two months after discharge, she visited the outpatient department with complaints of exertional dyspnea, dry cough, and fatigue for one month. She also reported an episode of exertional syncope. Her vitals revealed blood pressure of 140/90 mmHg, pulse rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 88% without any oxygen support. On examination, her jugular venous pressure raised 13 cm of H2O; left parasternal heave, and wide splitting of the second heart sound was noted. All the relevant blood tests were ordered along with a CXR, electrocardiography (ECG), and a SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. The ECG suggested right axis deviation, and the blood test results are presented in Table 1. A RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative which ruled out re-infection. The lung CXR demonstrated right atrial enlargement and some fibrotic changes (Fig. 1A). A high-resolution CT-scan revealed massive fibrosis, diffuse symmetrical ground glass opacities involving both lung fields along with septal thickening and traction bronchiectasis most consistent with post-COVID-19 changes (Fig. 1B).
To further investigate the cause of patient problem, transthoracic echocardiography was ordered which showed right ventricular systolic blood pressure (RVSP) 59 mmHg, tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity (TRV) 4.5 m/s, pulmonary artery diameter was 31 mm with normal left side heart parameters. Based on echocardiographic findings and clinical presentation of the patient, the diagnosis of PAH group 3 was made in accordance with the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Respiratory Society (ERS). The patient was commenced on epoprostenol infusion (25 ng/kg/min, repeated every week), montelukast 10 mg/day, oxygen therapy, and spironolactone 100 mg/day. In addition, all routine vaccinations including pneumococcal and influenza vaccines offered to the patient, and a follow-up visit was scheduled with a multidisciplinary team consisting of a pulmonologist, pulmonary rehabilitation team, and a cardiologist. Partial improvement was recorded in the subsequent visit (improved exercise tolerance, oxygen saturation, and decreased pulmonary arterial pressure to 45 mmHg).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old female presenting with fever, shortness of breath, dry cough, chest pain, nausea, and generalized body aches for seven days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 7-day history of fever, worsening dyspnea, dry cough, chest pain, nausea, and myalgias. Upon hospital presentation, she was severely hypoxemic and placed on oxygen via simple face mask at 5 L/min. During hospitalization, she developed mild acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring CPAP support, staying in the hospital for 18 days until clinical improvement and discharge on room air. Two months post-discharge, she presented to the outpatient clinic with a 1-month history of exertional dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and an episode of exertional syncope.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior history of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) or related chronic cardiopulmonary comorbidities.

objective.physical_examination: Initial hospital presentation: Blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 77% on room air; lung auscultation revealed bilateral coarse crackles in both lower lung fields. Outpatient presentation (2 months post-discharge): Blood pressure 140/90 mmHg, pulse rate 90 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air; jugular venous pressure elevated to 13 cm H2O; cardiac examination revealed a left parasternal heave and wide splitting of the second heart sound.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission labs: Hemoglobin 11 g/dL, WBC count 17,000/mm3 (90% polymorphonuclear neutrophils, 7% lymphocytes), LDH 900 U/L, serum ferritin 1,100 ng/mL, C-reactive protein 12 mg/L, PT 14 sec, INR 1.1, aPTT 32 sec, ALT 57 U/L, AST 78 U/L, total bilirubin 2 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, blood urea 40 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas (initial): pH 7.6, PaO2 42 mmHg, PaCO2 22 mmHg (respiratory alkalosis and hypoxemia), PaO2/FiO2 ratio 250. Initial chest radiograph: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Outpatient follow-up chest radiograph: Right atrial enlargement and fibrotic parenchymal changes. Follow-up ECG: Right axis deviation.
objective.advanced_workup: High-resolution CT (HRCT) of chest (post-discharge): Diffuse symmetrical ground-glass opacities involving both lung fields, massive fibrosis, septal thickening, and traction bronchiectasis. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) 59 mmHg, tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity (TRV) 4.5 m/s, pulmonary artery diameter 31 mm, with normal left heart parameters.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia with ARDS) confirmed by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR, complicated two months post-discharge by severe secondary Group 3 pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and pulmonary fibrosis. Repeat RT-PCR at outpatient presentation was negative, ruling out reinfection.
Plan & Outcome: Acute episode managed with oxygen support, CPAP, IV azithromycin (500 mg/day), IV ceftriaxone (75 mg/kg/day), subcutaneous enoxaparin sodium (40 mg q12h), IV dexamethasone (6 mg/day), vitamin C, and zinc, leading to discharge on day 18 with room air SpO2 of 92% and negative RT-PCR. Post-COVID PAH managed with continuous intravenous epoprostenol infusion (25 ng/kg/min weekly titration), oral montelukast 10 mg/day, spironolactone 100 mg/day, supplemental oxygen therapy, pneumococcal and influenza immunizations, and multidisciplinary pulmonary rehabilitation. Subsequent follow-up demonstrated improved exercise tolerance, improved oxygenation, and reduction of pulmonary arterial pressure to 45 mmHg.

raw_case_text: A 20-year-old young male was admitted to our hospital with a chief complaint of progressively increasing weakness of all the four limbs for 1 day. He had the history of high-grade fever for 5 days which responded to antipyretic with generalised body ache. The patient reported that his weakness started first from lower limbs, and within hours it progressed to involve upper limbs also. There was no history of neck pain, sensory symptoms in limbs, recent vaccination, diarrheal illness, recent vigorous exercise or heavy carbohydrate meal. On general examination, he was afebrile and rest of his vitals were normal. On neurological examination, only finding was grade 1-2/5 power in both upper and lower limb with diminished reflexes. There was no cranial nerve involvement, sensory deficit or any evidence of bladder, bowel, or bulbar dysfunction. His single breath count was 35. There was no past or family history of similar weakness or any episodic weakness. Blood investigations on admission were as follows: hemoglobin was 13.8 g/dl, total leucocyte count was 8.8 x 103/mul with 44% polymorphs, 54% lymphocytes and 2% monocytes. The platelet count was 1,00,000/mm. His blood biochemistry revealed serum potassium 1.82 mmol/l, sodium 139 mmol/l, and a normal creatinine kinase value, the arterial blood gas analysis showed a pH of 7.34, bicarbonate 16.7 mmol/l and anion gap 5.1 mmol/l. His renal and thyroid function tests were completely normal, and the liver function test showed a normal serum bilirubin with SGOT and SGPT of 90 and 100 IU/l, respectively. Urine analysis showed a pH of 6 with normal specific gravity and no proteinuria or glycosuria, and spot urinary sodium potassium and calcium were within normal limits, the hospital stay was uneventful. After 7 days, a challenge test performed with heavy carbohydrates diet and strenuous exercise, followed by rest, failed to produce any weakness. For the challenge test, the patient was hospitalized, and the procedure was explained to him. An informed consent was obtained. It was undertaken in an intensive care setting. His nerve conduction velocity (NCV)/electromyography (EMG) was completely normal, ECG showed prominent U waves [Figure 1], his dengue NS1 antigen ELISA as well as dengue IgM antibody test were positive. A diagnosis of dengue fever with thrombocytopenia with hypokalemic motor paralysis was made and the patient was given intravenous potassium chloride infusion. His motor power improved rapidly and at 10 h of starting treatment his power was completely normal. On the second day of treatment, his repeat serum potassium was 3.9 meq/l. The patient was not given any treatment for thrombocytopenia and was kept under observation as no signs of bleeding diathesis were present. At the end of first week, his platelet count became completely normal. The patient was discharged on 5th day of admission with advice for follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male presented with acute, progressively increasing quadriparesis for 1 day following a 5-day febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced high-grade fever and generalized body aches for 5 days that responded to antipyretics. One day prior to admission, he developed rapidly progressive muscle weakness starting symmetrically in the bilateral lower extremities and ascending to involve the upper extremities within hours. He had no neck pain, numbness, paresthesias, recent vaccination, diarrhea, heavy carbohydrate ingestion, or strenuous exertion.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior history or family history of episodic paralysis or muscle weakness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported generalized body aches and limb weakness. Denied sensory loss, diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria, shortness of breath, bowel or bladder incontinence.

objective.physical_examination: Patient was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurological examination revealed symmetric motor weakness with muscle power grade 1-2/5 across all four limbs and generalized hyporeflexia (diminished deep tendon reflexes). Cranial nerves were intact; bulbar, sensory, cerebellar, and autonomic functions were normal. Single breath count was 35.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 8,800/muL (44% polymorphs, 54% lymphocytes, 2% monocytes), platelet count 100,000/mm3 (normalized by 1 week).
Serum electrolytes & biochemistry: Serum potassium 1.82 mmol/L (severe hypokalemia), sodium 139 mmol/L, normal creatine kinase; arterial blood gas: pH 7.34, bicarbonate 16.7 mmol/L, anion gap 5.1 mmol/L.
Renal & liver function tests: Renal and thyroid function tests were completely normal; SGOT 90 IU/L, SGPT 100 IU/L, with normal total bilirubin.
Urinalysis: Urine pH 6.0, normal specific gravity, no proteinuria or glycosuria; spot urinary sodium, potassium, and calcium were normal.
Electrocardiogram: Prominent U waves characteristic of severe hypokalemia.
objective.advanced_workup:
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography (NCS/EMG): Normal motor and sensory nerve conduction velocities and waveforms without evidence of demyelinating polyneuropathy.
Provocative carbohydrate and exercise challenge test: Conducted under intensive care observation 7 days post-admission; high-carbohydrate feeding and strenuous exercise followed by rest failed to elicit muscle weakness, ruling out familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue fever presenting with secondary severe acute hypokalemic quadriparesis and mild transaminitis, confirmed by positive dengue NS1 antigen ELISA and positive dengue IgM antibody serology. Familial periodic paralysis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, renal tubular acidosis, and thyrotoxic periodic paralysis were ruled out.
Treatment and outcome: Treated with intravenous potassium chloride infusion. Motor strength improved rapidly, returning to grade 5/5 full power within 10 hours of initiation. Serum potassium normalized to 3.9 mEq/L on day 2, thrombocytopenia resolved spontaneously, and he was discharged in good health on hospital day 5.

raw_case_text: A thirty-five-year-old female presented with complaints of per rectal bleeding mixed with stools. She had recurrent episodes associated with crampy lower abdominal pain over a period of five days. Upon further enquiry, she also reported a history of productive cough for three months, night sweats, and weight loss of ten kilograms over the same period. Her medical history was significant for rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation. The patient had a surgical history of mitral valvuloplasty two years prior to her current presentation. Her regular medications included warfarin 5 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily. The examination revealed a sick-looking middle-aged female who had pallor, bipedal edema, and no palpable lymphadenopathy. The precordial examination was positive for features of mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation. Abdominal examination did not elicit any tenderness or palpable mass. Investigations done included a complete blood count with the following results: white cell count 9.24 x 109/L, hemoglobin 5.30 g/dL, and platelets 572 x 109/L. The prothrombin time was prolonged, and the international normalized ratio (INR) was 2.78. Renal and hepatic function tests were normal. Initial management involved withholding of warfarin and transfusion of three units of packed red cells. An urgent colonoscopy performed to evaluate hematochezia revealed segmental inflammation of the ascending colon with ulcerations and polyps covered with yellowish exudate, a distended ileocecal junction, and an aberrant vascular pattern with mucosal edema extending to the hepatic flexure (Figure 1). At endoscopy, the differential diagnoses were tuberculosis or CD. In view of her respiratory complaints and accompanying systemic symptoms, a computed tomography (CT) of the chest and abdomen was performed, which demonstrated right lung consolidation, focal subsegmental consolidations in the left lung, and subcentimeter-sized lymph nodes in the small bowel mesentery (Figure 2). Given her history of chronic cough and chest imaging findings, a sputum test was requested whose staining was acid-fast bacilli (AFB) positive. Biopsies of the samples obtained during colonoscopy revealed lymphocytic infiltration, necrotizing granulomas, and positivity for AFB (Figure 3). Serologic testing for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) was negative. A diagnosis of pulmonary and extra pulmonary tuberculosis with gastrointestinal involvement was established. The patient was initiated on the intensive phase of antituberculous therapy consisting of rifampicin (600 mg/day), isoniazid (300 mg/day), ethambutol (800 mg/day), and pyrazinamide (1 g/day). Warfarin 5 mg daily was reinstituted prior to her discharge after a five-day hospital admission. The culture in Lowenstein-Jensen medium later isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which was susceptible to the first-line drugs. She is followed up at the outpatient clinic with regular INR checks to ensure a therapeutic INR range of 2.0-3.0. Her warfarin dosage was increased from the initial 35 mg/week to 52.5 mg/week by the fourth week after discharge.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old female presented with crampy lower abdominal pain and rectal bleeding mixed with stools for five days, accompanied by productive cough, night sweats, and a 10 kg weight loss over three months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 35-year-old female presented with recurrent episodes of lower gastrointestinal bleeding mixed with stool and crampy lower abdominal pain over 5 days. On systemic questioning, she also reported a 3-month history of productive cough, night sweats, and 10 kg weight loss. She had a background of rheumatic heart disease on chronic anticoagulation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation, atrial fibrillation; status-post surgical mitral valvuloplasty 2 years prior. Regular medications: warfarin 5 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, furosemide 40 mg daily. Denies known TB contact or travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports crampy lower abdominal pain, hematochezia, productive cough, night sweats, 10 kg weight loss; denies fever, dyspnea, or hemoptysis. Home medications: warfarin, carvedilol, furosemide. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Sick-looking middle-aged female with pallor and bilateral pitting pedal edema; no palpable lymphadenopathy. Precordial exam revealed murmurs consistent with mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation. Abdominal examination soft, non-tender, without palpable masses.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 9.24 x 10^9/L; Hemoglobin: 5.30 g/dL; Platelets: 572 x 10^9/L; Prothrombin time: prolonged; INR: 2.78; Renal and hepatic function tests: normal; HIV serology: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Urgent colonoscopy: segmental inflammation of ascending colon with ulcerations and polyps covered with yellowish exudate, distended ileocecal junction, and mucosal edema with aberrant vascular pattern extending to hepatic flexure. Colonic biopsy histology: lymphocytic infiltration and necrotizing granulomas. CT chest and abdomen: right lung consolidation, focal subsegmental consolidations in left lung, and subcentimeter mesenteric lymph nodes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis and gastrointestinal (ileocecal) tuberculosis presenting with severe lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage and profound anemia, in a patient on warfarin for rheumatic heart disease.
Confirmation: Sputum microscopy was acid-fast bacilli (AFB) positive; colonoscopic biopsies revealed necrotizing granulomas with positive AFB staining; culture in Lowenstein-Jensen medium isolated Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex susceptible to first-line agents.
Differentials ruled out: Crohn's disease (excluded by necrotizing granulomas, AFB positivity, and MTB culture), colonic neoplasia, HIV infection (seronegative).
Treatment & Outcome: Warfarin temporarily held; 3 units of packed red blood cells transfused with resolution of bleeding. Intensive phase anti-TB therapy initiated with rifampicin (600 mg/day), isoniazid (300 mg/day), ethambutol (800 mg/day), and pyrazinamide (1 g/day). Warfarin 5 mg daily reinstituted prior to discharge on day 5. Due to rifampicin-mediated CYP induction, warfarin was titrated up from 35 mg/week to 52.5 mg/week by week 4, maintaining therapeutic INR 2.0-3.0.

raw_case_text: In May 2002, a 33-year-old Italian man presented to our outpatient clinic complaining of fever, weight loss, and diarrhea. He had mucocutaneous lesions highly suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma (KS). On physical examination he had hepatosplenomegaly; laboratory tests showed pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. He tested HIV positive. His CD4+ T-cell count was 17 cells/muL and HIV RNA viral load was 225,181 copies/mL. A bone marrow smear showed the presence of Leishmania spp. amastigotes. As a consequence, diagnosis of VL was made and treatment with meglumine antimoniate at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day was given for 30 days. Moreover, HAART with Lamivudine-Stavudine-Lopinavir/ritonavir was started. The patient clinically improved, with progressive resolution of KS lesions and good virological response to antiretroviral therapy. Six months later, the patient suffered a clinical relapse of VL and was treated with intravenous liposomal Amphotericin B (L-AMB) at a dose of 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days and then weekly at the same dose for 4 weeks. However, several relapses of VL occurred over the following years. Each relapse was treated with the aforementioned drug schedule. In February 2008, it was decided to start maintenance therapy with L-AMB at a dose of 4 mg/kg/day once a month, in an attempt to prevent further relapses. At this time, his HAART regimen consisted of Abacavir-Lamivudine-Lopinavir/ritonavir; HIV viral load was stably below 50 copies/mL and CD4+ T-cell count was 125 cells/muL. Some weeks after starting secondary prophylaxis with L-AMB, a maculopapular and nodular rash appeared on his trunk and upper limbs (Figure 1). The rash gradually worsened and, four months later, treatment with L-AMB was stopped and a cutaneous biopsy was performed. Histology revealed the presence of a granulomatous infiltrate, with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages, most of which contained Leishmania amastigotes. Restriction fragment length polymorphism-polymerase chain reaction (RFLP-PCR) was positive for L. infantum. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of PKDL. In September 2008, the patient started complaining of fever, diarrhea, and night sweats. Paradoxically, cutaneous lesions markedly improved. On the basis of his symptoms, a relapse of VL was suspected and confirmed by bone marrow aspirate, which showed the presence of Leishmania amastigotes. Treatment with meglumine antimoniate was restarted at a dose of 20 mg/kg/day for 30 days. The patient experienced a rapid clinical response and complete disappearance of cutaneous rash. Unfortunately, the patient had several relapses of VL over the following years, though the interval between them has become wider after restarting maintenance therapy with L-AMB 4 mg/kg/day once a month. At the last followup in December 2013, the patient was in good health and was still receiving secondary prophylaxis with L-AMB. He was taking HAART with Abacavir-Lamivudine-Lopinavir/ritonavir-raltegravir with his last CD4+ T-cell count being 98 cells/muL and HIV RNA < 20 copies/mL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male presented with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and mucocutaneous lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In May 2002, a 33-year-old male presented to an outpatient clinic with fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and mucocutaneous lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma. He was diagnosed with HIV infection and a systemic parasitic disease and received targeted antimicrobial therapy and HAART. Six months later, he experienced a clinical relapse and was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) at 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days, then weekly for 4 weeks. Several relapses occurred over subsequent years, each managed with the same regimen. In February 2008, secondary prophylaxis with monthly L-AMB (4 mg/kg/day) was started. Weeks later, he developed a maculopapular and nodular rash on the trunk and upper limbs, which gradually worsened over 4 months, leading to L-AMB discontinuation and skin biopsy. In September 2008, he developed fever, diarrhea, and night sweats while the rash improved. Relapse was diagnosed and treated with antimonials, resulting in rapid symptom resolution and rash clearance. Subsequent relapses occurred with longer inter-relapse intervals on monthly L-AMB. At follow-up in December 2013, he remained in good health on secondary prophylaxis.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed in 2002; Kaposi's sarcoma. Prior antiretroviral therapy: initial HAART with lamivudine, stavudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir; switched in 2008 to abacavir, lamivudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir; later intensified with raltegravir. Prior antimicrobial therapy with antimonials and liposomal amphotericin B.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, weight loss, diarrhea, night sweats, maculopapular and nodular skin rash. Denied other acute complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Hepatosplenomegaly present on abdominal examination; mucocutaneous lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma. Subsequent examination revealed a maculopapular and nodular rash distributed across the trunk and upper limbs.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory testing revealed pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Initial CD4+ T-cell count: 17 cells/muL; HIV RNA viral load: 225,181 copies/mL. In February 2008: CD4+ T-cell count: 125 cells/muL; HIV RNA viral load stably < 50 copies/mL. In December 2013: CD4+ T-cell count: 98 cells/muL; HIV RNA viral load < 20 copies/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Cutaneous biopsy histology demonstrated a dermal granulomatous infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages containing intracellular microorganisms. Serial bone marrow aspirates and smears demonstrated hypercellularity with macrophages containing intracellular protozoal forms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Recurrent visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) in a patient with advanced HIV-1 coinfection.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Initial bone marrow smear (May 2002) revealed Leishmania spp. amastigotes. Cutaneous biopsy histology showed macrophages containing Leishmania amastigotes, and RFLP-PCR was positive for Leishmania infantum, confirming PKDL. September 2008 relapse confirmed by repeat bone marrow aspirate demonstrating Leishmania amastigotes.
Differentials Ruled Out: Kaposi's sarcoma (mucocutaneous lesions initially suspected; resolved with HAART), other opportunistic infections, and drug eruptions.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Initial VL treated with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) and HAART (lamivudine-stavudine-lopinavir/ritonavir) with clinical improvement. Relapses treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB; 4 mg/kg/day for 5 days then weekly for 4 weeks). In February 2008, secondary prophylaxis with monthly L-AMB (4 mg/kg/day) was initiated. September 2008 relapse treated with meglumine antimoniate (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with complete rash clearance and symptom resolution. Monthly L-AMB maintenance was resumed, successfully widening relapse intervals. In December 2013, the patient was clinically well on L-AMB prophylaxis and abacavir-lamivudine-lopinavir/ritonavir-raltegravir.

raw_case_text:
A 49 year-old man of Chinese descent with no medical history presented in mid-January to our hospital for a history of fever (102.5 F), myalgias, and severe bilateral calf pain that began six days prior.
He had a 30 pack-year history of cigarette smoking, drank four to six beers almost every day for two years and smoked marijuana occasionally. He denied recent travel, owned two healthy pets and worked as a construction worker. The patient denied any recent travel outside the USA. He denied recent antibiotic exposure or sick contacts.
Vital signs in the emergency department were notable for a temperature of 101 F, pulse of 120 beats/min and blood pressure of 156/63 mm Hg. The patient was alert and oriented. The ocular examination was notable for scleral icterus. The skin appeared jaundiced, the lungs were clear to auscultation, the abdomen was soft, bilateral lower extremity tenderness was noted and dorsal pedal pulses were present bilaterally.
Initial laboratory study results were notable for a creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, platelets of 58,000 cells/mm3, hemoglobin of 12.8 G/dL, white blood cell count of 8.9 x 103 cells/mm3 with lymphopenia of 2.4%, total bilirubin of 4.3 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 2.6 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 143 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 201 U/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 246 U/L, and creatine kinase of 1219 U/L. The urine analysis showed moderate hematuria but no proteinuria. Results of lower extremity Doppler ultrasonography and chest radiography were negative, and electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm at 76 beats/min.
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for sepsis and multiorgan dysfunction. Intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone and vancomycin were initiated with aggressive fluid resuscitation.
The following day, the patient's acute renal failure, hyperbilirubinemia, anemia and thrombocytopenia worsened. Serologic test results for acute hepatitis A, B and C infections were negative. A peripheral smear showed no schistocytes. Levels of C3, C4, antinuclear antibodies, anti-dsDNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies were within normal limits. Renal ultrasonography results were normal. Computed tomography of the abdomen showed pancolitis, cholelithiasis and nephromegaly.
On the third day, the patient had worsening oxygenation with slight hemoptysis and developed new inferior bilateral infiltrates. Physical examination revealed the development of fine crackles at the bases of his lungs. Arterial blood gas on 2 L of oxygen revealed a pH of 7.45, PCO2 (partial pressure of carbon dioxide) of 28, PO2 (partial pressure of oxygen) of 55, oxygen saturation of 90% and bicarbonate of 19.5. The antibiotic regimen was broadened to IV cefepime, and vancomycin was continued. The right upper quadrant sonogram showed thickening of the gallbladder wall. Urine legionella antigen and serum HIV antibody results were negative. Initial blood cultures and sputum culture results were negative. The patient's acute renal failure, hyperbilirubinemia, anemia and thrombocytopenia continued to deteriorate. The patient was started on 125 mg of methylprednisone every six hours for five days and desmopressin for suspicion of alveolar hemorrhage in the presence of renal failure.
On the fourth hospital day, a nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A was conducted, and results were positive. All antibiotics were stopped, and the patient received one dose of oseltamivir. The patient's clinical status and renal failure started to improve, but the cholestatic picture was worsening, with a total bilirubin of 64.7 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 44.8 mg/dL, AST of 87 U/L and ALT of 121 U/L.
On the fifth day, the patient developed a maculopapular, nonpruritic rash on the face, torso, abdomen and upper extremities involving the palms. Biopsy was done and showed lichenoid dermatitis (drug reaction). Serum leptospira antibodies were sent to the NYC Board of Health for specialized testing. While the patient was taking corticosteroids, the hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, hemoptysis and renal failure resolved over the next few days. The final laboratory study results were notable for a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL, total bilirubin of 1.8 mg/dL and platelets of 165 cells/mm3. There was a near complete resolution of the chest radiography findings. Furthermore, the rash and the patient's calf pain gradually improved, and the patient was subsequently discharged.
Two weeks later, the NYC Board of Health reported the antibodies for leptospira as positive. A microagglutination test (MAT) confirmed the serovar Leptospira icterohaemorrhagiae, with the titers 1:6400. The patient was recalled for insertion of an indwelling catheter for a 14-day course of IV ceftriaxone after which he improved. Retrospectively, after having been asked about any epidemiologic factors that placed him at risk for contracting leptospirosis, the patient admitted to having been in contact with rat urine with his bare hands at a construction site in NYC.
