raw_case_text: A man who was on second-line ART and had a history of TB four times prior presented with weight loss, fatigue and diffuse, hypopigmented skin lesions suggestive of a superficial fungal infection (see Table 1 for more information). The patient was classified as meeting the WHO 'seriously ill' criteria and an AlereLAM revealed a strongly positive (4+) result; he was therefore started on TB treatment. A sputum and urine sample were collected, and both of these later cultured Mycobacterium kansasii. Once the two samples had isolated M. kansasii, a dual infection of M. tb and M. kansasii was diagnosed and azithromycin was added to the patient's regimen. Unfortunately, the patient disengaged from treatment after one year and died as an inpatient two years after initial presentation. Blood culture on that admission was positive for Mycobacterium kansasii. No Xpert MTB/RIF or cultures identified M. tb.

subjective.chief_complaint: An adult male presented with weight loss, fatigue, and diffuse hypopigmented skin lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A man with HIV on second-line antiretroviral therapy and a history of four prior tuberculosis episodes presented with fatigue, weight loss, and widespread hypopigmented skin lesions. He met the WHO 'seriously ill' criteria and was evaluated for opportunistic mycobacterial disease.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection on second-line ART; four previous episodes of tuberculosis. Other past medical history, travel, or animal exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports weight loss, fatigue, and diffuse hypopigmented cutaneous lesions; denies acute cough, hemoptysis, or chest pain. Home medications: second-line ART. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Met WHO 'seriously ill' criteria. Dermatologic examination revealed diffuse, hypopigmented superficial cutaneous lesions suggestive of superficial fungal infection.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection with Mycobacterium kansasii dual infection / cross-reactivity in advanced HIV.
Confirmation: Urine AlereLAM assay was strongly positive (4+); sputum and urine cultures subsequently isolated Mycobacterium kansasii; blood culture on subsequent admission grew M. kansasii; Xpert MTB/RIF and mycobacterial cultures did not detect M. tuberculosis.
Differentials ruled out: Superficial fungal infection considered for skin lesions; Mycobacterium tuberculosis excluded on negative Xpert MTB/RIF and cultures.
Treatment & Outcome: Initially started on anti-tuberculosis therapy based on strongly positive AlereLAM; azithromycin was added once M. kansasii was isolated. Patient disengaged from treatment after 1 year, was readmitted 2 years after presentation with M. kansasii bacteremia, and expired as an inpatient.

raw_case_text: A 46-year-old man originating from Morocco, with a medical history of end-stage renal disease secondary to type 2 diabetes mellitus presented with chills during haemodialysis (HD) sessions on January 2011. The patient was on HD since 2007, and in 2009, he was included in a prospective study to evaluate the utility of HBHA-IGRA, compared to TST for the detection of LTBI in HD patients (Dessein et al, manuscript in preparation). The QFT-G-IT was highly positive (13.58 IU/ml) as were the PPD- and HBHA-IGRAs with respectively 18,972 pg/ml and 7,287 pg/ml IFN-gamma. These results, especially the high IFN-gamma response to the latency antigen HBHA, indicated that the patient was latently infected with Mtb. During a January 2011 HD session, the patient presented with chills and fever, but no abnormalities were noted upon physical examination, except a weight loss of 4 Kg over the previous weeks. Blood cultures remained negative. A chest radiography revealed no infiltrates, cavities or calcifications. The patient denied prior exposition to Mtb, but the QFT-G-IT was still positive, with values similar to those found two years earlier (14.36 IU/ml), whereas the HBHA-IGRA had become totally negative. However, depletion of the CD4+ regulatory T cells from the PBMC, performed as described previously and based on CD25high T cell depletion by positive immunomagnetic selection, resulted in the re-appearance of a low but positive IFN-gamma response to HBHA stimulation (134 pg/ml). At that time, the IGRA values to rESAT-6 were very high (3,855 pg/ml) so that the HBHA/rESAT-6 ratio was 0.001. Since these results strongly suggested that the patient had progressed from latent Mtb infection to active TB disease, a PET Scan analysis was done demonstrating a strong metabolic captation of cervical and mediastinal lymph nodes. A jugular lymph node was surgically removed and revealed the presence of a granuloma with caseous necrosis. Anti-tuberculosis treatment was immediately initiated (Nicotibine, Rifadine, Tebrazid, Myambutol) and resulted in progressive clinical improvement. Thirty-two days later, the lymph node culture was positive for drug-sensitive Mtb.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old male on maintenance hemodialysis presenting with fever and chills during hemodialysis sessions and recent weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a Moroccan man on chronic maintenance hemodialysis since 2007, presented during a hemodialysis session in January 2011 with acute rigors and fever. Over the preceding weeks, he had noted an unintentional weight loss of 4 kg. He had been enrolled in a prospective latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) study in 2009, which documented positive interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), and he now presented with symptomatic reactivation.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease (ESRD) secondary to type 2 diabetes mellitus, maintained on chronic hemodialysis since 2007. Born in Morocco; denied known direct exposure to active tuberculosis. Documented latent TB infection in 2009 with strongly positive QFT-G-IT (13.58 IU/mL), PPD-IGRA (18,972 pg/mL IFN-gamma), and HBHA-IGRA (7,287 pg/mL IFN-gamma).
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, chills during dialysis, 4 kg weight loss over recent weeks. Denies cough, dyspnea, night sweats, or localizing pain.

objective.physical_examination: Patient was febrile and chilling during dialysis; physical examination was otherwise unremarkable with no peripheral adenopathy or organomegaly noted; documented 4 kg weight loss.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood cultures were repeatedly negative. Plain chest radiograph revealed no infiltrates, cavitations, or calcifications.
objective.advanced_workup: Repeat QFT-G-IT remained positive (14.36 IU/mL). Standard HBHA-IGRA was negative (<50 pg/mL); however, following positive immunomagnetic selection depletion of CD4+CD25high regulatory T cells from PBMCs, a low positive IFN-gamma response to HBHA was restored (134 pg/mL); rESAT-6 IGRA was markedly elevated (3,855 pg/mL), yielding an HBHA/rESAT-6 ratio of 0.001 indicative of active disease. 18F-FDG PET scan demonstrated intense hypermetabolic uptake in cervical and mediastinal lymph nodes. Excisional biopsy of a cervical jugular lymph node was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis manifesting as active cervical and mediastinal tuberculous lymphadenitis in an end-stage renal disease patient on hemodialysis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Excisional jugular lymph node biopsy demonstrated necrotizing caseating granulomas; mycobacterial culture of the lymph node yielded drug-sensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis at 32 days of incubation, concordant with active-TB biomarker shift (elevated rESAT-6 IGRA with suppressed HBHA response) and PET hypermetabolism.
Management and outcome: Immediately initiated on 4-drug antituberculosis chemotherapy: Nicotibine (isoniazid), Rifadine (rifampicin), Tebrazid (pyrazinamide), and Myambutol (ethambutol). Treatment resulted in rapid, progressive clinical recovery and resolution of constitutional symptoms.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old man presented with history of a left-sided neck swelling for 20 days which was progressive in nature associated with odynophagia and hoarseness. He gave history of chronic nonproductive cough for three months with loss of appetite. There was no history of fever or hemoptysis. His past history was insignificant except for a residual left hemiparesis due to a cerebrovascular accident 7 years ago.
Examination revealed an ill-defined swelling on the left anterior aspect of the neck, approximately 4 x 3 cms which was cystic, fluctuant, and nontender. There were no palpable neck nodes, and oral cavity was normal.
Flexible nasal endoscopy (Olympus flexible endoscope) revealed a normal laryngopharynx except for a mucosal swelling on the left side of vallecula.
A provisional diagnosis of neck abscess was made. We aspirated the abscess with an 18G needle and drained 20 mL of pus. The pus was sent for routine culture, fungal smears, and AFB (acid fast bacilli) smears which did not yield any positive result.
Three samples of sputum for AFB were sent in view of a cavity seen in the left upper zone on the chest X-ray (Figure 1), which were negative. Blood investigations done showed no immunocompromised status or other sources of infection.
A contrast enhanced computed tomography of the neck and thorax revealed an enhancing ill-defined osteolytic lesion of the body of hyoid with peripherally enhancing collection. The collection extended anteroinferiorly beneath the strap muscles along the anterior aspect of the thyroid cartilage (Figure 2).
Posteriorly the collection was found to protrude into the preepiglottic space (Figure 3). An incision and drainage of the abscess were planned. However as the patient suddenly developed a muffled voice, an elective tracheostomy was performed in anticipation of an impending airway compromise.
Intraoperatively there was a necrotic tissue with sero-sanguineous collection in the preepiglottic space. About 20 mL of fluid was drained. The body and the greater and lesser cornu of hyoid bone on the left side were found to be necrotic.
Histopathology of the hyoid revealed fibrocollagenous tissue with many discrete and confluent granulomas composed of epitheloid histiocytes and Langhans-type multinucleate giant cells rimmed by lymphocytes. Special stains done for fungal organisms were negative. A polymerase chain reaction study confirmed the diagnosis of tuberculosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male presenting with a left-sided neck swelling, odynophagia, and hoarseness for 20 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 20-day history of a progressively enlarging left anterior neck swelling associated with odynophagia and hoarseness. He also reported a 3-month history of chronic nonproductive cough and anorexia. He denied fever or hemoptysis. Following initial evaluation, he developed acute muffled speech, raising concern for impending upper airway obstruction that required urgent airway stabilization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Residual left hemiparesis following a cerebrovascular accident 7 years previously. Denied prior history of tuberculosis, immunosuppression, or diabetes.
subjective.review_of_systems: Progressive neck swelling, odynophagia, hoarseness, chronic nonproductive cough, anorexia. Denies fever, night sweats, or hemoptysis.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-defined cystic, fluctuant, nontender swelling measuring approximately 4 x 3 cm on the left anterior neck. No palpable cervical lymphadenopathy; oral cavity was normal. Flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy revealed a mucosal swelling on the left side of the vallecula with an otherwise normal laryngopharynx. Development of muffled voice prompted elective tracheostomy for impending airway compromise.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood investigations showed no evidence of immunocompromise or systemic infection. Three sputum specimens for acid-fast bacilli were negative. Chest radiograph showed a cavitary lesion in the left upper zone. Diagnostic needle aspiration of the neck swelling with an 18G needle drained 20 mL of pus; routine bacterial cultures, fungal smears, and acid-fast bacilli smears were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of neck and thorax revealed an enhancing, ill-defined osteolytic lesion of the body of the hyoid bone surrounded by a peripherally enhancing fluid collection extending anteroinferiorly deep to the strap muscles over the thyroid cartilage and protruding posteriorly into the preepiglottic space. Elective tracheostomy performed, followed by surgical incision and drainage of the preepiglottic collection (draining 20 mL of serosanguinous fluid) and debridement of necrotic bone from the hyoid body and left greater and lesser cornua. Histopathological examination of the debrided hyoid bone revealed fibrocollagenous tissue with discrete and confluent granulomas containing epithelioid histiocytes and Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells rimmed by lymphocytes; fungal stains were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Tuberculous osteomyelitis of the hyoid bone with preepiglottic and anterior neck cold abscess causing impending upper airway compromise, accompanied by cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay of resected hyoid tissue confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA; histopathology demonstrated discrete and confluent necrotizing granulomas with Langhans giant cells.
Management and outcome: Elective tracheostomy successfully secured the airway, followed by drainage of the preepiglottic abscess and surgical debridement of necrotic hyoid bone, confirming tuberculosis for definitive antitubercular chemotherapy.

raw_case_text: A twenty-nine-year-old male presented with a history of fever with chills and rigor for 19 days, evening rise in temperature, which responded to paracetamol. Pulse rate was 90 per minute, blood pressure was 112/78 mm of Hg, and SpO2 was 98% on room air. General examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory investigations showed hemoglobin of 12.3 gm/dL, and leucocyte counts of 8900/muL with a platelet count of 1.8 lakhs/muL and ESR was 98 mm/hr. Chest X-ray was normal. Urine routine examination was normal. Malarial smears were negative. Ciprofloxacin was given empirically outside for 5 days. Ceftriaxone was started empirically; blood cultures were sent which showed S. typhi growth on the third day with sensitivity to ceftriaxone. The patient didn't respond to sensitive antibiotics till day 7. Meanwhile, the Mantoux test was done which showed a 14 mm induration. We did a CT scan which showed terminal ileal concentric thickening of size 8 mm of length 9 cm. The patient underwent a colonoscopy which showed a normal colon till caecum, but the ileocecal valve showed multiple small superficial ulcers with whitish exudate on both lips. Ileum till 15 cm showed edematous, reddish bluish mucosa, less distensible, circumferential superficial ulcer near to ileocecal valve extending to the length of 3 cm with a few other small superficial ulcers till 30 cm (Fig. 1). Biopsies from the ulcer showed acute inflammation mixed with sheets of histiocyte infiltration (Fig. 2). No distortion of crypt architecture or well-defined epithelioid granuloma was noted. Ziehl Neelsen (ZN) stains did not reveal acid-fast bacilli, and Gene Xpert was negative. Intravenous antibiotics continued, and the patient improved on day 11. Antibiotics were continued for 5 more days. The patient was discharged, repeat colonoscopy was done 6 weeks later which showed normal ileum.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presented with a 19-day history of fever with chills and rigors.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with fever, chills, and rigors for 19 days, marked by evening temperature elevations that responded temporarily to paracetamol. Prior to hospital admission, he was empirically treated with oral ciprofloxacin for 5 days without clinical improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Received empirical oral ciprofloxacin for 5 days outside prior to admission. No other chronic illnesses reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports chills, rigors, and evening spikes in temperature. Denies other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Pulse rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 112/78 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air. General physical examination revealed no hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 12.3 gm/dL, leucocyte count 8900/muL, platelet count 1.8 lakhs/muL, and ESR 98 mm/hr. Chest X-ray was normal. Routine urinalysis was normal. Malarial smears were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Mantoux tuberculin skin test showed 14 mm induration. Abdominal CT revealed concentric thickening of the terminal ileum measuring 8 mm in wall thickness over a length of 9 cm. Colonoscopy showed normal mucosa up to the caecum; ileocecal valve exhibited multiple small superficial ulcers with whitish exudate on both lips; ileum up to 15 cm showed edematous, reddish-bluish, less distensible mucosa with a circumferential superficial ulcer (length 3 cm) near the ileocecal valve, and several small superficial ulcers extending up to 30 cm. Histopathological examination of ulcer biopsies showed acute inflammation mixed with sheets of histiocytic infiltration without crypt architecture distortion or well-defined epithelioid granulomas. Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain was negative for acid-fast bacilli and GeneXpert was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Salmonella typhi bacteremia (typhoid fever) confirmed by blood cultures demonstrating S. typhi growth on the third day of incubation, susceptible to ceftriaxone. Intestinal tuberculosis (Koch's disease) was ruled out based on negative ZN stain, negative GeneXpert, and absence of granulomas on biopsy; malaria was ruled out by negative smears.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous ceftriaxone. The patient did not respond to sensitive antibiotics through day 7, with clinical defervescence and improvement occurring on day 11. Ceftriaxone was continued for an additional 5 days (total 16 days). The patient was discharged, and a repeat colonoscopy at 6 weeks demonstrated a completely normal ileum.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old Saudi male from Jizan, with a comorbidity of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 6 years prior (well controlled by oral antidiabetic agents: metformin 1000 mg twice daily and gliclazide 30 mg once daily), presented with impaired renal function and hematuria. After basic laboratory investigations, kidney biopsy was performed. Histological examination with light microscope revealed a global sclerosed glomeruli, minimal interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy [Figure 1]. A diagnosis of glomerulonephritis of unknown etiology was made and treatment with mycophenolate (1 g PO twice daily) and prednisone (20 mg PO once daily) was initiated.
After 3 months, the patient presented with a 3-week history of fever, abdominal pain and fatigue. The fever was subjective, intermittent, associated with chills and rigors, especially at night, and not relieved by paracetamol. The abdominal pain was intermittent, diffuse and colicky in nature and was associated with nausea and vomiting without blood (2-3 times/day). During these 3 weeks, the patient's appetite decreased, owing to which he lost 7 kg in weight. In addition, the patient reported a history of animal contact (goat and sheep), ingestion of raw goat milk and swimming in the valley water. There was no history of rash, cough, hemoptysis, jaundice, diarrhea, constipation, dysuria, change in urine color, arthralgia, visual disturbances, oral ulcers, genital rash, discharge or contact with tuberculosis patients.
On physical examination, the patient was found to be obese, sweating, not jaundiced or cyanosed. He was conscious, alert and oriented to time, place and person. His vital signs were as follows: body temperature, 38.6 C; pulse rate, 98 beats/min; respiratory rate, 24 breaths/min; blood pressure, 125/85 mmHg; and oxygen saturation, 100% on room air. He was pale, with normal jugular venous pressure and no oral ulcers or thrush. Abdominal examination revealed mild epigastric tenderness and a palpable liver 4 cm below the costal margin with a 15-cm liver span. The rest of the examinations were within normal limits.
Laboratory investigations on admission revealed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 2.65/mcL (neutrophils, 72.1%; lymphocytes, 23.2%; monocytes, 4%; and eosinophils, 0.7%). Results of other hematological examinations were as follows: hemoglobin level, 8.8 g/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 88 mm/h; platelet count, 87,000/mcL; and reticulocyte count, 1.28%. Level of ferritin was 1000 ng/mL, with a transferrin saturation of 11.22 mg/dL. Estimation of electrolytes showed sodium 138 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L and bicarbonate 25 mmol/L. Liver function tests showed that total protein was 6.1 g/dL, albumin 3.2 g/dL, total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, alanine transaminase 71 IU/L, aspartate transaminase 42 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 179 IU/L and gamma-glutamyl transferase 447 IU/L. International normalized ratio was 0.8. Renal function tests showed that blood urea nitrogen was 12 mg/dL and creatinine 2.15 mg/dL. Level of lactate dehydrogenase was 732 U/L and C-reactive protein 53 mg/L. Urine analysis showed 2-5 WBCs/high-power field and 10-25 red blood cells/high-power field with no nitrites. Sickling test and direct/indirect Coombs test were negative, and the stool test result was normal.
Chest X-ray and electrocardiogram were normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed an enlarged liver (16.2-cm liver span) and a mildly enlarged spleen (14 cm in length). Kidneys were normal in size, with a mild increase in the echogenicity of renal parenchyma, but no hydronephrosis or ascites.
The serological tests for viral hepatitis, human immunodeficiency virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, Toxoplasma and Brucella were negative. Rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, antiglomerular basement membrane antibody, anti-Sjogren's syndrome A and B antibodies and cryoglobulin were negative. Malaria smear and blood cultures were also negative.
The patient's condition continued to deteriorate and he developed continuous fever of up to 40.5 C. Repeated tests after 5 days revealed the following: WBC, 1.4/mcL; hemoglobin, 6.7 g/dL; platelet, 55,000/mcL; creatinine, 3.3 mg/dL; C-reactive protein, 151 mg/L; total bilirubin, 2.9 mg/dL; alkaline phosphatase, 460 IU/L; alanine aminotransferase, 80 IU/L; aspartate aminotransferase, 138 IU/L; gamma-glutamyl transferase, 651 IU/L; albumin, 2.5 g/dL; and lactate dehydrogenase, 1400 U/L.
Bone marrow aspirate showed mild hypocellular marrow with no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy. Bone marrow culture for Brucella was negative. Further, Leishman-Donovan bodies were not detected by light microscope. Polymerase-chain reaction test for the diagnosis of tuberculosis, serological tests for dengue fever and Q fever as well as beta-D-Glucan and galactomannan antigen tests were all negative. Liver biopsy showed granulomatous hepatitis with extramedullary hematopoiesis. After 1 week of admission, the patient was treated empirically with broad-spectrum antibiotic (meropenem intravenously, 1 g every 8 h for 6 days); however, there was no improvement.
Additional serological testing using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) releveled the presence of anti-Leishmania antibodies. Based on this, the patient was started on liposomal amphotericin B course as a treatment for VL (4 mg/kg intravenous on Days 1-5, 10, 17, 24, 31 and 38), despite the lack of a definitive diagnosis. After 1 week, the patient improved clinically, the fever subsided, the laboratory parameters began to improve and at the end of liposomal amphotericin B course, all tests returned to normal.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presented with a 3-week history of subjective intermittent fever, colicky abdominal pain, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-week history of subjective intermittent fever with chills and night rigors (unrelieved by paracetamol), diffuse intermittent colicky abdominal pain, nausea, non-bloody vomiting 2-3 times daily, anorexia, fatigue, and 7 kg weight loss over 3 weeks. Three months earlier, he had been diagnosed with glomerulonephritis of unknown etiology by kidney biopsy and was placed on immunosuppressive therapy with mycophenolate and prednisone. During hospitalization, he deteriorated with high-grade continuous fevers up to 40.5 C and progressive cytopenias. Empiric intravenous meropenem (1 g q8h for 6 days) produced no clinical improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension; type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 6 years prior; biopsy-confirmed glomerulonephritis of unknown etiology (light microscopy showed globally sclerosed glomeruli, minimal interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy) diagnosed 3 months prior. Epidemiological exposure: resident of Jizan, Saudi Arabia; animal contact with sheep and goats; consumption of raw unpasteurized goat milk; swimming in valley water. No contact with tuberculosis patients.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue, anorexia, 7 kg weight loss, diffuse colicky abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting. Denies rash, cough, hemoptysis, jaundice, diarrhea, constipation, dysuria, hematuria, arthralgia, visual changes, oral ulcers, or genital lesions. Home medications: metformin 1000 mg PO BID, gliclazide 30 mg PO daily, mycophenolate 1 g PO BID, prednisone 20 mg PO daily. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: General appearance: obese, pale, sweating, conscious, alert, oriented x 3, non-jaundiced, non-cyanotic. Vital signs: Body temperature: 38.6 C (peaked at 40.5 C during hospital course); Pulse: 98 beats/min; Respiratory rate: 24 breaths/min; Blood pressure: 125/85 mmHg; Oxygen saturation: 100% on room air. Head and neck: normal JVP, no oral ulcers or thrush. Abdomen: mild epigastric tenderness, palpable liver 4 cm below costal margin with a 15-cm liver span. Rest of exam unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission hematology: WBC: 2.65/mcL (neutrophils 72.1%, lymphocytes 23.2%, monocytes 4%, eosinophils 0.7%); Hemoglobin: 8.8 g/L; Platelets: 87,000/mcL; Reticulocytes: 1.28%; ESR: 88 mm/h; Ferritin: 1000 ng/mL; Transferrin saturation: 11.22 mg/dL. Chemistry: Na 138 mEq/L, K 3.2 mEq/L, HCO3 25 mmol/L, BUN 12 mg/dL, Creatinine 2.15 mg/dL. Liver function: Total protein 6.1 g/dL, Albumin 3.2 g/dL, Total bilirubin 1.2 mg/dL, ALT 71 IU/L, AST 42 IU/L, ALP 179 IU/L, GGT 447 IU/L, INR 0.8, LDH 732 U/L, CRP 53 mg/L. Urinalysis: 2-5 WBC/hpf, 10-25 RBC/hpf, no nitrites. Day 5 repeat labs: WBC 1.4/mcL, Hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL, Platelets 55,000/mcL, Creatinine 3.3 mg/dL, CRP 151 mg/L, Total bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL, ALP 460 IU/L, ALT 80 IU/L, AST 138 IU/L, GGT 651 IU/L, Albumin 2.5 g/dL, LDH 1400 U/L. Infectious serologies/tests: negative for viral hepatitis, HIV, EBV, CMV, Toxoplasma, Brucella, dengue, Q fever, beta-D-glucan, galactomannan, sickling test, Coombs test, malaria smears, blood cultures, and stool test. Autoimmune markers: ANA, RF, ANCA, anti-GBM, anti-SSA/SSB, and cryoglobulins all negative. Imaging: Chest X-ray and ECG normal. Abdominal ultrasound: hepatomegaly (16.2 cm span), mild splenomegaly (14 cm length), normal sized kidneys with mildly increased parenchymal echogenicity, no hydronephrosis or ascites.
objective.advanced_workup: Prior kidney biopsy: globally sclerosed glomeruli, minimal interstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy. Bone marrow aspirate: mild hypocellular marrow without dysplasia or malignancy; Brucella marrow culture negative; PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis negative. Liver biopsy: granulomatous hepatitis with extramedullary hematopoiesis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) in an immunosuppressed patient (on mycophenolate and prednisone), complicated by bicytopenia, acute kidney injury, and granulomatous hepatitis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Serologic testing by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) demonstrated anti-Leishmania antibodies (initial bone marrow light microscopy did not visualize amastigotes).
Differentials ruled out: Brucellosis (negative serology and marrow culture), viral hepatitis, HIV, EBV, CMV, toxoplasmosis, malaria, systemic mycoses (negative galactomannan and beta-D-glucan), Q fever, dengue, tuberculosis (PCR negative), autoimmune disease, and secondary bacterial sepsis (empiric meropenem failure).
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg IV on days 1-5, 10, 17, 24, 31, and 38). Within 1 week, fever resolved, cytopenias normalized, renal and liver function recovered, and all laboratory parameters completely normalized by completion of therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old male soldier in the French Foreign Legion, who returned from Djibouti, was hospitalized in September 1999 after his chest x-ray showed abnormal findings. He was a nurse and had been occasionally in charge at the Djibouti Hospital for 2 years. His medical history was unremarkable. Eight months before he returned to France, he experienced asthenia, anorexia, and a weight loss of 3 kg. The symptoms resolved spontaneously after 2 months, and he had been asymptomatic since then. He had no history of cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, dyspnea, fever, or night sweats.
Results of a clinical examination and of laboratory studies were normal (Table), except for hypereosinophilia. Serologic tests for schistosomiasis, hydatidosis, distomiasis, amebiasis, toxocariasis, and trichinosis were negative, and parasites were not found in stool samples. Thoracic radiographs performed when he came back from Djibouti showed parenchymal consolidation of the right upper lobe with small cavities. Sputum was not produced. A gastric aspirate smear was negative for acid-fast bacilli, and a bronchial aspiration smear was positive for acid-fast bacilli. HIV serology was negative, and no other site of the infection was found. Drug therapy was initiated with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 2 months. Cultures of bronchial aspirates were positive within 14 days; later, cultures of two gastric aspirates were positive for acid-fast bacilli. An M. tuberculosis subsp. canetti isolate was identified, which was susceptible to all primary antituberculous drugs. The treatment was then extended for 4 months with rifampicin and isoniazid. The patient's response to treatment was favorable.
The following methods were used to identify the etiologic agent. First, the samples were decontaminated with N-acetyl-L-cysteine/NaOH. Acid-fast bacilli were detected by auramine staining, the positive smears also were stained with Ziehl-Nielsen stain. The samples were then seeded onto Lowenstein-Jensen and Coletsos slants and also into a liquid system, the BBL Mycobacterial Growth Indicator Tube (MGIT, BD Diagnostic Systems, Sparks, MD).
The mycobacteria were identified by using a specific DNA probe (Gen-Probe, Gen-Probe Incorporated, San Diego, CA) and by performing the usual biochemical tests (nitrate reduction, 68 C catalase resistance, niacin production).
The Pasteur Institute of Paris used two methods for typing: restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis and spoligotyping. In RFLP analysis, after digestion of the M. tuberculosis strain's genomic DNA with PvuII restriction enzyme and agarose gel migration, the DNA was transferred on a membrane, according to the Southern method, and then hybridized with an insertion sequence IS6110 probe. In the spoligotyping method, after DNA direct repeat amplification, the labeled polymerase chain reaction product was used as a probe to hybridize with 43 synthetic spacer oligonucleotides (DNA sequences derived from the direct repeat [DR] region of M. tuberculosis, H37Rv and M. bovis BCG P3), which were attached to a carrier membrane. The sensitivity to antituberculous drugs was determined by the indirect proportion method.
MGIT results were positive for the two cultures in 9 and 12 days, respectively. On Lowenstein-Jensen slants, the cultures were positive in 12 and 14 days, respectively. The white, smooth, and glossy colonies were characteristic of M. tuberculosis subsp. canetti (Figure 1). The two strains had the same phenotypic and genotypic pattern; 68 C catalase was negative, and they reduced nitrate, as do other M. tuberculosis species, but they did not produce niacin. The DNA probe, Gen-Probe, confirmed that these strains belonged to the M. tuberculosis complex.
These strains contained two copies of IS6110. Spoligotyping showed that they shared only 2 of the 43 oligonucleotides reproducing the spacer DNA sequences of M. tuberculosis, H37Rv and M. bovis BCG P3. This profile is characteristic of M. tuberculosis subsp. canetti (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old male presenting for hospital evaluation following an abnormal screening chest radiograph.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a French Foreign Legion nurse returning from Djibouti, was hospitalized following detection of parenchymal consolidation on routine chest radiography. Eight months prior to return, he had experienced asthenia, anorexia, and an unintentional weight loss of 3 kg, which resolved spontaneously after 2 months. He had remained asymptomatic since that time and denied cough, sputum expectoration, hemoptysis, dyspnea, fever, or night sweats.
subjective.past_medical_history: Soldier and nurse in the French Foreign Legion with occupational exposure in charge at the Djibouti Hospital for 2 years. Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Resolved asthenia, anorexia, and 3 kg weight loss (8 months prior). Denies current fever, night sweats, cough, sputum, hemoptysis, or shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination was completely normal; vital signs within normal limits.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine laboratory investigations were normal except for hypereosinophilia. Serologies for schistosomiasis, hydatidosis, distomiasis, amebiasis, toxocariasis, and trichinosis were negative; stool examinations were negative for ova and parasites. HIV-1 and HIV-2 serology was negative. Chest radiograph showed parenchymal consolidation of the right upper lobe with small cavitations.
objective.advanced_workup: Gastric aspirate smear: negative for acid-fast bacilli. Bronchial aspiration performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsp. canetti.
Diagnostic confirmation: Bronchial aspiration smear positive for acid-fast bacilli (detected by auramine and Ziehl-Neelsen staining); mycobacterial liquid culture (MGIT) positive at 9 and 12 days, and Lowenstein-Jensen slants positive at 12 and 14 days, yielding white, smooth, glossy colonies; subsequent gastric aspirate cultures also grew acid-fast bacilli. Biochemical profiling showed positive nitrate reduction, negative 68 °C catalase, and negative niacin production. Gen-Probe DNA probe confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. IS6110 RFLP demonstrated 2 insertion copies, and spoligotyping showed hybridization with only 2 of 43 spacer oligonucleotides, establishing Mycobacterium tuberculosis subsp. canetti. Susceptibility testing via indirect proportion method demonstrated full susceptibility to all first-line antituberculous agents.
Management and outcome: Treated with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months (total 6 months). Favorable clinical response with complete recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 72-year-old man was admitted to hospital for right upper quadrant abdominal pain, generalized body aches, night sweats, chills, subjective fever at night, and weakness for three days.
One month before presenting, patient travelled to his native African country Ghana for a two-week trip. Ten days after returning back to the United States, he developed the symptoms. Initially, he took over the counter common cold medication without any relief. He denied sick contacts, vomiting diarrhea, shortness of breath, chest pain, or any other symptoms.
Patient was also taking mefloquine for malaria prophylaxis during his visit.
Patient's past medical history included hypertension treated for five years, high cholesterol, gout, and chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertension. The patient had no surgeries in past and had no known allergies. He denied smoking, alcohol intake, or drug abuse. Patient's home medications included allopurinol, losartan, amlodipine, labetalol, furosemide, and simvastatin.
On physical examination, temperature was 39.3 degrees of Celsius, blood pressure was 184/86 mm of Hg, respiratory rate was 18 breaths per minute, and heart rate was 76 beats per minute. Patient looked in acute distress and was shivering. He was awake, alert, and oriented to time, place, and person. Neck was supple. Lungs were clear and heart sounds regular on auscultation. No murmur, rubs, or gallop was appreciated. Abdomen was soft and nontender and bowel sounds were audible in all four quadrants. No leg edema was noted.
Initial blood tests in the emergency room showed a normal complete blood picture including white count with differential, platelet count and a hemoglobin of 12.3 grams/dL. On metabolic profile, patient's creatinine was found to be 2.09 mg/dL that was higher than baseline of 1.5 mg/dL recorded six months earlier. Urea nitrogen was 30 mg/dL with glomerular filtration rate of 38. Liver function tests were normal except for albumin of 2.6 g/dL and total bilirubin of 1.6 mg/dL. Creatinine kinase was 514 IU/L. Amylase was 54 U/L and lipase 35 U/L.
Initially, patient was admitted to medical floor and started on broad spectrum empiric antibiotics. Blood culture, urine cultures, and nasal swab for influenza were sent. Because of the acute kidney injury, furosemide and losartan were stopped and intravenous fluids were given. A urinary catheter was placed and urinalysis along with urine electrolytes was ordered.
On the second day of hospitalization, patient continued to have abdominal pain and fever. An abdominal computerized tomography scan without contrast showed findings concerning acute pancreatitis or acalculous cholecystitis.
On the third day, his serum creatinine rapidly increased to 4.17 mg/dL with GFR of 17. Urine analysis showed dark colored, cloudy, and concentrated urine with small amount of bilirubin, large blood, large protein, no white blood cells, and red blood cells of 3-5/hpf. No casts were seen on urine sediment. Urine electrolytes showed a fractional excretion of sodium of 1.2% and urine creatinine of 157 mg/dL. A urine protein to creatinine ratio of 7929.41 was calculated. Patient's urinalysis one year ago showed trace protein and total protein of 34 mg/dL and creatinine of 144 mg/dL.
An abdominal ultrasound was done that was suggestive of acalculous cholecystitis. There was newly increased renal echogenicity but no hydronephrosis.
From days three to five, patient's urine output declined and serum creatinine continued to rise from 4.75 mg/dL up to 8.74 mg/dL and patient was started on Hemodialysis. Laboratory tests for different glomerulopathy causes resulted negative (Table 1).
In view of recent travel, a blood smear for malaria was done that showed crescentic shaped gametocyte which is usually the shape of Plasmodium falciparum and parasitemia of 1.64% (Figure 1).
Patient was then started on Coartem (Artemether: 20 mg and Lumefantrine: 120 mg) for malaria. This is considered as the treatment of acute malarial infections due to Plasmodium falciparum in geographical regions where chloroquine resistance has been reported.
Finally, the kidney biopsy was done (Figure 2) that was consistent with severe collapsing glomerulopathy. It showed collapse of the glomerular tufts and prominent hyperplasia of overlying epithelial cells, acute injury of the tubules, interstitial fibrosis and arteriosclerosis, complete foot process effacement, and tubular degenerative changes.
Patient's symptoms improved after starting the antimalarials and he was discharged after few days, but his kidney function never returned to his baseline and he continues to use renal replacement therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old male presenting with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nocturnal fevers, chills, diaphoresis, and severe acute-on-chronic renal failure 10 days after returning from Ghana.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Ten days after returning from a 2-week trip to Ghana, the patient developed right upper quadrant abdominal pain, generalized body aches, night sweats, nocturnal fevers, and profound fatigue. Over-the-counter cold medications provided no relief. Upon hospital admission, he was pyrexial and hypertensive with acute kidney injury superimposed on chronic kidney disease. Over hospital days 3 to 5, his serum creatinine escalated rapidly from 2.09 mg/dL to 8.74 mg/dL with oliguria and nephrotic-range proteinuria, necessitating emergency hemodialysis initiation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertension (baseline serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL), essential hypertension (5 years), hypercholesterolemia, and gout. Reported taking mefloquine chemoprophylaxis during his 2-week trip to Ghana. Home medications: allopurinol, losartan, amlodipine, labetalol, furosemide, simvastatin. Allergies: none known.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for subjective nocturnal fevers, chills, night sweats, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, generalized body aches, and weakness. Negative for nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, shortness of breath, chest pain, or dysuria.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39.3 C, blood pressure: 184/86 mmHg, heart rate: 76 beats/min, respiratory rate: 18 breaths/min. Patient appeared in acute distress and was shivering; awake, alert, and oriented. Neck supple. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. Heart: Regular rhythm without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Abdomen: Soft, nontender with audible bowel sounds in all four quadrants; no peripheral leg edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count on admission: Hemoglobin: 12.3 g/dL, normal white blood cell count and differential, normal platelet count. Serum creatinine: 2.09 mg/dL rising to 4.17 mg/dL on day 3, 4.75 mg/dL on day 4, and 8.74 mg/dL on day 5 (eGFR declining from 38 to 17 mL/min/1.73m2); blood urea nitrogen (BUN): 30 mg/dL. Serum albumin: 2.6 g/dL, total bilirubin: 1.6 mg/dL, creatine kinase (CK): 514 IU/L, serum amylase: 54 U/L, serum lipase: 35 U/L. Urinalysis: Dark, cloudy, concentrated, large blood, large protein, small bilirubin, RBC 3-5/hpf, no WBCs, no casts on sediment. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR): 7,929.41 mg/g (nephrotic range). Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa): 1.2%, urine creatinine: 157 mg/dL. Bacterial blood and urine cultures: Sterile. Nasal influenza PCR swab: Negative. Extensive glomerulopathy / vasculitis serologic workup: Negative. Abdominal ultrasound: Suggestive of acalculous cholecystitis; diffusely increased renal parenchymal echogenicity without hydronephrosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast abdominal CT scan: Imaging findings suspicious for acute pancreatitis or acalculous cholecystitis. Percutaneous renal biopsy: Severe collapsing glomerulopathy (collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis) characterized by global and segmental collapse of glomerular capillary tufts, marked hyperplasia and hypertrophy of overlying podocytes/visceral epithelial cells, acute tubular degenerative injury, diffuse foot process effacement on electron microscopy, interstitial fibrosis, and arteriolar sclerosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria (breakthrough infection on mefloquine prophylaxis) complicated by severe collapsing glomerulopathy (collapsing FSGS) with nephrotic-range proteinuria and dialysis-dependent acute renal failure.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated classic crescent-shaped gametocytes of Plasmodium falciparum with 1.64% parasitemia. Glomerular collapse and podocyte hypertrophy were histopathologically confirmed on renal biopsy. Viral etiologies of collapsing glomerulopathy (HIV, Parvovirus B19, Hepatitis B/C) were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Discontinued ACE inhibitors and loop diuretics; initiated intravenous fluid hydration and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics. Initiated hemodialysis for progressive oliguric renal failure. Targeted antimalarial treatment administered with oral artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem: artemether 20 mg / lumefantrine 120 mg). Parasitemia cleared and systemic febrile symptoms resolved; however, renal recovery did not occur, and the patient remained permanently dependent on maintenance hemodialysis.

raw_case_text:
In late March 2021, a 22-year-old female, Filipino, was brought to the emergency room due to headache followed by loss of consciousness. The patient was apparently well until 1 day prior to admission, when she allegedly complained of headache, uncharacterized. No associated trauma, no cough, no vomiting, nausea, fever, diarrhea, body malaise,or weakness of the extremities. Patient self-medicated with Paracetamol tablet. Then 1 h prior to consult, patient sent a text message to her brother asking for help due to her headache. However, her brother found her unconscious, lying on the bed, hence she was immediately brought to the emergency room.
Past medical history of the patient was unremarkable. No history of taking antiplatelet or anticoagulant medications, and no previous bleeding problems. No illicit drug use and no alcohol abuse.
Patient's vital signs: BP 110/70, CR 64, RR 19, T 36.6, and SpO2 98% at room air, with capillary blood glucose of 146 mg/dL. Patient was drowsy, disoriented, and inconsistently answered questions and followed commands appropriately. Pupils were anisocoric, 2 mm on the right and 4 mm on the left, equally reactive to light. Primary gaze was at midline. Patient had brisk corneal reflex, no facial asymmetry, with intact gross hearing, and withdrew to pain on all extremities.
Immediate non-contrast computerized tomography scan (Figure 1) revealed an acute subdural hemorrhage, left cerebral convexity (1.9 cm maximal thickness), with compression of the adjacent cortical sulci and left lateral ventricle, with rightward subfalcine herniation (1.2 cm). Computerized tomography angiography revealed no aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation.
Ideally, patient should have been screened for coagulation factors deficiency, but such tests were not readily available. Baseline blood counts, coagulation tests, and inflammatory markers were within normal (Table 1).
The patient was referred to neurosurgery service, and a left frontotemporoparietal craniotomy with evacuation of subdural hematoma was done. Decompressive hemicraniectomy was not done because brain parenchyma was not edematous on inspection post-evacuation of hematoma. No identifiable source of bleeding and no noted cerebral vessel malformation. Medical decompression was started after surgery. Postoperatively, patient became fully awake, oriented, followed command, answered appropriately without motor or sensory deficit. Patient's reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction tested positive for COVID-19, but chest X-ray was unremarkable, and she had no respiratory symptoms. Hence, the patient completed 14 days of quarantine in the hospital and was discharged without neurologic deficits.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old female presenting with acute severe headache followed by sudden loss of consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 22-year-old female with no prior symptoms developed an uncharacterized headache one day prior to presentation, for which she self-medicated with paracetamol without relief. Approximately one hour prior to presentation, she sent a text message requesting help for severe headache and was subsequently found unconscious in bed by her brother.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable medical history. Denied history of bleeding diathesis, head trauma, antiplatelet or anticoagulant medications, illicit drug use, or alcohol abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute severe headache and loss of consciousness. Negative for fever, cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, malaise, or extremity weakness. Home medications: paracetamol. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 36.6 °C, pulse rate: 64 beats/min, blood pressure: 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate: 19 breaths/min, SpO2: 98% on room air. Neurologic: drowsy, disoriented, inconsistent response to questions and commands; pupils anisocoric (right 2 mm, left 4 mm, both equally reactive to light); primary gaze midline; brisk corneal reflexes; no facial asymmetry; intact gross hearing; withdrew all extremities to pain. Postoperative examination: fully awake, alert, oriented, following commands appropriately with no focal motor or sensory deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Capillary blood glucose: 146 mg/dL. Complete blood counts, coagulation parameters (PT/INR, PTT), and baseline inflammatory markers were all within normal limits. Chest X-ray: unremarkable lung fields.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast head CT: acute subdural hematoma along the left cerebral convexity measuring up to 1.9 cm in maximal thickness, with effacement of adjacent cortical sulci, compression of the left lateral ventricle, and 1.2 cm of rightward subfalcine herniation. CT angiography (CTA) of the head: negative for intracranial aneurysm, arteriovenous malformation, or vascular malformation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Spontaneous acute subdural hematoma with left-to-right subfalcine herniation occurring in the setting of asymptomatic COVID-19 infection, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). Structural vascular etiologies (aneurysm, AVM) and underlying coagulopathy were ruled out. Management & Plan: Emergency left frontotemporoparietal craniotomy with evacuation of the subdural hematoma and postoperative medical decompression. The patient had complete neurological recovery without motor or sensory deficits, completed 14 days of inpatient isolation for COVID-19, and was discharged in stable condition.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old female presented with a painless lump in her right breast for 1 month duration. She gave history of low grade fever off and on for the last 2 weeks. There were no other complaints like weight loss, loss of appetite, and any cough. She was unmarried and there was no positive family history of breast tuberculosis. On local examination, a non-tender lump of size 3 x 4 cm was felt in lower quadrant of the breast [marked with a line as a - Figure 1]. It was freely mobile and no axillary nodes were present. Another 1 x 1.5 cm swelling was present in infra-mammary area just below and medial to the above mentioned lump [marked by line b; Figure 1]. Her systemic examination was non-contributory.
On routine blood investigations, total leucocyte count was 12,000 mm3 and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 60 mm at the end of 1 h, and HIV test was negative. Her fasting blood sugar and blood urea levels were normal. Chest X-ray was normal. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the breast and infra-mammary lump showed granulomas, epitheloid cells, and mixed inflammatory cells [Figure 2]. Background consisted of necrotic material and ZN stain for acid fast bacilli (AFB) was positive in the FNAC of both lumps. Mountex test was not done as on FNAC diagnosis already was made. Final diagnosis made as breast TB.
She was put on a 6-month course of anti-tubercular therapy with a 2 month intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide followed by a consolidation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid for another 4 months. The lump size was decreased within 3 weeks of initiation of ATT and at 3 month follow-up the patient remains asymptomatic and both lumps disappeared. She was advised to continue treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old female presenting with a painless right breast lump for one month and intermittent fever for two weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-month history of an enlarging, painless lump in her right breast. Over the preceding 2 weeks, she had noticed intermittent low-grade fever. She reported no weight loss, anorexia, or cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unmarried; no positive personal or family history of breast tuberculosis or malignancy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Intermittent low-grade fever. Denies weight loss, anorexia, cough, or nipple discharge.

objective.physical_examination: Right breast examination revealed a nontender, freely mobile lump measuring 3 x 4 cm in the lower quadrant. A second distinct swelling measuring 1 x 1.5 cm was palpated in the inframammary region just inferior and medial to the primary lump. No axillary lymphadenopathy was present. Left breast and systemic examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Total leukocyte count 12,000/mm3, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 60 mm/1st hr. HIV serology was negative. Fasting blood sugar and blood urea levels were normal. Chest radiograph was normal. Mantoux tuberculin skin test was omitted due to cytological confirmation.
objective.advanced_workup: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of both the right breast lump and the adjacent inframammary swelling showed granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid cells, mixed inflammatory cells, and necrotic background debris.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Primary breast and inframammary tuberculosis (tuberculous mastitis).
Diagnostic confirmation: Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain of fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) smears from both the right breast lump and the inframammary lesion demonstrated acid-fast bacilli (AFB) amidst necrotizing epithelioid cell granulomas.
Management and outcome: Treated with a 6-month course of antituberculosis therapy (ATT): 2-month intensive phase comprising rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide, followed by a 4-month continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid. Both masses significantly regressed within 3 weeks of initiating therapy; at 3-month follow-up, both lumps had completely resolved and the patient remained entirely asymptomatic, continuing treatment to completion.

raw_case_text:
A 60-year-old man with hyperlipidemia and with no history of hypertension, diabetes, or heart disease boarded the cruise ship 16 days before it went into quarantine. He noticed fever (day 0), RT-PCR positive was observed on day 4, and he was admitted to our hospital on day 7. His family members that had been in close contact with him tested negative. On admission, he had a fever and cough but had no difficulty in breathing. The physical examination showed no abnormalities. The results of blood examination were as follows: white blood cell (WBC) count 6,900/muL, lymphocyte count 1,056/muL, sodium level 131 mmol/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 4.45 mg/dL.
Following continuous fever for 7 days, on day 13, oxygen saturation suddenly decreased to 88% at room air without any obvious symptoms such as dyspnea. We started oxygen inhalation, which had to be increased. Chest X-ray demonstrated infiltrative shadows at the bilateral lower lung, and chest computed tomographic (CT) scan revealed bilateral ground-glass opacity (GGO) and a crazy-paving appearance, and we diagnosed him with COVID-19 pneumonia. Blood examination showed a slight elevation of WBC count, with decreased absolute lymphocyte counts, hyponatremia, hiper-ferritinemia, and a high CRP level: WBC 7,900/muL, lymphocyte 711/mL, sodium level 132 mmol/L, Ferritin level 866 ng/mL, CRP 12.21 mg/dL. Due to the abrupt oxygen requirement, which had to be increased, and the results of the CT scan, Lopinavir/Ritonavir was started on day 13. Simvastatin 50 mg once daily for hyperlipidemia was switched to pravastatin due to contraindication of simvastatin during treatment with LPV/r. The body temperature and oxygen requirement decreased and lymphopenia normalized within 2 days, followed by improvements in other measures. Chest-CT images showed that subpleural curvilinear shadow, ground-glass pattern, and consolidation were improved on day 16. He was discharged from the hospital after testing RT-PCR negative twice.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male presenting with a 7-day history of fever and cough following exposure on a quarantined cruise ship.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 60-year-old man developed a fever (illness day 0) after boarding a cruise ship that subsequently underwent quarantine. A viral respiratory swab was positive on illness day 4, and he was admitted to the hospital on illness day 7 presenting with persistent fever and cough without dyspnea. On illness day 13, following seven days of continuous fever, he developed sudden silent hypoxemia with oxygen saturation dropping to 88% on room air, necessitating escalating supplemental oxygen therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hyperlipidemia. No history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or cardiovascular disease. Epidemiological exposure: boarded a cruise ship 16 days prior to quarantine with known outbreak exposure; close family contacts tested negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and cough. Negative for dyspnea on initial presentation. Home medications: simvastatin 50 mg once daily. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission (day 7): febrile; physical examination was otherwise unremarkable with clear chest auscultation. On illness day 13: acute silent hypoxia with SpO2 88% on ambient air.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs (illness day 7): WBC count: 6,900/muL; absolute lymphocyte count: 1,056/muL; serum sodium: 131 mmol/L; C-reactive protein (CRP): 4.45 mg/dL. Illness day 13 labs: WBC count: 7,900/muL; absolute lymphocyte count: 711/muL; serum sodium: 132 mmol/L; serum ferritin: 866 ng/mL; CRP: 12.21 mg/dL. Chest X-ray (day 13): infiltrative opacities in bilateral lower lung zones.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest computed tomography (CT) on day 13: bilateral ground-glass opacities (GGO) with a crazy-paving pattern. Follow-up chest CT on day 16: significant improvement in bilateral ground-glass patterns, subpleural curvilinear shadows, and consolidations.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR on day 4. Management & Plan: Supplemental oxygen therapy initiated on day 13. Antiviral therapy with lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) was commenced on day 13; home simvastatin (50 mg daily) was switched to pravastatin to prevent drug-drug interactions with LPV/r. Defervescence and reduction of oxygen requirements occurred within 2 days, accompanied by normalization of lymphopenia and inflammatory markers. Successfully discharged following two consecutive negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR tests.

raw_case_text:
A 74-year-old gentleman, known to have hypertension and diabetes mellitus, presented to our emergency department with a 4-day history of intermittent subjective fever of no specific periodicity and rigors associated with generalized headache, altered mentation, body malaise, nausea, and vomiting. He reported no history of loss of consciousness, abdominal pain, or change in stool habits/urine color. The patient denied history of recent trauma or falls, and the rest of the systemic review was unremarkable. The patient resided in a malaria-endemic region and reported to have previous uncomplicated malarial infections that were successfully treated with oral anti-malarials.
On clinical examination, he was an elderly gentleman febrile (38.7  C), tachypneic, and disoriented with good nutritional status. He was not jaundiced or cyanosed. Initial vitals were pulse rate of 103 beats/min in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min, with slightly borderline low blood pressure of 96/60 mmHg and saturating at 98% on room air. On systemic examination he had normal vesicular breath sounds and a normal abdominal examination. While awaiting initial work up, in view of the findings the patient received intravenous (IV) resuscitation and analgesia.
The complete blood count (CBC) revealed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 8.2 x 103/muL, hemoglobin (Hb) of 11.5 g/dL, and thrombocytopenia of 46,000/mm3. The renal profile revealed elevated creatinine 117 mumol/L and BUN 10.5 mmol/L with slightly low sodium of 131 mmol/L. The rest of serum electrolytes, liver, and coagulation profile were normal. Chest X-ray was normal. Peripheral blood smear for malaria demonstrated P. falciparum with high parasitemia with more than 1000 trophozoites/200 WBC, HPF (high power field). He was subsequently admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) as a case of severe malaria evident by high parasitemia and altered mentation.
He was then commenced on an intravenous artesunate-based regimen as per the national malaria treatment protocol with other supportive measures. With marked improvement in both clinical status and lab parameters, he was subsequently shifted to the general ward after 3 days of ICU stay. While in the ward (day 5 post admission), he acutely developed features of acute abdomen characterized by progressive, dull, constant generalized abdominal pain more so on the left upper quadrant associated with nausea and several episodes of non-bilious vomiting. The rest of the review was unremarkable.
On review, he was lying still in bed, anxious, afebrile, diaphoretic, tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypotensive but saturating well on room air. He had a slightly distended abdomen which was tender on superficial palpation with inaudible bowel sounds on auscultation. In view of the above, urgent CBC, grouping/crossmatch, formal abdominal ultrasound, and contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen were performed. CBC revealed a low Hb of 7.1 g/dL (compared to 8.9 mg/dl the day prior). Ultrasound showed hypoechoic nodular cystic area (Figure 1A and B) and CT scan revealed hyperdense intrasplenic hematoma surrounded by hypodense subcapsular hematoma. Post-contrast CT images demonstrated splenic laceration on the superolateral aspect in addition to the hematoma as well as intraperitoneal free fluid. These findings were in line with grade 3 splenic injury (Figure 2A and B).
The findings of spontaneous splenic rupture were attributed to the consequence of severe malaria due to P. falciparum infection as there was no evidence of other documented etiologies such as trauma or other infectious causes. Blood products were mobilized, adequate resuscitation was done, and after thorough discussion with the patient and family the patient was taken to the operating theatre for explorative laparotomy and splenectomy.
Intra-operatively 2.5 L of frank blood without purulence was evacuated. The spleen was enlarged and very firm with a long laceration on the upper pole extending laterally involving the fine covering capsule and not much of the splenic parenchyma. Splenectomy was done. He had an uneventful postoperative period and 7 days later he was discharged home fully recovered with scheduled clinic visits for post-splenectomy care.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 74-year-old male presenting with intermittent fever, rigors, headache, altered mentation, malaise, nausea, and vomiting for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 74-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of intermittent subjective fever, rigors, generalized headache, confusion, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. He reported no loss of consciousness, abdominal pain, trauma, or falls. Following intensive care admission and initial treatment, his condition improved and he was transferred to the ward on day 3. On hospital day 5, he acutely developed severe, progressive, dull left upper quadrant abdominal pain and recurrent non-bilious vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, diabetes mellitus. Resides in a malaria-endemic region with a history of previous uncomplicated malaria episodes successfully treated with oral medications. Denied history of trauma or falls.
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized headache, altered mentation, malaise, nausea, vomiting; on day 5 developed acute left upper quadrant abdominal pain and recurrent non-bilious vomiting. Denied loss of consciousness, changes in bowel habits, or hematuria.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Febrile (38.7 °C), tachypneic (RR 23 breaths/min), tachycardic (pulse 103 beats/min in sinus rhythm), borderline blood pressure 96/60 mmHg, SpO2 98% on room air. Disoriented; no jaundice or cyanosis; chest and abdominal examinations unremarkable. Day 5: Anxious, afebrile, diaphoretic, tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypotensive. Abdomen slightly distended, tender to superficial palpation, with inaudible bowel sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: WBC 8.2 x 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, platelet count 46,000/mm^3. Serum creatinine 117 μmol/L, BUN 10.5 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L; serum electrolytes, liver enzymes, and coagulation profile normal. Chest X-ray normal. Day 5: Hemoglobin dropped acutely to 7.1 g/dL (down from 8.9 g/dL on prior day). Formal abdominal ultrasound showed a hypoechoic nodular cystic area in the spleen.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen: Hyperdense intrasplenic hematoma surrounded by hypodense subcapsular hematoma with superolateral splenic laceration and intraperitoneal free fluid (hemoperitoneum), consistent with Grade 3 splenic injury.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria with hyperparasitemia and cerebral involvement, complicated by delayed spontaneous Grade 3 splenic rupture and hemoperitoneum. Admission peripheral blood smear demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum with high parasitemia (> 1,000 trophozoites/200 WBC per high-power field). Trauma and other etiologies were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Initial severe malaria managed in the ICU with intravenous artesunate-based regimen and supportive care. Following splenic rupture on day 5, urgent fluid/blood resuscitation was administered, and emergent exploratory laparotomy and splenectomy were performed. Intraoperatively, 2.5 L of frank hemoperitoneum was evacuated from an enlarged, firm spleen with a superior pole laceration. Discharged fully recovered on postoperative day 7 with scheduled clinic visits for post-splenectomy care.

raw_case_text:
A 61-year-old immunocompetent Italian man, born and residing in Abruzzo, presented to our observation because of the persistence of multiple ulcerative nodules on the skin of his right cheek (larger nodule measured 2 cm in maximum diameter), partially covered by scaly scabs.
A complete blood picture was normal. The patient referred no travels and had received several topical treatments (antibiotics, antimycotics, steroids), which had failed. After cleaning off the excess blood, cytology smears were performed by sampling cells from the ulcer with a sterile lancet and by smearing the sample directly onto glass slides. Pathological examination showed the presence of a large number of intra- and extracellular Leishmania promastigotes and a massive histiocyte infiltration, laden with amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) [Figure 1].

subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with chronic, persistent ulcerative nodules on his right cheek, partially covered by scabs, that failed to respond to multiple courses of topical antibiotics, antifungals, and corticosteroid therapies.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immunocompetent. Born and residing in Abruzzo, Italy, with no travel history. Prior failed topical treatments including antibiotics, antimycotics, and corticosteroids.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic examination revealed multiple ulcerative nodules on the skin of the right cheek, partially covered with scaly scabs, the largest measuring 2 cm in maximum diameter.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count (CBC): normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Direct scraping cytology of right cheek ulcer: smears demonstrated massive histiocytic infiltration with intracellular and extracellular flagellated and aflagellated protozoan organisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Cytology smears from the right cheek ulcer demonstrated a large number of intra- and extracellular Leishmania promastigotes and a massive histiocytic infiltrate laden with Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies), confirming cutaneous leishmaniasis. Differential diagnoses of bacterial, fungal, and non-infectious inflammatory dermatoses were excluded by clinical failure of topical antimicrobials and cytological visualization of parasites. Management and Outcome: No specific treatment regimen or follow-up details documented in the provided text.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old previously healthy female was admitted to a local hospital in Sri Lanka with a history of fever (38.9 C) associated with myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and abdominal pain for two days. She was diagnosed as DF with a positive Dengue NS 1 antigen test on day 3. She was managed for five days in the medical ward with close monitoring and cautious fluid management as per Sri Lankan national guideline on management of DF. Her condition remained stable throughout the initial five days without evidence of leaking or bleeding with a dropping but above 100 x 109/l platelet count. However, on the 6th day of fever, she was diagnosed to have entered the critical phase with clinical evidence of leaking and her packed cell volume (PCV) rose to 50. By this time, platelet count had also dropped to 57 x 109/l. During the same episode, her behavior was altered and she developed an episode of generalized tonic clonic convulsion that resolved spontaneously in two minutes. As her conscious level further deteriorated to a GCS of six, she was intubated and neuroprotective ventilation was commenced suspecting an intracranial haemorrhage. She was transferred to a tertiary-care unit, for CT brain and further specialized management. She progressed to a circulatory shock state despite several crystalloid and colloid boluses, as per guidelines. Meanwhile, serum calcium, sugar, and acidosis were corrected. Noradrenalin infusion was commenced to maintain mean arterial pressure more than 70 mmHg. Although the clinical picture was strongly suggestive of dengue haemorrhagic fever with leaking, there was no definite evidence of significant fluid collection in the lung bases or abdomen on ultrasound examination except for a mild gall bladder wall oedema. Possibility of a significant bleeding was less likely as her PCV and hemoglobin were rising. The bedside 2D echocardiogram reveled a low ejection fraction of 30-35% with globally hypokinetic left ventricle. T inversions and ST changes were evident on ECG and troponin I titre was elevated, all pointing towards a diagnosis of dengue myocarditis.
CT brain revealed an SAH of Fishers grade 3 with diffuse cerebral oedema. Because of the high risk of bleeding with a persistently low platelet count of 30-40 x 109/l and haemodynamic instability, decision was taken to manage conservatively without performing a decompressive craniotomy. Hence, neuroprotective ventilation was continued with the implementation of intracranial pressure-reducing strategies.
Due to SAH, platelet count needed to be maintained close to 100 x 109 mm3. Despite platelet transfusion, the platelet count remained below 40 x 109/l. There was no evidence in the blood picture to suggest disseminated intravascular coagulation or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Hence, she was investigated on the line of HLH. Serum ferritin was 1500 mug/l, and LDH was 1247 mu/l. Bone marrow biopsy confirmed HLH. She was treated with immunoglobulin 20 g daily and high-dose dexamethasone as for HLH.
Even though she initially developed stage 1 acute kidney injury, on the second day of ICU admission, she developed polyuria (3.2 ml/kg/hr), with high serum osmolality and urinary sodium of 160 mmol/l. In the context of raised ICP following SAH, CDI was diagnosed along with urinary studies. Polyuria and hypernatremia further complicated the fluid management making bedside 2D echo and point-of-care ultrasound scanning a valuable tool to guide fluid therapy. Desmopressin nasal puffs were also used to control CDI.
Her condition continued to deteriorate despite the active multidisciplinary management. She expired on the third day of admission to the tertiary-care unit.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old female presenting with fever (38.9 °C), myalgia, arthralgia, headache, and abdominal pain for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 41-year-old previously healthy female was hospitalized with a 2-day history of high fever (38.9 °C), headache, body aches, and abdominal pain. She remained stable under guided fluid therapy until fever day 6, when she entered the critical phase with signs of plasma leakage and hemoconcentration. Simultaneously, she developed acute behavioral changes and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting two minutes. Her conscious level rapidly deteriorated to GCS 6, necessitating emergent endotracheal intubation and neuroprotective mechanical ventilation for suspected intracranial hemorrhage. Following transfer to a tertiary ICU, she developed refractory circulatory shock, severe acute myocarditis, and central diabetes insipidus.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; no prior medical comorbidities.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, myalgia, arthralgia, headache; no overt gastrointestinal or external bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Day 6: Acute deterioration of consciousness (GCS 6), postictal state following generalized tonic-clonic convulsion. ICU admission: Circulatory shock requiring high-dose vasopressor support (norepinephrine); signs of increased intracranial pressure.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 6 labs: Packed cell volume (PCV) rose to 50% (severe hemoconcentration), platelet count dropped to 57 x 10^9/L (subsequently persistently low at 30-40 x 10^9/L despite platelet transfusions). Hemoglobin rising alongside PCV. Blood smear: No evidence of DIC or TTP. HLH workup: Serum ferritin 1,500 microg/L, LDH 1,247 U/L. Renal function: Initial stage 1 AKI; on day 2 of ICU, developed polyuria (3.2 mL/kg/h) with elevated serum osmolality and urinary sodium 160 mmol/L (central diabetes insipidus). Cardiac biomarkers: Elevated troponin I. ECG: T-wave inversions and ST-segment changes. Point-of-care ultrasound: Mild gallbladder wall edema without significant pleural effusion or ascites. Bedside 2D echocardiogram: Globally hypokinetic left ventricle with severely depressed ejection fraction (EF 30-35%), consistent with acute myocarditis.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT: Fisher grade 3 subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) with diffuse cerebral edema. Bone marrow biopsy: Confirmed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (severe dengue / dengue hemorrhagic fever with plasma leakage) complicated by catastrophic Fisher grade 3 subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), diffuse cerebral edema, cardiogenic/circulatory shock secondary to acute dengue myocarditis, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and central diabetes insipidus (CDI). Dengue confirmed by positive Dengue NS1 antigen on day 3. DIC, TTP, and major systemic occult bleeding were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Neuroprotective mechanical ventilation and intracranial pressure-lowering strategies were instituted; decompressive craniotomy was withheld due to high surgical bleeding risk and refractory thrombocytopenia. Hemodynamics supported with targeted crystalloid/colloid boluses, electrolyte/acidosis correction, and norepinephrine infusion (targeting MAP > 70 mmHg). Repeated platelet transfusions were administered. HLH treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 20 g daily) and high-dose dexamethasone. CDI managed with desmopressin nasal puffs and echo-guided fluid titration. Despite aggressive multidisciplinary ICU care, her condition deteriorated, and she succumbed on the third day of tertiary ICU admission.

raw_case_text:
We contacted 31 pemphigus patients routinely followed-up in our hospital in Rome who received RTX in the 12 months preceding the COVID-19 pandemic. Among them, a 45-year-old woman (professional nurse, living in Northern Italy) confirmed having COVID-19.
She was affected by pemphigus foliaceous, as assessed by clinical examination and direct immunofluorescence microscopy ( Figure 1A ), from January 2019 and received a cycle of RTX (500 mg x 4 weekly infusions) in May 2019 reaching complete remission off-therapy in November 2019 ( Figure 2 ). Two months later, a relapse occurred; therefore, on January 23 2020, she received an additional 500 mg RTX infusion and started prednisone 50 mg/day. Disease control was reached two weeks after infusion, prednisone was gradually tapered to 5 mg and lesions completely resolved at the beginning of March when B cells were still depleted. By the 15th of March, she developed mild flu-like symptoms (fever up to 37.5 C, asthenia and some cough). She was treated with azithromycin 500 mg/day for 3 days without clinical improvement. On the 21st of March, a nasopharyngeal swab was performed, resulting in negative SARS-CoV-2 result. She was started on Co-amoxiclav 875/125 mg bid for 6 days. During antibiotic treatment she experienced hyposmia, ageusia, dry cough, nocturnal dyspnea and hyperpyrexia (up to 39.5 C). As symptoms persisted, on March 27 a second nasopharyngeal swab was performed, resulting in positivity for SARS-CoV-2 ( Figure 2 ). She was admitted to the Geriatric-COVID-19 Unit of the referral hospital in Bolzano-Bozen. At admission, the patient's oxygen saturation was 94% on room air, ABG revealed pO2 61.9 mmHg, pCO2 34 mmHg, pO2(a)/FO2(l) 295 mmHg and pH 7.49. Laboratory tests showed lymphopenia (940 cells/microL, n.v. 1100-4500), slightly increased LDH (337 U/L, n.v. 123-230), increased CRP (11.03 mg/dl, n.v. < 0.05) and increased IL-6 (51.7 pg/ml, n.v. <7.0). The chest radiograph showed interstitial pneumonia with bilateral airspace opacities ( Figure 1B ). She was started on hydroxychloroquine (200 mg bid for 8 days), lopinavir/ritonavir (200/50 mg qd for 8 days) and enoxaparin 0.4 ml qd. Oxygen therapy (from 3 up to 8 l/min) was administered. Despite this, her fever persisted, dyspnea worsened and on April 1, she was transferred to the Infectious Diseases Unit of the same hospital.
