Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) at 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days were administered. Neurological improvement was noted with resolution of upper extremity weakness, improved lower extremity tone/power, and GCS recovery to 14/15. On day 6, prior to scheduled extubation, the patient suffered accidental self-extubation, rapid decompensation, and refractory cardiac arrest leading to death despite CPR.

raw_case_text:
A 78 yr old man from a rural area at the western of Iran referred to Razi Hospital Dermatology Clinic, Tehran for multiple ulcerative and exudative lesions on mid face, dorsal aspect of hands and the posterior aspect of heels (Fig. 1, 2).
Informed consent was taken from the patient.
Lesions initiated three years before with papules on the dorsal aspect of the hands then progressively enlarged above the upper lip, anterior portion of the nasal fossa, above the eyebrows and heels and became ulcerative.
During the past 3 yr, the lesions of hands were so developed that destroyed the tendons and soft tissue of fifth finger in the right hand so led to amputation of this finger. There was no history of comorbid condition, drug consumption, systemic symptoms, weight loss, fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or any signs of systemic involvement in physical examination and laboratory survey.
Multiple treatments in order to some heterogenic diagnosis such as pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis were tried without any improvement in lesions.
In Razi Hospital Dermatology Clinic, initial Skin biopsy revealed necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern that suggested infections etiology but the smear of lesions for fungal and mycobacteria and Leishmania was negative. In order to result of PPD test with 27 mm induration, anti-tuberculosis treatment including isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide was started.
A month after initiating drugs for tuberculosis, the smear of leishmaniasis repeated that was positive this time, the second biopsy revealed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and infiltration of the dermis by mixed inflammatory cells and Leishman bodies compatible with leishmaniasis.
Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) PCR was carried out on DNA extraction was carried out with QIAGEN Kit according to the manufacturer's instruction using two primers, LITSR (5-GTG CAG GAT CAT TTT CCG ATG) and L5.8s: 5-TGA TAC CAC TTA TCG CAC TT was designed for LTS1-PCR and cutting with and HaeIII enzyme. Positive controls containing DNA of L. major, L. tropica and a negative control containing distilled water were included. The PCR-RFLP on specimens of lesions proved L. major as the pathogenic agent (Fig. 3).
From the left side, the 2 bands show L. major, the second 2 bands show L. tropica, the 5th one is the specimens of lesions that compatibles with L. major and the last one show L. tropica.
Treatment initiated with 3 gr per day of meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime ) until 1 wk followed by 4.5 gr per day for another week, in spite of good response to meglumine antimoniate after 2 wk of treatment we forced to discontinue of drug because of cardiac toxicity (Figs. 4, 5).
The patient was informed about publishing his figures whit covering eyes.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old male presented with a 3-year history of multiple ulcerative and exudative lesions on his mid-face, dorsal hands, and heels.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with chronic skin lesions that started 3 years earlier as papules on the dorsum of both hands, which progressively enlarged and ulcerated over the upper lip, anterior nasal fossa, eyebrows, and posterior heels. The hand lesions progressively destroyed tendons and soft tissue of the right fifth digit, leading to its amputation. Prior empiric therapies for presumed pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and leishmaniasis had failed. At the dermatology clinic, an initial skin biopsy showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation, but initial smears were negative; due to a positive PPD test (27 mm induration), anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) was initiated for 1 month without improvement. Repeat smear and biopsy were subsequently performed.
subjective.past_medical_history: No comorbid chronic conditions; prior amputation of right fifth digit due to soft tissue and tendon destruction from skin lesions. Epidemiological exposure: resident of a rural area in western Iran.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies fever, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Home medications: anti-tuberculosis therapy for 1 month prior to admission. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic examination revealed multiple ulcerative and exudative lesions over the mid-face (above upper lip, anterior nasal fossa, above eyebrows), dorsal aspect of both hands, and posterior aspect of heels. Right fifth finger was amputated. No peripheral lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or signs of systemic involvement.
objective.routine_investigations: Tuberculin skin test (PPD): 27 mm induration. Routine laboratory survey: normal with no signs of systemic involvement.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial skin biopsy: necrotizing and palisading granulomatous tissue pattern; initial lesion smears negative for fungi, mycobacteria. Second skin biopsy: pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and dermal infiltration by mixed inflammatory cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania major.
Diagnostic confirmation: Repeat lesion smear demonstrated Leishmania amastigotes; second skin biopsy revealed dermal infiltration with mixed inflammatory cells and Leishman bodies; PCR-RFLP analysis targeting ITS1 (primers LITSR and L5.8s, digested with HaeIII) confirmed Leishmania major as the etiologic agent.
Differentials ruled out: Cutaneous tuberculosis (unresponsive to 1 month of 4-drug anti-TB therapy; mycobacterial smear negative), pyoderma gangrenosum, sarcoidosis, and deep fungal infections (fungal smear negative).
Treatment and clinical course: Initiated on meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) at 3 g/day for 1 week, increased to 4.5 g/day for the second week with favorable lesion regression. However, therapy was discontinued after 2 weeks due to cardiotoxicity.

raw_case_text:
A 58-year-old Caucasian man presented with a one-month history of fever, night sweats, progressive fatigue, dyspnea, abdominal pain, and swelling. He had a past medical history of chronic hepatitis C and HIV disease/AIDS which was found 8 months prior to his presentation. He was started on HAART prior to this hospital visit and had a CD4 count of 83 cells/muL and a viral load of 214 copies/mL at the time of his presentation. His initial examination findings were significant for a middle-aged Caucasian male in moderate distress that was tachycardic at rest with a heart rate of 110 beats/min and febrile with a temperature of 101.6 F with generalized peripheral adenopathy, anasarca, and splenomegaly and decreased breath sounds in bilateral lung bases. Initial laboratory investigations revealed that he was pancytopenic with hemoglobin of 6.7 g/dL, white blood cell (WBC) count of 2700/muL, and a platelet count of 64000/muL. His complete metabolic panel showed that he was hypoalbuminemic with albumin of 2.3 g/dL; the remainder of his panel was within normal limits. Computerized Tomography (CT) imaging was performed on his chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast which showed diffuse bulky adenopathy, marked splenomegaly with evidence of portal hypertension, moderate ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions (Figure 1). The initial management was directed at treating him for possible sepsis and he was placed on broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics which did not improve his symptoms and blood and urine cultures returned negative.
A core needle biopsy was performed on an enlarged left axillary lymph node on the third day of hospitalization which demonstrated features consistent with MCD with focal features of early development of a plasmablastic microlymphoma. The pathology report highlighted the presence of numerous plasma cells seen mainly in the mantle zone and interfollicular area showing nuclear HHV-8 positivity. The plasma cells were evaluated using mRNA in situ hybridization (ISH) studies which were polyclonal for kappa/lambda. CD staining was performed which demonstrated a background of T-cells with occasional microscopic foci of lambda restricted plasmablast (HHV-8+), variably expressing CD20 seen invading follicles. A unilateral bone marrow aspirate and biopsy was subsequently done which showed a hypercellular marrow with evidence of hemophagocytosis in a background of plasma cell infiltration consistent with involvement by MCD. Additional laboratory studies revealed markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 229 mg/L (reference range: <5 mg/L) and an elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and beta2 microglobulin which were 282 U/L (reference range: 126-266 U/L) and 9.7 mg/L (reference range: 0.6-2.4 mg/L), respectively. His serum protein electrophoresis showed hypergammaglobulinemia and hepatitis B was found to be negative.
Prior to starting treatment, this patient was evaluated for skin lesions suggestive of Kaposi's sarcoma and no lesions were identified. He was also started on treatment with ganciclovir for HHV-8 but this was subsequently discontinued due to worsening cytopenias. His laboratory studies suggested worsening of his organ function since his admission with a decrease in his platelet count to 10000/muL; his albumin was further decreased to 1.7 g/dL; both his creatinine and his bilirubin had risen from previous normal values to 1.39 mg/dL and 1.5 mg/dL, respectively. He required multiple transfusions while in hospital and had a total of 9 units of packed red blood cells and 4 units of platelets. Given his declining performance status (PS) which was considered to be Eastern cooperative oncology group PS grade 3 (ECOG PS grade 3), he was not considered to be a candidate for chemotherapy and was offered treatment with rituximab only.
On day 10 of his hospitalization, treatment with rituximab was initiated at 375 mg/m2 with plans for weekly administration for a total of 4 cycles. This patient tolerated treatment with rituximab without any adverse effects. Within days of completing therapy, there was an observed clinical response with the resolution of his fever, night sweats, and anorexia as well as rapid improvement of his cytopenias. He completed all 4 cycles of rituximab in hospital. His posttreatment CT with contrast of the abdomen showed a marked reduction in the size of his enlarged intra-abdominal lymph nodes and splenic size (Figure 2). A follow-up PET (positron emission tomography)/CT study was done 2 months after completing therapy with rituximab which showed complete resolution of his previously seen bulky adenopathy and pleural effusions. Clinically, his performance status improved to ECOG PS grade 0 with no limitations in his activity level. Laboratory studies demonstrated resolution of his pancytopenia and hypoalbuminemia. Approximately 8 months after completing his treatment with rituximab, he remains in clinical remission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old male presenting with fever, night sweats, progressive fatigue, shortness of breath, and abdominal distension for one month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-month history of fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnea, abdominal pain, and swelling. Following admission, he was initially treated empirically with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for suspected sepsis without clinical improvement. Over his hospital course, he developed worsening pancytopenia requiring multiple blood product transfusions and profound functional decline.
subjective.past_medical_history: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection / AIDS diagnosed 8 months prior (maintained on HAART, with baseline CD4 count 83 cells/microL and viral load 214 copies/mL at presentation); chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fevers, night sweats, fatigue, dyspnea, abdominal pain and distension, and anasarca; denies focal rashes or focal neurological deficits.

objective.physical_examination: General: Moderate distress, anasarcous. Vitals: Temperature 101.6 °F (38.7 °C), heart rate 110 beats/min (tachycardia). Respiratory: Decreased breath sounds at bilateral lung bases. Abdomen: Distended with ascites and palpable splenomegaly. Lymphatics: Generalized peripheral lymphadenopathy. Performance status: ECOG grade 3.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 2,700/microL, platelet count 64,000/microL (platelet nadir 10,000/microL during admission). Comprehensive metabolic panel: Serum albumin 2.3 g/dL (nadir 1.7 g/dL), serum creatinine rising to 1.39 mg/dL, total bilirubin rising to 1.5 mg/dL. Inflammatory markers & Serology: C-reactive protein (CRP) 229 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 282 U/L, beta-2 microglobulin 9.7 mg/L; serum protein electrophoresis showed polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; hepatitis B surface antigen negative; blood and urine bacterial cultures sterile.
objective.advanced_workup: CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast: Diffuse bulky mediastinal, retroperitoneal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy, marked splenomegaly with portal hypertension, moderate ascites, and bilateral pleural effusions. Core needle biopsy of left axillary lymph node: Interfollicular and mantle zone expansion by sheets of plasma cells with nuclear HHV-8 positivity and occasional microscopic foci of lambda-restricted plasmablasts (HHV-8+) variably expressing CD20 invading follicles, consistent with multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) with features of early plasmablastic microlymphoma. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy: Hypercellular marrow with hemophagocytosis in a background of plasma cell infiltration. Follow-up PET/CT (2 months post-treatment): Complete resolution of bulky adenopathy and pleural effusions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection / AIDS (CD4 count 83 cells/microL) complicated by Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)-associated multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) with early plasmablastic microlymphoma, secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), and chronic hepatitis C.
Plan & Outcome: Broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics discontinued after sterile cultures. Antiviral therapy with ganciclovir was trialed but stopped due to worsening myelosuppression. Supported with transfusions of 9 units packed red blood cells and 4 units platelets. Due to poor performance status (ECOG grade 3), chemotherapy was deferred and single-agent rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses) was initiated on hospital day 10. The patient achieved rapid clinical and laboratory remission with resolution of fevers, cytopenias, and organomegaly, achieving ECOG grade 0 performance status and sustained complete remission at 8 months follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old male patient was commenced on ART in September 2010, at seven years of age. His baseline CD4 count was 145 cells/muL. His first-line ART regimens were stavudine/lamivudine (3TC)/nevirapine, followed by stavudine/3TC/efavirenz (EFV), followed by zidovudine/3TC/EFV. Viral load (VL) results were not available until 2014, at which time he was noted to have virological treatment failure. An HIV genotypic resistance test done in January 2015 showed significant nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) DRMs with no protease inhibitor resistance (see Table 1 for DRMs and sensitivity results). In January 2015 he was switched to second-line treatment with abacavir (ABC)/3TC/lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), which was later simplified to ABC/3TC/Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATZ/r). Virological suppression was maintained for the duration of protease inhibitor therapy. In August 2019 he was switched to a single tablet regimen of tenofovir (TDF)/3TC/DTG; his VL was suppressed at the time of switch.
Virological rebound occurred 11 months after initiation of the InSTI regimen. The patient reported a history of suboptimal adherence to TDF/3TC/DTG; no other risk factors for virological failure were identified. Despite adherence counselling his VL remained high, and an HIV genotypic resistance test taken 14 months after TDF/3TC/DTG initiation showed persistent NRTI and NNRTI DRMs, and extensive InSTI DRMs (see Table 1 for mutations and sensitivity analysis).

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old male presenting for longitudinal evaluation of antiretroviral treatment failure and drug resistance.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented for therapeutic monitoring following documented virological rebound 11 months after transition to an integrase strand transfer inhibitor-based single-tablet regimen. He acknowledged suboptimal medication adherence. Despite structured adherence counseling, high-level viral replication persisted, prompting specialized resistance profiling.
subjective.past_medical_history: Receiving antiretroviral therapy since 7 years of age (September 2010); previously treated with sequential first-line regimens (stavudine/lamivudine/nevirapine, stavudine/lamivudine/efavirenz, and zidovudine/lamivudine/efavirenz) until treatment failure in 2014; second-line protease inhibitor regimens (abacavir/lamivudine/lopinavir/ritonavir and abacavir/lamivudine/atazanavir/ritonavir) from 2015 to 2019 with virological suppression; switched in August 2019 to tenofovir/lamivudine/dolutegravir.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports feeling clinically well; denies opportunistic symptoms, weight loss, fever, or chronic diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Patient is an 18-year-old male in good general health without acute distress; physical examination was clinically unremarkable without focal signs of opportunistic disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Virological rebound and emergent integrase strand transfer inhibitor (InSTI) resistance complicating long-standing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (initial baseline CD4 count 145 cells/microL). Diagnostic confirmation: HIV genotypic resistance testing at 14 months post-InSTI switch revealed emergent multidrug resistance with extensive InSTI drug-resistance mutations (DRMs), alongside persistent nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) DRMs, following initial genotypic testing in 2015 showing dual NRTI/NNRTI resistance without protease inhibitor resistance. Plan & Outcome: Provided adherence counseling and reassessed salvage antiretroviral therapy options based on genotypic sensitivity profile.

raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old male with no previous medical comorbidities was brought to the Emergency Department (ED) with increasing tachypnea and dyspnea over the previous day. The accompanying partner reported that the patient had been intermittently warm to the touch for the past week, complaining of myalgia and headache. He has never used any medications. The pair had just returned to Canada from two weeks in Costa Rica, where the patient had begun feeling unwell one day before flying home. Immediately upon returning to Canada, the patient saw his primary care physician, who believed he had influenza. In the following days, the patient's condition worsened and he presented to the ED with the following vital signs: blood pressure of 125/75 mmHg, heart rate (HR) of 110 beats/min, respiratory rate (RR) of 35 breaths/minute, temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation of 82%. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15/15. He was in obvious respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. A portable chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral opacities (Figure 1). The patient was placed on a nonrebreather (FiO2 of 1), but his work of breathing did not substantially improve, and he remained hypoxemic. Therefore, the patient was intubated in the ED and an arterial line was inserted. ED bloodwork revealed a pO2 of 65 mmHg on 100% oxygen, but normal electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, and coagulation parameters. Following ICU transfer, the patient was diagnosed with ARDS due to his severely depressed PaO2/FiO2 ratio (110 upon ICU admission), bilateral opacities, and no signs that would suggest cardiac dysfunction (i.e., normal blood pressure, no peripheral edema, and normal electrocardiogram). He was ventilated with a standardized ARDSNet protocol that focused on low tidal volume (5 mL/kg of ideal body weight and a target pH > 7.25), plus a positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) increased to 10 mmHg. While the etiology for ARDS was unclear, it was presumed infectious in origin, given his fevers and travel. Blood and urine cultures were performed, along with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Bronchoscopy did not show any pulmonary hemorrhage or purulent secretions. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest confirmed bilateral edema but did not reveal any lobar infiltrate consistent with bacterial pneumonia. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal biventricular function, with no vegetation or valvular regurgitation.
Infectious Diseases consultation led to initiation of broad-spectrum antimicrobials (piperacillin-tazobactam, azithromycin, and vancomycin). Initial blood, urine, and BAL cultures grew no pathogens. Malaria thick and thin smears were performed several times and were negative. Dengue serology was also negative, as was human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis A, B, and C. Despite broad antimicrobial treatment, the patient's respiratory status worsened, which led to prone positioning.
Given the recent travel history to Costa Rica, the diagnosis of leptospirosis was considered, but after a delay of 48 hours from presentation. The clue was that, following further questioning, the patient's partner reported that she and the patient had spent several days swimming in freshwater, which they had also drunk. Both are sources of leptospirosis transmission. Leptospirosis serology was sent (specifically, an IgM-detection enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay). Given the prolonged time required to establish leptospirosis diagnosis via serology, the patient was empirically treated with ampicillin and penicillin G.
Over the next 48 hours, the patient's condition substantially improved. He became afebrile, his hypoxemia resolved, and his chest radiograph improved. Otherwise, his blood work remained largely unchanged, with normal renal, hepatic, and coagulation function. He was extubated on postadmission day five, was transferred to the medicine ward on day six, and was discharged home on day eight. Diagnosis was confirmed but not until after discharge: due to a positive IgM for Leptospira and a Leptospira canicola titer of 1 : 200. Diagnosis was further confirmed with microscopic agglutination testing (MAT). He was seen in follow-up by the Infectious Diseases service and never demonstrated any renal dysfunction, hepatic dysfunction, or coagulopathy suggesting Weil's disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old man presented with acute tachypnea, severe dyspnea, and hypoxemia after 1 week of fever, myalgias, and headache following travel to Costa Rica.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient became unwell with fever, myalgias, and headache 1 day prior to returning from a 2-week vacation in Costa Rica. After initial evaluation for suspected influenza, his symptoms rapidly deteriorated over subsequent days with increasing tachypnea and dyspnea, culminating in severe hypoxemic respiratory failure upon emergency presentation requiring urgent endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous medical comorbidities. Has never taken medications. Travel and epidemiological exposures: 2-week trip to Costa Rica with extensive swimming in and accidental ingestion of freshwater; no other animal exposures documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, myalgias, headache, and severe shortness of breath. No home medications or allergies.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.6 °C; blood pressure: 125/75 mmHg; heart rate: 110 beats/min; respiratory rate: 35 breaths/min; oxygen saturation: 82% on room air. Glasgow Coma Scale: 15/15. Patient was in obvious respiratory distress with accessory muscle use. No peripheral edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Arterial blood gas (on 100% O2): pO2 65 mmHg; PaO2/FiO2 ratio: 110 upon ICU admission. Electrolytes, renal function, liver enzymes, and coagulation parameters were normal. Portable chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral opacities. Electrocardiogram was normal. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed normal biventricular function with no vegetation or valvular regurgitation. Blood, urine, and BAL fluid cultures were negative. Thick and thin malaria smears were negative. Dengue, HIV, and hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: confirmed bilateral pulmonary edema without lobar infiltrates. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL): no pulmonary hemorrhage or purulent secretions visualized.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Acute pulmonary leptospirosis presenting as isolated acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) without hepatic, renal, or hematologic manifestations (no Weil's disease). Diagnosis was confirmed post-discharge by positive Leptospira IgM ELISA and microscopic agglutination test (MAT) with a Leptospira canicola titer of 1:200. Influenza, malaria, dengue, viral hepatitis, HIV, bacterial pneumonia, and infective endocarditis were ruled out. Treatment & Outcome: Initially treated with piperacillin-tazobactam, azithromycin, and vancomycin, low-tidal-volume ARDSNet mechanical ventilation (5 mL/kg, PEEP 10 cm H2O), and prone positioning. Following consideration of leptospirosis, empiric treatment with intravenous ampicillin and penicillin G was initiated. The patient showed rapid clinical improvement within 48 hours, was extubated on day 5, transitioned to the ward on day 6, and discharged home on day 8 with full recovery and no subsequent organ dysfunction on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 16-year-old, previously healthy teen presented to emergency department with complaints of high-grade intermittent fever for a week followed by severe periumbilical pain with multiple episodes of loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice for 3 days. He did not have history of drug or alcohol abuse and never received blood transfusions in the past. He did not have history of recent travel or trauma.
On examination, he looked ill and toxic but was conscious and well oriented. He was icteric and mildly dehydrated although hemodynamically stable. Temperature was recorded to be 101 F. He was in mild respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 32/min and SpO2 of 98% on O2 at 4 litres per minute via face mask. Abdominal examination revealed tenderness with guarding over the periumbilical region and hepatosplenomegaly. Rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. The investigations revealed a deranged LFT with direct hyperbilirubinemia (total 4.6 mg/dl, direct 2.3 mg/dl) and elevated enzymes (ALP 273 mu/l, AST 214 mu/l, ALT 123 mu/l, and G-GT 294 mu/l). The pancreatic enzymes were also elevated (Amylase-548 mu/l and Lipase-415 mu/l), whereas renal function tests and hemogram were both normal.
Plain abdominal radiographs showed colon cut-off and sentinel loop signs as shown in Figures 1 and 2. Ultrasound abdomen revealed hyperechoic pancreas, distended gall bladder, and splenomegaly. Further evaluation with an abdominal contrast enhanced computed tomography showed bulky pancreatic tail and body with mild soft tissue stranding in the peripancreatic fat, distended gall bladder with minimal pericholecystic fluid, and minimal ascites with hepatosplenomegaly. There was also bilateral minimal pleural effusion with subsegmental atelectasis of posterobasal segment of both lower lung lobes. Features favored acute interstitial pancreatitis: Modified Computed Tomography Severity Index (CTSI) score of 4 as shown in Figures 3-9.
Aided by Revised Atlanta Classification of AP 2012, a clinicoradiological diagnosis of interstitial edematous pancreatitis without pancreatic necrosis was made. Severity and mortality assessment done using Ranson's criteria at admission and within 48 hours predicted an associated mortality of 0-3%.
He was admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit (PICU), with a diagnosis of AP with impending septic shock and jaundice. Based on clinical findings, infective etiology was considered, and broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated after sending blood culture and serological tests. He was kept nil by mouth, given intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesics, and antipyretics.
After 4 days of intensive monitoring and supportive care, his fever and pain subsided. He could be gradually started on oral fluids and then on to fat-free diet. On day 6, he was stable to be transferred to the general ward, where he received a complete course of antibiotics for ten days and made an uneventful recovery.
LFT, serum proteins, and pancreatic enzymes were followed up till discharge and at 2 months, wherein gradual normalization in all was noted as shown in Figures 10-13.
Laboratory findings during hospitalization and at 2 months follow-up:
The serological tests for hepatitis B, C, leptospira, malaria antigen, and dengue were all reported negative, while the Widal test yielded positive for S. typhi "O" (1 : 320) and "H" (1 : 320). Based upon growth of "Salmonella enterica serovar typhi" on the blood culture 72 hours later, a final complete diagnosis of AP and AH secondary to Salmonella typhi infection was made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old male presented with high-grade intermittent fever for 1 week followed by severe periumbilical pain, loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice for 3 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: High-grade intermittent fever started 1 week prior to presentation. Four days later, he developed severe periumbilical pain, multiple episodes of loose stools, vomiting, and jaundice over the preceding 3 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Denied alcohol or drug abuse, blood transfusions, recent travel, or trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Loose stools, vomiting, jaundice, mild shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Ill and toxic-looking but conscious and oriented; icteric and mildly dehydrated; hemodynamically stable. Temperature: 101 °F. Mild respiratory distress with respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min oxygen via face mask. Abdomen: tenderness and guarding over the periumbilical region; hepatosplenomegaly. Rest of systemic examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver function tests: total bilirubin 4.6 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.3 mg/dL, ALP 273 mU/L, AST 214 mU/L, ALT 123 mU/L, GGT 294 mU/L. Pancreatic enzymes: amylase 548 mU/L, lipase 415 mU/L. Renal function tests and hemogram: normal. Plain abdominal radiographs: colon cut-off and sentinel loop signs. Abdominal ultrasound: hyperechoic pancreas, distended gallbladder, splenomegaly. Serology: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, leptospira, malaria antigen, and dengue tests all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT: bulky pancreatic tail and body with mild soft tissue stranding in peripancreatic fat, distended gallbladder with minimal pericholecystic fluid, minimal ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and bilateral minimal pleural effusion with subsegmental atelectasis of posterobasal segments of lower lung lobes; Modified Computed Tomography Severity Index (CTSI) score of 4, consistent with interstitial edematous pancreatitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Acute interstitial edematous pancreatitis and acute hepatitis secondary to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi infection (typhoid fever), complicated by impending septic shock. Blood cultures grew Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi at 72 hours, and Widal test was positive for S. typhi O (1:320) and H (1:320). Managed in the PICU: kept NPO, received IV fluid resuscitation, analgesics, antipyretics, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics. Fever and abdominal pain resolved after 4 days; oral fluids and fat-free diet were initiated. Transferred to the general ward on day 6 and completed a 10-day antibiotic course with uneventful recovery. Follow-up LFTs, serum proteins, and pancreatic enzymes gradually normalized and were completely normal at 2-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 51-year-old man who arrived at our facility complaining of fever, chills, myalgia, and generalized weakness that had begun 5 days before coming to the hospital. His fever was continuous, and he reported that his eyes have been yellow for the previous 3 days; he also complained of a headache in the frontal area. He is a fishery officer and works in the rice paddies as well. He reported severe vomiting 4 to 5 times per day and a decreased appetite and a change in urine color during the previous few days.
The patient had no significant familial history of any disease. Except for one capsule of Omeprazole (20 mg) each day for heartburn; he reported no other current medications and no history of drug abuse history. The patient's physical examination showed the following vital signs: blood pressure 120/80 mmHG, pulse of 80, respiratory rate of 18, and temperature of 38 C. 
His conjunctiva was congested. No neck stiffness was detected. On both arms multiple petechia and, purpura were observed, but there was no sign of ecchymosis. The heart beat was normal. No organomegaly was detected in an abdominal examination. The lower limbs had normal appearance and function. 
The laboratory data are shown in Table 1.
After a brain CT scan the radiologist reported "multiple hemorrhagic lesions in the temporal and parietal lobes, especially in the left side" (see Figure 1).
The patient's chest X-ray was normal, and he tested negative for HBs Ag and HBs AB.
His diagnosis was reviewed, and in view of the deranged hepatorenal functions and seasonal prevalence (recent floods in the area where the patient resided), leptospirosis was clinically suspected, which was further confirmed by the positive serum IgM-ELISA (IgG value of 100 and an IgM value of 20). Epidemics of leptospirosis in our region and unavailability of Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) made us to consider IgM-ELISA for confirmation of leptospirosis. 
In an abdominal sonography, 70 cc of fluid were found in Morison's pouch, and the liver exhibited hepatitis-like changes. An MRI showed intracranial hemorrhage, especially in the left lobe.
With intracranial hemorrhage care and Ceftriaxone (1 mg/day) and Dexamethasone (8 mg two times daily) for 1 week and 15 unit platelets, his condition improved. After 26 days of hospital care with a normal platelet count and normal renal function the patient was discharged from hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 51-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of continuous fever, chills, myalgias, generalized weakness, frontal headache, and 3 days of jaundice.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 5 days prior to admission with continuous fever, chills, generalized myalgias, and profound weakness. Frontal headache and yellow discoloration of the sclerae developed 3 days before presentation. He also experienced frequent vomiting (4 to 5 times per day), decreased appetite, and dark discoloration of his urine over the preceding few days.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant family history of disease. Denied history of substance abuse. Home medications: omeprazole 20 mg orally once daily for heartburn. Occupation and epidemiological exposure: fishery officer working in rice paddies in an area with recent flooding.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for frontal headache, jaundice, dark urine, anorexia, severe vomiting (4-5 episodes/day), chills, and generalized myalgias. Denied neck stiffness, chest pain, or focal limb weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38 °C; blood pressure: 120/80 mmHg; pulse: 80 beats/min; respiratory rate: 18 breaths/min. HEENT: conjunctival congestion, scleral icterus, no nuchal rigidity. Cardiovascular: normal heart sounds, regular rhythm. Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no organomegaly. Extremities: multiple petechiae and purpura on both arms without ecchymosis; lower limbs normal in appearance and function.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission laboratory evaluation revealed deranged hepatorenal functions and thrombocytopenia, both of which normalized prior to discharge (normal platelet count and normal renal function). Chest X-ray was normal. Serology: negative for HBsAg and HBsAb. Abdominal ultrasound: 70 cc of fluid in Morison's pouch and hepatitis-like parenchymal changes in the liver.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT: multiple hemorrhagic lesions in the temporal and parietal lobes, prominent on the left side. Brain MRI: confirmed intracranial hemorrhage, especially in the left temporal/parietal lobe.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis complicated by multifocal intracranial hemorrhage (temporal and parietal lobes), acute hepatorenal impairment, and severe thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis was confirmed by positive serum IgM-ELISA (IgG: 100, IgM: 20) in the setting of regional epidemic prevalence. Acute hepatitis B was ruled out. Treatment & Outcome: Managed with intracranial hemorrhage protocol, 15 units of platelet transfusion, intravenous ceftriaxone (reported as 1 mg/day) and intravenous dexamethasone (8 mg twice daily) for 1 week. After 26 days of inpatient hospitalization, his condition substantially improved with full normalization of platelet count and renal function, allowing successful discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 17-month-old boy was admitted to West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, in March of 2022 for the insidious onset of fever, ecchymosis of skin, anhelation, and pancytopenia. On admission, blood routine examination results were as follows: white blood cell (WBC) 2.5 x 109/L, hemoglobin (Hb) 60 g/L, platelet (PLT) 45 x 109/L, and immature granulocytes found in peripheral blood smears. Subsequently, bone marrow morphology, immunophenotyping, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics were carried out. Based on the above testing, the boy was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL, L2, ETV6-PEX5 fusion gene positive, KRAS A146V and KRAS A146T mutation, IKZF1-8 heterozygous deletion, 45, XY, der (7; 12) (q10; q10)(5)/46, XY (15). Then, according to ALL-low risk (ALL-LR) of the Chinese Children's Cancer Group study ALL 2020 (CCCG-ALL-2020), conventional and continuous therapy was administered. After the remission induction regimen of 4 weeks, complete remission (CR) was reached. Subsequently, the child was supposed to receive consolidation therapy according to CCCG-ALL-2020 with three courses after 4 weeks of achievement of CR.
On October 2022, which was also the interval between the first consolidation treatments, the patient was hospitalized again for a repeated fever of 13 days and coagulopathy after the second cycle of consolidation chemotherapy. Laboratory tests are shown in Table 1. Color Doppler ultrasonic examination showed swollen liver and spleen. The above results suggested that the infant had chemotherapy-related bone marrow suppression, infection, and coagulation dysfunction. Vancomycin, imipenem, and voriconazole were used for empirical antibiotic therapy. Fresh frozen plasma, fibrinogen, and prothrombin complex were used for improving coagulation function. Seven days after therapy, the patient still had a fever (38.4-39.4 C), and his liver and spleen were enlarged. CRP and PCT levels were 125.5 mg/L and 3.99 mg/L, respectively (Table 1). No microorganisms were detected by blood culture.
Then, mNGS was carried out in peripheral blood. After DNA was extracted from 200 mul of peripheral blood, the DNA library was built and sequenced on Nextseq 550 platform (Illumina, USA). All human host DNA was filtered out, and the valuable reads were aligned to Microbial Genome Databases (ftp://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genomes/) using BWA. Finally, a number of 196123 special reads of L. donovani were detected, and the coverage of the genome and relative abundance of L. donovani was 39.43 and 97.9%, respectively (Figure 1), which was indicative of L. donovani infection. In addition, 1 special read of Klebsiella pneumoniae was detected and defined as a background bacteria. Examination of patients' demographic information revealed the following: ever since birth, he resided in Jiuzhaigou county of Sichuan province, which is known as an endemic leishmaniasis region. Subsequently, microscopy of the bone marrow showed a larger number of Leishmania spp amastigotes, while phagocytic phenomena of histiocytes were found in all smears (Figure 2). All bone marrow smears from confirmed leukemia were reviewed, revealing no Leishmania spp amastigote in microscopy. Furthermore, RK39 antigens were also positive by immunochromatography. Thus, VL was diagnosed, and sodium stibogluconates were used as an anti-leishmanial drug. Nevertheless, after 10 days of anti-leishmanial therapy, 356 special reads of L. donovani were detected in peripheral blood by mNGS (Figure 3), and Leishmania spp amastigotes were also observed in the bone marrow. Subsequently, the anti-leishmanial drug Amphotericin B was used as rescue therapy. After completion of therapy, there was no Leishmania spp amastigote in the bone marrow. Finally, the child was discharged 56 days after admission. He was subsequently referred to the hematological clinic for leukemia and follow-up. On February 2023, he was readmitted to the hospital for chemotherapy, when mNGS test for peripheral blood was performed, and no reads of L. donovani were detected.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-month-old male with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia presented with recurrent fevers for 13 days and coagulopathy during consolidation chemotherapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, previously diagnosed with B-cell ALL and in complete remission following induction therapy, presented during consolidation chemotherapy with a 13-day history of recurrent high fevers (38.4-39.4 °C) and bleeding diathesis. He was treated empirically with intravenous vancomycin, imipenem, and voriconazole along with coagulation support for 7 days without clinical improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) diagnosed at 17 months of age, in complete hematologic remission following CCCG-ALL-2020 protocol induction and first consolidation. Epidemiological history: lifelong resident of Jiuzhaigou County, Sichuan Province, an endemic region for leishmaniasis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports persistent high fevers, tachypnea/anhelation, and bleeding tendencies; denies vomiting or diarrhea.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile infant (temperature 38.4-39.4 °C) with cutaneous ecchymoses and dyspnea/anhelation. Abdominal examination revealed marked hepatomegaly and splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission blood tests: WBC: 2.5 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin: 60 g/L, platelets: 45 x 10^9/L, with immature granulocytes on peripheral blood smear. Recurrent admission labs (day 7 post-antibiotics): CRP: 125.5 mg/L, procalcitonin (PCT): 3.99 mg/L, accompanied by coagulopathy. Blood cultures: negative for bacterial and fungal growth.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal color Doppler ultrasound: marked hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Bone marrow examination: histiocytic phagocytosis and hypocellularity without leukemic relapse.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of peripheral blood identified 196,123 specific reads of Leishmania donovani (39.43% genome coverage, 97.9% relative abundance). Bone marrow aspiration demonstrated numerous intracellular Leishmania spp. amastigotes within histiocytes, and rK39 immunochromatographic dipstick test was positive, establishing visceral leishmaniasis complicating chemotherapy. Bacterial sepsis and leukemic relapse excluded. Management and Outcome: Initial empirical vancomycin, imipenem, voriconazole, and blood products yielded no response. Sodium stibogluconate was initiated; follow-up mNGS at day 10 showed persistent L. donovani reads (356 reads) and persistent bone marrow amastigotes. Therapy was escalated to rescue amphotericin B, achieving complete clearance of bone marrow amastigotes. Discharged after 56 hospital days; repeat blood mNGS 4 months later showed zero L. donovani reads, permitting resumption of leukemia chemotherapy.

raw_case_text:
A 58-year-old Omani man with known hypertension controlled with lisinopril, from Barka, South Batinah governorate, presented to a nearby polyclinic in the early morning of April 24, 2019, with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and severe copious watery, non-bloody diarrhoea that had lasted for 12 hours. The patient was sick-looking and severely dehydrated, with reduced skin turgor and Kussmaul breathing. Oxygen saturation was 85% in room air, and his blood pressure was 85/65 mmHg, with a body temperature of 37 C. The patient was started on intravenous fluid through 2 inserted lines. Laboratory investigations were performed, with the following results: haemoglobin, 20.41 g/dL; white blood cells, 13.81 k/muL; creatinine, 396 mumol/L; urea, 6.3 mmol/L; sodium, 142 mmol/L; potassium, 3.47 mmol/L; and estimated glomerular filtration rate, 14.4 mumol/L. He received a total of 1,500 mL of normal saline before being escorted to the regional secondary hospital for further evaluation and management.
The initial evaluation at the secondary hospital immediately raised a suspicion of cholera based on the severe and persistent gastroenteritis and a more detailed history taken from the patient, revealing that he had arrived from Pakistan in the previous afternoon. An electronic notification of suspected cholera was immediately sent to the appropriate authorities, and the regional public health team became involved in further investigation of the case. The patient was also placed under strict enteric precautions. The stool examination showed a watery-rice consistency, and the rapid diagnostic test (RDT) (Crystal VC, immunochromatographic One Step Rapid Test for Vibrio cholerae; Dipstick, Arkray Health Care Private, Surat, India) was positive. The stool culture result, which was released on April 28, showed growth of V. cholerae O1 E1 Tor, subtype Inaba, which was fully sensitive to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. The patient had already received a dose of doxycycline (300 mg, stat) on April 25, and ultrasonography of the kidney, ureter, and bladder had been performed with normal results.
As the patient's condition worsened, he was moved to the intensive care unit and started on haemodialysis in order to manage his acute kidney injury. Two days after admission, the patient's condition had improved thanks to extensive rehydration therapy and haemodialysis. The vomiting, abdominal pains, and diarrhoea ceased slowly, and his good recovery led him to be discharged on May 6. Follow-up appointments and blood investigations revealed improved renal function.
An investigation team consisting of an epidemiologist, infection control staff, and a health inspector contacted the patient's family and arranged for an urgent home visit on April 26. The family was counselled about the suspicions of cholera in the father and the team obtained further details.
The patient and his wife had been on a 2-week trip to Karachi in Pakistan. Throughout their stay, they had no medical illnesses, and no sick people had stayed at their lodgings or been among their friends and relatives. They had cooked food in their house and had not eaten fast food from street restaurants. They had also bought bottled water for drinking, although they used the local water supply for cooking and showering. They both commented that the local water had not appeared safe to drink, and that it tasted salty. The patient and his wife had arrived in Oman in the afternoon of April 23 in good condition. The patient then started to complain of gastro-intestinal symptoms later that night, about 8 hours after arrival. The patient had multiple episodes of nausea, vomiting, and loose bowel movements, and his wife had to clean up the resulting mess. The patient was then taken to the polyclinic by his daughter and son, who accompanied him at the polyclinic before he was escorted to the secondary hospital. Importantly, the daughter helped with cleaning her father by removing vomitus and secretions directly from his mouth and body. All family contacts (12 members) were thus requested to provide stool samples for screening for cholera by RDT, and 10 samples were received. All contacts were placed under symptom monitoring. Advice was provided to the family, particularly with regard to hand washing, and using disinfectant cleaners to clean the house.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old male presenting with acute severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and copious watery diarrhea for 12 hours.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to a polyclinic in Oman on the morning of April 24, 2019, with sudden-onset severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and copious watery, non-bloody diarrhea lasting 12 hours. Symptoms began approximately 8 hours after returning from a 2-week trip to Karachi, Pakistan. He was severely dehydrated, sick-looking, and in hypovolemic shock with Kussmaul respirations. He received 1,500 mL normal saline and was urgently transferred to a regional secondary hospital under strict enteric precautions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Essential hypertension controlled with lisinopril. Epidemiological history: 2-week trip to Karachi, Pakistan, returning April 23, 2019; cooked food at home, drank bottled water, but utilized local municipal tap water for cooking and showering (noted water tasted salty and appeared unsafe).
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe abdominal cramping pain, nausea, persistent vomiting, voluminous watery diarrhea; denies bloody stools.

objective.physical_examination: Sick-looking, severely dehydrated, markedly reduced skin turgor, Kussmaul breathing. Oxygen saturation 85% on room air, blood pressure 85/65 mmHg, body temperature 37.0 C.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: severe hemoconcentration with hemoglobin 20.41 g/dL, white blood cells 13.81 k/muL. Renal panel and electrolytes: serum creatinine 396 mumol/L, blood urea 6.3 mmol/L, sodium 142 mmol/L, potassium 3.47 mmol/L, estimated glomerular filtration rate 14.4 mumol/L (mL/min). Stool macroscopic examination: watery-rice consistency. Bedside ultrasound of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB): normal findings.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cholera due to Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 biotype El Tor, serotype Inaba: Stool rapid diagnostic test (Crystal VC immunochromatographic dipstick) was positive; stool culture released on April 28 confirmed Vibrio cholerae O1 El Tor, subtype Inaba, fully sensitive to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Antimicrobial therapy: Oral doxycycline 300 mg single stat dose on April 25. Resuscitation and intensive care: 1,500 mL normal saline initially, intensive intravenous fluid rehydration in the intensive care unit, and intermittent hemodialysis for severe acute kidney injury. Diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain resolved, renal function improved, and the patient was successfully discharged on May 6. Public health and infection control teams initiated household contact tracing, quarantine, and screening.

raw_case_text:
The patient is from the municipality of Sao Bernardo do Campo and was admitted to a public hospital of the same city in July 2018, showing clinical symptomatology compatible with an arbovirus: fever, myalgia and headache.
Biochemical, serological and molecular tests were requested to detect arboviruses. Serum RNA was extracted using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), and the RNA was then converted into cDNA using the QuantiNova Reverse Transcription kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) and multiplex qRT-PCR composed of two platforms to determine the virus (platform A: four viral serotypes of dengue, yellow fever, Zika, chikungunya; and platform B: Mayaro, Rocio, St Louis and West Nile) was performed in an ABI 7500 thermal cycler. Primers and probes were designed with the assistance of the IDT First Design program (PrimerQuest program, IDT, Coralville, IA, USA).
Laboratory tests revealed a leukocytosis of 20.9 103 mm-3, an increase in direct bilirubin of 0.9 mg dl-1, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 68 mu l-1, aspartate transaminase (AST) of 60 mu l-1, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) of 301 mu l-1 and C-reactive protein (C-PR) of 240.59 mg dl-1 (Table 1). Haemoculture and urine cultures were both negative. Serology for hepatitis B, C and HIV I and II were all negative, while IgG was positive for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus. Rapid antibody tests for dengue (IgM and IgG) and viral protein NS1 were negative, while the test for YFV IgM was inconclusive. In multiplex qRT-PCR, genetic material from DENV2 and YFV was detected.

subjective.chief_complaint: A patient presenting with fever, myalgia, and headache compatible with an acute arboviral syndrome.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient from São Bernardo do Campo was admitted to a public hospital in July 2018 presenting with fever, myalgia, and headache compatible with an acute arboviral illness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of the municipality of São Bernardo do Campo, São Paulo, Brazil. Prior medical history not documented.

objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests: Leukocytosis 20.9 x 10^3 mm^-3, direct bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL, ALT 68 U/L, AST 60 U/L, GGT 301 U/L, C-reactive protein 240.59 mg/dL. Blood culture and urine culture: Both negative. Viral serologies: Hepatitis B, C, and HIV I/II all negative; IgG positive for toxoplasmosis, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed arboviral co-infection of Dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2) and Yellow Fever virus (YFV) detected via serum RNA extraction, cDNA conversion, and multiplex quantitative RT-PCR on an ABI 7500 thermal cycler. Rapid antibody tests (IgM and IgG) and viral protein NS1 for dengue were negative, while YFV IgM was inconclusive. Bacterial sepsis and viral hepatitides/HIV were ruled out by negative blood/urine cultures and nonreactive serologies.
Plan & Outcome: Hospital admission and supportive clinical management based on laboratory and molecular confirmation of dual flavivirus infection.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a male aged 56 years with comorbidities of diabetes and HIV. This individual was clinically and laboratory-compensated. The patient was using tenofovir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. His TCD4 lymphocyte count was measured at 1,163 cells, with a viral load that remained undetectable for a long period of time. However, hospitalization was required due to the onset of both dyspnea and asthenia. While a laboratory investigation via reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) showed negative results for SARS-CoV-2 infection, a computed tomography (CT) examination of the chest showed a radiological pattern typically reported following the pulmonary involvement of SARS-CoV-2. Based on immunochromatographic analysis, the patient evolved as a reagent for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. The patient was clinically compensated for respiratory infection, initially treated with ceftriaxone and clarithromycin for 3 days, and did not require other therapeutic measures to control the respiratory condition. Two days after hospital discharge (around 20 days after the beginning of respiratory symptoms) the patient developed complete hemiparesis with a predominance in the right arm and conduction aphasia. At that time, the patient scored 11 on the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale. An electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia, while a Doppler echocardiogram showed results within the normal range. Lumbar puncture was performed for cerebrospinal fluid (CS) analysis and was not compatible with a central nervous system infection or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. 
Imaging examinations were also conducted, with CT of the skull showing a loss of differentiation between the white-gray substance, hypoattenuation of deep nuclei, and an extensive area of vascular territory in the left middle cerebral artery (Figure 1). 
A T1-weighted magnetic resonance sequence showed an area of hypointensity, with a high intrinsic cortical signal, and hyperintensity in the T2 sequence (Figure 2). A Doppler velocimetric study of the left carotid artery determined total/critical sub occlusion. These findings corroborated the clinical diagnosis of subacute ischemic stroke, with an estimated duration of 15 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male presenting with acute dyspnea and asthenia, followed 20 days later by right-sided hemiparesis and conduction aphasia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 56-year-old male was initially hospitalized for dyspnea and asthenia in the setting of acute respiratory infection treated with ceftriaxone and clarithromycin for three days. Two days after discharge (approximately 20 days from initial symptom onset), he acutely developed complete right-sided hemiparesis predominant in the right upper extremity and conduction aphasia, prompting emergent re-hospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus; underlying chronic viral infection on long-term combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz); clinically and laboratory-compensated prior to index illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Dyspnea, asthenia, acute right arm and leg weakness, and speech impairment (conduction aphasia); denies fever or seizure.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination: Complete right hemiparesis with predominance in the right arm, conduction aphasia; National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 11. Cardiovascular: Regular rhythm, sinus tachycardia.
objective.routine_investigations: Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia. Doppler echocardiogram: Normal left ventricular function and structure. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis: Unremarkable, ruled out central nervous system infection or acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. Infectious serology: Positive for anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgM and IgG antibodies by immunochromatography; initial nasopharyngeal RT-PCR was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Ground-glass radiological pattern typical of SARS-CoV-2 pulmonary involvement. Cranial non-contrast CT: Loss of gray-white matter differentiation, hypoattenuation of deep nuclei, and an extensive ischemic territorial infarct in the left middle cerebral artery (MCA). Brain MRI: T1-weighted sequence showed hypointensity with high intrinsic cortical signal, and hyperintensity on T2-weighted sequence in the left MCA territory. Carotid Doppler ultrasonography: Critical sub-occlusion / total occlusion of the left internal carotid artery.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Subacute large-vessel ischemic stroke involving the left middle cerebral artery territory secondary to critical sub-occlusion/occlusion of the left internal carotid artery (NIHSS 11), occurring as a post-infectious thrombotic complication of SARS-CoV-2 infection (confirmed by positive IgM and IgG serology), in a patient with diabetes mellitus and well-controlled human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; baseline CD4 count 1,163 cells/microL, undetectable viral load on tenofovir, lamivudine, efavirenz).
Course & Outcome: Respiratory infection stabilized following ceftriaxone and clarithromycin. Neurological deficits were managed supportively for subacute ischemic stroke with an estimated duration of 15 days.

raw_case_text: An 83-year-old male Hispanic patient with a history of controlled diabetes mellitus, hypertension, sleep apnea, and a history of smoking called the outpatient clinic stating that he had a severe headache, sore, dry throat with a burning sensation, a slight cough, and congestion for the last 24 hours. He was on lisinopril for hypertension, using a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) device for sleep apnea, and received three doses of the COVID-19 vaccine 40 days prior to study. On presentation to the clinic, a COVID-19 antigen test was performed, which tested positive. The patient-reported experiencing severe headache, sore throat, dry throat with a burning sensation, coughing, and nasal congestion for the last 24 hours. Additionally, the patient reported malaise, fever, and fatigue. Treatment was started with Vitamin C 1000 mg twice a day, zinc 100 mg once a day, Vitamin D3 5000IU once a day, and ibuprofen or acetaminophen as needed, plus daily follow-up. Treatment with oral CPM spray was started. The patient reported significant improvement in the burning sensation immediately after the spray was applied, and by the end of the first day, he felt somewhat better from hoarseness. On day 2, the doctor added fluticasone nasal spray for treatment, but sore throat, hoarseness, and burning improved by more than 50% as reported by the patient. The fever lasted three days, and the muscle pain for about six days. By day 7, the patient recovered (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: An 83-year-old male presenting with a 24-hour history of severe headache, sore throat with burning sensation, mild cough, and nasal congestion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An 83-year-old male called the outpatient clinic with a 24-hour history of acute severe headache, sore and dry throat with a distinct burning sensation, slight cough, and nasal congestion. He additionally reported systemic malaise, fever, and fatigue. Following clinical presentation and diagnostic testing, he was managed with a topical antiseptic throat spray, fluticasone nasal spray, and supportive oral therapies, experiencing prompt improvement in throat symptoms and complete recovery by day 7.
subjective.past_medical_history: Essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (well-controlled), obstructive sleep apnea on continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy, and remote history of tobacco smoking. Current medications: lisinopril. Vaccinated with three doses of pandemic respiratory vaccine 40 days prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe headache, sore throat, dry throat with burning sensation, hoarseness, cough, nasal congestion, fever, malaise, fatigue, and myalgias.

objective.physical_examination: Outpatient physical examination: Patient in mild discomfort due to pharyngeal irritation, afebrile or low-grade pyrexia, hemodynamically stable without respiratory distress. Oropharynx revealed mucosal erythema.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Mild COVID-19 upper respiratory tract infection (confirmed by positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test on presentation) in an elderly patient with hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and sleep apnea.

Management and outcome: Managed as an outpatient with topical cetylpyridinium chloride (CPM) oral spray, fluticasone nasal spray added on day 2, vitamin C 1,000 mg BID, zinc 100 mg daily, vitamin D3 5,000 IU daily, and as-needed ibuprofen/acetaminophen with daily outpatient follow-up. Burning throat pain resolved immediately after initial spray; hoarseness and sore throat improved by > 50% by day 2. Fever resolved after 3 days, muscle aches lasted 6 days, and complete recovery was achieved by day 7.

raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old uneducated male of low socioeconomic status was scheduled for amputation of toes. To start with, he had complaint of fever associated with chills and rigors for 3 weeks. He consulted a local practitioner who prescribed some tablets about which patient could not give the details. He noticed blackening of toes of both the feet, which was slow and progressive over 1 week. As he was not responding to the treatment, he was rushed to our medical college. There was no history of trauma, significant drug ingestion particularly ergot, alcohol consumption or smoking. On physical examination, he was febrile, dehydrated, and had pallor; there was no icterus, cyanosis, edema, or significant lymphadenopathy. A pulse rate of 120/min, respiratory rate of 24/min, and blood pressure of 90/70 mmHg was recorded. All peripheral pulses were palpable. On systemic examination, mild hepatosplenomegaly was present and rest of the systemic examination was normal. On local examination, there was blackish discoloration of all toes, extending up to malleoli [Figures 1 and 2]. Intavenous line was secured. Ringer lactate was started and investigations were sent for. Reports were as follows [Table 1].
Peripheral blood smear showed ring forms of P. falciparum with occasional gametocytes. Three consecutive blood cultures for bacteria were negative. Color Doppler study of the lower limbs revealed normal flow in both the femorals and the popliteal, with slightly reduced flow in tibial and dorsalis pedis artery with hypoechogenic shadow in its lumen.
The patient was given i.v. quinine, loading dose of 20 mg/kg followed by a maintenance dose of 10 mg/kg thrice a day for 2 days. Then, the patient was shifted to oral quinine (dose 10 mg/kg) thrice a day and oral paracetamol 500 mg thrice a day for 5 days. Two units of packed cell transfusion were also given. Fever subsided within 5 days of treatment. His peripheral smear for malarial parasite became negative after 7 days of quinine course. Line of demarcation did not progress any further. For management of gangrene, amputation was planned. All repeated blood investigations were within normal limits except prothrombin time 16.5 s, fibrinogen level 2.9 g/L (normal value 1.5-4 g/L), and D-dimer 1.7. The surgery was done under total i.v. anesthesia.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presenting with a 3-week history of fever with chills and progressive blackish discoloration of all toes of both feet for 1 week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced fever with chills and rigors for 3 weeks and took unspecified oral tablets from a local practitioner without relief. Over the preceding week, he noticed slow, progressive blackening of all toes on both feet. Upon presentation, he was dehydrated and hypotensive with bilateral symmetrical peripheral digital gangrene.
subjective.past_medical_history: Low socioeconomic background. Denied history of trauma, ingestion of ergot alkaloids or other vasospastic drugs, tobacco smoking, or alcohol consumption.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, and bilateral toe pain and blackish discoloration. Negative for chronic peripheral vascular symptoms or Raynaud's phenomenon. Medications: unspecified tablets from local practitioner. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, dehydrated, marked pallor; no icterus, cyanosis, edema, or significant lymphadenopathy. Pulse rate: 120 beats/min, respiratory rate: 24 breaths/min, blood pressure: 90/70 mmHg. All peripheral pulses were palpable. Abdomen: Mild hepatosplenomegaly. Local examination: Symmetrical blackish discoloration (dry gangrene) of all toes extending up to the malleoli bilaterally.
objective.routine_investigations: Three consecutive bacterial blood cultures: Negative. Repeat laboratory panel post-stabilization: Prothrombin time (PT): 16.5 seconds, serum fibrinogen: 2.9 g/L (reference: 1.5-4 g/L), D-dimer: 1.7.
objective.advanced_workup: Color Doppler ultrasonography of lower limbs: Normal flow in bilateral femoral and popliteal arteries; slightly reduced flow in tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries with hypoechoic luminal thrombus/shadow.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by symmetrical peripheral digital gangrene of bilateral feet and microvascular thrombosis.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum with occasional gametocytes (smear cleared and became negative after 7 days of quinine). Bacterial blood cultures were negative; ergotism, Raynaud's disease, and macrovascular thromboembolism were excluded clinically and by duplex ultrasonography.
Plan & Outcome: Initial hemodynamic resuscitation with intravenous Ringer's lactate and transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells. Treated with intravenous quinine (loading dose of 20 mg/kg followed by maintenance dose of 10 mg/kg three times daily for 2 days), transitioned to oral quinine (10 mg/kg three times daily) with paracetamol (500 mg three times daily) for 5 days. Defervescence occurred within 5 days and parasite clearance at 7 days. Once the gangrenous line of demarcation stabilized, bilateral toe amputations were successfully performed under total intravenous anesthesia.

raw_case_text:
We present a case of a 53-year-old man who came to our department for a large multinodular goiter with multiple suspicious nodules on ultrasound. The diagnosis was made in 1999 during hospitalization for an episode of thyrotoxicosis. The patient was diagnosed as HIV-positive in 1994 and began antiretroviral treatment with AZT (zidovudine) and Ddi (didanosine) with minimal initial benefit; however, subsequent worsening of the immunological condition was noted. Therefore, beginning in June 1997, therapy was switched to d4T (stavudine) plus 3TC (lamivudine) and IDV (indinavir); this achieved excellent viral replication control and improved the immunological condition. In 1999, a change in HIV treatment was necessary due to the presence of an important lipid dysmetabolism with hypertriglyceridemia, modification of the habitus with an important lipohypertrophy of the cervicodorsal region (buffalo hump and taurine neck) and loss of subcutaneous fat of the legs (Fig. 1A-D). Therapy with AZT (zidovudine)+ 3TC (lamivudine) + EFV (efavirenz) enabled control of viral replication and stability of the lipodystrophic picture. The patient had undergone multiple liposuctions, but they were not effective, likely due to the excessive accumulation of adipose tissue. In our opinion, the most relevant clinical aspect to consider was the large buffalo hump and taurine neck due to lipodystrophy. He also presented with negative thyroid autoimmunity, with normal calcitonin and calcemic blood values. The ultrasound exam showed struma with partial retrosternal engagement and multiple thyroid nodules increasing in size relative to a previous check, as well as suspicious features for neoplasia. The patient had undergone several needle aspirations, which failed due to the thickness and abundancy of the adipose tissue.
Patient comorbidities were mainly based on the alteration of glucose metabolism (due to diabetes mellitus), alteration of bone metabolism (due to osteopenia), severe obesity (body mass index, BMI, of 34.6), and hypertension, as well as slight limitation in running, weightlifting and playing intense sports. He also reported that a previous HCV hepatopathy had been treated with Harvoni. The indication to remove the thyroid glands was suggested by the patient's endocrinologist, primarily due to the suspicious nodules. Preoperative anesthesia evaluation predicted an American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) anesthetic risk of 3, requiring complex intubation for the patient's habitus and for the shrinkage of the trachea. Indeed, preoperative chest X-ray showed an ovalization of the tracheal lumen (11 mm) to a plane passing through C7 (Fig. 2).
After careful positioning (Fig. 3A and B), the patient underwent total thyroidectomy by anterior cervicotomy. Total thyroidectomy was performed with technical difficulties: first, intubation of the patient was required for the operation due to the hyperextension of the neck; second, access to the goiter was difficult due to the amount of adipose tissue, as well as the buffalo hump and taurine neck. Thyroid isolation was complicated on the right side of the gland for the increased volume, particularly due to difficulty in recurring laryngeal nerve isolation. No intraoperative complications and no bleeding loss were observed during or after surgery. The drains were removed on the second postoperative day. Despite the patient's HIV infection, no complications were noted after surgery, especially around the wound. Calcium blood values stayed in the normal range after surgery. The patient presented with dysphonia; therefore, direct laryngoscopy was performed, which showed fixation of the right vocal string with good phonatory compensation, as well as consistency of the respiratory space. Therefore, the patient was sent to logopedic rehabilitation after discharge from the hospital.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old male presenting for surgical evaluation and management of a large multinodular goiter with multiple suspicious thyroid nodules and severe cervicodorsal lipodystrophy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 53-year-old male was evaluated for surgical management of a long-standing large multinodular goiter, first diagnosed in 1999 during an admission for thyrotoxicosis. Serial ultrasonography demonstrated enlarging thyroid nodules with suspicious neoplastic features and retrosternal engagement. Multiple prior fine needle aspiration attempts had failed due to excessive cervical adipose tissue. The patient also experienced progressive dysmorphic changes including cervicodorsal lipohypertrophy ('buffalo hump' and 'taurine neck') and peripheral fat loss refractory to multiple liposuctions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral condition managed with long-term antiretroviral therapy (initially zidovudine and didanosine in 1994, switched to stavudine, lamivudine, and indinavir in 1997, and subsequently transitioned in 1999 to zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz due to severe antiretroviral-associated lipodystrophy and hypertriglyceridemia); history of thyrotoxicosis (1999); diabetes mellitus; osteopenia; severe obesity (BMI 34.6 kg/m2); hypertension; chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) hepatopathy successfully treated with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir (Harvoni); multiple prior liposuctions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Dysphonia postoperatively; slight functional limitation in running, weightlifting, and intense sports; denies acute compressive airway obstruction symptoms preoperatively.

objective.physical_examination: Physical habitus: Severe obesity (BMI 34.6 kg/m2); massive cervicodorsal lipohypertrophy ('buffalo hump' and 'taurine neck') with loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue in the lower extremities. Neck: Marked adipose accumulation, large multinodular goiter palpable. Preoperative ASA class 3. Postoperative direct laryngoscopy: Fixation of the right vocal cord with good phonatory compensation and preserved respiratory space.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory studies: Thyroid autoimmunity negative; serum calcitonin and calcium levels within normal limits preoperatively and postoperatively. Preoperative chest X-ray: Tracheal compression with ovalization of tracheal lumen (11 mm) at C7 plane.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck ultrasound: Struma with partial retrosternal extension and multiple thyroid nodules increasing in size with suspicious features for neoplasia. Multiple failed fine-needle aspirations. Direct laryngoscopy: Right vocal cord paresis/fixation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Large multinodular goiter with retrosternal engagement and suspicious features for neoplasia, complicated by severe antiretroviral-induced lipodystrophy syndrome (taurine neck, buffalo hump, peripheral lipoatrophy, hypertriglyceridemia) in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; diagnosed 1994, virologically controlled on zidovudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz), diabetes mellitus, osteopenia, hypertension, and treated hepatitis C.
Surgical Management & Outcome: Patient underwent total thyroidectomy via anterior cervicotomy; procedure was technically challenging due to difficult airway intubation, excessive adipose tissue, and difficult right recurrent laryngeal nerve isolation. Surgical drains were removed on postoperative day 2 without hematoma or wound infection. Postoperative right vocal cord palsy was documented on direct laryngoscopy, managed with logopedic speech rehabilitation following discharge.

raw_case_text:
A 49-year-old female with no known comorbidities presented with history of fever, generalized body weakness and loss of appetite and who had been diagnosed with dengue fever after positive results of NS1 antigen and was under oral Paracetamol 500 mg per oral (as per required) presented to emergency room with retention of urine after 5 days of her initial symptoms. She was discharged with Foley's catheter in situ. Two days following this, she presented to ER again with inability to stand and walk which was associated with weakness and tingling sensation of bilateral lower limbs. She also complained of burning sensation over dorsal aspect of right foot for 3 years but had no history of any known comorbidities like diabetes, hypertension, or thyroid disorders.
Her vitals were stable and central nervous system examination showed intact higher mental functions. There were no signs of meningeal irritation. Muscle power was normal in the upper limb whereas it was decreased bilaterally in the lower limb. Her sensory examination revealed intact fine and crude touch but vibration and joint position sensation were reduced on bilateral lower limbs, abdomen and chest below T2 level. Superficial abdominal reflex was abolished and knee and ankle reflex were absent bilaterally with plantar reflexes bilaterally upgoing. Neurological examination of upper limbs, the cranial nerves and cerebellar examination were normal. Ophthalmological examination were also within normal limits.
Laboratory investigations showed normal complete blood counts and no growth on blood culture. Her HIV serology was nonreactive and blood sugar, electrolytes, kidney function tests, vitamins level were within normal limits. CSF analysis and auto immune panel also did not point us toward any pathological condition. Patient clinical profile did not guide us to perform serological evidence of anti-aquaporin 4 (NMO-IgG) to rule out neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD). As shown in Figure 1, MRI Brain did not reveal any significant finding. However, MRI dorsal spine (Figure 2) showed mild disc bulge at the L4/5 and L5/S1 levels, mild bilateral neural foraminal stenosis without major neural impairment, and lumbar spondylosis-like characteristics.
