Provisional diagnosis of TM was made based on patient's symptoms and correlating with the examination and investigations. MRI report of mild disc bulge at L4/L5 could not explain the examination findings of reduced vibration and joint position sensation in chest, abdomen and bilateral lower limbs below T2 level.
She was admitted and managed with analgesics and IV methylprednisolone 1 g intravenously once a day for 5 days and then changed to oral prednisolone 60 mg per oral once a day. Bladder catheterization was removed after 5 days. Physiotherapy was also started in hospital. Her symptoms of weakness improved dramatically with starting of steroids and she could walk with assistance. She was discharged after 8 days of hospital stay and advised to follow-up in OPD (outpatient department). As per advice, on neurophysician consultation, her steroids were tapered gradually over 30 days but for her burning sensation, she was started and advised to continue capsule gabapentin 100 mg, three times a day. In the follow-up after 2 weeks, the patient had no difficulty walking in level ground and her condition drastically improved. She is under regular follow up in our OPD.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old female presented with acute urinary retention followed by bilateral lower limb weakness, tingling, and inability to walk for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially experienced acute fever, generalized body weakness, and loss of appetite, managed with paracetamol. Five days following symptom onset, she developed acute urinary retention requiring Foley catheterization at an emergency room. Two days later, she returned with acute inability to stand or ambulate, progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness, and numbness/tingling.
subjective.past_medical_history: Three-year history of a burning sensation over the dorsal aspect of the right foot. No prior history of diabetes mellitus, systemic hypertension, or thyroid disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever, anorexia, urinary retention, bilateral lower extremity weakness, numbness, tingling, and chronic right foot burning. Denied upper extremity weakness, visual changes, or bowel incontinence. Home medications included oral paracetamol 500 mg as needed.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were stable. Higher mental functions intact; no signs of meningeal irritation. Cranial nerves, upper limb motor and sensory examination, cerebellar functions, and ophthalmologic exam were normal. Lower extremity motor power was bilaterally decreased. Sensory examination demonstrated intact fine and crude touch, but bilateral loss of vibration and joint position sensation in lower limbs, abdomen, and chest below the T2 level. Superficial abdominal reflexes were abolished; patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes were absent bilaterally; plantar reflexes were bilaterally extensor (upgoing).
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood counts: Normal cell lines.
Biochemistry & renal/metabolic panels: Blood glucose, serum electrolytes, kidney function tests, and vitamin levels were within normal limits.
Microbiology & infectious serologies: Blood cultures showed no growth; HIV serology non-reactive; autoimmune serologic panel unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup:
Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis: Normal opening pressure, cell counts, protein, and glucose; autoimmune CSF panel negative.
MRI Brain: Unremarkable.
MRI Dorsal/Lumbar Spine: Mild disc bulges at L4/L5 and L5/S1 with mild neural foraminal stenosis and lumbar spondylosis, without cord compression explaining the T2 sensory level.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Post-infectious acute transverse myelitis (TM) associated with dengue fever, previously confirmed by a positive dengue NS1 antigen test. Ruled out compressive myelopathy (MRI spine did not account for T2 level), intracranial demyelination (normal brain MRI), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), HIV, and systemic autoimmune disease.
Treatment and outcome: Treated with IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days, followed by oral prednisolone 60 mg daily with a 30-day gradual taper, analgesics, physiotherapy, and capsule gabapentin 100 mg three times daily for neuropathic burning. Foley catheter was removed on hospital day 5. Discharged after 8 days ambulating with assistance; at 2-week follow-up, she was ambulating independently on level ground with resolved weakness.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old male complained of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms in the spring for the previous 10 years, together with pruritus of the roof of the mouth and the ears following the consumption of drupes, nuts, apples, and carrots. Treatment of these symptoms with oral antihistamines, nasal GCs, and antihistamine eye drops was only partially effective. The patient was reportedly sensitized to tree, weed and grass pollen, but had no symptoms during weed and grass pollination season. The patient was HIV-positive and had been refused AIT for many years. When the patient consulted in our institution, he underwent a comprehensive allergologic and immunologic work-up. Total IgE was 375 IU/ml. The Immunocap assay confirmed sensitization to tree 74.9 IU/ml (5 class), weed 18.6 IU/ml (4 class) and grass pollen 14.3 IU/ml (3 class). The patient was diagnosed with severe intermittent allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, he had been receiving active HART for 8 years, and the disease progression had been monitored by an infectious disease specialist.
In view of the incomplete symptom control with pharmacologic therapy and the absence of signs of viral replication or clinically significant changes in lymphocyte subsets (i.e. a CD4+ count within the normal range), we recommended birch pollen sublingual AIT. After the patient had given his written, informed consent, he underwent two courses of pre- and co-seasonal therapy Staloral  Birch from Stallergenes (Antony, France); daily maintenance dose: 300 IR) from December to May. CD4+ cell counts and PCR tests for the HIV load were performed at 3-month intervals during the first year of treatment, and then at 6-month intervals during the second year. As in case #1, no positive PCR results and no negative trends in the CD4+ cell count were observed at any time during treatment and follow-up.
During the treatment period, the patient experienced the local adverse reactions commonly associated with sublingual AIT (pronounced pruritus and moderate edema in the sublingual region starting 1 or 2 minutes after administration and persisting for 25 minutes). However, the symptoms were managed with antihistamines and did not modify require modification of the AIT regimen. No systemic reactions were reported.
Based on the patient diary, an improvement was noted following the first course of pre- and co-seasonal AIT: mild rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms were successfully managed with standard doses of oral antihistamine, and the patient did not require topical GCs or topical antihistamines. Following the second course of AIT, the patient noted a further reduction in the severity and duration of rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms, which were fully controlled with oral antihistamines. The patient was advised to continue AIT, to monitor the viral load and CD4+ cell count, and to keep a diary of symptoms and concomitant medications (Table 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old male presenting with a 10-year history of springtime rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms and oral pruritus upon eating drupes, nuts, apples, and carrots.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 10-year history of recurring springtime rhinoconjunctivitis, along with itching of the palate and ears provoked by the consumption of drupes, nuts, apples, and carrots. Prior pharmacotherapy with oral antihistamines, intranasal glucocorticoids, and antihistamine ophthalmic drops yielded only partial symptom relief. Allergen immunotherapy had previously been withheld for many years. He experienced local adverse reactions to sublingual therapy consisting of pronounced sublingual pruritus and moderate edema onsetting within 1-2 minutes and lasting 25 minutes, which responded to antihistamines without systemic reactions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral infection on active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) for 8 years, monitored regularly by an infectious disease specialist; known sensitization to tree, weed, and grass pollens.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pruritus of the roof of the mouth and ears following ingestion of stone fruits, nuts, apples, and carrots; denies rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms during weed and grass pollination seasons.

objective.physical_examination: Localized examination following sublingual therapy demonstrated pronounced pruritus and moderate edema in the sublingual region lasting 25 minutes; no systemic adverse reactions observed.
objective.routine_investigations: Total IgE: 375 IU/ml. ImmunoCAP specific IgE assay: Sensitization to tree pollen 74.9 IU/ml (class 5), weed pollen 18.6 IU/ml (class 4), and grass pollen 14.3 IU/ml (class 3).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe intermittent allergic rhinoconjunctivitis with pollen-food allergy syndrome in a patient with well-controlled human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection on antiretroviral therapy (HAART). HIV monitoring: CD4+ T-cell count remained within normal range and HIV RNA PCR demonstrated no viral replication or negative CD4+ trends at 3-month intervals during year 1 and 6-month intervals during year 2 of treatment. Plan & Outcome: Initiated on birch pollen sublingual allergen immunotherapy (SLIT; Staloral Birch, daily maintenance dose 300 IR) administered pre- and co-seasonally from December to May across two courses. Local sublingual edema and pruritus were managed with oral antihistamines. Following two courses, rhinoconjunctivitis symptoms markedly decreased and were fully controlled with oral antihistamines alone, eliminating the need for topical corticosteroids or topical antihistamines. Advised to continue SLIT and longitudinal monitoring.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old Thai female with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection who had received TIV for 2012-2013 in August 2013 presented at the Bamrasnaradura Infectious Diseases Institute (BIDI) complaining of 2 days of fever, malaise, headache, cough, and sore throat in April 2014. She had been diagnosed with HIV infection confirmed by machine-based assay (ArchiTECT, Abbott, chemiluminescent test), particle agglutination test (Serodia HIV, Fujirebio), and immunochromatography test (Allere Determine or TriLine) at BIDI. Approximately 13 years prior to presentation, she received zidovudine (AZT) plus didanosine (ddI) from 2001 to 2005; AZT, ddI, and efavirenz (EFV) from 2005 to 2007; and has been receiving EFV plus lopinavir/ritonavir in combination (LPV/r) from 2007 to present. Before TIV was given in 2013, she had a CD4 count of 922 cell/microL (31%), plasma HIV-1 RNA <40 copies/mL by quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), a body weight of 85.7 kg, and a height of 165 cm. She received TIV 2011-2012 on August 1, 2012, and TIV 2012-2013 on August 28, 2013. TIV in 2012-2013 included the A/California/7/2009 (H1N1)-derived strain using NYMC X-179A, the A/Victoria/361/2011 (H3N2)-like strain using IVR-65, and the B/Wisconsin/1/2010-like strain using NYMC BX-39 derived from the B/Hubei-Wujiagang/158/2009 strains. At presentation of influenza-like illness symptoms, the physical examination was unremarkable except for a body temperature 38.5 C and body mass index of 31.48 kg/m2. Because of a positive rapid influenza test (Quidel QuickVue Influenza A+B test), the patient was given oseltamivir for 5 days and the clinical symptoms resolved The positive rapid influenza test result was from the BIDI, Nonthaburi, Thailand, with a confirmatory PCR result from the Siriraj Influenza Cooperative Research Center, Department of Microbiology, Faculty of Medicine, Siriraj Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand. The specimen was identified by the amino acid sequence of full hemagglutinin (HA) gene to evaluate the match between the influenza infection and TIV strains.
To perform nucleotide sequencing, total RNA was extracted using a QIAamp viral RNA mini kit (Qiagen) from direct nasal swab specimens of a vaccinated person who had developed a PCR-confirmed influenza illness from the 2009 pandemic virus. The RNA sample was amplified for the complete influenza HA gene, and the amplified product was subjected to nucleotide sequencing. The sequence was edited, aligned, and translated into an amino acid sequence by BioEdit program (version 7.1.11; available at http://www.mbio.ncsu.edu/bioedit/bioedit.html). The sequence was submitted to the GenBank database with the accession number of KU144591.
Table 1 shows the percentage of identity match of amino acid sequences of the full HA gene. The specimen of the present case matches TIV strains CA 07 vaccine strain, H1N1 A/Nonthaburi/102/2009, and H1N1 A/Thailand/104/2009 by 97%, 98%, and 98%, respectively. The matches of the specimen for H1N1 2014 isolates are 99% to 100%.
To perform phylogenetic analysis, the HA amino acid sequence of virus from the case was analyzed for its correlation with the sequences from A/California/07/2009 (H1N1) vaccine strain, 2 Thai virus isolates obtained from the first epidemic wave (A/Nonthaburi/102/2009 and A/Thailand/104/2009), and 2 more virus isolates from 2014 (A/Thailand/NMA_1/2014 and A/Thailand/BKK_1/2014) See Figure 1. The results demonstrate a closer relationship between the causative virus and the circulating strains rather than the vaccine strain closely related to the Thai viruses from the first epidemic wave.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old female presenting with fever, malaise, headache, cough, and sore throat for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in April 2014 with an acute 2-day history of influenza-like illness comprising fever, general malaise, headache, cough, and sore throat, occurring approximately eight months following seasonal trivalent influenza immunization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Perinatally acquired human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection diagnosed in early childhood, on continuous combination antiretroviral therapy for 13 years: zidovudine (AZT) plus didanosine (ddI) from 2001 to 2005; AZT, ddI, and efavirenz (EFV) from 2005 to 2007; and efavirenz plus lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) from 2007 to present. Documented CD4 count of 922 cells/microL (31%) and undetectable plasma HIV-1 RNA (< 40 copies/mL) prior to recent immunization. Vaccination history: Trivalent influenza vaccine (TIV 2011-2012) on August 1, 2012, and TIV 2012-2013 on August 28, 2013.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache, sore throat, cough, malaise, fever; denies dyspnea, chest pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Home medications: Efavirenz and lopinavir/ritonavir. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature 38.5 °C; weight 85.7 kg, height 165 cm, body mass index 31.48 kg/m2 (obesity); general physical and cardiopulmonary examinations were unremarkable.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Influenza A vaccine breakthrough infection (pandemic influenza A [H1N1]pdm09) in a virologically suppressed HIV-1 infected adolescent with robust CD4 counts (922 cells/microL, HIV-1 RNA < 40 copies/mL) following vaccination with 2012-2013 trivalent influenza vaccine.
Confirmatory Virological Testing: Initial positive rapid influenza test (Quidel QuickVue Influenza A+B test) confirmed by RT-PCR for influenza A at a national reference center. Complete hemagglutinin (HA) gene sequencing (GenBank KU144591) revealed 97% amino acid identity to the A/California/07/2009 vaccine strain and 99-100% homology to circulating 2014 Thai epidemic strains (A/Thailand/NMA_1/2014 and A/Thailand/BKK_1/2014), confirming vaccine mismatch/antigenic drift.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on oral oseltamivir for 5 days alongside continuation of baseline antiretroviral therapy (efavirenz and lopinavir/ritonavir). Complete resolution of clinical symptoms was achieved.

raw_case_text: The patient, a 38-year-old woman, presented with acute onset bilaterally symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of both large and small joints over a period of 20 days. She had no previous comorbidities. In addition, she had no history of antecedent events or substance abuse. Clinical examination revealed multiple tender joints with bilateral ankle tenosynovitis. Notably, she exhibited hyperpigmented, nonpruritic skin lesions over the tip of the nose with cutaneous thickening (A). Additional areas of hyperpigmentation were observed over the palms (B), knuckles, beneath the ear lobes, and on the pinnae. Further evaluation revealed high markers of inflammation (erythrocyte sedimentation rate 68 mm/1st hour, C-reactive protein 40 mg/L) with positive chikungunya serology (anti-chikungunya IgM). Her hormonal profile and autoimmune panel were normal. She was diagnosed with post chikungunya arthritis with classical CHIK sign (A and B). The patient was initiated on nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and low-dose glucocorticoids, leading to symptomatic improvement. Post chikungunya arthritis is a common clinical scenario in tropical countries. Nasal hyperpigmentation, initially thought to be a unique manifestation of chikungunya infection, has also been rarely observed in dengue. Increased intraepidermal melanin dispersion or retention triggered by virus is likely the cause of hyperpigmentation. A recent case series of six patients from India had described a phenotype named "COVID-19 nose" resembling "chik sign." Although both viral diseases are associated with brownish black nasal hyperpigmentation with post-infective arthritis, there was a significant delay in the presentation in COVID-19 than chikungunya, which appears one to three weeks after fever defervescence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old woman presented with acute-onset bilaterally symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of large and small joints for 20 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute-onset bilaterally symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis involving both large and small joints over a period of 20 days prior to presentation. She had no history of antecedent events.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous comorbidities; no history of substance abuse.

objective.physical_examination: Multiple tender joints with bilateral ankle tenosynovitis. Hyperpigmented, nonpruritic skin lesions over the tip of the nose with cutaneous thickening. Additional areas of hyperpigmentation were observed over the palms, knuckles, beneath the ear lobes, and on the pinnae.
objective.routine_investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 68 mm/1st hour; C-reactive protein: 40 mg/L. Hormonal profile and autoimmune panel were normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Positive serology for anti-chikungunya IgM, confirming post-chikungunya arthritis with classical 'chik sign' (nasal and acral hyperpigmentation). Treatment and course: Initiated on nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and low-dose glucocorticoids, leading to symptomatic improvement.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 10-month-old girl was admitted to our emergency department for abdominal pain, accompanied by irritability, decreased oral intake, intermittent crying and two episodes of non-biliary vomiting during the previous 24 h. No fever or presence of bloody stools were referred in previous days.
On physical examination, she presented apyretic with good general conditions and normal vital signs. An abdominal distension was clearly observable, with crying and pain evoked by the palpation of the left lower quadrant. No signs of dehydration or respiratory distress were noted. A rectal probe was applied, which showed the presence of blood traces. Laboratory tests performed on admission showed a normal white blood cell count and a mild increase of C-reactive protein of 10.2 mg/L (normal value <5 mg/L). Renal, liver function tests and electrolytes resulted normal as well. Blood gas analysis was normal. A coproculture and research for adenovirus and rotavirus on stool sample were performed and subsequently resulted negative. Urine analysis did not show signs of urinary tract infection.
Due to patient's age and clinical presentation, an abdominal ultrasound was performed, showing the presence of a massive ileocolic intussusception, with increased thickness of the intestinal wall and accompanying mesentery, and enlarged lymph nodes (Figure 1A). A subsequent contrast enema, using Gastrografin  (diatrizoate meglumine and diatrizoate sodium solution) diluted with saline, was successfully performed reducing the invagination (Figure 1B). No complications occurred during the procedure.
No history or signs of SARS-CoV-2 infection was documented in the patient and in close relatives, but, due to the pandemic period, the patient and her mother were tested for SARS-CoV-2 with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) molecular testing on nasopharyngeal aspirate and swab, respectively. The mother resulted positive for SARS-CoV-2, while the patient resulted negative. A subsequent nasopharyngeal aspirate performed 24 h after the first test was performed and it confirmed the negativity for SARS-CoV-2. The patient, admitted to the ward, underwent intravenous antibiotic treatment with ceftriaxone (100 mg/kg/day) and metronidazole (20 mg/kg/day in 3 doses) until discharge.
An intravenous fluid replacement was administered for 2 days and then progressively reduced and interrupted on day 4 following adequate oral intake and tolerance. During the first 4 days of hospitalization, the patient experienced recurrent episodes of spiking colicky pain with spontaneous resolution in few minutes, and on day 5 an abdominal ultrasound evidenced a recurrence of the ileocolic intussusception at the level of the splenic flexure. A new non-surgical hydrostatic reduction procedure was attempted but several relapses occurred during this procedure (Figure 2). A surgical reduction was therefore indicated. Before performing the procedure, a further SARS-CoV-2 PCR molecular testing on nasopharyngeal aspirate was then obtained, with negative result. Laparotomy with manual reduction of the ileocolic invagination and ileocecopexy was subsequently performed. Macroscopically, numerous enlarged abdominal lymph nodes, especially among celiac and mesenteric ones, near the ileocecal junction, were found. Due to the COVID-19 exposure, and the persistent negativity of SARS-CoV-2 PCR molecular testing on nasopharyngeal aspirate, a molecular test was performed on a bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) sample, a parietal peritoneum biopsy and a stool sample obtained during surgery, respectively. Positivity for SARS-CoV-2 was detected on BAL and biopsy, while stools were negative. The postoperative course was uneventful and the patient was discharged after a total of 11 days of hospitalization. A timeline of clinical course, laboratory test for SARS-CoV-2, radiological investigations and treatment of intussusception is summarized in Figure 3. During the hospital course, the patient did not develop any respiratory symptoms or signs of SARS-CoV-2 infection other than the intussusception. No further nasopharyngeal aspirate was performed for SARS-CoV-2 as the patient was completely asymptomatic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-month-old female presenting with abdominal pain, irritability, poor feeding, and vomiting for 24 hours.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 24-hour history of colicky abdominal pain, irritability, intermittent crying, decreased oral intake, and two episodes of non-biliary vomiting, without antecedent fever or diarrhea. Non-surgical reduction via Gastrografin enema was initially successful, but colicky abdominal pain recurred on hospital day 5 with ultrasound-confirmed recurrent ileocolic intussusception that failed repeat hydrostatic reduction, necessitating exploratory laparotomy with manual reduction and ileocecopexy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no chronic illnesses. Epidemiological exposure: Mother tested positive on admission screening for viral respiratory infection.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Apyretic, good general condition, normal vital signs, no signs of dehydration or respiratory distress; abdominal examination revealed abdominal distension with localized tenderness and crying elicited by palpation of the left lower quadrant; rectal exam showed traces of blood.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Normal white blood cell count; C-reactive protein mildly elevated at 10.2 mg/L (normal < 5 mg/L); renal function tests, liver function tests, electrolytes, and venous blood gas were normal; urinalysis showed no infection; coproculture and stool rapid antigen tests for rotavirus and adenovirus were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal ultrasound: Initial scan showed massive ileocolic intussusception with intestinal wall and mesenteric thickening and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes; day 5 ultrasound demonstrated recurrent ileocolic intussusception at the splenic flexure. Diagnostic and therapeutic contrast enema (Gastrografin): Initial successful non-surgical reduction; repeat attempt on recurrence was unsuccessful. Surgical findings: Laparotomy demonstrated ileocolic invagination and prominent celiac and mesenteric lymphadenopathy near the ileocecal junction.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection manifested as recurrent ileocolic intussusception and mesenteric lymphadenitis without respiratory symptoms. Nasopharyngeal aspirate RT-PCR was negative on three separate occasions (admission, 24 hours, and preoperative), but SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by positive RT-PCR on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid and parietal peritoneum biopsy obtained intraoperatively (stool RT-PCR negative). Rotavirus and adenovirus were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous hydration, IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day and metronidazole 20 mg/kg/day), initial contrast enema reduction, and subsequent open laparotomy with manual reduction and ileocecopexy upon recurrence. The postoperative course was uneventful without respiratory symptoms, and the patient was discharged in good health on hospital day 11.

raw_case_text:
A 12-year-old boy presented with 5 days continuous high-grade fever with chills and rigor, severe headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting for 3 days, neck stiffness for 2 days, and drowsiness for 1-day. However, there was no history of loss of consciousness and convulsion.
His GCS was E4M6V5 on admission. On neurological examination, he had only neck rigidity with positive Kernig sign. Rest of the CNS examination was within normal limit. Other systems were also within normal limit.
MRI of the brain done on the 6th day of fever showed no detectable abnormality. A diagnosis of dengue meningitis was made based on the clinical presentation that is, fever and neck rigidity, MAC ELISA positivity for dengue, and the suggestive CSF profile.
His clinical condition improved gradually on conservative management with IV fluids and paracetamol. Neck rigidity disappeared after 10 days. He was discharged from the hospital after 2 weeks of hospital stay in a stable condition.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old boy presenting with a 5-day history of high-grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, severe headache, anorexia, vomiting, neck stiffness, and drowsiness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Continuous high-grade fever with chills and rigors began 5 days prior to admission. Anorexia, nausea, and vomiting developed 3 days prior, followed by neck stiffness for 2 days and progressive drowsiness for 1 day. He had no history of convulsions or loss of consciousness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, neck stiffness, and drowsiness. Negative for convulsions or loss of consciousness. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Drowsy, GCS score E4M6V5 (15/15). Nuchal rigidity present with positive Kernig's sign. Remainder of central nervous system and other systemic examinations within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture / CSF profile: Cytochemical profile suggestive of viral/aseptic meningitis. Brain MRI on day 6 of fever: Normal; no detectable brain parenchymal abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue viral meningitis. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue IgM by MAC-ELISA, supportive CSF cytochemical profile, and normal brain MRI ruling out parenchymal encephalitis.
Plan & Outcome: Managed conservatively with intravenous fluids and paracetamol for fever and symptom relief. Nuchal rigidity resolved completely after 10 days, clinical recovery was uneventful, and the patient was discharged in stable condition after a 2-week hospital stay.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old boy, medically free, with history of unpasteurized milk ingestion, living in Shaqra (a village 200 km far from Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia), presented to our emergency department with fever, vomiting, and malaise for 2 weeks followed by 5-day history of left hypochondrial pain. He lost 9 kgs in the preceding two months. He had no history of trauma or surgery. He was admitted to a peripheral hospital where he received a course of antibiotics with no improvement. On clinical examination, he looked ill, in pain with a temperature of 38.4 degree Celsius; pulse rate of 116 beats per minutes; blood pressure 111/68 mmHg; and respiratory rate of 21 breaths per minute. Abdominal examination revealed moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium, no organomegaly on palpation and normal bowel sounds.
 Laboratory investigation showed white blood cell count 4.12 x 109/L; hemoglobin 11.80 g/dL; platelet count 364 x 109/L; ESR 61 mm/H; CRP 66.5 mg/L; amylase 509 U/L; lipase 471 U/L; alanine transaminase 45 U/I; aspartate transaminase 32 U/I; alkaline phosphatase 162 U/I; gamma GT 86 U/I; total bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL; albumin 39 g/L; creatinine 0.5 mg/dL; urea 3.2 mmol/L; and lactate dehydrogenase, 303 U/I. Chest X-ray was normal. Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia. Abdominal X-ray showed no evidence of intestinal obstruction. Computed tomography of abdomen showed multiple irregular peripheral hypodense splenic lesions suggestive of splenic infarcts and borderline splenomegaly, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis and patent splenic veins with no thrombosis (Figure 1). Blood culture grew Brucella species after 88 hours of incubation. Brucella serology using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay was positive for IgM. Transesophageal echocardiography was negative. Lupus anticoagulant and anti-cardiolipin antibodies were negative. Proteins C and S were negative. JAK2 mutation was negative.
 Treatment of brucellosis with rifampicin 600 mg daily (for 6 weeks), doxycycline 100 mg twice daily (for 6 weeks), and gentamycin 300 mg daily (for 7 days) was given to him.
On the 8th day of admission, fever and abdominal pain resolved. High amylase and lipase were normalized and the patient was discharged home in good condition. After 3-month follow-up in outpatient clinic, the patient remained well with significant improvement of splenic infarcts on computed tomography (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of fever, vomiting, and malaise, followed by a 5-day history of left hypochondrial pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed fever, vomiting, and malaise 2 weeks prior to presentation, followed by the onset of left hypochondrial pain 5 days prior. He had lost 9 kg over the preceding 2 months. He was initially admitted to a peripheral hospital and given a course of antibiotics without improvement before presenting to the emergency department.
subjective.past_medical_history: Medically free with no history of trauma or surgery. Residence: Shaqra village (200 km from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia). Epidemiological exposure: history of unpasteurized milk ingestion. Prior course of ineffective antibiotics at peripheral hospital.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, vomiting, malaise, left hypochondrial pain, 9 kg weight loss over 2 months. Home medications: prior ineffective antibiotic course (specific agents not documented). Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Appeared ill and in pain. Temperature: 38.4 °C; pulse rate: 116 beats/min; blood pressure: 111/68 mmHg; respiratory rate: 21 breaths/min. Abdomen: moderate tenderness in the left hypochondrium; no organomegaly palpated; normal bowel sounds.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 4.12 x 10^9/L; Hemoglobin: 11.80 g/dL; Platelets: 364 x 10^9/L; ESR: 61 mm/h; CRP: 66.5 mg/L; Amylase: 509 U/L; Lipase: 471 U/L; ALT: 45 U/L; AST: 32 U/L; ALP: 162 U/L; GGT: 86 U/L; Total bilirubin: 0.2 mg/dL; Albumin: 39 g/L; Creatinine: 0.5 mg/dL; Urea: 3.2 mmol/L; LDH: 303 U/L. ECG: sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray: normal. Abdominal X-ray: no evidence of intestinal obstruction.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) of abdomen: multiple irregular peripheral hypodense splenic lesions suggestive of splenic infarcts and borderline splenomegaly, with no evidence of acute pancreatitis and patent splenic veins without thrombosis. Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE): negative for vegetations. Thrombophilia panel: Lupus anticoagulant, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, protein C, protein S, and JAK2 mutation were all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Systemic brucellosis complicated by multiple peripheral splenic infarcts, borderline splenomegaly, and secondary pancreatic enzyme elevation.
Confirmation: Blood culture grew Brucella species after 88 hours of incubation; Brucella serology by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was positive for IgM.
Differentials ruled out: Infective endocarditis (negative TEE); acute pancreatitis (normal pancreatic parenchyma on CT); hereditary or acquired thrombophilia/hypercoagulable state (negative antiphospholipid antibodies, protein C, protein S, and JAK2 mutation).
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with oral rifampicin (600 mg daily for 6 weeks), oral doxycycline (100 mg BID for 6 weeks), and parenteral gentamicin (300 mg daily for 7 days). On day 8 of admission, fever and abdominal pain resolved, elevated amylase and lipase normalized, and he was discharged home; at 3-month follow-up, he remained asymptomatic with significant CT improvement of splenic infarcts.

raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old Chinese male presented to a local hospital with right ankle pain and limited mobility 23 months ago and underwent a synovectomy of the ankle. Specimen culture revealed brucellosis infection in sheep. The patient came to the department of Orthopaedics of our hospital 18 months ago because his symptoms did not improve. His case history indicated that he had worked in a Sheep farm for 9 months. We, therefore, suspected that he might have acquired Brucella infection through ingestion or contact with injured skin. A 37 C temperature, no sweating, weight loss, and no personal or family history of tuberculosis were all present on admission. Physical examination showed significant tenderness on the lateral side of the right ankle without fever. Blood flow to right toe is good, right ankle varus pressure test is positive. Laboratory tests were as follows: Hemoglobin (Hb) 136 g/L, Red blood cell count (RBC) 4.25x1012/L, White blood cell (WBC) 10.09x109/L accompanied by neutrophil elevation, Platelet 363x109/ L, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 31 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) 32 mg/L. Rose-Bengal Plate Agglutination Test (RBPT) was positive.
Anteroposterior and lateral X-ray of the right ankle showed arrowed joint spaces (Figure 1A and B). CT showed multiple cysts were noted below the articular surface of the right ankle, and the articular surface of the talus collapsed (Figure 2A-D). MRI showed the right ankle joint space was significantly narrowed, the articular surface was coarse, the articular cartilage was thinned, the talus articular surface collapsed, and multiple cysts were found in the subchondral bone (Figure 3A-D). Joint synovial fluid of right ankle was extracted by joint aspiration and sent to the laboratory for Real-time PCR examination, and the results showed that there was B. melitensis in the synovial fluid (Figure 4). The HE staining of ankle fluid revealed inflammatory cell infiltration, while acid-fast staining was negative (Figure 5A and B). We concluded that the patient had recurrent Brucella ankle arthritis and was treated with doxycycline (0.1 g po bid), rifampicin (0.6 g po qd) and cefotaxime-sulbactam (2.25 g ivgtt q8h) for six weeks during hospitalization. ESR and CRP levels declined significantly after drug treatment, returning to normal levels of 17.00 mm/h and 7.88 mg/L, respectively.     
The right ankle movement of the patient was basically normal at discharge, and the pain was significantly reduced. Laboratory tests after drug treatment showed erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels of 17.00 mm/h and 7.88 mg/L, respectively, significantly decreased and returned to normal. At following-up 18 months later, the patient had no discomfort in the right ankle and all inflammatory markers were normal. RBPT was negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male presented with persistent right ankle pain and restricted mobility for eighteen months following prior ankle surgery.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially developed right ankle pain and stiffness 23 months prior and underwent an ankle synovectomy at an outside hospital. Due to lack of clinical improvement over the subsequent 18 months, he was referred for orthopedic evaluation of persistent pain and joint dysfunction, without constitutional fevers or night sweats.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of right ankle synovectomy 23 months prior for septic arthritis. Denied personal or family history of tuberculosis. Epidemiological exposure/Occupation: Worked on a sheep farm for 9 months with potential percutaneous or mucosal exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies fever, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. Home medications: None documented. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right ankle: Significant localized tenderness over the lateral aspect of the right ankle, restricted range of motion, and positive ankle varus stress test. Peripheral perfusion: Intact distal pulses and capillary refill in the right toes. Afebrile (temperature 37.0 °C).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Hemoglobin 136 g/L, RBC 4.25 x 10^12/L, WBC 10.09 x 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, platelets 363 x 10^9/L, ESR 31 mm/h, CRP 32 mg/L. Post-treatment labs (6 weeks): ESR normalized to 17.00 mm/h and CRP normalized to 7.88 mg/L. Follow-up labs (18 months): Normal inflammatory markers.
objective.advanced_workup: Right ankle X-ray: Marked narrowing of the tibiotalar joint space. Right ankle CT: Multiple subchondral cyst formations below the articular surface with collapse of the talar dome. Right ankle MRI: Severe joint space narrowing, irregular and eroded articular surfaces, severe cartilage thinning, subchondral cysts, and talar collapse. Synovial fluid analysis: H&E staining demonstrated acute-on-chronic inflammatory cell infiltration; acid-fast bacilli staining was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Recurrent chronic brucellar septic arthritis of the right ankle with secondary talar osteonecrosis and subchondral collapse, confirmed by real-time PCR detection of Brucella melitensis in right ankle synovial aspirate, positive Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT), and prior synovial culture from first surgery growing Brucella from sheep contact. Tuberculosis excluded by negative acid-fast stain.
Plan & Clinical Course: Received 6 weeks of inpatient combination antimicrobial therapy comprising oral doxycycline 0.1 g twice daily, oral rifampicin 0.6 g once daily, and IV cefotaxime-sulbactam 2.25 g every 8 hours. The patient experienced marked pain relief, restoration of normal ankle motion, normalization of ESR and CRP, and at 18-month follow-up remained completely asymptomatic with negative RBPT serology.

raw_case_text:
Patient is a 26-year-old female with a past medical history of HIV. She was infected at age 15 and showed poor adherence to antiretroviral medication. She reported the combined use of Tenofovir, Emtricitabine, and Efavirenz intermittently, mostly because she did not seek adequate healthcare due to feelings of shame about being associated with the disease. She also missed most of her follow-ups in the last year, and had no CD4 counts or viral load tests performed in over 6 months. She also suffered from intermittent episodes of coughing, bloody stools, and weight loss during this time; however, she didn't seek any medical attention.
She presented to our emergency room with a 10-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, biliary vomits and asthenia. Approximately 24 h prior to admittance, the pain became worse. On clinical examination, a dehydrated, hypotensive and tachycardic patient was encountered. Her abdomen was diffusely tender, and the pain became more intense on touch. Laboratory exams revealed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. An arterial gasometry revealed metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia.
In view of these findings, surgical consultation was requested and a diagnosis of diffuse peritonitis was reached. Aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids was started and an emergency laparotomy was decided. At surgery, the peritoneal cavity was filled with 500 ml of pus and 2 bowel perforations were identified: a 1 x 1 cm perforation in the terminal ileum, 50 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, and a 3 x 2 cm perforation in the cecum (Fig. 1A-C).
A right colectomy was decided, however, the surgical team had doubts about restoring bowel continuity. Nonetheless, since the patient became stable after reanimation and surgery, restoration was considered feasible. Given the context of an HIV patient with poor controls who would be unlikely able to handle an ileostomy, a primary anastomosis with close surveillance was decided. Resection began 10 cm proximal to the ileal perforation and ended near the hepatic flexure of the colon. Then, a side-to-side ileotransverse anastomosis was performed with 75 mm staples (ETHICON Linear Cutter NTLC75, Johnson & Johnson). Extensive washing of the peritoneal cavity was completed and the remainder of the procedure was performed without complications. Based on the historical, clinical, and laboratory data obtained, we initially considered intestinal perforation due to cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection as the probable etiology of peritonitis, and the differentials included, mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma. However, definitive pathology tests for the cause of the perforation were delayed due to the unavailability of an in-house pathologist. Furthermore, other essential tests including CD4 counts and HIV viral loads and antibodies (both IgM and IgG) were not available at our institution.
This situation was further complicated by the lack of resources from the patient and our hospital; nonetheless, we managed to send a blood sample to a nearby hospital for testing. Even under these harsh conditions, the patient had a good recovery. She was placed under broad-spectrum antibiotics (Piperacillin/Tazobactam) and was given a 3-day cycle of Ganciclovir. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) was initiated as well. Meanwhile, sips of liquids were initiated on the second postoperative day without complications. She didn't have any episodes of fever, nausea, vomiting or signs of anastomosis leak.
At the 7th postoperative day, the patient requested to leave against medical advice (AMA), she signed the hospital consents and left our facility.
Two days after the patient went AMA, CD4 and HIV viral load results arrived along with the pathology report, revealing chronic inflammation of the resected bowel, and multiple ulcers affecting the mucosa of the ileum and the cecum. Also, multiple granulomas surrounded by inflammatory tissue were recognized, as well as some granulomas within the lymph nodes. Bowel perforation due to tuberculosis was confirmed as the final diagnosis, CD4 cell counts were estimated at 94 cells/mm3, and the viral load was estimated at over 106 genome copies (Fig. 2A-C).
Since tuberculosis in Ecuador is a mandatory declaration disease, we searched for the patient and found her in the coastal region of the country. Fortunately, she was stable and without complications. She was taken by the national healthcare system and admitted to a tertiary hospital for HIV and tuberculosis treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old female presenting with worsening lower abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, nausea, and asthenia for ten days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 26-year-old female presented with a 10-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, and severe asthenia. Over the preceding months, she had experienced intermittent cough, hematochezia, and weight loss without seeking medical care. Approximately 24 hours prior to admission, her abdominal pain acutely intensified and generalized, prompting emergency department presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic immunosuppression diagnosed at age 15 with poor medication adherence and intermittent use of tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz; missed clinical follow-up for over one year.
subjective.review_of_systems: Intermittent cough, hematochezia, unintentional weight loss, nausea, bilious vomiting, asthenia, generalized severe abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Dehydrated, hypotensive, and tachycardic. Abdomen: Diffusely tender with marked guarding and peritoneal signs accentuated by superficial palpation.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia. Arterial blood gas: Metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency exploratory laparotomy: Purulent peritonitis with 500 mL of peritoneal pus, identifying two intestinal perforations: a 1 x 1 cm perforation in the terminal ileum (50 cm proximal to ileocecal valve) and a 3 x 2 cm perforation in the cecum. Resected right hemicolectomy specimen: Multiple mucosal ulcers in the terminal ileum and cecum with chronic inflammation and extensive necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with granulomas in mesenteric lymph nodes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Gastrointestinal tuberculosis (TB) causing terminal ileal and cecal perforations with secondary purulent peritonitis and septic shock in a patient with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; CD4 cell count 94 cells/mm3, HIV viral load > 10^6 copies/mL) and severe medication non-adherence.
Surgical and Medical Plan: Emergency right hemicolectomy with primary stapled side-to-side ileotransverse anastomosis and peritoneal lavage. Postoperative management included crystalloid resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam), a 3-day course of ganciclovir, and resumption of ART (tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz). The patient left against medical advice on postoperative day 7 prior to pathology and immunology results. She was subsequently traced via the national tuberculosis surveillance registry in coastal Ecuador and admitted to a tertiary care center for integrated anti-tuberculosis therapy and antiretroviral management.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old Taiwanese female contracted DENV-1 infection during the 2023 endemic in Taiwan and was confirmed by positive results of dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen assay and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) examination. The platelet count reached the nadir at 102,000 cells/L on day 7 after the onset of DF (Post Symptom Onset Day 7, PSO 7). She had a history of optic neuritis (ON) in the left eye (oculus sinister, OS) more than 10 years ago. This time, she suffered from sudden onset blurred vision OS on PSO 10 with a white blood cell count of 7,600/mul and a platelet count of 272,000 cells/L. There were no pain or limitations in the eye movement.
The ophthalmic examination on PSO 11 revealed her best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) being 1.0 per glass (PG) right eye (oculus dexter, OD) and 0.05 PG OS. There was minimal relative afferent pupillary defect OS. The color plate test was 11/15 OD and 5/15 OS. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 8.8 millimeters of mercury (mmHg) OD and 9.5 mmHg OS. The slit lamp showed no remarkable findings. Fundus examination (Figures 1A, B) and optical coherence tomography (OCT, Figures 2A, B, 3) showed macular edema, disc hyperemia on both eyes (Oculus Uterque, OU) with ellipsoid zone (EZ) infiltration, and probably involving the choriocapillaris OS. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head was also performed, but no evidence of active ON is present (Supplementary Figure 1). She was then diagnosed with dengue maculopathy OU, with OS more severe than OD.
Systemic survey accidentally found type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and hypertriglyceridemia, while excluding human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and syphilis, and yielded a negative result in antinuclear antibodies, anti-phospholipid autoantibodies, and the connective tissue disease screening panel (Anti-CTD screen).
She received pulse therapy with intravenous 250 mg of methylprednisolone four times daily for 1 day, followed by intravenous dexamethasone 5 mg once, along with oral aspirin 100 mg daily, and topical prednisolone.
However, blurred vision persisted, and a new central scotoma OS was noted on PSO 15. A follow-up examination found worse BCVA (0.6 OD and 0.0125 OS) and new mild vitreous haze (2+) OS. Therefore, oral prednisolone 40 mg daily was given for 1 week and was tapered down gradually over 2 months. Color fundus (Figures 1C, D) on PSO 16 found macular and perimacular edema. Fluorescent angiography (Figures 1E-H) and OCT (Figures 2C, D) on PSO 16 showed capillary leakage, vitreous opacity OS, and late staining at disc OU. Visual field examination (Figures 1I, J) on PSO 17 showed an enlarged blind spot OS with a mean deviation (MD) of -4.86 decibels (dB). All evidence, including vitritis, small vessel vasculitis-related maculopathy, and optic disc inflammation, are consistent with the diagnosis of AMN.
With treatment, the color plate test soon normalized, no more vitreous cell was found, and BCVA gradually improved within a week. Follow-up BCVA was 0.7 OD and 0.05 OS on PSO 29 and 1.0 OD and 0.1 OS on PSO 38. During her latest follow-up, color fundus and OCT showed less hyper-reflective material with residual EZ disruption and the BCVA improved to 0.16 OS. The patient is currently on low-dose oral corticosteroids with a maintenance dosage of 5 mg on PSO 59 (Figure 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old female presented with sudden-onset painless blurred vision in the left eye 10 days after the onset of an acute febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed an acute febrile illness during an endemic viral outbreak. On post-symptom onset day (PSO) 7, her platelet count reached a nadir of 102,000 cells/muL. On PSO 10, she developed sudden-onset painless blurred vision in the left eye without ocular pain or restricted motility. On PSO 15, she developed a new central scotoma in the left eye with worsening visual acuity.
subjective.past_medical_history: Optic neuritis of the left eye diagnosed over 10 years prior. Newly identified type 2 diabetes mellitus, systemic hypertension, and hypertriglyceridemia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported acute painless vision loss and central scotoma in the left eye. Denied eye pain, headache, diplopia, fever at ophthalmic presentation, rash, or joint pain.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic examination (PSO 11): Best-corrected visual acuity was 1.0 in the right eye and 0.05 in the left eye. Minimal relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye. Ishihara color plate test: 11/15 right eye, 5/15 left eye. Intraocular pressures were 8.8 mmHg OD and 9.5 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy was unremarkable. Funduscopy showed bilateral macular edema and optic disc hyperemia, more prominent in the left eye. On PSO 15, left eye visual acuity dropped to 0.0125 with 2+ vitreous haze.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood counts: On PSO 7, platelet count nadir was 102,000 cells/muL; on PSO 10, white blood cell count was 7,600/muL and platelet count was 272,000 cells/muL.
Systemic serologies & screens: Non-reactive for HIV and syphilis; antinuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, and connective tissue disease screening panel were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup:
Brain MRI: No evidence of active optic neuritis or intracranial demyelination.
Optical coherence tomography (OCT): Bilateral macular edema and optic disc hyperemia with disruption and infiltration of the ellipsoid zone and choriocapillaris in the left eye.
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FA): Retinal capillary leakage, vitreous opacity in the left eye, and late hyperfluorescent staining of the bilateral optic discs.
Humphrey visual field perimetry: Enlarged blind spot in the left eye with a mean deviation of -4.86 dB.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue maculopathy and acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN) OU (OS > OD), secondary to Dengue virus serotype 1 (DENV-1) infection confirmed by positive NS1 antigen assay and RT-PCR. Syphilis, HIV, and autoimmune retinopathies were excluded.
Treatment and outcome: Treated initially with pulse IV methylprednisolone (250 mg four times daily for 1 day), IV dexamethasone (5 mg once), oral aspirin (100 mg daily), and topical prednisolone. Following development of vitritis and scotoma on PSO 15, high-dose oral prednisolone (40 mg daily) was instituted and tapered over 2 months. Color vision normalized, vitritis cleared, and left eye visual acuity recovered from 0.0125 to 0.16 on maintenance prednisolone (5 mg daily).

raw_case_text: We describe a clinical case of a 56-year-old woman from Angola, with diabetic end-stage kidney disease under maintenance hemodialysis and chronic anemia with frequent blood transfusion requirements, who presented with lumbar back pain and lower extremity muscle weakness for 3 months. The patient reported myalgia, rigors, and epigastric pain for 1 month, which had worsened in the previous 7 days, at which time she travelled to Portugal. At presentation, the patient's vital signs were normal, and physical examination was remarkable for pallor and proximal weakness of the lower limbs. Blood tests on admission revealed anemia (hemoglobin 6 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 67.1 fL, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration 20.5 pg, hematocrit 19.6%, and red cell distribution width 28%), leukocyte count 8.6 x 109/L and platelet count 77 x 109/L, C-reactive protein 26.88 mg/dL, creatinine 8.36 mg/dL, and urea 141 mg/dL, with no evidence of hemolysis. The peripheral blood smear revealed trophozoites and schizonts of Plasmodium malariae, and the patient was treated with artemether/lumefantrine for 3 days, under cardiac monitoring with electrocardiogram and blood potassium monitoring. No infected erythrocytes were identified on peripheral blood smear after treatment conclusion, and no adverse events were reported.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old female presenting with myalgias, rigors, and epigastric pain worsening over seven days, on a background of three months of back pain and leg weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient reported a 3-month history of lumbar back pain and lower extremity weakness. Over the preceding month, she developed progressive generalized myalgias, rigors, and epigastric pain, which sharply worsened over the seven days prior to presentation following her travel from Angola to Portugal.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease (ESRD) secondary to diabetic nephropathy on maintenance hemodialysis; chronic anemia requiring frequent blood transfusions; type 2 diabetes mellitus. Epidemiological history: Resident of Angola, recently traveled to Portugal.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were within normal limits. General appearance: Severe mucosal pallor. Neuromuscular examination: Symmetrical proximal muscle weakness of the lower extremities; lumbar spinal tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 6 g/dL, hematocrit 19.6%, MCV 67.1 fL, MCHC 20.5 pg, RDW 28%; white blood cell count 8.6 x 10^9/L; platelet count 77 x 10^9/L; C-reactive protein 26.88 mg/dL; serum creatinine 8.36 mg/dL; blood urea 141 mg/dL; absence of biochemical hemolysis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Uncomplicated Plasmodium malariae infection (quartan malaria) in a patient with diabetic end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis. Peripheral blood smear examination demonstrated characteristic trophozoites and schizonts of Plasmodium malariae.
Plan & Outcome: Hospitalized and treated with oral artemether/lumefantrine for 3 days, accompanied by continuous cardiac telemetry and frequent serum potassium monitoring. Repeat blood smear after treatment completion confirmed complete parasite eradication without adverse cardiac or metabolic events.

raw_case_text:
We report on a 32 year-old male with a history of contact eczema, residing at Djelfa town, in Algeria.
The patient reported a 6-week history of painless, and non-healing skin lesions on his right hand, he admitted having applied topical corticosteroids and antiseptics without any improvement, and then he had received two courses of antibiotics (pristinamycin, amoxicillin + clavulanic acid), with no significant results, moreover, there was an extension of the lesions leading to an imperative reevaluation of the condition. After being referred to our institution, the patient presented limited erythematous-papular plaque of 8 cm of diameter, located on the dorsal side of the right hand, the lesion was formed by the confluence of several papules (Fig. 1), with satellite lesions on the periphery, the initial plaque was associated with several firm and painless subcutaneous nodules 0.5-1.5 in diameter, following a lymphatic drainage to the elbow joint (Fig. 2). The patient didn't remembered being bitten by an insect, and other body surfaces did not reveal similar lesions. Furthermore examination of the other systems was unremarkable. Parasitological examination revealed abundant amastigote forms of Leishmania sp (Fig. 1), while direct mycological examination as well as the culture on Sabouraud medium at 25  C, and on the BHI medium (Brain Heart Infusion) at 37  C were both negative for fungal presence. In addition, culture on NNN medium (Novy- MacNeal-Nicolle), associated to species identification based on isoenzyme electrophoresis revealed Leishmania major as etiological agent.
The patient was started on Meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime ) as first line treatment 60 mg/kg/day for 15 days, which induced a reduction of the lesions after 10 days (Fig. 3), and favorable outcome at day 15 of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old male presented with a 6-week history of a painless, non-healing erythematous plaque on the right hand with ascending nodular lesions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a painless skin lesion on the dorsal aspect of his right hand 6 weeks prior to presentation. Despite application of topical corticosteroids and antiseptics and two oral antibiotic courses (pristinamycin and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid), the lesion progressively enlarged and developed satellite subcutaneous nodules ascending toward the elbow.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of contact eczema; resident of Djelfa town, Algeria; denied recollection of insect or vector bites.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies fever, pain, or lesions on other body surfaces.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination of the right upper extremity revealed an 8-cm well-demarcated erythematous-papular plaque on the dorsum of the right hand formed by confluent papules with peripheral satellite lesions, accompanied by several firm, painless subcutaneous nodules (0.5 to 1.5 cm in diameter) ascending along the lymphatic drainage tract to the right elbow joint. Other body surfaces were clear, and systemic examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Direct mycological examination and fungal cultures on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 °C and brain heart infusion (BHI) medium at 37 °C were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of sporotrichoid cutaneous leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania major: direct microscopic examination of dermal smears demonstrated abundant Leishmania amastigote forms; promastigote culture on Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) medium followed by isoenzyme electrophoresis confirmed Leishmania major. Deep fungal sporotrichosis was ruled out by negative mycological cultures. The patient was treated with intramuscular meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) at 60 mg/kg/day for 15 days. Lesion regression was noted by day 10, achieving complete healing and an excellent clinical outcome at day 15 of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old man from center of Iran noted a small pimple on eyelid 4 months before presentation. The eyelid lesion enlarged slowly. It was as a well-defined, firm, nontender, and subcutaneous skin-colored nodule. The lesion measured 1 cm x 1 cm in diameter (Figure 1).
The lesion had been enlarging slowly and had slightly erythematous, raised borders and was crusty and painless. CBC (complete blood cell count), ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein), and blood chemistries gave results within normal limits. Sample culture of the lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus. Various treatments with cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin-claulanate, and steroids failed to heal the lesion. These treatments were performed for 10 days Although there was cutaneous leishmaniasis in the patient's residence, and also because lack of response to treatment, cutaneous leishmaniasis or basal cell carcinoma was proposed as a differential diagnosis for him.
A slit-skin smear was taken from the edge of the nodule before a biopsy could be taken. Giemsa stain of the sample showed numerous leishman bodies within the macrophages (Figure 2), and the diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis was confirmed. The patient was treated with meglumine antimonate (glucantime) in a dose of 20 mg/kg/body weight intramuscularly for 20 days, with slow but definite improvement of the lesion. The patient reported mild arthralgias and mild myalgias but otherwise tolerated the meglumine antimonate well. After one year of followup, there has been no relapse or new lesion.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male presented with a slowly enlarging, painless nodule on his eyelid of 4 months duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient noticed a small pimple-like lesion on his eyelid 4 months prior that gradually enlarged into a firm, crusted, non-tender nodule with raised erythematous borders. Multiple 10-day courses of oral antibiotics (cephalexin, cloxacillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate) and corticosteroids failed to heal the lesion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior antibiotic therapies: cephalexin, cloxacillin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate. Epidemiological history: resident of central Iran (an endemic region for cutaneous leishmaniasis).
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports the eyelid lesion is completely painless; denies fever, visual disturbance, or constitutional symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic/dermatologic examination: well-defined, firm, non-tender, subcutaneous skin-colored nodule on the eyelid measuring 1 cm x 1 cm, featuring slightly erythematous raised borders and a crusted center.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood cell count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and serum chemistries: all within normal limits. Bacterial culture of lesion exudate: grew Staphylococcus aureus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Giemsa stain of a slit-skin smear from the margin of the eyelid nodule revealed numerous intracellular Leishmania amastigotes (Leishman bodies) within macrophages, confirming cutaneous leishmaniasis. Basal cell carcinoma and primary bacterial pyoderma were ruled out (S. aureus growth represented secondary colonization). Management and Outcome: Treated with intramuscular meglumine antimonate (Glucantime) at 20 mg/kg/day for 20 days. The patient experienced mild, self-limited arthralgias and myalgias, with slow but complete lesion resolution and no recurrence at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 16-year-old female patient was admitted during the summer with a 4-day history of diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, and chills. On admission, the patient looked pale and icteric, with tachycardia (123/min), palpable liver 1 cm below the right costal border, and the spleen was not palpable. The patient's blood pressure was normal. Arterial oxygen saturation in room air was 99%. The patient had Sbeta+-thalassemia (genotype S/thal beta), and the average laboratory data from outpatient follow-up was serum hemoglobin concentration (Hb) 11.7 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 62 fL, leucocyte count of 6.7 x 109/L, and platelet count of 123 x 109/L. The patient did not use hydroxyurea.
The initial laboratory test results are presented in Table 1. Metabolic acidosis was detected (pH 7.29; pCO2 28 mmHg; HCO3 13.8 mmol/L). Serology for viral hepatitis (A, B, and C) was non-reactive. Abdominal ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly, moderate ascites, and bilateral pleural effusion without detection of gallstones or dilatation of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Based on the local epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory data for a SCD patient along with serological confirmation of dengue (IgM reagent - risk group D according to the criteria of the Brazilian Ministry of Health), the diagnosis of SCIC associated with dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever) was considered. The patient was treated with vigorous hydration, analgesia, transfusion of packed red blood cells to achieve a target hemoglobin S (HbS) concentration < 30% (exchange transfusion), and intravenous antibiotic therapy (ceftriaxone 2 g/day).
Twelve hours after admission, the clinical condition worsened with the onset of respiratory distress, drowsiness, and intensification of abdominal pain with rapidly increasing hepatosplenomegaly (spleen and liver palpable at the level of the iliac crests). Laboratory parameters deteriorated with intensifying anemia, elevated LDH, and kidney and liver dysfunction (Table 1). Further management included maintenance of packed red blood cell transfusion (achieved HbS 19.8%) and supportive measures such as hemodialysis and mechanical ventilation in the intensive care unit. There was worsening organ failure, and the patient died eight days later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old female presenting with diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, and chills for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 16-year-old female with Sbeta+-thalassemia presented with a 4-day history of diffuse myalgia, retro-orbital headache, abdominal pain, fever, and chills. On admission, she was tachycardic, pale, and icteric with hepatomegaly. Twelve hours following admission, she developed acute clinical deterioration with severe respiratory distress, drowsiness, worsening abdominal pain, and massive rapid hepatosplenomegaly extending to the iliac crests, progressing to multi-organ failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle cell-beta+-thalassemia (genotype S/thal beta); baseline labs: hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, WBC 6.7 x 10^9/L, platelets 123 x 10^9/L; not on hydroxyurea.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, chills, retro-orbital headache; no history of baseline vaso-occlusive crises on hydroxyurea.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Pale, icteric, heart rate 123 bpm (tachycardia), blood pressure normal, SpO2 99% on room air; liver palpable 1 cm below the right costal margin, spleen not palpable. Deterioration (at 12 hours): Drowsy, acute respiratory distress, severe abdominal distention with massive hepatosplenomegaly (liver and spleen palpable to the level of the iliac crests).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: Metabolic acidosis (pH 7.29, pCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 13.8 mmol/L). Serial labs: Progressive severe anemia, markedly elevated LDH, acute renal failure, and severe hepatic dysfunction. Viral serologies: Hepatitis A, B, and C non-reactive. Abdominal ultrasound: Hepatosplenomegaly, moderate ascites, and bilateral pleural effusion, without gallstones or biliary ductal dilatation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (dengue hemorrhagic fever with plasma leakage, polyserositis, and severe thrombocytopenia) triggering fatal sickle cell intrahepatic cholestasis (SCIC) and acute splenic sequestration in a patient with sickle-beta+-thalassemia. Confirmatory testing showed Dengue IgM reagent (Risk Group D). Viral hepatitis A, B, and C and biliary obstruction were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with vigorous intravenous hydration, analgesia, empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g/day), and exchange blood transfusions targeting HbS < 30% (achieved HbS 19.8%). Following rapid decompensation with refractory lactic acidosis, multi-organ failure, and massive hepatosplenomegaly, she was transferred to the ICU, intubated for mechanical ventilation, and placed on continuous renal replacement therapy / hemodialysis. Despite maximal intensive supportive therapy, multi-organ dysfunction worsened, and she succumbed eight days after admission.

raw_case_text: A 47-year-old man, surgeon in "Hopital de l'Esperance," a private hospital in the north of Togo about 550 km from Lome, the capital, consulted in the same hospital on February 12, 2016, for fever. He was vaccinated against yellow fever. The thick smear performed was positive for malaria and received artemether/lumefantrine without any favorable clinical course after six days. Due to the persistence of high-grade fever and a generalized weakness, he was hospitalized in a private room and a nurse was designated for his care. On day 6 after consultation, he complained of fever, chills, malaise, headaches, pharyngitis hypoacusis, and diffuse abdominal pain. Laboratory tests showed leukopenia (1,100 cells/mm3) and thrombocytopenia (65,000/mm3). His epigastric pain gradually exacerbated. Based on syndromic abdominal pain with febrile illness, an exploratory laparotomy was conducted, which was followed by a bleeding on the operative wound. He was thus air-lifted using an air ambulance from Togo to Cologne, Germany, on day 13. Before the evacuation, the patient was transfused with two units of packaged red blood cells in the airport as his hemoglobin dropped to 6.8 g/dL with evidence of hemolysis symptoms. Despite intensive medical care in Germany, the patient's condition deteriorated rapidly on the second day of admission, and he died on day 14. A postmortem diagnosis of Lassa fever was confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in Germany.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old male presenting with persistent fever and generalized weakness for six days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a surgeon working in northern Togo, developed fever on February 12, 2016, and was prescribed outpatient oral antimalarial therapy. After six days of treatment without clinical improvement, he was hospitalized for high-grade fever, chills, malaise, headaches, pharyngitis, hypoacusis, and worsening diffuse abdominal pain localized primarily to the epigastrium.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: Surgeon at Hopital de l'Esperance in northern Togo (~550 km from Lome). Vaccinated against yellow fever. No other prior medical history documented.

objective.physical_examination: General appearance: Severe generalized weakness, high-grade fever. Abdomen: Progressive severe epigastric tenderness and guarding prompting exploratory laparotomy; post-procedure examination revealed bleeding from the surgical wound.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukopenia with WBC count 1,100 cells/mm3; thrombocytopenia with platelet count 65,000/mm3; hemoglobin subsequently decreased acutely to 6.8 g/dL with clinical and laboratory signs of active hemolysis.
objective.advanced_workup: Exploratory laparotomy: Performed for acute syndromic surgical abdomen, followed by postoperative wound hemorrhage.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Lassa fever (viral hemorrhagic fever) confirmed postmortem by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) in Germany, with initial thick smear positive for malaria (malaria coinfection or background parasitemia).
Plan & Outcome: Initially treated with oral artemether/lumefantrine for 6 days without clinical response. Exploratory laparotomy was performed for syndromic abdominal pain, complicated by wound hemorrhage and severe hemolytic anemia. Transfused with 2 units of packed red blood cells and air-evacuated to Cologne, Germany, on Day 13. Despite intensive medical therapy in the intensive care unit, he suffered catastrophic multiorgan failure and died on Day 14.

raw_case_text: A ten-year-old girl with sickle cell disease (SCD) (combined heterozygosity for the abnormal hemoglobin S and abnormal HbC; HbSC) presented to our clinic with a history of four days fever, malaise, and a generalized tonic-clonic convulsion. At presentation she was alert, nauseous, and complained of headache and retro-orbital pain. Temperature was 38.0 C, heart rate (HR) 135/min, blood pressure (BP) 94/62 mmHg, respiratory rate (RR) 20/min; minor hepatosplenomegaly and upper-quadrant abdominal tenderness were present. No further abnormalities were reported on physical examination. Initial lab results revealed a moderate increase of CRP, anemia, thrombocytopenia, prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and prothrombin time (PT), increased liver enzymes, and decreased albumin and hematocrit (Ht) (Table S1). On day two, during defervescence she became hypotensive and was treated with fluid resuscitation and inotropic agents. Blood products were transfused to correct anemia and thrombocytopenia. Hemolysis and acute hemorrhage with gastrointestinal, vaginal, and later on venipuncture sites bleeding developed. Splenic sequestration was also considered as the cause of anemia, but could not be confirmed with abdominal ultrasound. Pleural effusion, gallbladder wall thickening, and ascites were seen. On day three, she lost vision. A brain CT scan revealed no abnormalities. Lumbar puncture was deferred and antibiotic treatment was adjusted to cover possible meningitis. Hereafter she developed acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring mechanical ventilation. Dengue serology was positive for IgM (titer: 3.26) and IgG (3.26) (Focus Diagnostics), and RT-PCR showed dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2). Her clinical situation deteriorated with an increased hemorrhagic tendency, and blood, clotting products, and clotting factors were administered. In time multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (MODS) developed. Blood cultures remained negative for bacteria, but antibiotics were administered anyway. Candida was cultured and antifungals were initiated. Despite intensive treatment the patient did not recover, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) progressed and kidney function did not return. Consequently further treatment was discontinued and the patient died, 28 days after admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old girl with sickle cell disease (HbSC) presenting with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, and a generalized tonic-clonic convulsion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 4-day history of fever, malaise, and an acute generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On arrival, she was alert and nauseous with headache and retro-orbital pain. On hospital day 2, during defervescence, she developed severe hypotension requiring inotropic support, accompanied by extensive capillary leak and acute hemorrhage (gastrointestinal, vaginal, and venipuncture sites). On day 3, she experienced acute bilateral visual loss, followed by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) requiring mechanical ventilation and progressive multiorgan dysfunction.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle cell disease (combined heterozygosity for hemoglobin S and hemoglobin C; HbSC).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, nausea, headache, retro-orbital pain, convulsions, acute visual loss, and multi-site bleeding. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.0 C, heart rate: 135 beats/min, blood pressure: 94/62 mmHg, respiratory rate: 20 breaths/min. Alert, nauseous. Abdominal exam revealed minor hepatosplenomegaly and upper-quadrant abdominal tenderness. Subsequent exam: Hypotensive shock during defervescence, acute blindness, multi-site hemorrhages (GI, vaginal, venipuncture sites), and respiratory failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: Moderate elevation of CRP, anemia, thrombocytopenia, prolonged aPTT and PT, elevated liver enzymes, decreased serum albumin, and decreased hematocrit. Blood bacterial cultures: Negative. Fungal cultures: Candida isolated. Abdominal ultrasound: Gallbladder wall thickening, ascites, and pleural effusion; excluded splenic sequestration.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT scan: No abnormalities detected. Lumbar puncture: Deferred due to severe coagulopathy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue (dengue hemorrhagic fever / dengue shock syndrome) in a patient with underlying HbSC sickle cell disease, complicated by profound plasma leakage, severe hemorrhage, ARDS, multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (MODS), refractory disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and secondary candidemia. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue serology with IgM titer 3.26 and IgG titer 3.26 (Focus Diagnostics); RT-PCR confirmed dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2). Bacterial blood cultures were negative.
Plan & Outcome: Managed in intensive care with mechanical ventilation, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, inotropic support, broad-spectrum antibiotics adjusted for possible meningitis, antifungal therapy for Candida, and multiple transfusions of blood products, platelets, clotting products, and clotting factors.
