subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old female noticed a gradually enlarging, painful swelling over the right sternoclavicular joint for 2 months without sinus discharge. Pain was dull, continuous, and localized. Over the preceding 4 months, she had also experienced neck stiffness, pain on neck motion, chronic cough, low-grade fever, anorexia, weight loss, and nocturnal pain cries. She had received multiple antibiotic and analgesic courses at another clinic without symptomatic improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of previous tuberculosis, contact with an open case of tuberculosis, or prior trauma. Prescribed empirical antibiotics and analgesics without benefit.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cough, weight loss, low-grade fever, night pain cries, neck stiffness, and neck pain. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: 2 x 3 cm swelling over right sternoclavicular joint with mild tenderness, erythema, and local warmth, without discharging sinus. Neck stiffness and pain on neck movement. Remainder of physical examination normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 10.4 gm%, total leukocyte count 10,300/mm3, ESR 34 mm/1st hr. HIV ELISA negative. Plain radiograph: destruction with sclerosis at medial end of right clavicle and diffuse pulmonary infiltrate.
objective.advanced_workup: MRI: bilateral upper lobe pulmonary infiltrates with right sternoclavicular arthritis and regional fluid collection; destruction of atlanto-axial junction and D7-8 intervertebral disc space with pus collection extending from D5 to D8. Fine needle aspiration of right sternoclavicular lesion: chronic inflammation with caseating granulomas.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Multifocal tuberculosis involving lungs, right sternoclavicular joint, atlanto-axial junction, and thoracic spine (D5-D8 spondylodiscitis with cold abscess), confirmed by positive Ziehl-Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on early morning sputum smear and sternoclavicular FNAC demonstrating caseating granulomas with AFB on ZN smear (mycobacterial culture was negative). Management & Outcome: Started on 4-drug antitubercular chemotherapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) for 3 months, then de-escalated to 3 drugs (rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol). Demonstrated good clinical response within 6 weeks; complete clinical, hematological, and radiological resolution achieved at 1 year. ATT was continued for a total duration of 18 months. Disease-free without recurrence at 2-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old farmer from rural South India, who was previously well, presented to the emergency services with high-grade, intermittent fever for 4 days, which was associated with chills and rigors. He also complained of headache with retro-orbital pain, myalgia and right upper abdominal pain. On examination, he was afebrile with a pulse rate of 112/min, a blood pressure of 100/60 mmHg and a respiratory rate of 28/min. He had a diffuse, blanching erythematous rash over the trunk with no eschar. There was evidence of third space fluid loss, in the form of bilateral pleural effusions and ascites, with tender hepatomegaly. There was no neck stiffness, and fundus examination was negative for papilloedema. Clinical differentials of dengue, rickettsial illness, malaria, leptospirosis and viral hepatitis were considered. The patient's biochemical and hematological investigations during the hospital admission and follow-up are listed in Table 1. Initial evaluation revealed hemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, elevated white cell count, elevated liver enzymes and renal dysfunction. As the patient had significant hepatic dysfunction, ischemic hepatitis, toxin-induced and viral hepatitis were also considered and ruled out. A diagnosis of dengue hemorrhagic fever was made as serological tests were positive for IgG and IgM antibodies to dengue virus. 
The patient was admitted to the high-dependency unit where he was managed conservatively. He was given isotonic intravenous fluids cautiously, with close monitoring of the hematocrit and urine output. At admission, he had deranged coagulation parameters, with no overt bleeding, and was given fresh frozen plasma and platelet concentrates. He responded well to the above measures and was shifted to the ward as his clinical condition improved. His fever resolved, and there were a rise in platelet count, fall in hematocrit and improvement of biochemical and renal parameters.
However, while in the ward, the patient had recurrence of high-grade fever, and he developed features of systemic inflammatory response syndrome. He also developed worsening ascites and pleural effusions, the analysis of which was suggestive of an exudate (Fig. 1). There were no features of fluid overload. Initially, a hospital-acquired infection was suspected, and the patient was evaluated thoroughly for the same. Catheter-related blood stream infection, urinary tract infection, hospital-acquired pneumonia, infected pressure sores, deep-seated collections and drug fever were also looked for and ruled out. Serial cultures failed to isolate any organism. Broad-spectrum antibiotics were initiated, but the fever persisted despite the same. At this stage, a drop in white cell count and hemoglobin was noted, with a resolution of thrombocytopenia (Day 15, Table 1). Occult and overt blood losses were looked for, and hemolysis was ruled out. Hemodilution was unlikely as the patient had been off IV fluids. Further evaluation revealed elevated ferritin (17 386 ng/ml) and triglycerides (297 mg/dl), whereas lactate dehydrogenase persisted to be elevated (Table 1). The fibrinogen levels dropped from 171 to 124 mg/dl, and C-reactive protein was elevated (41.1 mg/l). Despite renal parameters and liver function tests showing an improving trend, the patient appeared toxic with features of hemodynamic instability. In view of the clinical picture, along with bicytopenia and elevated inflammatory markers, hemophagocytosis was considered. 
The patient underwent a bone marrow biopsy on Day 15 of the illness, which showed foci of hemophagocytosis with no evidence of malignancy or infiltrative disease (Fig. 2a and b). The patient thus fulfilled clinical, laboratory and histopathological diagnostic criteria for reactive hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH-2004 trial), with dengue infection being the trigger. As the patient was acutely ill with deteriorating respiratory and hemodynamic parameters, a decision was made to initiate him on steroid therapy. On Day 17, he was started on intravenous corticosteroids, as per the HLH-2004 protocol (dexamethasone 10 mg/m2). There was a dramatic response to the same with resolution of fever and improvement of blood cell counts (Day 20, Table 1). The pleural effusions and ascites gradually improved. In view of the good response, no second-line chemotherapeutic agent was added, and the steroids were tapered over a course of 8 weeks. At 1-month follow-up, the patient was doing well with no further signs of reactivation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old male presenting with a 4-day history of high-grade intermittent fever, chills, rigors, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, and right upper abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 29-year-old previously healthy farmer presented with high-grade intermittent fever with chills and rigors of 4 days' duration, accompanied by headache with retro-orbital pain, generalized myalgia, and right upper abdominal pain. Following initial stabilization on isotonic fluids, he developed recurrent high-grade fever in the ward with features of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), worsening ascites, and exudative pleural effusions unresponsive to broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: Farmer from rural South India. Previously well with no prior chronic medical conditions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for intermittent fever, chills, rigors, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and dyspnea. Negative for neck stiffness, overt bleeding, or papilledema. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Pulse rate: 112 beats/min, blood pressure: 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate: 28 breaths/min, afebrile on admission. Skin: Diffuse blanching erythematous rash over trunk; no eschar. Abdomen: Tender hepatomegaly, ascites. Chest: Bilateral pleural effusions. Neurological: No neck stiffness; fundus examination negative for papilledema. Follow-up: Toxic appearance with hemodynamic instability.
objective.routine_investigations: On admission: Hemoconcentration, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, elevated liver enzymes, deranged coagulation parameters, and renal dysfunction. Day 15: Drop in WBC count and hemoglobin with resolving thrombocytopenia; ferritin: 17,386 ng/mL, fasting triglycerides: 297 mg/dL, LDH: elevated, fibrinogen: dropped from 171 to 124 mg/dL, CRP: 41.1 mg/L. Pleural fluid analysis: Exudative effusion. Serial bacterial blood and urine cultures: Sterile. Workup ruled out catheter-related bloodstream infection, UTI, hospital-acquired pneumonia, pressure sores, deep collections, drug fever, and hemolysis.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow biopsy (day 15): Foci of hemophagocytosis with no evidence of malignancy or infiltrative disease.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) complicated by secondary reactive hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) fulfilling HLH-2004 criteria. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus serology (IgG and IgM antibodies); bone marrow biopsy demonstrating hemophagocytosis; negative serial microbial cultures ruling out secondary bacterial sepsis. Ischemic, toxin-induced, and viral hepatitis ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initially managed in high-dependency unit with cautious isotonic IV fluids, fresh frozen plasma, and platelet concentrates. Following development of reactive HLH, initiated on IV corticosteroids per HLH-2004 protocol (dexamethasone 10 mg/m2) on day 17. Dramatic clinical and laboratory response with fever defervescence, rising blood counts, and resolution of pleural effusions and ascites. Steroids tapered over 8 weeks without cytotoxic agents; doing well with no reactivation at 1-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 84-year-old female patient with a large nodular lesion in the forehead, with a pre-diagnosis of lymphoma, in a private hospital in Hatay applied to the Dermatology Outpatient Clinic of Hatay Mustafa Kemal University Faculty of Medicine. In the previous punch biopsy report, basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris and pseudolymphoma were stated in the clinical pre-diagnosis, and the punch biopsy material was sent to the Department of Pathology for consultation. Microscopic examination revealed dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis. In the cytoplasm of histiocytes, small, round structures similar to Leishmania amastigotes were noted. In the immunohistochemical study, reactive T lymphocytes were stained with a cluster of differentiation (CD) 3 and CD5, and reactive B lymphocytes were stained with CD20. Large clusters of histiocytes were stained with CD68. No staining was observed with CD30. In the report submitted, it was recommended to investigate the aetiology of granulomatous dermatitis, especially CL [Figures 1 and 2].
Dermal scraping from the lesion and diagnosis has been directed to the parasitology department.
Dermal scraping was performed with scalpel number 15 in the parasitology department with a depth of 1-2 mm to reach the upper dermis 0.5 cm long from the edge of the lesion. Smears were prepared. Leishmania amastigote forms were seen in the Giemsa-stained preparations in x 100 immersion lens, and the diagnosis of CL was made [Figure 3].
DNA extraction was performed from smear preparations prepared from the lesion. DNA extraction was carried out according to the protocol recommended in the kit (QIAamp DNA Mini Kit, QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany). The resulting DNA, Real-Time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR), was studied using primary probes specific to the ribosomal internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS-1) gene region that separates genes that encode small subunit ribosomal ribonucleic acid (ssu rRNA) and 5.8S rRNA of the Leishmania parasite. In the rotor-gene device, melting analysis was performed. The sample was typed as L. infantum by comparing it to reference strains [Figure 4].
The informed consent form was obtained from the patient. The patient was referred to the Provincial Health Directorate and received twice doses of intralesional meglumine antimonate treatment a week [Figure 5].

subjective.chief_complaint: An 84-year-old female presented with a large nodular lesion on her forehead.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to a dermatology clinic with a large nodular forehead lesion initially evaluated at an outside hospital under clinical pre-diagnoses of lymphoma, basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, lupus vulgaris, or pseudolymphoma, prompting referral and histological consultation.

objective.physical_examination: Large nodular lesion located on the forehead.
objective.advanced_workup: Forehead punch biopsy: dense nodular and diffuse lymphohistiocytic cell infiltration within the dermis, with cytoplasm of histiocytes showing small round intracellular structures. Immunohistochemistry: CD3 and CD5 positive in reactive T lymphocytes, CD20 positive in reactive B lymphocytes, CD68 positive in large clusters of histiocytes, and CD30 negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Giemsa-stained smears of dermal scrapings from the forehead lesion demonstrated Leishmania amastigote forms under 100x oil immersion. Real-Time PCR targeting the ribosomal internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS-1) gene region followed by melting curve analysis definitively typed the isolate as Leishmania infantum, confirming cutaneous leishmaniasis. Lymphoma, basal cell carcinoma, sarcoidosis, and lupus vulgaris were excluded. Management and Outcome: Referred to the Provincial Health Directorate and treated with twice-weekly intralesional meglumine antimonate injections.

raw_case_text:
A 32-year old man, previously living in Copenhagen, with a history of obesity (BMI 44.4) and untreated hypertension was found dead in his apartment in December 2020 (Table 1). The last known contact was the day before. During isolation due to a positive PCR test for SARS-CoV-2, he had reported fatigue, dizziness and difficulties sleeping and walking.
Post-mortem CT-scan (PMCT) showed bilateral consolidation of the lung tissue with extensive, evenly distributed ground glass opacities and traction bronchiectasis in both upper lobes. PMCT of the brain was unremarkable.
The autopsy revealed brain oedema with slight flattening of the gyri. The brain weighed 1860 g (normal weight 1250 +- 20 g). On gross examination there were no macroscopic signs of inflammation in the meninges or the brain tissue. The lungs were heavily congested and oedematous with diffuse consolidation. Total weight of the lungs was 1826 g (normal weight 840 g; upper limit of normal 1300 g). The lung tissue was generally hyperaemic. Extensive histological sampling from the brain and lungs (formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded, FFPE) were examined using histochemical stains. Brain samples were further examined using immunochemical stains. Tissue examined from the brain and the lungs is listed in Supplemental Table S2. There were no microscopic signs of inflammation, necrosis, thrombosis or haemorrhage in the leptomeninges or in the brain parenchyma. Immunohistochemistry staining for SARS-CoV-2 were negative in all tested areas of the brain. The histopathology of the lungs revealed consolidated tissue with severe diffuse alveolar damage in acute stage with hyaline membranes and type 2 pneumocyte hyperplasia. Interstitial organization was seen locally. The bronchi were with acute bronchitis. The large vessels were diffusely infiltrated with thrombi and the small vessels with microthrombi containing fibrin and platelets.
Toxicologic analysis of blood and vitreous fluid for medication, illicit drugs and alcohol and diabetes-related analyses showed only low treatment-related concentration of paracetamol.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old male found deceased in his home during self-isolation, following reports of fatigue, dizziness, and difficulty sleeping and walking.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 32-year-old man was found deceased in his apartment in December 2020. The last known contact was the preceding day. During home isolation following a positive viral respiratory test, he had reported worsening fatigue, dizziness, and difficulty sleeping and walking.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe obesity (BMI 44.4 kg/m^2) and untreated essential hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pre-mortem reported symptoms: Fatigue, dizziness, insomnia, and impaired ambulation.

objective.physical_examination: Post-mortem forensic examination: Body of an obese male found dead. Autopsy: Cerebral edema with slight flattening of cerebral gyri; brain weight 1,860 g (normal 1,250 ± 20 g). Grossly no macroscopic signs of meningeal or brain tissue inflammation. Lungs heavily congested, hyperemic, and edematous with diffuse consolidation; combined lung weight 1,826 g (normal 840 g; upper limit of normal 1,300 g).
objective.routine_investigations: Toxicology: Blood and vitreous fluid analysis negative for illicit drugs, alcohol, and diabetes-related abnormalities, showing only low therapeutic concentration of paracetamol.
objective.advanced_workup: Post-mortem CT (PMCT): Bilateral consolidation of lung tissue with extensive, evenly distributed ground-glass opacities and traction bronchiectasis in both upper lobes. PMCT of the brain was unremarkable. Histopathology: Lungs showed acute diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) with hyaline membranes, type 2 pneumocyte hyperplasia, focal organizing interstitial fibrosis, acute bronchitis, diffuse large vessel thrombi, and extensive small vessel microthrombi containing fibrin and platelets. Brain histology: No microscopic signs of inflammation, necrosis, thrombosis, or hemorrhage in leptomeninges or parenchyma. Immunohistochemistry: Negative for viral antigens in all tested areas of the brain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Fatal COVID-19 infection (confirmed pre-mortem by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR during isolation) presenting as sudden at-home death in a severely obese patient, caused by severe acute diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), bilateral pulmonary thromboembolism, and extensive microvascular thrombosis leading to massive pulmonary edema and secondary acute cerebral edema.

Outcome: Death at home; autopsy and post-mortem histopathology confirmed acute COVID-19 diffuse alveolar damage and extensive pulmonary microthrombi without evidence of direct central nervous system viral invasion.

raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old girl presented with a progressive bulging mass 2 x 3 cm2 in size, mildly tender, and soft without any fluctuation in 3 weeks located in her rib inter-space 1-2 near the left border of the sternum. She was living in the urban area and was healthy otherwise, except for a history of unpasteurized cheese usage. Intermittent low-grade fever (at night) and sweating were the only complaints. CXR was normal and ultrasonography reported the mass as a lymphadenopathy. Brucella seroagglutination tests, Wright, and 2ME were requested.
Laboratory data showed: WBC = 11,200: Neut = 78%, Lymph = 20%, Mono = 2%, Hb = 11.1, Wright = 1/640, 2ME = 1/80, ESR = 9. Other lab data were not remarkable.
Biopsy of the lesion showed nonspecific inflammation of the lymph node. She was treated with Cap. Doxycycline (100 mg/BID/Po) and Tab. Rifampin (600 mg/day/Po). After 2 months, lymphadenopathy disappeared and no relapse was reported after 1 year follow-up.
The third case was an 18-month-boy referred with a history of multiple, firm, and tender parasternal nodules (about 1.5 x 2 cm2 in size). He showed no constitutional symptoms.
There was no clear history of using unpasteurized dairy products. Wright and Coomb's Wright and all workups were negative. Routine laboratory exams revealed normal results. As a diagnostic approach, excisional biopsy was performed. Grossly, the lesion was cartilaginous with no evidence of necrosis or tumoral involvement. Microscopic examination revealed chronic nonspecific inflammatory process. The smear and culture of biopsied material were negative for tuberculosis or other bacteria. Due to persistent signs and symptoms, follow-up was done by repeated serologic tests which showed four-fold rising in brucella titer (8 weeks later). Treatment was started by Tab. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (trimethoprim, 8 mg/kg/Po) and Tab. Rifampin (10 mg/kg/Po) and continued for 8 weeks. Good response to therapy was achieved.

subjective.chief_complaint: Case 1: An 18-year-old female presented with a 3-week history of a progressive, mildly tender parasternal chest wall mass, nocturnal low-grade fever, and sweating. Case 2: An 18-month-old boy referred for multiple firm, tender parasternal nodules without constitutional symptoms.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Case 1: An 18-year-old female presented with a 3-week history of a progressive bulging mass near the left sternal border, accompanied by nocturnal low-grade fever and sweating. Case 2: An 18-month-old male presented with persistent multiple, firm, and tender parasternal nodules that failed to resolve, leading to excisional biopsy and subsequent serologic monitoring.
subjective.past_medical_history: Case 1: Urban resident, previously healthy; epidemiological history of unpasteurized cheese consumption. Case 2: No documented prior illnesses; no clear history of consuming unpasteurized dairy products.
subjective.review_of_systems: Case 1: Positive for nocturnal low-grade fever and night sweats. Case 2: Negative for constitutional symptoms. Home medications and allergies not documented for either patient.

objective.physical_examination: Case 1: Bulging mass measuring 2 x 3 cm^2 located in the left 1st-2nd intercostal space near the sternal border, mildly tender, soft, and non-fluctuant. Case 2: Multiple firm and tender parasternal nodules, approximately 1.5 x 2 cm^2 in size.
objective.routine_investigations: Case 1: WBC 11,200/mm^3 (neutrophils 78%, lymphocytes 20%, monocytes 2%), Hb 11.1 g/dL, ESR 9 mm/1st hour; CXR normal; ultrasonography reported the mass as lymphadenopathy. Case 2: Routine laboratory examinations revealed normal results.
objective.advanced_workup: Case 1: Biopsy of the lesion showed nonspecific lymph node inflammation. Case 2: Excisional biopsy revealed a cartilaginous lesion without evidence of necrosis or tumoral involvement, with histology demonstrating a chronic nonspecific inflammatory process; smear and culture were negative for tuberculosis or other bacteria.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Parasternal lymphadenopathy and chest wall granulomatous masses secondary to Brucellosis in both patients.
Confirmation:
Case 1: Wright agglutination titer of 1/640 and 2-mercaptoethanol (2ME) titer of 1/80.
Case 2: Initial Wright, Coombs-Wright, and routine workups were negative; repeat serologic testing at 8 weeks revealed a diagnostic four-fold rise in Brucella titer. Smears and cultures were negative for tuberculosis and other bacteria.
Treatment & Outcome:
Case 1: Treated with capsule doxycycline (100 mg BID orally) and tablet rifampin (600 mg/day orally) for 2 months; lymphadenopathy completely resolved with no relapse at 1-year follow-up.
Case 2: Treated with tablet trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (trimethoprim 8 mg/kg/day orally) and tablet rifampin (10 mg/kg/day orally) for 8 weeks, with good clinical response and complete resolution.

raw_case_text: A 25-year-old female was admitted after 3 days of progressive abdominal pain located in the epigastrium of a stabbing type intensity 9/10, associated with vomiting. Physical examination showed a distended abdomen, increased frequency of bowel sounds, and tenderness in the upper abdominal area on palpation. Dry mucous membranes, skin and sclera with jaundice ++/+++. The following laboratory tests were performed: complete blood count, amylase, lipase, liver profile (albumin, globulins, total and fractionated bilirubin, glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase GOT, glutamic pyruvic transaminase GPT, alkaline phosphatase), urea, creatinine, and urine test. Leukopenia 3500 cells/mul, hemoglobin 11.2 g/dl, hematocrit 33.6%, platelets 175,000 cells/mul, total bilirubin 4.76 mg/dl, direct bilirubin 4.58 mg/dl, albumin 3.4 g/dl, GOT 1989, GPT 2540, leukocytes in urine >100 cells/field and bilirubin in urine 1+ and reactive hepatitis A virus antibodies were found. She was hospitalized and given hydration, antiemetics and analgesics. During her hospital stay, vomiting decreased in frequency, but nausea and fever persisted. On her 5th day of hospitalization, a reactive result was obtained for IgM IgG for dengue positive and NS1 negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old female presented with severe epigastric abdominal pain and vomiting for 3 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-day history of progressive, severe stabbing epigastric abdominal pain rated 9/10 in intensity, accompanied by frequent vomiting. During hospitalization, she was treated with intravenous hydration, analgesics, and antiemetics; vomiting improved, but low-grade fever and nausea persisted through hospital day 5.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting. Denied diarrhea, hematemesis, or melena.

objective.physical_examination: Dry mucous membranes with cutaneous and scleral jaundice (++ / +++). Abdomen was distended with increased bowel sounds and marked tenderness on palpation over the upper abdominal region without reported rebound tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Leukocyte count 3,500 cells/muL (leukopenia), hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, hematocrit 33.6%, platelet count 175,000 cells/muL.
Liver function tests: Total bilirubin 4.76 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 4.58 mg/dL, AST (GOT) 1,989 U/L, ALT (GPT) 2,540 U/L, serum albumin 3.4 g/dL.
Urinalysis: Bilirubin 1+, urinary leukocytes >100 cells/high-power field.
Viral serologies: Reactive hepatitis A virus antibodies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue fever complicated by acute hepatitis / severe transaminitis and concurrent reactive hepatitis A serology, confirmed on hospital day 5 by positive dengue virus IgM and IgG serology (NS1 antigen negative).
Treatment and outcome: Managed supportively with intravenous fluid resuscitation, analgesics, and antiemetic therapy with gradual clinical stabilization.

raw_case_text:
A 63-year-old man presented a transient loss of consciousness and muscle strength with spontaneous recovery while walking in the street. He was a current smoker and had a past medical history of myotonic dystrophy type 1, also known as Steiner disease, and hiatal hernia. The patient denied fever, cough, sputum production, dyspnea, chills, muscle pain, loss of taste/smell or any other symptoms. He also denied excessive decrease in physical activity during the last week or any other risk factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE). Vital signs at admission were: arterial blood pressure 123/93 mm Hg, temperature 35.6C, heart rate 115/minute, respiratory rate 23/minute, and oxygen saturation 94% at room air. His physical examination revealed a contusion and hematoma in right supraciliary arch, shallow breathing without respiratory distress. The rest of the physical examination was unremarkable.
Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia and complete right bundle branch block. Chest X-ray showed no relevant alterations. Complete blood count and basic metabolic panel results were within normal ranges. Arterial blood gas analysis results were as follows: pH 7.40, PaCO2 39 mmHg, PaO2 64 mmHg and HCO3- 24 mmol/L. Dimer D was raised (4850 mug/mL). A multidetector computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography was performed to exclude pulmonary artery embolism. It demonstrated an obstruction of the posterior-basal and anterior-basal segmental branches of the right lower lobe (RLL) (Figure 1), with no associated areas of consolidation, crazy-paving or ground-glass opacities. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin, B-type natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP) and echocardiography were normal. Anticoagulation with enoxaparin (1mg/kg/12 hours) was initiated.
Taking into account the current pandemic due to COVID-19 and despite the absence of specific symptoms, we decided to perform a PCR for SARS-CoV-2. The results were positive and COVID-19 related to acute pulmonary embolism was diagnosed. Lactic Acid Dehydrogenase (LDH) was 242 U/L, interleukin 6 (IL-6) 15 pg/mL and ferritin 106 ng/mL. Inpatient hospitalization took an adequate course with no incidents. Hypercoagulability and autoimmune panel ruled out any other associated disease or factor. After seven days, the patient was discharged with home isolation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 63-year-old man presented with sudden transient loss of consciousness and loss of muscle strength while walking.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 63-year-old male experienced a transient loss of consciousness and muscle strength with spontaneous recovery while walking in the street. He denied fever, cough, sputum production, dyspnea, chills, myalgias, loss of taste or smell, or recent reduction in physical activity.
subjective.past_medical_history: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (Steiner disease) and hiatal hernia. Current smoker. Denied prior risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
subjective.review_of_systems: Systemic review negative for fever, chills, cough, sputum production, shortness of breath, muscle aches, anosmia, or ageusia. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: blood pressure 123/93 mmHg, temperature 35.6°C, heart rate 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. Physical exam showed a contusion and hematoma over the right supraciliary arch, and shallow breathing without overt respiratory distress. Remainder of physical examination was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Electrocardiography: sinus tachycardia, complete right bundle branch block. Chest X-ray: no relevant alterations. Complete blood count and basic metabolic panel: within normal ranges. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.40, PaCO2 39 mmHg, PaO2 64 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mmol/L. D-dimer: elevated at 4850 µg/mL. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin: normal. B-type natriuretic peptide (pro-BNP): normal. Echocardiography: normal. Lactic acid dehydrogenase (LDH): 242 U/L. Interleukin-6 (IL-6): 15 pg/mL. Ferritin: 106 ng/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: Multidetector computed tomography (CT) pulmonary angiography: demonstrated obstruction of the posterior-basal and anterior-basal segmental branches of the right lower lobe, without associated consolidation, crazy-paving, or ground-glass opacities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Acute pulmonary embolism associated with COVID-19, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Hypercoagulability and autoimmune panels ruled out underlying thrombophilia or autoimmune etiologies. Therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin (1 mg/kg every 12 hours) was administered. Hospital course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged in stable condition after 7 days for home isolation.

raw_case_text:
A 35-years-old male patient, originally from Russia, attended the Dermatology Service of the General Hospital in Mexico due to two ulcerative skin lesions with a semi-dry appearance, active borders, one of which was in the lower left pre-atrial region and the other in the dorsal region of the left forearm (Figure 1A). The patient referred having travelled to different Middle Eastern countries (Israel, Turkey), and to the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia) and Russia, between May and June 2019. In August of the same year, he detected red and indurated papules, leading him to seek medical attention in San Cristobal de las Casas, located in the Mexican State of Chiapas, in late August. Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was applied to the lesions, leading to their temporary reduction in size. After a renewed flare-up of the lesion edges, the patient was attended at the Tropical Medicine Center (UNAM/Hospital General de Mexico), where he was clinically diagnosed as having localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL). For the confirmation, Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion and ELISA tests for L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana were carried out. Additionally, an aspirate of the lesion was performed and the recovered material was grown in NNN medium (Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle) and in 199 Hank's culture medium (Cat. 12350039, Gibco, Burlington, Ontario, Canada), supplemented with 10% decomplemented fetal bovine serum- FBS (Cat. 16000044, Gibco, Burlington, Ontario, Canada). The quickly growing promastigotes were used for species identification. To this end, promastigote DNA was extracted with DNeasy Blood & Tissue kit (QIAGEN Inc., Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer's guidelines. For the PCR analysis, a 589 bp segment of the alanine aminotransferase gene (ALAT), a 350 bp of the heat shock protein 70 (hsp70) and 300 bp of the internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1) were amplified using 25 microL QIAGEN Master mix (QIAGEN Inc., Hilden, Germany), 1 microL (10 microM) of each primer (ALAT: Fwd 5 -GTGTGCATCAACCCMGGGAA-3 and Rvs 5 -CGTTCAGCTCCTCGTTCCGC-3 ; Hsp70: Fwd 5 -GGACGAGATCGAGCGCATGGT-3  and Rvs 5 -TCCTCCGACGCCTCCTGGTTG-3 ; ITS1: Fwd 5 -CTGGATCATTTTCCGATG-3  and Rvs 5 -TGATACCACTTATCGCAC-3  ), 2-3 microL of extracted DNA and bi-distilled sterile water in a final volume of 50 microL. Additionally, L. mexicana DNA and bi-distilled sterile water were used as positive and negative controls, respectively. We followed the amplification conditions previously reported. The PCR products were run on a 1% agarose gel stained with Smartglow (Cat. E4500-PS, Accuris Instruments, Edison, NJ, USA). The PCR products were purified using the Agencourt AMPure XP kit (Cat. A63882, Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA). Amplicons were sequenced using the BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Cat. 4337455, Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA). The sample was purified by the BigDye XTerminator (Cat. 4376486, Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, USA) prior to loading on the ABI 3730xL DNA analyzer (Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA, US). Sequencing was carried out at the Sequencing Unit of the National Institute of Genomic Medicine. Chromatograms were visualized and a consensus sequence was generated using the Chromas software (version 5, Technelysium, South Brisbane, QLD, Australia). The consensus sequence was compared to reference sequences deposited in GenBank using the BLASTn tool (National Center for Biotechnology Information, Bethesda, MD, USA). Sequences of validated Leishmania species were downloaded and a global alignment was conducted using the Clustal W algorithm (Informer Technologies, Inc., Dallas, US) with the software Bioedit (Informer Technologies, Inc., Dallas, US). Finally, a Maximum Likelihood phylogenetic reconstruction was carried out using the Tamura-three parameters model with invariant sites (I) with 10,000 Bootstrap replicates in Mega 6.0. Gaps were excluded from the analysis. Sequences were deposited in GenBank under the accession numbers MT157311, MT157312, and MT140349.
The Giemsa-stained smears of the lesion showed abundant amastigotes within macrophages. The ELISA analyzed the patient's serum revealing some degree of cross reactivity between four Leishmania species: L. braziliensis, L. infantum/chagasi, L. major and L. mexicana, yet higher antibody levels were recorded for L. major and L. mexicana antigens (Table 1). The isolated parasites were used for the PCR evaluation and a successful amplification of the three genes was achieved (Figures 2A, 2B and 2C). Using the BLAST analysis, these consensus sequences were 99% (538/544 bp), 100% (323/323 bp), and 100% (277/277 bp) identical to the corresponding sequences of the ALAT (MH455379), hsp70 (LN907846), and ITS1 (FN677341), genes respectively, of L. tropica from Israel and Russia. For the phylogenetic analyses, we only included fragments of 540, and 320 bp of the ALAT, and hsp70 genes, respectively. The Maximum Likelihood analysis confirmed that the parasite recovered from the patient corresponded to L. tropica (Figures 2D and 2E). The patient was treated with intralesional applications of 1 mL of glucantime per lesion at 5-day intervals with outpatient monitoring for 4 weeks. The case resolved favorably, the lesions healed adequately and the patient was discharged (Figure 1B).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male presented with two chronic ulcerative skin lesions on his left pre-auricular region and left dorsal forearm.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 35-year-old male originally from Russia who traveled to Israel, Turkey, Armenia, Georgia, and Russia between May and June 2019. In August 2019, he noted red, indurated papules on his face and arm. He sought medical care in Chiapas, Mexico, in late August, where liquid nitrogen cryotherapy was applied, resulting in only temporary lesion reduction. Following flare-up and ulceration of the lesion edges, he presented to the Tropical Medicine Center in Mexico City for definitive diagnosis and treatment.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent international travel to the Middle East (Israel, Turkey), the Balkan region (Armenia, Georgia), and Russia (May-June 2019). No chronic medical conditions documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies fever, weight loss, or systemic symptoms. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic examination demonstrated two ulcerative cutaneous lesions with a semi-dry appearance and active erythematous borders: one located in the lower left pre-auricular/pre-atrial region and the other on the dorsal aspect of the left forearm.
objective.advanced_workup: Lesion aspirate and culture: material cultivated in Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle (NNN) and Hank's 199 medium with 10% fetal bovine serum yielded rapidly growing promastigotes. Giemsa-stained smears of the skin lesions: performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Old World localized cutaneous leishmaniasis (LCL) caused by Leishmania tropica.
Diagnostic confirmation: Giemsa-stained smears demonstrated abundant intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages; parasite culture yielded promastigotes; PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing of the alanine aminotransferase (ALAT, 589 bp), heat shock protein 70 (hsp70, 350 bp), and internal transcribed spacer 1 (ITS1, 300 bp) genes demonstrated 99-100% sequence identity to Leishmania tropica from Israel and Russia; Maximum Likelihood phylogenetic analysis confirmed Leishmania tropica; ELISA confirmed anti-Leishmania antibody cross-reactivity.
Differentials ruled out: Endemic New World leishmaniasis (e.g., L. mexicana, L. braziliensis), cutaneous tuberculosis, deep fungal infections (sporotrichosis), and cutaneous malignancy.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with intralesional meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime, 1 mL per lesion) administered at 5-day intervals with outpatient monitoring over 4 weeks, resulting in complete lesion healing and favorable clinical resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old German Caucasian truck driver presented to the ophthalmologist with unilateral visual loss. Upon eye examination, visual acuity was 0.8 in the right eye and 0.02 in the left eye (normal visual acuity = 1). Fundoscopic examination showed swelling of the optic disk and serous retinal detachment in the left eye (Figure 1, upper image). Slit lamp exam did not reveal any additional pathology. Therefore, the diagnosis of unilateral papillitis was retained. Additionally, oral ulcers and thrush were identified (Figure 2, upper left image), hence an HIV test was ordered. HIV-serology was positive and the patient was referred to the infectious disease department of the University Hospital of Giessen.
Regarding his medical history, the patient had been asthenic and anorectic for 7 weeks and had lost 12 kg. He received a course of oral antibiotics (3 days of azithromycin) three weeks prior to presentation due to sinusitis. He had a burning pain when swallowing, but no other complaints. Apart from sinusitis no pre-existing medical conditions were known. The risk factor for HIV infection was MSM contacts.
On admission the patient had a mild fever of 38.5 C but the other vital signs were normal. Clinical examination was unremarkable except for a moderately enlarged liver and oral ulcers. In addition to the oral lesions, multiple painless, hard-edged ulcers and oedematous swelling were found on the penis and scrotum (Figure 2, upper right image). No anal lesions were present. Signs of fluid overload such as peripheral oedema were absent. No abnormalities were found upon neurological examination, there being no signs of meningismus.
Serum laboratory values on admission showed increased inflammation markers C-Reactive Protein (CRP) and procalcitonin, moderately elevated liver enzymes, moderate hypoalbuminemia and severe hyponatremia (Table 1). Moreover markedly reduced levels of Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH), thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) were noted, indicative of a centrally-induced hypothyroidism. Creatinine and uric acid levels were subnormal. Urine analysis revealed high osmolality and sodium, consistent with the Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH).
Laboratory diagnosis of syphilis in this patient included serology and a Real-Time Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) assay against the polA gene of Treponema pallidum . Serologic tests revealed a reactive Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR)-titer of 1:32, a T. pallidum haemagglutination assay (TPHA) titer of 1:2560 and positive T. pallidum IgM and IgG immunoblots (recomBlot, Mikrogen, Germany). The RT-PCR detected the presence of T. pallidum DNA in the swabs from oral and genital lesions, but not from the anal swab. All other bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial cultures of this patient were negative. Surrogate markers of the HIV infection showed a viral load of 2 x 105 c/ml and a CD4 count of 191/mul. Additional virological studies revealed chronic HBV and HCV infection with viral loads of 55 c/ml (12 IU/ml HBV-s-NAT) and 107 IU/ml (HCV-NAT).
CSF analysis indicated increased blood-brain-barrier permeability with an elevated white blood cell count of 6/mul (normal <4/mul) and protein level of 0.59 g/l (normal <0.45 g/l). No blood contamination was detected (red blood cell count <1/mul). The T. pallidum IgG immunoblot from the cerebrospinal fluid was also positive showing the presence of additional and higher-intensity bands compared to the serum sample. This indicated intrathecal antibody production and suggested neurosyphilis. HIV load in CSF was 2 x 104 c/ml, while PCR based testing for JC Virus (JCV), Herpes Simplex Virus 1/2 (HSV 1/2), Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV) and Cytomegalovirus (CMV) were negative.
Sonography found a normal thyroid size and structure, however, a discrete reduction of the perfusion was noted. A computed tomography (CT) scan showed generalized lymphadenopathy, moderate enlargement of liver and spleen, and extension of the genital oedema to the lower abdominal wall (Figure 2, lower image). Cerebral Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) including pituitary imaging showed no abnormalities apart from sinusitis. Of note, no signs of elevated intracranial pressure were detected. CSF pressure was not measured during lumbar puncture.
The patient was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g/d for 14 days due to a reported allergy to penicillin. Prednisolone at 50 mg/d (tapering scheme over 4 weeks) was added on the recommendation of the ophtalmologist in order to treat papillitis. Fluconazole was included for oesophageal thrush, and trimethoprim-sulfomethoxazole for pneumocystis prophylaxis. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) was started after completion of ceftriaxone. Because of the high viral load in the CSF, a regimen with a high CNS Penetration-Effectiveness rank was chosen, consisting of Lopinavir/Ritonavir (LPV/r), Tenofovir (TDF), Lamivudine (3TC), Zidovudine (AZT).
A therapeutic response to syphilis treatment was observed with normalization of sodium levels (Figure 3), healing of oral ulcers and improvement of the patient's general condition within one week. TSH levels normalized within 3 weeks without any additional specific thyroid treatment, whereas T4 and T3 remained low for longer (Table 2). Visual acuity also improved markedly from 0.02 to 0.2 and papillitis was no longer present after 3 weeks of treatment (Figure 1, lower image).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old male presenting with acute unilateral left-eye vision loss preceded by a 7-week history of asthenia, anorexia, and a 12-kg weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced progressive asthenia, anorexia, and 12-kg weight loss over 7 weeks, along with burning odynophagia. Three weeks prior, he received a 3-day course of oral azithromycin for sinusitis. He subsequently developed acute visual loss in the left eye, prompting ophthalmologic evaluation where unilateral papillitis, oral ulcerations, and mucosal thrush were discovered.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of sinusitis treated with oral azithromycin 3 weeks prior; no other pre-existing medical conditions. Epidemiological history notable for high-risk sexual behavior (men who have sex with men [MSM] contacts).
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for odynophagia, profound asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss; negative for respiratory, abdominal, or anal complaints. Home medications: unmentioned. Allergies: reported allergy to penicillin.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.5 °C; other vital signs normal. Abdomen: moderately enlarged liver (hepatomegaly). Genitourinary: multiple painless, hard-edged ulcers with indurated borders and edematous swelling involving the penis and scrotum; no anal lesions. HEENT: oral ulcers and mucosal thrush; ophthalmic exam: visual acuity 0.8 in the right eye and 0.02 in the left eye (normal = 1); fundoscopy: optic disc swelling and serous retinal detachment in the left eye; slit-lamp examination: unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures: negative. Thyroid ultrasound: normal thyroid size and structure with discretely reduced perfusion. Complete blood counts, electrolytes, and endocrine tests showed hyponatremia and abnormal thyroid function (low free T3 and T4, elevated TSH).
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: CSF opening pressure not measured; CSF white blood cell count 6/mcL (normal < 4/mcL), protein 0.59 g/L (normal < 0.45 g/L), red blood cell count < 1/mcL. CSF PCR for JC virus, HSV-1/2, VZV, and CMV: negative. CT scan: generalized lymphadenopathy, moderate hepatosplenomegaly, and soft tissue edema of the external genitalia extending into the lower abdominal wall. Brain MRI with pituitary protocol: unremarkable except for sinus mucosal thickening; no intracranial mass or signs of elevated intracranial pressure.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Neurosyphilis with ocular syphilis (syphilitic papillitis and serous retinal detachment), secondary genital syphilis, and oropharyngeal candidiasis, in newly diagnosed advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infection (viral load 2 x 10^5 copies/mL, CSF viral load 2 x 10^4 copies/mL, CD4+ count 191/mcL) with chronic hepatitis B and C co-infection (HBV DNA 55 copies/mL [12 IU/mL], HCV RNA 10^7 IU/mL). Syphilis confirmed by reactive serum RPR titer 1:32, TPHA titer 1:2560, positive T. pallidum IgM and IgG immunoblots, positive T. pallidum IgG immunoblot in CSF demonstrating intrathecal synthesis, and positive T. pallidum polA real-time PCR from oral and genital lesions. Management & Outcome: Due to penicillin allergy, treated with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 14 days, oral prednisolone 50 mg/day tapered over 4 weeks for papillitis, oral fluconazole for esophageal thrush, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PCP prophylaxis. Antiretroviral therapy with high CNS penetration (lopinavir/ritonavir, tenofovir, lamivudine, zidovudine) was initiated following ceftriaxone. Achieved complete healing of genital/oral lesions, resolution of hyponatremia and thyroid abnormalities, resolution of papillitis, and marked visual acuity recovery in the left eye from 0.02 to 0.2.

raw_case_text:
On January 9, 2021, a 52-year-old female patient who lives in Jiuzhaigou in the Sichuan province of China was admitted to another hospital because of an unprovoked high fever (Table 1). The body temperature reached 39.6 C, accompanied by coughing, sputum expectoration, tiredness, anhelation, chilly, and shivering. A mass of rash was seen on the face, chest, and groin. She was checked by ultrasound in urinary system, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan, and chest computed tomography (CT), but no significant abnormality was seen. Based on the above symptoms, antibiotics ceftriaxone sodium and clindamycin were used for anti-infection, and methylprednisolone was administered as an anti-asthmatic drug.
On January 11, 2021, the concentration of folic acid (FOL), vitamin B12 (VB12), and serum ferritin (SF) was determined, with the level of SF on the high side. On January 13, 2021, the bone marrow aspiration smear showed a low proliferation rate of nucleated cells, a downside of granulocyte/erythrocyte ratio, and some erythroblasts presented with abnormal morphology. In addition, a significant reduction of iron content in the bone marrow was seen, and the platelet production by megakaryocytes was poor. Scattered and clustered platelets could be seen in the bone marrow. After administering drugs for a week, she recovered from symptoms like coughing, sputum expectoration, tiredness, and shortness of breath. However, the fever was not on the mend. On January 14, 2021, the results of the blood routine indicated decreased levels of white blood cells (WBC), red blood cells (RBC), hemoglobin (HGB), and platelet (PLT). The timeline of diagnosis and treatment of case 1 is demonstrated in Table 2.
On January 15, 2021, she was admitted to our hospital (The Third People's Hospital of Chengdu) and confirmed a history of hypertension, diabetes, and anemia, together with thalassemia in her daughter. Based on the medical history and physical examination results, the patient was tentatively diagnosed with "a fever pending for diagnosis, with moderate anemia, chronic nephritis, hypertension of grade 2, and type 2 diabetes." Chest CT showed splenomegaly, and the abdominal B-mode ultrasound revealed hepatosplenomegaly. After admission, the patient was administered piperacillin sodium/tazobactam sodium and moxifloxacin for anti-infection, oseltamivir for anti-influenza, folic acid tablets, and vitamin B12 as the hematopoietic raw materials, and clexane for preventive anticoagulant.
On January 19, 2021, the bone marrow aspiration smear showed active bone marrow hyperplasia and some dysplastic changes (>10%) in erythroid cells. The patient's fever had not been remitted. On January 20 and 21, no significant abnormality was seen in the bone marrow chromosome karyotyping and gene mutation analysis in myeloid blood diseases.
On January 24, 2021, peripheral blood mNGS was performed, and 11,552 reads of Leishmania genus-specific sequence were detected in microbial cell-free deoxyribonucleic acid (mcfDNA), and 7,509 reads were detected in microbial cell-free ribonucleic acid (mcfRNA) (Table 3), with a genome coverage of 2.7% (Figure 1). The sequencing data were deposited in the database under the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) accession number PRJNA850821. On January 26, the RK39 antibody test showed a positive result. After repeated examinations on the bone marrow aspiration smears, Leishmania was found (Supplementary Figure 1). Finally, the patient was diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis, sepsis, moderate anemia, rash, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, grade 2 hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
On January 26, 2021, a sodium stibogluconate regimen (6 ml/vial, course of treatment for 14 days, D1 3 ml antimonials & 7 ml glucose and sodium chloride injection iv, D2-D14 6 ml antimonials & 4 ml glucose and sodium chloride injection iv) was administrated, and her fever was remitted on that day. On March 2, 2021, the decreased WBC had been resolved, but splenomegaly remained. On March 7, the peripheral blood was collected again for mNGS detection, and 73 reads of the leishmania-specific genus sequence were detected in mcfDNA, but none was seen in mcfRNA (Table 3). Meanwhile, the rash on the face, chest, and groin disappeared utterly.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 52-year-old female presented with high fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, and a widespread maculopapular rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: On January 9, 2021, the patient developed unprovoked high fever up to 39.6 °C accompanied by chills, shivering, cough, sputum expectoration, fatigue, and breathlessness, with a prominent rash over the face, chest, and groin. Outpatient therapy with ceftriaxone, clindamycin, and methylprednisolone improved cough and dyspnea, but high fevers persisted and pancytopenia developed, prompting tertiary hospital admission on January 15, 2021.
subjective.past_medical_history: Confirmed medical history of grade 2 hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and chronic anemia; family history notable for thalassemia in her daughter; resident of Jiuzhaigou, Sichuan Province, China.
subjective.review_of_systems: Cough, sputum expectoration, fatigue, exertional shortness of breath, chills, and shivering.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature: 39.6 °C. Skin: extensive maculopapular rash distributed across the face, chest, and bilateral groins. Abdomen: palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia with decreased WBC, RBC, hemoglobin, and platelets. Elevated serum ferritin, reduced bone marrow iron content, low folic acid and vitamin B12 levels. Urinary tract ultrasound was normal; abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly. Empiric therapy with piperacillin-tazobactam, moxifloxacin, oseltamivir, hematinics, and enoxaparin was initiated.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI showed no significant abnormalities; chest CT revealed splenomegaly without acute pulmonary lesions. Initial bone marrow aspirate showed hypocellularity, decreased granulocyte/erythrocyte ratio, dysplastic erythroblasts, and impaired megakaryocyte platelet production. Repeat bone marrow aspirate on January 19 demonstrated active hyperplasia with dysplastic erythroid changes (>10%); bone marrow chromosome karyotyping and myeloid blood disease gene mutation panels showed no abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) complicated by secondary sepsis, moderate anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and diffuse exanthem: peripheral blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) on January 24 detected 11,552 reads of Leishmania genus-specific mcfDNA and 7,509 reads of mcfRNA (2.7% genome coverage; SRA PRJNA850821); rK39 antibody test was positive on January 26; targeted re-examination of bone marrow aspirates confirmed intracellular Leishmania amastigotes. Myelodysplastic syndrome was ruled out by normal cytogenetics and mutation profiling. Treated with intravenous sodium stibogluconate (SSG; 14-day regimen: day 1 3 mL antimonial in 7 mL glucose-saline, days 2-14 6 mL antimonial in 4 mL glucose-saline). Fever resolved on the first day of SSG; leukopenia and cutaneous rash completely disappeared; follow-up blood mNGS on March 7 demonstrated complete clearance of mcfRNA and reduction of mcfDNA to 73 reads.

raw_case_text:
A 41-year-old HIV-negative male presented to a regional hospital in Cape Town, South Africa with a 5-day history of non-bloody and non-mucoid diarrhoea. He was unemployed and lived in an informal dwelling without access to municipal water and sanitation. He denied any recent exposure to river and dam freshwater or floodwaters. He denied any recent travel history, headache, fever, vomiting, sore throat or respiratory symptoms. He also complained of lower limb weakness that initially affected his ankles and then progressed to involve his knees, to the point where he was unable to walk. He denied any symptoms of bladder or bowel incontinence or retention. He denied any significant past medical or surgical history, alcohol or drug abuse and was not taking medication prior to presentation.
On admission to hospital, his diarrhoea had resolved, and on examination, he had a blood pressure of 86/54 mmHg, pulse 101, temperature 36.5 C, oxygen saturation on room air of 94% and respiratory rate of 18. He was jaundiced, dehydrated and without rash or lymphadenopathy. On neurological examination, he was alert and orientated, his cranial nerves were normal and he had no neck stiffness or muscle wasting. He had decreased tone in both lower limbs with symmetrical weakness (Medical Research Council grade 2/5 power) extending from L1 to S1 myotomes. He had absent ankle and patellar reflexes bilaterally, as well as loss of sensation (light touch and pain) extending up to L1 dermatome in both lower limbs. His upper limb power and reflexes were normal, his anal sphincter tone was normal and he had no cerebellar signs. His cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.
His chest X-ray, 12-lead electrocardiography and urine dipstick showed no abnormalities. His blood results showed bicytopaenia (anaemia and thrombocytopenia), acute kidney injury, conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and a mild transaminitis (see Table 1). His international normalised ratio, vitamin B12 and thyroid functions were normal, and serological testing for viral hepatitis A, B and C was negative. His sputum geneXpert  (Cepheid, CA, USA) was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and his blood cultures were negative. His cerebrospinal fluid showed an elevated protein of 1.31 g/L, glucose of 3.9 mmol/L, polymorphs 4/uL, lymphocytes 7/uL, erythrocytes 25/uL. The gram stain, bacterial culture, TB culture and TB geneXpert  on his cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were negative. His serum Leptospira Enzyme Linked Immunosorbant Assay (ELISA) IgM was positive (titre of 3.8). Contrast Tomography (CT) scans of his head, chest and abdomen were normal and an Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of his spine showed no signs of arachnoiditis or other spinal cord or nerve root pathology. Nerve conduction study findings were compatible with a sensorimotor polyradiculopathy possibly because of AIDP (Table 1 and Table 2).
In summary, our patient was diagnosed with leptospirosis complicated by AIDP. He was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone, intravenous 0.9% saline at 84 mL/h and had regular monitoring of his full blood count, renal function and liver profile. He received daily physiotherapy, thromboprophylaxis and close monitoring for any indication for haemodialysis. He was ambulatory by day 2 in hospital and at discharge, approximately 2 weeks after admission, his renal function and liver profile had improved significantly. When seen at the hospital outpatient department 2 weeks later, his renal function and liver profile were almost normal, and he was ambulating independently.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old male presenting with progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness resulting in inability to walk, preceded by acute diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five days prior to admission, the patient developed acute non-bloody, non-mucoid diarrhea which subsequently resolved. Concurrently, he developed progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness starting distally at the ankles and ascending to the knees, resulting in complete inability to ambulate. He denied fever, headache, vomiting, sore throat, respiratory symptoms, or bowel or bladder dysfunction.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical or surgical history. HIV-negative. Unemployed, residing in an informal settlement without access to municipal water and sanitation. Denied exposure to freshwater bodies, dams, rivers, or floodwaters. Denied recent travel. Denied alcohol or illicit drug abuse. Medications prior to presentation: none.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports resolved non-bloody diarrhea and lower extremity weakness. Denies headache, fever, vomiting, sore throat, cough, dyspnea, urinary or fecal retention, or incontinence. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: blood pressure 86/54 mmHg, pulse 101 beats/min, temperature 36.5 °C, SpO2 94% on room air, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min. General: jaundiced and clinically dehydrated; no rash or lymphadenopathy. Neurological: alert, oriented; cranial nerves intact; no neck stiffness or muscle wasting. Motor: decreased tone in bilateral lower extremities with symmetrical flaccid weakness (MRC grade 2/5 power) extending from L1 to S1 myotomes; absent bilateral patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes. Sensory: loss of light touch and pinprick sensation up to L1 dermatome bilaterally. Normal upper limb motor power and reflexes; normal anal sphincter tone; no cerebellar signs. Cardiovascular, respiratory, and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest X-ray, 12-lead ECG, and urine dipstick showed no abnormalities. Blood tests revealed bicytopenia (anemia and thrombocytopenia), acute kidney injury, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and mild transaminitis. INR, vitamin B12, and thyroid function tests were normal. Sputum GeneXpert was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Blood cultures were negative. Viral hepatitis A, B, and C serologies were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: cerebrospinal fluid protein elevated at 1.31 g/L, glucose 3.9 mmol/L, polymorphs 4/mcL, lymphocytes 7/mcL, erythrocytes 25/mcL; CSF Gram stain, bacterial culture, TB culture, and TB GeneXpert were negative (demonstrating albuminocytological dissociation). Contrast CT scans of head, chest, and abdomen: normal. MRI of the spine: normal with no signs of arachnoiditis, cord compression, or nerve root pathology. Nerve conduction studies: confirmed sensorimotor polyradiculopathy compatible with acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis complicated by acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP / Guillain-Barré syndrome), acute kidney injury, jaundice, and bicytopenia. Confirmed by positive serum Leptospira ELISA IgM with a titer of 3.8. Differential diagnoses ruled out: pulmonary and meningeal tuberculosis (negative GeneXpert and cultures), bacterial meningitis, viral hepatitis A/B/C, HIV, compressive spinal cord myelopathy, and vitamin B12 deficiency.
Plan & Treatment: Intravenous ceftriaxone, intravenous 0.9% normal saline at 84 mL/h, daily physiotherapy, thromboprophylaxis, and regular monitoring of hematologic, renal, and hepatic profiles.
Outcome: Regained ability to ambulate by hospital day 2; discharged approximately 2 weeks post-admission with substantial recovery of renal and hepatic functions; ambulating independently with near-normal renal and liver profiles at 2-week outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
An 86-year-old Cameroonian male was brought to our district hospital with complaints of fever for 4 weeks and abdominal pain and diarrhoea for 2 weeks. The fever was of low grade, intermittent, and without associated symptoms. He automedicated himself with suboptimal doses of amoxicillin, metronidazole, and ibuprofen tablets which were bought over the counter from a drug store. After 2 weeks of continuous use of these drugs, the fever was persistent and became associated with abdominal pain and diarrhoea. The pain was a mild burning intermittent hypogastric pain which was of gradual onset and with no relieving or aggravating factors. The diarrhoea was of gradual onset and started a few hours after the onset of abdominal pain. It was watery and intermittent, and he passed out small quantities of blood-stained yellowish stool about 4 times on average each day. He was taken to a traditional healer who gave him concoctions for 2 weeks during which there was progressive onset of a severe frontal throbbing headache, loss of appetite, and general weakness. The severity of the abdominal pain was increasing. He was then brought to our hospital after 4 weeks of illness.
His past history was significant for moderate arterial hypertension, which was controlled with hydrochlorothiazide. He frequently used nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for chronic low back pain. His past history was otherwise unremarkable.
On admission, the patient was wasted and prostrated and had sunken eyeballs. His Glasgow coma score was 15/15. His vital signs were: blood pressure 100/60 mm/Hg, pulse 124 beats/minute (regular, rapid, and thready), respiratory rate 29 breaths/min and regular, and temperature 39 C. The capillary refill time was 3 seconds. His conjunctivae were mildly pale, and his sclerae were anicteric. There was no palpable enlarged lymph node. His buccal cavity was dry. The abdomen was symmetrically distended and moved slightly with respiration. There was guarding and rebound tenderness at the hypogastrium. Digital rectal examination was without particularity but for an empty rectum. Bowel sounds were faint and hypoactive. The rest of the physical examination was normal.
An erect chest X-ray which revealed air beneath the right hemidiaphragm and distended small-bowel loops.
The Widal test which was positive with a titre of <1/160 for both somatic and flagellar antibodies.
White cell count that showed leucocytosis at 16,000 cells/mm3 with 72% neutrophils.
Haemoglobin level which was 11.8 g/dL.
In view of these, a diagnosis of localized peritonitis with severe sepsis was made. Aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids was started. The patient was put on nil per os, and a nasogastric tube was inserted. Copious thick greenish fluid was brought out by the nasogastric tube. A urinary catheter was placed, and the urine output was monitored. The patient was placed on intravenous ceftriaxone (1 g, 8 hourly), gentamicin (160 mg daily), metronidazole (500 mg, 8 hourly), and paracetamol (1 g, 8 hourly). The following laboratory investigations were requested:
Blood cell indices were not fully assessed because our hospital could not do a complete blood count. Based on the historical, clinical, and laboratory data obtained, we considered intestinal perforation due to typhoid fever as the probable aetiology of peritonitis, and the aetiological differentials included perforated peptic ulcer and perforated appendix. However, we could not perform blood or stool culture in our primary care hospital to confirm typhoid fever.
Four hours after admission and continuous resuscitation, the vital signs were blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min (regular and bounding), respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, and temperature 37.5 C. The patient remained haemodynamically stable the following 3 hours. Urine output was 32 ml/hr. His physical status score at the time of surgery was American Society of Anaesthesiology class IV. Intravenous ceftriaxone alongside other preoperative medication was administered to the patient, and an emergency exploratory laparotomy through a vertical midline incision was performed under general anaesthesia. Intraoperatively, distended small-bowel loops denuded of serosa on multiple spots were observed. Abundant greenish peritoneal fluid mixed with exudate and faecal material was obvious. The operative wound was rated as Altemeier class IV. On further inspection, multiple perforations were observed in the ileum (Figure 1).
A total of 15 perforations scattered over about 26 cm of the distal ileum were found. The perforation closest to the ileocaecal junction was less than 2 cm from the junction. The peritoneal cavity was thoroughly cleaned with warm saline. About 28 cm of the distal ileum including the section with perforations was segmentally resected (Figure 2) to leave clean margins, and then, a manual 2-layer end-to-side anastomosis of the proximal edge of the ileum and the transverse colon was performed.
The distal edge of the ileum was closed as a stump over the caecum, and the ascending colon left as a blind loop. Two abdominal drains were inserted to drain both the paracolic gutters and the rectovesical pouch through the right (Figure 3) and left lower quadrants of the abdomen.
The abdomen was closed layer by layer. Portions of the resected ileum were sent for histopathological analysis in a tertiary hospital. The patient was monitored in the recovery room for 30 minutes during which he remained haemodynamically stable. He was sent to the ward where close monitoring was continued.
Postoperatively, the patient was maintained on intravenous infusions of dextrose-saline, as well as intravenous ciprofloxacin (400 mg, 12 hourly), metronidazole (500 mg, 8 hourly), omeprazole (40 mg, 24 hourly), and intramuscular diclofenac (150 mg daily) for 10 days. Early ambulation was encouraged upon recovery from general anaesthesia. Enteral feeding with fluid diet was started after 26 postoperative hours, and routine postoperative care in the ward was continued. The abdominal drains were removed on the 6th postoperative day. On the 8th postoperative day, bowel sounds could not be perceived. A probable diagnosis of the postoperative paralytic ileus was made. The nasogastric tube was maintained, and enteral feeding halted till the tenth postoperative day when bowel sounds were appreciated. On the tenth postoperative day, suppuration was noticed at the surgical site which necessitated removal of the stitches and opening of the wound at the bedside. The wound was dressed for 3 weeks. Serial (four) Widal tests done at 3 days' interval remained positive with a titre of <1/160 for both somatic and flagellar antibodies. Histopathology of the resected intestinal tissue revealed diffuse aggregates of enlarged irregular pale cells, with eccentric nuclei, and abundant acidophilic cytoplasm, with phagocytic characteristics. Chronic inflammation of the Peyer patches was also noted. These findings confirmed that the multiple ileal perforations were due to typhoid fever. The patient was discharged home on the thirty-fifth postoperative day and scheduled for regular visits. No other complications were observed after 6 months of follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 86-year-old Cameroonian male presented with low-grade fever for 4 weeks and abdominal pain and diarrhea for 2 weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Low-grade, intermittent fever began 4 weeks prior to admission without associated symptoms. He self-medicated with over-the-counter amoxicillin, metronidazole, and ibuprofen for 2 weeks. Fever persisted and became associated with mild burning intermittent hypogastric pain and watery, blood-stained yellowish diarrhea (~4 times daily). He then consumed herbal concoctions from a traditional healer for 2 weeks, during which he developed severe frontal throbbing headache, anorexia, general weakness, and progressively worsening abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Moderate arterial hypertension controlled with hydrochlorothiazide. Frequent use of NSAIDs for chronic low back pain. Otherwise unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe frontal throbbing headache, loss of appetite, general weakness. Home medications: hydrochlorothiazide and frequent NSAIDs.

objective.physical_examination: Wasted, prostrated, with sunken eyeballs; Glasgow Coma Scale 15/15. Capillary refill time 3 seconds. Mildly pale conjunctivae, anicteric sclerae, dry buccal cavity, no palpable lymphadenopathy. Admission vitals: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 124 beats/min (regular, rapid, thready), respiratory rate 29 breaths/min (regular), temperature 39 °C. Post-resuscitation vitals: blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min (bounding), respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, temperature 37.5 °C; urine output 32 mL/h. Abdomen: symmetrically distended, moved slightly with respiration; guarding and rebound tenderness at hypogastrium; faint, hypoactive bowel sounds. DRE: empty rectum.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count: 16,000 cells/mm3 with 72% neutrophils. Hemoglobin: 11.8 g/dL (full red cell indices unavailable). Erect chest X-ray: air beneath right hemidiaphragm and distended small-bowel loops. Nasogastric aspirate: copious thick greenish fluid.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency exploratory laparotomy: distended small-bowel loops denuded of serosa on multiple spots, abundant greenish peritoneal fluid mixed with exudate and fecal material (Altemeier class IV operative wound), and 15 perforations scattered over ~26 cm of the distal ileum (closest perforation <2 cm from ileocecal junction).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Multiple ileal perforations with peritonitis and severe sepsis secondary to typhoid fever. Confirmed by histopathology of resected ileum demonstrating diffuse aggregates of enlarged irregular pale cells with eccentric nuclei and abundant acidophilic cytoplasm (phagocytic characteristics) and chronic inflammation of Peyer patches; serial (four) Widal tests showed titers of <1/160 for somatic and flagellar antibodies (cultures were unavailable). Differentials considered: perforated peptic ulcer and perforated appendix. Treatment: Aggressive fluid resuscitation, NPO, NGT decompression, Foley catheter; preoperative IV ceftriaxone (1 g every 8 h), gentamicin (160 mg daily), metronidazole (500 mg every 8 h), and paracetamol (1 g every 8 h). Segmental resection of 28 cm distal ileum with manual 2-layer end-to-side ileotransverse anastomosis, ileal stump closure, and two abdominal drains. Postoperative therapy: IV ciprofloxacin (400 mg every 12 h), metronidazole (500 mg every 8 h), omeprazole (40 mg every 24 h), and IM diclofenac (150 mg daily) for 10 days; IV dextrose-saline. Drains removed on POD 6. Postoperative paralytic ileus managed conservatively until POD 10. Bedside wound debridement and dressings performed for wound suppuration on POD 10. Discharged on POD 35 with complete recovery and no complications at 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
On October 29th 2005, a 56-year-old German tourist living in Haiti, with a history of heavy alcohol use and 2 malaria infections treated with chloroquine, developed symptoms of fever, headache, nausea, and diarrhea. On November 3rd he visited a local hospital in Cotes des Arcadins and was diagnosed with P. falciparum infection by peripheral blood smear. The patient was treated with chloroquine and doxycycline the same day but developed altered mental status and was hospitalized. Despite falling parasite counts, the patient's neurological condition continued to worsen and he was mechanically ventilated. Seizures, bloody stools, hematemesis, and decreased urinary output were also documented. Due to his worsening condition, he was transferred to a hospital in Miami the following day, November 4th.  At the time of hospital admission in Miami, the patient had thrombocytopenia, diffuse intravascular coagulation, electrolyte imbalance, and acute renal failure. Blood smears showed few malaria parasites, but treatment with antimalarial agents was continued.  Bronchoalveolar lavage was positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomas aeruginosa, and yeast forms.
Blood culture on November 4th was positive for C.  perfringens. Vancomycin, amphotericin, piperacillin, phenytoin, lorazepam, and hydrocortisone were added to the treatment regimen. On November 5th blood culture revealed Candida tropicalis. An encephalitis panel was also negative. The patient continued to decline clinically and he expired on November 7th, 10 days after symptom onset.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 56-year-old male presenting with fever, headache, nausea, diarrhea, followed by progressive altered mental status, seizures, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 56-year-old male tourist living in Haiti developed fever, headache, nausea, and diarrhea on October 29, 2005. On November 3, he presented to a local hospital in Haiti and was prescribed antimicrobial therapy. However, he developed acute altered mental status and was hospitalized and intubated for mechanical ventilation. He developed generalized seizures, hematemesis, melena/hematochezia, and oliguria, prompting emergency air medical evacuation to Miami on November 4.
subjective.past_medical_history: German tourist residing in Haiti. History of heavy alcohol use and two prior malaria infections treated with chloroquine. Pre-transfer medications: chloroquine and doxycycline initiated on November 3.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, nausea, diarrhea, hematemesis, bloody stools, seizures, and altered sensorium. Medications: chloroquine, doxycycline. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Critically ill, comatose/altered mental status on mechanical ventilation. Hemodynamically unstable, oliguria/anuria. Abdomen: distended with signs of gastrointestinal bleeding (hematochezia and hematemesis via gastric tube). Skin: petechiae/purpura.
objective.routine_investigations: Thrombocytopenia, diffuse intravascular coagulation (DIC), severe electrolyte imbalances, and acute renal failure. Serial peripheral blood smears performed. Encephalitis panel: negative. Blood cultures: positive for Clostridium perfringens on November 4; repeat blood culture positive for Candida tropicalis on November 5. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) culture: positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and yeast forms.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and lumbar puncture with viral/encephalitis panel.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by cerebral malaria, multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (DIC, acute renal failure, respiratory failure), gastrointestinal hemorrhage, Clostridium perfringens bacteremia, Candida tropicalis fungemia, and polymicrobial ventilator-associated pneumonia.
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial peripheral blood smear in Haiti demonstrating Plasmodium falciparum; subsequent blood smears in Miami demonstrating low-level intraerythrocytic parasites; blood cultures confirming Clostridium perfringens bacteremia and Candida tropicalis fungemia; BAL cultures yielding K. pneumoniae, A. baumannii, and P. aeruginosa.
