objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: 4,000 cells/mm3, total leukocyte count: 3,000 cells/mm3, lymphocyte count: 12%, serum albumin: 3 g/dL, hemoglobin: 14.2 g/dL, hematocrit: ~44%. Coagulation: Prothrombin time (PT) was normal, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) was elevated.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) presenting with severe oral mucosal hemorrhagic plaques, diffuse palatal erosion, and profound thrombocytopenia. Diagnostic confirmation: Detection of dengue IgM antibodies by antibody-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (MAC-ELISA) performed 8 days after symptom onset.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted to the intensive care unit and managed with intravenous fluid resuscitation and platelet transfusions. Oral mucosal lesions and thrombocytopenia resolved, and the patient made a complete recovery within 1 week.

raw_case_text: A 75-year-old male presented to our hospital with fever, productive cough, and fatigue for 3 days. His medical history was significant for hypertension and hyperlipidemia. In the emergency department, he was found to be hypoxic to 78% on room air. He was also tachypneic at 26 respirations per minute and tachycardic at 110 beats per minute. His temperature was 38.8 C. Physical exam demonstrated crackles at the right and left lung bases. His laboratory tests revealed a C-reactive protein concentration of 88 mg/L (normal range 0.00-4.9 mg/L), D-dimer value 1.60 mg/L (normal range < 0.5 mg/L, serum ferritin 1300 ng/mL (normal range 30-400), Complete blood count 9500 cells per microL (normal range 3900-11 000), lymphocyte count 950 (normal range 700-4500) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) 226 pg/mL (normal range 5-15 pg./mL). Nasopharyngeal severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2(SARS-C0V-2) reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction was positive. Chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed bilateral patchy consolidations (Figure 1). Echocardiography was normal. He was treated with antibiotics, corticosteroids, prophylactic anticoagulation, and remdesivir. He was placed on supplemental oxygen. During his hospitalization, he continued to have an increased need for oxygen. On day 6 of his hospitalization, he developed worsening dyspnea despite maximum non-invasive oxygen support, a chest CT scan was ordered and demonstrated pneumopericardium without subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, or pneumothorax (Figure 2). Because of an absence of pericardial compressive symptoms, a conservative approach to our patient is suggested. He continued to receive consistent respiratory therapy and daily echocardiography was performed to diagnose tension pneumopericardium. The patient did not show any signs of tension pneumopericardium during hospitalization. On day 7 of hospitalization, he had acutely increased work of breathing and had desaturations. He was intubated. Two days later the patient died of severe respiratory insufficiency secondary to the adult respiratory distress syndrome.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old male presenting with fever, productive cough, and fatigue for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-day history of fever, productive cough, and progressive fatigue. On emergency presentation, he was found to have marked hypoxemia (SpO2 78% on room air) and respiratory distress requiring high-flow supplemental oxygen. Over the course of hospitalization, his respiratory distress progressed despite maximal non-invasive support, and repeat imaging on hospital day 6 demonstrated acute spontaneous pneumopericardium. On hospital day 7, acute decompensation necessitated endotracheal intubation, followed by refractory respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Temperature 38.8 °C, heart rate 110 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 78% on room air. Chest auscultation: Crackles auscultated at bilateral lung bases. Day 7: Acutely increased work of breathing with severe desaturations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Complete blood count 9,500 cells/microL, absolute lymphocyte count 950/microL, C-reactive protein 88 mg/L, D-dimer 1.60 mg/L, serum ferritin 1,300 ng/mL, interleukin-6 (IL-6) 226 pg/mL. Initial and serial echocardiograms: Normal cardiac function, no evidence of tamponade or tension pneumopericardium.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT on admission: Bilateral patchy pulmonary consolidations. Chest CT on day 6: Pneumopericardium without subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum, or pneumothorax.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia with ARDS) confirmed by nasopharyngeal RT-PCR, complicated by spontaneous pneumopericardium and refractory hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with supplemental oxygen escalating from non-invasive support to invasive mechanical ventilation via endotracheal intubation, remdesivir, systemic corticosteroids, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and prophylactic anticoagulation. Spontaneous pneumopericardium was managed conservatively with serial echocardiographic surveillance given the absence of cardiac tamponade. Despite intensive interventions, the patient succumbed to severe ARDS on hospital day 9.

raw_case_text:
A 58-year-old male, a farmer by occupation presented with persistent watering and intermittent discharge for 1 year. He had had multiple consultations earlier and was treated with topical antibiotics. Ocular examination showed edema of the right lower eyelid localized to the medial aspect with a pouting punctum. Canalicular curettage revealed the presence of pus and concretions which were sent for microbiological evaluation. Gram's stain of the smear showed Gram-positive branching filamentous organisms and Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Nonhemolytic nonpigmented small gray colonies [Figure 3] grew on blood agar. These were identified as Brucella melitensis. Staphylococcus epidermidis and Actinomycetes were also isolated from culture. The organisms were sensitive to chloramphenicol [Table 1].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 58-year-old male presented with persistent watering and intermittent discharge from the right eye for one year.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1-year history of persistent right eye tearing (epiphora) and intermittent discharge. He had sought multiple medical consultations previously and was treated empirically with courses of topical ophthalmic antibiotics without lasting symptom resolution.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of prior topical ophthalmic antibiotic therapy for chronic eye symptoms. Epidemiological exposure/Occupation: Farmer.

objective.physical_examination: Ocular examination: Localized edema of the medial aspect of the right lower eyelid with a pouting lacrimal punctum.
objective.routine_investigations: Diagnostic canalicular curettage: Pus and concretions expressed. Gram stain smear: Demonstrated Gram-positive branching filamentous organisms and Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
objective.advanced_workup: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing: Isolated organisms demonstrated in vitro susceptibility to chloramphenicol.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Chronic canaliculitis with polymicrobial infection, confirmed by bacterial culture of canalicular concretions growing nonhemolytic nonpigmented small gray colonies identified as Brucella melitensis, alongside Staphylococcus epidermidis and Actinomyces species. Isolates were sensitive to chloramphenicol.
Plan & Clinical Course: Treated with surgical canalicular curettage and removal of concretions along with targeted topical antimicrobial therapy guided by chloramphenicol susceptibility.

raw_case_text:
We report the case of an 11-year-old Nigerian boy, living in Italy since 2010. On August, 26th he flew back from a one-month stay in Nigeria, and two days later he started presenting fever. On August, 31st he complained vomiting and abdominal pain and was then conducted to the Emergency Room of our Hospital. Here, after an initial suspect of appendicitis, a diagnosis of Plasmodium falciparum malaria was made, and the patient was admitted to the Infectious Diseases ward. Body temperature was 38 C, while other vital signs were normal. His complete blood count showed leukopenia (WBC 4060, nv 4500-10800) and thrombocytopenia (PLT 59,000, nv 100,000-400,000), while hemoglobin was 13 g/dL (nv 13-16.5 g/dL). His chemistry profile showed hyperbilirubinemia (2.93 mg/dL, nv 0.2-0.5 mg/dL), AST 136 UI/L and ALT 122 UI/L (nv 13-51 UI/L and 15-47 UI/L, respectively), creatinine was 1.06 mg/dL (nv 0.3-0.9 mg/dL) and an increase of LDH values (657 U/L) was present (nv 120-330 U/L); C-reactive protein was 85.6 mg/L (nv <5 mg/L). He started therapy with piperachin/diidroartemisin 320/40 mg, 3 tablets qd, and as long as he kept presenting well-localized right upper quadrant abdominal pain, an ultrasound (US) was performed on September, 1st. The exam showed a starred sky appearance of the liver associated with a slightly enlarged gallbladder, with transonic content and thickened walls, suggestive of cholecystitis. A slight increase of the spleen's dimensions (pole-to-pole diameter 11 cm) was present, and in its context a hypo-anechoic, inhomogeneous ovalar lesion (diameter 1.5 cm) was found, raising a diagnostic doubt (Abscess? Hematoma? Cyst?). The pediatric surgeon confirmed a non-surgical approach for cholecystitis and antibiotic therapy with piperacilline/tazobactam 4.5 g tid (body weight of 42 Kg) was undertaken. As long as he kept presenting fever (Figure 1) although therapy for malaria was considered over (piperachin/diidroartemisin 320/40 mg, 3 tablets qd, from August, 31st to September, 2nd) and hemoscopy resulted negative, as suggested by the radiologist, the next day the US was repeated, showing multiple splenic abscesses. Therefore, serologies for Bartonella, Echinococcus and Entamoeba and blood cultures were sent.
Quantiferon test and coproparasitologic exam were executed, resulting both negative. An echocardiogram showed no endocarditic vegetations. On September, 5th the boy was transferred to the Pediatrics ward for cholecystitis and splenic abscesses. Antimicrobial spectrum was broadened with Claritromicine 250 mg bid per os. Blood tests were performed, including peripheral blood smear, quantitative Ig, total IgE, lymphocyte typing, hemoglobin electrophoresis and dihydrorhodamine 123 test, in order to evaluate any underlying hematologic diseases. On September, 8th, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen was performed, confirming the presence of seven focal areas of signal alteration, with prevalent peripheral subcapsular distribution (maximum size 1.7 mm).
The morphology of the formations, especially of the most voluminous, was a pyramidal wedge with the apex pointing towards the hilum, and the base of the splenic capsule, while profiles looked finely irregular (Figure 2 and 3). The radiographic appearance then made it less likely the possibility of splenic abscesses, in favour of a diagnosis of recent post-infarction outcomes or hematomas in a subacute phase. While all other requested exams resulted negative, on September, 13th, hemoglobin electrophoresis showed a percentage of HbS of 40.6%, HbA was 55.2% while HbA2 and HbF were respectively 3.5 and 0.7%. A diagnosis of SCT was then made.
On September, 15th the boy was discharged, with recommendations to radiologic follow-up and preconception counseling for him and his parents and without further antibiotic therapy.
On October, 13th the boy repeated the US, which showed a normal spleen. The timing of regression is compatible with the diagnosis of splenic infarction.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old boy presenting with fever for three days, followed by vomiting and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient returned from a 1-month stay in Nigeria on August 26 and developed a fever two days later. On August 31, he presented to the emergency room with vomiting and abdominal pain, where acute appendicitis was initially suspected. He was admitted to the hospital and continued to experience persistent fever and well-localized right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: Nigerian boy living in Italy since 2010; epidemiological exposure: 1-month travel to Nigeria, returning on August 26. No prior chronic medical illnesses documented.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature 38.0 °C; other vital signs were normal. Abdominal examination revealed well-localized right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: WBC 4,060/mm3 (reference 4,500-10,800/mm3), platelets 59,000/mm3 (reference 100,000-400,000/mm3), hemoglobin 13 g/dL (reference 13-16.5 g/dL). Chemistry: Total bilirubin 2.93 mg/dL (reference 0.2-0.5 mg/dL), AST 136 UI/L (reference 13-51 UI/L), ALT 122 UI/L (reference 15-47 UI/L), serum creatinine 1.06 mg/dL (reference 0.3-0.9 mg/dL), LDH 657 U/L (reference 120-330 U/L), C-reactive protein 85.6 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L). Blood cultures were negative. Serologies for Bartonella, Echinococcus, and Entamoeba were negative. Quantiferon test and stool coproparasitologic examination were negative. Transthoracic echocardiogram: No endocarditic vegetations. Hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbS 40.6%, HbA 55.2%, HbA2 3.5%, HbF 0.7% (confirming sickle cell trait). Abdominal ultrasound (September 1): Starred sky appearance of the liver, slightly enlarged gallbladder with transonic content and thickened walls suggestive of acalculous cholecystitis, slight splenomegaly (pole-to-pole diameter 11 cm) with a 1.5 cm hypo-anechoic inhomogeneous ovalar splenic lesion. Repeat ultrasound (September 2): Multiple hypoechoic splenic lesions.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal MRI (September 8): Seven focal areas of signal alteration with prevalent peripheral subcapsular distribution (maximum size 1.7 mm) demonstrating pyramidal wedge morphology with apex towards hilum and base at capsule, consistent with recent splenic infarction or subacute hematomas.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute splenic infarction and acalculous cholecystitis in a child with newly recognized sickle cell trait (SCT). Appendicitis, infective endocarditis, and other parasitic/bacterial etiologies (Bartonella, Echinococcus, Entamoeba, tuberculosis) were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Treated for malaria with oral piperaquine/dihydroartemisinin 320/40 mg (3 tablets once daily for 3 days, August 31 to September 2), achieving negative hemoscopy. Cholecystitis and splenic infarction were managed conservatively without surgery, receiving IV piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g three times daily (weight 42 kg) and oral clarithromycin 250 mg twice daily. Discharged on September 15 without antibiotics, with recommendations for preconception counseling and follow-up imaging. Follow-up abdominal ultrasound on October 13 confirmed complete resolution with a normal spleen.

raw_case_text:
A 62-year-old male with past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and arthritis was readmitted via emergency department for worsening chest pain, productive cough, and shortness of breath. His chest pain was pleuritic. He was discharged a week earlier from a 1-day hospital stay on a 10-day course of dexamethasone for coronavirus disease-2019 (COVID-19) infection, which he was unable to take. He was maintaining oxygen saturation of 88% on 6 L nasal cannula. Initial blood work was remarkable for leukocytosis 25.86 (ref: 3.1-8.50 x 103/uL) with bands elevated at 9%, anion gap 15, lactic acid elevated 3.3 (ref: 0.5-2.0 mmol/L), mild transaminitis with aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 113, and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 153. Physical examination was remarkable for decreased air entry with bilateral crepitation. Computed tomography pulmonary embolus study confirmed presence of bilateral acute pulmonary emboli with possible right heart strain and bilateral infiltrates consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia. He was treated with heparin infusion, remdesivir, dexamethasone, 1 dose of vancomycin, and piperacillin-tazobactam as well as supportive breathing treatments consisting of albuterol nebulization as needed. He was then admitted to the medical floors for further management.
Echocardiogram obtained later was resulted as normal left ventricular function with ejection fraction 55% to 65% with normal right ventricular pressure and no evidence of right ventricular dysfunction. Heparin infusion, remdesivir, and dexamethasone were continued. Vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam were given the initial 2 days to cover for superimposed bacterial pneumonia and later deescalated to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid on days 3 and 4 of hospitalization. Ultrasound abdomen done on day 4 showed no abnormalities within the liver or gallbladder.
During hospitalization, patient was noticed to have worsening of liver enzymes which peaked at ALT 721 IU/L (normal <55 U/L) and AST 305 IU/L (normal value < 35 U/L). Other laboratory values were gamma-glutamyl transferase 114 IU/L (ref: 12-64 IU/L), albumin 2.7 g/dL (ref: 3.4-4.8 g/dL), alkaline phosphatase 49 IU/L (ref: 56-119 IU/L), and international normalized ratio 1.5. Further workup showed pro-calcitonin minimally elevated at 0.28 (ref: <0.05 ng/mL), d-dimer elevated at 12.89 (ref: <0.5 mg/dL), and fibrinogen was normal. His blood alcohol and acute hepatitis panel were negative on day 2 of hospital admission. Acetaminophen levels obtained on hospital day 4 were <0.6 (ref 0.00-50.0 microg/mL). At that point, remdesivir was discontinued on day 2 of admission as it was thought to have contributed to worsening of liver function. Antibiotics were discontinued as bacterial infection was less likely and it was thought amoxicillin-clavulanic acid could also have contributed to liver enzyme abnormalities. Computed tomography abdomen and pelvis with contrast (day 8) showed mild splenomegaly with no abnormalities noted in the liver or gall bladder.
Despite discontinuation of remdesivir, antibiotics, and improving oxygen requirements, his liver function continued to worsen (see Table 1) and additional workup including autoimmune work up with anti-smooth muscle antibodies, systemic lupus erythematosus, and vasculitis panel were done and reported negative. Further testing with EBV and cytomegalovirus (CMV) serology were done, which revealed EBV viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM positivity. He was also positive for EBV VCA IgG, EBV early antigen (EA) IgG, and EBV nuclear antigen (NA) IgG. EBV polymerase chain reaction was reported positive. CMV IgM antibody was negative; however, CMV IgG antibody was positive with reported value >10 (ref: 0.00-0.059). He remained stable with improving oxygen requirements and was eventually discharged home without the need for supplemental oxygen.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 62-year-old male presenting with worsening pleuritic chest pain, productive cough, and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had been discharged one week prior following a 1-day hospitalization and prescribed a 10-day course of dexamethasone, which he was unable to take. He was readmitted via the emergency department for worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain, presenting with severe hypoxemia requiring 6 L/min nasal cannula oxygen. During admission, he developed marked hepatocellular injury in the setting of acute pulmonary embolism and viral coinfection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, and arthritis.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Oxygen saturation 88% on 6 L/min nasal cannula; chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry with bilateral crepitations.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Leukocytosis 25.86 x 10^3/microL (reference: 3.1-8.50 x 10^3/microL) with 9% bands, lactic acid 3.3 mmol/L (ref: 0.5-2.0 mmol/L), anion gap 15, AST 113 U/L, ALT 153 U/L. Peak liver enzymes: ALT 721 IU/L (normal < 55 U/L), AST 305 IU/L (normal < 35 U/L), GGT 114 IU/L (ref: 12-64 IU/L), albumin 2.7 g/dL (ref: 3.4-4.8 g/dL), alkaline phosphatase 49 IU/L (ref: 56-119 IU/L), INR 1.5. Inflammatory and coagulation markers: Procalcitonin 0.28 ng/mL (ref: < 0.05 ng/mL), D-dimer 12.89 mg/dL (ref: < 0.5 mg/dL), fibrinogen normal. Toxicology & viral serology: Acetaminophen level < 0.6 microg/mL, blood alcohol negative; acute viral hepatitis panel negative. Abdominal ultrasound (day 4): Normal liver and gallbladder parenchyma. Echocardiogram: Normal left ventricular systolic function (ejection fraction 55-65%) with normal right ventricular pressure and no right ventricular strain.
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography: Bilateral acute pulmonary emboli with possible right heart strain and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Abdominal and pelvic CT (day 8): Mild splenomegaly with normal liver and gallbladder.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia complicated by acute bilateral pulmonary thromboembolism, alongside acute hepatocellular injury secondary to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reactivation versus drug-induced liver injury. Infectious and autoimmune evaluation: Autoimmune markers (anti-smooth muscle antibodies, SLE panel, vasculitis panel) were negative; EBV reactivation was confirmed by positive EBV VCA IgM, EBV VCA IgG, EBV EA IgG, EBV NA IgG, and positive EBV PCR; CMV IgG was positive (> 10) with negative CMV IgM.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with therapeutic unfractionated heparin infusion, systemic dexamethasone, and supportive albuterol nebulization. Antiviral remdesivir was started and discontinued on hospital day 2 due to worsening transaminases. Empiric IV antibiotics (vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam) were de-escalated to oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and then discontinued. Transaminases improved, oxygen requirements resolved, and the patient was discharged home on room air.

raw_case_text:
A 30-year-old man presented with a background of end-stage renal failure secondary to birth asphyxia and with a donation after brainstem death renal transplant (baseline creatinine 290 micromol/l), maintained on sirolimus and tacrolimus. This was the patient's second transplant, the first being complicated by graft rejection, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and requiring graft nephrectomy in 2013. The current transplant had taken place >1 year before the current presentation, of which he had had one episode of BK viral nephropathy treated with CSs. He had been stable after this, with no significant infections. He presented with a 14-day history of feeling unwell with fevers, and a 5-day history of a cough, sore throat and difficulty breathing.
Initial oxygen saturation was 80% on room air, which improved to 100% on 35% oxygen via a venturi face mask. His blood pressure was 127/73 mmHg, heart rate 95 beats/min, temperature 38 C and respiratory rate 21 breaths/min. Chest X-ray (CXR) showed bilateral patchy consolidation, and nasopharyngeal swab (NPS) confirmed SARS-CoV-2. Blood tests revealed ferritin of 24617 microg/l, creatinine 519 micromol/l and CRP 92 mg/l.
Oxygen was titrated to keep his saturations >94%, and he was initiated on co-amoxiclav. After 2 days, with increasing oxygen requirements and progressive CXR consolidation, he was transferred to the ICU, where he was commenced on continuous positive airway pressure. The sirolimus was stopped, but he remained on tacrolimus. Ferritin at the time was 23 788 microg/l, CRP 73 mg/l and procalcitonin 17.27 mug/l (normal range <0.5 mug/l). Microscopy from blood cultures and urine cultures was negative, and CMV and EBV viraemias remained very low level. Given the increasing oxygen requirement and persistent inflammatory state, anakinra 200 mg i.v. was initiated (Table 1). A marked improvement in ferritin was seen within 2 days; CRP steadily decreased (Fig. 1), creatinine improved, and his respiratory effort stabilized. After 3 days of continuous positive airway pressure, he was weaned off and stepped down to the ward. Anakinra i.v. was stopped on day 10, when the ferritin was 4969 microg/l. He was discharged on day 12 with a creatinine of 371 micromol/l and CRP 7 mg/l and remained on tacrolimus.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old male renal transplant recipient presenting with a 14-day history of fevers and a 5-day history of cough, sore throat, and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 30-year-old male renal transplant recipient presented with a 14-day history of malaise and fevers, and a 5-day history of cough, sore throat, and progressive dyspnea. Initial room-air oxygen saturation was profoundly reduced at 80%, requiring 35% oxygen via Venturi mask. Over the initial 48 hours of admission, oxygen requirements escalated alongside progressive radiographic consolidation, necessitating transfer to the intensive care unit for continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

Prior BK virus nephropathy treated with corticosteroids; baseline serum creatinine: 290 mcmol/L. Immunosuppressive regimen: sirolimus and tacrolimus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fevers, malaise, cough, sore throat, and shortness of breath. Negative for gross hematuria or lower urinary tract symptoms. Home medications: sirolimus and tacrolimus. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.0 °C, blood pressure: 127/73 mmHg, heart rate: 95 beats/min, respiratory rate: 21 breaths/min, SpO2: 80% on room air (correcting to 100% on 35% Venturi face mask). Lungs: bilateral coarse breath sounds with increased work of breathing.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum ferritin: 24,617 mcg/L (peaked at 23,788 mcg/L in ICU; declining to 4,969 mcg/L by day 10); serum creatinine: 519 mcmol/L (baseline: 290 mcmol/L; improving to 371 mcmol/L at discharge); C-reactive protein (CRP): 92 mg/L (ICU: 73 mg/L; declining to 7 mg/L at discharge); procalcitonin: 17.27 mcg/L (reference: <0.5 mcg/L). Blood and urine bacterial cultures: negative. Viral surveillance: low-level CMV and EBV viremias. Chest X-ray: bilateral patchy consolidations showing interval radiographic worsening prior to CPAP.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute graft dysfunction and hyperferritinemic hyperinflammatory cytokine storm (secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis-like syndrome) in a renal allograft recipient, confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Bacterial superinfections ruled out by sterile blood and urine cultures. Management & Outcome: Initiated on empiric intravenous co-amoxiclav, noninvasive respiratory support with CPAP for 3 days, and discontinuation of sirolimus while maintaining tacrolimus. Targeted anti-cytokine therapy with intravenous anakinra (200 mg daily) was administered for 10 days, resulting in rapid decline of serum ferritin and CRP, stabilization of allograft function (creatinine 371 mcmol/L), successful weaning from CPAP, and discharge on hospital day 12.

raw_case_text:
A 9-year-old girl was presented to our hospital on referral from a peripheral hospital with a one-week history of darkish discoloration of both feet and her left hand and a six-day history of a purulent feculent discharge from an exploratory laparotomy wound. She had presented to the referring hospital eight days earlier, with a two-week history of high-grade fever and a one-week history of a generalized abdominal pain and diarrhea. She had an exploratory laparotomy at the referring hospital. Intraoperative findings include a feculent intraperitoneal collection and a single perforation on the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum. An intraoperative diagnosis of perforated typhoid enteritis was made, and the perforation was closed in two layers. One unit of blood was transfused postoperatively. On the first day of postsurgery, the patient developed darkish discoloration of the left hand and both feet which were associated with pain. She was not a known sickle cell disease patient and had no past histories suggestive of intermittent claudication. On the second day of postoperation, a purulent discharge from the lower aspect of the laparotomy wound was noted, and there was darkening of the feet and duskiness of the distal one-third of both legs. Due to the progressive worsening of the patient's condition, she was referred to our hospital on the seventh day of postoperation.
At presentation to our unit, she was acutely ill looking, febrile with a temperature of 38.1 C, dehydrated, not pale, and anicteric. Her respiratory rate was 30/minute with reduced air entry and coarse crepitations in both lower lung fields. She had a pulse rate of 130/minute, which was regular and of moderate volume. Only first and second heart sounds were heard. Her abdomen was full, and did not move with respiration, and had a midline dressing soaked with a feculent fluid. There was a complete wound dehiscence of the abdominal wound, with both edges being necrotic. There was no bowel evisceration. Both feet were dark and cold, with duskiness of the skin of the distal one-third of both legs (Figure 1). There was loss of sensation in the feet and absent dorsalis pedis, anterior and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally. Popliteal pulses were palpable bilaterally. The left hand was dark, dry, and shriveled up to the wrist. The radial pulse was however present. The right upper limb was normal. A diagnosis of complete wound dehiscence, fecal fistula with peripheral gangrene of both feet and left hand in a patient who had surgery for typhoid intestinal perforation, was made. The patient was commenced on intravenous (IV) fluid resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole). She was placed on nil per os (NPO) and nasogastric decompression of the stomach. A consult was sent to the orthopedic surgery team who advised that the gangrene be allowed to demarcate before any decision could be taken on the limbs.
Hematological investigations after fluid resuscitation showed a hematocrit of 23.9% and a white blood cell count of 18.9 x 109/l and a hemoglobin genotype of AS. She was transfused with 200 ml of packed cells, in preparation for a wound exploration. She was however noted to be making scanty urine, and due to her unstable clinical condition, the surgery was postponed while IV fluid resuscitation and local wound care continued. By the fourth day of admission in our unit, the left upper limb gangrene had extended to the distal forearm, while on the lower limbs, the gangrene had extended to the middle aspect of the legs. The patient's condition continued to deteriorate in spite of efforts at resuscitation. She died on the eighth day of admission in our unit.

She underwent exploratory laparotomy at a referring hospital 8 days prior, where feculent intraperitoneal fluid and a single antimesenteric terminal ileal perforation were closed in two layers, followed by 1 unit blood transfusion. On postoperative day 1, she developed painful dark discoloration of both feet and the left hand. On postoperative day 2, purulent wound discharge was noted, with progressive darkening and duskiness extending up the distal one-third of both legs, prompting transfer on postoperative day 7.

Respiratory: rate 30/min, reduced air entry and coarse crepitations in bilateral lower lung fields. Cardiovascular: pulse rate 130/min (regular, moderate volume), normal S1 and S2. Abdomen: full, did not move with respiration, midline dressing soaked with feculent fluid; complete wound dehiscence with necrotic edges; no bowel evisceration. Extremities: both feet dark and cold with duskiness of skin over distal one-third of bilateral legs; absent sensation in feet; dorsalis pedis, anterior and posterior tibial pulses absent bilaterally; popliteal pulses palpable bilaterally. assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Complete abdominal wound dehiscence, fecal fistula, and symmetrical peripheral gangrene of both feet and left hand secondary to septic shock following surgery for perforated typhoid enteritis. Managed with intravenous fluid resuscitation, NPO, nasogastric decompression, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole), and transfusion of 200 mL packed red blood cells. Orthopedic consult advised conservative observation pending gangrene demarcation. Surgical exploration was postponed due to oliguria and hemodynamic instability. Gangrene extended to the left distal forearm and bilateral mid-legs. Despite resuscitation, she deteriorated and died of septic shock on day 8 of admission.

raw_case_text:
Patient information: the patient was a 17-year-old female who is a known asthmatic and presented to the emergency room with a week s history of persistent post-prandial epigastric pain associated with vomiting, diarrhea, and fever. She had reported to a peripheral clinic where she was given analgesics without relief.
Clinical results: at presentation, the patient was lethargic, had a tinge of jaundice, pallor, and had a mild tenderness in the epigastrium, with no palpable abdominal organ. Her temperature was 37.8 C and her pulse rate was 109 beats per minute. Blood pressure (BP) and oxygen saturation were normal. Laboratory results showed malaria parasites of 600,000/mul, reduced haemoglobin level and low platelets, and normal renal function test (Table 2).
Diagnostic approach and therapeutic intervention: a diagnosis of severe malaria with thrombocytopenia and anaemia was made. The patient was started on IV artesunate 125 mg at 0, 12, 24 hours and IV paracetamol 1g every 8 hours for 24 hours and subsequently continued with artemether/lumefantrine 80/480 twice daily for 3 days. The patient s temperature, BP, pulse rate, and other vital signs were monitored every 4 hours, as the patient s temperature continued to rise. Within 12 hours, the highest temperature recorded was 39 C, the BP dropped to 68/38 mmHg and the patient started experiencing respiratory distress. On examination, the patient had a respiratory rate of 35 cycles per minute and flaring of the ala nasi. Chest examination revealed adequate air entry bilaterally, vesicular breath sounds, and bilateral wheezes. Oxygen saturation on room air was 45%. The impression made was severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) with a differential diagnosis of septic shock, and acute exacerbation of asthma, to rule out COVID-19. The patient was propped up in bed at 45 C, given oxygen at 10 liters/minute via a non-rebreather mask, and intravenous paracetamol, and was resuscitated with intravenous fluids. A urethral catheter was passed to monitor urine output. She was nebulized with 5 mg of salbutamol for 3 cycles and was given 200 mg of intravenous Hydrocortisone. Oxygen saturation improved to between 75-77% on oxygen, BP 132/78 mmHg, and respiratory rate 40 cpm. The patient was started on intravenous ceftriaxone 2g daily and nebulization with 5 mg of salbutamol was continued.
On the third day of admission, dyspnea had improved, the temperature was 37 C, the pulse rate was 111 bpm, and oxygen saturation of 96% on the non-rebreather mask with the patient propped at an angle of 45 . A chest X-ray taken showed heterogenous opacifications at the upper right lung zones and homogenous opacifications at the lower lung zones. Repeated blood film for malaria parasites showed a reduction in the parasite load (Table 2). The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 100 ml/fall/hr.
On day four of admission, the temperature was 36.7 C, pulse rate 132 bpm, blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation was 91%. The impression made was severe malaria complicated by thrombocytopenia, intravascular hemolysis, and acute respiratory distress syndrome with a differential diagnosis of COVID-19. Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal samples were taken for COVID-19 testing and the ESR and full blood count were repeated. At this point, the patient was started on tab azithromycin 500 mg immediately and 250 mg daily for 7 days, IV dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 72 hours then tab dexamethasone 6mg daily for 7 days, tab zinc 40 mg daily for 14 days and tab vitamin C 1000 mg daily for 14 days.
On admission day 5, the patient had no new complaints. Vital signs recorded were a temperature of 37.2 C, pulse rate of 83 bpm, blood pressure of 89/62 mmHg, respiratory rate of 32 cpm, and 26 cpm off oxygen and on oxygen, respectively. Oxygen saturation was between 82-84% off oxygen and 96-97% on a non-rebreather mask at 10 L/min. Examination of other systems was unremarkable. All medications were continued.
On day 6, ESR of 100 ml fall/hour. The full blood count showed raised WBC, low haemoglobin level, and higher platelets than on day one (Table 2). The patient s RT-PCR for COVID-19 was confirmed positive on day 9 of admission. The patient had no complaints and no other symptoms. The patient was jaundiced and warm to touch on examination. Vital signs were a temperature of 36.6 C, pulse rate of 101bpm and blood pressure of 105/75mmHg. Air entry was reduced in the lower lung zones with no added sounds. The rest of the examination was unremarkable. Patient was prescribed tab folic acid 5 mg daily, tab cefuroxime 500 mg every 12 hours, tab artemether/lumefantrine 80/480 mg every 12 hours, tab azithromycin 250 mg daily, syp bioferon 15 ml every 8 hours and tab zinc 30 mg daily.
Follow-up: the patient was discharged home on day 17 post-admission. The patient did not report back with any condition.
Informed consent: this was obtained from the adult patient and parents of the child. Approval was obtained from the authorities of the University Hospital, KNUST to use data from the patient s medical records. Privacy, safety, and confidentiality of the patients were strictly ensured.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old female presenting with persistent post-prandial epigastric pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and fever for one week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 17-year-old female presented with a one-week history of persistent post-prandial epigastric pain associated with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. She had attended an outpatient peripheral clinic where analgesics afforded no relief. Within 12 hours of hospital admission, her fever escalated to 39 C, blood pressure precipitously dropped to 68/38 mmHg, and she developed severe respiratory distress with dyspnea, nasal flaring, bilateral wheezing, and profound hypoxemia (SpO2 45% on room air). She required emergent fluid resuscitation, in-bed propping at 45 degrees, and non-rebreather mask oxygenation. Respiratory symptoms gradually improved by day 3, and she remained stable through discharge.

At 12 hours: temperature 39 C, blood pressure 68/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 35 cycles/min, flaring of ala nasi, bilateral vesicular breath sounds with diffuse wheezes, SpO2 45% on room air (improving to 75-77% on 10 L/min non-rebreather mask, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 40 cpm). Day 3: temperature 37 C, pulse 111 bpm, SpO2 96% on non-rebreather mask. Day 4: temperature 36.7 C, pulse 132 bpm, BP 90/60 mmHg, SpO2 91%. Day 5: temperature 37.2 C, pulse 83 bpm, BP 89/62 mmHg, RR 32 cpm off O2 and 26 cpm on O2, SpO2 82-84% off O2 and 96-97% on non-rebreather mask at 10 L/min. Day 6: temperature 36.6 C, pulse 101 bpm, BP 105/75 mmHg, warm, jaundiced, reduced air entry at bilateral lung bases without adventitious sounds.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 100 mm/hr (100 ml/fall/hr). Chest X-ray: heterogeneous opacifications in right upper lung zone and homogeneous opacifications in bilateral lower lung zones. Full blood count on day 6: leukocytosis, low hemoglobin, and improving platelet count.
