assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by hyperparasitemia, severe thrombocytopenia, intravascular hemolysis, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), with concurrent COVID-19 infection and acute asthma exacerbation.
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial peripheral blood film showing Plasmodium falciparum with 600,000 parasites/muL, with sequential smears showing progressive parasite reduction and clearance; nasopharyngeal RT-PCR positive for SARS-CoV-2 on day 9.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with intravenous artesunate 125 mg at 0, 12, and 24 hours followed by oral artemether/lumefantrine 80/480 mg twice daily for 3 days (second course administered on day 9), IV paracetamol 1 g q8h, IV fluid resuscitation, urinary catheterization, high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask (10 L/min), salbutamol nebulization (5 mg for 3 cycles and continued), IV hydrocortisone 200 mg, IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily, oral azithromycin (500 mg load, then 250 mg daily for 7 days), IV dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 72 hours transitioned to oral dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 7 days, oral zinc, vitamin C, folic acid 5 mg daily, cefuroxime 500 mg q12h, and iron syrup (Bioferon). Oxygen was successfully weaned and the patient was discharged in good health on hospital day 17.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy, Caucasian, 18-year-old man presented at our Department of Emergency Medicine for watery diarrhoea, high-grade fever, and severe malaise. Stool samples performed by the family physician had been negative, including testing for Salmonella species (spp.). Five days after returning from travelling to various countries, e.g. India and Nepal, he developed fever, chills, cough, sore throat, and headaches, which lasted for 3 days before diarrhoea started. The total duration of the disease on admission was 7 days.
day 1: Germany
day 2-4: Kingdom of Bahrain
day 4-8: United Arab Emirates
(Dubai: day 4-6; Abu Dhabi: day 6-8)
day 8-11: Kathmandu, Nepal
day 11-13: Delhi, India
day 13-16: Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
day 16-18: Singapore
day 19-23: Melbourne, Australia
day 24-26: Taipei, Taiwan
day 26-28: Manila, Philippines
day 28-29: Kuwait City, Kuwait
During his travels, he experienced gastroenteritis while he was in Delhi (oral antibiotic therapy and electrolyte solution resulted in cure after 3 days), and multiple mosquito bites in malaria-endemic countries. He denied tick bites and animal contact of all kinds. Although he had received pre-travel medical advice, he did not respect alimentary precautions (he preferred vegetables and salad in local restaurants), and had refused malaria prophylaxis due to fear of side effects. The patient did not receive any vaccination against cholera or typhoid fever.
Apart from signs of exsiccosis, a thorough physical examination was unremarkable. The patient was fully conscious, had a relative bradycardia (95/min), hypotension (95/60 mmHg), high-grade fever (39 C), and normal oxygen saturation. Electrocardiogram was normal and abdominal ultrasound was consistent with diagnosis of gastroenteritis. A differential blood count demonstrated a normal white blood count, aneosinophilia and discrete thrombocytopenia (126/microl, normal: 140-200/microl). Laboratory examination revealed an elevated CRP level (93 mg/dl; normal: <5 mg/dl) and slightly elevated ALT (48 U/l, normal: <40 U/l), AST (59 U/l, normal: <41 U/l) and LDH (461 U/l, normal: <250 U/l). Creatinine levels, blood gas and urine analysis were normal. Malaria was ruled out using thick smears and rapid testing. Blood, urine, and stool cultures were performed. The latter two showed no growth.
Due to suspected typhoid fever, we started intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g once daily), fluid supplementation (2.500 ml per day), and oral antipyretics (750 mg metamizole four times daily). Liver enzymes increased to ALT 97 U/l and AST 83 U/l on day 8 after disease onset; to ALT 196 U/l and AST 165 U/l on day 9 after disease onset. Diarrhoea subsided to 15-20 times per day; fever subsided as well. On day 11 after disease onset, blood cultures revealed Gram-negative bacteria. By the time, the patient's condition had not improved. We suspected a Gram-negative sepsis and changed the antibiotic regime to intravenous meropenem, 1 g three times per day. One day later, Salmonella enterica Serovar Typhi was identified (susceptibility testing: Table 2 (Tab. 2)), and the therapy was continued with meropenem. Liver enzymes peaked on day 12 after the onset of initial symptoms: LDH 756 U/l, ALT 544 U/l, AST 263 U/l, alkaline phosphatase (AP) 168 U/l (normal: 55-149 U/l), and Gamma-GT 196 U/l (normal: <60 U/l). Bilirubin remained normal; abdominal ultrasound displayed mild hepato- and splenomegaly. We ruled out hepatitis A/B/C/D/E (serologic tests), entero-haemorrhagic Escherichia coli, and amoebic liver disease (stool samples), and continued the treatment regime. On day 16 after disease onset (day 9 of antibiotic therapy), the patient's condition improved, both his body temperature and his liver enzymes decreased. On day 14 of treatment (4 days ceftriaxone; 10 days meropenem), the patient had fully recovered (including complete normalization of laboratory parameters). One week after treatment, 3 stool samples (obtained on 3 different days) were negative for S. Typhi.
During a family visit in Dresden 14 days after completion of initial treatment, the patient was hospitalised again (Department of Infectious Diseases and Tropical Medicine, Stadtisches Klinikum Dresden) for high-grade fever, crampy abdominal pain, and watery diarrhoea. Abdominal ultrasound revealed extended mesenteric lymph nodes. The colleagues ruled out schistosomiasis and HIV (serology), as well as helminthic infections, other parasites, and Clostridium difficile (stool analyses). Blood cultures revealed S. Typhi (susceptibility testing: Table 2 (Tab. 2)). Urine analysis, performed because of dysuria and pollakiuria, yielded a urinary tract infection (UTI) due to Escherichia coli (4-MRGN (German Classification of Gram-negative bacteria indicating resistance to 4 clinically relevant groups of bactericidal antibiotics: cephalosporine and acylureidopenicilline antibiotics, carbapenems and fluoroquinolones), OXA-48 positive; Colony forming units: 106/ml).
Consequently, the colleagues administered a combination antibiotic therapy according to susceptibility testing using intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g daily dose maintained for 28 days to address relapse) and oral sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (800/160 mg daily dose, maintained for 10 days to address the UTI). The patient fully recovered. Again, 3 stool samples following treatment were negative for S. Typhi. The patient has been free of relapse for 9 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old Caucasian male presented with watery diarrhea, high-grade fever, and severe malaise 5 days after returning from international travel.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Five days after returning from a multi-country trip (including Bahrain, UAE, Nepal, India, Malaysia, Singapore, Australia, Taiwan, Philippines, and Kuwait), he developed fever, chills, cough, sore throat, and headaches lasting 3 days, followed by watery diarrhea (disease duration of 7 days on admission). Outpatient stool testing by a family physician was negative. Fourteen days after completing initial treatment, he experienced a disease relapse with high-grade fever, crampy abdominal pain, watery diarrhea, dysuria, and pollakiuria leading to rehospitalization.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Traveled across multiple countries in the preceding month; experienced an episode of gastroenteritis in Delhi treated with oral antibiotics and rehydration for 3 days. Multiple mosquito bites in malaria-endemic areas; denied tick bites or animal contact. Did not follow alimentary precautions (ate raw salads/vegetables); refused malaria prophylaxis; unimmunized against endemic travel diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Chills, cough, sore throat, headaches, severe malaise, watery diarrhea; dysuria and pollakiuria during relapse.

objective.physical_examination: Signs of exsiccosis (dehydration); relative bradycardia (pulse rate 95/min with high fever 39 °C), blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, normal oxygen saturation. Fully conscious. Remainder of physical examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood count: normal; aneosinophilia; discrete thrombocytopenia (platelet count 126/microL, normal 140-200/microL). CRP: elevated at 93 mg/dL (normal <5 mg/dL); LDH: 461 U/L (peaked at 756 U/L on day 12). LFTs: ALT 48 U/L (rose to 97 U/L on day 8, 196 U/L on day 9, peaked at 544 U/L on day 12); AST 59 U/L (rose to 83 U/L on day 8, 165 U/L on day 9, peaked at 263 U/L on day 12); alkaline phosphatase peaked at 168 U/L; GGT peaked at 196 U/L; normal bilirubin. Creatinine, blood gas, and initial urine analysis normal. Malaria ruled out by thick smears and rapid tests. Hepatitis A/B/C/D/E serology negative. Initial stool and urine cultures showed no growth; stool negative for enterohemorrhagic E. coli, amoebic disease, parasites, and C. difficile; HIV and schistosomiasis negative. Abdominal ultrasound: initially consistent with gastroenteritis; follow-up showed mild hepatosplenomegaly; relapse ultrasound showed extended mesenteric lymph nodes.
objective.advanced_workup: Electrocardiogram: normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi bacteremia) with subsequent relapse and concurrent complicated urinary tract infection due to 4-MRGN OXA-48-positive Escherichia coli (10^6 CFU/mL). Initial blood cultures revealed Gram-negative bacilli on day 11, identified as Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Repeat blood cultures at readmission again yielded S. Typhi. Initial treatment: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily, IV fluid hydration (2500 mL/day), and oral metamizole (750 mg 4 times daily); switched on day 11 to IV meropenem 1 g 3 times daily for 10 days (total 14 days antibiotics: 4 days ceftriaxone, 10 days meropenem), resulting in full recovery and 3 negative post-treatment stool cultures. For relapse and UTI: combination regimen of IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily for 28 days and oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (800/160 mg daily) for 10 days. Fully recovered with 3 subsequent stool cultures negative for S. Typhi; free of relapse at 9-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old HIV-positive male, who was not on antiretroviral treatment, presented with a right-sided conjunctival mass for an uncertain period of time. On examination, he was in good health and did not have any soft-tissue masses elsewhere. Ophthalmic examination revealed right eye hyperaemia together with a raised conjunctival lesion noted on the medial aspect, extending on to the cornea. He was found to have normal vision. The clinical assessment was that of an invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
The patient underwent a monoblock excision of the mass with cryotherapy applied to the base. Clinically, the margins were thought to be free of tumour. The tissue was submitted for histopathological evaluation. The patient had not returned for his follow-up appointment.
The excised specimen submitted for histopathological examination consisted of a single, unorientated fragment of tissue measuring 7 mm x 4 mm x 3 mm. The specimen was processed in its entirety.
Microscopic examination revealed a single portion of tissue surfaced by intact squamous mucosa. At one edge of the surface mucosa, mild dysplasia was noted. Within the underlying tissue, however, a spindle cell proliferation was present. This proliferation consisted of fascicles of spindle cells displaying varying degrees of atypia. The cells were large and hyperchromatic. Focally, tumour cells contained perinuclear vacuoles. Mitotic activity was apparent with up to 14 mitotic figures noted in 10 high-powered fields (Figure 1). Definitive lymphovascular and perineural infiltration was not documented in the submitted specimen. The tumour measured 2 mm in thickness and was clear of the peripheral surgical resection margins.
Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratins (AE1/3, MNF116, 34BE12, CK5/6) and a p63 stain were negative, thus excluding the most likely diagnosis of a spindle cell carcinoma. Melanocytic markers (S100, MiTF, Melan-A and HMB-45) were negative and excluded a diagnosis of a malignant melanoma. Kaposi sarcoma was excluded with negative staining for Human Herpes Virus-8 (HHV8) and CD31. A desmin stain was positive in the neoplastic cells. Smooth muscle actin (SMA), muscle-specific actin (MSA) and h-Caldesmon stains were positive in tumour cells (Figure 2). Myogenin and Myo-D1 stains were both negative, thus excluding a rhabdomyosarcoma. Epstein-Barr encoding region (EBER) in-situ hybridisation was negative. A final diagnosis of a conjunctival leiomyosarcoma was rendered.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old male presenting with a painless, raised mass on the right conjunctiva of uncertain duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a slowly enlarging, painless mass involving the medial aspect of the right eye for an uncertain duration. He reported no visual disturbance, ocular trauma, foreign body sensation, or prior ophthalmologic interventions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, untreated (not currently receiving antiretroviral therapy); otherwise in good health with no known chronic medical conditions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Right ocular hyperemia and visible growth; denies eye pain, diplopia, reduced visual acuity, systemic soft-tissue masses, constitutional symptoms, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: General physical examination: Good general health, no peripheral lymphadenopathy or cutaneous soft-tissue lesions. Ophthalmologic examination: Visual acuity normal bilaterally; right eye demonstrated conjunctival hyperemia with a raised, fleshy conjunctival lesion on the medial aspect extending across the limbus onto the cornea.
objective.advanced_workup: Surgical pathology of excised conjunctival lesion (7 mm x 4 mm x 3 mm, tumor thickness 2 mm): Histopathology demonstrated intact overlying squamous mucosa with focal mild dysplasia, overlying a fascicular spindle cell proliferation exhibiting nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, focal perinuclear vacuolization, and high mitotic activity (up to 14 mitoses per 10 high-power fields), with clear surgical margins and absence of lymphovascular or perineural invasion. Immunohistochemistry: Positive for desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), muscle-specific actin (MSA), and h-caldesmon; negative for cytokeratins (AE1/3, MNF116, 34betaE12, CK5/6), p63, melanocytic markers (S100, MiTF, Melan-A, HMB-45), vascular/Kaposi markers (HHV-8, CD31), skeletal muscle markers (myogenin, Myo-D1), and Epstein-Barr virus-encoded RNA (EBER in-situ hybridization).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Primary conjunctival leiomyosarcoma (smooth muscle malignancy) in an untreated HIV-positive male; squamous cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, Kaposi sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma were ruled out by immunohistochemistry.
Plan & Outcome: Managed with complete wide local monoblock surgical excision of the conjunctival mass with adjuvant cryotherapy applied to the surgical bed, achieving microscopically negative resection margins. The patient was scheduled for routine oncologic and ophthalmologic surveillance, but was subsequently lost to follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old male presented to the hospital emergency with fever associated with chills for the past 5-6 days. He also had complaints of abdominal pain and vomiting. The patients did not have any complaints of rash, joint pains, cough, difficulty in breathing, and any feature suggestive of urinary tract infection. The history of seizures and bleeding from any site was ruled out. There was no past history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, tuberculosis, smoking, or alcohol intake. The patient did not give a history of previous treatment or self-medication. The patient resided in a slum area in east Delhi with a drain near his house.
On examination, the patient was sick and his general condition was poor. He was conscious and oriented and had severe pallor. His heart rate was 110 beats/min, respiratory rate was 16 breaths/min, and blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg. On per abdominal examination, abdomen was soft and nontender. Hepatomegaly and massive splenomegaly was detected. On central nervous system examination, patient was lethargic, but no other abnormality was present. On chest and cardiovascular examination, no significant abnormality was detected. On the basis of these findings, a provisional diagnosis of acute undifferentiated fever was made with a differential diagnosis of malaria, dengue fever, and enteric fever. The patient was admitted in the department of internal medicine, and the case was further investigated.
The hemoglobin of the patient was 5 g/dL, total leukocyte count was 3,900/mm3, and platelet count was 78,000/mm3 on Day 0 and 30,000/mm3 on Day 2. Peripheral blood smear (PBS) showed microcytic hypochromic anemia with tear drop cells and thrombocytopenia. Micro-hematuria was detected on urine routine examination. His liver and renal function tests were within normal limits. Tube Widal test titers were <1:40 for TO, TH, and AH. Serum RK-39 was negative. Chinkungunya immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay was negative. Dengue immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (NIV, Pune, India) was reactive. Rapid malaria antigen test (RMAT) (Ybio, Goa, India) on Day 0 was positive for P. vivax only. However, on PBS examination, rings of P. vivax and rings and gametocytes of P. falciparum were seen. Parasite density for P. falciparum was found to be 2% (Figure 1). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay confirmed the presence of both the species (P. falciparum and P. vivax) in the patient. Abdominal ultrasound showed enlarged spleen (30 cm in size), mild hepatomegaly, and ascites. Bilateral pleural effusion was also noted.
A final diagnosis of mixed malarial infection (P. vivax and P. falciparum) with dengue fever coinfection with pancytopenia was made.
The patient was prescribed intravenous (IV) artesunate 2.4 mg/kg on Day 0 then at 12 h and 24 h. He was also administered IV ceftriaxone 600 mg b.d., IV fluids, IV paracetamol, and IV ondansetron and pantoprazole as supportive management on Day 0 of admission. The next day, the patient was switched to oral ACT (1 tablet of artesunate 200 mg and 2 tablets of sulfadoxine/pyrimthamine 750 mg/37.5 mg on Day 1 followed by artesunate 200 mg for next 2 days).
By Day 3 of treatment, the patient's condition had improved, but fever persisted (>37.5 C).
RMAT and PBS were reperformed on Day 3. On PBS, ruptured schizonts of P. vivax, rings and gametocytes of P. falciparum were seen, with a rise in parasitemia to 5%. (Figure 1). RMAT was now positive for both P. vivax and P. falciparum.
Unfortunately, the patient left the hospital against medical advice and was lost to follow-up.
As the patient had rise in parasitemia with fever of (>37.5 C) on Day 3 of treatment, he was diagnosed as a case of early treatment failure (ETF) according to the National Vector Borne Diseases Control Programme guidelines. The patient's blood spots were inoculated on Whatman filter paper no. 1 for further molecular analysis.
Genomic DNA extraction of the patient sample collected on Day 0 and Day 3 was done from filter paper blood spots using a QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (QiagenInc., Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Diagnostic confirmation of Plasmodium species was done by 18S rRNA PCR assay, which confirmed the results of microscopy and RMAT, showing mixed infections of P. falciparum and P. vivax in the patient (Figure 2). The samples were also genotyped for the drug resistance genes viz: chloroquine resistance (pfcrt), multidrug resistance (pfmd-r1), sulfadoxine (pfdhps), pyrimethamine (pfdhfr), and artemisinin resistance (keltch 13). Single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in pfcrt, pfmdr1, pfdhfr, pfdhps, and keltch 13 genes were assessed by PCR-RFLP and sequencing as described previously. Restriction site for ApoI enzyme for K76T mutation associated with chloroquine resistance in the pfcrt gene and N86Y SNP for restriction enzyme AflIII in pfmdr-1 gene were seen in both the samples of the patient (Figure 2). Two mutations in pfdhfr gene at C59R and S108N were observed and there was one mutation in the pdhps gene at A437G. One SNP was seen on aligning with wild-type sequences of pfdhfr (GenBank accession no. 9221804) and pfdhps (GenBank accession no. 2655294) using Clustal W of the BioEdit 7.0 and MEGA (Molecular Evolutionary Genetics Analysis; http://www.megasoftware.net/) 4.0 programs (Table 1). Since this case was diagnosed as a case of ETF and artesunate resistance was suspected, sequence analysis to detect the presence of any SNP in kelch13 was also carried out. However, no SNPs were detected in this region (Table 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever with chills and rigors for 1.5 months, and abdominal pain with distension for one month.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 1.5-month history of high-grade intermittent fever associated with chills and rigors. Over the preceding month, he developed progressive abdominal distension, dull abdominal pain, and lower extremity swelling.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of alcohol consumption for 10 years; no known chronic medical illness. Occupation: Daily wage laborer residing in Delhi, India.

objective.physical_examination: General appearance: Severe mucosal pallor, icterus, and bilateral pitting pedal edema. Abdominal examination: Distended with positive shifting dullness and fluid thrill; non-tender hepatosplenomegaly with spleen palpable 20 cm and liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margins.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 5 g/dL; total leukocyte count 3,900/mm3; platelet count 78,000/mm3 on Day 0, falling to 30,000/mm3 on Day 2. Peripheral blood smear: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with tear drop cells and thrombocytopenia. Urinalysis: Micro-hematuria. Liver function tests and renal function tests: Within normal limits. Serologies: Tube Widal titers <1:40 for TO, TH, and AH; serum rK-39 test negative; Chikungunya IgM ELISA negative; Dengue IgM ELISA reactive. Abdominal ultrasound: Splenomegaly (spleen length 30 cm), mild hepatomegaly, ascites, and bilateral pleural effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Mixed Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax malaria coinfection with Dengue fever presenting with pancytopenia and early treatment failure (ETF). Day 0 rapid malaria antigen test (RMAT) was positive for P. vivax; peripheral blood smear demonstrated P. vivax rings, P. falciparum rings and gametocytes (P. falciparum parasitemia 2%), and 18S rRNA PCR confirmed mixed species infection. Visceral leishmaniasis (rK-39), enteric fever (Widal), and Chikungunya were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg (at 0, 12, and 24 hours), IV ceftriaxone 600 mg BID, IV fluids, paracetamol, and supportive therapy, transitioned on Day 1 to oral ACT (artesunate 200 mg plus sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine 750/37.5 mg, then artesunate 200 mg daily for 2 days). On Day 3, persistent fever (>37.5 °C) and repeat smear showed ruptured P. vivax schizonts, P. falciparum rings/gametocytes, and parasitemia rising to 5% with RMAT positive for both species, fulfilling ETF criteria. Drug resistance genotyping demonstrated pfcrt K76T, pfmdr1 N86Y, pfdhfr C59R/S108N, and pfdhps A437G mutations (kelch13 wild-type). Patient left against medical advice on Day 3.

raw_case_text:
A two months old Saudi Arabian male infant was admitted to the pediatric ward of maternity and children's hospital, Buraidah, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for the management of multiple ulcers on his face. The ulcers was observed by the parents at the age of one month and progressively increased in size with no history of fever. He was the third child of healthy unrelated boduin Saudi Arabian parents, the mother's age was 35 and the father's age was 40. There was no history of perinatal or postnatal complication. The child was delivered in a tent in the desert where his parents live.
On physical examination, there was severe disfigurement of the face with 3 crusty ulcers Surrounded by a notable erythematous reaction, the biggest one presents on the right cheek and measures 2 x 2 cm. The second ulcer presents on the right lower eye lid and measures 1 x 1.5 cm. The third ulcer presents on the forehead and measures 0.5 x .5 cm (figure 1). The examination also revealed no lymphadenphathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
On first look to the face of our case, it was difficult to recognize the facial features of Down syndrome because of severe disfigurement of the face, the ulcers were surrounded by extensive edema that caused the eyes to be closed most of the times so the upslanting palpebral fissures which is a very characteristic feature of Down syndrome was not so obvious, in addition the presence of an ulcer near the nasal bridge added more difficulty to recognize the facial features but the presence of hypotonia, flat occiput, short neck, low set ears, short broad hands; clinodactyly of fifth finger; bilateral simian creases of the hands and gap between the first and second toes, directed us to request karyotyping. The result of karyotyping confirmed our suspicion and the diagnosis of Down syndrome was confirmed.
Blood count and immunological study were normal except for the presence of lymphopenia and inverted CD4/CD8 ratio. The baseline erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal. Liver, kidney, and thyroid function tests (TSH, T3, and T4) were within normal limits. Histopathologic examination of the ulcers' sections stained with hematoxylin and eosin showed a superficial reticular dermis occupied by large pale histiocytes with leishmania. With the Giemsa stain technique multiple leishmania were seen confirming the diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis. After the diagnosis of leishmaniasis, sodium antimony gluconat was administered intravenously along with other antibiotics, the condition started to improve but unfortunately after two weeks of treatment the child was discharged from the hospital under the request and insistence of his parents. The parents were seeking cautery treatment for the ulcers which is a common practice in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia; the parents refused all medical advices to continue the treatment in the hospital. The child was discharged and was never seen again.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-month-old male infant presented with multiple progressively enlarging facial ulcers of 1-month duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant's parents noted the appearance of three facial ulcers at 1 month of age, which progressively enlarged over the subsequent month. The parents reported no history of fever or systemic distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born in a tent in the desert to healthy Bedouin parents without perinatal or postnatal complications. Phenotypic features of Down syndrome confirmed by karyotyping.
subjective.review_of_systems: Absence of fever, feeding difficulties, or respiratory distress reported by parents.

objective.physical_examination: General: dysmorphic features including flat occiput, short neck, low-set ears, hypotonia, short broad hands, fifth-finger clinodactyly, bilateral simian creases, and wide sandal gap between first and second toes. Dermatologic: severe facial disfigurement with three crusted ulcers with prominent surrounding erythematous margins: right cheek (2 cm x 2 cm), right lower eyelid (1 cm x 1.5 cm), and forehead (0.5 cm x 0.5 cm). No peripheral lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count and immune panel: lymphopenia with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): normal. Liver function tests, renal function tests, and thyroid function tests (TSH, free T3, free T4): all within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: Ulcer histopathology (H&E): superficial reticular dermis heavily infiltrated by large pale histiocytes containing intracellular organisms. Karyotype analysis: confirmed trisomy 21 (Down syndrome).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Giemsa staining of facial ulcer biopsy sections revealed multiple intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within histiocytes, establishing the diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis in an infant with confirmed Down syndrome. Management and Outcome: Administered intravenous sodium stibogluconate (sodium antimony gluconate) alongside systemic antibiotics with initial clinical improvement. After 2 weeks of therapy, the infant was discharged against medical advice due to parental insistence on traditional desert cautery treatment, and was lost to further medical follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 42-year-old male presented to the medical emergency department with complaints of weakness and significant weight loss over 1 year. He had episodes of low-grade fever in the past year, for which the patient was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years back. At present, he was again put on antitubercular therapy (ATT) for the past 1 month; however, no improvement was noted and hence the patient was referred to our hospital. There was no significant family history. On general physical examination, the patient was found to be thin built, pale, and afebrile with abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were enlarged and measured 1.5 cm in diameter. Mild hepatosplenomegaly was noted, however no fluid thrill could be discerned. Ultrasound abdomen revealed enlarged multiple conglomerate of mesenteric lymph nodes with the largest node measuring 22 mm x 18 mm. Clinical chemistry revealed A:G reversal with total protein of 9.5 g%, albumin of 2.0 g%, globulin of 7.5 g%, and A:G ratio of 1:3.75. Other parameters of liver function test and kidney function test were found to be within normal limits. Complete hemogram revealed pancytopenia with hemoglobin: 6 g%, total leukocyte count: 1800/muL, differential leukocyte count: polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%, eosinophils 1%, monocytes 1%, platelets: 48,000/muL, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear revealed the presence of rouleaux; however, no hemoparasite was noted.
Fine needle aspiration cytology was performed on the left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes, which yielded thick aspirate. Smears prepared showed few epithelioid cell granulomas interspersed with discrete and aggregates of histiocytes in a background of reactive lymphoid cells and many plasma cells. Numerous intracellular as well as extracellular amastigote forms of Leishmania species were seen [Figure 1]. In view of strong clinical suspicion, Ziehl-Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) was also done which came out to be negative. Both polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and AFB culture yielded negative result. Later on, rK39 antigen was also found to be positive. Bone marrow examination (both aspirate and biopsy) revealed a prominence of plasma cells and histiocytes along with infiltration by numerous intracellular as well as extracellular amastigote forms of Leishmania spp. Average parasite density (APD) of 5+, i.e., 10-100 Leishman-Donovan (LD) bodies/field, was noted in the bone marrow aspirate (BMA) [Figure 2]. In view of high APD, the patient's human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) status was evaluated which showed positive serology. Immune status evaluation revealed a low CD4 count; 28/muL (reference range: 400-1600/muL). The patient was started on intravenous amphotericin B along with highly active antiretroviral therapy. Improvement was noted after 14 days of treatment (CD4 count: 36/muL). Subsequent bone marrow evaluations revealed a significant fall in APD and clinical improvement in patient's health; weight gain, improved appetite, and rise in CD4 counts.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presented with progressive weakness, significant weight loss, and low-grade fever for 1 year.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 42-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a 1-year history of weakness, significant unintentional weight loss, and recurrent episodes of low-grade fever. He had been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years previously. For the preceding month, he had been restarted on empirical antitubercular therapy (ATT) without improvement, prompting referral to a tertiary care hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 2 years prior; recent 1-month course of empirical antitubercular therapy. Family history non-contributory. Prior other medications and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized weakness, marked weight loss, low-grade fever, abdominal distension. Denied cough, hemoptysis, diarrhea, or rash.

objective.physical_examination: Thin-built, pale, afebrile male with abdominal distension. Left submandibular and left axillary lymph nodes were palpable, measuring 1.5 cm in diameter each. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly without fluid thrill.
objective.routine_investigations: Pancytopenia on complete hemogram: hemoglobin 6.0 g/dL, total leukocyte count 1,800/muL (polymorphs 47%, lymphocytes 51%, eosinophils 1%, monocytes 1%), platelets 48,000/muL, ESR 50 mm/h. Peripheral smear showed rouleaux formation without hemoparasites. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed marked A:G reversal: total protein 9.5 g/dL, albumin 2.0 g/dL, globulin 7.5 g/dL (A:G ratio 1:3.75). Liver and kidney function tests otherwise normal. HIV serology was positive; CD4+ T-cell count was 28/muL (reference range 400-1,600/muL).
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal ultrasonography showed multiple enlarged conglomerate mesenteric lymph nodes (largest 22 x 18 mm) and hepatosplenomegaly. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of left submandibular and axillary lymph nodes revealed epithelioid granulomas, discrete histiocytic aggregates, plasma cells, and numerous intracellular and extracellular microorganisms; Ziehl-Neelsen stain for acid-fast bacilli was negative; PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and AFB cultures were negative. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy showed prominent plasma cells and histiocytes with abundant intracellular and extracellular microorganisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with generalized lymphadenopathy in a patient with newly diagnosed advanced HIV-1 coinfection (AIDS).
Diagnostic Confirmation: FNAC of lymph nodes and bone marrow aspirate/biopsy demonstrated abundant intracellular and extracellular Leishmania amastigotes (average parasite density 5+, 10-100 LD bodies/field in BMA); rK39 rapid antigen test was positive; HIV serology positive with CD4+ count of 28/muL.
Differentials Ruled Out: Recurrent/disseminated tuberculosis and tuberculous lymphadenitis (negative ZN stains, negative MTB PCR, negative AFB culture, clinical failure on ATT), lymphoma, and visceral histoplasmosis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Empirical ATT was discontinued. Initiated on intravenous amphotericin B combined with HAART. After 14 days of therapy, CD4+ count improved to 36/muL. Follow-up bone marrow aspirates demonstrated significant clearance of parasite density, accompanied by appetite recovery, weight gain, hematologic reconstitution, and progressive immune recovery.

raw_case_text:
The source patient was a 28-weeks' pregnant, 30-year-old woman of Kenyan origin who resided in France; she had visited Kenya and returned to France on June 1, 2001. On June 21, she was admitted to the gynecology-obstetrics emergency room at a greater Paris area hospital with fever and malaise. Blood sampling and thin and thick blood smears were performed by the nurse. The source patient's level of parasitemia was estimated at 0.05 per 100 erythrocytes, and oral quinine was initiated. The physician who interviewed the nurse after the needlestick injury verified that the source patient was HIV- and HCV-antibody negative and that the nurse was immunized against HBV. On June 23, although the results of her test for Plasmodium were negative, she was transferred to another tertiary care center where IV quinine was administered for nausea and vomiting, and she could be monitored more closely. She recovered fully and was discharged on June 27. Unfortunately, all blood samples or smears from the source patient had been discarded by the time the injured nurse became ill.
P. falciparum is a bloodborne pathogen, and malaria is a well-documented complication of transfusion. Malaria has also been diagnosed after intravenous drug use (,) and breaches in infection control procedures (-), as well as occupational exposures (-). Occupational P. falciparum infection after a needlestick injury may be rare; however, such an injury can be potentially severe in nonimmune healthcare workers in countries where malaria is not endemic, especially if the occupationally infected person is pregnant. This situation may also become more common as malaria spreads and as increasing international travel brings potential source patients to hospitals in malaria-endemic countries.
HBV, HCV, and HIV are the pathogens most often transmitted in documented cases of occupational infection following needlestick injuries in industrialized countries. Testing for infection by these pathogens does not include all the possible infections that can result from occupational exposure (,,). Although conducting a thorough investigation of the circumstances surrounding any needlestick injury is a challenge in the daily clinical setting, an investigation should always be carried out. As in this case-patient, the treatment of occupational P. falciparum infection may be delayed because physicians do not immediately consider malaria as a possible diagnosis. Furthermore, healthcare workers with neurologic symptoms caused by P. falciparum malaria may be too ill to tell the treating physician about their occupational exposure. Such infections must be diagnosed promptly as they are potentially lethal, and presumptive treatment is readily available and well tolerated. Clinicians managing healthcare or laboratory workers with a febrile illness or in a postexposure setting should consider the probability of occupational P. falciparum malaria.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old pregnant female presenting at 28 weeks' gestation with fever and malaise following recent travel to Kenya.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 30-year-old pregnant female at 28 weeks' gestation of Kenyan origin residing in France returned from Kenya on June 1, 2001. On June 21, she presented to an obstetric emergency department with acute fever and malaise. Blood smears were drawn (during which a treating nurse sustained a needlestick injury). Oral antimalarial therapy was started. On June 23, due to severe nausea and persistent vomiting precluding oral medication, she was transferred to a tertiary center for parenteral therapy and closer fetal-maternal surveillance.
subjective.past_medical_history: 28 weeks' gestation (gravida). Kenyan origin, residing in France. Travel to Kenya returning June 1, 2001. Baseline post-exposure contact serologies: HIV antibody negative, hepatitis C virus antibody negative.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, malaise, nausea, and vomiting. Negative for vaginal bleeding, rupture of membranes, uterine contractions, or dysuria. Medications: oral quinine initiated. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Pregnant female at 28 weeks' gestation. Febrile on presentation, nauseated. Vital signs stable. Obstetric examination confirmed reassuring fetal status; systemic physical examination otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline hematology and biochemistry. Thin and thick blood smears performed. Negative maternal HIV and HCV serologies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in pregnancy (28 weeks' gestation) complicated by hyperemesis/intolerance of oral medication. (Source patient for an accidental needlestick transmission to a treating nurse).
Diagnostic confirmation: Initial blood smears demonstrating Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia of 0.05 per 100 erythrocytes (0.05%); repeat blood smears upon transfer were negative for circulating parasites. HIV and HCV antibodies confirmed negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with oral quinine, switched to intravenous quinine upon transfer due to persistent vomiting. Monitored with serial fetal-maternal assessments. Experienced full symptom resolution, completed therapy, and was discharged in stable condition on June 27.

raw_case_text:
A 14-year-old previously healthy boy presented with fever, headache, generalized body aches, and retro-orbital pain for 5 days duration. As he had symptoms of dengue, he underwent dengue NS1 antigen testing and blood counts on day 3 of fever. Complete blood count (CBC) revealed a platelet count of 170 x 103/cumm and white cell count of 5.7 x 103/cumm. Following NS1 antigen was detected positive, he had serial blood counts and supportive care during initial stage as guided by the general practitioner (GP). Patient was advised to have oral fluids approximately 75-100 ml per hour. On day 5 of fever, platelet count dropped to 98 x 103/cumm and white cell count dropped to 4.2 x 103/cumm, and he was admitted for in-patient observation and management. On admission to hospital, he had stable vital signs which included pulse rate of 140 beats per minute, blood pressure:100/70mmg, capillary refill time of less than 2 s, and hematocrit rise of 16.7% from baseline (42% on admission with baseline hematocrit being 36%). During initial 24 h following admission, he developed vomiting and abdominal pain but had no bleeding manifestations.
Physical examination revealed generalized flushing, right hypochondrial tenderness, 3 cm hepatomegaly, and no signs of leakage. Point of care ultrasound revealed a mild pleural effusion and thickened gall bladder wall. Investigations revealed leucopenia (2.2 x 103/cumm), thrombocytopenia (platelet count:68 x 103/cumm), and deranged liver functions (Alanine aminotransferase-88 U/L, Aspartate transaminase-124 U/L). C-reactive protein and renal functions were normal. Subsequently, he was managed as for dengue hemorrhagic fever in high dependency care unit. Platelets further dropped to the lowest count of 6 x 103/cumm on day 7. However, there were no bleeding manifestations during the course of illness. Dengue serology including both IgM and IgG were positive on day 7 of illness. He recovered on day 11 of illness with evidence of rise of platelet counts. The cell indices at discharge on day 11 were white blood cells:7.5 x 103/cumm and platelet counts:52 x 103/cumm. Follow-up was arranged with local GP to review platelet counts in 3 days and patient was also requested for a follow-up appointment at the tertiary care hospital in 2 weeks.
Platelet counts were followed up to ensure complete recovery although platelet count remained at 47 x 103/cumm at 2-week post-discharge review at the tertiary care hospital. He was subsequently admitted as in-patient for further evaluation although no significant abnormality was found. Platelet count at one-month post-discharge was 100 x 103/cumm. Unfortunately, his parents defaulted follow-up as investigations were normal apart from thrombocytopenia and the patient re-presented with multiple purpura for 1 week duration at 1-year post-discharge. The parents had managed by their own to repeat blood counts over period they defaulted clinic follow-up, and the records revealed persistent thrombocytopenia (ranged from 30 to 45 x 103/cumm).
He was investigated in-depth at this point for persistent thrombocytopenia. Average absolute lymphocyte over the period of 1 year was 3.26 x 103/cumm (based on five previous records during the period they defaulted treatment), and the latest lymphocyte count was 2.6 x 103/cumm. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 15 mm/1st hour. Anti-nuclear antibody, anti-double standard DNA, and anti-phospholipid antibodies were negative. Mycoplasma, influenza cytomegalovirus, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, human immunodeficiency virus, and Epstein-Barr virus serology were also negative. Past medical history was not supportive of immunodeficiency and baseline immunodeficiency screen (serum immunoglobulins and complement levels) was negative. There was no recent history of MMR (mumps-measles-rubella) vaccination or use of platelet lowering medications prior to first detection of thrombocytopenia. Blood film showed normal morphology of cells including platelets and showed only thrombocytopenia. Bone marrow examination showed megakaryocytes but was otherwise completely normal. The clinical evaluation and investigations ruled out differential diagnosis confirming the diagnosis of chronic ITP secondary due to dengue infection. Since the child had persistent thrombocytopenia for over 12 months, he was managed as for chronic ITP. The child was commenced on corticosteroids and currently being followed-up at pediatric hematology clinic.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-year-old male presenting with fever, headache, generalized body aches, and retro-orbital pain for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 14-year-old previously healthy boy developed fever, headache, body aches, and retro-orbital pain 5 days prior to admission. Serial outpatient blood counts showed progressive decline in platelets and white blood cells. On day 5 of fever, he was admitted for inpatient observation. In the first 24 hours of hospitalization, he developed vomiting and abdominal pain without bleeding manifestations. Following supportive care in the high-dependency unit, he clinically recovered by day 11 and was discharged. However, post-discharge follow-up revealed persistent thrombocytopenia, and at 1 year post-discharge he re-presented with multiple purpura of 1 week duration, prompting extensive hematological evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy; no prior medical history supportive of immunodeficiency; no recent history of MMR vaccination or platelet-lowering medications prior to first detection of thrombocytopenia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Vomiting and abdominal pain during initial admission; multiple purpura at 1-year follow-up; absence of overt bleeding manifestations during acute phase.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Pulse rate 140 beats/min (tachycardia), blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, capillary refill time < 2 seconds. Generalized flushing, right hypochondrial tenderness, 3 cm hepatomegaly, no signs of overt plasma leakage. Re-presentation at 1 year: Multiple purpura.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 3 of fever: Platelet count 170 x 10^3/cumm, white cell count 5.7 x 10^3/cumm. Day 5: Platelet count 98 x 10^3/cumm, WBC 4.2 x 10^3/cumm, hematocrit 42% (16.7% rise from baseline of 36%). Hospital labs: Leucopenia (2.2 x 10^3/cumm), thrombocytopenia (platelet count 68 x 10^3/cumm; lowest nadir 6 x 10^3/cumm on day 7), ALT 88 U/L, AST 124 U/L; normal CRP and renal functions. Point of care ultrasound: Mild pleural effusion and thickened gallbladder wall. Discharge indices (day 11): WBC 7.5 x 10^3/cumm, platelets 52 x 10^3/cumm. Follow-up counts: Platelets 47 x 10^3/cumm at 2 weeks, 100 x 10^3/cumm at 1 month, persistent thrombocytopenia (30-45 x 10^3/cumm) over the subsequent year. One-year workup: Absolute lymphocyte count 2.6 x 10^3/cumm (1-year average 3.26 x 10^3/cumm), ESR 15 mm/1st hour; ANA, anti-dsDNA, and antiphospholipid antibodies negative; serologies negative for Mycoplasma, influenza, CMV, HBV, HCV, HIV, and EBV; serum immunoglobulins and complement levels normal; peripheral blood film showed normal morphology of cells and platelets with isolated thrombocytopenia.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow examination: Adequate megakaryocytes without dysplasia or malignant infiltration, otherwise completely normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (dengue hemorrhagic fever) complicated by secondary chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (chronic ITP) persisting for over 12 months. Dengue diagnosis confirmed by positive Dengue NS1 antigen on day 3 of fever and positive Dengue IgM and IgG serology on day 7. Primary immunodeficiencies, systemic lupus erythematosus/antiphospholipid syndrome, hematologic malignancies, and other viral/atypical infections were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Acute infection managed with oral and intravenous fluid resuscitation and close monitoring in high dependency care unit, achieving clinical recovery by day 11 without bleeding manifestations or blood transfusions. For chronic post-dengue ITP at 1 year, oral corticosteroids were commenced, resulting in clinical stabilization with ongoing pediatric hematology follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 22-year-old female with a past medical history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which included fibrotic lupus pneumonitis, grade IV lupus nephritis, and pericardial tamponade, presented to the hospital due to fevers and progressive shortness of breath. Initial oxygen saturations on room air were in the low 80s. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the lungs showed granular and interstitial ground glass opacities with chronic interstitial lung fibrosis (Figure 1). At presentation, the differential diagnosis included an acute exacerbation of chronic lupus pneumonitis and COVID-19 interstitial pneumonia. As a result, the first test performed was a COVID-19 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test. To evaluate for an acute lupus flare, anti-dsDNA and C3/C4 serum complement levels were ordered, which showed anti-dsDNA at 19 IU/mL (reference interval: <10 IU/mL). Serum complement levels C3/C4 were mildly decreased at 84 mg/dL and 9 mg/dL, respectively (reference interval: C3 [88-201 mg/dL]; C4 [10-40 mg/dL]). Additionally, proteinuria was not detected on urinalysis. Other initial laboratory findings showed lymphopenia, elevated D-dimer levels, elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, and a negative upper respiratory PCR viral panel. Atypical pneumonia sputum culture was also negative. The patient's home medications including hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolic acid as a part of her outpatient management of SLE were continued. Due to the diagnostic dilemma between acute lupus pneumonitis and COVID-19 interstitial pneumonia, the patient was not given any steroids initially. The patient required up to 6 L of oxygen via nasal cannula, maintaining an oxygen saturation of 94%. After 24 hours of admission with no improvement, the patient was started on 60 mg of intravenous methylprednisolone 3 times daily, which resulted in improved respiratory status and decreased oxygen requirements to 2 L via nasal cannula to maintain oxygen saturation of 94%. Eventually, results of the COVID-19 PCR test returned as positive. On day 5 of her hospital admission, the steroids were tapered down to a total 60 mg of oral prednisone daily, and a repeat CT scan showed significant improvement (Figure 2). The patient was subsequently removed from the nasal cannula with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air and was discharged home.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with fever, progressive shortness of breath, and acute hypoxia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 22-year-old female with known systemic lupus erythematosus presented with progressive shortness of breath and fevers. On room air, her oxygen saturation was in the low 80s, requiring escalation of supplemental oxygen up to 6 L/min via nasal cannula to maintain target saturations.
subjective.past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) complicated by fibrotic lupus pneumonitis, class IV lupus nephritis, and prior pericardial tamponade. Home medications: hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolic acid. No epidemiological exposures or allergies documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and progressive dyspnea. Negative for gross hematuria or active arthralgias. Home medications: hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolic acid. Drug allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: febrile; respiratory rate increased; SpO2 in the low 80s on room air, improving to 94% on 6 L/min via nasal cannula. Follow-up examination: SpO2 95% on room air following steroid taper.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation: absolute lymphopenia; elevated D-dimer; elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). SLE flare serology: anti-dsDNA antibody elevated at 19 IU/mL (reference: <10 IU/mL); serum complement C3 decreased at 84 mg/dL (reference: 88–201 mg/dL); serum complement C4 decreased at 9 mg/dL (reference: 10–40 mg/dL). Urinalysis: negative for proteinuria. Respiratory microbiology: upper respiratory multiplex PCR viral panel negative; atypical pneumonia sputum cultures negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial chest CT: granular and interstitial ground-glass opacities superimposed on chronic interstitial lung fibrosis. Follow-up chest CT (hospital day 5): significant interval resolution and clearance of ground-glass infiltrates.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Acute COVID-19 interstitial pneumonia in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus and chronic fibrotic lupus pneumonitis, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Acute severe lupus flare was deemed less likely given absent proteinuria and only mild complement depression, though mild SLE activity may have coexisted. Management & Outcome: Continued baseline hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolic acid. Due to lack of improvement after 24 hours of oxygen therapy, high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (60 mg three times daily) was administered, resulting in marked clinical stabilization and decrease of oxygen requirement to 2 L/min. Tapered to oral prednisone (60 mg daily) on hospital day 5; successfully weaned to room air (SpO2 95%) and discharged home.

raw_case_text: The likely source of laboratory worker 1's infection was found after reassessing Gram stains performed in laboratory 1 in August, September, and October 2001. A 76-year-old woman visited the emergency room served by laboratory 1 in early September 2001. The patient had had fever (temperature 38.3oC) for 1 day and headache for 3 weeks. She received one dose of ciprofloxacin for a possible urinary tract infection and was discharged. After 4 days of incubation, a Gram stain of this patient's blood culture specimen showed tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, reported as coryneform bacilli. As part of the investigation for the source of infection for laboratory worker 1, this patient's prepared Gram stain slide was referred to the Wadsworth Center, where small, gram-variable cocci were identified. More than 1 year after being seen in the emergency room, this patient was offered Brucella SAT and a repeat blood culture. She refused Brucella SAT, and her physician did not identify symptoms consistent with brucellosis. Six months after this identification, further experimental analysis by the Wadsworth Center with polymerase chain reaction tests performed on Gram stain material detected B. melitensis DNA (Wadsworth Center, NYSDOH, unpub. data). The patient was again contacted, and Brucella SAT (>1.5 years after her initial blood culture) showed a titer of 1:80 (indeterminate). Repeat blood cultures were negative. Upon interview, the patient denied any visits outside the United States since 1989, when she emigrated from Peru. She also denied consuming any unpasteurized products from the United States or abroad. An additional interview was scheduled, but the patient died unexpectedly.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 1-day history of fever (38.3 °C) and a 3-week history of headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in early September 2001 with a 3-week history of headache and 1 day of fever (38.3 °C). She was evaluated for a suspected urinary tract infection, administered a single dose of oral ciprofloxacin, and discharged. Blood cultures were collected at that time. More than 1 year later, an epidemiologic trace-back investigation of laboratory-acquired febrile illness led to re-evaluation of her historical blood culture specimen.
subjective.past_medical_history: Emigrated from Peru in 1989; denied travel outside the United States since 1989. Denied consuming unpasteurized dairy products from the United States or abroad. Prior medical history and comorbidities not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache for 3 weeks; fever for 1 day. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.3 °C. Other vital signs and physical examination findings not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood culture (September 2001): incubated for 4 days; Gram stain showed tiny gram-negative coccobacilli, originally reported as coryneform bacilli. Repeat blood cultures performed >1.5 years later were negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis caused by Brucella melitensis.
Confirmation: Review of the original prepared Gram stain slide by the Wadsworth Center identified small gram-variable cocci; experimental PCR analysis of Gram stain material performed at Wadsworth Center detected Brucella melitensis DNA. Repeat Brucella serum agglutination test (SAT) performed >1.5 years later showed an indeterminate titer of 1:80.
Differentials ruled out: Suspected urinary tract infection; coryneform contamination ruled out by PCR confirmation of B. melitensis DNA.
Treatment & Outcome: Received a single dose of ciprofloxacin in the emergency department in 2001. Found to be asymptomatic when evaluated >1 year later. An additional follow-up interview was planned, but the patient died unexpectedly from an unrelated cause.

raw_case_text: A 17-year-old male recipient of matched-sibling donor transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome, on immunosuppressive agent, presented with fever and body ache on day +317. Donor chimerism at day +180 was >90%. At presentation, CBC showed Hb = 16.5 g/dL, hematocrit (HCT) = 48%, platelet = 90 x 109/L. Physical examination revealed harsh vesicular breathing. Dengue NS1 antigen was detected. Blood cultures were negative. He was managed conservatively for 1 week as inpatient with intravenous hydration, analgesics, and antipyretics. Platelet count dropped to 24 x 109/L followed by recovery without need for transfusion.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old male post-allogeneic stem cell transplant presented with fever and body ache on post-transplant day +317.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, on immunosuppressive therapy following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, presented on day +317 post-transplant with acute-onset fever and generalized body aches. During inpatient management, his platelet count declined to a nadir of 24 x 10^9/L before spontaneous recovery.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underwent matched-sibling donor stem cell transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome (donor chimerism >90% at day +180). Maintained on immunosuppressive therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported fever and generalized body aches. Denied bleeding manifestations, chills, cough, or dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: Chest examination revealed harsh vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. No petechiae, ecchymoses, or mucosal bleeding were identified.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count at presentation: Hemoglobin 16.5 g/dL, hematocrit 48%, platelet count 90 x 10^9/L (nadir: 24 x 10^9/L).
Microbiology: Blood cultures showed no bacterial growth.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue fever presenting in an allogeneic stem cell transplant recipient with acute thrombocytopenia, confirmed by positive Dengue NS1 antigen detection. Bacterial bloodstream infection was ruled out with negative blood cultures.
Treatment and outcome: Managed conservatively as an inpatient for 1 week with intravenous fluid hydration, analgesics, and antipyretics. The platelet count recovered spontaneously without requiring platelet transfusions, and he recovered uneventfully.

raw_case_text: A 24-year-old male presented with a fever for 16 days mild abdominal pain and a weight loss of 4 kg. He was treated outside with cefixime for five days at suboptimal doses. Routine investigations revealed a leucocyte count of 3400/muL with ESR 87 mm/hr with slightly elevated SGOT (62 IU/dL) and SGPT (58 IU/dL), rest parameters were normal. He was evaluated for dengue, malaria, and typhus fever and all workups were negative. Ultrasound showed ileal thickening with few mesenteric lymph nodes (LN) triggering suspicion of Koch's disease. Meanwhile, he underwent a CT abdomen that showed terminal ileal thickening with mesenteric LN of maximum size 12-14 mm and was non-necrotic. In between blood cultures grew S. typhi. He was started antibiotic ceftriaxone, but there was no response till day 7 which prompted us to colonoscopy which showed multiple superficial ulcers with whitish exudate with surrounding erythema in the ascending colon and caecum. The ileocecal valve and ileum showed multiple superficial ulcers with whitish exudate with surrounding erythema. Mucosa edematous, erythematous with a bluish hue seen till 20 cm (Fig. 3). Histopathology revealed diffuse active ileitis with lymphoid hyperplasia and prominent histolytic inflammatory infiltrate. Acid-fast staining did not reveal acid-fast bacilli and Gene Xpert for mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative. The patient responded to ceftriaxone on day 9th and was discharged after 5 days of more intravenous antibiotics. At the 2-month follow-up, the ultrasound was repeated which showed a resolution of ileal thickening.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male presented with a 16-day history of fever, mild abdominal pain, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with fever of 16 days' duration, accompanied by mild abdominal pain and an associated 4 kg weight loss. Prior to admission, he was treated outside with suboptimal doses of cefixime for 5 days without clinical benefit.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated with a 5-day course of suboptimal oral cefixime prior to admission. No other prior medical history reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports mild abdominal pain and a 4 kg weight loss. No other complaints reported.

objective.routine_investigations: Leucocyte count 3400/muL, ESR 87 mm/hr, SGOT 62 IU/dL, and SGPT 58 IU/dL; remaining baseline laboratory parameters were normal. Diagnostic evaluations for dengue, malaria, and typhus fever were all negative. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated ileal thickening with a few mesenteric lymph nodes.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT showed terminal ileal thickening with non-necrotic mesenteric lymph nodes measuring up to 12-14 mm. Colonoscopy revealed multiple superficial ulcers with whitish exudate and surrounding erythema in the ascending colon and caecum; the ileocecal valve and ileum showed multiple superficial ulcers with whitish exudate and surrounding erythema, with edematous, erythematous mucosa and a bluish hue extending up to 20 cm. Histopathology revealed diffuse active ileitis with lymphoid hyperplasia and prominent histiocytic inflammatory infiltrate. Acid-fast staining was negative for acid-fast bacilli and GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Salmonella typhi bacteremia (typhoid fever) confirmed by blood cultures growing S. typhi. Dengue, malaria, typhus fever, and abdominal tuberculosis (Koch's disease) were ruled out based on negative diagnostic panels, negative AFB staining, and negative GeneXpert.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on intravenous ceftriaxone. The patient did not show clinical response through day 7, with defervescence occurring on day 9 of ceftriaxone therapy. Intravenous antibiotics were continued for 5 additional days prior to discharge. At 2-month follow-up, repeat ultrasound confirmed complete resolution of ileal thickening.

raw_case_text:
A 29-year-old woman from Kumba, Cameroon, was admitted in January 2004 to St. John's Hospital and Maternity, Kumba, with a five-day history of fever, emesis, poorly localized abdominal discomfort, myalgias and hepatosplenomegaly. Her total leukocyte count was 1.7 x 109/l, (neutrophils 51%, lymphocytes 43%, monocytes 5%). Urinalysis was normal and thin and thick film examinations of the peripheral blood were negative for malaria. The patient also tested negative for HIV. A blood Widal test however, showed a titre of 80 against "O" (somatic) antigen and 160 against the "H" (flagella) antigen of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (recommended cut-off titre in our hospital: >= 1:80 and >= 1:160 for the "O" and "H" antigens respectively). Blood culture grew Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi. Two months prior to her illness, she had suffered from an attack of suspected typhoid fever and had been treated with chloramphenicol 500 mg every 6 hours for 14 days.
Antibiogram of the isolated S. enterica serovar Typhi was performed by disc diffusion techniques as recommended by NCCLS guidelines, Minimum inhibitory concentrations (MIC) of nalidixic acid and ciprofloxacin were determined by agar dilution method. The antibiotic discs used included ampicillin 10 mug (Beecham), co-trimoxazole 1.25/23.75 mug (Roche), chloramphenicol 30 mug (Antibioticos SA), ciprofloxacin 5 mug (Bayer), nalidixic acid 30 mug (Sigma) and ceftriaxone 30 mug (Roche). The isolate was found resistant to nalidixic acid, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole and chloramphenicol, but susceptible to ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin by disc diffusion test. The MICs of ciprofloxacin and nalidixic acid were 0.5 mug/ml and 32.0 mug/ml respectively. The patient remained febrile after 7 days of oral administration of 500 mg ciprofloxacin every 12 hours. Thereafter, the patient was administered 1 g ceftriaxone every 12 hours intravenously, which rendered her afebrile within four days. Treatment was continued for another 3 days. The patient did not relapse on follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old woman presenting with a 5-day history of fever, emesis, and poorly localized abdominal discomfort.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute fever five days prior to admission in January 2004, accompanied by recurrent emesis, poorly localized diffuse abdominal discomfort, and generalized myalgias. Her symptoms progressively worsened over the five-day period prompting hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Two months prior to current presentation, she experienced an attack of suspected typhoid fever treated with oral chloramphenicol 500 mg every 6 hours for 14 days. She resides in Kumba, Cameroon.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports generalized myalgias and gastrointestinal distress (emesis, abdominal discomfort). No other constitutional complaints detailed.

objective.physical_examination: Abdominal examination revealed palpable hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Patient was clinically febrile upon admission.
objective.routine_investigations: Total leukocyte count markedly decreased at 1.7 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 51%, lymphocytes 43%, monocytes 5%, demonstrating leukopenia). Urinalysis was normal. Peripheral blood thin and thick smears were negative for Plasmodium falciparum (malaria). HIV rapid screening was negative. Blood Widal serology showed a diagnostic titre of 1:80 against Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi 'O' somatic antigen and 1:160 against 'H' flagella antigen (meeting hospital cut-off criteria).
objective.advanced_workup: Antibiogram via NCCLS disc diffusion demonstrated multidrug resistance to nalidixic acid, ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, and chloramphenicol, with apparent disc susceptibility to ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. Agar dilution MIC testing revealed nalidixic acid MIC of 32.0 mcg/mL (resistant) and ciprofloxacin MIC of 0.5 mcg/mL (reduced susceptibility).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi bacteremia (typhoid fever) based on blood culture growth, presenting as nalidixic acid-resistant S. enterica serovar Typhi (NARST) with reduced ciprofloxacin susceptibility. Differential diagnoses of malaria and HIV were definitively ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initially treated with oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg every 12 hours; patient experienced clinical treatment failure, remaining febrile after 7 days. Regimen was switched to intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g every 12 hours, achieving defervescence within four days. Ceftriaxone was continued for a total of 7 days, resulting in complete clinical recovery with no relapse on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
We report the case of a 17-month-old female patient from Berkane, born from a consanguineous marriage with the notion of the death of a sister at the age of 6 (unknownetiology), with no other pathological history. She presented for an anarchic fever evolving for 3 months with the anemic syndrome and hemorrhagic syndrome made up of epistaxis with stature retardation. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 39   C, lower limbsedema, paleness of skin and mucous membranes, gingival petechiae, bleached hair and hepatosplenomegaly. Other exams are unremarkable.
The complete blood count showed pancytopenia made up of deep aregenerative normochromic normocyticanemia at 3 g/dL, with reticulocyte count at 76.700/mm3, leukocytes at 4860/mm3 made up of neutropenia at 680/mm3 and thrombocytopenia at 12.000/mm3. The blood smear showed no abnormality. We also observed a hypoalbuminemia at 13 g/L, hypertriglyceridemia at 4.57 g/L, hyperferritinemia at 626ug/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level at 337IU/L, low prothrombin time (PT) at 56 %, and fibrinogen level at 1 g/L. The direct Coombs test was also positive. The hepatic assessment and the renal function are without abnormality. (Table 1) in front of these clinical and biological features, the clinicians taking charge of the patient evoked the diagnosis of MAS. Thus, a cytological study of the bone marrow in search of the features of hemophagocytosis was necessary to confirm the diagnosis. Careful examination of the myelogram revealed the presence of leishmania bodies with figures of hemophagocytosis (Fig. 1, Fig. 2). The diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis associated with a MAS was retained.
The patient was put on liposomal amphotericin B and corticosteroid therapy with good clinical and biological progress and good therapeutic tolerance.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-month-old female presented with a 3-month history of chaotic fever, severe anemia, epistaxis, and growth delay.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with irregular, anarchic fever evolving over 3 months, associated with progressive anemic syndrome, hemorrhagic manifestations including recurrent epistaxis, and stature retardation leading to hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born to consanguineous parents in Berkane, Morocco; family history notable for the death of an older sister at age 6 years of unknown etiology; no other prior personal pathological history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Recurrent epistaxis and growth retardation.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature: 39 °C. Marked paleness of skin and mucous membranes, gingival petechiae, lower limb edema, bleached hair, and hepatosplenomegaly. Other physical examination findings were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed profound pancytopenia: aregenerative normochromic normocytic anemia with hemoglobin: 3 g/dL and reticulocyte count: 76,700/mm^3; leukopenia with WBC: 4,860/mm^3 and absolute neutropenia: 680/mm^3; severe thrombocytopenia with platelets: 12,000/mm^3. Peripheral blood smear: no morphological abnormalities. Serum albumin: 13 g/L (hypoalbuminemia), triglycerides: 4.57 g/L (hypertriglyceridemia), serum ferritin: 626 ug/L (hyperferritinemia), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): 337 IU/L, prothrombin time (PT): 56%, fibrinogen: 1 g/L. Direct Coombs test: positive. Hepatic transaminases and renal function tests: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Cytological study of the bone marrow aspirate (myelogram) demonstrated prominent features of hemophagocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) associated with macrophage activation syndrome (MAS): careful microscopic examination of the bone marrow myelogram revealed the presence of characteristic Leishmania bodies (amastigotes) alongside active hemophagocytic histiocytes. The patient was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B and systemic corticosteroid therapy, resulting in excellent therapeutic tolerance and rapid clinical and biological recovery.

raw_case_text:
Patient is a 26-year-old female with a past medical history of HIV. She was infected at age 15 and showed poor adherence to antiretroviral medication. She reported the combined use of Tenofovir, Emtricitabine, and Efavirenz intermittently, mostly because she did not seek adequate healthcare due to feelings of shame about being associated with the disease. She also missed most of her follow-ups in the last year, and had no CD4 counts or viral load tests performed in over 6 months. She also suffered from intermittent episodes of coughing, bloody stools, and weight loss during this time; however, she didn't seek any medical attention.
She presented to our emergency room with a 10-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, biliary vomits and asthenia. Approximately 24 h prior to admittance, the pain became worse. On clinical examination, a dehydrated, hypotensive and tachycardic patient was encountered. Her abdomen was diffusely tender, and the pain became more intense on touch. Laboratory exams revealed mild leukocytosis and neutrophilia. An arterial gasometry revealed metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia.
In view of these findings, surgical consultation was requested and a diagnosis of diffuse peritonitis was reached. Aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids was started and an emergency laparotomy was decided. At surgery, the peritoneal cavity was filled with 500 ml of pus and 2 bowel perforations were identified: a 1 x 1 cm perforation in the terminal ileum, 50 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, and a 3 x 2 cm perforation in the cecum (Fig. 1A-C).
A right colectomy was decided, however, the surgical team had doubts about restoring bowel continuity. Nonetheless, since the patient became stable after reanimation and surgery, restoration was considered feasible. Given the context of an HIV patient with poor controls who would be unlikely able to handle an ileostomy, a primary anastomosis with close surveillance was decided. Resection began 10 cm proximal to the ileal perforation and ended near the hepatic flexure of the colon. Then, a side-to-side ileotransverse anastomosis was performed with 75 mm staples (ETHICON Linear Cutter NTLC75, Johnson & Johnson). Extensive washing of the peritoneal cavity was completed and the remainder of the procedure was performed without complications. Based on the historical, clinical, and laboratory data obtained, we initially considered intestinal perforation due to cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection as the probable etiology of peritonitis, and the differentials included, mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma. However, definitive pathology tests for the cause of the perforation were delayed due to the unavailability of an in-house pathologist. Furthermore, other essential tests including CD4 counts and HIV viral loads and antibodies (both IgM and IgG) were not available at our institution.
This situation was further complicated by the lack of resources from the patient and our hospital; nonetheless, we managed to send a blood sample to a nearby hospital for testing. Even under these harsh conditions, the patient had a good recovery. She was placed under broad-spectrum antibiotics (Piperacillin/Tazobactam) and was given a 3-day cycle of Ganciclovir. Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) was initiated as well. Meanwhile, sips of liquids were initiated on the second postoperative day without complications. She didn't have any episodes of fever, nausea, vomiting or signs of anastomosis leak.
At the 7th postoperative day, the patient requested to leave against medical advice (AMA), she signed the hospital consents and left our facility.
Two days after the patient went AMA, CD4 and HIV viral load results arrived along with the pathology report, revealing chronic inflammation of the resected bowel, and multiple ulcers affecting the mucosa of the ileum and the cecum. Also, multiple granulomas surrounded by inflammatory tissue were recognized, as well as some granulomas within the lymph nodes. Bowel perforation due to tuberculosis was confirmed as the final diagnosis, CD4 cell counts were estimated at 94 cells/mm3, and the viral load was estimated at over 106 genome copies (Fig. 2A-C).
Since tuberculosis in Ecuador is a mandatory declaration disease, we searched for the patient and found her in the coastal region of the country. Fortunately, she was stable and without complications. She was taken by the national healthcare system and admitted to a tertiary hospital for HIV and tuberculosis treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old female with HIV presented with a 10-day history of worsening lower abdominal pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, and asthenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 10-day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, and asthenia, with acute exacerbation of pain 24 hours prior to admission. She noted intermittent cough, bloody stools, and weight loss over the preceding months.
subjective.past_medical_history: HIV infection diagnosed at age 15, with poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy (intermittent tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz). Resides in Ecuador.
