objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Tachycardic, normotensive, hypoxemic. Cardiovascular: Distant heart sounds. Lymphatics: Palpable left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy and multiple palpable axillary lymph nodes. Extremities: Right calf tenderness and ankle swelling.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count: 13,500 cells/mm3 with 78% neutrophils. D-dimer: 20 microg/mL FEU (normal: 0.00-0.48 microg/mL FEU). Cardiac troponin: 0.286 ng/mL (normal: 0.0-0.034 ng/mL). Chest radiograph: Cardiomegaly without acute pulmonary infiltrates. Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia. Echocardiogram: Moderate pericardial effusion with normal left ventricular ejection fraction. Pericardiocentesis fluid: Serosanguinous fluid with normal WBC count and negative Gram stain. Venous duplex ultrasound of right lower extremity: Deep vein thrombosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT angiogram: Negative for pulmonary embolism; demonstrated right paratracheal lymphadenopathy, right hilar mass, and subcarinal lymph nodes. CT abdomen/pelvis: Bilateral breast masses, bilateral pleural effusions, bilateral adrenal nodules, and vertebral translucency. Brain MRI: Two lesions located in the cerebellum and left frontal lobe consistent with metastases. Excision biopsy of left supraclavicular lymph node: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of lung origin, mucin stain positive, thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1) positive, GATA-3 negative. Pericardial fluid cytology: Malignant large epithelioid cells favoring metastatic adenocarcinoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (Stage IV with metastases to lymph nodes, pericardium, brain, adrenals, and vertebrae) complicated by malignant pericardial effusion, impending cardiac tamponade, and right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis, in a patient with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; absolute CD4 count 116 cells/microL [normal 500-1750], CD4 percentage 7% [normal 30-61%], CD4/CD8 ratio 0.11 [normal 0.86-5.00]).
Management & Outcome: Managed with unfractionated heparin infusion for DVT, prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, continued ART, and therapeutic pericardiocentesis. Due to rapid pericardial re-accumulation and refractory respiratory failure, a surgical pericardial window was performed; however, the patient experienced acute clinical decompensation and expired shortly after surgery.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old man diagnosed with malaria in the summer of 2015 presented in May 2016 with a five-day history of symptoms. He noted that five days prior to presentation, he started feeling generalized weakness. Four days before presenting, he felt lightheaded and had one episode of nonbilious, nonbloody vomiting, later developing right upper quadrant pain. He also endorsed several bouts of nonbloody diarrhea for the three days prior to arrival with associated fevers up to 102 F. On review of systems, the patient endorsed frontal headaches and dark urine. He denied any recent travel or sick contacts.
However, the patient's symptoms had actually begun almost a year before. During July of 2015, after the patient spent twenty days in a Venezuelan jungle, he had a seizure and was taken to local health clinic where he was treated with an unknown regimen of antimalarial pills for fourteen days. After a brief period of resolution, the patient experienced his second clinical episode and went to a rural town where he was again treated with an unknown regimen of antimalarial medications.
After returning to the U.S., during October of 2015, the patient remained asymptomatic until he experienced a third episode of malarial symptoms for which he was treated in Miami, Florida (though unable to recall/establish precise regimen). On November of 2015, the patient endorsed a fourth clinical episode with the same symptoms including fever, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and right upper quadrant pain. At that time, he was admitted to Elmhurst Hospital in Queens, New York. He was diagnosed by blood smear analysis with both P. falciparum and P. vivax during that hospitalization. He was treated with quinine for five days, doxycycline for seven days, and primaquine for fourteen days.
He was readmitted and retreated at Elmhurst Hospital for malaria during both January and February of 2016 with the same medication regimen stated previously; but during February, the dose of primaquine was doubled and he was enrolled in directly observed therapy (DOT) in Elmhurst Hospital ID Clinic to ensure compliance. After completion of his last regimen of primaquine on March 10, 2016, he reported to be asymptomatic.
On May 8, 2016, he was readmitted to Elmhurst Hospital for recurrent malaria (at which point he was treated by study authors). This was his seventh episode of malaria over the course of one year. By his seventh presentation, he had completed an approved treatment regimen, endorsed compliance, and had no risk for reexposure. The CDC was then contacted by study authors via CDC Malaria Hotline, given multiple relapses, at which point it was suggested genotyping be sent for CYP2D6. When tested for the CYP2D6 allele during his May 8th admission, he was found to have a *4/*5 allele variation, which corresponds to a poor metabolizer. There are numerous alleles rendering CYP2D6 inactive, and *4/*5 are among those "null alleles".
DNA analysis of the cytochrome P4502D6 gene was performed at North Shore-LIJ Core Laboratories located in Lake Success, NY. Testing was completed on the Tm Bioscience/Luminex Universal Array platform using primer extension chemistry. Multiplex PCR-amplified fragments containing alleles aforementioned and the primer extension then generated a biotin-labeled product that hybridized to complementary bead-immobilized probes to permit flow-sorted detection of both normal and variant sequences. This testing is available through the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by contacting the CDC Malaria Hotline, information for which is readily available online.
Using the CDC guideline, the patient was started on chloroquine for 48 hours and discharged. After completion of the chloroquine regimen, he was placed on weekly chloroquine prophylaxis for 1-2 years. Since completion of the aforementioned treatment, he has remained malaria free.
The patient suffered an attack of P. vivax after he travelled to an endemic area. He was treated twice with unknown medications while abroad. However, upon his return, he was treated with four full courses of appropriate medications. After failure of resolution and continued relapses, a genetic screen was ordered, and it was determined that the patient had a mutation of the CYP2D6 allele rendering him a "poor metabolizer," thereby explaining his treatment failure.
Previous studies established the pivotal role of CYP2D6 hepatocyte enzyme on primaquine metabolism and P. vivax eradication. Those who were intermediate and poor metabolizers were considered for alternate therapy with chloroquine, artemether, or lumefantrine. Our case validates previous claims on the crucial role that genetic variations of the CYP450 have on proper therapy. After numerous failed treatments and a genetic screen, second-line therapy was initiated successfully eradicating the P. vivax infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old male presenting with fever up to 102 °F, generalized weakness, right upper quadrant pain, and diarrhea for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 5-day history of generalized weakness, lightheadedness, one episode of nonbilious nonbloody vomiting, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Over the preceding three days, he had nonbloody diarrhea and fevers reaching 102 °F. He noted frontal headaches and dark urine, denying recent travel or sick contacts. This represented his seventh clinical episode of recurrent fever and abdominal pain over the course of one year despite multiple completed courses of antimalarial therapy with directly observed administration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposure: Spent 20 days in a Venezuelan jungle in July 2015 where he developed a seizure and received a 14-day antimalarial regimen. Experienced multiple recurrent episodes: July 2015 (Venezuela), August 2015 (Venezuela), October 2015 (Miami, FL), November 2015 (Elmhurst Hospital, NY), January 2016 (Elmhurst Hospital), and February 2016 (Elmhurst Hospital; treated with directly observed double-dose primaquine). No other prior medical illnesses.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for frontal headaches, dark urine, generalized weakness, lightheadedness, nausea, vomiting, right upper quadrant pain, and diarrhea; negative for cough, shortness of breath, or rash.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature up to 102 °F. Abdominal examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Urinalysis demonstrated dark-colored urine.
objective.advanced_workup: Cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) gene genotyping (Tm Bioscience/Luminex Universal Array platform using multiplex PCR and primer extension chemistry): Identified a *4/*5 allele variation, confirming that the patient is a CYP2D6 'poor metabolizer' with inactive null alleles.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Recurrent relapsing Plasmodium vivax malaria secondary to CYP2D6 poor metabolizer status (*4/*5 null alleles) causing primaquine bioactivation failure. Prior admissions documented P. falciparum and P. vivax on blood smears.
Plan & Outcome: Consulted the CDC Malaria Hotline. The patient was treated with an acute course of oral chloroquine for 48 hours and discharged, followed by weekly chloroquine chemoprophylaxis for 1 to 2 years to suppress hypnozoite reactivation. Following completion of therapy, he remained completely asymptomatic and free of malaria relapses.

raw_case_text:
A 13-year-old boy was referred to our hospital with complaints of high-grade fever, non-bilious, non-bloody projectile vomiting, light headedness, generalized weakness, reduced appetite and passing black-coloured urine. Prior to his admission, the child was febrile (40  C) with blood pressure of 110/40 mmHg (considered to be low as per guidelines of the National Institute of Health), along with thrombocytopaenia (28 000 mm-3 blood; normal: 1.5-4.5 mm-3 blood), low haematological parameters of haemoglobin (12.3 g dl-1; normal: 10-15.5 g dl-1), haematocrit (35.8 %; normal: 35-44 %), mean corpuscular volume (66.1 fl; normal: 80-95 fl) and mean corpuscular haemoglobin (22.7 pg; normal: 32-36 pg). Blood urea (62 mg dl-1; normal: 5-18 mg dl-1) and random blood sugar (204 mg dl-1; normal: 70-140 mg dl-1) levels were significantly raised. Peripheral blood smear examination was positive for P. vivax. Other tests such as Dengue (Non-structural protein 1) NS1, scrub typhus card tests, Widal test and COVID 19 reverse transcriptase (RT)-PCR were negative. Despite thrombocytopaenia, the child had no bleeding manifestations and was administered a first dose of intravenous artesunate and intravenous fluids.
With the impending hypovolaemia, and persistent hypotension with an episode of loss of consciousness for 20 min, the child was referred to our hospital. He was afebrile, hypotensive (88/36 mmHg), with high pulse rate (110 bpm) and facial swelling. There was reduction in urine output of around 150 ml per day, but the oxygen saturation (SpO2) was well maintained. Liver was enlarged up to 2 cm below the right costal margin. Other systemic examinations were within normal limits. Upon laboratory investigations, his haemoglobin level was 11 g dl-1, with a low haematocrit (34.2 %), mean corpuscular volume (71 fl) and mean corpuscular haemoglobin (22.9 pg) values with platelet count of 36 000 mm-3 blood. Serum direct bilirubin and liver enzymes were elevated. Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smears revealed normal sized erythrocytes with microgametocytes containing malarial pigments (Fig. 1). Quantitative buffy coat (QBC) examination detected gametocytes of non-falciparum species. Blood sample was subjected to a multiplex nested PCR assay using published primers (Table 1), and an amplified product of 121 bp corresponding with P. vivax was detected by 1.5 % agarose gel electrophoresis using a molecular ladder of 100 bp (Thermo Scientific Gene Ruler 100 bp ladder) (Fig. 2). Buffer used for the agarose gel cast and running buffer in the gel electrophoresis tank was 10x Tris boric acid EDTA (TBE). The child was treated with injectable inotropes, intravenous fluids, oxygenation, the remaining two doses of artesunate and injectable antibiotics (ceftriaxone and vancomycin). Antibiotics were discontinued after malaria was reported. A repeat complete haemogram showed a fall of platelets to 19 000 mm-3 blood after 7 h of treatment, but the child became stable after 22 h with the same regimen and was discharged with advice to continue artemether-lumefantrine combination without any other drugs and/or antibiotics.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 13-year-old boy presenting with high-grade fever, projectile vomiting, lightheadedness, weakness, and passage of black-colored urine.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 13-year-old boy presented with high-grade fever, projectile non-bilious non-bloody vomiting, lightheadedness, generalized asthenia, anorexia, and passing black-colored urine. At a primary healthcare facility, he was documented to have high fever (40 C), hypotension (110/40 mmHg), and severe thrombocytopenia. Following initial resuscitation and antipyresis, he developed persistent refractory hypotension, impending hypovolemic shock, and an episode of loss of consciousness lasting 20 minutes, prompting urgent referral to a tertiary hospital.
subjective.past_medical_history: No documented chronic illnesses. Pre-admission administration of one dose of intravenous artesunate and intravenous fluids at referring center.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, projectile non-bloody non-bilious vomiting, lightheadedness, generalized weakness, anorexia, dark black urine, facial swelling, and transient syncope. Negative for active mucosal or cutaneous bleeding manifestations. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Afebrile, hypotensive with blood pressure 88/36 mmHg, pulse rate 110 beats/min, SpO2 well maintained on room air. Facial swelling present. Urine output markedly reduced to approximately 150 mL/day (oliguria). Abdominal examination revealed tender hepatomegaly palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin. Other systemic examinations were unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-referral laboratory tests: hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL, hematocrit 35.8%, MCV 66.1 fL, MCH 22.7 pg, platelet count 28,000/mm3, blood urea 62 mg/dL, random blood sugar 204 mg/dL. Tertiary admission laboratory tests: hemoglobin 11 g/dL, hematocrit 34.2%, MCV 71 fL, MCH 22.9 pg, platelet count 36,000/mm3 (declining to 19,000/mm3 at 7 hours post-treatment), elevated direct bilirubin, and elevated transaminases. Negative investigations: Dengue NS1 antigen, scrub typhus card test, Widal agglutination test, and SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Peripheral blood smears and quantitative buffy coat (QBC) performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium vivax malaria complicated by blackwater fever (intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria), severe thrombocytopenia, oliguric acute renal failure, and impending hypovolemic/septic shock.
Diagnostic confirmation: Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear demonstrating microgametocytes containing malarial pigments; QBC detecting non-falciparum gametocytes; multiplex nested PCR confirming a 121-bp amplicon specific for Plasmodium vivax. Dengue NS1, scrub typhus, Widal, and COVID-19 tests were negative.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed with intravenous fluid resuscitation, injectable inotropic support, oxygenation, completed remaining two doses of intravenous artesunate, and empiric IV ceftriaxone and vancomycin (discontinued once diagnosis confirmed). Thrombocytopenia nadired at 19,000/mm3 at 7 hours, followed by hemodynamic stabilization, recovery of urine output by 22 hours, and discharge on oral artemether-lumefantrine combination therapy with complete recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old male patient presented to the Medicine Department with a history of low-grade fever, weight loss, and anorexia for the past 6 weeks. General examination revealed mild pallor, splenomegaly, and mild hepatomegaly with discrete enlarged lymph nodes at the right epitrochlear area and right cervical region. He was advised for all necessary investigations including FNAC of the lymph nodes. All biochemical tests were within normal limits, except mild elevation of liver enzymes (serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase - 60 IU/L, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase - 53 IU/L, lactic dehydrogenase - 370 IU/L). On hematological examination, he had a hemoglobin level of 10.2 g% and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was elevated (ESR - 68 mm/h). On serology screening, he was reactive to HIV I.
FNAC was performed from both cervical and epitrochlear lymph nodes with a 24G needle attached with 20 cc syringe. The smears were stained with Leishman-Giemsa stain and Ziehl-Neelsen stain. The smears showed polymorphous cell population, comprised of reactive lymphoid cells, histiocytes, isolated epithelioid cells, many tangible body macrophages, and macrophages filled with leishmania amastigote form [Figures 1 and 2]. Subsequently, he had undergone bone marrow examination and the smears revealed high parasitic load of amastigote form of leishmania in the bone marrow smears (parasite load - [5+]). The diagnosis was established as visceral leishmaniasis with leishmanial lymphadenitis with HIV-reactive status. He was treated with stibogluconate for 28 days with antiretroviral therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old male presented with a 6-week history of low-grade fever, weight loss, and anorexia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the Medicine Department with a 6-week history of persistent low-grade fever accompanied by progressive weight loss and anorexia. Diagnostic evaluations including biochemical testing, hematologic surveys, fine-needle aspiration cytology of peripheral lymph nodes, and bone marrow examination were recommended.

objective.physical_examination: General examination revealed mild pallor. Abdominal examination demonstrated splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly. Lymphatic examination showed discrete enlarged lymph nodes in the right epitrochlear area and right cervical region.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 10.2 g%; Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 68 mm/h. Liver enzymes: serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT) 60 IU/L, serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) 53 IU/L, lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) 370 IU/L. Other biochemical tests: within normal limits. Serology screening: reactive for HIV-1.
objective.advanced_workup: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of right cervical and epitrochlear lymph nodes (24G needle, Leishman-Giemsa and Ziehl-Neelsen stains): smears showed a polymorphous cell population comprised of reactive lymphoid cells, histiocytes, isolated epithelioid cells, and numerous tingible body macrophages. Bone marrow examination: bone marrow aspirate smears obtained.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis presenting with leishmanial lymphadenitis in an HIV-1-reactive patient.
Diagnostic confirmation: FNAC of cervical and epitrochlear lymph nodes revealed macrophages filled with Leishmania amastigote forms. Bone marrow smears demonstrated a high parasitic load of Leishmania amastigotes (parasite load 5+).
Differentials ruled out: Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Ziehl-Neelsen stain negative for acid-fast bacilli), lymphoma, and other opportunistic infections.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with sodium stibogluconate for 28 days in conjunction with antiretroviral therapy (ART).

raw_case_text: Although the role of HHV8 in KD is demonstrated in the occurrence of KD, cofactors remain poorly understood. We report here a case of KD occurring after a 10-year-old vascular trauma on a patient from Central Africa with HIV infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A patient from Central Africa presenting with localized lesions developing after a vascular trauma ten years prior.
subjective.past_medical_history: Vascular trauma sustained 10 years prior. Epidemiological origin: Central Africa.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Kaposi disease (KD) associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection occurring in a patient from Central Africa at the site of vascular trauma sustained 10 years previously.

raw_case_text:
A 57-year-old man with a past medical history of controlled diabetes mellitus (DM), and no prior ophthalmic examination was referred due to gradually bilateral vision loss six days before the presentation which was accompanied by ocular pain in recent days. Eighteen days before the onset of visual symptoms, the patient was diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2 by a positive real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) of a nasopharyngeal swab specimen and symptoms of high fever, persistent cough, and shortness of breath. The patient was admitted for two weeks and received systemic Dexamethasone and Remdesivir. At presentation, his viral and systemic symptoms were resolved. There was no history of headache, scalp tenderness, fever, weight loss, and muscle weakness.
On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was light perception for the right eye (RE) and no light perception for the left eye (LE). Examination of the pupils revealed nonreactive pupils to light; therefore, the relative afferent pupillary defect was not assessable. Extraocular movements were normal. Intraocular pressure was measured 28 mmHg for the RE and 42 mmHg for the LE. Slit-lamp examination findings indicated bilateral shallow anterior chambers (360  peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) was found on gonioscopic examination), corneal microcystic edema, and nuclear sclerosis 1+ cataract in both eyes. A bilateral optic disk swelling was detected in fundus examination via undilated pupils. The patient was admitted, and after medical IOP reduction, peripheral laser iridotomy was done. Then, dilated fundoscopic examination performed, and bilateral optic disk swelling was found. Optic disks were small-sized. Also, an intraretinal macular hemorrhage in the RE was seen (Figure 1A,D). Peripapillary retinal swelling was documented in retinal nerve fiber layer optical coherence tomography (RNFL OCT) (Figure 1B,E). Analysis of blood tests including complete blood test (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and C-reactive protein (CRP) was not remarkable. Prothrombin, partial thromboplastin time, antithrombin, protein C, proteinS, lupus anticoagulant, and lipid profile all resulted within the normal range. The HbA1c was 7.2%. According to optical biometry, axial length was 21.79 mm in the RE and 20.89 mm in the LE. The refraction of the RE was [+2.00  -1.00 @83] and [+6.75 -0.50 @ 13] for the LE. Increased choroidal thickness was noted in enhanced depth imaging OCT (EDI-OCT), especially in the LE (Figure 1C,F). In fluorescein angiography, no sign of ischemia or peripheral vasculitis was detected (Figure 2). Indocyanine green angiography (ICG) confirmed severe choroidal ischemia (Figure 3). Color Doppler sonography of carotid and vertebral arteries and transthoracic echocardiography were unremarkable. No pathologic finding was reported in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Neurologist consult was done, and no evidence of giant cell arteritis and systemic vasculitis was found. Intravenous methylprednisolone (one gr daily) for three days was prescribed. In follow-up examination, there was no improvement in visual acuity, IOP was controlled with topical medication, and optic disk swelling was resolved (Figure 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male presenting with progressive bilateral visual loss for 6 days accompanied by recent severe ocular pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Eighteen days prior to visual symptoms, the patient developed high fever, persistent cough, and shortness of breath, testing positive for acute viral respiratory infection, for which he was hospitalized for 2 weeks and treated with remdesivir and dexamethasone. His systemic respiratory symptoms resolved. Six days prior to ophthalmologic evaluation, he noted insidious bilateral loss of vision, followed in subsequent days by bilateral ocular pain. He denied headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, fever, weight loss, or muscular weakness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus. No prior ophthalmologic history or previous ocular surgery. Recent 2-week hospitalization for viral pneumonia.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports bilateral vision loss and ocular pain. Denies headache, temporal tenderness, systemic fevers, myalgias, arthralgias, or respiratory symptoms at presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic exam: Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was light perception (LP) in the right eye (RE) and no light perception (NLP) in the left eye (LE). Pupils: Bilaterally non-reactive to light (relative afferent pupillary defect not assessable). Extraocular motility normal. Intraocular pressure (IOP): Elevated at 28 mmHg in RE and 42 mmHg in LE. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy: Bilateral microcystic corneal edema, shallow anterior chambers, 360-degree peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) on gonioscopy, and 1+ nuclear sclerotic cataract bilaterally. Fundus examination: Small optic discs with bilateral marked optic disc swelling; intraretinal macular hemorrhage in the right eye.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood tests: CBC, ESR, and CRP unremarkable. Coagulation and thrombophilia profile: Prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, antithrombin, protein C, protein S, and lupus anticoagulant normal. Lipid panel normal. HbA1c 7.2%. Optical biometry: Axial length 21.79 mm in RE, 20.89 mm in LE. Refraction: RE [+2.00 -1.00 @ 83], LE [+6.75 -0.50 @ 13].
objective.advanced_workup: Retinal nerve fiber layer optical coherence tomography (RNFL OCT): Marked peripapillary retinal swelling bilaterally. Enhanced depth imaging OCT (EDI-OCT): Increased choroidal thickness, more prominent in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography: No evidence of retinal ischemia or peripheral vasculitis. Indocyanine green angiography (ICG): Severe choroidal ischemia bilaterally. Color Doppler ultrasound of carotid and vertebral arteries: Unremarkable. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Normal. Brain MRI: Normal without intracranial pathology.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Bilateral acute angle-closure glaucoma (AACG) and non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) with severe choroidal ischemia and optic disc edema following COVID-19 infection (confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal RT-PCR 18 days prior). Underlying risk factors included hyperopia, shallow anterior chambers, short axial length, and diabetes mellitus. Giant cell arteritis and systemic vasculitis were excluded clinically and serologically.

Management and outcome: Initial medical lowering of intraocular pressure followed by bilateral peripheral laser iridotomy, topical antiglaucoma medications, and intravenous pulse methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days. Follow-up examinations demonstrated normalization and control of intraocular pressure and complete resolution of optic disc swelling; however, bilateral severe visual impairment persisted (light perception RE, no light perception LE).

raw_case_text: Patient 1: 64-year-old male, diabetes mellitus, dyslipaemia, and arthrosis with lumbar discopathy, attending the emergency department showing fever and dry cough, with a blood pressure of 160/90, a heart rate of 85 beats per minute, a SpO2 measure of 94%, and elevated D-Dimer levels. Chest X-ray: Faint opacities in the upper right and lower left lobes were seen, suggesting the presence of infectious and viral processes and atypical germs. Confirmation of COVID-19 was made by RT-PCR using a throat swab. The patient was treated with lopinavir-ritonavir, hydroxychloroquine (for 5 days), and lithium carbonate (starting on day 5, initial dose of 200 mg/12 h and after 48 h increased to 400 mg/12 h). He was also was treated with prednisolone (day 14, 40 mg/8). The patient was discharged after 27 days.

subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 64-year-old male presented to the emergency department with fever and dry cough.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diabetes mellitus, dyslipaemia, and arthrosis with lumbar discopathy.

objective.routine_investigations: Elevated D-Dimer levels. Chest X-ray: Faint opacities in the upper right and lower left lobes were seen, suggesting the presence of infectious and viral processes and atypical germs.

The patient was treated with lopinavir-ritonavir, hydroxychloroquine (for 5 days), lithium carbonate (starting on day 5, initial dose of 200 mg/12 h and after 48 h increased to 400 mg/12 h), and prednisolone (day 14, 40 mg/8). raw_case_text:
A 3.5-year-old male child born in April 2012 was brought to a private hospital in Mumbai in April 2015. The child had a history of parotitis and a 3-month long history of recurrent fever, cough, and symptoms suggestive of respiratory tract infection in March 2015. The child was found to be infected by HIV. His absolute CD4+ count (CD4%) and plasma viral load were 388 cells/mm3(13.4%) and 191,000 copies/ml, respectively. This signified severe immunosuppression for his age and suggested that the HIV infection had not been acquired recently. Both the parents were tested and found to be HIV negative. The discordant result of mother and child was baffling, and an explanation was sought for alternate source of infection.
The parents had a nonconsanguineous marriage, and the child was delivered vaginally at term without any complications. He was immunized appropriately for his age. There was no history of sexual abuse, blood transfusion, tattooing, or piercing of body parts of the child. There was no history of surrogate breastfeeding to the child and sharing of a toothbrush or nail clipper. There was no history of premastication according to the family members.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 3.5-year-old male presenting with a three-month history of recurrent fever, persistent cough, and symptoms of respiratory tract infection.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 3-month history of recurrent fevers, cough, and frequent respiratory infections. He had a prior documented episode of acute parotitis. Following persistent illness, diagnostic serological evaluation revealed advanced immunodeficiency, prompting an investigation into non-vertical routes of transmission given negative parental serologies.
subjective.past_medical_history: Full-term normal vaginal delivery without perinatal complications to non-consanguineous parents; fully immunized for age; episode of acute parotitis. Negative history for blood transfusions, child abuse, skin puncture/tattooing, surrogate breastfeeding, premastication of food, or sharing of sharp personal items.
subjective.review_of_systems: Recurrent fevers, productive cough, parotid swelling; denies chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, seizures, or rash.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Advanced pediatric human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection (CDC Category 3 severe immunosuppression for age: absolute CD4+ count 388 cells/microL [13.4%], plasma HIV-1 RNA 191,000 copies/mL) acquired via a non-vertical, household route, with confirmed seronegativity in both biological parents.
Plan & Outcome: Comprehensive epidemiological and molecular phylogenetic investigation initiated to identify household transmission sources, alongside enrollment into pediatric HIV specialty care for initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy.

raw_case_text: A 23 yearold male patient (whose verbal consent was taken for reporting this case) presented in our outpatient department (OPD) with a history of decreased sleep, odd behavior, wandering about, frequent irrelevant talks, fearfulness, referential thinking, and persecutory ideas for 2 days with a history of being HIV positive for 5 years. This was the first episode. He was treated with tablet olanzapine 5 mg, which was increased up to 10 mg. He improved in a month. After 2 months, he presented with sadness, decreased interaction, crying spells, and hopelessness. Hence, along with tablet olanzapine, antidepressant tablet escitalopram 5 mg was started which was gradually increased to 10 mg. He improved in about 2 months and maintained well for about 11 months. He was compliant to the treatment and was followed up once a month in the OPD. After 11 months, he presented with a history of decreased sleep, increased talk, irritability, and cheerfulness. Hence, escitalopram was stopped, and he was continued with tablet olanzapine 10 mg. He recovered in 15 days and maintained well for further 8 months, and tablet olanzapine was gradually reduced to 5 mg. A diagnosis of "bipolar affective disorder, current episode mania without psychotic symptoms" was made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old male presenting with decreased sleep, odd behavior, wandering, irrelevant speech, fearfulness, and persecutory ideas for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 23-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with a 2-day acute onset of psychiatric symptoms including reduced sleep, odd behavior, wandering, irrelevant talk, fearfulness, referential thinking, and persecutory ideation, representing his first psychotic manic episode. He was treated with olanzapine (5 mg titrated to 10 mg daily) with remission within one month. Two months later, he experienced an episode of severe depression with sadness, psychomotor withdrawal, crying spells, and hopelessness, managed by adding escitalopram (5 mg titrated to 10 mg daily) with recovery over two months. After 11 months of euthymia, he developed an acute manic relapse characterized by decreased sleep, logorrhea, irritability, and elevated cheerfulness.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic viral infection diagnosed 5 years previously; no prior psychiatric hospitalizations or episodes prior to index presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Decreased sleep, irrelevant speech, referential thinking, persecutory ideas, episodic sadness, crying spells, hopelessness, irritability, and logorrhea; denies concurrent focal neurological deficits or physical complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Mental status examination: Disorganized behavior, wandering, pressured irrelevant speech, fearfulness, referential and persecutory delusions during initial acute episode; cheerful mood, irritability, and increased talkativeness during subsequent manic relapse.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Bipolar affective disorder, current episode mania without psychotic symptoms (subsequent relapse), following an initial episode of acute mania with psychotic features and an intermediate depressive episode, occurring in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection diagnosed 5 years prior.
Management & Clinical Course: Initial psychotic mania treated with olanzapine (5 mg titrated to 10 mg daily) with resolution in 1 month. Depressive episode treated with escitalopram (5 mg to 10 mg daily) alongside olanzapine. Upon emergence of mania at 11 months, escitalopram was discontinued, and olanzapine was increased to 10 mg daily, achieving full symptom remission in 15 days. Olanzapine was subsequently maintained and tapered to 5 mg daily with sustained stability for over 8 months.

raw_case_text:
We present the case of a previously healthy 35-year-old female, who presented to our emergency department (ED) complaining of high-grade fever of waxing-and-waning nature for five days, associated with vomiting, body aches and sleepiness. She works at a local bank and developed fever during her mandated hotel quarantine upon return from a holiday in Sudan seven days ago, during which she was not on malaria prophylaxis. COVID-19 PCR from nasopharyngeal swab was negative. She did not improve despite anti-pyretics and anti-emetics during the hotel quarantine, and sought medical advice at a private clinic where she tested positive for malaria and was referred to our hospital for inpatient management.
Patient reported that she had previous history of malaria 10 years ago but not as severe. She had no other sick contact in her family or friends.
Her initial labs showed hemoglobin of 12.1 gm/dl, normal white blood cell count of and platelets of 150 with elevated AST and ALT of 58 and 57U/L, respectively and high total bilirubin of 26 mumol/L. Malarial smears were positive for Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitemia level of 27 %. She was admitted to medical intensive care unit (MICU) for further management under close monitoring due to severe malaria with overlapping features of sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In line with guidelines for malaria management, she was started on parenteral artesunate, which was administered until the parasite level decreased to less than 1%. She was then started on oral artemether-lumefantrine for five days thereafter, and the malaria parasite level at the end of the treatment was less than 0.1 %. In the meantime, she received other supportive treatment including intravenous fluids, antiemetics, antipyretics and antibiotics.
She was transferred to medical ward after MICU care, and had significant improvement in her condition, except for persistent fever and a gradual decline in her hemoglobin.
Labs later in the hospital course revealed continuous gradual drop in hemoglobin from 12 g/dL to 6.5 g/dL and she received multiple packed red blood cell transfusions. Her hemoglobin would initially increase post-transfusions, followed by a decrease again within one to two days. Figure 1 shows the trend of hemoglobin levels during the hospitalization along with blood transfusions throughout the admission. Later in her clinical course, her platelets dropped from 160 to 70 x 103/muL, but improved without intervention. Liver transaminases also increased up to 150sU/L and total bilirubin was 35 mumol/L. Labs revealed increased lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 595 U/L (reference range: 135-214 U/L) and low haptoglobin reported as less than 10 mg/dl (30-200 mg/dl). Coombs' test was positive with low complement 4 (C4). Subsequently, all liver function tests improved within one week.
She continued to spike fever at least once per day and temperatures ranged from 38.5 to 40C and she was on as-needed paracetamol infusion. Sepsis workup including blood cultures and urine culture were negative. She had bilateral pleural effusion, more prominent on the right side associated with dyspnea and increased requirement for oxygen supplementation, thus piperacillin-tazobactam was initiated empirically and she underwent therapeutic and diagnostic thoracentesis on the left side - as the right-sided effusion was complicated with consolidation and collapse. Pleural fluid analysis revealed exudative effusion with predominantly neutrophilic leukocytosis.
In the next few days, she continued to spike fever and had persistent drop in hemoglobin, due to which antimicrobial coverage was escalated to tigecycline to treat suspected empyema, for which right-sided effusion was drained by interventional radiologist, and pleural fluid analysis showed the same results as those from left pleural effusion. Once the results of all cultures from pleural fluid and peripheral blood were negative, the antibiotics were discontinued.
Despite all measures, there was no further improvement in her fever. Further workup to investigate possible fever of unknown origin included ultrasound of the abdomen to evaluate for any intrabdominal collections and it showed an ill-defined hypoechogenicity in the pancreatic head (Fig. 2) and multiple ill-defined hypoechoic lesions in the spleen and recommended for further evaluation by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The ultrasound also incidentally noted multiple gallbladder polyps, minimal pelvic free fluid and bilateral pleural effusion. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the abdomen confirmed multiple splenic infarcts, mildly enlarged liver and annular pancreas with no focal pancreatic lesion.
As no significant improvement was noted in her clinical condition, further workup was performed to exclude connective tissue disease, involving ANA which was positive. Direct antiglobulin test was also positive, along with high LDH and low haptoglobin, confirming autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Bone marrow aspiration (BMA) was not performed as the patient declined the procedure after discussion of benefits of BMA in diagnosis and potential risks of the procedure including hematoma and bleeding, especially considering thrombocytopenia. After ruling out all other causes including hemolytic anemia due to autoimmune etiologies or related to sepsis, along with resolution of the fever, the delayed autoimmune hemolytic anemia was deemed most likely attributable to parenteral artesunate in our case.
After one-week follow-up, she had stable hemoglobin and her fever chart showed no more spikes with good over all condition as per the patient.
As per our conclusions, with accumulating available information, it appears our patient had a rare case of artesunate-induced delayed hemolysis by exclusion of all other possible diagnoses and we highlight the challenges of diagnosis of PADH due to its rare occurrence and as the concept is not yet well-recognized.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old female presenting with fluctuating high-grade fever, vomiting, body aches, and drowsiness for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 35-year-old female presented with a 5-day history of waxing-and-waning high fevers, vomiting, body aches, and drowsiness during mandatory hotel quarantine 7 days after returning from Sudan without chemoprophylaxis. She failed to respond to antipyretics and antiemetics and was evaluated at an outpatient clinic before referral for inpatient care. Following initial intensive care management, she developed persistent daily fever spikes and progressive drop in hemoglobin requiring multiple blood transfusions, followed by right-sided dyspnea.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. History of uncomplicated malaria 10 years prior. Travel history: Returned from Sudan 7 days prior without malaria prophylaxis. Denied sick contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Vomiting, body aches, drowsiness, dyspnea; denies sick contacts.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing, drowsy, in respiratory distress requiring oxygen supplementation; persistent daily fever spikes between 38.5 °C and 40.0 °C. Decreased breath sounds at lung bases, more prominent on the right.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: Hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, normal WBC, platelets 150 x 10^3/μL, AST 58 U/L, ALT 57 U/L, total bilirubin 26 μmol/L. Hospital course: Progressive hemoglobin decline from 12.0 g/dL to 6.5 g/dL despite repeated packed red blood cell transfusions; platelets nadired to 70 x 10^3/μL; AST/ALT rose to ~150 U/L, total bilirubin to 35 μmol/L. Hemolysis workup: LDH 595 U/L (ref: 135-214 U/L), haptoglobin < 10 mg/dL (ref: 30-200 mg/dL), direct Coombs test positive with low C4; ANA positive. COVID-19 PCR negative. Blood and urine cultures sterile. Pleural fluid analysis (bilateral thoracenteses): Exudative effusion with neutrophilic leukocytosis; sterile cultures. Abdominal ultrasound showed ill-defined hypoechoic lesions in the spleen and pancreatic head, gallbladder polyps, trace pelvic fluid, and bilateral pleural effusions.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI: Confirmed multiple splenic infarcts, mild hepatomegaly, annular pancreas with no focal mass, and bilateral pleural effusions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria (initial parasitemia 27%) with ARDS and sepsis features, complicated by post-artemisinin delayed autoimmune hemolytic anemia (PADH) with positive direct antiglobulin test and multiple splenic infarctions. Initial malarial smear confirmed Plasmodium falciparum with 27% parasitemia. Empyema, occult bacteremia, and primary connective tissue disorders were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initial severe malaria treated in MICU with intravenous artesunate until parasitemia dropped below 1%, followed by oral artemether-lumefantrine for 5 days (final parasitemia < 0.1%). Empirical IV piperacillin-tazobactam and tigecycline with bilateral pleural drainage were discontinued once cultures proved sterile. PADH was managed with supportive care and blood transfusions. Hemoglobin stabilized, fever resolved, and she was in good condition at 1-week outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old femalepresented with widespread painful crusted skin lesions over both palms and digits [Figure 1]. The largest lesion ranged from 3 cm x 5 cm and the smallest from 2 cm x 2 cm. They were preceded by discrete deep-seated vesicles 2 weeks earlier, which ruptured within a day or two and coalesced to form plaques with minimal discharge. On examination, well-demarcated plaques were present, associated with thick, adherent reddish yellow crusts, accompanied by a foul-smelling odor and tenderness. Contracture of the middle finger of the right hand was observed owing to similar lesions in the past.
Further, genital examination revealed numerous painful genital ulcers over the labia majora, labia minora, and inner aspect of the thigh covered with a pale creamy discharge [Figure 2]. The inguinal lymph nodes were enlarged and tender. The lesions over the hand and genitalia appeared simultaneously.
The history of a similar episode was present 2 years ago; however, the treatment details could not be traced. She was diagnosed to be HIV positive 10 years ago and has been on regular "highly active antiretroviral treatment" since then. Her CD4 count at the time of presentation to us was 236 cells/mm.
Bacterial and fungal cultures failed to show any growth. Biopsy displayed nonspecific features and the laboratory parameters were unremarkable except for hemoglobin of 9.2 g%. The serological test for HSV IgM was strongly positive. Polymerase chain reaction and viral cultures could not be carried out due to unavailability and cost constraints.
Episodic treatment with tablet acyclovir 400 mg per oral, 5 times daily, was started for 2 weeks until the lesions healed completely.
One month later, she presented again with vesicles over the palms and with genital ulcers, and contractures from the previous episode were evident [Figure 1]. Biopsy of the vesicle for histopathological examination was consistent with herpes virus infection revealing an intraepidermal vesicle containing balloon cells, neutrophils, nuclear debris, and fibrin strands. Balloon cells were noted to have pale gray nuclei, some being multinucleated. Dense mononuclear infiltrate was present in the upper dermis [Figure 3].
The patient was commenced on suppressive therapy with tablet acyclovir 400 mg orally, 2 times daily, to which she responded satisfactorily. Follow-up at 6 months showed no new lesions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old female presenting with painful, foul-smelling, crusted skin plaques over both hands and painful genital ulcers for two weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-week history of painful lesions simultaneously erupting on both hands and the genital region. The hand lesions began as discrete, deep-seated vesicles that ruptured within 1 to 2 days and coalesced into tender, foul-smelling, crusted plaques. She reported a similar episode 2 years prior that had resulted in a flexion contracture of her right middle finger. Following treatment and complete healing, she presented one month later with recurrent palmar vesicles and genital ulcerations.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic retroviral illness diagnosed 10 years earlier, maintained on regular highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART); history of a similar blistering and ulcerating episode 2 years prior resulting in digital contracture.
subjective.review_of_systems: Painful cutaneous and genital lesions, foul-smelling discharge, and local tenderness; denies systemic fever, chills, or gastrointestinal complaints.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic/Extremities: Well-demarcated plaques measuring from 2 cm x 2 cm up to 3 cm x 5 cm over both palms and digits, covered with thick, adherent reddish-yellow crusts, foul-smelling discharge, and local tenderness; flexion contracture of the right middle finger. Genitourinary: Numerous exquisitely painful ulcers over the labia majora, labia minora, and inner thighs covered with pale creamy exudate. Lymphatics: Tender bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 9.2 g%; remaining routine laboratory hematologic and biochemical parameters were unremarkable. Bacterial and fungal cultures: No microbial growth.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin biopsy of initial lesion: Non-specific inflammatory changes. Skin biopsy of recurrent palm vesicle: Intraepidermal blister containing balloon cells with pale gray nuclei and multinucleation, neutrophils, nuclear debris, and fibrin strands, accompanied by dense upper dermal mononuclear infiltrate, consistent with viral cytopathic changes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe, atypical, recalcitrant herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection causing synchronous crusted palmar plaques (herpetic geometric ecchymosis/whitlow) and genital herpes in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4 cell count 236 cells/mm3). Diagnostic confirmation: Strongly positive serum HSV IgM serology, supported by classic cytopathic histopathologic features of multinucleated balloon cells on repeat lesional biopsy; bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. Management & Outcome: Acute episode treated with oral acyclovir 400 mg 5 times daily for 2 weeks, resulting in complete lesion re-epithelialization. Upon clinical recurrence 1 month later, initiated on chronic oral acyclovir suppressive therapy at 400 mg twice daily, achieving satisfactory remission without new lesions at 6 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old man was admitted at a secondary-care hospital in the Brazilian Amazon with acute abdominal pain after jumping from a tree denying to have suffered any direct abdominal trauma. A diagnosis of spleen rupture and intra-abdominal haemorrhage was performed. He was submitted to splenectomy, during which a large spleen of 1,300 grams with a capsule rupture in the colic surface was obtained. The patient lived in an urban area of Manaus and denied previous episodes of malaria. For the last month before the traumatic event he had been working in a building project in a rural area where malaria transmission is endemic and referred that in the two days preceding surgery he had been feeling feverish and complaining of mild headache and asthenia. After surgery, he developed high fever, chills, and generalized myalgia. The initial diagnostic investigation performed by the Surgery Department only revealed anemia (Hb 8.7 g/dL) and thrombocytopenia (66,000 platelets/mm3). The patient was then transferred to a tertiary-care infectious diseases reference center.
A thick blood smear disclosed P. vivax infection with a semiquantitative parasitemia between 10.000 and 100.000 parasites/mm3. Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from the peripheral blood confirmed P. vivax monoinfection. Treatment was initiated with chloroquine (1,500 mg divided in 3 days) and primaquine (30 mg/day during 7 days). Both fever and parasitemia were cleared within 48 hours. The patient was discharged in the third day of treatment, and he did not develop any relapse nor had any other complications through a 1-year follow-up.
The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Fundacao de Medicina Tropical Heitor Vieira Dourado and the National Committee of Ethics in Science and Technology (CONEP Process No.: 25.001.011.792/2009-15), and the patient consented his case to be published.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male presenting with acute abdominal pain following a jump from a tree, followed postoperatively by high fever and chills.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was admitted to a secondary-care hospital after jumping from a tree with acute severe abdominal pain, denying direct trauma. He was diagnosed with splenic rupture and hemoperitoneum and underwent emergency splenectomy. He reported experiencing low-grade feverishness, mild headache, and asthenia for 2 days prior to the traumatic event. Following surgery, he developed high fevers, shaking chills, and generalized myalgia, with anemia and thrombocytopenia prompting transfer to an infectious disease reference center.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resided in urban Manaus; worked on a construction project in an endemic rural area for 1 month prior to presentation. Denied prior episodes of acute febrile parasitic disease. Denied direct abdominal trauma.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, mild headache, asthenia, generalized myalgia, and acute abdominal pain. Negative for direct abdominal trauma. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Post-surgical status post-splenectomy with healing surgical abdomen; febrile with chills and myalgias. General appearance was acute and uncomfortable.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 8.7 g/dL, platelet count: 66,000 platelets/mm3 (thrombocytopenia).
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency laparotomy / surgical pathology: Splenectomy specimen weighing 1,300 grams with capsule rupture along the colic surface and documented intra-abdominal hemorrhage.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute Plasmodium vivax infection manifesting with massive acute splenomegaly (1,300 g) and pathological/atraumatic splenic rupture with severe intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
Diagnostic confirmation: Thick blood smear disclosed Plasmodium vivax infection with semiquantitative parasitemia between 10,000 and 100,000 parasites/mm3; real-time PCR from peripheral blood confirmed Plasmodium vivax monoinfection.
Plan & Outcome: Emergency surgical splenectomy. Antimalarial therapy initiated with oral chloroquine (1,500 mg divided over 3 days) and oral primaquine (30 mg/day for 7 days). Fever and parasitemia cleared within 48 hours. Discharged on day 3 of antimalarial therapy with no relapses or complications during 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text: The case is of a 65-year-old migrant from Sierra Leone who has been living in the United States for more than a decade. The patient has had history of multiple episodes of malaria infection in childhood but no reported episode after emigrating to the United States. The patient had last been to the malaria endemic region of Sierra Leone in 2009 and denied any sickness during her trip or immediately after returning to the United States. She had her first episode of malaria in August of 2010 during which she was treated with full course of quinine and clindamycin. Her blood smears examined for parasites were reported as positive for Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites with very low parasite titer. The patient was readmitted in September of 2012 with complaint of recurrent fever and chills. She had no interval history of travel to any malaria endemic region. Blood smears obtained on the second hospitalization were reported showing Plasmodium malariae trophozoites. The patient's peripheral blood smears from the current and prior hospitalization were reviewed by the hospital's chief pathologist to answer why two different malariae species were identified on the two occasions without any evidence of reexposure. The final pathology report stated that the malaria parasite seen on both occasions was that of Plasmodium malariae and the initial reports of the parasite being Plasmodium falciparum were flawed. After this report the patient was treated with full course of chloroquine with resolution of fever and parasitemia. At 2-month followup a blood smear was obtained which did not show any parasites in her blood.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old female presenting with recurrent fevers and chills 3 years after last residing in West Africa and 2 years following an incompletely characterized parasitic episode.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who emigrated from Sierra Leone over a decade earlier and last visited in 2009 without acute illness, presented in August 2010 with fever and was treated with oral quinine and clindamycin. In September 2012, she was readmitted with recurrent paroxysmal fevers and chills without any interval travel to endemic regions. Comparative pathology review of peripheral smears was requested to adjudicate disparate diagnostic findings between admissions.
subjective.past_medical_history: Emigrated from Sierra Leone over a decade prior; last travel to Sierra Leone in 2009. History of multiple childhood febrile illnesses. Treated with oral quinine and clindamycin in August 2010 for a febrile illness. No interval travel between 2010 and 2012.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent fevers and chills. Negative for localized pain, cough, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile during paroxysms; general and systemic physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood investigations unremarkable except for microscopic evaluation of peripheral blood films.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Recrudescent quartan malaria due to chronic persistent Plasmodium malariae infection, originally misidentified as Plasmodium falciparum.
Diagnostic confirmation: Formal pathology review by the hospital's chief pathologist of peripheral blood smears from both the August 2010 and September 2012 admissions confirmed identical Plasmodium malariae trophozoites on both occasions, correcting the initial erroneous identification of P. falciparum.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with a full standard therapeutic course of oral chloroquine. Fevers and parasitemia resolved promptly. Repeat peripheral blood smear at 2-month follow-up confirmed complete parasite clearance with no detectable intraerythrocytic organisms.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old previously healthy African male medical intern sustained a needle-stick injury from a wide bore needle (gauge 18) to his little finger while performing a lumbar puncture on a HIV-infected patient. He sustained a small lesion that bled a little and he immediately washed it with water and soap. He was immediately started on postexposure prophylaxis Anti-Retroviral drugs (ARVs): Zidovudine, Lamivudine and Kaletra for 28 days as per the Kenya National AIDS Control Program protocol. His initial rapid HIV test (Determine) test was negative and so was a PCR done on completion of the ARVs. He had no significant past medical history.
The patient source, an African Female, was WHO clinical stage 4, not on ARVs and was being investigated for meningitis died soon the lumbar puncture and her results were not followed up until several months later.
Two weeks after the injury, the intern had swelling of the little finger associated with a persistent dull ache for which he sought surgical intervention. Pus was aspirated from the finger and incision and drainage were done under local anesthesia. Culture of the pus grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin on which he was started.
His little finger now had an open wound that persisted for several months despite debridement and different antibiotic regimens: levofloxacin, clindamycin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin. The intern continued to clean and dress his wound daily.
He developed painless axillary lymphadenopathy 6 weeks after the injury. For the next 6 months, there was persistent swelling of the little finger which seemed to be spreading to the hand (Fig.1). This was accompanied with low-grade fever, night sweats, and subjective weight loss. He underwent a surgical debridement 6 months after the injury and was started on levofloxacin. Intraoperatively necrotic debris was found.
Radiographic examinations done during the course of illness showed no bone involvement. Serial blood counts done in the course of illness showed persistently elevated lymphocytes and a raised ESR. Liver function test and renal tests were normal.
Ten months later and with no improvement of symptoms, he underwent yet another surgical debridement. Histological examination of the tissue taken revealed a chronic inflammatory process (Fig.2), granulomatous tubercles with epithelioid cells (Fig.3), giant cells of Langerhans (Fig.4), and a mononuclear infiltrate but no acid-fast bacilli (AFB) were demonstrated on Ziehl-Nelson stain.
He was started on rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for duration of 2 months to be followed by a 4-month course of rifampicin and isoniazid. The intern had complete recovery by the end of the 6 months. A rapid HIV test done at the end of the anti-TB treatment was negative.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male medical intern presented with a non-healing open wound and swelling of the little finger spreading to the hand for 10 months following an occupational needle-stick injury.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 27-year-old male medical intern sustained an accidental needle-stick injury to his little finger with an 18-gauge needle while performing a lumbar puncture on an HIV-infected patient with suspected meningitis (source patient died shortly after). He washed the wound immediately and completed a 28-day antiretroviral post-exposure prophylaxis course. Two weeks later, the finger became swollen and painfully aching; incision and drainage was performed, yielding pus that grew S. aureus. Despite drainage and sequential courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics, the open wound persisted for 10 months and spread to the hand, accompanied by painless axillary lymphadenopathy at 6 weeks, low-grade fever, night sweats, and weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Needle-stick injury to little finger from an 18-gauge needle; received 28 days of post-exposure prophylaxis (zidovudine, lamivudine, Kaletra) with negative baseline rapid HIV test and post-PEP HIV PCR. Treated sequentially with flucloxacillin, levofloxacin, clindamycin, ceftriaxone, and vancomycin. No other significant past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for low-grade fever, night sweats, subjective weight loss, and persistent dull aching pain in little finger. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Swelling and chronic open wound of the little finger extending into the hand; painless axillary lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial blood counts showed persistently elevated lymphocytes and elevated ESR. Liver function and renal function tests normal. Radiographs showed no bone involvement. Initial wound culture grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin. Repeat rapid HIV test at end of treatment remained negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Surgical debridement at 6 months revealed necrotic debris. Repeat surgical debridement at 10 months: histological examination revealed a chronic inflammatory process, granulomatous tubercles with epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and mononuclear infiltrates; Ziehl-Neelsen stain was negative for acid-fast bacilli.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Cutaneous inoculation tuberculosis (tuberculosis verrucosa cutis / cutaneous TB) of the finger contracted via occupational needle-stick injury during lumbar puncture of a patient with tuberculous meningitis, confirmed by histopathology demonstrating granulomatous tubercles with epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells, clinical indolence despite multiple antibacterial regimens, and rapid curative response to antitubercular therapy. Tissue ZN stain was negative for acid-fast bacilli. Management & Outcome: Treated with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for 4 months (total 6 months). Achieved complete wound healing and clinical recovery; follow-up HIV rapid test was negative.

raw_case_text: A 14-month-old female infant was admitted with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, bicytopenia, hypoxemia, and increased serum ferritin. A myelogram revealed Leishmania spp. and hemophagocytosis. She presented liver failure, and lipossomal amphotericin B and corticosteroid were started. She was treated with cefepime and vancomycin due to sepsis (blood cultures revealed Klebsiella spp., and she had skin lesions). After 12 days, she was discharged from the hospital and continued oral corticosteroid therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 14-month-old female infant presented with fever, abdominal distension, and respiratory distress.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant presented with persistent fever, progressive abdominal distension secondary to hepatosplenomegaly, bicytopenia, hypoxemia, and acute hepatic failure complicated by secondary sepsis.

objective.physical_examination: Hepatosplenomegaly, hypoxemia, and presence of skin lesions.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory evaluation revealed bicytopenia, elevated serum ferritin, and acute liver failure. Blood cultures yielded Klebsiella spp. bacteremia.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow myelogram demonstrated prominent features of hemophagocytosis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis complicated by secondary hemophagocytosis, acute liver failure, and Klebsiella spp. sepsis: bone marrow myelogram demonstrated Leishmania spp. amastigotes. The patient was treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B, systemic corticosteroids, intravenous cefepime, and intravenous vancomycin for bacterial sepsis. Following stabilization and clinical improvement, she was discharged home after 12 days of hospitalization to complete oral corticosteroid therapy.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male traveling from Bangladesh was admitted with fever and joint pain at Nakasero Hospital on 09 Sep 2017. Date of initial symptom onset of illness was 08 Sep 2017. The patient had no significant past medical history, was on no regular medication, and had received yellow fever specific travel-related vaccination. The patient, whose final destination was the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) where he worked, became ill while in transit in Dubai before traveling to Uganda. Once in Uganda and at Nakasero Hospital, a blood sample was collected on 09 Sep 2017 and transported to the arbovirus laboratory at UVRI.
Less detailed information is available for case report 2 involving two sisters who traveled to Ethiopia to visit their father for about 6 weeks. They became ill but got better after a week with treatment in Ethiopia. Their father had been diagnosed with a case of DF 2 months prior to them falling sick. They traveled back to Uganda on 27 Aug 2017. They arrived at the UVRI clinic on 03 Oct 2017, and a blood sample was collected from each person, approximately 5 weeks post-travel. They looked well but requested a DF test to confirm test results performed in Ethiopia.
A total of 284 serum samples collected in 2017 were tested for yellow virus (YFV), West Nile virus (WNV), DENV1-4, CHIKV and Zika virus (ZIKV) antibodies by IgM capture ELISA. Only the diagnostic testing results for arbovirus infections of the three travel-related cases are shown and summarized in Table 1. All serological testing in case report 1 (ARB01183/Uganda) were negative, while high neutralizing antibodies against DENV2 were found for both sisters that traveled to Ethiopia in case report 2 (ARB01227UVRI and ARB01228UVRI). 
Virus culture on Vero cell monolayers was performed in T25 flasks. The serum sample from the Bangladeshi traveler exhibited prominent and characteristic 100% CPE on day 2 post-infection. RNA extracted from harvested virus supernatant and tested by group-specific RT-PCR was positive for alphavirus and negative for flavivirus and bunyavirus. Further testing by real-time RT-PCR using CHIKV, ONNV and Semliki Forest virus (SFV) specific primers, yielded positive results for CHIKV. Next generation sequencing of the RNA isolated from cell culture supernatant of the CPE-positive culture sample identified a CHIKV genome that genetically clustered within a CHIKV clade containing predominantly Asian CHIKV strains (Fig. 1). The CHIKV strain most related to the virus isolated from ARB01183/Uganda was from Bangladesh collected in 2017 (MF77773566, Fig. 1 insert).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented with acute fever and joint pain of 1 day's duration during travel.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old male traveling from Bangladesh to the Democratic Republic of the Congo fell ill with acute fever and joint pain while in transit in Dubai on September 8, 2017, and was admitted to Nakasero Hospital upon arrival in Uganda the following day.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history; yellow fever travel vaccination received; travel route: Bangladesh through Dubai to Uganda and DRC.

objective.physical_examination: Fever and joint pain noted on admission; further physical examination details not documented.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Acute serum viral isolation on Vero cell monolayers showed 100% cytopathic effect (CPE) on day 2; group-specific RT-PCR was positive for alphavirus (negative for flavivirus and bunyavirus), and real-time RT-PCR was positive for Chikungunya virus (negative for O'nyong-nyong and Semliki Forest viruses). Next-generation sequencing confirmed a CHIKV genome clustering with Asian lineage strains (closely matching a 2017 Bangladesh isolate). Acute IgM capture ELISA for YFV, WNV, DENV 1-4, CHIKV, and ZIKV was negative (drawn on day 2 of illness before seroconversion). Management and course: Inpatient supportive care upon diagnosis.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old male patient returned to a rural region of Colombia on 17 December 2020, from Africa, where he lived for 10 months in the city of Gul, Uganda. He went to the emergency room on 26 December 2020 due to 10-day history of fever, holocranial headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and retroocular pain associated with sudden onset epistaxis and choluria. Physical examination revealed blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, heart rate 89 beats/minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths/minute, temperature 39 C, oxygen saturation 97% room air, cold and sweaty skin without jaundice or skin lesions, with adequate ventilatory dynamics, with hepatosplenomegaly 5 cm below the costal margin, and without any neurological compromise.
Laboratory analysis showed anemia (hemoglobin 10 g/dl reference value 12-14 mg/dl), thrombocytopenia (platelets 97 000/mm3 reference value 150 000-400 000/mm3) and abnormal serum transaminase. Various laboratory investigations were conducted to exclude any other likely cause of the fever and presence of an infection, including those for hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody, both came out normal. Serologic tests for dengue performed on the acute-phase serum (collected 10 days after onset of symptoms) showed the presence of immunoglobulin (Ig) M (titers 1:800) and IgG (titers 1:400; Table 1). Diagnosis of dengue virus infection with warning signs (Group B) was made and admitted to hospitalization for management with intravenous hydration, antipyretic, and total abdominal ultrasound. Ultrasound scan shows pleural effusion in addition to moderate free fluid in the peritoneal cavity surrounding urinary bladder and gallbladder wall thickening, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and pleural effusion. A 72 hours after admission, the patient persisted with fever and presented a decrease in hematocrit (34.4%) with an increase in hemoglobin 12 g/dL and platelets to 137 000/mm3 (Table 1).
Although dengue virus infection had been diagnosed, parasitic tests were performed because the patient had returned from an endemic country with persistent prolonged febrile syndrome, a thick and thin blood smear stained with Giemsa was performed and revealed the characteristic intraerythrocytic ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum (trophozoites: a total of 215 000 parasites/mul, parasitemia index of 2.3% and gametocytes), which confirmed the diagnosis of malaria as uncomplicated. Antimalarial management was started with artemether-lumefantrine 20/120 mg twice a day for 3 days. To rule out false positives, the asexual parasites load was performed on the peripheral blood smear and MAC-ELISA (considering more than 5 days illness) was positive for dengue virus type 2 (DENV-2). The MAC-ELISA is based on capturing human IgM antibodies on a microtiter plate using anti-human-IgM antibody followed by the addition of dengue virus antigens. The antigens used for this assay are derived from the envelope proteins of the 4 dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1-4). Considering IgG detection by ELISA in a single serum sample is not useful for diagnostic testing because it remains detectable for life after a dengue virus infection, the patient was asked if he had had dengue infection before, which he denied, and IgG was negative. Therefore, a diagnosis of concurrent malaria and dengue infection was established.
The patient completed antimalarial treatment with clinical and paraclinical improvement, afebrile, without new episodes of epistaxis or obvious bleeding, without skin lesions or jaundice, normalization of platelets and transaminases with normal total abdominal ultrasound. PCR (molecular test) was performed to confirm the presence of dengue virus in the blood, being positive. After 7 days at hospital, he was fully discharged.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting with fever, holocranial headache, myalgia, arthralgia, retro-ocular pain, sudden-onset epistaxis, and choluria for ten days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 34-year-old male returned to Colombia from Uganda and presented 10 days later with persistent fever, holocranial headache, retro-ocular pain, myalgias, arthralgias, choluria, and sudden-onset epistaxis. Inpatient ultrasound revealed polyserositis (pleural effusion and ascites), splenomegaly, and gallbladder wall thickening. Further investigation for persistent febrile syndrome in a returned traveler identified concurrent parasitic and arboviral infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior history of similar arboviral illness. Epidemiological history: Colombian resident who lived for 10 months in Gulu, Uganda, Africa, returning to rural Colombia 9 days prior to emergency evaluation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Sudden-onset epistaxis, choluria, holocranial headache, retro-ocular pain, myalgia, arthralgia; absence of jaundice.

objective.physical_examination: Body temperature 39 °C, blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, heart rate 89 beats/minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths/minute, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Skin cold and diaphoretic, without jaundice, petechiae, or cutaneous lesions. Respiratory: Normal respiratory dynamics. Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly palpable 5 cm below the costal margin. Neurological: Intact, no neurological deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: Hemoglobin 10 g/dL (reference value: 12-14 mg/dL), platelet count 97,000/mm3 (reference: 150,000-400,000/mm3), elevated serum transaminases. Follow-up (72 hours): Hematocrit 34.4%, hemoglobin 12 g/dL, platelet count improved to 137,000/mm3. Total abdominal and thoracic ultrasound: Moderate free fluid in the peritoneal cavity surrounding the urinary bladder (ascites), gallbladder wall thickening, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and pleural effusion; repeat ultrasound at discharge was normal. Infectious serologies: Hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody negative. Peripheral blood Giemsa thick and thin smears: Intraerythrocytic ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum (trophozoites: 215,000 parasites/microL, parasitemia index 2.3%, and gametocytes).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Concurrent co-infection of Dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2 with warning signs, Group B) and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a returned traveler from Uganda. Dengue confirmed by positive acute-phase serum IgM (titer 1:800) and IgG (titer 1:400), MAC-ELISA positive for DENV-2, and confirmatory blood Dengue RT-PCR; malaria confirmed by Giemsa-stained blood smear demonstrating P. falciparum trophozoites (215,000 parasites/microL, 2.3% parasitemia) and gametocytes. Acute hepatitis B and C were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Admitted for intravenous hydration, antipyretics, and supportive monitoring. Antimalarial therapy initiated with oral artemether-lumefantrine (20/120 mg twice daily for 3 days). The patient achieved complete defervescence, cessation of epistaxis, resolution of polyserositis on repeat ultrasound, normalization of transaminases and platelet count, and clearance of parasitemia, and was discharged in fully recovered condition after 7 days.

raw_case_text:
Case presentation. A 41-year-old Caucasian male with laryngeal and facial mucocutaneous leishmaniasis in treatment with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B was admitted to our hospital because of elevated creatinine kinase (CK):more than 100 upper limit of normal:in the absence of myalgia or muscle weakness. He was born to non-consanguineous parents. His father died in his 60s from gastric adenocarcinoma, while his mother was in good health. His brother died at 20 years of age from an unspecified lymphoproliferative disease. He had three sisters, and one of them suffered from chronic myalgias ( Figure 1A ). He worked as a construction worker. He lived in a small town in the province of Florence, Italy, and reported having previously traveled in Spain and France for vacation, while he denied having never traveled outside Europe. His past medical history was notable for visceral leishmaniasis at age 13, recurrent otitis and an episode of bronchopneumonia during childhood, and unexplained elevated CK on several occasions that were attributed to his occupation and to boxing that he played in his spare time. In 2013, at the age of 35, the patient developed periorbital swelling of the left side of the face, associated with mild erythema and skin thickening that was diagnosed as Morbihan's disease. The swelling did not improve with retinoid treatment and transiently responded to low-dose steroid ( Figure 1B ).
