At this time, blood tests showed worsening pancytopenia (anemia 7.0 g/dL, platelets count 50 G/L, neutropenia 600/mm3), hyperferritinemia, elevated liver enzymes and mild elevated triglyceridemia. We hypothesized that the patient had a hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by an acute primary HIV infection. Sternal bone marrow aspiration was performed showing signs of macrophages activation without hemophagocytosis. No Leishmania was found on bone marrow aspirate smears and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex PCR was negative. An empiric treatment with intravenous immunoglobulins 1 g/kg for 2 days was administered; no clinical response was observed.
Finally, a bone marrow biopsy was performed showing hemophagocytosis, confirming HLH, and moreover, revealing the presence of Leishmania spp ( Figure 1 ), with a low parasitic load. Serology was also positive for Leishmania infantum antibodies by immune-enzymatic screening technique, confirmed by Western-Blot assay. Molecular species identification confirmed a Leishmania infantum strand.
Intravenous liposomal amphotericin B was administered at 4 mg/kg/day on five consecutive days followed by five weekly administrations, allowing complete clinical recovery and pancytopenia recovery. Patient was discharged, no secondary prophylaxis against VL was prescribed. Viral load decreased to 75 copies/mL and CD4+ T-cells count increased to 213/mm3 two months after cART initiation and viral load was undetectable with CD4+ T-cells count at 345/mm3 after 6 months ( Figure 2 ), with no sign of VL relapse. After 24 months of follow-up, no VL relapse was observed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented with acute psychotic symptoms, fever, cough, and generalized asthenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency room with a sudden onset of paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, severe anxiety, fever, cough, and asthenia 10 days after returning from a 1-week trip to Greece. He was diagnosed with acute primary HIV-1 infection and initiated on neuroleptic medications (cyamemazine, risperidone), benzodiazepines, combination antiretroviral therapy (cART: tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir), and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. He developed neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) with bilateral muscular rigidity requiring ICU admission. Following cessation of neuroleptics, his rigidity resolved, but he experienced persistent high-grade fevers, chills, night sweats, and progressive pancytopenia. Workup for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and opportunistic pathogens was undertaken; empiric IVIG (1 g/kg for 2 days) produced no clinical response.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical or psychiatric history aside from anxious personality; mild tobacco and cannabis use. Normal lymphocyte count (1.4 G/L) one year prior. Epidemiological history: 1-week travel to Greece returning 10 days before symptom onset; unprotected sex with a male partner 2 months prior and during travel (partner recently diagnosed with HIV). Resident of Paris, France.
subjective.review_of_systems: Paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, anxiety, cough, asthenia, chills, night sweats. Home medications: cART (tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir), cotrimoxazole. Allergies: Severe adverse drug reaction to neuroleptics (neuroleptic malignant syndrome).

objective.physical_examination: General: febrile (temperature 38.5 C). HEENT: pharyngitis and oral candidiasis. Dermatologic: generalized erythematous skin rash. Neurologic: severe bilateral muscular rigidity (during NMS episode, later resolving). Abdomen: palpable hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology and Chemistry: Hemoglobin: 10.5 g/dL declining to nadir of 7.0 g/dL; Platelets: 90 G/L declining to 50 G/L; Neutrophils: 600/mm3; Absolute lymphocyte count: 500/mm3; Reticulocytes: 37 G/L; C-reactive protein: 18 mg/L; Elevated ferritin, elevated liver transaminases, and mild hypertriglyceridemia. HIV-1 diagnostics: HIV-1 serology positive, immunoblot positive (gp120, gp41 reactivity); initial plasma HIV viral load 5.47 million copies/mL rising to 6.85 million copies/mL; CD4+ T-cell count 90/mm3 declining to 30/mm3; viral genotype CRF19-cpx strain. Infectious screen negative: HAV, HBV, HCV, HEV, Toxoplasma, syphilis, EBV, CMV, Pneumocystis jirovecii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (negative sputum and BAL).
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture, EEG, and brain MRI: normal. Thoraco-abdomino-pelvic CT: homogenous hepatosplenomegaly and sparse interstitial micronodules/reticulations. Sternal bone marrow aspiration: macrophage activation without frank hemophagocytosis; aspirate smear negative for parasites, MTB PCR negative. Core bone marrow biopsy: performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania infantum) complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) in a patient with acute primary HIV-1 infection.
Diagnostic confirmation: Core bone marrow biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytosis confirming HLH and revealed the presence of intracellular Leishmania spp. amastigotes (low parasite load); serology was positive for Leishmania infantum antibodies by EIA and confirmed by Western blot; molecular species identification confirmed Leishmania infantum.
Differentials ruled out: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, tuberculosis, viral hepatitides (HAV/HBV/HCV/HEV), neurosyphilis/syphilis, toxoplasmosis, EBV/CMV infection, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome (resolved after neuroleptic withdrawal). Empiric IVIG produced no response.
Treatment and clinical course: Treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (4 mg/kg/day on days 1-5, followed by five weekly infusions) alongside cART and cotrimoxazole. Achieved complete clinical recovery, resolution of fever and hepatosplenomegaly, and full hematologic recovery of all cell lines. At 2 months, HIV viral load suppressed to 75 copies/mL (CD4 213/mm3); at 6 months, HIV viral load was undetectable (CD4 345/mm3). No relapse of visceral leishmaniasis observed over 24 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text: Twenty-six-year-old male patient referred from general hospital and admitted to our center with a history of Brucella aortic valve endocarditis, accompanied by hypotension and chest pain. Chest radiography showed moderately enlarged cardiac silhouette and mediastinum. Results of laboratory tests made on admission were as follow: White blood cell count, 19000/mm-3 with 91% neutrophils; platelet count, 89000/mm-3 ; hemoglobin, 8 g/dl; c-reactive protein, 54 mg/dl; erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 80 mm/h; blood urea nitrogen (BUN), 40 mg/dL; creatine (Cr), 2.9 mg/dL; and urinalysis revealed no any hematuria and 24-hour urinalysis (U.A) revealed proteinuria). Antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA ), anti-double stranded DNA, rheumatic factor (RF), anticardiolopin antibody, lupus anticoagulant were all negative. Serum agglutination tests were positive (titer>1:1500), and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay tests for anti-Brucella IgG and IgM antibodies were strongly positive (133 U/ml and 31.7 U/ml; 30 U/ml and 20 U/ml, respectively). In addition, Brucella melitensis was isolated from 2 of 3 consecutive blood cultures. No significant alterations were observed in the electrocardiogram. TEE revealed normal aortic diameter at the mid-ascending aorta, severe aortic regurgitation, aortic ring abscess in noncoronary sinus, large vegetation in noncoronary sinus leaflet with preserved ventricular function and moderate pericardial effusion (Figure 1A and  1B). Aortic wall fistula from ring abscess to pericardium temporary was blocked by intra fistula vegetation. Intraoperative finding revealed large vegetation and perifistula hematoma in aortic wall. The fistula tract starting from aortic ring (Figures 2 and 3) and extended to aortic wall as intramural tract in a distance of 15 mm above the ring and ending to external aortic wall as a crater of fistula (Figure 4). We think that initial bleeding from fistula tract to pericardium was blocked by vegetation that confirmed intra operatively. The patient then underwent conventional surgical treatment with extracorporeal circulation (ECC), and replacement of aortic valve with prosthetic valve (carbomedic, sorin group, 23 mm size) and resection of aortic wall containing fistula site and its replacement with fresh pericardial patch (Figure 5). Patient treated with ceftriaxone 2 g and gentamicin 3 mg/kg prior to culture report. Therapy with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily with gentamicin 3 mg/kg intravenus in 2 divided doses with oral rifampin 600 mg once daily for 6 weeks was started after confirmation of Brucella endocarditis. The patient recovered uneventfully and was discharged in the 15th postoperative day.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male presented with chest pain and hypotension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred from a general hospital and admitted with hypotension, chest pain, and clinical features of acute aortic valve endocarditis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior medical history, comorbidities, and animal/dairy exposure not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Chest pain, hypotension. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Hypotension; other vital signs and systemic physical examination details not documented beyond signs of acute endocarditis.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 19,000/mm^3 (91% neutrophils); Platelet count: 89,000/mm^3; Hemoglobin: 8 g/dL; CRP: 54 mg/dL; ESR: 80 mm/h; BUN: 40 mg/dL; Creatinine: 2.9 mg/dL. Urinalysis: no hematuria; 24-hour urine collection revealed proteinuria. Autoimmune/vasculitis panel: ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, rheumatoid factor (RF), anticardiolipin antibody, and lupus anticoagulant were all negative. Chest radiography: moderately enlarged cardiac silhouette and widened mediastinum. ECG: no significant alterations.
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): normal mid-ascending aortic diameter, severe aortic regurgitation, aortic ring abscess in the noncoronary sinus, large mobile vegetation on the noncoronary cusp, preserved left ventricular function, moderate pericardial effusion, and an aortic wall fistula tract from the ring abscess extending 15 mm into the aortic wall and ending as a crater on the external aortic wall, temporarily plugged by intra-fistula vegetation. Surgical procedure: emergent open heart surgery under cardiopulmonary bypass with resection of the aortic wall containing the fistula tract, fresh autologous pericardial patch repair of the aortic wall defect, and aortic valve replacement with a 23 mm Carbomedics mechanical prosthesis. Intraoperative findings confirmed large vegetation and perifistula hematoma in the aortic wall.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar native aortic valve infective endocarditis complicated by aortic ring abscess, aorto-pericardial fistula, severe aortic regurgitation, and secondary acute glomerulonephritis/renal impairment.
Confirmation: Brucella melitensis isolated from 2 of 3 consecutive blood cultures; standard tube agglutination test positive at titer >1:1500; ELISA anti-Brucella IgG (133 U/mL; UNL 30) and IgM (31.7 U/mL; UNL 20) strongly positive.
Differentials ruled out: Autoimmune vasculitis and systemic lupus erythematosus ruled out (negative ANA, ANCA, anti-dsDNA, RF, anticardiolipin, and lupus anticoagulant).
Treatment & Outcome: Initially treated empirically with ceftriaxone 2 g and gentamicin 3 mg/kg. Upon confirmation, switched to oral doxycycline (100 mg BID), intravenous gentamicin (3 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses), and oral rifampin (600 mg daily) for 6 weeks, alongside emergency surgical aortic valve replacement and pericardial patch repair. Recovered uneventfully and was discharged on postoperative day 15.

raw_case_text:
A 73-year-old female patient presented to the Security Forces Hospital in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, with fever and general body fatigue complaints for two weeks. She also complained of generalized body rashes and one episode of gingival bleeding; however, there was no epistaxis, hematemesis, or melena. Unfortunately, we did not take images of her rash because it was a usual rash with common viral diseases in our area, for example, dengue fever. In addition, the patient had left knee pain for one week before admission. Previous medical track record revealed hypertension which was treated with perindopril and amlodipine. Also, osteoarthritis was reported to be controlled with hydroxychloroquine and celecoxib for the past two years. The patient's family history was unremarkable. There was no history of weight loss and drinking, smoking, or illegal drug usage.
On day 0 of the patient's admittance, physical examination revealed the following vital signs: an initial temperature of 37 C, arterial blood pressure of 110/68 mmHg, heart rate of 94/min, and respiratory rate of 17/min. Anticyclic citrullinated peptides antibody of 0.80 U/ml was reported as normal (0.00-5.00). Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing was positive, whereas anti-dsDNA antibody 95.4 IU/mL was reported as normal (0.0-200.0). Normal levels of complement C3, 1.03 g/L (normal 0.83-1.93), and complement C4, 0.21 g/L (normal 0.15-0.57), were detected. Both the CXR and ECG were normal. The abdomen was examined with ultrasound and found to be normal. Other physical examinations were ordinary, including a normal heart sound with no murmur or rub, equal air entry bilaterally on chest examination, and normal cranial nerves; power and sensation were intact. Rheumatoid factor, as well as the COVID-19 PCR test, was confirmed as negative. Multiple joint abnormalities exist in both the hands, and there was a left knee effusion with hotness and pain, as well as a skin scar over the right knee from a prior knee replacement. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 19 mg/L, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 85 mm/h. Renal and liver function tests were normal, including sodium, potassium, total protein, and albumin levels. She never developed CNS or renal features. Antiviral antibody tests were negative for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, anti-HIV, and hepatitis B and C.
Since the patient has a history of consuming raw milk, ingesting unpasteurized dairy products, and lives in a brucellosis-endemic area (the western region of Saudi Arabia), brucellosis was suspected. Therefore, the blood culture was sent to the microbiology laboratory for further examination.
On day 1, the patient was admitted to the hospital with critically low thrombocytopenia. Platelet counts were only 1 x 10e3/mu L with generalized body rash in the form of purpura and petechiae and gum bleeding. The initial impression was idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). The hematological assessment revealed that hemoglobin was 13.5 g/dL, hematocrit was 40.1 percent, and the white blood cell count was 6.4 x 10e3/Ul, with an average differential in the initial laboratory tests. The platelets count was 1 x 10e3/mu L. Normal Hb and RBCs were confirmed in peripheral blood film assessment. There were some reactive lymphocytes, significant thrombocytopenia, and no aberrant cells. Prothrombin time (PT) is 12.6 seconds, while activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) is 36.3 seconds. Initially, the patient received six units of platelets, dexamethasone (40 mg IV daily) for five days, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) as an urgent intervention for her critically low platelets.
On day 7 of admittance to the hospital, the patient's platelets count went up slowly to 18 x 10e3/mu L, as shown in Figure 1, so the hematological team decided to start eltrombopag (thrombopoietin receptor agonist) at 50 mg tablet daily.
On day 8 of admission, hemoglobulin started to drop from 13.5 g/dL to 10.6 g/dL; a repeat peripheral blood film showed mild normocytic normochromic anemia; RBCs showed mild rouleaux and polychromasia, mild polymorph nuclear leukocytosis (bands = 5%), moderate monocytosis, and marked thrombocytopenia. A hemolytic anemia workup was sent; haptoglobin was low <0.08 g/L, reticulocytes were high at 2.9% (normal 0-2), and direct antiglobulin was confirmed as positive. Indirect bilirubin was elevated at 15 from a total bilirubin of 23. The patient was diagnosed with autoimmune hemolytic anemia based on a hemolytic workup and severe critically low thrombocytopenia, possible ITP.
On day 10, her platelet count remained low at 12 x 10e3/mu L, and her hemoglobin was 9.5. The diagnosis of Brucella was made based on the presence of the organism in blood and high Brucella serology. The serological analysis showed the Brucella antibody titer to be positive (titer, 1 : 2560). Hence, for immediate and effective treatment, the patient was started on doxycycline and rifampicin as a case of brucellosis. At this point, the hematology team decided to stop eltrombopag and IVIG.
The patient underwent bone marrow aspiration on day 10, which revealed high normocellular marrow, normal granulopoiesis and erythropoiesis, normal megakaryocytes, and reduced platelet. No remarkable evidence of malignancy or dysplasia. On day 12 of admission (two days after starting Brucella treatment), the platelet count was raised to 42 x 10e3/mu L. Three days after Brucella treatment (day 13 of admission), the platelet counts improved to 106 x 10e3/mu L. After five days of Brucella treatment (day 15 of admission), it returned to normal 306 x 10e3/mu L. On day 16, the blood culture grew Gram-negative coccobacilli (Brucella species).
On day 18, after normalization of the platelet count, the patient underwent right knee arthrocentesis, and synovial joint fluid was obtained. Synovial culture grew Gram-negative coccobacilli (Brucella species) upon microbial analysis, as shown in Figure 2. The patient was discharged home to be continued on rifampicin and doxycycline. Upon outpatient follow-up five days later, her platelet count remained within the normal range of 301 x 10e3/mu L. Her hemoglobin went up to 12.1 g/dL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old female presented with fever, fatigue, generalized petechial rash, and gingival bleeding for two weeks, accompanied by left knee pain for one week.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-week history of fever, severe generalized fatigue, petechial and purpuric rash, and an episode of gingival bleeding, along with left knee pain and swelling for 1 week. She was admitted with critical thrombocytopenia (platelet count 1 x 10^3/muL) initially treated as refractory immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) with platelets, high-dose IV dexamethasone, and IVIG, and subsequent eltrombopag. On hospital day 8, she developed acute autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Evans syndrome). Following identification of the underlying infectious etiology and commencement of targeted antimicrobials on day 10, her cytopenias rapidly normalized within 5 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension treated with perindopril and amlodipine; osteoarthritis managed with hydroxychloroquine and celecoxib for two years; prior right total knee arthroplasty. Epidemiological exposure: Regular ingestion of raw milk and unpasteurized dairy products; resident of western Saudi Arabia (endemic area).
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized petechial and purpuric skin rash, gingival bleeding, and left knee pain; denies epistaxis, hematemesis, melena, or weight loss. Home medications: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydroxychloroquine, celecoxib. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Temperature 37.0 °C, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, heart rate 94 beats/min, respiratory rate 17 breaths/min. Skin: Generalized purpuric and petechial rash. Musculoskeletal: Left knee effusion with local erythema, warmth, and tenderness; surgical scar over the right knee; chronic osteoarthritic changes of hand joints. Systemic: Normal heart sounds without murmur; lungs clear bilaterally; cranial nerves, motor, and sensory examinations intact.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission hematology: Platelet count 1 x 10^3/muL, Hb 13.5 g/dL, hematocrit 40.1%, WBC 6.4 x 10^3/muL, PT 12.6 s, aPTT 36.3 s. Peripheral blood smear: Severe thrombocytopenia with reactive lymphocytes, no blast cells. Day 8 hemolysis workup: Hb dropped to 10.6 g/dL (nadir 9.5 g/dL on day 10), haptoglobin <0.08 g/L, reticulocytes 2.9%, direct antiglobulin test (Coombs) positive, indirect bilirubin 15 umol/L (total bilirubin 23 umol/L); blood film showed normocytic normochromic anemia with rouleaux, polychromasia, 5% bands, and monocytosis. Inflammatory and serological tests: CRP 19 mg/L, ESR 85 mm/h; ANA positive, anti-dsDNA normal (95.4 IU/mL), anti-CCP normal (0.80 U/ml), normal C3 (1.03 g/L) and C4 (0.21 g/L); negative rheumatoid factor, COVID-19 PCR, and viral hepatitis/HIV/EBV/CMV panels. Renal and liver function tests normal. Chest X-ray, ECG, and abdominal ultrasound normal. Follow-up: Platelets rose to 42 x 10^3/muL on day 12, 106 x 10^3/muL on day 13, 306 x 10^3/muL on day 15, and 301 x 10^3/muL (Hb 12.1 g/dL) at outpatient follow-up.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration (day 10): Hypercellular to normocellular marrow with active granulopoiesis, erythropoiesis, and adequate megakaryocytes, with marked reduction in circulating platelets, without evidence of malignancy, granuloma, or myelodysplasia. Left knee arthrocentesis: Yielded purulent synovial fluid for microbial analysis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis with Brucella septic monoarthritis complicated by secondary Evans syndrome (immune thrombocytopenia and Coombs-positive autoimmune hemolytic anemia). Brucellosis confirmed by positive blood cultures growing Gram-negative coccobacilli (Brucella species), synovial fluid cultures growing Brucella species, and high Brucella serological antibody titer (1:2560).
Plan & Clinical Course: Received urgent initial therapy with 6 units of platelets, IV dexamethasone 40 mg daily for 5 days, IVIG, and eltrombopag 50 mg daily without significant platelet recovery. Following confirmation of Brucellosis on day 10, eltrombopag and IVIG were stopped and targeted therapy with oral doxycycline and rifampicin was initiated. Platelets dramatically surged to 42 x 10^3/muL within 48 hours, reached 106 x 10^3/muL at day 3, and normalized to 306 x 10^3/muL at day 5 of antibiotic therapy, with complete resolution of hemolysis (Hb improved to 12.1 g/dL). Patient was discharged on oral doxycycline and rifampicin with full hematological and joint recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 60-year-old previously healthy male farmer presented to the First Affiliated Hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University with a 6-month history of intermittent fever. Five months ago, he was diagnosed with VL and treated with sodium antimony gluconate (SAG) (0.6 g/d) for 6 days. The patients' condition improved, and he was discharged from the hospital. However, he was readmitted to our hospital because of recrudesce fever. He had a history of working in coalmines and current hypertension treated with oral therapy. There was no complication related to hypertension. Medical, surgical, pharmacological and family histories were not significant. His body weight was 70 kg. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly, no superficial lymphadenopathy, and no edema of the lower limbs. Blood cultures as well as tests for bacteria, fungi, tuberculosis, parasites, and brucellosis agglutination were all negative. His laboratory findings included pancytopenia with a C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 82.8 mg/L and procalcitonin (PCT) level of 0.88 ng/mL. The patient's liver function and coagulation function were abnormal. Computed tomography of the abdomen confirmed the presence of splenomegaly. Examination of bone marrow aspirate revealed amastigotes, which is the typical sign of leishmaniasis. PACE-seq metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) (Hugobiotech, Beijing, China) detected 5,074 specific reads of Leishmania in the blood sample, also indicating leishmaniasis (Figure 1). The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test of the bone marrow aspirate confirmed the diagnosis. He was thus diagnosed with recurrent VL.
Because the patient experienced relapse after treatment with antimonials, he received L-AmB. The starting dose of L-AmB was 10 mg/day (~0.15 mg/kg). Then dose escalation of the L-AmB for the patient is presented in Figure 2. On the 17th day of the treatment protocol when the accumulated dose reached 500 mg (10 mg/kg), PCR of the bone marrow aspirate of Leishmania was negative. The patient's blood cell counts (red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets) increased gradually, and his spleen size decreased gradually. During the treatment, patient's liver function remained normal. There was no recurrence of VL at the 1-year follow-up visit. The patient's temperature and L-AmB dose were presented in Figure 2, and his basic information was summarized in Table 1.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male farmer presented with a 6-month history of intermittent fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced intermittent fevers over the preceding 6 months. He had temporarily defervesced following outpatient therapy several months earlier but was readmitted due to recrudescence of high fevers.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior hospitalization 5 months earlier for fever of unknown origin treated with heavy metal antimicrobial therapy (0.6 g/day for 6 days) with transient remission; history of employment in coalmines; essential hypertension controlled with oral antihypertensive therapy without complications; no significant surgical or family history.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight: 70 kg. Abdomen: marked splenomegaly. Superficial lymphadenopathy was absent, and there was no peripheral edema of the lower extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Pancytopenia, C-reactive protein (CRP): 82.8 mg/L, procalcitonin (PCT): 0.88 ng/mL. Hepatic transaminases and coagulation parameters were abnormal. Blood cultures and microbiological diagnostic tests for bacteria, fungi, tuberculosis, other parasites, and brucellosis tube agglutination were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen confirmed marked splenomegaly. Bone marrow aspirate was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of relapsed/recurrent visceral leishmaniasis (VL): bone marrow aspirate examination revealed intracellular Leishmania amastigotes; blood PACE-seq metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected 5,074 specific reads of Leishmania; bone marrow aspirate polymerase chain reaction (PCR) confirmed Leishmania. Secondary bacterial, fungal, mycobacterial, and brucellosis infections were excluded. Because of antimonial relapse, he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) starting at 10 mg/day (~0.15 mg/kg) followed by dose escalation. On day 17 at an accumulated dose of 500 mg (10 mg/kg), repeat bone marrow aspirate Leishmania PCR turned negative. Peripheral blood counts gradually normalized, splenomegaly regressed, liver enzymes remained stable, and no VL recurrence was observed at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text: A 47-year-old man experienced 2 months of progressive unilateral nasal blockage and recurrent anterior epistaxis. He denied other symptoms such as fever, malaise, weight loss, tinnitus, and diplopia. He was initially diagnosed with a nasal polyp and underwent resection. An initial pathological examination indicated malignancy, and he was referred to our centre. He had a history of 5 repeated falciparum malaria infections within 8 years period during occupational placement in Congo and Papua Island, both of which are malaria-endemic regions. He always received complete treatment for every episode of infection and had not experienced symptoms of malaria for the past 2 years. He lived on Java Island, which is not a malaria-endemic region and where our centre is located. He had no other significant comorbidities, including autoimmune disease and immunodeficiency. Data for previous infection by potential lymphomagenic viruses were not available since examination for these viruses was not available in our region. Upon presentation at our centre, he had a WHO performance status of 0 with an unremarkable physical examination. A repeat biopsy and pathological examination showed CD20 (+), highly proliferative DLBCL (Fig. 1a-c). Contrast CT scan showed a mass on the right maxillary sinus, destroying the posteromedial wall of the maxillary sinus, extending to the nasal cavity, ethmoid sinus, and masticator space, with metastasis to right cervical lymph nodes (Fig. 2a-c). Intracranial spread and distant metastasis were not detected. He was treated with six cycles of R-CHOP every 3 weeks (rituximab 375 mg/m2, cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2, doxorubicin 50 mg/m2, vincristine 1.4 mg/m2, and prednisone 40 mg/m2 for 5 days) with G-CSF support as needed. He experienced no significant adverse event during chemotherapy. A repeat CT scan was performed 1 month after the completion of chemotherapy, showing a complete response (Fig. 3a-e). One month after CT scan, he experienced shivering, fever, sweating, and a return to normal temperature, which repeated irregularly for roughly 1 week, suggesting malaria. His complete blood count showed haemoglobin of 8 g/dL, haematocrit of 27.6%, leucocyte of 2,000 cells/muL, and platelet count of 10,000 cells/muL. The presence of falciparum malaria was confirmed through immunochromatographic testing of malarial antigen (Plasmotec Malaria-3, Indec Diagnostics, Jakarta, Indonesia). This case was considered a relapse since our centre is not in the malaria-endemic region. He was treated with a fixed drug combination of dihydroartemisinin (40 mg)-piperaquine (320 mg) 4 tablets qd on day 1-3 and primaquine 15 mg qd on day 1 (bodyweight of 61 kg). The patient completed the anti-malarial regimen without any adverse event. He experienced complete symptom resolution, and normalization of complete blood count, with no detected plasmodium on blood smear evaluation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old male presenting with irregular fever, shivering, and sweating of approximately one week's duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a one-week history of cyclical shivering, fever, profuse sweating, and defervescence repeating irregularly roughly one month following completion of chemotherapy. Two months prior to chemotherapy, he had presented with unilateral nasal blockage and epistaxis, leading to resection of a suspected polyp which demonstrated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), for which he completed 6 cycles of chemoimmunotherapy with confirmed complete remission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of right maxillary sinus (CD20-positive, stage II with cervical lymph node involvement) in complete remission following 6 cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab 375 mg/m2, cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2, doxorubicin 50 mg/m2, vincristine 1.4 mg/m2, and prednisone 40 mg/m2 for 5 days) completed one month prior. Occupational history: lived on Java Island (non-endemic); prior occupational placement in Congo and Papua Island (malaria-endemic regions) within the past 8 years with 5 treated episodes of malaria, asymptomatic for 2 years prior. No autoimmune disease or known immunodeficiency.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denied malaise, weight loss, tinnitus, diplopia, cough, or dyspnea. Home medications: recent R-CHOP and G-CSF. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: WHO performance status 0. Vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable, without focal lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: hemoglobin 8 g/dL, hematocrit 27.6%, leukocytes 2,000 cells/muL, and platelets 10,000 cells/muL. Peripheral blood smear performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic tumor biopsy: CD20 (+), highly proliferative DLBCL. Head and neck contrast-enhanced CT (staging and post-treatment): initial CT showed destructive mass of right maxillary sinus extending into nasal cavity, ethmoid sinus, masticator space, and right cervical lymph nodes; post-treatment CT at 1 month showed complete radiographic response.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Relapse of Plasmodium falciparum malaria secondary to chemotherapy-induced immunosuppression (R-CHOP) in a patient with DLBCL.
Diagnostic confirmation: Positive immunochromatographic malarial antigen test (Plasmotec Malaria-3), with subsequent negative post-treatment blood smear evaluation confirming parasite clearance.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with fixed-dose oral dihydroartemisinin (40 mg)-piperaquine (320 mg) 4 tablets once daily on days 1-3 and primaquine 15 mg once daily on day 1 (patient weight 61 kg). The patient completed the regimen without adverse events, resulting in complete resolution of fever, normalization of complete blood counts, and eradication of parasitemia.

raw_case_text: The infant clinically improved. Hemoglobin rose to 91 g/L. Septic workup and HIV screen were negative. Malaria smears showed parasite clearance at 72 h. The infant was transitioned to oral quinine and clindamycin for a total 7-day course. She remained well in follow-up, with no parasite recrudescence or post-artesunate delayed hemolysis. The mother was assessed by the local Tropical Disease Unit. She was clinically well, and malaria thick and thin blood films and rapid diagnostic test were negative. Given the diagnosis of congenital P. ovale malaria in her child, she was treated with 3 days of oral atovaquone-proguanil followed by 14 days of oral primaquine 30 mg (base) per day, following G6PD testing. Infant G6PD testing was not done due to recent red blood cell transfusion and cessation of breastfeeding prior to maternal primaquine course.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-week-old female infant presenting for post-resuscitation monitoring and completion of antimicrobial therapy for congenital parasitic infection.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Continuation of inpatient management for a 5-week-old infant who demonstrated rapid clinical improvement following emergency transfusion and parenteral antiparasitic therapy. Her feeding, vigor, and hemolytic parameters stabilized, with complete microscopic resolution of acute intraerythrocytic inclusions. Concurrently, the infant's mother was referred to and evaluated at the regional Tropical Disease Unit for maternal screening and radical cure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Infant: severe congenital neonatal infection successfully treated with blood transfusion and intravenous artesunate. Mother: treated for gestational malaria in Nigeria and Canada, peripartum fever. Infant G6PD testing was deferred due to recent red blood cell transfusion.
subjective.review_of_systems: Infant: alert, active, feeding vigorously without desaturations or seizures. Mother: asymptomatic, denies fever, chills, night sweats, or fatigue. Medications: infant completed IV artesunate; mother: none currently. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Infant: clinically improved, well-perfused, pink, clear breath sounds, normal heart sounds without murmurs, soft non-tender abdomen without palpable organomegaly. Mother: afebrile, normotensive, systemic examination completely normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Infant: hemoglobin rose from 55 g/L to 91 g/L post-transfusion. Full septic workup and HIV screening: negative. Serial thick and thin blood smears performed at 72 hours. Mother: thick and thin blood films negative; rapid diagnostic test negative; G6PD enzymatic screening performed and normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Complete parasitological clearance of severe congenital Plasmodium ovale malaria in the infant, and maternal latent hepatic carriage of Plasmodium ovale requiring radical hypnozoitocidal therapy.
Diagnostic confirmation: Infant peripheral blood smears confirmed complete parasite clearance at 72 hours; maternal blood smears and rapid antigen tests were negative, consistent with dormant hypnozoite carriage; maternal G6PD screening confirmed normal enzymatic activity.
Treatment & Outcome: Infant was transitioned to oral quinine and clindamycin to complete a total 7-day course, resulting in sustained recovery without parasite recrudescence or post-artesunate delayed hemolysis. Mother discontinued breastfeeding and was treated with oral atovaquone-proguanil for 3 days followed by oral primaquine 30 mg (base) daily for 14 days for radical cure. Both mother and infant remained healthy and free of relapse on outpatient follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old male presented with a 1-day history of fever, chills and severe vomiting, associated with myalgia, frontal headache and arthralgia. He tested positive for dengue NS1 antigen and was dengue IgM positive on the second day of fever. The patient progressed to a lower level of consciousness over 12 h after admission.
Brain MRI revealed an oval-shaped lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum, which was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images and showed no post-contrast enhancement (Figures 5a-c). The lesion revealed increased signal on diffusion imaging with corresponding low values on ADC and no blooming on GRE images (Figures 5e-f).
The patient was managed conservatively with intravenous fluid, antipyretics and close clinical monitoring. He recovered completely and was released from the hospital on the 14th day of his illness. A follow-up MRI revealed complete resolution of the splenial lesion. A diagnosis of transient lesion of the splenium of corpus callosum, also known as reversible splenial lesion syndrome (RESLES), was made.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male presenting with fever, chills, severe vomiting, myalgia, frontal headache, and arthralgia for one day, followed by decreased consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 20-year-old male presented with a 1-day history of acute fever, chills, intractable vomiting, frontal headache, myalgia, and arthralgia. Within 12 hours of hospital admission, his clinical condition progressed to encephalopathy with a decreased level of consciousness. Under supportive care, his sensorium improved, and he recovered completely by day 14 of illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe vomiting, frontal headache, myalgia, arthralgia, chills.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Febrile; within 12 hours of admission developed lethargy and decreased level of consciousness.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: Well-circumscribed, oval-shaped lesion in the splenium of the corpus callosum showing hyperintensity on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, without post-contrast enhancement, with marked restricted diffusion (high DWI and low ADC) and no blooming on GRE images. Follow-up Brain MRI (day 14): Complete resolution of the splenial lesion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Reversible splenial lesion syndrome (RESLES / transient lesion of the splenium of the corpus callosum) secondary to confirmed Dengue virus infection. Confirmed by positive Dengue NS1 antigen and positive Dengue IgM antibody on day 2 of fever.
Plan & Outcome: Managed conservatively with intravenous fluid therapy, antipyretics, and close neuromonitoring. He achieved complete clinical recovery and was discharged on day 14 of illness with follow-up neuroimaging demonstrating complete resolution of the corpus callosum lesion.

raw_case_text: A 22-month-old girl presented to us with 8-day fever (40 C), and mild cough. On examination, she had hepatosplenomegaly. Past medical history included failure to thrive, but normal neurological development. She was the first child of a non-consanguineous marriage. She had normal brown hair and normal skin. There was no family history of albinism. On physical examination, she was stunted, pale, and had non-tender hepatomegaly of 5-6 cm; the spleen was palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin as confirmed by abdominal ultrasound. The WBC count was 5100/mm3 (ANC 1200/mm3), Hb 9.1 g/dl, and platelets 47.000/mm3. She had mild hypertransaminasemia and hypoalbuminemia. Ferritin was 1134 ng/ml. Soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25) was 3183 UI/ml. Blood cultures were negative. Serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets were normal. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) serology yielded seroreactivity (positive IgM and IgG anti-VCA) with negative IgG anti-EBNA. EBV viral load was 637 copies/ml. Leishmania serology showed both negative immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence. Conversely, serum ELISA was slightly positive. Leishmanial antigen in the urine was negative. Bone marrow aspiration revealed hemophagocytosis. The patient worsened clinically, with persistent malaise, progressive splenomegaly, and petechial rash on her chest and legs. Subsequent investigations were WBC 4800/mm3 (ANC 800/mm3), Hb 6.8 g/dl and platelets 27000/mm3, triglycerides 686 mg/dl, ferritin 3849 ng/ml, and sCD25 3596 UI/ml with normal clotting tests as well as perforin expression by flow-cytometry. Hair microscopy was not performed because clinical features of albinism were not present neither in our patient nor in her family. HLH-2004 protocol was started. The following day, Leishmania Polymerase Chain Reaction was done where Leishmanial DNA was detected by nested PCR.) This was confirmed on a bone marrow aspirate as well. Standard therapy with liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day IV on days 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 14, and 21) was given. The patient completed HLH-2004 protocol, except for 2 doses of etoposide due to clinical and laboratory improvement without evidence of underlying primary HLH. At 30 month follow up, there is no evidence of relapse. As CD107a degranulation assay was not performed (just normal intracytoplasmic pattern of perforin staining), primary HLH is not absolutely discarded as a differential diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-month-old female presented with high fever (40 °C) and mild cough for 8 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 22-month-old girl presented with an 8-day history of high fever up to 40 °C and mild cough. During hospitalization, she deteriorated clinically with persistent malaise, progressive splenomegaly, and a new petechial rash on her chest and legs. Laboratory testing demonstrated worsening cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, and hypertriglyceridemia, fulfilling criteria for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Protocol HLH-2004 was initiated. Subsequent molecular testing established an underlying parasitic infection, and targeted antileishmanial therapy was instituted.
subjective.past_medical_history: First child of non-consanguineous parents. Past history of failure to thrive with normal neurological development. Normal brown hair and skin; no family history of albinism. Prior antibiotic therapy not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: High-grade fever, mild cough, progressive malaise, petechial rash on trunk and legs. Denied vomiting, diarrhea, seizures, or jaundice.

objective.physical_examination: Stunted and pale infant; body temperature: 40 °C. Abdominal exam revealed non-tender hepatomegaly measuring 5-6 cm and splenomegaly palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin. Developing petechial rash on chest and lower extremities. Brown hair, normal skin pigmentation; no features of albinism.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: WBC 5,100/mm^3 (ANC 1,200/mm^3), hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL, platelets 47,000/mm^3; mild hypertransaminasemia, hypoalbuminemia; serum ferritin 1,134 ng/mL; soluble IL-2 receptor (sCD25) 3,183 UI/mL. Blood cultures: negative. Normal immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets. EBV serology: positive IgM and IgG anti-VCA, negative IgG anti-EBNA; EBV viral load 637 copies/mL. Repeat labs during clinical deterioration: WBC 4,800/mm^3 (ANC 800/mm^3), hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL, platelets 27,000/mm^3, triglycerides 686 mg/dL, ferritin 3,849 ng/mL, sCD25 3,596 UI/mL; normal coagulation tests. Flow cytometry: normal intracytoplasmic perforin expression. Urine parasite antigen: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal ultrasonography confirmed hepatomegaly (5-6 cm) and splenomegaly (4 cm below costal margin). Bone marrow aspiration revealed prominent hemophagocytosis. Leishmania serology: immunochromatography and indirect immunofluorescence negative; serum ELISA weakly positive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) triggering secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), with concurrent low-level EBV reactivation.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Detection of Leishmania DNA by nested PCR from peripheral blood and bone marrow aspirate.
Differentials Ruled Out: Primary (familial) HLH (normal perforin expression, though CD107a degranulation assay not done), Griscelli syndrome and Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (normal hair and skin pigmentation, no albinism), acute bacterial sepsis (sterile blood cultures), and primary EBV-induced HLH.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Patient initiated on HLH-2004 protocol. Following PCR confirmation, standard intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day on days 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 14, and 21) was administered. Completed HLH-2004 protocol with omission of the final 2 doses of etoposide due to rapid clinical and laboratory recovery. The patient remains in complete remission without relapse at 30-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male presented with complaints of decreased vision in the right eye of 4 months duration. There was pain in the right eye at onset and the visual loss progressed to complete loss of vision within 6 weeks of onset of symptoms. There was no history of seizures or focal limb weakness. There were no systemic features like fever, loss of appetite, or weight. Previous treatment history for the visual loss included a short course of oral steroids; no improvement was noted with the same.
He presented to us nearly 4 months after onset of visual symptoms and nearly 10 weeks after manifesting complete visual loss. On examination, there was no light perception in the right eye. Relative afferent pupillary defect and optic disc pallor were noted. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain and orbit at this time (16 weeks after onset of symptoms) revealed a homogenously enhancing, diffusely thickened optic nerve [Figure 1a] with nodular enhancing lesions in the right parietal and frontal lobes. [Figures 2a1 and a2]. Human immunodeficiency virus enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (HIV ELISA) was negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis including cultures was noncontributory. There was no significant lymphadenopathy. Chest X-ray and abdomen ultrasonography were noncontributary. As there was still significant enhancement of the optic nerve, possibility of an infiltrative optic neuropathy due to an infectious (tuberculosis, cysticercosis) or inflammatory condition (sarcoidosis) was considered most likely. Infiltrations from lymphomatosis, gliomatosis, and other compressive optic neuropathies were considered less likely especially considering the brain lesions. At this stage, he was asymptomatic for the brain lesions and had already completely lost his vision in the right eye. Initiation of empiric antituberculous therapy was strongly contemplated. However, considering the risk of missing other diagnosis in which different treatment will be required, it was decided to go ahead with a biopsy for definitive diagnosis. The options included an optic nerve biopsy versus brain biopsy.
While awaiting the biopsy in the ward, mild impairment of dexterity of the left hand was noted. Antituberculous therapy (ATT) (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) with dexamethasone was started after a repeat imaging. A repeat MRI brain revealed conglomerate ring enhancing lesions in right frontal and parietal lobes with perilesional edema, mass effect, and midline shift. [Figure 2b] There was also a 30 x 21 mm ring enhancing lesion in the right optic nerve [Figure 1b] with associated thickening. Biopsy from the right parietal lesion revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with numerous acid fast bacilli. Pansensitive mycobacterium tuberculosis was grown on culture. ATT with steroids was continued. Decompression of optic nerve lesion was not done as he already had complete loss of vision with optic atrophy. The mild weakness of the left hand improved completely. Repeat imaging at 2 months follow up revealed subtle increase in the size of the right optic nerve necrotic rim enhancing lesion [Figure 1c]. There was remarkable increase in the size, number, and perilesional edema of the brain lesions as well consistent with paradoxical worsening. [Figure 2c] The dosage of steroids was hiked up and ATT was continued. Repeat MRI at 18 months showed significant resolution of the intracranial lesions. [Figure 2d] The optic nerve lesion persisted, though there was a decrease in the size and degree of enhancement [Figure 1d]. Hence, ATT was continued.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented with decreased vision in the right eye of 4 months duration, with initial eye pain progressing to complete loss of vision within 6 weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, a 40-year-old male, noted onset of right eye pain and decreased vision 4 months prior to presentation. The visual loss progressively worsened, culminating in complete loss of vision within 6 weeks of onset. He presented approximately 10 weeks after total vision loss. While admitted awaiting diagnostic biopsy, he developed mild impairment of left hand dexterity.
subjective.past_medical_history: Short course of oral steroids administered previously for visual loss without improvement. No other prior medical history, hospitalizations, or exposures documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right eye pain at onset and subsequent mild left hand clumsiness. Negative for fever, loss of appetite, weight loss, seizures, and focal limb weakness at presentation. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Right eye: no light perception, relative afferent pupillary defect, optic disc pallor. Mild impairment of left hand dexterity noted during admission. No significant peripheral lymphadenopathy. Remainder of physical examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasonography noncontributory. HIV ELISA negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis including routine cultures noncontributory.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain and orbit MRI (16 weeks post-onset): diffusely thickened, homogeneously enhancing right optic nerve with nodular enhancing lesions in right parietal and frontal lobes. Repeat brain MRI: conglomerate ring-enhancing lesions in right frontal and parietal lobes with perilesional edema, mass effect, and midline shift, alongside a 30 x 21 mm ring-enhancing lesion in right optic nerve with thickening. Follow-up MRI at 2 months: subtle enlargement of necrotic rim-enhancing optic nerve lesion and interval increase in size, number, and perilesional edema of intracranial lesions. Repeat MRI at 18 months: marked resolution of intracranial lesions with persistent but decreased size and enhancement of optic nerve lesion. Right parietal lesion biopsy: necrotizing granulomatous inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Central nervous system and ocular tuberculosis (tuberculoma of the right parietal and frontal lobes and right optic nerve tuberculoma), confirmed by histopathology of the right parietal brain biopsy demonstrating necrotizing granulomatous inflammation with numerous acid-fast bacilli and tissue culture growing pansensitive Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Differential diagnoses considered included infiltrative optic neuropathy secondary to cysticercosis, sarcoidosis, lymphomatosis, gliomatosis, and compressive optic neuropathies. Management & Outcome: Initiated on antituberculous therapy (ATT: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) with dexamethasone. Decompression of the optic nerve was withheld given pre-existing complete blindness and optic atrophy. Left hand weakness resolved completely. Development of paradoxical expansion of intracranial and optic nerve lesions at 2 months was managed with escalation of steroid dosing and continuation of ATT. At 18-month follow-up, intracranial lesions had significantly resolved and optic nerve enhancement had decreased; ATT was continued.

raw_case_text:
In mid-January, a 38-year-old man went duck hunting in flooded rice fields in Butte County; he also stayed in a trailer that had stood vacant for some time, where he recalled cleaning up rodent droppings. On January 27, jaundice, pulmonary infiltrates, and renal failure developed. Laboratory studies showed bilirubin of 48 mg/dL and platelets of 13,000/muL.
Serologic testing for hantavirus was negative. IHA for leptospirosis at a private laboratory 9 days later yielded an initially ambiguous titer of 1:50, and a second test 11 days after that yielded a titer of 1:800 (Table 2), greater than the fourfold rise required to confirm the diagnosis. He was treated successfully with doxycycline.
In 2000, the largest known common-source outbreak of leptospirosis in California involved three men vacationing on a houseboat in the New Melones Lake in Tuolomne County May 5-7. Three of eight men who shared the houseboat reported swimming to a remote cove and hiking along a creek draining into the main reservoir on May 7. They were exposed there to muddied waters after an overnight thundershower. Each of these three men went individually to his own doctor and independent health system in Redwood City 10-15 days later, with a constellation of signs and symptoms including fever, headache, myalgias, nausea, and vomiting. In each, the salient common clinical feature of renal failure developed, manifested by elevated creatinine levels that in one case required hemodialysis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old man presented with acute onset of jaundice, pulmonary infiltrates, and acute renal failure following an outdoor hunting trip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In mid-January, the patient went duck hunting in flooded fields and stayed in a vacant trailer. On January 27, he developed acute jaundice, pulmonary infiltrates, and oliguric renal failure necessitating immediate medical evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposures: duck hunting in flooded rice fields in Butte County, California, and cleaning rodent droppings in a long-vacant trailer. Prior medical history, home medications, and allergies are unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination demonstrated profound jaundice. Complete vital signs and detailed physical examination findings are not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Total bilirubin: 48 mg/dL; platelets: 13,000/muL. Laboratory testing confirmed acute renal failure. Chest imaging revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Serologic testing for hantavirus was negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting with profound jaundice, acute renal failure, severe thrombocytopenia, and pulmonary infiltrates. Confirmed by indirect hemagglutination assay (IHA) demonstrating a greater than fourfold rise in antibody titers from an initial ambiguous titer of 1:50 (drawn 9 days post-presentation) to 1:800 (drawn 11 days later). Hantavirus infection was excluded serologically. Treatment & Outcome: Successfully treated with oral doxycycline, achieving complete clinical recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 35 year-old male, with hypertension, post-LRRT on triple immunosuppression, and telmisartan 40mg daily, and 5 years posttransplant, was admitted with high grade fever for 5 days and few episodes of vomiting since morning. BP was 104/70 with tachycardia (Pulse: 110/minute). The patient received IV fluid resuscitation on arrival and his antihypertensive medication was withheld. Viral serology for CMV, BKV was negative and the result of urine examination was normal. His last serum creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL (2 months ago) and it was 2.3 mg/dL during hospitalization. There was lymphopenia (14% lymphocytes) with normal haemoglobin of 12g/dL. There was a 3-fold increase in AST and ALT with normal bilirubin in liver function test. X-ray chest and abdominal ultrasound and graft was normal. Blood and urine cultures were sterile. RT PCR from nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV2. The patient was continued on tacrolimus 1mg (morning) and 0.5mg (evening). Prednisolone was increased from 5mg OD to 20 mg OD. 
 Mycophenolate sodium was stopped. Oral azithromycin, along with hydroxychloroquine and oseltamivir, was given and haemodynamic and fluid status were closely monitored. The patient became afebrile on day 4 and serum creatinine gradually decreased to 1.1 mg/dL on day 15. RT PCR was negative on day 21. He was given antihypertensive medication again and continued the dual immunosuppression at hospital discharge. On follow-up (telephonic), the patient was doing well. His tacrolimus level was 7ng/mL and leukopenia had completely settled. The patient was resumed on triple immunosuppression with the same dose of tacrolimus, prednisolone 10mg, and mycophenolate sodium 360 mg, BD, and is doing well with the latest creatinine of 1mg/dL.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever for five days and vomiting since the morning of presentation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is a 35-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation who presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever and several episodes of vomiting starting on the morning of presentation. He received intravenous fluid resuscitation on arrival, and his antihypertensive therapy was temporarily withheld.
subjective.past_medical_history: Live-related renal transplant (LRRT) 5 years prior; hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: Triple immunosuppression regimen including tacrolimus, prednisolone 5 mg once daily, and mycophenolate sodium; telmisartan 40 mg daily. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure 104/70 mmHg; pulse 110 beats/min (tachycardia).
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 12 g/dL; differential revealed lymphopenia (14% lymphocytes); serum creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL two months prior); liver function tests showed a 3-fold elevation in AST and ALT with normal total bilirubin; urinalysis was normal; viral serologies for CMV and BKV were negative; blood and urine cultures were sterile; chest X-ray was normal; abdominal and renal allograft ultrasound was normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19) confirmed by nasopharyngeal swab RT-PCR, complicated by acute kidney injury. Serologies for CMV and BKV, and blood and urine cultures were negative.
Plan & Outcome: Immunosuppression was adjusted: mycophenolate sodium was discontinued, prednisolone increased from 5 mg once daily to 20 mg once daily, and tacrolimus continued at 1 mg morning / 0.5 mg evening. Antimicrobial and antiviral therapy was administered with oral azithromycin, hydroxychloroquine, and oseltamivir, with close monitoring of hemodynamic and fluid status. The patient became afebrile on day 4, and serum creatinine decreased to 1.1 mg/dL by day 15. Nasopharyngeal RT-PCR turned negative on day 21. Antihypertensive therapy was resumed, and he was discharged on dual immunosuppression. On follow-up, he remained well with a tacrolimus trough of 7 ng/mL, resolved leukopenia, normal creatinine of 1 mg/dL, and successful resumption of triple immunosuppression (tacrolimus same dose, prednisolone 10 mg daily, and mycophenolate sodium 360 mg BID).

raw_case_text: A 53-year-old woman with no significant underlying medical history was admitted to our hospital with a 1-month history of intermittent fever. She ever picked Zanthoxylum seeds in Hancheng, China 8 years ago, and she had a history of mosquito bites. She had a history of esophageal cancer and received surgical treatment one and a half years ago, and there was no recurrence after operation. Past medical, past surgical, drug and family histories were not significant. Her body weight was 55 kg. Physical examination revealed splenomegaly and axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Laboratory tests revealed high levels of CRP (97.3 mg/L; reference value, <10.0 mg/L), as well as elevated liver enzyme levels, abnormal coagulation, and pancytopenia. Her PCT level was 1.24 ng/mL. Antibodies against Leishmania were detected in her blood. A positive PCR result for Leishmania in bone marrow aspirate confirmed the diagnosis of VL. She received prompt treatment with L-AmB at an initial dose of 5 mg (~0.10 mg/kg) on the first day. The L-AmB protocol for the patient is presented in Figure 3. During L-AmB dose escalation, laboratory tests of renal functions and electrolytes uncovered no particular abnormality during treatment. Routine blood parameters gradually normalized during therapy, and her spleen size gradually decreased. No VL recurrence was observed at the 1-year follow-up visit.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old female presented with a 1-month history of intermittent fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed intermittent fevers evolving over 1 month without localizing infectious symptoms, leading to hospital evaluation.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of esophageal carcinoma treated with surgical resection 1.5 years prior without postoperative recurrence; epidemiological exposure: harvested Zanthoxylum seeds in Hancheng, Shaanxi Province, China 8 years earlier with a history of insect and mosquito bites; past medical, surgical, drug, and family histories otherwise non-contributory.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight: 55 kg. Abdomen: splenomegaly. Lymphatic: palpable axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia. C-reactive protein (CRP): 97.3 mg/L (reference <10.0 mg/L), procalcitonin (PCT): 1.24 ng/mL. Elevated liver enzymes and abnormal coagulation parameters. Serial renal function tests and serum electrolytes showed no abnormality during treatment.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow aspiration was performed for diagnostic evaluation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis (VL): anti-Leishmania antibodies were detected in peripheral blood; bone marrow aspirate polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was positive for Leishmania. Malignancy recurrence was ruled out. She was treated promptly with liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) at an initial dose of 5 mg (~0.10 mg/kg) on day 1 followed by protocol dose escalation. During therapy, renal function and electrolytes remained entirely normal, routine blood cell counts normalized, splenomegaly gradually resolved, and no VL recurrence was detected at 1-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
In August 2016, a 78-year-old man living in the San Juan metropolitan area with a medical history of hypertension (for which he was taking amlodipine), diabetes, asthma, and prostate cancer visited a hospital emergency department with a 4-day history of worsening paresthesia of the lower and upper extremities and progressive bilateral lower and upper extremity weakness (Figure 1). Computed tomography without contrast of the head found no acute intracranial or other abnormalities. The patient was given albuterol nebulizer treatment, ipratropium bromide, and ceftriaxone and discharged home on the same day. Three days later, the patient returned to the emergency department with worsened weakness. He was admitted to the intensive care unit with respiratory distress and was intubated. Hospital staff suspected GBS due to monophasic illness progression, symmetric weakness, and loss of deep tendon reflexes. A 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (30 g/d) was initiated, and serum and urine specimens were collected for Zika virus diagnostic testing. On day 7 after onset of neurologic illness, the patient had acute kidney injury and hyperuricemia. Electrodiagnostic studies performed 10 days post-onset identified demyelinating polyneuropathy consistent with GBS (Technical Appendix). Given clinical features and electrophysiologic findings, the patient met level 2 of the Brighton Collaboration Criteria for GBS diagnostic certainty.
The patient was mildly responsive by day 15 and thereafter became unresponsive but hemodynamically stable. On day 16, pneumonia was diagnosed, and a course of vancomycin was started. Multidrug-resistant forms of Acinetobacter baumanii were found in sputum (collected on day 14) and fecal samples (collected on day 18), and multidrug-resistant Enterobacter aerogenes and Klebsiella pneumoniae were isolated from sputum (collected on day 27). Computed tomography of the chest performed on day 20 indicated multifocal pneumonia with parapneumonic effusions involving the entire right lung and part of the left lung. Following an episode of cardiac arrest on day 23, tracheostomy for chronic respiratory failure was performed on day 24. The patient died on day 37 due to cardiac arrest and respiratory failure complicated by bilateral pneumonia, sepsis, and acute renal failure.
An autopsy was performed, and external evaluation noted edema of the left hand, scrotum, penis, legs, and feet, as well as decubitus ulcers on the back and in the gluteal area. Internal examination showed bilateral pleural effusions, hepatic congestion, ascites, and cardiomegaly. Microscopic examination showed focal pneumonia, acute tubular necrosis, and prostate adenocarcinoma. Brain examination showed subacute watershed infarcts of the left cerebral hemisphere; occasional perivascular lymphomononuclear cell infiltrates were also observed.
We detected Zika virus RNA by reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) in urine and Zika virus and dengue virus IgM antibodies in serum (both collected on day 7). Additional laboratory testing of premortem specimens was negative for Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, enteropathic isolates, Campylobacter jejuni, Legionella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, HIV, influenza A and B, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus. We performed Zika virus RT-PCR and immunohistochemical (IHC) assays on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded autopsy tissue specimens. We detected neither RNA nor antigen for Zika virus in any autopsy specimens tested (Zika virus RT-PCR, cranial nerve VII, sciatic nerve, and spinal cord including cauda equina; IHC, brain, spinal cord, sciatic nerve, and multiple solid organs).
We analyzed postmortem specimens of the peripheral and central nervous system and specimens from other organs by microscopic examination and special stains. A section of cranial nerve IV showed mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate and mild myelin loss, while sections of the sciatic nerve showed inflammation-associated myelin loss. Myelin loss was highlighted by luxol fast blue staining (Figure 2). IHC staining for CD68 demonstrated an abundance of macrophages. Cranial nerves I, II, III, V, VI, and VII and spinal cord showed no substantial histopathologic findings. Pathology findings in lung, prostate, and spleen tissues were consistent with comorbid conditions. Findings for heart, testicle, adrenal gland, gastrointestinal system, and thyroid specimens were unremarkable.

subjective.chief_complaint: 78-year-old male presenting with a 4-day history of worsening paresthesias and progressive bilateral weakness of all four extremities, followed by acute respiratory distress.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 78-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of worsening paresthesias and progressive bilateral weakness of the upper and lower extremities. Following initial emergency evaluation, head CT, and nebulizer treatment, he was discharged home. Three days later, he returned with severe progression of weakness and acute respiratory distress requiring ICU admission and endotracheal intubation. On day 7 post-neurologic onset, he developed acute kidney injury and hyperuricemia. By day 15 he was only mildly responsive and subsequently became unresponsive. On day 16, hospital-acquired pneumonia was diagnosed. He suffered a cardiac arrest on day 23, underwent tracheostomy on day 24, and died on day 37 from respiratory failure, bilateral pneumonia, sepsis, and acute renal failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, asthma, prostate adenocarcinoma; resident of San Juan metropolitan area, Puerto Rico.
subjective.review_of_systems: Extremity paresthesias, dyspnea, progressive generalized weakness. Home medication: amlodipine. Allergies unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: At ICU admission: Severe respiratory distress, symmetric quadriparesis, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Post-intubation course: Hemodynamically stable but unresponsive by day 16. Postmortem external exam: Edema of left hand, scrotum, penis, legs, and feet; decubitus ulcers on the back and gluteal area.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 7 post-onset: Serum chemistry showed acute kidney injury and hyperuricemia.
objective.advanced_workup: Head CT without contrast (day 4): No acute intracranial or other abnormalities. Electrodiagnostic studies (day 10): Demyelinating polyneuropathy consistent with Guillain-Barré syndrome (Brighton Criteria level 2). Chest CT (day 20): Multifocal pneumonia with parapneumonic effusions involving the entire right lung and part of the left lung. Autopsy examination: Internal examination revealed bilateral pleural effusions, hepatic congestion, ascites, and cardiomegaly; microscopic exam showed focal pneumonia, acute tubular necrosis, and prostate adenocarcinoma; brain exam showed subacute watershed infarcts of the left cerebral hemisphere and occasional perivascular lymphomononuclear infiltrates; cranial nerve IV showed mononuclear lymphocytic infiltrate and mild myelin loss; sciatic nerve showed inflammation-associated myelin loss on luxol fast blue and abundant CD68+ macrophages; cranial nerves I, II, III, V, VI, VII and spinal cord showed no substantial histopathologic abnormalities.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Guillain-Barré syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, Brighton level 2) triggered by acute Zika virus infection, complicated by nosocomial pneumonia, multidrug-resistant bacterial sepsis, acute kidney injury, and fatal cardiopulmonary arrest. Zika virus RNA was detected by RT-PCR in urine collected on day 7, with positive Zika virus IgM and dengue virus IgM in serum. Premortem testing ruled out Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter jejuni, Legionella, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, HIV, influenza A/B, CMV, and EBV. Autopsy RT-PCR and IHC for Zika virus RNA and antigen were negative in cranial nerves, sciatic nerve, spinal cord, brain, and solid organs. Sputum and stool cultures grew multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, and sputum grew multidrug-resistant Enterobacter aerogenes and Klebsiella pneumoniae. Treatments included IVIG (30 g/day for 5 days), IV vancomycin, albuterol, ipratropium, ceftriaxone, mechanical ventilation, and tracheostomy; patient died on hospital day 37.

raw_case_text: A 60-year-old man who has sex with men was diagnosed with HIV in 2001 (Table 1). At the time of presentation, the plasma RNA HIV viral load was 29 079 copies/mL. The nadir CD4 T-cell count was 190 cells/microL. No baseline genotyping was done at the time. He was started on HAART in 2002. The patient suffered from chronic intestinal parasitosis with Entamoeba coli and Blastocystis hominis, which was completely treated in 2004. The patient never developed an AIDS-defining illness. In 2007, he developed chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to IgA nephropathy. His antiretroviral therapy at that time was abacavir, lamivudine, and efavirenz. His CKD progressed to ESRD over the following 5 years, and hemodialysis was initiated in 2012, time at which he was also evaluated for a kidney transplantation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male with end-stage renal disease presenting for maintenance renal replacement therapy and kidney transplantation evaluation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with progressive renal dysfunction initially diagnosed in 2007. Over the subsequent five years, renal failure steadily progressed to end-stage renal disease, necessitating the initiation of chronic hemodialysis in 2012 and formal nephrological evaluation for kidney transplantation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection diagnosed in 2001; baseline plasma HIV RNA viral load 29,079 copies/mL and nadir CD4 T-cell count 190 cells/microL; started on HAART in 2002; antiretroviral regimen consisted of abacavir, lamivudine, and efavirenz in 2007. Chronic intestinal parasitosis with Entamoeba coli and Blastocystis hominis completely eradicated in 2004. Biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy diagnosed in 2007 progressing to ESRD. Never developed an AIDS-defining illness. Epidemiological history: Man who has sex with men (MSM).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: End-stage renal disease (ESRD) secondary to biopsy-confirmed IgA nephropathy in an HIV-1-infected patient on established combination antiretroviral therapy (HAART) without history of AIDS-defining opportunistic infections.
Plan & Outcome: Commenced on chronic maintenance hemodialysis in 2012. Antiretroviral therapy was maintained (abacavir, lamivudine, and efavirenz with appropriate dosage adjustments for hemodialysis). The patient was evaluated and approved for kidney transplantation.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male presented with a history of fever and cough for the last three days with a history of close contact with a COVID-19 confirmed case. He did not have any GI complaints during the presentation. He denied any addiction and his past history was unremarkable. He was vitally stable. He was tested with a throat swab for COVID-19 PCR, which came positive. According to the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidelines, he was categorized as having a mild COVID-19 infection. His saturation on admission was 99% and baseline investigations were also normal (Table 1).
He was admitted for isolation and started on tablet hydroxychloroquine. He improved after treatment and his complaints settled down. By the fifth day of treatment, he started complaining of seven to eight episodes of bloody diarrhea associated with fever. He was febrile (temperature - 100.6 F) with a pulse rate of 124/min. There was no abdominal pain or vomiting. The rectal examination was normal, and the proctoscopy revealed red velvety rectal mucosa. However, his repeat swab of COVID-19 came negative. Due to the short history, the patient was evaluated for infective colitis. Stool examination revealed 90-100 red blood cells/HPF and 18-20 pus cells/HPF. His hemoglobin dropped from 10.3 g/dL to 8.2 g/dL during the hospital course. Entamoeba and Clostridium difficile stool toxins were negative, while his CRP was >100 mg/L. His fecal calprotectin level was also elevated (2,300 microg/g). A computed tomography scan of the patient showed wall thickening involving the cecum to the rectum with vascular engorgement and surrounding peri-colic fat stranding (Figures 1A, 1B).
He underwent a colonoscopy, which revealed edematous, erythematous mucosa complete loss of vascularity with multiple superficial and deep ulcerations, the largest measuring 1.5 X 1 cm which bleeds on touch involving the sigmoid colon and rectum (Mayo Grade 3 changes) (Figure 2).
Biopsies were taken and further advancement of the colonoscope was deferred due to severe changes in the sigmoid colon and rectum. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen showed loss of mucin, mucosal ulcerations, basal plasmacytosis, dense mixed infiltrate with cryptitis, crypt abscesses, crypt distortion, and cryptic hyperplasia (Figures 3A-3C).
Based on clinical and histopathological findings, he was diagnosed with ASUC, probably triggered by COVID-19 infection. His Truelove-Witt's Score (TLW) and UC Disease Activity Index (UCDAI) scores were severe and 10 respectively. He was started on intravenous steroids and he improved clinically in form of decreased stool frequency (2-3 times/day) and no blood in stool on the fifth of treatment initiation. Repeat stool examination revealed occasional red blood cells and CRP also dropped down to 7 mg/L. He was started on maintenance therapy with 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA). He was discharged on oral tapering dosages of steroids with 5-ASA.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presenting with a 3-day history of fever and cough, followed five days later by acute bloody diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 28-year-old previously healthy male presented with a 3-day history of fever and cough following close contact with a known respiratory infection case. He had no gastrointestinal symptoms on admission and was isolated for mild disease. His respiratory complaints resolved with hydroxychloroquine. On hospital day 5, he developed 7 to 8 episodes of bloody diarrhea per day accompanied by fever. There was no abdominal pain or vomiting. Evaluation revealed severe inflammatory colitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical and surgical history. Denies any addiction, tobacco, alcohol, or illicit substance use. Epidemiological history: Known close contact with a confirmed viral respiratory case.
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial presentation: Fever, cough. Denied initial GI symptoms. Day 5: Frequent bloody diarrhea (7–8 bowel movements/day), recurrent fever. Denies abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Vitally stable; SpO2 99% on room air. Day 5 (colitis onset): Febrile (T 100.6 °F), tachycardia (HR 124 beats/min), BP normal. Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly. Digital rectal examination: Normal. Rigid proctoscopy: Hyperemic, red velvety rectal mucosa.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission: Baseline hematology and biochemistry were within normal limits, SpO2 99%. Day 5 labs: Stool microscopy showed 90–100 RBCs/HPF and 18–20 pus cells/HPF. Stool tests for Entamoeba histolytica and Clostridium difficile toxins: Negative. Inflammatory markers: CRP > 100 mg/L; fecal calprotectin markedly elevated at 2,300 μg/g. Hemoglobin dropped from 10.3 g/dL to 8.2 g/dL during hospitalization. Follow-up stool exam showed only occasional RBCs, and CRP decreased to 7 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal CT: Marked mural thickening involving the cecum through the rectum, with prominent vascular engorgement and surrounding pericolonic fat stranding. Colonoscopy: Edematous, erythematous mucosa with complete loss of normal vascular pattern and multiple superficial and deep ulcerations (largest 1.5 x 1 cm) that bled easily on touch throughout the sigmoid colon and rectum (Mayo grade 3). Further advancement was deferred due to perforation risk.
