Rapid wet mount microscopic examination of liver aspirate showed motile unicellular organisms with pseudopodia characteristic of amoebic trophozoites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Amebic liver abscess complicated by concurrent Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhi and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serotype Typhimurium pyogenic co-infection, with secondary transdiaphragmatic rupture into the pleural space (empyema), in a patient with newly diagnosed HIV/AIDS (CD4 count 163.4 cells/muL). Pre-antibiotic blood cultures (3 of 4 bottles positive) and drained hepatic abscess fluid grew Salmonella Typhi (identified by API 20E and confirmed via MALDI-TOF MS). Broth microdilution and disc diffusion demonstrated susceptibility to ceftazidime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), cefepime (MIC <= 1 mug/mL), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (MIC <= 1/19 mug/mL), piperacillin-tazobactam (MIC 8 mug/mL), and aztreonam (MIC <= 1 mug/mL). Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) of pleural and liver fluids detected Entamoeba histolytica; liver fluid mNGS also identified S. Typhi and S. Typhimurium sequences.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with continuous catheter drainage, IV ceftriaxone 2000 mg every 24 hours for 26 days, metronidazole 750 mg every 8 hours for 10 days, and luminal cyst eradication with paromomycin 500 mg three times daily for 10 days (started on day 16). Discharged in stable condition to complete a 4-week course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, achieving complete clinical recovery, normalization of inflammatory markers, and radiographic resolution of the abscess.

raw_case_text: A 28 year old female, known to have type I DM presented to the emergency room (ER) with history of backache and lower limb weakness. Contrast MRI of the lumbosacral region demonstrated loss of disc space with paraspinal collection at L3-4 extending into bilateral iliopsoas muscle suggesting tuberculosis. After work up, the patient was started on four anti-tubercular drugs (ATT) regime of HRZE as per the protocol. After initial improvement in clinical and neurological status, the patient returned with relapse of back pain after 5 months of therapy. The repeated radiology demonstrated re-collection of organised pus. The needle aspiration of pus along with Xpert MTB/RIF and liquid culture (MGIT) both showed the presence of MTB resistant to rifampicin. Under USG guidance, a malecot catheter was inserted for drainage of the abscess. Patient was started on modified ATT and planned for surgical intervention and fixation in case of non-improvement or deterioration. After 2 months, the patient presented with high grade fever and discharge from the abscess site for which she was brought to the emergency department. MRI lumbosacral spine revealed infective pathology at L3/L4 segment with associated intra and extra-spinal abscesses causing neural compression in comparison with that of previous scans report (Fig. 1). Suspecting secondary infection, pigtail insertion was done to drain the abscess and cultures were sent for two consecutive days. Aerobic culture of the sample did not show growth of any bacteria and anaerobic culture showed growth of bacteria sensitive to metronidazole. The latter was identified as   Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus   in both the samples by MALDI-TOF MS. Antibiotic sensitivity was put up by agar dilution method according to CLSI guidelines M11-A8 2012 which was sensitive to clindamycin, cefoxitin, metronidazole, imipenem and piperacillin-tazobactam with MIC breakpoints of 0.25, 4, 0.25, 0.031 and 0.125 (mg/L) respectively. With the culture report, the patient was started on metronidazole I/V 500 mg TDS and the patient's clinical symptoms like discharge of pus and fever drastically improved. Metronidazole was continued for a period of 14 days along with ATT. At the end of 14 days, patient had no signs of active pus discharge and there was complete resolution of fever. Follow up MRI after 14 days also revealed significant reduction in the loculated abscesses in the right iliopsoas muscles while the rest of the findings grossly remained the same (Fig. 2). Patient was discharged with continuation of oral metronidazole for five more weeks along with anti-tubercular drugs and insulin and surgical intervention once the secondary infection settled.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old female presented to the emergency room with back pain and lower extremity weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 28-year-old female presented with back pain and lower limb weakness. Contrast MRI demonstrated L3-4 disc space narrowing with paraspinal fluid collections extending into bilateral iliopsoas muscles. She was commenced on HRZE with initial clinical and neurological improvement, but relapsed with recurrent back pain after 5 months. Repeat imaging showed re-collection of organized pus; malecot catheter drainage was performed under USG guidance and modified therapy was initiated. Two months later, she re-presented to the emergency department with high-grade fever and active purulent discharge from the abscess drainage site.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 1 diabetes mellitus; spinal infection treated with HRZE for 5 months, followed by modified therapy after relapse. Denies other chronic illnesses, travel, or animal exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports severe back pain, lower extremity weakness, high-grade fever, and purulent drainage from catheter site; denies bowel or bladder dysfunction, cough, or hemoptysis. Home medications: modified ATT, insulin. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile (high grade). Examination of lumbosacral region: active purulent discharge from previous catheter drainage site. Neurological: lower extremity motor weakness with signs of neural compression.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial contrast MRI lumbosacral spine: loss of disc space at L3-4 with paraspinal collection extending into bilateral iliopsoas muscles. Repeat lumbosacral MRI (at 7 months): infective pathology at L3/L4 with intra- and extra-spinal abscesses causing neural compression. USG-guided malecot catheter insertion, followed by pigtail catheter placement. Aerobic abscess culture: no growth. Anaerobic abscess culture: isolated Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus on two consecutive days identified by MALDI-TOF MS; agar dilution susceptibility (CLSI M11-A8) showed sensitivity to clindamycin (MIC 0.25 mg/L), cefoxitin (MIC 4 mg/L), metronidazole (MIC 0.25 mg/L), imipenem (MIC 0.031 mg/L), and piperacillin-tazobactam (MIC 0.125 mg/L). Follow-up MRI at 14 days: significant reduction in loculated right iliopsoas abscesses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Relapsed rifampicin-resistant tuberculous spondylodiscitis (Pott's disease) at L3-L4 with bilateral iliopsoas abscesses and neural compression, complicated by secondary anaerobic superinfection with Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus.
Confirmation: Needle aspirate pus was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to rifampicin by both Xpert MTB/RIF and liquid culture (MGIT). Anaerobic culture of drained pus on two consecutive days grew Peptoniphilus asaccharolyticus confirmed by MALDI-TOF MS.
Differentials ruled out: Aerobic pyogenic bacterial spondylodiscitis (aerobic cultures negative).
Treatment & Outcome: Pigtail catheter abscess drainage; IV metronidazole 500 mg TDS for 14 days combined with modified anti-tubercular therapy. Fever resolved and active purulent discharge ceased completely within 14 days; follow-up MRI showed marked abscess regression. Discharged on oral metronidazole for 5 additional weeks, continuation of modified ATT and insulin, with elective spinal surgical stabilization planned following resolution of infection.

raw_case_text: A 44-year-old man was admitted to the infectious disease department of our hospital for fever and abdominal distension. The CT-scan evidenced a 6.5 cm abdominal lymph node mass with peritoneal infiltration. Patient was found HIV-1 infected and the CT driven lymph node biopsy led to the diagnosis of Burkitt lymphoma. At that time, CD4+ T cell count was 55/mul, HIV-RNA copies were 232.000/ml and patient was proven positive for anti-Toxoplasma IgG antibodies. Combined antiviral therapy (cART) with emtricitabine/tenofovir/lopinavir and prophylaxis for Toxoplasmosis/Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia and disseminated Mycobacterium Avium Complex infection with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and azithromycin at standard doses were undertaken. In the meanwhile, patient underwent chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma, according to the Magrath protocol, consisting of the administration of two regimens: CODOX-M (Cyclophosphamide 800 mg/m2 i.v.day 1; Vincristine 1.5 mg/m2 i.v. days 1, 8 and 15; Doxorubicin 40 mg/m2 i.v. day 1, Cytarabine 70 mg i.t. days 1 and 3; Cyclophosphamide 200 mg/m2 i.v.days 2-5; Methotrexate 1200 mg/m2 i.v. over 1 hour and then 240 mg/m2 i.v. each hour over 23 hours, day 10; Leucovorin 192 mg/m2 i.v. day 11 at hour 36 after methotrexate and then 12 mg/m2 i.v. every 6 hours until methotrexate level was not detectable; Methotrexate 12 mg i.t. day 15) and IVAC (Ifosfamide 1500 mg/m2 i.v. days 1-5; Mesna 360 mg/m2 mixed with ifosfamide i.v. and then 360 mg/m2 i.v. 3 hourly for seven doses, Etoposide 60 mg/m2 i.v. days 1-5, Cytarabine 2 g/m2 i.v. 12 hourly for a total of four doses, days 1-2, Methotrexate 12 mg i.t.day 5). G-CSF was administered at dose of 5 mug/kg s.c. daily, from day 15 after CODOX-M and from day 7 after IVAC regimen, until neutrophil granulocyte count reached 0,5 x 109/l. Overall, the patient received two alternating CODOX-M/IVAC courses and four Rituximab administrations at 375 mug/m2 i.v. dose over a six month period. A total body CT scan performed at the end of therapy, showed normal lymph node, liver and spleen size. The complete remission of the lymphoma was subsequently confirmed by a 18-FDG-PET scan. The CD4+ T cell count arose progressively to normal values and the HIV-RNA copies became persistently undetectable. Four months after the end of the therapy, the patient started to complain progressive weakness of legs, and, afterwards, sudden urinary retention. He was still on prophylaxis with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole without interruption; CD4+ T cell count was 270/mul and HIV-RNA was undetectable (< 50 copies/ml). Neurologic examination revealed absent ankle reflexes, reduced strength (3/5) in lower limbs and saddle sensory deficit. The spine MRI with Gadolinium showed a focal lesion of the conus medullaris, involving the proximal portion of the cauda equina nerve roots. The lesion was hyper-intense on T2-weighted images and showed marked contrast-enhancement (Figure 1a-c, white arrows). The patient was then admitted to our department: the brain MRI demonstrated an additional lesion in the deep right frontal region (0.5 cm), with signal alterations similar to that of the spinal cord. The cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) examination showed a slight increase of protein and cell concentrations (199 mg/dl and 56/mm3, respectively), with any evidence of immature lymphoid cells. The flow cytometry analysis of CSF samples revealed that cells were CD19 positive B lymphocytes, without kappa or lambda light chain restriction. PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis-DNA, Epstein Barr virus (EBV)-DNA and cytomegalovirus-DNA on CSF were all negative. The search for Cryptococcus antigen was negative, as well. Whereas both brain and spinal lesions were highly suggestive for lymphoma localizations, the total body CT scan showed no liver, spleen or lymph node enlargement consistent with the systemic relapse of the Burkitt lymphoma. Indeed, in the suspicion of an isolated CNS relapse, the patient underwent open biopsy of the conus medullaris lesion. The histological examination revealed numerous Toxoplasma tachyzoites surrounded by inflammatory cells (Figure 1d). Actually, the patient referred that he owned a cat who lived with him. Indeed, the proper treatment with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine was undertook with marked improvement of neurologic conditions in few weeks. The patient showed the full neurologic recovery and the MRI scan performed after 4 months demonstrated the definite disappearance of both spinal and brain lesions.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 44-year-old male presenting with fever and progressive abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with fever and abdominal distension and was found to have an extensive retroperitoneal/abdominal mass and newly diagnosed retroviral infection, for which he received combined antiretroviral therapy, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, and intensive chemotherapy (CODOX-M/IVAC plus rituximab), achieving complete remission. Four months following completion of chemotherapy, while maintained on trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, he developed subacute progressive weakness of the lower extremities followed by acute urinary retention.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (Burkitt lymphoma) treated with two alternating cycles of CODOX-M/IVAC and four doses of rituximab, achieving complete remission confirmed by PET-CT. Chronic retroviral disease diagnosed during initial presentation. Pre-existing seropositivity for Toxoplasma gondii IgG antibodies. Resided at home with a pet cat.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever and abdominal fullness initially; later positive for bilateral leg weakness, numbness in the saddle distribution, and acute urinary retention; negative for headache or altered sensorium. Home medications: emtricitabine/tenofovir/lopinavir, trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, azithromycin. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Initial exam: abdominal distension, palpable abdominal mass, febrile. Second admission: afebrile; neurologic exam revealed lower extremity paraparesis with motor strength 3/5 bilaterally, absent Achilles deep tendon reflexes bilaterally, and saddle sensory anesthesia.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial workup: positive anti-Toxoplasma IgG antibodies. Follow-up workup during neurologic relapse: CD4+ T-cell count: 270/mcL; serum HIV-RNA undetectable (< 50 copies/mL). CSF analysis: protein elevated at 199 mg/dL, leukocyte count 56/mm3 without immature lymphoid cells; CSF flow cytometry: polyclonal CD19+ B lymphocytes without light chain restriction; CSF PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA, EBV DNA, and CMV DNA: negative; CSF Cryptococcus antigen: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial abdominal CT: 6.5 cm abdominal lymph node mass with peritoneal infiltration; CT-guided lymph node biopsy: Burkitt lymphoma. Post-chemotherapy total body CT and 18F-FDG PET: complete remission. Spinal MRI with gadolinium: focal T2-hyperintense, intensely contrast-enhancing lesion of the conus medullaris involving cauda equina nerve roots. Brain MRI: 0.5 cm contrast-enhancing lesion in deep right frontal subcortical white matter. Total body CT: no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Open surgical biopsy of conus medullaris lesion: histopathological demonstration of numerous intracellular and extracellular Toxoplasma gondii tachyzoites surrounded by inflammatory cells.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Central nervous system toxoplasmosis (myeloradiculopathy of the conus medullaris and brain lesion) in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infection (initial CD4 55/mcL, viral load 232,000 copies/mL; post-cART CD4 270/mcL, viral load <50 copies/mL) and Burkitt lymphoma in complete remission. CNS lymphoma relapse ruled out by open conus medullaris biopsy showing Toxoplasma tachyzoites without neoplastic cells, polyclonal CSF flow cytometry, and negative staging CT. CNS tuberculosis, cryptococcosis, CMV, and EBV ruled out by negative CSF PCR and antigen. Management & Outcome: cART with emtricitabine/tenofovir/lopinavir maintained. Treated for toxoplasmosis with oral pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine, leading to rapid neurological improvement over several weeks, complete neurological recovery with resolution of paraparesis and urinary retention, and documentation of complete radiographic resolution of spinal and brain lesions on 4-month follow-up MRI.

raw_case_text:
A 26-year-old girl presented with high-grade continuous fever associated with chills and rigor for 5 days, severe headache anorexia, nausea, multiple episodes of vomiting for 4 days, and disorientation for 2 days. There was a history of one episode of GTCS convulsion day before admission. There was no similar illness in the past.
On neurological examination, she had neck rigidity with positive Kernig sign. GCS Score was E4M5V3. No cranial nerve abnormality was noted. Motor function, sensory function, reflexes, cerebellar function, and autonomic function were all within normal limit. Planter was bilateral extensor.
MRI scan of brain (plain and contrast) done on 6th day of fever, showed mild diffusion restricted nonenhancing altered signal intensity (hypointense in T1, hyperintense in T2 and FLAIR) in both thalamic and left medial temporal lobe suggestive of encephalitis [Figure 4]. The patient was diagnosed as dengue meningoencephalitis.
Patient was treated only with IV fluid and paracetamol as antipyretic. Patient improved gradually with normal sensorium gained on the 10th day of hospital stay with no neck rigidity. He had uneventful hospital stay thereafter and was discharged after 2 weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old female presenting with a 5-day history of high-grade continuous fever with chills and rigors, headache, vomiting, disorientation, and a generalized tonic-clonic convulsion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 5 days prior to admission with continuous high-grade fever, chills, and rigors. Severe headache, anorexia, nausea, and repeated vomiting developed 4 days prior, followed by disorientation for 2 days and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 1 day prior to presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No similar illness in the past.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, rigors, headache, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, and convulsions. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination: GCS score E4M5V3 (12/15). Nuchal rigidity present with positive Kernig's sign. Bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski positive bilaterally). Cranial nerves, motor strength, sensory exam, deep tendon reflexes, cerebellar function, and autonomic function were normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI (plain and contrast) on day 6 of fever: Mild diffusion-restricted non-enhancing altered signal intensity (hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR) in both thalami and the left medial temporal lobe, suggestive of viral encephalitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute dengue meningoencephalitis with bilateral thalamic and left medial temporal lobe encephalitis. Diagnosed clinically, serologically, and neuro-radiologically during an epidemic dengue outbreak.
Plan & Outcome: Managed supportively with intravenous fluids and paracetamol as an antipyretic. The patient improved gradually, regaining normal sensorium and complete resolution of nuchal rigidity by hospital day 10. The remainder of the hospital stay was uneventful, and she was discharged in stable condition after 2 weeks.

raw_case_text:
A 50-year-old man working as an employee was admitted to neurosurgery clinic with severe low back, radicular right leg pain and hypoesthesia in right L4-5 dermatomes for 2 months. His past history revealed that he had weight loss, night sweats and chills, fatigue and severe malaise for 4 months, and he consumed unpaesteurized milk and dairy products. On neurological examination there was 3/5 motor strength of right ankle dorsiflexion and hypoesthesia in distribution of right leg L4-5 dermatomes. Brucellosis was common in the area where the patient was living and brucella tube agglutination (Wright) test was routinely studied in suspected patients coming from that area. Brucella tube agglutination (Wright) test was studied in serum sample of the patient and was positive with a titer of 1/640. Brucella melitensis was isolated from blood culture. X-ray of the lumber spine showed massive collapse of L4 vertebral body (Fig. 1A). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed fracture and collapse of the body of L4 vertebrae (Fig. 1B, C). The spinal canal was narroved by posterior elements of the vertebrae, therefore neural tissue was compressed (Fig. 1D).
The patient was taken to the operation emergently a posterior midline approach and bilateral hemilaminotomy were done. Grey-yellow colored pathologic specimen was obtained from vertebral body and epidural space. Neural tissue was decompressed and then posterior L3-5 short segment transpedicular screw fixation and stabilization was performed (Fig. 2). Tricortical iliac crest wedge obtained from the same patient (autograft) was used for fusion. Neurological signs and symtoms of the patient were recovered after the operation. Brucella melitensis was isolated from microbiologic culture of pathologic specimen. Antibiotic therapy was given for brucellar infection as doxycycline 200 mg/day and rifampicin 600 mg/day for 6 months.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old male employee presented with a 2-month history of severe low back pain, radicular right leg pain, and right L4-L5 hypoesthesia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced fatigue, severe malaise, night sweats, chills, and weight loss over a 4-month period. For the preceding 2 months, he developed progressively severe low back pain radiating into his right lower extremity accompanied by sensory loss and motor weakness, prompting neurosurgical admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Occupation: employee residing in an endemic zoonotic region. Epidemiological exposure: consumed unpasteurized milk and dairy products. Prior medical conditions not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Severe low back pain, radicular right leg pain, right leg numbness, fatigue, severe malaise, night sweats, chills, weight loss. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination: motor strength of right ankle dorsiflexion reduced to 3/5; hypoesthesia in the distribution of right L4-L5 dermatomes. Vital signs not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Lumbar spine plain radiography: massive collapse of the L4 vertebral body.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar MRI: fracture and collapse of the L4 vertebral body with spinal canal narrowing caused by posterior vertebral elements and compression of neural tissue. Emergent neurosurgery: posterior midline approach with bilateral hemilaminotomy, debridement of grey-yellow pathologic specimen from vertebral body and epidural space, neural decompression, posterior L3-L5 short-segment transpedicular screw fixation, and autograft fusion using tricortical iliac crest wedge.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar spondylodiscitis with massive L4 vertebral body collapse, spinal canal stenosis, and neural compression.
Confirmation: Brucella tube agglutination (Wright) test positive at a titer of 1/640; blood culture isolated Brucella melitensis; intraoperative culture of vertebral and epidural pathologic specimens grew Brucella melitensis.
Treatment & Outcome: Emergent surgical decompression and posterior L3-L5 transpedicular screw fixation with autograft fusion; targeted antibiotic therapy administered with oral doxycycline 200 mg/day and rifampicin 600 mg/day for 6 months. Neurological signs, motor strength, and sensory symptoms completely recovered after surgery.

raw_case_text:
A 38 years-old moderate hemophiliac A male patient was diagnosed to be co-infected with HIV (Subtype B, CCR5+) and HCV (Subtype 4), both transmitted by a blood transfusion received in 1982 during hip surgery for a fracture. Diagnoses of these infections were respectively ascertained in 1988 and 1998.
Since 1989, he received different lines of anti-retroviral treatment (ART) then HAART (Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy) with poor compliance, voluntary interruption until 2008, and correct compliance since then. A 215S mutation of the HIV virus reverse transcriptase, which induces resistance to the anti-retroviral drug azidothymidine was consequently identified. His HCV infection (Metavir score A0A1-F1F2 determined by biopsy and checked regularly by noninvasive markers of hepatitis inflammation/fibrosis) was never treated. Moreover his hepatic assessment, as observed with L-aspartate aminotransferase (ASAT), L-alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) and gammaGT gamma-glutamyltransferase markers is not so much disrupted (Figure 1A).
The patient received prosthesis of the left eye in 1996 after a paintball accident and a hip replacement in 2011 for osteo-necrosis known since 1982. None of these surgeries were accompanied by infectious side effects. Indeed, over these 30 years and despite an extremely low number of T lymphocytes, the patient displayed neither opportunistic infections, nor HIV-related cancer, nor HCV-hepatitis damages. In 1989 his initial CD4+ T-cells count was 196/mm3 and since 1995 remains between 5 and 59/mm3 (Figure 1B). HIV viral loads have been mostly undetectable (below 40 copies/mL) or very low (matching deliberate HAART interruptions) since 2008 (Figure 1B).
Over the past two years, the immunophenotypic and functional status of his CD3-CD56+ NK-cells were explored by multi-parameter flow cytometry (reagents from Becton Dickinson, MountainView, CA, Figures 2A-D). Surprisingly, an abnormally high percentage of NK-cells has been steadily observed, representing approximatively 40% of peripheral lymphocytes and characterized by an expansion of the CD56bright subset (~30 to 50% of NK-cells) (Figures 2A and 2B). The percentage of CD56bright cells seems to increase when the number of CD4 decreases moreover HIV viral load is below 40 copies/ml when % of CD56bright cells is the more important (Figure 2B). These cells display high levels of natural cytotoxicity receptors NCR1 (NKp46), NCR3 (NKp30) and NKG2D compared to CD56dim cells, and have a low expression of NCR2 (NKp44) and CD69, with no labeling for CD57 nor CD25 (data not shown). The inhibitory CD94/NKG2A receptor is expressed by all CD56bright cells and a majority of CD56dim NK-cells while there is a low expression of CD158b on CD56dim and CD56bright NK-cells and a faint labeling with CD158a (Figure 2C).
Surprisingly, the NK degranulation potential (% of CD107a) that correlates with target cytolysis, usually exerted by the CD56dim NK subset, is here mainly performed by CD56bright NK-cells. Strikingly, these cells did not produce IFN-gamma following NK activation by K562 (Figure 2D).
In addition, no Th1/Th2 cytokines (TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-10) have been detected in the patient's serum (data not shown).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old male with hemophilia presenting for routine immunological surveillance and evaluation of long-term disease non-progression despite severe CD4 lymphopenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had moderate hemophilia A and acquired chronic retroviral and hepatitis C infections via contaminated blood transfusion during orthopedic surgery in 1982. Over 30 years of infection, despite severe and persistent CD4 lymphopenia (<50 cells/mm3 since 1995), he exhibited remarkable clinical resilience without ever developing opportunistic infections, malignancies, or hepatic failure, prompting comprehensive natural killer (NK) cell immunophenotypic investigation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Moderate hemophilia A. Chronic retroviral disease diagnosed in 1988, treated intermittently with ART/HAART (documented 215S reverse transcriptase mutation conferring zidovudine resistance; intermittent noncompliance until 2008, good compliance thereafter). Chronic hepatitis C (Subtype 4) diagnosed in 1998, untreated (liver biopsy Metavir score A0A1-F1F2). Left eye prosthesis placed in 1996 following trauma; right total hip arthroplasty performed in 2011 for post-traumatic osteonecrosis without infectious complications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, cough, dyspnea, diarrhea, focal neurologic complaints, or bleeding episodes. Home medications: combination antiretroviral therapy, factor VIII concentrate as needed. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Well-developed, well-nourished male in no acute distress; vital signs normal; left ocular prosthesis in place; well-healed surgical scars; no oral thrush; no peripheral lymphadenopathy; abdomen soft, non-tender, without hepatosplenomegaly; musculoskeletal exam showed intact range of motion in replaced hip.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver function tests (AST, ALT, gamma-GT): minimally elevated or near-normal; serum Th1/Th2 cytokines (TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-10): undetectable; baseline CD4+ T-cell count: 196 cells/mm3 in 1989, persistently between 5 and 59 cells/mm3 since 1995.
objective.advanced_workup: Liver biopsy: Metavir score A0A1-F1F2. Multi-parameter flow cytometry of peripheral blood: marked steady expansion of CD3-CD56+ NK cells representing approximately 40% of peripheral lymphocytes, with high expansion of CD56bright NK cells (30-50% of NK subset) expressing high levels of natural cytotoxicity receptors NCR1 (NKp46), NCR3 (NKp30), and NKG2D, low NCR2 (NKp44) and CD69, negative for CD57 and CD25, with inhibitory receptor CD94/NKG2A expressed uniformly, performing predominant CD107a degranulation without IFN-gamma secretion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Chronic human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1 Subtype B, CCR5-tropic) infection and chronic hepatitis C (HCV Subtype 4) co-infection with unique natural killer (NK) cell-mediated long-term non-progression / opportunistic infection resistance despite profound CD4+ T-lymphopenia (CD4 5-59/mm3). Confirmed by HIV Western blot, RT-PCR (viral loads undetectable <40 copies/mL on adherent HAART), and reverse transcriptase genotypic resistance testing (215S AZT mutation). Management & Outcome: Maintained on adherent HAART without opportunistic complications or liver decompensation, with expanded cytolytic CD56bright NK cells maintaining protective innate immune surveillance.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old man went to the hospital emergency department 13 days after the houseboat excursion, with fever of 37.8 C, tea-colored urine, myalgias, chills, headache, anorexia, nausea, and abdominal pain. He was admitted to the hospital with oliguric acute renal failure. Peak elevated laboratory values included a creatinine of 17.3 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 82 mg/dL, urobilinogen 4+ EU/dL, and urine protein 100 mg/dL. His leukocyte count was within normal range at 5.6 k/muL.
Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, C, rickettsiae, and ehrlichiae were negative. Renal biopsy 17 days post exposure showed acute tubulointerstitial nephritis (Figure 2A), which is reported to be the most characteristic renal lesion observed in leptospirosis. Ultrasonography showed bilateral pleural effusions and echogenic kidneys. He received broad-spectrum antimicrobials and dialysis and remained hospitalized for almost a month. His acute renal failure resolved, and he made a full recovery. MAT and IgM-ELISA results for leptospirosis were processed at CDC; titers from serum taken 23 days and 44 days postexposure were most strongly positive with serovars from L. interrogans serogroup Mini (Table 2). Immunohistochemical assay for leptospira was performed at CDC and showed granular immunostaining of leptospira in the kidney biopsy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old man presented with fever of 37.8 °C, tea-colored urine, myalgias, chills, and oliguric acute renal failure 13 days after a house-boating trip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Thirteen days after a house-boating excursion, the patient developed fever of 37.8 °C, dark tea-colored urine, generalized myalgias, chills, headache, anorexia, nausea, and abdominal pain. He presented to the emergency department with severe oliguria and acute renal failure necessitating immediate admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposure: house-boating trip to New Melones Reservoir, California, with direct exposure to storm runoff and freshwater creeks. Past illnesses, chronic medications, and drug allergies are unmentioned.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, headache, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, myalgias, and tea-colored urine with marked oliguria. Home medications and allergies are unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 37.8 °C. Physical examination notable for oliguria and abdominal tenderness. General appearance and other organ systems are not further detailed in the record.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count: 5.6 x 10^3/muL (normal range). Renal panel: peak creatinine: 17.3 mg/dL; blood urea nitrogen: 82 mg/dL. Urinalysis: urobilinogen: 4+ EU/dL; urine protein: 100 mg/dL. Ultrasound: echogenic kidneys and bilateral pleural effusions. Serologies for viral hepatitis A, B, and C, Rickettsia, and Ehrlichia were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Renal biopsy (17 days post-exposure): histopathology demonstrated marked acute tubulointerstitial nephritis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis complicated by acute tubulointerstitial nephritis and profound oliguric renal failure. Confirmed by: (1) positive granular immunostaining for Leptospira on renal biopsy via immunohistochemical assay at the CDC, and (2) positive IgM-ELISA and MAT seroconversion at 23 and 44 days post-exposure at the CDC, with titers most strongly reactive against Leptospira interrogans serogroup Mini. Viral hepatitis, Rickettsia, and Ehrlichia were ruled out. Treatment & Outcome: Managed in-hospital for nearly a month with hemodialysis, empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, and supportive care. Renal function completely recovered, allowing discontinuation of dialysis with full clinical recovery.

raw_case_text: A 21-year-old female from hilly area of Kashmir, presented with pus discharge of from two openings on the right breast for last 6 years. These aberrant openings on breast had often spontaneous pus discharge followed by cessation of discharge on its own. There were neither any constitutional symptoms nor any discharge or any abnormality of the nipple. She had already taken antitubercular therapy (ATT) thrice but was defaulter all times and reluctant for further antitubercular therapy (ATT) intake. Systemic examination was normal. Local examination showed no abnormality in left breast. A 1.5 centimeter opening was seen in inferior and outer quadrant breast, through which whitish pus was discharging along with a scar superior to discharging sinus which used to discharge pus 2 weeks before. (Figure 1). No swelling was palpable. Two firm tracts, inferior one with length of 4 cm, superior with 2.5 cm, were run posterior-superiorly ending on fifth rib. No axillary lymphadenopathy was evident. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was raised. Montoux test was positive (16x14 mm). X-ray chest showed an osteolytic lesion in anterior part of fifth rib. Computed tomography scan of chest could not reveal any foci of tuberculosis in lungs; only two sinus tracts in breast tissue and the necrosed rib were seen. Purulent aspirate was sterile for tubercle bacilli. Breast ultrasound showed ill-defined sinus tract and opening. Given the reluctance to antitubercular therapy (ATT) intake and recurrent disease coupled with apprehension of further followup, surgical intervention was done through fifth intercostal space. Excision of fibrous tract and resection of involved rib were carried out. (Figures 2 and 3) About 12 cm of rib containing pus and necrosed tissue were resected. Histopathology of specimen was chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate, with areas of caseous necrosis, giant cells (Figure 4). After proper counseling and understanding the nature of disease by patient and her parents the affected woman was motivated for antitubercular therapy (ATT) intake and with daily dose of 300 mg isoniazid, 600 mg rifampicin, 1500 mg pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and 10 mg pyridoxine for 9 months. She had regularly attended our followup clinics during last two years, with no recurrence of disease being recorded.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old female presenting with chronic pus discharge from two right breast sinuses for six years.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-year history of persistent whitish pus discharge from two abnormal sinuses on her right breast. The sinuses discharged spontaneously with intermittent temporary cessation followed by recurrence. She noted no nipple discharge or retraction and no constitutional symptoms. She had previously been prescribed antitubercular therapy on three separate occasions, but had defaulted treatment each time due to reluctance to take medications.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resides in a hilly area of Kashmir. History of breast tuberculosis with three prior defaulted courses of antituberculosis therapy (ATT). Denies other chronic medical conditions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pus discharge from right breast sinuses. Denies fever, chills, night sweats, weight loss, anorexia, breast pain, or nipple discharge.

objective.physical_examination: Systemic physical examination was normal. Left breast examination was normal. Right breast examination revealed a 1.5 cm cutaneous sinus in the inferior-outer quadrant discharging whitish pus, with a healed scar superior to it from a previous sinus tract. No palpable breast masses. Two firm subcutaneous tracts were palpated coursing posterosuperiorly toward the chest wall (inferior tract 4 cm, superior tract 2.5 cm) terminating on the fifth rib. No axillary lymphadenopathy was palpable.
objective.routine_investigations: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was elevated. Mantoux tuberculin test was positive (16 x 14 mm induration). Chest radiograph showed an osteolytic lesion in the anterior aspect of the right fifth rib. Breast ultrasound showed ill-defined sinus tracts and cutaneous openings.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT scan showed no active pulmonary parenchymal tuberculous lesions, confirming two sinus tracts traversing the breast tissue and osteolytic necrosis of the fifth rib. Purulent sinus aspirate was sterile for pyogenic bacteria and tubercle bacilli on routine culture. Excisional surgery through the fifth intercostal space was performed, with complete resection of the fibrous sinus tracts and 12 cm of the involved necrotic fifth rib containing pus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Secondary breast tuberculosis with tuberculous osteomyelitis of the fifth rib and chest wall cold abscess forming chronic discharging fistulae, in a multi-defaulting patient.
Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathological examination of the resected rib and sinus tracts demonstrated chronic inflammatory infiltrate with extensive caseous necrosis and Langhans giant cells, alongside radiographic osteolytic rib destruction and positive Mantoux test.
Management and outcome: Radical excision of sinus tracts and en bloc resection of 12 cm of necrotic rib. Following extensive adherence counseling, the patient was successfully initiated on a 9-month daily antituberculosis regimen: isoniazid 300 mg, rifampicin 600 mg, pyrazinamide 1500 mg, ethambutol, and pyridoxine 10 mg. She regularly attended follow-up clinic for 2 years with complete wound healing and no recurrence.

raw_case_text:
A twenty-five-year-old male patient from Paicandu, Parana, sought the health care unit of his city because of an ulcer on the lower lip that was treated as herpes labialis without wound healing or improvement. In August 2015, after thirty days of the ulcer appearance, the patient was referred to the LEPAC (Laboratorio de Ensino e Pesquisa em Analises Clinicas) at the Universidade Estadual de Maringa. During examination of the lower lip, an ulcerated lesion was observed, it was erythematous with raised edges and there was the presence of granulomatous, purulent and crusty contents characteristic of mucosal leishmaniasis (Figure 1A). In a patient interview, he described that he frequently fished in the Ivai river, an endemic region for Leishmania (Viannia) sp. and several acquaintances acquired leishmaniasis in the same place.
The conducted laboratory tests were Montenegro skin test, direct parasite search in the scraping from lesion edges and in the patient's blood sample an indirect immunofluorescence for anti-Leishmania IgG antibodies was performed. The Montenegro skin test was reactive with an induration of 6 mm in diameter, indirect immunofluorescence was positive for anti-Leishmania IgG antibodies with titer of 1:80 and the direct parasite search was also positive (Figure 1B). Detection of the parasite in the scraping from lesion edges and in the patient's blood sample were made by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using primers to amplify a 70-bp fragment of the kinetoplast minicircle DNA (kDNA) from parasites belonging to Leishmania (Viannia) sp. subgenera. Only the scraping material was positive (Figure 1C).
The initial therapeutic regimen for treating leishmaniasis was Glucantime , three ampoules per day (1.215 mg) with four cycles of treatment: 20 and 30 days with an interval of 12 weeks, and two extra-cycles of 40 and 30 days with a break of approximately 10 days. This therapeutic scheme used by the patient is actually the one recommended to cutaneous leishmaniasis, since, according to what is suggested by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the duration of the first cycle is 20 days with 10-20 mg/kg/day of Glucantime , respecting the limit of three ampoules per day, being repeated for more 30 days in case of failure with an interval of 12 weeks. At this stage, the patient was followed up by a new medical team, who decided not to use the therapeutic regimen recommended by the Ministry of Health, prescribing other two cycles of Glucantime , 40 and 30 days with an interval of approximately 10 days between them. The treatment with Glucantime  was unsuccessful, because the lesion reappeared with nodular aspect followed by ulceration. The side effects reported by the patient were present only on the first day of Glucantime  administration (seasickness and fever). Electrocardiogram was used to monitor the treatment side effects. In this situation, amphotericin B administration was necessary and 1 mg/kg/day was administered during 30 days with an interval of three days every 10 days, respecting the maximum of 50 mg (one flask) per administration.
Delayed diagnosis and treatment failure led the patient to episodes of depression. In March 2017, three months after treatment with amphotericin B and 19 months after correct diagnosis, the patient was in remission and under observation (Figure 1D). The project received the approval of the Project Management System (process No 1505/1997) of the Universidade Estadual de Maringa and the patient signed an informed consent form and a photograph consent form.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented with a 30-day non-healing ulcer on his lower lip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 25-year-old male from Paiçandu, Paraná, Brazil presented with an ulcer on his lower lip that had persisted for 30 days. It was initially treated as herpes labialis without improvement, prompting referral to LEPAC at Universidade Estadual de Maringá in August 2015. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime, 3 ampoules/day) across four extended cycles (20, 30, 40, and 30 days), but treatment failed as the lesion recurred as a nodule that re-ulcerated. He experienced reactive depression due to diagnostic delay and repeated therapeutic failure, before successful second-line antimonial salvage.
subjective.past_medical_history: Frequent recreational fishing in the Ivaí river, an endemic area for Leishmania (Viannia) sp., where acquaintances had contracted leishmaniasis. No prior chronic diseases. Prior topical/systemic antiherpetic therapy without effect.
subjective.review_of_systems: Lower lip ulceration, nausea/seasickness and fever on first day of antimonial administration, depressive symptoms. Denied systemic fever, weight loss, or adenopathy.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination of the lower lip revealed an erythematous ulcerated lesion with raised borders and granulomatous, purulent, and crusty exudate. Serial electrocardiograms (ECG) performed during antimonial therapy remained normal without QT prolongation.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial electrocardiograms (ECG) performed to monitor potential antimonial cardiotoxicity showed normal tracings.
objective.advanced_workup: Scraping from the lesion margins stained with Giemsa: microscopic examination revealed intracellular microorganisms. Blood and scraping samples subjected to molecular testing.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Mucosal leishmaniasis of the lower lip caused by Leishmania (Viannia) sp., refractory to pentavalent antimony.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct parasite search in lesion scraping revealed Leishmania amastigotes; Montenegro skin test was reactive (induration 6 mm); indirect immunofluorescence was positive for anti-Leishmania IgG (titer 1:80); PCR amplifying a 70-bp kDNA minicircle fragment of subgenus Leishmania (Viannia) was positive on lesion scraping (negative in blood).
Differentials Ruled Out: Herpes labialis (initial misdiagnosis, unresponsive to antivirals), squamous cell carcinoma, paracoccidioidomycosis, and primary syphilis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Patient failed extensive therapy with Glucantime (3 ampoules/day = 1,215 mg over 4 cycles of 20, 30, 40, and 30 days) with lesion recurrence. Salvage therapy with intravenous amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day, maximum 50 mg/day, for 30 days with 3-day intervals every 10 days) was instituted, resulting in complete mucosal healing and sustained remission at 19-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 47-year-old man living in the countryside with a history of exposure to cattle was admitted to our hospital with a 2-week history of abdominal distension and a 9-day history of fever. Initially, the patient also presented with fatigue, myalgia, and joint pain. Within 2 weeks, he lost 7.5 kg of body weight. His temperature reached 38.9 C for 9 days. Before he came to our hospital, he was treated in a local hospital for 9 days. His local test results showed that his blood culture was negative, and abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed splenic infarction and portal vein enlargement. The Brucella serum tube agglutination test (SAT) was negative (1:25). His symptoms had no improvement with 6-day ceftriaxone [2.0, quaque die, intra-veineuse drip (QD, iv. D)] treatment. Then, he was discharged from the local hospital and visited our hospital.
At admission, his physical examination results were as follows: blood pressure, 132/72 mmHg; high-grade fever, 39.0 C; tachycardia, 102 beats/min; submandibular, cervical, and axillary enlarged lymph nodes were 10-20 mm, soft, freely moveable, and nontender; he had hepatomegaly, with the liver felt 2.0 cm below the ribs; and splenomegaly, with the spleen felt 5.0 cm below the ribs.
The laboratory results were as follows: white blood cell counts of 3.2 x 109/L (normal range: 3.5-9.5) and hemoglobin of 100 (normal range: 130-175) g/L. Liver enzymes and cardiac enzymes were increased: aspartate aminotransferase of 329.9 (normal range: 15-40) U/L, alanine aminotransferase of 217.1 (normal range: 9-50) U/L, alkaline phosphatase of 417.4 (normal range: 45-125) U/L, and lactate dehydrogenase of 284 (normal range: 120-250) U/L. Pancreatic enzymes were increased: amylase of 151.8 (normal range: 35-135) U/L and lipase of 127.8 (normal range: 0-79) U/L. The tumor marker carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9 level was obviously increased at 240.1 (normal range: 0-37) U/mL. Brucella serum tests were sent again, and the results were as follows: STA was weakly positive (1:100), and Brucellosis antibody IgG was positive. Inflammatory marker levels were increased: C-reactive protein of 17.0 (normal range: 0-10) mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 72 (normal range: 0-15) mm/h, and ferritin of 897.3 (normal range: 20-300) mug/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and multiple low-density lesions in the spleen. Enhanced abdominal CT showed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, multiple low-density lesions in the spleen (prone to splenic infarction), portal vein enlargement, and a small amount of effusion in the pelvis ( Figure 1 ). Brucella abortus was cultured and isolated from blood after 5 days.
Because of the concerns about his long-term exposure to cattle, treatment after admission was started and consisted of doxycycline [0.1, bis in die, per os (BID, p.o.)] and streptomycin [15 mg/kg, quaque die, intramuscular injection (QD, IM)]. After verifying Brucella abortus infection by blood culture, rifampicin (0.6, QD, p.o.) was added to the combination therapy ( Figure 2 ). The body temperature of the patient recovered to the normal level after anti-brucellosis treatment for 6 days. After 8 days of treatment, blood tests and abdominal ultrasound were performed. The blood test results were as follows: CA 19-9 decreased to 70.1 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and no low-density lesions in the spleen. The subsequent treatment with streptomycin was administered for 2 weeks, and the other two medicines were taken for 6 weeks. After 1 month of treatment, pancreatic enzymes levels and liver enzymes recovered to normal levels: the amylase 66 U/L, the lipase 55.2 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 20 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 18 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L. After 6 weeks of treatment, CA 19-9 recovered to normal levels. Abdominal CT showed that the low-density lesions in the spleen were much less than the former ( Figure 3 ).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of abdominal distension and a 9-day history of fever reaching 38.9 C.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 47-year-old man presented with abdominal distension for 2 weeks and fever up to 38.9 C for 9 days, accompanied by fatigue, myalgia, and arthralgia, resulting in a 7.5 kg weight loss. Prior to presentation, he was hospitalized locally for 9 days and treated empirically with intravenous ceftriaxone 2.0 g daily without clinical improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Residence in the countryside with a history of exposure to cattle. Prior antibiotic therapy: ceftriaxone 2.0 g IV daily for 6 days at a local hospital. Other chronic illnesses and allergies not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal distension, fatigue, myalgia, joint pain, and 7.5 kg weight loss over 2 weeks. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure: 132/72 mmHg, body temperature: 39.0 C (high-grade fever), pulse rate: 102 beats/min (tachycardia). Lymph nodes: submandibular, cervical, and axillary lymph nodes enlarged (10-20 mm, soft, freely moveable, nontender). Abdomen: hepatomegaly (liver palpable 2.0 cm below ribs) and splenomegaly (spleen palpable 5.0 cm below ribs).
objective.routine_investigations: WBC: 3.2 x 109/L (normal range: 3.5-9.5 x 109/L); Hemoglobin: 100 g/L (normal range: 130-175 g/L). AST: 329.9 U/L (normal range: 15-40 U/L); ALT: 217.1 U/L (normal range: 9-50 U/L); ALP: 417.4 U/L (normal range: 45-125 U/L); LDH: 284 U/L (normal range: 120-250 U/L). Pancreatic enzymes: amylase 151.8 U/L (normal range: 35-135 U/L) and lipase 127.8 U/L (normal range: 0-79 U/L). Tumor marker CA 19-9: 240.1 U/mL (normal range: 0-37 U/mL). CRP: 17.0 mg/L (normal range: 0-10 mg/L); ESR: 72 mm/h (normal range: 0-15 mm/h); Ferritin: 897.3 mug/L (normal range: 20-300 mug/L). Initial local blood culture: negative. Abdominal ultrasound: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and multiple low-density lesions in the spleen.
objective.advanced_workup: Enhanced abdominal CT: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, multiple low-density lesions in the spleen suggestive of splenic infarction, portal vein enlargement, and small amount of pelvic effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellosis (Brucella abortus infection) complicated by splenic infarction, acute pancreatitis, and hepatitis.
Confirmation: Brucella abortus cultured and isolated from blood after 5 days; serum tube agglutination test (STA) weakly positive at 1:100 (initial local SAT had been negative at 1:25) and Brucellosis antibody IgG positive.
Differentials ruled out: Pancreaticobiliary malignancy (CA 19-9 normalized with antimicrobial therapy), common bacterial pyogenic sepsis (initial blood culture negative and refractory to ceftriaxone).
Treatment & Outcome: Initially started on oral doxycycline (0.1 g BID) and intramuscular streptomycin (15 mg/kg daily). Upon blood culture confirmation of Brucella abortus, oral rifampicin (0.6 g daily) was added to complete triple therapy. Body temperature normalized within 6 days of targeted therapy. Streptomycin was completed for 2 weeks, while doxycycline and rifampicin were continued for 6 weeks. At 1 month, pancreatic and liver enzymes normalized (amylase 66 U/L, lipase 55.2 U/L, AST 20 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, ALP 88 U/L). At 6 weeks, CA 19-9 normalized and follow-up CT demonstrated resolution of most splenic infarct lesions.

raw_case_text:
Patient information: a 32-year-old woman in her fifth pregnancy with three children alive and one first trimester miscarriage was referred to our hospital, a tertiary institution, from a provincial hospital. She had a previous C/S, and had presented late at an estimated menstrual gestational age of 42 completed weeks and four days. On work-up for C/S at the referring hospital, she was noted to have a severe thrombocytopenia of 34x103/microL. The reasons for referral were the absence of blood products and appropriately qualified anaesthesiologists at that hospital. On systemic enquiry at presentation, she reported generalised body weakness in the preceding three-to-four days that she attributed to advanced pregnancy and did not bother to seek medical attention. She had no fever, chills and rigors, joint pains nor headaches, and the rest of her systemic enquiry was non-contributory. The pregnancy was booked, and she had six antenatal care (ANC) visits. She was HIV negative, and had no other chronic illnesses. No ultrasound scan (USS) was done due to financial constraints. She was on hematinic supplements from the booking visit; however, she did not receive IPT for malaria, and did not take any other medicines. In the first trimester, she was treated for slide-positive symptomatic malaria with a complete course of co-artemether (artemether/lumefantrine). She had a history of one C/S performed for fetal distress in her last pregnancy in 2015, after two vaginal deliveries and a first trimester miscarriage. She stayed with her family in Burma Valley, which is malaria-endemic.
Clinical findings: she looked rather unwell, pale and dehydrated, with no jaundice or lymphadenopathy. The blood pressure was 110/56 mmHg with a heart rate of 119 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 14 breaths per minute and a temperature of 36.5  C. Chest, cardiovascular, central nervous system and skin examinations were unremarkable, and she did not have epigastric tenderness on abdominal examination. She had a Pfannenstiel scar. The symphysis-fundal (SFH) was 38 cm, with a singleton foetus in longitudinal lie and cephalic presentation. The foetal heart rate was 132 beats per minute.
Diagnostic assessment: the problems noted were the severe thrombocytopenia, one previous C/S and post-term pregnancy. Laboratory investigations revealed a pancytopenia, and numerous ring forms of P. falciparum. However, no level of parasitemia was provided. The white cell count was 2.0x103/microL, haemoglobin level was 9.8 g/dl and platelet count was 29x103/microL, with a mean corpuscular volume of 81.1 fL. The urea, electrolytes and liver enzymes were all normal with an alanine transaminase (ALT) of 13 iU/l and an aspartate transaminase (AST) of 36 iU/l. Both total and direct bilirubin were within normal limits. Bedside clotting time was prolonged at 13 minutes. Despite low normal BPs, urinalysis was done and was negative for proteins.
Therapeutic intervention: diagnoses of P. falciparum malaria, one previous C/S and post-term pregnancy were made. Treatment for malaria with intravenous (IV) artesunate 2.4 mg/kg body weight once daily, ceftriaxone 1 g IV once daily, and paracetamol 1 g IV three times a day was commenced. An emergency C/S was done under platelet cover and tranexamic acid 1 g infusion, and a live baby weighing 3195 g with Apgar scores of 8/10-9/10 was delivered. However, post C/S the patient was noted to be actively bleeding per vagina, and a re-laparotomy was done, proceeding to a supra-cervical hysterectomy after she had continued bleeding despite uterotonics, traexamic acid infusion and uterine massage. The total estimated blood loss was 2500 ml, and the patient was transfused three units of packed cells, 6 units of platelets and 6 units of fresh frozen plasma.
Follow-up and outcomes: post-operatively, the patient remained anaemic, with a haemoglobin level of 7 g/dl, and she was transfused two more units of packed cells. She had a good urine output of 1800 mls of clear urine in the first 24 hours, and started mobilising on the first day. The repeat malaria thin slide was negative, and she was discharged on co-artemether (artemether/lumefantrine), paracetamol and oral antibiotics on the fifth day. For further postnatal follow-up, she was referred back to the referring hospital to minimise the costs and need for travelling.
Patient s perspective: the patient was very grateful that both her and the baby were well on discharge, and was also grateful that she had been diagnosed of malaria before she had developed fatal complications.
Informed consent: the patient provided signed written informed consent for case publication. However, the Medical Research Council of Zimbabwe and the Joint Research Ethics Committee do not require approvals for case reports.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old pregnant female (gravida 5, para 3, abortus 1) at 42 weeks and 4 days of gestation presenting with generalized body weakness, post-term pregnancy, and severe thrombocytopenia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 32-year-old female (G5P3A1) with one previous cesarean section presented post-term at 42 weeks and 4 days of gestation. She was referred from a provincial hospital after routine pre-operative workup revealed severe thrombocytopenia (34 x 10^3/μL) in the absence of local blood banking facilities. She reported generalized weakness for 3-4 days, which she had attributed to advanced pregnancy. She denied fevers, chills, rigors, arthralgias, or headaches.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida 5, para 3, abortus 1 (previous C-section in 2015 for fetal distress; two vaginal deliveries; one first-trimester miscarriage). Booked pregnancy with 6 antenatal visits; received hematinics but did not receive intermittent preventive therapy (IPT) for malaria. Treated in the first trimester for slide-positive symptomatic malaria with oral artemether-lumefantrine. HIV-negative, no other chronic illnesses. Resides in Burma Valley (malaria-endemic region).
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized fatigue/weakness; denies fevers, chills, rigors, joint pains, headaches, or epigastric discomfort.

objective.physical_examination: Unwell-appearing, pale, dehydrated, anicteric, no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Blood pressure 110/56 mmHg, heart rate 119 beats/min (tachycardia), respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.5 °C. Normal heart sounds and clear lungs. Abdomen: Pfannenstiel scar, non-tender without epigastric tenderness. Symphysis-fundal height 38 cm; singleton fetus in longitudinal lie and cephalic presentation with fetal heart rate 132 beats/min.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Pancytopenia with WBC 2.0 x 10^3/μL, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelet count 29 x 10^3/μL (confirmed thrombocytopenia), MCV 81.1 fL. Bedside clotting time prolonged at 13 minutes. Serum ALT 13 IU/L, AST 36 IU/L; total and direct bilirubin normal; urea and electrolytes normal. Urinalysis negative for protein.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Post-term pregnancy (42 weeks 4 days) with prior cesarean scar and asymptomatic Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by pancytopenia, severe thrombocytopenia (29 x 10^3/μL), prolonged clotting time, and severe intrapartum/postpartum hemorrhage requiring emergency peripartum hysterectomy. Diagnosis confirmed by peripheral blood smear demonstrating numerous intraerythrocytic ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum. Preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome ruled out by normal liver enzymes, normal blood pressure, and absence of proteinuria.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on IV artesunate (2.4 mg/kg daily), IV ceftriaxone (1 g daily), and IV paracetamol. Emergency cesarean section performed under platelet transfusion cover and IV tranexamic acid (1 g), delivering a healthy live infant (3,195 g, Apgar 8/10-9/10). Intractable postpartum hemorrhage occurred despite uterotonics and uterine massage; emergency relaparotomy and subtotal/supracervical hysterectomy were performed (estimated blood loss 2,500 mL). Transfused total 5 units PRBCs, 6 units platelets, and 6 units FFP. Postoperative hemoglobin stabilized at 7.0 g/dL with good urine output (1800 mL/24h). Repeat malaria thin blood film was negative, and she was discharged on day 5 on oral artemether-lumefantrine, paracetamol, and antibiotics.

raw_case_text: The patient is a 33-year-old Chinese male. He was diagnosed with brucellosis in a local hospital in October 2017 due to right hip pain and wavy fever. Following the administration of anti-brucellosis drugs, the fever subsided, but the pain in the right hip did not. In January 2018, the patient visited the orthopedic department of our hospital due to aggravation of right hip pain and decreased hip joint mobility. History indicates that the patient's family raised sheep for a long time, and there was no history of trauma, alcohol consumption, or hormone use. The physical examination revealed severe tenderness in the right hip region, longitudinal percussion pain in the right lower limb, and limited passive and active movement of the right hip. There was no abnormality in the chest X-ray or CT. X-ray of the hip joint showed low signal on the right femoral head, joint narrowing and even invagination of the joint space (Figure 3A). CT showed cavity necrosis and low-density patches of shadows in the right femoral head (Figure 3B). MRI of the hip joint indicates effusion of the right hip joint complicated by necrosis of the right femoral head, and the inflammatory fluid diffused with extra-articular (Figure 3C). Blood tests indicated WBC 4.60x109/L with neutrophils accounting for 61.1%, CRP59.3mg/L, ESR29.0mm/hr, and procalcitonin (PCT) 0.05ng/mL. T-SPOT.TB assay (T-SPOT), as well as serum anti-tuberculosis antibody tests, were negative. RBPT was positive, and SAT was positive at a titer of 1:640. The above examination eliminated tuberculosis, and a preliminary diagnosis of brucellar hip arthritis and osteonecrosis of the femoral head was made. Despite taking anti-brucellosis medications for two weeks, which included rifampicin (0.6g po qd; Guangdong Hengjian Pharmaceuticals), doxycycline (0.1g po bid; Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceuticals), and levofloxacin (0.2g ivgtt bid; Yangtze River Pharmaceuticals), the right hip's symptoms did not improve. This patient underwent puncture and irrigation of the right hip joint and core decompression with bone grafting of the femoral head. Using real-time PCR, B. melitensis was detected in joint effusions and osteonecrosis of the femoral head. HE staining in osteonecrosis of the femoral head revealed partial dead bone and inflammatory cellulose exudate (Figure 4A); Giemsa staining showed scattered positive Brucella (Figure 4B). When discharged from the hospital three weeks after surgery, the patient's right hip pain was significantly reduced; blood tests showed a CRP level of 24.7mg/L and an ESR level of 18.00mm/hr. The antibiotic regimen was adjusted to rifampicin (0.6g po qd; Guangdong Hengjian Pharmaceuticals) and doxycycline (0.1g po bid; Jiangsu Lianhuan Pharmaceuticals) after discharge, with a total therapy duration of six months. Following a follow-up four years later, the pain in the right hip had completely disappeared, and the hip joint was no longer limited in movement; neither the blood tests nor the imaging examinations (Figure 3D-F) revealed any abnormalities.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male presented with worsening right hip pain and decreased joint mobility for three months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed undulant fever and right hip pain in October 2017. Although the fever subsided following antimicrobial therapy, the right hip pain progressively worsened and joint mobility declined over the subsequent three months. He was admitted to orthopedics in January 2018 for surgical decompression and targeted antimicrobial treatment.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of undulant fever treated with antimicrobial therapy three months prior; denied history of trauma, alcohol consumption, or corticosteroid therapy. Epidemiological exposure: Longstanding family occupation of raising sheep.

objective.physical_examination: Right hip: Severe localized tenderness in the right hip region, positive longitudinal axial percussion tenderness along the right lower limb, and marked restriction of both active and passive motion of the right hip.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC 4.60 x 10^9/L (61.1% neutrophils), CRP 59.3 mg/L, ESR 29.0 mm/hr, procalcitonin (PCT) 0.05 ng/mL. T-SPOT.TB and anti-tuberculosis antibody tests: Negative. Chest X-ray and thoracic CT: Normal. Postoperative labs (3 weeks): CRP decreased to 24.7 mg/L, ESR decreased to 18.00 mm/hr. Four-year follow-up: Normal inflammatory markers.
objective.advanced_workup: Right hip X-ray: Low density of the right femoral head with joint space narrowing and acetabular invagination. Hip CT: Cavitary osteonecrosis and mottled low-density shadows in the right femoral head. Hip MRI: Joint effusion with avascular necrosis of the right femoral head and extra-articular extension of inflammatory fluid. Histopathology: H&E staining revealed non-viable bone trabeculae and fibrinous inflammatory exudate; Giemsa staining showed scattered coccobacilli. Four-year follow-up CT/MRI: Complete osseous remodeling and resolution of effusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar septic arthritis complicated by avascular osteonecrosis of the right femoral head, confirmed by real-time PCR detection of Brucella melitensis in hip joint fluid and necrotic femoral head tissue, positive Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT), Standard Tube Agglutination Test (SAT titer 1:640), and Giemsa staining demonstrating Brucella organisms. Tuberculosis was excluded.
Plan & Clinical Course: Received preoperative triple therapy with oral rifampicin 0.6 g daily, oral doxycycline 0.1 g twice daily, and IV levofloxacin 0.2 g twice daily for two weeks without symptomatic relief. He then underwent surgical puncture and irrigation of the right hip joint, core decompression, and autologous bone grafting. Discharged 3 weeks postoperatively on oral rifampicin 0.6 g daily and oral doxycycline 0.1 g twice daily for 6 months. At 4-year follow-up, right hip pain and mobility limitation were completely resolved with normal radiographic findings.

raw_case_text:
A 32 years old woman was admitted during labor, to the Department of Gynecology of the Moroccan Field hospital deployed in South Sudan. The patient was gravida 3, para 2, abortus 1 (2 living children) at the 39th week of gestation, prenatal screening tests were not performed. The clinical examination showed normal fundal height, with perception of uterine contractions and normal fetal heart activity, the cervix was effaced and dilated to 4cm. Trans-abdominal ultrasound was performed; the placenta was localized in the posterior side of the fundus; the amniotic fluid and the fetal growth were normal. A healthy male infant weighing 2600g was successfully delivered via spontaneous vaginal delivery, the apgar score was 8/9/10 with no blood loss during delivery, and no congenital abnormality was detected. 24 hours after delivery, the mother presented acute fever associated to chills and excessive sweating; she had anemia with hemoglobin 8.2g/dl, hematocrit 25.8%, MCV 86.1fl, MCH 28.5pg, MCHC 31.5g/dl, total leucocyte count 5.5x103/ul and platelet count was low 56,000/ul. C-reactive protein (CRP) was normal (5,2mg/l), with normal range of serum electrolytes. Blood and urine cultures were sterile and peripheral blood smear showed malarial parasites of Plasmodium falciparum parasitemia at 4%.
The mother reported after evaluation a possible malaria infection in the 32th week of pregnancy, managed with unspecific treatment. The newborn baby was healthy and vigorous, exclusively breastfed, the clinical examination was normal; biological analysis showed hemoglobin 16.3g/dl, total leucocyte count 7.5x103/ul and platelet count 72,000/ul. C-reactive protein (CRP) was normal (< 5mg/l), with normal range of serum electrolytes. Peripheral blood smear was negative for malaria parasites; unfortunately, the other methods of diagnosis (Detection of PfHRP2 antigen, DNA detection and quantification) were not available for further investigations, the newborn was placed under close observation and a second examination of the peripheral blood, was done within 3 days; a thick and thin blood film revealed P. falciparum trophozoites, with a parasitaemia of 1,5%. The mother was treated according to local guidelines with arthemeter + lumefantrine and the infant was treated by oral chloroquine 10mg/kg for two days and 5mg/kg in the third day. Four days after treatment haemoparasites were cleared, with normal follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old parturient female (gravida 3, para 2, abortus 1) admitted in labor at 39 weeks gestation who presented postpartum with acute fever, chills, and excessive sweating.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 32-year-old pregnant woman (G3P2A1) presented at 39 weeks of gestation in active labor. Transabdominal ultrasound showed a fundal posterior placenta with normal amniotic fluid and fetal growth. She underwent an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of a healthy male infant weighing 2600 g (Apgar 8/9/10). Twenty-four hours post-delivery, the mother acutely developed fever, chills, and profuse diaphoresis. Clinical examination of the newborn was initially normal, with close monitoring initiated.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida 3, para 2, abortus 1 (2 living children). Prenatal screening tests were not performed. Reported a possible febrile illness in the 32nd week of pregnancy managed with non-specific treatment. Location: Deployed in South Sudan.
subjective.review_of_systems: Chills and excessive sweating accompanying fever; no blood loss during delivery.

objective.physical_examination: Mother on admission: Normal fundal height, uterine contractions palpable, cervix effaced and dilated to 4 cm. Postpartum: Acute fever. Newborn: Healthy and vigorous, weight 2600 g, Apgar scores 8/9/10; systemic physical examination normal without congenital abnormalities.
objective.routine_investigations: Mother (24h postpartum): Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, hematocrit 25.8%, MCV 86.1 fL, MCH 28.5 pg, MCHC 31.5 g/dL, total leukocyte count 5.5 x 10^3/μL, platelet count 56,000/μL. CRP 5.2 mg/L; serum electrolytes normal. Blood and urine cultures sterile. Transabdominal ultrasound showed placenta in posterior fundus, normal amniotic fluid, and normal fetal growth. Infant initial labs: Hemoglobin 16.3 g/dL, total leukocyte count 7.5 x 10^3/μL, platelet count 72,000/μL, CRP < 5 mg/L, serum electrolytes normal; initial neonatal peripheral blood smear was negative for hemoparasites.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Maternal and congenital Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Maternal peripheral blood smear demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum with 4% parasitemia. Repeat neonatal thick and thin blood films on day 3 of life revealed Plasmodium falciparum trophozoites with 1.5% parasitemia (PfHRP2 antigen and PCR testing unavailable). Bacterial blood and urine cultures were sterile.
Plan & Outcome: Mother was treated with oral artemether-lumefantrine according to local protocols. Neonate was treated with oral chloroquine (10 mg/kg daily for two days, then 5 mg/kg on the third day). Complete clearance of hemoparasites was confirmed on repeat smear 4 days post-treatment, with normal clinical follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old lady presented with fever, headache, arthralgia, and myalgia, after returning from the Philippines. She recalled mosquito bite one week before. Investigations showed lymphopenia, increased hepatic enzymes, C-Reactive-Protein (CRP), normal renal function (Table 1), and prominent spleen (11.6 cm) on ultrasonogram. Empirical antibiotic was given. Septic workup was negative. Her fever subsided and hepatic enzymes were improving. Dengue-virus IgM/specific nonstructural (NS1) protein antigen, chikungunya virus (CHIKV) IgM, and blood malaria parasite were not detected. She was discharged on day 10 with stable condition.
Eight weeks later she was readmitted for fever, malaise, and persistent symmetrical polyarthritis involving both wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, shoulders, hips, and knees, mimicking RA. She reported no recent hiking, no rash, and no oral ulcer. Clinical examination revealed more than ten tender and swollen joints over hands, wrists, and knees. There was no lymphadenopathy and no focal neurological deficit. Blood tests showed elevated liver enzymes, ferritin, and persistent high CRP level (Table 1). Hepatitis A, B, and C serology, anti-HIV, autoantibodies including rheumatoid factor, anticyclic-citrullinated peptide, anti-nuclear antibody, antidouble-stranded-DNA, anti-neutrophil-cytoplasmic antibody, anti-smooth-muscle antibody, and anti-mitochondrial antibody were all negative. C3 and C4 levels were normal. There was no erosion on hands and knees radiographs and her chest X-ray was clear. She was covered with Augmentin and Doxycycline for fever. No vegetation was detected on echocardiogram. Hepatic ultrasonogram showed prominent periportal echogenicity. Musculoskeletal ultrasound demonstrated wrists extensors and flexors tenosynovitis with increased Doppler signals, effusion, and synovial proliferation in knees (Figure 1). A total 25 mL fluid was aspirated from left knee suprapatellar recess. Gram stain, bacterial culture, and acid-fast-bacilli smear were negative. Fever persisted for two weeks. Liver biopsy was suggested to look for infective or infiltrative causes but patient refused. Septic workup was all unrevealing. CHIKV serology was rechecked. This time CHIKV-IgM was detected and CHIKV-polyvalent-antibody titre had risen from 1 : <10 to 1 : 1280. The first CHIKV-IgM negative sample was reexamined and was CHIKV-PCR positive (Table 1). The diagnosis of CHIKV-related arthritis was made. She was treated with supportive measures. Liver enzymes slowly reduced but joint symptoms persisted. Patient requested discharge-against-medical-advice after 3 weeks of hospital stay.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female presented with fever, headache, arthralgia, and myalgia after returning from the Philippines, with subsequent readmission 8 weeks later for persistent polyarthritis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old female presented with fever, headache, arthralgia, and myalgia following travel to the Philippines. Initial symptoms and transaminases improved, and she was discharged on day 10. Eight weeks later, she was readmitted with persistent fever, malaise, and symmetrical polyarthritis affecting bilateral wrists, MCP joints, shoulders, hips, and knees mimicking rheumatoid arthritis. Fever persisted for 2 weeks during readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Travel to the Philippines; recall of mosquito bite one week prior to initial presentation. No recent hiking. Prior empiric antibiotic exposure during initial admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Malaise, headache, myalgia, arthralgia; denies rash or oral ulcers. Home medications and allergies: Not documented.

objective.physical_examination: More than 10 tender and swollen joints involving hands, wrists, and knees. No lymphadenopathy; no focal neurological deficits.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial admission: Lymphopenia, elevated hepatic enzymes, elevated CRP, normal renal function; abdominal ultrasound showed splenomegaly (11.6 cm). Readmission: Elevated liver enzymes, elevated ferritin, persistent high CRP. Normal C3 and C4 levels. Viral hepatitis (HAV, HBV, HCV), anti-HIV: negative. Autoimmune serologies: RF, anti-CCP, ANA, anti-dsDNA, ANCA, ASMA, and AMA all negative. Plain radiographs of hands and knees: no erosions. Chest X-ray: clear. Arthrocentesis of left knee (25 mL aspirated): Gram stain, bacterial culture, and AFB smear negative. Malaria smear: negative. Septic workup: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Musculoskeletal ultrasound: Extensor and flexor tenosynovitis of bilateral wrists with increased Doppler signals; synovial proliferation and joint effusion in bilateral knees. Transthoracic echocardiogram: No vegetations. Hepatic ultrasound: Prominent periportal echogenicity.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV)-related chronic symmetrical polyarthritis confirmed by seroconversion and PCR. Initial acute sample (negative for CHIKV IgM and Dengue IgM/NS1) was retrospectively positive for CHIKV PCR; convalescent CHIKV serology at readmission was positive for CHIKV IgM with a polyvalent antibody titer rise from <1:10 to 1:1,280. Management and course: Empirically treated with Augmentin and doxycycline for persistent fever, followed by supportive care. Liver enzymes gradually normalized, but articular symptoms persisted; patient requested discharge against medical advice after a 3-week stay.

raw_case_text:
A 41 year old Malay female with no prior medical illness, was admitted to medical ward with the complain of fever, headache and reducing platelet and increasing hematocrit for 3 days duration. Her Dengue NS-1 antigen was reactive which confirms dengue virus infection. She was diagnosed to have 'dengue fever with warning signs' based on WHO classification of levels of severity.
