On admission she complained of right eye blurring of vision for 1 day. Fundus examination was done by medical officer in Medical ward and was documented normal. Therefore she was not referred to Ophthalmology department during the hospital stay. She was treated with fluid resuscitation and was discharged after 5 days. However, right eye blurring of vision persisted and then she was referred to the ophthalmologist. She presented to our eye clinic with right eye blurring of vision for 8 days. It was sudden in onset and non-progressive.
On examination, patient was alert, comfortable and vital signs were stable. Ocular examination noted best corrected visual acuity in right eye was <20/1000 and left eye was 20/25. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes. Relative pupillary afferent defect was detected in the right eye. Right eye fundus showed typical features of CRVO:dilated, tortuous retinal veins and retinal hemorrhages in all four quadrants, optic disc swelling, cotton wool spots and macular edema. Left eye examination was normal (Fig. 1). 
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of right eye macula disclosed cystoid spaces with edema, retinal thickening and subretinal fluid (Fig. 2). 
Further assessment to identify the risk factors for CRVO were done. She was not on any hormonal contraception. Blood investigations were done namely fasting serum lipid, fasting blood sugar, renal profile, full blood count (post recovery), anti-cardiolipin antibodies (ACA), Anti-Beta-2-Glycoprotein 1 (2GP1), Protein C activity, Protein S activity, Antithrombin activity, Activated Protein C Pathway which were normal. Serum electrophoresis shows no paraprotein band and no immune paresis. Her full blood count (FBC) trend during hospital stay showed increasing hematocrit and reducing platelet which peaked on day 6 of illness and then gradually improved (Table 1). Her symptoms onset was during early period of the illness when her hematocrit and platelet levels were still acceptable. 
Six weeks later, fundus fluorescein angiography was done and there was delayed venous filling, less than ten disc diameter area of capillary dropout and areas of masking by retinal hemorrhages (Fig 3). Patient was planned for repeat FFA, however her right eye progress to develop proliferative retinopathy:new vessels elsewhere on the posterior pole which was treated with panretinal photocoagulation. There was no new vessels on the iris or angle noted. The macular edema improved drastically and was monitored with OCT imaging. Unfortunately, her vision did not improve. Her best corrected visual acuity of right eye is 20/400 and left eye 20/25.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old female presenting with fever, headache, thrombocytopenia, and hemoconcentration for 3 days, alongside acute painless blurring of vision in the right eye for 1 day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 41-year-old female presented with 3 days of fever, headache, hemoconcentration, and progressive thrombocytopenia, accompanied by acute onset of painless right eye visual blurriness of 1 day's duration. Initial fundoscopic examination was reported normal and she received intravenous fluid resuscitation, defervescing and discharging after 5 days. However, right visual blurring persisted, prompting ophthalmic evaluation 8 days after visual symptom onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical illnesses. Not taking hormonal contraception.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, and right eye visual disturbance. Negative for systemic thrombosis or bleeding. Medications: IV fluid resuscitation during acute admission. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Alert, comfortable, vital signs stable. Ophthalmic examination: Right eye best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) <20/1000; left eye BCVA 20/25. Intraocular pressures normal bilaterally. Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) present in right eye. Right eye fundoscopy: Dilated tortuous retinal veins, retinal hemorrhages in all four quadrants, optic disc swelling, cotton wool spots, and macular edema, consistent with central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). Left eye fundoscopy was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: FBC trend: Increasing hematocrit and falling platelet count peaking on day 6 of illness before gradual normalization. Thrombophilia and systemic workup (post-recovery): Fasting lipids, fasting glucose, renal panel, complete blood count, anti-cardiolipin antibodies, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein 1, Protein C activity, Protein S activity, antithrombin activity, activated protein C pathway: All normal. Serum protein electrophoresis: Normal with no paraprotein band or immune paresis.
objective.advanced_workup: Right eye macular Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): Cystoid macular edema with retinal thickening and subretinal fluid. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) at 6 weeks: Delayed venous filling, capillary dropout <10 disc diameters, and areas of blocked fluorescence from retinal hemorrhages.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue fever complicated by unilateral central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) with macular edema and subsequent proliferative retinopathy. Diagnostic confirmation: Reactive dengue NS1 antigen test. Extensive thrombophilia and vasculitis screening was negative.
Plan & Outcome: Fluid resuscitation during acute phase. Ophthalmic management: Observation with serial macular OCT monitoring showed drastic resolution of macular edema; subsequent development of new retinal vessels elsewhere on posterior pole was treated with panretinal photocoagulation (PRP). Right eye visual acuity improved to 20/400 (left eye 20/25).

raw_case_text:
We present the case of a 65-year-old Caucasian male, without any significant medical history, admitted to our clinic with bilateral lower limb motor deficit and distal paresthesia in all limbs, with an onset of ~3 weeks prior. The patient also complained of sudden bilateral decreased visual acuity, more severe on the right side, which preceded the motor deficit by approximately 10 days and had a spontaneously favorable evolution and was partially remitted by the time of admission.
An ophthalmologist in another service evaluated the patient approximately 7 days from the onset of the visual symptoms, where he tested positive for SARS-CoV-2. At that moment, he had had mild respiratory symptoms (slight cough and rhinorrhea) for a~2 days. The interval between the onset of the neurological and COVID-19 symptoms was ~5 days.
The ophthalmological examination noted VOS Presbyopia 0.5 sc (0.7 c), VOD PHM, with a regular fundus examination in both eyes. At that time, sight in the left eye was already spontaneously improving, and the diagnosis was right retrobulbar optic neuritis. He was not started on any therapy and received a recommendation for a neurological evaluation and a brain MRI scan. The patient chose to isolate himself at home for 14 days, per the local recommendations at the time.
Approximately 3 days into the isolation period, he developed lower limb paresthesia, followed by paraparesis and ataxia, which progressively worsened until he could no longer walk.
Our initial clinical examination showed a slight loss of visual acuity in the right eye (he could read a newspaper), asymmetric paraparesis (3/5 MRC on the right, 4/5 MRC on the left), bilateral Babinski sign, distal paresthesia in all limbs, severe bilateral lower limb myoarthrokinetic and vibratory hypoesthesia, with important secondary ataxia, and a T10 sensory level on the left side; walking was impossible.
The full spine MRI revealed a non-enhancing, T2 and STIR hyperintense cervical demyelinating lesion extending from C4 to C7 levels (Figures 1A,B), cervical spondylotic changes, and degenerative lumbar stenosis at L4-L5 levels. The cerebral MRI was unremarkable except for a slight STIR hyperintense signal affecting the right ON, extending posteriorly into the optic chiasm (Figure 2).
The patient was evaluated extensively for autoimmune disorders associated with myelitis, testing negative for ANA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, anti-Ro, anti-La, and anti-neuronal antibodies. The infectious screening was negative except for the incidental presence of IgG against HCV. Testing for HIV, syphilis, and borreliosis was negative. The B12 serum level was normal. Serum anti-AQP4 antibodies and anti-MOG antibodies were both positive. The AQP4 was tested by indirect immunofluorescence with a titer of 1:1,000 (N < 1:10). The MOG testing was Western Blot.
The CSF had elevated protein levels (albumin 0.44 g%, positive Pandy test) without pleocytosis (6 elements/muL) and no oligoclonal bands. The IgG index was normal (0.63).
Given the patient's history of optic neuritis, longitudinal extensive cervical myelitis, positive tests for anti-AQP4 and anti-MOG antibodies, and the exclusion of other possible causes that could have caused central nervous system demyelination, a diagnosis of neuromyelitis optica was reached.
The patient had been treated with iv Methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 5 days with significant improvement of motor function (4-/5 MRC bilaterally) and partial remission of the paresthesia but with the persistence of the objective sensory deficits. The patient was able to walk using a Zimmer frame. He was discharged with oral prednisone at 1 mg/kg/day.
At the 2-month checkup, the patient had continued to improve, presenting with normal visual acuity, asymmetric paraparesis (4-/5 MRC on the right, 4+/5 MRC on the left), bilateral lower limb paresthesia up to the lower half of the thighs, and crural proprioceptive hypoesthesia, still requiring a frame for walking. The cervical MRI showed a slightly favorable evolution of the cervical lesion (Figures 1C,D). As a corticoid-sparing treatment, he was started on Azathioprine (AZA), gradually reaching a dose of 150 mg per day.
He was seen again at the 1-year mark, being stationary from a neurological point of view, with the persistence of the asymmetric paraparesis and sensory anomalies. The cervical MRI examination was discreetly improved, as the intramedullary pathological signal had continued to decrease in area and intensity (Figure 1F). AZA was continued in the same doses while prednisone tapering was initiated.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presenting with progressive bilateral lower extremity weakness and distal paresthesias in all limbs of approximately 3 weeks' duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Approximately 3 weeks prior to admission, the patient developed distal paresthesias in all limbs and bilateral lower extremity motor deficits. This was preceded by approximately 10 days by sudden bilateral decreased visual acuity (worse on the right), which had partially improved spontaneously. Approximately 7 days after visual symptom onset (5 days prior to neurological motor deficit onset), he experienced mild respiratory symptoms (slight cough, rhinorrhea) and was diagnosed with retrobulbar optic neuritis. During a 14-day home isolation period, his lower extremity paresthesias progressed rapidly to severe paraparesis and ataxia, rendering him completely unable to walk.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant prior medical or surgical history. No prior neurological disorders.
subjective.review_of_systems: Visual impairment, limb paresthesias, lower extremity weakness, gait ataxia, mild cough, rhinorrhea. Denies bowel or bladder incontinence.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological: Slight reduction in visual acuity in right eye (able to read newspaper). Motor: Asymmetric spastic paraparesis (MRC muscle strength 3/5 right lower limb, 4/5 left lower limb); bilateral Babinski signs. Sensory: Distal paresthesias in all four limbs, severe bilateral lower limb myoarthrokinetic and vibratory hypoesthesia, sensory level at T10 on the left. Coordination/Gait: Severe sensory ataxia; ambulation impossible without assistance. Ophthalmologic exam (initial): VOS presbyopia 0.5 sc (0.7 c), VOD PHM, normal fundoscopy; diagnosed as right retrobulbar optic neuritis.
objective.routine_investigations: Lumbar puncture / CSF: Elevated protein (albumin 0.44 g%, positive Pandy test) without pleocytosis (cell count 6 elements/μL), absent oligoclonal bands, normal IgG index (0.63). Serum B12 normal. Autoimmune and vasculitis panel negative: ANA, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, anti-Ro, anti-La, and anti-neuronal antibodies. Infectious screening: Negative for HIV, Treponema pallidum (syphilis), and Borrelia burgdorferi; incidental positive hepatitis C IgG.
objective.advanced_workup: Spine MRI: Non-enhancing, T2 and STIR hyperintense longitudinally extensive cervical demyelinating lesion extending from C4 to C7 levels; concurrent cervical spondylosis and L4-L5 lumbar stenosis. Brain MRI: Unremarkable except for slight STIR hyperintense signal affecting the right optic nerve extending posteriorly into the optic chiasm. Autoantibody serology: Serum anti-aquaporin-4 (AQP4) antibodies positive by indirect immunofluorescence (titer 1:1,000; normal < 1:10); serum anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies positive by Western blot. Follow-up cervical MRI (2 months and 1 year): Marked reduction in size and intensity of intramedullary cervical lesion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) with double-positive anti-AQP4 and anti-MOG antibodies, presenting as sequential optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM), triggered by mild COVID-19 infection (confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 test during initial prodromal respiratory illness).

Management and outcome: Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 5 days, resulting in significant motor improvement (MRC strength 4-/5 bilaterally) and ability to walk with a Zimmer frame. Discharged on oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. At 2-month follow-up, visual acuity normalized, motor strength improved to 4-/5 right and 4+/5 left, and azathioprine was added (titrated to 150 mg/day). At 1-year follow-up, neurological status remained stable with persistent mild paraparesis and sensory changes; MRI showed further regression of the cervical cord lesion, and prednisone was successfully tapered.

raw_case_text:
On July 10, 2022, a 40-year-old woman was admitted to the first affiliated hospital of Xi'an Jiaotong University due to intermittent fever for 2 months. Two months prior, her temperature fluctuated between 37.4 and 38.4 C in the afternoons, and chills and a dry cough accompanied this symptom. She had previously undergone examination and symptomatic treatment at a regional hospital. However, the treatment was ineffective. Furthermore, arthralgia and fatigue gradually appeared, with no chest pain and tightness, or rash. A month and a half prior, she was diagnosed with depression and treated with escitalopram oxalate, and magnesium valproate sustained-release tablets at a hospital. The symptoms slightly improved after treatment. Half a month prior, a B-ultrasonic examination showed lymphadenopathy throughout her body. Therefore, lymphoma was suspected but she did not get any treatment. One day prior to her arrival at our hospital, the patient suddenly developed hemoptysis of approximately 2 ml, which occurred four times for no reason. Past medical history revealed that she was diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) in 2014 and developed cirrhosis a year later. Her CHB was well-controlled by a long-term oral antiviral treatment with Entecavir. In addition, she had lost 5 kg over the past 3 months.
On admission, her temperature was 37 C, respiratory rate was 19 breathe min-1, heart rate was 70 beat min-1, and blood pressure was 103/72 mmHg. The liver, spleen, lymph nodes of the neck, and axillary lymph nodes were enlarged with moderate activity and no tenderness. Rough breath sounds were detected in both lungs with dry and wet rales. All other clinical examination results were negative.
Laboratory examination revealed inflammation and liver dysfunction: red cell count, 4.27 x 1012/L (4-4.5 x 1012/L); white cell count, 4.87 x 109/L (5-12 x 109/L); platelet count 89 x 109/L (125-350 x 109/L), hypersensitive C-reactive protein 9.81 mg/L (0-3 mg/L), direct bilirubin 6.2 mumol/L (0-3.4 mumol/L), aspartate aminotransferase, 54 U/L (13-45 U/L); alanine aminotransferase, 20 U/L (7-40 U/L); alkaline phosphatase, 164 U/L (35-100 U/L); gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase, 82 U/L (7-45 U/L), albumin 33.8 g/L (40-55 g/L).
B-scan ultrasonography revealed bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathies. Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed multiple pulmonary nodules in both lungs, with a small amount of pleural effusion (Figure 1) and enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral axilla. To effectively confirm the nature of the lesion, we performed needle biopsies of pulmonary nodules and lymph nodes. The results implied an infectious disease, while the detection of T cells in tuberculosis infection was negative. Therefore, suspicions of tumors and tuberculosis were excluded.
Interestingly, we noticed that the patient came from Ningxia province, which is famous for animal husbandry. The patient reluctantly informed us that she raised cattle and had come into contact with neighboring sheep without vaccination. Consequently, Brucella infection was suspected. On the fourth day of admission, the serum agglutination test (SAT) result was 1:800, and the rose-bengal plate agglutination test (RBPT) result was positive. Furthermore, the blood culture for Brucella melitensis was positive on the tenth day after admission. Characteristic rod-shaped gram-negative bacteria could be observed under a microscope. Subsequently, the patient was definitively diagnosed with brucellosis.
Following the brucellosis diagnosis, she received antibiotic therapy with rifampicin (600 mg/dose, once a day) and doxycycline (100 mg/dose, twice a day) for 3 months from the fourth day of the course. Furthermore, due to the poor medical conditions of the patient's residence and excessive complications, including multipulmonary nodules, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy, moxifloxacin and ceftriaxone sodium were added from the sixth day of the course to prevent the possibility of developing drug-resistant brucellosis after discharge. During treatment, the patient and her family were highly cooperative. At discharge, fever, cough, arthralgia, depression and fatigue were relieved. After 2 months of follow-up, the fever and cough were gone, as was fatigue and arthralgia. In addition, the number of multiple nodules in both lungs was reduced. At the same time, liver function test results also indicated that the patient was recovering well. After 3 months of follow-up, her weight had increased and her depression symptoms were alleviated. The entire process of diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes is shown in Figure 2.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female presented with intermittent afternoon fevers, chills, dry cough, generalized lymphadenopathy, arthralgia, and acute hemoptysis for two months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced a 2-month history of fluctuating afternoon fevers (37.4-38.4 °C), chills, and nonproductive cough that failed symptomatic therapy at an outside clinic. Over the preceding six weeks, she developed progressive fatigue, arthralgia, a 5 kg weight loss, generalized lymphadenopathy, and secondary depression treated with psychiatric medications. One day prior to admission, she experienced four episodes of hemoptysis (approximately 2 mL each). She was admitted for evaluation of suspected disseminated infection versus lymphoma, achieving full resolution following targeted multi-agent antimicrobial therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic hepatitis B diagnosed in 2014 with compensated cirrhosis diagnosed in 2015, well-controlled on long-term oral entecavir; depression diagnosed 1.5 months prior. Epidemiological exposure: Native of Ningxia province, raised cattle, and had direct contact with unvaccinated neighboring sheep.
subjective.review_of_systems: Chills, nonproductive cough, hemoptysis, arthralgia, fatigue, depressed mood, and 5 kg weight loss; denies chest pain or cutaneous rash. Home medications: Entecavir, escitalopram oxalate, and magnesium valproate. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals: Temperature 37.0 °C, respiratory rate 19 breaths/min, heart rate 70 beats/min, blood pressure 103/72 mmHg. Head and neck: Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy (enlarged, mobile, non-tender). Pulmonary: Coarse breath sounds bilaterally with dry and wet rales. Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly without tenderness. Lymph nodes: Bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Red blood cell count 4.27 x 10^12/L, white blood cell count 4.87 x 10^9/L, platelet count 89 x 10^9/L, hypersensitive C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) 9.81 mg/L (normal 0-3 mg/L). Hepatic panel: Direct bilirubin elevated at 6.2 umol/L (normal 0-3.4 umol/L), AST 54 U/L, ALT 20 U/L, ALP 164 U/L, GGT 82 U/L, serum albumin 33.8 g/L. Ultrasound: Bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathies. Mycobacterial testing: T-cell interferon-gamma release assay for tuberculosis was negative. Follow-up labs (2-3 months): Normalization of liver enzymes and inflammatory markers.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: Multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, small pleural effusion, and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Percutaneous needle biopsies of lung nodules and lymph nodes: Histopathology demonstrated infectious granulomatous changes, excluding lymphoma and malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated Brucellosis with pulmonary nodules, hemoptysis, hepatosplenomegaly, and generalized lymphadenopathy, confirmed by blood cultures growing Brucella melitensis (Gram-negative rods), positive Rose Bengal Plate Agglutination Test (RBPT), and Serum Agglutination Test (SAT titer 1:800). Tuberculosis and lymphoma were ruled out by negative biopsy and negative IGRA.
Plan & Clinical Course: Initiated on oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for a 3-month course. Given the presence of diffuse pulmonary nodules, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy, IV ceftriaxone and oral moxifloxacin were added on day 6. The patient improved rapidly, with resolution of fever, cough, hemoptysis, arthralgia, and fatigue by discharge. At 2-month follow-up, pulmonary nodules regressed on CT, and at 3-month follow-up, she regained lost weight and achieved complete clinical cure.

raw_case_text:
A 7-year-old boy presented to the Emergency Department of Hasan Sadikin Hospital with a history of difficulty arousing from sleep, confusion, and incoherent speech for 1 day before admission. The patient experienced sudden onset of fever for 2 days prior to admission accompanied by coffee ground vomiting. There was no history of other bleeding episodes or seizures. Physical examination showed an obese, drowsy patient with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 13, fever of 38.3 C, normal blood pressure, and no circulatory problems. Abdominal examination revealed no signs of hepatomegaly, abdominal tenderness, or petechiae. Ocular tests revealed normal pupils. Neurological examination showed no facial asymmetry, motor weakness, abnormal movements, nor posture. Reflexes were normal, and the Babinski was negative. Nuchal rigidity, Kernig, and Brudzinski signs were absent.
Laboratory examination showed hemoglobin and hematocrit levels were within normal range with leukocyte count of 1.9 x 103/uL, and lower platelet count of 129 x 103/uL. Liver transaminases were high with 446 U/L for aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and 204 U/L for alanine aminotransferase (ALT). Patient electrolytes were within normal limits with sodium of 141 mmol/L, potassium of 3.9 mmol/L, and non-fasting blood glucose of 139 mg/dL. CSF showed clear fluid, negative for Nonne's and Pandy's test and protein of 26.9 mg/dL which indicated CSF protein was within normal limits, cell count of 4 cells/uL, and glucose of 98 mg/dL. CSF gram and acid-fast bacilli stains were negative. Neuroimaging was not conducted. A presumptive diagnosis of viral CNS infection was given based on neurological manifestations as well as laboratory parameters.
During follow-up, conscious level improved to GCS 15 on day 4 and defervescence occurred on day 3 of hospitalization. Hematocrit dropped to 34.3% on the day 5 while nadir platelet count occurred on day 3 of hospitalization. Supportive treatment was given with antipyretics and fluid replacement. The patient continued to improve and was discharged on the sixth day following admission with dengue encephalitis as the final diagnosis. On the 1-month follow-up, the patient had completely recovered without any neurological sequelae.
Additional laboratory examination confirmed the presence of DENV serotype 1 RNA by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) in CSF taken on admission day and in the serum specimen taken on the second day of hospitalization (Table 1). Molecular screening was conducted by genus-specific flavivirus RT-PCR, followed by DENV serotyping RT-PCR and whole genome sequencing. Obtained sequence was submitted to the GenBank with accession number MW559478.1. Anti-DENV immunoglobulin M (IgM)   was positive in both serum specimens from the second and the sixth day of hospitalization, while samples collected on day 6 showed immunoglobulin G (IgG) seroconversion (Dengue Virus IgG DxSelect, Focus Diagnostics, USA). Other classical neurotropic pathogens including Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), chikungunya virus, human herpesviruses, enteroviruses, Streptococcus pneumonia and Haemophilus influenzae were negative using PCR testing algorithms   as well as an anti-JEV IgM assay.   Both CSF and blood samples were inoculated onto Vero E6 cells to attempt for virus isolation; no virus was isolated from these efforts. A phylogenetic tree was constructed based on E gene aligned to the top 20 sequence matches in NCBI BLASTn database (Figure 1). The DENV-1 strain from this study belonged to genotype IV and appeared to be closely related to strains previously identified in Indonesia. None of the GenBank DENV-1 strains analyzed in the phylogenetic tree were reported to be associated with CNS manifestations.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old male presenting with acute confusion, incoherent speech, and difficulty arousing from sleep for one day, following two days of fever and coffee-ground emesis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 7-year-old boy experienced sudden onset of fever and coffee-ground vomiting 2 days prior to admission. One day before admission, he developed progressive encephalopathy characterized by difficulty arousing from sleep, confusion, and incoherent speech. There was no history of seizures or other bleeding manifestations. Following supportive inpatient therapy, defervescence occurred on hospital day 3, consciousness improved to GCS 15 on day 4, and he made a full recovery by discharge on day 6.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant medical history; obese habitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Coffee-ground vomiting; absence of seizures, rash, or other bleeding manifestations.

objective.physical_examination: General: Obese child, drowsy with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 13. Vitals: Temperature 38.3 °C, blood pressure normal, hemodynamics stable without circulatory collapse. Abdomen: Soft, no hepatomegaly, no tenderness. Dermatologic: No petechiae or rash. Neurologic: Pupils normal and equal; no facial asymmetry, motor weakness, abnormal movements, or abnormal posturing; deep tendon reflexes normal; Babinski sign negative; absence of nuchal rigidity, Kernig, and Brudzinski signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Hemoglobin and hematocrit within normal range; leukocyte count 1.9 x 10^3/microL; platelet count 129 x 10^3/microL (platelet nadir occurred on hospital day 3; hematocrit dropped to 34.3% on day 5). Liver transaminases: AST 446 U/L, ALT 204 U/L. Serum electrolytes and glucose: Sodium 141 mmol/L, potassium 3.9 mmol/L, random glucose 139 mg/dL. Lumbar puncture / Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: Clear fluid, cell count 4 cells/microL, protein 26.9 mg/dL (normal limits), glucose 98 mg/dL; Nonne and Pandy tests negative; Gram stain and acid-fast bacilli stain negative; viral/bacterial CSF cultures negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus encephalitis (DENV serotype 1, genotype IV) manifesting as acute encephalopathy with transaminitis and leukopenia. Confirmed by detection of DENV serotype 1 RNA via genus-specific and serotype-specific RT-PCR in admission CSF and in day 2 serum, with whole-genome sequencing (GenBank accession MW559478.1), along with positive serum anti-DENV IgM on days 2 and 6 and IgG seroconversion on day 6. Classical neurotropic pathogens including Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV), chikungunya, herpesviruses, enteroviruses, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae were excluded by negative PCR and serology assays.
Plan & Outcome: Managed conservatively with antipyretics, intravenous fluid maintenance, and neurological monitoring. Consciousness normalized to GCS 15 by day 4, platelet counts recovered, and he was discharged on hospital day 6. At 1-month follow-up, he achieved complete recovery without neurological sequelae.

raw_case_text: A 23-year-old female presented to medical clinics with history of cough, sore throat, and high grade fever for last 7 days. The fever was high grade (101-103 F) and was not associated with chills and rigor. On reviewing the history, she did not have any other comorbid illness. On investigations, she was found to have positive serology for dengue and her platelet count was 20,000/mm3. She was admitted in the medical ward, and 6 hours later her blood pressure dropped to 82/42 mm Hg. After adequately resuscitating her with intravenous fluids, she was started on dopamine infusion and titrated at 5 mug/kg/min to maintain her blood pressure at 106/62 mm Hg. She was shifted to intensive care unit for further management. The patient's respiratory rate increased to 35/minute. Her chest X-ray revealed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates suggestive of acute respiratory distress syndrome. Her oxygen saturation (SpO2) was 88% on oxygen by face mask. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed a paO2 of 55 mm Hg. She was given a trial of noninvasive ventilation but she could not maintain oxygen saturation (SpO2:84-86%). She was tracheally intubated and started on mechanical ventilation. Her repeat platelet count was 12,000/mm3. Other laboratory investigations revealed haemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, total leucocyte count (TLC): 10,800/mm3, differential leucocyte counts: neutrophil: 85%, lymphocytes: 13%, sodium: 144 mg/L, potassium: 3.6 mg/L, blood urea: 48 mg/dL, serum creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL and total bilirubin: 0.9 mg/dL. Her international normalized ratio (INR) was 1.2, d-dimer and fibrin degradation products were negative. She was transfused with 4 units of platelet concentrate. Her condition further deteriorated requiring escalation of inotropic support to noradrenaline 0.4 mug/kg/min, dopamine 10 mug/kg/min. A final diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and dengue hemorrhagic shock was made. Viral markers for HCV, HBV, and HIV were negative. Electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia with peaked P wave. Echocardiography revealed ejection fraction of 45%, mild left ventricular global hypokinesia, mild tricuspid regurgitation with a pressure gradient of 30 mm Hg. Serum cardiac enzymes: creatine phosphokinase MB levels were 116 I.U/L (normal up to 20) and lactic acid dehydrogenase was 2489 u/L (normal up to 260). Tropnin-T was negative. An additional diagnosis of viral myocarditis was made. Dobutamine was started and noradrenaline was tapered off and subsequently stopped. Patient required an FiO2 of 0.8-1 to maintain of SpO2 > 90%. So, patient received intermittent prone ventilation to keep FiO2 less than 0.6% for first three days (6-8 hours each day). Central venous pressure (CVP) of 6 to 8 cm of H2O was maintained as further increase in CVP manifested in pulmonary edema twice. Patient had an episode of pulseless ventricular tachycardia which was managed with electrical therapy once and subsequently required 300 mg bolus amiodarone followed by 45 mg/hr infusion. By third day, patient platelet count improved and reached 66,000 and then 1,20,000/mm3 by 5th day. But a continuous falling trend of leucocyte count was observed from 9800 on first day to 800/mm3 by 5th day. She also had persistent fever of 102 to 104 F, despite being given coverage of broad-spectrum antibiotics and persistently negative cultures report (blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, CSF). When her leucocyte count dropped to less than 4000, intravenous hydrocortisone 50 mg BD was started. Despite this her leucocyte count dropped to 800/mm3 with differential count of polymorpholeucocytes of 46% and fever persisted. On 6th day, after written and informed consent from patients guardian, a trial of intravenous filgrastim 150 mug was given for two days. Her leucocyte counts improved to 9000/mm3 on seventh day and 15,000/mm3 on eighth day. Platelet count was 1.5 x 103/mm3. Clinically, her fever also subsided. She was weaned off from ventilator and inotropic support within next three days. Patient shifted to high dependency unit on 9th day. She was discharged uneventfully on 15th day with advice to follow-up in medical clinics.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old female presented with high-grade fever, sore throat, and cough for 7 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 7-day history of high-grade fever (101-103 F) without chills or rigors, accompanied by a cough and sore throat. Six hours after admission, she developed hypotensive shock (blood pressure 82/42 mmHg) and severe tachypnea with refractory hypoxemia (PaO2 55 mmHg, SpO2 88%), requiring tracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). During ICU admission, she experienced an episode of pulseless ventricular tachycardia requiring electrical defibrillation and amiodarone, followed by profound leukopenia and persistent fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior comorbid medical conditions documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported high-grade fever, cough, and sore throat. Denied chills, rigors, hemoptysis, or prior cardiac symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Upon clinical deterioration: Blood pressure 82/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 35 breaths/min, SpO2 88% on face mask. Following intubation and resuscitation, examination showed central venous pressure maintained at 6-8 cmH2O and absence of peripheral edema.
objective.routine_investigations:
Chest X-ray: Bilateral diffuse pulmonary infiltrates consistent with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).
Complete blood counts: Initial platelet count 20,000/mm3, nadir 12,000/mm3, recovering to 66,000/mm3 on day 3 and 120,000/mm3 on day 5. Hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, initial leukocyte count 10,800/mm3 (85% neutrophils, 13% lymphocytes), which declined precipitously to 800/mm3 (46% neutrophils) on day 5 before rising to 9,000/mm3 on day 7 and 15,000/mm3 on day 8.
Biochemistry & renal panel: Sodium 144 mg/L, potassium 3.6 mg/L, blood urea 48 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, total bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL.
Coagulation profile: INR 1.2; D-dimer and fibrin degradation products negative.
Cardiac enzymes: CPK-MB 116 IU/L (normal up to 20 IU/L), LDH 2,489 U/L (normal up to 260 U/L), Troponin-T negative.
Electrocardiogram: Sinus tachycardia with peaked P waves; pulseless ventricular tachycardia.
Transthoracic echocardiogram: Ejection fraction 45%, mild left ventricular global hypokinesia, mild tricuspid regurgitation with pressure gradient 30 mmHg.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture and CSF analysis: Sterile CSF cultures; negative for infectious pathogens.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue / dengue hemorrhagic shock syndrome complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute myocarditis with pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and severe post-infectious leukopenia/agranulocytosis. Confirmed by positive dengue serology. Blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and CSF cultures were repeatedly sterile; viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV) and HIV serologies were negative.
Treatment and outcome: Managed in the ICU with invasive mechanical ventilation (including intermittent prone positioning), intravenous fluid resuscitation, inotropes and vasopressors (dopamine, noradrenaline, dobutamine), electrical cardioversion and amiodarone infusion (300 mg bolus, 45 mg/hr maintenance), 4 units of platelet concentrate transfusions, broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV hydrocortisone (50 mg twice daily), and IV filgrastim (150 mcg daily for 2 days). The patient achieved complete clinical and hematologic recovery, was weaned off mechanical ventilation and inotropes, transferred to HDU on day 9, and discharged on day 15.

raw_case_text: A 16-year-old boy, with severe aplastic anemia, presented in transplant emergency with high-grade fever associated with shivering, pain in right hypochondrium and loose watery stools for 2 days, on day +88 posttransplant. Pan cultures and other infective workup were negative while Dengue NS1 antigen was detected. His platelet count declined rapidly with rising hematocrit level. He was managed aggressively with supportive care, intravenous hydration, and platelet transfusions during critical phase. He also had slightly deranged renal function and liver enzymes were elevated two times upper normal limit. However, the coagulation profile was normal. Mild pleural effusion and moderate ascites were also observed on ultrasound. He stayed in the hospital for 15 days for management of dengue fever.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old male post-allogeneic stem cell transplant presented with high-grade fever, shivering, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and diarrhea for 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, at day +88 post-allogeneic stem cell transplantation for severe aplastic anemia, presented to the transplant emergency department with a 2-day history of acute high-grade fever with rigors, right hypochondrial abdominal pain, and loose watery stools. During hospitalization, his hematocrit rose as platelet counts dropped precipitously during the critical plasma leakage phase.
subjective.past_medical_history: Severe aplastic anemia status post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (day +88 post-transplant).
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported high-grade fever, rigors/shivering, right hypochondrial pain, and watery diarrhea. Denied dysuria, cough, or gross bleeding.

objective.physical_examination: Right hypochondrial tenderness on abdominal palpation. No active cutaneous bleeding documented on initial exam.
objective.routine_investigations:
Complete blood count: Hemoconcentration with rising hematocrit levels and rapid decline in platelet counts (severe thrombocytopenia).
Biochemistry & organ function: Mildly deranged renal function parameters; serum transaminases elevated to two times the upper limit of normal; normal coagulation profile.
Microbiology: Pan-cultures (blood, urine, stool) and comprehensive infectious disease workup yielded no bacterial or fungal pathogens.
Abdominal/chest ultrasound: Demonstrated moderate ascites and mild pleural effusion consistent with plasma leakage.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue / dengue hemorrhagic fever with plasma leakage (ascites, pleural effusion), hepatitis, and acute kidney injury occurring in a post-transplant recipient. Confirmed by positive Dengue NS1 antigen detection. Bacterial pan-cultures and other infectious screens were negative.
Treatment and outcome: Managed aggressively in the inpatient setting for 15 days with meticulous intravenous crystalloid resuscitation, supportive care, and platelet transfusions during the critical phase, achieving clinical recovery and discharge.

raw_case_text:
A healthy 30-year-old pregnant woman, gravida 6, para 4 (1 fetal death), with a history of premature rupture of membranes (PROM) at 20 weeks in a previous gestation, a scarred uterus, and osteoarthritis, was admitted, at 31 weeks of gestation, to the obstetric emergency room 4 days after the onset of the following symptoms: shortness of breath, fever at 38.5 C, and persistent dry cough promptly complicated with PROM.
Physical examination revealed tachypnea with a respiratory rate (RR) of 30 breaths/min, a 92% oxygen saturation (SpO2), tachycardia with a heart rate (HR) of 109 beats/min, and blood pressure of 96/50 mmHg. She was quickly put on nasal cannula oxygen support at a flow of 3 L/min and improved her oxygen saturation to 98%. Her uterine height was 28 cm with no sign of uterine contraction. Vaginal examination demonstrated ruptured membranes and a cephalic presentation. Ultrasound was performed, showing active fetal movements, normal fetal morphology, normal amniotic fluid quantity, and an estimated fetal weight of 1960 g. A chest computed tomography scan detected bilateral condensation opacities reaching 50 to 75 percent suggesting a viral infection, as shown in Figure 1. A nasopharyngeal swab returned positive for SARS-CoV-2 using reverse transcription polymerase chain reactions (RT-PCR).
Healthcare professionals wore appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), according to each level of contamination risk. The patient was hospitalized in an isolated room in the reserved COVID-19 maternity ward, wearing a surgical mask during her stay. Initially, the patient received intravenous fluids, acetaminophen, and prophylactic 3rd-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone). The patient also received corticosteroids (betamethasone) to ensure fetal pulmonary maturation. A complete blood panel demonstrated an intense inflammatory status displayed by hyperferritinemia and an elevated level of CRP as shown in Table 1.
After 24 hours, the patient became hypoxemic with a SpO2 of 89%, RR of 38/min, and hyperthermia of 39.0 C. She was instantly admitted to the COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU). She was administered high-flow oxygen (10 L/min) via a non-rebreather mask and placed in a lateral decubitus position. She received azithromycin, hydroxychloroquine, and a curative dose of tinzaparin sodium (Figure 2), and as she failed to improve, we added methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day. Echocardiogram did not find any abnormalities (Figure 3).
The patient reported intense and frequent uterine contractions as she went into labor. The fetal heart rate monitoring found acute fetal distress. Consequently, an urgent caesarian section was performed. The healthcare team transported the patient, following the COVID-19-dedicated hallways, to an operating room with negative pressure.  Figure 4 portrays anesthesiologists and an obstetrician surgeon wearing level 3 PPE and an aerosol protective shield for a potential intubation. The patient received oxygen support on nasal cannula at flow of 5 L/min while being routinely monitored. She underwent single-shot spinal anesthesia using bupivacaine (10 mg), morphine (100 mug), and fentanyl (25 mug). A lower segment cesarean section was performed without any incident, as she remained stable.
Postoperative pain was handled by spinal morphine analgesia that lasted 16 hours. The patient improved her respiratory function with an RR of 15 breaths/min, a SpO2 of 94%, and a temperature of 38.2 C. However, vaginal examination found foul-smelling mucopurulent lochia associated with a delayed uterine involution and an increased serum level of CRP to 204.2 mg/L.
Under the light of these findings, we suspected postpartum endometritis which was treated by an association of metronidazole and gentamycin, along with prior ceftriaxone. After 7 days, the patient's evolution was marked by a full clinical recovery; her last blood panel showed a decreased serum level of CRP to 37.42 mg/L with a white blood cell count of 10.16 x 109/L. She was discharged to the maternity ward, after being negative for SARS-CoV-2 nasopharyngeal swab two days in a row.
The premature newborn, weighted 1700 g with an Apgar score of <7 at 1 min and at 5 min. The neonate was immediately isolated and transported to the COVID-19 neonatal intensive care unit; no skin-to-skin contact was made with the mother. The newborn experienced severe asphyxia, failing to improve under ventilation. At 1 hour of life, a nasopharyngeal swab viral test was performed, returning negative for SARS-CoV-2 using RT-PCR. The initial blood panel, as portrayed Table 2, demonstrated a white blood cell count of 21.27 x 109/L with a CRP of 90.29 mg/L, whereas blood culture remained sterile. The neonate's condition continued to deteriorate due to septic shock and respiratory failure and died after 5 days of birth.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 30-year-old pregnant female at 31 weeks of gestation presenting with fever up to 38.5 °C, dry cough, shortness of breath, and premature rupture of membranes for 4 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 30-year-old multiparous female at 31 weeks gestation presented with a 4-day history of fever reaching 38.5 °C, persistent nonproductive cough, and dyspnea, acutely complicated by spontaneous premature rupture of membranes (PROM). Twenty-four hours post-admission, her respiratory condition deteriorated into severe respiratory failure with tachypnea of 38 breaths/min and oxygen desaturation to 89% on ambient air, requiring intensive care transfer. Soon thereafter, she entered active labor complicated by acute fetal distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Gravida 6, para 4 (one prior fetal demise), scarred uterus (previous cesarean delivery), prior history of PROM at 20 weeks gestation in a prior pregnancy, and osteoarthritis. No documented drug allergies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, nonproductive cough, shortness of breath, amniotic fluid leakage, painful uterine contractions, and postpartum foul-smelling lochia. Home medications: none documented. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon presentation: temperature: 38.5 °C; respiratory rate: 30 breaths/min; heart rate: 109 beats/min; blood pressure: 96/50 mmHg; SpO2: 92% on room air (correcting to 98% on 3 L/min nasal cannula). Obstetric examination: fundal height 28 cm without initial contractions; speculum/vaginal exam revealed clear amniotic fluid pooling confirming ruptured membranes, cephalic presentation. ICU deterioration (24 h): temperature: 39.0 °C; respiratory rate: 38 breaths/min; SpO2: 89% on room air. Postoperative examination: RR: 15 breaths/min; SpO2: 94% on supplemental oxygen; temperature: 38.2 °C; uterine fundus subinvoluted with foul-smelling mucopurulent lochia.
objective.routine_investigations: Obstetric ultrasound: single viable fetus, active fetal movements, normal fetal anatomy, normal amniotic fluid index, estimated fetal weight: 1,960 g. Cardiotocography/fetal heart monitoring: acute non-reassuring fetal heart tracing/fetal distress. Transthoracic echocardiogram: normal cardiac chambers and function. Maternal laboratory tests: admission CRP elevated; post-cesarean CRP peaked at 204.2 mg/L; convalescent labs showed CRP decreasing to 37.42 mg/L and WBC normalizing to 10.16 x 10^9/L. Neonatal labs: WBC count: 21.27 x 10^9/L, CRP: 90.29 mg/L, sterile blood cultures.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest computed tomography (CT): extensive bilateral ground-glass and consolidative opacities involving 50% to 75% of the pulmonary parenchyma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure at 31 weeks gestation, complicated by preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), acute fetal distress, and secondary postpartum bacterial endometritis, confirmed by positive maternal nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR (neonate tested negative at 1 hour of life). Management & Outcome: Intensive care admission with high-flow oxygen (10 L/min via non-rebreather mask), prone/lateral positioning, azithromycin, hydroxychloroquine, therapeutic tinzaparin sodium, and intravenous methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg/day). Emergency lower segment cesarean section performed under spinal anesthesia (bupivacaine 10 mg, morphine 100 mcg, fentanyl 25 mcg) delivering a 1,700 g neonate. Postpartum endometritis treated with triple antibiotic therapy (intravenous ceftriaxone, metronidazole, and gentamicin). Maternal symptoms and inflammatory markers fully normalized, and she was discharged following two consecutive negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR tests. The premature neonate experienced severe birth asphyxia and refractory septic shock, expiring on day 5 of life.

raw_case_text:
In this case, the blood culture was taken from an 8-year-old boy from rural Mpumalanga, South Africa who was admitted to the Steve Biko Academic Hospital on 23 September 2016 and was being investigated for a bladder mass and a 2-year history of enuresis (Figure 1). For this case isolate, the chocolate plate had pure growth of fine grey colonies after 14 h of incubation. This isolate was sent for Vitek 2 for identification and was identified as B. melitensis. Once this identification was noted, all further processing was done in a biological safety cabinet class 2 using Biosafety Level 3 precautions, as recommended by the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A Gram stain from the culture plates revealed Gram-negative coccobacilli which were catalase and oxidase positive and indole negative which was in keeping with a preliminary identification of Brucella species. The positive B. melitensis culture was sent to the National Institute of Communicable Diseases in Sandringham, South Africa on 24 September 2016, where the identification of the organism was confirmed using matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionisation time of flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry. The instrument used in this case was the Vitek MS (bioMerieux, Marcy-l'Etoile, France), Instrument software version 1.5.0.4, MYLA version 4.5.1, Knowledge Base (Database) version 3.2 (bioMerieux, Marcy-l'Etoile, France).
The blood culture was taken as part of 'routine' investigations as the child had no symptoms or clinical signs which may have led one to consider brucellosis as a possible differential diagnosis. The child was discharged once the blood samples were obtained. The outbreak response unit of the National Institute of Communicable Diseases was alerted to the case on 25 September 2016 and began further investigations and follow-up of affected individuals and possible contacts. It was discovered that the child's family had been consuming unpasteurised cow's milk from a local farmer for many years. This farmer's cattle were tested in late October/early November 2016 using standard South African veterinary testing guidelines. Sixty-eight cows were tested and 13 were found to be positive for B. melitensis, using the Rose Bengal test, complement fixation test and serum agglutination test, all of which are serology-based tests. The affected cattle were then isolated, sent to an abattoir and slaughtered as stipulated in the control programme of brucellosis in animals of South Africa - Animal Diseases Act (Act No. 35 of 1984 ss. 9.1, 9.2, 11). The farmer was instructed to send his milk to another local farm for pasteurisation until this farmer was able to pasteurise effectively on his own farm.
The patient was treated with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and rifampicin 600 mg daily for six weeks. He commenced treatment in the first week of November 2016. The treatment was initiated by the clinicians in his hometown and it was uncertain why he was started on the treatment six weeks following the initial blood culture result. Soon after commencing with treatment, the patient reported side effects which included abdominal pain and vomiting. These were managed symptomatically, and the patient was able to complete treatment. The affected patient's family was tested serologically for brucellosis and were found to be negative. Prophylaxis was given to those family members who consented to receive it.
The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's brucellosis laboratory exposure risk stratification tool was used to screen for exposed staff and staff exposures were stratified as minimal risk, low risk and high risk using these guidelines. Twenty-one of seventy-two staff members were identified, who had either directly handled the specimen on an open bench or were within 1.5 metres of the person who handled the specimen on an open bench, thus rendering them at high risk for acquiring brucellosis. Baseline serology was performed on all potentially exposed staff members and standard prophylaxis was provided by the employer. This comprised of rifampicin 600 mg oral daily for three weeks as well as doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for three weeks. One staff member was pregnant (in her second trimester) at the time, and subsequently received trimethroprim-sulfamethoxazole (160/800 mg) twice daily for three weeks. Exposed staff were advised to undergo follow-up serology at 0, 6, 12, 18 and 24 weeks post-exposure. Weekly symptom watch forms were completed and daily fever self-checks were done for six weeks as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization. None of the staff members reported any symptoms for the duration of the symptom check.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old boy presented for investigation of an incidental bladder mass and a 2-year history of enuresis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-year history of enuresis and an incidental bladder mass discovered during workup. He was completely asymptomatic with regard to systemic infection, exhibiting no fever, chills, sweats, weight loss, or arthralgia. Routine admission blood cultures yielded unexpected bacterial growth following discharge.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of enuresis for 2 years and a recently diagnosed bladder mass under urological investigation. Epidemiological exposure: lived in rural Mpumalanga, South Africa; family had consumed unpasteurized cow's milk from a local dairy farmer for many years.
subjective.review_of_systems: Enuresis; denied fever, chills, night sweats, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, or joint pain. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Completely afebrile without clinical signs of systemic infection or distress. Physical examination was unremarkable; vitals not documented.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine blood cultures drawn on admission. Chocolate agar demonstrated fine grey colonies at 14 hours of incubation; smear revealed Gram-negative coccobacilli that were catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, and indole-negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal/pelvic imaging (Figure 1): demonstrated a bladder mass under ongoing investigation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Asymptomatic Brucella melitensis bacteremia detected incidentally during investigation of a bladder mass and enuresis. Confirmed by blood culture isolate identified as Brucella melitensis by Vitek 2 and verified by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry (Vitek MS) at the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD). Veterinary investigation confirmed Brucella melitensis in 13 of 68 dairy cows from the family's milk provider via Rose Bengal test, complement fixation test, and serum agglutination test.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and oral rifampicin 600 mg once daily for 6 weeks. Treatment-emergent gastrointestinal adverse effects (nausea, abdominal pain, and vomiting) were managed symptomatically with full completion of antimicrobial therapy. Hospital and laboratory personnel at risk received post-exposure prophylaxis.

raw_case_text:
A 22-year-old student from Paris, France, with no previous medical history, was taken by local authorities to the health center in Saul (3 55'18''N, 53 18'02''W), a small village with around 100 inhabitants, located in the center of French Guiana, about 180 km southwest of Cayenne.
Saul is a popular tourist destination for hiking in the middle of the rainforest, which is only accessible by walking through the forest or by plane.
The patient was taken to the health center after he fainted during his walk. He was in poor general condition and manifested fever, vomiting and diarrhea
He had returned from a 4-month stay in Cameroon eleven days earlier, and was drinking A. annua herbal tea daily for malaria prophylaxis. He reported a first malaria episode in Cameroon which was treated with artesunate, and a second episode a month earlier which was treated with tablets that he could not identify. These malaria attacks occurred while he was taking an alternative treatment of A. annua herbal tea obtained from a local store in Cameroon. He strongly believed in the effectiveness of these tea infusions, and he associated these attacks with forgetting to take the decoction.
The symptoms started during his stopover in Paris, 5 days prior to the consultation at the Saul health center. He consulted a general physician 24 h later in Kourou (5 09'29." N, 52 38'33" W), a city located 60 km from the capital of French Guiana (Cayenne), where he was diagnosed through thick and thin blood smears that were positive for P. falciparum. However, the patient left for Saul, without taking the prescribed medicine. He continued drinking A. annua herbal tea. As soon as he arrived in Saul, he started a walk in the deep forest. Three days later, he was found by the local police several kilometers away from the village, in a poor clinical condition. He was febrile and couldn't walk anymore. The police carried him to the health center.
There, the physical examination showed no sign of sepsis, bleeding, hypoglycemia or dyspnea. His neurological examination was normal. The malaria rapid diagnostic test was positive with 2 bands, Pf and PAN. Treatment was started with artemether/lumefantrine (20/120 mg) and the patient was then transferred by helicopter to a hospital in Cayenne (Centre Hospitalier de Cayenne Andree Rosemon) (4 56'13.6"N, 52 19'32.9"W).
Thick and thin blood smears were positive for P. falciparum with a parasitemia of 1.62% of erythrocytes. Other laboratory tests showed: hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 8 G/L, platelet count 19 G/L, alkaline reserve 20.8 mmol/L, urea blood level 16.4 mmol/L (normal 2.8-8.1 mmol/L), creatinine blood level 135 micromol/L (normal 59-104 micromol/L), bilirubin 45.8 micromol/L (normal < 21 micromol/L) and CRP 205.4 mg/L (normal < 5mg/L).
He had watery diarrhea but no more vomiting (he had received metoclopramide in Saul).
A new blood draw showed worsening of the renal function with creatinine dosed at 325 micromol/L and urea at 26.1 mmol/L for an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 22 mL/min/1.73 m2 (normal > 90 mL/min/1.73 m2). A dosage of lactate returned normal at 1.6 mmol/L. There were no other signs of severe malaria apart from the acute renal failure, established by the severely reduced glomerular filtration rate.
The treatment with artemether/lumefantrine (20/120 mg) was continued for a total of 3 days as recommended by the French guidelines  . It was decided not to switch treatment for IV artesunate (recommended treatment in severe malaria)   because the patient's clinical state was already improving after the first dose of artemether/lumefantrine.
Parasitemia on day 3 was still positive but had diminished considerably (only the thick blood smear was positive). A new control on day 9 came back negative. Stool cultures as well as stool parasitology were screened and no pathogens were found.
Symptoms improved rapidly and the patient was discharged 5 days after the beginning of treatment. Renal function improved significantly with IV saline solution (0.9/1,000) but creatinine levels remained above normal values (121 micromol/L) on day 10. Follow up was done in outpatient consultations on days 9 and 28 post treatment.
Despite the severity of his clinical condition and the manifest lack of efficacy of this alternative treatment, he was still convinced the herbal tea could work as a malaria treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old male presenting with syncope, fever, vomiting, and diarrhea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 22-year-old male student fainted during a rainforest hike in Saül, French Guiana, and was brought to the local health center by authorities in poor general condition with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. Symptoms had begun 5 days earlier during a stopover in Paris following a 4-month stay in Cameroon. Four days prior to presentation, he consulted a physician in Kourou, where testing was performed and medication prescribed, but he declined conventional therapy and instead consumed Artemisia annua herbal tea. Three days after arriving in Saül, he collapsed in the deep forest and was unable to ambulate. After initial stabilization and antiemetic administration, he was medically evacuated by helicopter to the hospital in Cayenne.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous medical history. Travel history: 4-month stay in Cameroon, returning 11 days prior. Had two previous malaria episodes in Cameroon (one treated with artesunate, one with unspecified tablets), occurring while consuming A. annua herbal tea for prophylaxis. Continued consuming A. annua tea instead of prescribed medication.
subjective.review_of_systems: Vomiting (treated with metoclopramide), watery diarrhea, syncope, profound fatigue.

objective.physical_examination: Saül health center: Febrile, poor general condition, unable to walk; no neurological deficits; no clinical signs of sepsis, active bleeding, or respiratory distress. Cayenne hospital: Persistent watery diarrhea, hemodynamically stabilized.
objective.routine_investigations: Cayenne admission labs: Hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, WBC 8 x 10^9/L, platelet count 19 x 10^9/L (severe thrombocytopenia), bicarbonate (alkaline reserve) 20.8 mmol/L, serum urea 16.4 mmol/L, serum creatinine 135 μmol/L, total bilirubin 45.8 μmol/L, CRP 205.4 mg/L. Repeat renal panel showed worsening acute renal failure: serum creatinine 325 μmol/L, urea 26.1 mmol/L, eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m^2. Serum lactate normal at 1.6 mmol/L. Stool cultures and stool parasitology negative for enteric pathogens.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe imported Plasmodium falciparum malaria complicated by acute renal failure (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m^2) and severe thrombocytopenia (19 x 10^9/L), occurring after failure of Artemisia annua herbal tea prophylaxis/self-treatment. Malaria rapid diagnostic test was positive (Pf and PAN bands), and thick and thin blood smears confirmed Plasmodium falciparum with 1.62% parasitemia. Enteric pathogens were excluded by negative stool cultures and parasitology.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on oral artemether-lumefantrine (20/120 mg) for 3 days alongside vigorous intravenous hydration with normal saline. Intravenous artesunate was withheld as rapid clinical improvement occurred following the initial artemether-lumefantrine dose. Parasitemia diminished markedly by day 3 (thick smear only) and was completely cleared on day 9. Renal parameters improved significantly (creatinine 121 μmol/L on day 10). Discharged on day 5 with complete symptom resolution and outpatient follow-up at days 9 and 28.

raw_case_text:
A 36-year-old Caucasian, homosexual male with known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection for the past 15 years presented with a disseminated skin eruption over 6 weeks. The patient had been without antiretroviral medications for the past 8 years, defaulted on follow-up, and was uncertain of his last CD4 count or viral load.
The eruption was composed of annular, scalene papules and plaques, some of which were ulcerated (Figure 1). Lesions were distributed on the trunk, extremities, and face. A few lesions demonstrated a thick, ostraceous crust consistent with the skin eruption described in "malignant" syphilis.
Constitutional symptoms included night sweats, decreased appetite, and fatigue. The patient also complained of joint pains at both hands and feet. He denied recent travel, walks in the woods, and recent environmental changes. He could not recall any sick contacts.
Of note, he was allergic to penicillin. The allergy was ascribed since childhood and he could not recall the specific reaction but did emphasize that he was strongly advised against taking any penicillin-containing antibiotics. He denied recent sexual interaction but stated that he contracted HIV via anal intercourse.
The patient looked unwell on general examination. He had pink, but dry mucous membranes and was mildly tachycardic with otherwise unremarkable vital signs. White, adherent plaques were noted in the mouth. The diffuse skin eruption was noted as above. Joint swelling and tenderness were also noted at the wrist and ankles. Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurological examinations were noncontributory.
Initial hematologic workup was significant for mild pancytopenia, leukocyte count 3.4 x 103/mm3, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and platelet count 123 x 103/mm3. The CD4 count was 57 cells/muL and HIV RNA was 365,000 copies/mL. Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor assays were both negative.
Evaluation for additional sexually transmitted infections revealed a negative acute hepatitis panel but a positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) with a titer of 1 : 64. Confirmatory testing with Treponema pallidum antibody (TP-PA) testing was positive. A call to the department of health confirmed no previously reported syphilis infection. Subsequent lumbar puncture was not consistent with infection, specifically a negative VDRL. Blood cultures and wound swabs were negative, and the sedimentation rate was 132 mm/hr.
Punch biopsies were performed on the skin lesions at the left forearm and the left thigh. The histopathologic features were those of psoriasiform lichenoid dermatitis, typical for secondary syphilis. Plasma cells were not readily identified in the infiltrate. Because of the concern for syphilis, a modified Steiner stain was performed which demonstrated several spirochetes within the epidermis.
Plain radiography of the hands and feet revealed polyostotic cortical irregularities of the right foot and both hands, without joint involvement. Roentgenogram of the legs and forearms demonstrated cortical irregularities of the ulnar and radial diaphyses and of the tibial and fibular diaphyses, bilaterally (Figure 2). Roentgenogram of the skull was negative for bony lesions. Follow-up bone scintigraphy was impressive for bilateral, extensive polyostotic uptake within the hands, feet, forearms, and tibiae/fibulae (Figures 3(a)-3(e)).
Based on the positive serology and bone imaging findings, the patient was diagnosed with secondary syphilis osteitis and also now with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).
Given his penicillin allergy, the decision was made to treat the patient with an oral regimen: doxycycline 100 mg twice per day for a total of 6 weeks. He commenced receiving Atovaquone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. Prior to discharge (hospital course, day 8), a repeat RPR was performed, with a declining titer of 1 : 32.
The patient was subsequently referred to a HIV clinic where he commenced antiretroviral therapy with Darunavir/Cobicistat, Dolutegravir, and Tenofovir/Emtricitabine. He had one additional follow-up with the HIV clinic and was noted to be compliant with the medications and tolerating them well. He was followed up by his primary care provider at 2 and 6 weeks. During and upon completion of the course of doxycycline, the patient noted considerable improvement in bone pains and joint swelling, which was corroborated on physical examination. At this time, the skin eruption was completely resolved (Figure 4). A follow-up blood count revealed an improvement in the cytopenias. The patient was referred for repeat imaging and RPR titers but defaulted on additional follow-up. Multiple attempts at communication were unsuccessful, and the patient is yet to return to either the HIV clinic or his primary care provider.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 36-year-old male presenting with a widespread ulcerating skin eruption for six weeks, accompanied by joint pain, night sweats, and fatigue.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-week history of a progressively spreading cutaneous eruption over his face, trunk, and extremities that developed ulcerated and heavily crusted plaques. He concurrently experienced worsening constitutional symptoms including drenching night sweats, fatigue, anorexia, and bilateral joint pains involving both hands and feet. He reported no recent travel, outdoor exposures, or sick contacts.
subjective.past_medical_history: Known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection for 15 years, off antiretroviral therapy for the past 8 years due to loss to follow-up; contracted via anal intercourse. Childhood penicillin allergy with strict recommendation to avoid penicillin-containing antibiotics.
subjective.review_of_systems: Constitutional night sweats, fatigue, decreased appetite, joint pains in hands and feet; denies fever, visual symptoms, headache, or genital chancres.

objective.physical_examination: General: Ill-appearing, mildly tachycardic, vitals otherwise unremarkable. HEENT: Pink but dry mucous membranes; adherent white mucosal plaques in the mouth. Dermatologic: Diffuse eruption of annular, scaly papules and plaques with central ulceration and thick, ostraceous crusts across the trunk, extremities, and face. Musculoskeletal: Symmetrical swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists and ankles. Neurologic and cardiopulmonary exams: Noncontributory.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukocytes 3.4 x 10^3/mm3, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, platelet count 123 x 10^3/mm3 (mild pancytopenia). Inflammatory markers: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 132 mm/hr. Autoimmune serology: Antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) negative. Infectious serology: Acute hepatitis panel negative; blood cultures and wound swabs negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: Lumbar puncture opening pressure and analysis normal; CSF VDRL negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin punch biopsy (left forearm): Epidermal ulceration with dense dermal lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and endothelial swelling. Skeletal radiography and whole-body bone scintigraphy: Multifocal cortical thickening, periosteal reactions, and increased radiotracer uptake involving the distal radius, ulna, tibia, fibula, and tarsal bones bilaterally, consistent with multifocal osteitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS; CD4 count 57 cells/microL, HIV RNA 365,000 copies/mL) complicated by severe secondary syphilis manifesting as malignant syphilis (lues maligna), bilateral syphilitic osteitis, and oral candidiasis in a penicillin-allergic patient.
Confirmatory Testing: Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) reactive at a titer of 1:64, confirmed by positive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TP-PA); Warthin-Starry silver staining of skin biopsy demonstrated characteristic spirochetes.
Plan & Outcome: Due to documented penicillin allergy, treated with oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks, atovaquone for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis, and oral antifungal therapy for thrush. Pre-discharge day 8 RPR declined to 1:32. Antiretroviral therapy was initiated with darunavir/cobicistat, dolutegravir, and tenofovir/emtricitabine. Follow-up at 2 and 6 weeks showed complete resolution of skin lesions, marked improvement in bone pain and joint swelling, and hematologic recovery; the patient subsequently defaulted from ongoing care.

raw_case_text: A 66-year-old German woman presented in a university hospital with nasal obstruction. Clinically the patient showed nodular and ulcerative lesion at the nasal septum. Histology of the left nasal septum biopsy revealed necrosis, chronic inflammation and intracellular amastigote that was suggestive of leishmaniasis (Figure 1). The molecular-pathological detection of parasite DNA was positive for leishmania infantum. The medical history includes hypothyroidism and rheumatoid arthritis for which she was under continuous immunosuppressive treatment with methotrexate and anti-TNF-blocker (Humira ) several years ago. Moreover, she was treated for cutaneous leishmaniasis in the left elbow after a travel history in Mallorca five years ago (4 weeks, amphotericin B). The patient successfully retreated as a case of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis receiving at first liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks. Under the treatment showed the patient an increased level of creatinine, therefore, the therapy was changed to a phospholipid (Hexadecylphosphocholin = Miltefosin ) for 4 weeks with a side effect of vomiting. Follow up visits showed significant improvement with no recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old female presented with progressive nasal obstruction and an ulcerative lesion of the nasal septum.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to a university hospital with progressive nasal obstruction. Clinically, she was noted to have a nodular and ulcerative lesion involving the nasal septum. She was admitted for biopsy and microbiological identification.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hypothyroidism; rheumatoid arthritis on long-term immunosuppressive therapy with methotrexate and adalimumab (Humira, anti-TNF blocker) for several years; history of cutaneous leishmaniasis of the left elbow 5 years prior following travel to Mallorca (treated with amphotericin B for 4 weeks). Origin: Germany.
subjective.review_of_systems: Nasal obstruction. Home medications: methotrexate, adalimumab, levothyroxine. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Otolaryngologic examination revealed a nodular and ulcerative lesion located at the nasal septum.
objective.routine_investigations: Renal function testing: increased serum creatinine levels documented during liposomal amphotericin B therapy.
objective.advanced_workup: Biopsy of left nasal septum: histopathology showed tissue necrosis and chronic active inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis of the nasal septum caused by Leishmania infantum in an immunosuppressed patient.
Diagnostic confirmation: Histology of the left nasal septum biopsy demonstrated necrosis, chronic inflammation, and intracellular Leishmania amastigotes; molecular-pathological PCR testing confirmed Leishmania infantum DNA.
Differentials ruled out: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), nasal squamous cell carcinoma, lymphoma, and fungal rhinosinusitis.
Treatment and clinical course: Initially treated with liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, which was complicated by nephrotoxicity (elevated serum creatinine). Therapy was switched to oral miltefosine (hexadecylphosphocholine) for 4 weeks, complicated by transient vomiting. Follow-up examinations revealed significant clinical improvement with complete resolution and no disease recurrence.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old Guinea-Bissau born male, living in Portugal for 16 years, was admitted to our institution because of vomiting, hiccups, weight loss (about 16 kg), occasional nocturnal sweating, and dry cough, lasting for 1 month. He had a past medical history of recurrent episodes of intestinal worm infection and excessive alcohol consumption (100-120 g/day). He was screened for tuberculosis due to prior contact with pulmonar tuberculosis. Laboratory blood tests were normal except for a high sedimentation rate (79 mmh). A bilateral bronchial reinforcement was observed on chest X-ray. Mediastinal enlarged lymph nodes and a nodular lesion at inferior left pulmonary lobe were noted on chest CT (computerized tomography) scan. A brain CT showed a small corticosubcortical ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe. He was diagnosed with HIV-1 infection (323/8,3% T-CD4 + lymphocytes/muL) and HBV chronic infection (AgHBs positive, Ac anti-HBc positive, and AgHBe negative).
Inspection revealed good general condition, with papular lesions scattered throughout the body. On brain MRI a single round lesion with 7 mm was seen, with perilesional oedema, suggesting tuberculoma (Figures 1(a)-1(b)).
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cytochemical evaluation was normal. Bronchoscopy showed nonspecific inflammatory findings. Bacteriological and mycobacteriological (direct and cultural examination) analysis of respiratory products tested negative. Bronchial histology showed inflammatory infiltrate, with no granuloma or neoplastic tissue. Patient was discharged from hospital clinically stable, with no signs of infection.
One month later he manifested persistent deterioration of general condition, with vomiting, abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant, myalgias, and fever. Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, C-reactive protein 12,2 mg/dL, and sedimentation rate >120 mmh. On chest CT scan a bulky right adrenal gland mass was disclosed. Abdominal sepsis was considered and treatment with intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone (1 g bid) was empirically started. Blood, urine, and stool cultural exams were negative, as well as Schistosoma spp. and Taenia solium serology. He completed a 14-day cycle of antibiotic treatment with clinical and analytical improvement. He was also treated with oral fluconazole (200 mg id) during 14 days for esophageal candidiasis. One week after ceftriaxone suspension a worsening of headache and inaugural seizures were observed. MRI brain-scan presented multiple well-defined annular lesions. Nocardia versusfungal abscesses was hypothesized (Figures 1(c)-1(d)). Empirical treatment with IV ceftriaxone (2 g bid), liposomal B amphotericin (4 mg/Kg id), and valproic acid was started. Adrenal mass was punctured; culture of purulent material revealed Nocardia spp. Characterization of bacterial species and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were not possible, neither by microbiologic methods nor by protein chain reaction (the sample was deteriorated when it arrived at reference laboratory; in Portugal, characterization of Nocardia spp. and antimicrobial susceptibility testing are made at reference laboratory, National Health Institute, Dr. Ricardo Jorge). ACTH and cortisol were within normal limits. As skin nodules persisted, a skin biopsy was performed; histology revealed superficial acute folliculitis and no microorganisms were seen with special stains; microbiological study was missed. The diagnosis of disseminated nocardiosis with brain, adrenal, and possibly lung and skin involvement was assumed. Based on literature, IV treatment was started with cotrimoxazole 1440 mg 8/8 h, amikacin (dosage adjusted to the serum levels), and ceftriaxone (2 g bid); liposomal B amphotericin was stopped.
