A brain MRI revealed frontal, parietal and mesial bilateral temporal cortical and subcortical altered signals with restricted diffusion and similar abnormalities in the posterior thalamus, midbrain and cerebellar vermis, and no enhancement was noted. These findings were compatible with a diffuse encephalitis. Further CSF analysis (day 12 of the disease) revealed pleocytosis (98 cells/mm with 68% of lymphocytes and 12% of monocytes), high protein (161 mg%), normal glucose (81 mg%) and high adenosine deaminase level (47.9 international units (UI)/L, normal < 4.5 UI/L). Negative results were obtained for syphilis and the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies and polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, herpes virus types 1 and 2 were carried out. CSF and serum were positive for IgM antibodies to CHIKV (using the IgM antibody capture ELISA [MAC-ELISA] and commercial ELISA [Euroimmun, Lubeck, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany], respectively). A clinical deterioration of the patient was identified and despite the absence of sedative drugs, he remained in a coma and died on day 24 after onset of the illness.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male presented with high-grade fever, arthralgia, asthenia, vomiting, acute behavioral changes, and seizures for 8 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 57-year-old male agricultural worker experienced high-grade fever, arthralgia, asthenia, and vomiting over 8 days prior to hospital admission. On day 8, he acutely developed psychomotor agitation, behavioral changes, and seizures, followed by progressive neurological deterioration with depressed consciousness and acute respiratory distress requiring emergent endotracheal intubation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, arterial hypertension; occupation as an agricultural worker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Vomiting, asthenia, psychomotor agitation. Home medications and allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Admission vitals/status: Hypotension, bradycardia, reduced level of consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale: 11), acute severe dyspnea necessitating endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Laboratory tests revealed acute renal dysfunction managed conservatively without hemodialysis. Serology for syphilis and HIV: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT (without contrast): No acute abnormalities. Brain MRI: Frontal, parietal, and bilateral mesial temporal cortical and subcortical altered signals with restricted diffusion, with similar findings in posterior thalamus, midbrain, and cerebellar vermis without contrast enhancement, compatible with diffuse encephalitis. Lumbar puncture / CSF analysis (initial, day 8): Pleocytosis 240 cells/mm3 with 72% neutrophilia, high protein, and normal glucose. CSF analysis (repeat, day 12): Pleocytosis 98 cells/mm3 (68% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes), protein 161 mg%, glucose 81 mg%, adenosine deaminase (ADA) 47.9 UI/L (normal < 4.5 UI/L). CSF PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, HSV-1, and HSV-2: all negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Detection of Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) IgM antibodies in both CSF (by MAC-ELISA) and serum (by commercial ELISA), confirming Chikungunya viral encephalitis. Management and course: Initially placed on mechanical ventilation and continuous sedation; treated with ceftriaxone 1 g, modified on day 2 to add ampicillin 1 g and acyclovir 250 mg, alongside antiepileptic medications. The patient experienced progressive neurological decline, remained comatose despite cessation of sedation, and died on day 24 after illness onset.

raw_case_text: Case 6: A 29 year old patient that reported exanthema and pruritus in the second trimester of gestation. Her IgM serology was positive for Zika and the PRNT90% was positive for neutralizing antibodies. At 38 weeks of gestation, her baby girl was born by cesarean that presented a cephalic circumference of 30 cm.

subjective.chief_complaint: 29-year-old pregnant female in the second trimester of gestation presenting with exanthema and pruritus.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced acute onset of a pruritic exanthema during the second trimester of pregnancy. The pregnancy progressed until 38 weeks of gestation, when she delivered a baby girl by cesarean section who presented with microcephaly.
subjective.past_medical_history: Second trimester of pregnancy; no prior medical illnesses reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pruritus; denies other systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Maternal: Cutaneous exanthema. Neonatal: Female infant delivered at 38 weeks gestation by cesarean section with a cephalic circumference of 30 cm (microcephaly).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Congenital Zika syndrome manifest as neonatal microcephaly following maternal second-trimester Zika virus infection. Maternal infection was confirmed by positive Zika IgM serology and positive PRNT90% for neutralizing antibodies. Delivery occurred at 38 weeks gestation with the neonate demonstrating microcephaly (head circumference 30 cm).

raw_case_text:
This is a case of a 20-year-old patient with no particular pathological history, originally from the province of Taounate and moving between this province and the province of Meknes. However, he was infected in the province of Taounate, especially in the rural sector of Ghafsai where he carries out his agricultural activities. He consulted for a skin lesion in the nose. The disease started around May 2018 with a small localized lesion (Figure 1). Four months later, the lesion has spread over the entire lobe of the nose and appeared erythematous (Figure 2).
In front of all these clinical elements, the patient had received antibiotic treatment without improvement. After that, several diagnoses were suggested, namely, sarcoidosis and leishmaniasis, and the observational clinical examination had suspected cutaneous mucosal leishmaniasis. The pathological anatomy results performed in a private center showed an inflammatory reaction composed of mononuclear cells, sometimes epithelioid with a vaguely granulomatous arrangement without caseous necrosis. However, these same results showed the absence of a formal argument for sarcoidosis as well as the absence of an obvious Leishmania body. As for the X-ray results, no lysis of the specific bones of the nose was detected and no damage to the underlying mucosa was observed (Figure 3). One month later, the patient was presented to the national leishmaniasis reference laboratory at the national institute of hygiene in order to confirm the diagnosis of CL. Clinical examination revealed an ulcerative, infiltrated, and poorly limited erythematous placard (Figure 4).
The microscopic diagnosis from skin samples showed the presence of Leishmania amastigotes within the macrophages. These results were confirmed by molecular diagnosis using the ITS1 PCR-RFLP technique. In addition, the enzymatic digestion carried out by MN1-I enzyme made it possible to compare the sample received and the three Leishmania species circulating in Morocco, namely, L. tropica, L. major, and L. infantum. However, the results showed that the electrophoretic profile was comparable to that of L. tropica (Figure 5).
Lane 1-2: patient smears and lane WM: weight marker 100 bp. Positive controls: Lt, L. tropica; Li: L. infantum; Lm: L. major; and NTC: negative control. The electrophoretic profile of the strain isolated in the patient was comparable to the L. tropica profile.
Immediately after laboratory confirmation and after an X-ray of the healthy liver and lungs, treatment with meglumine antimonate (Glucantime ) was initiated according to the protocol described by the Ministry of Health, generally 20 mg of SB5+/kg, without exceeding 2 ampoules, for 3 weeks. For our patient, two ampoules/injection (one ampoule = 5 ml) of antimony salt were administered intramuscularly. Due to the extent and location of the lesion, the duration of treatment was one month.
The initiation of treatment had shown good tolerance and satisfactory results (Figure 6). A week later, a clear clinical improvement was noticed and the skin lesion healed completely without relapse (Figure 7). Nevertheless, the patient still retains partial healing of the lesion (Figure 8). However, cosmetic surgery was subsequently mandatory to remove the residue from the lesion. This was the consequence of late treatment because the patient did not come to the leishmaniasis reference center (INH) until after having consulted quite a few private centers.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old male presented with a 5-month history of an expanding, non-healing erythematous skin lesion on the nose.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: In May 2018, the patient developed a small localized papular lesion on the nose that progressively enlarged over 4 months to involve the entire nasal lobe, appearing as an infiltrated, erythematous, ulcerative placard. Multiple empirical courses of oral antibiotics produced no clinical improvement, prompting referral to a reference center.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Taounate Province and Meknes, Morocco; actively engaged in agricultural activities in the rural sector of Ghafsai (endemic focus); no other pathological or surgical history.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatological examination revealed an ulcerative, infiltrated, and poorly circumscribed erythematous placard covering the entire lobe of the nose. Physical examination of other organ systems was unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial external skin biopsy revealed an epithelioid mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate with a vaguely granulomatous arrangement lacking caseous necrosis or visible microorganisms. Plain radiographs of the nasal bones showed no bone lysis or underlying mucosal destruction; chest and abdominal radiographs demonstrated clear lung fields and healthy hepatic contours.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) caused by Leishmania tropica: direct microscopic examination of dermal scrapings from the lesion margins revealed intracellular Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages; molecular identification using ITS1 PCR-RFLP technique with MN1-I restriction enzyme digestion confirmed an electrophoretic band profile identical to Leishmania tropica. Sarcoidosis and mucosal leishmaniasis were ruled out. The patient was treated with intramuscular meglumine antimonate (Glucantime; 2 ampoules [10 mL] daily, corresponding to 20 mg Sb5+/kg/day) for 1 month. Therapy was well tolerated with rapid improvement within 1 week and complete lesion healing without relapse; residual scarring subsequently underwent elective cosmetic surgical excision.

raw_case_text:
In July 2013, a 25-year-old male presented to the ED with complaints of a 4-day history of fever, myalgia, bone pain, headache, malaise, chills, and nausea (Table 1). Two days earlier he had sought care at a local health center where he was found to be dehydrated and was given intravenous (IV) fluids. Upon presentation to the ED, he was afebrile, and laboratory results demonstrated thrombocytopenia and mildly elevated liver function tests (LFTs) (Tables 2 and 3). He was given a provisional diagnosis of viral syndrome with a rule-out of dengue, given acetaminophen and IV fluids, and admitted for care.
On the first day of hospitalization, he remained afebrile and developed nausea, vomiting, and dry cough. His lungs were consistently clear to auscultation and chest X-rays were unremarkable. Repeat laboratory values on the third day of hospitalization demonstrated worsening thrombocytopenia. Additional laboratory results obtained the following day demonstrated leukocytosis and improving thrombocytopenia. He was discharged home on day 4 of hospitalization with a diagnosis of dengue.
A serum specimen collected on day 5 of illness was positive by MAT with a reciprocal titer of 100 against serogroup Icterohaemorrhagiae (serovar Mankarso). Serum collected upon discharge 8 days after illness onset had a reciprocal MAT titer of 3,200 against serovar Mankarso.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presenting with a 4-day history of fever, myalgia, bone pain, headache, malaise, chills, and nausea.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented in July 2013 with a 4-day history of fever, myalgia, bone pain, headache, malaise, chills, and nausea. Two days prior to presentation, he visited a local health center for dehydration and received intravenous fluids. He presented to the emergency department and was admitted for suspected viral syndrome with a rule-out of dengue. On hospital day 1, he remained afebrile and developed nausea, vomiting, and a dry cough, which subsequently resolved with supportive management until discharge on hospital day 4.
subjective.past_medical_history: Received intravenous fluids for dehydration at a local health center two days prior to presentation. No other medical history documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon emergency department presentation, the patient was afebrile and remained afebrile on day 1 of hospitalization. Bilateral lung fields were consistently clear to auscultation.
objective.routine_investigations: Emergency department presentation: Thrombocytopenia and mildly elevated liver function tests (LFTs). Chest X-rays: Unremarkable. Day 3 of hospitalization: Worsening thrombocytopenia. Day 4 of hospitalization: Leukocytosis and improving thrombocytopenia.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed leptospirosis based on microscopic agglutination test (MAT) seroconversion: reciprocal MAT titer of 100 on illness day 5 rising to 3,200 on illness day 8 against Leptospira serogroup Icterohaemorrhagiae (serovar Mankarso). Initially managed under a provisional diagnosis of viral syndrome / dengue rule-out and discharged with a clinical diagnosis of dengue.
Plan & Outcome: Managed supportively with acetaminophen and intravenous fluids. Symptoms resolved, laboratory abnormalities improved, and the patient was discharged home on hospital day 4.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old Caucasian man went to an urgent care clinic twice before being admitted to the hospital with fever as high as 39.4 C, myalgias, and renal insufficiency later. Additional symptoms included headache, photophobia, nausea, and anorexia, starting 10 days after returning from the boating trip. Signs included subtle diffuse flushing and conjunctival suffusions. Initial laboratory values showed a mild hepatitis with a rising creatinine that increased daily to peak at 4.0 mg/dL. Liver enzymes were elevated with peak values of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 258 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 189 U/L, and bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL. Results of examination of the cerebrospinal fluid were normal. Leukocyte count was within normal range at 4.7 k/muL. By the third day of hospitalization, after IV rehydration and broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents, the patient's fever subsided with improvement of his myalgias and headache. He was discharged and given doxycyline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days. He had no clinical sequelae.
Serologic tests for infectious hepatitis A, B, C, and brucella, and a Monospot test were negative. MAT and IgM-ELISA for leptospirosis were processed at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the California Department of Health Services (CDHS), respectively. Titers from serum drawn 15 days after the initial exposure were negative; however, convalescent-phase serum drawn 17 days later tested positive for leptospira by IgM-ELISA at CDHS, and MAT at CDC showed the strongest reaction with serovars from L. interrogans serogroups Australis and Mini (Table 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old man presented with fever up to 39.4 °C, severe myalgias, and acute renal insufficiency 10 days after a recreational boating trip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 10 days after returning from a boating trip with high fever up to 39.4 °C, myalgias, headache, photophobia, nausea, and anorexia. He was evaluated at an urgent care clinic twice before being admitted to the hospital due to persistent symptoms and rising renal function markers.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological exposure: participated in a recreational house-boating trip to New Melones Reservoir, California, with exposure to muddied creek and runoff waters. Baseline medical history, medications, and allergies are unmentioned.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, headache, photophobia, generalized myalgias, nausea, and anorexia. Home medications and allergies are unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: up to 39.4 °C. General appearance showed subtle diffuse facial and bodily flushing. Eyes: prominent bilateral conjunctival suffusion.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC count: 4.7 x 10^3/muL (normal range). Renal panel: rising serum creatinine increasing daily to a peak of 4.0 mg/dL. Hepatic panel: ALT: 258 U/L; alkaline phosphatase: 189 U/L; total bilirubin: 3.5 mg/dL. Serologic tests for hepatitis A, B, and C, Brucella, and Monospot test were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis demonstrated normal findings.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis manifesting with fever, conjunctival suffusion, acute kidney injury, and hepatitis. Confirmed by CDC and CDHS serologic testing: acute serum (drawn 15 days post-exposure) was negative, but convalescent serum (drawn 17 days later) tested positive by IgM-ELISA at CDHS and by microscopic agglutination testing (MAT) at CDC, reacting most strongly with Leptospira interrogans serogroups Australis and Mini. Acute viral hepatitis A, B, C, Brucella, and Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis were excluded. Treatment & Outcome: Managed with intravenous rehydration and empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents for 3 days, leading to defervescence and resolution of headache and myalgias. Transitioned at discharge to oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days, achieving complete recovery without clinical sequelae.

raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 9-year-old boy (whose mother was recently found to be HIV-positive) presented to the hospital with 1 week of right-sided hemiplegia and right-sided facial palsy. Past medical history included psoriasis, diagnosed 4 years prior. His only HIV exposure was perinatal. On exam the patient weighed 22 kilograms, and vitals signs were within normal limits. He was alert and oriented with a normal level of consciousness and responded appropriately to questions. His speech was slowed and slurred, but this was his baseline according to his mother. He had right-sided facial palsy and right-sided tongue deviation; otherwise cranial nerves were intact. The boy had 3/5 strength in the right upper extremity and 4/5 strength in the right lower extremity. Left-sided strength was 5/5. The patient was able to walk with limited difficulty. Deep tendon reflexes were 2+ and 3+ throughout. Babinski's sign showed dorsiflexion of the right 1st toe. Sensation was intact throughout. The patient also had clusters of 1-2 mm skin colored papules on his forehead and left cheek in addition to diffuse mild psoriatic scaling. Immunizations were up to date. The patient was admitted for a workup of these symptoms.
Laboratory studies showed complete blood count: hematocrit 31.6%, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 5000 cells/muL (N 41%, L 35%, E 12%, M 6%, B 1%, atypical L 1%), and 157 000 platelets/muL. HIV-antibody test was positive with a CD4 T-cell 0.21% (4 cells/muL) and plasma HIV RNA virus of 185 976 copies/mL (log 5.27). Tests for Cryptococcus antigen, Toxoplasmosis antigen, Ebstein Barr virus IgG and IgM, Cytomegalovirus IgG and IgM, Hepes Simplex virus polymerase chain reaction (PCR), Japanese encephalitis as well as cultures for tuberculosis and fungi (plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, CSF) were all negative. Plasma and CSF samples were positive for JCV by real time PCR with a plasma RNA level of 226 copies/mL.
Three days after admission a brain computerized tomography (CT) scan was performed and showed frond-like hypodense lesion at the left frontal lobe with mild effacement of the left frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) regimen was subsequently started 10 days after admission, consisting of GPOvir-Z (coformulated zidovudine 250 mg, lamivudine 150 mg, and nevirapine 200 mg). Clinically, the patient deteriorated during the 1st and 2nd weeks of HAART with fever and increased right leg weakness, but immunologic and virologic improvement was seen (CD4 T-cell count 0.8%, 10 cells/muL, and a plasma HIV RNA viral level of 26 532 copies/mL, log 4.42). CT (Figure 1) and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI; Figure 2) scans were subsequently performed. The scans showed progressive of white matter lesions with asymmetrical deep and subcortical white matter lesions over the left frontotemporoparietal region and the right frontal lobe. The lesion on the left hemisphere involved internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, and genu of corpus callosum and anterior cerebellar hemisphere. There were no enhanced areas after the contrast study.
The patient was discharged 7 weeks after the first admission. Upon discharge he was able to walk with assistance, but was unable to speak.
The patient was readmitted one day after discharge due to autonomic nervous system dysfunction (nausea, vomiting, and loss of bowel and bladder tone). Deep tendon reflexes were 4+ throughout, and Babinski was positive bilaterally. Continued improvement of immunologic (CD4 T-cell count 2.0%, 30 cells/muL) and virologic (HIV RNA level 3220 copies/mL, log 3.51) measures were seen. Due to progressive neurologic symptoms HAART was ceased. The second MRI (Figure 3) scan was performed and showed a progressive lesion in the same regions as described in the previous MRI, but also found new lesions over the midbrain, pons, and medulla predominantly on the left. The patient was discharged approximately 3 weeks after admission.
The patient was readmitted 1 month later (100 days after onset of symptoms). Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS) was suspected, and the boy was treated with methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day) for 5 days. Despite HAART suspension and administration of steroids, his clinical symptoms worsened. The third MRI (Figure 4) scan showed new lesions in the regions of the right brainstem and right hemisphere with gyral enhancement. The patient's mother refused further treatment, he was discharged home, and he subsequently died 1 year later.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 9-year-old boy presenting with a 1-week history of right-sided hemiplegia and right-sided facial palsy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute progressive weakness of the right upper and lower extremities and right facial droop over a 1-week period. He had a baseline of slowed and slurred speech according to his mother. Ten days after admission, he was started on combination antiretroviral therapy; during the 1st and 2nd weeks of therapy, he experienced clinical deterioration with fever and worsening right leg weakness despite virologic and immunologic improvement. He was discharged after 7 weeks, but readmitted one day later with autonomic nervous system dysfunction (nausea, vomiting, and urinary and fecal incontinence), and again at 100 days with progressive neurocognitive decline.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of psoriasis diagnosed 4 years prior. Perinatal exposure to maternal retroviral infection (mother recently tested positive for retroviral disease). Immunizations up to date.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right-sided weakness, facial droop, slurred speech, mild psoriatic scaling; later positive for nausea, vomiting, and bowel and bladder incontinence; negative for sensory loss or seizures. Home medications: unmentioned. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Weight: 22 kg; vital signs: within normal limits on admission. Mental status: alert and oriented with normal level of consciousness, responding appropriately; speech slowed and slurred (baseline). Cranial nerves: right-sided facial palsy and rightward tongue deviation; other cranial nerves intact. Motor: right upper extremity strength 3/5, right lower extremity strength 4/5, left-sided strength 5/5; ambulatory with limited difficulty. Reflexes: deep tendon reflexes 2+ to 3+ throughout (escalating to 4+ on second admission); Babinski sign: dorsiflexion of the right 1st toe (bilateral on readmission). Sensory: intact throughout. Dermatologic: clusters of 1-2 mm skin-colored papules on forehead and left cheek, with diffuse mild psoriatic scaling.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: hematocrit 31.6%, hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL, white blood cell count 5,000 cells/mcL (neutrophils 41%, lymphocytes 35%, eosinophils 12%, monocytes 6%, basophils 1%, atypical lymphocytes 1%), platelets 157,000 cells/mcL. Plasma and CSF tests: negative for Cryptococcus antigen, Toxoplasma antigen, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) IgG and IgM, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgG and IgM, Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) PCR, and Japanese encephalitis virus; plasma and CSF cultures for fungi and Mycobacterium tuberculosis: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT (day 3): frond-like hypodense lesion in left frontal lobe with mild effacement of the left frontal horn of the lateral ventricle. Repeat brain CT and MRI: progressive asymmetrical deep and subcortical white matter lesions over the left frontotemporoparietal region and right frontal lobe, involving left internal capsule, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, genu of corpus callosum, and anterior cerebellar hemisphere, without contrast enhancement. Second MRI: progressive lesions in previously described areas with new lesions in left midbrain, pons, and medulla. Third MRI (day 100): new lesions in right brainstem and right cerebral hemisphere with gyral enhancement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) complicated by PML-Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (PML-IRIS) in a child with perinatally acquired advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS. Confirmatory testing: HIV-antibody test positive, initial CD4+ T-cell count 0.21% (4 cells/mcL), plasma HIV RNA 185,976 copies/mL (5.27 log10 copies/mL); JC virus (JCV) confirmed positive by real-time PCR in both CSF and plasma (plasma viral load 226 copies/mL). Alternative etiologies (tuberculosis, fungal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV, EBV, HSV, Japanese encephalitis) excluded by negative serology, PCR, and cultures. Management & Outcome: Initiated on HAART (GPOvir-Z: zidovudine 250 mg, lamivudine 150 mg, and nevirapine 200 mg) on day 10. Experienced paradoxical clinical deterioration despite virologic/immunologic response (CD4 rising to 0.8% [10 cells/mcL] and 2.0% [30 cells/mcL]; viral load declining to 26,532 copies/mL and 3,220 copies/mL). HAART was discontinued due to progressive neurotoxicity, and methylprednisolone (2 mg/kg/day for 5 days) was administered for suspected IRIS. Neurologic deficits worsened progressively; palliative discharge was provided, and the patient died 1 year later.

raw_case_text: A 65-year-old male came to our hospital complaining of abdominal pain in the right lumbar region for 2 months with lethargy. He had history of loss of appetite for one month with no history of fever, diabetes, tuberculosis, weight loss, or any surgeries. He has been a chronic alcoholic for the last 30 years. He had a history of dark-colored stools for a week. The patient did not receive BCG vaccination at his birth. Pallor was present in the palpebral conjunctiva, cardiovascular and respiratory system has no abnormality. On abdominal examination, mild tenderness in the right lumbar region otherwise the abdomen was soft on palpation with no organomegaly. His haemoglobin level was 8%, peripheral smear showed normocytic, normochromic anemia with few microcytes, and stool examination revealed occult blood. HIV and HBsAg tests were negative. Colonoscopy showed a circumferential ulcerated, narrowed ileocecal valve with a pulled-up caecum suggestive of abdominal tuberculosis. Multiple biopsies were taken to rule out dysplasia. The anal canal, rectum, sigmoid colon, descending colon, transverse colon, and ascending colon were visualized and their mucosa appeared normal. Computed tomography of abdomen showed mesenteric lymph node enlargement suggestive of intestinal tuberculosis. Interferon-gamma release assay, polymerase chain reaction, and Mantoux test were positive suggestive of tuberculosis, and fecal calprotectin level was normal. Chest X-ray revealed no abnormalities. The patient started with antitubercular therapy (ATT) according to national protocol i.e. rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol were prescribed for four months, followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for two months along with vitamin B6.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 65-year-old male presenting with right lumbar abdominal pain and lethargy for two months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of right lumbar abdominal pain associated with generalized lethargy. He noted reduced appetite over the past month and dark-colored stools for one week prior to presentation. He denied fever, unintentional weight loss, nausea, or vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic alcohol consumption for 30 years. Did not receive BCG vaccination at birth. Denied past history of tuberculosis, diabetes mellitus, or prior surgical interventions.
subjective.review_of_systems: Right lumbar pain, lethargy, anorexia, melenic/dark-colored stools. Denies fever, weight loss, cough, chest pain.

objective.physical_examination: Pallor present in palpebral conjunctiva. Cardiovascular and respiratory system examinations were normal. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right lumbar region; abdomen was otherwise soft, non-distended, with no palpable organomegaly or masses.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 8 g/dL (reported as 8%); peripheral blood smear showed normocytic normochromic anemia with few microcytes. Stool examination positive for occult blood. Fecal calprotectin level normal. Serology for HIV and HBsAg negative. Chest radiograph revealed no abnormalities. Mantoux tuberculin skin test was positive.
objective.advanced_workup: Colonoscopy showed a circumferential ulcerated, narrowed ileocecal valve with a pulled-up cecum; anal canal, rectum, sigmoid colon, descending colon, transverse colon, and ascending colon visualized with normal mucosa; multiple biopsies obtained to rule out dysplasia. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed mesenteric lymph node enlargement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Abdominal / intestinal tuberculosis involving the ileocecal valve and mesenteric lymph nodes.
Diagnostic confirmation: Positive interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA), positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, positive Mantoux test, and classical colonoscopic findings (circumferential ulceration with narrowed ileocecal valve and pulled-up cecum) alongside CT mesenteric lymphadenopathy; dysplasia ruled out on biopsy.
Management and outcome: Initiated on antitubercular therapy according to national protocol: 4-drug intensive phase with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 4 months, followed by continuation phase with rifampicin and isoniazid for 2 months, along with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation.

raw_case_text:
A 46-year-old female from Hulunbeir City, Inner Mongolia, presented with a two-month history of intermittent high fever (up to 40.1 C) accompanied by persistent neck, shoulder, and back pain. Despite having no direct contact with cattle, sheep, dogs, or consumption of raw meat and dairy products, her symptoms persisted. She reported a weight loss of 2.5 kg, normal bowel habits, and poor sleep due to pain, without any signs of fatigue or night sweats. Upon her initial consultation at our hospital Orthopedics Outpatient Department on June 1, 2021, she was admitted for suspected cervical brucellosis spondylitis. Physical examination revealed significant tenderness at the C7 spinous process and paravertebral areas, limited cervical spine mobility, and radiating pain to the right upper limb. Neurological examination showed reduced right triceps tendon reflex and a muscle strength of grade 3 in the right upper limb. Diagnostic tests were performed to clarify her condition. The Rose Bengal plate agglutination test was positive, suggesting brucellosis. Concurrently, tuberculosis screening via T-SPOT showed increased spots of interferon alpha and beta, and a positive PPD test, though tuberculosis antibodies were negative, and no acid-fast bacilli were detected in sputum smears. Initial investigations showed leukopenia (WBC 4.57x109/L) with relative neutrophilia (51.3%), and anemia with a hemoglobin level of 103 g/L. Inflammatory markers were mildly elevated (CRP 0.5 mg/L, ESR 7mm/hr). Imaging studies, including X-rays, CT, and MRI scans of the cervical spine, demonstrated destructive spondylitis at the C7 vertebral level with paravertebral abscess formation (Figure 1). Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Brucella cervical spondylitis was confirmed.
Treatment began with a two-week regimen of antibiotics, including doxycycline, rifampin, levofloxacin, and ceftazidime-sulbactam. Surgical intervention was deemed necessary due to the persistence of symptoms and imaging findings. The patient underwent anterior cervical debridement and decompression, C7 subtotal corpectomy, and titanium mesh bone graft fusion, with a cervical titanium plate for internal fixation (Figure 2). The surgery involved meticulous removal of the infected tissue and decompression of the cervical spine. Postoperative care included continued antibiotic therapy, nourishment for nerve recovery, and precautions to prevent esophageal and respiratory complications. Pathology from intraoperative samples confirmed extensive Brucella involvement via Gram staining and RT-PCR, while tuberculosis was excluded (Figure 3). Follow-up at six months showed significant improvement in pain, recovery of muscle strength to grade 5 in the right upper limb (Figure 4), and normalization of inflammatory markers.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 46-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of intermittent high fever and persistent neck, shoulder, and back pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced intermittent high fevers peaking up to 40.1 °C accompanied by persistent neck, shoulder, and back pain for 2 months. She reported poor sleep due to pain and a weight loss of 2.5 kg since symptom onset. Bowel habits were normal, and she denied fatigue or night sweats.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Hulunbeir City, Inner Mongolia. Denied direct contact with cattle, sheep, or dogs, and denied consumption of raw meat or unpasteurized dairy products. No prior medical illnesses or chronic conditions reported.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports poor sleep due to pain and weight loss of 2.5 kg. Denies fatigue, night sweats, or changes in bowel habits.

objective.physical_examination: Significant tenderness at the C7 spinous process and paravertebral areas; limited cervical spine mobility; radiating pain to the right upper limb. Neurological examination: diminished right triceps tendon reflex; muscle strength of grade 3/5 in the right upper limb.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count (WBC): 4.57 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 51.3%), hemoglobin: 103 g/L, C-reactive protein (CRP): 0.5 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 7 mm/hr. Plain cervical X-ray showed destructive changes at C7.
objective.advanced_workup: CT and MRI scans of the cervical spine demonstrated destructive spondylitis at the C7 vertebral level with paravertebral abscess formation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Rose Bengal plate agglutination test was positive; intraoperative pathology confirmed extensive Brucella involvement by Gram staining and reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), confirming Brucella cervical spondylitis with paravertebral abscess. Differential diagnosis: Tuberculosis investigated and excluded; T-SPOT showed increased spots of interferon alpha and beta, and PPD was positive, but serum tuberculosis antibodies were negative and sputum smears showed no acid-fast bacilli. Management and Outcome: Preoperatively received a 2-week course of doxycycline, rifampin, levofloxacin, and ceftazidime-sulbactam. Underwent anterior cervical debridement and decompression, C7 subtotal corpectomy, titanium mesh bone graft fusion, and anterior cervical titanium plate fixation. Postoperatively, antibiotic therapy and nerve nourishment were continued. At 6-month follow-up, she demonstrated significant pain relief, recovery of right upper limb strength to grade 5/5, and normalization of inflammatory markers.

raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old man was admitted 11 days after having a donation after brainstem death renal transplant for end-stage renal failure secondary to IgA nephropathy. The transplant itself was uneventful. His other past medical history consisted of transfusion dependent beta-thalassaemia intermedia (baseline ferritin was 2236 mug/l) and splenectomy. He was discharged on tacrolimus, MMF and prednisolone.
He was re-admitted 6 days later with a 2-day history of dry cough, dyspnoea and self-recorded pyrexia of 38 C. Examination revealed coarse crepitations predominantly on the right, saturation of 97% in room air, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min and blood pressure 161/84 mmHg. Blood tests showed a ferritin of 4054 mug/l, CRP 84 mg/l and procalcitonin of 1.71 mug/l. CXR showed consolidation in the right mid and lower zones, and NPS confirmed SARS-CoV-2. Ceftriaxone was initiated.
On day 2, his oxygen requirement increased, with worsening bilateral mid zone air space shadowing. He was commenced on continuous positive airway pressure 5 days after admission and underwent endotracheal intubation on day 7. Given the clinical deterioration and rising CRP (170 mg/l), he was commenced on anakinra 200 mg i.v. once a day (Table 1). After initiation of anakinra, inotropes were weaned within 24 h, and significant improvement in his blood parameters was noted (ferritin 2687 microg/l and CRP 26 mg/l).
His ICU admission was complicated by an Enterococcus faecium bacteraemia on day 9 of admission, for which he completed 7 days of teicoplanin. Anakinra was reduced and stopped after 21 days. After a successful tracheostomy wean, he was discharged on day 45.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old male renal transplant recipient presenting with a 2-day history of fever up to 38 °C, dry cough, and shortness of breath.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 48-year-old male who had undergone a deceased-donor renal transplant 17 days prior presented with a 2-day history of dry cough, dyspnea, and pyrexia of 38.0 °C. On hospital day 2, his hypoxemia progressed alongside expanding bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. He was placed on CPAP on day 5 and required endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation on day 7 due to progressive respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: End-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy status post recent deceased-donor renal transplantation (17 days prior), transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia intermedia (baseline ferritin: 2,236 mcg/L), and splenectomy. Maintenance immunosuppression: tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), and prednisolone.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for pyrexia, nonproductive cough, and shortness of breath. Negative for gastrointestinal symptoms. Home medications: tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisolone. Allergies: none documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.0 °C, blood pressure: 161/84 mmHg, respiratory rate: 18 breaths/min, SpO2: 97% on ambient air upon arrival (rapidly declining over subsequent days). Lungs: coarse crepitations/crackles auscultated predominantly over the right hemithorax.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: serum ferritin: 4,054 mcg/L; C-reactive protein (CRP): 84 mg/L (peaking at 170 mg/L on day 7; declining to 26 mg/L post-treatment); procalcitonin: 1.71 mcg/L. Convalescent ferritin: 2,687 mcg/L. Blood cultures: positive on day 9 for Enterococcus faecium bacteremia. Serial chest radiographs: initial CXR revealed airspace consolidation in the right mid- and lower lung zones; day 2 showed worsening bilateral mid-zone airspace shadowing.
objective.advanced_workup: Tracheostomy performed during prolonged invasive mechanical ventilation for successful ventilator weaning.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and hyperinflammatory cytokine release syndrome in a recent renal allograft recipient with underlying beta-thalassemia intermedia, confirmed by positive nasopharyngeal SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR; complicated by nosocomial Enterococcus faecium bloodstream infection. Management & Outcome: Initiated on intravenous ceftriaxone. Escalated to continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and endotracheal intubation on day 7 with inotropic support. Intravenous anakinra (200 mg daily) was administered for 21 days, allowing prompt discontinuation of inotropes within 24 hours and dramatic reduction of ferritin and CRP. Enterococcal bacteremia was treated with 7 days of intravenous teicoplanin. Following tracheostomy creation and gradual ventilatory weaning, the patient was successfully decannulated and discharged on hospital day 45.

raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old Mexican patient presented to Donghai Hospital with complaints of fever (39.3 C), anorexia, and watery diarrhea three to four times a day. About 16 days prior to the onset of these symptoms, he arrived in Yantai, China. His condition improved after 2 days of antipyretic and antidiarrheal treatment (clindamycin 900 mg, etimicin 100 mg, anisodamine 10 mg, dexamethasone 5 mg, and antondine 2 ml). Unfortunately, the patient developed abdominal pain (paroxysmal colic) and diarrhea on the third day after discharge, and the symptoms gradually worsened. Two days later, the patient went to Yeda Hospital. On admission, he appeared ill and jaundiced but was alert. Initial vital signs were temperature 37 C, blood pressure 120/65 mmHg, heart rate 100 beats/min, and respiratory rate 18/min. Abdominal physical examination revealed right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound tenderness, liver percussive pain, Murphy's sign, no kidney percussive pain, and no rash. Initial investigation (Table 1) showed acute infectious, hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases, and thrombocytopenia. The hepatitis panel was negative. Rapid tests for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 were also negative. Chest computerized tomography (CT) showed bilateral inferior lobar foci, right pleural hypertrophy, and adhesion. Abdominal CT indicated hepatosplenomegaly and cholecystitis. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) showed gallbladder enlargement and wall thickening, cholecystitis not excluded, bilateral pleural effusion, and a small amount of ascites. Blood culture revealed the growth of Gram-negative rod. After admission, he received a combined therapy of levofloxacin and imipenem. Due to his serious condition, he was transferred emergently to Yuhuangding Hospital at 9 pm the next day after admission.
On arrival at Yuhuangding Hospital, his vital signs were temperature 35.8 C, blood pressure 114/59 mmHg, heart rate 89 beats/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. Blood tests (Table 1) were notable for elevated transaminases, prolonged prothrombin time (15.2 s, activity 53.9%), high international normalized ratio (1.32), elevated D-Dimer, elevated serum amyloid A and procalcitonin, thrombocytopenia, and eosinopenia. Chest CT showed bilateral pneumonia and bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal CT showed fatty liver, hepatosplenomegaly, thickening of the horizontal duodenal wall, multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the mesentery, cholecystitis, and a small amount of ascites (Figure 1). The following test results were negative: the full panel for hepatitis; serologic tests for hantavirus, EB virus, and TORCH (Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and other pathogenic microorganisms); nucleic acid assay for cytomegalovirus, EB virus, and the new Bunya virus; fecal bacterial isolation of V. cholerae O1/O139 and Escherichia coli O157:H7. The patient received intravenous meropenem 1.0 g per 8 h. On the second night after the transfer, the patient had bloody stools with clots three times within 3 h, about 50, 100, and 300 ml, respectively. Three urgent blood tests showed a continuous decrease in hemoglobin and platelet count from 126 g/L and 42 x 109/L to 101 g/L and 26 x 109/L, respectively. Blood pressure dropped to 96/45 mmHg. He was rendered norepinephrine (400 mug/h), somatostatin (250 mug/h), vitamin K1 (20 mg, ivgtt), and hemocoagulase agkistrodon (2 IU, iv). The patient had another bloody stool about 200 ml 8 h after the first bloody stool. The electrocardiograph (ECG) monitor showed blood pressure 115/54 mmHg, heart rate 107 beats/min, blood oxygen saturation 99%, and respiration 24 beats/min. Urgent blood test showed hemoglobin 83 g/L, platelet count 43 x 109/L, prothrombin time 17.0 s, activity 46.0%, and fibrinogen 1.68 g/L. The patient received human prothrombin complex 600 IU and two infusions of O-type RH-positive RBCs (2.0 units and 1.5 units, respectively) without any transfusion side effects. On the third morning in Yuhuangding Hospital, Yeda Hospital reported the result of blood culture initiated at the time of admission, which was identified as S. Typhi. Transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) refused by the patient initially was performed after 3 days of conservative treatment failed. Hemostasis was achieved and the patient continued to receive total parenteral nutrition and symptomatic support treatment (Figure 2). Unexpectedly, the patient had three more bloody stools (about 350 ml in total) with no obvious cause on the fourth day after TAE. Urgent blood test showed hemoglobin 66 g/L, neutrophil count 1.55 x 109/L, K 3.22 mmol/L, Na 134.7 mmol/L, Ca 1.86 mmol/L, Mg 0.64 mmol/L, glucose 8.07 mmol/L, creatinine 48 mumol/L, urea 1.47 mmol/L, uric acid 157 mumol/L, prothrombin time 13.1 s, D-Dimer 12.6 mg/L, and procalcitonin 0.466 ng/ml. The patient was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) and underwent TAE again. On the second day in the ICU, he had bloody diarrhea again. The hemoglobin level increased from 66 to 97 g/L after 4.0 units of RBC transfusion. On the third day in the ICU, the patient developed severe leukopenia (1.78 x 109/L) and was treated with recombinant human granulocyte stimulating factor (GSF; 100 mug subcutaneous injection) promptly. After 5 days of intensive care in the ICU, his vital signs stabilized. The patient was discharged after another week of comprehensive treatment in the general ward. He returned to Mexico immediately after discharge and did not receive follow-up examinations as prescribed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old Mexican male presented with fever of 39.3 °C, anorexia, and watery diarrhea, followed by severe paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Fever (39.3 °C), anorexia, and watery diarrhea (3-4 times daily) started 16 days after arriving in Yantai, China. He received 2 days of outpatient antipyretic/antidiarrheal therapy with temporary relief, but developed severe paroxysmal colicky abdominal pain and recurrent diarrhea 3 days post-discharge, which progressively worsened over 2 days. He presented to a secondary hospital and was transferred to a tertiary center. On hospital night 2, he developed massive lower gastrointestinal bleeding (bloody stools with clots totaling ~450 mL over 3 hours, and another 200 mL 8 hours later) with hemorrhagic shock. Four days after initial embolization, he experienced recurrent lower GI bleeding (350 mL), followed by recurrent bloody diarrhea in the ICU.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent international travel: arrived in Yantai, China from Mexico 16 days prior to symptom onset. Prior therapy for current illness: clindamycin 900 mg, etimicin 100 mg, anisodamine 10 mg, dexamethasone 5 mg, antondine 2 mL for 2 days.
subjective.review_of_systems: Anorexia, colicky abdominal pain, watery and subsequent massive bloody stools with clots. No allergies documented.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-appearing, jaundiced, alert. Vitals: temperature 37 °C initially (35.8 °C on transfer); blood pressure 120/65 mmHg initially, dropping to 96/45 mmHg during bleed, and 115/54 mmHg post-resuscitation; heart rate 100 beats/min initially, 89 beats/min on transfer, and 107 beats/min during bleed; respiratory rate 18-24/min; SpO2 99%. Abdomen: right upper quadrant tenderness without rebound tenderness, liver percussive pain, positive Murphy's sign, no kidney percussive pain; no rash.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematology: thrombocytopenia (platelets 42 x 10^9/L falling to 26 x 10^9/L) and eosinopenia; hemoglobin decreased from 126 g/L to 101 g/L, then 83 g/L, nadir 66 g/L (increased to 97 g/L after transfusion); neutrophil count 1.55 x 10^9/L; severe leukopenia in ICU (WBC 1.78 x 10^9/L). Coagulation: prolonged PT 15.2 s (activity 53.9%) to 17.0 s (activity 46.0%), INR 1.32, fibrinogen 1.68 g/L, elevated D-Dimer (12.6 mg/L). Inflammatory markers: elevated serum amyloid A, elevated procalcitonin (0.466 ng/mL). LFTs & Biochemistry: hyperbilirubinemia, elevated transaminases; K 3.22 mmol/L, Na 134.7 mmol/L, Ca 1.86 mmol/L, Mg 0.64 mmol/L, glucose 8.07 mmol/L, creatinine 48 umol/L, urea 1.47 mmol/L, uric acid 157 umol/L. Infectious workup: rapid tests and fecal isolation for Vibrio cholerae O1/O139 and E. coli O157:H7 negative; full hepatitis viral panel negative; serologies for hantavirus, EBV, and TORCH negative; PCR for CMV, EBV, and new Bunya virus negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest CT: bilateral inferior lobar foci, right pleural hypertrophy and adhesion, progressing to bilateral pneumonia and bilateral pleural effusion. Abdominal CT: fatty liver, hepatosplenomegaly, thickening of horizontal duodenal wall, multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, cholecystitis, and small amount of ascites. MRCP: gallbladder enlargement and wall thickening, cholecystitis not excluded, bilateral pleural effusion, and small ascites. Interventional angiography: emergency transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) performed twice for active/recurrent intestinal bleeding.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi bacteremia) complicated by massive lower gastrointestinal hemorrhage, hemorrhagic shock, acute acalculous cholecystitis, bilateral pneumonia, and secondary myelosuppression (severe leukopenia). Confirmed by blood culture yielding Gram-negative rods identified as Salmonella Typhi. Antimicrobial therapy: initially IV levofloxacin and imipenem, switched to IV meropenem 1.0 g every 8 hours. Resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock: norepinephrine (400 mcg/h), somatostatin (250 mcg/h), IV vitamin K1 (20 mg), hemocoagulase agkistrodon (2 IU), human prothrombin complex (600 IU), multiple packed red blood cell transfusions (total 7.5 units), and total parenteral nutrition. Hemostasis achieved via two separate transcatheter arterial embolizations (TAE). Recombinant human G-CSF (100 mcg SQ) administered for severe leukopenia. Stabilized after 5 days in the ICU and 1 week in the general ward; discharged clinically recovered.

raw_case_text:
This male infant was born at term and had uneventful perinatal and postnatal periods until about 4 months of age. His birth weight was 2.8 kg. Unfortunately, he was not screened for the presence of TREC at birth, as current national neonatal screening programs in the UAE does not include testing for primary immunodeficiencies. At birth, he received the routine BCG and hepatitis B vaccines. At 2 and 4 months of age, he received the routine DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus, acellular pertussis), HiB (haemophilus influenzae type b conjugate), and 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate, rotavirus (RV1,Rotarix ), and oral IP (inactivated polio) vaccines. At 41/2 months, he developed severe respiratory infection and refractory diarrhea, which required hospitalization and intravenous antibiotics. His blood and stool cultures were negative. The stool was positive for rotavirus. His chest radiographs showed bilateral infiltrations, and the thymus was not visible (Figure 1(a)). On admission, his neutrophil count was 10.5 x 109/L and lymphocyte count was 10.4 x 109/L, with a normal hemoglobin concentration and platelet count. His serum IgE and IgA were unmeasurable, IgG <0.5 g/L (normal, 3.5 to 12.2), and IgM = 0.14 (normal, 0.18 to 1.08). He was started on a regular intravenous gammaglobulin infusion. The results of his lymphocyte immunophenotyping were as follows: total lymphocyte count, 3,715/microL; CD3+, 96 cells/microL (normal: 2,530 to 4,510); CD4+, 82 cells/microL (normal: 1,640 to 2,980); CD8+, 1 cell/microL (normal: 780 to 1,500); CD19+, 3,000 cells/microL (normal: 1,160 to 2,420); and NK, 514 cells/microL.
Diagnostic (whole) exome sequencing revealed two pathogenic variants: homozygous NM_000732.4(CD3D):c.128G > A, p.Trp43* (VCV000643120.1; pathogenic; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/CCDS/CcdsBrowse.cgi?REQUEST=CCDS&DATA=CCDS8394) and hemizygous NM_001287344.1 (BTK):c.80G > A, p.Gly27Asp (novel). Pathologic variants of CD3D (CD3 antigen, delta subunit, autosomal recessive; MIM#186790) cause "immunodeficiency type 19" (MIM#615617). His CD3D variant creates a premature stop-gain, resulting in a loss-of-function due to absent protein product. Pathologic variants of BTK (Bruton agammaglobulinemia tyrosine kinase; MIM#300300), on the other hand, cause "agammaglobulinemia, X-linked 1 (MIM#300755) and "isolated growth hormone deficiency, type III, with agammaglobulinemia" (MIM#307200). His novel BTK variant had conflicting predictions of interpretation: MutationTaster: 0.810 (pathogenic), LoFtool: 0.953 (pathogenic), and CADD: 7.6 (benign).
The parents, second cousins, had four healthy boys and one healthy daughter. They also had a daughter who passed away at the age of 4 months of an undetermined disease. The mother had four miscarriages in the first trimester. In addition, she and six of her sisters had hypothyroidism; one sister also had autoimmune hepatitis.
Over the following six weeks, he continued to suffer from high-fever, dyspnea (requiring oxygen), maculopapular rash, severe oral thrush, poor feeding, severe diarrhea, failure-to-thrive, and E. coli urosepsis. On physical examination, he had moderate hepatomegaly, mild splenomegaly, and palpable left axillary lymph nodes; the largest measured about 2 cm in diameter. Neck, chest, and abdominal CT scans confirmed generalized lymphadenopathy, including his left axillary lymph nodes (Figure 1(b)). Excisional left axillary lymph node biopsy showed numerous acid-fast bacilli (AFB), consistent with tuberculous (TB) lymphadenitis (Figure 2). As expected, IGRA (Interferon Gamma Release Assay) was negative.
His BCG-related lymphadenitis and systemic TB infection were treated with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyridoxine. He was maintained on regular immunoglobulin infusion, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis, fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. His brother was a 10/10 HLA match. Bone marrow transplantation was performed before 8 months of age.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4.5-month-old male infant presented with severe respiratory infection, refractory diarrhea, and failure to thrive.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born at term with uneventful early infancy; received BCG and hepatitis B vaccines at birth and routine infant vaccinations at 2 and 4 months. At 4.5 months, developed severe respiratory tract infection and refractory diarrhea requiring hospitalization. Over the subsequent six weeks, experienced persistent high fevers, oxygen-dependent dyspnea, maculopapular rash, oral thrush, failure to thrive, and E. coli urosepsis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born at term (birth weight 2.8 kg) in the United Arab Emirates. Parents are second cousins (consanguineous); family history notable for infant death of a sibling at 4 months, maternal history of four first-trimester miscarriages, and familial hypothyroidism. Received routine BCG vaccination at birth.
subjective.review_of_systems: Poor feeding, diarrhea, maculopapular rash, and dyspnea. Home medications: prior broad-spectrum antibiotics. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: High fever, tachypnea, oxygen dependence, severe oral thrush, generalized maculopapular eruption, moderate hepatomegaly, mild splenomegaly, and palpable left axillary lymphadenopathy (largest node measuring 2 cm).
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: absolute neutrophil count 10.5 x 10^9/L, lymphocyte count 10.4 x 10^9/L, with normal hemoglobin and platelet counts. Serum immunoglobulins: IgG <0.5 g/L (normal 3.5-12.2), IgM 0.14 g/L (normal 0.18-1.08), IgA and IgE undetectable. Lymphocyte immunophenotyping: total lymphocytes 3,715/uL, CD3+ T cells 96/uL (normal 2,530-4,510), CD4+ T cells 82/uL (normal 1,640-2,980), CD8+ T cells 1/uL (normal 780-1,500), CD19+ B cells 3,000/uL, NK cells 514/uL (consistent with T-B+NK+ severe combined immunodeficiency). Stool rotavirus antigen: positive; blood and stool bacterial cultures: sterile. Chest radiograph: bilateral pulmonary infiltrations and absent thymic shadow.
objective.advanced_workup: Whole exome sequencing: identified homozygous pathogenic nonsense mutation in CD3D (c.128G>A, p.Trp43*) confirming T-B+ severe combined immunodeficiency (immunodeficiency type 19), along with hemizygous variant in BTK (c.80G>A, p.Gly27Asp). CT scans of neck, chest, and abdomen: generalized lymphadenopathy, prominently involving the left axillary chain. Excisional left axillary lymph node biopsy: histopathology demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous lymphadenitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated BCG-osis / tuberculous lymphadenitis and systemic mycobacterial infection in an infant with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID, T-B+NK+ phenotype) secondary to homozygous CD3D mutation. Excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrated numerous acid-fast bacilli (AFB) on special staining; interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) was falsely negative due to profound T-cell lymphopenia. E. coli urosepsis and rotavirus gastroenteritis were also treated.
Treatment & Outcome: Treated with antitubercular therapy consisting of rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyridoxine, along with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) substitution, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PCP prophylaxis, fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Underwent successful allogeneic bone marrow transplantation from a 10/10 HLA-matched sibling before 8 months of age.

raw_case_text: A 29-year-old female patient, referred from general medicine department was presented with asymptomatic purplish and black colored skin lesions over the face (around lips) and extremities since past 15 days. Patient was a known and treated case of pulmonary tuberculosis and had taken complete anti-tubercular treatment 2 years back. Three months back, before the development of skin lesions, patient came to our hospital with complains of continuous cough and heaviness in chest. 2 D echo was carried out, which showed blocking in left pulmonary artery due to thrombus with right ventricular enlargement. Patient was put-on oral Warfarin 2.5 mg once daily to dissolve the thrombus. At that time her sputum was negative for acid fast bacilli (AFB). Two and half months later the patient came back with worsening of her chest complaints and on investigation she was found to have reactivation of pulmonary tuberculosis (sputum positive for AFB). She also had the above mentioned skin lesions for which she was referred to skin out patient department (OPD). General examination revealed her poor general condition with multiple purple to black ecchymotic patches around mouth, upper, and lower extremities [Figures 1 and 2]. Skin over right knee revealed black eschar surrounded by ecchymotic patch and erythema [Figure 3]. She also had resolving grouped vesicular lesions involving right L3, 4 dermatome, and clinically, suggestive of Herpes zoster. Routine investigations were within normal limits. Prothrombin time international normalized ratio (PTINR) of patient was carried out, which initially was not recordable as it was very high. We advised enzyme linked immune sorbent assay (ELISA) for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) antibodies taking in to consideration her reactivation of pulmonary tuberculosis, drug reaction, and herpes zoster. ELISA for HIV antibodies was reactive. Then the patient was admitted in medicine ward. Oral Warfarin was stopped and she was given two units of FFP on two alternate days. After giving one FFP, PTINR came down to 4 min, however, the patient died on the 4th day of admission.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old female presenting with asymptomatic purplish-black cutaneous ecchymoses over the face and extremities for 15 days, in conjunction with worsening cough and chest heaviness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed continuous cough and chest heaviness 3 months prior and was diagnosed with a left pulmonary artery thrombosis and right ventricular enlargement, for which oral warfarin was prescribed. Sputum AFB was negative at that time. Two and a half months later, she returned with worsening respiratory complaints, reactivation of pulmonary tuberculosis (sputum AFB positive), and newly erupted asymptomatic purple-to-black ecchymotic patches over her perioral area and extremities of 15 days' duration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pulmonary tuberculosis treated with full course of anti-tubercular therapy completed 2 years prior. Left pulmonary artery thrombus with right ventricular enlargement diagnosed 3 months prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for continuous cough, chest heaviness, purpuric skin lesions, and resolving localized dermatomal rash; negative for fever, hemoptysis, or spontaneous mucosal hemorrhage. Home medications: oral warfarin 2.5 mg once daily. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: General: poor general condition. Dermatologic: multiple purple-to-black ecchymotic patches around the mouth (perioral) and across upper and lower extremities; skin over the right knee demonstrated a necrotic black eschar surrounded by an ecchymotic patch and erythema; resolving grouped vesicular lesions along the right L3-L4 dermatome consistent with herpes zoster. Systemic examination: chest heaviness; other systemic findings unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline routine investigations: within normal limits. Coagulation profile: prothrombin time international normalized ratio (PT/INR) markedly elevated and initially unrecordable (supratherapeutic), decreasing to 4 after fresh frozen plasma transfusion. Baseline sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear: positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
objective.advanced_workup: Transthoracic 2D echocardiography: left pulmonary artery thrombosis causing vascular obstruction, with right ventricular enlargement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe warfarin-induced skin necrosis / coumarin necrosis with supratherapeutic coagulopathy, multi-dermatomal herpes zoster (VZV reactivation), and reactivated pulmonary tuberculosis, in newly diagnosed advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. HIV confirmed by reactive ELISA for HIV antibodies. Tuberculosis confirmed by positive sputum acid-fast bacilli smear. Management & Outcome: Oral warfarin was immediately discontinued, and patient was admitted to the medical ward and administered 2 units of fresh frozen plasma (FFP) on alternate days. PT/INR improved to 4, but the patient experienced rapid clinical decline and succumbed on the 4th hospital day.

raw_case_text:
A 12-year-old Indian boy was admitted to our institution with a prolonged fever of 1 month duration, with maximum temperatures above 40 C. This was associated with watery, nonbloody diarrhea, with intermittent vomiting and abdominal pain. There was a travel history to India for 1 month, and the patient had returned to Singapore 1 week prior to the admission. The patient had visited several rural areas in Kerala and Bangalore during his travel. There was no history of raw food intake or animal contact. His vaccinations were up-to-date according to the national immunization schedule, but he had not received the typhoid vaccine prior to travel. At this time, his 21-year-old older sister was also admitted to another hospital with fever and diarrhea. There was no prior treatment with antibiotics. No significant past illnesses were reported.
On admission, the child was alert and oriented and no pallor or jaundice was noted. Mucosal membranes appeared dry but perfusion was good with a capillary-refill time of less than 2 seconds. His temperature was 38.2 C, with a pulse rate of 150 bpm and a blood pressure of 90/48 mm Hg. On examination, his heart sounds were dual and breath sounds were vesicular, with no added sounds. His abdomen was soft, with mild tenderness over the right hypochondrium, and there was no guarding or rigidity. He had no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. There was no rash or eschar noted. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable. Heart rate and blood pressure responded well to a fluid bolus given in the emergency department and subsequently remained stable. He was started empirically on intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day for presumptive enteric fever.
The aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi, which were sensitive to ampicillin, co-trimoxazole and ceftriaxone. Widal Weil Felix (WWF) serology showed titers of 1/160 for S typhi O-AB, 1/640 for S typhi H-AB, 1/80 for Salmonella paratyphi A O-AB, 1/320 for S paratyphi A H-AB, and 1/80 for S paratyphi B O-AB. Proteus OXK AB and Proteus OX19 AB were not detected. The full blood count showed pancytopenia, with a hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dL, white blood cell count of 3.47 x 109/L and a platelet count of 90 x 109/L. Liver function tests revealed elevated transaminases with an alanine transaminase level of 188 U/L and an aspartate transaminase level of 186 U/L. An ultrasound of the abdomen showed cecal and terminal ileal bowel wall thickening with enlargement of mesenteric lymph nodes.
The patient continued to be persistently febrile despite 9 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Repeat blood cultures were negative for bacterial growth. Oral co-trimoxazole 4 mg/kg BD was added to provide added cover for typhoid fever. Table 1 shows the timeline of his hematological and biochemical investigations. Microbiological investigations performed are summarized in Table 2.
On day 16 of ceftriaxone and oral co-trimoxazole, the patient remained persistently febrile. Diarrhea was also persistent although noted to be on an improving trend. At this point, a further infective workup was done, which included blood film for malaria parasite, Rickettsia typhi serology and Orientia tsutsugamushi serology. Two days later, Orientia tsutsugamushi serology results returned positive at IgG >=64. The patient was started on oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole were stopped. Fever resolved on day 2 of doxycycline, and the patient was discharged after being afebrile for more than 24 hours, to complete a 7-day course of doxycycline. Subsequent follow-up revealed a well child with complete resolution of fever and symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-year-old Indian boy presented with prolonged fever of 1 month duration with temperatures exceeding 40 °C, accompanied by watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced prolonged fever for 1 month with maximum temperatures above 40 °C, associated with watery, nonbloody diarrhea, intermittent vomiting, and abdominal pain. His 21-year-old sister was concurrently hospitalized elsewhere with fever and diarrhea. No prior antibiotic therapy had been administered.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past illnesses. Vaccinations were up to date according to national schedule, but had not received travel-specific immunizations prior to departure. Travel history: 1-month travel to rural areas in Kerala and Bangalore, India, returning to Singapore 1 week prior to admission. Denied raw food intake or animal contact.
subjective.review_of_systems: Watery nonbloody diarrhea, intermittent vomiting, and abdominal pain as noted in HPI.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and oriented; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill time <2 seconds; no pallor or jaundice. Temperature: 38.2 °C, pulse rate: 150 bpm, blood pressure: 90/48 mmHg (stabilized after fluid bolus). Cardiovascular: dual heart sounds, no murmurs. Respiratory: vesicular breath sounds without added sounds. Abdomen: soft with mild tenderness over right hypochondrium; no guarding, rigidity, hepatomegaly, or splenomegaly. Skin: no rash or eschar noted.
objective.routine_investigations: Full blood count showed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, white blood cell count 3.47 x 10^9/L, platelet count 90 x 10^9/L. Liver function tests: ALT 188 U/L, AST 186 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound showed cecal and terminal ileal bowel wall thickening with mesenteric lymph node enlargement. Blood film for malaria parasite: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Proteus OXK AB and Proteus OX19 AB were not detected.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Typhoid fever (enteric fever) with concurrent Orientia tsutsugamushi (scrub typhus) coinfection. Aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures grew Salmonella typhi sensitive to ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, and ceftriaxone. Widal Weil Felix serology demonstrated titers of 1/160 for S. typhi O-AB, 1/640 for S. typhi H-AB, 1/80 for Salmonella paratyphi A O-AB, 1/320 for S. paratyphi A H-AB, and 1/80 for S. paratyphi B O-AB. He received empiric IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg/day, with oral co-trimoxazole 4 mg/kg twice daily added on day 9 for persistent fever (repeat blood cultures were negative). Due to fever persistence on day 16, Orientia tsutsugamushi serology was obtained and returned positive (IgG >=64; Rickettsia typhi serology was evaluated). Ceftriaxone and co-trimoxazole were stopped, and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily was initiated. Fever resolved on day 2 of doxycycline, and he completed a 7-day course with complete symptom resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 17-year-old boy living in a care home due to his cerebral palsy was referred to "Imam Khomeini Hospital Complex":a tertiary care educational hospital in Tehran, Iran:with a two-month history of fever, abdominal pain, and constipation. A VP shunt had been inserted for him at age four for treating hydrocephalus and subsequent refractory seizures. His recent symptoms had an intermittent pattern subsiding transiently with symptomatic therapies such as antipyretics and laxatives. Empiric antibiotics too, including parenteral ceftriaxone, were prescribed for the patient several times, but no response was achieved.
At presentation, the physical exam revealed a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg, a pulse rate of 100/min, a temperature of 38.5 C, and generalized tenderness in the abdominal palpation. The initial laboratory findings revealed increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) and a mild leukocytosis (Table 1).
Although physical examination was not compatible with peritonitis, we asked for a confirmatory abdominal X-ray which was unrevealing. The abdominal ultrasound done for more evaluation of pain showed a pseudocyst exactly at the distal end of the VP shunt. To evaluate the shunt infection, cerebrospinal fluid samples were taken from lumbar and shunt punctures and sent for analysis and culture simultaneously (Table 1). To rule out any possible contraindication for lumbar puncture (LP), we ordered a brain computed tomography (CT) scan without contrast which showed normal results for the patient and his history.
The analysis of CSF obtained from VP shunt reservoir and spinal canal was suggestive of a bacterial shunt infection (Table 1). Considering the previous antibiotic administration, and for the coverage of both Gram-positive and Gram-negative microorganisms, we treated the patient empirically with meropenem and vancomycin.
Five days later, the result of CSF and blood cultures (Bact/Alert 3D Microbial Identification System) was reported: Brucella spp. We then tested the blood for Wright, Coombs Wright, 2 Mercapto Ethanol agglutination test, and anti-Brucella IgG (ELISA), all of which were compatible with diagnosis of brucellosis (Table 1). Since this was an unusual result, we decided to take a more detailed history from the patient's caretakers. The notable finding was consumption of unpasteurized cheese before the symptoms had started.
According to abovementioned findings, anti-Brucella treatment with oral rifampicin (15 mg/kg), oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazol (5 mg/kg trimethoprim component twice a day) and parenteral ceftriaxone (1000 mg twice a day for covering CNS infection) was started for the patient with diagnosis of VP shunt infection with Brucella spp. Considering our patient's condition that suffered from cerebral palsy and could not take enough care against esophagitis as an adverse effect of doxycycline (one of the first line drugs in treating brucellosis), we avoided including this medication in our regimen.
As our hospital is one of the busiest centers in the country and our patient needed intensive care before and after any surgery, it took three weeks to replace his shunt with extraventricular drain (EVD). His EVD was removed after 5 days when CSF culture was negative, and our neurosurgeons inserted a new VP shunt for the patient. Following six weeks of triple therapy, the patient was discharged on oral antibiotic therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazol and rifampicin while he was fine and symptom-free. We planned to continue antibiotic therapy for six months and to have three follow-up visits during this period, after which a lumbar puncture will be done to confirm the disease has eradicated.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 17-year-old boy with cerebral palsy and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt presented with a 2-month history of intermittent fever, abdominal pain, and constipation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of intermittent fever, recurrent abdominal pain, and constipation. Symptoms transiently subsided with symptomatic therapies including antipyretics and laxatives. Multiple previous empiric courses of antibiotics, including parenteral ceftriaxone, failed to elicit a clinical response.
subjective.past_medical_history: Cerebral palsy, seizure disorder, and hydrocephalus status post ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement at age 4. Lives in a care home. Multiple prior courses of empiric antibiotics including IV ceftriaxone. Epidemiological exposure: caretakers disclosed history of consuming unpasteurized cheese prior to symptom onset.
subjective.review_of_systems: Abdominal pain, constipation, fever. Home medications: prior empiric antibiotics, antipyretics, and laxatives. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.5 °C, blood pressure: 90/60 mmHg, pulse rate: 100 beats/min. Abdomen: generalized tenderness to palpation without frank peritoneal signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Mild leukocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) (Table 1). Plain abdominal radiography: unrevealing. Abdominal ultrasonography: identified an abdominal pseudocyst located precisely at the distal peritoneal tip of the VP shunt.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT without contrast: compatible with baseline shunt-treated hydrocephalus with no acute intracranial process or contraindication to lumbar puncture. CSF analysis (from both VP shunt reservoir and lumbar puncture): pleocytosis and elevated protein consistent with bacterial shunt infection (Table 1).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Brucellar ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt infection with distal abdominal pseudocyst and bacteremia. Confirmed by CSF and blood cultures growing Brucella species on Bact/Alert 3D system, corroborated by positive Wright, Coombs Wright, 2-mercaptoethanol (2-ME), and anti-Brucella IgG ELISA serologies. Other pyogenic bacterial pathogens ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initial empiric vancomycin and meropenem were transitioned to targeted triple therapy: IV ceftriaxone (1000 mg twice daily), oral rifampicin (15 mg/kg/day), and oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (5 mg/kg trimethoprim component twice daily); doxycycline was deliberately avoided due to high esophagitis risk in severe cerebral palsy. VP shunt was externalized to an external ventricular drain (EVD) and subsequently revised with a new VP shunt once CSF cultures documented sterility. Following 6 weeks of initial therapy, patient was discharged symptom-free on oral rifampicin and TMP-SMX to complete a 6-month antimicrobial course.

raw_case_text:
A 5.5-year-old girl presented with six-day fever up to 38.5 C with spikes mostly in the afternoon, accompanied by pain at the right wrist joint and right elbow joint. The girl's parents are stockbreeders and homemade dairy products had been offered to the child. Three days prior to her admission in our department, she was examined in another hospital, where no remarkable findings from the joints or other systems were noted. As shown in Table 1, laboratory tests were white blood cells 7.2 x 109/L, platelets 180 x 109/L, hemoglobin 131 g/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 19 mm/h, C-reactive protein (CRP) 10 mg/L, monotest negative, alanine aminotransferase (AST) 62 U/L, positive Wright agglutination reaction (title 1/1280), and negative Rose Bengal. Based on the symptoms and the positive Wright reaction, treatment for brucellosis was initiated. Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) (10 mg/kg/day) and rifampicin (15 mg/kg/day) were administered orally.
On the third day of treatment, generalized purpuric lesions were noted accompanied with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 3 x 109/L) and the child was referred to our hospital.
