On admission the child was febrile (38.8 C) and generalized petechial/purpuric rash, bruising, wet purpura on the palate, and gingival bleeding were noted, while the spleen and the liver were palpable 2 cm below the subcostal margin at the midclavicular line. Examination of the joints and the other systems did not reveal any pathological signs.
Laboratory tests showed white blood cells 7.5 x 109/L (neutrophils 45%, lymphocytes 52%, and monocytes 3%), platelets 1 x 109/L, hemoglobin 120 g/L, ESR 15 mm/h, CRP 7 mg/L, AST 64 U/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 92 mumol/L, and total bilirubin 12 mumol/L. Wright agglutination reaction was positive (title 1/1280), as well as the specific IgM, IgA antibodies against Brucella melitensis. The specific IgG antibodies were negative. Blood cultures were sterile. Direct and indirect Coombs were negative. The quantification of immunoglobulins IgG, IgM, and IgA and complements C3 and C4 was within normal range. Antinuclear antibodies, anti-double stranded DNA antibodies, and rheumatoid factor were negative, while the antiplatelet antibody test was positive. Clotting time and fibrinogen were normal (Table 1).
Due to the very low platelet count and the mucous membrane hemorrhage, treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (1 gr/kg/day for two days) was initiated, combined with antibiotic therapy with amikacin intravenously (15 mg/kg/day for seven days) and oral rifampicin. TMP/SMX treatment was stopped due to the suspicion of drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
The patient responded with a gradual increase in the number of platelets up to 218 x 109/L five days after treatment. At this stage, oral TMP/SMX administration was reinitiated, without any negative effect on the platelet count. On the contrary, a rise in platelet number up to 503 x 109/L was observed. Fever resolved at the second day of treatment and no new bleeding manifestations appeared. The patient was discharged with rifampicin and TMP/SMX as maintenance therapy for a total six-week treatment. She completed the treatment without further complications and during the regular follow-up platelet counts were normal (Table 1).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5.5-year-old girl presented with a 6-day history of fever up to 38.5 °C, right wrist and right elbow joint pain, and acute onset of generalized purpuric rash and mucosal bleeding.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 6-day history of fever up to 38.5 °C with afternoon spikes, accompanied by pain in the right wrist and right elbow joints. Three days prior to admission, she was evaluated at an outside hospital, found to have joint pain and initiated on oral trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) and rifampicin. On the third day of treatment, she developed generalized purpuric lesions and severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 3 x 109/L), prompting referral with active mucosal bleeding (palatal wet purpura and gingival bleeding).
subjective.past_medical_history: Evaluated at an outside hospital 3 days prior to admission where no initial joint or systemic findings were noted; started on oral TMP/SMX and rifampicin. Epidemiological history: parents are stockbreeders, and the child was fed homemade unpasteurized dairy products.
subjective.review_of_systems: Petechial/purpuric rash, bruising, wet purpura on palate, gingival bleeding, right wrist and elbow arthralgia. Home medications: TMP/SMX (10 mg/kg/day) and rifampicin (15 mg/kg/day). Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.8 °C. Skin and mucous membranes: generalized petechial/purpuric rash, bruising, wet purpura on the palate, and gingival bleeding. Abdomen: spleen and liver palpable 2 cm below the subcostal margin at the midclavicular line (hepatosplenomegaly). Examination of the joints and other systems revealed no pathological signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Outside hospital labs: WBC 7.2 x 109/L, platelets 180 x 109/L, hemoglobin 131 g/L, ESR 19 mm/h, CRP 10 mg/L, AST 62 U/L, Monotest negative. Admission labs: WBC 7.5 x 109/L (45% neutrophils, 52% lymphocytes, 3% monocytes), platelets 1 x 109/L, hemoglobin 120 g/L, ESR 15 mm/h, CRP 7 mg/L, AST 64 U/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 92 mumol/L, total bilirubin 12 mumol/L. Coagulation: clotting time and fibrinogen normal. Autoimmune and serology: direct and indirect Coombs tests negative; IgG, IgM, IgA, C3, and C4 normal; ANA, anti-dsDNA, and rheumatoid factor negative; antiplatelet antibody test was positive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute brucellosis complicated by severe immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and peripheral arthritis. Confirmed by Wright agglutination reaction positive at 1/1280 titer (Rose Bengal negative initially), and positive specific IgM and IgA antibodies against Brucella melitensis (specific IgG negative). Blood cultures were sterile. Autoimmune vasculitis, EBV mononucleosis, and consumptive coagulopathy ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initial TMP/SMX was withheld due to suspicion of drug-induced thrombocytopenia. Treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 1 g/kg/day for 2 days), IV amikacin (15 mg/kg/day for 7 days), and oral rifampicin (15 mg/kg/day). Platelet count increased to 218 x 109/L after 5 days. Oral TMP/SMX was safely reintroduced without adverse effect on platelets, which rose to 503 x 109/L. Fever resolved on day 2. Discharged on oral rifampicin and TMP/SMX to complete a 6-week course with complete recovery and normal platelet counts on follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 26-year-old man with a past medical history of unspecified hepatomegaly at birth, and alcohol use disorder since he was 20 years of age, went to the Emergency Department complaining of 5 days of throbbing headache, arthralgias, myalgias, and a documented fever (40.4 C) that partially improves with ibuprofen and with no response to paracetamol.
The clinical course was exacerbated on day 2 of the initiation of symptoms by crampy (colicky) abdominal pain in the epigastrium with radiation to the right upper quadrant, accompanied by nausea and vomiting.
Admission physical exam revealed blood pressure (BP) of 120/90 mmHg, heart rate (HR) of 56 bpm, respiratory rate (RR) of 20 rpm, oxygen saturation of 97% in room air, and temperature of 36.6 C. Disseminated petechiae were observed on the patient's face, trunk, and extremities. Cardiac and lung exams revealed normal heart sounds, without rhythm alterations, no murmurs, and lung fields were clear, without wheezing, rhonchi, rales, or crepitus. Examination of the abdomen revealed scattered petechiae, increased abdominal perimeter (95 centimetres), tenderness to palpation in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, without hepatosplenomegaly, and no guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds were present. The pulses in the extremities were regular, and there was no edema.
Laboratory tests (Table 1) performed on the patient's hospital admission revealed a hematocrit of 49%, platelet count of 23.000, C-reactive protein (CRP) of 29.2, glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (GOT) of 747 U/L, glutamic pyruvic transaminase (GPT) of 509 U/L, amylase of 229 U/L, lipase of 258 U/L, gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) of 604 U/L, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 208 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) of 995 U/L, and lactic acid of 3.4 mmol/l, triglycerides of 267 mg/dl, cholesterol of 158 mg/dl, mild hypophosphatemia of 2.4 mg/dl, and albumin of 3.7 g/dl and glucose of 112 mg/dl.
Ultrasonography of the abdomen revealed an enlarged liver, with increased diffuse echogenicity and reinforcement of the periportal vessels, homogeneous structure, and fluid at the level of the left hepatic border that extended to Morrison's space. Gallbladder with walls of normal thickness, without endoluminal images, nondilated bile ducts, slightly hypoechoic pancreas, preserved shape and structure, and scant perisplenic fluid, slight bilateral pleural effusion associated with a consolidation process with air bronchogram was also seen.
Having ruled out the biliary cause of pancreatitis and searching for other causes, there were no calcium abnormalities, hypertriglyceridemia, endocrine abnormalities, or use of drugs associated with pancreatitis. Due to a history of fever and being a resident of an endemic area of the dengue virus, a viral panel was requested, resulting in positive IgM and IgG antibodies for dengue, with negative NS1 antigen (Table 2), qualifying it as dengue with warning signs.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old male presenting with high fever (40.4 °C), throbbing headache, arthralgia, and myalgia for five days, with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 26-year-old male presented with a 5-day history of throbbing headache, arthralgias, myalgias, and high fever (40.4 °C) partially responsive to ibuprofen and unresponsive to paracetamol. On illness day 2, he developed severe crampy epigastric pain radiating to the right upper quadrant, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Hospital evaluation revealed acute pancreatitis and acute hepatitis alongside petechial rash and hemoconcentration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unspecified hepatomegaly at birth; alcohol use disorder since age 20. Resident of a tropical arbovirus-endemic area.
subjective.review_of_systems: Crampy epigastric and right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting; absence of hematemesis or melena.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 120/90 mmHg, heart rate 56 beats/min (bradycardia), respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on room air. Dermatologic: Disseminated petechiae over face, trunk, and extremities. Cardiopulmonary: Normal heart sounds, lungs clear bilaterally without crackles or wheezing. Abdomen: Increased abdominal girth (95 cm), scattered petechiae, exquisite tenderness to palpation in epigastrium and right upper quadrant, without hepatosplenomegaly, guarding, or rebound tenderness; normal bowel sounds. Extremities: Peripheral pulses regular, no peripheral edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: Hematocrit 49% (hemoconcentration), platelet count 23,000/microL, CRP 29.2 mg/L, GOT/AST 747 U/L, GPT/ALT 509 U/L, amylase 229 U/L, lipase 258 U/L, GGT 604 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 208 U/L, LDH 995 U/L, lactic acid 3.4 mmol/L, triglycerides 267 mg/dL, cholesterol 158 mg/dL, serum phosphorus 2.4 mg/dL, albumin 3.7 g/dL, glucose 112 mg/dL. Abdominal and thoracic ultrasound: Enlarged liver with increased diffuse echogenicity and periportal cuffing/vessel reinforcement; free fluid along the left hepatic border extending to Morison's pouch; gallbladder of normal wall thickness without gallstones; non-dilated intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts; slightly hypoechoic pancreas with preserved parenchymal shape; scant perisplenic fluid; mild bilateral pleural effusions with consolidation and air bronchograms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (dengue with warning signs and severe plasma leakage) complicated by acute pancreatitis (elevated lipase and amylase), acute hepatitis, and polyserositis (ascites and bilateral pleural effusions). Confirmed by positive Dengue IgM and IgG antibodies by viral panel (with negative NS1 antigen). Biliary obstruction, choledocholithiasis, severe hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, drug-induced pancreatitis, and alcoholic pancreatitis etiologies were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Inpatient admission for guided intravenous fluid resuscitation, multimodal analgesia, pancreatic rest, gastroprotection, and close monitoring of hematological and hemodynamic parameters.

raw_case_text: This 57-year-old man was referred for a 2-month history of progressive development of imbalance, dizziness, and vomiting. On examination, he presented with wide-based gait, uncoordinated limb movements, and nystagmus on extreme gaze. Radiological investigations disclosed two bilateral hemispheric cerebellar lesions, suggestive of metastases [Figure 1]. On April 2020, he was then admitted to the C. Besta Neurological Institute (Milan, Italy), which was appointed as reference center for the treatment of neurooncological patients from other departments in Lombardy during the COVID-19 emergency period. In line with our triage protocol, the patient performed a nasopharyngeal swab for viral RNA of SARS-CoV-2 detection with reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) by Allplex  2019-nCoV Assay (Seegene Inc., Seoul, Korea) for amplification of RdRP, N and E genes. The test was positive and SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed. The patient had a history of family exposure (the two daughters tested positive) and reported in the previous month only hyposmia and hypogeusia without rhinorrhea or nasal obstruction, which had resolved at the time of admission. Blood tests at admission revealed no significant abnormalities. A chest computed tomography (CT) reported a left pulmonary lesion suggestive of tumor in the absence of inflammatory changes [Figure 2]. According to our classification of urgency in category A+, meaning patients with intracranial tumors with mass effect or with progressive neurological deficit, without deterioration of consciousness, for which treatment is deferred for up to 10 days, two swabs were resampled after 7 days and both were still positive. Considering the neurological and radiological stability, it was established to perform three new swabs after a period of 7 days with negative results, leading the way to surgery. The two cerebellar lesions were then surgically removed with a pathological result of pulmonary adenocarcinoma metastases. In the early post-operative period, the patient manifested acute onset of psychotic symptoms with hyperactive delirium. He was admitted to the intensive care unit, and antipsychotic therapy was administered with quetiapine (up to 1 g/day); chlorpromazine and sedation with propofol and dexmedetomidine until control of the neuropsychiatric picture were obtained. Four days after surgery, the patient suddenly developed fever (up to 38.5 C) and acute respiratory failure. Another chest CT scan disclosed a radiological pattern of ground-glass opacities in the lower lobes bilaterally, suggesting a viral pneumonia [Figure 2]. Laboratory findings revealed an increased inflammatory response with higher white blood cell counts (15.94 x 109/L), higher neutrophil counts (14.54 x 109/L), lower lymphocyte counts (0.79 x 109/L), lower platelet count (66 x 109/L), increased D-dimer (1.77 mg/L), and C-reactive protein (229.8 mg/L) levels. Serological tests were performed using LIAISON  SARSCoV-2 S1/S2 IgG kit (Diasorin S.p.A, Saluggia, Italy), an indirect chemiluminescent immunoassay serology test for detecting IgG antibodies against S1/S2 antigens. An antibody level of 133 kAU/L was found (positive: >15.0 kAU/L). The RT-PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab was negative. Under the strong radiological and laboratory suspicion of pneumonia from COVID-19, a new RT-PCR was performed after 72 h which confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. Oxygen therapy with alternating cycles of high-flow nasal cannula and low-flow venturi mask was administered until full recovery.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 57-year-old male presenting with a 2-month history of progressive imbalance, dizziness, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-month history of progressive dizziness, gait imbalance, and vomiting secondary to intracranial mass lesions. Following admission and neurosurgical resection of cerebellar metastases, he developed acute hyperactive delirium in the early postoperative period. Four days after surgery, he developed sudden-onset high fever up to 38.5 °C and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Bilateral hemispheric cerebellar metastases secondary to a primary left pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Epidemiological exposure: Household contact with symptomatic sick contacts (two daughters tested positive for viral infection). Transient hyposmia and hypogeusia without rhinorrhea or nasal obstruction one month prior to admission, resolved upon presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Admission neurological examination: Wide-based gait, uncoordinated limb movements, and nystagmus on extreme gaze. Postoperative evaluation: Body temperature up to 38.5 °C, acute respiratory failure, and hyperactive delirium with psychotic features.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission blood tests: No significant abnormalities. Postoperative acute respiratory failure labs: White blood cell count 15.94 x 10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count 14.54 x 10^9/L, absolute lymphocyte count 0.79 x 10^9/L, platelet count 66 x 10^9/L, D-dimer 1.77 mg/L, C-reactive protein 229.8 mg/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Preoperative neuroimaging: Two bilateral hemispheric cerebellar lesions suggestive of metastases. Admission chest CT: Left pulmonary lesion suggestive of neoplasm without inflammatory changes. Postoperative chest CT: Bilateral ground-glass opacities in the lower lobes suggestive of viral pneumonia. Histopathology: Metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma confirmed from resected cerebellar lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (COVID-19 pneumonia) confirmed by repeat nasopharyngeal RT-PCR 72 hours postoperatively following an initial negative postoperative test (with preoperative positive screening swabs and positive SARS-CoV-2 S1/S2 IgG antibody titer of 133 kAU/L [cutoff > 15.0 kAU/L]).
Plan & Outcome: Postoperative delirium was treated with quetiapine (up to 1 g/day), chlorpromazine, and sedation with propofol and dexmedetomidine. Acute respiratory failure was managed with oxygen therapy using alternating cycles of high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) and low-flow Venturi mask until achieving full clinical recovery.

raw_case_text: A 13-month-old male child from Koraput district, Orissa, was diagnosed to have malaria with smear positive for PF. He was treated with a 3-day course of oral artesunate-SP. In view of persistent fever and failure of parasite clearance after 3 days, he was administered second course of 3 days oral artesunate-SP. He was referred to our hospital in view of severe anemia and persistence of ring forms of PF in blood smear. He was started on parenteral quinine along with clindamycin and a dose of primaquine was administered. Serial peripheral smears were performed which showed parasitological clearance after 48 h of initiating therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 13-month-old male infant presenting with persistent fever and severe pallor following two courses of antimalarial therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child presented with persistent fever and failure of parasite clearance after completing a 3-day course of oral artesunate-sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine, followed by a second 3-day course of the same regimen. He was referred to tertiary care due to worsening severe anemia and persistent fever.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Koraput district, Orissa, India. Received two consecutive 3-day courses of oral artesunate-sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine prior to referral.

objective.physical_examination: Persistent fever and severe clinical pallor on physical examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Severe anemia documented on laboratory evaluation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Artesunate-resistant Plasmodium falciparum malaria with persistent parasitemia and severe anemia (treatment failure after two courses of oral artesunate-SP). Peripheral blood smears confirmed persistence of P. falciparum ring forms.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on parenteral quinine combined with clindamycin, along with a single dose of primaquine. Serial peripheral blood smears documented complete parasitological clearance within 48 hours of starting therapy.

raw_case_text:
A forty-year-old housewife, from a very low socio-economic status group, presented with history of gradually progressive weakness of left lower limb of 6 months duration, rapidly progressive weakness of right lower limb of 8 days duration and urinary incontinence of 6 months duration. She had been living near a very unhygienic abattoir and admitted to drinking unpasteurised goat's milk. There was history of fever on and off with night sweats. There was no history trauma or past history of tuberculosis. On examination, she was moderately built and nourished. General physical examination was normal. She was febrile with a temperature of 99 F (37.2 C). Vital parameters were normal. Neurologically she was conscious, alert and orientated. Cranial nerve examination was normal. There was no papilledema and meningeal signs were absent. She had flaccid areflexic paraplegia with power 0/5 (MRC grade). She had impaired sensations in both lower limbs with a level at T10. Perianal sensations were impaired and she had poor anal tone. Routine haematological parameters revealed a total white blood cell (WBC) count of 13,980/cu mm with neutrophil predominance. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate ESR (Westergreen) was 50 mm in 1 hour. Standard agglutination test (tube) titer was 1:320 and 2-mercaptoethanol agglutination test titer was 1:80. Plain radiograph of lumbosacral spine was normal. MRI scan of the spine showed a lesion in the spinal cord extending from lower part of T12 to L2. It was hyper-intense on T1WI and iso-intense on T2WI There was cord edema extending cranially up to T10 (figure 1).
She underwent T11 to L3 laminectomy. The lower end of the cord and the conus medullaris were swollen and the cauda equina nerve roots were pushed to the right side. Myelotomy was done at the conus level. At a depth of about 0.5 cm, purulent fluid was encountered, which was sent immediately for microbiological analysis. Under operating microscope the abscess cavity was visualized through the limited myelotomy (fig 2). The abscess was completely evacuated, after which the cord and conus had become lax and pulsating well. Dura was closed completely.
Pus revealed gram-negative bacilli. It was inoculated aerobically [Brucella agar, chocolate and MacConkey media], and anaerobically [Kanamycin-vancomycin laked sheep blood agar (KVLB) and Bacteroides bile esculin agar (BBE)]. Brucella agar and CA were incubated in CO2 jar and after 2 days minute translucent colonies were seen. Gram stain from culture showed gram-negative bacilli. Oxidase, catalase, and urease test were positive. There was no H2S production and it was resistant to dye inhibition. The organism was confirmed as Brucella melitensis . The organism isolated in blood culture taken preoperatively, also was identified as Brucella melitensis.
Postoperatively she had fever, headaches and vomiting lasting for about 1 week. It subsided once antibiotics were instituted. She was started on injection streptomycin 1 gm once a day for 1 month with oral doxycycline 100 mgm twice a day for 1 month. After one month she received oral rifampicin 450 mgm once a day with oral doxycycline 100 mgm twice a day for 1 month. Dexamethasone was given only perioperatively and was rapidly tapered and stopped in the post-operative period. Post operatively she gradually improved in neurological status. At 2-year follow up she had grade 3/5 power in both lower limbs and was mobilising on a wheel chair. The urinary symptoms did not resolve and she continues to be on Foley catheter. She refused a repeat MRI scan, as she could not afford it.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old female presented with progressive weakness of the left lower limb and urinary incontinence of 6 months duration, and rapidly progressive weakness of the right lower limb of 8 days duration.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed insidious, progressive weakness in her left lower limb accompanied by urinary incontinence 6 months prior to presentation. Eight days prior to admission, she experienced rapidly progressive weakness in her right lower limb, leaving her bedbound. She also noted intermittent fevers accompanied by night sweats. She denied any history of trauma.
subjective.past_medical_history: Housewife of low socioeconomic status living near an unhygienic abattoir. Dietary exposure: regular consumption of unpasteurized goat's milk. Denied history of trauma or past history of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports intermittent fever and night sweats. Denies trauma or history of tuberculosis.

objective.physical_examination: Moderately built and nourished; febrile with temperature of 99 °F (37.2 °C); vital parameters otherwise normal. Neurological: conscious, alert, and oriented; cranial nerves intact; no papilledema; meningeal signs absent. Motor: flaccid areflexic paraplegia with muscle power 0/5 (MRC grade) in both lower limbs. Sensory: impaired sensation in both lower limbs with a sensory level at T10; impaired perianal sensation and poor anal sphincter tone.
objective.routine_investigations: Total white blood cell (WBC) count: 13,980/cu mm with neutrophil predominance; erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, Westergren): 50 mm in 1 hour. Plain radiograph of the lumbosacral spine was normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Spinal MRI showed an intramedullary lesion extending from the lower part of T12 to L2, hyperintense on T1WI and isointense on T2WI, with surrounding cord edema extending cranially up to T10. Surgical exploration via T11-L3 laminectomy revealed a swollen lower spinal cord and conus medullaris with cauda equina roots displaced to the right; myelotomy at the conus level drained purulent fluid from an intramedullary abscess cavity at 0.5 cm depth.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Standard tube agglutination test titer was 1:320 and 2-mercaptoethanol agglutination test titer was 1:80. Smear of intramedullary pus showed gram-negative bacilli. Culture on Brucella agar and chocolate agar grew minute translucent colonies after 2 days; biochemical testing revealed oxidase-positive, catalase-positive, urease-positive, negative H2S production, and resistance to dye inhibition, confirming Brucella melitensis. Preoperative blood culture also grew Brucella melitensis, confirming intramedullary spinal cord abscess and neurobrucellosis. Tuberculosis was excluded clinically and microbiologically. Management and Outcome: Complete surgical evacuation of the abscess was performed via T11-L3 laminectomy and conus myelotomy. Postoperative fever, headache, and vomiting resolved with antimicrobial therapy. Regimen consisted of intramuscular streptomycin 1 g once daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 1 month, followed by oral rifampicin 450 mg once daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 1 month; perioperative dexamethasone was rapidly tapered and discontinued. At 2-year follow-up, motor strength improved to grade 3/5 bilaterally and she was wheelchair-mobile, with persistent neurogenic bladder requiring long-term Foley catheterization.

raw_case_text: A 41-year-old, White British, man who has sex with men (MSM) presented complaining of drenching night sweats and fatigue of recent onset. He reported unprotected oral and anal intercourse with casual partners and had recently been diagnosed with hepatitis C virus (HCV). He gave no travel history of note. He was diagnosed with and treated for early, secondary syphilis. His HCV genotype was 1a (HCV RNA: 3.87 x 104 copies/mL) and his HIV serology testing was negative. Four weeks later, he presented with night sweats, anorexia and dysphagia. Oesophageal candidiasis was suspected and treated with fluconazole 50 mg once daily for seven days. HIV-1 antibodies were positive (HIV viral load [VL]: 10 million copies/mL, Log10 >5.8, CD4 count: 263 x 106/L, 21%). Acute HIV sero-conversion syndrome was diagnosed. Sequencing of protease (PR) and first 234 amino acids of the reverse transcriptase (RT) genes indicated a fully antiretroviral-susceptible HIV-1 subtype B strain with minor PR and RT differences to the HIV reference strain HXB2 (K20R, E35D, N37E, L63P; V8I, V90I, I142T, S162D, I178M). HCV RNA was undetectable, suggesting spontaneous clearance of the HCV. Sixteen weeks later, despite initial recovery, the CD4 had declined to 185 x 106/L (12%). The HIV-1 VL was 167,200 copies/mL (Log10 5.2). Abacavir, lamivudine and nevirapine were commenced and the VL suppressed to 270 copies /mL (Log10 2.4) at 12 weeks. Four weeks later, the patient presented feeling unwell with night sweats. On examination, he had right-sided inguinal lymphadenopathy and enlarged liver and a palpable spleen. A pale macular rash was visible on the trunk and extremities. He was diagnosed with rectal Neisseria gonorrhoeae and urethral Chlamydia trachomatis, his HCV RNA remained negative. However, the HIV VL had risen to 14,900 copies/ml (Log10 4.2) despite good reported adherence and tolerance. HIV genotyping revealed HIV-1 subtype B with multiple new mutations: PR: K14R, R83K, RT: A98S, K101E, M184I, G190A, T215D, I135T, D177E, I178L, V179I, T200A, I202V, Q207K, R211K. This virus, showed high-level resistance to lamivudine and nevirapine and low-level resistance to abacavir. The sequences were highly divergent exhibiting 45 nucleotide differences of which 20 were non-synonymous including the four resistance-associated mutations (Figure 1). Considering the history of repeated unprotected sex and co-infections with sexually transmitted infections together with the number of changes in non-resistance mutations HIV superinfection was suspected. This was confirmed by phylogenetic analysis. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) was changed to abacavir, lamivudine, zidovudine and boosted atazanavir. The HIV VL was <50 copies/mL (log10 1.6) within three weeks. Fifteen months later, routine tests revealed newly raised AST (73IU/L) and bilirubin (89 micromol/L) levels and HCV RNA levels of 2.6 x 106 copies/mL. The two HCV strains were identical in the 135 base region of the 5' NCR. Considering the previous HCV RNA negative tests and ongoing unprotected sex, HCV reinfection was thought to be more likely than reactivation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 41-year-old male presenting with drenching night sweats and fatigue of recent onset.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with recent-onset drenching night sweats and fatigue following high-risk sexual exposures. Four weeks after an initial presentation where viral serology was negative, he developed recurrent night sweats, anorexia, and dysphagia. Following initial stabilization and antiretroviral therapy initiation, he re-presented 16 weeks later with malaise, night sweats, and a new cutaneous rash accompanied by acute urethral and rectal symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Hepatitis C virus (HCV genotype 1a, HCV RNA: 3.87 x 10^4 copies/mL) with spontaneous clearance; early secondary syphilis (treated). Epidemiological risk: Man who has sex with men (MSM) reporting unprotected oral and anal intercourse with casual partners; denied travel history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Drenching night sweats, fatigue, anorexia, dysphagia, rectal discharge, and urethral discharge.

objective.physical_examination: Right-sided inguinal lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, palpable spleen, and a pale macular rash visible on the trunk and extremities.
objective.routine_investigations: Liver biochemistry: Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 73 IU/L, total bilirubin 89 micromol/L. Serial HCV RNA was undetectable during initial monitoring.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute HIV-1 infection (subtype B) followed by documented HIV-1 superinfection with a drug-resistant strain, co-occurring with rectal Neisseria gonorrhoeae, urethral Chlamydia trachomatis, and late HCV reinfection.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Initial seroconversion confirmed by positive HIV-1 antibodies, plasma HIV-1 RNA > 10,000,000 copies/mL (Log10 > 5.8), and CD4 count 263 x 10^6/L (21%), with baseline sequencing demonstrating a fully susceptible subtype B strain with minor polymorphisms (PR: K20R, E35D, N37E, L63P; RT: V8I, V90I, I142T, S162D, I178M). Superinfection confirmed by viral rebound to 14,900 copies/mL (Log10 4.2) and emergence of 45 divergent nucleotide substitutions (20 non-synonymous) including high-level resistance mutations to lamivudine and nevirapine and low-level resistance to abacavir (PR: K14R, R83K; RT: A98S, K101E, M184I, G190A, T215D, I135T, D177E, I178L, V179I, T200A, I202V, Q207K, R211K), confirmed by phylogenetic tree analysis. STI testing confirmed rectal gonorrhea and urethral chlamydia. Late HCV reinfection confirmed at 15 months with AST 73 IU/L, bilirubin 89 micromol/L, and HCV RNA 2.6 x 10^6 copies/mL.
Plan & Outcome: Suspected esophageal candidiasis treated with fluconazole 50 mg daily for 7 days. Initial ART of abacavir, lamivudine, and nevirapine was modified upon superinfection to abacavir, lamivudine, zidovudine, and boosted atazanavir, achieving rapid suppression to < 50 copies/mL (Log10 1.6) within 3 weeks. STI coinfections were treated.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male patient with a previous history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), diagnosed six years ago but had stopped had treatment approximately five years ago, was hospitalized with clinical and epidemiological diagnosis of arbovirus infection (fever, asthenia, myalgia and arthralgia). On admission, thrombocytopenia (12,000/mm3) and anemia (8.0 g/dL) were observed (Table 1). Oral corticosteroid therapy was started with prednisone 1 mg/kg/day. On the third day of hospitalization, he had headache with vomiting, associated with mental confusion and, subsequently, motor aphasia and right hemiplegia. Considering the sudden worsening of the patient's overall conditions, he was referred to the intensive care unit. Nuclear magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed to rule out acute ischemic or hemorrhagic events. The neuroimaging examination showed no alterations. Faced with an acute neurological worsening, the possibility of TTP was considered. Analysis of the peripheral smear showed innumerable schizocytes, confirming the presence of TMA. Plasmapheresis and pulse therapy with methylprednisolone were started due to the hypothesis of TTP.
Serological results were IgM positive for chikungunya and dengue viruses, and initially, the presence of IgG only raised to chikungunya virus (Euroimmun Medizinische Labordiagnostika, Lubeck, Germany). Serological tests for hepatitis virus B and C were negative, as well as for retroviruses (only HIV). Regarding retroviruses, other representatives are not routinely investigated and, in this case, they were not suspected. The patient also had negative results for antinuclear antibody (ANA) (Table 2). During the follow-up, serological results for dengue and chikungunya were confirmed, at this time showing the presence of IgG antibodies to chikungunya as well as to dengue virus. The serological test for zika virus was not performed following guidelines from Brazilian Ministry of Health, which recommend not to test zika virus when serological tests for dengue and chikungunya are positive.
There was a decrease in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) (Table 1). Plasmapheresis was maintained until platelet counts remained higher than 150,000 for three consecutive days (Figure 1). Complete remission of neurological signs occurred after the first plasmapheresis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male with a history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura presenting with acute fever, asthenia, myalgia, arthralgia, severe thrombocytopenia, and anemia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 28-year-old male with a history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) diagnosed 6 years prior presented with acute fever, asthenia, myalgia, and arthralgia. On hospital day 3, while receiving oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day), he developed acute headache, vomiting, mental confusion, and rapidly progressed to motor aphasia and right hemiplegia. Emergent peripheral smear revealed abundant schistocytes, prompting ICU transfer for suspected thrombotic microangiopathy.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) diagnosed 6 years prior, discontinued treatment approximately 5 years prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, asthenia, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, vomiting, confusion, aphasia, and right hemiplegia. Home medications: none prior to admission. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological examination on hospital day 3: Mental confusion, expressive motor aphasia, and right-sided hemiplegia. Following the first session of plasmapheresis, neurological signs exhibited complete remission.
objective.routine_investigations: On admission: Platelet count 12,000/mm3, hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL. Peripheral blood smear: Innumerable schistocytes, confirming thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). Serum LDH: Markedly elevated, declining with therapy. Serology: Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: Normal without evidence of acute infarction, hemorrhage, or intracranial mass lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) / secondary thrombotic microangiopathy triggered by acute co-infection with Dengue and Chikungunya viruses in a patient with underlying ITP. Diagnostic confirmation: Serology positive for Dengue virus IgM (with subsequent IgG seroconversion) and Chikungunya virus IgM and IgG; peripheral smear demonstrating innumerable schistocytes and elevated LDH; exclusion of viral hepatitis, HIV, and SLE.
Plan & Outcome: Managed in ICU with pulse methylprednisolone therapy and daily therapeutic plasma exchange (plasmapheresis). Achieved complete neurological recovery following the initial plasma exchange session. Plasmapheresis was discontinued after platelet counts sustained >150,000/mm3 for three consecutive days, leading to full clinical and hematological recovery.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old Latinx male with known HIV, diagnosed 6 years prior and nonadherent with his ART for over 2 years presented to the emergency department with persistent fevers, bilateral flank pain, nausea, and vomiting for 5 days. Social history revealed a male who has sex with male both insertive and receptive and significant alcohol abuse. He denied any travel outside of the United States or exposure to any animals.
Upon further questioning, the patient revealed a similar constellation of symptoms of fever and abdominal pain 3 years ago, was found to have pancytopenia and generalized lymphadenopathy, and admitted to an outside facility. At that time, a left axillary lymph node biopsy was performed which revealed benign lymphoid hyperplasia with no malignancy and a right inguinal lymph node excisional biopsy that revealed fibroadipose tissue with focal lymphoid hyperplasia. Flow cytometry of the samples showed many lymphoid cells but no evidence of monoclonality in B cell population. A bone marrow biopsy showed slightly hypocellular marrow with no evidence of lymphoma or myelodysplastic syndrome. His symptoms improved after he became adherent to his ART.
Upon this presentation, vital signs were significant for a temperature of 38.8 C, blood pressure of 161/96 mm Hg, heart rate of 145 beats per minute, and respiratory rate of 22 breaths per minute. Examination showed hepatosplenomegaly, and nontender axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
Laboratory work up revealed pancytopenia, high HIV viral load, elevated sedimentation rate, positive cytomegalovirus (CMV) immunoglobulin G (IgG) and ParvoB19 IgG, and negative CMV and Parvo B19 DNA polymerase chain reaction (Table 1). Patient was empirically started on broad spectrum antibiotics but continued to have fevers. A decision to discontinue antibiotics was made when all cultures continued to remain negative. Imagings were significant for bilateral diffuse axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly (Figures 1-4).
Differential diagnosis at this time remained very broad from infectious etiologies including viral, fungal, mycobacterial, or parasitic on one side, and AIDS-associated malignancies such as lymphoma on the other side.
His CD4 cell count came back as 27 cells/microL (6%) and HIV viral load of 98 200 copies/mL. HIV genotype results showed no transmissible resistance, so he was restarted on his previous ART regimen with Bictegravir/Emtricitabine/Tenofovir AF (Biktarvy).
Bone marrow biopsy and aspirate showed normocellular marrow with megakaryocytic hyperplasia, decreased iron, no evidence of acid-fast or fungal organisms, pancytopenia, and no evidence of parvovirus or malignancy. CT-guided right inguinal lymph node core biopsy resulted in scant fragments of lymphoid and fibrous tissue and was nondiagnostic.
His hospital course was complicated with clostridioides difficile colitis with diarrhea, which resolved with oral vancomycin therapy.
After a nonrevealing exhausting work up, the decision was made to perform a right inguinal excisional biopsy. Histopathology showed interfollicular plasma cells and germinal centers with vascularization and "onion-skin" hyaline vascular appearance. HHV-8 immunostaining showed presence of HHV-8 (Figures 5-7). Serum revealed an elevated level of HHV-8 of 2 288 277 copies/mL (nmL <1000). Therefore, a diagnosis of HHV-8-associated MCD was reached.
The patient was started on 6 cycle of rituximab chemotherapy and transitioned to outpatient therapy. He improved clinically. Positron emission tomography (PET) scan showed decreased splenomegaly from 17 to 15 cm in axial dimension and diminished his diffuse lymphadenopathy. He also responded to ART and his HIV viral load dropped to 40 copies/mL.
Three months later, he became nonadherent to his ART due to heavy alcohol abuse. He was readmitted due to jaundice and fever and found to have elevated bilirubin and transaminases with negative work up for biliary obstruction and bacterial cholangitis. Due to fever, recurrence of pancytopenia and high index of suspicious for recurrence of MCD, he was restarted on another 8 cycles of weekly rituximab followed by doxorubicin liposomal. He was also placed back on his previous ART.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presenting with persistent fevers, bilateral flank pain, nausea, and vomiting for five days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 5-day history of persistent high-grade fevers, bilateral flank pain, nausea, and emesis. Three years prior, he experienced a similar syndrome of fever, abdominal pain, pancytopenia, and generalized lymphadenopathy that resolved following compliance with antiretroviral medications. During the current admission, his course was complicated by healthcare-associated diarrhea secondary to Clostridioides difficile colitis, which resolved with oral vancomycin. Three months post-discharge, he developed recurrent fever, jaundice, and cytopenias in the setting of heavy alcohol intake.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying chronic retroviral infection diagnosed six years prior, with medication non-adherence for over two years; prior generalized lymphadenopathy and pancytopenia three years prior with non-malignant lymph node biopsies (benign lymphoid hyperplasia) and bone marrow evaluation. Social history: Men who have sex with men (MSM); significant chronic alcohol abuse; denies travel outside the United States or animal exposures.
subjective.review_of_systems: Persistent fevers, bilateral flank and abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea; denies focal cough or dysuria.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals: Body temperature 38.8 °C, blood pressure 161/96 mmHg, pulse rate 145 beats/min (marked tachycardia), respiratory rate 22 breaths/min. Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly. Lymphatics: Diffuse, nontender bilateral axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Severe pancytopenia. Inflammatory markers: Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Serology & Virology: CMV IgG and Parvovirus B19 IgG positive; CMV DNA PCR and Parvovirus B19 DNA PCR negative; bacterial and fungal blood cultures sterile. Stool testing: Positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin.
objective.advanced_workup: CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis: Marked bilateral diffuse axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy and pronounced hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy: Normocellular marrow with megakaryocytic hyperplasia, decreased iron stores, absence of acid-fast or fungal pathogens, and no malignancy. Percutaneous core needle biopsy of right inguinal lymph node: Scant non-diagnostic lymphoid fragments. Right inguinal excisional lymph node biopsy: Interfollicular plasma cell sheets and germinal centers with penetrating vascularity and classic concentric 'onion-skin' hyaline-vascular architecture; submitted for specialized immunohistochemical evaluation. Positron emission tomography (PET): Marked diffuse adenopathy and splenic enlargement (17 cm axial diameter), which reduced to 15 cm following therapy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8)-associated multicentric Castleman disease (MCD) in a patient with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4+ T-cell count 27 cells/microL [6%], HIV-1 viral load 98,200 copies/mL) complicated by secondary Clostridioides difficile colitis. Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathology of excisional lymph node biopsy demonstrating characteristic hyaline-vascular and plasma-cell features with positive HHV-8 immunostaining, accompanied by extremely high serum HHV-8 DNA quantitative viremia of 2,288,277 copies/mL (reference < 1,000 copies/mL); HIV genotypic testing confirmed no transmissible resistance. Plan & Outcome: Treated for C. difficile colitis with oral vancomycin. Restarted on combination ART with bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Biktarvy), with viral load dropping to 40 copies/mL. Received 6 cycles of intravenous rituximab leading to clinical resolution, reduction in spleen size, and regression of lymphadenopathy. Following disease flare three months later linked to medication non-adherence, successfully retreated with 8 cycles of weekly rituximab followed by liposomal doxorubicin and re-establishment of ART.

raw_case_text:
A 33-year-old international male student studying in England traveled to Japan and stayed with a friend in Tokyo during July-September 2014. In late August, an acute high fever (39.7 C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, malaise, and loss of appetite developed. He did not have cough, sputum, or rhinorrhea. He returned to England 3 days after symptoms developed. On day 5 after symptom onset, the man noticed a scattered papular erythematous rash on the anterior chest wall. His symptoms had improved substantially. One week later, he experienced exacerbation of the same symptoms (again without cough, sputum, or rhinorrhea), which continued for a few days until he sought care 12 days after initial onset. He had no significant medical history or known allergies and had not traveled to any countries other than Japan.
On examination, the man appeared ill and had a high fever (38.5 C). His lungs were clear, but his pharynx was markedly swollen and erythematous with cervical lymphadenopathy. Despite his severe symptoms, results of laboratory tests showed no or only mild elevations: normal leukocyte count and differentials (6,700 cells/mm3 [reference 4,000-11,000] with neutrophils 60% and lymphocytes 26%) and slightly elevated C-reactive protein (0.9 mg/dL [reference 0.0-1.0 mg/dL]) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (14 mm/h [reference 1-10 mm/h]). Liver enzyme levels were elevated: lactate dehydrogenase 623 IU/L (reference 125-243 IU/L), alanine aminotransferase 78 IU/L (reference 0-55 IU/L), aspartate aminotransferase 58 IU/L (reference 5-45 IU/L), and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase 81 IU/L (reference 12-64 IU/L), with normal total bilirubin (1.0 mg/dL [reference 0.2-1.2 mg/dL]). Mild hyponatremia (sodium 132 mmol/L [reference 135-145 mmol/L]) also was noted; otherwise the test results were unremarkable, including normal platelet count and coagulation panel. Serologic tests were positive for anti-dengue virus IgM but negative for anti-dengue virus IgG: viral RNA was not detected.
The patient was hydrated with intravenous fluid and discharged with acetaminophen as needed for fever and pain. He was instructed to avoid nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs because of possible bleeding risk. The sore throat resolved within 1 day, and his pain and fever were well controlled with acetaminophen.
This dengue outbreak in Japan started in Yoyogi Park, a public park in the Tokyo metropolitan area. From August 26, 2014, when the first case was identified, through October 30, a total 160 autochthonous dengue fever infections occurred. The patient reported here stated that the house where he stayed in Japan is a 2-minute walk from Yoyogi Park and that he was bitten multiple times by mosquitos in late August, although he did not enter the park or other implicated parks.
This outbreak has several possible causes. First, Aedes albopictus mosquitoes:1 of 2 main vector mosquitoes of dengue virus:are widespread in Japan. Although the other species, A. aegypti, has not been established in Japan, it was once identified at Tokyo International Airport. Second, the worldwide dengue fever incidence has increased exponentially during the past 50 years, and the number of cases imported to Japan has increased steadily since 1999. Third, increased international travel, trade, and shipping, in addition to global warming, might have contributed to geographic expansion of the vectors.
Why this dengue fever outbreak started from Yoyogi Park remains unknown. One possibility is the popularity of Yoyogi Park, which holds  100 events annually, including many international events. In July and August 2014, just before the first case was identified, Yoyogi Park hosted multiple festivals of countries in dengue-endemic regions, including Southeast Asia and South and Central America (http://www.yoyogipark.info/ad2014/). Dengue virus could have been spread from infected visitors by mosquitoes in the park. Any events that include persons from dengue-endemic regions and held where the vectors are prevalent could be the source of spread.
This case highlights the possible risk for a dengue outbreak in countries to which dengue is not endemic but where the vectors are present. and thus the potential exists for travelers to become infected. Physicians need to be aware of the possibility of dengue fever in patients returning from non-tropical/subtropical countries, obtain a full travel history, and keep apprised of the latest epidemic information.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 33-year-old male presenting with a recurrent acute febrile illness, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, malaise, anorexia, pharyngeal swelling, and rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: While visiting Tokyo, Japan in late August 2014, the patient developed acute high fever (39.7 C), severe headache, retro-orbital pain, malaise, and loss of appetite, without respiratory symptoms. He returned to England 3 days later. On day 5 of illness, he developed a scattered papular erythematous rash on the anterior chest wall, followed by substantial symptom improvement. One week later, symptoms recurred with severe headache, retro-orbital pain, fever, and severe sore throat, leading him to seek care 12 days after initial onset.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant medical history or known allergies. Travel history: Visited Tokyo, Japan (stayed in an apartment a 2-minute walk from Yoyogi Park) from July to September 2014; recalled multiple mosquito bites in late August. No other international travel.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, malaise, anorexia, severe sore throat, and rash. Negative for cough, sputum, or rhinorrhea. Medications: none. Allergies: no known allergies.

objective.physical_examination: Appeared ill, high fever with temperature 38.5 C. Lungs: Clear to auscultation. Pharynx: Markedly swollen and erythematous with cervical lymphadenopathy. Skin: Scattered papular erythematous rash on the anterior chest wall.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukocyte count 6,700 cells/mm3 (neutrophils 60%, lymphocytes 26%), normal platelet count. Inflammatory markers: CRP 0.9 mg/dL (reference: 0.0-1.0 mg/dL), ESR 14 mm/h (reference: 1-10 mm/h). Liver enzymes: LDH 623 IU/L (reference: 125-243 IU/L), ALT 78 IU/L (reference: 0-55 IU/L), AST 58 IU/L (reference: 5-45 IU/L), GGT 81 IU/L (reference: 12-64 IU/L), total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL (reference: 0.2-1.2 mg/dL). Electrolytes: Serum sodium 132 mmol/L (mild hyponatremia). Coagulation panel: Normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Autochthonous acute dengue fever with a biphasic clinical course, acquired in Tokyo, Japan. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive anti-dengue virus IgM and negative anti-dengue virus IgG; dengue viral RNA RT-PCR was negative (consistent with late presentation at day 12).
Plan & Outcome: Treated with intravenous fluid rehydration and oral acetaminophen for symptom relief; NSAIDs were strictly avoided due to potential bleeding risks. Sore throat resolved within 24 hours, fever and pain were well controlled, and the patient made a full recovery.

raw_case_text: A 28-year-old male from Santarem, Para, Brazil, with a history of leisure activities in a rural area, tractor driver, a known carrier of the HIV virus since 2010, however without previous follow-up, contacted us for the first time at Fundacao de Medicina Tropical Dr. Heitor Vieira Dourado, Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil, for investigation of left knee chronic monoarthritis associated with tegumentary lesions. He had been using zidovudine, lamivudine, lopinavir/ritonavir for three weeks, this being the first antiretroviral regimen used. He had never used prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. He denied being a smoker or alcohol user. He reported that the left knee arthritis appeared after local trauma identified five months before, preceding the tegumentary lesions that appeared two months after the fact. During the clinic exam, polymorphism of skin lesions was noted with pustules of follicular distribution, papules with central necrosis, erythematous-infiltrated plaques covered with pustules and ulcerated plaques, located on the face, trunk, abdomen and limbs, associated with left knee arthritis (Figures 1, 2 and 3A). Oral and genital mucosa were spared. Lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly were not observed. Blood cultures for aerobes, mycobacteria, fungi and leukocyte cream were negative. VDRL resulted non-reagent. The Leishmaniasis screening exam was negative. The analysis of synovial fluid suggested infectious arthritis. Left knee x-ray showed reduction of joint space and osteolytic patellar lesion (Figure 3B). Patient underwent surgical cleansing of joint, biopsy of synovial membrane and skin. Both exams identified round cells, birefringent, with multiple buddings compatible with P. brasiliensis (Figure 4). Culture of synovial tissue confirmed the finding. Complementary propedeutics suggested pulmonary involvement and the Xpert/MTB RIF  sputum test was negative. At the time of diagnosis T CD4+ count was 44 cells/mm3 . Patient was treated with Amphotericin B deoxycholate 50mg/day (cumulative dose of 650mg) but despite the therapy, his clinical condition worsened, progressing to death on the 20th day of hospitalization. Necropsy revealed involvement of lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, adrenals and bone marrow, in addition to the previously described sites (Figure 5).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presenting with chronic left knee monoarthritis for 5 months and polymorphic cutaneous lesions for 3 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive pain and swelling in the left knee following local trauma 5 months prior. Two months later, he noticed the appearance of polymorphic skin lesions that progressively spread across his face, trunk, abdomen, and extremities. Three weeks prior to consultation, he initiated his first combination antiretroviral regimen.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic retroviral illness diagnosed in 2010 without prior clinical follow-up or opportunistic prophylaxis; initiated on zidovudine, lamivudine, and lopinavir/ritonavir 3 weeks prior. Denied tobacco or alcohol consumption. Occupation: tractor driver; epidemiological exposure: leisure activities in a rural area of Santarém, Pará, Brazilian Amazon.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left knee pain, swelling, and diffuse skin lesions; negative for oral or genital ulcers, fever, or weight loss. Home medications: zidovudine, lamivudine, lopinavir/ritonavir. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Dermatologic: extensive polymorphic cutaneous eruption consisting of pustules in a follicular distribution, papules with central necrosis, erythematous-infiltrated plaques covered with pustules, and ulcerated plaques over face, trunk, abdomen, and limbs; oral and genital mucosa completely spared. Musculoskeletal: inflammatory monoarthritis of the left knee with effusion, warmth, and restricted range of motion. Lymph nodes and abdomen: no lymphadenopathy; no hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood cultures for aerobes, mycobacteria, fungi, and leukocyte buffy coat: negative. Syphilis VDRL: non-reactive. Leishmaniasis screening test: negative. Sputum Xpert MTB/RIF: negative for tuberculosis. Synovial fluid analysis: cloudy fluid consistent with infectious arthritis. Left knee plain radiograph: joint space narrowing with an osteolytic patellar lesion.
objective.advanced_workup: Arthroscopic surgical debridement and synovial membrane biopsy; skin punch biopsy. Histopathology of skin and synovium: round, birefringent yeast cells with multiple peripheral buddings ('pilot wheel' / 'mariner's wheel' appearance) characteristic of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis. Synovial tissue culture: confirmed Paracoccidioides brasiliensis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis presenting with chronic osteoarticular infection (patellar osteolytic monoarthritis), severe polymorphic cutaneomucosal lesions, and pulmonary involvement in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS (CD4+ T-cell count 44 cells/mm3). Visceral leishmaniasis, syphilis, tuberculosis, and pyogenic/bacterial septic arthritis excluded by negative serology, cultures, and sputum Xpert MTB/RIF. Paracoccidioidomycosis confirmed by biopsy of synovial membrane and skin showing birefringent multiple-budding yeast cells and positive synovial fungal cultures. Management & Outcome: Underwent surgical joint cleansing and received intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate 50 mg/day (cumulative dose 650 mg). Despite antifungal therapy, clinical condition deteriorated with multisystem failure, leading to death on hospital day 20. Post-mortem necropsy confirmed disseminated paracoccidioidomycosis involving lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, adrenal glands, bone marrow, synovium, and skin.

raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old male presented with complaint of blurring of vision in the left eye (LE) and headache for 15 days. He had a history of DF 22 days before the presentation. The DF was confirmed by positive immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay serology for the Dengue virus. His best-corrected-visual-acuity (BCVA) was (right eye [RE]) 6/9 and (LE) finger counting 0.5 m. On examination, (LE) fundus revealed focal constriction of arteries and veins, soft exudates, dot-blot and flame-shaped hemorrhages in branch vein distribution, attempt at macular fan formation, and area of macular edema [Figure 1]. (LE) optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed neurosensory detachment with cystoid macular edema [Figure 2]. Central macular thickness was 1018 mu.
Complete blood count revealed platelet count: 84,000 (thrombocytopenia). Based on history, thrombocytopenia and clinical findings, diagnosis of dengue retinopathy was made. The patient was given intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide (4 mg/0.1 ml).
At 2 months, BCVA (RE) was 6/6 and (LE) 6/18. Since (LE) visual acuity did not normalize, fundus fluorescein angiography (FA) and OCT angiography (OCTA) were done. FA LE showed normal foveal avascular zone (noted in the early phase of angiogram), few areas of the delayed filling (inferotemporal vascular arcade) with capillary leakage. Disc leakage was also noted [Figure 3]. OCT showed cystoid spaces, intraretinal exudates with back-shadowing, disruption of the external limiting membrane, the ellipsoid zone, and the interdigitation zone in the foveal region. There was the subfoveal area of hyperreflectivity and retinal thinning [Figure 4]. (RE) OCTA was normal. OCTA (LE) showed distortion of retinal superficial and deep capillary plexus (SCP-DCP) inferotemporal to foveal center [Figure 5]. The features on OCT and OCTA were suggestive of AMN.
Six months visit revealed complete resolution of fundus features, visual acuity of both eyes on Snellen's 6/6, but with persistent micropsia. OCT revealed retinal thinning with the restoration of retinal layers. Distortion of SCP-DCP on OCTA persisted, which was the only persistent defect explaining the visual complaint of the patient [Figure 2].

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old male presented with blurring of vision in the left eye and headache for 15 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 15-day history of left eye visual blurring and headache following an acute febrile illness that occurred 22 days prior to presentation. Visual impairment in the left eye had progressed to counting fingers at close distance.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of an acute febrile illness 22 days prior to ophthalmic presentation. No other chronic medical illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reported blurred vision in the left eye and persistent headache. Denied ocular pain, redness, flashes, floaters, or active systemic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic examination: Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/9 in the right eye and finger counting at 0.5 m in the left eye. Left eye fundus examination revealed focal constriction of retinal arteries and veins, soft exudates, dot-blot and flame-shaped hemorrhages in a branch vein distribution, an attempt at macular fan formation, and prominent macular edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Platelet count 84,000/muL (thrombocytopenia).
objective.advanced_workup:
Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of left eye (presentation): Neurosensory detachment with cystoid macular edema; central macular thickness was 1018 mu.
Follow-up at 2 months: BCVA was 6/6 in right eye and 6/18 in left eye. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FA) of left eye showed normal foveal avascular zone in early phase, delayed filling in the inferotemporal vascular arcade with capillary leakage, and optic disc leakage. Left eye OCT showed cystoid spaces, intraretinal exudates with back-shadowing, disruption of external limiting membrane, ellipsoid zone, and interdigitation zone in foveal region, with subfoveal hyperreflectivity and retinal thinning. Right eye OCT angiography (OCTA) was normal; left eye OCTA showed distortion of superficial and deep capillary plexus (SCP-DCP) inferotemporal to foveal center, consistent with acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN).
Follow-up at 6 months: OCT showed retinal thinning with layer restoration; persistent distortion of SCP-DCP on OCTA.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue retinopathy with acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN) secondary to Dengue virus infection, confirmed by positive immunoglobulin M (IgM) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) serology for Dengue virus.
Treatment and outcome: Treated with intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide (4 mg/0.1 mL). At 2 months, left eye BCVA improved to 6/18. At 6 months, complete resolution of fundus hemorrhages and exudates occurred with BCVA restoring to 6/6 OU on Snellen chart, accompanied by mild persistent micropsia corresponding to residual capillary plexus distortion on OCTA.

raw_case_text:
The patient was a 73-year-old man who had a myocardial infarction (MI) about a month prior to the onset of COVID-19 symptoms. He underwent a percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for the MI, and a stent was subsequently inserted into his left circumflex artery. On March 3, he visited the emergency room of a COVID-19 center in a hospital in Isfahan City in Iran with chief complaints of fever and chills. He reported that for several days, he was suffering from anorexia, nausea, and diarrhea. He had a 38.5 C fever and his oxygen saturation level was at 85% at room air. According to the protocol for the COVID-19 epidemic, a high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest was performed, indicating the involvement of both lungs manifested as ground-glass opacity (GGO) (Figure 1). He was admitted and transferred to a COVID-19 ward, and the therapeutic regimen for COVID-19, including Tamiflu  (Oseltamivir), hydroxychloroquine, and KALETRA  (lopinavir/ritonavir), and a superinfection battery, including levofloxacin and linezolid, were administered for the patient by an infectious disease specialist.
To confirm the diagnosis, a throat swab sample was analyzed using a molecular test (RT-PCR), and the result was positive for COVID-19.
During the first day of admission, his breathing became harder and his O2 saturation reduced to 94% while using a nasal cannula. During the first two days of admission, his oxygen saturation decreased further over time. Hence, a facial mask and then a non-rebreather mask (NRB) were prescribed for the patient. On the third day of admission, he developed respiratory distress, while his oxygen saturation decreased below 90%, and some impairments of consciousness were observed. Therefore, he was transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) with suspected superinfection, and meropenem was added to his antibiotic regimen. His impairments of consciousness became more pronounced, and his systolic blood pressure fluctuated between 70 mmHg and 160 mmHg. Moreover, it was difficult to maintain his oxygen saturation over 89%. His status was designated as severe sepsis, and even septic shock. On March 9 (day 6 of admission), he underwent endotracheal intubation, and he was connected to a ventilator with high positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) (10-15 cmH2O) with a fraction of inspired oxygen (fiO2) of 100%. Nevertheless, his O2 saturation did not exceed 90%. During ICU hospitalization, his creatinine level increased from 1.2 to 1.7, and an acute kidney damage (stage one) was observed. Thus, a jugular vein access was established by a surgeon for potential future actions.
Interestingly, his symptoms were getting worse in an episodic manner during day and night. His temperature increased to 39 C while he had chills, and he developed tachycardia with up to about 160 beats per minute. Moreover, he developed respiratory distress, O2 saturation drop, and diarrhea. During these episodes, his blood pressure became more unstable. Furthermore, each consequent episode became worse than the one before, where he would experience more severe symptoms.
On the evening of the sixth day of admission, he underwent hemoperfusion (HA230 cartridge, Jafron ) for 4.5 hours due to suspicion of autoimmune dysfunction and cytokine storm. We used Heparin 50 mg/kg (intravenous bolus over 10 minutes) before hemoperfusion, and 15-20 mg/kg/h (intravenous infusion) during hemoperfusion. During hemoperfusion, his symptoms improved significantly and his need for oxygen therapy was reduced. His fever disappeared, while his heart rate and respiratory rate decreased. We report the details of his status on an hour-by-hour basis in Figure 2.
On the 7th day of admission, based on the improvement in his clinical status, the medical team decided to perform another hemoperfusion for 6 hours. As a result, his status improved even more, and we were able to reduce mechanical ventilation support. Finally, on day 8 of admission, the patient was extubated, and he was able to breathe independently. His status and detailed laboratory data are reported in Table 1. 
On day 13 of admission, he was discharged with a satisfactory general condition, without fever, and with normal breathing.
It should be noted that he developed fever and decreased oxygen saturation 26 days after discharge. We performed another CT scan, which showed segmental pulmonary thromboembolism. He was administered anticoagulant therapy (Enoxaparin, 60 mg, subcutaneous, every 12 hours for 1 week, followed by Rivaroxaban, 20 mg, once daily), and his condition became stable after 6 days.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 73-year-old male presenting with fever, chills, anorexia, nausea, diarrhea for several days, and acute hypoxemia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 73-year-old male presented with a several-day history of fever, chills, nausea, anorexia, and watery diarrhea. Upon presentation, he was profoundly hypoxemic with an oxygen saturation of 85% on ambient air. Despite sequential oxygen escalation from nasal cannula to face mask and non-rebreather mask, he developed progressive respiratory distress and altered consciousness by hospital day 3, leading to ICU transfer. On hospital day 6, he developed septic shock and refractory hypoxemic respiratory failure, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent acute myocardial infarction (one month prior) status post percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with a drug-eluting stent placed in the left circumflex coronary artery. Denied prior renal disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, nausea, anorexia, watery diarrhea, progressive dyspnea, and confusion. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Upon presentation: temperature: 38.5 °C, SpO2: 85% on room air. ICU admission (day 3–6): fluctuating systolic blood pressure between 70 and 160 mmHg, paroxysmal spikes of hyperpyrexia up to 39.0 °C accompanied by tachycardia up to 160 beats/min, severe tachypnea, episodic desaturations (<90% on FiO2 1.00), and obtundation/altered level of consciousness.
objective.routine_investigations: Serum creatinine: increased from baseline 1.2 mg/dL to 1.7 mg/dL (stage 1 acute kidney injury); arterial blood gases demonstrated severe hypoxemia with PaO2/FiO2 ratio < 100 mmHg on 100% FiO2 and PEEP 10–15 cmH2O.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) at admission: bilateral extensive ground-glass opacities (GGO). Chest CT angiography (26 days post-discharge): segmental pulmonary thromboembolism. Therapeutic hemoperfusion: two sessions using HA230 cartridges (4.5 hours on day 6 and 6 hours on day 7) under systemic heparin anticoagulation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe COVID-19 pneumonia with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), hyperinflammatory cytokine storm, septic shock, and stage 1 AKI, complicated post-discharge by acute segmental pulmonary thromboembolism; confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR from a throat swab. Management & Outcome: Initial pharmacotherapy included oseltamivir, hydroxychloroquine, lopinavir/ritonavir, levofloxacin, linezolid, and meropenem. Following mechanical ventilation and refractory shock, two sessions of HA230 hemoperfusion yielded rapid resolution of fever, stabilization of hemodynamics, and dramatic pulmonary recovery, allowing successful extubation on day 8 and hospital discharge on day 13. Late post-discharge pulmonary embolism was successfully managed with therapeutic enoxaparin (60 mg subcutaneous q12h for 1 week) transitioned to rivaroxaban (20 mg daily).

raw_case_text:
The patient is a 48-year-old female who was diagnosed with schizophrenia in 2014. Initially, multiple antipsychotics were consolidated due to her severe symptoms, and the regimen has been in place ever since due to the presence of residual symptoms (Table 1). Her residual symptoms have been stable and included auditory hallucinations with intact insight and reality testing. Since the first episode, she has displayed good treatment compliance and never experienced relapse. The clinical global impression-severity was 2 (borderline ill) and clinical global impression-improvement was 1 (marked improvement from initial encounter). The patient functioned stably in her housekeeping duties.
Her medical history was significant for HIV infection, which was diagnosed in 2012. Initial CD4+ count at the time of diagnosis was 72 cells/ul, which rose to 377 cells/ul in the first year of treatment with lamivudine, stavudine, and efavirenz. She never had any opportunistic infection. Past self-reported pill counts indicated excellent compliance. Antiretroviral regimen was changed once owing to changes in locally available formulary (Table 1) to lamivudine, zidovudine, and efavirenz in 2020. In the past 3 yearly laboratory investigations, her CD4+ cell counts were between 1163-1935 cells/ul and viral loads were all < 20 copies/mL. She had no other underlying diseases.
The current relapse began 2 months prior. Her daughter noted that the patient started to respond to (the ever present) hallucinations while becoming more irritable, yet displayed slower responses to stimuli; these symptoms did not show any signs of fluctuation, nor were disorientations noted. The patient reported that her hallucinations occurred more frequently, and that she lost the ability to differentiate between hallucinations and reality. She also complained of fatigue, headache, and cold intolerance. Noncompliance was ruled out as the daughter noted that the patient regularly took her medicines and went for monthly injections while remaining pill counts were consistent with follow-up visit date. The patient was brought to the emergency department twice for her somatic complaints. In both instances, two separate physicians focused more on the relapse of psychotic symptoms and only prescribed intramuscular haloperidol without performing laboratory investigation before discharging the patient. The patient later came for a regular psychiatric follow-up visit and reported the relapse and somatic symptoms. The psychiatrist ascertained that there was no compliance issue, nor was there comorbid use of tobacco, alcohol, or illicit substances that could have triggered a psychotic episode or affected pharmacokinetics of the prescribed medication. Examination was positive for systolic ejection murmur. There was no thyroid enlargement, peripheral edema, or abnormalities in lung auscultation. Neurological examination was normal. Investigation revealed a hemoglobin level of 4.7 g/dl with multiple microspherocytes seen in peripheral blood smear; there was no history of hereditary spherocytosis or notes of spherocytes in complete blood counts in the past 10 years. Direct Coomb's test was positive (3+). Reticulocyte count, however, was not elevated (reticulocyte 0.24%, absolute count 3000 cells/ul). Iron studies were normal. Vitamin B12 level was within intermediate range and was deemed unexplanatory of the low reticulocyte count. (The cause of borderline low vitamin B12 was attributed to her self-medication with omeprazole for dyspepsia). Combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia and pure red cell aplasia attributed to zidovudine was provisionally diagnosed. Infectious specialist ruled out possibilities of anemia and psychotic symptoms from HIV, as her infection had been under good control. As her homocysteine level, the marker of abnormality in one-carbon metabolism pathway and the implicated mechanism of psychosis from vitamin B12 deficiency, was within normal range, psychosis from the vitamin status was ruled out. No abnormalities were seen in serum electrolyte panels, thyroid functions, and liver functions, nor was there rhabdomyolysis as evaluated by serum creatine phosphokinase, lactate dehydrogenase and urine myoglobin, ruling out their contribution to psychosis and somatic symptoms.
Transfusion with 2 units of leukocyte-poor packed red blood cells was initiated. After her hemoglobin level rose to 7.8 g/dl over the course of the night the transfusion was carried out, her psychotic symptoms promptly abated: frequency of hallucination became rare, insight and reality testing returned, and mood and affect became euthymic. The recovery was maintained throughout the admission. No adjustment in psychiatric medication was necessary. As zidovudine was implicated as etiology of anemia, the anti-HIV regimen was changed to tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz. 60 mg/d of prednisolone was given for immunohemolysis. At 2-week follow-up her hemoglobin level was similar to post-transfusion (7.3 g/dl) without any ongoing signs of hemolysis in blood smear, and schizophrenia symptoms were stable. At 3-months, and 6-months follow-ups, her schizophrenia remained in quiescence and her anemia gradually improved (Table 1). Self-reported compliance and leftover pill counts indicated good compliance.
From the psychiatric perspective, a disease relapse is a function of risk factors. For schizophrenia, common risk factors are medication discontinuation and substance use, which were not present in this case. Another strong factor is the disease's chronicity, which is assumed to be accompanied by ongoing pathological processes such as low-grade systemic inflammation and brain function deterioration. Moreover, the chronic use of antipsychotics and the patient's sedentary lifestyle could have led to metabolic derangements, potentially worsening the inflammatory condition. Her HIV infection, although well controlled, can also exert subtle inflammatory disturbances that chronically deteriorate brain function and adds to the predisposition. These factors are then precipitated into a syndromic relapse by the emergence of severe anemia.
From her course of physical symptoms and relatively preserved level of consciousness, it was suspected that her anemia may have been gradually progressing over the past two months, concurrent with the re-emergence of psychotic symptoms. Due to the absence of symptom fluctuation and disorientation, the psychosis was unlikely a part of delirium. Therefore, the re-emergence of symptoms was diagnosed as schizophrenia relapse. Her reality testing, insight, and auditory hallucination recovered to baseline after transfusion raising hemoglobin level from 4.2 to 7.8 g/dl. The rapid improvement of insight could be a product of recovery of sensitive cognitive functions, similar to situations observed in iatrogenic normovolemic anemia experiments. Hallucination has been postulated as a disorder of brain regions generating inner speech, while the insight or the ability to tell hallucination apart from reality is an amalgam of self-certainty, self-reflection, executive functions, and memories.
