Resuscitation with CPR and defibrillation achieved return of spontaneous circulation after 30 minutes; however, recurrent cardiac arrest occurred while preparing for emergency transfer for plasmapheresis, and the patient expired.

raw_case_text: A 22-year-old male of Caribbean descent presented to our clinic with complaints of diminished vision, pain, and photosensitivity in the right eye (OD) for several weeks. He was currently suffering through the acute phase of dengue fever, which had been diagnosed by his primary care provider and confirmed with serology. The patient had severe arthralgia, malaise, headache, pyrexia, and severe dehydration. There was no thrombocytopenia. His dengue infection was confirmed with an elevated dengue fever IgM performed at a contract reference laboratory (LAbCorp, Tampa, FL, USA) on two separate occasions separated by several weeks. His visual acuity, unimproved with refraction, was 20/80 OD and 20/60 in the left eye (OS). Intraocular pressures were 46 mmHg OD and 44 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination was notable for pronounced ciliary flush; large, nongranulomatous keratic precipitates; scattered anterior synechiae; and 3+ anterior chamber cell OD, while the slit-lamp exam of the left anterior segment was unremarkable except for mild ciliary flush. There was an anterior vitritis present in both eyes, with significantly greater vitreous opacity OD than OS. Dilated fundus examination revealed a dense core vitritis, pars planitis, and significant neuroretinitis OD, with a milder vitritis, mild neuroretinal folds, and mild pars planitis OS. Both optic nerves appeared to have enlarged cup-to-disc ratios, although examination was limited due to vitreous opacity. The presumptive diagnosis of bilateral panuveitis was made, and a comprehensive lab workup was initiated to locate any other causative etiology. After a normal chest radiograph, treatment was started with oral prednisone 80 mg orally once a day (PO QD), topical timolol, topical acetazolamide, and topical cycloplegia. Response to oral steroid was excellent, and a follow-up examination at 1 week showed nearly complete resolution of the vitritis and neuroretinitis. The intraocular pressures, however, had risen to over 60 mmHg in both eyes, and there was persistent anterior chamber cell and flare OD. Topical timolol was continued along with the initiation of an oral prednisone taper, and oral acetazolamide was added. After another week with no change in oral prednisone dosage at 60 mg PO QD, the vitritis and retinitis returned OU with worsening vision to CF OD, 20/100 OS, and persistently elevated pressures. While increasing the oral and topical steroid over the following 2 weeks was effective at resolving the inflammation, oral acetazolamide and maximal topical hypotensives were inadequate to control the rising intraocular pressures. It was presumed that there was both an inflammatory glaucoma and a steroid-induced glaucoma response. Steroid-sparing therapy was a primary goal and, for this reason, mycophenolate mofetil was added and raised to 3 g per day. It was decided that the complete cessation of oral steroid was an important treatment goal given what we believed to be a mixed-mechanism glaucoma with some contribution from a hypertensive steroid response in a very young patient. As the oral steroids were tapered, every time the dose was decreased to 60 mg PO QD or lower, the inflammation again returned, and oral cyclosporine A was added in addition to the mycophenolate mofetil. With addition of cyclosporine A, the inflammation was completely controlled. Combination treatment with both mycophenolate mofetil and cyclosporine A allowed us to completely taper off oral prednisone and topical prednisolone without the recurrence of any inflammation. The intraocular pressures decreased from the sixties to the forties, but still could not be medically managed to an acceptable range. In our practice, we generally prefer Ahmed glaucoma valve implants as first-line drainage procedures in inflammatory glaucomas due to their long-term lower incidence of postoperative hypotony compared to Baerveldt implants. Bilateral Ahmed implants (FP7) were placed 4 days apart OD and OS. The intraocular pressure was stabilized in the low teens without the need for topical or oral hypotensives. Visual acuity returned to 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS within 1 month of Ahmed glaucoma implantation. All anterior and posterior inflammation has to date been controlled without the need for further topical or systemic corticosteroid therapy.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 22-year-old male presenting with diminished vision, ocular pain, and photophobia in the right eye for several weeks following an acute febrile illness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient suffered an acute febrile illness characterized by high fever, severe arthralgia, malaise, headache, and severe dehydration without thrombocytopenia. Concurrently over several weeks, he experienced diminished visual acuity, ocular pain, and photophobia in the right eye. Following ophthalmologic presentation, he was diagnosed with bilateral panuveitis and secondary ocular hypertension.
subjective.past_medical_history: Caribbean descent. No other chronic illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for decreased visual acuity, eye pain, photophobia, fever, severe arthralgias, malaise, headache, and dehydration. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Best-corrected visual acuity: 20/80 in the right eye (OD) and 20/60 in the left eye (OS). Intraocular pressures (IOP): 46 mmHg OD and 44 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp examination: OD showed marked ciliary flush, large nongranulomatous keratic precipitates, scattered anterior synechiae, and 3+ anterior chamber cells; OS showed mild ciliary flush and unremarkable anterior segment. Dilated fundus examination: Bilateral anterior vitritis (dense core vitritis OD > OS), bilateral pars planitis, marked neuroretinitis OD, and mild neuroretinal folds OS; enlarged cup-to-disc ratios bilaterally.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: No thrombocytopenia. Chest radiograph: Normal. Comprehensive infectious and inflammatory workup: Negative for other systemic etiologies.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe bilateral panuveitis, pars planitis, and neuroretinitis complicated by secondary mixed inflammatory and corticosteroid-induced glaucoma, secondary to acute dengue fever. Diagnostic confirmation: Significantly elevated dengue fever IgM detected by serology on two separate occasions separated by several weeks; other infectious and autoimmune etiologies ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Initial therapy with oral prednisone (80 mg daily) and topical ocular hypotensives/cycloplegics achieved near-complete resolution of vitritis/neuroretinitis, but IOP escalated to > 60 mmHg. Initiated steroid-sparing immunosuppression with mycophenolate mofetil (titrated to 3 g daily) and oral cyclosporine A, allowing complete tapering and cessation of systemic and topical steroids without inflammatory recurrence. Persistent ocular hypertension (40s mmHg) refractory to maximal medical therapy required bilateral Ahmed glaucoma valve (FP7) implantation placed 4 days apart. Following surgery, IOP stabilized in the low teens without medications, and visual acuity improved to 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS with sustained quiescence of ocular inflammation.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old female underwent transcranial surgery for pituitary macroadenoma. She underwent the right frontotemporal craniotomy. The lesion was approached through right subfrontal and pterional transsylvian corridor. Postoperatively, she was recuperating well in the neurosurgical intensive unit. She was fully conscious and oriented with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 15/15. Computed tomography (CT) scan done at this juncture was uneventful with only postoperative changes [Figure 1]. She had mild fever which manifested on the 4th postoperative day which lasted for few days and subsided. All routine investigations were done which were equivocal and cultures were negative. After 2 days, we noticed a swelling over the craniotomy site which gradually increases by the 10th day to involve upper part of the face. A CT scan was repeated which showed subgaleal and extradural hematoma (EDH) beneath the craniotomy site with mild midline shift of 3 mm [Figure 2]. In view of the recent epidemic of Dengue in our region, we investigated her for NS1 antigen and Dengue IgM antibodies both of which turned out to be positive. Her platelet counts during this time were alarmingly low, 19,000/mm3. Further investigation revealed her activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) was 59 s and international normalized ratio (INR) 1.3. Her blood group was "O" negative, and accordingly, she received multiple platelet concentrate transfusions without a notable rise in her platelet counts. By the 11th day her GCS deteriorated to 10/15 and there were multiple petechial hemorrhages all over the body. During this time, it was noticed that her left arm was swollen due to underlying hematoma at the venipuncture site. The radial pulse in her left arm disappeared due to ongoing compartment syndrome. She also started to develop anisocoria consequent to uncal herniation. Platelet count during this time was 40,000/mm3. In this life-threatening situation, it was decided to go ahead with emergency life and limb-saving surgery. She underwent craniotomy and evacuation of the EDH and fasciotomy of the left upper limb. Multiple transfusions of fresh blood, plasma, and platelets were given during the surgery as there was profuse bleeding from both sites. Hemostasis at the craniotomy site was achieved by the use of Floseal, a hemostatic matrix (Baxter Healthcare Inc.). After fasciotomy, the radial pulse in her hand reappeared and the wound was packed loosely with mop and dressing after achieving hemostasis; however, there was mild diffuse oozing from the dressing site.
After surgery, she regained consciousness to a GCS of 13/15 and her platelet count showed mild increase to 50,000/mm3. A repeat CT scan was taken which showed recollection of EDH [Figure 3]. Since she was conscious and alert we decided to wait and watch. But again, after 2 days she deteriorated in her consciousness and a repeat CT revealed the size of the EDH had further increased with mass effect on the brain [Figure 4]. She underwent emergency surgery during which there was diffuse ooze from the underlying dura. A meticulous hemostasis was achieved with bipolar cautery and surgical. She was given multiple platelet concentrate transfusions during this time. Postoperatively, she improved in her consciousness to a GCS of 12/15 and platelet counts rose to 65,000/mm3. A repeat CT scan was take after 3 days of second reexploration which showed that there was no further bleeding [Figure 5]. The fasciotomy site wound which had diffuse oozing also stopped by this time.
After the second resurgery, she developed chest infection and went into adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). She was transferred to the critical care unit and was weaned off from the ventilator gradually. She recovered well from the ARDS and was discharged after 4 weeks with a Glasgow outcome scale of 5/5.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old female post-craniotomy for pituitary macroadenoma presenting with mild postoperative fever, progressive craniotomy swelling, profound thrombocytopenia, and acute uncal herniation.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 24-year-old female underwent elective right frontotemporal craniotomy for pituitary macroadenoma with an initially uneventful recovery (GCS 15/15). On postoperative day 4, she developed mild fever lasting several days. On postoperative day 6, swelling appeared over the craniotomy site and progressively expanded over the next 4 days to involve the upper face. On postoperative day 11, during an ongoing regional febrile epidemic, she acutely deteriorated to GCS 10/15 with diffuse petechial hemorrhages, anisocoria from uncal herniation, and left upper limb compartment syndrome secondary to hematoma at a venipuncture site.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pituitary macroadenoma status post elective transcranial right frontotemporal craniotomy via subfrontal and pterional transsylvian corridor. No prior bleeding disorder.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for postoperative fever, surgical site swelling, upper extremity swelling, petechiae, and declining consciousness. Medications: postoperative neurosurgical medications, blood products. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Postoperative day 11: GCS 10/15, anisocoria consistent with uncal herniation, extensive petechial hemorrhages over the body. Head: Large tense subgaleal swelling over craniotomy site extending to upper face. Left upper extremity: Marked swelling, tense compartment, and absent radial pulse secondary to puncture hematoma. Radial pulse returned following emergency fasciotomy.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: 19,000/mm3 (lowest nadir), remaining 40,000/mm3 despite multiple platelet concentrates; aPTT: 59 sec; INR: 1.3; blood group: O negative. Repeat cultures: Sterile.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial Brain CT scans: Immediate postoperative CT was normal; Day 10 CT demonstrated subgaleal and extradural hematoma (EDH) with 3 mm midline shift; repeat CT showed increasing EDH with brain mass effect requiring re-evacuation; Day 3 post-reexploration CT confirmed complete hemostasis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue infection occurring in the acute postoperative neurosurgical period, complicated by severe coagulopathy, profound refractory thrombocytopenia, massive extradural and subgaleal hematoma, uncal herniation, upper limb compartment syndrome, and secondary ARDS. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus NS1 antigen and dengue IgM antibodies occurring during a regional dengue outbreak.
Plan & Outcome: Emergency decompressive craniotomy, EDH evacuation, Floseal hemostatic matrix placement, and left upper extremity fasciotomy under aggressive transfusion of platelets, fresh blood, and plasma. Required second emergency re-exploration for recurrent EDH. Developed postoperative ARDS requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU care. Successfully weaned from ventilator and discharged at 4 weeks with a Glasgow Outcome Scale of 5/5.

raw_case_text:
A 4-year-old boy was presented to our unit on referral with a three-week history of high-grade fever and a five-day history of generalized abdominal pain and abdominal distension. There was an associated history of headaches and body weakness. He had no history of jaundice. He had several episodes of vomiting which was initially none bilious, but later became bilious. There was an associated history of passage of diarrhea stools two days before presentation, although the patient had not passed stools on the day of presentation. He had no history of passage of melena or of hematochezia. His parents complained that he had been passing scanty urine for about five days before presentation. He had been receiving medications from the referring hospital for about two weeks before presentation.
At presentation, he was chronically ill looking with a toxic facie, febrile (temperature 38.5 C), pale, dehydrated, anicteric, and had no pedal edema. His respiratory rate was 28/minute; he had reduced air entry on both lung bases posteriorly. His pulse rate was 128/minute, which was regular but of small volume. Only first and second heart sounds were heard. Abdominal examination showed a distended abdomen which did not move with respiration. He had generalized tenderness with guarding. The bowel sounds were absent. A digital rectal examination showed an empty rectum with a full and tender rectovesical pouch. An initial assessment of a generalized peritonitis was made. The patient was placed on NPO with nasogastric tube for gastric decompression. He was commenced on IV fluid resuscitation and broad spectrum IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone and metronidazole) and was worked up for surgery. Initial laboratory investigations showed a hematocrit of 24% and hypokalemia (2.5 mmol/l) and a serum urea of 10 mmol/l. After an initial fluid resuscitation and correction of serum potassium, he had 300 ml of whole blood transfused. He had an exploratory laparotomy on the second day of admission. At surgery, about 600 ml of a feculent peritoneal fluid was drained, and a single perforation on the antimesenteric border of the terminal ileum was closed in two layers. An intraoperative diagnosis of perforated typhoid enteritis was made. Blood and tissue cultures were not done. He was continued on IV fluids and the same empiric antibiotics after the surgery.
On the third day of postoperation, the abdominal wound had a purulent discharge from the distal end. The wound was opened and stitches were removed from the site of drainage, with the institution of daily wound dressing. By the fifth day of postsurgery, a dark patch was noticed to have developed in the skin over the right iliac fossa and measured about 5 cm in its widest diameter. At about the 7th day of postoperation, the dark dry patch had extended to the right hypochondrium, and a similar patch had appeared along the edges of the abdominal incision and the left iliac fossa. A diagnosis of anterior abdominal wall gangrene was made. On the 8th day of postsurgery, the patient was noticed to have developed a complete wound dehiscence (Figure 2) and a fecal fistula. He had fluid resuscitation and was taken back to the theatre on the 10th day after the first surgery, for wound exploration and debridement of the anterior abdominal wall gangrene. A new intestinal perforation was seen at about 2 cm from the initial perforation. The intestinal perforation was exteriorized as an ileostomy, and the abdominal wound closed with tension sutures. Postoperatively, the patient's condition remained unstable, with intractable shock. He died six days after the reexploration of septic shock.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 4-year-old boy presented with a 3-week history of high-grade fever and a 5-day history of generalized abdominal pain and abdominal distension.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: High-grade fever started 3 weeks prior, accompanied by headaches and generalized weakness. Five days prior to presentation, he developed generalized abdominal pain, progressive abdominal distension, vomiting (initially non-bilious, becoming bilious), and scanty urine output. He passed diarrheal stools 2 days before presentation (no bowel movement on presentation day). Denied melena or hematochezia. He had received outpatient medications from a referring facility for approximately 2 weeks.
subjective.past_medical_history: Received outpatient medications from referring facility for 2 weeks prior to presentation. No history of jaundice.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headaches, body weakness, vomiting (initially non-bilious, then bilious), diarrhea, oliguria.

objective.physical_examination: Chronically ill-looking with toxic facies, febrile (temperature 38.5 °C), pale, dehydrated, anicteric, no pedal edema. Respiratory: rate 28/min, reduced air entry at bilateral lung bases posteriorly. Cardiovascular: pulse rate 128/min (regular, small volume), normal S1 and S2. Abdomen: distended, did not move with respiration, generalized tenderness with guarding, absent bowel sounds. Digital rectal examination: empty rectum, full and tender rectovesical pouch.
objective.routine_investigations: Hematocrit: 24%; serum potassium: 2.5 mmol/L; serum urea: 10 mmol/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Exploratory laparotomy (hospital day 2): evacuation of 600 mL feculent peritoneal fluid and two-layer primary closure of a single antimesenteric terminal ileal perforation. Re-exploration laparotomy (day 10 post-first surgery): wound exploration, extensive debridement of full-thickness anterior abdominal wall gangrene, identification of a recurrent ileal perforation 2 cm from the initial site exteriorized as an ileostomy, and abdominal wall closure with tension sutures.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Generalized peritonitis, recurrent ileal perforation, complete abdominal wound dehiscence, fecal fistula, and anterior abdominal wall gangrene secondary to perforated typhoid enteritis (cultures were not performed). Medical management: NPO, nasogastric decompression, fluid resuscitation, potassium correction, transfusion of 300 mL whole blood, and broad-spectrum intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Wound complications began on POD 3 with purulent drainage managed by stitch removal and daily dressings. On POD 5, a 5 cm dark patch developed over the right iliac fossa, extending to the right hypochondrium, incision edges, and left iliac fossa by POD 7, with complete dehiscence and fecal fistula on POD 8. Following re-exploration and ileostomy creation on day 10, the patient remained in intractable shock and died of septic shock 6 days after the second surgery.

raw_case_text:
A 10-year-old male presented with a 12-day history of high-grade fever and chills. He also had headaches, retro-orbital pain and occasional episodes of vomiting. He developed an acute onset of right upper and lower limb weakness five days later, followed by weakness of the left upper limb and a decreased level of consciousness. Haematological investigations revealed a platelet count of 80 000/microl with anti-dengue positive IgM and negative IgG status. Dual antigen for malaria and serology markers for Japanese encephalitis and herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) were negative.
Brain MRI revealed multiple patchy hyperintense areas on T2-weighted and FLAIR images in the left temporoparietal lobe and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, involving the cortex and subcortical white matter, the body of the corpus callosum and the lower medulla (Figures 3a-e). The lesions showed no diffusion restriction and no enhancement on post-contrast T1FS images (Figure 3f). MRI screening of the spine revealed T2 hyperintense signal in the inferior part of the medulla, at the cervicomedullary junction and spinal cord up to the C3 vertebral level as well as in the terminal dorsal cord and conus medullaris from the T11 to the L1 vertebral level (Figure 4a-c).
A diagnosis of acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) secondary to dengue infection was made based on the clinical history, laboratory findings and typical MRI findings.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 10-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever and chills for 12 days, followed by acute-onset asymmetric limb weakness and decreased consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 10-year-old male presented with a 12-day history of high-grade fever, chills, headache, retro-orbital pain, and vomiting. Five days after fever onset, he developed acute-onset right hemiparesis (upper and lower extremity weakness), followed sequentially by left upper extremity weakness and progressive obtundation/decreased consciousness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, chills; absence of sensory complaints or bowel/bladder dysfunction.

objective.physical_examination: Decreased level of consciousness/altered sensorium; asymmetric quadriparesis with prominent weakness of the right upper and lower extremities and left upper extremity.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count: 80,000/microL. Diagnostic serologies: Dual antigen for malaria negative; serological markers for Japanese encephalitis virus and herpes simplex virus (HSV-1) negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI: Multiple patchy hyperintense lesions on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences in the left temporoparietal lobe and bilateral cerebellar hemispheres involving cortex and subcortical white matter, corpus callosum body, and lower medulla, without diffusion restriction or post-contrast enhancement on T1FS images. Whole spine MRI: T2 hyperintense signal in the inferior medulla, cervicomedullary junction, cervical cord up to C3 vertebral level, and terminal dorsal cord/conus medullaris (T11 to L1 vertebral levels).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) with extensive brainstem and spinal cord involvement secondary to confirmed Dengue virus infection. Confirmed by positive anti-Dengue IgM antibody with negative IgG antibody. Malaria, Japanese encephalitis, and HSV-1 were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Inpatient neurocritical care and immunomodulatory supportive management based on neuroimaging confirmation of post-infectious demyelination.

raw_case_text:
A 45-year-old South Asian male farmer with no significant medical history presented to the emergency department with chest pain and generalized myalgias. He was exposed to "flood waters" a week before admission. He also reported fever and "flu-like" symptoms, which seemingly resolved 2 days before seeking medical care. He was a lifelong nonsmoker and denied using alcohol or any illicit substances. There was no pertinent travel or pet history.
His vital signs on admission were blood pressure of 86/58 mm Hg, heart rate of 102 beats per minute, pulse-oximetry 94% on room air, random blood glucose 184 mg/dL, and temperature of 36.4  C. On physical examination, he was noted to be severely icteric. He had an S3 with no murmurs. Air entry was decreased, and there were occasional scattered crackles bilaterally. His abdomen was mildly distended, however, nontender. He was alert and oriented without any neurological deficits, and there was no anasarca with mild pitting edema to the tibial tuberosity bilaterally. His chest radiography revealed borderline cardiomegaly with mild interstitial edema, and initial admission 12-lead electrocardiogram indicated sinus rhythm at 94 beats per minute with no acute dynamic changes. The patient was immediately resuscitated with intravenous crystalloid infusion, and his electrolytes were repleted judiciously. His coronavirus rapid antigen test returned a negative result.
He was subsequently admitted to the medical intensive care unit, where he was empirically initiated on renally-dosed intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam and tigecycline for suspected leptospirosis infection. He also received the routine management bundle for severe sepsis, excluding corticosteroid therapy. The following day, the patient incurred respiratory failure with severe hypoxemia and was commenced on high-flow noninvasive ventilation. A bedside 2-dimensional transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a moderate global hypokinesis with an estimated ejection fraction of 30% to 35% and mild-moderate mitral regurgitation. A noncontrast computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed basilar, bilateral air-space disease suggestive of aspiration pneumonitis. Eventually, his serologies returned positive for leptospirosis infection (Table 1).
The patient endured a rocky clinical course. He alternated rapidly between AT, AF with rapid ventricular response, and VT, for which he was defibrillated and started on low-dose amiodarone infusion at 0.5 mg/min with vigilant hepatic function monitoring (Image 1). During his ensuing hospitalization, he remained clinically unstable and could not undergo further diagnostic testing to clinch or ascertain his tentative diagnosis of nonischemic cardiomyopathy and myocarditis. He deteriorated into a vicious spiral of septic and cardiogenic shock for which he was admitted on multiple inotropic supports; however, he ultimately succumbed to his illness due to multiorgan failure.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 45-year-old male presenting with chest pain and generalized myalgias following floodwater exposure one week prior.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week prior to admission, the patient was exposed to floodwaters. He subsequently developed fever and 'flu-like' symptoms, which appeared to resolve 2 days before seeking care. He presented to the emergency department with acute chest pain and generalized myalgias. Following admission, he rapidly deteriorated into severe hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring high-flow noninvasive ventilation, followed by complex cardiac arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock, and multiorgan failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant prior medical history. Farmer by occupation. Lifelong non-smoker, denied alcohol or illicit substance use. No pertinent travel or pet history. Epidemiological exposure: direct exposure to floodwaters one week prior to admission.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports generalized myalgias, acute chest pain, and prior flu-like symptoms. Denies illicit substance or alcohol use. Home medications: none. Allergies: not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals on admission: blood pressure 86/58 mmHg, heart rate 102 beats/min, pulse oximetry 94% on room air, random blood glucose 184 mg/dL, temperature 36.4 °C. General: severely icteric, alert and oriented without neurological deficits. Cardiovascular: S3 gallop present, no murmurs heard. Respiratory: decreased air entry bilaterally with occasional scattered crackles. Abdomen: mildly distended, non-tender. Extremities: no anasarca, mild pitting edema extending to bilateral tibial tuberosities.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest radiography showed borderline cardiomegaly with mild interstitial edema. Initial 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 94 beats/min with no acute dynamic changes; subsequent ECGs revealed rapid alternation between atrial tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, and ventricular tachycardia (defibrillated). Bedside 2D transthoracic echocardiogram showed moderate global hypokinesis with an estimated ejection fraction of 30% to 35% and mild-to-moderate mitral regurgitation. Coronavirus rapid antigen test was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Noncontrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed basilar, bilateral air-space disease suggestive of aspiration pneumonitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospirosis infection confirmed by positive serologies, complicated by severe sepsis, acute non-ischemic cardiomyopathy/myocarditis, malignant cardiac arrhythmias (atrial tachycardia, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, ventricular tachycardia), cardiogenic and septic shock, and acute respiratory failure with aspiration pneumonitis. COVID-19 infection was ruled out.
Plan & Treatment: Emergent intravenous crystalloid resuscitation and judicious electrolyte repletion; empirical renally-dosed IV piperacillin-tazobactam and tigecycline; routine severe sepsis management bundle (corticosteroids withheld); high-flow noninvasive ventilation; electrical defibrillation and low-dose amiodarone infusion at 0.5 mg/min with hepatic monitoring; multiple inotropic supports for refractory shock.
Outcome: Patient developed refractory mixed cardiogenic and septic shock and succumbed to multiorgan failure.

raw_case_text:
Participant 3: A.A, a 42-year-old married commercial bus driver admitted with a two-day history of recurrent focal seizures involving the left lower limb. He was brought in with an altered level of consciousness on the second day. No history of long-standing fever or weight loss. He was not a previously known patient with seizure disorder, head injury, and was not a known hypertensive or diabetic patient. He smoked several sticks of cigarette and consumed large amounts of alcohol daily. At entry, he was restless, with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 8/15, afebrile to touch, not pale (PCV 36%) and anicteric. There were bilateral planter blisters sustained from the use of hot plates to stimulate him after episodes of seizures at home. There was left hemiparesis, power was 2 in the right upper and lower limbs with facial nerve palsy. The chest was clear. The blood pressure was 130/70mm/Hg, no heart murmurs. Abdominal examination was unremarkable. He tested positive for HIV 1. The random blood glucose was 110mm/dl (6.1mmol/l). Cranial CT and other requested investigations were not done for financial reasons. He was commenced on parental anticonvulsant and cerebral decompression with minimal improvement.
Outcome: relatives requested for transfer to another facility for proximity and financial reasons.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 42-year-old male presenting with recurrent focal seizures involving the left lower limb for two days and acute depression of consciousness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-day history of recurrent focal motor seizures initially involving the left lower limb. On the second day of illness, his mental status deteriorated into restlessness and obtundation, prompting emergency admission. Family members had applied heated plates to his soles at home in an attempt to revive him during seizure episodes. Denied prior history of chronic fever or weight loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior history of seizures, head injury, hypertension, or diabetes mellitus. Social history: Commercial bus driver; daily heavy alcohol consumption and regular cigarette smoking.
subjective.review_of_systems: Focal seizures and altered sensorium; denies pre-existing fevers, chronic cough, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: General: Restless, obtunded with Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 8/15; afebrile to touch, anicteric, no conjunctival pallor. Vitals: Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, heart rate regular, no murmurs; chest clear to auscultation; abdomen unremarkable. Dermatologic: Bilateral plantar burn blisters secondary to thermal stimulation. Neurologic: Facial nerve palsy, left hemiparesis, muscle power grade 2/5 in limbs.
objective.routine_investigations: Packed cell volume (PCV): 36%. Random blood glucose: 110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: New-onset focal status epilepticus with acute encephalopathy secondary to suspected intracranial opportunistic infection or focal mass lesion in a patient with newly confirmed human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive serological testing for HIV-1; advanced neuroimaging (cranial CT) was precluded by financial constraints. Plan & Outcome: Managed with parenteral anticonvulsant therapy and medical cerebral decompression with osmotic agents, achieving minimal clinical improvement. At the request of his relatives, the patient was transferred to another healthcare facility due to financial and logistical considerations.

raw_case_text:
A 38-year-old woman who is from and lives in Central Africa consulted for solid lesions and purple-colored patches on her right leg and foot that had been evolving for six months. The patient's interview revealed a notion of pain of the affected limb, an antecedent of trauma of the same limb in a road accident that had occurred ten years before and that resulted in a leg lymphoedema. The physical examination found the patient in good general condition, without fever. Locally, there were infiltrated purple macula associated with angiomatous papulo-nodules and lymphoedema of the right leg. The external part of the lower third of the same leg is the seat of an unsightly and atrophic scar and erosion of the external malleolus (Figure 1). At palpation of the pulse, there was no thrill or associated breath at auscultation. The mucous were unharmed. There was no sign of impairment of other organs. So, the diagnosis of endemic KD was evoked in view of the geographical origin of the patient, with a pseudo-Kaposi of Stewart-Bluefarb and an epidemic KD being differentially diagnosed. Hemogram revealed nothing particular. C-reactive protein was positive at 35  mg/L. The histopathology of the lesions and the ultrasonography of the affected limb have not been performed. HIV serology was positive to HIV1. The CD4 count was 600 cells/mm3. The diagnosis of epidemic KD on an anteriorly traumatized leg in a patient from Central Africa was retained.
The patient was put on a combination of antiretrovirals including two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (emtricitabine-tenofovir) and a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (efavirenz). The development was marked by the complete disappearance of the pain and an important regression of the lesions after six months of treatment, with however the persistence of residual lymphoedema (Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 38-year-old woman presenting with solid lesions, purple patches, and pain on her right lower extremity evolving for six months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 38-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of painful, progressive nodular and purpuric cutaneous lesions involving her right leg and foot. Ten years prior, she sustained lower extremity trauma in a motor vehicle accident that resulted in chronic post-traumatic lymphedema of the affected limb.
subjective.past_medical_history: Prior limb trauma sustained in a road traffic accident 10 years earlier resulting in chronic right leg lymphedema. Epidemiological origin: Born and residing in Central Africa.
subjective.review_of_systems: Pain in the right lower extremity; denies constitutional symptoms, fever, mucosal lesions, or symptoms in other organ systems.

objective.physical_examination: Good general condition, afebrile. Dermatologic / Extremities: Right lower extremity showed infiltrated purple macules with angiomatous papules and nodules, accompanied by lymphedema; lower third of right lateral leg showed an unsightly atrophic scar with erosion of the external malleolus. Vascular: Peripheral pulses palpable without thrill or audible bruit on auscultation. Mucous membranes: Intact, uninvolved. No evidence of systemic organ involvement.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count (hemogram): Normal / unremarkable. C-reactive protein (CRP): Positive at 35 mg/L.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Epidemic Kaposi disease (KD) occurring on a previously traumatized and lymphedematous limb in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection.
Diagnostic Evaluation: HIV-1 serology positive, CD4 count 600 cells/mm3. Differentials considered and ruled out included endemic Kaposi disease and Stewart-Bluefarb pseudo-Kaposi sarcoma. Histopathology and Doppler ultrasound were not performed.
Treatment & Outcome: Initiated on combination antiretroviral therapy comprising emtricitabine, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, and efavirenz. At six months of treatment, the patient achieved complete pain resolution and substantial regression of vascular lesions, with persistent residual lymphedema.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old male with sickle cell anemia, being treated with folic acid, presented to the emergency department of Samtah General Hospital, Jizan, Saudi Arabia, with fever, nausea, headache, and yellowish discoloration of sclera. Patient was living in Jizan, an endemic area of malaria, which raised suspicion of malaria infection. Patient looked unwell, conscious, and alert. His vital signs were normal except the temperature which was high (38.5 degree C). Chest examination was normal and the cardiovascular system showed normal first and second heart sounds with no added sound. Fundus examination was normal. Other systemic reviews were unremarkable. Patient was admitted in the medical ward, and baseline laboratory investigations revealed the following remarkable laboratory values: white blood cells 12 x 109/L (normal range: 4.5 to 11.0 x 109/L); hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL (normal range: 13.8 to 17.2 g/dL); mean corpuscular volume 72 fL/red cell (normal range: 80-96 fL/red cell); platelet count 62 x 103/muL (normal range: 150-400 x 103/muL); reticulocyte 2.6% (normal range: 0.5% to 2.5%); aspartate transaminase 89 U/L (normal range: 10 to 40 U/L); alanine transaminase 78 U/L (normal range: 7 to 56 U/L); total bilirubin 600 mumol/L (normal range: 1.71 to 20.5 mumol/L); direct bilirubin 200 mumol/L (normal range: less than 5.1 mumol/L); and sodium 149 mmol/L (normal range: 136-145 mmol/L), whereas the following laboratory values were found to be in normal ranges: alkaline phosphatase 120 IU/L (normal range: 44 to 147 IU/L); random blood glucose 7.2 mmol/L (normal range: 4.4-8.9 mmol/L); potassium 4.9 mmol/L (normal range: 3.6-5.2 mmol/L); magnesium 0.9 mmol/L (normal range: 0.6-1.1 mmol/L); calcium 2.3 mmol/L (normal range: 2.2-2.7 mmol/L); phosphate 1.4 mmol/L (normal range: 1.12-1.45 mmol/L); creatinine 78 mmol/L (normal range: 60-110 mmol/L); and urea 3.7 mmol/L (normal range: 2.5-7.1 mmol/L).
ECG initially showed normal sinus rhythm, and chest X-ray was normal. The patient had no previous history of cardiac arrhythmias, and his baseline ECG was normal (Figure 1(a)). Peripheral blood smear revealed P. falciparum (ring form) with parasitemia index 10%. His body weight was 74 kg and height 166 cm.
Patient was diagnosed with severe P. falciparum malaria based on clinical presentation and laboratory investigations and started on intravenous artesunate 170 mg (2.4 mg/kg) bolus slowly over 2 minutes at 0 hour, 12 hours, and 24 hours, and every 24 hours thereafter for 5 days. The powder for injection was reconstituted with 5% sodium bicarbonate and diluted in an equal volume of normal saline. He was started on paracetamol 500 mg tablet orally as needed every 6 hours. Patient was clinically improving and temperature subsided. After 4 hours of the third dose of artesunate, the patient became sick, faint, and suddenly arrested. Resuscitation was done for 32 minutes, ECG was done and showed wide complex ventricular tachycardia, and QTc (Bazett) was 516 msec (Figure 1(b)). Electrolytes were in the normal limits: sodium 136 mmol/L; potassium 4.3 mmol/L; magnesium 0.8 mmol/L; and calcium 2.1 mmol/L. Tachycardia was managed by administration of amiodarone (150 mg i.v. for 10 minutes). The patient revived and kept in ICU for further observation. There was no worsening of hemolytic anemia during and after the treatment with artesunate. The treatment plan was not changed; the next dose of artesunate was after 24 hours of the third dose (last dose given before event happened). The patient clinically improved, fever subsided, and the temperature decreased with paracetamol to 37.4 C, and he was walking and conversing normally. The treatment was completed by oral artesunate 100 mg + sulfadoxine 500 mg/pyrimethamine 25 mg tablets (3-day course).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male presenting with fever, headache, nausea, and yellowing of the eyes.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute onset of fever, headache, nausea, and progressive scleral icterus. Following admission and initiation of parenteral therapy, his fever began to improve; however, four hours after his third antimalarial dose, he experienced sudden syncope and cardiac arrest requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Sickle cell anemia on maintenance folic acid therapy; resident of Jizan, Saudi Arabia (malaria-endemic area). No prior history of cardiac arrhythmias or structural heart disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications: Folic acid. Positive for nausea and headache; negative for chest pain, palpitations prior to arrest, or shortness of breath.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.5 °C, body weight 74 kg, height 166 cm; patient appeared unwell but was conscious and alert. HEENT: Marked scleral icterus/jaundice; fundus examination normal. Cardiovascular: Normal S1 and S2 without murmurs or gallops. Respiratory: Clear breath sounds bilaterally. Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no focal tenderness. Sudden in-hospital cardiac arrest occurred with documented pulseless wide-complex ventricular tachycardia.
objective.routine_investigations: White blood cell count 12 x 10^9/L (reference 4.5-11.0 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL (reference 13.8-17.2 g/dL), MCV 72 fL/red cell (reference 80-96 fL), platelet count 62 x 10^3/microL (reference 150-400 x 10^3/microL), reticulocyte count 2.6% (reference 0.5-2.5%). Liver function tests: Total bilirubin 600 micromol/L (reference 1.71-20.5 micromol/L), direct bilirubin 200 micromol/L (reference <5.1 micromol/L), AST 89 U/L (reference 10-40 U/L), ALT 78 U/L (reference 7-56 U/L), alkaline phosphatase 120 IU/L. Electrolytes and renal function: Sodium 149 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, magnesium 0.9 mmol/L, calcium 2.3 mmol/L, phosphate 1.4 mmol/L, serum creatinine 78 micromol/L, blood urea 3.7 mmol/L, random blood glucose 7.2 mmol/L. Post-arrest electrolytes: Sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, magnesium 0.8 mmol/L, calcium 2.1 mmol/L. Chest radiograph: Normal. Initial 12-lead ECG: Normal sinus rhythm.
objective.advanced_workup: Event 12-lead ECG (post-arrest): Wide-complex ventricular tachycardia with prolonged QTc interval (Bazett) of 516 msec.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe hyperparasitemic Plasmodium falciparum malaria (parasitemia index 10%) complicated by acute drug-induced QTc prolongation and malignant ventricular tachycardia leading to cardiac arrest, in a patient with underlying sickle cell anemia. Peripheral blood smear confirmed P. falciparum ring forms.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on intravenous artesunate (170 mg [2.4 mg/kg] at 0, 12, and 24 hours) along with oral paracetamol. Following sudden cardiac arrest from ventricular tachycardia with QTc prolongation (516 ms), cardiopulmonary resuscitation was performed for 32 minutes and the arrhythmia was successfully terminated with IV amiodarone (150 mg over 10 minutes). Transferred to the ICU for hemodynamic monitoring; IV artesunate was resumed at 24 hours post-event without recurrent arrhythmia or worsening hemolysis. Therapy was completed with a 3-day course of oral artesunate (100 mg) combined with sulfadoxine 500 mg / pyrimethamine 25 mg, resulting in complete clinical recovery.

raw_case_text: Female, 31 years old, Caucasian, unemployed, from Salvador, State of Bahia, was diagnosed (Montenegro positive test) with American Tegumentary Leishmaniasis in October, 2011. The patient was treated with Glucantime, 20 mg/kg/day for 30 days. A lesion in her back region was partially healed. In 2012, two episodes of recurrence occurred and restarted treatment with Glucantime in January and May. In a third recurrence episode (August, 2012), due to the maintenance of the lesion, a lesion biopsy was performed and Leishmania braziliensis was diagnosed. Treatment with amphotericin B was initiated at a dose of 250 mg/d up to a maximum dose of 2,400 mg, resulting in wound healing. In 2013, the patient was admitted with submandibular lymphadenopathy and ulcerated lesions in the lower lip frenulum ( Figure 1d), gingiva, nasal septum and in the back region. She was hospitalized for diagnosis and treatment of lesions with liposomal amphotericin B. Due to persistence of the lesions, HIV serology was performed. The patient was HIV positive and antiretroviral therapy was started (efavirenz 600mg, tenofovir 300mg, lamivudine 300mg, per day, one tablet containing the three drugs). Excisional biopsies of oral lesions were performed with unspecific result. Microbiological analysis for fungi was negative. Two months later, the patient was discharged and a maintenance dose of liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg/day) was prescribed.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old female with HIV co-infection presented with recurrent ulcerated lesions on her lower lip frenulum, gingiva, nasal septum, and back.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 2-year history of recurrent American tegumentary leishmaniasis. She was diagnosed in October 2011 with a back lesion and treated with Glucantime (20 mg/kg/day for 30 days) with partial healing. In 2012, she experienced two recurrences treated with Glucantime, followed by a third relapse in August 2012 where biopsy confirmed Leishmania braziliensis; she was treated with amphotericin B (250 mg/day up to 2,400 mg cumulative) with lesion healing. In 2013, she presented with submandibular lymphadenopathy and new ulcerated lesions on her lower lip frenulum, gingiva, nasal septum, and back. Due to recurrence and persistence, an HIV screening test was performed and returned positive.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recurrent cutaneous and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis since 2011; multiple courses of Glucantime and amphotericin B; newly diagnosed HIV infection. Resident of Salvador, Bahia, Brazil.
subjective.review_of_systems: Recurrent oral and cutaneous ulcerations, localized discomfort. Home medications: none prior to HIV diagnosis. Allergies: None documented.

objective.physical_examination: Lymphatic: submandibular lymphadenopathy. Mucocutaneous: ulcerated lesions on the inferior labial frenulum, gingival mucosa, nasal septum, and dorsal back region.
objective.routine_investigations: Serology: HIV antibody positive. Microbiological analysis: fungal cultures and fungal microscopy negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Excisional biopsies of oral mucosal lesions: demonstrated non-specific chronic inflammatory changes. Prior August 2012 lesion biopsy: performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Relapsing mucocutaneous and disseminated leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania braziliensis in an HIV-coinfected patient.
Diagnostic confirmation: Biopsy of lesion previously confirmed Leishmania braziliensis; Montenegro intradermal reaction positive; fungal cultures negative.
Differentials ruled out: Histoplasmosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, oral Kaposi sarcoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and syphilis.
Treatment and clinical course: Initiated on combination antiretroviral therapy (fixed-dose single tablet of efavirenz 600 mg, tenofovir 300 mg, and lamivudine 300 mg daily) and inpatient intravenous liposomal amphotericin B. Discharged after 2 months on maintenance liposomal amphotericin B (150 mg/day).

raw_case_text: A 49-year-old female patient was diagnosed with stage III HIV infection 11 years back after presenting with smear negative pulmonary tuberculosis and oropharyngeal candidiasis with a baseline CD4+ count 74 cells/mm3. She was covered with fluconazole as antifungal therapy. She was treated with anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) for 6 months and declared treatment completed. ART (AZT-3TC-NVP) and CPT were started two weeks after ATT initiation. She had records of undetected viral load after 2 years of ART initiation. The ART regimen was shifted to TDF-3TC-DTG after 10 years as recommended by the National Comprehensive HIV Care Guideline. She was diagnosed with hypertension and dyslipidemia on follow-ups, and advised on lifestyle modification. She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes after presenting with polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue and blurred vision, and hyperglycemia (RBS=313 g/dl) which occurred after 1 year of the DTG-based ART regimen (Table 1). No documented preceding infections. No personal or family history of diabetes mellitus. Serum C-peptide level, anti-insulin antibody or anti-GAD antibody were not determined due to limited clinical setup. No documented plasma glucose level prior to changing ART regimen. She was started on NPH insulin 24 IU s/c daily, which later changed to metformin 1 gm po daily. Good glycemic control (FBS=109-135 mg/dl) was achieved with metformin, while the DTG-based ART regimen was continued.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 49-year-old female presenting with polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, and blurred vision.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 49-year-old female presented with progressive polyuria, polydipsia, generalized fatigue, and blurred vision developing one year after transitioning her long-standing antiretroviral therapy regimen to a dolutegravir-based combination. She had no preceding infectious symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Underlying retroviral illness on long-term antiretroviral therapy (treated with AZT-3TC-NVP and cotrimoxazole preventive therapy for 10 years, transitioned to tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir [TDF-3TC-DTG]); history of smear-negative pulmonary tuberculosis successfully treated with 6-month anti-tuberculosis therapy; history of oropharyngeal candidiasis treated with fluconazole; hypertension; dyslipidemia; no personal or family history of diabetes mellitus.
subjective.review_of_systems: Polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue, blurred vision; denies fever, weight loss, nausea, or vomiting.

objective.routine_investigations: Blood glucose: Random blood sugar (RBS) 313 mg/dL. (Serum C-peptide, anti-insulin antibodies, and anti-GAD antibodies were not determined due to clinical setup limitations; pre-switch plasma glucose not documented).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: New-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus associated with dolutegravir (DTG) therapy in a patient with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV; diagnosed 11 years prior with stage III disease, baseline CD4 74 cells/mm3, sustained virological suppression on ART), hypertension, and dyslipidemia.
Plan & Outcome: Initially managed with subcutaneous NPH insulin 24 IU daily, subsequently transitioned to oral metformin 1 g daily. DTG-based ART (TDF-3TC-DTG) was continued. Good glycemic control was successfully achieved (fasting blood sugar 109-135 mg/dL) on metformin monotherapy.

raw_case_text:
A 24-year-old Indian male patient who arrived in Singapore from Mumbai, India, in October 2012 for employment presented at the National University Hospital (NUH) in May 2013 with a history of high grade fever associated with chills and rigor the last 4 days. Physical examination was unremarkable except for the presence of fever. The history and clinical examination suggested possible malaria infection with dengue fever as a differential diagnosis and specific laboratory tests were requested. Full blood count revealed thrombocytopenia at 24 x 109/L (references: 132-372 x 109/L) and lymphopenia at 0.33 x 109 (references: 0.94-3.08 x 109/L) but was otherwise normal. G6PD was normal and Dengue IgM/IgG/NS1 were negative. Malaria microscopy was positive. The test results thus confirmed the initial suspicion of Plasmodium infection and identified the parasites as Plasmodium vivax with a parasitemia of 0.4%.
Since malaria is a notifiable disease with a surveillance program in Singapore, the case was notified to the Ministry of Health (MOH) and, at the same time, two thin blood films and residual EDTA whole blood were sent for further investigation to the Malaria Reference Centre at the National Public Health Laboratory (MRC-NPHL). During interview the patient declared that he originated from West Bengal, India, and he had an onset of P. vivax malaria in Aug 2012 there prior to his relocation to Singapore. As he was living in a nonmalaria susceptible transmission area of Singapore and based on his declarations the case was classified by MOH as an imported relapsing case. Morphological and molecular tests for routine malaria surveillance were performed in MRC-NPHL as described previously. Both methods were congruent and confirmed the P. vivax infection. In the meantime, the patient was treated in NUH with chloroquine 600 mg stat, followed by 3 doses of 300 mg 6 h, 24 h, and 48 h after to cure his malaria infection and the fever lysed and the parasite count rapidly dropped to 0.05%. The patient was discharged the day after admission with planned out-patient follow-up.
During the follow-up appointment in NUH in June 2013, the patient was asymptomatic and a thick blood film was prepared and found negative for malaria but unexpectedly showed the presence of several microfilaria. Intrigued and surprised by this finding and also uncertain about the morphological features to identify this parasite, the hospital laboratory staffs sent the thick film and residual of whole EDTA blood to the MRC-NPHL. Microscopist prepared additional blood films stained with Giemsa according to standard procedure and protected them with coverslip mounted with Eukitt  (Sigma-Aldrich). The blood films were entirely screened at low magnification (100x) to detect the MF that were studied in detail at higher magnifications (x400 to x1000) with an Olympus CX31 microscope (Olympus). Morphometric measurement and microphotographs were taken with a Nikon Eclipse 80i microscope equipped with a Nikon DS Ri1 camera and Nikon NIS Element D Imaging Software (Nikon).
The parasites illustrated in Figures 1(a)-1(k) were identified as MF of Wuchereria bancrofti based on their morphological characteristics such as presence of sheath unstained or lightly stained with Giemsa stain (Figures 1(a), 1(c), and 1(j)), cephalic space proportions (Figures 1(a)-1(c), 1(e), and 1(f)), and tail that tapers to delicate point without nucleus at the tip (Figures 1(a), 1(d), 1(e), 1(i), and 1(j)) as well as morphometric measurements: 272.9 +- 16.4 x 6.6 +- 1.2 microm (range 234.6-292.57 x 4.57-8.34 microm; n = 10) for length and width (three points' measurement), respectively.
As alternative confirmatory approach, the sample was subjected to molecular testing. DNA was extracted and stored as described previously. Amplification of the filarial parasite DNA was carried out by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting the cox1 and the 12S rRNA genes from the parasite mitochondrion according to the protocols developed by Casiraghi et al.. PCRs were run on Veriti  Thermal Cycler (Applied Biosystem ) and the PCR products were visualized after electrophoresis performed with the QIAxcel  Advanced instrument (Qiagen ) equipped with QIAxcel DNA Screening Kit (Qiagen). The 12S rRNA gene reactions did not generate any results despite repeats. PCR products obtained for the cox1 gene were purified using the QIAquick  PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen) and stored at -30 C until usage. Purified PCR products were sequenced in both directions using the appropriate oligonucleotide primers as described previously. Alignment and cross-checking of the sequences were performed with CLC Main Workbench 7.7 software (CLC Bio, Qiagen) and consensus sequences of 655 bp of the cox1 gene were obtained. Comparison of the sequences using Basic Local Alignment Tool (BLAST) confirmed the identity of the MF as W. bancrofti. The sequence has been deposited in GenBank under the following accession number: KY883763. A multiple sequences alignment of the cox1 gene including 37 sequences of common human parasitic roundworms retrieved from GenBank and KY883763 was generated by multiple sequences comparison by log-expectation (MUSCLE) algorithm. A phylogenetic analysis was performed using the Maximum Likelihood (ML) method based on GTR+Gamma model. The most appropriate model of nucleotide substitution for ML was selected based on Akaike's Information Criterion value. This analysis showed that the cox1 sequence of the W. bancrofti strain presented here clustered with other sequences from India and Sri Lanka (Figure 2), corroborating the epidemiological data and the idea of an imported parasite.
Based on the confirmed presence of W. bancrofti MF in the blood of the patient, a retrospective investigation of his P. vivax positive blood sample taken a month earlier and archived in MRC-NPHL was initiated. The two original thin blood films provided by NUH laboratory were entirely screened at low magnification and revealed the presence of one MF in each blood film within the thick part of the smear (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). This result confirms that the patient was already infected with detectable MF of W. bancrofti that were missed out by medical technologists in both NUH and MRC-NPHL as they only focused on the tail of the blood films for the malaria investigations at that time.
This laboratory finding was notified to the clinician in charge of the patient who informed him and prescribed a course of Albendazole (400 mg) + Ivermectin (200 microg/kg). The patient responded well to the treatment.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 24-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever, chills, and rigors for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with a 4-day history of high-grade fever accompanied by chills and rigors. He sought medical care in Singapore, where acute tropical febrile infections including malaria and dengue fever were considered in the differential diagnosis.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of treated malaria infection in August 2012 in West Bengal, India; relocated to Singapore from Mumbai, India, for employment in October 2012.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination was unremarkable except for the presence of fever.
objective.routine_investigations: Full blood count: Platelets 24 x 10^9/L (reference 132-372 x 10^9/L), lymphocytes 0.33 x 10^9/L (reference 0.94-3.08 x 10^9/L); remaining cell lines were normal. G6PD screen: Normal. Dengue serology and antigen (IgM, IgG, NS1): Negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Relapsing Plasmodium vivax malaria (0.4% parasitemia) with incidental co-infection by Wuchereria bancrofti microfilaremia (filariasis). Dengue infection was ruled out. Malaria microscopy and reference PCR confirmed P. vivax. Subsequent blood film morphometry and mitochondrial cox1 gene PCR/sequencing (GenBank KY883763) confirmed W. bancrofti microfilariae.
Plan & Outcome: Hospitalized and treated for malaria with oral chloroquine (600 mg stat, followed by 300 mg at 6, 24, and 48 hours), leading to rapid defervescence, reduction in parasitemia to 0.05%, and discharge the following day. At one-month follow-up, repeat thick blood film was negative for malaria but revealed W. bancrofti microfilariae; he was successfully treated with oral albendazole (400 mg) and ivermectin (200 microg/kg) with excellent clinical response.

raw_case_text:
We received a bone marrow biopsy measuring 2 cm in length in the Hematology Unit of the Department of Pathology along with the requisition form mentioning the following clinical details: 7-year-old girl, resident of New Delhi, India, and clinical features - fever on and off associated with weakness and abdominal distension for the past 3 weeks. Physical examination revealed pallor and hepatosplenomegaly with no significant lymphadenopathy. Laboratory data showed pancytopenia with a hemoglobin level of 8.7 g/dl, the total leukocyte count of 3400/mm3, and a platelet count of 44,000/mm3. Peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic blood picture. Bone marrow aspiration finding reported from an outside center was of hypocellular marrow. Human immunodeficiency virus serology, hepatitis B surface antigen, antibodies against hepatitis C virus, the Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, measles, Widal test, K39 test for visceral leishmaniasis, and rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for malarial antigen were negative. Her blood, urine, sputum, and stool cultures were sterile. The chest X-ray and the cerebrospinal fluid study were normal.
The bone marrow biopsy that we received was routinely histoprocessed and stained with hematoxylin and eosin stain. Low power microscopic examination of the sections revealed an adequate bone marrow in length with normal bony trabeculae. The marrow was normocellular for the age [Figure 1a]. High-power view of the trephine biopsy exhibited sheets and clusters of histiocytes. These were large cells with abundant pale staining bubbly cytoplasm and a small nucleus. No pleomorphism or any prominent nucleoli were seen. These histiocytes were seen admixed with an increased number of erythroid precursors and lymphocytes. The rest of the marrow hematopoietic elements were suppressed [Figure 1b]. Many of these marrow macrophages demonstrated phagocytosis of red cells, white cells, platelets as well as immature myeloid and erythroid cells (hemophagocytosis) [Figure 2a]. Some of these histiocytes also revealed the presence of a brown-colored pigment [Figure 2b]. Based on these findings, a tentative diagnosis of a mononuclear phagocytic system disorder/histiocytosis was made. Special stains and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were applied for ruling out various differentials under this category of disorder such as storage histiocytosis, dendritic cell-related, inflammatory, and malignant histiocytosis. On IHC, the histiocytes were positive for CD68 and negative for CD1a, S100, CD3, CD20, epithelial membrane antigen, and pancytokeratin, confirming the histiocytic nature of these large cells and ruling out the possibility of dendritic cell-related (Langerhans cell histiocytosis) and malignant histiocytosis [Figure 3a-c]. However, on IHC, a finding that was evident was the CD3 positive immunoexpression of the increased lymphocytes [Figure 3d]. Among the special stains, the periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain, Oil red O stain, and Perl's iron stain were put. These histiocytes were negative for both the PAS stain as well as the Oil red O stain [Figure 4a], thus ruling out any storage histiocytosis. Another finding that was revealed on Perl's iron stain was that not all histiocytes containing the brown pigment demonstrated hemosiderin, and in most of them, the brown pigment remained unstained [Figure 4b]. Based on all these findings, we arrived at a diagnosis of inflammatory histiocytosis HLH.
A detailed clinical history as well as examination of the child was done as she came with her father to fetch the bone marrow report as her condition was deteriorating day by day. Her birth, family, and past medical or any treatment history was non-contributory. There was no history of contact with tuberculosis, measles, allergy, or any blood transfusion. Currently, she appeared lethargic and had fever with abdominal distention. On physical examination, she was febrile with a temperature of 39.5 C, pale, and had a palpable spleen (6 cm below the left costal margin) and a liver (liver span of 15 cm). The rest of the clinical examination was unremarkable. Her blood sample was taken for hematological investigations. The current complete blood count revealed pancytopenia with hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL, total leukocyte count of 2500/mm3 (differential being N - 30%, L - 60%, M - 9%, and E - 1%), and a platelet count of 50,000/mm3. Other indices included were red blood cell count of 2.7 million/mm3, mean corpuscular volume - 59 fl, mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) - 20.3 pg, MCH content - 27.8 g/dl, red cell distribution width - 20.7%, and a corrected reticulocyte count of 3.9%. The peripheral smear revealed fragmented red blood cells and on careful examination, schizonts of P. vivax [Figure 5a]. Biochemical tests revealed elevated ferritin (989 mg/dL) and lactate dehydrogenase levels (1022 mu/L) with high triglyceride at 4 mmol/L. Serum haptoglobin and plasma fibrinogen levels were reduced (0.02 g/l and 132 mg/dl, respectively). Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity was normal. Renal function tests were normal; however, the liver function tests were deranged. Ultrasonography revealed enlarged liver and spleen. Meanwhile, the trephine biopsy was treated with alcoholic ammonium hydroxide, to which the brown pigment responded by getting bleached, hence, confirming the nature of this pigment to be that of malarial pigment (hemozoin) [Figure 5b]. Based on the clinical, hematological, histopathological, and immunohistochemical parameters, a final diagnosis of pancytopenia due to HLH as a result of P. vivax infection was estabilished. Due to the cost and unavailability, local perforin mutation studies and soluble interleukin (IL) level estimation tests were not performed. The child was administered oral chloroquine and primaquine along with iron supplements. Her condition dramatically improved within few days as she became afebrile, her laboratory parameters such as serum ferritin and fibrinogen levels improved gradually, and the liver and spleen reduced in size. She was discharged in a stable condition (hemoglobin of 10.8 g/dl, total leukocyte count of 10,600/mm3, and a platelet count of 198,000/mm3), and so far, her follow-up period has been uneventful.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 7-year-old girl presenting with intermittent fever, progressive weakness, and abdominal distension for three weeks.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 7-year-old girl presented with a 3-week history of fluctuating fever, weakness, and abdominal distension. Initial evaluation elsewhere revealed pancytopenia and a hypocellular bone marrow aspirate. Over subsequent days, her condition progressively deteriorated with increasing lethargy, high fevers, and worsening abdominal enlargement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Non-contributory birth, family, and past medical or treatment history. No history of contact with tuberculosis or measles, no allergies, and no blood transfusions. Resident of New Delhi, India.
subjective.review_of_systems: Progressive weakness, abdominal distension, lethargy; denies cough or focal pain.

objective.physical_examination: Lethargic, pale, and febrile with a temperature of 39.5 °C. Abdomen distended with palpable splenomegaly (6 cm below the left costal margin) and hepatomegaly (liver span 15 cm). No significant lymphadenopathy. Remainder of physical examination unremarkable.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial labs: Hemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, total leukocyte count 3,400/mm^3, platelet count 44,000/mm^3; peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic blood picture. Repeat CBC: Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, total leukocyte count 2,500/mm^3 (neutrophils 30%, lymphocytes 60%, monocytes 9%, eosinophils 1%), platelet count 50,000/mm^3, RBC count 2.7 million/mm^3, MCV 59 fL, MCH 20.3 pg, MCHC 27.8 g/dL, RDW 20.7%, corrected reticulocyte count 3.9%. Serum ferritin 989 mg/dL, LDH 1022 mU/L, triglycerides 4 mmol/L, serum haptoglobin 0.02 g/L, plasma fibrinogen 132 mg/dL. Deranged liver function tests; normal renal function tests; normal G6PD activity. Blood, urine, sputum, and stool cultures sterile. Serologies negative for HIV, HBsAg, anti-HCV, EBV, CMV, measles, Widal test, and rK39 test for visceral leishmaniasis. Chest X-ray and CSF analysis normal. Abdominal ultrasound confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.advanced_workup: Bone marrow trephine biopsy: Normocellular marrow with sheets and clusters of large CD68-positive histiocytes demonstrating extensive hemophagocytosis of red cells, white cells, platelets, and immature precursors, accompanied by CD3-positive lymphocytes and hematopoietic suppression. Histiocytes were negative for CD1a, S100, CD20, EMA, cytokeratin, PAS, and Oil Red O. Perl's iron stain showed unstained brown pigment within histiocytes that bleached completely upon exposure to alcoholic ammonium hydroxide, confirming hemozoin (malarial pigment).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) induced by Plasmodium vivax malaria, manifesting with severe pancytopenia, hyperferritinemia (989 mg/dL), hypofibrinogenemia (132 mg/dL), hypertriglyceridemia (4 mmol/L), and bone marrow hemophagocytosis. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for malarial antigen were initially negative, but meticulous review of peripheral blood smear identified Plasmodium vivax schizonts, and hemozoin bleaching confirmed intra-histiocytic malarial pigment on bone marrow biopsy. Viral, bacterial, and leishmanial causes were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with oral chloroquine, oral primaquine, and iron supplementation. Defervescence was achieved within days, organomegaly regressed, and hematologic indices steadily normalized. Discharged in stable condition (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 10,600/mm^3, platelet count 198,000/mm^3) with uneventful follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 35-year-old multiparous woman in 36th week of gestation with no significant past history presented to emergency with a short history of 8 days of malaise, chills, myalgia, jaundice, abdominal pain, and asthenia. At admission, the clinical parameters were - heart rate 120/min, blood pressure 105 / 66 mmHg, respiratory rate 17/min, axillary temperature 38 C, and oliguria of 500 ml in last 24 hours. The patient was conscious but irritable with dark icterious conjunctive and bruises in all extremities.
Earlier during her pregnancy both systolic and diastolic arterial pressures were noted to be stable. There was no history of travel abroad, contact with animals, or fever. The obstetrical examination did not reveal any genital bleeding. The laboratory parameters were: hemoglobin 10 g/dL; leukocyte count: 15,2 x 109/L including 75% neutrophils, platelets count: 40 x 109/L; C reactive protein (CRP): 115 mg/L, glucose: 0,92 g/L, creatinine: 18 mg/L and urea: 1.05 g/L, AST: 165 U/L, ALT: 145 U/L, bilirubin total: 7 mg/dl, conjugated bilirubin: 5,8 mg/dl. A moderate coagulopathy was found (PT 45%, ACT 220 seconds, D-dimer 600 ng/ml, fibrinogen 1,5 g/L), CPK: 355 U/L, troponin Ic: 0.4., Blood and urine cultures were sterile, and the serology tests for hepatitis A, B, C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV were all negative. Leptospira IgM antibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay were positive at 1/300 dilution. The electrocardiogram revealed negative T waves in DII, DIII, and AVF. Ultrasound showed a single live pregnancy with oligohydramnios; Kidneys, spleen, and liver were normal and without any dilatation of the biliary canaliculi. The fetal cardiotocography was reactive. The interview of the family revealed that the patient had visited a public bath 15 days earlier. The initial management in the intensive care unit consisted of intravenous Penicillin G at 4 000 000 UI four times daily, hydration with crystalloid solutions, oxygenation by facemask. 10 hours after admission, she became severely icteric and developed severe respiratory distress with crackles on pulmonary auscultation requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. An emergency cesarean section was performed. A healthy female weighing 2.9 kg was delivered with an Apgar of 6 and 8 respectively at 1 min and 2 min after delivery. Postoperatively, X-ray chest showed bilateral diffuse opacities; blood gases showed PaO2/FiO2 < 200 and transthoracic echocardiography showed absence of increased left filling pressures fulfilling the American-European criteria for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). PAOP was not measured in the absence of Swan Ganz.
The post delivery treatment included mechanical ventilation with intravenous sedation, central venous pressure monitoring, restriction of fluid infusion and antibiotics (penicillin G). 4 days after delivery, the laboratory tests showed: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, leukocytes: 11 x 109/L, CRP: 52 mg/L, platelet: 106 x 109/L, PT: t 60%, fibrinogen: 3.5 g/l, urea: 0.55 g/L, creatinine: 11 mg/L, AST: 60 U/L, ALT: 52 U/L, troponin Ic: 0,08. Five days later, the patient's neurological and respiratory status improved, and 1 week later, she was discharged discharged from the ICU with antibiotics continued for 12 days. At follow up after 1 month of discharge the blood and urine were negative for leptospira and the neonate showed no signs of active infection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 35-year-old pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation presented with an 8-day history of malaise, chills, myalgias, jaundice, abdominal pain, and oliguria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 8 days prior to presentation with malaise, chills, myalgias, asthenia, abdominal pain, and progressive jaundice, accompanied by oliguria (500 mL in the prior 24 hours). Ten hours after ICU admission, she deteriorated acutely with worsening jaundice and severe respiratory distress with diffuse crackles, requiring emergency endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and urgent cesarean section.
subjective.past_medical_history: Multiparous at 36 weeks of gestation with stable arterial blood pressure throughout pregnancy and no significant past medical history. Epidemiological exposure: visited a public bath 15 days prior to presentation. Denied travel abroad or direct animal contacts.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for malaise, chills, myalgias, asthenia, abdominal pain, jaundice, and dark oliguric urine. Denied vaginal/genital bleeding. Home medications and allergies are unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Heart rate: 120 beats/min; blood pressure: 105/66 mmHg; respiratory rate: 17 breaths/min; axillary temperature: 38 °C; 24-hour urine output: 500 mL. Conscious but irritable. Ocular: dark icteric conjunctivae. Skin: ecchymoses and bruises across all extremities. Obstetrical exam: no genital bleeding; reactive fetal cardiotocography. Ten hours post-admission: developed severe icterus and diffuse bilateral lung crackles with respiratory distress.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL (post-delivery: 9.8 g/dL); WBC: 15.2 x 10^9/L with 75% neutrophils (post-delivery: 11 x 10^9/L); platelets: 40 x 10^9/L (post-delivery: 106 x 10^9/L); CRP: 115 mg/L (post-delivery: 52 mg/L); glucose: 0.92 g/L; urea: 1.05 g/L (post-delivery: 0.55 g/L); creatinine: 18 mg/L (post-delivery: 11 mg/L); AST: 165 U/L (post-delivery: 60 U/L); ALT: 145 U/L (post-delivery: 52 U/L); total bilirubin: 7 mg/dL (conjugated: 5.8 mg/dL); PT: 45% (post-delivery: 60%); ACT: 220 seconds; D-dimer: 600 ng/mL; fibrinogen: 1.5 g/L (post-delivery: 3.5 g/L); CPK: 355 U/L; troponin Ic: 0.4 ng/mL (post-delivery: 0.08 ng/mL). Blood and urine cultures: sterile. Viral hepatitis A, B, and C, cytomegalovirus, and HIV serologies: negative. ECG: negative T waves in leads DII, DIII, and aVF. Ultrasound: single live intrauterine pregnancy with oligohydramnios; kidneys, spleen, and liver normal without biliary dilatation. Postoperative CXR: bilateral diffuse opacities. Blood gases: PaO2/FiO2 < 200. Transthoracic echocardiogram: normal left filling pressures.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease) presenting in the third trimester of pregnancy, complicated by acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), acute kidney injury, hepatic dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, and consumptive coagulopathy. Confirmed by positive Leptospira IgM antibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) at a 1/300 dilution. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C), CMV, HIV, and bacterial sepsis were excluded. Treatment & Outcome: Managed in the ICU with intravenous penicillin G (4,000,000 UI four times daily), crystalloid hydration, emergency cesarean section delivering a healthy 2.9 kg infant (Apgar scores 6 and 8), mechanical ventilation with sedation, central venous pressure monitoring, and fluid restriction. Antimicrobial therapy was continued for 12 days. The patient experienced steady neurological and respiratory improvement, being discharged from the ICU after 1 week. Follow-up at 1 month confirmed negative Leptospira testing in blood and urine, with the infant remaining healthy and free of infection.

raw_case_text: A 29-year-old female patient was diagnosed with HIV infection in June 2017 and commenced on TDF/3TC/EFV. Her baseline CD4 count and VL are unknown. Three years later, she was switched to ABC/3TC/ATZ/r following virological failure. Four weeks after treatment switch, she developed pulmonary tuberculosis and in error was given rifampicin with ATZ/r for two months.
