For treatment optimisation reasons, the ART regimen was switched to ABC/3TC/DTG, but DTG was dosed at 50 mg daily with rifampicin for four months instead of twice daily according to current guidelines. The VL at switch to ABC/3TC/DTG is unknown. The clinical response to treatment was poor and she was referred to Newlands Clinic. A VL taken after seven months on ABC/3TC/DTG was 6540 copies/mL, despite adherence counselling. A genotypic resistance test taken 10 months after initiation of DTG showed extensive NRTI DRMs and one major InSTI DRM (see Table 1 for mutations and sensitivity analysis). This patient admitted to inconsistent adherence both to tuberculosis treatment and ART.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 29-year-old female presenting with poor clinical response and virological failure during concomitant antiretroviral and antituberculosis therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred for evaluation of persistent treatment failure following sequential antiretroviral switches and dosing errors during concurrent treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis. Four weeks after switching to second-line protease inhibitor therapy, she contracted pulmonary tuberculosis and erroneously received unboosted atazanavir with rifampicin for two months. She was subsequently transitioned to a dolutegravir-based regimen, but dolutegravir was underdosed at 50 mg once daily instead of twice daily with rifampicin for four months. She exhibited a poor clinical response with persistent viral replication despite adherence support.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated with first-line tenofovir/lamivudine/efavirenz (TDF/3TC/EFV) from June 2017 to 2020; switched to abacavir/lamivudine/atazanavir/ritonavir (ABC/3TC/ATZ/r) in 2020 for treatment failure; complicated by active pulmonary tuberculosis receiving rifampicin-based therapy. Patient admitted to inconsistent adherence to both antitubercular medications and antiretrovirals.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fatigue and persistent respiratory complaints; denies acute hemoptysis or focal neurological deficits.

objective.physical_examination: Patient appeared chronically ill with signs of poor response to medical therapy; vital signs and specific examination parameters not documented in raw text.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Drug-resistant human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) virological failure with emergent integrase strand transfer inhibitor (InSTI) and NRTI resistance, precipitated by pharmacotherapeutic dosing errors during concurrent rifampicin-based pulmonary tuberculosis treatment. Diagnostic confirmation: Quantitative HIV viral load demonstrated persistent viremia of 6,540 copies/mL at 7 months; genotypic drug resistance testing at 10 months post-DTG confirmed extensive NRTI drug-resistance mutations (DRMs) and one major InSTI DRM selected by subtherapeutic dolutegravir exposure (50 mg once daily rather than 50 mg twice daily with rifampicin). Plan & Outcome: Patient was referred to Newlands Clinic for adherence counseling and optimization of salvage antiretroviral therapy and completion of tuberculosis management.

raw_case_text:
During the period of March 2009 till Febraury 2010, 75 PCNLs were performed in our unit. The standard technique followed for the procedure is explained in brief. Retrograde catheter (5fr.) was placed in the ipsilateral ureter under fluoroscopy in supine position. The patient was then placed in the prone position and the puncture was made using a three-part needle (Angiomed1.3 mm (17.5G)) under fluoroscopy control after retrograde opacification of the pelvicaliceal system via the ureteral catheter. An angle tip terumo wire (Radifocus; Terumo wire) was then positioned in the upper ureter. The tract was then dilated, initially using serial Teflon dilators up to 10fr. followed by placement of Alken's rod. The subsequent dilatation was achieved using serial Alken metal dilators and an Amplatz sheath (Cook Surgical) of adequate caliber used (Size 26/28/30 Fr.). The PCNL was then completed using Wolf nephroscope (24fr.) and pneumatic lithotripsy. An adequate-size nephrostomy was placed at the end of the procedure. All our patients recovered well. Nephrostomy was removed on the second postoperative day after the check X-ray KUB The nephrostomy tract site was then dressed with sterile dressing. Patient was discharged with instructions to remove the dressing after 72 h and follow up after one month if asymptomatic.
To keep the cost of the procedure reasonable we reuse the puncture needle, Teflon dilators, and the Amplatz sheath. All of these were rinsed adequately immediately after the end of the procedure and blow-dried. They were then placed along with the nephroscope in a 2% glutaraldehyde solution for a minimum of 45 min prior to the next procedure.
Six of our 75 patients presented with persistent discharge from the nephrostomy site. "Non-healing" was defined as nephrostomy sites that had not healed within three to four weeks after nephrostomy removal. [Table 1] gives the clinical details and mode of presentation of these patients. Average age of presentation was 39.2 + 12 years. Of the six patients four were males and two females. Four patients had undergone the procedure on the right side and the remaining two on the left side. None of the patients had a previous history suggestive of TB and had a normal chest X-ray. Average time of presentation was 35.5 + 6.8 days. The commonest symptom was mild pain and minimal but persistent discharge for the nephrostomy site.
On examination, initially it appeared like a simple wound infection with erythema [Figure 1a and b]. Patients were initially started on anti-staphylococcal medication (Linizolid 600 mg twice a day) with wound dressing. The wound did show signs of healing on subsequent dressings but then again erupted with discharge. The wounds were then explored under local anesthesia and the tissue excised was sent for histopathology. The histopathology of the tissue was suggestive of TB, with caseating granuloma that contained Langerhan's giant cells [Figure 2a and b].
Patients were then started on antitubercular medication:four drugs, (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for the first two months and then two drugs (rifampicin and isoniazid) for the remaining four months:in consultation with a dermatologist and this is in accordance with the current literature. Subsequently the wounds healed as the patients responded to the antitubercular medication. Average time to complete wound healing was 22 + 6 days after the start of antitubercular medication. All these patients have completed six months' follow-up and are doing fine.

subjective.chief_complaint: Six patients (mean age 39.2 ± 12 years; 4 males, 2 females) presenting with persistent discharge from nephrostomy tract sites following percutaneous nephrolithotomy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six out of 75 patients who underwent percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) presented at an average of 35.5 ± 6.8 days post-procedure with mild pain and persistent, non-healing discharge from their nephrostomy tract sites that failed to close 3 to 4 weeks after catheter removal. Four patients had right-sided and two had left-sided procedures. They were initially treated with oral linezolid (600 mg twice daily) and local wound dressings for suspected staphylococcal surgical site infection, demonstrating transient improvement followed by recurrent persistent discharge, leading to surgical wound exploration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) for renal calculi using puncture needles, Teflon dilators, Amplatz sheaths, and nephroscopes reprocessed via 45-minute immersion in 2% glutaraldehyde. None of the patients had a prior history suggestive of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Mild local wound pain, persistent cutaneous discharge from nephrostomy site. Denies fever, weight loss, hematuria, or pulmonary symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Nephrostomy wound sites exhibited erythema and continuous minimal to moderate seropurulent discharge without systemic signs of sepsis.
objective.routine_investigations: Postoperative check plain radiographs of kidneys, ureters, and bladder (KUB) were satisfactory. Chest radiographs were normal in all six patients.
objective.advanced_workup: Local surgical wound exploration was performed under local anesthesia with complete excision of the non-healing sinus tracts and surrounding granulation tissue for histopathological examination.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Iatrogenic cutaneous tuberculosis of the nephrostomy tract secondary to contaminated reused surgical instruments (inadequate glutaraldehyde disinfection of PCNL equipment).
Diagnostic confirmation: Histopathological examination of excised nephrostomy tract tissue demonstrated characteristic caseating granulomas with Langhans multinucleated giant cells diagnostic of tuberculosis.
Management and outcome: Initial empiric anti-staphylococcal therapy with linezolid failed. Initiated on standard antitubercular therapy: 4-drug intensive phase (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol) for 2 months, followed by a 2-drug continuation phase (rifampicin and isoniazid) for 4 months. Complete wound healing was achieved at a mean of 22 ± 6 days following initiation of ATT. All six patients completed 6 months of follow-up without recurrence.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old African man was referred to our hospital because of microscopic hematuria identified at an annual health checkup at his workplace. The patient had no significant past medical history and was not taking any medications. The patient gave written informed consent to be included in this case report.
Upon initial routine workup, the patient's HIV test was positive. Subsequent blood tests showed CD4 count was 139 cells/muL and viral load was 5.1x104/mm3. The patient's serum creatinine level was 0.86 mg/dL, with blood urea nitrogen of 10.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis showed red blood cell (RBC) 3+ and urinary sediment showed dysmorphic RBCs (>100/high power field) with RBC casts and absence of white blood cells. Urine beta2-microglobulin was 913 mug/L, urine N-acetyl-beta-d-glucosaminidase was 14.9 U/L, and urine protein was 0.217 g/d. The patient was subsequently diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and was treated with a standard regimen including four drugs for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months.
Because of persistent hematuria, the patient was hospitalized to undergo renal biopsy. The histopathological analysis revealed focal interstitial infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells in the renal cortex as well as in the corticomedullary junction, accompanied by mild tubulitis without microcysts (Figure 1). No tubular necrosis was observed, with erythrocytic casts and flattened tubular epithelium (Figure 2). Analysis of glomeruli showed no evidence of podocyte hypertrophy, glomerular collapse, or endocapillary hypercellularity (Figure 2). These findings were consistent with the diagnosis of focal and mild tubulointerstitial nephritis. Ziehl-Neelsen staining of the biopsied specimens was negative, and there were no pathological findings suggestive of tuberculosis.
Two weeks after the initiation of treatment for tuberculosis, antiretroviral therapy (ART), including lamivudine, abacavir, and dolutegravir, was started. The 6-month treatment for tuberculosis was completed successfully. Eight months after the initiation of ART, urinary levels of beta2-microglobulin and N-acetyl-beta-d-glucosaminidase normalized and microscopic hematuria resolved completely.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting asymptomatic following detection of microscopic hematuria on annual occupational screening.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient was referred following the incidental detection of microscopic hematuria during an annual workplace health checkup. He had no history of gross hematuria, dysuria, flank pain, or fever. Following documentation of persistent glomerular hematuria and active urinary sediment, he was admitted for diagnostic percutaneous renal biopsy.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant past medical history; not taking any home medications.

objective.routine_investigations: Renal biochemistry: Serum creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 10.1 mg/dL. Urinalysis: Red blood cells 3+, protein 0.217 g/day; urinary sediment showed dysmorphic red blood cells (> 100 per high-power field) with red blood cell casts and absence of white blood cells. Tubular markers: Urinary beta-2 microglobulin 913 microg/L, urinary N-acetyl-beta-D-glucosaminidase (NAG) 14.9 U/L.
objective.advanced_workup: Renal cortical biopsy: Light microscopy revealed focal interstitial lymphoplasmacytic infiltration in the cortex and corticomedullary junction with mild tubulitis, erythrocytic casts, and tubular epithelial flattening without tubular necrosis or microcysts; glomeruli showed normal cellularity without podocyte hypertrophy, capillary collapse, or endocapillary hypercellularity, diagnostic of focal and mild tubulointerstitial nephritis; tissue Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacilli.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (CD4 count 139 cells/microL, viral load 5.1 x 10^4 copies/mm3) presenting with biopsy-proven focal tubulointerstitial nephritis (TIN) manifesting as persistent isolated microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs and casts, and concurrent pulmonary tuberculosis.
Plan & Outcome: Treated for pulmonary tuberculosis with standard quadruple therapy (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months, followed by isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months. Two weeks after initiating antitubercular therapy, antiretroviral therapy (ART) was commenced with abacavir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. The 6-month tuberculosis treatment was completed successfully. By 8 months post-ART initiation, microscopic hematuria had completely resolved and urinary tubular biomarkers (beta-2 microglobulin and NAG) normalized.

raw_case_text: A 50-year-old married female from Chitwan District presented with fever for 9 days which was high grade, intermittent, measuring up to 104 degrees Fahrenheit and associated with chills, rigors, and sweating. Also she gave history of body ache, weakness, nausea, vomiting, headache, and yellowish discoloration of eyes. She noticed small rash over her right shoulder a few days after first episode of fever which gradually took the shape of cigarette burn eschar. She gave history of regular visit to jungle for cutting wood and grazing cattle. With these symptoms she first visited OPD on 6th day of illness where few tests were run; follow-up was done on 7th day where diagnosis of dengue was made and admitted for one day at local hospital where she received injection ceftriaxone and tablet azithromycin. The investigations revealed low platelets count for which two-pint PRP were transfused. With persistent symptoms and low platelets count, she was referred to our centre the next day. At presentation, she was well oriented to time, place, and person. Her blood pressure was 100/60 mm of Hg, pulse rate was 98 beats per minute, temperature was 100 F, and respiratory rate was 22 per minute. On general physical examination she was icteric with palpable axillary lymph nodes bilaterally and pitting edema was present. Eschar was visible on right deltoid with necrotic centre forming scab and erythematous periphery (Figure 1). Also similar eschar was found on Rt waist (Figure 2). There was hepatosplenomegaly with liver span of 16 cm and spleen was palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin. Occasional crackles were heard in right infra-axillary and inframammary region. Apart from these the other systemic examination revealed no abnormalities. Laboratory investigations revealed leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia. Her LFTs were deranged with raised total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, SGOT, SGPT, ALP, and LDH. Her PT was prolonged. Sodium and potassium were below normal. Values of all these parameters are listed in Table 1. The peripheral blood smear did not show malarial parasite. Serology was nonreactive for HIV, HBS Ag, and HCV. USG showed hepatomegaly with fatty liver grade II and right pleural effusion. CXR showed right pleural effusion. ECG was normal. With these findings empirical treatment was started with iv ceftriaxone and tablet doxycycline. Further reports showed that IgM/IgG antibody for Leptospira was negative, IgM/IgG antibody for dengue was positive (method: immunochromatography), and Widal agglutination test for Salmonella typhi and S. paratyphi was negative. Intravenous fluid and electrolytes were supplemented while oral doxycycline was continued. Report for scrub typhus was awaited. The test result was obtained on 5th day of admission from National Public Health Laboratory, Teku. Scrub typhus was positive (method: ELISA). She was discharged on 7th day of admission and advised for follow-up in a week. But the patient was followed up only after two weeks at local hospital in her hometown where lab investigations were carried out and were normal. She has been doing well since then and this was confirmed by telephone conversation.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 50-year-old female presenting with high-grade fever for 9 days, chills, rigors, sweating, headache, vomiting, jaundice, and two eschars.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 50-year-old female presented with a 9-day history of high-grade intermittent fever (up to 104 F) with chills, rigors, and sweating, alongside body aches, weakness, headache, nausea, vomiting, and scleral icterus. A few days after fever onset, she noted a skin lesion on her right shoulder that enlarged into a cigarette-burn eschar, and another lesion on her right waist. She was seen at a local clinic on day 6 and hospital on day 7 where she received IV ceftriaxone, oral azithromycin, and 2 pints of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) for thrombocytopenia before transfer due to persistent fever and cytopenias.
subjective.past_medical_history: Epidemiological history: Regular visits to the jungle for cutting wood and grazing cattle in Chitwan District. Prior medical history otherwise unremarkable.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever, chills, rigors, diaphoresis, generalized body aches, weakness, nausea, vomiting, headache, jaundice, and skin lesions. Negative for chest pain or cough. Prior medications: IV ceftriaxone, oral azithromycin, and 2 units PRP at local hospital. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 100 F, blood pressure: 100/60 mmHg, pulse rate: 98 beats/min, respiratory rate: 22 breaths/min. Alert and oriented x3. Icteric. Bilateral palpable axillary lymphadenopathy and peripheral pitting edema present. Skin: Cigarette-burn eschar with necrotic center, black scab, and erythematous periphery on right deltoid and right waist. Abdomen: Hepatosplenomegaly (liver span 16 cm; spleen palpable 2 cm below left costal margin). Respiratory: Occasional crackles in right infra-axillary and inframammary regions.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukocytosis and thrombocytopenia. LFTs: Raised total bilirubin, direct bilirubin, SGOT, SGPT, ALP, and LDH. Coagulation: Prolonged PT. Electrolytes: Hyponatremia and hypokalemia. Peripheral blood smear: Negative for malaria parasites. Serology: Nonreactive for HIV, HBsAg, HCV, Leptospira (IgM/IgG), and Widal test (Salmonella typhi/paratyphi negative). Chest X-ray: Right pleural effusion. Abdominal ultrasound: Hepatomegaly with grade II fatty liver and right pleural effusion. ECG: Normal.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute co-infection of Dengue fever and Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) with hepatosplenomegaly, transaminitis, jaundice, and right pleural effusion. Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue virus IgM and IgG serology (immunochromatography) and positive Scrub typhus ELISA (confirmed by National Public Health Laboratory, Teku); negative malaria smears and Leptospira/Widal/viral hepatitis serology.
Plan & Outcome: Treated with IV ceftriaxone, oral doxycycline, IV fluid and electrolyte repletion. Discharged on day 7 of admission in improved condition; normal laboratory values at 2-week follow-up at local hospital and doing well.

raw_case_text: A 40-year-old male, agriculturist, smoker, nonalcoholic, native of Ravi river valley area (altitude 996 meters above the mean sea level) in Chamba district of Himachal Pradesh, India was admitted in September 2014 with history of fever for 1 month. Fever was high grade recorded up to 105 F and associated with chills without rigors. The patient had history of malaise and easy fatigability for last 3 weeks. Review of other systems was normal. He had no significant past history. Treatment records revealed that he received a course of antibiotic from his primary care physicians without any relief. He denied ever visiting any endemic area of VL. On examination, pallor was present and he was febrile. No icterus and lymphadenopathy were present. His body mass index was 21. Per abdomen examination revealed massive splenomegaly (palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin) and hepatomegaly (liver span 16 cm). Rest of the examination was normal. On hematological investigations, pancytopenia was observed. Hemoglobin was 6.7 g%, leukocyte count was 600 mm3 (neutrophils-41%, lymphocytes-42%, and monocytes-14%), platelet count was 36,000 mm3, and corrected reticulocyte count was 1.2%. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 102 mm/h. Peripheral smear showed macrocytic normochromic picture and was negative for malaria parasite. The results of serial hemogram and biochemistry are shown in Table 1. A prothrombin time of 16 s was recorded (international normalized ratio 1.34), with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time. Blood glucose and renal function were normal. Hepatitis B surface antigen, anti-hepatitis C virus, and human immunodeficiency virus serology were negative. Chest X-ray was normal. Ultrasound of the abdomen showed hepatosplenomegaly and dilated portal vein (15.3 mm). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal. Empiric treatment for neutropenic fever was prescribed. Blood and urine culture were sterile. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed. Bone marrow morphology was normocellular with normoblastic erythropoiesis. M:E ratio was 1.5:1. Myeloid and megakaryocytic series were normal in maturation and morphology. There was a marked increase in histiocytes with a prominent hemophagocytosis. Amastigote forms of Leishmania donovani were seen both intracellularly and extracellularly [Figure 1]. Serum ferritin was significantly raised (18,500 ng/ml) and triglycerides were 274 mg/dl. The diagnosis of HLH was established as 6 out of 8 diagnostic criteria (5 out of 8 are required) were fulfilled; fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hemophagocytosis in the bone marrow. The final diagnosis of VL with secondary hemophagocytic syndrome was made. The patient was started with amphotericin B 1 mg/kg on alternate days and given 15 infusions. The patient became afebrile after the first dose of amphotericin B. At discharge, spleen tip was just palpable and liver span was normal. Hematological and biochemical parameters at discharge are shown in Table 1. The patient remained asymptomatic at the end of 3 months and 6 months during follow-up.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented with high-grade fever up to 105 °F for 1 month, accompanied by malaise and fatigability.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 40-year-old male agriculturist presented in September 2014 with a 1-month history of high-grade fever recorded up to 105 °F associated with chills without rigors, and 3 weeks of malaise and easy fatigability. He received an empirical course of antibiotics from primary care physicians without relief. He denied travel to known endemic areas for visceral leishmaniasis.
subjective.past_medical_history: Smoker, non-alcoholic. Agriculturist residing in the Ravi river valley (altitude 996 m), Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh, India. Denied travel to known endemic visceral leishmaniasis zones. Prior empirical antibiotic therapy without improvement. No other past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: High-grade fever up to 105 °F, chills, malaise, easy fatigability. Denied rigors, cough, dysuria, abdominal pain, diarrhea, or bleeding manifestations.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile, marked pallor; anicteric; no peripheral lymphadenopathy. Body mass index: 21 kg/m^2. Abdominal examination revealed massive splenomegaly palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin and hepatomegaly with a liver span of 16 cm. Remainder of examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Severe pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL, leukocyte count 600/mm^3 (neutrophils 41%, lymphocytes 42%, monocytes 14%), platelet count 36,000/mm^3, corrected reticulocyte count 1.2%. ESR: 102 mm/h. Peripheral blood smear: macrocytic normochromic erythrocytes, negative for malaria parasites. Prothrombin time: 16 s (INR 1.34), normal aPTT. Fasting blood glucose, renal function tests normal. Serum ferritin markedly elevated at 18,500 ng/mL; serum triglycerides elevated at 274 mg/dL. Sterile blood and urine cultures. Serologies negative for HBsAg, anti-HCV, and HIV. Chest X-ray normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdominal ultrasonography showed marked hepatosplenomegaly and dilated portal vein (15.3 mm). Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal without varices. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy: normocellular marrow with normoblastic erythropoiesis (M:E ratio 1.5:1), normal myeloid/megakaryocytic maturation, marked increase in histiocytes with prominent hemophagocytosis, and intracellular and extracellular microorganisms.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).
Diagnostic Confirmation: Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy demonstrated intracellular and extracellular amastigote forms of Leishmania donovani. Fulfilled 6 of 8 HLH diagnostic criteria: fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias (Hb 6.7 g/dL, WBC 600/mm^3, platelets 36,000/mm^3), hyperferritinemia (18,500 ng/mL), hypertriglyceridemia (274 mg/dL), and hemophagocytosis in bone marrow.
Differentials Ruled Out: Malaria (negative smear), viral hepatitis B/C, HIV, enteric fever / bacterial sepsis (sterile blood and urine cultures), and cirrhosis/portal hypertension (normal endoscopy).
Treatment & Clinical Course: Empiric treatment for neutropenic fever was prescribed initially. Specific therapy with intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg on alternate days for 15 infusions) was initiated. The patient defervesced following the first infusion. At discharge, the spleen tip was barely palpable, liver span normalized, and cytopenias and biochemical derangements resolved. The patient remained completely asymptomatic at 3- and 6-month follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old female presented to our clinic with fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, and muscle ache for two days. In addition hematemesis and epistaxis started on the day of admission. Her medical history revealed sickle cell anemia (SCA) (homozygosity for abnormal HbS; HbSS). On examination she was alert, with a temperature of 37 C, BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 100/min, and RR 15-20/min. She had right upper-quadrant abdominal tenderness. No other abnormalities on physical examination were found. Initial lab results revealed moderate increase of CRP, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and increased liver enzymes. NS1-antigen tested positive and dengue serology was negative for IgM (0.41) and positive for IgG (5.71), and RT-PCR showed DENV-2. Shortly after admittance she became hypotensive, with distension of her abdomen. Intravenous fluid resuscitation was started and further intervention was implemented on the basis of the monitoring of hematocrit, urine output, and blood glucose. Profuse abdominal bleeding was suspected, with marked decrease of Hb, low platelets, severe disrupted coagulation parameters, and intra- and retro-abdominal free fluid with fibrin strands on ultrasound. Moreover extensive capillary leakage and anuria developed. She was intubated due to seizures and following sedation. Although in the course of time shock and bleeding stabilized, she continued to develop MODS and both pupils became progressively less reactive to light until nonreactive. CT brain imaging could not be performed. On day four, she died due to cardiac arrest.
No autopsies were performed on either of the patients. Written informed consent for publication of the disease histories was obtained from the direct relatives of both patients.
During the past decades dengue has been reported to occur in Curacao. Until now fatal cases were never documented. However the 2010-2011 outbreak with 1,822 serologically confirmed cases was associated with four deaths (personal communication). Two of these patients had been previously diagnosed with SCD type HbSC and SCA. SCD is not uncommon in Curacao, with a prevalence of approximately 0.25%. Although chronic diseases such as SCD are considered to be a risk factor for development of severe dengue, few cases of children or adolescents have been reported.
The clinical findings of the two cases described here are difficult to interpret because of the apparent complementary vascular endothelial damage in SCD, SCA, and severe dengue. As proposed in the model of dengue pathogenesis by Martina et al., DENV might replicate in selective endotheliocytes. In SCD, endothelial dysfunction is known to occur. There is no direct evidence from fatal dengue cases that dengue virus replicates in endothelial cells. Nonetheless, damage to endothelial cells as reflected by increased vascular permeability is central to the dengue vascular permeability syndrome (DHF/DSS). Vascular endothelial cells (VEC) play an important roll in inflammation and coagulation. By damaging the VEC either through infection of DENV or by sickling of erythrocytes, the permeability of the vascular endothelial layer can increase, which may induce plasma leakage, release of cytokines, and cause profound shock. Based on these findings, we hypothesize an essential role for endothelial cells to contribute to disease severity. The similarities between the cases are striking: shock, plasma leakage, hemorrhage, and MODS. However plasma leakage predominated in case 1, whereas hemorrhage did in case 2. The onset of vaso-occlusion with SCD and SCA is often triggered by inflammation, as is the case in a DENV infection. Severe bleeding seldom happens in children, but only in cases of profound shock, and no thrombotic complications are seen. In treating dengue patients with underlying SCD or SCA, the treating physician is facing a dilemma. In SCD and SCA, it is preferred to maintain a low Ht to reduce the risk of vaso-occlusion. Treating physicians may be reluctant to perform blood transfusions in SCD patients because of concerns of excessive accumulation of iron, transfusion reactions, and alloimmunization. However severe anemia as a result of SCD or dengue may necessitate blood transfusion. The WHO reports an increase of Ht as a sign of plasma leakage with subsequently a decrease that may be due to hemorrhage. Both cases showed a continuing decrease of Ht, associated with hemorrhage with plasma leakage also predominating, suggesting Ht should not be used as a marker in patients with SCD or SCA. Iatrogenic interstitial fluid overload in patients with SCD, SCA, and severe dengue, due to preexisting vascular endothelial damage, is not just a theoretical hazard. Whether the clinical manifestations would just have been the result of secondary DENV infection only, despite SCD or SCA, remains a matter for debate. To further address this issue, we suggest that a case-control study should be performed to further elucidate the proposed association between severe dengue and SCD or SCA.
This report is based on two fatal cases of severe dengue with underlying SCD/SCA in Curacao during the 2010-2011 epidemic. Currently no guidelines exist on how to treat such patients. In populations with a high prevalence of SCD, SCA, and dengue activity, clinicians should be aware of the challenges in clinical management.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe dengue (dengue shock syndrome / dengue hemorrhagic fever) in a patient with homozygous sickle cell anemia (HbSS), complicated by profuse intra- and retro-abdominal hemorrhage, massive plasma leakage, severe coagulopathy, seizures, and multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (MODS). Diagnostic confirmation: Positive dengue NS1 antigen; dengue serology negative for IgM (0.41) and positive for IgG (5.71), consistent with secondary dengue infection; RT-PCR confirmed dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2).
Plan & Outcome: Resuscitated with aggressive intravenous fluids guided by monitoring of hematocrit, urine output, and blood glucose. Underwent sedation and endotracheal intubation for seizures. Despite temporary stabilization of shock and bleeding, multiorgan dysfunction syndrome progressed, leading to unreactive pupils and fatal cardiac arrest on hospital day 4.

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old female presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of progressive neck stiffness, severe headache, fever, and loss of weight. She reported no other neurological symptoms. She had no medical history of TB but was diagnosed with HIV two years ago. At a visit to her local clinic about 3 weeks before this admission, laboratory tests showed a CD4 cell count of 76 cells/muL. She was subsequently started on antiretroviral therapy:with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and efavirenz. Targeted screening for cryptococcal antigenemia was not yet offered by her clinic. The physical examination revealed tachycardia, pyrexia, conjunctival pallor, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Neck stiffness was present, but no confusion, focal neurologic deficit, papilledema, or cranial nerve involvement was evident on neurological examination. No pulmonary or dermatological changes were noted. The remainder of the systemic examination was otherwise normal.
The initial CSF opening pressure was raised (28 cm H20). CSF was clear in appearance, and further analysis revealed lymphocytes of 34 cells/muL, neutrophils of 5 cells/muL, protein of 1.83 g/dL (normal: 0.15-0.45 g/dL), and glucose of 1.9 mmol/L (normal: 2.8-4.4 mmol/L). Gram's stain of the CSF was negative. The cryptococcal latex antigen test (CLAT) and India ink were, however, positive. CSF CrAg titres are not routinely performed in South Africa, as antifungal treatment is standardised and fungal burden at the time of diagnosis is invariably high. Other laboratory tests showed a positive peripheral blood CrAg LFA and a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin: 9.2 g/L). Chest radiography was normal.
A diagnosis was made of cryptococcal meningitis with raised intracranial pressure and unmasking HIV-associated IRIS. ART was continued in the ward, and antifungal therapy was started with amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day IV) and high dose fluconazole of 800 mg daily. Fluconazole is used in South Africa, as flucytosine is presently unavailable. Intravenous antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone was also started. To avoid nephrotoxicity and electrolyte abnormalities, she was prehydrated and given potassium and magnesium supplements. No nephrotoxicity or worsening of anaemia was noted during admission. Therapeutic lumbar puncture was performed three times a week to relieve symptoms of raised intracranial pressure, and paracetamol was given for further analgesia. Corticosteroids were also added to the regimen. By hospital day 14, her symptoms had improved greatly. Intravenous amphotericin was stopped and the dose of fluconazole was changed to 400 mg daily. She was discharged from hospital 3 weeks after admission. At her 2-month follow-up visit, she was maintained on fluconazole of 200 mg daily as secondary prophylaxis. She is currently well and reports no recurrence of her symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old female presenting with a 1-week history of severe headache, progressive neck stiffness, fever, and weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed worsening severe headaches, progressive neck stiffness, fever, and involuntary weight loss over a 1-week period, approximately two weeks after initiating combination antiretroviral therapy. She reported no focal neurological deficits, visual changes, or seizures.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic retroviral infection diagnosed 2 years prior; initiated on antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz) 3 weeks prior when CD4 cell count was 76 cells/mcL. No prior history of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for severe holocephalic headache, neck stiffness, pyrexia, and weight loss; negative for visual loss, confusion, nausea, vomiting, cough, or dyspnea. Home medications: tenofovir, emtricitabine, efavirenz. Allergies: unmentioned.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs: tachycardia, pyrexia/fever. General: conjunctival pallor, generalized lymphadenopathy. Neurologic: prominent neck stiffness / nuchal rigidity; alert, oriented, no confusion; no papilledema; cranial nerves intact; no focal motor or sensory deficits. Lungs and skin: clear, no cutaneous or pulmonary findings.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (transcribed 9.2 g/L). Chest radiograph: normal.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: opening pressure elevated at 28 cm H2O; CSF clear; lymphocytes: 34 cells/mcL, neutrophils: 5 cells/mcL, protein elevated at 1.83 g/dL (normal: 0.15-0.45 g/dL), glucose depressed at 1.9 mmol/L (normal: 2.8-4.4 mmol/L); CSF Gram stain: negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Cryptococcal meningitis with intracranial hypertension secondary to unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) / AIDS (baseline CD4 count 76 cells/mcL). Confirmed by positive cerebrospinal fluid India ink examination, positive CSF cryptococcal latex antigen test (CLAT), and positive serum cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assay (CrAg LFA). Bacterial meningitis ruled out by negative Gram stain. Management & Outcome: Continued on antiretroviral therapy; treated with intravenous amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day) plus high-dose oral fluconazole (800 mg daily) and empiric IV ceftriaxone, accompanied by prehydration and electrolyte supplementation (potassium and magnesium). Systemic corticosteroids were added for IRIS. Raised intracranial pressure was managed with serial therapeutic lumbar punctures three times weekly and paracetamol. Marked clinical improvement achieved by day 14, allowing discontinuation of amphotericin B and transition to oral fluconazole 400 mg daily. Discharged after 3 weeks, and maintained on fluconazole 200 mg daily secondary prophylaxis at 2-month follow-up without symptom relapse.

raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old woman, married, working as a school housekeeper, presented to the emergency department with a one-day history of abdominal pain. This pain started as a vague, mild generalized pain, then localized to the right iliac fossa and became severe and constant. She denied any change in her bowel motions. It was associated with nausea and recurrent episodes of nonprojectile food content vomiting for 3 days.
She had a febrile sensation, has not been recorded, and a lack of appetite for the last 3 days, but there was no history of nasal congestion, runny nose, sore throat, cough, or chest pain. The patient did not report any contact with sick patients or recent travel to epidemic areas. The patient was previously healthy with no history of chronic medical conditions of relevance. She was afebrile and vitally stable. She had a peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) of 100 % on ambient air, a respiratory rate (RR) 17 breath per minute, a heart rate (HR) 72 beats per minute, and blood pressure 123/85 mmHg. The abdomen was not distended and soft, but there was tenderness and rebound tenderness at the right iliac fossa. There was no organomegaly. The examination of the chest and the other systems were normal. Her routine blood examination showed leukopenia with WBC 3000/muL, lymphopenia 800/muL, a microcytic hypochromic anemia with hemoglobin 9.6 g/dl (normal range 12-15), a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 62.6 fl (normal range 83-101), and platelet level was normal.
Kidney and liver functions were normal, C-reactive protein 14.4 mg/l (normal range 0-5), and procalcitonin was normal. Pregnancy test was negative. Chest x ray was completely normal initially and after 3 days (Fig. 1).
Based on the history, physical examination and laboratory results, Alvarado score assessment for acute appendicitis was done (5/10) which supported the diagnosis of appendicitis. CT abdomen was ordered to rule out acute appendicitis. The image revealed that the appendix is normal, but there are bilateral patchy peripheral lung basal consolidations and ground-glass attenuations (Figs. 2 and 3 ). Given the current pandemic of COVID-19, the CT scan findings suggested the possibility of COVID-19. Therefore, nasal and throat swabs from the patients were tested for COVID-19. The results of the reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) came back positive for SARS-CoV-2.
She was admitted to communicable diseases center (CDC) under airborne isolation and started on a COVID-19 pneumonia treatment local protocol; azithromycin 500 mg IV daily for 10 days, ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 10 days, oseltamivir 150 mg q 12 h for 10 days and darunavir/cobicistat (800/150 mg) for 14 days. She has improved and her symptoms have resolved. The CT chest (image 4 and 5) was repeated after 2 weeks of management to confirm the improvement and it showed almost complete resolution of the previously noted patchy lower lung zones consolidation and ground glass opacities without obvious residual significant ground glass opacity or consolidation could currently be appreciated, however, minimal dependent possible congestive changes still noticed. PCR test was repeated after 2 weeks and still positive (Figs. 4 and 5 ).
