assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Atypical/autochthonous visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania siamensis in an immunocompetent host.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Bone marrow aspirate demonstrated Leishmania amastigotes. Serology: Rapydtest (rK39 RDT) was negative; direct agglutination test (DAT) was weakly positive (1:3,200; cutoff 1:1,600). Leishmania-specific PCR produced positive amplicons from kinetoplast minicircle, genomic HSP70, and ITS1 targets; ITS1 sequencing revealed 99-100% identity to Leishmania siamensis, clustering monophyletically with 100% bootstrap support.
Differentials Ruled Out: Hematologic malignancy (lymphoma, multiple myeloma), HIV infection, viral hepatitis B/C, and strongyloidiasis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) at 3 mg/kg given on days 1-5, followed by 7-day courses starting on days 10 and 20. Developed mild reversible renal impairment during therapy, with complete return of blood counts to reference values and no relapse during 10 months of follow-up.

raw_case_text:
A healthy 37-year-old Caucasian Australian male presented to medical services in Cambodia with fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and severe headache. He was diagnosed clinically with dengue fever, which was subsequently confirmed on haematological investigations. On day 3 of his illness, he developed sudden onset painless, patchy, clouding of vision (right worse than left), and left eye floaters. This coincided with the nadir of his platelet count at 44 x 109/L (normal > 150 x 109/L). A paucity of other symptoms and signs led to an initial diagnosis of dengue fever-associated retrobulbar optic neuritis, which has been described.
He presented for ophthalmic review in Australia 4 days later with symptoms unchanged. An ocular history and systems review for other autoimmune conditions proved noncontributory. His best-corrected visual acuity was 6/6-1 (right eye, using eccentric vision) and 6/4 (left eye). Central and paracentral scotomas were noted on Amsler grid testing, worse in the right eye, and confirmed with Humphrey visual field testing (Figure 1). Pupils were equal and reactive to light with no relative afferent pupillary defect. His intraocular pressures were normal. His left eye showed mild ciliary congestion and occasional anterior chamber inflammatory cells with minimal flare but no keratic precipitates. There was mild vitritis with vitreous condensations inferiorly. Neither disc was swollen but there was surrounding hyperaemia and the retinal veins appeared tortuous and beaded. Multiple, perimacular, and intraretinal haemorrhages with occasional cotton wool spots were seen in both eyes (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography (OCT) was performed which confirmed the fundoscopic findings of intraretinal haemorrhage (Figure 3(a)) and demonstrated hyperreflective lesions involving the outer nuclear layer (Figures 3(a) and 3(b)) and photoreceptor outer segments, encroaching onto the retinal pigment epithelial layer indicating an acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN) picture as part of a clinical panuveitis complex (Figure 3(b)). The patient declined investigation with fluorescein angiography preventing us from characterising the microangiopathy further. Routine uveitis screening blood tests were noncontributory.
Based on these new posterior pole findings and normal colour vision testing and normal brightness saturation, his diagnosis was changed to dengue fever-associated maculopathy bilaterally with left panuveitis. As his platelet count was recovering, he was managed conservatively with tapering topical steroids and cycloplegia. The anterior chamber inflammatory reaction as well as the vitritis and retinal haemorrhages resolved over the following month as his platelet count returned to normal. He is now fortunately symptom-free with visual acuity recovery to 6/6-1 (right eye) and maintained at 6/4 (left eye) best-corrected. Further characterization of his recovery was not able to be performed as he deemed follow-up Amsler grid and visual field testing as well as OCT not necessary.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male presenting with acute painless clouding of vision and left eye floaters on day 3 of fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and severe headache.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old Caucasian Australian male presented to medical services in Cambodia with acute fever, myalgia, arthralgia, and severe headache. On day 3 of illness, coinciding with platelet nadir, he developed sudden painless patchy clouding of vision (right greater than left) and left eye floaters. He presented for specialized ophthalmic review in Australia 4 days later with stable ocular symptoms and resolving systemic complaints.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Recent travel to Cambodia. Denied prior ocular or autoimmune diseases.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, severe headache, myalgia, arthralgia, blurred vision, and floaters. Negative for eye pain, photophobia, or red eyes. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Ophthalmic examination: Best-corrected visual acuity 6/6-1 (right eye, eccentric fixation) and 6/4 (left eye). Central and paracentral scotomas on Amsler grid and Humphrey visual fields (OD > OS). Pupils equal and reactive without RAPD. Intraocular pressures normal. Left eye: Mild ciliary congestion, trace anterior chamber cells with minimal flare (no keratic precipitates), mild vitritis with inferior vitreous condensations. Fundoscopy bilaterally: No optic disc swelling, peripapillary hyperemia, tortuous/beaded retinal veins, and multiple perimacular and intraretinal hemorrhages with occasional cotton wool spots.
objective.routine_investigations: Platelet count nadir on day 3: 44 x 10^9/L (normal >150 x 10^9/L), recovering to normal over 1 month. Routine uveitis screening blood panel: Noncontributory.
objective.advanced_workup: Optical coherence tomography (OCT): Bilateral intraretinal hemorrhages and hyperreflective lesions involving the outer nuclear layer and photoreceptor outer segments encroaching onto retinal pigment epithelium, consistent with acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN). Humphrey visual field testing: Central and paracentral visual field defects. Fluorescein angiography: Declined by patient.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Dengue virus-associated maculopathy with acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN) and left eye panuveitis. Diagnostic confirmation: Hematologically and serologically confirmed dengue fever contracted during travel in Cambodia; characteristic optical coherence tomography (OCT) findings; negative autoimmune/uveitis screening.
Plan & Outcome: Conservative ophthalmic management with topical tapering corticosteroid drops and cycloplegic agents. Over the subsequent month, anterior uveitis, vitritis, and retinal hemorrhages resolved completely as platelet counts normalized, with BCVA recovering to 6/6-1 (right eye) and maintained at 6/4 (left eye).

raw_case_text:
A 15-day-old girl was brought to the emergency center with a 2-day recurrent fever after contracting confirmed cases of COVID-19. The peak temperature was 38.1 C. Besides fever, she had a stuffy nose and a mild cough. She did not develop diarrhea and vomiting during the course. She had no complicated perinatal history. Her examination was febrile at 38.1 C with a respiratory rate of 48 breaths/min and oxygen saturation of 98%-100%. She had normal respiratory effort, and coarse breath sounds could be heard in all lung fields. Lab data of the WBC, CRP, blood gas, transaminase levels, and bilirubin levels were all in the normal range. The PCR test was positive for SARS-CoV-2 without other positive findings of other pathogens [RSV, EBV, TORCH, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus (CA16/CVB), influenza A/B, adenovirus, mycoplasma, chlamydia, HIV, Human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, and hepatitis B/C virus]. After admission, the baby was given the nebulization treatment of budesonide and ipratropium bromide, using normal saline and nasal drops to relieve nasal congestion and keep the nasal cavity clean (see Table 1).
The baby returned to normal temperature and developed frequent coughs over the days. Her lung examination demonstrated scattered crackles on the back side, and then, phlegm and wheezing sounds could be heard in the following days. Chest x-rays showed that bilateral lung markings increased and blurred, with patchy shadows on the right upper lung field (see Figure 1). The piperacillin/tazobactam for pneumonia was administered on the fourth day after admission. Since then, her symptoms and signs of respiratory improved gradually.
The baby got better on the 6th day after admission with wild nasal congestion. Laboratory tests showed that ALT and AST increased significantly (see Table 2 and Figure 2). She was also administered hepatoprotective treatment of glycyrrhizin and bicyclol. After a 2-week treatment, the liver function recovered totally.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-day-old female infant presenting with a 2-day history of recurrent fever up to 38.1 °C, stuffy nose, and mild cough.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 15-day-old female infant presented with a 2-day history of recurrent fever with a peak temperature of 38.1 °C, accompanied by nasal congestion and a mild cough. She had no history of vomiting or diarrhea. Following admission, she became afebrile but developed an increasingly frequent cough, progressive wheezing, and phlegm production.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uncomplicated perinatal history. Epidemiological exposure: contact with individuals confirmed to have a viral respiratory illness.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, nasal congestion, and cough. Negative for vomiting and diarrhea. Home medications and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 38.1 °C, respiratory rate: 48 breaths/min, SpO2: 98%–100%. Respiratory effort: normal without distress; coarse breath sounds audible across all lung fields. Follow-up lung examination: scattered crackles over posterior lung fields, with subsequent rhonchi/phlegm and wheezing.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs: WBC count, CRP, arterial blood gas, transaminases (ALT/AST), and total bilirubin were within normal ranges. Day 6 labs: significant elevation of serum ALT and AST, with total normalization achieved after two weeks of therapy. Chest X-ray: increased and blurred bilateral lung markings with patchy consolidative opacities in the right upper lung field. Pathogen panel: negative for RSV, EBV, TORCH pathogens, ECHO virus, Coxsackie virus (CA16/CVB), influenza A/B, adenovirus, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, HIV, human metapneumovirus, rhinovirus, and hepatitis B/C viruses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Neonatal COVID-19 pneumonia with acute secondary transaminitis/hepatic injury, confirmed by positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR. Other common neonatal and viral respiratory pathogens were excluded by comprehensive PCR/serological panel. Management & Plan: Inhaled nebulized budesonide and ipratropium bromide, normal saline nasal toilet, decongestant nasal drops, and intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam initiated on hospital day 4 for bacterial superinfection/pneumonia. Glycyrrhizin and bicyclol were administered for elevated hepatic transaminases. Complete resolution of respiratory symptoms and normalization of liver enzymes achieved following 2 weeks of treatment.

raw_case_text:
The team was informed that the rapid diagnostic stool test for the patient's daughter, who was 31 years old, was positive. As every family member denied suffering any symptoms on the first field visit, another visit was conducted to further investigate the possibility of a secondary case in the family. On interviewing the patient at her home, although she looked well and was not dehydrated, she confirmed that she had begun to experience frequent loose bowel movements and moderate to severe abdominal pain on April 26, and that she had sought medical consultation at a nearby health center, where she was given supportive treatment and discharged. When asked why she had not reported this to the public health team, she answered that she thought her symptoms were irrelevant to her father's condition. The patient was then given a 300 mg stat dose of doxycycline along with hyoscine butyl bromide. She was advised to use a designated toilet, and the need for strict hand washing was emphasised. In 2 more days, the patient's condition had improved, and her symptoms had disappeared. Her culture report was released on May 1; this also showed growth of a similar isolate of her father, V. cholerae O1 E1 Tor, subtype Inaba, fully sensitive to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Figure 1 presents an overview of the 2 patients' clinical progress, the tests performed, and their management.
The initial workup of the stool samples in the regional hospital laboratory revealed a Gram-negative non-lactose-fermenter coccobacilli curved shape. The stool samples analysed in the regional hospital laboratory were positive on the rapid cholera antigen test. Stool samples were cultured and the growing isolates were sent to the Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL) on MacConkey agar for identification and confirmation, susceptibility testing, and serotyping. At the CPHL, the isolates were sub-cultured on blood agar and thiosulfate-citrate-bile-salts-sucrose agar and incubated in air at 35-37 C for 18-24 hours. Fermentation of sugars such as glucose, maltose, mannitol, and sucrose tested positive using the Vitek system (Vitek-2 Compact; bioMerieux, Marcy-l'Etoile, France). Most strains were also motile at 37 C, metabolized lysine and ornithine, and showed a positive string test. The isolates were identified using a matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization biotyper (Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA), which indicated that the bacteria were a Vibrio species. Vitek was used for identification and it gave a 98% probability that the isolates were V. cholerae.
The agglutination test (V. cholerae antisera) used was positive for V. cholerae serogroup O1 serovar Inaba. Since the growth showed haemolysis of colonies, the strain was most probably El Tor V. cholerae. Antibiotic susceptibility testing was done using disc diffusion for ampicillin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole according to the relevant guidelines (M100, 29th edition, Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute).
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying images.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old female presenting with frequent loose stools and moderate-to-severe abdominal pain for approximately 1 day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is the daughter of an index patient hospitalized with severe acute gastrointestinal illness. Following her father's return from Pakistan, she directly assisted with cleaning his vomitus and oral secretions from his mouth and body without protective equipment. She subsequently developed frequent loose bowel movements and moderate to severe abdominal pain on April 26, 2019. She sought outpatient evaluation at a local health center where supportive care was given. During secondary household contact tracing following an initial positive stool screening test, she confirmed active gastrointestinal symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Household secondary contact of an index case with severe acute diarrheal illness; directly handled and cleaned infectious vomitus and oral secretions without protective measures. No prior chronic illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Frequent loose bowel movements, moderate to severe abdominal pain; denies vomiting, fever, or hematochezia.

objective.physical_examination: Clinically well-appearing, hydrated, no signs of dehydration or systemic instability.
objective.advanced_workup: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing via disc diffusion (CLSI M100, 29th edition): isolate fully sensitive to ampicillin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of secondary cholera transmission due to Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 biovar El Tor, serotype Inaba: Stool rapid diagnostic antigen dipstick (Crystal VC) was positive; stool culture grew curved Gram-negative non-lactose-fermenting coccobacilli on MacConkey agar; subculture on TCBS agar grew yellow sucrose-fermenting colonies and blood agar revealed colonies with hemodigestion; motile at 37 C, positive string test, metabolized lysine and ornithine; Vitek-2 Compact confirmed glucose, maltose, mannitol, and sucrose fermentation (98% probability V. cholerae); Bruker MALDI-TOF biotyper confirmed Vibrio species; slide agglutination confirmed V. cholerae serogroup O1 serovar Inaba. Antimicrobial therapy: Oral doxycycline 300 mg single stat dose along with oral hyoscine butylbromide for abdominal cramps. Advised on strict enteric precautions, dedicated toilet use, and meticulous hand hygiene. Symptoms completely resolved within 48 hours.

raw_case_text:
An 18-year-old male patient presented with the signs and symptoms of continuous, high-grade fever without chills and rigors since one week. He also had associated vomiting, altered sensorium, and was unconscious with delirium of one-day duration. On examination, the patient was unconscious, pulse: 82/minute, respiratory rate: 14/minute, blood pressure (BP): 110/60 mm of Hg. On auscultation, S1 and S2 were heard, and lungs were clear. There was no organomegaly, but tenderness in the right hypochondrium was present. Plantars were downgoing; he was started on antimalarial therapy. As per altered sensorium and deterioration, mechanical ventilation and intubation were done.
Basic laboratory investigations were done. Hemoglobin was 12.9g/dL, total leukocyte count was normal with normal differential count, and there was severe thrombocytopenia. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was normal. Plasmodium falciparum ring forms: 1/1000 RBC were seen. Complete urine examination showed trace amount of albumin. Biochemical analysis showed elevated serum bilirubin (2.4mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase, and transaminases. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) profile showed prolonged prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), fibrinogen -64mg/dL, and markedly reduced platelets. Lactate dehydrogenase was raised significantly.
The patient received blood components and platelets, and requested for fresh frozen plasma in view of DIC. Transfusion therapy received by the patient from day one of admission until death was reviewed [Table 1] and the description of the anaphylactic reaction [Table 2] was taken into consideration for investigating the adverse reaction. During the same period, plasma units of the same implicated platelet components were transfused to three different patients with bleeding, without any adverse transfusion reactions.
Investigation of transfusion reaction included clerical check of patient identification; labels of blood components, and grouping and typing, along with requisition forms revealed no misidentification. Visual inspection of the postreaction sample of the patient was negative for hemolysis. Pretransfusion testing done on day one of admission revealed 'O', Rh-positive blood group and negative antibody screening. On day five, the patient was transfused with 'O', Rh-positive platelets and no pretransfusion sample was available. Direct Coomb's test and IgG monospecific antibody were positive in the post-transfusion sample. In view of the positivity of the direct Coomb's test, antibody screening for any irregular or clinically significant red cell antibody was done to rule out immune-mediated hemolytic transfusion reaction. Indirect Coomb's test was negative. Antibody screening by commercial three red cell panel was also negative. Based on this workup, the possibility of immune-mediated hemolytic transfusion reaction was ruled out.
Blood components as well as the sample of the patient were submitted for culture, and the result was negative for both. The activity of anti-IgA, IgG, and IgM was tested by gel column hemagglutination method. Gel column hemagglutination was positive for IgG antibodies and negative for IgA [Figure 1]. Serum imunoglobulins were measured by capture sandwich immunoassay using direct chemiluminescent technology and the results showed raised IgE antibody levels [Table 3].
Signs and symptoms of transfusion reaction such as rashes all over the body, bronchospasm, endotracheal secretions, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and breathlessness developed immediately after the platelet transfusions. As the gel hemagglutination assay was positive for IgG and serum IgE levels were raised, we considered non-IgA-mediated or IgE- and IgG-mediated severe anaphylactic transfusion (alternate pathway) reaction.
Based on some of the pulmonary signs and symptoms like breathlessness, hypoxia, and chest radiograph with lung infiltrates, transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) might have been considered as the important differential diagnosis. However, the underlying critical illness of the patient with ventilator-associated pneumonia may explain the cause for acute lung injury. Subsequent transfusion of the plasma units of the implicated platelet components was uneventful.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 18-year-old male presenting with a 1-week history of continuous high-grade fever, vomiting, altered sensorium, and delirium progressing to coma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Continuous high-grade fever without chills or rigors began 1 week prior to admission, accompanied by recurrent vomiting. Over the 24 hours preceding presentation, he developed acute delirium, rapid neurological deterioration, and coma. Following admission, he was intubated and mechanically ventilated for airway protection. During hospitalization for disseminated intravascular coagulation, he received multiple blood and platelet transfusions and suffered an acute severe anaphylactic reaction immediately following platelet infusion on day 5.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, vomiting, delirium, altered sensorium, and right hypochondriac tenderness. Medications and allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Unconscious, comatose; heart rate: 82 beats/min, respiratory rate: 14 breaths/min, blood pressure: 110/60 mmHg. S1 and S2 present, lung fields clear bilaterally. Abdomen: Tenderness in the right hypochondrium; no organomegaly. Neurological: Comatose, plantars downgoing (flexor). Post-transfusion exam on day 5: Diffuse erythematous body rash, bronchospasm, endotracheal secretions, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and severe breathlessness.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 12.9 g/dL, total leukocyte count: normal with normal differential, severe thrombocytopenia (markedly reduced platelets), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): normal. Urinalysis: Trace albumin. Serum bilirubin: 2.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase: elevated, transaminases: elevated. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH): significantly raised. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) panel: Prolonged prothrombin time (PT), prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), fibrinogen: 64 mg/dL. Bacterial cultures of blood and blood components: Negative. Pretransfusion testing: Blood group O Rh-positive, negative antibody screen. Post-reaction evaluation: Visual inspection negative for hemolysis; direct Coombs test positive (IgG monospecific positive), indirect Coombs test negative, red cell antibody screen negative. Gel column hemagglutination: Positive for IgG, negative for IgA. Serum IgE: Elevated. Chest radiograph: Pulmonary infiltrates.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe cerebral malaria complicated by acute hepatic dysfunction, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and fatal non-IgA-mediated (IgE- and IgG-mediated) severe anaphylactic transfusion reaction.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood smear demonstrated Plasmodium falciparum ring forms (1/1000 RBC). Immune-mediated hemolytic transfusion reaction was ruled out by negative indirect antiglobulin testing; bacterial sepsis was excluded by negative blood and product cultures.
Plan & Outcome: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. Initiated on antimalarial therapy along with supportive intensive care, fresh frozen plasma, and platelet transfusions for DIC. Following platelet transfusion on day 5, the patient suffered an acute severe anaphylactic reaction with bronchospasm and refractory hypoxemia, which proved fatal.

raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old man from Hulunbuir City, Inner Mongolia, presented with severe lower back pain and a fever that had persisted for 6 months, along with reduced mobility and difficulty walking that had developed over the last 2 months. His temperature had peaked at 40.1 C, accompanied by significant pain in the chest, waist, and back. A positive Rose Bengal plate test (RBPT) and an MRI revealed inflammatory changes and structural destruction in the lumbar vertebrae 1 and 2, leading to a diagnosis of brucellosis spondylitis (Figures 1G-L). The patient's close contact with sheep in a pastoral region was a critical factor in his medical history. After 20 days of hospital treatment in a local hospital with oral doxycycline and rifampicin, along with intravenous levofloxacin, his body temperature normalized, but the severe back pain persisted. This prompted his transfer to our hospital for further diagnosis and specialized treatment. Upon admission, the patient reported poor sleep and a weight loss of approximately 2.5 kg since the onset of the disease. His physical examination revealed thoracolumbar segment tenderness, pressure pain, and radiating pain in the right lower limb, with significantly limited lumbar motion. Laboratory assays showed a leukocyte count of 4.57 x 109/L with 51.30% neutrophils, a CRP of 14.9 mg/L, and an ESR of 20 mm/h. The comprehensive diagnostic workup included a negative tuberculosis antibody test and sputum smear, highlighting the specificity of the brucellosis infection.
Before surgical intervention, the patient was placed on a robust triple anti-brucellosis regimen consisting of oral doxycycline and rifampicin, supplemented by intravenous ceftazidime-sulbactam, adhering to principles of long-term, sufficient, and combined multi-route administration. Once his inflammatory markers stabilized, he underwent lumbar posterior debridement and decompression, internal fixation, and bone graft fusion under general anesthesia, facilitated by an intervertebral foramen endoscope. During the operation, the patient was positioned prone, and the surgical site was accessed through a layered skin incision. Paravertebral muscles were stripped, and a total of eight pedicle screws were inserted across T1, L1, L2, and L3. The upper and lower articular processes of L1-L2 were removed, and the intervertebral foraminal sleeve was positioned under C-arm X-ray fluoroscopy. Continuous saline irrigation was used to thoroughly remove abscess tissue, concurrently relieving nerve root compression. Diseased intervertebral disk material was meticulously cleared using a bone file and curette, with rifampicin and bone graft particles implanted into the intervertebral space to ensure stability and promote healing (Figures 2J-O). HE staining clearly shows the extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells, which is a hallmark of Brucella spondylitis (Figure 3B), and Gram staining revealed numerous Brucella (Figure 3D). The real-time PCR tests identified the DNA of both Brucella melitensis and Brucella bovis (Brucella abortus in cattle), confirming the dual infection (Figure 3F). Following surgery, the patient continued the anti-brucellosis medication for 6 weeks at the same preoperative dosage; 4 weeks postoperatively, the patient returned for follow-up, where X-rays and a three-dimensional CT scan of the lumbar spine showed substantial relief from pain, and he reported free movement of the lower limbs, marking a significant improvement in his quality of life (Figure 3H).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old man presented with severe lower back pain and fever persisting for 6 months, along with reduced mobility and difficulty walking for the past 2 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced fever peaking at 40.1 °C, accompanied by significant pain in the chest, waist, and back 6 months prior to presentation, followed by reduced mobility and progressive difficulty walking over the subsequent 2 months. He received 20 days of inpatient treatment at a local hospital with oral doxycycline, rifampicin, and intravenous levofloxacin, which normalized his body temperature; however, severe back pain persisted, prompting transfer for specialized care.
subjective.past_medical_history: Past medical history is notable for living in a pastoral region in Hulunbuir City, Inner Mongolia, with close contact with sheep. Prior antibiotic therapy: 20-day course of oral doxycycline, oral rifampicin, and intravenous levofloxacin at an outside hospital.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports poor sleep and an unintended weight loss of approximately 2.5 kg since the onset of the disease.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed thoracolumbar segment tenderness, pressure pain, and radiating pain in the right lower limb, with significantly limited lumbar motion.
objective.routine_investigations: Leukocyte count: 4.57 x 10^9/L (51.30% neutrophils), C-reactive protein (CRP): 14.9 mg/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR): 20 mm/h.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar MRI revealed inflammatory changes and structural destruction in lumbar vertebrae L1 and L2. Intraoperative intervertebral foramen endoscopy revealed abscess tissue with nerve root compression and diseased intervertebral disk material. Histopathology (HE staining) showed extensive infiltration of inflammatory cells. Postoperative X-rays and three-dimensional CT scan of the lumbar spine demonstrated internal fixation across T1, L1, L2, and L3 with bone graft fusion.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmation: Positive Rose Bengal plate test (RBPT); intraoperative tissue Gram staining revealed numerous Brucella; real-time PCR tests identified DNA of both Brucella melitensis and Brucella bovis (Brucella abortus), confirming dual Brucella spondylitis infection. Differential diagnosis: Tuberculosis excluded via negative tuberculosis antibody test and negative sputum smear. Management and Outcome: Preoperatively treated with oral doxycycline, oral rifampicin, and intravenous ceftazidime-sulbactam until inflammatory markers stabilized. Underwent lumbar posterior debridement, decompression, internal fixation with eight pedicle screws across T1, L1, L2, and L3, and bone graft fusion with local rifampicin implantation. Postoperatively continued oral doxycycline, rifampicin, and IV ceftazidime-sulbactam for 6 weeks. At 4-week follow-up, imaging confirmed good positioning, back pain was substantially relieved, and he regained free movement of the lower limbs.

raw_case_text: On January 6, 2018, a 5-month-old male presented with a 4-day history of fever to the emergency room at the Jurua Regional Hospital and was diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum by microscopy. The patient was treated following the Brazilian Ministry of Health national treatment guidelines: 3 days of twice daily Coartem (fixed combination of artemether (20 mg) and lumefantrine (120 mg)).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-month-old male presenting with a four-day history of fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 5-month-old male presented to the emergency room at Jurua Regional Hospital with a 4-day history of fever.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Plasmodium falciparum malaria, confirmed by microscopic identification on peripheral blood smear.
Plan & Outcome: Treated following the Brazilian Ministry of Health national treatment guidelines with a 3-day course of twice-daily oral artemether (20 mg) and lumefantrine (120 mg) fixed-dose combination (Coartem).

raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old male presented with on-and-off fever (102 degrees F) for four days and generalized weakness in both upper and lower limbs. All necessary investigations were performed. On evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with dengue fever with thrombocytopenia. On examination, the patient was conscious and coherent with the following vital signs: blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, pulse rate of 54 bpm, and saturation of peripheral oxygen (Spo2) of 95%. Neurological examination revealed sensory loss below the T4 level with absent deep tendon reflexes. The patient had a Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 15 without any signs of meningeal irritation. The pupillary size and reaction were normal. Serological tests for malaria and typhoid infection were negative. He had a hematocrit of 46%, and thrombocytopenia (1.01 lakhs/cumm) with an increased total leukocyte count (19,400 cells/cumm) and a normal coagulation profile (prothrombin time (PT) 14.1 sec, international normalized ratio (INR) 1.2). The rest of the laboratory results were unremarkable.
The patient was started on intravenous antibiotics (doxycycline 100mg), analgesics, and other supportive medications. His weakness gradually progressed with the inability to walk or stand. The patient was referred for a spine MRI, which showed long-segment spinal epidural hemorrhage in the cervical and dorsal spine (up to D8 level) causing mild to moderate lateral compression and anterior displacement of the cord at these levels (Figures 1, 2). An MRI of the brain was also performed which revealed mild diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage with subtle dependent hemorrhage in the bilateral occipital horns of the lateral ventricles which correlated with CT (Figure 3). After the radiology report, a neurosurgeon was consulted regarding the MRI findings and explained the grave risk and poor prognosis in relation to the radiological findings. Since the epidural hemorrhage was a long-segment (cervicodorsal spine epidural hematoma from C2 to D7 level) and not focal, surgical treatment was not possible and conservative management was advised. The patient was intubated due to unresponsiveness on day 10 of the dengue fever diagnosis. On the same day, the patient's family members decided to have the patient discharged against medical advice. Subsequently, the patient died of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male presenting with intermittent fever (102 °F) and generalized weakness in all four extremities for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of intermittent fever (102 °F) and progressive generalized weakness of both upper and lower limbs. On admission, he was alert and coherent but had sensory loss below T4 level and areflexia. Despite antibiotic and supportive therapy, neurological weakness rapidly progressed to complete paraplegia and inability to stand or walk, followed by unresponsiveness on day 10 requiring endotracheal intubation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized weakness in all four limbs; sensory level loss below T4; absent deep tendon reflexes; absence of bowel/bladder details.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals: Blood pressure 180/100 mmHg, pulse rate 54 bpm (bradycardia), SpO2 95% on room air. Neurologic: GCS 15 initially, alert and coherent; pupils equal and reactive; absence of meningeal irritation. Sensory exam revealed sensory level loss below T4. Motor/Reflexes: Absent deep tendon reflexes in all limbs, with rapid progression to flaccid paralysis; subsequently deteriorated to unresponsiveness (day 10) requiring tracheal intubation.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hematocrit 46%, total leukocyte count 19,400 cells/cumm (leukocytosis), platelet count 1.01 lakhs/cumm (thrombocytopenia). Coagulation profile: PT 14.1 sec, INR 1.2 (normal). Infectious serology: Malaria smear and typhoid serology negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Whole spine MRI: Extensive, long-segment spinal epidural hemorrhage in the cervical and dorsal spine extending from C2 to D7/D8 level, causing mild-to-moderate lateral cord compression and anterior spinal cord displacement. Brain MRI and non-contrast CT: Mild diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage with subtle dependent intraventricular hemorrhage in the bilateral occipital horns of the lateral ventricles.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (dengue fever with thrombocytopenia) complicated by extensive non-traumatic long-segment cervicothoracic spinal epidural hematoma (C2 to D8), spinal cord compression, diffuse intracranial subarachnoid hemorrhage, and intraventricular hemorrhage. Malaria and typhoid were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on intravenous antibiotics (doxycycline 100 mg), analgesics, and supportive neurocritical therapy. Urgent neurosurgical consultation deemed surgical decompression unfeasible due to the extensive non-focal multi-segmental hematoma (C2-D7/D8) and grave operative risk; conservative management was advised. Due to progressive neurological deterioration and unresponsiveness, the patient was intubated for mechanical ventilation on hospital day 10. The family opted for discharge against medical advice, and the patient subsequently succumbed.

raw_case_text: A 26 year-old woman with no medical history of personal or family tuberculosis was admitted for a left sub-mandibular swelling which had appeared 12 months earlier. It began small then gradually increased in volume without alteration of the general condition. Many broad-spectrum antibiotics were attempted without any improvement. Examination showed a 5 cm painless, elastic left parotid mass, adherent to the skin and deeper layers, with mild inflammation of the overlying skin but without fistula or facial paralysis (Figure 1). Moreover, we found ipsilateral sub-mandibular lymphadenopathies. The contralateral parotid region was unremarkable. Otoscopy was normal and oral cavity examination showed neither left tonsillar deviation nor purulent secretions from the left Stensen's duct. The MRI showed a 4.6 cm, irregular and heterogeneous tumoral process of the deep lobe of the left parotid gland with a T1 hyposignal and a T2 hypersignal, and heterogeneous enhancement after gadolinium injection (Figure 2). Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the mass was inconclusive. We, therefore, decided an exploratory extrafacial parotidectomy. In preoperative, parotid tissue appeared necrotic and purulent by places (Figure 3). Frozen section showed tuberculous lesions in both parotid and sub-mandibular lymph nodes. We, therefore, restricted surgery to a left lower pole parotidectomy. A check-up looking for second location tuberculosis (clinical examination, chest X ray, sputum analysis) was negative. The tuberculin skin test was positive at 12 mm. A prolonged (9 months) four drug antituberculous regimen (H: isoniazid, E: ethambutol, R: rifampicin and Z: pyrazinamid) was then started according to our usual protocol: 2 RHZE/7 RH. The evolution was satisfactory with no relapse after six years.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 26-year-old female presented with a left submandibular swelling that had been present and enlarging for 12 months.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 26-year-old female noticed a small swelling in the left submandibular area 12 months prior to admission that gradually increased in volume without constitutional symptoms. Multiple empirical courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics failed to reduce the mass.
subjective.past_medical_history: No personal or family history of tuberculosis. Multiple courses of broad-spectrum antibiotics without improvement.
subjective.review_of_systems: Denied weight loss, fever, or alteration of general health. Other systems, home medications, and allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: 5 cm painless, elastic left parotid mass adherent to skin and deeper planes with mild inflammation of overlying skin; no fistula or facial nerve palsy. Ipsilateral submandibular lymphadenopathy present. Contralateral parotid normal. Otoscopy normal; oral cavity showed no tonsillar deviation or purulent discharge from Stensen duct.
objective.routine_investigations: Chest X-ray and sputum analysis showed no active pulmonary focus. Tuberculin skin test positive with 12 mm induration.
objective.advanced_workup: MRI: 4.6 cm irregular, heterogeneous tumoral process involving deep lobe of left parotid gland (T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, with heterogeneous gadolinium enhancement). Fine needle aspiration cytology was inconclusive. Exploratory extrafacial parotidectomy revealed necrotic and purulent parotid tissue intraoperatively; frozen section demonstrated necrotizing granulomatous lesions in parotid gland and submandibular lymph nodes. Restricted to left lower pole parotidectomy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Primary parotid tuberculosis with ipsilateral submandibular tuberculous lymphadenitis, confirmed by frozen section and histopathology demonstrating characteristic caseating granulomatous tuberculous lesions in parotid and nodal tissue in conjunction with a positive tuberculin skin test (12 mm induration). Workup for secondary pulmonary or systemic focus was negative. Management & Outcome: Underwent left lower pole parotidectomy followed by a 9-month 4-drug antituberculous regimen (2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol followed by 7 months of rifampicin and isoniazid: 2RHZE/7RH). Achieved complete clinical cure with no recurrence at 6-year follow-up.

raw_case_text:
On August 29, 2014, The Minister of Health officially announced the First Ebola virus disease case in Senegal. It was related to a 21-year-old national from Guinea, who had been in contact in Guinea with members of his family who had contracted the disease and eventually passed away. He entered Senegal by road, before the second restricted access of frontiers on August 22. He had used an overnight public transport vehicle from August 13 through 14 in order to reach Dakar. At that time, and all along his trip, he had presented no single fever-type symptom. Three days after his arrival, he started showing signs of fever, vomiting and diarrhea with no bleeding, and then decided to consult in a suburban health centre where he had been taken in charge for three days. Due to persisting symptoms, he approached the infectious diseases service at Fann University Hospital, where he was subsequently hospitalized. During all those consultations, he had never informed practitioners as regards the contacts he likely had with other people affected by the Ebola virus disease. Senegal had been alerted by some WHO authorities based in Guinea that a contact-case had probably travelled to Senegal; the investigation undertaken revealed that it was related to the patient hospitalized at the Fann Hospital Infectious Disease Service. He was then immediately placed in an isolation room and some fluid samples were gathered. On August 28, the test operated on the blood sample by the Dakar Pasteur Institute returned as Zaire-Ebola-virus-positive. The investigations undertaken helped identify 74 individuals who had been in contact with the patient (34 in his family and 40 health workers). The reopening of the interrogation of both the patient and his caretaker, with a focus on their itinerary, facilitated the identification of all the family members and the health centre staff. At the level of the hospital, the patient's record was reviewed, along with the list of all personnel on duty. This helped identify all individuals who had been in contact with the patient or his biological samples. All the contacts were put in quarantine inside their homes and were monitored twice a day by the medical district teams in their respective areas, conducting temperature checks and patient questioning. Senegal, since the declaration of the outbreak in Guinea, had implemented a three-step response plan: pre-epidemic, epidemic and post-epidemic. Since the month of March, the National Committee for Epidemics Administration has held weekly meetings in order to implement the pre-epidemic phase activities. This is a permanent committee meeting anytime a threatening epidemic situation occurs in Senegal.
During the pre-epidemic phase, all activities essentially deal with the communication of health workers to populations, the training of healthcare personnel, the capacity-building of healthcare workers and the reinforcement of frontiers surveillance. As soon as the case was signified, the epidemic phase was launched and ten commissions were implemented adding to the National Committee for Epidemics Management. A coordination committee supervised by the Healthcare Executive Director including commission presidents and their reporters, along with some partners would meet every morning. The multi-sectorial approach was used as a guide for the commissions' implementation. Epidemiological Investigation and Surveillance Commission: in charge of the monitoring of the 74 contact cases and alert management; social Intervention and Behavior Commission: in charge of the patient's and contacts' psychosocial care; media and Communication Commission: in charge of all aspects dealing with communication; patients' Clinic Care and Infection Control Commission: in charge of the monitoring of the patient's care and also the supervision of healthcare structures; logistics Commission: in charge of the management of all necessary products, facilities and material; security Commission: in charge of patients and contacts security and frontier surveillance; research and ethical aspects commission: in charge of all research and ethical issues related to the epidemic: hygiene and Sanitation Commission: in charge of the decontamination and sanitation healthcare sites; fund-raising Commission: in charge financial resources management. Mobile Intervention Commission: in charge of the transportation and the sampling of all suspect cases.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old male presenting with fever, vomiting, and diarrhea for 3 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient traveled by road and overnight public transport from Guinea to Dakar, Senegal, from August 13 to 14, 2014, remaining asymptomatic during transit. Three days after arrival in Dakar, he developed fever, vomiting, and diarrhea without hemorrhagic manifestations. He attended a suburban health center where he was managed for 3 days before presenting to the infectious diseases service at Fann University Hospital due to persistent symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: National of Guinea. Documented epidemiological exposure in Guinea with family members who had contracted a fatal febrile illness and died. No other prior medical history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Fever, vomiting, watery diarrhea; denies overt bleeding or hemorrhagic manifestations.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of Ebola virus disease (Zaire ebolavirus): Blood specimen tested positive for Zaire ebolavirus by RT-PCR at the Dakar Pasteur Institute on August 28, 2014. The patient was placed in strict biocontainment isolation in the infectious disease service at Fann University Hospital. Comprehensive contact tracing identified 74 contacts (34 family members and 40 healthcare workers), all of whom were quarantined at home with twice-daily temperature checks and symptom monitoring. The national epidemic response plan was activated across ten multi-sectoral commissions. The patient recovered, representing the index and only confirmed imported case in Senegal with zero secondary transmissions.

raw_case_text:
A 27-year-old male with no past medical history presented to the emergency department with headache for the past 2 days. He also endorsed photophobia, chills, night sweats, decreased appetite, 10-pound unintentional weight loss, and fevers. The patient reported being sexually active with men only with the last unprotected sexual intercourse 2 weeks ago. He denied any illicit drug use.
In the emergency department, the patient had a temperature of 38.2  C, a heart rate of 103 beats/minutes, respiratory rate of 20 breaths/minutes, blood pressure of 100/60 mm Hg, and O2 saturation of 100% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable with no meningeal signs. Given his headache and a fever of 38.3  C, the patient was started on empiric meningitis treatment with vancomycin and ceftriaxone. Computed tomography of the head without contrast showed no acute intracranial process. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with and without contrast was unremarkable.
Initial laboratory findings (Table 1) were significant for leukopenia of 2.2 x 103/microL, thrombocytopenia of 81 x 103/microL, hemoglobin of 12.3 g/dL, transaminitis, elevated C-reactive protein of 3.16 mg/dL, and hypoalbuminemia. Chest X-ray did not reveal any active infection or any other pathology. Blood cultures were negative. Lumbar puncture revealed the following: white blood cells 3 cells/cm2, red blood cells 378 cells/cm2, glucose 54 mg/dL, and elevated protein 51 mg/dL. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was negative for cryptococcal antigen, herpes simplex virus, and CSF VDRL. Accordingly, vancomycin was discontinued. Ceftriaxone was decreased to 1 g every 24 hours for 2 weeks, followed by intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 3 million units to treat presumed neurosyphilis due to elevated protein in the CSF. HIV antigen/antibody test was positive, with an HIV-RNA level over 10 000 000 copies/mL, CD4 T-cell count of 201 cells/microL, and CD8 T-cell count of 93 cells/microL. These results along with fatigue, fever, pancytopenia, and transaminitis supported the diagnosis of acute retroviral syndrome; therefore, ART was initiated consisting of darunavir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide.
Additional laboratory values (Tables 1 and 2) showed hyperferritinemia >40 000 ng/mL, D-dimer >5000 ng/dL, bi-cytopenia, transaminitis, and hypertriglyceridemia, which raised concern for HLH. H-score showed a 93% to 96% probability of having HLH (Table 3). A collaborative decision was made by the patient and the physicians to defer bone marrow biopsy and we chose to confirm our suspicion by performing noninvasive tests such as interleukin (IL)-2 receptor and natural killer (NK) cell activity.
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed borderline prominent right hepatic lobe, slight hypodensity of the liver suggesting fatty hepatocellular changes, and mesenteric adenitis. The patient's symptoms of headache had self-resolved on the third day of admission and he left against medical advice. Following discharge, IL-2R returned >4000 pg/mL. The suspicion of HLH secondary to acute HIV was confirmed as the patient met 4/8 criteria for the diagnosis including fever, bi-cytopenia of thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, elevated ferritin, elevated IL-2R along with the high probability of H-score. The patient followed-up outpatient and he reported complete resolution of his symptoms.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 27-year-old male presenting with headache, photophobia, chills, fever, night sweats, and weight loss for two days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 27-year-old male presented with a 2-day history of persistent headache accompanied by photophobia, subjective fevers, chills, night sweats, anorexia, and a 10-pound unintentional weight loss. Due to persistent headache and fevers reaching 38.3 °C, he was admitted to the emergency department for evaluation of suspected meningitis.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history; denies illicit drug use. Epidemiological risk: Sexually active with men only, reporting unprotected sexual intercourse two weeks prior to presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Headache, photophobia, chills, night sweats, decreased appetite, 10-pound unintentional weight loss, and fatigue; denies neck stiffness, rash, or focal weakness.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 38.2 °C (fever up to 38.3 °C), heart rate 103 beats/min (tachycardia), respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Neurological: Normal examination, no meningeal signs or nuchal rigidity. General: Alert, oriented.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Leukopenia of 2.2 x 10^3/microL, thrombocytopenia of 81 x 10^3/microL, hemoglobin 12.3 g/dL. Serum biochemistry: Transaminitis, hypoalbuminemia, elevated C-reactive protein of 3.16 mg/dL, ferritin > 40,000 ng/mL, D-dimer > 5,000 ng/dL, hypertriglyceridemia. Blood cultures: Negative. Chest X-ray: No active pulmonary infection or pathology. Lumbar puncture: CSF WBC 3 cells/mm3, RBC 378 cells/mm3, glucose 54 mg/dL, protein elevated at 51 mg/dL; CSF cryptococcal antigen, HSV PCR, and VDRL were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Non-contrast CT head: No acute intracranial process. Brain MRI (with and without contrast): Unremarkable. Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis: Borderline prominent right hepatic lobe, mild hepatic steatosis, and mesenteric adenitis. Serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R): > 4,000 pg/mL. H-score: 93% to 96% probability of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Bone marrow biopsy: Deferred.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Acute retroviral syndrome (ARS) secondary to primary human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection complicated by secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH; met 4/8 diagnostic criteria with fever, bi-cytopenia, ferritin > 40,000 ng/mL, sIL-2R > 4,000 pg/mL, and H-score 93-96%) and presumed neurosyphilis.
Confirmatory Testing: Positive 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody test, plasma HIV RNA > 10,000,000 copies/mL, CD4 T-cell count 201 cells/microL, CD8 T-cell count 93 cells/microL.
Treatment & Outcome: Initially treated empirically with vancomycin and ceftriaxone for meningitis; vancomycin stopped following negative CSF gram stain/cultures. Ceftriaxone was transitioned to 1 g IV daily for 2 weeks followed by benzathine penicillin G 3 million units IM for presumed neurosyphilis. Antiretroviral therapy (darunavir/cobicistat/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide) was initiated. Headache resolved by day 3; the patient left against medical advice but attended outpatient follow-up with complete symptom resolution.

raw_case_text:
A 34-year-old Sri Lankan Tamil male, was presented to a tertiary care hospital in Northern Province of Sri Lanka with a history of high-grade fever of 3-days duration which was associated with myalgia, arthralgia and retro-orbital pain. He also had vomiting and loss of appetite for preceding 3 days. He never experienced an abdominal pain or distention. He had no mucocutaneous bleeding manifestations on presentation. He had no symptoms suggestive of either respiratory or urinary tract infection. There was no past medical history of note. He is an ethanol user, consuming 16 units per week for last 10 years. He did admit a history of binge drinking during the initial course of the illness to relieve his pain.
On arrival, he was conscious and rational. He was febrile with a temperature of 38.6 C. He was not pale or icteric. His capillary refilling time was less than 2 s. There were no peripheral lymphadenopathy, petechial rashes, ecchymotic patches or stigmata of chronic liver disease.
His pulse rate was 84 beats/min and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg without a significant postural drop. There was no clinical evidence of pleural effusion or free fluid in the abdomen. Abdomen was soft, non-tender, and there was no hepatosplenomegaly. There were no features of neurological deficit or meningeal irritation. Rest of the clinical examination was unremarkable including the optic fundus.
Initial full blood count showed white blood cells (WBCs) of 3.91 x 109cells/L with neutrophil 3.22 x 109/L and lymphocytes 0.37 x 109/L. Hemoglobin, hematocrit and platelet were 16.1 g/dL, 46.1% and 142 x 109/L, respectively. Initial liver biochemistry showed alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 3760 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 9352 U/L. Prothrombin time was 16.3 s (standard: 10-13 s). Renal function and urine full report were normal. The dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen in serum became positive on day 3 of illness (day of admission).
He was managed in the ward during the initial 48 h with usual supportive care in addition to the standard fluid therapy according to the national dengue management protocol. During this 48 h, the clinical parameters remained within the normal limits.
Although he had defervescence on day 5, he became restless. His conscious state, pulse rate blood pressure and capillary blood glucose were normal, and there was no postural drop or bleeding manifestations. Abdominal examination revealed mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Full blood count showed WBC 4.17 x 109cells/L (neutrophil 64%, lymphocytes 30%), hemoglobin 17.6 g/dL, hematocrit 46.8% and platelet count 27 x 109cells/L. Liver biochemistry was as follows: ALT of 8648 U/L, AST of 28,373 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 155 U/L (range: 46-116), albumin 37 g/L and total bilirubin 55.1 mumol/L with direct bilirubin 30 mumol/L. Prothrombin time was elevated to 21.3 s. His other routine biochemical investigations such as blood glucose, renal function tests, serum calcium and venous blood gas were within normal range. A bed side ultrasound scan did not reveal any evidence of plasma leakage.
On the same day night, ceiling of medical care was escalated and patient was transferred to High Dependency Unit. At this point of care, he was diagnosed with acute liver failure with grade III hepatic encephalopathy evidence by deranged liver biochemistry, coagulopathy and altered level of sensorium, and he was started on intravenous NAC infusion (150 mg/kg in 250 mL of 5% dextrose over 15 min, then 50 mg/kg in 500 mL 5% dextrose over 4 h followed by 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL of 5% dextrose over 16 h). Furthermore, he also received lactulose and metronidazole as a part of the treatment for hepatic encephalopathy. Throughout the course of illness, he had never experienced a shock and his vitals were stable except the altered level of consciousness. He was never given supra-therapeutic dose of paracetamol, any other medicines, herbals or traditional medicines that could cause liver injury. He had no clinical, laboratory or radiology evidence of plasma leakage throughout the course of illness. Furthermore, he also developed features of alcohol withdrawal and it was managed with intravenous thiamine and short acting benzodiazepines.
With the above treatment, his cognitive state started to improve. AST and ALT started to decline gradually from the day 6 of the illness as shown in Table 1. On day 7 of illness, the dengue serology (both immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM)) was positive. Even though co-existence of alcoholic hepatitis was considered, however, it does not explain the degree of elevation of transaminases in this patient. Since the clinical scenario and the serological evidence confirmed a dengue infection, we did not explore for an alternate cause of hepatic injury other than the work up for co-infections with primary hepatitis virus A, B and C which all became negative. On day 15, patient was sent home after complete recovery.
On review a month later, he was asymptomatic and had successfully abstained from alcohol. His follow-up liver profile and ultrasound scan of the abdomen showed no abnormalities except mild fatty liver.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 34-year-old male presenting with high-grade fever, myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, and loss of appetite for three days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 34-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of high-grade fever associated with myalgia, arthralgia, retro-orbital pain, vomiting, and anorexia. He received supportive care and intravenous fluid therapy. On day 5 of illness following defervescence, he became acutely restless and developed right upper quadrant tenderness with severe hepatic encephalopathy (grade III) and coagulopathy, necessitating transfer to the High Dependency Unit. Throughout admission, he had no episodes of shock or evidence of plasma leakage.
subjective.past_medical_history: No significant medical history. Alcohol consumption of 16 units per week for 10 years, with a history of binge drinking during the initial course of illness to relieve pain. No history of supratherapeutic paracetamol, herbal medicines, or traditional remedies.
subjective.review_of_systems: Loss of appetite, vomiting; denies abdominal pain or distension on presentation, mucocutaneous bleeding, respiratory symptoms, or urinary tract symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Admission: Conscious and rational. Temperature 38.6 °C, pulse rate 84 beats/min, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg without postural drop, capillary refill time < 2 seconds. No pallor, icterus, peripheral lymphadenopathy, petechiae, ecchymoses, or stigmata of chronic liver disease. Abdomen soft, non-tender, without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Respiratory examination normal; no pleural effusion. Neurological examination unremarkable with normal optic fundi. Day 5 (HDU transfer): Restless, altered level of consciousness (grade III hepatic encephalopathy), mild right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness, vitals stable without postural drop or bleeding.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 3 (admission): WBC 3.91 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 3.22 x 10^9/L, lymphocytes 0.37 x 10^9/L), hemoglobin 16.1 g/dL, hematocrit 46.1%, platelet count 142 x 10^9/L; ALT 3,760 U/L, AST 9,352 U/L, prothrombin time 16.3 seconds (standard: 10-13 seconds); renal function and urinalysis normal. Day 5: WBC 4.17 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 30%), hemoglobin 17.6 g/dL, hematocrit 46.8%, platelet count 27 x 10^9/L; ALT 8,648 U/L, AST 28,373 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 155 U/L (reference: 46-116 U/L), albumin 37 g/L, total bilirubin 55.1 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 30 micromol/L, prothrombin time 21.3 seconds; blood glucose, renal function tests, serum calcium, and venous blood gas normal. Bedside ultrasound: No evidence of plasma leakage, ascites, or pleural effusion; repeat ultrasound at 1 month showed mild fatty liver. Viral serologies: Acute hepatitis A, B, and C negative.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe Dengue virus infection (expanded dengue syndrome) manifested by acute liver failure with massive transaminitis (AST > 28,000 U/L, ALT > 8,000 U/L), grade III hepatic encephalopathy, and coagulopathy in the absence of plasma leakage or shock, complicated by concurrent alcohol withdrawal. Confirmed by positive serum Dengue non-structural protein 1 (NS1) antigen on day 3 of illness and positive Dengue serology (IgM and IgG) on day 7. Viral hepatitis A, B, and C, acetaminophen toxicity, and alternative causes of acute liver injury were ruled out.
Plan & Outcome: Transferred to High Dependency Unit. Managed with standard intravenous fluid resuscitation, intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) infusion protocol (150 mg/kg in 250 mL 5% dextrose over 15 min, then 50 mg/kg in 500 mL over 4 h, followed by 100 mg/kg in 1000 mL over 16 h), lactulose, and metronidazole for hepatic encephalopathy. Alcohol withdrawal managed with intravenous thiamine and short-acting benzodiazepines. The patient showed gradual neurological and biochemical recovery, transaminases steadily declined, and he was discharged on day 15. At 1-month follow-up, he remained completely asymptomatic with normalized liver enzymes and sustained alcohol abstinence.

raw_case_text: An antiretroviral therapy (ART)-naive woman was asymptomatic for tuberculosis (TB) at presentation and started on first-line ART (see Table 1 for more information). She rapidly deteriorated and presented again after 10 days with night sweats, a cough, and abdominal pain. She met the criteria for AlereLAM testing on this date, which revealed a strongly positive (4+) result. The patient was placed onto TB treatment and sputum was sent for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and mycobacterial culture, along with urine for mycobacterial culture.

subjective.chief_complaint: An ART-naive woman presented with night sweats, cough, and abdominal pain ten days after initiating first-line antiretroviral therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: An ART-naive woman with newly diagnosed HIV was asymptomatic for tuberculosis at baseline and started on first-line antiretroviral therapy. She deteriorated rapidly over the subsequent 10 days, presenting with night sweats, cough, and abdominal pain, fulfilling clinical criteria for urinary lipoarabinomannan testing.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recently diagnosed HIV infection, ART-naive until initiating first-line antiretroviral therapy 10 days prior. Prior medical history, travel, or TB exposures not documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports night sweats, cough, and abdominal pain; denies hemoptysis, vomiting, or diarrhea. Home medications: first-line ART. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Assessed and met WHO clinical criteria for rapid diagnostic lipoarabinomannan testing; specific physical examination findings not documented.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Disseminated tuberculosis unmasked by immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (unmasking TB-IRIS) following first-line antiretroviral therapy initiation.
Confirmation: AlereLAM urine assay was strongly positive (4+); sputum and urine specimens were submitted for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and mycobacterial culture.
Differentials ruled out: Acute antiretroviral adverse reaction and alternative opportunistic infections.
Treatment & Outcome: Promptly started on standard anti-tuberculosis therapy alongside continued antiretroviral therapy and supportive care.
